1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ The lock file pins the graph: the package manager records resolved versions and verifies them on install (Y2)
⚠️ The interpreter is not pinned by the project: the language runtime version is left to a version manager or an image (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ The registry records signatures: a published package carries a verifiable statement of the publisher (Y3)
❌ The registry is a flat name space: a name is a first claim, and a dependency can be redirected without a change in the consumer’s source (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ The instrumentation standard publishes an implementation: traces and metrics have a stable expressed form (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit is the run: no build step sits between a change and its effect (Y7)
✅ An incremental analyser answers as the code is typed: the editor resolves types and references without a full build (Y8)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A general foreign-function interface exists: a native addon calls the platform’s C ABI in process (Y9)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ A published conformance suite exists: Test262 runs against every engine, so the language’s meaning is testable outside one implementation (Y17)
✅ A published parser exists: the engine’s parser and the compiler API expose the syntax (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Dart (3.12)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Dart in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 70.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Sound null safety: String and String? are distinct types, and Dart 2.12 and later check the difference at compile time
✅ Static typing with inference: var, final, and const infer a type, and that type is checked everywhere the value is used
✅ Sealed classes give exhaustive matching: A sealed class hierarchy lets the analyser check a switch expression for exhaustiveness
✅ Records give structural data: (int, String) is a value type with no class declaration, and its fields are named or positional
✅ Pattern matching decouples destructuring from accessors: An object, list, or record pattern pulls values apart without getter calls
✅ Extension methods add behaviour outside the type: An extension on String adds methods without subclassing or changing the class
❌ String is documented as UTF-16 code units; length counts units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ late decouples initialisation from construction: A late final field is initialised on first access, so the constructor need not compute it
✅ Factory constructors decouple construction from allocation: A factory constructor can return a cached instance, a subtype, or a constant instead of a fresh object
✅ const constructors build compile-time constants: A const value is canonicalised, so equal constants share one instance
✅ State lives in the object: The language forces no global mutable state, and an instance is the natural unit of state
✅ Named and optional parameters state the construction contract: Point({required int x, int y = 0}) names each argument at the call site
⚠️ A library-level var is global mutable state: Mutable top-level variables are permitted, so global coupling needs discipline rather than the compiler
❌ One value, many names: every Dart object is reached by reference; a field, a parameter, and a closure share one instance, and const pins the binding, not the object (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The VM collects garbage: Allocation and reclamation are automatic, and the program cannot choose when a pause happens (M2)
❌ No RAII: The language has no scope-exit destructor, so an opened File or socket must be closed by hand or in a try/finally (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow model: Aliasing is unrestricted, so two references can hold the same mutable object and the VM alone tracks its lifetime (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: Ordinary Dart never frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur in managed code
✅ Each isolate owns a separate heap: An isolate collects its own garbage, so a pause is confined to one isolate
⚠️ Finalizer and weak references are best effort: Finalisation runs when the collector decides, not at a moment the program chooses



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: throw accepts any object and no signature declares what a function can throw, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
⚠️ try/on/catch/finally gives a structured path: The recovery path is separate from the normal path, but the caught type is matched at run time
⚠️ Error and Exception are a convention: Error marks a programming fault and Exception a recoverable condition, and nothing enforces the split
✅ finally separates cleanup from recovery: The block runs whether the body succeeds, throws, or returns
✅ Future failures stay inside the chain: async/await routes a thrown object to the awaiting caller, and catchError handles it beside the value
✅ assert states a precondition in development mode: An assertion runs in development and JIT mode, so a violated invariant fails early



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Isolates share no memory: Each isolate has its own heap and communicates only by message, so a data race between isolates cannot occur
✅ Future and async/await suspend without blocking: An await yields the event loop instead of holding a thread
✅ Stream composes asynchronous sequences: await for and stream transformers chain events without callback nesting
❌ No race detection inside an isolate: The event loop runs each callback to completion, and the language provides no lock or race checker for shared mutable state (K3)
✅ Isolate.run and ports marshal by copy: A message is copied or transferred, so a value cannot be shared accidentally
✅ One event loop per isolate removes most synchronisation: Application code on a single isolate needs no lock



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Ahead-of-time compilation to native code: dart compile exe and the Flutter release build produce native ARM and x64 binaries with no interpreter
✅ Web targets are first class: dart compile js and dart2wasm emit JavaScript and WebAssembly for browsers
✅ The development VM supports hot reload: The kernel VM and the JIT path give an edit-and-reload cycle without a rebuild
✅ No vendor runtime lock-in: One source runs on the Dart VM, as native code, and in a browser
⚠️ Flutter is the dominant consumer: Server use through Shelf and Dart Frog is real but far smaller



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ecosystem outside Flutter is small: Most packages target Flutter, so a non-UI project has fewer libraries; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
Null-safety migration of old packages is unfinished: An unmigrated package carries an unsound boundary, and opting out with a // @dart=2.x comment is a legacy choice
JIT in development and AOT in production is a tooling split: Hot reload needs the JIT, and a release build needs the AOT compiler
Familiar syntax is a familiarity choice: The C-style grammar is close to Java and TypeScript, which lowers the barrier but is not a coupling property
dart:ffi reaches native code: FFI is an explicit escape hatch, so the memory-safety guarantees of managed code do not extend across it
Dart is a general-purpose language with a UI-heavy reputation: The reputation follows Flutter, not a scope limit in the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Production code is compiled ahead of time: The Flutter release toolchain and dart compile emit native machine code, so the hot path holds no interpreter
✅ Startup is fast: An AOT binary starts without a warm-up phase, which matters for a mobile cold start
✅ The JIT optimises development runs: The development VM profiles and recompiles hot functions, so hot reload keeps speed
❌ The collector pauses the mutator: The generational garbage collector stops execution during a collection, which appears as a frame-time spike (R2)
⚠️ Throughput is good but not hand-tuned C: AOT output is close to a native compiler’s, but a numeric kernel has no SIMD or arena control in the language



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ dart pub and pub.dev are mature: Version constraints, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the SDK
✅ The SDK ships the toolchain: dart analyze, dart format, dart test, and dart fix need no extra install
✅ Google backs the language: Funding and staff come from one large vendor, which keeps the toolchain coherent
❌ The package ecosystem is small outside Flutter: The great majority of packages are Flutter plugins, so a server or CLI project finds fewer libraries (Ec3)
⚠️ Null-safety migration is still in progress for old packages: An unmigrated dependency weakens the soundness guarantee at the boundary
⚠️ A single vendor holds the roadmap: The language specification and the Flutter release train come from one company
✅ Native code reaches Dart through the FFI’s C interface, whose ABI the platform publishes [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Dart 3 unified the language at 100% null safety: One soundness model now applies to all migrated code
✅ Language versions are declared per library: A // @dart=3.0 comment pins a library to a language version, so a migration can be staged
✅ dart fix --apply automates migrations: Mechanical rewrites for deprecations ship with the SDK
✅ The language changes on a predictable cadence: Releases follow the Flutter stable train, so a team can plan an upgrade
⚠️ Older packages may lag the current release: A dependency that targets an older language version keeps its old semantics
❌ Build variants multiply: const fromEnvironment with –define, plus URI-conditional imports, select which code the compiler keeps (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for cross-platform UI: Flutter renders one widget tree on iOS, Android, web, and desktop from one source
✅ Server-side use is supported: Shelf and Dart Frog provide HTTP servers and routing on the same runtime
✅ Browser output works through JavaScript and WebAssembly: dart compile js and dart2wasm cover the web target
✅ Command-line tools are a supported target: dart compile exe produces a standalone binary
⚠️ Non-Flutter use is uncommon: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward UI development



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is familiar: The C-style grammar and the type annotations resemble Java, C#, and TypeScript
✅ Inference keeps annotations light: var, final, and collection literals let a beginner write working code early
✅ The official documentation is thorough: dart.dev carries a language tour, codelabs, and the effective-Dart guides
✅ Null safety gives a clear first rule: The compiler’s null-safety errors teach the distinction between T and T? quickly
⚠️ Dart 3 features are recent: Records, patterns, and sealed classes postdate many tutorials, so older material omits them



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Familiar C-style syntax: Braces, semicolons, and the . member operator match the mainstream
✅ Expression-oriented switch: A Dart 3 switch expression returns a value and reads as a mapping from case to result
✅ String interpolation is built in: "value: $x" embeds an expression without a concatenation call
✅ Named arguments make call sites self-documenting: theme: dark, dense: true states the intent at the call
⚠️ Asynchronous code colours functions: An async function returns Future<T>, so a caller must be asynchronous to await it
⚠️ Null-aware operators add punctuation: ?., !, and ?? are concise but stack up in dense expressions



1.2.7 Testing

✅ package:test is the standard runner: dart test discovers files under test/ and reports structured failures
✅ flutter_test covers widget tests: WidgetTester pumps frames and finds widgets by key or text
✅ The analyser catches errors before the test run: dart analyze reports type and null-safety faults without executing code
✅ Asynchronous and golden tests are supported: expectLater and matchers handle Future and Stream results
⚠️ There is no single mocking standard: mockito with code generation and mocktail without it are both common



1.2.8 Security

✅ Sound null safety removes null dereference: A String? cannot be used as a String without a check or an explicit !
✅ Static typing rejects type confusion at compile time: The analyser rejects an assignment the type system forbids
✅ Bounds checking is always on: An index outside a list’s range throws RangeError rather than reading adjacent memory
✅ No eval and no dynamic code execution: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
⚠️ Web output inherits browser risks: A compiled script still runs inside the browser’s security model
❌ VM integers are 64-bit two’s-complement wraparound; the web backend carries the JavaScript double rule (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Pub resolves dependency versions from the registry at get time; the lockfile is discipline. (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Pub packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The pub name space is flat. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; DevTools observes the running app. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ Dart DevTools ships with the SDK. (Y13)
✅ dart run starts with no build. (Y7)
⚠️ Editor analysis rides the analysis server.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ dart:ffi is the in-process foreign interface to C. (Y9)
✅ The compilers target the common desktop, mobile, and web platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ The language specification is published, and the semantics of the unspecified corners rest on the shipped SDK; the SDK’s tests are a development suite, not a conformance suite (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Dart’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling. Sound null safety, inference, records, patterns, and sealed classes decouple the type from absence and from shape, and isolates remove shared-memory races entirely. Main strengths: AOT native compilation with fast startup, an explicit late and factory construction model, and a compiler that rejects null-safety faults before the program runs. Main weaknesses: the collector and the absence of RAII make resource release non-deterministic, exceptions are unchecked, there is no race detection inside an isolate, and the package ecosystem is small outside Flutter.

title: Lean 4 (4.31)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Lean 4 in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 94.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 86.3/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Dependent types let a type name a value: Vector α n and Fin n carry the length in the type, so a length mismatch and an out-of-range index are rejected at elaboration
✅ Propositions are types, so a proof is a term: The Curry–Howard correspondence puts a theorem and a program in one system, and the same kernel checks both
✅ A structure type names its fields and their types: structure with typeclass fields gives a record whose construction is checked, and where supplies the values by name
✅ Typeclass resolution is checked instance search: An instance is found by the declared class at compile time, so a missing instance is an elaboration error rather than a run-time lookup
✅ Subtype couples a value to its proof: {x // p x} is a pair of a value and a proof that the predicate holds, so an invariant is carried by the term itself
✅ unsafe marks the one escape from the logic: A declaration that bypasses the kernel must be named unsafe, so the boundary is visible in the source



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Construction runs through the kernel, so an invariant cannot be skipped: A value of an inductive type is built by its constructors, and a term that does not fit the type fails elaboration
✅ where puts the field values beside the type: An instance of a structure is written with named fields, so a reader does not count an argument list
✅ macro and syntax extend the surface at the definition site: A notation for the domain is declared once and then used like a built-in
✅ deriving generates the mechanical instances: Repr, BEq, Hashable, and Inhabited are produced by the elaborator, so a type does not repeat boilerplate
✅ do notation builds the effectful value: Construction in IO, Option, or Except is written as a sequence of binds
⚠️ Termination is an obligation on every definition: A recursive def must be shown to terminate structurally or by a decreasing measure, so a natural formulation of an algorithm can need a proof before it compiles



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The compiler inserts the reference counting: Borrow inference decides which arguments are borrowed and which are owned, and emits the retain and release operations, so a pure definition never writes one
✅ There is no tracing collector: A value is reclaimed when its last reference goes away, so there is no collection pause to plan around
✅ A value of an inductive type is immutable: No term updates a field in place, so sharing is safe by construction
⚠️ A reference cycle is not collected: A mutable reference cell (IO.Ref) whose value points back to the cell keeps its storage alive, because reference counting has no cycle detector
⚠️ Allocation is not controllable from the source: The allocator is not a parameter and there is no placement control, so a program cannot choose where a value lives
⚠️ A deeply shared structure still pays a count per reference: A persistent structure that shares a subtree is counted at every edge, and the compiler removes many but not all of those operations



1.1.4 Error

✅ Option α and Except ε α are the error types: A partial function returns a value that states the failure, and do notation sequences the recovery path
✅ A total function cannot fail by definition: In the pure fragment the type states that the function returns, and partial is required to opt out of that guarantee
✅ Decidable turns a proposition into a branch that is total: if h : p then ... else ... computes from a proof of decidability, so the two branches cover the cases by construction
✅ There are no exceptions in the logic: An error is a value in the return type, so a computation that can fail carries the failure in its signature rather than raising out of it
⚠️ panic! and an IO failure leave the kernel’s guarantee: An abort at run time is not a term in the logic, and the type of the function does not mention it
⚠️ Error-freedom is a theorem, not an automatic result: To state that a function never fails, you prove it; the compiler does not derive the property



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The pure fragment has no shared mutable state: A mathematical term is a value with no location, so two proofs cannot race by construction
✅ Task gives structured, joinable parallelism in IO: A task is a value that can be awaited, so a spawned computation is joined through its result
⚠️ There is no concurrency construct in the language: Parallelism lives in the IO monad through Task and the promise cell, so a concurrent program is an IO program like any other
⚠️ A promise carries a value between tasks and the program orders its use: Nothing in the type states when the value becomes available
✅ The runtime owns the thread pool: The scheduler and its thread count are runtime settings, so the language does not expose a thread object
⚠️ The kernel says nothing about a task’s behaviour: A theorem about a function does not constrain the parallel schedule that runs it



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Lean 4 is the only implementation: The language is defined by its own elaborator and kernel, so there is no second independent compiler to test the specification against (P1)
✅ The trusted kernel is small and portable: The elaborator is written in Lean and the kernel is a compact checker, so the language does not rest on a large run-time
✅ @[extern] and @[export] make the foreign boundary a declaration: A call out to C is written and recorded, so the escape from the language is visible in the source
✅ The output is C, so the target set is the C compiler’s: The compiler emits C and hands it to a C back end, so a Lean program runs where a C program runs
⚠️ A native build needs a C toolchain and the Lean runtime: The build environment is part of the platform, and a deployed binary carries the runtime
⚠️ The toolchain moves in nightly steps: A project pins its version in lean-toolchain, and a dependency may require a different one



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Proof work is a separate effort from programming: A def is not obliged to carry a proof, and requiring one is the author’s decision
The kernel is deliberately small and the tactics are not trusted: A tactic produces a term that the kernel rechecks, which is a decision about where trust sits
partial and unsafe are the intended escape hatches: A non-terminating or pointer-touching definition is expressible, at the cost of its guarantee
Typeclass search is a proof search with a cost: An instance can be ambiguous or expensive to find, and that is an elaboration property rather than a run-time coupling
The library is one large shared body: mathlib’s definitions belong to the community, so a development inherits its choices instead of buying a library
The audience is mathematics and verification: The adoption of the language follows from that, and it is a market fact rather than a mechanism of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits C, and a native optimiser then compiles it: The generated C passes through a mature C back end, so the run-time cost benefits from that pipeline
✅ Borrow inference removes most reference-count traffic: The compiler’s borrow analysis turns many retain and release pairs into nothing, so a pure functional definition stays close to imperative cost
✅ @[inline] and @[specialize] remove an abstraction at the seam: A monomorphic specialisation of a polymorphic definition is generated on request
✅ Compile-time evaluation removes run-time work: A proof discharged by decide or native_decide is computed while the project is built
⚠️ Elaboration dominates the build time: Typeclass search, tactic execution, and proof checking are spent at compile time, so a large development builds slowly even when its binary is small
⚠️ A count is not free on a shared structure: A persistent structure counted at each edge still pays for the sharing the compiler cannot prove away



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The package universe is small: Dependencies are resolved from git by lake, and the practical library set is mathlib, the core library, and a few support packages (Ec3)
✅ lake is a standard build tool and dependency resolver: lakefile.lean or lakefile.toml declares a package, lake build builds it, and lake-manifest.json records the resolved revisions
✅ The editor integration is first class: The Lean 4 server speaks LSP and the infoview shows the goal, the hypotheses, and the diagnostics beside the source
✅ mathlib is one of the largest libraries of formalised mathematics: It is developed in the open and its continuous integration checks every proof
⚠️ The community is academic and small: The centre of gravity is mathlib, the Zulip chat, and the university groups, and industrial use is rare
⚠️ A project’s revision set is tight against the toolchain: mathlib tracks recent Lean releases, so a project that pins an older toolchain cannot use the current mathlib



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A project pins its toolchain and its dependency revisions: lean-toolchain names the version and lake-manifest.json names the commits, so a build is reproducible without a separate lock convention
✅ Lean 4 is the stable line and its minor releases are backward compatible: A project on a pinned version is not moved by a release it did not take
✅ The language and its libraries are open and publicly discussed: The request-for-comments archive and the community chat record why a feature changed
⚠️ Lean 4 replaced Lean 3 with a different language: A Lean 3 development is a porting project, and the mathematical libraries moved with the new language
⚠️ The ecosystem moves in nightly steps: A feature can land in a nightly build and reach a stable release later, so a dependency may require a version the project has not taken



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Proof engineering and formalised mathematics are the native domain: theorem, by, simp, and mathlib are built for that work
✅ Verified systems programming is supported: A verified algorithm compiles to C and ships as an ordinary binary, which is the growing use of the language
✅ It is a general-purpose functional language beside the proof assistant: A def with no proof obligation is ordinary functional code
❌ The domain lock-in is the point of the tool: The language expects a proof-carrying artifact, and a program that states no theorem gets little from the system (D1)
⚠️ mathlib is a shared global body rather than a set of packages: A mathematical development is expected to build on its definitions, so the notation and the lemma names belong to the community
⚠️ A formalisation is a research and maintenance commitment: A proof tracks the definitions it is about, so a change to one of them can invalidate a development



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The curve is very steep: Dependent types, the elimination rules, and the elaborator’s inference model are new to a working programmer (L1)
❌ Proof writing is a second skill on top of programming: Tactic scripts, the simp sets, and the explicit proof term are a subject of their own
❌ The elaboration is not visible in the source: Why a by simp succeeded, or why an instance was not found, must be read from the goal state and the options (L3)
✅ The infoview shows the goal and the hypotheses at the cursor: The state is displayed rather than inferred by the reader
✅ The libraries supply the lemmas: An algebra or order fact is used without being reproved
⚠️ The documentation trail is uneven: The reference manual is complete for the language, but much elaboration behaviour is documented in the source, and the community’s books are a growth area



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Term syntax reads like mathematics: ∀ x, P x → Q x, ∃, fun x => ..., and infix notation for the relations the library defines
✅ Notation is declared and hygienic: notation, infix, and macro add a form where it is defined, so the surface can match the domain
✅ do notation sequences effects as statements: let, if, and for inside do read like an imperative body over a monad
✅ Pattern matching is checked for exhaustiveness: A missing constructor is a compile-time error, so a case is not forgotten
⚠️ Layout is significant: do, by, and where blocks are delimited by indentation, so a re-indentation changes the parse
⚠️ A macro can change what a line means: macro and elab rewrite the surface, so the reader must know the notation the library installed



1.2.7 Testing

✅ #eval runs a term in the file: A definition can be evaluated and printed beside its proof, and #check reports its type
✅ example and by decide state a checked claim inline: A decidable proposition is proved by evaluation, and an example block is a test the elaborator runs
✅ lake test runs the project’s test executable: A test driver is declared in the package and run by the build tool
✅ #print axioms reports the assumptions behind a theorem: A proof that used sorry or an extra axiom shows the dependency, so an unchecked step is discoverable
⚠️ native_decide extends the trusted base: It closes a goal by evaluating compiled code, so the compiler and the runtime, not only the kernel, are relied on
⚠️ An IO program is outside the logic: The behaviour of a program that reads a file or a socket is tested as an ordinary program rather than proved



1.2.8 Security

✅ The kernel rechecks every proof term: A theorem that elaborates cannot be invalid, so a claimed property is a checked one
✅ sorry is visible and reportable: The placeholder closes any goal with a warning, and #print axioms shows that it was used, so an unfinished proof is discoverable rather than hidden
✅ unsafe names the escape from the logic: A declaration that bypasses the kernel is marked, so the boundary can be found in the source
✅ No pointer type exists in the language surface: A term written without unsafe cannot express an address, so the memory-safety class of bugs is outside the pure fragment
⚠️ The trusted base is wider than the kernel in a native binary: The runtime, the C compiler, and the runtime’s primitives are all in the path of a compiled program
⚠️ There is no capability model: IO gives a program the authority of the operating system, and the sandbox is the operating system’s

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Lake resolves dependency versions from the manifest at build time. (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Reservoir packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The package registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Lean packages. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ IO.println carries no structure. (Y6)
❌ A panic prints a message and exits; no post-mortem is written. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the toolchain. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs on the platforms the release toolchains cover. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Lean FRO and the community govern in the open. (Y11)
✅ The reference manual is public. (Y12)
✅ The compiler and the theorem prover are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

Verdict: Lean 4’s design produces the highest core score here, because its constructs are separating by construction. Dependent types let a type state a property of a value, propositions-as-types puts the specification and the program in one term, and the kernel rechecks every proof, so an invalid claim does not elaborate. Reference counting with borrow inference keeps the memory story deterministic and out of the source. Main strengths: an exact fit to mathematics and verification, a small trusted kernel, and a first-class editor and library. Main weaknesses: the language has a single implementation, the library universe beyond mathlib is small, the toolchain moves in nightly steps, and the curve is among the steepest.

title: Tag Index: Snapshots by Tag
text:
Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown · the Scoreboard · the Scoring Model
The scores rank snapshots. The tags classify them. A tag is a membership claim with a stated test, drawn from a closed vocabulary: nothing here is a score, and a tag never moves a page or changes a band. Tags answer a different question — what kind of thing is this snapshot — so a reader can find every snapshot that runs on one platform, carries one paradigm, or sits at one lifecycle stage.
No primary use. A snapshot carries every use tag it has. The analysis does not pick one headline use, because the same snapshot is genuinely used for several: Java is an application language, a server language, a desktop language, and a mobile language at once. Lifecycle, memory, and typing are single-valued, because a snapshot has exactly one of each at its analysis date.
How the tags are derived. Typing and its strength follow the Type verdicts: T2 makes the snapshot statically weak, T1 without T2 makes it dynamic, and the absence of both makes it statically strong. The verification use tag follows the proof and certification evidence on the page. Memory follows the Memory verdicts and the page: a collector appears where the page records one, explicit deallocation where the page records it, and runtime-managed storage where the language hands the allocator to its host. Use and platform tags follow deployment facts — which hosts the snapshot runs on, and what the standard or the toolchain ships — and each use tag cites a source, or an observation the page carries. Lifecycle is an editorial judgment tied to the snapshot’s analysis date, and every page states the date beside it.
Scope. Every snapshot on the site carries tags. A snapshot with nothing to say in a namespace simply shows no line for it: interpreted languages with no fixed deployment target carry no Platform tag, and a language used for one purpose carries one Use tag rather than a ranked list. The tags describe the snapshot that was assessed, not every release of the family: Java 26 and Java 27 carry the same uses and differ in lifecycle.

title: Rust (1.99 / 2024 edition)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Rust in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 89.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 68.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Traits decouple without inheritance: Interface + implementation separate
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Monomorphization prevents abstraction coupling to runtime cost
✅ No null: Option<T> makes absence explicit
✅ Ownership prevents aliasing: Can’t have multiple mutable references, eliminates coupling
✅ Associated types in traits: Decouple trait from concrete types
✅ C-variadic definitions are stable: A Rust function can now define, not only call, a C-variadic function, so a library can expose a variadic C API without a C shim
⚠️ Orphan rules couple trait implementations: Can’t impl external trait on external type



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors are just functions: new() is convention, not special
✅ Builder pattern zero-cost: Type-state pattern at compile time
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction can’t couple to globals
✅ Drop trait separates cleanup: Destruction logic separate from construction
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation states HashMap’s order varies with a per-process random seed; the ordered BTreeMap is the opt-in (C5)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Ownership system prevents memory coupling: Compiler prevents use-after-free and double-free at compile time
✅ No GC, no pauses: Deterministic deallocation via RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, via the Drop trait)
✅ Lifetime tracking decouples: References can’t outlive referents
✅ Zero-cost abstractions for memory: Box, Rc, Arc explicit about allocation strategy
✅ Allocator parameter support: Can decouple allocation strategy from data structures
✅ No implicit copies: Move semantics by default prevent accidental copying
⚠️ Reference cycles with Rc: Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles require Weak to break (M7)
⚠️ Lifetimes can couple: Complex lifetime constraints create dependencies between regions
⚠️ Unsafe blocks bypass memory-safety guarantees: Can violate all guarantees, but explicit
❌ Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles leak (the standard-library documentation names it); Weak is the discipline (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Result<T, E> makes errors explicit: Can’t ignore errors without .unwrap()
✅ ? operator composes: Error handling doesn’t obscure logic
✅ No exceptions: All errors in type system
✅ Panics are rare: Explicit unwrap/expect, or Result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Ownership prevents data races: Compiler enforces Send/Sync
✅ Async/await with explicit futures: Concurrency in types
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples concurrent tasks
✅ No shared mutable state without explicit synchronization: Arc/Mutex make coupling visible



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor lock-in: Compiles to native code for every major platform
✅ Broad target support: Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, and bare-metal no_std
✅ Static linking by default: A binary does not couple to a platform’s runtime or shared libraries
✅ The target list keeps widening: 1.98 promoted the thumbv7a and thumbv7r families to Tier 2, and 1.99 promoted riscv64-unknown-linux-musl to Tier 2 with host tools



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Safety vs. Flexibility: Borrow checker rejects valid programs that don’t fit ownership model
Lifetime Complexity: Complex lifetime bounds couple function signatures to caller context
Async Colored Functions: async fn creates two function worlds (sync/async), couples call sites
Trait Coherence vs. Modularity: Orphan rules prevent implementing external traits on external types
Compile Times vs. Zero-Cost: Monomorphization couples build time to generic instantiation count
Learning Curve vs. Productivity: Steep learning curve couples team productivity to expertise




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Zero-cost abstractions: No runtime overhead
✅ No GC: Deterministic performance, no pauses
✅ Predictable: WYSIWYG performance model
✅ Compile-time optimization: LLVM 23 backs the 1.99 compiler, so inlining and vectorisation arrive without a source change
⚠️ Binary size: Can be large without optimization



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Cargo is excellent: Best-in-class package manager
✅ Great IDE support: Rust-analyzer, IntelliJ, VSCode
✅ Strong ecosystem: crates.io growing rapidly
⚠️ Smaller than JVM/npm: Fewer libraries than established ecosystems
✅ Excellent docs: Rustdoc, The Book
✅ Crates ship source, and Rust-to-Rust binaries do not cross a producer boundary; exported symbols cross to C consumers on the platform ABI [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Editions system: Breaking changes isolated to editions
✅ cargo fix: Automated migration
✅ Strong stability: Post-1.0 stability guarantee
⚠️ Async runtime: Tokio is the de facto standard; async support has stabilized at the language level (2024 edition)
❌ An edition can change what existing code means (V1): Edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of impl Trait, required unsafe extern, and reserved gen, so a crate that adopts it must be revisited
⚠️ The last three releases changed what existing code meets: 1.97 removed the accidental deref coercion in pin! and deprecated the std::char constants, 1.98 turned some ambiguous glob imports into a hard error, and 1.99 made no_mangle_generic_items a hard error and fully deprecated the legacy integral modules
❌ Build variants multiply: cfg attributes and cfg!(…) blocks select which items compile, and –cfg flags set the space (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Memory safety without GC
✅ Great for embedded: No runtime, predictable
✅ Strong for CLI tools: Single binary, fast startup
✅ Good for WebAssembly: First-class WASM support
⚠️ Backend less common: Growing but smaller than Java/Go



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Ownership, lifetimes, borrowing
❌ Compiler fights you: Borrow checker takes time to internalize
✅ Excellent docs: The Book, Rustlings, error messages
❌ Lifetime complexity: Advanced patterns very difficult



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Expression-oriented: Everything returns a value
⚠️ Lifetime annotations: <'a, 'b> syntax noisy
✅ Pattern matching: Powerful, expressive
⚠️ Macro syntax: ! and #[] can be confusing



1.2.7 Testing

✅ cargo test: Built-in testing
✅ Integrated benchmarking: Cargo bench
⚠️ Debugging async code: Can be challenging
✅ gdb/lldb support: Standard debuggers work
⚠️ Symbol names changed by default: 1.97 made v0 mangling the default, so a debugger or profiler with an older demangler prints raw symbol names



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: Ownership prevents use-after-free, double-free
✅ Thread safe: Send/Sync prevent data races
✅ No null: Option prevents null pointer derefs
⚠️ Unsafe blocks: Can bypass safety (but explicit)
❌ The release build wraps in two’s complement (documented); the debug panic is a mitigation, priced (Q4)

Verdict: Rust’s design yields exceptionally low language-imposed coupling. The ownership system prevents aliasing and use-after-free at compile time. Result types make errors explicit and composable. Traits decouple interface from implementation without inheritance. Concurrency safety is enforced by the compiler through Send and Sync. Main strength: the compiler detects coupling that other languages defer to runtime. Main weakness: the learning curve is real, and complex lifetime constraints couple function signatures to their callers’ contexts.

title: Nim (2.2)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Nim in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 69.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 77.0/100 · Engineering readiness 61.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Distinct types: Create new types from existing without coupling
✅ Concepts: Generic constraints like Rust traits
✅ Method call syntax: Uniform function call, decouples OOP from functional style
⚠️ Macros powerful but complex: Can create coupling in generated code, and can hide it behind opaque expansion



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Objects, tuples, refs separate: Multiple data representation strategies
⚠️ GC for refs: Garbage collection couples to runtime
✅ Destructors for non-GC: Can manage resources explicitly
❌ Collection order is unpinned: Table and HashSet iterate in documented-unspecified order; OrderedTable is opt-in (C5)
❌ One value, many names: ref targets and var parameters alias the target (the aliasing model documents the hazard); sink is the opt-in, not the default (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

⚠️ Multiple GC modes: Can choose GC strategy (ARC, Boehm, etc.)
✅ Ref vs value types: Can choose between GC (ref) and stack (value)
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Depends on the GC mode, so allocation timing cannot be controlled precisely
✅ Destructors for deterministic cleanup: =destroy hook for custom cleanup
⚠️ ARC mode has cycles: Automatic reference counting needs manual cycle breaking
✅ No GC mode available: Can compile without GC for embedded
⚠️ Manual memory management possible: alloc/dealloc available but error-prone
✅ Implicit initialization is the default: every variable starts at its default(T) value, and {.noinit.} is the opt-out named at the declaration that takes it (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: the manual defines cast as type punning, like reinterpret_cast, available in ordinary code (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a nil dereference and an out-of-bounds index in the release build end the process — the checks are a debug-build flag, and a flag is a mitigation (Er6)
❌ refcounted objects leak cycles; the manual makes cycle-breaking the user’s job (M7)



1.1.4 Error

⚠️ Exceptions exist: Not as explicit as Result types
✅ Can return Option/Result: Libraries support explicit errors
⚠️ Effect system planned: Future feature for tracking errors/effects
❌ A fault ends the process: an unhandled exception in a thread terminates it (documented) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Multiple models: Threads, async/await, channels
⚠️ GC complicates: Shared heap couples concurrent operations (K2)
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Compiles through C, C++, or JavaScript: Nim emits source for a language the target platform already supports, so it reuses that platform’s compiler and libraries instead of requiring its own runtime
✅ No vendor owner: The compiler is developed in the open by the Nim project, so no company controls the language
✅ No platform-specific build service: The standard library ships with the compiler and Nimble fetches packages directly, so a build needs no vendor infrastructure
✅ Runs on every mainstream platform: One source base targets Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded devices through the portable C and C++ backends



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Indentation is significant: Blocks are marked by layout, a syntax decision that shortens code and makes the parser and the editor extra important
seq and string copy on assignment: The built-in containers have value semantics, trading accidental aliasing for a copy unless a move or sink parameter is used
The default memory manager changed: Nim 2.0 moved the default to the ARC/ORC family, so code from the 1.x era assumed a different collector — a project decision with a migration cost
The language spans two levels: High-level abstraction sits beside raw pointers and alloc, a deliberate breadth whose cost is that a codebase may mix idioms
The manual is the specification: Nim’s behaviour is defined by its manual and its compiler rather than by a separate standard — a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiles to C: Good performance
⚠️ GC overhead: Non-deterministic pauses (but tunable)
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Templates compile away
✅ Predictable: C backend makes performance transparent
⚠️ GC tuning needed: Couples performance to GC configuration



1.2.2 Ecosystem

⚠️ Small ecosystem: Nimble packages limited
✅ Nimble package manager: Works well
⚠️ IDE support: Limited (Nimsuggest, VSCode)
⚠️ Small community: Fewer resources
✅ Good docs: Manual is comprehensive
✅ Nim reaches other code through the platform C ABI, which the target publishes [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ Breaking changes: v1.0 to v2.0 had issues, and language evolution couples code to a version
✅ Stable now: Post-1.0 more stable
⚠️ Small team: Development pace couples to resources
✅ Active: Regular improvements
❌ Build variants multiply: when defined(…) selects which statements compile, and -d flags set the space (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Good for systems: Compiles to C, performance
✅ Great for scripting: Python-like syntax
✅ Strong for CLI tools: Single binary
⚠️ Limited adoption: Niche use cases
⚠️ Web backend: Possible but uncommon



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Python-like syntax: Familiar, gentle
⚠️ Macro system: Powerful but complex
✅ Good docs: Tutorial, manual
⚠️ Small community: Fewer learning resources



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean, readable: Python-influenced
✅ UFCS: Uniform function call syntax elegant
✅ Expressive: Macros, templates
⚠️ Indentation-based: Not everyone’s preference



1.2.7 Testing

✅ unittest module: Built-in testing
⚠️ Debugging: Gdb works but not ideal
⚠️ Limited tooling: Fewer profilers
✅ Compile-time checks: Good error messages



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
⚠️ C interop: FFI can introduce unsafety
✅ Type safe: Static typing
⚠️ Exceptions: Less explicit than Result types
❌ The release build wraps; overflow checks are an off-by-default switch, a priced mitigation (Q4)

Verdict: Nim provides flexible coupling support (distinct types, concepts, UFCS) but GC and macros create coupling. UFCS (Uniform Function Call Syntax) decouples method syntax from type definitions. title: Crystal (1.15)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Crystal in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 73.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 87.9/100 · Engineering readiness 59.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing with full inference: The compiler infers every local and parameter type, so the code reads like Ruby while the type is known at compile time
✅ Nil is a type, not a universal value: T? is T | Nil, and the compiler forces a nil? check or an explicit not_nil! before a member is reached
✅ Union types name the alternatives: Int32 | String is a declared type that a case narrows, so an alternative is expressed rather than encoded
✅ Modules mix in behaviour at compile time: include and extend add a module’s methods to a type, so composition is the ordinary route and the class hierarchy stays shallow; a reopened class is fixed when the program is compiled, so there is no runtime monkey-patching
✅ Generics are specialised per instantiation: Array(T), Hash(K, V), and generic classes produce a specialised type, so a collection carries its element type
⚠️ Operator overloading is per type and unchecked in cost: +, <=>, and [] are ordinary method definitions, so the notation can hide the call (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ new is generated from initialize: Construction is an ordinary method call, and a struct is built where it is declared
✅ Structs are value types: A struct is copied on assignment and passed by value, so construction does not allocate or alias
✅ record generates a value type in one line: record Point, x : Int32, y : Int32 creates the getters, the constructor, ==, and hash
✅ Named arguments separate the call from the parameter order: foo(b: 1, a: 2) names each argument at the call site
✅ A block binds a resource to its construction: File.open(path) { |f| ... } opens the resource around the block and closes it at the end
⚠️ Mutability is the default: An instance variable is writable unless the class prevents it, so immutability is a convention rather than a declared property (C2)
❌ One value, many names: objects move by reference; a field, a parameter, and a closure reach the same instance (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The collector owns deallocation: Crystal uses a conservative garbage collector, and a collection runs on the collector’s schedule rather than the program’s (M2)
⚠️ No RAII: File.open with a block closes through ensure, but no destructor runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow checking: Aliasing and lifetime are unchecked, and a value stays alive while any reference to it exists (M4)
✅ Structs keep small values off the heap: A struct is stored in place, so an ordinary value does not involve the collector
✅ The unsafe boundary has its own types: Pointer(T), Slice(T), and StaticArray(T, N) name a raw region explicitly, so an unsafe access is visible in the type
⚠️ A conservative collector retains conservatively: Any bit pattern on the stack that looks like a pointer keeps an object alive
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild-pointer trap in the unsafe pointer operations ends the program, and the crash is outside the exception surface (Er6)
❌ A pointer cast reinterprets with no check and no mark: Pointer#as converts between pointer types, and the reference states that no runtime check runs — the same as operator performs a checked cast for unions, so the unchecked case reads like the checked one (M6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: raise needs no declaration in the signature, and the compiler does not require a handler (Er2)
✅ begin/rescue/else/ensure is the structured path: Each clause separates one stage of the recovery
✅ ensure runs on every exit path: A normal return, a raised exception, and an explicit return all run the ensure clause
✅ T? makes absence a value, not an error: A method that may not produce a value returns T?, and the caller must handle Nil
✅ An exception hierarchy is ordinary classes: class MyError < Exception declares a new error type
⚠️ A bare raise "message" creates a plain Exception: A rescue clause that names a specific type does not catch it, so the message-only form is a coarse signal
❌ A fault ends the program: an unhandled exception raises to the program and terminates it (documented) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Fibers are lightweight concurrency: spawn starts a fiber with its own stack and no operating-system thread
✅ Channels pass messages between fibers: Channel(T) with send/receive implements CSP-style communication, so two fibers hand off a value without a shared lock
✅ select waits on several channels at once: The first ready message is taken
✅ A completion channel expresses a join: A Channel(Nil) closed by the worker is the ordinary signal that a fiber has finished
❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection: Mutex, Atomic, and WaitGroup are library types, and the compiler checks no locking discipline (K3)
⚠️ One fiber runs at a time by default: The runtime is single-threaded until parallel multi-threading is enabled at build time, so a CPU-bound fiber blocks the others between yields



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The compiler uses the LLVM backend and emits native code: The toolchain produces machine code rather than bytecode
✅ The output is one self-contained binary: A Crystal program links to a single executable with no runtime installed separately
✅ C bindings are direct: A lib declaration with a @[Link(...)] annotation calls a C function from the shared library
✅ The standard library covers the system surface: HTTP, JSON, YAML, sockets, and cryptography are in the distribution
⚠️ Windows support lags: The Windows target is less complete than Linux and macOS, so a Windows-first program takes the harder path
⚠️ A “self-contained” binary still follows the platform: The Crystal runtime is linked into the executable, but libc is linked dynamically unless --static and the linker flags say otherwise, so portability depends on the build



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Ruby-like syntax with compile-time typing is the design bet: Readability with safety, and the price is a long compile
A single-threaded runtime by default is a deliberate choice: Simplicity and predictable behaviour before parallel throughput
Compile-time macros instead of runtime monkey-patching: The flexibility is available at the build, not after it
The conservative collector is a pragmatic pick: There is no borrow checker to satisfy, and the cost is a collector that can pause
The small ecosystem is an adoption fact: A market outcome, not a construction of the language
Limited IDE support is a tooling fact: An editor plugin cannot infer the whole program as the compiler does




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Native code from LLVM: The optimisation pipeline used for C and C++ applies to Crystal
✅ There is no interpreter and no JIT warm-up: A compiled binary starts and stays at its compiled speed
✅ The whole program is visible to the compiler: The compiler sees every call site, so it can inline and devirtualise across files
✅ Concrete types dispatch directly: When the type is known, a method call is a direct call, and a union type dispatches on a type identifier
⚠️ Compile time is long: Whole-program type inference and LLVM optimisation make a build heavy, which slows the edit-build-run loop



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small: shards is the dependency manager, and the available libraries are far fewer than Ruby’s or Go’s (Ec3)
✅ shards is a standard dependency manager: shard.yml declares the dependencies, and shards install resolves them
✅ The standard library is high quality: An HTTP server, JSON, YAML, cryptography, and concurrency are in the box
✅ Kemal and Lucky are established web frameworks: A program has a real web path on the language
✅ The toolchain is one command: crystal compiles and runs, crystal tool format formats, and crystal docs generates documentation
⚠️ The community is small but active: The project depends on a small contributor base, so a package is more likely to be left unmaintained than in a large ecosystem



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The 1.x line has held a stability promise: Crystal 1.0 established the compatibility expectation, and the 1.x series has kept it
✅ An experimental feature is gated behind a flag: Parallel multi-threading is enabled at build time, so an unstable feature is opt-in
✅ A formatter keeps the style stable across versions: crystal tool format removes a class of style change
✅ Deprecations precede removals: A method is marked deprecated for a series and then removed
⚠️ The 0.x line was a breaking series: The stability promise begins at 1.0, so code older than 1.0 needed a migration
⚠️ The Windows target is still maturing: The platform’s support level changes across releases
❌ Build variants multiply: flag?(…) selects which code compiles, and the flags arrive at the command line (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ CLI tools are a strong fit: A single native binary with immediate start-up
✅ Web services are a strong fit: Kemal and Lucky cover the service layer
✅ Network daemons are a strong fit: Fibers and channels give cheap concurrent connection handling
✅ C interoperability work is a strong fit: A lib declaration calls a C library without a wrapper generator
⚠️ Large application backends are less proven: The library pool and the hiring pool are both smaller
⚠️ Windows-first desktop work is not the target: The platform support is the constraint



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a Ruby or Python developer: The syntax is familiar, and the type annotations are usually inferred
✅ The compiler teaches the type model: A union-type error names the case that was not handled
✅ The standard library reads like the language: The same block and ? conventions appear throughout
⚠️ Flow-sensitive typing is the real subject: A union type and Nil narrowing must be understood to use the language well
⚠️ The macro system is a second language: Compile-time macros use their own {% %} and { } syntax
⚠️ The build loop is slow: A long compile makes each experiment expensive



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Ruby-like and readable: Method calls, blocks, and string interpolation follow the familiar shape
✅ Type annotations are optional in most positions: Inference removes the declaration
✅ Blocks are the call idiom: do ... end and { ... } pass a closure, so resource handling and iteration look alike
✅ ? and ! name a method’s contract: nil? asks a question and not_nil! asserts the answer
⚠️ The macro syntax sits beside the ordinary syntax: {% ... %} and { ... } appear only inside a macro
⚠️ A union type is written in the type position: T? is shorthand for T | Nil, which must be read correctly



1.2.7 Testing

✅ crystal spec is built in: The standard library’s Spec module gives describe, it, and expect, with a runner
✅ Specs live under spec/ by convention: The compiler builds a spec target from the project
✅ The compiler checks the test code: A spec that calls a method with the wrong type fails the build
✅ The ? and ! convention carries into assertions: Absence is tested explicitly rather than caught as an exception
⚠️ The standard library has no mocking layer: A double, a stub, or a property test comes from a third-party shard
⚠️ The compile time is paid again for the spec target: A slow build slows the test loop as well



1.2.8 Security

✅ No null reference: Nil is a type, and a member is reached only after a check
✅ Memory safety is the runtime’s: The collector and the index checks remove the use-after-free and out-of-bounds classes
✅ There is no runtime eval: The program is compiled, so a string cannot become code at run time
✅ Static typing removes dynamic type confusion: A value’s type is known before the program runs
⚠️ Pointer(T) and LibC are the unsafe surface: They are declared escapes and must be reviewed by hand
⚠️ A macro expands to code the reader cannot see: The compiled program differs from the source text at the macro site
❌ The release build wraps; debug traps are a mitigation, priced (Q4)

❌ Shards resolve versions at install time; the shard.lock is opt-in discipline. (Y1)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)

1.3.6 Governance

✅ The language reference is public. (Y12)
✅ The compiler source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Crystal’s design separates what the language itself controls, and the score is held back mainly by the runtime it inherits. The Memory dimension carries the largest cost, because the collector schedules its own pauses, no destructor is tied to a scope, and no ownership or borrow check exists; manual synchronisation and unchecked exceptions are the other significant marks. Inference gives static types with a light syntax, Nil and union types make absence and alternatives explicit, and compile-time macros keep metaprogramming out of the runtime. title: C++ (C++11)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C++11 in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 53.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.7/100 · Engineering readiness 43.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A conversion narrows in silence: the conversion table is a shared resource no reader is forced to hold, so a checked expression cannot be told from a narrowed one (T2)
❌ No sum type in the standard: std::variant arrives in C++17, so a union plus a tag remains the encoding and every consumer re-derives which member is live (T4)
❌ An operator takes its meaning from the operand types: << shifts and inserts, and a reader resolves the type to know which (T8)
❌ A pointer may be null and the type does not say so: each consumer writes the guard, and an omission stays invisible (T10)
❌ A header is the only surface, and import does not exist: a module boundary arrives in C++20, so a header’s declarations are all public (T11)
❌ A signature states no effects: a call may write a file, mutate a global, and throw, and the signature names only the return type (T12)
❌ extern "C" is a hand-written promise: argument order, layout, and lifetime cross a boundary that neither compiler validates (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A binding is mutable until the code says otherwise: const is opt-in, and every holder reconstructs who may write (C2)
✅ Placement construction separates storage from construction: an object is built in storage the caller already holds (C3)
⚠️ The hash container ships with an unpinned order: std::map keeps key order and std::unordered_map does not, so a program that reaches for the hash container keeps the ordering discipline itself (C5)
❌ One value, many names: a pointer, a reference, a member, and a parameter reach one object, and the declaration names none of the sharers (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: a converting constructor and a conversion operator run from the contexts the standard names, not from a call the source shows (C7)
❌ The static initialization order fiasco: namespace-scope init order across translation units is implementation-defined [5] (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Destructors run at scope exit: the release is deterministic, and unique_ptr and shared_ptr put the owner in the type
❌ A raw pointer still names no owner: two pointers can share one buffer with no way to say which frees it (M4)
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: default-initialization leaves scalars indeterminate, and reading one before a write is undefined behaviour (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: a reinterpret_cast and an unchecked downcast reinterpret storage with no check (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer’s trap ends the program outside every catch clause (Er6)
❌ shared_ptr cycles leak; the standard requires the cycle to be broken by hand (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A structured path exists: throw and catch carry a failure from where it is raised to where it is handled (Er1)
❌ A failure may arrive undeclared: throw needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it (Er2)
❌ A failure is not an ordinary value: nothing folds a fallible operation into an expression, so each level rebuilds the pair (Er4)
❌ A fault ends the program: an uncaught exception in a thread calls std::terminate, and the thread is not an isolation unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Threads are in the standard: std::thread runs a second computation inside the program’s own structure (K1)
⚠️ Shared state is the default: nothing marks a value thread-local or immutable (K2)
⚠️ Nothing detects a race: the locking discipline is an agreement across files that no tool checks (K3)
⚠️ No scope joins a task: a thread started without a scope can outlive the code that started it (K4)
✅ Locks, atomics, and futures are in the standard: std::mutex, std::atomic, and std::async state the protocol in the source (K5)
❌ A concurrent task is an operating-system thread: each task holds a thread for its whole life, and a blocked task holds one too (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owner: the language is standardised by ISO/IEC, and independent compilers implement it
✅ No required runtime: a program compiles to native code and needs no vendor service
✅ Every mainstream target is supported: compilers exist for the operating systems and embedded targets of the era



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Zero-cost abstraction vs. reading time: templates and inline code remove runtime cost and add ceremony at every declaration
Placement construction vs. readability: building an object in storage the caller chose is a precise control, and the reader reconstructs where that storage came from




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled to native code: no interpreter dispatch sits in the hot loop
✅ No collector: release timing is the program’s, not a runtime component’s



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: a dependency is resolved by a build script or by the platform’s toolchain, so two checkouts can disagree about the graph (Ec1)
❌ Fragmented tooling: the language is split across platform toolchains with different extensions and warning sets (Ec2)
❌ No cross-release binary promise: libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Build variants multiply: the preprocessor’s #ifdef tree selects which declarations reach the compiler, so a translation unit is a flag outcome (V7)
✅ A three-year cadence begins: C++11 was the first feature revision after thirteen years, and the committee has shipped one every three years since
✅ Additive: the revision removed almost nothing, so C++98 code compiles under it



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Close to the machine: the language serves systems, games, and embedded work
⚠️ Not a web or scripting language: the work it fits least is the work it is least used for



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Steep: templates, multiple inheritance, manual memory, and undefined behaviour build on nothing a mainstream background supplies (L1)
❌ Several paradigms at once: procedural, object-oriented, and generic code all remain available for the same task (L2)
✅ An authoritative standard text and a large literature: the reference is public and complete



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Nested instantiations tax the reader: a template argument can itself be an instantiation, and the reader unfolds the chain to know the type it produces
✅ Declarations state types once: the reader resolves a type at its declaration rather than at each use



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ Testing arrives from outside the toolchain: assert is in the library and no runner is, so a framework and a runner are adopted per project
✅ A mature debugger exists for every platform: the toolchain is the platform’s, and it steps through the source
✅ A monotonic clock is in the standard: std::chrono::steady_clock publishes an elapsed reading that the program can call (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Memory-unsafe: a buffer overflow, a use-after-free, and a double free all compile, and any pointer suffices (Q1)
❌ The inherited C rule: signed overflow undefined, unsigned modulo; the optimizer exploits both (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default: timestamps and absolute paths reach the artifact, so a third party cannot confirm it matches the source (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No registry, so no signed provenance: a dependency is a source tree or a library, and its origin is taken on trust (Y3)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ A failure leaves no post-mortem by default: without a debugger and an enabled core dump, an unhandled failure prints nothing (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ A change pays a slow build: templates and a long link step sit on the critical path of every edit (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A general foreign-function interface exists: the platform’s C ABI is the boundary, and the language calls it directly (Y9)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ An open standard with no conformance suite: the standard lists implementation-defined behaviour, and the committee publishes no suite an independent implementation runs (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [7], [8]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [9].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [10], [11].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.
