title: C (C23)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 36.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.5/100 · Engineering readiness 52.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Structs separate data: Pure data, no methods
✅ Function pointers enable polymorphism: Can pass behavior as data
❌ No encapsulation: Everything is public
❌ No generics: Void pointers couple to type casting
✅ No inheritance: Can’t create coupled hierarchies
❌ Header files couple: Includes create compilation dependencies
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope
❌ No namespaces: Global namespace pollution



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Explicit memory management: Allocation separate from initialization
✅ Designated initializers: Can initialize specific fields
❌ No constructors: Manual initialization couples to usage
❌ Global state common: Static variables couple modules
❌ One value, many names: pointers alias freely, restrict is an opt-in promise the compiler does not check, and an assignment shares the object the pointer addresses (C6)
❌ File-scope initializers elaborate in an order unspecified across translation units (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Manual control enables precise memory strategy: Can separate memory management from logic
✅ Explicit allocation/deallocation: malloc/free make lifetime visible
❌ No safety: Use-after-free, double-free, memory leaks all possible
❌ No RAII: Must manually track and free resources
✅ Predictable: No GC pauses, deterministic performance
❌ Pointer arithmetic couples to memory layout: Buffer overruns couple to hardware, with no abstraction over memory
✅ Custom allocators: Can decouple allocation strategy (arena, pool, etc.)
❌ Undefined behavior on errors: Buffer overruns, null derefs, and other memory-safety violations are UB
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: reading an automatic object before initialization is undefined behaviour, and malloc returns bytes nobody wrote, so every read depends on a write the code must prove happened on every path (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: a union member, a pointer cast, or a char* read reinterprets storage with no check, and only the effective-type rule separates the honest puns from the undefined ones (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer’s trap ends the program, and the language’s failure surface is values — the trap is not a value (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Explicit error codes: Return values make errors visible
❌ No enforcement: Can ignore return values
❌ errno couples: Global error state couples functions
❌ NULL everywhere: Pointer errors couple all code
❌ A fault ends the program: a trap or an illegal access ends the process, and the language publishes no recoverable unit — setjmp jumps out of frames, it isolates nothing (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ pthreads manual: All synchronization explicit
❌ Shared mutable state default: No protection
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No prevention
⚠️ Explicit is predictable: At least coupling is visible
❌ A thread is an operating-system thread: pthread_create reserves one for the task’s whole life, and a blocked task holds it (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No platform owner: The language is standardised by ISO/IEC and implemented independently by GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so no single vendor controls it
✅ No required platform runtime: A conforming program depends only on the C standard library, not on a vendor runtime
✅ Every mainstream platform has a C compiler: Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded targets all have conforming implementations, and operating systems expose a C ABI to other languages
✅ No single-implementation dependence: Source compiles under more than one compiler, so the loss of one implementation does not strand the code



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Power vs. Safety: Complete control couples to complete responsibility for safety
Simplicity vs. Safety: No abstractions means manual discipline required to control coupling
Performance vs. Correctness: Optimization couples to unsafe patterns (buffer tricks, pointer arithmetic)
Portability vs. Platform Access: Platform-specific code couples to hardware/OS
Manual Memory Management: Must couple resource acquisition to every usage site
Undefined Behavior Everywhere: Memory errors couple entire program to runtime environment
Header Dependencies: Changes to one header couple to all files that include it (transitively)




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Maximum performance: No abstraction overhead
✅ No GC: Deterministic, predictable
✅ Full control: Manual everything
✅ Predictable: What you write is what runs
✅ Minimal runtime: Runs anywhere



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Ubiquitous: Available on every platform
⚠️ Build systems: Make, autotools, CMake fragmentation
✅ Mature tooling: GCC, Clang, debuggers
⚠️ No package manager: Manual dependency management
✅ Stable ABI on a given platform: A platform’s C ABI is long-stable, so binaries built by ABI-compatible compilers interoperate on that platform (the C standard itself defines no ABI, and compatibility is not guaranteed across compilers or targets)
✅ Objects cross compilers on the platform’s published C ABI [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Extremely stable: C89/C99/C11/C17/C23 all backward compatible
✅ No breaking changes: Code from 1980s still compiles
✅ Conservative: Changes are minimal
⚠️ Slow evolution: New features take decades
❌ Build variants multiply: the C preprocessor’s #ifdef tree selects which statements exist, so the shipped binary is one selection from a space no suite covers, and every guard must agree with every combination that ships (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: OS kernels, drivers
✅ Great for embedded: Minimal footprint
✅ Strong for performance: No overhead
✅ Good for portability: Runs everywhere
⚠️ Not for application dev: Too low-level



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Simple language: Small, learnable
❌ Hard to master: Undefined behavior, pointers
✅ Lots of resources: K&R, tutorials
❌ Many footguns: Easy to shoot yourself



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Simple, direct: Minimal syntax
❌ No abstractions: Manual everything
❌ Pointer syntax: int *(*fp)(void) confusing
✅ Explicit: Clear what’s happening



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ Testing frameworks: Check, Unity, cmocka
✅ Excellent debuggers: Gdb, lldb
❌ Manual memory tracking: Valgrind needed
⚠️ UB makes debugging hard: Anything can happen



1.2.8 Security

❌ Memory unsafe: All memory bugs possible
❌ Buffer overflows: No bounds checking
❌ Undefined behavior: Security vulnerabilities
❌ No protection: Manual everything
❌ Fixed-width integers wrap; signed overflow is undefined, so the optimizer deletes the checks that catch it; unsigned is modulo 2^W by definition (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds embed include paths, library state, and preprocessor definitions; no byte-reproducible default exists. (Y1)
❌ Libraries resolve from the system and toolchain state at build time. (Y2)
❌ The distribution records no compiler version per project. (Y14)
✅ The makefile (or build description) is the contract the builder reads. (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ System packages and vendored sources carry no signed provenance by default. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to the libraries a program links. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ printf and syslog carry no structure by contract. (Y6)
❌ A fault ends in a signal; core dumps are a platform setting, not a language default. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with a compiler; gdb and lldb are separate projects. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ The C FFI is the language itself: any library with a header is callable. (Y9)
✅ C compilers target every common architecture and platform. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The standard enumerates the corners, and a suite runs: C’s implementation-defined behaviors are listed (J.2), and the NCAR C conformance suite runs against independent compilers (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [9], [10].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: C provides no coupling prevention mechanisms but also imposes few forced coupling constructs — the language itself is neutral. With discipline, developers can separate concerns through function pointers, explicit error codes, and manual memory management. Without discipline, globals, macros, and undefined behavior couple everything. Main insight: coupling in C is entirely up to the programmer. The same language can produce extremely low or extremely high coupling depending on how it is used.

title: Zsh (5.9)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Zsh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 51.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with no static check: A scalar, an array element, and an associative-array value all hold text, and no declaration states what kind of thing a name holds (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative is a word plus a convention, and typeset -A gives a mapping rather than a tagged choice (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional arguments, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
❌ One flat namespace: Functions and parameters share the global space, and local only narrows a name inside a function body, so nothing hides a library’s internals from the process (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to nothing by default: setopt nounset turns the reference into an error, but the option is off unless it is requested, and an empty value still passes (T10)
✅ typeset -T ties two parameters together: typeset -T PATH path makes the scalar PATH and the array path one value in two shapes, so colon-separated data is edited as a list



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: An assignment writes the global unless local or typeset narrows it, and no binding is immutable unless readonly is applied (C1, C2)
❌ No constructor or validation on a plain parameter: Nothing checks a value when it is bound; validation exists only where setopt or an explicit test is applied (C4)
✅ local in a function body is a real scope: A parameter declared local is restored when the function returns, so working state stays with the routine
✅ autoload -Uz separates definition from call: A function body is loaded from $fpath on first reference, so the name is declared without the implementation being read
✅ Configuration files are layered and sourced by role: .zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc, .zlogin, and .zlogout each hold one kind of setup, so interactive configuration does not reach a script
✅ emulate -L zsh fixes the option set inside a function: The options are reset for the function’s duration and restored on return, so a routine does not inherit settings from the caller



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; parameters are allocated and released by the shell
✅ Scope and unset bound a lifetime: A local parameter disappears when its function returns, so working state does not persist by accident
✅ Associative arrays are managed by the shell: typeset -A allocates and grows its own storage, so no capacity handling is written
⚠️ Assignment copies the value: An array is duplicated on assignment, and referencing one without copying requires an explicit indirection
⚠️ Command substitution is materialised whole: $(cmd) collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large result is held in memory
⚠️ always blocks hold their state until the block ends: The try and always blocks are kept for the duration of the construct, so a long-running trap delays release



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: $?, TRAPZERR, and the always block are the apparatus, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ The error trap is global and undifferentiated: TRAPZERR runs for the whole script, it receives no description of the failure, and it fires only where a non-zero status is not consumed (Er3)
❌ Errors cannot be returned: A function’s outcome is an exit status, so an error carries no payload and cannot be combined with another (Er4)
✅ { ... } always { ... } guarantees cleanup: The always block runs after an error, a break, or a continue, so teardown is attached to the construct rather than to a global trap
⚠️ The always block does not survive a parse error: A syntax error in the try list aborts during parsing, so the always list never runs
⚠️ setopt errexit is fragile: The option does not fire inside && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes error behaviour



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no lock, channel, mutex, or await; the only parallel construct is a background job (K5)
✅ zmodload zsh/system adds real synchronisation: The module provides a zsystem builtin with file locking and a sysread/syswrite pair, so a race over a shared file can be avoided in the language
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
✅ Coprocesses give two-way communication: coproc starts a child that print -p and read -p can drive, so a long-running program is not restarted per iteration
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the environment: A & job shares every global parameter, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ wait returns a status, not a value: A result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a coprocess



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One implementation defines the language: Zsh exists as the zsh project’s own C implementation, with no independent implementation of the same specification to compare against (P2)
✅ zsh is packaged for every UNIX-like system: Linux distributions, the BSDs, and macOS all ship it, and it is the default interactive shell on macOS
✅ The implementation runs on POSIX systems and Windows: The same code base builds on Linux, the BSDs, Solaris, and through Cygwin or MSYS2 on Windows
⚠️ emulate sh is a compatibility mode, not POSIX compliance: The shell can be invoked as sh or ksh and behave closer to them, but the mode is offered for convenience rather than as a conformance claim
⚠️ Open-source governance is project-led: The language is directed by its maintainers in a public repository, with no standards body and no formal change process
⚠️ No second implementation is likely: With a very large option and module surface, an independent implementation would be a research project



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The large option set is a deliberate design: setopt lets a user choose behaviour that other shells fix, and the price is that a script must state which behaviour it expects
The completion system is a language of its own: compinit, _arguments, and zstyle make completion programmable, which is a feature rather than a coupling mechanism
Modules are optional capability: zmodload adds zsh/mathfunc, zsh/datetime, and zsh/system on demand, so a script chooses its own surface
1-indexed arrays were a compatibility decision: The offset differs from Bash and ksh, and KSH_ARRAYS exists for users who want the other convention
oh-my-zsh is a distribution, not the language: The framework owns configuration and the prompt, so its coupling is to the user’s setup rather than to zsh itself
zsh is not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, which is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT (R1)
✅ A native implementation with a fast path for common work: Expansion, globbing, and arithmetic are executed in C rather than by calling an external command
✅ Floating-point arithmetic is built in: (( ... )) handles real numbers, so a numeric calculation does not need awk or bc
✅ zmodload zsh/mathfunc adds the C math library: Trigonometric and logarithmic functions are available inside arithmetic expressions
⚠️ Start-up sources several configuration files: An interactive shell reads .zshenv, then .zprofile or .zshrc, so a large oh-my-zsh setup costs time on every new shell, which zsh/zprof can measure
⚠️ The completion system builds a cache: compinit scans $fpath and writes ~/.zcompdump, so the first shell after a change pays for the scan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager in the language: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins arrive through third-party frameworks such as oh-my-zsh, prezto, zinit, or antigen (Ec1)
✅ The plugin ecosystem is one of the largest in the shell world: Prompt themes, completions, and syntax-highlighting plugins exist for most command-line tools
✅ The bundled completion system is extensive: _arguments definitions ship for hundreds of commands, and compinit makes them all available without an add-on
✅ vcs_info provides a git-aware prompt in the standard distribution: Version-control state is read by a shipped module instead of a script
✅ Documentation is complete and versioned: The manual is shipped as man pages and as a searchable HTML manual
⚠️ Frameworks own the configuration: oh-my-zsh and its alternatives take over .zshrc, so a user’s setup depends on a third-party project



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: New releases add features, and the project documents the few changes that affect existing configuration
✅ emulate pins behaviour: A script can fix the option set with emulate -L zsh, so a change of defaults does not silently alter it
✅ The project ships regular releases: The 5.x series has been maintained for many years with ongoing fixes
✅ Options are the compatibility mechanism: A new behaviour is normally introduced behind a setopt, so the old behaviour remains available
⚠️ Change depends on the maintainers: The language is directed by its project team rather than by a committee with a published process
⚠️ Frameworks must track the language: A plugin that depends on internal behaviour can break when a release changes it, which is a risk of the ecosystem rather than of the language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for interactive use: The completion system, prompt substitution, and vcs_info make the terminal the primary domain
✅ Strong for text and path processing: Glob qualifiers such as *(.) for plain files, recursive **/, and setopt extendedglob express selection that other shells delegate to find
✅ Arrays and associative arrays fit scripting that needs structure: typeset -A and array slicing cover indexed and keyed data inside the language
✅ Emulation covers other shells when needed: emulate sh and emulate ksh run foreign syntax in a nested scope
⚠️ A zsh script needs zsh: An interpreter that is not installed on every host, so a portable bootstrap script cannot be written in zsh
⚠️ The most useful features are interactive: Completion, prompt themes, and autosuggestions do not travel into a script



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Bash knowledge transfers: The core syntax, expansions, and pipelines are familiar to a Bash user
✅ Documentation is complete and searchable: The manual covers the language, the builtins, the options, and the modules
⚠️ Parameter expansion is more complex than in Bash: ${(flags)name} and the setopt-controlled variations each have their own rule
⚠️ The option set is very large: The behaviour of a script depends on which options are set, and a reader must know the current set
⚠️ Framework configuration hides the setup: An oh-my-zsh user learns the framework before the language



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Arrays are first-class with slicing: $a[2,-1] expresses a range that other shells express with a loop
✅ Glob qualifiers replace external tools: *(.), *(/D), and **/*.c select files by kind and recursion in the pattern itself
✅ No word splitting by default: An unquoted $var expands as one word even when it contains spaces, so fewer quotes are needed
⚠️ Parameter expansion flags are dense: ${(q)var}, ${(j:,:)a}, and ${(k)assoc} pack quoting, joining, and keys into a short notation
⚠️ setopt changes the reading of the text: The same script behaves differently under shwordsplit, nomatch, or extendedglob
⚠️ Arrays may be 0-indexed or 1-indexed: The default is 1-indexed while KSH_ARRAYS changes it, so an array index is not always portable between zsh configurations



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped parameter or a bad array index is found during the run (G3)
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: zsh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ functions -T traces a selected function: Tracing can be limited to the function under test instead of the whole script
✅ TRAPDEBUG gives a debugger hook: A function bound to the DEBUG trap runs before each command, which supports a stepping harness
✅ The test set can be isolated with emulate -L zsh and a subshell: Each case runs with known options in a child process



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic typing removes a check the shell cannot make: A value that should be a path, a number, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object (Q2)
⚠️ Text can re-enter the interpreter: A value assembled from data and passed to eval, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code
⚠️ nomatch controls a failure mode rather than removing it: An unmatched glob either errors or expands literally, so the script must choose which surprise it prefers
✅ setopt nounset turns an unset reference into an error: A misspelled parameter is reported instead of expanding to nothing
✅ ${(q)var} quotes a value for re-input: The expansion flag makes safe quoting explicit instead of leaving it to hand-written escaping
✅ setopt noclobber protects existing files: The option makes > refuse to overwrite a regular file
❌ Arithmetic is 64-bit and wraps in two’s complement (Q4)

Verdict: Zsh keeps the core coupling of a word-based shell — one namespace, no static typing, and an exit status in place of an error value — so its core score stays low, but it removes real friction inside that model: typeset -T ties PATH to the path array, { ... } always { ... } guarantees cleanup, autoload -Uz separates a name from its body, and glob qualifiers express selection that other shells leave to find. The ecosystem score reflects the strongest interactive tooling in the family: a large bundled completion system, shipped modules such as vcs_info and zsh/system, and documentation that keeps pace with the releases. The remaining cost is that zsh is one implementation, its option set is large, and a framework usually owns the configuration.

title: PowerShell (7.6)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PowerShell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 62.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 63.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ A typed variable or parameter is checked at the boundary: [int]$n and a typed param() block make the binder convert and reject a bad call
✅ Object-oriented: Everything is an object (not strings like Bash)
✅ Classes: PowerShell 5+ has classes
❌ Dynamic typing is the default (T1): A variable takes its type from the value assigned, so a type error is reported only when the statement runs
✅ Interfaces: Can use .NET interfaces
⚠️ Module scope pollution: Import-Module can overwrite commands
❌ Verb-Noun naming: While helpful, couples to conventions
❌ Inherits the CLR rule: Char is a UTF-16 code unit (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors: Classes have constructors, [PSCustomObject] for ad-hoc
✅ Factory patterns: Common with New-Object cmdlets
✅ Pipeline objects: Objects flow through pipelines
⚠️ Hashtables: Often used for construction, less structured
⚠️ Global scope: Can create global variables
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation states a hashtable’s keys enumerate in no guaranteed order (C5)
❌ One value, many names: .NET objects move by handle through the pipeline, and the variable table shares instances across scopes (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: dynamic method invocation (the string-typed command name, Invoke-Expression) runs text as code at sites that show a value (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ .NET GC: Automatic garbage collection
✅ Dispose pattern: IDisposable for resources
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic .NET GC
⚠️ Disposal is explicit: There is no using block for a resource, so a value is released with try/finally, or by the clean block that a PowerShell 7.3 function runs when it ends



1.1.4 Error

✅ Try/Catch/Finally: Structured exception handling
✅ Typed exceptions: Can catch specific .NET exceptions
⚠️ Terminating vs non-terminating: Two error types, confusing
✅ $ErrorActionPreference: Control error behavior
⚠️ Silent failures: Default is to continue on errors
❌ A fault ends the pipeline: a terminating exception aborts the runspace (documented); the language declares no recoverable unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Jobs: Background jobs with Receive-Job
⚠️ Workflows are Windows PowerShell only: The workflow keyword is not implemented in PowerShell 7
⚠️ Runspaces: Low-level threading, complex
⚠️ No async/await: The language has no await keyword, even in PowerShell 7
✅ ForEach-Object -Parallel: PowerShell 7+ parallel pipelines
⚠️ Pipeline variable: $_ implicit like Perl



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The runtime is open source under the MIT licence: PowerShell 7 is developed in the open at github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell and has no proprietary runtime component
✅ The engine is .NET: PowerShell 7 runs on .NET (formerly .NET Core), so one runtime assembly runs on every platform .NET supports
✅ Builds ship for Windows, macOS, and Linux: Microsoft publishes a Windows installer, a signed macOS package, and packages for Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL, and Alpine
✅ A module is a portable .NET assembly: A cmdlet written in C# against the .NET API loads on any host running the Core runtime
✅ Nothing in the core language names a Windows API: The built-in cmdlets cover files, processes, and text, so a script that avoids WMI, COM, and the registry providers runs unchanged off Windows



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The type system is borrowed: The types are .NET types, so the language adds convenience syntax and inherits .NET’s type behaviour rather than defining a model of its own
The language ships with a host and a remoting layer: PowerShell is a shell, a session, and a language in one product, so its scope reaches past programming into administration
Help is part of the runtime: Get-Help and Get-Command read metadata from the loaded modules, a design decision that ties documentation to the session rather than to a separate manual
Aliases ship as part of the surface: ls, cd, and cat map to cmdlets, a convenience whose meaning depends on what the session has loaded
Two products share the name: Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships with Windows while PowerShell 7 is the cross-platform line, so a script states which one it targets — a version split, not a language dependency




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled
⚠️ .NET overhead: JIT warmup, GC pauses
✅ Object pipelines: More efficient than text parsing
⚠️ Startup time: Slow to launch



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ PowerShell Gallery: Central repository
✅ Excellent Windows integration: WMI, COM, .NET
✅ VSCode: PowerShell extension excellent
⚠️ Smaller than npm/PyPI: But growing
✅ Cross-platform: PowerShell Core runs everywhere
✅ Binary dependencies arrive as CLR assemblies under the runtime’s published format [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Active development: Regular improvements
✅ PowerShell Core: Open source, cross-platform
⚠️ Windows PowerShell frozen: v5.1 last version
✅ Mostly compatible: Migration path exists



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for Windows administration: Best-in-class
✅ Good for DevOps: Configuration management, automation
✅ Azure/Office 365: First-class support
⚠️ Linux: Works but less common
❌ Not for applications: Scripting language



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Discoverable: Get-Command, Get-Help
✅ Consistent: Verb-Noun naming
⚠️ Large surface area: Many cmdlets to learn
⚠️ .NET knowledge helps: But not required



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable: Verb-Noun is clear
⚠️ Verbose: Get-ChildItem vs ls
✅ Aliases: Shortcuts available
⚠️ Pipeline syntax: | familiar but object-based



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Pester: Testing framework mature
✅ Debugger: Set-PSBreakpoint, step-through
✅ ISE/VSCode: Integrated debugging
✅ Verbose/Debug streams: Good diagnostics



1.2.8 Security

✅ Execution policy: Script signing available
✅ .NET security: Inherits .NET protections
⚠️ Code injection: Still possible with Invoke-Expression
✅ Constrained language mode: Restrict capabilities
❌ A calculation overflowing Int64 promotes to Double: the value loses precision without a word (Q4)

title: Ksh (kSH 93u+)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ksh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 51.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with run-time attributes: typeset -i, -F, -E, -l, and -u decide how a name is read and written, but the parser performs no static check and the attribute is enforced when the value is used (T1)
❌ No sum types: A tagged alternative is a word plus a convention, because typeset -T gives a named structure rather than a choice between variants (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional parameters, and behaviour is selected by the string in $0 or by the command name, never by a declared type (T5, T9)
❌ One flat global namespace: typeset inside a function body makes a name local, but a plain assignment writes the global, and no module boundary hides anything from the process (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name reads as empty by default: set -o nounset turns a reference to an unset name into an error, but the option is off by default and nothing forces a variable to be initialised (T10)
⚠️ typeset -T defines a real named type: A type can own discipline functions (.get, .set, .unset) and a create routine invoked for each instance, which is more than text binding — yet an instance is still a compound of words with no static check



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: A plain assignment writes the global namespace, and no binding is immutable unless readonly or typeset -r is applied (C1, C2)
⚠️ Validation is not attached to a plain variable: A name accepts any word, and the checking that exists comes from an attribute or from a discipline function added with typeset (C4)
✅ function bodies get local variables: A variable declared typeset in a function body is local, so a routine keeps its working state out of the caller’s namespace
✅ Discipline functions are real set and get hooks: x.set, x.get, and x.unset run on assignment and reference, so a rule about a value is attached to the value’s name instead of to every write site
✅ Name spaces and FPATH separate a library’s names: namespace lib { ... } keeps internal names out of the flat space, and a function on FPATH is loaded on first reference
✅ typeset -n gives a nameref: A function can operate on a caller’s variable by name without string concatenation and eval



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer, no address, and no deallocation builtin; the shell owns every value
✅ Scope and unset bound a lifetime: A local variable disappears when its function returns, and unset drops a name, so working state does not persist by accident
✅ Associative arrays are managed by the shell: typeset -A allocates and grows its own storage, so no capacity handling is written
⚠️ Assignment copies compound values: A typeset -T instance and a compound variable are copied on assignment, so a large structure is duplicated in full
⚠️ Parsed functions stay resident: ksh93 compiles a script to an internal tree and caches it, so a long session keeps the parsed definitions in memory
⚠️ typeset -E, -F, and -X choose a representation, not a lifetime: The attribute pins a value to double, float, or long-double storage, which couples the number to a precision decision made once



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: $? and trap ... ERR are the whole apparatus, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ The ERR trap is global and undifferentiated: One handler covers the whole script, it receives no description of the failure, and it fires only where an explicit check or set -o errexit applies (Er3)
❌ Errors cannot be returned: A function’s outcome is its exit status, so an error carries no payload and cannot be combined with another (Er4)
⚠️ set -o errexit is fragile: The option does not fire inside && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes error behaviour
✅ trap covers named signals and EXIT: Cleanup can be attached to EXIT and to specific signals, so a script releases resources on any exit path
✅ $? is unambiguous at the test, and pipefail extends it: The status of the last command is read directly, and set -o pipefail makes a mid-pipeline failure visible



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no lock, channel, or await; the only parallel construct is a background job (K5)
✅ Coprocesses give two-way communication: cmd |& with print -p and read -p keeps a child in conversation without a named pipe or a temporary file
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the global environment: A & job shares every global variable, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ wait returns a status, not a value: The join exists, but a result must travel through a pipe, a file, or a coprocess
⚠️ No structured concurrency: Nothing guarantees that a job started inside a function finishes before the function returns



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One lineage defines ksh93: The language comes from AT&T’s KornShell and its maintained fork ksh93u+m, while the BSD-derived pdksh and mksh implement an older dialect, so behaviour is not interchangeable (P2)
✅ POSIX with extensions: A script written to the POSIX shell language runs under ksh93, so it can move between systems that have a KornShell
⚠️ Two dialects share the name ksh: mksh and pdksh lack associative arrays, discipline functions, and floating point, so #!/bin/ksh means different things on different systems
⚠️ Availability is not uniform: ksh93 ships on AIX and Solaris and is packaged for Linux, but it is not the default shell on any mainstream Linux distribution
✅ A manual and a test suite define the language: The ksh93 manual and the AT&T test suite, now maintained in ksh93u+m, are the reference for behaviour
⚠️ One implementation carries the extensions: With no standard covering them, an omission or a defect in ksh93 is a property of the language as practised



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ksh88 lineage is a separate language: mksh and pdksh continue the older design on BSD and Android, and that divergence is a history of implementations rather than a coupling mechanism
Rich builtins are a deliberate choice: print, typeset, and the .sh.* variables lengthen the learning curve to remove whole categories of external command
The floating-point attribute is a representation choice: typeset -E, -F, and -X select storage precision, which is a modelling decision about the numbers a script handles
Discipline functions are a heavy mechanism: A .get hook runs on every reference, so encapsulation is paid for with an unpredictable per-access cost
namespace is not a module system: It prevents name collisions inside one script but hides nothing from the process, which is a scope decision
POSIX mode is available but not the goal: set -o posix narrows ksh to the standard, and a script that wants the extensions rightly leaves it off




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with an internal compile step: A script is parsed into a tree and cached, so a function body is not re-parsed on every call, but there is no artifact to precompile (R1)
✅ A native implementation with an optimised parser: ksh93 was designed with performance in mind, and the maintained fork continues to fix hot paths
✅ Coprocesses avoid repeated process creation: A child started once with |& is driven with print -p and read -p, so a loop does not fork per iteration
✅ Builtins cover most text work: print, printf, [[ ... ]], and ${var/pat/rep} avoid an external process for common operations
⚠️ Path hashing and tracked aliases are opt-in: alias -t records a resolved command path, so a script without it rescans PATH
⚠️ A .get discipline runs on every read: A hook on a variable adds work to each reference, so encapsulation has a per-access price



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no dependency resolver or module registry for ksh, so shared code is sourced from a directory on FPATH (Ec1)
⚠️ The ecosystem is smaller than Bash’s or Zsh’s: Few libraries and completions target ksh93 specifically
⚠️ The user base is declining: Bash is the default on Linux and absorbed most of ksh’s ideas, so new ksh93 code is rare
✅ The maintained fork revived the project: ksh93u+m restarted development and fixed defects that had stood for years
✅ Documentation is complete: One manual documents the language, the builtins, and the discipline mechanism
✅ The historical influence is documented: Ksh is the source of [[ ... ]], $'...', select, typeset, printf, and pipefail in other shells



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: New features arrive as extensions, and a ksh88-style script still runs
✅ set -o posix pins the dialect: A script can fix POSIX behaviour so that a change in an extension does not silently alter it
✅ The extensions are stable to the point of immobility: A construct such as typeset -A has behaved the same way for decades
⚠️ The 93v- development line was abandoned: The ksh2020 line never reached a stable release, and ksh93u+m carried the language instead
⚠️ Development rests on a small group: The maintained fork is a volunteer effort, so the pace of change is outside user control
⚠️ The older dialect is frozen in place: AIX and other systems ship a ksh88-era shell, so the language as practised is fragmented



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Good fit for POSIX system scripting with extras: ksh93 covers portable shell code and adds associative arrays, floating point, and coprocesses where the standard stops
✅ Strong for text and record processing: ${var/pat/rep}, ${var:offset:length}, [[ ... =~ ... ]], and printf keep string handling inside the language
✅ Associative arrays fit lookup and configuration work: typeset -A and compound variables model keyed data without a temporary file or an external tool
✅ Coprocesses suit long-running children: A child started once can be driven from a loop instead of through a named pipe
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so a program with real data structures belongs elsewhere
⚠️ The most advanced features are not portable: Discipline functions, name spaces, and typeset -T exist only in ksh93



1.2.5 Learning

✅ POSIX knowledge transfers: A Bash or sh user can write ksh on the first day
✅ Functions are more capable than in sh: function name { } with typeset locals is a familiar and predictable form
⚠️ The surface is large: typeset has many attributes, and [[ ... ]], (( ... )), print, whence, and the .sh.* variables each need their own reference
⚠️ The documentation is a specification, not a tutorial: There is little introductory material for the ksh93-specific features
⚠️ The dialect trap is invisible: A script written for ksh93 runs under mksh until it reaches an associative array or a float



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ POSIX surface with familiar extensions: if, case, for, and while are the standard forms, and (( ... )) and [[ ... ]] read like C
✅ ${var/pat/rep} handles substitution inline: A replacement no longer needs sed in a pipeline
⚠️ $'...' and typeset attributes add notation: Quoting, justification, case conversion, and numeric attributes each add their own spelling
⚠️ function and name() differ quietly: The two definition forms have different scoping behaviour, so the choice of syntax changes the semantics
⚠️ print and printf overlap: Two output builtins with different escape handling coexist



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or report facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad attribute is found during the run (G3)
✅ The DEBUG trap gives a command-by-command trace: trap ... DEBUG runs after each command, which makes a failure locatable in a long script
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: ksh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ set -o xtrace shows the expansion: set -x prints the expanded command, so an argument built from several variables can be inspected
✅ typeset -f and whence -v inspect the loaded program: A test can assert on a function’s definition and on how a name resolves



1.2.8 Security

❌ Unquoted expansion is re-parsed: A word is split and globbed again, so untrusted text can change the argument count unless it is quoted (Q2)
⚠️ eval and indirect expansion re-enter the interpreter: Text assembled from data and passed to eval, or a name resolved through a nameref, becomes code or a name the parser decides
⚠️ No memory-safety defect class, but no confinement either: Values are interpreter-managed, yet the shell has no capability or sandbox model beyond its restricted mode
✅ [[ ... ]] does not word-split: The test construct evaluates its operands directly, so a value cannot become extra operands or a pattern
✅ A restricted mode exists: rksh93 blocks cd, redirection, and assignment to SHELL, ENV, and PATH, so an untrusted script can be run with fewer powers
✅ readonly and typeset -r freeze a value: A name can be fixed against later assignment and against unset
❌ Arithmetic is 64-bit and wraps in two’s complement (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the shell reads: requirements live in the script text and the invocation, and the shell validates nothing (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A script depends on the caller’s environment; nothing signs what it invokes. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers the commands a script calls. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists; set -x is the instrument. (Y5)
❌ print and echo carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A failure leaves an exit status. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the shell. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Other languages are reachable only by starting a process. (Y9)
❌ The script runs where a ksh implementation runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ ksh 93u+ is developed as open source with a public history. (Y11)
✅ The ksh manual is public. (Y12)
✅ The ksh source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Ksh is a POSIX shell with the most complete set of extensions in the family, and its own constructs buy real separation: typeset gives a function local scope, discipline functions attach validation to a name, |& keeps a child in two-way conversation, and name spaces keep a library’s internals out of the flat namespace. The core score stays low because the value model is still words with run-time attributes, an error is still a status code, and a plain assignment still writes the global namespace. The platform side is stronger at 68, since ksh93 is standard-compliant, well documented, and the source of many constructs other shells adopted, while its weakness is that the most advanced features exist in one implementation and the user base is shrinking.

title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses the C shell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 68.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73.8/100 · Engineering readiness 46.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Every value is a word list: set binds a list of words to a name, and no declaration states what the name holds, so the same variable carries a path on one line and a number on the next (T1)
❌ No sum types: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is one string, and the reader must decode the convention (set flag versus set flag=0) to tell them apart (T4)
❌ No generics: A command is specialised only by the words passed to it, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data (T5)
❌ Arithmetic is a second grammar: @ and if ( expr ) evaluate C operators over words, so a number is a word that is re-parsed at each use, a null or missing argument counts as 0, and a non-numeric word raises Badly formed number
❌ One flat namespace: set variables and setenv environment variables form two flat spaces with no lexical scope, so a sourced file cannot hide a name from its caller (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to empty: Csh has no nounset option — its letters are -bcefimnstVvXx — so a misspelled variable becomes an empty argument instead of an error (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ No function scope: A variable set in a script is visible to every command the script runs, and a sourced file writes directly into the caller’s namespace (C1)
❌ No immutability by default: Every name is writable everywhere, so a value read at the top of a script can change before it is used (C2)
❌ Aliases are the only reuse mechanism: An alias is textually substituted with \!* arguments, so its body is expanded in the caller’s context instead of a protected one
❌ Recursion re-enters the script: With no function call, a recursive routine re-invokes $0, which couples the logic to the script path and to the positional parameters
⚠️ tcsh can freeze a variable: set -r marks a name read-only, but this is a tcsh extension and it is never the default
✅ path is tied to PATH: Assigning the path word list re-exports PATH, so the search path is edited as a list rather than by string editing



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation syntax: The language has no pointer, no address, and no free, so word lists are allocated by the interpreter on assignment
✅ No deallocation to manage: unset drops a name and the interpreter reclaims the words, so a script has no free order and no double free to avoid
⚠️ Assignment copies the list: set b = ($a) duplicates every word, so a large list is held twice while the assignment runs
⚠️ Global scope extends lifetime: Because every variable is global, data created early in a session stays resident until it is explicitly unset
✅ Word lists are the only aggregate: There are no user-visible buffers or arenas, so memory layout never enters a script



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: Csh gives onintr for interrupts and $status for the last exit code, but there is no exception, no error value, and no handler that can return a result (Er1)
❌ $status is lost by the next command: Any command resets it, so a test placed between a failure and its check silently discards the error (Er3)
❌ Errors do not compose: A failure is a global word rather than a value that can be returned, combined, or stored, so recovery cannot be factored into a routine (Er4)
⚠️ Diagnostics are short and late: The parser is ad hoc, so a fault such as 0: Event not found. reaches the user only when the line runs and names nothing beyond the command
⚠️ The parser reads a command at a time: A syntax error later in a file is reported when execution reaches it, so earlier side effects are already committed
⚠️ onintr couples cleanup to a label: The handler is a named target in the script rather than a scope, so cleanup cannot be attached to the thing it cleans up



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: & and job control start and steer jobs, but there is no lock, channel, or await, so coordination is done by signals and exit codes (K5)
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: The language models concurrency as separate processes joined by pipes, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
✅ Job control isolates the terminal: Csh introduced job control, so a foreground or background decision does not require the script to manage the terminal itself
⚠️ wait is the only join: wait blocks for all jobs or one named job and returns no value, so a result must travel through a file or a pipeline
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the whole environment: A & job shares every global variable and the current directory, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No coprocess: Unlike ksh’s |&, csh offers no supported two-way conversation with a child, so a pipeline stage cannot be driven interactively



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Two implementations of one lineage: The language is defined by the frozen BSD csh 8.2 and by tcsh, so there is no third implementation to check behaviour against (P2)
⚠️ The frozen and maintained dialects differ: set -r, bindkey, and the completion system are tcsh additions, so a script that uses them is not a csh script
⚠️ No standard to be portable to: The POSIX committee chose KornShell, so csh has no specification and its contracts live in two manuals
✅ tcsh is packaged nearly everywhere: Tcsh ships on the BSDs, Linux, and macOS, where csh normally resolves to tcsh, so an interpreter is usually present
✅ Interactive configuration transfers within the family: alias, history, !!, tilde expansion, and the directory stack behave the same in csh and tcsh
⚠️ Scripting support is frozen: New portable automation targets other shells, so csh is maintained rather than extended



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Interactive first, scriptable second: The design targets the terminal, so a weak scripting surface is a priority choice rather than a defect in the language
The C-like expression grammar is a deliberate borrowing: @ and if ( expr ) give a C programmer a familiar evaluation model; the cost is a second grammar, not a forced dependency
The 1993 freeze is a maintenance decision: Original csh is complete and unmaintained while tcsh continues the line, so the freeze is a project decision rather than a coupling mechanism
set and setenv are two commands by history: The split mirrors the shell-variable and environment-variable distinction that every shell must represent somehow
The ad-hoc parser is one implementation’s shortcut: A different implementation could parse the same language properly, so the parser defect is not part of the language contract
csh is not a general-purpose language: An interpreter plus a set of external commands is the assumed platform, which is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation step: Every command line is parsed and evaluated as text at run time, so a loop over files pays parser cost per iteration (R1)
⚠️ Builtins are a short list: cd, set, @, and echo avoid a process, and almost everything else forks and executes
✅ Path hashing avoids repeated search: rehash and hashstat keep a table of resolved command paths, so command lookup does not rescan PATH
✅ Scripts start without interactive configuration: Tcsh reads .tcshrc for interactive shells only, so a script pays no start-up cost for prompt and completion setup
⚠️ Arithmetic is re-parsed per evaluation: @ evaluates its expression each time it runs, so a numeric loop is far slower than compiled code
⚠️ The shell is rarely the bottleneck: Time goes to the external commands it spawns, so interpreter overhead matters mainly in arithmetic-heavy loops



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no distribution channel for csh code, so shared routines are copied between scripts or vendored as files (Ec1)
⚠️ The user base is small and narrowing: Csh survives as a login-shell option on the BSDs and macOS, and new scripting rarely targets it (Ec3)
✅ Documentation is complete and stable: The csh and tcsh manuals describe the language fully and have changed little in decades
✅ Interactive tooling is mature in tcsh: bindkey, complete, and the set toggles are documented and widely configured
⚠️ No static analysis: ShellCheck does not analyse csh or tcsh, so a csh script has no mainstream linter
✅ Scripts are the interchange format: csh is invoked from make, cron, and login configuration without a binding layer



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is total: Tcsh runs csh scripts unchanged and adds behaviour through new builtins and set variables
✅ No version treadmill: No breaking change can arrive for frozen csh, and decades-old scripts still run
⚠️ Fixes arrive only in tcsh: A defect or an unhelpful message in csh stays, and the remedy is to install tcsh and let csh point at it
⚠️ Two dialects share one manual: The tcsh manual marks tcsh-only behaviour with (+), so a reader must know which shell they have
⚠️ No standardisation track: With POSIX committed to KornShell, no committee can modernise the language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Adequate as an interactive login shell: History, aliases, tilde notation, the directory stack, and job control cover terminal work
⚠️ Weak as a scripting language: foreach, while, if, and switch cannot be piped into one another, so a data-processing script must be rebuilt around that limit
⚠️ Text handling calls out to other tools: There are no associative arrays and no substring operators beyond the :r, :e, :h, and :t modifiers, so sed and awk do the work
⚠️ Arithmetic is integer only in csh: @ and expr cover integers, so floating-point calculation leaves the shell
✅ Configuration files are the native domain: .cshrc, .login, and .logout express an interactive environment directly
⚠️ Legacy maintenance persists: Csh remains a login shell on some BSD and macOS accounts, so its configuration files still need care



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The interactive surface is gentle: History substitution, aliases, and tilde notation are learnable in an afternoon
✅ The grammar resembles C: if ( $#argv > 1 ) and @ arithmetic read as expected to a C programmer
⚠️ The scripting limits are learned by failure: A beginner discovers that a control structure cannot be piped only when the pipeline fails
⚠️ Word modifiers must be memorised: :r, :e, :h, :t, :g, and :q are a compact but unguessable syntax for path and quoting work
⚠️ set and setenv confuse newcomers: Two binding commands with different rules produce silent mistakes when the wrong one is used



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Block terminators disagree: if closes with endif, switch with endsw, and foreach and while with end
⚠️ set, setenv, and alias follow different rules: Three ways to bind a name use three argument conventions
⚠️ No separate stderr redirection: >& merges the two streams and |& pipes both, so a stream cannot be redirected on its own
✅ Terse for its work: foreach f (*.c) with if (-e $f) expresses a loop and a test in a few characters
✅ Word modifiers are short and local: $file:r.c and $path:h perform path surgery inline
⚠️ @ and if ( expr ) add a second reading of a line: The same word is a string in one place and an expression in another



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that calls the code and compares $status, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Debugging is echo and set -x: Csh prints commands with set echo and the -x option, but has no breakpoint, no state inspection, and no debugger (G2)
❌ Faults appear only in the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad foreach pattern is found during the test run (G3)
⚠️ A hand-built harness is possible: $status and onintr allow a script to record an outcome and report it
✅ Exit status is a usable oracle: After a command, if ($status == 0) tests the one outcome the language reports reliably
⚠️ Interactive behaviour needs a terminal: History, completion, and prompt behaviour are tty-driven, so they resist automated checks
❌ No monotonic reading published: the shell reads date, and the elapsed counter POSIX defines for the sh family is not here (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Unquoted expansion is re-parsed: Because a value is a word list, an unquoted $var splits and globs, so untrusted text can change the number of arguments a command receives (Q2)
⚠️ eval and $< feed outside text to the parser: Both re-enter the interpreter with text that is not validated
⚠️ No restricted mode: Csh offers no sandbox and no capability model, so a script’s protection is the file permissions of its user
✅ set noclobber protects existing files: The option makes > refuse to overwrite, so a mistake cannot silently destroy data
✅ Environment changes are explicit: setenv and unsetenv are named builtins, so a script’s effect on its children is visible in the text
✅ No memory-safety surface: There are no pointers and no manual allocation, so memory defects belong to the programs csh runs
❌ Arithmetic follows the C rule: overflow wraps, signed undefined (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the shell reads: requirements live in the script text and the invocation, and the shell validates nothing (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A script depends on the caller’s environment; nothing signs what it invokes. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers the commands a script calls. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists; verbose and echo modes are the instruments. (Y5)
❌ echo carries no structure. (Y6)
❌ A failure leaves an exit status. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the shell; -x tracing is the aid. (Y13)
⚠️ The C shell’s own quoting and parsing quirks are the documented debugging burden.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Other languages are reachable only by starting a process. (Y9)
❌ The script runs where a csh or tcsh runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the implementation: POSIX defines the standard sh-family shells, not this one, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Awk in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 65.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.4/100 · Engineering readiness 63.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A variable is dynamically typed: A name holds a string or a number, and the context decides (T1)
❌ There are no sum types (T4)
❌ There are no generics (T5)
❌ There are no namespaces: Every function and variable is global (T6)
❌ An unset variable is the empty string and zero: Nothing distinguishes absent from empty (T10)
❌ There is no module boundary: A program is one file or a set of includes (T11)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A global variable is the default: A variable at the top level is shared by every rule (C1)
❌ A value is mutable by default (C2)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ There is no scope-exit release: A file is closed by hand or at exit (M3)



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no exception path: A failure is a message and a nonzero exit (Er1)
❌ An error can be ignored: A failed getline returns −1, and nothing forces the check (Er3)
❌ A fault ends the program: a runtime error exits (documented); no recoverable unit exists (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ One process is the whole program: There is no second thread (K1)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The standard is public: awk is defined by POSIX.1-2024



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A rule is the program: A pattern selects a record and an action transforms it
The fields are the data model: $1 to $NF is the record, and an array is the only structure
The standard is the portability: A POSIX script runs on every Unix
The language is deliberately small: A longer program wants a different tool




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ The interpreter executes the program: A pattern is matched per record (R1)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is tiny: A program is a script, and a library is rare (Ec3)
✅ The standard is the portability: The same script runs on the system awk



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: POSIX 2024 is the first revision in years (V4)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The domain is a text stream: A record, a field, and a rule
⚠️ A general program is out of scope: There is no data structure beyond an array



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The model is three parts: A pattern, an action, and a field



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Pattern-action and functions share one grammar: A rule and a function are different forms (S2)
❌ The punctuation is dense: $1, NF, FS, and ~ (S3)



1.2.7 Testing

❌ A type error is found at run time: The interpreter has no static check (G3)
❌ No monotonic reading published: systime() is the wall second, and the reference ships no elapsed reading (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ system() runs a command: A string from input is a command path (Q3)
❌ The integer path of the numeric ladder (since 2008) is 64-bit with wraparound; above it the double rule applies (Q4)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown · the Scoreboard and the full per-language data · the scoring model

Every language on this site is measured against one inventory of 99 mechanisms — the same list, with the same weights, and the same arithmetic, for all 125. The inventory has three parts: Core coupling (46 mechanisms, 350 points), Ecosystem coupling (34 mechanisms, 256 points), and Engineering readiness (19 mechanisms, 171 points). No language gets a private criterion, and no mechanism is applied to one language and then set aside for another. That is what makes the comparison a comparison: a difference between two scores is a difference in which mechanisms are present, never a difference in how strictly the two languages were judged.
This page explains each criterion. For every mechanism it gives what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, how harmful it is — the weight tier that removes the points — and a concrete example. The Scoreboard publishes the other half: which mechanisms each language has, and the score that follows. The scoring model gives the arithmetic and the tests that decide presence.
Read every entry as a harm. The inventory of 99 mechanisms contains no features, no positives, and no offsets. A mechanism is in the list because a maintainer pays for it when the mechanism is present, and a language’s score is what remains once the present share is subtracted from that axis inventory. One mechanism, V5, carries the Recorded severity: it states a fact and removes no points. The same practice appears on the pages that record a boundary no current document decides: Turbo Pascal and SAS, where a delivery row marked recorded, not priced states a crossing release boundary, and PHP, where a data row marks the format the manual names without a version field or a cross-release rule — a format the probe harness has round-tripped across the 8.0 to 8.4 release pairs without reproducing a break, which tests the format and still promises nothing.


Two parts of a program are coupled where they must agree about one shared thing: a type, a heap, a lock, a name space, a platform ABI, a runtime. The agreement is the cost. It has to be established when the code is written, it has to be maintained while the code lives, and it has to be re-established whenever either side changes.
A language mechanism is a coupling criterion when it forces agreement that the programmer cannot refuse. Three properties decide how much that costs:








Property
Question
Effect on the weight




Breadth
How much of the program has to agree — one call site, one module, or the whole program?
A wider agreement costs more


Escape
Can a programmer opt out of the mechanism locally?
No escape costs more


Silence
Does the language say so, or must a reader discover it?
A silent obligation costs more



A mechanism that makes the whole program agree, with no local way out, and nothing in the language that records the agreement, is High. A mechanism that forces agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a convention that the whole codebase must keep, is Moderate. A mechanism whose agreement is confined to a boundary, and removable by a contained workaround, is Minor.
That is the whole rationale for the weights. The tier is a judgment about breadth, escape, and silence — not a count of incidents, and not a substitute for measurement.
Every entry names its coupling. After the tier, each entry states the kind of coupling the mechanism imposes and why it cannot be refused: which two parties must agree, what they must agree about, and which property of the language forces the agreement. The kind is the name of the shared resource — a type, a call target, a heap, a schedule, a version, a supply — so the entries read as a catalogue of shared resources rather than as a list of complaints.












Tier
Weight
What the tier asserts
Cost on Core when it is alone




High
−15
Agreement across the whole program, no local escape, and nothing in the language that records it
−4.6


Moderate
−8
Agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a whole-codebase convention
−2.5


Minor
−4
Agreement confined to a boundary, removable by a contained workaround
−1.2


Recorded
0
The event is a fact the reader must know, and its direction is not mechanically determinable
0 — it never enters a sum



The fourth tier is not a weight. A price has one direction: the same presence must always mean the same cost. Where the direction is not fixed, no single number can state the cost. A mechanism whose sign varies cannot enter the sum without making that sum incomparable across languages and across releases — the same mark would have to mean a gain and a loss at once, so two scores would no longer be arithmetically comparable, and two analysts would no longer reach the same number. The model therefore records such a mechanism: the mark is present or absent, the observation beside it states what changed, why, and how a deployment reverses it, and the score is untouched. V5 is the only mechanism in this tier.
Within one dimension the present weights are summed, and each mechanism contributes its share of the axis inventory: a mechanism of weight w costs 100 × w ÷ inventory weight score points, and the dimension cost is the sum over its present mechanisms. There is no cap and no curve. The share is a rubric choice, not a measurement: it stays additive because a maintainer pays every forced coupling, it stays bounded because the numerator can never exceed the inventory, and it is monotone, so removing a mechanism always moves the number. The inventory weight states what the model knows about the axis, not a ceiling on what the axis can cost.



Each entry gives the mechanism’s code and tier, what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, an example, and — where the criterion is easy to misread — what its presence does not mean.
Presence is a factual question about the language: does the language hand the programmer this construct? It is not a judgment about the code. Every language permits a global; C1 asks whether a global is the default home for state.
Who imposes the mechanism. Every entry carries one tag: Imposed by: language, runtime, or context. A language mechanism is decided by the compiler — the construct is in the source, and the compiler accepts or rejects it. A runtime mechanism is decided by the executor: the memory manager, the compiler that runs later, the thread scheduler, or a default the platform chooses. A context mechanism is decided by the surroundings: the vendor, the toolchain, the market, the documentation, or the standard. The tag is meta-information and never changes a weight. It tells a reader where a remedy would have to happen: in the code, in the deployment, or outside both.
A check behind a project switch. Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch. The mark uses the configuration the language’s own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. tsc --init writes "strict": true (which sets strictNullChecks), so TypeScript is not charged T10; dotnet new writes <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, so C# is not charged T10; Visual Basic’s compiler default is Option Strict Off and the SDK template sets no OptionStrict, so the narrowing conversion is charged T2. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — that is what T1 already says about mypy in CI.
A mitigation is not an absence. Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism — @CompileStatic in Groovy, try-with-resources in Java, reified in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged, because the default code still pays it and avoiding it needs knowledge the language does not force. The model measures what the language imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on the same language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the language page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above.

Ecosystem coupling (34) Performance (3) — R1 · R2 · R3 Ecosystem (9) — Ec1 · Ec2 · Ec3 · Ec4 · Ec5 · Ec6 · Ec7 · Ec8 · Ec9 Evolution (6) — V1 · V2 · V3 · V4 · V5 · V7 Domain (2) — D1 · D3 Learning (3) — L1 · L2 · L3 Syntax (3) — S1 · S2 · S3 Testing (4) — G1 · G2 · G3 · G4 Security (4) — Q1 · Q2 · Q3 · Q4
Engineering readiness (19) Reproducibility (4) — Y1 · Y2 · Y14 · Y18 Supply chain (3) — Y3 · Y4 · Y16 Observability (3) — Y5 · Y6 · Y15 Feedback (3) — Y7 · Y8 · Y13 Interop (2) — Y9 · Y10 Governance (4) — Y11 · Y12 · Y17 · Y19





What the Type dimension asks: can the language keep the meaning of a value in one place, or must every reader reconstruct it?


Imposed by: language.
High · −15. A value carries its type at run time, so nothing checks that an operation suits its operand until the operation runs. The meaning of every value becomes a shared agreement between the site that produces it and every site that consumes it, and no tool holds that agreement: it lives in the tests and in the reader’s memory.
Coupling imposed. Type-identity coupling across the whole program: producer and consumer agree on what a value is, and on every operation that may apply to it, and nothing in the source records that agreement. Because the check happens when the operation runs, the agreement survives only while both sides are read together, so a change to one reaches all the others at once.
Example. Python accepts n = 1 and then n = "one", and n + 1 fails only on the path that reaches it, and only for the inputs that take that path. MATLAB, R, SAS, Lua, and every POSIX shell behave the same way.
Presence does not mean a checker is unavailable. The criterion asks whether the language enforces a check. A program that runs mypy --strict in CI has a check the language did not give it, and the score still records the language.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The compiler knows the types, but it converts between them implicitly, so a check that would catch a mistake becomes a silent conversion. The conversion rules become the shared resource: every expression depends on a table that nothing forces a reader to know.
Coupling imposed. Conversion coupling: every expression that mixes types agrees with the language’s conversion table rather than with its neighbour. The table is the shared resource, so a reader who does not hold it cannot tell a checked expression from a silently narrowed one, and an implicit conversion hides the moment the meaning changed.
Example. C compiles int i = 3.7; and discards the fraction, and lets an integer stand in for a pointer. COBOL converts between two different PICTURE clauses on a MOVE without complaint. Visual Basic’s Option Strict Off default admits a narrowing conversion and a late-bound call.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Which code a call reaches is decided by the value’s run-time type rather than by a declared contract. The set of operations a value must answer becomes a shared agreement that no declaration holds, so a rename in one module breaks a caller in another — and only at run time.
Coupling imposed. Call-target coupling: a caller and a callee agree on a name and an arity that no declaration enforces, and the agreement must hold for every type that can arrive at the call site. Because the target is chosen from the value, the coupling spans types the author of the call never named.
Example. Erlang resolves Mod:Fun(Args) when it is called, so a missing function fails there; Elixir and Clojure choose a protocol or a pattern clause from the value they receive; Ruby and Python resolve an attribute at the moment of the call.
Presence does not mean T1. Objective-C is statically typed at the pointer level and still dispatches every message at run time, so it is charged T3 and not T1. TypeScript is statically typed and still reaches a method through the prototype at run time, so it is charged the same way. Duck typing is about which code runs; T1 is about what a value is.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language cannot declare that a value is one of several alternatives and have the compiler track which one. The alternatives are encoded by convention, so the tag and its payload are a shared resource that every consumer re-derives, and the compiler cannot prove that a consumer handles every case.
