Moderate · −8. The ecosystem carries versions, APIs, or idioms that must still be supported, so old and new coexist. The compatibility surface becomes a shared resource that every new feature has to respect, so no part of the ecosystem can change freely.
Coupling imposed. Compatibility coupling: every new feature must agree with every version still in service, because the ecosystem will not drop them. The agreement is longitudinal — it runs between old and new code rather than between modules.
Example. Java’s enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2026 one, and a library has to keep both working. Ruby’s ecosystem pins older runtimes through older gems, so an upgrade has to wait for the slowest dependency.
Ec7 is the twin of V1. V1 is the language changing under the code; Ec7 is the ecosystem refusing to change.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. A compiled unit of the language reaches a consumer who links it without rebuilding it, and no published promise says that the producer’s release and the consumer’s release agree. The agreement is the toolchain release. Nothing in the source of either side names it. Where a check exists, it fires at load or at link, after both sides are already built. The failure names a mismatch, and the consumer still works out which side to rebuild.
Coupling imposed. Release-boundary coupling at a published binary: a wheel, a plugin, a MEX file, an extension, a package, a library, or a model package names the release that built it, and every consumer who cannot rebuild carries the whole cost. The agreement runs between independently released parts, so one release in one part forces rebuilds in all the others. A source-shipped package resolves the same agreement inside the consumer’s own build, and a published promise settles it: the class-file rules a language specification publishes, the assembly format and compatibility rules a runtime publishes. Neither is charged.
Example. A Python wheel names the interpreter, ABI, and platform tags, and the installer loads that binary. A Go plugin must be built with the same toolchain as the application that opens it. MathWorks requires a MEX file to be rebuilt for a new release. libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another.
Delivery targets decide this mechanism, target by target. Every language page lists its delivery targets at the end of its Ecosystem coupling section: what ships, whether a compiled unit reaches a consumer who does not rebuild it, and whether a published promise covers it. The mechanism is present exactly when one target crosses with no promise. Kotlin is charged on .klib and not on the JVM jar. JavaScript is charged on a node-gyp addon and not on a Node-API addon. Go is charged on its plugin path and not on its module proxy. Rust, Dart, Julia, Swift, and Zig are not charged: their package managers ship source, and the compiled paths they publish carry a promise. C and the Java family are not charged on objects that travel on a published format.
A promise must be published, and a charge needs a document. A de-facto convention settles nothing: an ecosystem that mostly works across releases is not exempted by practice, and an ecosystem with no document at all is not charged on practice either. Each charged verdict names the document it rests on, and each exemption names the guarantee it claims; no verdict is priced from practice alone. Where a vendor document is out of print and no current document decides, the page records the fact in the delivery table and the score stays untouched.
T14 prices a different agreement. T14 charges the hand-written declaration a developer maintains at a foreign-language boundary. This mechanism charges the release boundary of a unit that crosses as a binary. A plugin host and a foreign binding are two facts, and they are charged once each.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. State the program writes outlives the program: a serialized value, a workspace image, a compiled snapshot, a project archive, a saved model. The file carries a format header naming the release that wrote it, and the only reader is the toolchain. The boundary crosses time in one direction the consumer cannot rebuild: the data is years old, the release is today’s. Where a version check exists, it fires when the file opens. Where the vendor withdraws a reader, files written years ago have no reader at all on the current release, and the failure is not a link error to fix — it is the data.
Coupling imposed. Release-boundary coupling at stored state: the agreement runs across time, between the release that wrote the file and the release reading it now. The upgrade of a toolchain is safe for old data only when the vendor has promised it, and a promise is published in one direction. A format with a version field and a published reading rule settles the agreement — the reader checks the header and reads; the file is not charged. A format that records its writer in the header, states no rule, and leaves the maintainer to discover the reading by opening the file keeps the agreement unpromised, and that is what the mechanism charges.
Example. Microsoft disables BinaryFormatter in .NET 8 and removes the in-box implementation in .NET 9, so payloads written on an older runtime have no reader on the current one. R states that serialization format 3, the default for save() and saveRDS() since 3.6.0, cannot be read by versions of R prior to 3.5.0. Python reserves the right to change the marshal format, which .pyc files carry, in non-backwards compatible ways. MATLAB states that releases R2006b and later all support all MAT file versions, and Java’s serialization specification publishes the stream protocol, its versions, and the serial version UID.
Data-format targets decide this mechanism, target by target. Every language page that stores state lists its data formats at the end of its Ecosystem coupling section, under the delivery table: what the toolchain stores, whether the current release reads data written by an older one as a published promise, and whether the vendor states that data written now cannot be read by other releases. The mechanism is present exactly when one row carries a break: the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable elsewhere, or a break the probe harness has reproduced with pinned releases and a committed result. Python is charged on the marshal format its .pyc files carry and is not charged on pickle, which carries the published promise. The C# family is charged on BinaryFormatter payloads, which .NET 8 disabled and .NET 9 removed. R is charged on the format-3 default it states old readers cannot open. Ruby, Perl, Go, Java, Julia, MATLAB, Scratch, Erlang, Elixir, GameMaker, and SAS carry a published promise on the format they store and are not charged. PHP is recorded, not priced: the manual names the format, documents no version field, and states no cross-release rule, and the probe harness has reproduced no break across the tested release pairs — tested is not promised, so the row records and prices nothing.
A promise must be published, and a charge needs an affirmative fact. The discipline is the one the delivery table applies to compiled units: practice settles nothing. A charge rests on a published statement of a break, or on a break the probe harness has reproduced — never on a suspicion of one. An ecosystem whose old files mostly open is not exempted by habit, and a format with no document is not charged on suspicion either. Each charged row names the document stating the break, or the probe artifact that reproduced it; each exemption names the document publishing the promise; and a row nothing decides is recorded and removes no points.
Ec8 prices a different crossing. Ec8 charges a compiled unit that crosses from a producer to a consumer who links it without rebuilding it. This mechanism charges state that crosses from a release to the future: the consumer is not a second team, it is the same program on a later toolchain, and it cannot rebuild the file. A wheel is Ec8; the pickled cache the wheel’s program reads on first run is this mechanism. The two never charge one byte.
Ec7 prices a different burden. Ec7 charges the ecosystem that keeps old versions, APIs, and idioms in service, so new work must respect them. This mechanism charges the file that keeps the old release’s reader required. Long-lived stored data is one reason the legacy burden lands at all; the two price the staying and the crossing, and never the same byte.
V1 prices a language moving under the code. This mechanism prices a reader that no longer opens the data. The code changes under V1; the file’s reader changes under Ec9.




What the Evolution dimension asks: will the code still mean what it means after the language moves?


Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language, or its standard library, changes in a way that invalidates existing code. The language itself becomes the shared resource, so every consumer has to revisit code when the language moves.
Coupling imposed. Version coupling: the source must agree with one version of the language, because a later version may change the meaning it had. The agreement is temporal — the same file means different things to two compilers.
Example. Rust’s edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of impl Trait, required unsafe extern, and reserved gen, so a crate that adopts the edition has to be revisited. Scala’s 2-to-3 migration, Nim’s and Zig’s moving standard libraries, and Haskell’s library-level breakage put the same cost on their users.
An edition system is the mitigation, not the absence. Rust isolates the changes to an opt-in edition and is still charged, because the cost of the migration is real.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The language is complete and will not change further. “What the language will do next” becomes settled, which removes one shared uncertainty — and also means that a missing feature or a defect is permanent.
Coupling imposed. Definition coupling: the program must agree with a definition that will not move again, because the language is complete. The agreement is settled rather than absent, which is why a freeze can be a benefit and a trap at once.
Example. Objective-C 2.0 is effectively the last revision of the language, and platform-facing work moved to a successor. Turbo Pascal’s definition is frozen at 7.0.
Minor because a freeze is a promise. Nothing in the existing code will break.



Imposed by: context.
High · −15. The language has no vendor, no steward, and no expectation of another version. The language becomes a shared resource that will never be maintained again, so every defect and every security issue is permanent, and every dependency is a dead end.
Coupling imposed. Stewardship coupling: the program must agree with a language that no one maintains, because there is no second party left to renegotiate with. Every defect becomes a term of the agreement, and no local escape exists because a migration path would have to be supplied by the missing steward.
Example. Borland ended the Turbo Pascal line in the mid-1990s and moved it to a successor product. Microsoft announced VBScript’s deprecation in 2023, with removal from the operating system planned after 2027, so the remaining life of the language is a published countdown.
High because the cost is total and irreversible. There is no migration path inside the language, and none can be added.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The language is defined by a standard that revises on a multi-year cycle, so a needed feature waits for the committee. The definition becomes a shared resource whose revision schedule is not the user’s, and a program’s design is bounded by when the standard catches up.
Coupling imposed. Revision coupling: the program’s design must agree with a committee’s calendar, because the definition moves on a multi-year cycle. The agreement is with a date rather than with a decision, so no local act can advance it.
Example. SQL:2023 appeared seven years after SQL:2016, so a feature outside the standard stays an extension in the meantime. Ada 2022 followed Ada 2012 by a decade, and the POSIX shell specification moves slowly enough that a shell’s own extensions are the practical definition of its behaviour.
Minor because implementations commonly lead the standard with extensions — at the cost of portability, which is charged elsewhere, under P2 and Ec2.



Imposed by: runtime.
Recorded · no points removed. A default that the source does not name changes between releases of the runtime or the standard library, and nothing in the build reports it. The default is the shared resource: the code and the platform must agree on a value the code never wrote down, and the platform may choose it again in the next release. No compiler error, no signature change, and no type carries the old value, so the agreement is discovered when the behaviour of the running program moves.
Coupling imposed. Default coupling: a deployment must agree with a default it does not name, and the agreement is one-sided — the platform sets it, the code inherits it, and the next release may set it again. The agreement is silent in both directions: the code records neither the value it relies on nor the fact that it relies on one.
Example. Java 27 changed two such defaults. ML-KEM and ML-DSA private keys now encode as a seed rather than an expanded key, so a key this JDK writes is unreadable by an older release unless jdk.mlkem.pkcs8.encoding is set before the key is made. G1 replaced the Serial selection on small machines, so a deployment that never named a collector now runs a different one. Both are documented in the release notes and both can be reversed — by a security property or by -XX:+UseSerialGC — and both still move the behaviour of code that no one edited.
This mechanism is recorded, not priced. A price has a fixed direction: the same presence must always mean the same cost, or the sum stops being an arithmetic and becomes an opinion. The direction of a default change is not fixed. G1 everywhere helps a one-CPU container by the JEP’s own measurements and moves the latency profile of a service that was measured under Serial; the seed encoding is better interoperability by RFC 9935 and a break for a peer on an older release. The same presence can therefore mean a gain or a loss, and a mechanism whose sign varies cannot enter a sum without making that sum incomparable across languages and across releases. Pricing it would also make the inventory anti-evolution by construction: a release that improves every default and changes no construct could only lose points. The model records the event here, states its direction in the observation beside the mark, and leaves the score to the mechanisms whose sign is fixed.
Presence is per assessed release. An empty mark records that no such change appears in this analysis for the release shown — not that none exists. The analysis date and the assessed version are stated on every page.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The toolchain ships a documented source-level facility that selects which source reaches the compiled artifact: a preprocessor’s #ifdef tree, a build constraint, a reader conditional, a compile-time when, a code-generating %IF. The flag set is a shared resource that every guarded part of the program must agree with, and no source fully names it. A program is no longer one program: it is a space of selections, and the binary a maintainer ships is one selection. The states nobody builds are nobody’s problem until a change touches a guard — then the agreement has to be reconstructed for every combination, and tested for the one that ships.
Coupling imposed. Compile-time-configuration coupling: each guard is an agreement between the source and a flag set that lives in project files, command lines, and toolchain defaults, not in the source the reader sees. The agreement multiplies: n independent flags name 2^n programs, and the suite runs one of them. A change to shared code must respect every selection that ships, and the untested selections compile wrong in silence — the failure is a build that no one ran, not a test that no one passed.
Example. The C preprocessor and its #ifdef tree; Go’s //go:build constraints; Rust’s cfg; Common Lisp’s #+/#- reader conditionals; Racket’s read-conditional barbs; Clojure’s reader conditionals; Delphi’s {$IFDEF}; Erlang’s -ifdef; Oracle PL/SQL’s IF/IF/THEN; SAS’s macro %IF; X++’s #if; GHC’s -XCPP; Nim’s when defined; Zig’s build options feeding inline-if — the release build the consumer runs compiles a program the debug suite never saw.
V1 prices the language moving; this prices the flags multiplying. V1 charges a release changing under the code, so consumers revisit source when the language moves. This mechanism charges one release’s source meaning different programs under different flags. Both agreements run along time; the first is against a release, this one against a configuration.
G1 prices the missing tooling; this prices the space the tooling faces. G1 charges the absence of a test framework, assertion, or runner. This mechanism charges the number of programs a suite must face. A strong suite against ten flag states still pays ten states; a weak suite pays them worse, and the two charges are separate facts.
The charge is the state space, not the facility’s usefulness. Conditional compilation exists to solve portability problems, and the model prices no feature. What it prices is the agreement the facility forces: every guarded file must agree with every combination that ships, the flag set lives outside the source, and the untested selections fail as silent builds. A language with no source-level selection pays none of this — Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, and the rest of the family carry no such facility, and the absence earns the absence of the mechanism, nothing more.
Context, not language: the toolchain ships it. A preprocessor, a build constraint, a reader conditional, a compile-time evaluation hook — the facility is a toolchain fact, decided by the vendor, so the tag is context: the remedy is outside both code and language, in what the toolchain chooses to ship. Each charged page names the facility in the observation beside the mark.




What the Domain dimension asks: is the language shaped for one target so tightly that adopting it means adopting that target?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. The language exists to serve one domain or one vendor’s product, so adopting it is also adopting that target. The domain’s model becomes the shared resource, and every abstraction in the program has to be expressible in it.
Coupling imposed. Domain-model coupling: every abstraction must agree with one target’s model, because adopting the language is adopting the target. The agreement reaches the design and not only the deployment, so a choice of language settles what the program can say.
Example. MATLAB’s library set targets one vendor’s platform, so adoption is a procurement decision as much as a technical one. PL/SQL exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain. SAS’s data-step model is the SAS library. Transact-SQL’s domain is one database engine, and Solidity’s is one blockchain’s execution model. Rocq’s, SPARK’s, and Lean’s domain is machine-checked proof.
D1 and P1 ask different questions. P1 is where the artifact can run; D1 is what the language is for. MATLAB is charged D1 and not P1: the vendor’s platform is the language’s purpose, and the artifact is not confined to one machine.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The idiomatic way to use the language is inside a host framework whose execution model decides the program’s structure. The framework’s callbacks, lifecycles, and conventions become the shared resource, so the program’s architecture is set by a third party.
Coupling imposed. Architecture coupling: the program’s structure must agree with a host framework’s lifecycle, callbacks, and conventions, because the idiomatic path into the language runs through the framework. The agreement sits above the code — changing it means changing what calls the code, not what the code does.
Example. A Java program is idiomatically assembled as a Spring application, so its wiring, its transactions, and its entry points follow the framework’s model. A C# program follows the same path through ASP.NET. In Groovy the build script and the pipeline run inside a host’s execution model and obey its conventions. Go’s project layout and module conventions are conventions the toolchain assumes.
Moderate because the framework is hard to leave: the code is written against the framework’s lifecycle, not merely called by it.




What the Learning dimension asks: what does a practitioner pay to become productive, and who bears that cost?


Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. A practitioner has to learn concepts that build on nothing else they already know. That knowledge becomes a shared resource with a narrow entry, so the onboarding cost is borne by every team and every hiring decision.
Coupling imposed. Onboarding coupling: productivity must agree with a body of concepts that the practitioner’s background does not supply, because the language builds on nothing familiar. The agreement is with people rather than with code, so it is paid again at every hire.
Example. Erlang asks for functional programming, the actor model, and OTP at once, on top of a Prolog-derived syntax. Rust asks for ownership, borrows, and lifetimes. Haskell asks for type classes, monads, and laziness. Lean and Rocq ask for dependent types and proof engineering. Ada’s language and its annexes are large enough that a team learns them for a while.
L1 measures distance from the mainstream, so a language whose concepts are unusual is charged even when the concepts are excellent. The cost is real even when the design is good.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The language is large, or it supports several paradigms at once, so there are many ways to write the same thing. “The way we do it here” becomes the shared resource, and it has to be written down, because the language will not narrow the choice.
Coupling imposed. Idiom coupling: each contributor must agree with the team on which of several available ways to write the same thing, because the language refuses to narrow the choice. The agreement is a document rather than a check — the language will not enforce it.
Example. Ada’s standard library, annexes, and profiles add to a large core. C++ mixes four paradigms and several generations of idiom. Scala, Kotlin, F#, Elixir, Erlang, Nim, and Swift each admit both object and functional styles. PowerShell mixes cmdlets, .NET calls, and pipelines.
Minor because a team can cut the surface with a style guide — but the guide is the team’s, not the language’s.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The reference material is thin, or it omits the knowledge a practitioner actually needs. The understanding of the language becomes a shared resource held privately, so it is rediscovered by each practitioner in turn.
Coupling imposed. Knowledge coupling: understanding must agree with whoever already holds it, because the reference does not supply it. The agreement is private, so it leaves when the practitioner leaves.
Example. In Lean 4, why a simp call succeeded, or why an instance was not found, has to be read out of the goal state and the option list rather than from a reference. Zig’s language reference is still evolving with the language, so the authoritative answer is sometimes the compiler’s source.
Minor because it is the cheapest criterion to fix externally: a book, a wiki, or a community can supply what the vendor did not.




What the Syntax dimension asks: how much of the reader’s attention does the notation itself consume?


Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The notation requires many words or lines to express a small idea. The reading surface grows, so a lower signal-to-noise ratio is a cost every reader pays on every review.
Coupling imposed. Reading-surface coupling: every reader must pay the same notation cost for the same idea, because the language requires the words. The agreement is uniform and unavoidable, which is why a local style cannot reduce it.
Example. A PL/SQL unit needs a declaration section, a BEGIN ... END block, and an exception section before it does anything. A SAS step is a list of KEYWORD option; lines, and LENGTH, FORMAT, and LABEL add lines before any data is touched. COBOL and Ada require a declaration before nearly every statement, and Fortran and Delphi carry a long legacy of required keywords.
S1 is not a style preference. It is charged where the language requires the words, not where a programmer chose them.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Comparable things are written differently, so there is no rule to learn, only cases. The syntax becomes a shared resource whose mapping is not predictable, so every reader has to look things up.
Coupling imposed. Mapping coupling: the reader must agree with a name’s behaviour through memorised cases rather than through a rule, because the language supplies no predictable mapping. The agreement is per name, so it grows with the library and never generalises.
Example. PHP’s standard library names follow no single rule: str_replace, strpos, and str_contains disagree on placement of the underscore and on argument order between neighbours. Perl’s built-ins read the current context, so $_, @_, and %+ change what a call does.
S2 is the most expensive syntax criterion because it cannot be automated away. A formatter normalises layout, not names.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The notation leans on dense delimiters, so the structure is carried by characters the reader has to match. Reading then requires tracking a delimiter stack, which couples comprehension to an editor’s matching and folding.
Coupling imposed. Delimiter coupling: the reader must agree with the editor on where a structure begins and ends, because the structure is carried by characters rather than by layout. The agreement is paid per reading, not per change, which is why tooling can absorb most of it.
Example. Common Lisp’s parentheses nest deeply, and the text is hard to read without an editor that matches them. Perl’s sigils add a character to nearly every variable reference.
Minor because tooling removes most of it, and because the cost is paid once per reading rather than once per change.




What the Testing dimension asks: how does the language help the program find its own mistakes, and how much of that work is left to the team?


Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language or its standard toolchain provides no test framework, assertion, or runner. The verification of the code becomes a shared resource that each project has to build and maintain for itself.
Coupling imposed. Verification coupling: each project must agree with its own harness about what “tested” means, because the language ships no framework, assertion, or runner. The agreement is local, so a result is only as meaningful as the harness that produced it.
Example. In Assembly a test is another program that runs and compares, and the harness lives outside the assembler. Scratch has no assertion and no runner, so a test is a manual run. Turbo Pascal ships no test framework, and neither do most shells beyond what an exit code can say.
G1 records what the language and its standard toolchain ship. A mature third-party framework can remove the practical cost without changing what the language provides — which is what the criterion is about.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. Finding a failure means reading machine state or log output rather than a named abstraction. The diagnosis becomes a shared resource held only by whoever can read the raw state, so debugging skill does not travel with the code.
Coupling imposed. Diagnosis coupling: whoever debugs must agree with the machine’s own state about what happened, because the language offers no named abstraction over it. The agreement is personal — it exists in one practitioner’s reading skill and nowhere in the code.
Example. A debugger that exposes registers and raw memory turns a fault into a machine-state question. Haskell’s laziness means the failing expression is not the one that produced the value. Zig’s comptime evaluation and Unison’s content-addressed code make the executed form differ from the source. Turbo Pascal’s IDE steps and watches variables, with no assertion or coverage support.
G2 is not G3. G2 is “you cannot see what happened”; G3 is “nothing told you beforehand”.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. A mistake of the kind a compiler could catch is deferred to the executed path. The correctness of an unexecuted path is then unknown, so coverage becomes the only evidence of safety — a shared resource that every contributor has to maintain.
Coupling imposed. Coverage coupling: the correctness of an unexecuted path must agree with whatever the tests happened to reach, because the compiler declined to decide it. The agreement is a property of the suite rather than of the source, so it changes when the tests change.
Example. A wrong block in Scratch is found by running the project. A type mistake in Elixir, Erlang, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, or Perl surfaces on the path that reaches it. TypeScript’s any re-opens the gap the language closes elsewhere. In Prolog a goal fails at run time, and in R a coercion fails when it is evaluated.
G3 is deliberately T1 counted again. The same language property costs once as coupling, under T1, and once as deferred verification, here. The model counts both because a program pays both — and the dimensions are separate because the remedies are separate.



Imposed by: runtime.
Minor · −4. The language publishes no monotonic clock the program can read. The time a program sees is the wall: the operator’s date, the machine’s calendar, the value that moves backward at a daylight-saving change and jumps at an NTP correction. A measurement taken across such a clock is a property of the operator’s calendar, not of the program, and a test that reads time has no stable thing to read.
Coupling imposed. Time coupling: every measured duration, every timeout, every ‘after this event’ guard must agree with a clock the vendor does not publish as a monotonic reading. The agreement sits in the machine’s calendar and the administrator’s corrections — outside the code, outside the deployment, outside the test. The model prices the published API: a vendor that publishes an elapsed reading settles the agreement, and the mechanism lifts.
Example. Java publishes System.nanoTime; C++ names steady_clock in the standard; Python’s time.monotonic and Rust’s Instant, Ruby’s Process.clock_gettime and .NET’s Stopwatch, Erlang’s monotonic_time and Fortran’s system_clock, Ada’s Real_Time and Tcl’s time command — all published elapsed readings, none charged. Against these: Lua publishes os.clock as CPU time only; the R7RS current-second is a wall second; R7RS Scheme ships no monotonic reading; Visual Basic’s Timer() is a wall-clock date value; SAS, X++, and the plain-SQL CURRENT_TIMESTAMP family name no monotonic reading; OCaml’s standard library ships Sys.time as CPU time with no monotonic companion in the stdlib.
M2 prices the collector’s schedule; this prices the wall clock. M2 charges the runtime’s own timing acting on the program (pauses, schedules). G4 charges the program’s only published time reading being the wall. A language can carry both (Java’s GC pauses and its published nanoTime: M2 present, G4 absent) and the facts do not touch.
Minor 4: the reading is one call site. The cost sits at each place a program reads time — the T7/M3 boundary shape. Languages that publish the reading pay nothing; languages that publish none pay 4, not 8: the diagnosis is a missing API, not a missing architecture.
The exemption is a published elapsed reading, not a discipline. Stopwatch, nanoTime, steady_clock, monotonic_time, system_clock, Real_Time, tic, current_second with a documented monotonic companion — the vendor’s own reference names them and the program can call them. A team’s decision to wrap time in a helper is a mitigation and never an exemption: the model measures what the language publishes, not what a disciplined team builds around it.




What the Security dimension asks: does the language make a whole class of exploit possible, or a whole class of mistake silent?


Imposed by: language.
High · −15. The language permits access to memory outside the bounds of an object, and to storage that has already been freed. Every pointer becomes a shared resource with no owner and no bound, so a fault in one module can corrupt another module’s data.
Coupling imposed. Memory-bound coupling: every pointer must agree with the object it addresses, because the language keeps no record of the bound. The agreement crosses module and trust boundaries alike, which is why a violation is an exploit rather than a defect.
Example. In C a buffer overflow, a use-after-free, a double free, and an out-of-bounds write are all possible, and nothing in the language prevents them. In C++ the same faults compile: reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic, and manual new/delete remain available, and the standard library is safe only where a program uses it. Zig keeps manual memory management and undefined behaviour, so a use-after-free and a mistyped @ptrCast are reachable. In Assembly an address is a number, with no abstraction in between.
Q1 prices a class of vulnerability, and carries the top weight for it. The others price maintainability; Q1 prices an exploit, and any pointer suffices. M6 prices the sibling class — type confusion — at Moderate, because it needs a pun site and a type with invariants to break.
The safe subset is the default, or the charge stands. A language is charged when the violation is reachable in what a new project writes without a decision. Rust and Swift are not charged: the safe subset is the default, and the unsafe paths are explicit and delimited per site. C# is not charged: unsafe blocks are opt in. Zig is charged: the safety checks that hold in a debug build are removed in the release build the consumer runs, so the shipped binary is the unchecked one. A flag, a lint, or a coding standard is a mitigation and never an exemption.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. A value from an untrusted source arrives with no declared type, so keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer’s check. The trust boundary becomes a shared resource that the type system does not mark, so a missing check leaves no trace.
Coupling imposed. Trust-boundary coupling: a value from outside must agree with the dangerous operation it will reach, because the type system does not mark which values are trusted. The agreement is written by hand at the boundary and leaves no trace when it is missing.
Example. In Python, Ruby, JavaScript, and PHP a request value is whatever the input made it, so a check has to be written and kept. A Prolog term carries no declared type, so a value from an untrusted source is separated from a goal only by an explicit test. In Smalltalk a type confusion is discovered at run time, so an unexecuted path stays unchecked.
Q2 is Q1’s sibling for dynamic languages. The same missing type information costs once as coupling, under T1 or T2, and once as a security surface here.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language turns text into code or commands as an ordinary operation, so concatenated input is an injection path. The code’s own text becomes a shared resource reachable from data, so a data path can become a control path.
Coupling imposed. Data-to-control coupling: text from a data path must agree with the parser that will execute it, because the language supplies conversion from text to code as a built-in operation. The agreement is available to whoever controls the text, so the boundary that matters is the input rather than the code.
Example. PL/SQL’s EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and DBMS_SQL build a statement as text. R’s eval(parse(text = ...)), do.call on a string, and system() turn text into code or into a command. A shell’s eval sends a quoted variable back through the parser. In Transact-SQL and SQL a statement assembled by concatenation carries the caller’s text. PowerShell’s Invoke-Expression does the same.
Q3 records the language-level facility, not its misuse. Parameterised queries and prepared statements are the mitigation, and the criterion is charged because the facility remains available and remains the path of least resistance.



Imposed by: language.
High · −15. The type promises a range, and arithmetic leaves it with no defined failure. A counter, a length, an index, a price passes the maximum, and the program continues on the wrapped bit pattern. Size becomes a shared resource whose meaning is decided by an operation that records no bound, so the check written above the arithmetic agrees with a quantity that no longer measures what the check checks. Integer overflow is a standing member of the CWE Top 25, and the fuzzing literature calls integer arithmetic errors a major source of software vulnerabilities [5].
Coupling imposed. Range coupling: every consumer of the value — a bounds check, an allocation size, a loop bound, a protocol field width — must agree that the arithmetic stayed inside the type, because the language records the bound nowhere. The agreement is invisible, so one input larger than the type turns the program’s own guard into the attacker’s entry point.
Example. Java defines integer arithmetic as two’s-complement wraparound (JLS 15.7.2), silent by specification; Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Spark, and the JVM family carry Java’s answer. C leaves signed overflow undefined, and the optimizer removes the checks that guard it; unsigned arithmetic is modulo 2^W by definition. The EVM runs arithmetic on raw 256-bit add and sub opcodes that wrap in silence, the rule the Solidity security documentation names as the overflow pitfall; a language compiles to it directly whenever it defines no guard [6]. JavaScript, TypeScript, PureScript, SAS, GML, Scratch, VBScript, and R carry every number as a double, so integers above 2^53 change value in silence. PHP and Perl promote an overflowing integer to float in place. PowerShell promotes a calculation that overflows Int64 to Double. MATLAB saturates to the type bounds without a word. The shells wrap 64-bit integers; Ladder logic wraps modulo the IEC 61131-3 type width; Ghostscript promotes to an inexact real. Go, Zig, Rust, Nim, Crystal, Julia, Lua, OCaml, Haskell’s Int, D, Eiffel, Turbo Pascal, and Delphi (range checks off by default) all define the wrap. Against these: Swift traps on the default operators, and the wrapping &+ is the opt-in; Ada raises Constraint_Error under the default checks; Solidity reverts on overflow by definition; ABAP raises CX_ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW; the SQL family raises an arithmetic-overflow error; Python, Ruby, Erlang, Elixir, Clojure, Gleam, Common Lisp, Scheme, Racket, Tcl, Prolog, Smalltalk, and R carry exact integers, so the value never leaves its range; Visual Basic 6 raises a loud Overflow; Assembly has no numeric promise for arithmetic to betray, the M6 boundary.
The trap prices nothing; the wrap prices everything. A defined, loud failure on the ordinary path — Swift’s trapping operators, Ada’s Constraint_Error, Solidity’s revert, the SQL family’s raised error, VB6’s Overflow — records no charge, the boundary the M5 note draws for zero-initialization. Debug-build panics are a mitigation, never an exemption (Rust, Zig, Nim, Crystal): the shipped build is the ordinary path, as the M1 note states for manual freeing. Exact promotion is absence, not mitigation: Python, Ruby, Clojure, and the BEAM languages promote to arbitrary precision, so the harm never occurs. Lossy promotion is presence, not absence: PHP, Perl, PowerShell, JavaScript, and SAS convert the integer to a float or double and the value changes. A language with no fixed-width numeric promise prices nothing, the M6 boundary.





The readiness axis uses the same three tiers and the same severity-share arithmetic as coupling. It asks a different question: not how much the language forces two parts of a program to agree, but whether the artifact can be rebuilt, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to another language, and governed openly. Breadth, escape, and silence decide the tier here too.


What the Reproducibility dimension asks: can you rebuild the artifact and get the same thing?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. Two builds of the same source do not produce the same artifact. The build environment — timestamps, absolute paths, file order, a random seed — becomes an input the source does not name, so the artifact is tied to the machine that made it and no third party can confirm that it matches the source.
Coupling imposed. Build-environment coupling: the artifact must agree with inputs that the source does not name — timestamps, paths, file order, a seed — because the build records them rather than normalises them. The agreement is invisible in the source and fixed at build time.
Example. Maven, PyPI, and RubyGems packages are largely unreproducible as published, because archive metadata and build paths leak into the artifact; Cargo and npm fix those values and reach reproducible builds [7]; the general problem is surveyed in [8].
The criterion records the default of the language’s own build tool, not what a careful team can arrange.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The dependency set is not pinned, so the build resolves to different versions at two points in time. The resolved graph is a shared resource that the source does not record, and the build that passed is not the build that ships.
Coupling imposed. Resolution coupling: the build must agree with the index about which versions exist, because nothing in the source fixes the answer. The agreement is made at build time and then forgotten, so two builds of one source can differ.
Example. A Python requirements.txt without hashes, or a setup.py that names ranges, leaves the resolution to the index. Cargo’s Cargo.lock, npm’s package-lock.json, and Go’s go.sum pin the graph.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The official distribution offers no way to record the language’s own version in the repository, so a repeatable environment needs a third-party version manager or a container image. The compiler version is a shared resource that no file in the project names.
Coupling imposed. Toolchain-version coupling: every machine and every build agent agree on a compiler version that the repository never states, so the agreement is rebuilt by memory or hidden inside a container image.
Example. Rust records the toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml through rustup, Go records it in the toolchain directive of go.mod, .NET records it in global.json, and Lean records it in lean-toolchain; Python, Ruby, Node.js, and Java leave it to pyenv, rbenv, nvm, and SDKMAN.
A container image is not a pin. The dependency set may be pinned while the compiler that built it is not, and the repository still names no version that a reader can check.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The toolchain reads no declared project contract. No shipped artifact names the dependencies with version ranges, the toolchain the build expects, the source encoding, in a form the compiler, the runtime, or the shipped package tool validates. The project’s requirements live in a README, a CI shell block, or a team’s memory — where a change arrives as behavior, not as a diff, and no tool refuses the mismatch before the build runs.
Coupling imposed. Contract coupling: the build’s requirements are a shared resource the toolchain never checks, so every producer and consumer carries them by convention. A dependency that moved, a compiler that advanced, a file re-encoded — none of these fail the contract, because there is no contract to fail. The agreement is the reason version drift arrives as behavior in production: the machine-read manifest is the place a mismatch stops at the build.
Example. Go’s go.mod is read by the go command; Rust’s Cargo.toml by cargo; Dart’s pubspec.yaml by pub; Elixir’s mix.exs by mix; Erlang’s .app resource files are read and validated by the code loader; npm reads package.json; pip reads pyproject; the .NET SDK reads the project file and global.json; R’s loader validates DESCRIPTION version requirements; OCaml’s opam/dune, Haskell’s cabal, Clojure’s clj launcher, Julia’s Project.toml, Swift’s Package.swift, Zig’s build.zig.zon, Tcl’s pkgIndex.tcl, MATLAB’s .prj, ABAP’s validated packages, X++’s model manifests, GML’s package registry, TwinCAT’s library registry, Scratch’s project format, Fortran’s module-dependency files: the contract is machine-read. Against these: the Java platform ships no manifest its own compiler reads — Maven and Gradle are third-party tooling, and javac reads only what the command line names. The same runs for Kotlin, Scala, CFML, PHP (composer is not shipped with the runtime), COBOL (JCL names the datasets, not the toolchain’s contract), Turbo Pascal, FoxPro, VB6, the POSIX shells, awk, assembly, Prolog, R7RS Scheme, Rocq, Goose, and SAS. Unison is the counter-case: its codebase pins every dependency by exact content hash, so it charges nothing here.
Y2 prices unpinned dependencies; Y14 prices the unpinned toolchain; this prices no contract at all. The three are cumulative, not exclusive: with no manifest, dependencies cannot be pinned, so a snapshot charged here usually carries Y2 as well — each mechanism prices its own agreement, and this one prices the missing artifact.
The charge follows the dependencies, not the manifest. Scratch declares nothing to pin and charges nothing; the shells and awk keep no manifest, but a script’s dependencies are the programs it calls, so they charge. The charge lands where a project has dependencies and the toolchain reads no contract about them.
Context: the toolchain decides. The tag names the remedy’s home: the vendor ships a manifest reader, or ships none. A language family inherits the parent’s answer — the JVM languages share the JDK’s (no manifest javac reads), the .NET family shares the SDK’s (global.json read), the BEAM languages share the release system’s (.app files read), the shells share POSIX’s silence.




What the Supply chain dimension asks: can you verify what you shipped?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. A published package carries no verifiable statement of who built it and from what source. The artifact’s origin is a shared resource that the consumer must take on trust, so a compromised build is indistinguishable from a genuine one.
Coupling imposed. Origin coupling: the consumer must agree with the publisher’s build, because the artifact carries no evidence of who made it or from what. The agreement rests on trust in a supply chain the consumer cannot inspect.
Example. npm and PyPI can attach Sigstore-signed provenance, and Maven Central now validates Sigstore signatures [9], [10]. A bare checksum gives integrity against corruption, not against substitution.
Presence is “no signing or provenance facility”, not “no Sigstore”. Maven Central requires a PGP signature, npm ships registry signatures, PyPI ships TUF metadata and opt-in attestations, RubyGems and NuGet have their own signing, and Go’s checksum database is a signed transparency log. A registry that offers only a bare checksum, and a language with no registry, are charged.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The package registry has one flat name space and no ownership model, so a name can be claimed or confused. The name is the shared resource, and a dependency can be redirected to a different author without a change in the consumer’s source.
Coupling imposed. Name-ownership coupling: the consumer must agree with whoever holds the name, because the registry records a first claim rather than an author. The agreement can be reassigned without the consumer’s code changing at all.
Example. PyPI, npm, crates.io, RubyGems, Hex, NuGet, and pub.dev reserve a flat name first-come, and npm and PyPI have both suffered dependency-confusion and typosquatting attacks. Maven Central’s group coordinates, Go’s module paths, CPAN’s nested namespaces, SwiftPM’s scope.package-name, and Packagist’s vendor/package carry a namespace. A language with no package registry is not charged: the mechanism is about a name space that exists.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The ecosystem maintains no advisory database joined to package versions, so a known vulnerability in a dependency is found by reading release notes or by a scanner that guesses. The vulnerability state of the dependency set is a shared resource that no feed records.
Coupling imposed. Advisory coupling: every consumer must track the vulnerability state of its own dependency graph, because no shared feed joins an advisory to the versions it affects. Each team builds the same map, and the maps disagree.
Example. OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database cover npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems, Packagist, Cargo, Go, Hex, Pub, and Swift; CPAN, Hackage, CRAN, the Julia General registry, LuaRocks, and dub have no equivalent maintained feed.
A scanner without an advisory database is not a feed. A tool that reports what a registry’s metadata implies does not record a vulnerability that a maintainer disclosed somewhere else.




What the Observability dimension asks: can you see what the program does in production?


Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language and its standard library provide no agreed way to emit traces and metrics, so each project invents one. The instrumentation contract is a shared resource, and a distributed call cannot be followed across a service the project did not write.
Coupling imposed. Instrumentation-contract coupling: every service must agree with every other on a format for traces and metrics, because no standard supplies one. The agreement is invisible until a call crosses a boundary the project does not own.
Example. OpenTelemetry ships stable tracing for C++, C#, Erlang/Elixir, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, and Swift, beta for Rust, and development status for Kotlin [11]. A language on the JVM or the CLR can use the stable Java or .NET implementation.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. Diagnostics are free text, and the standard library exposes no structured record of them. The program’s state is a shared resource held in an unstructured log, so a question about a running system requires a new deployment to answer.
Coupling imposed. Log-schema coupling: the running system must agree with whoever parses its output on a format, because the standard library records no structure. The agreement is informal and unwritten, so it breaks when a message changes.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. A failed run leaves no stack trace with source locations and no post-mortem artifact, so a failure in production cannot be reconstructed after the fact. The state at the moment of failure is a shared resource that the runtime discards.
Coupling imposed. Post-mortem coupling: the incident must be reproduced before it can be understood, because the runtime keeps no record of where the program stopped. Reproduction depends on an environment that has already changed.
Example. Python, Java, Go, C#, JavaScript, and Ruby print a stack trace with source locations on an unhandled failure; C and C++ print nothing without a debugger and an enabled core dump; Rust prints a backtrace only when RUST_BACKTRACE is set, and OCaml only when OCAMLRUNPARAM=b is set.
A trace that only a special build produces is not present. The criterion asks what an ordinary build does when it fails, because that is the build that runs in production.




What the Feedback dimension asks: how fast is the edit-build-test loop?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. A change costs a long rebuild, and the rebuild repeats work it did not need to. The build is a shared resource on the critical path of every edit, so the feedback loop is set by the compiler rather than by the size of the change.
Coupling imposed. Feedback coupling: every edit must agree with the compiler’s rebuild cost, because the build repeats work that the change did not require. The agreement is paid on every edit that ends in a build, whatever the size of the change.
Example. A large C++ translation unit and a large Rust crate both pay a long codegen and link step. Go and a scripting language pay almost none.



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The language has no incremental analyser that answers a question about the code as it is typed. The type and reference information is a shared resource available only after a full build, so the editor cannot answer while the author is working.
Coupling imposed. Answer-latency coupling: the editor must agree with a full build about what the code means, because no incremental analyser holds the answer. The agreement arrives after the fact, so the author works without it.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language’s official toolchain ships no source-level debugger, so a failing run is examined by reading the source and adding print statements. The procedure for inspecting a running program is a shared resource held outside the distribution, and each team assembles it for itself.
Coupling imposed. Diagnosis coupling: every failure must be reconstructed from the source and the logs, because the toolchain cannot stop the program and show its state. The team agrees with whichever external debugger it installs, and no file in the repository records that agreement.
Example. Python ships pdb, Java ships jdb, and Ruby bundles debug; Go ships no debugger and points to delve, C and C++ leave it to gdb or lldb, and PHP leaves it to Xdebug.
Presence is the official distribution. A commercial IDE with a debugger does not lift the charge: the criterion asks what the language itself installs, because that is what every new team starts from.




What the Interop dimension asks: can the language work with code written in another language?


Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language has no in-process foreign-function interface: a library written in another language is reachable only by starting a process or through an external binding. Every library must be reimplemented in the language, so the program is coupled to the ecosystem of one language and cannot reuse the rest. This is the mirror of T14: T14 prices an unchecked boundary, and Y9 prices the absence of one.
Coupling imposed. Ecosystem-reach coupling: the program must agree to live inside one language’s library supply, because no in-process path reaches another language. The agreement is with a community rather than with a component, so a library choice cannot renegotiate it.
Example. A shell reaches another language only by starting a process. Scratch, Solidity, and Rocq reach none. SQL is not charged: PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server each load native code through a user-defined function (LANGUAGE C, extproc, SQLCLR).



Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The program cannot be compiled to a portable target, so it runs only where the language’s own runtime runs. The deployment surface is a shared resource fixed by the runtime.
Coupling imposed. Deployment-target coupling: the program’s reach must agree with the runtime’s reach, because the language compiles only to its own execution environment. The agreement is fixed by the implementation, so a new target is a new implementation rather than a new build flag.
Example. Popcorn and AtomVM compile Erlang and Elixir to WebAssembly; GHC, wasm_of_ocaml, Pyodide, php-wasm, webR, and SwiftWasm cover their languages. Julia has no maintained official target.




What the Governance dimension asks: will the language be maintained, and by whom?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. One company decides the language’s direction, and no independent body can change it. The language’s future is a shared resource held by a commercial owner, so the program’s roadmap follows that owner’s priorities.
Coupling imposed. Roadmap coupling: the program’s future must agree with one owner’s priorities, because no independent body can change the language’s direction. The agreement runs one way — the program adapts to the owner’s schedule, never the reverse.
Example. MATLAB, SAS, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, Objective-C, Delphi, and VBScript are governed by one vendor, and Swift’s project lead is appointed by Apple. Rust, Python, JavaScript, PHP, Kotlin, C#, and Eiffel sit with an independent foundation or a standards body.



Imposed by: context.
High · −15. The language has no public, complete definition that an independent implementation could follow. The meaning of a program is a shared resource held by one implementation, so portability and third-party tooling depend on reverse engineering.
Coupling imposed. Specification coupling: the program must agree with one implementation’s behaviour, because there is no public definition to agree with instead. The agreement is discovered by experiment, and third-party tooling is built on the same experiment.
Example. ISO C, ISO SQL, Ada, Fortran, and Scheme have published standards. MATLAB, SAS, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, and Objective-C do not.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language’s meaning lives in the behavior of the dominant implementation. The vendor’s documentation describes what the shipped toolchain does; implementation-defined corners are not enumerated as a list; and no published conformance suite exists for an independent implementation to run. A program’s correctness is then a toolchain property, not a language property: the only oracle of what the code means is the compiler everyone already ships.
Coupling imposed. Conformance coupling: every consumer of the language’s semantics depends on one implementation’s choices, documented after the fact. The agreement is between the program and a toolchain nobody can test independently, so a second implementation is a compatibility gamble, a bug in the dominant one becomes the language’s behavior, and the code has no external standard to return to.
Example. The C standard lists its implementation-defined behaviors (J.2) and the NCAR suite runs against independent compilers, so C is not charged. Java marks implementation-defined corners in the JLS, and the conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation. Haskell publishes a test suite that independent implementations run. Against these: Perl, Clojure, Erlang, and Elixir are documented as the behavior of their implementations, and no published conformance suite exists; C++ lists its implementation-defined behavior in the standard and the committee publishes no suite; MATLAB, R, Julia, SAS, ABAP, X++, Scratch, and GML document the semantics of the product the vendor ships.
Y12 prices the closed specification; this prices the open one with no checkable core. Y12 charges a specification that is not public. This mechanism charges a public document whose semantics rest on the dominant implementation, with no enumerated implementation-defined list and no published conformance suite for an independent implementation to run. Both are governance facts; the first closes the document, this one leaves the oracle a single toolchain.
V4 prices the standard moving glacially; this prices no standard testable at all. A language can have a published standard with a slow committee (V4) and still ship a conformance suite — C does. A language can have no committee at all and a published suite — JavaScript ships Test262. The two facts are independent, and this mechanism charges only the second absence.
A development suite is not a conformance suite. A repository’s tests validate the reference implementation’s own behavior; they are run by maintainers, not by independent implementations, and they do not settle the unspecified corners. The mechanism charges when no published suite exists for an independent implementation to run against the language’s semantics. The published suites that settle it: Test262 (JavaScript), the TCK (Java), ACVS (Ada), the NIST suites (C, COBOL, SQL, Fortran-77), the R6RS and ANSI-CL test suites, the Haskell Test Suite, the Go suite that gccgo runs, the CLI conformance suite behind C# and VB.NET.
Context, not language. The tag says where the remedy lives: the vendor’s governance of its own specification, not the programmer’s code. A language family inheriting a parent’s conformance mechanism inherits this verdict from the parent: the JVM languages carry Java’s answer, the .NET languages carry the CLI suite, the BEAM languages share the BEAM’s status, and the shells follow POSIX’s scope for sh-family shells and the absence of any standard for the rest.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The vendor publishes no parser the analysis tools can use. The grammar is informal prose in a manual, and the shipped parser lives only inside the compiler, closed. Anyone who wants the program’s structure — a linter, a formatter, a security scanner, an editor, a migration tool — reverse-engineers the syntax from behavior, and the community’s parser is a guess the vendor never tests, never answers to, never has to keep current.
Coupling imposed. Syntax coupling: the language’s surface is a shared resource every analysis tool touches, and its contract is unpublished. The tooling agrees with a guess; the vendor moves the syntax; the agreement breaks silently and the repair falls on the third-party authors who never owned the grammar. The code a team writes is read by software the vendor does not answer for.
Example. Published parsers, published grammars, published source: Go ships go/parser; the JDK exposes its syntax tree through com.sun.source; TypeScript’s compiler API is the parser; CPython ships ast and its PEG source is public; Ruby ships prism; Elixir’s Code.string_to_quoted; Erlang’s epp/erl_parse; PHP’s tokenizer; Rust’s proc-macro token stream; OCaml’s parser.mli; the open-source compilers whose source is the published parser (Zig, Haskell’s GHC, Swift’s swift-syntax, .NET’s Roslyn, Clang, GCM, the shells). Against these: MATLAB ships no parser and its grammar is prose in function docs; SAS ships none; Delphi’s compiler is closed and its grammar is diagrams in prose; Turbo Pascal, FoxPro, VB6, COBOL on the IBM line, ABAP, X++, GameMaker’s GML and the TwinCAT compilers ship no parser an independent analysis can run, and Adobe ColdFusion’s engine is closed; Lucee, the other CFML engine, publishes its compiler source, which is why CFML charges nothing here.
Y12 prices the closed specification; this prices the closed parser. Y12 charges the language document nobody outside the vendor can read. Y19 charges the syntax artifact nobody outside the compiler can run. A language can publish its specification and ship no parser (COBOL: the ISO standard is public, the compilers’ parsers are closed) — Y12 absent, Y19 present — and the two facts do not merge.
L3 prices thin documentation; this prices the missing artifact. A language with a rich manual and a closed parser (MATLAB) charges Y19 and not L3; a language with a published grammar and an open-source compiler charges neither. The manual’s depth and the parser’s availability are different absences.
Open source counts as published, and says why. A compiler whose source is published publishes its parser: the source is the artifact tools read (the Zig, Clang, GHC, Roslyn, and shell verdicts). The charge lands on closed compilers with no published grammar normative beyond prose and no shipped parser API — a test a reader can check from the vendor’s own distribution, in both halves.
Context, not language. The parser is a toolchain artifact; the vendor ships it in source, as an API, in a package, not at all. The remedy lives in the vendor’s distribution decision, not in the program.

The inventory prices the language, before any design decision, and it is honest about its limits.

Not design quality. Two programs in the same language differ more from each other than the languages differ from one another. A program can cluster what the language scatters, and a good design decision is exactly that act. The score is the raw material, not the outcome.
Not team skill or process. A discipline that a team keeps — a checked build, a mandatory code review of ownership, a lint rule — can hold a High mechanism at bay in practice. The model charges it anyway, because the discipline is not in the language and cannot be relied on by the next team.
Not severity in a particular system. The weight judges breadth, escape, and silence. A Minor mechanism in a hot path can cost more than a High one in a corner of the program, and the model deliberately does not try to price that. A weight is a property of the mechanism; a cost is a property of a system.
Not the last word on any one language. Every mechanism mark is a factual claim about the language, and a factual claim can be wrong. When one is, the mark is corrected, and every score, table, and ranking derived from it is regenerated. The Scoreboard carries the data so that the claim can be checked rather than trusted.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
Two parts of a program are coupled where they must agree about one shared thing: a type, a heap, a lock, a name space, a platform ABI, a runtime. The agreement is the cost. It has to be established when the code is written, it has to be maintained while the code lives, and it has to be re-established whenever either side changes.
A language mechanism is a coupling criterion when it forces agreement that the programmer cannot refuse. Three properties decide how much that costs:








Property
Question
Effect on the weight




Breadth
How much of the program has to agree — one call site, one module, or the whole program?
A wider agreement costs more


Escape
Can a programmer opt out of the mechanism locally?
No escape costs more


Silence
Does the language say so, or must a reader discover it?
A silent obligation costs more



A mechanism that makes the whole program agree, with no local way out, and nothing in the language that records the agreement, is High. A mechanism that forces agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a convention that the whole codebase must keep, is Moderate. A mechanism whose agreement is confined to a boundary, and removable by a contained workaround, is Minor.
That is the whole rationale for the weights. The tier is a judgment about breadth, escape, and silence — not a count of incidents, and not a substitute for measurement.
Every entry names its coupling. After the tier, each entry states the kind of coupling the mechanism imposes and why it cannot be refused: which two parties must agree, what they must agree about, and which property of the language forces the agreement. The kind is the name of the shared resource — a type, a call target, a heap, a schedule, a version, a supply — so the entries read as a catalogue of shared resources rather than as a list of complaints.

The fourth tier is not a weight. A price has one direction: the same presence must always mean the same cost. Where the direction is not fixed, no single number can state the cost. A mechanism whose sign varies cannot enter the sum without making that sum incomparable across languages and across releases — the same mark would have to mean a gain and a loss at once, so two scores would no longer be arithmetically comparable, and two analysts would no longer reach the same number. The model therefore records such a mechanism: the mark is present or absent, the observation beside it states what changed, why, and how a deployment reverses it, and the score is untouched. V5 is the only mechanism in this tier.
Within one dimension the present weights are summed, and each mechanism contributes its share of the axis inventory: a mechanism of weight w costs 100 × w ÷ inventory weight score points, and the dimension cost is the sum over its present mechanisms. There is no cap and no curve. The share is a rubric choice, not a measurement: it stays additive because a maintainer pays every forced coupling, it stays bounded because the numerator can never exceed the inventory, and it is monotone, so removing a mechanism always moves the number. The inventory weight states what the model knows about the axis, not a ceiling on what the axis can cost.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
Each entry gives the mechanism’s code and tier, what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, an example, and — where the criterion is easy to misread — what its presence does not mean.
Presence is a factual question about the language: does the language hand the programmer this construct? It is not a judgment about the code. Every language permits a global; C1 asks whether a global is the default home for state.
Who imposes the mechanism. Every entry carries one tag: Imposed by: language, runtime, or context. A language mechanism is decided by the compiler — the construct is in the source, and the compiler accepts or rejects it. A runtime mechanism is decided by the executor: the memory manager, the compiler that runs later, the thread scheduler, or a default the platform chooses. A context mechanism is decided by the surroundings: the vendor, the toolchain, the market, the documentation, or the standard. The tag is meta-information and never changes a weight. It tells a reader where a remedy would have to happen: in the code, in the deployment, or outside both.
A check behind a project switch. Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch. The mark uses the configuration the language’s own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. tsc --init writes "strict": true (which sets strictNullChecks), so TypeScript is not charged T10; dotnet new writes <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, so C# is not charged T10; Visual Basic’s compiler default is Option Strict Off and the SDK template sets no OptionStrict, so the narrowing conversion is charged T2. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — that is what T1 already says about mypy in CI.
A mitigation is not an absence. Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism — @CompileStatic in Groovy, try-with-resources in Java, reified in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged, because the default code still pays it and avoiding it needs knowledge the language does not force. The model measures what the language imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on the same language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the language page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
What the Type dimension asks: can the language keep the meaning of a value in one place, or must every reader reconstruct it?


Imposed by: language.
High · −15. A value carries its type at run time, so nothing checks that an operation suits its operand until the operation runs. The meaning of every value becomes a shared agreement between the site that produces it and every site that consumes it, and no tool holds that agreement: it lives in the tests and in the reader’s memory.
Coupling imposed. Type-identity coupling across the whole program: producer and consumer agree on what a value is, and on every operation that may apply to it, and nothing in the source records that agreement. Because the check happens when the operation runs, the agreement survives only while both sides are read together, so a change to one reaches all the others at once.
Example. Python accepts n = 1 and then n = "one", and n + 1 fails only on the path that reaches it, and only for the inputs that take that path. MATLAB, R, SAS, Lua, and every POSIX shell behave the same way.
Presence does not mean a checker is unavailable. The criterion asks whether the language enforces a check. A program that runs mypy --strict in CI has a check the language did not give it, and the score still records the language.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The compiler knows the types, but it converts between them implicitly, so a check that would catch a mistake becomes a silent conversion. The conversion rules become the shared resource: every expression depends on a table that nothing forces a reader to know.
Coupling imposed. Conversion coupling: every expression that mixes types agrees with the language’s conversion table rather than with its neighbour. The table is the shared resource, so a reader who does not hold it cannot tell a checked expression from a silently narrowed one, and an implicit conversion hides the moment the meaning changed.
Example. C compiles int i = 3.7; and discards the fraction, and lets an integer stand in for a pointer. COBOL converts between two different PICTURE clauses on a MOVE without complaint. Visual Basic’s Option Strict Off default admits a narrowing conversion and a late-bound call.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Which code a call reaches is decided by the value’s run-time type rather than by a declared contract. The set of operations a value must answer becomes a shared agreement that no declaration holds, so a rename in one module breaks a caller in another — and only at run time.
Coupling imposed. Call-target coupling: a caller and a callee agree on a name and an arity that no declaration enforces, and the agreement must hold for every type that can arrive at the call site. Because the target is chosen from the value, the coupling spans types the author of the call never named.
Example. Erlang resolves Mod:Fun(Args) when it is called, so a missing function fails there; Elixir and Clojure choose a protocol or a pattern clause from the value they receive; Ruby and Python resolve an attribute at the moment of the call.
Presence does not mean T1. Objective-C is statically typed at the pointer level and still dispatches every message at run time, so it is charged T3 and not T1. TypeScript is statically typed and still reaches a method through the prototype at run time, so it is charged the same way. Duck typing is about which code runs; T1 is about what a value is.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language cannot declare that a value is one of several alternatives and have the compiler track which one. The alternatives are encoded by convention, so the tag and its payload are a shared resource that every consumer re-derives, and the compiler cannot prove that a consumer handles every case.
Coupling imposed. Encoding coupling: producer and consumer agree on how an alternative is written down — a tag beside a payload, a nil, a nullable column — rather than on the alternative itself. The encoding is the shared resource, so a new case has to be taught to every reader of it, and exhaustiveness stays a convention.
Example. Go has no sum type, so “a value or a failure” is a pair and a nil check stands in for a match. SQL models an alternative as nullable columns, and the caller must know the encoding. Rust’s enum and C++’s std::variant are the constructs whose absence is charged.
Minor because it is containable. A constructor plus its accessors can confine the cost to one place — but never to zero, because exhaustiveness stays unchecked.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language cannot write an algorithm once over a type parameter, so it duplicates the code per type or falls back on one universal representation. That representation becomes the shared resource, and every user casts out of it, so the type is known by convention.
Coupling imposed. Representation coupling: every use of the algorithm agrees on the one representation it can carry — void *, Object, interface{} — and casts back out by hand. The universal representation is the shared resource, so the real type of a value becomes knowledge held by the programmer rather than a fact held by the compiler.
Example. Pre-generics Java needed (String) list.get(0) from an Object container; C passes void * with a callback; Go before 1.18 used interface{}; SQL has no type parameter at all and generates DDL per column type instead.
Presence does not mean the checking half of generics. A language with generics whose parameters cannot be constrained still leaves a gap — but that gap is charged under T2 or T3. T5 records only the absence of the type parameter itself.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language has a single flat name space, so two declarations with the same name collide whichever module they live in. The global name space is the clearest shared resource there is: every name is a claim on it, and a new module can break an unrelated one.
Coupling imposed. Name coupling over one flat space: every declaration competes for the same set of identifiers, so two modules that never call each other are coupled through the name they both want. The name space is the shared resource, and nothing local bounds a claim on it, which is why the convention that resolves it — a prefix — must be kept by the whole codebase.
Example. Two C libraries that both define init cannot be linked without renaming one, which is why C libraries prefix their symbols (gl_, png_). Lua keeps every global in one shared table. An assembler puts every global symbol in one flat symbol table.
Presence asks about the mechanism, not the idiom. MATLAB is not charged, because +pkg folders scope a name, and R is not charged, because a package declares a NAMESPACE. C is charged, because a header’s declarations all land in one translator-level name space.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The type parameter is present in the source and gone from the artifact, and the program can inspect and alter its own structure at run time. The erased type is a shared resource that no longer travels with the value, so a consumer must recover it by convention — and reflection turns every private field into a reachable one.
Coupling imposed. Type-recovery coupling at the boundary: the consumer agrees with the producer on a type argument that the artifact no longer carries. The agreement sits where the cast is written, so it holds per call site and cannot be checked back at the place the value was made.
Example. Java’s List<String> is a List at run time, so get(0) returns Object and the cast is unchecked. Objective-C’s id carries no compile-time type at all. TypeScript’s types exist in the editor and the build, and not in the running program.
Minor because the cost sits at the boundary where the type is recovered — a cast, a Class<T> token, an isKindOfClass: test — not in the body of the algorithm.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. A symbol such as +, ==, or [] takes its meaning from the operand types. A symbol is a shared resource with one meaning by default, and overloading makes that meaning depend on a lookup the reader has to perform.
Coupling imposed. Symbol-meaning coupling: the reader agrees with the definer on what + or == does for the type at hand. The meaning is resolved by a lookup at the use, so the coupling is real but bounded to one expression — the reader resolves one type and the answer arrives.
