Example. C++’s << both shifts and inserts into a stream. Scala’s + on a Set performs a union. Racket’s + accepts exact and inexact numbers and returns whichever type the operands dictate.
Minor because the operator still carries a type signature, so its meaning is discoverable by resolving one type — unlike a macro, which can mean anything at all.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The only way to use two types through one interface is to place both in an inheritance chain. The base type becomes a shared resource that the types must be placed into, which forces an “is-a” commitment wherever the domain has only “does-this”, and a change to the base changes every subtype.
Coupling imposed. Hierarchy coupling: a type agrees to be placed under the interface it will be used through, so it inherits its base’s identity and its base’s future changes. The chain is the shared resource, so a change at the root reaches every leaf, and an unrelated type must be moved into the chain before it can play the role.
Example. Eiffel’s polymorphism runs through its inheritance and genericity rules. C approximates it with a struct holding function pointers, or with a void * and a convention. TclOO expresses a shared protocol as a class or a mixin rather than a declared type.
Minor, and the cheapest to remove. Go’s implicit interfaces, Rust’s traits, and Elixir’s protocols supply polymorphism without a chain, so those languages are not charged.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Any reference can be the absent value, and nothing in the type says whether it is. “May be absent” becomes a shared resource that every consumer must guard, and no signature records the guard, so each reader repeats the check or forgets it.
Coupling imposed. Absence coupling: every consumer agrees with every producer about whether a reference may be missing, and no signature records the answer. The unwritten agreement is the shared resource, so each guard is written per use and each omission stays invisible until the missing value arrives.
Example. Java compiles String s = null; s.length(). SQL’s NULL is compatible with every domain and propagates through three-valued logic, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL. In PL/SQL a variable that is never assigned is NULL. A null pointer in Assembly is a zero register, and a load from it is an ordinary instruction.
Presence does not mean “the language has an absent value”. Kotlin’s String? against String, Swift’s optionals, Rust’s Option<T>, and TypeScript’s string | null under strict are exactly the construct whose absence is charged, which is why those languages are not charged T10.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. There is no construct that declares what a module exposes and what it keeps. The boundary is the shared resource, and its absence means every declaration is reachable by every consumer, so an internal change can break an unrelated caller.
Coupling imposed. Visibility coupling in its total form: every declaration is a public fact, so a consumer may depend on anything a producer contains. The missing boundary is what makes the coupling unbounded — a change to an internal name travels to callers the module never intended to have.
Example. A C header makes everything it declares public, and static is the only file-scoped boundary. A POSIX shell script sources another script into the same variable space. VBScript’s ExecuteGlobal writes into the same global scope. Scratch exposes every sprite’s blocks with no declared interface.
Presence does not mean “no files”. Splitting code across files is not a boundary. Go is not charged, because a package-level unexported name is a real boundary, and neither is MATLAB, whose +pkg and private folders hide what they do not export.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. A call’s signature says what it returns, not what it does. The effects a call may perform — input and output, mutation of shared state, exceptions, randomness — are a shared resource that no declaration carries, so every caller learns them by reading the body or by testing. A change to an effect is invisible to every caller [1].
Coupling imposed. Effect coupling: a caller agrees with a callee on what the call may do, and reads that agreement from the body rather than from the signature. Because the effect set is unwritten, every caller is exposed to every effect the implementation may later acquire.
Example. Haskell’s IO, PureScript’s Effect, and Unison’s abilities put the effects in the type, so a function cannot hide a socket behind a pure signature. In Java, Python, Go, and C a function that writes a file, mutates a global, and throws looks like any other function.
Held at Moderate, not High. The breadth is the whole program — any call may perform any effect — but nothing breaks when the effect set is wrong. The cost is the reading and refactoring work an untracked effect adds, not a missed check, so the mechanism does not carry a High mechanism’s weight.
Presence records whether the type states the effects. Every language has effects. Haskell, PureScript, Unison, Lean 4, and Rocq carry them in the type; so do Nim (its raises and tags lists are part of a proc type) and D (pure, nothrow, and @nogc are constituents of the function type). Java’s throws clause is a signature annotation, not part of the method type, so Java is charged.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language has two kinds of function — one that may suspend and one that may not — and the two do not compose. A synchronous function cannot call an asynchronous one without a bridge, so the kind spreads outward through the call graph and every caller must agree on it. The kind is a shared resource that a change in one function imposes on the whole chain [2].
Coupling imposed. Function-kind coupling along the call chain: a caller must share the kind of its callee, so the kind propagates from the smallest suspending leaf to the entry point. The kind is the shared resource, so adopting it at one site is a decision that the whole chain must repeat.
Presence records a function-kind split, not the existence of concurrency. Go’s goroutines and Erlang’s processes are concurrency without a second function kind, so neither is charged.
Example. In JavaScript, C#, and Dart an async function returns a future, and a plain function that calls it must itself become async or block. Rust’s async fn returns a Future that only an executor drives, Nim’s {.async.} proc can be awaited only inside another async proc, and Python’s async def and Kotlin’s suspend draw the same line.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language can call code outside its own type system, and nothing checks that the two sides agree. The foreign interface — argument order, ownership, layout, lifetime, and error convention — is a shared resource held by a hand-written declaration, so a mismatch is found at run time or not at all.
Coupling imposed. ABI coupling at the foreign boundary: the two sides agree on argument order, layout, ownership, and error convention through a hand-written declaration that neither compiler validates. The declaration is the shared resource, so the agreement holds until run time and then fails as corruption rather than as a diagnostic.
Example. Rust’s extern "C" block is an unchecked promise. Python’s ctypes and Ruby’s Fiddle accept any signature. JNI requires the C side to agree by hand, and a Java exception that crosses the boundary unwinds nothing on the other side.
Minor because the boundary is containable to one module — but never zero, because the compiler cannot check across it.
Covers the native boundary, not a boundary inside one runtime. Unison 1.0 added a C FFI, so it is charged. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server can load native code through a user-defined function, so the procedural SQL dialects are charged with them. Solidity calls only inside the EVM, and a shell reaches foreign code by starting a process, so neither is charged. The readiness axis prices the other side of the same boundary, under Y9: a language is charged there for having no interface, and here for the interface being unchecked. Both can be charged at once.
A safe language’s guarantees stop at the crossing. The host pays this mechanism: the hand-written declaration carries layout, ownership, lifetime, and the error convention across the boundary, and it is the host’s own construct. The language on the far side pays Q1 for the unsafety that crosses with it, on its own page. A third mechanism charging the host for its partner’s unsafety would price one fact twice, once where the construct lives and once on every page that calls it, so the analysis prices each fact once: T14 on the host, Q1 on the partner.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The string API counts text and moves it by position, and the values it hands are units of an encoding. A character above the Basic Multilingual Plane occupies two UTF-16 units, so a count that names a character counts a unit, an index that names a position can cut between the halves of a pair, and a boundary that names a character can split one. The representation is the unit, the promise is the character, and the API names the promise while it ships the unit. When Twitter moved its post limit from 140 to 280 characters in 2017, the new limit counted an emoji as two: the count, the API, and the user all named characters, and the type shipped units.
Coupling imposed. Character coupling: every API that counts text — a length, an index, a slice, a regex, a protocol field width, a posting limit — must agree on what one character is, because the type’s name says character and the value says unit. The agreement lives in the name, so every count is a count of units wearing the word character, and the first value outside the plane splits in silence.
Example. ECMA-262 defines a String as a sequence of UTF-16 code units, and length, charAt, and substring are unit operations; PureScript and TypeScript inherit the engine. Java’s char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units, the split the code-point APIs document; Scala, Groovy, Clojure, Spark, and the JVM languages carry Java’s answer. C# documents Char as a UTF-16 code unit, and the .NET family carries that answer. Kotlin documents Char as a 16-bit code unit. Dart documents String as UTF-16 code units and length as a unit count. Delphi’s Char is a WideChar unit; Objective-C’s NSString counts UTF-16 units. Against these: Go documents strings as UTF-8 byte slices and indexes bytes; Rust validates UTF-8 at construction and documents len() as bytes, so the named fact matches the shipped fact; Swift defines Character as an extended grapheme cluster and iterates String by graphemes; Python documents str as a sequence of Unicode code points; Ruby tags strings with an encoding and documents length in that encoding; Haskell, OCaml, Racket, Scheme, Common Lisp, Ada, Erlang, Elixir, Gleam, Julia, MATLAB, R, Tcl, and Smalltalk name the code point, char, byte, or grapheme they ship; Assembly and Ladder logic ship no text abstraction with a character promise.
The mechanism charges the mismatch, not the encoding. A language that names bytes and ships bytes (Go, C, C++, Lua, Perl, PHP, SAS, the shells) records no charge; a language that names code points and ships them (Python, Haskell, Ada, Racket, Julia, Ruby) records no charge; a language that names characters and ships units (JavaScript, Java, C#, Kotlin, Dart, Scala, Groovy, Clojure, Delphi, Objective-C) is charged, with the family answers inherited per the Y17 pattern. Documenting the unit fact is a mitigation, never an exemption: the M5 note prices compiler warnings, and this prices documentation.




What the Construction dimension asks: can the language keep state local, and can a value only come into existence through a path that establishes its invariant?


Imposed by: language.
High · −15. The default home for a value is a global that any code can read and write; state is local only when the programmer asks for it. The global is the widest shared resource there is — the whole program is its consumer — so any module can change it, and any change can surprise any reader.
Coupling imposed. State coupling to one cell: every reader and every writer of the global agrees on its meaning at each instant, and the whole program is a party to that agreement. Because the cell has no owner, no module can change its own behaviour without the possibility of changing another’s.
Example. Python’s module-level names and global. MATLAB’s base workspace, and R’s global environment with <<-. A POSIX shell, where x=1 inside a function can write the caller’s variable. COBOL’s WORKING-STORAGE. A PL/SQL package variable, which lives for the whole session.
Presence asks whether a global is the default. Every language permits a global. Kotlin and Rust make top-level state immutable unless it is declared otherwise, so neither is charged.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. A binding, and the value behind it, can be changed unless the programmer says otherwise. “Who may write this?” then has no default answer, so every reader has to trace the writes.
Coupling imposed. Write-permission coupling: every holder of a binding must know which other holders may change it, and the language states no default answer. The permissive default makes the coupling silent at the definition and forces it to be reconstructed at every read.
Example. Java fields are mutable unless they are final; C++ members unless they are const; a MATLAB array is mutable with no const at all; a SAS DATA step may overwrite the dataset it is reading.
Minor because immutability is usually a local decision. A language that inverts the default — Rust’s let with mut, Haskell’s bindings — is not charged.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. Creating a value and obtaining its storage are one act, and the construction cannot be redirected to different storage. The storage site becomes a shared resource, so a caller cannot choose where a value lives, and the code that builds a value cannot be separated from the code that reserves it.
Coupling imposed. Storage coupling: the constructor and the caller must agree on where the value will live, because the language offers no way to separate the act of construction from the act of reservation. The agreement is narrow — one allocation site — which is why a single indirection removes it.
Example. In C a value exists only because storage was reserved and then filled, and a constructor is a naming convention over malloc. In Assembly the reservation is a register or a stack slot, and nothing constructs.
Minor because one indirection restores the separation. C++’s placement construction and allocator-aware containers, and Rust’s Box and Vec::with_capacity, build in storage that already exists, so those languages are not charged.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. A value of the type can exist without having passed any validating path. The invariant becomes a shared resource that nothing enforces, so every consumer either re-validates or simply trusts.
Coupling imposed. Invariant coupling: every consumer must agree with every producer that a value is valid, because no constructor stands between the type and its instances. The agreement is silent — a consumer cannot tell a validated value from an unvalidated one.
Example. A C struct is uninitialized memory until each field is assigned. A Fortran variable can be referenced before it is set. A Solidity contract without a constructor is deployed with whatever the default state is. In a POSIX shell a variable comes into existence on first assignment, and no construct can state an invariant about it.
Minor because the invariant can often be re-established cheaply — a smart constructor, a factory, a private field plus a validating entry point. The criterion is the same either way.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The key-value container the source uses iterates in an order the source does not state: the specification leaves map iteration unspecified, and the default type in the shipped library is the unordered one. Code that assembles output, report text, a serialized payload, or a join order from an iteration is agreeing with a hash function. Go and Rust randomize the order between runs on purpose, Perl randomizes it to catch the agreement, Scala switches from insertion order to hashed order when the fifth entry arrives — documented, and silent.
Coupling imposed. Order coupling at iteration sites: the sequence of a traversal is a shared resource between the container’s internals and every consumer of its order. The source cannot pin it, the type does not name it, and a change to a key set, a capacity, or a seed moves the output of a program nobody changed. The fix is a discipline — choose the ordered container, sort the keys, never rely on the order — and a discipline is what the model prices as present.
Example. The Java specification states the iteration order of HashMap need not be constant; the Go specification states map iteration receives no order guarantee, and the runtime randomizes the seed each run; Rust’s HashMap documents the per-process random seed; Perl’s documentation states the hash order is the implementation’s and varies; Lua’s reference says pairs() walks in an order ‘decided by the internal data structures’; the CLHS states hash iteration is unspecified; Swift documents Dictionary order as ‘not specified’; Microsoft documents Dictionary order as not to be relied on.
V5 prices a default that drifts; this prices an order the source never owned. V5 charges a build-time default changing between releases; C5 charges a run-time order not pinned in the source. The two combine in the story the model records for the Go gob: the order of a map the source serialized changes between runs, so an encoding built on iteration order is unstable by the language’s design.
Y1 prices bytes, this prices sequence. Y1 charges a build that is not byte-reproducible. C5 charges the run-time sequence a program cannot pin. An artifact built once from pinned inputs can still print its map in three orders on three runs.
The exemption is a specified order, not a discipline. Insertion-order-guaranteed defaults are exempt: Python’s dict (specified since 3.7), Ruby’s Hash, PHP’s array, Kotlin’s mapOf, Dart’s Map, Elixir’s and Erlang’s maps (key term order), Haskell’s Map (key order), Crystal’s Hash, Tcl’s dicts, JavaScript’s object key order (ES specification) and Map (insertion order). Where the unordered container is the opt-in and the ordered type is the default, the page records no charge. Where the unordered type is the default and the ordered type the opt-in, the mechanism is present, as the mitigation rule prices it.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. A value is reachable through more than one name, and the declaration names no alias set. A parameter, a field, a closure, and a return can all reach the same object, and the write that matters is the one through the name the reader was not watching. The code shows the names; it does not show the sharing. In the languages where every object moves by reference, sharing is the default condition of data, not a construct a programmer reaches for.
Coupling imposed. Alias coupling: every reader of a mutated value must agree on which of its names are aliases of one storage, and the type system records the names, not the edges. The agreement is per mutation site — invisible, uncounted, and reconstructed by reading the whole reachability set — so a change at one reader must assume the writer list the declaration never stated. Where the language names the borrow, the list is in the type; where it does not, the list is folklore.
Example. In Java every object variable is a reference, and an array’s buffer is shared by assignment (a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type). In C, pointers alias freely and restrict is an opt-in promise the compiler does not check. Fortran’s argument association passes the caller’s storage to the callee. COBOL CALL USING passes parameter addresses. VB6 parameters are ByRef by default. Go’s slices and maps share backing structures — append to a slice can write a buffer another name reads. Against these: Rust’s &mut names the exclusive path; Pascal’s VAR names the alias; ABAP’s BY VALUE and BY REFERENCE are written in the declaration; IEC 61131-3 names REF_TO; SPARK proves flow.
M4 prices the owner; this prices the visible write. M4 charges the missing record of who frees storage — a lifetime fact, removed by a collector. C6 charges the missing record of which names reach one value — a mutation-visibility fact, which a collector does not remove: a garbage-collected Java program needs no owner story and keeps the alias story.
K2 prices the thread crossing; this prices the sequential pair. K2 charges concurrent sharing by default. C6 charges that a write through one name is visible through another on one thread. A language can be K2-clean and C6-charged (Clojure’s immutable data with explicit refs), and the two are charged on different facts.
C1 prices the global; this prices the pair. C1 charges mutable state any module can reach. C6 charges the local graph: names in one program unit reaching one value with no declared alias set. Both are agreements over who writes what; the scopes differ.
The exemption is named semantics, not immutability of style. Immutable-by-default languages (Haskell, Erlang, Elixir, Clojure’s persistent data, PureScript, Gleam, Unison, Rocq, Lean) reach no mutable sharing: the harm has no site. Value-semantics languages (PHP’s arrays, R and MATLAB copy-on-modify, Tcl’s value copies, ABAP’s named BY VALUE/BY REFERENCE, Pascal’s named VAR, Rust’s borrows, IEC’s REF_TO, SPARK’s contracts) name the alias where the alias is allowed, and the naming settles the agreement. The mitigation rule prices the default code: Java’s clone, C#‘s readonly, Kotlin’s val, a team’s copy convention — all disciplines on a shared default. Assembly carries no charge here: it makes no binding declarations for the sharing to appear in — the same ’no typed promises’ boundary that exempts it from M6.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language runs code the source does not name at the site that triggers it. An implicit conversion writes a call to a user-defined operator the text never shows; a string argument names a function the source never mentions; data built at run time names the code that runs. The reader follows execution by reading calls; these transfers carry no call, and the agreement about what runs and when lives in the rules the reader must carry in their head, file by file.
Coupling imposed. Transfer coupling: at each site the reader must know which language rules start code — conversion operators, dynamic invocation, string evaluation — because the site names none. The agreement is per construct, and it is read from the standard, not from the file. A change at one site re-derives the whole rule set: which conversions exist, which strings execute.
Example. C++ performs user-defined conversions without a call: an implicit constructor, a conversion operator, and overload selection run code the source does not name; std::function construction from a lambda is an implicit user-defined conversion. .NET runs user-defined implicit conversion operators at assignment and argument sites. MATLAB’s function handles take string names — str2func builds the call from text the reader must resolve at run time. PHP’s unserialize runs __ unserialize magic at a site the source shows as data. Scala 2’s implicit conversions (deprecated in Scala 3, present in the shipped language) insert user-defined calls silently. Against these: Go names its deferred calls (the defer statement is the call), Rust names conversions as explicit trait calls, Java’s checked exceptions and numeric widening carry no user code, Kotlin ships no user-defined implicit conversion, Swift’s conversions are named constructs and its dynamic member lookup is an opt-in protocol the source’s own name routes, Clojure, Elixir, Haskell, and Erlang name their calls (a macro expands at a named site).
T8 prices operators you define for syntax; this prices code that runs with no syntax. T8 charges operator overloading (a named construct redefines the operator). C7 charges the transfers with no site — implicit conversions, string-built calls. C++ carries both, on different facts, and the entry keeps them apart.
M2 prices the collector’s schedule; this prices the call. Finalizer and destructor timing is the collector’s or the object model’s schedule acting on declared code — M2’s fact, priced on every collector language, which is why the JVM and the CLR pay it there and not here. This mechanism charges the transfer with no call site: the implicit conversion, the string-built call, the data-built goal.
Er2 prices exceptions raised from no declaration; this prices every transfer, including the non-exceptional ones. Er2 charges the unchecked-exception surface. C7 charges conversions, dynamic invocation, and string evaluation. A language can be Er2-clean and C7-charged (MATLAB charges both on different facts: Er2 for the MException that propagates until something catches it, C7 for its string-built function handles), and a language can charge Er2 with C7 absent (Go: a panic crosses frames unchecked, and every transfer it makes is written at the site).
C5 prices the unpinned order; this prices the unpinned call. C5 charges an iteration sequence the source cannot pin. C7 charges a code path the source cannot name. Delphi’s abs overload (an operator the source shows) is T8; its SysUtils string execution is C7’s class — the charged set names the fact per page, not per family.
Language: the transfers are the language’s rules. The tag says the compiler decides which silent transfers exist; the remedy is a language that names its calls (Go’s defer, Rust’s explicit traits, Kotlin’s absent implicit conversions). A team’s discipline of always writing the explicit form is a mitigation, charged by the mitigation rule.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Module state initializes when the loader reaches it, and the loader’s order across modules appears in no line of source. A module-level value whose initializer reads another module’s module-level value reads whatever state that module happened to hold when the loader came. The program’s starting state is a property of link order and file order, so a rename, a new import, or a build-tool change flips a value that no code ever wrote. The C++ literature names the case the static initialization order fiasco [3].
Coupling imposed. Initialization coupling: every module that touches another module’s state while it initializes must agree with the loader on who ran first, because the source names no order. The agreement lives in the build, so each reader reconstructs it from the loader’s rules, and one added dependency silently changes the sequence.
Example. C++ leaves the order of namespace-scope initialization across translation units implementation-defined: a global that reads a global from another unit is the fiasco [3]. C leaves elaboration order across translation units unspecified; Objective-C and D inherit the rule. Java initializes a class at first active touch, and JLS 12.4.1 documents the circular case: a thread reaching a class under initialization proceeds, observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock; the JVM family carries Java’s answer. C# defines static-constructor order as unpredictable (ECMA-335); Scala, Groovy, and the JVM family carry Java’s class-init answer, and VB .NET carries the C# rule. Kotlin runs top-level initializers at file-module load, in loader order. Python executes each module once, in first-import order, and a circular import hands the importer the half-initialized module. Ruby, PHP, Perl, and Lua load code at require time, and a cyclic require re-enters a half-loaded file; Smalltalk freezes the sequence in the image; Visual Basic 6 runs module initialization by startup form; GameMaker runs scripts in room-load order. Against these: the Go specification initializes packages in dependency order, variables before init(), in source order within a package; Rust has no global constructors, and lazily-initialized statics decide order at first use; Swift runs top-level code once, in main, and global storage initializes on first use; OCaml links modules in dependency order; Racket’s and Scheme’s require graph defines the sequence; the ECMAScript module system defines evaluation order as a post-order walk of the import graph, so the JavaScript family records no charge; Delphi and Turbo Pascal units initialize in uses order, a name the source states; Erlang’s loader enforces dependency order; F# module initialization follows the compile order the project file lists; Ada elaborates packages under the Reference Manual’s rules, with pragma Elaborate as the source-visible control; Unison content-addressing removes module load order entirely; Fortran, COBOL, Assembly, Ladder logic, the shells, SAS, ABAP, the SQL family, and Solidity ship no cross-module global-initialization construct.
Presence follows where the order lives, not how long the sequence is. An order the source names prices nothing (the Delphi uses clause, OCaml’s dependency link, the Go specification, the ECMAScript module graph, F#’s project order, Unison’s content addressing); initialization tied to first use prices nothing (Scala, Rust, Swift); initialization with a defined, source-visible rule prices nothing (the Solidity constructor, Ada’s elaboration pragma, Erlang’s dependency-loading loader); an order recorded only in the loader’s behavior is the charge. Where a language inherits a parent’s rule (the JVM languages carry Java’s answer, as the Y17 note states for conformance), the family carries the verdict.




What the Memory dimension asks: can the language state when storage and other resources are released, and who owns them?


Imposed by: runtime.
High · −15. The programmer decides when storage is released, and the program is wrong if the decision is wrong in either direction — a missed release leaks, and a doubled release corrupts. The heap becomes a shared resource, and “who frees this, and when” is a question that every path through the program must answer identically.
Coupling imposed. Lifetime coupling: every path that holds a value must agree on when it stops being valid, because the decision is written per path rather than once for the value. The agreement is global in effect and local in expression, so one divergent path corrupts what the others still trust.
Example. malloc and free in C. A stack frame plus malloc plus free in Assembly. New and Dispose in Turbo Pascal. Zig’s allocator.free. In Fortran, allocate and deallocate are written by hand for a pointer, and a missing statement leaks.
Presence follows the ordinary path. A language with an optional collector for one allocation class is charged when the ordinary path is manual, because the ordinary path carries the cost.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. Memory returns when the collector decides, not when the last reference goes away. The heap becomes a shared resource whose release schedule the program cannot name, so a latency-sensitive path is coupled to a component it never calls.
Coupling imposed. Schedule coupling: every path that depends on latency and the runtime must agree on when memory returns, because the release is the collector’s decision and not the program’s. The agreement is unavoidable and unnamed: no declaration states the schedule that the path is relying on.
Example. The JVM family (Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Clojure), the CLR (C#, F#), Go, Crystal, D, Nim, OCaml, Haskell, Dart, Unison, and the Lisp family (Common Lisp, Racket, Scheme). Elixir, Erlang, JavaScript, and Ruby each collect on their own runtime’s schedule, and TypeScript inherits the JavaScript runtime’s.
Presence does not mean “the language has a collector for one thing”. Reference counting is deterministic and is not M2: Swift’s ARC and Delphi’s strings and interfaces release at the last reference, and Delphi on Windows frees objects explicitly, so neither is charged. Objective-C is charged, because an autorelease pool defers a release past the last reference and a Core Foundation handle is released by hand.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. Nothing runs automatically when a scope ends, so a resource is released in a finally, by a project convention, or not at all. The resource — a lock, a file, a connection — is shared, and its release depends on every path remembering.
Coupling imposed. Release coupling: every exit path must run the same release, because no scope boundary runs it for them. The agreement is duplicated on every branch, so its cost grows with the number of paths rather than with the resource.
Example. C reaches a release path through goto cleanup. R uses on.exit and MATLAB uses onCleanup. Java’s try-with-resources was added precisely to supply the destructor the language lacks. Python’s with covers context managers, but only the ones that exist.
Minor because one convention removes it, and because a missed release is often caught in testing. Rust’s Drop and Zig’s defer run at scope exit by construction, so neither is charged.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language does not track which of several handles owns a resource, and aliasing is unrestricted. “Who may free or mutate this?” becomes a shared resource that the program states in comments rather than in the type, and every reader has to reconstruct the answer.
Coupling imposed. Ownership coupling: every holder of a handle must agree on who may free it and who may mutate it, because the type records neither. The agreement is left to prose, so it cannot be reviewed and does not survive the author.
Example. In C, two pointers can share one buffer with no way to say who owns it. In C++ a raw pointer and a reference alias the same object. Go offers no way to declare that a value moves, so a slice and its backing array stay aliased. In C# and Java, any two references can reach the same mutable object.
Presence does not mean “the language has references”. Rust is not charged: moves, borrows, and lifetimes are exactly the construct whose absence M4 records.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Storage exists before the program fills it, and the language permits a read of the bytes nobody wrote. A local variable, a raw allocation, or an unfilled buffer arrives carrying whatever the previous user of that memory left, so the value a read returns is a property of the heap’s and stack’s history, which no reader of the code can see. The behavior is not a language error — it is undefined, which is the strongest way a language can decline to say.
Coupling imposed. Initialization coupling: every read must agree with a write that happened earlier on every path that reaches it, because the language keeps no record of the write. The agreement is invisible — no type, no signature, and no contract names it — so each reader reconstructs the history from the call graph, and one new path that skips the write silently reopens the question.
Example. In C, reading an automatic object before initialization is undefined behaviour, and malloc returns bytes nobody wrote. Fortran locals without SAVE or an initializer are undefined at entry. COBOL data items without a VALUE clause hold undefined content at program start. Java gives every field a zero value and requires assignment before a local is read; C# has definite assignment; Zig zero-initializes and makes undefined an explicit opt-in.
Q1 prices the address, not the content. Q1 charges access outside an object’s bounds and access to freed storage — both read memory the program never owned. This mechanism charges memory the program owns but has not written. The two are the classic pairing: an uninitialized length feeds an out-of-bounds write, and one violation causes the other, but each is a distinct fact and they are charged once each.
M1 prices the release, not the first write. M1 charges the decision about when storage is freed. This mechanism charges the state of the storage before the first assignment. A collector removes M1 and leaves this one untouched: Java’s collector never frees early and never leaves a read uninitialized.
M4 prices the owner, not the origin. M4 charges the missing record of who may free or mutate. This mechanism charges the missing write before the first read.
The boundary is the written value, not the warning. Managed runtimes that zero-initialize (the Java and .NET families, Go, Python, the dynamic languages) are not charged. Languages that initialize some types and leave others indeterminate (Delphi’s managed strings against its plain records) are charged, and the page states the split. Languages that make undefined an explicit opt-in (Zig) are not charged, because the opt-out is named at every use site. A compiler warning is a mitigation and never an exemption.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language permits the same storage to be read and written through unrelated types. A union member, a pointer cast, a redefining data clause, or a reinterpret intrinsic takes the bytes of one type and hands them to another, and no check runs. The value does not satisfy the target type’s constraints, and the language’s own guarantee — that a value of a type is a valid value of that type — ends at the pun, unmarked, in ordinary code.
Coupling imposed. Representation coupling: every reader of the storage must agree on which type’s rules govern it now, because the language records no switch. The agreement is invisible at the use site — the pun and the ordinary use of the type look identical — so each reader reconstructs which invariants still hold from the history of the bytes, and one new writer under the other type silently invalidates them all.
Example. C unions and pointer casts; C++ reinterpret_cast and unchecked downcasts; COBOL REDEFINES; Fortran EQUIVALENCE and the TRANSFER intrinsic; Pascal and Delphi variant records and absolute declarations; D’s cast between unrelated pointer types, which the specification hands to the programmer as undefined behaviour; Nim’s cast, which the manual defines as type punning, like reinterpret_cast. Against these: Java and C# check every cast at run time; Rust confines it to the marked transmute; Go to unsafe.Pointer; Swift to unsafeBitCast; Ada names every conversion as an Unchecked_Conversion instantiation over one type pair.
Q1 prices the address, this prices the type. Q1 charges storage the program never owned — out of bounds, already freed. This mechanism charges storage the program owns, interpreted under rules it does not satisfy. The classic pairing runs one way into the other: pun the type, break the invariant, corrupt the memory. Each is a distinct fact and they are charged once each.
Q2 prices the trust boundary, this prices the program’s own types. Q2 charges untyped data arriving from outside. This mechanism needs no untrusted input: the types lie to each other inside one program, under one programmer.
T7 prices the type parameter that is gone, this prices the type that is present and lied about. T7 charges erasure and reflection — types unreachable or alterable at run time. This mechanism charges concrete storage reinterpreted under an unrelated layout, with every type still present in the source.
The boundary: a marked escape, a checked cast, or no invariant to break. A checked cast prices nothing — the run time rejects the mismatch loudly (the Java and C# cast checks). A marked escape prices nothing — transmute, unsafe.Pointer, unsafeBitCast, and Ada’s named Unchecked_Conversion instantiation put the crossing in the source, where review and proof can find it. Reinterpretation between plain-data types prices nothing — where every bit pattern is a valid value of the target type, no invariant can break, which is why Julia’s size-checked reinterpret over bitstypes is not charged. And a language with no typed promises prices nothing — Assembly has no type system for the bytes to betray.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. The language permits faults outside its declared failure surface, and no catch reaches them. A wild pointer’s trap, a nil force-unwrap, a safety panic, a bounds violation outside the declared error path, a stack overflow in the recursive evaluation — the run time takes the program down with no path back, because the failure is not a value the program was told to expect. The declared failures (the exception, the error value, the Result) cover the faults the language names; this mechanism charges the fault class the language cannot name.
Coupling imposed. Fault-surface coupling: the recoverable boundary ends where the declared failure ends, and the undeclared class crosses it freely. Every recovery the team writes is a bet that the real fault lands inside the declared surface — a bet with no enforcement, because the fault class that ends the program has no site in the source. The maintainer’s recovery plan and the fault’s actual class are two shared resources that never meet.
Example. C and C++ trap on a wild pointer, and no signal handler is a language construct (the POSIX signal story is C’s answer, and it is not a catch). Swift’s force-unwrap trap and out-of-range crash are fatal by design (documented: fatal error; process abort). Zig’s safety panics abort (the panic handler ends the process; the error-value mechanism covers fallible operations, not safety faults). BEAM’s unsafe atom-table overflow ends the node (documented: atom table exhaustion is a node failure — the atom table’s unbounded growth is the fault the language cannot catch). Ada’s Program_Error is raised outside catchable scope at storage exhaustion (documented: the exception can end the partition). Fortran’s STOP, COBOL’s ABEND, VB6’s uncatchable runtime errors. Against these: JVM languages throw OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError as catchable values (documented, Java 1.4 onward — the 1.4-era memory-exhaustion patch made the class declared), and .NET added OutOfMemoryException’s contract to the catchable surface.
Er5 prices the missing unit; this prices the uncatchable class. Er5 charges that no published unit survives a fault (Go’s panic ends the process). Er6 charges the fault class no catch reaches inside a surviving unit (Java: the thread survives a fault, and the wild-pointer class does not exist in Java at all; a JVM crash from JNI is the partner’s Q1). The two land on different faults; C++ pays both on the wild pointer (Er6) and the thread-wide uncaught exception (Er5), and the notes keep them separate.
Er3 prices ignored declared errors; this prices the class the declaration cannot name. Er3 charges the language culture of dropping the failure value it returned. Er6 charges the fault outside the returned values. A language can charge both (Perl: Er3 for the failure values its culture drops, Er6 for the memory-exhaustion crash no eval reaches), and the two facts are the dropped declaration and the undeclared class.
T10 prices the null possibility; this prices the crash it causes. T10 charges references that may be absent unstated. Er6 charges the runtime’s answer being fatal. Swift’s optionals (T10 absent, nil is stated) and its traps (Er6 present) prove the facts separate: the stated nil and the uncatchable crash are two agreements, and Java’s NullPointerException is a stated nil’s catchable answer (T10 present, Er6 absent).
Language: the fault surface is the language’s declaration. The tag says the language decides which faults enter its declared surface. A runtime that patches the class (Java 1.4’s OutOfMemoryError, .NET’s OutOfMemoryException) moves the verdict with the runtime’s promise; the family’s verdict follows the parent’s patch, and the entry names the release.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. Reference counting releases at the last reference, and a cycle has no last reference. A parent and its child, a closure and the environment that created it, keep each other’s counts above zero for the life of the program. The leak is a property of the graph’s shape, not of any path, so the release the counting promises is a release no path can reach. The reference-counting survey names the cycle problem the scheme’s standing limit [4].
Coupling imposed. Retention coupling: every holder of a counted handle must agree that the reachability graph has no cycle, because the release fires only at zero, and a cycle never reaches zero. The agreement is a shape constraint no type states, so the leak is invisible at the site that creates it and surfaces, if at all, as process memory that never returns.
Example. Swift documents strong reference cycles in the Automatic Reference Counting chapter and prescribes weak and unowned as the discipline. The Rust standard-library documentation states that Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles leak memory and that Weak breaks them. The C++ standard library requires shared_ptr cycles to be broken by hand; Objective-C ARC documents the same. Delphi documents interface reference cycles under ARC; Nim’s manual carries the cycle-breaking obligation for its counting mode; Perl’s internals document reference-count loops and the opt-in collectors; D counts class references by default, its cycle collector a runtime mode; Visual Basic 6 leaks COM circular references. Against these: the collecting runtimes — Java, C#, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Clojure, JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Go, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lua, Erlang, Elixir, OCaml, Haskell, Racket, Scheme, Common Lisp, R, MATLAB, Julia — reclaim the cycle by default, charging the schedule through M2 and leaving this leak uncharged.
M2 excuses counting from the collector’s schedule; this charges the schedule’s limit. The two mechanisms are the two halves of one design decision, and a language pays exactly the half it leaves exposed: a runtime charged the collector schedule pays that charge, and a counting runtime pays M7. weak, Weak, __weak, and hand-broken back-pointers are a mitigation, never an exemption: the ordinary path holds strong references. A default-on cycle collector removes the harm, in the M5 zero-init style; Perl’s opt-in collectors are mitigation-priced. Languages that ship no counted handles price nothing; the manual-memory class is M1’s decision.




What the Error dimension asks: can a failure travel from where it is detected to where it can be handled, and does anything require a caller to decide?


Imposed by: language.
High · −15. The language has no construct that carries a failure from where it is detected to where it is handled. The failure travels by side channel — a return code, an out-parameter, a log line, a global status flag — so every caller must remember to check it, and nothing checks that a caller did.
Coupling imposed. Failure-signalling coupling: producer and consumer must agree that a particular value means failure, because the language gives the failure no type. The agreement is a convention that every call site repeats, so it is invisible where it is skipped.
Example. C returns a sentinel and sets errno. A shell returns an exit code that nothing reads unless set -e is set. Fortran reports through iostat=, and COBOL through FILE STATUS. SAS writes a note to the log and moves to the next observation. VBScript’s On Error Resume Next turns a failure into a silent continuation.
Presence records the path, not its enforcement. A language whose ordinary failure path is an exception is charged Er2 instead.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. A failure can be raised without the signature saying so, and no caller is required to handle it. The set of failures a call can produce becomes a shared resource that the type system does not carry, so a caller discovers it in production.
Coupling imposed. Failure-enumeration coupling: the caller must agree with the callee on the set of failures that may arrive, because no signature lists them. The agreement is learned from production, so it is discovered after it is needed.
Example. A MATLAB MException propagates until something catches it, and nothing must. An R condition is signalled and carried on. D’s throw needs no declaration, and nothrow is an opt-in promise that no caller sees. Go’s panic is unchecked and recover is optional. Java’s unchecked exceptions carry the failures that actually occur — NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException — even though the language also has checked ones.
Presence does not mean “the language has no checked failures”. The criterion is charged when the failures that arrive in practice are the unchecked ones, because those are the ones no signature can enumerate.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language lets a failure pass without any decision, and it does not force exhaustiveness. “Handled or not” becomes a shared decision that nothing records, so a caller’s silence is indistinguishable from its approval.
Coupling imposed. Handling-decision coupling: each caller must agree with the rest of the system that silence is an adequate response, because nothing forces the decision to be recorded. The agreement is indistinguishable from neglect, so review cannot separate the two.
Example. In C a return value and an errno value carry no consequence until the code branches on them, and a switch over an enum may leave cases unhandled without a diagnostic. In Haskell a non-exhaustive pattern compiles and fails only when reached. A -1 from an Assembly call is a value, not a signal.
Minor because one discipline removes it locally — a checked return, a total switch, an exhaustive match — but the discipline has to be written down, and the language will not check that it is kept.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. A failure cannot be carried as an ordinary value through an ordinary expression, so it cannot be threaded, combined, or returned from a helper. The success-and-failure pair has to be rebuilt at every level, through out-parameters, sentinel values, or a global status, so the shape of the error path becomes a shared convention.
Coupling imposed. Error-shape coupling: every level must agree on where a failure travels, because no value can carry it through an expression. The agreement is repeated at each boundary, so a change to the shape changes every signature in the chain.
Example. Ada reports through raise, so a fallible operation cannot be folded into an expression. In C the pair is an out-parameter or errno. In Go it is a second return value, which cannot be mapped or chained without a second statement. In Assembly there is no value that can carry “this failed”.
Minor because the cost is syntactic rather than structural — but it is the difference between an error path that composes and one that is everywhere a special case. Rust’s Result, Haskell’s Either, and C++’s std::expected are the constructs whose absence is charged.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. A fault has no declared survivable unit. The language raises and catches inside one frame chain; the runtime publishes no supervision unit whose failure the program survives. An uncaught fault in a thread takes the process with it (the .NET and C++ and OCaml documentation says so in plain terms), a Go panic unwinds every goroutine, a Swift trap aborts, a PLC task crash is the runtime’s problem, an ABEND ends the program. The maintainer has no named recoverable boundary: the choices are a process restart set up by the deployment, or a catch in a frame that is already unwound.
Coupling imposed. Fault-boundary coupling: the agreement between a unit of work and its survivability is held nowhere in the program. Recovery discipline — wrap the worker loop, restart the service, keep the shared state recoverable — is an untyped convention across the codebase, and every failure mode the convention missed is a full restart. Where the runtime publishes a supervision unit the program declares, the agreement moves into a declared structure, and the charge lifts.
Example. The .NET runtime documents that an unhandled exception terminates the process. C++ documents std::terminate for a thread with an uncaught exception. The Go specification: an unrecovered panic terminates the program. Swift traps abort. OCaml, Nim, Crystal, and D document the thread-wide end. Fortran STOPs; COBOL abends. Against these: the BEAM publishes the supervision tree — a process fault restarts the process under a declared strategy; the JVM documents thread death as the end of the thread; Python’s threading documentation ends the thread, not the process; Ada’s RM 11.1 terminates the task that raises and the partition survives; Common Lisp’s restarts are first-class recovery points; JavaScript publishes Workers.
Er1 prices the missing structured path; this prices the missing boundary. Er1 charges a language with no structured failure mechanism at all. A language can ship exceptions (Er1 absent) and publish no survivable unit — C++, PHP, the .NET family — and a language can ship a unit with a blunt path. The two facts are separate: raising and surviving are different agreements.
K4 prices the concurrency scope; this prices fault containment. K4 charges the lack of structured concurrent scoping. Er5 charges that a fault in a unit of work is not contained by a unit the runtime publishes. BEAM languages carry both answers (supervision is the published unit); a thread-isolated runtime (JVM, Python) answers containment without publishing supervision; a process-abort runtime (Go, Swift, .NET) carries the charge.
Runtime, not language. The tag says the executor decides: which unit survives a fault is the runtime’s published contract, not the source text. The published exemptions the model honors: BEAM supervision trees (Erlang, Elixir, Gleam), JVM thread death (Java family), Python’s threading contract, Ada task termination (RM 11.1), Julia’s failed tasks, Common Lisp’s restarts, JavaScript Workers, Lua coroutines, Tcl interpreters, SQL transactions, EVM transactions, PLC tasks, R’s session, SAS’s step, ABAP’s internal session, Scratch’s script, FoxPro’s ON ERROR, VB6’s On Error, Prolog’s queries (an uncaught exception fails the query and the toplevel continues, documented in the standard systems), and GML’s script termination (a script error ends the script, documented in the manual). The declaration-shaped exemption is the program naming the unit; a convention is not a unit.




What the Concurrency dimension asks: can the language express parallel work, and can it keep that work from touching shared state unintentionally?


Imposed by: runtime.
High · −15. The ordinary execution model offers no second thread of control: running two computations at once needs a worker, a separate process, or a native extension. “How much may run at once” is fixed by the runtime, so every part of the program that wants throughput is coupled to that one decision.
Coupling imposed. Throughput coupling: every part of a design that needs concurrency must agree with the runtime on how a second thread may exist, because the execution model is fixed outside the language. The agreement cannot be made locally: a second core is available only by leaving the program’s own structure behind.
Example. Python’s global interpreter lock serialises bytecode execution, so a CPU-bound program must leave the language — multiprocessing, a native extension — to use a second core. JavaScript and PHP take a request or an event as the unit of work. Solidity runs a transaction on one EVM thread, and PureScript and TypeScript inherit the single-threaded JavaScript runtime.
Presence is about what the language can express, not about what a library can reach. A language whose only route to a second core is a separate process or a native extension is charged, because the program’s structure is then not the language’s.



Imposed by: language.
Moderate · −8. Concurrency shares memory by default, and nothing marks a value as thread-local, immutable, or owned. The shared cell becomes the resource, and every reader has to reconstruct which lock protects it.
Coupling imposed. Shared-cell coupling: every thread that reaches a value must agree on its content, because the default offers no privacy and no immutability. The agreement is unbounded — a thread’s correctness depends on code it does not contain.
Example. An Assembly store to a global is visible to every core, with no privacy notion attached to the address. A PL/SQL package variable is shared by every program unit in the session. In T-SQL, SET options and session-scoped state are visible to code the caller did not write. A C file-scope object is shared by every thread that reaches it.
Presence records the default. K2 and K3 often appear together, and they are different claims: K2 says the shared state is the default, and K3 says the language gives no help in finding the resulting races.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. Locks and atomics are library types, and the language neither proves the locking discipline nor detects a race. The discipline becomes an agreement across every file that touches the data, and the compiler checks none of it.
Coupling imposed. Protocol coupling: every file that touches the data must agree on one locking discipline, because the language supplies primitives but no proof. The agreement is horizontal — it runs across files that never call each other — so no compiler can hold it and no test can localise a violation.
Example. Java’s synchronized, C#’s lock, Go’s sync.Mutex, Kotlin’s @Synchronized, and Scala’s synchronized blocks serialise access but do not find a missing lock. D’s core.atomic and Crystal’s Mutex and WaitGroup are libraries over the same primitive. A lock prefix on one x86-64 instruction is the whole of Assembly’s provision.
Presence is about detection, not about threads. A language that proves thread safety at compile time is not charged, even though it has threads.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language gives no construct that scopes a task’s lifetime to a block, so nothing guarantees that a task has finished when the block ends. The task’s lifetime becomes a shared resource that the program tracks by hand, and a scope can end while work it started is still running.
Coupling imposed. Task-lifetime coupling: the block that starts work must agree with the work about when it ends, because nothing scopes the two together. The agreement is kept by hand, so every starter must also be the joiner.
Example. C’s threads and Zig’s threads have no scope that joins them. Perl’s threads leaves the task tree to the program. A Groovy executor service is joined by hand or not at all. In Assembly a thread is a clone or pthread_create call with nothing around it.
Minor because a scope construct can be added by convention, and because the failure it causes — work outliving its scope — is usually visible in testing. Kotlin’s coroutineScope and Swift’s task groups are the constructs whose absence is charged.



Imposed by: language.
Minor · −4. The language has no first-class lock, channel, or await, so concurrent work is started and steered outside the language. The synchronisation becomes a shared resource that lives in signals, exit codes, or a foreign library, so no declaration states the protocol.
Coupling imposed. Coordination coupling: the concurrent units must agree on a protocol, because the language supplies no first-class lock, channel, or await to state it. The agreement is carried by the operating system’s facilities rather than by the program’s declarations.
Example. A shell starts a job with &, steers it with signals, and communicates through exit codes, with no lock and no channel anywhere in the language. Turbo Pascal 7.0 in DOS reaches concurrent work through an interrupt procedure, and its synchronisation is the hardware’s.
Presence is the complement of K1. K1 is a runtime that forbids parallelism; K5 is a language that offers nothing to coordinate it.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. A concurrent task is an operating-system thread, so each task holds a thread for its whole lifetime. The number of tasks a program may run at once becomes a platform limit, and a task that blocks holds a thread that another task could have used.
Coupling imposed. Scale coupling: the program’s concurrency structure is fixed by the runtime’s mapping from task to thread, so a design that reads well at ten tasks is a liability at ten thousand.
Example. Java before virtual threads gives each request a platform thread, so a blocking call consumes one. Kotlin’s coroutines, Swift’s tasks, Go’s goroutines, Erlang’s processes, and Haskell’s green threads multiplex many tasks onto a few threads, so none is charged. Java 21’s virtual threads remove the charge for Java 21 and later.
Presence asks whether the ordinary unit is an OS thread. A single-threaded event loop is not charged, because no task holds a thread. An implementation that multiplexes tasks onto threads — green threads, coroutines, goroutines, processes — is not charged either, because the mapping is the runtime’s and it is cheap.




What the Platform dimension asks: can the artifact run anywhere other than where it was built for?


Imposed by: context.
High · −15. The program runs only inside one vendor’s product or one domain, so the deployment unit is that platform. The platform is the widest shared resource of all: every line is coupled to a runtime, an API surface, and a release cycle the program does not control.
Coupling imposed. Platform coupling: the whole program must agree with an environment it cannot change, because the deployment unit and the artifact are the same thing. Nothing in the source stands outside the agreement, which is what makes the tier High.
Example. A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database and deploys as a schema. SAS needs a SAS installation and deploys as a library on a SAS host. Transact-SQL needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE. A Rocq development runs only after extraction to another language. An x86-64 Assembly artifact runs only where that instruction set runs. A Solidity contract runs only on an EVM.
Presence is about the artifact. A language whose compiler runs anywhere but whose programs run in one place is still charged.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language has a single dominant implementation or platform, even though alternatives exist in principle. The toolchain, the library set, and the release schedule of one vendor become the program’s agreed reality.
Coupling imposed. Implementation coupling: a single implementation’s compiler, libraries, and release cycle become the agreement every consumer makes, because the alternatives are theoretical rather than practical. The escape exists on paper, and the working reality is one vendor’s.
Example. Groovy has no non-JVM implementation. Objective-C’s complete language, reference compiler, and flagship frameworks are one vendor’s. Most production COBOL runs on one mainframe platform with that vendor’s compilers. Eiffel’s practical toolchain is EiffelStudio, and Tcl’s is its own interpreter. Swift’s toolchain and frameworks are one platform’s.
P2 is a degree below P1. The artifact could in principle run elsewhere, and in practice does not.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The program targets a platform that is no longer developed, so the artifact is frozen with it. The platform’s limits — its word size, its memory model, its APIs — become permanent constraints on the program.
Coupling imposed. Era coupling: the program must agree with a platform whose own development has ended, because the artifact is frozen at that platform’s last state. The agreement has no revision path, only an exit.
Example. Turbo Pascal 7.0 compiles real-mode DOS executables, and it was the last release of that line: the target, not just the tool, has ended.
P3 is not P1. P1 is one live vendor with one domain; P3 is a platform whose own life has ended. Assembly on x86-64 is charged P1 for its instruction-set lock-in, and not P3, because that instruction set is current.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The language is a bad fit for ordinary application work, because the constructs it lacks make ordinary logic expensive. Every abstraction the program needs has to be built from primitives, so the program’s structure becomes a local invention rather than a shared convention.
Coupling imposed. Expressiveness coupling: every ordinary abstraction must agree with the primitives the language supplies, because nothing above them is standard. The agreement is made per project, so two programs in the language share a language and little else.
Example. Assembly has no types, no data abstraction, and no error path, so application logic is expensive to write and to change. Scratch has no file access, no network, and no general library, so it is not usable for a production application. Prolog’s computation model fits relational search and resists ordinary imperative application code. Ada’s and Fortran’s constructs fit their own problem classes first.
Presence is judged against general-purpose use, not against the language’s intended domain — otherwise every domain-specific language would be charged twice, once for its fit and once for its narrowness.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
What the Performance dimension asks: is there a cost the program pays at run time that its source does not show?


Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. The source is executed by an interpreter or a virtual machine rather than compiled to the machine’s code ahead of time. The execution model becomes a shared resource fixed by the runtime, so the shape of every hot loop is decided by the interpreter’s dispatch rather than by the algorithm.
Coupling imposed. Execution-model coupling: the shape of every hot path must agree with the interpreter’s dispatch rather than with the algorithm, because the runtime decides how a statement is executed. The agreement is invisible in the source, so a hot loop is tuned by leaving the language rather than by rewriting it.
Example. A Prolog goal is a search over the clause database through the engine’s instruction set, so a tight arithmetic loop trails a compiled equivalent. A shell parses and evaluates text at run time, so a loop over files pays parser cost per iteration. Base R and base MATLAB execute an interpreted form, and Perl’s reference interpreter has no JIT. Ruby is charged because its JIT is opt-in, so a default run stays interpreted.
Presence does not mean “slow”. The criterion is about the absence of an ahead-of-time path, which is why a language with a mature library behind it (MATLAB’s BLAS and LAPACK calls) can still be charged while remaining fast where it matters.



Imposed by: runtime.
Moderate · −8. A collector’s pause is part of the program’s timing, and the program cannot state when it will occur. The heap’s release schedule becomes a shared resource decided outside the program, so a latency target couples to the runtime’s collector.
Coupling imposed. Timing coupling: a latency budget must agree with the collector’s pause, because the program cannot schedule the pause. The agreement is temporal rather than structural — it constrains when the program runs, not what it contains.
Example. Dart’s generational collector stops the mutator, which shows as a frame-time spike. SBCL and CCL stop the program to collect Common Lisp, GHC pauses to collect Haskell, and Nim’s collector stalls its mutator. The JVM’s pause reaches Java, Kotlin, Scala, and Groovy alike, and the CLR’s reaches C#, F#, and the Visual Basic runtime. JavaScript pauses the one event loop it has, so a pause blocks every pending callback, and TypeScript and PureScript inherit that runtime. Go’s pause is short but present, Eiffel’s and D’s collectors remain a latency risk, and Unison’s own runtime collects on its own schedule.
R2 is not M2. M2 records that the heap’s schedule is not the program’s; R2 records that the schedule is observable — a pause a latency budget has to absorb. The two are marked independently: a language can hold M2 without R2, because a collector whose pause the page does not record as a cost (Python’s, Ruby’s, Crystal’s, Racket’s) is not charged. Where the page records the pause as a cost, the mechanism is charged — which is what keeps the charge set checkable against the pages themselves.



Imposed by: runtime.
Minor · −4. The first execution of a function compiles it, so the code’s speed depends on which path runs first and on how long the process has been up. Measurement itself becomes the shared convention: a benchmark has to agree on a warm-up, and a short-lived process never reaches the optimized state.
Coupling imposed. Measurement coupling: a benchmark, a latency target, and the compiler must agree on what “steady state” means, because the first execution compiles the code. The agreement must be written down, so a short-lived process and a long-lived one are not measuring the same program.
Example. Julia compiles a method on its first call, so latency depends on which path runs first. The JVM and the CLR tier their compilation, so Groovy, Clojure, Kotlin, F#, C#, Java, and PowerShell are slower on their first requests than in steady state.
Minor because a long-running process amortises it, and because it can be pre-warmed.




What the Ecosystem dimension asks: does the surrounding supply of libraries, tools, and people make the language’s own costs worse?


Imposed by: context.
Minor · −4. The language has no standard way to declare, fetch, and resolve a dependency. The build’s dependency graph becomes a shared resource owned by the build system rather than the language, so a project’s dependencies are a local convention that no tool can check.
Coupling imposed. Dependency-graph coupling: a project’s dependencies must agree with a build script rather than with a resolver, because the language defines no way to declare them. The agreement is local and unchecked, so two checkouts can disagree about the graph.
Example. In Assembly a dependency is an object file or a linked library resolved by the build script. The C and C++ standard defines no distribution, so the platform’s toolchain supplies one. Prolog’s standard defines no distribution, so each system ships its own. A shell has no dependency declaration beyond what the script itself probes for.
Minor because the cost is confined to the build — but the build’s convention is the whole program’s convention.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. No single toolchain covers the language, so every tool targets a dialect, a version, or a vendor. The workflow becomes a shared resource with several incompatible owners, and a team’s tooling choices must agree file by file.
Coupling imposed. Toolchain coupling: a project’s tools must agree with a dialect or a version rather than with the language, because no single toolchain covers the whole of it. The agreement is assembled per tool, so each choice constrains the next one.
Example. ORMs, migration tools, linters, and formatters each target one SQL engine’s dialect, so there is no single SQL toolchain. C and C++ are split across platform toolchains with different extensions and different warning sets. Go’s module and build conventions grew in parallel with the wider Go toolchain, so a project’s conventions are partly its own.
Moderate because the fragmentation is structural — it comes from the language’s reach, not from anyone’s neglect.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The library pool, the hiring market, or the vendor’s investment is small, so more code is written than found. The library surface is a shared resource the whole community draws on, and when it is thin, each project re-invents and the local convention becomes the only one.
Coupling imposed. Supply coupling: the program must agree to write what the community does not supply, because the library pool is thin. The agreement is with a market as much as with a language — hiring, support, and examples move with it.
Example. dub’s registry is far smaller than crates.io, npm, or Maven, so a D project is likelier to write a library than to find one. SAS’s market shrank against R and Python, so new packages arrive more slowly. Tcl, Eiffel, Prolog, Delphi, Crystal, and Lua sit in the same position. This criterion is charged in just over half the inventory, and it is deliberately held at Moderate: a niche language is a cost, not a defect.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The engine, the tooling, and the documentation come from one vendor under licence. The right to continue becomes a shared resource owned by a licensor, so the program’s future depends on a commercial decision.
Coupling imposed. Licence coupling: the program must agree with a commercial owner’s terms, because the engine, the tools, and the documentation come under one licence. The agreement reaches past the code into procurement and support.
Example. MATLAB’s toolboxes, editor, and reference documentation come from one vendor under licence. PL/SQL’s engine, tooling, and support come from Oracle. SAS, COBOL, Eiffel, Transact-SQL, Objective-C, and VBScript are in the same position, and so is any language whose manuals are behind a paywall.
Moderate because the licence is a structural dependency, not merely a price: the artifacts, the formats, and the support channel are all the vendor’s.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The build, the debugger, or the package tooling runs on one operating system or one runtime only. The development environment becomes a shared resource the team cannot choose, so the workflow is coupled to a platform.
Coupling imposed. Environment coupling: the team’s build, debugger, and package tools must agree with one operating system, because the toolchain is written for it alone. The agreement constrains the team rather than the program — the artifact may still be portable.
Example. Swift’s toolchain, its debugger, and its frameworks belong to one platform, so a Swift team outside it works with a second-class toolchain.
Ec5 is not P2. P2 is about where the program runs; Ec5 is about where the tools run.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. One framework, library, or runtime dominates to the point that the alternatives are not really alternatives. The dominant choice becomes a shared resource with one owner, so the whole community’s assumptions move together — and a defect or a policy change in that one component reaches everything.
Coupling imposed. Concentration coupling: the community’s assumptions must agree with one dominant component, because the alternatives are not maintained enough to be escapes. The agreement delivers consistency and removes the exit at the same time.
Example. Elixir’s ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP, so alternatives to the dominant framework are few. Java’s and C#’s enterprise worlds, PHP’s web stack, and Ruby’s Rails are each dominated by one framework family.
Moderate because the concentration is a risk, not a defect: it delivers consistency, and it removes the escape route.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. The ecosystem carries versions, APIs, or idioms that must still be supported, so old and new coexist. The compatibility surface becomes a shared resource that every new feature has to respect, so no part of the ecosystem can change freely.
Coupling imposed. Compatibility coupling: every new feature must agree with every version still in service, because the ecosystem will not drop them. The agreement is longitudinal — it runs between old and new code rather than between modules.
Example. Java’s enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2026 one, and a library has to keep both working. Ruby’s ecosystem pins older runtimes through older gems, so an upgrade has to wait for the slowest dependency.
Ec7 is the twin of V1. V1 is the language changing under the code; Ec7 is the ecosystem refusing to change.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. A compiled unit of the language reaches a consumer who links it without rebuilding it, and no published promise says that the producer’s release and the consumer’s release agree. The agreement is the toolchain release. Nothing in the source of either side names it. Where a check exists, it fires at load or at link, after both sides are already built. The failure names a mismatch, and the consumer still works out which side to rebuild.
Coupling imposed. Release-boundary coupling at a published binary: a wheel, a plugin, a MEX file, an extension, a package, a library, or a model package names the release that built it, and every consumer who cannot rebuild carries the whole cost. The agreement runs between independently released parts, so one release in one part forces rebuilds in all the others. A source-shipped package resolves the same agreement inside the consumer’s own build, and a published promise settles it: the class-file rules a language specification publishes, the assembly format and compatibility rules a runtime publishes. Neither is charged.
Example. A Python wheel names the interpreter, ABI, and platform tags, and the installer loads that binary. A Go plugin must be built with the same toolchain as the application that opens it. MathWorks requires a MEX file to be rebuilt for a new release. libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another.
Delivery targets decide this mechanism, target by target. Every language page lists its delivery targets at the end of its Ecosystem coupling section: what ships, whether a compiled unit reaches a consumer who does not rebuild it, and whether a published promise covers it. The mechanism is present exactly when one target crosses with no promise. Kotlin is charged on .klib and not on the JVM jar. JavaScript is charged on a node-gyp addon and not on a Node-API addon. Go is charged on its plugin path and not on its module proxy. Rust, Dart, Julia, Swift, and Zig are not charged: their package managers ship source, and the compiled paths they publish carry a promise. C and the Java family are not charged on objects that travel on a published format.
A promise must be published, and a charge needs a document. A de-facto convention settles nothing: an ecosystem that mostly works across releases is not exempted by practice, and an ecosystem with no document at all is not charged on practice either. Each charged verdict names the document it rests on, and each exemption names the guarantee it claims; no verdict is priced from practice alone. Where a vendor document is out of print and no current document decides, the page records the fact in the delivery table and the score stays untouched.
T14 prices a different agreement. T14 charges the hand-written declaration a developer maintains at a foreign-language boundary. This mechanism charges the release boundary of a unit that crosses as a binary. A plugin host and a foreign binding are two facts, and they are charged once each.



Imposed by: context.
Moderate · −8. State the program writes outlives the program: a serialized value, a workspace image, a compiled snapshot, a project archive, a saved model. The file carries a format header naming the release that wrote it, and the only reader is the toolchain. The boundary crosses time in one direction the consumer cannot rebuild: the data is years old, the release is today’s. Where a version check exists, it fires when the file opens. Where the vendor withdraws a reader, files written years ago have no reader at all on the current release, and the failure is not a link error to fix — it is the data.
