Presence is a factual determination about the language a programmer can write, not about a team’s house style or a third-party tool. Four coupling determinations need a stated rule:

A check behind a project switch. Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch that the project file sets. The mark uses the configuration the language’s own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. tsc --init writes "strict": true, and strict sets strictNullChecks, so TypeScript is not charged T10. dotnet new writes <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, so C# is not charged T10. Visual Basic’s compiler default is Option Strict Off and the SDK template sets no OptionStrict, so the narrowing conversion is charged T2. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — the mypy case under T1.
M2 — the collector’s schedule. Present when the run time reclaims memory on its own schedule rather than at the last reference, so the program cannot name when the heap shrinks. Deterministic reclamation is not charged: Swift’s ARC and Delphi’s strings and interfaces release at the last reference, and Delphi on Windows frees objects explicitly. Objective-C is charged, because an autorelease pool defers a release past the last reference and a Core Foundation handle is released by hand. The collector must be the one that reclaims the language’s own objects: a language that compiles to another scored language inherits that language’s collector (TypeScript inherits JavaScript’s), while a language whose artifact is consumed by a host rather than executed as its own objects is not charged here (a Rocq term is checked by the kernel, and a Scratch project runs inside the Scratch VM).
R2 — the collector’s pause. Present when the page records the collector’s pause as a cost the program must absorb — a ⚠️ or ❌ bullet on the pause itself, on a stop-the-world cycle, or on the program’s lack of control over the pause. Absent when the page names no collector cost at all, and absent when the page records the opposite (bounded collector steps, per-process collection, a collector mode stated as a strength). The mark is thus the page’s own assessment of its collector, which is what keeps the charge set checkable: where the page states the pause as a cost, the mechanism is charged.
Data rows for stored state — the two directions. A data-format row names the state the toolchain writes that outlives the program. Reading: present when the vendor publishes that the current release opens data written by an older one. Writing: present when the vendor publishes that data written now cannot be read by other releases. Ec9 charges a row whose evidence is a break — the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable, or a break the probe harness has reproduced with pinned releases and a committed result — and a format whose stored state carries a published version rule and a documented reading path is not charged. A row nothing decides is recorded on the page and prices nothing; a row the probe has tested without finding a break states the test and still prices nothing, because tested is not promised.

A mitigation is not an absence. Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism: @CompileStatic in Groovy, try-with-resources in Java, reified in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged. The default code still pays it, and avoiding it needs knowledge that the language does not force. That is deliberate: the model measures what the language imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve with the same language. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on one language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above: what a new project gets without a decision is the language’s; what the developer must know to turn on is a discipline.



Every mechanism carries one tag: Imposed by: language, runtime, or context. A language mechanism is decided by the compiler, so a remedy is a change to the code. A runtime mechanism is decided by the executor — the memory manager, the compiler that runs later, the thread scheduler, or a default the platform chooses — so a remedy is a change to the deployment, to a flag, or to the version. A context mechanism is decided by the surroundings, so a remedy is outside both: a different vendor, toolchain, market, or standard. The tag is meta-information. It never enters a score, and it makes one thing visible: a release can change a runtime fact and no language fact, and the page will say so.



V5, silent default drift, is in the inventory and carries no weight. A default that the source does not name changes between releases; nothing in the build reports it, so a deployment discovers the change when the behaviour of the running program moves. That is a real coupling — the agreement exists, and the code never wrote it down — but its direction is not fixed. The same change can help one workload and hurt another: G1 as the default everywhere helps a one-CPU container and moves the latency profile of a service that was measured under Serial, and a new default key encoding can be better interoperability and a break for an older peer. A price has to point one way, or the sum stops being arithmetic. So the model records the event, states its direction in the observation beside the mark, and prices nothing. The same rule keeps execution quality — footprint, throughput, energy — out of the score entirely. A delivery row, or a data row for stored state, marked recorded, not priced follows the same rule as V5: a crossing release boundary that no current document decides is recorded, and it removes no points.
All three axes are scored the same way. Readiness is a scored axis exactly like Core and Ecosystem: every mechanism carries a weight, a present mechanism removes that weight, the dimension subtotals sum to the axis cost, and the axis score is 100 minus that cost over the axis inventory. Presence is a factual determination on every axis, decided by a stated test rather than by a severity judgment. The readiness tests are stated with each mechanism in the Criteria — “build not reproducible” is present when the language’s own build tool does not default to byte-reproducible output, and “no signed provenance” is present when the registry ships no default attestation — so a reader can check a mark and regenerate the score, exactly as on the other two axes.

title: 1 The Scoring Model
text:
Every score on this site is reported on its own axis. The ranking score is the one place where two axes meet, and coupling leads it. The rule is declared here:








Term
Role
Why




Core coupling
Primary
The coupling the language’s own constructs force into the code.


Engineering readiness
Modifier, at most 15% of the coupling score
A toolchain, registry, and observability stack can be fixed by process; coupling written into the code cannot.


Ranking score
core × (0.85 + 0.15 × readiness / 100)
Readiness lifts the coupling score by at most 15% of that score, so a full 0-to-100 readiness swing is worth 15 points at a core of 100 — about 3.3 High mechanisms on the Core scale — and proportionally less below that. Rows that tie share a rank; the table lists them by Core coupling, then readiness, then the name.



Ecosystem coupling does not enter the ranking. It is a dependency context, not a quality: a near-monoculture ecosystem lowers risk through consistency, so its band can disagree with its number (JavaScript scores 80.1 there and 54.0 on Core). It stays a lens, and the table sorts by it, but it does not decide the order.
Coupling is primary; readiness is a modifier. Once the code is written, the code is what remains, and a maintainer faces it for most of a system’s life. A language that forces accidental coupling into every line has damaged that artifact permanently. Readiness surrounds the code rather than entering it, and it is remediable by process: a toolchain, a registry, and an observability stack can be fixed, while coupling in the code cannot. So readiness does not weigh against coupling as a peer. Readiness earns its lift the way every axis earns ground: as the absence of present harms. A language lifts the ranking by having fewer readiness mechanisms present, never by having a feature. The remedy for a readiness gap is a process change; the measurement is the language’s own default toolchain, not a team’s discipline.

title: 1 The Scoring Model
text:
To reproduce any score: read the language’s present mechanisms for one axis, sum their weights, and divide by the axis inventory weight — 350 on Core, 256 on Ecosystem, 171 on Readiness. The score is 100 × (1 − present weight ÷ inventory weight), rounded to one decimal. Repeat for each axis. The three axes are scored apart: no score is ever added to another, though several mechanisms share one underlying fact and the axes are correlated in practice.

title: Turbo Pascal (7.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Turbo Pascal in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 67.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69.5/100 · Engineering readiness 25.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Strong static typing is enforced at compile time: Every variable, parameter, and function result has a declared type, and an assignment between incompatible types is rejected
✅ Enumerated and subrange types state a value domain: type TDay = (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri) and a subrange such as 1..31 narrow the domain in the declaration
✅ A typed pointer names what it addresses: ^T is a pointer to T, so an assignment between pointers of different types is an error
❌ A variant record is an unchecked union: record ... case Tag: T of ... end names the alternatives, but the compiler does not require the tag to be tested before a field is read (T4)
❌ No generics: A container is written for one element type, or it stores Pointer values and casts them, so reuse across types is untyped (T5)
✅ A unit is the namespace and a real module boundary: The interface section is what a uses clause sees, and the implementation section is private to the unit



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A uses clause states each dependency: The compiler rejects a call into a unit that is not listed, so the dependency edge is written in the source
✅ interface and implementation separate the contract from the code: A caller compiles against the declarations only
✅ An object declares its own construction and destruction: An object type declares constructor Init and destructor Done, and New(P, Init) runs the constructor together with the allocation
✅ Unit initialization and finalization run in dependency order: A unit’s startup code runs before the program body and its shutdown code runs after it
❌ Mutability is the default: A var is writable and reassignable, and only a const marks a value fixed (C2)
⚠️ A class hierarchy couples a derived object to its base: Object-oriented programming arrived in version 5.5, and an object type derives from one base, so shared behaviour is reached through that single-inheritance chain



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Every heap allocation is manual: New and Dispose, or GetMem and FreeMem, are the ways to use the heap, and the programmer writes the matching release (M1)
❌ Nothing runs when a variable leaves its scope: There is no release tied to scope, and a destructor is a method the programmer must call (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A typed pointer may alias, dangle, or be disposed twice, and the compiler does not track it (M4)
✅ The run-time library owns the heap: New, Dispose, Mark, and Release give a defined heap with a stack-like mark and release discipline
✅ A String value carries its own length: A String[255] short string stores its length in the first byte, so a string operation needs no terminator
⚠️ Real-mode addressing bounds the heap: In the 16-bit memory models the heap lies in the data segment, so the model’s segment limit caps one allocation
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: local variables hold indeterminate content until assigned, and only the managed types of later dialects initialize themselves (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: variant records overlay one storage with unrelated field layouts, unchecked (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a pointer trap is a runtime error that exits the program (the RTL’s runtime-error path), with no recovery surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ The default failure path is a halt or an error code: An unhandled run-time error stops the program with a run-time error number, and an I/O failure is reported through IOResult when checking is off (Er1)
❌ No composable result type: A failure cannot be carried in the type of a function’s result, so the caller learns of it from an error code or an exception (Er4)
✅ try/except/finally is a structured path: Version 7 added exception handling, and the finally block runs on every exit from the statement
✅ raise names the failure: raise EDivByZero.Create raises an object from the SysUtils exception hierarchy
⚠️ The exceptions are unchecked: Nothing in a signature states which exceptions a routine may raise, so the recovery path depends on a convention
⚠️ Two error styles coexist: {$I-} with IOResult checks one call at a time, while try/except covers a block, so a program mixes both
❌ A fault ends the program: the runtime library exits on the runtime error (documented); no recoverable unit exists (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The language has no concurrency construct: There is no thread type, no task, and no synchronisation primitive; concurrent work in DOS is expressed with an interrupt procedure (K5)
⚠️ The only shared state is a global variable: With no concurrency construct in the language, a global variable is what the main code and an interrupt procedure both reach, and nothing guards the access
⚠️ A thread-local variable needs a successor compiler: threadvar gives a variable one copy per thread in Delphi and Free Pascal, but Turbo Pascal creates no thread and the DOS target has none
⚠️ An interrupt procedure must be declared as such: The interrupt directive saves the registers, and the protection is a declaration rather than a checked protocol
⚠️ Reentrancy is the programmer’s concern: An interrupt procedure that calls a library routine can corrupt state the interrupted code was using
⚠️ Cooperative concurrency came from an add-on: A terminate-and-stay-resident program or a library simulated multitasking outside the language



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The main target is 16-bit DOS: The compiler produces real-mode DOS executables, and version 7 was the last release of the line (P3)
❌ A compiled unit is a private object format: A .TPU file is Turbo Pascal’s own unit format, and no other language’s linker consumes it
✅ Free Pascal and Delphi compile the same source: Both accept Turbo Pascal units, so the source is not frozen to the original compiler
✅ The compiler is a self-contained toolchain: One executable compiles a program, and the IDE runs the edit-compile-run cycle
⚠️ The memory model is a compile-time choice: {$M} selects tiny, small, compact, large, or huge, and the model bounds the code and the data segments
⚠️ Real-mode addressing shows in the source: near and far pointers and segment arithmetic appear once a program leaves the small model



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The one-pass compiler is a deliberate speed choice: Compilation is nearly instant, and the price is a modest optimiser
The integrated IDE is the intended way to work: The compiler, the editor, and the debugger are one program
The 16-bit limit belongs to the target machine: The segment size is a property of the processor mode, not only of the language
Turbo Vision is supplied and not required: The text-mode GUI library is an optional dependency of the program
The goto statement remains in the language: A jump is available for the case where a structured form is awkward
Pascal is a teaching language by design: The readable syntax and the strong typing were written for instruction




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits native 8086 machine code: There is no interpreter and no run-time compiler between the source and the processor
✅ Compilation is very fast: The one-pass compiler makes the edit-compile-run cycle take seconds
✅ A compiled program starts immediately: A DOS .EXE needs no runtime initialisation beyond the loader
⚠️ The optimiser does little global work: The algorithm and the data layout dominate the result
⚠️ The 16-bit target caps the work: The real-mode segment limit bounds the data one program can address
⚠️ A far pointer costs extra cycles: A segment override and a far access element are slower than a register operation



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is legacy and discontinued: Borland ended Turbo Pascal after version 7 in favour of Delphi, so the tool and package field is historical (Ec3)
✅ Free Pascal, Delphi, and Virtual Pascal continue the language: Each is a compatible implementation, so much Turbo Pascal code still compiles today
✅ A large body of published material exists: The era’s books, tutorials, and the Turbo Vision source remain available
✅ The compiler is a single small program: Nothing else must be installed to build a program
⚠️ Reuse is by source: A unit is shared as .PAS source rather than as a resolved package with a version
⚠️ The tooling runs in DOS or an emulator: The IDE and the debugger need a DOS machine or an emulator on a current computer



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language is discontinued: Borland ended the line in 1995 and moved it to Delphi and Object Pascal, so no version followed 7.0 (V3)
❌ The definition is frozen at 7.0: The language does not change, so a missing feature or a defect is permanent (V2)
✅ The reach of the tool was historically large: Over 400 000 copies were sold in the first two years, which made Pascal accessible to a generation of programmers
✅ The successors accept the source: Delphi and Object Pascal keep the unit, the static typing, and most of the syntax
✅ A port is an adjustment rather than a rewrite: Free Pascal compiles a unit with little change outside the platform-specific code
⚠️ The platform-specific part is real work: DOS interrupts, direct video memory, inline machine code, and .TPU linkage have no direct counterpart on a current target
❌ Build variants multiply: {$IFDEF} directives select which code compiles, and the flag set lives outside the source (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Structured programming instruction is the native domain: The readable syntax and the strong typing were designed for teaching
✅ DOS application and tool development fit the target: A compiled .EXE needed no runtime and ran on any PC of the era
✅ Turbo Vision covers text-mode GUI work: The bundled library provides windows, menus, and dialogs on a character screen
✅ A small number-crunching utility is a natural use: A scientific or engineering program was a common Turbo Pascal program
⚠️ New development does not choose it: The domain today is legacy maintenance and education
⚠️ Hardware access sits outside the language: A program that drives a device uses the BIOS, a DOS interrupt, or inline code



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is small and readable: begin/end, var, procedure, if/then/else, and for/to cover the language
✅ The compiler reports an error immediately: The short edit-compile-run cycle makes a mistake cheap to find
✅ The IDE integrates a debugger: Step, watch, and breakpoint are keystrokes away
⚠️ Pointers and manual memory are the hard part: The syntax is gentle and the heap discipline is not
⚠️ Real-mode addressing is a second subject: Near and far pointers and segments must be learned for system work
⚠️ The semicolon rule catches a beginner: A semicolon separates statements, so the last statement of a block takes none



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The syntax is verbose: begin/end, unit/interface/implementation, try/except/end, and every declaration keyword are spelled out (S1)
✅ Keywords are words rather than symbols: if, then, do, of, and end carry the structure
✅ Blocks are bracketed consistently: begin/end closes every compound statement, including the body of a procedure
✅ A declaration names the variable before its type: var Count: Integer reads in one direction
⚠️ A statement separator, not a terminator: The semicolon rule is a rule to learn rather than a decoration
⚠️ A nested field needs its qualifier or a with: Reading a record inside a record is verbose without the with statement



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework in the toolchain: A test is a program that runs and compares, and nothing in the distribution runs a suite (G1)
❌ The debugger is the era’s tool: The IDE steps and watches variables, with no assertion or coverage support (G2)
✅ A failed run-time check reports the detail: The run-time library prints the error number, the address, and the register contents
✅ A check is a few lines of Pascal: A comparison and a halt write a test without a framework
⚠️ A test suite is a program the programmer writes: No runner, no fixture loader, and no report come with the toolchain
❌ No monotonic reading published: the RTL’s clock is the BIOS wall time; no elapsed reading ships (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ The type system rejects a mismatch at compile time: A pointer to one type cannot take a pointer to another without a written cast
✅ The dangerous cast is one written site: Pointer and a type cast put the risk where the programmer wrote it
✅ A check can be switched on: {$R+} adds range checking to an array index and to a subrange assignment
⚠️ Manual memory management admits the classic faults: An overrun and a use-after-free are possible, and the compiler does not check them
⚠️ {$I-} disables an I/O check: After that directive a failed file operation must be tested through IOResult
⚠️ inline machine code bypasses the type system: An inline(...) statement writes raw opcodes into the compiled program
❌ Range checking ($R) is off by default, so arithmetic wraps the type bound in silence (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the compiler reads: the IDE compiles the units named, and no manifest declares dependencies, versions, or encoding (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Units and libraries move as disks and files with no provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed exists for the ecosystem. (Y16)
⚠️ The unit library is whatever the installation carries.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ Write and WriteLn carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A runtime error prints a code and stops; no post-mortem exists. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer exists beyond the compiler’s own errors. (Y8)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The executable runs where the DOS target runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the product documentation: the manuals defined the language, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)
❌ No parser published: the grammar is prose in the manuals, the compiler is closed, and no parser API ships (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Turbo Pascal’s core score is held down by the mechanisms of its era rather than by a missing idea: the heap is manual, no release is tied to scope, and a failure is a run-time error number or an unchecked exception. Its one strong structural feature is the unit, where interface and implementation draw a real boundary and the uses clause writes each dependency into the source. Main strengths: strong static typing, near-instant native compilation, a gentle readable syntax, and a live path to Free Pascal and Delphi. Main weaknesses: no generics, unchecked variant records, no concurrency construct in the language, and a 16-bit target whose toolchain, ecosystem, and platform are all historical.

title: COBOL (ISO/IEC 1989:2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses COBOL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 69.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 71.1/100 · Engineering readiness 40.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Typing is weak and static: A PICTURE clause fixes an item’s shape, but a MOVE between items with different pictures converts the value silently, so the declared type does not protect it (T2)
✅ The Data Division declares the shape once: Level numbers and PICTURE state each item’s size and category, and the Procedure Division uses that declaration without repeating it
✅ Group items give a structured record: Level numbers nest elementary items inside groups, so a record layout is one declaration
✅ Fixed decimal arithmetic is exact: COMP-3 packed-decimal operations do not accumulate binary floating-point error, so the numeric representation matches monetary values
⚠️ USAGE decides the representation: COMP-3 (packed decimal), COMP (binary), and DISPLAY differ, and a move between them converts without a type error
⚠️ An alphanumeric item accepts any character string: An X(n) item holds any text, so a category mistake is caught only by the program’s own checks



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Every data item is visible to every paragraph: A WORKING-STORAGE item can be read and modified from any procedure, and before COBOL-85 the language offered no way to restrict access to it (C1)
✅ The four divisions separate concerns: Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure give each declaration a fixed place, so data definition does not share a space with program logic
✅ CALL ... USING passes parameters to a subprogram: A called program receives its arguments explicitly, so a subprogram boundary is a declared interface
✅ LOCAL-STORAGE gives per-call state: It is allocated for each invocation, so a re-entrant call does not share the state held in WORKING-STORAGE
⚠️ PERFORM THRU names a range of paragraphs and passes nothing: The called region is a text span and the performed code communicates only through shared data items, with no parameter list and no call stack
⚠️ GO TO and ALTER break structured flow: The language permits control transfers that obscure which paragraph runs next
❌ One value, many names: CALL USING passes parameter addresses (documented), so the called program’s writes land in the caller’s storage (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: evaluate-on-name dispatch and the CALL ‘literal-name’ site resolve at run time to the program the string names (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Ordinary program data needs no allocator: WORKING-STORAGE and LOCAL-STORAGE come from a declared layout, so a program that uses only them calls no allocator and no free
✅ No garbage collector: Storage is fixed at compile time, so reclamation is deterministic and unobserved
✅ OCCURS declares fixed-size tables: The size of a table is known at compile time
⚠️ OCCURS DEPENDING ON varies a table’s length at run time: The logic then couples to the actual occurrence count
⚠️ ALLOCATE and FREE put deallocation back on the programmer: The 2002 standard added dynamic allocation for tables and objects, and release is an explicit statement
❌ Storage arrives undefined: a data item without a VALUE clause holds undefined content at program start, so every field the program does not initialize is a read of leftover bytes (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: REDEFINES lays a second data description over the same storage, and the program decides which layout governs (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: an ABEND (documented) ends the program below the ON EXCEPTION surface (the runtime abend is not an exception the program declared) (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Error handling has no structured path: USE AFTER STANDARD ERROR and other declaratives are declared globally in the DECLARATIVES section, and control may or may not return to the failing statement (Er1)
✅ The declaratives section is separated from the main procedure: Recovery code is declared apart from the normal path
✅ FILE STATUS reports I/O results as data: A file’s FILE STATUS item holds a two-character code that the program can test after each I/O statement
✅ INVALID KEY and AT END put the failure case at the statement: READ ... INVALID KEY ... NOT INVALID KEY and AT END handle the result inside the operation itself
❌ An error need not terminate the program: A declarative can return control after a failure, so a caller cannot rely on termination
⚠️ No value carries the failure: There is no exception object and no result type, so detail travels only through shared items
❌ A fault ends the program: a runtime error abends the program (documented); no recoverable boundary is declared (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency belongs to the transaction monitor: EXEC CICS and IMS link a program to a transaction environment instead of a language thread model
✅ Batch steps are single-threaded by design: A batch program runs to completion without shared-memory concurrency
✅ The 2023 standard defines asynchronous messaging: ISO/IEC 1989:2023 adds asynchronous message handling and transaction processing, so a program need not hand-roll that loop
⚠️ The language has no threads or synchronisation primitives: Any parallel work couples the program to the monitor
⚠️ Shared WORKING-STORAGE across transactions needs external discipline: A pseudo-conversational program must reset its state between transactions



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A large share of production runs on IBM mainframes: Much COBOL executes on z/OS with IBM compilers, so practice is largely one vendor’s (P2)
✅ The language is an ISO standard: ISO/IEC 1989:2023 is the current edition, so the language is not owned by a single vendor
✅ GnuCOBOL is an independent compiler: It is an open-source project separate from GCC and translates COBOL to C
⚠️ Vendor extensions bind a program to a compiler: EXEC CICS, EXEC SQL, and vendor libraries do not compile unchanged elsewhere
⚠️ Newer standard features are unevenly implemented: The 2002 object-oriented features and the 2023 additions are not uniformly available across compilers



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The small standard library is a scope decision: The standard specifies 43 statements, 87 functions, and one class, and adds no general-purpose library beyond them
The fixed reference format comes from the punched card: Columns 1–6 hold a sequence number and column 7 an indicator, and free format is now permitted, so the old constraint is optional
Mainframe batch orientation is a scope decision: COBOL assumes file and transaction processing in a monitor, which suits high-volume work and excludes systems programming
The PICTURE-driven fixed record suits flat files: The declared layout matches a fixed-length record, which is a modelling choice for the domain
The installed base is a business constraint: Retaining legacy programs is an organisational decision, not a property of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled ahead of time to native code: IBM Enterprise COBOL and GnuCOBOL (through generated C) produce machine code, so no interpreter and no JIT warm-up sits on the path
✅ USAGE selects the representation per item: COMP-3 packs two digits per byte where compact storage matters
✅ A batch step amortises start-up over millions of records: One run processes the whole job
⚠️ Tuning is platform-specific: IBM’s optimiser and GnuCOBOL produce different code, so a tuned program does not transfer unchanged
⚠️ Exact decimal arithmetic is slower than binary: COMP-3 operations cost more than native binary arithmetic



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is legacy and vendor-fragmented: IBM, Micro Focus, and GnuCOBOL each supply their own compiler, runtime, and tooling (Ec3)
❌ The mainframe tooling is proprietary: The compilers, monitors, and debuggers are commercial products (Ec4)
✅ GnuCOBOL is open source and maintained: It gives the language a free compiler
✅ A long-lived body of documentation exists: The ISO standard and the vendor manuals are complete and stable over decades
✅ The deployed base is enormous: Gartner reported over 200 billion lines of COBOL in 1997, and the language remains among the most widely deployed
⚠️ The skills base is shrinking: Retirements reduce the pool of maintainers, a risk exposed by the COVID-era unemployment-systems crisis
❌ A load module binds to a runtime release: IBM states that the COBOL Runtime Environment for AIX is required to deploy compiled COBOL applications into production and is ordered separately, and names the AIX releases its generated object programs run on [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The standard is backward compatible across decades: COBOL-74, -85, 2002, 2014, and 2023 code coexist, and programs written decades ago still compile
✅ ISO/IEC 1989:2023 added modern features: Asynchronous messaging, transaction processing, and dynamic-capacity tables join the language
⚠️ Revisions are infrequent: A new standard edition arrives at intervals of a decade or more, so a needed feature waits a long time
⚠️ Adoption of a new feature is uneven: A compiler may not implement a standard feature for years after publication



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Strong lock-in to mainframe transaction and batch processing: The language assumes fixed records, files, and a monitor runtime, so code carries that shape outside its home domain (D1)
✅ Superb for high-volume batch and transaction processing: The fit to financial and administrative workloads is close
✅ Still runs the bulk of card-payment background processing: The source reports COBOL behind most credit and debit-card swipe processing
✅ Fixed-point decimal arithmetic fits money: The data model matches monetary computation without floating-point error
⚠️ Poor for nearly everything else: Interactive, systems, and scientific work have little COBOL tooling



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep in practice: Verbosity and over 300 reserved words must be learned (L1)
✅ The syntax is English-like: MOVE A TO B, ADD ... GIVING, IF ... END-IF, and DISPLAY read close to prose
✅ The division structure is a fixed learning path: Four divisions in a defined order give a predictable place for each declaration
⚠️ The vocabulary is large: More than 300 reserved words, and each verb carries many optional clauses
⚠️ The tooling is not beginner-friendly: Mainframe editors, JCL, and compile procedures are learned separately from the language



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose: Every statement names its verb and its operands, and paragraphs need explicit names (S1)
✅ English-like and self-describing: The verb names the operation, so a statement is readable without symbol decoding
✅ END-IF, END-PERFORM, and END-READ bound a scope: Explicit terminators remove the ambiguity of implicit scope
⚠️ Fixed-format column rules still shape style: Column 7 is an indicator and the code sits in columns 8–72 in the classic reference format, and free format is an option
⚠️ The four-division prologue is long: Even a minimal program declares Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure



1.2.7 Testing

✅ FILE STATUS and INVALID KEY give checkable I/O outcomes: A test can assert on the status item after a file operation
✅ Compilers supply tracing and dump facilities: IBM Debug Tool and GnuCOBOL’s runtime tracing report execution, and COB_SET_TRACE enables a trace at run time
✅ GnuCOBOL runs on ordinary workstations: The open-source compiler executes test jobs locally
⚠️ No test framework is in the language or the standard: A harness is external, so a suite couples to the tooling
⚠️ A batch test needs representative data: The job needs real files and JCL, not just a unit of code
❌ No monotonic reading published in the language: the runtime functions IBM names are the wall, and the standard ships no elapsed reading (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Fixed PICTURE sizes bound every item: An oversized source value is truncated or padded on assignment rather than overrunning a buffer
✅ No pointers in the classic language: A COBOL program cannot forge an address
✅ The transaction monitor authorises access: CICS and RACF check a transaction’s resource use
⚠️ Truncation is silent: A value that does not fit an item is truncated without an error, so data can be lost quietly
⚠️ Dynamic SQL is injectable unless host variables are used: EXEC SQL with host variables is parameterised, but a statement built from a string re-opens SQL injection
❌ Arithmetic on a PICTURE-clause field truncates the high-order digits, defined by ISO COBOL and silent (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the compiler reads: JCL names the datasets for the run, and the compiler validates none of a project’s dependency or version contract (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Copybooks and mainframe artifacts move without signature checks. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to the runtime and tools. (Y16)
⚠️ The copybook library is the shared resource; its registry is the installation.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ DISPLAY is the whole logging surface. (Y6)
❌ Abends produce a dump only where the installation configures one. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the compiler; the mainframe interactive tools are separate products. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs where a COBOL compiler and runtime for the dialect exist. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ ISO/IEC WG4 maintains the standard through an open national-body process. (Y11)
✅ ISO/IEC 2002 (COBOL 2014… the 2023 revision) is published. (Y12)
✅ The NIST conformance suites historically checked COBOL compilers against the standard. (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 125 Languages Through Three Lenses
text:
Analysis date: October 2026. Later general-availability releases are added as they ship and state their own date: TypeScript 7.0 (8 July 2026), Dart 3.13 (12 August 2026), Go 1.27 (19 August 2026), Java 27 (15 September 2026), Rust 1.99 (1 October 2026), and Gleam 1.19 (5 October 2026). Three new families joined in October 2026. Goose (v2026.3, released 21 October 2026), a language whose repository was first published on 28 August 2026 and which sits outside the TIOBE top 50, is assessed against its own release date. So is G# (0.5.212, released 22 October 2026), a .NET language by David Obando whose repository dates to 2019-05-22, sat dormant from 2023-05-19 to 2026-05-17, and has released from v0.1.270 (2026-05-29) on a self-hosted compiler since v0.5.3; it too is assessed against its own release date. So is Kern (1.1.2, released 28 October 2026), a capability-secure backend language stewarded by PUA Group in the Netherlands, whose repository carries a normative specification, signed releases, and no published compiler binary — the installer builds from source; its Core score rests on capability tracking carried in the type (E0404), and its changelog states its own security fixes and known memory-safety defects; it too is assessed against its own release date. Three further families are assessed at a historical release beside their current one: C++98, C++11, and C++23; JavaScript ES5, ES2015, and ES2025; and Python 2.7 with Python 3.14. The older snapshot records the release of its era and states the constructs it did not have; the family’s current page assesses the release named there. The Java line is assessed release by release, from 1.4 through 27: the language releases move the mechanisms, and the runtime-only releases (6, 26, 27) record what changed without moving them. Every other language is evaluated against its latest stable version as of the October 2026 date. The TIOBE top 50 is covered as of October 2026.
Most language comparisons rank languages on adoption, adoption rate, and the feature list. Adoption counts the teams that chose a language. Adoption rate counts how fast that number moves. The feature list counts what a language offers the people who write in it. All three read the language from the side that gains: how many people want it, how quickly that group grows, and how much the language gives them.
This analysis reads the same 125 languages from the side that pays. It asks what a language brings with it when it is used: the agreements the code must keep, the shared resources the code must reach through, and the readiness gaps it leaves in the artifact. Each agreement a mechanism names is charged when it is present. Two facts are recorded and priced nothing: a mechanism whose direction the model cannot fix (V5), and a crossing delivery target whose promise no document decides.
The inversion is deliberate. Adoption and features are the language’s gain. The costs this analysis prices fall on the people who keep the code, and a popularity number does not price them: a demand count says how many teams chose the language, not what the code asks of the people who keep it.
Coupling is the cost that propagates, and accidental coupling is the part of it no requirement asked for. Coupling is access to a shared resource: when the producer of that resource changes, every consumer moves with it. The coupling analysis sets a floor — the shared-resource edges the system genuinely needs — and calls every edge above it a boundary defect or an accidental edge. Necessary coupling is made visible and governed. Accidental coupling is removed. The page develops the distinction below, in A coupling taxonomy: accidental vs. necessary: the accidental kind splits into the coupling a better design removes and the coupling only the language’s own constructs impose. The Core coupling axis prices the part of that list the language imposes: the agreements its own constructs force into ordinary code. The inventory names 43 of them, and an agreement the inventory does not name is not priced.
The model prices a different question: which named agreements a language forces on the code written in it, and which readiness gaps it leaves in the artifact. Its inventory of 99 mechanisms contains no features: the score removes points for a harm that is present, and pays nothing for a language being good at anything. What a change will cost a program, and whether its code is easy to change, stay outside the score.
This analysis examines each language on three scored axes — Core coupling (how much accidental coupling do the language’s own constructs force?), Ecosystem coupling (what do the platform, the tooling, and the release packaging cost?), and engineering readiness (can you rebuild the artifact, verify what you shipped, observe it, work in it quickly, connect it to other languages, and count on its governance?) — plus one unscored profile (what does it cost to run, how well do coding models and agents work in it, and is there a safety-certified path?).

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 125 Languages Through Three Lenses
text:
3 What is coupling?

3.1 A coupling taxonomy: accidental vs. necessary
Coupling falls into two fundamental kinds:








Kind
Definition
Origin




Necessary coupling
Dependencies the system cannot function without — its irreducible coupling floor. The floor is a property of the system and its domain, never of the language, and no score in this analysis measures a distance to it.
Domain artifacts


Accidental coupling
Dependencies that are not causally required — coupling that exists by developer choice, oversight, or language/platform constraint.
Design or platform



In any system, necessary coupling is the minimum possible: the inter-module communication the domain demands. Accidental coupling is everything beyond that — coupling introduced by design choice, oversight, or the language and platform itself. This taxonomy, and the coupling-floor idea it rests on, is developed in the coupling analysis: the definition of coupling as access to a shared resource [11], and the coupling floor as the coupling the domain demands [12].
Accidental coupling subdivides into two subtypes, which are the core of this language analysis:








Subtype
Definition
Fix




Avoidable accidental
Could be removed by better design within the language’s capabilities. The developer chose to couple unnecessarily.
Better design


Language-imposed
Unavoidable given the language’s constructs — the irreducible residuum of accidental coupling the language inflicts on all programs. Even optimal design cannot eliminate it.
Change language or version



A language can also couple elements in dimensions beyond structural dependency. Coupling has several dimensions: structural, temporal, concurrency, security, platform, and language (memory model, type system, module system). Each dimension carries its own dependency relation, and coupling decomposes into necessary and accidental components.
What this means for language comparison: This article evaluates languages along the language coupling dimension: how much language-imposed coupling does the language generate, and how well does it help you detect and eliminate avoidable accidental coupling? A language with a good coupling profile (a) minimizes language-imposed coupling (fewer constructs that force accidental edges) and (b) detects avoidable coupling at the earliest possible stage (compile time > static analysis > runtime > never).
The coupling scores answer: how much agreement does this language force on the code written in it? The readiness score answers a separate question, stated with it below. The profile is not scored. The ranking score is coupling, lifted by at most 15% for readiness — coupling is primary, because the code is what remains and readiness is remediable by process. The rule is stated on the Scoring Model.

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 125 Languages Through Three Lenses
section: 4 How the Scores Are Computed: Methodology
text:
4 How the Scores Are Computed: Methodology
Every language imposes some amount of accidental coupling that even optimal design cannot eliminate. Headers force compilation coupling. Unchecked null forces null-check coupling. A global interpreter lock forces concurrency coupling. Dynamic typing forces coupling detection to runtime. These are not design mistakes — they are language properties.
The scores in this analysis are computed by a fixed, mechanical rule, not by subjective impression:

A closed mechanism inventory — each coupling mechanism has a fixed weight.
A binary presence check — for each language, each mechanism is marked present or absent (a factual determination, not a severity judgment).
An arithmetic rule — the present weights are summed, and the axis score is 100 × (1 − present weight ÷ inventory weight), the share of the axis inventory the language forces.

Because the weights are fixed and the only per-language step is present/absent, any two analysts following these rules reach identical scores. The framework makes disagreement precise: to dispute a score, you must either contest a mechanism’s presence in a specific language, or propose changing a fixed weight and then recompute.
The full mechanism inventory (Core coupling: Type, Construction, Memory, Error, Concurrency, Platform; Ecosystem coupling: Performance, Ecosystem, Evolution, Domain, Learning, Syntax, Testing, Security; Engineering readiness: Reproducibility, Supply chain, Observability, Feedback, Interop, Governance), the detailed severity-share rule, and the tests that decide presence are on The Scoring Model. The ranked tables, the per-dimension sub-scores, and the complete per-language mechanism-presence data for all 125 languages — so any score can be reproduced from first principles — are on The Scoreboard.
What each mechanism means — what it is, what it forces to agree, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — is explained mechanism by mechanism, with examples, in the Criteria.
Three scores, not one. The comparison reports Core coupling (what the language’s own constructs force), Ecosystem coupling (what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost), and Engineering readiness (whether the artifact can be rebuilt, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to another language, and governed openly). The three scores are reported separately and are never summed. They are correlated in practice — a missing package registry affects both Ecosystem coupling and the supply chain — but each is scored on its own axis. Alongside them, an unscored profile records three axes a score cannot price — energy and cost, AI and agent readiness, and safety certification — language by language.

4.1 What the coupling score means
Because the model is a fixed inventory scored by severity share, the bands are thresholds over that share:

90+: under 10 points of cost — on Core, under 36 raw weight, usually in one dimension.
75–89: 10 to 25 points — on Core, 36 to 88 raw weight, across a few dimensions.
60–74: 25 to 40 points — on Core, 88 to 140 raw weight.
45–59: 40 to 55 points — on Core, 140 to 192 raw weight.
below 45: over 55 points of cost — on Core, over 192 raw weight; five or six dimensions carry a priced mechanism, and at least four reach 15 in raw weight. The language’s design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).

Five snapshots reach the 90+ band today — Rocq 95.7, Unison 95.4, Lean 4 94.6, Haskell 92.0, and Gleam 90.9. Rust 1.96 and Rust 1.99 sit at 89.7, PureScript at 88.9, and SPARK at 85.4, just below. None reaches 100: every language carries at least one priced mechanism, and the gap to 100 is the progression margin left to language design.


4.2 What the readiness score means
The readiness score uses the same arithmetic over its six dimensions, the same three tiers, and the same bands. Every readiness mechanism is priced by breadth, escape, and silence exactly as a coupling mechanism is: a readiness gap that runs across the whole artifact, that the team cannot close locally, and that nothing in the language records is High. Its inventory therefore totals 171 points, and its scores move in the same fractional steps as Core. A readiness band is still not comparable to a coupling band, because the two axes price different kinds of cost. The readiness bands are listed with the coupling bands under “By Score” below, and on the Scoreboard.

text:
7 The Verdict: Coupling Edition
Ranked by Core coupling from the model (severity share per axis); the numbers behind every grouping below are on the Scoreboard. Analysis date October 2026 — older versions of the same language can score significantly lower (e.g., C++98, Java 8).
If you need mathematical proof of correctness: Rocq, SPARK, Lean 4
If you want bulletproof low coupling by language design: Unison, Rocq, Rust, SQL
If you want low coupling with pragmatism: Haskell, PureScript, Zig, OCaml
If you want low coupling with discipline (modern versions): Elixir, Erlang, Clojure, Transact-SQL, Dart, Kotlin, Delphi, Go
Low coupling on a budget (ecosystem-driven): Tcl, F#, Scala, C++
Specialized excellence (unique coupling profiles): Erlang: Actor model with per-process isolation and let-it-crash. Elixir: Modern BEAM with macros and protocols. Julia: Multiple dispatch without inheritance. Eiffel: Design by Contract states each routine’s obligations in the source. Objective-C: Dynamic messaging plus categories, protocols, and blocks for decoupling. Turbo Pascal: Units give genuine interface/implementation separation rare among 1980s languages.
Domain-locked procedural database logic: PL/SQL, PL/pgSQL, SQL PL, SAP ASE, and Transact-SQL couple all logic to their database engines but offer real encapsulation (packages, modules, stored procedures). Structured exceptions are the norm, but SAP ASE’s Transact-SQL dialect carries no TRY ... CATCH, so its failure path is @@error checks. SAS uniquely separates the DATA step from PROC steps. Use them only where the logic must live inside the database or analytics engine.
Lowest forced coupling:

Rocq: Machine-checked proof as the unit of development
Unison: Content-addressed code, algebraic effects, distributed computing built-in
Rust: Ownership enforces separation, Result types compose, no null, traits decouple
Lean 4: Dependent types over a small trusted kernel
SPARK: A proved Ada subset, so the proof is part of the build

Low coupling with pragmatism (latest versions):

Haskell: Type classes, explicit effects, immutability
PureScript: Effect system separates effect types
Zig: Explicit everything, error unions, allocator parameters, comptime
OCaml: Module system, immutable data, exhaustive pattern matching

Highest forced coupling:

Assembly: No abstractions, manual everything, maximum coupling risk
C: Manual memory, weak typing, global state, undefined behavior
Perl: Dynamic, global state, primitive objects, GIL
JavaScript: Dynamic, global state, unchecked errors, no types
Ruby: Dynamic, global state, metaprogramming everywhere
PHP: Dynamic, weak typing, superglobals, no concurrency
TypeScript: JavaScript’s runtime coupling under a compile-time type layer

Neither helps nor hinders coupling:

C: With discipline, coupling can be low; without it, coupling is extreme
D: Better C++ with cleaner templates, contracts, and both GC and manual memory

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 125 Languages Through Three Lenses
text:
8 The Real Truth
Coupling scores depend heavily on which version of a language you’re using. C++23 is a fundamentally different language from C++98. Java 26 with records, sealed classes, and virtual threads is not the same as Java 8. Always check the version baseline.
Version aside, Coupling scores don’t determine project success. Context matters:

Team expertise trumps language coupling score
Ecosystem maturity often beats language elegance
Hiring availability is a real constraint
Performance requirements eliminate choices
Platform constraints narrow the field

But here’s what coupling analysis reveals:
Languages with proven separation (Lean 4, Rocq, SPARK) let a machine check a claim against a stated specification. The remaining risk moves to the specification, and the learning curve is steep.
Languages with enforced separation (Rust, Haskell, PureScript, OCaml) make coupling impossible to hide. You pay upfront in learning curve, gain long-term in maintainability.
Languages with optional separation (Swift, Kotlin, C#, modern Java, modern C++, Eiffel, Groovy) let you choose coupling level. Good for migration, requires discipline.
Languages with manual separation (C, D, Zig, COBOL, Turbo Pascal) put the separation burden on the programmer: the same language supports a carefully separated design and a tangled one. Expertise required.
Languages with runtime-only separation (JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Ruby, shells, VBScript) defer most coupling detection to testing. TypeScript moves a share of that detection to compile time, but its runtime coupling is JavaScript’s. Python 3.14 (free-threaded), PHP 8.4 (property hooks, fibers), and Ruby 4.0 (YJIT, pattern matching) have all made meaningful coupling-separation progress in recent versions.
Languages with domain-locked separation (Objective-C, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, SAS, Solidity) are coupled to a single platform or domain — the platform is the unit boundary, and the language’s coupling quality only matters within it.
One result worth stating plainly: the type layer now moves the number. TypeScript scores above JavaScript, because the type layer removes T1, T4, T5, and T10 and leaves T7: JavaScript carries T1, T3, T4, T5, T10, T12, T13, and T14; TypeScript carries T3, T7, T12, T13, and T14. JavaScript carries 59 Type severity points against TypeScript’s 40 — 19 raw points, worth 5.4 Core points — and TypeScript also drops M3, so the two snapshots sit 8.9 Core points apart: 54.0 against 62.9. The presence lists still carry the detail.
The lesson: Match language coupling capabilities to your context AND your version. C++23 with modern idioms is a different beast from C++98. Java 26 with virtual threads, records, and sealed classes is not Java 8. Don’t pick a language based on its worst version. Building life-critical systems? Use SPARK or Lean 4. Building a 20-year system with changing requirements? Invest in Rust. Building mobile apps? Swift or Kotlin. Building a weekend project? JavaScript is fine. Maintaining legacy code? TypeScript adds compile-time detection incrementally, though its runtime coupling is JavaScript’s. Need shell automation? PowerShell adds objects, Fish adds interactive polish, and Bash stays the portable default.
No language is best in every context. The scores show where a language matches your constraints and where it will charge you; design covers the rest.
The evidence points away from a single winner: different contexts need different coupling trade-offs, and the scores price them.
The scores are a starting point. The design work is yours.

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 125 Languages Through Three Lenses
text:
9 Learn More
The coupling account this analysis rests on is developed in the published coupling papers:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access [11] defines coupling as access to a shared resource, with the resource taxonomy and the three coupling modes.
A Self-Contained Derivation of the Optimal Modularization from Coupling [13] derives the modularisation directive from the coupling account alone.
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling [12] establishes the coupling floor and shows that correctly bounded coupling is a consequence of cohesion.

The link to knowledge — why a language that scatters or hides a module’s knowledge imposes coupling — is the knowledge-embodiment theorem: a maximally cohesive module embodies exactly the knowledge its class must hold. The theorem is developed in On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule [14], with the causal grounding in Causal Cohesion [15].

Which language’s coupling analysis surprised you? Which mechanisms did the analysis miss? Share your experience in the comments.

text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ladder Logic in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 69.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68.0/100 · Engineering readiness 32.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ The type is a PLC data type: BOOL, INT, and REAL are checked by the vendor compiler (T2)
❌ There are no sum types (T4)
❌ There are no generics (T5)
❌ There is no namespace: A global tag shares one controller-wide space, and a POU’s local variables are the only scope (T6)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ The I/O image is global: Every rung reads and writes the same process image (C1)
❌ A tag is writable from any rung (C2)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ There is no scope-exit release: A resource is a coil or an instruction the scan resets (M3)
❌ There is no ownership model: A tag is shared by every rung (M4)



1.1.4 Error

❌ A fault bit is the failure path: The program checks a bit, and no structure carries the failure (Er1)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The scan is the only thread: One pass reads the inputs, executes the rungs, and writes the outputs (K1)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A program runs on one controller family: The vendor’s runtime and I/O modules are the platform (P1)
✅ The standard is published: IEC 61131-3 defines the languages and the program model, and the text is sold by the IEC
❌ Ordinary application work is out of reach: There is no file, socket, or heap (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The rung is the program: A network of contacts and coils over one memory map
The scan is the contract: The cycle time bounds every response
The vendor is the platform: A project, a runtime, and an I/O module set come from one supplier
The standard is shared, the implementations are not: A program does not move between vendors




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A scan completes in a bounded time: The cycle is deterministic



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The toolchain is proprietary: A vendor sells the IDE and the runtime (Ec4)
❌ The IDE is locked to the vendor: A project does not move between vendors unchanged (Ec5)
❌ A controller runs a program for decades: The installed base keeps old firmware (Ec7)
❌ A compiled PLC library binds to a version: Beckhoff ships libraries as *.compiled-library with a four-part version, increments the major digit when a new version is incompatible with the previous one, and fixes the version a project uses when the configuration activates on the target [5], [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: The third edition is from 2013 (V4)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is industrial control: A machine, a line, or a process (D1)
❌ The scan and the I/O image set the architecture: A network of rungs over a fixed memory map (D3)



1.2.5 Learning

✅ An electrician reads a rung: The notation mirrors a relay circuit



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The notation is graphical and verbose: A network of contacts and coils (S1)



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The IDE simulates the controller: A rung is forced and watched



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ A tag has no access control inside the program
❌ IEC 61131-3 integer types wrap modulo the declared width, the scan cycle never seeing the carry (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ A project is downloaded to a controller: The artifact is a vendor project file (Y1)
❌ A dependency is a firmware version: Nothing in the program pins it (Y2)

❌ There is no portable target: A program runs on one controller family (Y10)

❌ Semantics rest on the standard-plus-vendor pair: the IEC standard enumerates implementation-dependent behavior, and no published conformance suite runs against the vendor’s runtime (Y17)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ No independent energy or time benchmark for the language is recorded.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse public training data: models write it less reliably than a mainstream language [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Scheme (R7RS)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Scheme in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 70.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 92.2/100 · Engineering readiness 42.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static type check: A binding has no declared type and a call is resolved when it runs, so a type error is reported at run time rather than at load time (T1)
❌ Dispatch is dynamic: An application checks its argument count and its operands’ types when it executes, so an over-application or an under-application is an error then (T3)
❌ No sum types and no generics in the core: An alternative is a tagged list whose tag the code must test by hand, and a reusable procedure accepts any object and documents its expectation in a comment (T4, T5)
⚠️ + and the other arithmetic procedures are ordinary bindings: A redefinition changes what (+ a b) means, so an expression can invoke code the syntax does not show (T8)
✅ Hygienic macros decouple a macro from its use site: syntax-rules renames the identifiers a template introduces, so a macro cannot accidentally capture a name from the caller
✅ Lexical scope is one small rule: A lambda binds its parameters and its internal definitions, and nothing else is visible



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors are ordinary procedures: A record constructor or a lambda that returns a list is built with the same mechanism, so construction does not couple to a class system
✅ define-record-type declares the shape once: The R7RS form generates the constructor, the type predicate, and the field accessors from one declaration
✅ Proper tail recursion is a language guarantee: A tail call reuses the current frame, so a loop written as a tail-recursive procedure runs in constant stack space
✅ let confines a binding to its body: A construction can build its state inside a let and expose only what it returns
⚠️ set! lets a construction mutate a captured binding: A closure can change state that its caller still holds, so a value built by a procedure is not automatically immutable
⚠️ A plain program has one top-level environment: R7RS define-library with explicit export confines a set of bindings, but a program’s top-level defines share a single scope
❌ One value, many names: pairs are shared, and set! mutates every name that reaches the cell (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ A garbage collector reclaims memory: The implementation chooses the collector, and the program cannot free an object or predict when it dies (M2)
❌ No RAII or scope-exit destructor: A resource is released by an explicit call, and dynamic-wind can wrap that call in a dynamic extent, but nothing runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow model: A reference is an untracked alias, and the collector alone knows when an object is unreachable (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: There is no free operation in the language, so a program cannot release a live object by mistake
✅ dynamic-wind binds a release to the dynamic extent: Its after thunk runs on every exit, including a non-local one
✅ R7RS pairs acquisition with release in the common cases: call-with-port, with-input-from-file, and with-output-to-file close what they open
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: recursion crashes the implementation below the handler surface (the implementation’s stack is not a declared failure) (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ A failure is raised and is not described by a signature: A procedure promises nothing about the conditions it may raise, so the failure set is not readable from the call (Er2)
✅ guard gives a structured handler: An R7RS guard clause names a condition and a recovery expression, and the handler returns a value to the guard
✅ with-exception-handler installs a handler for a dynamic extent: The handler is bound where it is installed, not at the raise point
✅ Condition types form a small hierarchy: error-object?, file-error?, and read-error? distinguish a raise by kind
✅ error carries a message and irritants: The offending values travel with the condition
⚠️ raise and raise-continuable differ: A non-continuable raise does not return to the raise point, so a handler must transfer control explicitly
❌ A fault ends the program: the standard leaves toplevel recovery to the implementation and declares no recoverable unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The core defines no shared-memory concurrency: R7RS specifies no threads, so the standard makes no promise about a race the language does not create
✅ Continuations separate control flow from the call stack: call/cc captures the current continuation as a procedure, so a coroutine, a generator, or a backtracking search is a library over it
⚠️ Parallelism is an implementation extension: SRFI-18 supplies threads and SRFI-21 supplies synchronisation, and an implementation may support neither
⚠️ A thread extension fixes no memory model: SRFI-18 defines a mutex and a condition variable, but the report it extends states no ordering guarantee for a shared object
✅ A cooperative scheduler is expressible in the language: A queue of continuations plus a trampoline gives green threads without a runtime thread



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No single implementation owns the language: The language is a published report, and Chez, Guile, Racket, CHICKEN, Gambit, MIT, and Chibi all implement it
✅ define-library is the portability unit: An R7RS library with explicit import and export moves between implementations with its source
✅ The core is small enough for a small runtime: The report’s language fits a microcontroller interpreter and an embeddable one
✅ A program runs under several evaluation strategies: A compiler such as Chez and a simple interpreter both accept the report’s subset
⚠️ The standard is a family of reports, not one: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS are not fully compatible, so the name “Scheme” alone does not say which report a program targets
⚠️ The library set beyond R7RS-small is the implementation’s: Each dialect ships a different collection, so portability in practice follows the chosen implementation



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The minimalist core is a deliberate trade: The report defines a small language and leaves libraries to the SRFIs, so a program chooses its extensions
The report split is a standards history: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS followed a disagreement about how large the language should be
Dynamic typing is a design choice: No type declaration is required, so the discipline is the programmer’s
call/cc is a powerful and uncommon operator: Full continuations make control flow harder to reason about, and the expressiveness is the return
The REPL-first workflow is a choice: A program is developed at the prompt, which suits exploration and is not required by the language
Niche adoption is a scope outcome: The language targets education and research rather than industry




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Native compilers are available: Chez Scheme, Gambit, and CHICKEN compile Scheme to native code, so a program need not be interpreted
✅ The core is small enough to compile well: A compiler sees the whole language, so a straightforward optimiser covers it
✅ Tail calls do not consume stack: A recursive loop compiles to a jump
✅ Numeric code is fast in the strong implementations: A fixnum loop compiles to machine operations when the compiler proves the operands are fixnums
⚠️ Performance varies significantly by implementation: The same program can be fast under Chez and much slower under a simple interpreter
⚠️ A dynamically typed call is a checked call: The compiler inserts checks the program did not write, and their cost depends on how well it can eliminate them



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and spread over implementations: R7RS-small ships no library set, and the shared material is the SRFI collection plus each implementation’s own packages (Ec3)
✅ The SRFIs are a portable library standard: A program requests a library by number, and an implementation reports the SRFIs it supports
✅ The implementation distributions are mature and maintained: Guile, Chez, Racket, Gambit, and CHICKEN are long-lived projects with their own package collections
✅ snow and the implementation indexes collect R7RS libraries: A portable library can be published for several implementations at once
⚠️ Package management is implementation-specific: raco pkg, chicken-install, and Guix each serve one dialect, and the report fixes no package manager
⚠️ A library that uses a dialect extension is not portable: A program written against one implementation’s collection usually needs editing for another



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ SRFIs extend the language without changing the report: A new facility arrives as a numbered request, and each implementation adopts it independently
✅ A program written to R7RS-small keeps its meaning: The small report is stable, so its subset does not move under the program
✅ define-library localises a change to its importers: An exported name is the interface, and a change inside a library is invisible to the code that imports it
⚠️ Three reports are in circulation and they differ: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS disagree on libraries, on the details of syntax-rules, and on some standard procedures
⚠️ An improvement reaches a program when an implementation adopts it: There is no single body that ships the language, so the timing is the implementation’s decision



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent as a teaching language: A dozen special forms cover the core, and SICP uses the language as a complete course
✅ Excellent for programming-language research: A small core with hygienic macros and first-class continuations is a substrate for experiments
✅ A real scripting and extension language: Guile is the extension language of GNU packages, including the Guix package manager
✅ Embedding is a real use: A small Scheme interpreter is embedded in applications for configuration and scripting
⚠️ Commercial application work is rare: Adoption is niche, so a team that picks Scheme for a product finds few precedents



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The distinctive abstractions take real effort: call/cc, continuation-passing style, and hygienic macro writing are each a skill that takes time (L1)
✅ The core is small enough to learn quickly: The special forms are few, and a complete course in them exists
✅ A REPL returns the value immediately: The read-eval-print loop gives feedback on each expression
✅ The report is precise about the language it defines: The specification states the required behaviour of each procedure
⚠️ The report is a specification, not a tutorial: A beginner needs a text such as SICP alongside it
⚠️ A continuation is easy to use outside its intended extent: Control that re-enters a captured continuation can surprise the programmer



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is uniform: A program is a sequence of S-expressions, so there is almost no grammar to learn
✅ Prefix notation removes precedence rules: (+ 1 (* 2 3)) states the order in brackets, so no operator-precedence table is needed
✅ Quasiquotation makes a template readable: `(a ,b ,@c) builds a list with holes at the point of use
✅ The reader recognises the literal syntaxes directly: #\a is a character, #(1 2) is a vector, and #; comments out the next datum
✅ A macro can add a readable form: define-syntax with syntax-rules introduces surface syntax without changing the core
⚠️ A deeply nested expression needs the editor’s indentation: The reader balances the brackets, and the human eye follows the layout



1.2.7 Testing

✅ SRFI-64 defines a portable test framework: test-begin, test-equal, and test-end run under any implementation that supports the SRFI
✅ error makes a check cheap to write: (unless test (error "..." x)) fails a check and reports the offending value
✅ The REPL is the first test loop: An expression is evaluated and its value is compared at the prompt
✅ The implementation supplies a tracer and a debugger: Chez, Guile, and Racket each expose a trace facility and an inspector
⚠️ No test framework is in the standard: A project depends on its implementation’s SRFI coverage rather than on the report
⚠️ A test exercises the paths it runs: An unexecuted branch is unchecked, and a dynamic error in it appears only when the branch is reached
❌ No monotonic reading published: the standard’s current-second is the wall; the program’s durations have no published clock (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ The implementation manages memory: The language exposes no pointer and no manual free, so a buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Scheme source
✅ Hygienic macros remove a class of capture defect: A macro cannot bind a name it did not intend to bind
✅ The core has no unsafe memory operation: The report defines no pointer arithmetic and no address
⚠️ eval and read execute data as code: (eval (read port)) runs whatever the input contains, so untrusted input must never reach it
⚠️ A continuation can cross an intended check: A continuation captured before a permission test can be re-entered after it
⚠️ A foreign-function interface leaves the safe subset: An FFI in an implementation reaches native code, and the memory-safety guarantee stops there
