1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the implementation reads: the R7RS import system names libraries, not versions, and no machine-read manifest ships (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Scheme library channels carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The library registries are flat name spaces. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Scheme libraries. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ display and write carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ An error lands in the REPL with no post-mortem artifact. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the standard toolchain. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs where its implementation runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Scheme Steering Committee runs the process in the open. (Y11)
✅ The R7RS-small report is published. (Y12)
✅ The R6RS test suite is published for independent implementations. (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Scheme’s minimalist, orthogonal core keeps language-imposed coupling low, and its platform cost is moderate. Proper tail recursion removes stack growth from a recursive loop, hygienic macros prevent name capture, first-class continuations separate control flow from the call stack, and define-library confines a set of bindings behind explicit exports. The core score is held down by dynamic typing, absent sum types and generics, garbage-collected memory with no ownership model or RAII, and unchecked exceptions. Main weakness: the ecosystem is small and the standard is fragmented across R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS.

title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server 2022)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Transact-SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 84.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 55.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and column has a declared type, and a block that violates it fails at parse or bind time
✅ Table variables and table-valued parameters carry a declared row type: DECLARE @t TABLE (...) and a user-defined table type pass a typed row set between units
✅ A procedure parameter declares its type and direction: @p int OUTPUT fixes the type and the direction, so a caller binds to a signature
⚠️ DECLARE @name defaults to NULL (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, so an unassigned variable is valid and propagates NULL into the expression
⚠️ NULL comparison needs three-valued logic: With ANSI_NULLS ON (the default, and the only supported setting since SQL Server 2017), @x = NULL is unknown, so a check needs IS NULL
⚠️ sql_variant is the one escape hatch: A column or variable of sql_variant holds values of different base types, and every consumer must discover the stored base type at run time



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A stored procedure provides modularity with a declared interface: CREATE PROCEDURE names the unit, its parameters, and its result, and can return a status value and OUTPUT parameters
✅ A view or an inline table-valued function separates consumers from the query: The exposed relation is stable while its defining query can change
✅ A table-valued parameter passes a row set without a shared temporary table: A user-defined table type plus a TVP parameter removes the need for a global temporary table
✅ Set-based statements compose without a cursor: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM, and MERGE express the whole transformation in one statement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: An AFTER or INSTEAD OF trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Session SET options change the meaning of a statement: ANSI_NULLS and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER are captured when a stored procedure is created, while DATEFORMAT applies when the statement runs, so the same text can parse or convert differently elsewhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The SQL Server buffer pool and the query workspace own the memory, and a batch never names an address
✅ The server grants memory to a query: The query’s memory grant comes from the server’s calculator or the Resource Governor, so the batch does not request bytes
✅ Buffer pool and tempdb behaviour are server configuration: max server memory, the tempdb files, and a Resource Governor pool are settings, not batch properties
⚠️ A sort or hash can spill to tempdb: An operation whose grant is too small writes to tempdb, which costs I/O even though the language hides allocation
⚠️ A cursor allocates per fetch: A row-by-row cursor uses workspace per fetch, so the memory pattern follows the loop



1.1.4 Error

✅ TRY ... CATCH gives a structured path: The CATCH block runs on error and exposes ERROR_NUMBER, ERROR_MESSAGE, ERROR_SEVERITY, and ERROR_LINE
✅ THROW and RAISERROR raise with a number and a message: THROW 50001, 'msg', 1 carries a number, so a handler can branch on it
✅ XACT_STATE() and @@TRANCOUNT tell the handler whether the transaction is committable: A doomed transaction is detectable inside CATCH
⚠️ Errors ignored or non-exhaustive (Er3): A CATCH block that swallows the error, or a skipped @@ERROR check, lets the batch continue past the failure
⚠️ Errors do not abort the batch by default: Without SET XACT_ABORT ON, a statement error rolls back that statement and the batch continues
⚠️ Severity decides whether the caller sees the error: A low-severity error is informational, so the same statement text can pass a caller by



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one
✅ Isolation levels are selectable and versioned: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, and SERIALIZABLE, while the database options READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT and ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION switch READ COMMITTED to row versioning and enable SNAPSHOT
✅ Snapshot isolation removes reader–writer blocking: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON, a reader uses row versions and does not block a writer
✅ Set-based statements reduce explicit locking: One UPDATE moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): SET options, CONTEXT_INFO, and a global temporary table ##t are visible to code the caller did not write
⚠️ A locking hint couples the query to the engine’s concurrency model: WITH (NOLOCK), UPDLOCK, and READPAST are engine-shaped and must agree with the application’s lock ordering



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Client interfaces are standard: ODBC, JDBC, OLE DB, and ADO.NET reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol
✅ Bulk interfaces are documented: bcp and BULK INSERT use a documented format, so data exchange is not tied to an application API
⚠️ Two implementations exist under separate vendors: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP ASE share a lineage and a core syntax, but the two diverge, and Microsoft and SAP document them separately
⚠️ Azure SQL is the same vendor with a different deployment: The managed service changes availability, administration, and some features, so code targets a specific surface
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): The language needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE
❌ The T-SQL surface is engine-specific: TOP, IDENTITY, GO, the sys catalog views, and the sp_ procedures are SQL Server features, so a port to another engine is a rewrite



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: Keeping a rule in the database guarantees it for every writer; the cost is that the rule now deploys and versions with the schema rather than with the application
A cursor is a deliberate trade for row-by-row work: It makes a per-row algorithm expressible, at the cost of the set-based model
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible query: sp_executesql and EXEC reach constructs a static statement cannot name; the cost is that the statement’s shape is known only when it runs
NOLOCK trades consistency for concurrency: A reader that accepts dirty reads avoids blocking




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A cost-based optimiser with a plan cache executes a statement: A procedure’s plan can be reused, so the caller does not choose an access path
✅ A columnstore index and batch mode scan analytically: CREATE COLUMNSTORE INDEX plus batch mode processes a large scan in vectorised batches
✅ Query Store records plans and regressions: An operator can see a plan change and force a previous plan
✅ In-memory OLTP tables are lock-free and memory-optimised: MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON tables and natively compiled procedures remove latch contention
⚠️ Parameter sniffing can choose a plan for the wrong input: A cached plan built for one parameter value can be poor for another
⚠️ A plan can regress without a query change: New statistics, a version upgrade, or a changed data volume can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Tooling is mature and first-party: SQL Server Management Studio, Azure Data Studio, and sqlcmd cover administration and query work
✅ The market and the hiring pool are large: SQL Server is widely deployed in Microsoft environments, so documentation, training, and consultants are abundant
✅ Cloud deployment is a first-party service: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance run the same engine with a managed administration model
❌ Proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Microsoft (and, for ASE, from SAP) under licence
⚠️ The ASE toolchain is separate from the SQL Server toolchain: SAP maintains its own documentation, tools, and support, so knowledge does not transfer freely



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The release cadence is regular and active: SQL Server ships a major release periodically, and Azure SQL receives continuous updates
✅ A compatibility level keeps old behaviour: A database at an older compatibility level keeps the older optimiser and syntax behaviour while the engine is upgraded
✅ The engine leads the standard: TRY ... CATCH, MERGE, window functions, and JSON support arrived as engine features, so users get them without waiting for the standard
⚠️ A deprecated feature is warned and then removed: The documentation lists deprecated features, and an upgrade can require edits
⚠️ Feature availability differs by edition and deployment: An Enterprise feature or an Azure-only feature may not exist on a local Standard edition



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for transactional and analytical logic in the database: A stored procedure runs beside the data with a plan and a transaction
✅ One language spans OLTP and analytics: Set-based DML, window functions, and a columnstore scan all live in the same language
✅ The surrounding pipeline is first-party: Integration Services, the Agent scheduler, and Reporting Services cover the rest of a data workflow
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists inside SQL Server or SAP ASE, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
⚠️ Procedural row logic reads poorly: A row-by-row algorithm in a cursor is verbose and slow beside its set-based equivalent
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: The language assumes a SQL Server database and a set-based workload



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a SQL developer: A procedure with BEGIN ... END, TRY ... CATCH, and SELECT ... INTO is readable to anyone who knows SQL
✅ Documentation and examples are complete: The Microsoft T-SQL reference documents every statement with examples
⚠️ The procedural and the set-based model coexist: A developer must choose between a cursor and a set-based statement, and the wrong choice shows up as a performance problem
⚠️ NULL handling must be learned: With ANSI_NULLS ON, = NULL never matches, and a comparison with NULL yields unknown
⚠️ Plan and locking behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Performance work means reading plans and lock waits rather than syntax
⚠️ The SAP ASE dialect diverges in details: Differences in GO, IDENTITY, and built-in functions mean knowledge transfers only in part



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE and BEGIN ... END read close to English
✅ A procedure is a readable unit: The parameter list, the body, and the RETURN value are declared in one CREATE PROCEDURE statement
✅ GO marks a batch boundary in a script: The client tool sends the batch, so the boundary is visible in the source
⚠️ SET options prefix every script: SET NOCOUNT ON, ANSI_NULLS ON, and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON are usually written at the top, so the boilerplate grows
⚠️ @ and @@ distinguish kinds of variable by convention: A local variable, a parameter, and a global function share the sigil, so a reader distinguishes them by spelling
⚠️ Identifier quoting depends on a setting: [name] and "name" both quote an identifier, and the second form needs QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON



1.2.7 Testing

✅ tSQLt is the established framework: An open-source unit-test framework runs test classes with mocked tables and assertions
✅ TRY ... CATCH makes a unit test expressible in the language: A test procedure asserts and THROWs on a mismatch
✅ A transaction wraps a test and rolls it back: The database is unchanged after the test
✅ Error metadata supports an assertion on a failure path: ERROR_NUMBER and ERROR_MESSAGE inside CATCH let a test check the rejection
⚠️ No test framework ships with the toolchain (G1): SSMS and sqlcmd provide no assertion or runner, so a suite depends on tSQLt or a hand-rolled harness
⚠️ A server-side suite needs a server: The harness needs a SQL Server instance, so the tests couple to infrastructure
❌ No monotonic reading published: GETDATE and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are wall readings (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ sp_executesql with parameters removes the injection surface: EXEC sp_executesql N'SELECT ... WHERE x = @p', N'@p int', @p = 1 passes the value out of band
✅ GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE with roles express least privilege: Access is declared per object, per schema, and per role
✅ Row-level security limits what a statement can see: A SECURITY POLICY with a predicate function filters rows by the caller’s identity
✅ EXECUTE AS makes the effective identity explicit: A procedure can run as its owner or as a named user
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): A statement built with EXEC (@sql) from concatenated input lets the input become code
⚠️ Dynamic SQL and owner-rights execution re-open the risk: EXEC on a built string, sp_OA* procedures, and xp_cmdshell where enabled defeat parameterisation

Verdict: Transact-SQL’s coupling follows its host engine. Stored procedures, views, and table-valued parameters give real modularity, TRY ... CATCH gives a structured failure path, and the optimiser, Query Store, columnstore, and in-memory OLTP carry performance work. Main strengths: a mature first-party toolchain, a regular release cadence, and standard client interfaces. Main weaknesses: the language only runs on SQL Server or SAP ASE, the useful surface is engine-specific, NULL starts in every declared variable, an unhandled CATCH continues the batch, cursor code paths are slow, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard.

title: Teradata SPL (Database Engine 20)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Teradata SPL (Database Engine 20) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 38.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL is a member of every domain: procedure parameters, locals, and warehouse columns carry NULL unannounced, and no signature states whether a value may be absent (T10)
⚠️ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column, a status value, or a separate procedure, and the caller learns the encoding by reading the body
❌ Statements state no effect: a procedure that loads tables, calls macros, and logs looks like any other in the DBC catalog (T12)
❌ C and Java ride the boundary: external stored procedures bind compiled code through declared signatures, and the agreement on layout and error convention is checked by neither side’s compiler (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The procedure is one block: CREATE PROCEDURE gathers DECLARE, flow, and SQL into one unit the database compiles into the catalog
⚠️ Macros sit beside procedures: an EXEC macro is a parameterized SQL batch with no flow at all, and the boundary between the two unit kinds is a design decision the language does not guide



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the engine’s: spool, AMP memory, and cursor state live in the database processes, and the procedure text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ The handler decides, or the request aborts: DECLARE … HANDLER routes conditions and SQLSTATE codes, RESIGNAL re-raises, and without a handler the failure ends the request — no value carries it (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception, results by OUT parameters and DYNAMIC RESULT SETS cursors, and neither composes through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session state is shared: volatile tables and session-scoped cursor results are visible across every procedure the session calls, and the engine’s workload management arbitrates the rest (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The procedure runs only in Teradata: the parser, the DBC dictionary, and the AMP architecture are the engine’s, and nothing in the language runs without a Vantage system (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside warehouse work: the language has no libraries or data abstraction beyond tables, so application logic builds every abstraction itself inside the warehouse (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic inside the warehouse: procedures remove client round trips and run under the engine’s workload management, and the price is application logic whose deploy, version, and license story is the platform’s
Result sets by cursor contract: DYNAMIC RESULT SETS returns cursors to callers through the standard CLI, and the price is that the result shape is a cursor convention, not a type
Macros and procedures share the stage: the same logic can live as a flowless macro or a procedural block, and the price is a design decision the language documents but does not settle
The engine line is a ratchet: 17.20’s announced end of life funnels deployments to Engine 20’s parity path, and the price is an upgrade calendar set by the vendor




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ EXPLAIN is the ordinary tool: the engine publishes the plan of any request, procedure statements included, and the docs treat it as the baseline cost instrument



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A niche commercial ecosystem: expertise and tooling concentrate in enterprise warehouse shops, and the license terms govern every deployment (Ec3)
❌ A proprietary stack: the engine, the tooling, and the support model are Teradata commercial products (Ec4)



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ The engine line turned over: Database Engine 20 replaces the 17.20 line (end of life announced for 2027), and deployments plan around the parity-and-upgrade path the release notes describe



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists to serve the warehouse: procedures, macros, and external routines deploy into the DBC catalog, and the workload management and storage model define what they can say (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ Warehouse concepts before syntax: AMP distribution, spool, and workload management decide whether a procedure performs, and the SPL book assumes that layer



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Standard-shaped, Teradata-flavored: statements read like ISO SQL, and DYNAMIC RESULT SETS, volatile tables, and macro calls are the engine’s own layer on top



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user procedures: the documented testing story is application-side tests against a live system, with EXPLAIN as the only published instrument (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and PREPARE run text assembled at run time, so concatenated user input reaches the parser, and the mitigation is the privilege model plus USING inputs (Q3)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A procedure is stored source: the same body on the same engine version and data reproduces the same result, and nothing is compiled ahead of the call
❌ No toolchain pin exists: the repository names no engine version — the executing release is a deployment fact the system records elsewhere (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published procedures or external packages: code moves through Teradata’s commercial channels, with no signature-checked public distribution (Y3)
❌ No public advisory feed for the engine’s dependencies: fixes land in Teradata release notes and support channels, with no CVE-mapped public advisory database (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: DBQL logging, Viewpoint, and EXPLAIN are platform features, and the procedure text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: SIGNAL text and the database’s own logs are the output surface, and no logging construct exists in SPL (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No maintained editor analysis ships with the engine: Teradata Studio’s editors are basic, and code assistance lives in third-party SQL tools (Y8)
❌ No procedure debugger ships with the engine: diagnosis goes through EXPLAIN, DBQL, handler instrumentation, and the error log (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the body compiles in one vendor’s engine, and nothing in the language runs without a Teradata system (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is Teradata Corporation: the release calendar, the EOL schedule, and the language’s direction are one company’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the SQL Stored Procedures book documents the implemented behavior of one product line, and no independent implementation follows from it (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the engine does: no conformance suite exists for SPL, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
❌ The parser is closed: the grammar lives as prose in the stored-procedures book and the parser inside the closed engine, so analysis tooling reads the manual and guesses (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the AMPs’: spool, distribution, and the warehouse’s license bill pay, and the reader’s levers are distribution and statement design the procedure exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Generated procedures appear in warehouse migration work, and the traps are the procedural layer: handler scope, result-set cursors, volatile state, and dynamic SQL no generated snippet prices.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the engine’s transaction, fallback, and recovery guarantees are Teradata’s, stated in its own documentation and support terms.

title: SQLite SQL dialect (3.54)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL dialect (SQLite 3.54) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 81.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68.0/100 · Engineering readiness 45.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ The value decides the type, not the column: type affinity coerces on write and comparison, one column stores numbers, text, and blobs side by side, and a mismatch is a data fact found at run time (T1)
❌ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column or a conventionally tagged value, and the consumer re-derives the encoding (T4)
❌ No generic parameter: queries are typed per statement, and a parameterized “any table” query does not exist in the language (T5)
❌ NULL is a member of every domain: any column accepts NULL unless declared, three-valued logic decides comparisons, and no signature records the guard (T10)
❌ Statements state no effect: an INSERT, an UPDATE, and a SELECT look alike to the caller, and nothing tracks what a statement touches (T12)
❌ The extension boundary is unchecked: load_extension() loads a compiled shared object in process, and the agreement on entry points and ABI is checked by neither side’s compiler (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ Any value fits any column by default: ordinary tables coerce or store whatever arrives, and STRICT tables — the construct that enforces declared types — are an opt-in the deployment must choose



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the library’s: pages, cache, and statement memory live inside the embedding process under the engine’s allocator, and the SQL text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

⚠️ Errors are integer codes out of the call: the language raises none and catches none — the result codes return to the host, and the SQL text carries no branch for them



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency is the engine’s: WAL mode, locking modes, and busy handlers decide what runs in parallel, and the SQL text names none of it



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The query runs only in SQLite-family engines: the dialect, the pragmas, and the file format are one engine’s, and nothing in the language runs without an embedding (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside application storage: the language has no stored procedures, no users, and no network story, and application logic beyond local persistence builds every abstraction itself (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One file is the whole database: the format is stable, cross-platform, and promised backward compatible for all future 3.x releases, and the price is a format whose forward direction is only “usually” compatible and whose rules live in one implementation
Flexibility by default, strictness by opt-in: any column accepts any value until STRICT is chosen, and the price is a schema that describes rather than enforces
The C boundary is the feature and the exposure: load_extension() and the amalgamation make embedding trivial, and the price is an unchecked ABI agreement and a supply line with no registry
Stability is the roadmap: decades of release notes document deliberate conservatism, and the price is that the dialect’s quirks — affinity, DQS quoting — are promised forward as behavior




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The plan is a statement away: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN are part of the published reference, so a query can be asked to show its plan before it runs



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager exists for extensions: load_extension() takes a path, distribution is find-the-URL-and-trust-it, and no registry, namespace, or signing channel stands behind the ecosystem (Ec1)



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ Conservatism is the stated policy: release notes document deliberate stability across decades, and the same policy promises forward the quirks — affinity and quoting — a new project might rather not inherit



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting SQLite SQL means adopting the file format: pragmas, affinity, and the single-file model define what a query can say, and the same vocabulary is the application’s storage design (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ The reference assumes the C embedder: the docs’ structure follows the library’s interfaces rather than a language course, and affinity and quoting rules live where a C programmer would look for them



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The same text means two things: double-quoted strings may be identifiers or literals depending on schema state and the DQS setting, and affinity decides whether ‘5’ equals 5 — inconsistencies the docs document as compatibility behavior (S2)



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user SQL: the project’s own TH3 and sqllogic tests are internal, and the documented testing story is application-side tests against the library (G1)
✅ The plan is queryable in the CLI: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN runs in the ordinary shell, published as part of the language reference (G2)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic typing is the security margin: affinity coercion meets attacker-shaped values at evaluation, and type confusions across the C boundary are the documented risk class (Q2)
❌ String-built SQL is the canonical injection: the docs’ own guidance exists because SQL text assembled by concatenation reaches the parser; the mitigation is bound parameters (Q3)
❌ Overflow promotes in silence: integer arithmetic that would overflow “perform[s] floating point arithmetic, per IEEE Standard 754”, so the value changes above 2^53 with no failure (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is text against a file: the same SQL on the same file and library version reproduces the same answer, and nothing is built
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution: the repository names no library version, and the embedding’s amalgamation or system copy decides semantics (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published extensions or builds: the download page publishes hashes of official artifacts, but extensions and third-party bindings carry no signature-checked distribution channel (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names the ecosystem’s dependencies: fixes land in release notes and the security page, with no CVE-mapped advisory database for extensions and bindings (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: the profile and trace callbacks are C API features, and the SQL text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: the error log is a C callback, and no logging construct exists in the SQL surface (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger exists for SQL: diagnosis goes through EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, the CLI’s dot commands, and result codes returned to the host (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the query runs on a SQLite-family engine, and nothing in the language runs without an embedding (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is one project lead and a small consortium: the direction, the releases, and the format promises are the SQLite project’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the language reference documents the implemented behavior of one engine, and no independent implementation follows from a published standard (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the library does: no conformance suite exists for the dialect, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the embedding process’s: the library’s cache and locks share the application’s fate, and the reader’s levers are schema and index design the SQL text exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ SQLite is a common agent-side store and SQL is the model-trained lingua franca — generated queries meet the traps: affinity coercion, three-valued logic, and pragma state the text never names.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; durability and atomicity are the engine’s guarantees, stated in its own documentation, with the project’s release discipline as the only contract.

Verdict: SQLite’s SQL dialect is the language of an embedded, public-domain library: standard-shaped SQL with type affinity instead of enforced types, opt-in STRICT tables, pragmas as the control plane, load_extension() as the only in-process escape, and one database file as the whole deployment. Its costs are the embedded model’s own: values decide types at run time, NULL in every domain, silent float promotion on integer overflow, a canonical string-built injection surface, and an extension ecosystem with no registry, namespace, or signing. Main strengths: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in the ordinary shell, a file format whose backward compatibility is an explicit published promise, decades-long stability as a stated policy, and public-domain source. Main weaknesses: no stored procedures, no debugger, no standard test harness, no structured logging or tracing in the language, single-project governance with no specification or conformance suite, and inconsistency the docs themselves carry as compatibility behavior.

title: SQL/PSM (MySQL 9.7)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL/PSM stored programs (MySQL 9.7 LTS) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 86.3/100 · Engineering readiness 45.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL is a member of every domain: a routine parameter, local, or OUT value carries NULL without a declaration, three-valued logic decides every comparison, and no signature states whether NULL is legal (T10)
⚠️ No sum types: an alternative is modeled by nullable OUT parameters, a status column, or separate routines, and the caller learns the encoding by reading the body
⚠️ No generic parameter: routines are typed per definition, and a routine over “any table” must take dynamic SQL or return one fixed shape
❌ Statements state no effect: a stored function that writes a table, calls a trigger, or reads the clock looks like any other in the catalog — only the DETERMINISTIC/NOT DETERMINISTIC declaration, which the docs state is trusted for replication rather than verified, says anything (T12)
❌ C code rides the boundary: the server loads native plugins and UDFs through its plugin interface, and the declaration the two sides agree on is checked by neither compiler (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The routine is one block: BEGIN … END gathers DECLARE, flow, and SQL into one deployable unit the catalog stores and parses
⚠️ Tables mutate in place: the routine body is ordinary DML, and every UPDATE is an in-place mutation with no immutability construct anywhere in the language



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the server’s: buffers, sort areas, and cursors live in mysqld, and the routine text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ The handler decides, or the statement dies: DECLARE … HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION routes a failure, and without a handler the routine aborts with an error to the caller — no value ever carries the failure (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception or error code, results by OUT parameters and SELECT result sets, and neither can thread through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ One session, one shared state: user variables, temporary tables, and session settings are visible across every routine the session calls, so two callers of the same routine share what it reads (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The routine runs only in MySQL-family servers: CALL speaks the server’s protocol, the body compiles in the server’s parser, and nothing in the language runs without mysqld (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside set work: the language has no data abstraction beyond tables, no libraries, and no error values, so application logic pays for every abstraction it builds (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic next to the data: routines remove the network round trip per statement and run inside the server’s transactions, and the price is application logic whose deploy, debug, and version story is the database’s
Handlers are optional by design: BEGIN … END with DECLARE … HANDLER gives structured recovery, and the price is that a routine without one fails at the first unhandled error, discovered by the caller
Session state is the shared resource: user variables and temporary tables make cross-routine state cheap, and the price is that every caller of a routine shares whatever the session already holds
The definer is a privilege decision: SQL SECURITY DEFINER lets one routine guard a table behind its owner’s rights, and the price is a trust edge the signature carries silently




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The plan is inspectable: EXPLAIN answers for the statements inside a routine through the ordinary session tools, and the optimizer answers per statement



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The installed base is one of the largest: drivers, ORMs, admin tooling, and managed offerings surround the server, and the community forums and docs answer the common questions



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ The LTS calendar governs the surface: 9.7 is the newest long-term-support line, the release model states that features change only in the first release of an LTS line, and maintenance arrives quarterly



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The routine exists to serve the database: the catalog, the privilege model, and the trigger/event system define what a stored program is, and moving the logic moves the engine (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

❌ SQL-92 roots with procedural grafts: the docs interleave ISO statements with MySQL-specific variables, handlers, and delimiters, and the traps (implicit commits, cursor scoping) get their own chapters



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The tool changes the text: DELIMITER is a client-side convention the server never sees, one of several places where the program’s meaning depends on which tool reads it
⚠️ Case rules differ per layer: table and column case follows the file system on some platforms while routine names follow the server, and the docs devote a page to identifier case sensitivity



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user routines: mysqltest serves the server’s own suite, and the documented testing story for stored programs is application-side tests against a live server (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: PREPARE and EXECUTE run SQL text held in a variable, so concatenated user input reaches the parser, and the documented mitigation is SQL-level privileges plus bound parameters (Q3)
⚠️ SQL SECURITY DEFINER runs as its owner: a definer routine executes with the owner’s privileges, so the catalog records a trust decision the body never states



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A routine is stored source: the same body on the same server version and data reproduces the same result, and nothing is compiled ahead of the call
❌ No toolchain pin exists: the repository names no server version — the executing release is a deployment fact a third-party manager must supply (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published routines or plugins: routines move as SQL dumps the server executes, and plugins install from distribution channels without signature checks (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names stored-program issues: fixes land in quarterly LTS release notes, and no published advisory database tracks the language surface the way Apache and CNCF projects publish theirs (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: the performance_schema and the general log are server features, and the routine text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: SIGNAL text and the server log are all a routine can emit, and no logging construct exists in the language (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No routine debugger ships with the server: diagnosis goes through SELECT scaffolding, handler instrumentation, and the error message (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the body compiles in one server family’s parser, and SQL/PSM conformance is a manual claim no suite checks (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is Oracle: the release model, the LTS calendar, and the language’s direction are one company’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the reference manual documents the implemented behavior of one server line, and no independent implementation follows from a published standard document (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what mysqld does: no conformance suite exists for the stored-program language, and a second implementation would be a compatibility gamble (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is mysqld’s: buffer pool, sort areas, and the event scheduler pay, and the reader’s levers are index and statement design the routine text exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Generated stored programs are common in migrations and admin tooling, and the traps are exactly the procedural layer: handler scope, implicit commits, definer rights, and cursor state that no generated snippet names.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; InnoDB’s ACID guarantees and the privilege model are the server’s, stated in its own documentation.

Verdict: MySQL’s stored-program language is SQL/PSM-shaped procedural SQL: BEGIN … END blocks over DECLARE, cursors, handlers, SIGNAL and dynamic PREPARE, deployed as procedures, functions, triggers, and events inside the server catalog. Its costs are the server family’s own: NULL in every domain with no null-safety, failures that travel only by exception or error code, session-wide user variables and temporary tables as the default shared state, and single-vendor governance with no specification and no conformance suite. Main strengths: one deployable block per program, structured handler-based recovery, EXPLAIN through the ordinary session tools, GPL-public source, and a release model (9.7 LTS, quarterly maintenance) the docs state plainly. Main weaknesses: no debugger or user-routine test harness, no structured logging or tracing in the language, string-built dynamic SQL as the standing injection surface, and logic whose reproducibility depends on a server version no repository file names.

title: Informix SPL (15.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SPL (IBM Informix 15.0) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 38.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL is a member of every domain: procedure variables and columns carry NULL unannounced — the INTO clause takes indicator variables to say a value was NULL — and no signature states whether a value may be absent (T10)
⚠️ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable return, a status value, or separate routines, and the caller learns the encoding by reading the body
❌ Statements state no effect: a procedure that updates tables, fires triggers, and writes files looks like any other in sysprocedures (T12)
❌ C code rides the boundary: EXTERNAL NAME declarations bind SPL to compiled shared objects through the C UDR interface, and the agreement on layout and error convention is checked by neither side’s compiler (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The routine is one block: CREATE PROCEDURE and CREATE FUNCTION gather DEFINE, flow, and SQL into one unit the server stores and parses
⚠️ WITH RESUME is a hand-rolled iterator: an SPL routine returns rows across calls where RETURN WITH RESUME runs, and the FROM TABLE(…) interface consumes the stream



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the server’s: buffers, cursors, and UDR memory live in the oninit process, and the SPL text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ ON EXCEPTION decides, or the error propagates: handlers catch by SQL error code and ISAM code, can nest, and RAISE EXCEPTION re-raises — without a handler the error leaves the routine, and no value carries it (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception and results by RETURNING clauses and OUT parameters, and neither composes through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session and global state is shared: DEFINE GLOBAL variables persist for the session’s global environment and the server does not save them in the database, and temporary tables are visible across every routine the connection calls (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The routine runs only in Informix: the parser, the sysprocedures catalog, and the Datablade extension model are the engine’s, and nothing in the language runs without one (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside set work: the language has no libraries, no data abstraction beyond tables and opaque types, and no error values (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Iterator routines are the abstraction: RETURN … WITH RESUME turns a procedure into a streaming source for FROM TABLE(…), and the price is control flow whose meaning sits in where the RETURN runs
Global variables are built in: DEFINE GLOBAL gives cross-routine session state by declaration, and the price is the widest shared state the language offers as a one-word feature
Decades of installed base: the same syntax runs across 12.10, 14.10, and 15.0 with parallel maintenance lines, and the price is documentation and tooling that carry every era at once
C UDRs are the escape hatch: opaque types, casts, and support functions bind compiled C into the engine, and the price is an ABI agreement neither side’s compiler checks




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The plan is a statement away: SET EXPLAIN publishes the query plans the server chooses, and the docs treat it as the ordinary tool for reading cost



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A niche, shrinking ecosystem: Informix’s tooling and expertise concentrate in its installed base, and the 15.0 line’s tooling follows the same narrow path (Ec3)
❌ A proprietary stack: the server, its tooling, and the support model are IBM/HCL commercial products under license terms (Ec4)



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ Parallel release lines carry the surface: 12.10, 14.10, and 15.0 are maintained side by side, and a routine’s available surface follows the line the deployment runs



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists to serve the database: routines, triggers, and opaque-type support functions deploy into the catalog, and the engine’s security and storage model define what they can say (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ The documentation predates the reader: SPL’s reference prose carries decades of releases in one voice, and the version selector decides which page a statement’s truth lives on



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ ESQL/C conventions inside the server language: INTO clauses, indicator variables, and colon-prefixed host markers shape SPL’s syntax from its embedded-SQL lineage



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user routines: the documented testing story is application-side tests against a live server, with TRACE statements as the language’s only instrumented aid (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and PREPARE run text assembled at run time, so concatenated user input reaches the parser, and the mitigation is the privilege model plus bound inputs (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A routine is stored source: the same body on the same server version and data reproduces the same result, and nothing is compiled ahead of the call
❌ No toolchain pin exists: the repository names no server version, and the executing release is a deployment fact a manager must supply (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published routines or Datablade modules: code moves through IBM Fix Central and commercial channels, with no signature-checked public distribution (Y3)
❌ No public advisory feed for the engine’s dependencies: security fixes arrive as IBM security bulletins per release, with no CVE-mapped public advisory database (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: onstat, the message log, and SET EXPLAIN are server tools, and the routine text carries no trace hook beyond its own TRACE statements (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: TRACE writes a debug file, and no structured logging construct exists in SPL (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No maintained editor analysis ships with the server: IBM’s Eclipse-era data tooling is discontinued, and code assistance lives in third-party and generic SQL editors (Y8)
❌ No routine debugger ships with the server: diagnosis goes through SET EXPLAIN, TRACE files, ON EXCEPTION instrumentation, and the message log (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the body compiles in one engine’s parser, and nothing in the language runs without an Informix server (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is IBM and HCL: the release calendar and the language’s direction are two companies’ agreement, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the Guide to SQL documents the implemented behavior of one product line, and no independent implementation follows from it (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the server does: no conformance suite exists for SPL, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
❌ The parser is closed: the grammar lives as prose in the Guide to SQL and the parser inside the closed engine, so analysis tooling reads the manual and guesses (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is oninit’s: buffers, cursors, and the installed hardware pay, and the reader’s levers are index and statement design the routine exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Generated SPL appears in migration work off the installed base, and the traps are the procedural layer: WITH RESUME placement, exception scope, global state, and indicator variables no generated snippet names.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the engine’s transaction and recovery guarantees are IBM’s and HCL’s, stated in their own documentation and support terms.

Verdict: Informix SPL is the stored procedure language of a long-lived proprietary engine: CREATE PROCEDURE and FUNCTION over DEFINE, FOREACH cursors, ON EXCEPTION handlers with RAISE EXCEPTION, RETURN … WITH RESUME iterator routines, DEFINE GLOBAL session variables, TRACE, and EXECUTE IMMEDIATE for dynamic SQL, with C UDRs bound through EXTERNAL NAME declarations. Its costs are the engine’s own: NULL in every domain with indicator-variable workarounds, failures that travel only by exception, built-in global session state, a niche proprietary ecosystem, and single-vendor governance with no specification or conformance suite. Main strengths: SET EXPLAIN query plans as an ordinary tool, one syntax across long-lived parallel release lines, and one-unit routines the catalog stores as source. Main weaknesses: no debugger, no maintained editor analysis, no standard test harness, no structured logging or tracing in the language, string-built dynamic SQL, and tooling whose continuity depends on two companies’ commercial roadmap.

title: Snowflake SQL (2026)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Snowflake SQL (2026-10 documentation state) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 80.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 43.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column or a VARIANT holding a shape by convention, and the consumer re-derives the encoding (T4)
❌ No generic parameter: queries and procedures are typed per definition, and a routine over “any table” needs dynamic SQL (T5)
❌ NULL is a member of every domain: columns, parameters, and scripting variables carry NULL unannounced, and no signature records the guard (T10)
❌ Statements state no effect: a procedure that loads tables, calls tasks, and sends emails carries nothing in its signature (T12)
❌ Three languages ride inside one function: UDFs and procedures can be defined in SQL, JavaScript, Python, Java, or Scala inline, and values cross between the SQL type system and each runtime with no checked boundary (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The query composes declaratively: WITH, lateral joins, and Snowflake Scripting blocks build on the same text, and the same statement replays against any role-authorized schema
⚠️ Tables mutate in place: DML rewrites micro-partitions, and time travel and cloning are the engine’s retention features rather than language constructs



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the warehouse’s: compute, spool, and cache live in the virtual warehouse, and the query text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ The handler decides, or the script dies: Snowflake Scripting’s EXCEPTION blocks route failures by condition, and without one the failed statement ends the script — no value carries the failure (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception and results by tables and variables, and neither threads through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session state is shared: session variables and temporary tables are visible across every statement and procedure the session runs (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The query runs only in Snowflake: the dialect’s functions, scripting, and role model are the service’s, and nothing in the language runs without an account (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside analytical work: the language has no general libraries or error values, and transactional application logic is the wrong shape for the warehouse (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Separation of compute and storage is the bill: warehouses scale per query and suspend per idle, and the price is a runtime whose size, credits, and release cadence are the vendor’s
Scripting turns SQL into a program: variables, loops, cursors, and EXCEPTION blocks deploy real logic, and the price is logic with no debugger and no test harness
Five UDF languages buy reach: Python, Java, Scala, and JavaScript bodies run beside SQL, and the price is an unchecked boundary per language inside one function
Structured logging exists where it matters: SYSTEM$LOG writes to event tables, and the price is that the event table is platform configuration a query cannot see




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The Query Profile states the plan: per-node timings, spill, and pruning are published per query in the web UI and retrievable by API



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A proprietary service end to end: the engine, storage, and governance are Snowflake products under commercial terms, with no self-hostable reference (Ec4)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Weekly releases move under the queries: behavior changes roll out on the vendor’s cadence with change notifications, and scheduled SQL can shift under a release the repository never named (V1)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting Snowflake SQL means adopting the account model: databases, roles, warehouses, and tasks define what a query can say, and the same vocabulary is the deployment and the bill (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

❌ SQL plus scripting plus five UDF languages: Snowflake Scripting adds blocks, cursors, and result sets, and UDF bodies may be JavaScript, Python, Java, or Scala — a surface well beyond the SQL a reader knows (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Standard-shaped, Snowflake-flavored: the core reads like ANSI SQL, and VARIANT columns, scripting, and the IDENTIFIER grammar are the dialect’s own layer



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for queries: the documented testing story is dbt and third-party frameworks against a billed account, and the language names no regression harness (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs text assembled at run time, and IDENTIFIER() interpolates names, so composed user input reaches the parser; the documented mitigation is binding and role-based access (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is request text: the same SQL on the same data and warehouse reproduces the same answer, and nothing is built
❌ The executing engine is unpinnable: the repository names no engine build — weekly releases decide semantics, and no file records them (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published queries or routines: shared objects and application packages move through the service under role terms, with no signature-checked public channel (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names the query surface: changes and fixes land in release notes and client advisories, with no CVE-mapped advisory database for the engine’s dependencies (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: the event table, history views, and account usage are platform features, and the query text carries no trace hook (Y5)
✅ The scripting layer can log: Snowflake Scripting publishes SYSTEMLOGanditsSYSTEMLOG and its SYSTEMLOG_ variants writing to the event table, with capture levels set through the LOG_LEVEL parameter, so a procedure can emit recorded diagnostics by calling documented functions (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger exists for scripts or procedures: diagnosis goes through the Query Profile, history views, and error messages (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the query runs on Snowflake, and nothing in the language runs without an account (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is one vendor: the dialect’s direction and weekly cadence are Snowflake’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the SQL reference documents the implemented behavior of one service, and no independent implementation follows from it (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the service does: no conformance suite exists for the dialect, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
❌ The parser is closed: the grammar lives as prose in the SQL reference and the parser inside the service, so community grammars are guesses the vendor never answers for (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the virtual warehouse and the credits bill: compute size, auto-suspend, and storage pay, and the reader’s levers are clustering and query shape the text exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ Cortex Analyst and document AI sit beside the dialect, and SQL is the model-trained lingua franca — generated queries still meet the traps: three-valued logic, VARIANT shape conventions, and scripting scope.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the service’s durability, governance, and isolation guarantees are Snowflake’s, stated in its own documentation and terms.

Verdict: Snowflake SQL is a cloud-warehouse SQL dialect — ANSI-shaped SQL over VARIANT semi-structured data, plus Snowflake Scripting’s blocks, cursors, and EXCEPTION handling, plus UDFs whose bodies may be SQL, Python, Java, Scala, or JavaScript — served by one proprietary engine on weekly releases. Its costs are the service’s own: NULL in every domain, failures that travel only by exception, session-wide state, an unpinnable engine, and single-vendor governance with no specification or conformance suite. Main weaknesses: no debugger or standard test harness, string-built dynamic SQL, a proprietary stack with no self-hostable reference, and scheduled SQL whose semantics move with releases the repository never named.

title: SAP ASE (ASE 16.1)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SAP ASE in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 48.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and column has a declared type, and a batch that violates it fails at parse or bind time
✅ A procedure parameter declares its type and direction: @p int output fixes the type and the direction, so a caller binds to a signature
⚠️ DECLARE @name defaults to NULL (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, so an unassigned variable is valid and propagates NULL into the expression
⚠️ NULL comparison needs three-valued logic: With ansinull on, @x = NULL is unknown, so a check needs is null, and the ansinull setting decides which semantics a batch gets
❌ A signature says what a procedure returns, not what it does (T12): A procedure that mutates tables, opens a remote connection, or changes session settings looks like any other procedure



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A stored procedure provides modularity with a declared interface: CREATE PROCEDURE names the unit, its parameters, and its return status, and can return result sets and output parameters
✅ A view separates consumers from the query: The exposed relation is stable while its defining query can change
✅ Set-based statements compose without a cursor: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM, and DELETE ... FROM express a whole transformation in one statement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Session set options change the meaning of a statement: ansinull and quoted_identifier alter how comparisons and identifiers parse, so the same text can behave differently elsewhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The ASE server owns its data caches and procedure caches, and a batch never names an address
✅ The server sizes the work areas: Sorts and hashes take their memory from the engine’s configuration, not from the batch
⚠️ A cursor allocates per fetch: A row-by-row cursor uses workspace per fetch, so the memory pattern follows the loop
⚠️ A #temp table is session-scoped, not procedure-scoped: It lives for the session and is dropped with it, not with the procedure that built it



1.1.4 Error

❌ Errors travel by global status (Er1): A statement’s outcome lands in @@error, and the next statement must check it; the language has no construct that carries a failure from where it is detected to where it is handled
⚠️ A skipped check is silent (Er3): A batch that never tests @@error runs past the failure, and nothing marks the missing check
❌ A failure cannot travel as a value (Er4): The failure shape is @@error, a procedure return status, and raiserror — rebuilt at every boundary, and never composable in an expression
⚠️ Severity decides the effect: A raiserror below severity 11 is informational, mid severities abort the statement, and the highest severities end the client session, so the same text behaves differently by number
⚠️ A failed statement can doom the transaction without ending the batch: The code must test @@trancount and roll back explicitly, so recovery is written statement by statement



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one
✅ Isolation levels are selectable in the statement: at isolation read uncommitted, read committed (the default), repeatable read, and serializable name the level a query needs
❌ Session state is shared by default (K2): set options, the @@ status globals, and session temp tables are visible to code the caller did not write
⚠️ Locking hints bind a query to the engine’s concurrency model: holdlock, noholdlock, and shared must agree with the application’s lock ordering
⚠️ Chained mode moves the transaction boundary: With set chained on, a transaction opens at the first statement, so the same batch commits differently by mode



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Cannot function outside one engine (P1): SAP ASE programs need SAP ASE, so the unit of deployment is an ASE database
⚠️ One lineage, two vendor branches: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP ASE share the 1980s Sybase core syntax, but the dialects diverged, and the vendors document them separately
⚠️ The server also parses SQLScript in SQLScript-mode databases: A separate dialect with handlers of its own serves HANA compatibility, but a Transact-SQL database cannot use it
⚠️ Extended stored procedures load native code (T14): An xp_ routine is a native library inside the server, crossing a boundary no signature check reaches
⚠️ CIS reaches remote servers through proxy tables: Component Integration Services maps a remote table into the local catalog, so a query’s real target is not visible in the query text
✅ Client interfaces are standard: Open Client, ODBC, and JDBC reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: A rule that runs beside its tables is enforced for every writer; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application’s test suite and profilers
A cursor is a deliberate trade for row-by-row work: It makes a per-row algorithm expressible, at the cost of the set-based model
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible filter: execute ('...') reaches names a static statement cannot; the cost is that the statement’s access path is chosen when it runs
Chained mode is a deliberate transaction default: It gives every statement a transaction boundary; the cost is that a script written in one mode commits differently in the other




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Plans are cached: A procedure’s compiled plan is reused per call, so the caller does not choose an access path
✅ The optimiser serves the data path: Plan selection and buffer caching are the engine’s job, not the procedure’s
⚠️ Row-by-row cursors pay per-fetch costs: A loop that fetches one row at a time runs far slower than its set-based equivalent
⚠️ Statistics and plan choice can regress a query without a code change: New data volumes or a changed configuration can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from SAP under licence
❌ A small market beside the mainstream engines (Ec3): Hiring, community material, and third-party tooling concentrate on the larger engines, so more is written than found
✅ The SAP stack integrates: ASE serves SAP Business Suite applications with first-party certification
⚠️ Documentation and fixes sit behind the SAP portal: Notes, manuals, and downloads require SAP access
⚠️ Tooling centres on the engine’s own tools: isql and the SAP ASE Cockpit carry the workflow, and the procedural language has no dedicated environment of its own



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Upgrades keep routines: A procedure written for ASE 15 compiles in 16.1
⚠️ Releases are infrequent: The ASE 16 line has carried for years through patch levels, so a new capability waits a long time
⚠️ A feature arrives with a patch level or a major release: Adoption follows the server a deployment can upgrade to
⚠️ SAP’s own decisions govern the change: The ASE reference manuals are the definition, and no independent standard bounds the dialect



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for SAP Business Suite data logic: ASE is certified for the Suite’s data tier, and a procedure runs beside its tables with SQL in the body
✅ A full procedural language inside SQL: Procedures, triggers, cursors, and dynamic SQL live beside the queries
❌ Domain lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside SAP ASE, so the ASE data tier is the only domain
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a long-running service belongs in another language beside ASE’s SQL
⚠️ Procedural row logic reads poorly beside its set-based equivalent: A row-by-row algorithm in a cursor is verbose and slow



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a developer who knows classic T-SQL: Procedures, batches, and triggers read like the Sybase-line originals
⚠️ The dialect diverges from the Microsoft branch in details: Error handling, catalog procedures, and built-in functions differ, so knowledge from SQL Server transfers only in part
⚠️ @@error checking is a discipline: Every statement that can fail needs the check written after it, and reviewing for it is part of learning the language
⚠️ Engine behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Locks, isolation modes, and page structure matter more than syntax for correct code
✅ The reference manuals are complete: The ASE manuals cover every statement with syntax and examples



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE and BEGIN ... END read close to English
✅ A procedure is a readable unit: The parameter list and the body are declared in one CREATE PROCEDURE statement
⚠️ @@ sigils distinguish kinds of variable by convention: A local, a parameter, and a global status share the sigil, so a reader distinguishes them by spelling
⚠️ set options prefix every script: set nocount on, ansinull, and quoted_identifier are usually written at the top, so the boilerplate grows
⚠️ go marks a batch boundary in a script: The client tool sends the batch, so the boundary is visible in the source but owned by the tool



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ No test framework ships with the toolchain (G1): isql and the SAP tools provide no assertion or runner, so a suite is hand-rolled or borrowed
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run inside a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database unchanged
✅ Error status supports assertion-style checks: @@error and raiserror inside a procedure can express an assertion and stop the test
⚠️ A suite needs a server: Tests run inside the ASE instance they exercise, so the harness depends on the server and on deployment rights
❌ No monotonic reading published: GETDATE is the wall clock (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ GRANT and roles express least privilege: Access is declared per object, per user, and per role
✅ Views plus grants scope what a role can see: A view over a table, with execution and select grants, is the row-scoping mechanism
⚠️ Dynamic SQL is string-built with no binding: execute ('...') runs a built string, and the language supplies no parameter-binding form, so values travel inside the text
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): A statement assembled by concatenation turns input into code, and the mitigation is validation at the call site
⚠️ A procedure runs with its creator’s permissions: A caller gains the owner’s access through the procedure, so the grant surface needs an audit



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The distribution records no toolchain version per project; the server version is a fact of the installation. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Module sources carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to Transact-SQL modules. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ print and raiserror carry no structure. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer ships with the server; editor analysis rides third-party tools. (Y8)
❌ No debugger ships with the server. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The module runs only in SAP ASE. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ SAP decides the language’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists; the manuals document one implementation. (Y12)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

❌ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: SAP ASE’s coupling follows its host engine and its Sybase lineage. Stored procedures, views, and cached plans give real modularity, isolation is selectable in the statement, and the SAP stack integration is first-party. Main strengths: classic T-SQL readability, engine-owned memory and plans, standard client interfaces, and a current 16.1 line with long-standing compatibility. Main weaknesses: the language only runs on SAP ASE, the dialect has no structured failure path — every statement’s outcome lands in @@error and the next statement must check it — dynamic SQL is string-built with no parameter binding, the market beside the mainstream engines is small, session state is shared by default, and no test framework ships with the toolchain.
