1 Assessment
This page assesses Redis Lua in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 45.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 46.1/100 · Engineering readiness 52.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ The embedded dialect is documented command by command: Redis ships one Lua 5.1 interpreter, and the Lua API reference names the libraries a script may use — string, table, math, os.clock, struct, cjson, cmsgpack, bit
❌ No static type check: types are decided at run time, and a nil from a missing key becomes a fault only when the line that touches it executes (T1)
❌ Dispatch follows the run-time value: ipairs, table.insert, and metatable __index chains resolve by what the value is when the call runs (T3)
❌ No sum types: a result carries one value, and a script signals an alternative with a nil, a boolean flag, or a table convention (T4)
❌ No generic type parameter: reusable script logic is copied between projects; a Functions library has no parameterised routine (T5)
❌ One global name space: Lua globals default to the shared global table, and Redis runs scripts and functions in one Lua state, so name collisions are a deployment fact (T6)
❌ Operators are metatable dispatch: +, .., and # on a table mean what its metatable says, so the call site’s meaning follows the data (T8)
❌ nil is a value on every path: a missing key’s reply, an absent table field, and an unset global all reach expressions, and indexing nil raises mid-script (T10)
❌ redis.call shows the command, not the effect: the script text names the command, not which keys it mutates, expires, or replicates (T12)
❌ The script-to-server boundary is unchecked: redis.call enters the server’s command dispatcher, and no check ties the command names, key arguments, and replies to the script’s expectations (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Atomic execution is the contract: Redis runs the script to completion before serving any other client, so all of the script’s effects commit together
❌ Globals persist across calls: scripts run in one shared Lua state, and a global written by a script stays visible to the next call — avoiding globals is a published Redis scripting practice (C1)
❌ Nothing is immutable by default: tables, KEYS, and ARGV are mutated in place, and function libraries share the state they mutate (C2)
❌ No constructor validates a shape: a result table is assembled field by field, and a missing field surfaces as a nil on the reader’s side (C4)
❌ Iteration order is the table’s, not yours: pairs() visits a hash-part table in an order the script cannot state (C5)
❌ One value, many names: a table handed to redis.call and kept in a global is the same table, and Lua 5.1 source shows no aliasing declaration (C6)
⚠️ Key-space notifications react outside the script: a script’s writes fire subscribers and module consumers that the script text never mentions



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the interpreter’s: scripts create tables and strings, and Redis’s bundled Lua collector reclaims them; no script frees memory
❌ The collector pauses the server: Lua’s collection work runs on the main thread during the script’s run, so collecting a big table is a latency spike every client sees (M2)
❌ Scope does not release: __gc runs when the collector decides, not at the end of a block, and a script cannot bind release to scope (M3)
❌ No ownership is expressed: tables move through redis.call replies and globals with no owner, and the collector decides lifetime (M4)
⚠️ A runaway script holds its memory to the end: SCRIPT KILL stops only a script that has not written, so a script past its write budget runs to completion



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: error() raises any value, pcall returns it untyped, and a script reporting ‘insufficient funds’ invents its own convention (Er1)
❌ Failures nobody is required to handle: redis.call on a wrong-type key raises, and a script with no pcall wrapper commits nothing and hands the fault to the client (Er2)
❌ A failure can be ignored: pcall’s false reply is discarded freely, and scripts commonly drop the flag (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: success values, nils, and raised strings share the return slot, so callers compose them by convention (Er4)
✅ The fault boundary is one call: a raised error aborts the script, the server keeps serving, and the blast radius is the current call



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No parallel execution: Redis runs one script at a time on its main thread, and every client waits for the script to finish (K1)
❌ Coroutines are unstructured: Lua 5.1 coroutine transfers control by hand, and no construct scopes a running child (K4)
✅ Atomicity is total: every effect commits before any other client runs, so a script needs no lock to compose a read-modify-write
⚠️ The budget is a wall: lua-time-limit decides when a read-only script may be stopped, and a script that has written runs to the end



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The language runs only inside Redis: Redis ships a single embedded scripting engine, the Lua 5.1 interpreter, and the Functions docs name it as the only engine present (P1)
❌ A poor fit for general application logic: scripts exchange replies with clients; HTTP, file I/O (the sandbox exposes os.clock only), and multi-pass algorithms belong to the client (P4)
⚠️ Redis 8 makes Functions engine-agnostic by design, and Lua 5.1 is the engine that ships: more engines are a plan, not a feature



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Code ownership: application-side (EVAL) versus server-side (Functions): scripts ship with the client code and reload after a restart, functions persist and replicate with the dataset — the server then carries application logic that the client no longer ships
Script-cache economics: EVALSHA keeps script text in the server, Redis’s own docs warn that value-embedded scripts ‘consume a large amount of memory over time’, and Redis 7.4’s LRU eviction means the cache budget now decides which scripts the next call must resend
Cluster key discipline: every key a script touches must arrive as an input argument, so scripts that derive key names from data are written out of clustered deployments
One roundtrip buys atomic composition: a conditional multi-key update ships as a single call with no lock and no client-side race, and the standing duty is reviewing every script for length, because Redis runs a writing script to completion




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Bytecode interpretation, no JIT: Redis bundles the Lua 5.1 interpreter, not LuaJIT, and a hot script loop pays per bytecode instruction (R1)
❌ Collector pauses are server latency: Lua’s GC steps run on the main thread, and a script’s big tables appear as latency spikes in every client’s timings (R2)
✅ Data locality is the point: the script reads and writes inside the server, and the docs call scripting ‘very efficient’ because the data never leaves



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager for scripts: a Functions library embeds its full source, the sandbox exposes only the libraries Redis pre-imports, and nothing installs into the server’s Lua (Ec1)
❌ Tooling fragments across clients: redis-cli --ldb, the ZeroBrane Studio plugin, and the per-language client libraries cover scripting at different levels (Ec2)
❌ A niche within a niche: Lua developers who write server-side Redis scripts are a small hiring pool (Ec3)
❌ RDB snapshots do not cross a version boundary backward: a snapshot written by a newer Redis cannot be loaded by an older one, and Redis’s knowledge base states it as the rule for upgrades (Ec9)
✅ **The server is open source (AGPLv3 since Redis 8), and the Lua API, Functions, and persistence docs are public



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Script behavior moved under scripts: Redis 7.0 shifted the recommended path from EVAL to Functions — changing how code is loaded, named, and persisted — and Redis 7.4 added eviction from the EVAL script cache (V1)
❌ The embedded dialect is frozen: Redis ships the same Lua 5.1 line it has used since 2012; upstream Lua 5.4’s changes — an integer subtype, a bitwise library, GC options — never reach scripts (V2)
✅ Scripts from Redis 2.6 run on Redis 8: EVAL with KEYS and ARGV has kept its contract across the whole line



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting Redis Lua means adopting Redis: scripts call the Redis command API, and the language exists to compose key operations on Redis data structures (D1)
✅ Redis Lua is used to script server-side read-modify-write logic over stored data: conditional updates across keys commit atomically inside the server
⚠️ Cluster rules travel with the script: every key a script touches must be an input key argument, and generated key names break cross-slot operation



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The language core is small: local, for, function values, and tables fit a short manual, and Redis’s own design notes call Lua ‘simple and easy to learn’
❌ Two domains at once: a scripter needs Lua’s table idioms and metatables, the Redis command API, the atomicity budget, and the key-argument rules together (L2)
⚠️ The sandbox’s shape is a page of rules: which globals exist, which os functions are exposed, and what SCRIPT KILL will stop



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Scripts read linearly: a short Lua script is a statement list, and redis.call renders as a plain function call
❌ Lua 5.1’s surface is uneven: table.insert(t, v) against table.concat(list, sep), methods as ('x'):rep(2), 1-based indexing, no ++, no ternary — the idioms are conventions to learn one by one (S2)



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test harness ships with the language: testing a script needs a running Redis, and every project wires its own harness; the debugger’s forked sessions are for authoring, not CI (G1)
❌ The debugger reaches scripts, not Functions: LDB steps, breakpoints, and variable inspection attach to EVAL, and the Functions docs name the debugger as the one capability functions lack (G2)
❌ Type faults surface only at execution: tonumber on a malformed ARGV value, indexing nil, and a wrong-type key all resolve when the line runs (G3)
❌ No monotonic clock in the sandbox: the os library exposes os.clock only, so elapsed-time tests read wall time (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Untrusted data enters untyped: values read back from keys are data, and every arithmetic, concatenation, and pattern use re-checks its type at run time (Q2)
❌ Embedding values in the script text is a documented abuse: Redis’s EVAL docs warn that value-embedded scripts generate a new script text on each call, and the parse follows the embedded value (Q3)
❌ Arithmetic leaves the range in silence: Lua 5.1 numbers are C doubles, integers past 2^53 lose precision quietly, and the bit library truncates to 32 bits by C cast (Q4)
✅ Passing data as ARGV keeps values out of the parse, and Redis’s docs make it the rule
✅ ACL categories gate scripting: the @scripting permission decides which clients may load and run scripts

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A script is source text: the same text on the same Redis version and dataset reproduces the same result, and there is no build artifact (Y1)
❌ Dependencies are not pinned: applications ship scripts beside client code, and no manifest names the Redis version a script expects (Y2)
❌ The distribution carries no toolchain pin for script code: Redis bundles its Lua line inside the server, and a deployment has no machine-read pair of server version to script version (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published drivers carry no signed provenance by default: redis-py on PyPI and ioredis on npm name their publishers, and a consumer must trust the package they install (Y3)
✅ Registries carry namespaces: PyPI and npm name each package’s owner, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
✅ Advisories exist: Redis publishes its CVE list for the server and stack components, and the GitHub advisory database covers the major Python and Node clients (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: a script reports through INFO counters and the server’s own telemetry (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the sandbox: redis.log writes a message and level into the server’s log format, and the debug console is debug-only (Y6)
✅ The server names a slow script: SLOWLOG records script executions past the latency threshold with their duration, and SCRIPT KILL is the documented stop path (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit-test loop is a text submission: redis-cli --eval /tmp/script.lua runs a file with no build step (Y7)
❌ Editors do not analyse Redis Lua: redis.call’s command names and key semantics are checked by the server at execution, and no incremental analyser ships for the language (Y8)
✅ LDB is a real debugger for scripts: step, breakpoints, backtrace, variable print, and Redis command tracing ship in redis-cli (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No foreign-function interface: the sandbox exposes no C library, os is reduced to os.clock, and extending Redis in compiled code is a C module’s job, outside the language (Y9)
❌ No portable target: scripts run on Redis’s embedded engine and nowhere else (Y10)
✅ The client boundary is the command API: a script’s reply converts to RESP, and every language’s Redis client can call EVAL



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is Redis-owned: the embedded engine, the Functions design, and script-cache behavior all follow Redis’s roadmap, and a second engine is stated as a plan (Y11)
✅ The engine is published: Redis bundles its Lua line as open source in the server repository, and the Functions docs describe the engine interface (Y12)
❌ Conformance is what Redis’s Lua fork does: the redis.call API, the library set, and the atomicity rules exist only in the server’s implementation, and no shared test suite runs an independent implementation (Y17)
✅ The parser is published: Redis’s bundled Lua source is the parser, readable and reusable by tooling (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on the Redis main thread: a long script is a server-wide latency spike, and the energy and time are the server’s, not the script’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ Lua 5.1 is small and richly represented in public code, and the Redis Lua API is documented command by command: current models write common scripts reliably, with the key-argument and atomicity rules needing review.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Redis Lua is coupling-heavy at the language level and cheap at the deployment level, and the two facts are the same fact. The language is a frozen Lua 5.1 line embedded in Redis’s main thread: dynamic typing with no static check, one shared global state, an unchecked redis.call boundary, no parallel execution, no FFI, no package boundary, and silent numeric range exits in a language built on C doubles. What the embedding buys is real: atomic read-modify-write where the data lives, a published remote debugger for scripts, a documented CVE feed, and EVAL contracts that have held since Redis 2.6. Main strengths: atomic execution, data locality, LDB, tiny language core. Main weaknesses: the dialect is frozen, Functions run where no debugger reaches, RDB snapshots cross a release boundary unpromised backward, and the language runs only inside Redis.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925201
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4], [5], [6].
Snapshot PromQL (Prometheus 3.15) — released October 2026 · lifecycle current
Family PromQL — shelf: Data and Science
The language’s primary object is a dataset or a numeric array, not a program loop. A shelf groups; it does not classify — the tags below carry every use, paradigm, and platform of this snapshot.
Trajectory Prometheus 0.x (November 2012 — the query language of the first Prometheus releases) · Prometheus 2.0 (January 2017 — the new TSDB arrives; the language grows the selector and modifier surface over the 2.x line) · Prometheus 3.0 (November 2024 — the first major in seven years: left-open ranges, newline regex semantics, UTF-8 names, and le-label normalization, each published in the migration guide) · 3.15.1 (October 2026 — assessed release; duration expressions ship by default and first_over_time is promoted to stable)

title: PromQL (Prometheus 3.15)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PromQL (Prometheus 3.15) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 70.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 47.7/100 · Engineering readiness 65.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ A typed value lattice: instants, vectors, matrices, scalars, and (from 3.0) strings are distinct expression kinds with published per-operator type rules
❌ No static check against the data: a query is typed against its own expression kinds, not against what the cluster stores — a selector that matches no series is legal, and the releases added warnings for exactly that pattern (T1)
❌ No sum types: a sample is a float64 (integer histogram samples arrive in the 3.x line behind documented type-coercion fixes), and histogram, string, scalar, and vector values coexist with conversions defined per operator, not a type the expression names (T4)
❌ No parameterization: an expression is not a function, recording rules publish a series by name in a flat YAML, and reusable logic is copied rule file by rule file (T5)
❌ One flat name space: metric names are global to the TSDB, __name__ carries the name as a label, and the 3.0 quoting syntax for UTF-8 names exists because dots and colons in names were once illegal (T6)
❌ Absence is not a value: a selector matching no series yields an empty vector, a lookback with no sample yields no element, and the 3.0 migration guide shows a 1m subquery turning into No Data on aligned systems — absence has no type to name (T10)
❌ No module boundary: a record rule publishes a series by name, and nothing in the language imports definitions from a file, a server, or a namespace (T11)
❌ No effects, because the language writes nothing: a query reads the TSDB, recording-rule files derive series the engine stores, and neither the expression nor the rule file states its effect (T12)
❌ The ingest boundary renames labels: the 3.14 notes add warnings and a counter for OTLP attribute names that collide into one Prometheus label after sanitization — series identity changes crossing the boundary, and no check in the language validates the result (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The query states the result: count by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) declares the vector to produce, and the engine builds the plan
❌ Series mutate with arrivals: samples append to the head, staleness markers rewrite a series’ state, and the out-of-order and reset-detection features of the 3.x line exist because the store is mutable in place (C2)
❌ No constructor validates label identity: sum by (l), label joins, and label_replace compose new label sets by regex, and the 3.0 migration guide shows the le/quantile normalization changing a series’ identity when the engine, not the expression, decides (C4)
❌ A vector’s order is not pinned: vectors are label-set collections with no declared order, and the sort() and sort_le() functions exist because the default order is unspecified (C5)
⚠️ Remote write and federation are config, not language: a query writes nothing to the TSDB, the deployment moves series by YAML beside it, and the language does not scope that



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the server’s: head blocks, mmap’d block files, and query results live in the Prometheus process, and the query text allocates nothing
⚠️ High-cardinality selectors materialize in RAM: aggregations over unbounded label sets are operations whose cost the operator plans — the 3.15-line notes fix query panics during series eviction after WAL replay, and head-series gauges track native-histogram buckets



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured path in the language: a query aborting on the sample-count and queue limits, a many-to-many match error, and a lookback that found no sample surface as API-level errors the expression cannot route around (Er1)
❌ NaN swallows silently: an expression fed by a NaN sample propagates NaN, and the 3.14 notes fix two silent behaviors in one release — mad_over_time returning 0 where NaN is right, and case-insensitive regex matchers silently dropping matching values (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: scalar, vector, matrix, and string values share expression slots with per-operator promotion rules, strings arrived in 3.0 with restricted usability, and success and absence compose by spec rules, not by a type (Er4)
✅ Warnings ride the response: advisory warnings for unanchored regex selectors and saturation signals arrive in the API result, so a caller reads a defined advisory with the data



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency is the server’s: scrape pools, query-queue limits, and remote-write shards run in the engine, and the language names no threads, channels, or tasks
⚠️ A range query steps the expression: each evaluation timestamp is an independent instant evaluation, and the 3.15-line notes fix a subquery @-modifier case — the scheduling the user faces is in the frontend, not the text



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A poor fit outside metrics: series, labels, sample windows, and counter-reset semantics assume a monitoring store, application logic lives in the dashboard and alert-rule layer, and the language is the query surface of the TSDB class — Prometheus, Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics, and Cortex read it, and nothing runs standalone (P4)
✅ The language ships with the stack: the UI, promtool, the API, and every feature flag arrive in the same Apache-2.0 binary, and a new cluster speaks the full language with no install



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The lookback window is the language’s load-bearing default: staleness markers make a series vanish when its scrape stops, rate() extrapolates at window edges, and the semantics that make queries cheap are the semantics a migrated dashboard must re-check
Feature flags graduate, no-op, and gate: the @ modifier, negative offsets, subqueries, duration expressions, and extended-API functions crossed the flag boundary across 2.x and 3.x, so the same expression can be valid on one server and a parse error on the next deployment
Many-to-one matching is a bargain per operator: vector joins align on labels by operator rules, and the release notes show the edges — duplicate-series errors, dropped metric names, NaN propagating through mad_over_time — expressiveness bought one operator at a time
A query is cheap; an evaluation is not: the text carries no cost model, and the engine’s sample limits, queue limits, and cardinality caps decide whether the one-liner lands




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Selectors are indexed lookups: the TSDB postings index serves label matchers, the 3.14 notes ship regex-set matching optimizations, and per-query statistics report the cost through the API
❌ Collector runtime is server latency: 3.0 auto-sets GOMEMLIMIT and GOMAXPROCS to container limits, and the 3.14 notes fix a 100%-CPU shutdown spin that ‘could delay graceful shutdown and trigger timeout-based kills’ — the Go runtime appears in scrape and query timings (R2)
⚠️ The tuning surface is engine limits: max samples per query, lookback window size, and subquery resolution are yaml and CLI knobs, and crossing them is an abort, not a plan choice



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments across the sub-ecosystem: promtool, thanos tools, mimirtool, vmctl, and Grafana each carry rule checkers, explorers, and monitors for the same query text (Ec2)
❌ A niche market: PromQL expertise concentrates in cloud-native observability, and the hiring pool is a fraction of SQL’s (Ec3)
❌ Flags are a compatibility layer: the 3.0 migration guide exists to retire seven-year-old feature flags, rename holt_winters, and repair regex semantics, and an old-ui flag keeps the prior UI alive — the language carries its own migration history (Ec7)
✅ The stack is open end to end: Prometheus (Apache-2.0, CNCF), the client libraries, promtool, and the exposition formats are published, with checksummed downloads on prometheus.io



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ 3.0 shipped published breaking changes: the migration guide names them — range selectors turned left-open, so a subquery that returned two points returns one and ‘No Data’; . now matches newlines; le and quantile labels normalize, so alerts referencing le="1" stop working; strict Content-Type fails v2-compatible scrapes (V1)
❌ Surface rides on feature flags: subqueries, the @ modifier, negative offsets, double_exponential_smoothing, duration expressions, and extended-API functions sit behind --enable-feature switches that graduate, no-op, or gate per release — 3.14 made duration expressions default and promoted first_over_time (V7)
✅ A predictable release rhythm: quarterly minor releases, named LTS lines (3.13, 3.5), a stability promise, and a published migration guide per major — the surface moves on months’ clocks



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting PromQL means adopting the pull-model TSDB: scrape intervals, label conventions, counter-reset semantics, and the default lookback window are the domain, and the language has no shape outside them (D1)
✅ PromQL queries stored metric time-series data: selectors, range windows, and aggregation produce the series that dashboards and alert rules consume
⚠️ Dashboards and rules travel with the language: recording rules, alerting YAML, and Grafana expressions are companion surfaces, and a team maintaining the queries maintains all three



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Four semantics a SQL reader must rebuild: vector matchers replace WHERE, range windows replace BETWEEN, counter resets drive rate() and increase() extrapolation, and label-set rules decide which joins the operators admit (L1)
❌ The surface is a lattice of clauses, functions, modifiers, and flags: the docs split basics, functions, aggregation, subqueries, modifiers, matching, and statements across pages, and experimental functions hide behind CLI switches (L2)
✅ The basics page is readable in one sitting: selectors, operators, and functions with worked examples, and a full published function list



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Operators share symbols with type-specific rules: + adds vector-to-vector under label-matching rules and scalar-to-vector on others, - is unary only on some value kinds, strings (3.0) barely join binary operations, and the bool modifier changes a comparison’s result type (S2)
❌ Punctuation carries meaning: { } for matchers, =~ and !~, : for subqueries, @ for time, [5m] with unit letters, __name__, quoted UTF-8 names in 3.x — and after the 3.0 regex change, a misread pattern still parses and matches more (S3)
✅ The core selector is four tokens: {job="api"} and rate(http_requests_total[5m]) state the common query in a line



1.2.7 Testing

❌ Faults surface at evaluation: many-to-many match errors, No Data from a short subquery after the 3.0 boundary change, and a regex selector that silently matches nothing report only when the query reaches the server (G3)
❌ Only the wall clock: timestamp() and time() read sample and evaluation time, the new start-timestamp function reads ingestion time, and the language names no monotonic clock for elapsed-time tests (G4)
✅ A published test harness ships with the tool: promtool test rules unit-tests alerting and recording rules against input series, an evaluation time, and expected outputs, and the 3.0 notes add debug printouts to it
✅ The UI explains the query: the 3.0 interface carries a PromLens-style explain tree and an Explain tab, and the API reports per-query statistics



1.2.8 Security

❌ Values coerce at evaluation: integer histogram bucket counts feed float64 arithmetic (the 3.14 notes fix sample-type conversions between float, integer-histogram, and float-histogram series), label_replace writes strings where a number was read, and histogram_quantile reads buckets the expression built by hand (Q2)
❌ Counters ride IEEE-754: samples are float64, the project’s own guidance treats counters above 2^53 as losing integer precision, and the 3.14 notes track integer histogram values crossing float encodings in compaction fixes (Q4)
❌ String-built expressions are the injection surface: dashboards and rule generators interpolate values into expressions — the Grafana templating docs publish regex-escaping guidance precisely because a raw value can inject label matchers and operators into the query — and the language has no escape mechanism of its own (Q3)
⚠️ Regex is RE2-linear: label matchers compile to RE2 with a fast literal matcher (3.14 performance work), so the catastrophic backtracking a PCRE selector would invite is structurally absent — the remaining risk is cardinality, not injection

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is a request text: the same expression on the same server version and TSDB reproduces the same samples, and there is no build artifact (Y1)
✅ Servers and consumers pin by version: the binary ships release versions (3.15.1 in late 2026) reported by the version API, and a Go consumer pins the module as an ordinary dependency (Y14)
⚠️ The deployment is the dataset: a result reproduces on a server with specific scrape config, retention, lookback, and out-of-order flags, not on the text alone



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published libraries carry no signed provenance by default: binaries and Docker images ship with SHA256 checksums, exporters and client libraries sit on Maven Central, Go, and PyPI registries, and a consumer trusts the package installed (Y3)
✅ Go module paths, Maven Central, PyPI, and quay.io namespace every artifact, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
✅ Advisories are published: the Prometheus repository maintains GitHub security advisories per release (the 3.15.1 notes bump dependency CVEs), and the Go advisory feed covers the module (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing standard is part of the language: exemplars link samples to trace IDs and the 3.0 OTLP receiver ingests OpenTelemetry metrics, but trace correlation is a deployment feature, and the query text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: the server moved to Go’s log/slog in 3.0, a published format change, and the expression defines no logging construct (Y6)
✅ The server reports its queries: per-query statistics in the API, the TSDB status page, and the query log name the queries, their costs, and the head state behind a result (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The UI is submit-and-run: the browser query page runs an expression instantly, and promtool check and exec subcommands validate rules and run queries with no build step (Y7)
❌ No analyzer the project maintains: an in-editor PromQL extension ships linting in VS Code as an IDE plugin, and full checks land when the query reaches the server on every other editor (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger: diagnosis goes through the explain tree, query statistics, and the server’s logs (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No function interface inside the language: the extended API is a feature-flagged integration point where a process exposes functions the engine calls, and that wiring is server code, not a function the language declares (Y9)
❌ No portable target: a query evaluates on a TSDB-backed server, and nothing runs on a machine without a Prometheus-compatible engine (Y10)
✅ HTTP and OTLP carry results out: the query API answers JSON, the OTLP receiver takes OpenTelemetry metrics, and remote write moves series to any receiver implementing the published protocol



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Governance is a CNCF project: the Prometheus maintainers and technical oversight committee run public design discussions on GitHub, and the feature-flag graduation process is documented (Y11)
✅ The semantics are published: the querying docs define the language per release, the migration guide states every 3.0 semantics change, and the source is Apache-2.0 (Y12)
❌ No conformance mechanism tests the ecosystem: Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics, and Cortex each assert PromQL compatibility with their own suites, and no published suite with implementation reports decides the claim (Y17)
✅ Published parsers: the promql package is Apache-2.0 Go source, the grammar lives in the parser, and remote-read proxies re-implement it from the published docs (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a Prometheus-class server: energy is the engine’s — scrape cadence, retention, and the query guards are the knobs a reader tunes.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A compact, heavily documented language: models write rate() and sum by queries reliably, and the published 3.0 migration notes are exactly what a generated 2.x-era query needs reviewed against.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; Prometheus feeds production alerting pipelines, and its safety record is operational — release-note fixes for CPU spin on shutdown and rule-leak series — not qualification.

Engineering readiness score: 65.5/100 — 59 of the 171 inventory points are present, so the axis cost is 100 × 59 ÷ 171 = 34.5 and the score is 100 − 34.5. Each dimension’s cost above is its share of the same denominator, and the raw weight sum follows in parentheses.
Verdict: PromQL is the most compact language in this analysis: selector syntax over a pull-model TSDB, read by a multi-vendor engine family — Prometheus, Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics, and Cortex — governed by a CNCF project with quarterly releases, named LTS lines, and a published migration guide that lists every 3.0 semantics change: the newline regex rule, the left-open range boundary, le-label normalization, and UTF-8 names all carry documented fixes. Its costs are the metric model’s own: absence is an empty vector, not a type; NaN propagates silently; label identity is composed by regex, rewritten at the OTLP ingest boundary, and paced by the Go runtime, with no constructor check; a vector has no pinned order; the surface rides on feature flags, so a valid parse depends on the deployment; and dashboards interpolate values into expressions the language cannot escape. Main strengths: promtool’s published rule-test harness, the 3.0 explain tree, fully documented breaking changes, a warnings channel in the API response, and ecosystem-wide parser publication. Main weaknesses: a niche beyond observability, no cross-engine conformance suite, no user-function mechanism inside the language, and float64 counters documented as exact only below 2^53.

Snapshot PL/SQL 26ai (Oracle 26ai) — released 14 October 2025 · lifecycle current (Oracle AI Database 26ai, the long-term-support release that replaces 23ai; on-premises general availability followed in January 2026.)
Family PL/SQL — shelf: Data and Science
The language’s primary object is a dataset or a numeric array, not a program loop. A shelf groups; it does not classify — the tags below carry every use, paradigm, and platform of this snapshot.

title: PL/SQL (Oracle 26ai)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PL/SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 41.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, constant, parameter, and function return declares a type, and a mismatch is a compilation error
✅ %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor a declaration to the schema: emp%ROWTYPE follows the table’s column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
✅ Subtypes declare a constrained domain once: SUBTYPE and a constrained type such as NUMBER(7,2) state a range or a shape and reuse it
❌ NULL is not type-safe absence (T10): An unassigned variable and an unused column are NULL, and NULL propagates through expressions, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL
✅ A REF CURSOR carries a row set without fixing its row type: SYS_REFCURSOR passes a result between program units, so the producer and the consumer need not share a record type



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The package separates specification from body: The spec declares the public interface — types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, and subprograms — and the body holds the implementation, so a consumer binds to the spec
✅ Subprogram overloading is available in a package: Two subprograms with one name differ by parameter list, so a family of operations shares one name
✅ A cursor FOR ... LOOP iterates the query result directly: Iteration ends at the result’s last row, so the code does not track a row count
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): A package variable is declared once and lives for the whole session, so every caller that touches the package sees and changes the same value
⚠️ Package initialisation runs on first use: An initialisation block in the body runs when the package is first touched in the session, so setup timing follows call order
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to an insert, update, or delete, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The Oracle server owns SGA and PGA memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
✅ The server sizes the work areas: Automatic PGA management gives a sort or a hash operation its memory from PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET, so the block does not reserve it
⚠️ A session-scoped collection holds its memory: An associative array or nested table kept in a package variable stays for the session, so retained state is a standing cost
⚠️ A bulk fetch needs a deliberate size limit: BULK COLLECT ... LIMIT bounds a fetch, and its absence can materialise a whole result set in PGA
✅ A cursor is released by CLOSE: The server reclaims the cursor’s memory, so the program does not track bytes



1.1.4 Error

✅ The block separates the normal path from the recovery path: DECLARE ... BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END; gives a named handler section
✅ Exceptions are matched by name: A predefined exception (NO_DATA_FOUND, TOO_MANY_ROWS, ZERO_DIVIDE) and a user-declared EXCEPTION are caught by name, and WHEN OTHERS catches the remainder
✅ RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR sets a code and a message: A custom failure carries a number in the application range −20000 to −20999, so a caller can branch on it
⚠️ WHEN OTHERS hides the class of the failure (Er3): A handler that catches everything without logging SQLCODE and SQLERRM, or that does not re-raise, lets the enclosing block see a normal return where the inner block failed
⚠️ No composable result type (Er4): A failure cannot be returned as a value the caller must inspect, so error information does not compose through a call chain



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions are the unit of concurrency: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT make a unit of work atomic, so a block does not coordinate with other sessions statement by statement
✅ An autonomous transaction decouples a log write: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION commits on its own, so the entry survives the caller’s rollback
✅ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE names the rows to lock: The lock is declared by the cursor text rather than by a separate call
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): A package variable is shared with every program unit that runs in the session, and nothing in the declaration marks it private
⚠️ Serialisation across sessions is the application’s to arrange: Where row locks do not apply, two sessions coordinate only through an explicit DBMS_LOCK call, and the ordering between them is nowhere declared
✅ DBMS_LOCK provides an explicit lock service: A named user lock serialises a critical section across sessions



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The block and package model follows the SQL/PSM shape: Persistent stored modules are specified in ISO/IEC 9075 Part 4, and the package and block model follows that concept, though the language itself has no public specification
⚠️ It is implemented outside Oracle Database: TimesTen and IBM Db2 support PL/SQL, so there is more than one implementation, though the dialects are not fully interchangeable
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database, so the unit of deployment is an Oracle schema
❌ The useful surface is Oracle-specific: DBMS_* server packages, ROWNUM, sequences, and SQL%ROWCOUNT are Oracle features, so the code cannot move to another engine unedited
⚠️ A port to Transact-SQL is a rewrite, not a translation: Feature differences and different concurrency and locking models separate the two dialects



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A session-scoped package variable is a deliberate cache: Keeping a value for the session avoids a repeated read; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the cached value when the underlying data changes
A trigger is a data-integrity mechanism: A rule kept in the database is enforced for every writer, where the same rule in the application would be visible at each call site
Logic beside the data is the purpose of the language: A procedure that runs in the database avoids shipping rows to a client; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application’s test suite and profilers
Dynamic SQL buys flexibility: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs DDL and changes object names in a statement, which static SQL cannot do; the cost is that the statement’s shape is known only when it runs




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compilation happens at deployment: A package or procedure is compiled once and the stored form is reused, so a call does not re-parse the source
✅ Native compilation is selectable: PLSQL_CODE_TYPE = NATIVE compiles to machine code, so a hot subprogram does not pay the interpreter
✅ Bulk processing amortises the SQL boundary: FORALL and BULK COLLECT move many rows per round trip, so per-row context switches do not dominate
✅ The optimiser and the SGA serve the data path: Plan selection and buffer caching are the server’s job, not the block’s
⚠️ Cost follows the plan and the retained state: A poorly chosen plan, or a package variable holding a large collection, is a cost the unit cannot see



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Oracle under licence
✅ Tooling is mature and long-established: SQL*Plus, SQL Developer, and third-party IDEs have existed for decades
✅ Published practice is extensive: The PL/SQL language reference, the database manuals, and decades of books and courses document the language in detail
⚠️ Capability follows the licence: Tooling, support, and advanced features are licensed per seat or per processor, so a team reaches only what it has bought
⚠️ Enterprise code bases are long-lived and heavy: A schema commonly spans many versions, so a change has to keep the oldest callers working



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A program written for an early Oracle release generally still compiles and runs in the current one
✅ Edition-based redefinition supports an online change: EDITIONABLE objects let a new version of a package be deployed and switched over without downtime
✅ Deprecation is announced before removal: Oracle documents deprecated features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
⚠️ A language feature arrives with a database release: Adoption timing therefore follows the customer’s upgrade cycle, not a separate language release
⚠️ A new feature is unavailable on a pinned older database: Code that must run on an old release cannot use a recent construct
❌ Build variants multiply: $IF and $THEN directives select which PL/SQL statements compile, evaluated against package state at compile time (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for data-centric business logic: A procedure operates on tables with SQL directly, so a rule runs where the data is
✅ The language is a full procedural language inside SQL: Loops, records, collections, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
✅ Server packages reach outside the schema: UTL_FILE, UTL_HTTP, and DBMS_SCHEDULER give file, network, and job facilities from inside the database
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain
⚠️ A trigger can hide a domain rule: An invariant implemented in a trigger is enforced for every writer, but a reader of the application source cannot see it
⚠️ The language is not a general-purpose runtime: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a high-rate service belongs in another language beside PL/SQL



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Moderate for a SQL-plus-Pascal background: The block structure follows Ada and Pascal, so a developer from those languages reads it quickly
⚠️ The SQL-to-PL/SQL boundary needs practice: A SELECT inside a block must return exactly one row, so NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS are everyday cases
⚠️ Package semantics take time: Spec versus body, per-session package state, and initialisation timing are not visible in the syntax
⚠️ Exception semantics reward careful reading: An exception in a nested block propagates to the enclosing handler unless it is handled there
✅ The reference documentation is complete: The Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference documents every construct with examples



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable and keyword-led: Statements read as verbs — INSERT INTO, FETCH, RAISE — so intent is visible
✅ Blocks nest visibly: An inner BEGIN ... END holds its own declarations and handler, so scope follows the indentation
❌ Verbose (S1): Even a small unit needs a declaration section, a BEGIN ... END, and an exception section, so the block structure adds lines to every subprogram
⚠️ END closes several constructs: END IF;, END LOOP;, and a package END must each be matched, so a long body is read against its terminators
⚠️ A large package body is one long file: The spec and the body are a unit boundary, not a file-per-subprogram rule



1.2.7 Testing

✅ utPLSQL is the established framework: An open-source test framework runs suites with assertions and reporting, so tests need not be hand-rolled
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run and ROLLBACK, leaving the database unchanged
✅ The toolchain traces execution: DBMS_PROFILER, DBMS_TRACE, and the hierarchical profiler report call counts and coverage
⚠️ A suite depends on grants and deployment: The framework is installed in the database it tests, so permissions and schema state are preconditions
❌ No monotonic reading published: SYSTIME and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are wall readings anchored per session (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Bind variables remove the injection surface: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ... WHERE x = :1' USING v passes the value out of band, so it cannot change the parse
✅ DBMS_ASSERT validates an identifier before interpolation: SIMPLE_SQL_NAME, QUALIFIED_SQL_NAME, and ENQUOTE_NAME check the string
✅ The rights model is explicit: AUTHID DEFINER and AUTHID CURRENT_USER select whether a unit runs with its owner’s privileges or the caller’s
✅ Privileges are granted per object: GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg TO role scopes access, and the package specification is the grantable interface
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and DBMS_SQL build a statement as text, so concatenated input can become code
⚠️ Definer’s-rights code can escalate: A unit that runs with its definer’s rights reaches more than the caller, so it needs an audit



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Compilation state lives in the dictionary; no reproducible build exists outside the database. (Y1)
❌ Units resolve dependencies against the schema at compile time. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Schema sources and third-party packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to PL/SQL libraries. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO is a convention. (Y5)
❌ DBMS_OUTPUT is the whole logging surface. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the database; the IDE debuggers are separate products. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The unit runs only in Oracle-family databases. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Oracle decides the language’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists; the manuals document one implementation. (Y12)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

❌ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: PL/SQL’s coupling is set by its host, not its syntax. The package separates a specification from its body, blocks and named exceptions give a structured failure path, and bind variables close the injection surface. Main strengths: interface and implementation are separable, error handling is structured, and server-side code runs beside its data. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside an Oracle database, a package variable is shared session state, every variable starts as NULL and NULL propagates, dynamic SQL turns concatenated text into code, and WHEN OTHERS is a standing invitation to swallow a failure.

title: N1QL (Couchbase 7.6 / SQL++)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses N1QL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61.3/100 · Engineering readiness 61.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No sum types: An alternative is encoded with MISSING, NULL, and discriminator fields, and expressions test the encoding by convention (T4)
❌ No generics: A query cannot be parameterised over a type, so reusable logic is copied, stored as a view, or wrapped in a JavaScript function (T5)
❌ MISSING and NULL are distinct values: An absent field and a null field compare unequal, and comparisons over them form a three-valued logic (T10)
❌ A call’s signature says what it returns, not what it does: A JavaScript user-defined function runs in the query service, and the statement shows the call, not the body’s effects (T12)
❌ User-defined JavaScript crosses into the query service unchecked: A function is declared by name, and the engine does not check its body against typed expectations (T14)
✅ Type expressions are checked at prepare time: SQL++ type expressions validate typed paths against the query’s declared types before execution



1.1.2 Construction

✅ NEST and UNNEST compose nested collections without shared state: A query flattens and groups embedded arrays inside its own clauses
⚠️ Keyspace semantics reach past the query: USE KEYS, USE INDEX, and covering-index clauses bind a statement to storage design
⚠️ Views store statements server-side: A stored view is a dependency a reviewer must fetch from the cluster to read a query in full



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The cluster owns allocation: Index entries, join buffers, and result streaming are managed by the services, not by the statement
⚠️ Large joins can exhaust service memory: An unbounded nested-loop join over big keyspaces streams results only after the join completes



1.1.4 Error

✅ Syntax and scope errors are caught at prepare time: Unknown keyspaces, malformed clauses, and bad aliases are reported before the statement runs
⚠️ Runtime failures depend on the data: Casts, arithmetic on strings, and array-index faults surface only when the matching document is reached



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group writes atomically: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK wrap N1QL writes in a distributed transaction
⚠️ Isolation is service-specific: The transaction service’s isolation levels decide what a concurrent statement observes



1.1.6 Platform

❌ N1QL runs only inside a Couchbase cluster: The query service, the index service, and the data services are one vendor’s product, and no other engine implements the dialect (P1)
❌ N1QL is a poor fit outside database work: General application logic, loops beyond queries, and external I/O are pushed to a host language (P4)
⚠️ SQL++ is the shared core, not the dialect: The standard’s scope covers the common language, while Couchbase’s clauses remain vendor-defined



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

SQL familiarity against document semantics: The SQL-shaped surface carries readers in fast; NEST, UNNEST, and keyspace clauses are new material the familiarity does not cover
MISSING and NULL keep absent fields honest: The document model distinguishes absent from null, and three-valued comparisons become a cost every reader pays
Vendor clauses buy performance: USE KEYS and covering-index directives buy plan control at the cost of binding a statement to one product’s storage
JavaScript functions extend the language: User-defined functions buy general computation at the cost of an unchecked boundary in the query service




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The query service compiles statements to a distributed plan: Index selection, join order, and partition pruning are planned before execution
⚠️ Plan quality depends on index design: A statement is fast with a covering index and a full keyspace scan without one



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments across editions and syntax generations: The Query Workbench, the cbq CLI, and the drivers target Couchbase versions at different support levels (Ec2)
❌ The N1QL ecosystem is niche: The library pool, hiring market, and third-party tooling are thinner than for SQL and the major document stores (Ec3)
❌ The server, the tooling, and the documentation come from Couchbase under licence: Enterprise features sit behind a commercial licence, and Community Edition ships under SSPL (Ec4)
❌ Pre-6.0 N1QL syntax is still accepted alongside SQL++: Two generations coexist in the query service, so every new feature inherits the compatibility surface (Ec7)
✅ Official SDKs cover the mainstream languages: Couchbase maintains SDKs for many ecosystems, installed through ordinary package managers



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Releases changed the language’s surface: The move from N1QL 5 syntax to SQL++-based 6.0, and deprecations across 7.x, put a version agreement under every statement (V1)
❌ The SQL++ standard moves on a committee cycle: The GDMC working group publishes drafts slowly, and Couchbase ships clauses engine-first (V4)
✅ Release notes name each query feature’s version: The documentation states which Couchbase release introduced each clause



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting N1QL means adopting the Couchbase platform: The language is tied to the document store, the query service, and the index service (D1)
✅ N1QL is used to query stored document data: SELECT ... FROM keyspace retrieves documents, and INSERT, UPDATE, and MERGE write them
⚠️ Nested-document joins are non-SQL: NEST, UNNEST, and USE KEYS carry document semantics a relational reader must learn separately



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The SQL-shaped surface transfers: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and joins read as SQL to anyone with SQL experience
❌ Advanced material is thin: Index design, planner behaviour, and join semantics are documented by example and by blog posts, not systematically (L3)
⚠️ Keyspace and index idioms take practice: Covering indexes, partial indexes, and scan directives are storage decisions a newcomer must learn alongside the language



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Comparable things are written differently: NEST and UNNEST pair where SQL uses subqueries, USE KEYS selects by key, and pre-6.0 statements used positional aliases (S2)
⚠️ Backtick-quoted keyspaces carry the names: ``travel-sample` ``, quoting keyspace names, reads as a delimiter convention
✅ Statements read as SQL clauses in order: A query’s shape is visible without learning a new dataflow model



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test harness ships with the language: Testing N1QL requires a running cluster and a harness each project builds for itself (G1)
⚠️ Plan review is standard practice: EXPLAIN reports the chosen plan, and the Query Workbench shows it while the author edits
❌ No monotonic clock is published in the language: now() and local_now() read the wall clock, so elapsed-time tests depend on cluster clocks (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ String-built statements are an injection surface: Concatenating untrusted input into a statement text lets that input change the parse (Q3)
❌ Documents arrive untyped at write time: Field types in a schemaless keyspace are data, so a query must re-check each type at every use (Q2)
✅ Parameterised statements remove the injection surface: Bound parameters carry data out of band, so a value cannot become syntax

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A statement is a request text: The same statement submitted to the same cluster version and dataset produces the same result, and there is no build artifact to reproduce (Y1)
⚠️ Statements live beside the application that submits them: A deployment stores no manifest naming the server version the statement was written against



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published SDKs carry no signed provenance by default: A consumer must trust the package they install (Y3)
✅ SDKs publish in registries with an ownership model: Package names on npm, PyPI, and Maven identify the publisher, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
✅ Couchbase publishes security advisories naming the affected product and version: A consumer reads a published CVE record to learn a server release or SDK version is affected (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: Observability is provided by the server’s own metrics services (Y5)
❌ No structured logging is defined in the language: Diagnostics are server log entries with their own format (Y6)
✅ Failed queries are recorded by the server: The query log and request status inspector name the statement, its duration, and its error (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit-test loop is a text submission: There is no compile step between editing a statement and running it (Y7)
❌ No fast in-editor analysis ships for N1QL: Syntax is checked when the statement is submitted; editors have no incremental analyser for the language (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger ships with the language: Debugging is done through explain plans, the query log, and Workbench traces (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ User-defined functions call host-language code: JavaScript functions extend the query service without leaving the process (Y9)
❌ The statement runs only inside a Couchbase cluster: The plan spans the query, index, and data services of one product (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is Couchbase-led: The dialect ships with the query service, and the roadmap follows the vendor (Y11)
✅ The SQL++ core has a public draft specification: The GDMC working group publishes the shared language for independent implementation (Y12)
❌ No conformance suite exists: SQL++ implementations cannot run a shared test suite against the draft standard (Y17)
✅ The N1QL parser is open source: Couchbase publishes the parser on GitHub, so third-party tools can parse statements (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a Couchbase cluster: energy and time are the services’, not the statement’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ SQL-shaped statements with public examples: current models write common N1QL queries reliably, though keyspace and index clauses need review.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: N1QL’s coupling is set by its host, not by its SQL-shaped surface. The clause structure transfers to anyone with SQL experience, prepare-time checks catch syntax and scope errors, and bound parameters close the injection surface a string-built statement opens. What the language charges: it runs only inside a Couchbase cluster, its vendor clauses sit beyond the SQL++ standard, two syntax generations coexist under the query service, and the ecosystem is niche behind a vendor licence. Main strengths: SQL-shaped access to nested JSON, distributed joins planned by the query service, and a public parser with a public draft standard for its core. Main weaknesses: single-vendor governance with no conformance suite, sparse advanced documentation on index and planner behaviour, and JavaScript user-defined functions that cross an unchecked boundary.

title: MATLAB (R2026a)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses MATLAB in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 72.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.8/100 · Engineering readiness 29.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A variable takes its type from the value assigned to it, so a type error is reported only when the statement runs
⚠️ A numeric value carries a class but no shape: double is the default for a literal, and a 1×1 scalar, a vector, and a matrix are the same class, so the type does not state the dimensions the algorithm needs
⚠️ Cell arrays and structs are weak structural types: They group heterogeneous values but declare no schema, so a consumer learns a struct’s fields from the code that fills it
⚠️ Only a package folder scopes a name: A +pkg folder gives its functions and classes their own namespace, but a plain function or script on the search path shares one flat name space with every other file on the path, so a collision is resolved by path order
⚠️ Argument validation is opt-in: An arguments block (R2019b+) checks class, size, and shape at call time, but a function without one accepts anything



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Toolboxes separate domain computation from the core language: Signal Processing, Control System, and Image Processing operations are ordinary function calls, so an algorithm does not embed its own filter or transform code
✅ A classdef file groups state with its operations: Properties and methods are declared in one unit, so a consumer binds to the class name
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): The base workspace and every shared function workspace hold variables that running code can read and overwrite at any time
❌ No immutability by default (C2): Every array is mutable, and there is no const-like freeze for ordinary data
⚠️ Constructors are ordinary methods with no enforced invariant: A class defines its own Name(...) constructor, so a well-formed instance depends on the author’s validation
⚠️ Scripts run in the caller’s workspace: A variable a script creates stays in the caller after the script returns, so a script couples to every caller’s variable names
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: string function handles (str2func, feval with a char name) resolve to code at run time, and the source names a string, not the call (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Copy-on-modify protects the reader: An assignment copies a value only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives an array does not change the caller’s value
⚠️ The collector runs on its own schedule (M2): Memory returns when the interpreter decides, so release timing is not owned by the code
❌ No RAII (M3): There is no block-scoped destructor, so a file handle, timer, or instrument connection stays open until delete or an onCleanup object runs
❌ No ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties an array’s storage to one owner
⚠️ clear and pack are manual controls: Freeing a large array and defragmenting the workspace are explicit calls, so the memory strategy is the programmer’s
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a Java-heap exhaustion inside the interpreter ends the session (documented), below the try/catch surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ try/catch gives a structured recovery path: A catch block receives the MException object, with its identifier, message, and stack, so recovery need not parse text
✅ error takes a stable identifier: error('pkg:func:reason', ...) sets MException.identifier, so a caller can branch on the code rather than on the message
❌ Unchecked exceptions only (Er2): A raised MException travels up until something catches it or the program stops, and no caller is required to handle it
⚠️ An empty catch is common in legacy code: A catch block with no body discards the failure without a trace
⚠️ Many failures are detected only at run time: An out-of-bound index, a class mismatch, or a singular matrix is reported when the statement executes



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Manual synchronisation with no race detection (K3): parfor, spmd, and parfeval leave the shared-variable reasoning to the programmer, and the language reports no data race
✅ parfor separates loop iterations: An independent loop is split across workers, so iteration order is not part of the result
✅ labSend and labReceive pass data between spmd workers: A worker sends a value to a named peer instead of writing into shared memory
⚠️ The parallel constructs need the Parallel Computing Toolbox: parfor, distributed arrays, and parpool are a separate licensed product
⚠️ A captured variable is broadcast to every worker: A parfor body sees a copy of the outer variable, and a reduction must use a supported form or a temporary variable



1.1.6 Platform

✅ GNU Octave is a compatible open implementation: Most MATLAB programs run under Octave, so a project is not bound to one vendor’s binary alone
⚠️ A licence still governs the base product: An installation of MATLAB itself needs a licence, so deployment and continuous integration depend on MathWorks’ terms and pricing
⚠️ Toolbox coverage is proprietary: Domain functions come from licensed MathWorks toolboxes, so portability depends on which toolboxes the code calls
⚠️ A compiled component still needs the MATLAB Runtime: MATLAB Compiler builds a library callable from C, C++, .NET, or Python, but the component runs against a version-matched MATLAB Runtime



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One-based indexing is a convention choice: Starting an array at index 1 is a documented decision, and the cost is re-learning for a user who comes from a zero-based language
The global workspace suits interactive work: A session-wide namespace is convenient at the command line, and the coupling it creates at scale follows from using session state as program state
Everything-is-an-array is a deliberate uniformity: One container for scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D arrays keeps the language small, and the loss of shape in the type is the price
The filename rule is a lookup convention: A function file is named for its entry point, and local functions in scripts (a later addition) reduce the constraint
A proprietary platform is traded for an integrated toolchain: The licence buys one install, one editor, and one support channel
Scripts are for session-scale tasks: Converting a script to a function removes the caller-workspace coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Matrix expressions call tuned BLAS and LAPACK libraries: A*B, A\b, and fft run in compiled libraries, so numerical throughput does not depend on hand-written loops
✅ Vectorisation removes per-element interpreter overhead: One array expression is one interpreted call, whatever the element count
⚠️ The interpreter performs no ahead-of-time compilation (R1): Base MATLAB executes an interpreted form, so a loop that cannot be vectorised is slower than its compiled equivalent
✅ The execution engine compiles eligible code just in time: The engine introduced in R2015b accelerates a repeated loop after warm-up
⚠️ Speed follows the shipped library, not the source: The cost of a signal-processing or control operation depends on the toolbox build and on the CPU it was tuned for



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): Toolboxes, the editor, and the reference documentation come from one vendor under licence
✅ The toolbox library covers most engineering fields: Optimization, Statistics and Machine Learning, Signal Processing, and Control System toolboxes are long-established products
✅ The Add-On Explorer installs packages by name: MathWorks and community add-ons are installed through one manager, so a project does not have to vendor source
✅ MATLAB Central File Exchange is a large community index: User-contributed functions and toolboxes are published together and searchable
⚠️ Toolboxes ship in lockstep with the release: A toolbox is versioned for the MATLAB release it targets, so an upgrade can require every toolbox to move
⚠️ Every tool in the chain assumes a licensed installation: Editors and continuous-integration integrations exist, but they resolve back to a licensed MATLAB
❌ A MEX file binds to a release: MathWorks requires MEX files to be rebuilt for a new release, on a compiler that release supports [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored data crosses on a published promise: releases R2006b and later all support all MAT file versions, and save can write an older version on request [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is a stated commitment: MathWorks keeps old syntax working and warns before a feature is removed, so a program from an earlier release generally still runs
✅ Two releases a year on a known cadence: R2026a and R2026b follow a predictable schedule, so an upgrade path can be planned
✅ verLessThan lets one source span two releases: A program can branch on the MATLAB version, so an old and a new release can be supported together
⚠️ An upgrade can change performance or a default: A new execution engine, a new library version, or a changed default can alter timing or output for code that relied on the old behaviour
⚠️ A deprecated function may stop working later: Deprecation is announced, but a function or toolbox marked for removal eventually goes away



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for numerical linear algebra: Matrix syntax, \ for a linear solve, and N-D arrays match the mathematics directly
✅ Signal processing, control systems, and image processing are first-class domains: Each ships as an endorsed toolbox with the reference algorithms
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language and its library set target one vendor’s platform, so adoption is also a procurement decision
⚠️ Simulink is a second modelling toolchain: A graphical model is not MATLAB source, so a control design that uses Simulink couples to a second product and file format
⚠️ General application work sits outside the design centre: File handling, text processing, and network code read as additions to a numerical language



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ Moderate at the start and steeper later (L1): A\b and 1:n are learnable in days, while vectorisation, the workspace model, and copy semantics take practice
⚠️ The workspace model confuses newcomers: A variable a script creates persists in the caller, so a beginner cannot tell where state lives
⚠️ One-based indexing diverges from most languages: Code ported from a C-family or Python source needs every index checked by hand
✅ Documentation is uniform and complete: Every function has a reference page with examples, and the language is taught in standard textbooks
⚠️ Toolbox knowledge is separate from language knowledge: Finding the right function means knowing which toolbox owns the domain



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Matrix-oriented and compact: A(:, 2) = A(:, 1) * 3; expresses a whole-column operation in one statement
✅ Keyword-light and readable: Most statements are operations on data, with few punctuation-only constructs
⚠️ Element-wise and matrix operators differ by one dot: * versus .* and ^ versus .^ are distinct operations, so a missing dot silently changes the computation
⚠️ end is overloaded: It terminates a block and marks the last index inside a subscript
⚠️ The semicolon controls output rather than the statement: A missing ; prints every intermediate result, which clutters a long run



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework ships in the base product: matlab.unittest.TestCase, functiontests, and runtests provide assertions, fixtures, and parameterised cases
✅ A failure reports the value and the assertion: The framework prints the constraint that failed and the observed value, so a failure is localised
✅ Mocking and coverage are part of the framework: matlab.mock creates replacement objects, and the code-coverage plugin reports unexecuted lines
⚠️ A test suite lives in function files beside the code: There is no separate test manifest, so a suite’s scope follows the folder layout
⚠️ Automated runs need a licence: Continuous integration needs a licence seat or a pre-built component with the MATLAB Runtime



1.2.8 Security

✅ No pointers and no manual memory access: The language offers no address arithmetic, so a buffer overflow cannot be written in MATLAB source
✅ External access is explicit in the source: fopen, readmatrix, and webread are visible calls, so a reader can see every file and network access
⚠️ eval, evalin, and str2func execute text as code: A string built from untrusted input can become a statement, which is the injection pattern
⚠️ load can introduce undeclared variables: Restoring a .mat file creates variables whose names the source does not state, and such a name can shadow a live variable
⚠️ Static proof of run-time error freedom needs a separate product: Polyspace Code Prover proves the absence of certain run-time errors, but it is licensed apart from the language
❌ The integer types saturate to the type bounds, documented; the clamp is silent (Q4)

Verdict: MATLAB’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling for numerical engineering work. Matrix operations remove per-element iteration from the source, and toolboxes separate domain algorithms from the core language. Main strengths: an excellent fit for linear algebra, signal processing, and control systems; a large library; and a strong backward-compatibility record. Main weaknesses: the base workspace and every script variable form one shared mutable namespace with no namespaces, typing is dynamic with no static check, indexing is one-based against most languages, and the whole platform is proprietary, so cost and portability follow MathWorks’ licence and pricing.
