title: Gremlin (Apache TinkerPop 3.7)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Gremlin in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 67.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are dynamically typed: A property or traversal result has no static type declaration, so a type fault appears when the step runs (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative is modelled with nullable properties, separate vertices, or explicit type labels (T4)
❌ No generics: A traversal cannot be abstracted over a type parameter, so reusable logic is copied or wrapped (T5)
❌ NULL and optional values are not type-safe: A step may produce null, and the next step fails only on the path that reaches it (T10)
❌ A traversal’s side effects are not tracked in its type: A sideEffect or lambda step may mutate state, and nothing in the traversal signature records it (T12)
❌ Lambdas and script bindings cross into the host language unchecked: A closure passed to the traversal is type-checked only by the host runtime, not by the graph engine (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A traversal composes by chaining steps: Each step returns a traversal, so a complex query is built from small, named operations
✅ Steps are referentially transparent at the language level: Reusing a traversal value does not introduce hidden mutable state
⚠️ Stateful side-effect steps require care: sideEffect, aggregate, and group introduce state that must be understood in the order of the traversal



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The traversal engine manages intermediate results: Bulksets, paths, and traversers are allocated and reclaimed by the engine
⚠️ Unbounded traversals can exhaust memory: A path step with no limit or a dense bulkset can still overflow the configured heap



1.1.4 Error

✅ Malformed traversal steps are caught when the traversal is built: Missing steps and unknown labels are reported early
⚠️ Type and arity failures surface at execution: A step that expects a vertex but receives a value fails only when that traverser is processed



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The traversal runs inside a transaction: The graph database provides atomicity and isolation
⚠️ Concurrency is an engine concern, not a traversal concern: The language itself has no construct for parallel traversal



1.1.6 Platform

✅ TinkerPop abstracts over many graph databases: Gremlin runs on Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph, Cosmos DB, and others
⚠️ Feature support varies by provider: Transactions, lambdas, and server-side scripts are not available on every backend
❌ The language is a poor fit outside graph traversal: General application logic and non-graph algorithms belong in a host language (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic typing keeps queries flexible: A traversal can navigate mixed property types, but type faults move to execution
Lambdas extend expressiveness: Host-language closures add power, but they also add an unchecked boundary and an injection path
Functional composition versus readability: Long chains of steps are powerful but can obscure the underlying graph pattern
Provider-specific optimisations trade portability: A traversal tuned for one backend may run poorly on another




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The graph computer framework can distribute traversals: OLAP traversals can run across a cluster for large graphs
⚠️ Traversal performance depends on the provider’s optimiser: A step chain that is idiomatic Gremlin may still be slow if the provider does not optimise it



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments by provider: Drivers, visualisers, and debugging tools often target one TinkerPop-enabled backend (Ec2)
✅ Gremlin language variants are available in many host languages: Gremlin-Python, Gremlin-Java, Gremlin-JavaScript, and others let the traversal live in the application language
⚠️ The ecosystem is smaller than SQL’s: Libraries, learning material, and practitioners are fewer than for relational query languages



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Apache TinkerPop releases are open and documented: Roadmaps and migration notes are published by the project
⚠️ Provider implementations advance at different speeds: A new TinkerPop feature may not be available on every backend immediately



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting Gremlin means adopting a graph database and a TinkerPop provider: The traversal language is tied to the graph data model (D1)
✅ Excellent fit for path and neighbourhood queries: Traversal steps such as out, in, both, and repeat match graph structure directly
⚠️ Set-based relational queries are less natural: Aggregations and tabular results are possible but read as workarounds
✅ Gremlin is used to query stored graph data: g.V().hasLabel(...) retrieves vertices and out() walks relationships



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Thinking in traversals is a different model: A developer must shift from set-based or imperative logic to step-by-step graph navigation (L1)
✅ Steps are small and composable: Each step does one thing, and a traversal can be read left to right
⚠️ Order and bulkset semantics must be understood: A step that looks imperative may behave differently under bulkset optimisation



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Fluent step chains are compact: g.V().hasLabel("person").out("knows").values("name") reads as a pipeline
⚠️ Long traversals can become deeply nested: Nested choose, coalesce, and repeat steps push indentation to the right



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Profile and explain steps are built in: profile() and explain() expose the chosen traversal strategy
❌ No monotonic clock is published: Timing a traversal relies on the host language’s wall clock or the engine profile timer (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ String-built traversals are an injection surface: Concatenating untrusted input into a script lets that input become code (Q3)
✅ Parameterised bindings separate data from code: Bind variables keep user values out of the traversal text
⚠️ Lambdas and script execution re-open the risk: A traversal that embeds host-language code can execute arbitrary logic

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A Gremlin traversal is a query text or a host-language expression: The same traversal submitted to the same engine version and dataset produces the same result (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published drivers and language variants carry no signed provenance by default: A consumer must trust the package they install (Y3)
✅ No package registry exists for Gremlin modules: There is therefore no registry namespace to confuse or hijack (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: Observability is provided by the engine and its drivers (Y5)
❌ No structured logging is defined in the language: Diagnostics are engine log entries with their own format (Y6)
✅ Failed traversals leave a query log and a stack trace: The engine records the traversal and the error location (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit-test loop is a text submission or a host-language build: There is no separate compile step for the traversal text (Y7)
✅ Editors and drivers provide fast syntax feedback: The traversal is parsed before it is executed (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger ships with the language: Debugging is done through profile steps, logs, and engine tools (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ Script and lambda steps can call host-language code: The engine is not closed to other languages (Y9)
❌ The traversal runs only inside a TinkerPop-enabled graph database: There is no portable target outside that context (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Apache TinkerPop governs the language through an open process: Roadmap and releases are decided in the open (Y11)
✅ The TinkerPop reference documentation is public: The language surface is documented and can be implemented by others (Y12)
❌ No conformance suite exists: Independent providers cannot run a shared test suite against the specification (Y17)
✅ Grammar and parser resources are published: Third-party tools can parse Gremlin without reverse engineering (Y19)

Verdict: Gremlin’s design yields low-to-moderate coupling for graph traversal. The functional step chain composes without shared mutable state, and the TinkerPop abstraction lets one traversal run on several backends. Main strengths: composable traversal steps, multi-provider portability, and strong fit for path queries. Main weaknesses: dynamic typing, no sum types or generics, side effects are not tracked, tooling fragments by provider, and lambdas or string-built traversals re-open injection and unchecked-boundary risks.

title: Fortran (2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Fortran in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 51.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.8/100 · Engineering readiness 52.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Typing is static but implicit typing is the default: Without implicit none, a name beginning with I–N is an integer and every other name is a real, so a misspelled variable becomes a new one rather than an error (T2)
❌ There are no sum types: An alternative is encoded as an integer tag beside the payload fields, and select case or select type must decode it, so nothing checks that the right branch was taken (T4)
⚠️ There are no generics, and a generic interface overloads a name instead: An interface block binds one name to several specific procedures and the compiler resolves the call by argument type, which is overloading without a type parameter (T5)
⚠️ Operator and assignment overloading is expressible: interface operator(+) and interface assignment(=) redefine + and = for a derived type, so the work behind an operator is invisible at the call site (T8)
✅ A module is a namespace with a selective import: use mymodule, only: a, b brings in two names and nothing else, so no flat global namespace is imposed
✅ class(t) and select type give checked run-time polymorphism: A polymorphic dummy argument dispatches on the dynamic type of the actual argument, and select type narrows it in a checked branch



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global mutable state is the default storage class: A module variable and a common block are shared by every procedure that names them, and a variable marked save keeps its value between calls (C1)
❌ There is no immutability by default: Only a parameter names a constant, and a module variable is writable by any user unless it carries the Fortran 2003 protected attribute (C2)
❌ A structure constructor validates nothing: t(a, b) fills the components in order or by keyword, and no invariant can be stated at the type, so a valid object exists only because the caller made it valid (C4)
✅ A pure procedure states the absence of side effects: It may not write a global, an intent(in) argument, or a saved variable, and the compiler enforces the rule
✅ intent(in), intent(out), and intent(inout) state the direction of an argument: The declaration says whether a routine reads, writes, or does both, and the compiler checks it at the call site
✅ elemental states an elementwise operation: An elemental procedure applies to each element of an array, so a scalar definition composes with array construction without a written loop
❌ One value, many names: argument association passes the caller’s storage to the callee (documented), so two names — one in each program unit — write one object (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: defined ASSIGNMENT and defined operators run user code at an assignment or operator site that names no call (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ allocate and deallocate are written by hand for a pointer: The language tracks no owner and no bound, so a pointer target is freed by an explicit statement and a missing one leaks (M1)
❌ There is no ownership model: A pointer may alias a target, dangle after deallocate, or be freed twice, and the compiler does not see the aliasing (M4)
⚠️ Release tied to scope is partial: An allocatable local and a derived-type component with a final procedure are released at scope exit, but a pointer is not, so the rule differs by variable kind (M3)
⚠️ An allocation failure must be tested: allocate(a(n), stat=ierr) returns a code the program has to check, and without stat= a failure aborts the program
✅ move_alloc transfers an allocation without a copy: call move_alloc(from, to) moves the storage and deallocates the source, so a result array is returned without duplication
✅ Allocatable locals are released at procedure exit: An allocatable array declared inside a procedure is deallocated when the procedure returns, which is a scope-tied release the language provides
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: a local without SAVE or an initializer is undefined at entry, and reading it is the classic source of nonzero garbage that changes between builds (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: EQUIVALENCE overlays unrelated declarations on one storage, and the TRANSFER intrinsic reinterprets any value’s bits as another type (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a runtime fault beyond STOP has no declared handler path — the standard names STOP, not recovery (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no exception mechanism: A failure is reported through a stat=/iostat= code or an err= label, and the caller has to test it (Er1)
❌ A returned code can be ignored: Nothing obliges a caller to look at iostat, so a failed read, allocate, or deallocate proceeds as though it had succeeded unless the program checks (Er3)
❌ There is no composable result type: No value carries either a result or an error, so error state travels in an extra out argument or in a saved flag (Er4)
✅ error stop gives a defined abort: Since Fortran 2008, error stop stops the program with a message or an integer stop-code, and Fortran 2018 added the optional quiet= specifier, so a fatal failure is stated rather than inferred from a negative status
⚠️ IEEE exceptional values are inspected through an intrinsic module: ieee_arithmetic and ieee_exceptions let a program test ieee_is_nan and select a halting mode, but the checks are ordinary calls rather than a language guarantee
✅ A pure procedure cannot perform I/O: An I/O failure is outside a pure procedure by construction, so a computational kernel has no I/O error channel to handle
❌ A fault ends the program: STOP ends execution (documented), and the standard publishes no recoverable unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Coarray images share memory by default: A coarray declared with codimension is written by one image and read by another, and nothing in the language prevents the race (K2)
⚠️ Synchronisation is manual: sync all, sync images, event post/event wait, and lock/unlock are image control statements the program must place at the right point
✅ do concurrent states an independent loop: The construct asserts that the iterations have no interdependencies, and Fortran 2018 adds local, local_init, and shared locality specifications, so the compiler may parallelise it
✅ atomic and critical give a defined atomic access: atomic define/atomic_ref and a critical construct express one update that must not interleave
⚠️ The practical parallel model sits outside the language: Coarray support varies across compilers, so most high-performance code uses OpenMP directives or MPI calls



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One standard source runs on every major compiler: gfortran, ifx, nagfor, Cray, and LLVM flang accept standard-conforming Fortran on Linux, Windows, macOS, and the large HPC systems
✅ iso_c_binding names the interoperable interface: c_int, c_double, c_ptr, and c_funptr let a Fortran routine be called from C and call C in return
✅ iso_fortran_env names the portable kinds and units: real64, int32, and input_unit state a portable choice where real(8) names one machine’s representation
✅ A compiled module is a binary interface: A module is compiled to a file a consumer imports, so the interface is checked when the consumer is compiled
⚠️ Vendor directives are common in working code: !DIR$ and !DEC$ directives, REAL*8, and STRUCTURE/RECORD appear in legacy HPC source, which binds it to one compiler
⚠️ Coarray support varies by compiler and platform: A coarray program depends on the compiler’s image implementation and its transport library, so its portability is weaker than that of a serial program



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

implicit none is the modern practice, not the standard default: A project chooses to require it, and the language permits implicit typing for the old source
Column-major order is a deliberate numerical choice: Array expressions follow Fortran’s storage order, which is what the linear-algebra kernels are written for
The aliasing rules are what the optimiser needs: The standard’s restrictions let the compiler vectorise a loop, which costs flexibility and buys speed
goto remains for compatibility: It is retained so that decades of code keeps compiling, and a new program need not use it
Whole-array syntax exists so the compiler chooses the loop nest: The programmer gives up per-loop control in exchange for vectorisation
The legacy corpus is working, tested numerical code: The aging ecosystem holds decades of validated physics and linear-algebra routines




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The program is compiled to machine code: gfortran, ifx, and flang emit native objects for the target CPU, and the performance of an array kernel rivals C
✅ Array syntax maps onto the machine’s loop nests: a = b + c over whole arrays lets the compiler fuse and vectorise the loops, and matmul and dot_product have library or instruction implementations
✅ Nothing between the source and the CPU interprets: A Fortran binary has no bytecode dispatch and no JIT warm-up
⚠️ The optimiser needs the aliasing facts: Without intent(in), contiguous, and pure, the compiler must assume a possible alias and cannot reorder the loops
⚠️ The floating-point contract is the compiler’s flags: -O3 with -ffast-math or -fp-model fast changes the order of the operations, so the measured speed depends on the build options



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ There is no standard package manager for the language: Dependencies are resolved by a language-agnostic manager such as Spack or Conda or by the system manager, and the fpm package manager is young and small (Ec3)
✅ The numerical libraries are mature and standard: BLAS, LAPACK, and the vendor-tuned kernels (MKL, ESSL) are callable from Fortran directly
✅ A compiler is available on every system: A Fortran compiler is installed on every HPC cluster and is packaged for every common Linux distribution
✅ Interoperation with the C and Python ecosystems is standard: iso_c_binding and the Python wrapper generators make a Fortran kernel callable from a Python array library
⚠️ Tooling beyond the compiler is thin: Formatting, lint, and documentation come from small community projects (fprettify, ford) rather than from a supported toolchain
⚠️ The community is aging: Adoption is declining and maintenance is concentrated in the HPC and numerical community



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The standard is backward compatible: Fortran 90 source mostly compiles with a Fortran 2023 compiler, and only a small set of features has been deleted
✅ The compilers retain the deleted features as extensions: arithmetic IF and PAUSE, both removed by the standard, are still accepted by the common compilers
✅ The intrinsic modules extend the language without editing it: iso_c_binding, iso_fortran_env, and the parallel features were added as modules and new syntax rather than as changes to existing syntax
⚠️ A revision takes about a decade: The editions are 2003, 2008, 2018, and 2023, so a needed feature waits years for the standard and lives as a compiler extension until then
⚠️ One program can hold several standards: A single codebase can mix a Fortran 77 common block with a Fortran 2008 module, so the version in use is a property of the file
⚠️ An extension can become load-bearing: A program that depends on a vendor directive cannot be moved to another compiler without an edit
❌ Build variants multiply: the compilers ship a documented preprocessor (-cpp, #define), and guarded source selects which statements compile (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Numerical and scientific computing is the design target: Array syntax, complex arithmetic, real kinds, and the IEEE intrinsic modules fit it directly
✅ High-performance computing is the deepest adoption: Weather, climate, and physics codes are written in Fortran, so the language dominates legacy HPC codebases
✅ submodule fits a large numerical codebase: A module can declare the interface and a submodule hold the implementation, so changing a kernel recompiles only that submodule (Fortran 2008)
✅ Coarrays put a parallel program in the language: A distributed-memory program is written without a call from a separate parallel library
⚠️ The language assumes a numerical, batch-shaped workload: Text handling, dynamic data structures, and event-driven logic get little support, and the standard library is mainly the intrinsic procedures
⚠️ A new project often keeps Fortran for the kernel only: The language is used where the inner loop must be native, and the orchestration moves to Python or C++



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The core is small once implicit none is in place: The statement forms, the intrinsic procedures, and the array expressions are a modest set
✅ The authoritative material is stable and complete: The ISO standard, the compiler references, and Modern Fortran Explained cover the language in one place
✅ The array idiom has a direct mathematical reading: A whole-array expression reads as the equation it computes
❌ Legacy syntax quirks create friction: Fixed-form source with its column rules, implicit typing, and common blocks must be read to work on an existing codebase (L1)
⚠️ The array and parallel idioms take practice: Array sections, where, and do concurrent read differently from an explicit loop, and the cost of a temporary array is easy to miss



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Fixed-form source is column-sensitive: In a .f file a label sits in columns 1–5, a continuation mark in column 6, and a statement starts in column 7, so the layout carries meaning
⚠️ The language is verbose: Kind, intent, and dimension accumulate on every dummy argument, and the internals of a procedure need their own contains block (S1)
✅ Whole-array expressions are compact: c = matmul(a, b) + alpha * c states a matrix update in one line
✅ Free-form source is line-oriented and readable: With implicit none and use, only:, a modern module reads close to the mathematics
⚠️ A common block’s storage is positional: Two declarations of the same block must list the fields in the same order with the same types, and the block’s layout is a convention rather than a checked interface



1.2.7 Testing

✅ error stop gives a test program a defined failure status: A failing check stops the program with a non-zero status that a harness can read
✅ Run-time checks can be compiled in: -fcheck=all (gfortran) and -check all (ifx) raise on an out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a shape mismatch
✅ The numerical libraries ship their own test suites: LAPACK and BLAS carry a published suite that exercises each routine, which is the numerical community’s model
❌ There is no test framework in the language: A test is a program that runs and compares, and a runner such as pFUnit or test-drive is a third-party library
⚠️ There is no assertion intrinsic: A check is an explicit if (cond) error stop, so its presence is a written decision
⚠️ The result depends on the flags and the hardware: The summation order, -ffast-math, and the fused multiply-add change the last bits, so a test must fix the build and compare with a tolerance



1.2.8 Security

❌ Memory safety depends on a checked build: an out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a mismatch between an actual and a dummy argument are found only when the compiler is asked to check them, and the standard requires no run-time check
✅ There is no dynamic evaluation of source text: The language has no eval, no reflective call by name, and no string-to-code path, so a value cannot become code
✅ intent(in) prevents a write through the callee: The compiler refuses an assignment to an intent(in) dummy argument, so the read-only direction is enforced
⚠️ The C interface hands safety to the neighbour: c_ptr and type(c_funptr) are raw addresses, and the guarantees of the C code on the other side become part of the program
⚠️ There is no capability model and no sandbox: A program runs with the authority of the process, and the mitigations come from the operating system and the linker
✅ A pure procedure cannot corrupt state through I/O or a global: The effect set of a pure procedure is empty by construction
❌ The standard requires no bounds check: an out-of-bounds subscript, a mismatched actual and dummy argument, and a disassociated pointer are undefined behaviour unless the compiler is asked to check, so the shipped program carries the violation (Q1)
❌ Integer overflow is undefined in the standard; a real build wraps in silence (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds embed compiler flags and library state; no reproducible default exists. (Y1)
❌ Libraries resolve from the system and module state at build time. (Y2)
❌ The distribution records no compiler version per project. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Numerical libraries carry no signed provenance in the build. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to the libraries a program links. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ PRINT carries no structure. (Y6)
❌ A runtime error stops with a message; post-mortems are a platform facility. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with a compiler; the platform debugger is separate. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ ISO_C_BINDING is the standard in-process interface to C. (Y9)
✅ The compilers target the HPC and workstation platforms in maintained ports. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ ISO/IEC WG5 maintains the standard through national bodies. (Y11)
✅ ISO/IEC 1539 is published. (Y12)
✅ The NIST Fortran test suites historically checked compilers against the standard. (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

Verdict: Fortran’s design produces a low core score, because the constructs that make the numerical work fast are the constructs that couple. Array expressions and pure procedures are real separations, and a module with a submodule separates an interface from its implementation. But implicit typing hides a misspelled variable, common blocks and module variables are global mutable state, a pointer is freed by hand with no owner, and an error is a code the caller may ignore. Main strengths: the fit to numerical computing is exact, array performance rivals C, and one standard source runs on every major compiler. Main weaknesses: the ecosystem is small and aging, the revision cycle is slow, and the syntax of a legacy file depends on column positions.

title: Firebird PSQL (5.0.4)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PSQL (Firebird 5.0.4) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 52.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL is a member of every domain: parameters and locals carry NULL unannounced, the NULL guide is its own documentation chapter, and no signature states whether a value may be absent (T10)
⚠️ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column, a domain, or an EXCEPTION raised by convention, and the consumer re-derives the encoding
❌ Statements state no effect: a selectable procedure that writes tables, fires triggers, and reads context looks like any other in the catalog (T12)
❌ The UDR boundary is hand-written: EXTERNAL NAME declarations bind PSQL to compiled modules through the UDR engine, and the agreement on layout and error convention is checked by neither side (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ One block, one unit: EXECUTE BLOCK and CREATE PROCEDURE gather DECLARE, flow, and SQL into one executable the server parses whole
⚠️ SUSPEND is a hand-rolled yield: a selectable procedure produces its rows where SUSPEND runs, and moving the statement moves the result set’s shape



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the engine’s: pages, statement memory, and cursor state live in the firebird process, and the PSQL text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ WHEN … DO decides, or the error propagates: EXCEPTION handlers catch by name, SQLSTATE, or ANY, and without one the error leaves the block — no value carries the failure (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception, results by output parameters and SUSPENDed rows, and neither composes through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Connection state is shared: session context variables and global temporary tables are visible across every PSQL unit the connection runs (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The block runs only in Firebird: the parser, the exceptions, and the catalog are the engine’s, and nothing in the language runs without a Firebird server (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside set work: the language has no libraries, no data abstraction beyond tables and domains, and no error values, so application logic builds every abstraction itself (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A community engine with an enterprise surface: packages, UDRs, and query profiling arrive without a vendor’s license meter, and the price is an ecosystem a fraction of the mainstream size
Selectable procedures are the abstraction: FOR SELECT … DO with SUSPEND builds streaming result sets inside the engine, and the price is control flow whose meaning sits in where SUSPEND runs
Exceptions are engine-wide: named EXCEPTIONs with custom messages give structured recovery, and the price is that unhandled ones leave the block as the engine’s error, with no value to catch
The UDR engine opens the door: EXTERNAL NAME declarations bind compiled modules into the database, and the price is an ABI agreement neither side’s compiler checks




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The engine ships its own profiler: Firebird 5.0 introduces SQL query profiling as a documented server feature, so a block’s statements can be timed inside the toolchain



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A niche ecosystem: Firebird’s tooling and hiring pool concentrate in its legacy application base, a fraction of the PostgreSQL or MySQL worlds (Ec3)
⚠️ Third-party tools carry the day: FlameRobin, IBExpert, and DBeaver fill the tooling space, and no official editor analysis or IDE ships with the server



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ Three lines maintained at once: 5.0, 4.0, and 3.0 receive simultaneous sub-releases, so a block’s available surface depends on which maintained line the deployment runs



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists to serve the database: procedures, triggers, and packages deploy into the catalog, and the security model and storage engine define what they can say (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ The Language Reference is one volume: the PSQL chapters cover statements, exceptions, and cursors with worked examples, and the wider engine documentation surrounds them



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ A dialect inside a dialect: PSQL shares syntax with Firebird SQL but adds SUSPEND, block-scoped DECLARE, and EXCEPTION handling that plain SQL statements do not accept



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user blocks: the project’s own QA is internal, and the documented testing story for PSQL is application-side tests against a live database (G1)
✅ Profiling is a server feature: the 5.0 query profiler answers what a block’s statements cost, so the instrument is part of the engine rather than a third-party tool (G2)



1.2.8 Security

❌ EXECUTE STATEMENT is string-built: dynamic SQL text assembled from parameters reaches the parser, and the mitigation is the statement-level privilege model plus bound inputs (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A block is stored source: the same text on the same engine version and data reproduces the same result, and nothing is compiled ahead of the call
❌ No toolchain pin exists: the repository names no engine version, and the executing release is a deployment fact a manager must supply (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published code: UDRs and client drivers move through distribution channels without signature checks, and a deployment trusts what it installs (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names the product’s dependencies: fixes land in release notes of three maintained lines at once, with no CVE-mapped advisory database (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: the trace and audit facilities are server configuration, and the PSQL text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: exceptions and the server’s firebird.log are the whole output surface, and no logging construct exists in PSQL (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No editor analysis ships with the server: isql is the official interface, and code assistance lives in third-party tools (Y8)
❌ No debugger ships with the engine: diagnosis goes through profiling output, exception messages, and logging tables the procedure itself must write (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the block compiles in one engine’s parser, and nothing in the language runs without a Firebird server (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ No public specification exists: the Language Reference documents the implemented behavior in detail, and no independent implementation follows from a published standard document (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the engine does: no conformance suite exists for PSQL, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
✅ The source is public and readable: the engine and the documentation build from public repositories under the IPL/IDPL, so the parser’s ground truth is inspectable (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the firebird process’s: page cache, sweep, and statement memory pay, and the reader’s levers are index and statement design the block exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Generated PSQL arrives in migration and admin tooling, and the traps are the procedural layer: SUSPEND placement, exception scope, and context variables that no generated snippet names.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the engine’s transaction model (read consistency options in 5.0) and its security classes are the project’s, stated in its own documentation.

Verdict: Firebird’s PSQL is the procedural SQL of a community-owned engine: EXECUTE BLOCK, stored procedures, functions, triggers, and packages over DECLARE, FOR SELECT … INTO … DO, SUSPEND, named EXCEPTIONs with WHEN … DO handlers, and EXECUTE STATEMENT for dynamic SQL, with the UDR engine binding compiled modules through EXTERNAL NAME declarations. Its costs are the engine family’s own: NULL in every domain, failures that travel only by exception, connection-wide session state, and a niche ecosystem with no conformance suite. title: DuckDB SQL (2.0.0 LTS)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL (DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS “Cinnamon Teal”) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column, a UNION type by convention, or a VARIANT holding a shape, and the consumer re-derives the encoding (T4)
❌ No generic parameter: queries and macros are typed per definition, and a routine over “any table” does not exist in the language (T5)
❌ NULL is a member of every domain: columns and macro parameters carry NULL unannounced, and no signature records the guard (T10)
❌ Statements state no effect: an INSERT in a data-modifying CTE and a SELECT in the same pipeline look alike, and nothing tracks what a statement touches (T12)
❌ Extensions ride the ABI: LOAD pulls compiled C++ modules agreed on an unpromised ABI, and the signature check that fires at load is about provenance, not layout (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Friendly SQL is the interface: FROM-first queries, data-modifying CTEs, and $variable shorthand let one pipeline read top to bottom without wrappers
⚠️ Triggers join the surface: 2.0 adds CREATE TRIGGER with transition tables, and audit logic now mutates beside the statements it watches



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the engine’s: buffer manager and hash tables live in the embedding process, and the query text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

⚠️ Errors abort the statement with a message: no handler, no error value, and no in-language recovery exist — the caller (shell, script, or client) decides what a failure means



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session state is shared: SET variables, temp tables, and ATTACHed databases are visible across every statement the session or process runs (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The query runs only in DuckDB: the dialect, the extensions, and the file format are one engine’s, and nothing in the language runs without it (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside analytical work: the language has no stored procedures, no error values, and no concurrency story, and application logic beyond analytics builds every abstraction itself (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

In-process is the feature and the exposure: queries run at memory speed inside the application, and the price is that the engine’s memory, threads, and crashes are the host program’s
Extensions are the package system: one INSTALL statement reaches signed, version-matched binaries, and the price is a compiled supply line whose ABI agreement is provenance-checked, not type-checked
2.0 is a feature ratchet: a new file format, parser, and triggers arrive with a migration guide and LTS support, and the price is that pre-2.0 engines cannot read what 2.0 writes
Friendly SQL is a dialect: FROM-first and implicit grouping read faster and port worse, and the price is paid at the next engine




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ EXPLAIN ANALYZE states the cost: the published statements return the plan with real timings, and the docs treat it as the ordinary instrument
⚠️ The process shares the application’s fate: in-process execution means the query’s memory and threads compete with the host program, and the language carries no budget construct



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The ecosystem moves on one engine: CLI, client libraries, extensions, and the file format are published together, so tooling agrees with the engine by release rather than by convention



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ 2.0 moved under the queries: the release publishes breaking changes — a new default file format, a new parser default, disabled lambda syntax — with a migration guide and a legacy escape hatch (V1)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting DuckDB SQL means adopting the engine: extensions, file format, and the in-process model define what a query can say, and the same vocabulary is the deployment (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ The friendly dialect is its own lesson: FROM-first order and implicit grouping read fast, and the docs’ “friendly SQL” page exists precisely because the surface diverges from what a SQL course taught



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ The friendly dialect bends SQL: FROM-first order, implicit GROUP BY columns, and alias reuse read well and diverge from the standard the rest of the industry speaks



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user queries: the project’s own sqllogic tests are internal, and the documented testing story is application-side tests against the library (G1)
✅ The plan is a statement away: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE are part of the published reference, so a query can be asked to show its cost before and during a run (G2)



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Injection lives in the caller: the language has no dynamic-SQL statement, and string-built queries are a host-language pattern, not a DuckDB construct

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is text against a file: the same SQL on the same database file and engine version reproduces the same answer, and nothing is built
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution: the repository names no engine version, and the CLI, library, and extension versions must agree from deployment memory (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ Extensions are signature-verified: distribution is signed against repository public keys the engine pins with a printed fingerprint, so provenance is checked at install rather than trusted (Y3)
❌ The flat extension registry is the supply line: community extensions are centrally listed by name with no namespace, so a name’s meaning is whatever the registry maps it to (Y4)
✅ The project publishes advisories: the duckdb repository runs a security-advisory feed with maintained CVE entries and patched-version ranges, so dependency-relevant disclosures have a documented home (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: EXPLAIN output is the query’s own report, and tracing lives in the host application or the client library (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: the engine logs to its host’s streams, and no logging construct exists in the SQL surface (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger exists: diagnosis goes through EXPLAIN ANALYZE, error messages with source locations from the new parser, and the CLI (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the query runs on a DuckDB engine, and nothing in the language runs without one (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is one company: DuckLabs sets the release calendar, the LTS lines, and the language’s direction, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the documentation describes the implemented behavior of one engine, and no independent implementation follows from a published standard (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the engine does: no conformance suite exists for the dialect, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the host process’s: the engine’s threads and buffer pool draw from the application that embeds it, and the reader’s levers are query shape and file layout the text exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ 2.0 ships an agent mode for coding agents that drive the CLI, and SQL is the model-trained lingua franca — the agent surface exists because generated analytics are already the common case.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the engine’s transaction and durability guarantees are the project’s, stated in its own documentation, with the LTS calendar as the support contract.

Verdict: DuckDB’s SQL is an in-process analytical dialect — friendly FROM-first syntax, LIST/STRUCT/MAP and VARIANT types, data-modifying CTEs, and as of 2.0 LTS triggers, CONNECT to remote engines, and an extensible PEG parser — executed inside the embedding application. Its costs are the in-process model’s own: NULL in every domain, no procedures or error values, session-wide state, an extension supply line of compiled version-matched binaries, and single-company governance with no specification or conformance suite. Main strengths: EXPLAIN ANALYZE as an ordinary published instrument, signature-verified extension repositories, precise parser diagnostics, MIT-licensed public source, and an LTS line with a stated support calendar. Main weaknesses: a published one-way file-format boundary (pre-2.0 engines cannot read 2.0 files), a flat extension namespace, no debugger or standard query-test harness, no structured logging or tracing in the language, and a dialect that bends SQL where it reads best.

title: Cypher (Neo4j 5.x / openCypher)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Cypher in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 89.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 59.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Property types come from the graph schema: Node and relationship properties are typed when a schema is declared, and the planner rejects type mismatches before execution
❌ No sum types: A property is a scalar, a list, or a map, and an alternative must be modelled with nullable properties or separate nodes (T4)
❌ No generics: A query cannot be parameterised over a type, so reusable logic is copied or wrapped in a procedure (T5)
❌ NULL is a value in every property type: Missing properties and optional matches produce NULL, and three-valued logic makes NULL = NULL unknown (T10)
❌ A CALLed procedure may perform effects the signature does not state: The query text shows the call, but it does not show whether the procedure writes, reads files, or invokes external systems (T12)
❌ User-defined procedures cross into the host runtime unchecked: A procedure is declared by signature, but the engine does not check its implementation against that signature (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Pattern matching is declarative: (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) states the shape of the result and leaves the traversal to the planner
✅ Subqueries compose without shared state: CALL { ... } and UNWIND let a query build intermediate results without imperative sequencing
⚠️ Triggers and transaction event handlers run implicitly: A write can fire code that is not visible in the query text



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The graph engine owns allocation: Buffers, index pages, and transaction state are managed by the database, not by the query
⚠️ Large pattern matches can exhaust engine memory: An unbounded variable-length path or a dense cartesian product can still exhaust the configured heap



1.1.4 Error

✅ Syntax and type errors are caught at prepare time: Unknown labels, missing variables, and type mismatches are reported before the query runs
⚠️ Runtime failures depend on the data: Division by zero, missing properties, and constraint violations surface only when the path is reached



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group writes atomically: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a set of updates commit or abort as one
⚠️ Isolation is engine-specific: READ COMMITTED is common, and write skew is possible unless the engine supports a stronger level



1.1.6 Platform

✅ openCypher provides a shared core: Pattern matching, MATCH, WHERE, CREATE, and RETURN are portable across Neo4j, Memgraph, and Amazon Neptune
⚠️ Vendor extensions diverge: Index hints, full-text search, and procedure libraries differ by engine
❌ The language is a poor fit outside property-graph workloads: Arbitrary algorithms and general application logic are usually pushed to a host language or a procedure (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Schema optional versus schema required: A flexible graph model allows ad-hoc properties, but the lack of enforced schema moves type agreements into code
NULL for missing values: Using NULL to mean “not present” widens the value set and brings three-valued-logic costs
Procedures extend the language: Calling a procedure buys expressiveness at the cost of an unchecked foreign boundary
Vendor-specific Cypher may be worth the portability cost: Engine extensions buy performance and features; the loss of portability is a deliberate trade




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Cost-based planners choose traversal strategies: The engine selects start nodes, index scans, and join orders without hand-tuning in the query
⚠️ Plan quality depends on the engine and the schema: The same query can be fast on one graph database and slow on another



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments by vendor: Visualisers, migration tools, and drivers commonly target one engine’s dialect and procedure set (Ec2)
✅ Multiple engines share the openCypher core: Neo4j, Memgraph, and Amazon Neptune keep the core portable
⚠️ The talent pool is narrower than SQL’s: Graph query expertise is common in graph-native teams but less so in general data teams



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The openCypher standard moves slowly: New features often appear first as vendor extensions and wait for standardisation (V4)
✅ The core pattern language is stable: Queries written to the openCypher core continue to run across releases



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting Cypher means adopting a property-graph store: The language is inseparable from the graph data model and the engine that runs it (D1)
✅ Excellent fit for connected data: Nodes, relationships, and pattern matches map directly onto graph-shaped problems
⚠️ Recursive or path-centric algorithms can be awkward: Some traversals read more naturally in a traversal language than in pattern-matching syntax
✅ Cypher is used to query stored graph data: MATCH retrieves nodes and relationships, and CREATE manipulates the graph



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Basic pattern queries are intuitive: (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) is readable after a short introduction
⚠️ Variable scoping and OPTIONAL MATCH semantics take practice: A newcomer must learn where a variable is bound and how NULL propagates



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ ASCII-art patterns are compact: A relationship and its direction are visible at a glance
⚠️ Complex queries grow long: Multiple patterns, subqueries, and aggregations can produce deeply indented text



1.2.7 Testing

✅ EXPLAIN and PROFILE are standard practice: Engines report the chosen plan and estimated or actual costs
✅ Constraints are executable invariants: Uniqueness, existence, and type constraints reject bad data at write time
❌ No monotonic clock is published in the language: datetime() reads the wall clock, so elapsed-time tests depend on the session clock (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ String-built queries are an injection surface: Concatenating untrusted input into a query text lets that input change the parse (Q3)
✅ Parameterised statements remove the injection surface: Bound parameters carry data out of band, so a value cannot become syntax
✅ Role-based access control limits data visibility: The engine grants or denies read and write access per label, type, and property



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.









Target

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A Cypher program is a query text: The same text submitted to the same engine version and dataset produces the same result (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published drivers and extensions carry no signed provenance by default: A consumer must trust the package they install (Y3)
✅ No package registry exists for Cypher modules: There is therefore no registry namespace to confuse or hijack (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: Observability is provided by the engine and its drivers (Y5)
❌ No structured logging is defined in the language: Diagnostics are engine log entries with their own format (Y6)
✅ Failed queries leave a query log and a stack trace: The engine records the query text and the error location (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit-test loop is a text submission: There is no compile step between editing a query and running it (Y7)
✅ Editors and drivers provide fast syntax feedback: The query is parsed before it is executed (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger ships with the language: Debugging is done through query plans, logs, and engine tools (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ User-defined procedures call host-language code: Java, Python, or other procedures extend the engine without leaving the process (Y9)
❌ The query runs only inside a graph database engine: There is no portable target outside that context (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is effectively Neo4j-led: openCypher provides a community specification, but the main implementation and roadmap follow Neo4j (Y11)
✅ The openCypher specification is public: The language surface is documented and can be implemented by others (Y12)
❌ No conformance suite exists: Independent implementations cannot run a shared test suite against the specification (Y17)
✅ Parser implementations and the grammar are available: Third-party tools can parse Cypher without reverse engineering (Y19)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a graph database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A well-documented query language with many public examples: current models write common patterns reliably.

What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Cypher’s design yields low language-imposed coupling for property-graph queries. The declarative pattern-matching model separates what a result is from how it is traversed, and the graph schema separates data structure from the queries that consume it. Main strengths: compact pattern syntax, portable openCypher core, and mature cost-based planners. Main weaknesses: no sum types or generics, NULL is not type-safe, tooling fragments by vendor, the standard moves slowly, and string-built queries remain an injection hazard unless parameters are used.

title: BigQuery Standard SQL (2026)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses GoogleSQL (BigQuery, 2026-10 documentation state) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 80.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.3/100 · Engineering readiness 45.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column, a STRUCT field checked by convention, or a JSON half-type, and the consumer re-derives the encoding (T4)
❌ No generic parameter: queries are typed per statement, and a routine over “any table” needs dynamic SQL or a fixed signature (T5)
❌ NULL is a member of every domain: columns, parameters, and scripting variables carry NULL unannounced, three-valued logic decides comparisons, and no signature records the guard (T10)
❌ Statements state no effect: an INSERT in a script, a CREATE in a loop, and an EXPORT look alike in the signature, and nothing tracks what a statement touches (T12)
❌ JavaScript rides the boundary: SQL UDFs can be defined in JavaScript inside the query, and values cross between GoogleSQL types and the JS runtime with no checked boundary (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The query is the program: WITH, scripting blocks, and table functions compose declaratively, and the same text replays against any authorized dataset
⚠️ Tables mutate in place: DML rewrites in place with no immutability construct, and time travel is the engine’s retention feature rather than a language construct



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the service’s: slots, spill, and shuffle live in Google’s fleet, and the query text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ The handler decides, or the script dies: BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN ERROR wraps a statement block, and without it the failed statement ends the script — no value carries the failure (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception and results by tables, arrays, and scalar variables, and neither threads through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session state is shared: session variables and temporary tables are visible across every statement and routine the session runs (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The query runs only in BigQuery: GoogleSQL’s functions, scripting, and authorization model are the service’s, and nothing in the language runs without it (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside analytical work: the language has no general libraries or error values, and transactional application logic is explicitly the wrong shape for the engine (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The bill is part of the language: bytes-scanned pricing makes column pruning and partitioning design decisions, and the price is a data model shaped by the meter
Serverless scale without a server: slots and shuffle absorb the workload, and the price is a runtime whose version, limits, and behavior are the service’s, never the repository’s
Scripting turns SQL into a program: variables, loops, transactions, and EXCEPTION blocks deploy real logic, and the price is logic with no debugger, no result type, and no test harness
JavaScript UDFs buy portability of logic: a function body moves to the query, and the price is an unchecked boundary between two type systems inside one statement




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The service states its own cost: query execution details break a query into per-stage timings and row counts, and INFORMATION_SCHEMA publishes the job’s plan
⚠️ The bytes are the bill: on-demand pricing charges scanned bytes, so a SELECT’s column list is a cost decision the syntax barely surfaces



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A proprietary service end to end: the engine, storage, and authorization are Google Cloud products under commercial terms, with no self-hostable reference (Ec4)
❌ Two dialects ride along: legacy SQL remains documented beside Standard SQL for old jobs, and the migration between them is a burden new work still meets (Ec7)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The service moves under the queries: release notes document deprecations and behavior changes on a continuous cadence, and SQL text that ran last quarter can shift under a scheduled job (V1)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting GoogleSQL means adopting BigQuery: datasets, authorized views, slots, and the storage model define what a query can say, and the same vocabulary is the deployment (D1)
❌ The cost and partitioning model dictates the schema: partitioned and clustered tables, denormalized nesting, and bytes-scanned pricing drive table design — the published guidance makes the data model follow what the engine bills (D3)



1.2.5 Learning

❌ SQL plus a scripting layer plus UDFs: GoogleSQL carries statements, procedural blocks, SQL and JavaScript routines, and TVFs, and the surface exceeds the SQL a new reader already knows (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Standard-shaped, Google-flavored: the core reads like ANSI SQL, and arrays, STRUCTs, scripting, and the qualifier grammar are the dialect’s own layer



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for queries: the documented testing story is dbt and third-party frameworks against a billed project, and the language names no regression harness (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs text assembled at run time in scripts, so concatenated user input reaches the parser, and the documented mitigation is parameterized queries and query parameters (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is request text: the same GoogleSQL on the same data and service state reproduces the same answer, and nothing is built
❌ The executing engine is unpinnable: the repository names no engine build — the service’s continuous releases decide semantics, and no file can record them (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published queries or routines: shared datasets, saved queries, and routines move through the service under IAM terms, with no signature-checked distribution channel (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names the query surface: changes and fixes land in release notes, with no CVE-mapped advisory database for the engine’s dependencies (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: Cloud Monitoring and audit logs are platform features, and the query text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: jobs log to the service, and no logging construct exists in GoogleSQL (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The vendor’s IDE completes the query: BigQuery Studio publishes SQL editing with autocompletion and run control as part of the service (Y8)
❌ No debugger exists for scripts: diagnosis goes through execution details, job information, and error messages (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the query runs on BigQuery, and nothing in the language runs without the service (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is Google: the dialect’s direction and cadence are one company’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the GoogleSQL reference documents the implemented behavior of one service, and no independent implementation follows from it (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what the service does: no conformance suite exists for GoogleSQL, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
✅ The parser is published: Google’s ZetaSQL, the open-source analyzer behind the dialect, publishes its grammar and analyzer source, so tooling can read a real parser for the language’s core (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is Google’s fleet and the project’s bill: slots, storage, and scanned bytes pay, and the reader’s levers are partitioning and column design the query text exposes but does not control.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ BigQuery ships agent-facing data surfaces (data canvas, Gemini-assisted SQL), and SQL is the model-trained lingua franca — generated queries still meet the traps: three-valued logic, bytes-scanned cost, and scripting scope.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the service’s durability, IAM, and audit guarantees are Google’s, stated in its own documentation and terms.

Verdict: BigQuery Standard SQL is GoogleSQL — analytical SQL with arrays and STRUCTs, a scripting layer with procedures, transactions, and EXCEPTION blocks, SQL and JavaScript UDFs, and table functions — served by one proprietary engine. Its costs are the service’s own: NULL in every domain, failures that travel only by exception, session-wide state, bytes-scanned pricing that shapes the data model, and continuous engine releases no repository can pin. Main strengths: per-stage execution details inside the service, vendor IDE tooling, a declarative core that composes cleanly, and one reference that states the whole surface. Main weaknesses: no specification or conformance mechanism, single-vendor governance, a proprietary stack with no self-hostable reference, no debugger or standard test harness, string-built dynamic SQL, and a legacy-SQL burden the docs still carry.
