title: Visual Basic 16 (.NET)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Visual Basic .NET in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 63.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.8/100 · Engineering readiness 88.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Option Strict Off is the default: Under it an implicit narrowing conversion and a late-bound Object call compile, and the type is resolved when the statement runs (T2)
✅ Option Strict On removes the late-bound path: The same code does not compile until the conversion or the reference is written explicitly
✅ Interface and Implements separate a contract from its implementation: A class names the interface members it supplies
✅ A nullable value type states an absence: Integer? is Nullable(Of Integer), and HasValue and Value test and read it
❌ Nothing is compatible with every reference type: A reference may be Nothing, no declaration requires a test before use, the language offers no nullable reference annotation, and for a string "" = Nothing is True (T10)
⚠️ A class hierarchy couples a derived class to its base: Inherits binds a class to the base’s virtual members, and an Interface with Implements is the alternative that avoids the chain
❌ Inherits the CLR rule: Char is a UTF-16 code unit (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Sub New is a real constructor: A class declares it, Overloads gives several signatures, and MyBase.New runs the base constructor
✅ ReadOnly and Const mark a fixed value: A ReadOnly field is set once, and a Const is fixed at compile time
❌ Mutability is the default: A Dim variable and a property are writable, and only an explicit ReadOnly or Const changes that (C2)
✅ A Structure is a value type with its own constructor: A copy of a structure is a copy of its values, and it is not collected
✅ Using bounds the life of a resource: The block calls Dispose on every exit path
⚠️ WithEvents binds the handler object to its source: A WithEvents field is tied to the events of one declared type, and Handles lists the events it answers, so the subscription is written into the declaration
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the .NET Dictionary carries the documented no-order guarantee to VB.NET’s collection defaults (C5)
❌ One value, many names: .NET objects move by handle, and no declaration names the alias set — ByVal pins the variable, not the object (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: .NET’s implicit conversion operators (Widening and Narrowing CType) run at unmarked sites (C7)
❌ VB .NET inherits the CLR rule: type-initializer order across modules is unpredictable (ECMA-335), the C# answer the .NET family carries (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The garbage collector decides when memory returns: A reference is reclaimed after it becomes unreachable, and a collection pause is possible (M2)
❌ No release runs at the end of a scope: A class has a finalizer at best, whose time is not defined, and there is no deterministic destructor (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A reference may alias, and nothing in the type states who releases the object (M4)
✅ Using gives deterministic release for an IDisposable: The block calls Dispose on every exit, including the exceptional one
✅ IDisposable is the stated protocol for a native resource: A type that holds a handle states its release method
⚠️ A finalizer delays the collection of its object: The object survives one extra collection while the finalizer queue is drained



1.1.4 Error

❌ The exceptions are unchecked: No method signature states the exceptions it may raise, so a Try is a convention (Er2)
❌ A failure can be discarded by design: On Error Resume Next and an empty Catch both let a failure pass with no effect (Er3)
✅ Try/Catch/Finally is a structured path: The Catch block holds the recovery code and Finally runs on every exit
✅ The failure is selected by type: Catch ex As IOException chooses by exception type, and ex.InnerException carries the cause
⚠️ The legacy On Error GoTo form remains: It binds the recovery to a line label and a sequence, beside the structured form
⚠️ An Async failure arrives at the Await: An exception in an awaited task surfaces at the await, so the Try block must span it
❌ A fault ends the process: an unhandled exception in any thread terminates the process (documented by the runtime) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection: SyncLock guards a block, and the compiler analyses no program for a race (K3)
✅ SyncLock is a language construct: It takes a lock on an expression and releases it at the end of the block
✅ Async and Await state the suspension point: An asynchronous call reads as a sequence, and the language marks where it yields
✅ The task and thread types come from the runtime: Task, Thread, and the thread pool are .NET types the language uses directly
⚠️ The lock order is not stated: SyncLock names a lock and not an order, so a deadlock is a design concern outside the language
⚠️ An event handler runs on the raising thread: An event raised on a worker thread runs the handler there, and the UI-thread rule is a framework convention
❌ Thread reserves an operating-system thread: Each task holds one for its whole life (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The compiler emits a portable .NET assembly: The resulting .dll or .exe runs wherever the .NET runtime runs
✅ The runtime runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS: The same assembly runs on each, so the language is not bound to one operating system
✅ The class library is reachable: An assembly with a public surface can be consumed from Visual Basic
✅ The project system is the common one: A .vbproj is an SDK-style project built by dotnet build
⚠️ A few newer features have no Visual Basic form: Nullable reference annotations and static abstract interface members have no equivalent syntax, so a consumer of a library that requires them needs a wrapper
⚠️ Windows Forms and WPF target Windows only: A GUI project on either framework runs on Windows



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Late binding is the pragmatic COM path: Option Strict Off around an Office object model avoids an interop reference, which is why the setting survives
The Visual Basic 6 heritage is deliberate: On Error, My, and the forms designer are continuity choices for the existing developer base
Verbosity buys explicitness: End If and End Sub are redundant, and the end of every block is visible
The design-time form designer is a tool: The layout is a tool feature rather than a language mechanism
A port to C# is mechanical: The constructs map closely, and the effort is the trade for leaving the language line
A frozen language is stable for existing code: No feature churn reaches a maintained program




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits IL and the runtime compiles it: The hot path becomes machine code through the just-in-time compiler
✅ The collector is generational: A short-lived object is reclaimed cheaply
✅ The runtime library supplies the fast paths: StringBuilder and the asynchronous I/O APIs are available to a Visual Basic program
⚠️ The first call of a method is the slowest: Compilation happens on first use, so start-up includes a warm-up
⚠️ Boxing and string concatenation allocate: An Object-typed value and a repeated & produce garbage on the heap
⚠️ A collection pause is possible on a large heap: The collector’s pause is outside the program’s control (R2)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ NuGet is the package manager: A dependency is declared in the project and restored by dotnet restore
✅ The IDE is Visual Studio: Editing, refactoring, debugging, and the designer are integrated, and the free edition supports Visual Basic
✅ The class library is large and documented: I/O, networking, collections, and UI are covered by the runtime
✅ The compiler ships with the platform: vbc is maintained with the .NET SDK
⚠️ The published example is usually C#: A library’s documentation and samples are C#, and a Visual Basic consumer translates them
⚠️ New libraries are rarely written in Visual Basic: The language’s share of new code is small
✅ CLR metadata carries a published promise: VB.NET compiles to IL under the runtime’s standardised format [5], [6] (Ec8)
❌ Stored payloads bind to the runtime: VB.NET runs on the .NET runtime, and from .NET 8 BinaryFormatter throws across nearly all project types, with .NET 9 removing the in-box implementation [7], [8] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language line is closed to new features: Microsoft has stated that Visual Basic will not be evolved for new workloads, and the language receives no new syntax (V3)
✅ The language remains supported for existing code: The compiler is maintained with the .NET SDK for bug fixes and platform compatibility
✅ The runtime advances under the language: An existing assembly runs on a current .NET, so the platform moves even though the language does not
✅ A migration path to C# exists and is close: The language improved substantially from Visual Basic 6, and the constructs and the object model map almost one to one onto C#
⚠️ A new framework feature can be C#-only: Nullable reference types and static abstract interface members arrived without a Visual Basic form
❌ Build variants multiply: #If blocks with compiler constants select which code the compiler emits (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Office and COM automation is a native domain: Object and late binding make an Office object model usable without an interop assembly
✅ Windows Forms is the rapid-desktop domain: The designer and the event model fit a business form application
✅ Console tools and services are straightforward: A short program builds into an .exe in the .NET toolchain
✅ The .NET library ecosystem is reachable: Any assembly with a public surface can be consumed
⚠️ Modern .NET UI frameworks are not offered for Visual Basic: The .NET MAUI and Blazor templates are C#, so a new Visual Basic GUI is a Windows Forms or WPF project
⚠️ It is not the choice for new development: The language remains less expressive than C# on the newer features, and the direction of the ecosystem is C#



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is readable and close to English: If ... Then, For Each ... In, and End Sub read as their meaning
✅ The curve is gentle from BASIC or Visual Basic 6: The surface carries over, and the runtime supplies the rest
✅ The reference documentation is complete: Microsoft documents every statement, keyword, and option
✅ The IDE guides a new user: IntelliSense and the compiler’s messages explain a construct as it is written
⚠️ Four Option statements change the language: Strict, Explicit, Infer, and Compare each alter what compiles or what a comparison means
⚠️ The large subject is the class library: The framework, not the syntax, is the bulk of the work



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The syntax is verbose: Every block closes with its own keyword pair such as End If, End Sub, and Next, and a declaration repeats Dim and As (S1)
✅ Keywords are words: The reading is close to English
✅ A line ends a statement: Continuation is explicit with _
✅ Attributes are written in angle brackets: <Serializable> and <Obsolete("...")> attach metadata to a declaration
⚠️ A file-level Option changes the parse: Option Strict On at the top of a file changes which lines compile
⚠️ The language is case-insensitive: myValue and MyValue name the same variable, so a rename is not caught by the case



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework is available from NuGet: MSTest, NUnit, and xUnit all run against the .NET test SDK
✅ dotnet test runs the suite: Discovery, execution, and the report come from the platform
✅ A test is written in Visual Basic: Attributes such as <TestMethod> mark a test method
✅ The debugger is integrated: A failed test can be stepped through in Visual Studio
✅ An assertion or mocking library is a package: NUnit’s assertions and Moq are consumed from NuGet
⚠️ The default Option Strict Off weakens the test itself: A test project with the default setting can pass a value of a wrong type and notice only at run time



1.2.8 Security

✅ The runtime is memory-safe: No use-after-free and no buffer overrun occurs in safe code, and the language has no pointer type
✅ No unsafe context exists in Visual Basic: The unverifiable memory operations of the runtime are out of reach
✅ The exception path keeps the failure in a value: ex.Message and ex.InnerException carry the detail to a handler
✅ Option Strict On removes the late-bound call: The member is resolved by the compiler rather than by name at run time
⚠️ On Error Resume Next can hide a failure that matters: A suppressed failure leaves the program in a state the next statement does not expect
⚠️ A COM interop boundary is outside the runtime’s checks: A late-bound call crosses into unmanaged code that the type system does not verify
❌ Inherits the CLR rule: integer arithmetic wraps unchecked by default (Q4)

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Package versions resolve from NuGet unless the restore pins them. (Y2)
✅ The project file and global.json are contracts the SDK reads and validates. (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The GitHub advisory database covers NuGet packages, not the registry itself.



1.3.3 Observability

✅ System.Diagnostics.Metrics and Activity ship in the base class library. (Y5)
✅ ILogger is the structured logging contract the platform ships. (Y6)
✅ Crash dumps and platform error reporting ship by default. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the SDK; the IDE debuggers are separate installs. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ P/Invoke is the in-process C interface; VB calls the whole .NET surface. (Y9)
✅ The runtime ships maintained builds for the common platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The .NET Foundation and the community stewards run the process in the open. (Y11)
✅ The Visual Basic language specification is published. (Y12)
✅ The VB compiler is public source in Roslyn. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [9]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [10].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [11].



1.4.3 Safety certification

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Visual Basic .NET reaches a mid-range core score by inheriting the .NET runtime’s separation of interface from implementation, its collected memory, and its checked types, while keeping the older Visual Basic defaults beside them. The losses are those defaults: Option Strict Off, a Nothing that fits every reference type, unchecked exceptions, a failure a caller may discard, and manual synchronisation. Main strengths: interfaces, Option Strict On, Using for deterministic release, the whole .NET class library, and a mechanical path to C#. text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Unison in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 95.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 77.0/100 · Engineering readiness 63.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Algebraic data types with exhaustive pattern matching: Like Haskell, separates cases explicitly
✅ Abilities (algebraic effects): Superior to monads for separating different effect types
✅ Content-addressed functions decouple code from names: Functions identified by hash of their implementation
✅ Structural typing for abilities: Can satisfy ability requirements without explicit declarations
✅ No orphan instances: Type classes (abilities) prevent distant coupling
✅ Distributed computing primitives: Remote ability separates local from distributed concerns



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Immutable data structures by default: No coupling through mutation
✅ Smart constructors via abilities: Construction effects tracked in type system
✅ No global state: Pure functions can’t have hidden dependencies
✅ Content addressing eliminates initialization order: Functions self-contained, no module load order coupling (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Runtime GC decouples memory: No manual memory management
✅ Immutability prevents reference cycles: Simpler GC, fewer leaks (M7)
✅ Distributed execution abstracts memory: Remote computation handles serialization automatically
⚠️ GC implementation details not public: Couples performance to runtime implementation



1.1.4 Error

✅ Abilities make errors explicit: {Exception} Result shows failure in type signature
✅ Algebraic effects compose: Can combine error handling with other effects naturally
✅ Pattern matching on Either/Result: Exhaustiveness checking prevents missed error paths
✅ No unchecked exceptions: All failure modes visible in types



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Distributed computing built-in: Functions can execute remotely without changing logic
✅ Content addressing enables safe deployment: Update function implementation without breaking callers
✅ Abilities separate concurrent operations: Concurrent, Remote abilities explicit in signatures
✅ Deterministic execution: Pure functions compose regardless of execution location



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Own runtime, no foreign VM: Unison ships its own runtime, so programs target no third-party virtual machine such as the JVM or the CLR
✅ Native binaries for the desktop platforms: UCM ships for macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), 64-bit Linux, and Windows
✅ Cloud is optional: A local codebase builds, tests, and runs with ucm alone; Unison Cloud and Unison Share are services you may adopt, not platform prerequisites
✅ Host-independent code identity: Because definitions are identified by a hash, a codebase binds to no filesystem layout or machine-specific package registry



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Content Addressing vs. Naming: Hash-based identity decouples from names but couples to implementation details (changing algorithm changes identity)
Distributed Transparency vs. Network Reality: Remote abstracts distribution but couples logic to serialization constraints
Immutability vs. Performance: Persistent data structures couple performance to structure sharing discipline
Ability Inference vs. Explicitness: Type inference can hide effect requirements, coupling understanding to compiler
Codebase Manager vs. Traditional VCS: Git independence decouples from version control but couples to Unison tooling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Own runtime: Predictable performance, its own runtime avoids JVM dependency
✅ Distributed execution: Can distribute computation across machines transparently
⚠️ GC pauses: Unison’s own runtime collects garbage, so pauses are non-deterministic (R2)
❌ Persistent data structures overhead: Immutability couples performance to structure sharing
⚠️ Network abstraction cost: Remote computation couples performance to serialization/network



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Very small ecosystem: Limited library availability couples a project to manual implementation or to the few libraries that exist
✅ Codebase Manager is innovative: Content addressing decouples from traditional VCS
✅ Excellent error messages: Compiler feedback decouples debugging from trial-and-error
⚠️ UCM learning curve: Novel workflow couples productivity to understanding new paradigm
✅ Share functionality built-in: Can publish/consume code via Unison Share without separate package manager



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Content addressing handles refactoring: Rename functions without breaking dependents (they reference by hash)
✅ Upgrade functions independently: Can use multiple versions of same function (different hashes)
⚠️ Pre-1.0 stability: Breaking changes still occur while the language evolves, coupling code to a language version
✅ Automatic migration tools: UCM helps update codebases when language changes
⚠️ Small team: Development pace couples to limited resources



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for distributed systems: Built-in remote execution separates logic from distribution
✅ Strong for backend services: Type safety + distributed primitives
⚠️ Limited frontend use: No browser runtime (yet)
⚠️ Immature for production: Ecosystem couples adoption to risk tolerance
✅ Great for exploratory programming: Content addressing enables fearless refactoring



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Novel paradigm: Content addressing + abilities + UCM workflow all new concepts
✅ Good documentation: Unison docs and tour explain concepts well
⚠️ Requires functional thinking: Learning couples to FP background
⚠️ UCM workflow different: Codebase management couples to unlearning Git habits and to understanding content addressing
✅ Interactive REPL: ucm makes exploration easier



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean syntax: Python/Haskell hybrid, minimal noise
✅ Significant whitespace: Indentation-based, reduces boilerplate
✅ Abilities integrate naturally: Effect syntax lightweight
⚠️ UCM commands: Learning curve for codebase operations
✅ Hash-qualified names optional: Can use readable names, hashes only when needed



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Watch expressions: Can add tests directly in code files
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No hidden state coupling
✅ Property testing support: Can write generative tests
⚠️ Debugging tools immature: Stack traces couple to runtime implementation
⚠️ Distributed debugging hard: Remote computation couples debugging to network
❌ No clock reading in the language: time lives in effects the host supplies (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safety: No null, no type confusion
✅ Content addressing: Function identity verified by hash, prevents tampering
✅ Ability system: Can control what effects functions perform
⚠️ Distributed execution risk: Remote computation couples security to network trust
❌ Int64 and Nat64 are fixed-width machine integers; the documentation demonstrates overflow wrapping (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ The codebase is the contract: dependencies are content-addressed by exact hash, and the compiler resolves them by hash, so a dependency cannot move under the build (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published libraries resolve by hash with no signature layer above it. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers published libraries. (Y16)
⚠️ The shared library market is the public codebase, content-addressed by hash.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ print and the ability boundary carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A failed ability request surfaces as a typed value, and no post-mortem is written. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ There is no build: running is fetching content-addressed definitions. (Y7)
⚠️ No analyzer ships; the editor integrations are the tooling.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs on the Unison deployment targets the runtime supports. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the reference implementation: the published specification defines the language as the reference implementation behaves, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Swift (6.2)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Swift in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 80.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 85.9/100 · Engineering readiness 55.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Protocols decouple interface from implementation: Similar to Rust traits
✅ Value types (structs) vs reference types (classes): Explicit separation
✅ Enums with associated values: Discriminated unions like Rust/F#
✅ Generics with constraints: <T: Equatable> decouples from concrete types
⚠️ Optional chaining: ?. syntax elegant but can hide nil propagation
❌ AnyObject/Any: Type erasure creates coupling escape hatch
❌ Force unwrap (!): Bypasses type safety, couples to runtime crashes
❌ Implicitly unwrapped optionals: String! hides nil possibility
❌ Dynamic dispatch overhead: Protocol witness tables couple performance



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Initializers separate from usage: init methods decouple construction
✅ Failable initializers: init? makes construction failure explicit
✅ Value semantics by default: Structs copy, preventing shared state coupling
⚠️ Classes allow inheritance: Can create coupling hierarchies
✅ Protocol-oriented programming: Composition over inheritance
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation states Dictionary’s iteration order is not specified, dependent on hashing; the ordered variants are opt-in (C5)
❌ One value, many names: classes move by reference (documented) — a property, a parameter, and a capture share one instance; copy-on-write protects the containers, not the objects (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Automatic Reference Counting (ARC): Deterministic, no GC pauses
⚠️ Retain cycles possible: Weak/unowned references needed for graphs
✅ Value types: No reference counting for structs
✅ Predictable: Deallocation timing known
❌ Objective-C interop: Foreign code can introduce manual memory management and can bypass Swift’s safety guarantees
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a force-unwrap of nil and an out-of-range index trap fatally (documented) — the typed optionals name the nil, the trap is not a value (Er6)
❌ ARC releases at the last reference; a strong reference cycle has no last reference, and the cycle leaks until the process ends; weak/unowned is the discipline (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Typed throws (Swift 6): throws(MyError) makes error types explicit in signatures — a major coupling improvement over untyped throws
✅ Do-try-catch: Explicit error handling, checked at call site
✅ Result<T, E> available: For functional-style composable error handling
⚠️ Failable initializers: init? returns nil instead of throwing
⚠️ Force unwrap: ! bypasses safety, couples to runtime crash
✅ Guard statements: Early exit decouples validation from logic
❌ A fault ends the process: a runtime trap is fatal (documented — precondition failures and force-unwrap nil abort); thrown errors recover fallible calls, not safety faults (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Swift Concurrency (async/await): Built-in, structured concurrency
✅ Actors: Data race prevention via isolation
✅ Sendable protocol + strict concurrency checking (Swift 6, on by default): Compile-time thread safety with full enforcement
✅ Task-based: Decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ Grand Central Dispatch (GCD): Legacy API still available, manual



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The toolchain is open source: The Swift compiler, standard library, and Swift Package Manager are developed in the open at github.com/swiftlang under the Apache 2.0 licence
✅ The language runs outside Apple platforms: Official Linux toolchains cover Ubuntu, Fedora, and Amazon Linux, and a Windows toolchain is distributed alongside macOS
✅ The package manager is platform-independent: SwiftPM resolves one manifest and builds the same targets on macOS, Linux, and Windows
✅ Server-side frameworks run on Linux: Vapor and Hummingbird target the Linux toolchain, so a non-Apple deployment does not need Apple hardware
❌ One vendor sets the language direction: Apple owns the evolution process and ships the complete toolchain in Xcode, so the platform a project depends on has a single centre (P2)
⚠️ The strongest tools are Apple-only: Instruments and the Xcode debugger have no full equivalent on Linux, so profiling and debugging off Apple platforms are weaker



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Value vs Reference: Structs vs Classes creates identity coupling decisions
ARC vs Manual: Retain cycles require weak/unowned discipline
Swift vs Objective-C: Interop couples to legacy patterns
Protocol Extensions: Default implementations can create hidden coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled: LLVM backend, native performance
✅ ARC: Deterministic, no GC pauses
✅ Value types optimized: Copy-on-write for arrays/strings
✅ Whole module optimization: Cross-module inlining
⚠️ Protocol witness tables: Dynamic dispatch overhead



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Swift Package Manager: Standardized, improving
✅ Xcode: Excellent IDE (on macOS)
⚠️ Apple ecosystem focus: Couples to Apple platforms primarily
✅ Growing server-side: Vapor, Kitura frameworks
⚠️ Smaller than Java/npm: But growing rapidly
✅ ABI stability is promised by the language: Swift 5 declares ABI stability, so an app built with one compiler links against a library built with another [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Swift Evolution process: Transparent, community-driven
⚠️ Breaking changes: Swift 2→3→4→5 had significant breaks
✅ Stable now: Swift 5+ has ABI stability
✅ Regular improvements: Annual updates with new features
❌ Build variants multiply: #if blocks with -D flags select which declarations compile, and the SPM build settings set the space (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for iOS/macOS: Native platform language
✅ Good for server-side: Linux support, growing ecosystem
⚠️ Limited cross-platform: Windows support improving but limited
✅ Good for embedded: Embedded Swift compiles to bare-metal ARM and RISC-V targets, dropping ABI stability, reflection, and unspecialized generics so that it links without the full Swift runtime
⚠️ Web frontend: SwiftUI for Web experimental



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Approachable: Cleaner than Objective-C
⚠️ Many concepts: Protocols, extensions, generics, concurrency
✅ Excellent docs: Swift.org, Apple documentation
⚠️ Rapid evolution: Older resources outdated



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean, modern: Minimal boilerplate
✅ Type inference: Often don’t need explicit types
✅ Trailing closures: Elegant for callbacks
⚠️ Attribute syntax: @available, @escaping can clutter



1.2.7 Testing

✅ XCTest: Built-in testing framework
✅ LLDB debugger: Powerful, integrated with Xcode
✅ Instruments: Excellent profiling tools (on macOS)
⚠️ Linux tooling: Less polished than macOS
✅ The published elapsed reading exists: ContinuousClock and the Clock protocol ship a monotonic reading the program declares (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: ARC prevents use-after-free
✅ Type safe: Strong static typing
✅ Optional safety: Prevents null pointer errors
⚠️ Force unwrap escape hatch: Can bypass safety
⚠️ Objective-C interop: Can introduce unsafety

Verdict: Swift combines protocol-oriented programming with value semantics for excellent coupling separation. Swift 6 adds typed throws (error types in signatures) and strict concurrency checking (Sendable enforced by default), significantly improving both error handling and concurrency coupling separation. Main strength: value types + protocols decouple without inheritance; actors + strict Sendable prevent data races at compile time. Main weakness: Objective-C interop creates safety escape hatches, force unwrap bypasses type system.

title: Scala (3.8 / 3.3 LTS)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Scala in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 71.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 81.9/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Traits enable composition: Multiple trait inheritance without diamond problem
✅ Implicit parameters decouple: Can pass context without threading parameters
✅ Higher-kinded types: Generic over type constructors (Map, List, Option)
⚠️ Implicits can create hidden coupling: Action-at-a-distance when implicit resolution is not obvious and resolution order matters
❌ Complexity allows many ways to couple: Language flexibility means discipline required
❌ Inherits the JVM answer: Char is a UTF-16 code unit (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Case classes separate data from construction: Immutable, auto-generated constructors
✅ Apply methods decouple construction syntax: Person("Alice", 30) instead of new Person(...)
⚠️ Can use Java-style mutable constructors: Interop allows coupled patterns
❌ Collection order is unpinned: immutable Map keeps insertion order through four entries, then switches to a hashed map — documented, and the switch is silent (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: Scala 2’s implicit conversions insert user-defined calls at unmarked sites (the documented deprecation to Scala 3 names the hazard) (C7)
❌ Scala compiles classes to JVM classes: class initialization is first active touch with the JLS-documented cycle, the Java rule the JVM family carries (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutable collections reduce GC pressure: Structural sharing, persistent data structures
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Stop-the-world pauses, though modern JVM GC improves (ZGC, Shenandoah)
⚠️ Object allocation overhead: Boxing/unboxing couples primitives to heap allocation
⚠️ Closure captures can extend lifetimes: Function closures hold references, preventing collection



1.1.4 Error

✅ Try/Either/Option separate concerns: Multiple error handling approaches
✅ For-comprehensions make error composition clear: for { a <- tryA; b <- tryB } yield f(a, b)
❌ Exceptions still common: Scala culture uses exceptions more than Haskell-style Result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Futures decouple async: Future[T] separates async from sync
✅ Akka actors separate concurrent operations: Message passing prevents shared state
✅ Immutable collections by default: Prevents concurrent modification coupling
⚠️ Can use Java threads: Interop allows traditional coupling



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Portable JVM target: Scala runs wherever a JVM runs — Linux, macOS, and Windows — rather than on one vendor’s runtime
✅ Multiple JVM implementations: OpenJDK builds from Oracle, Eclipse Adoptium, Amazon, and Azul all run Scala, so no single vendor controls the runtime
✅ Open-source compiler: The Scala 3 compiler is Apache-2.0-licensed and developed by EPFL’s Scala Center with the community
✅ Three backends, not one platform: Scala compiles to JVM bytecode, to JavaScript through Scala.js, and to native code through Scala Native



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Expressiveness vs. Simplicity: Multiple ways to solve problems couples team to arbitrary choices
Implicits as Magic: Implicit resolution hides dependencies, creating action-at-a-distance coupling
Compile Time vs. Development Speed: Type-level programming couples fast iteration to long compile times
OOP + FP Hybrid: Can use both paradigms, but mixing couples code to dual mental models
Library Fragmentation: Cats vs. Scalaz vs. ZIO couples projects to ecosystem factions




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JVM performance: JIT optimization, fast steady-state
⚠️ GC pauses: Inherits JVM GC characteristics (R2)
❌ Slow compilation: Couples development velocity to compiler speed
✅ Immutable collections optimized: Persistent data structures perform well
⚠️ Runtime reflection overhead: Implicits and type classes have runtime cost



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ JVM ecosystem: Access to massive Java library ecosystem
✅ sbt/Mill build tools: Standardized (though complex)
⚠️ IDE support mixed: IntelliJ good, others struggle
❌ Slow build times: Compilation couples to wait time, so build time affects iteration speed
✅ Active ecosystem: Libraries for most use cases
✅ The release line carries a published promise: Scala guarantees binary compatibility inside a line, checked with MiMa, so a consumer links the artifact built for its own line [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Scala 2 → 3 breaking changes: Major version couples code to rewriting effort
⚠️ Library fragmentation: Scala 2.12 vs 2.13 vs 3 couples to version matrix
✅ Active development: Regular improvements
❌ Binary compatibility issues: Cross-version compatibility couples deployment



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend/distributed systems: Akka, Spark, Play
✅ Strong for data engineering: Spark is industry standard
✅ Great for functional programming: Full FP support
⚠️ Less common for frontend: Scala.js exists but niche
✅ JVM deployment: Runs anywhere Java runs



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Implicits, type system complexity, multiple paradigms
❌ Too many ways to do things: Couples productivity to knowing “the right way”
⚠️ Scala 2 vs 3 differences: Learning couples to version
✅ Good books/resources: “Functional Programming in Scala” et al.



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Expressive: For comprehensions, pattern matching, case classes
❌ Symbol overload: =>, <-, _, * used in many contexts
⚠️ Implicit complexity: Hard to understand what’s happening
✅ Concise when done right: Less boilerplate than Java



1.2.7 Testing

✅ ScalaTest, Specs2: Mature testing frameworks
✅ Property testing: ScalaCheck available
⚠️ Debugging implicits hard: Stack traces couple to implicit resolution
✅ JVM tooling: Profilers, debuggers work



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: JVM GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safe: Strong static typing
⚠️ Java interop: null, exceptions can leak through
✅ Immutability by default: Prevents mutation bugs (if used)
❌ Inherits the JVM rule: Int/Long wraparound, unchecked (Q4)

title: Python (2.7)
text:
Analysis against Python 2.7 (released 2010-07-03, final release 2.7.18 on 2020-04-20): print is a statement, str is bytes, async does not exist, and dict iteration order is unspecified. The family’s Python 3.14 page assesses the current release.
This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].
Snapshot Python 2.7 — released 3 July 2010 · lifecycle retired (The Python 2 series ended on 2020-04-20 with 2.7.18; no further release or security fix is planned.)
Family Python — shelf: Application
The language’s main business is building general application software, with a managed runtime or a rich standard library. A shelf groups; it does not classify — the tags below carry every use, paradigm, and platform of this snapshot.

title: Python (2.7)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Python 2.7 in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 55.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.3/100 · Engineering readiness 79.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing: the type of a value is whatever the run time finds, so every agreement is deferred to execution (T1)
❌ The call target is chosen from the value: a method name must exist on every object that arrives at the site (T3)
❌ No sum type: an alternative is a sentinel, a None, or a tuple with a tag, and exhaustiveness stays a convention (T4)
❌ No type parameter: an algorithm over several types duplicates or falls back on one universal object (T5)
❌ None is an ordinary value: no signature says a value may be absent, and each consumer writes the guard (T10)
❌ A signature states no effects: a call may read a file, mutate a module global, and raise, and the signature names only the return value (T12)
❌ ctypes is an unchecked boundary: a hand-written declaration states the C layout, and nothing validates it (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A module-level name is a global: a function writes the caller’s namespace through global, and any module can reach the name (C1)
❌ Bindings are mutable by default: nothing states that a name or an attribute will not change (C2)
❌ Dictionary order is the hash’s: the 2.7 reference states that the order of dict keys is unspecified, and insertion order becomes a promise only in 3.7 (C5)
⚠️ __init__ may run side effects: construction and initialisation are one call, and a subclass shares the base’s path
❌ One value, many names: names bind objects, and a parameter, a closure, and an attribute can hold the same list (C6)
❌ The import system executes a module once, at first import; a circular import hands the importer the half-initialized module (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting reclaims at the last reference: most objects are released as soon as nothing names them
⚠️ A cycle needs the collector: a reference loop waits for the periodic pass
⚠️ __del__ timing is not a release path: a finalizer is unreliable for a resource
❌ No release runs at scope exit: with releases only the context managers that exist, and a lock or a file acquired outside one has no scope rule (M3)
⚠️ A module global extends a lifetime: a name held at module level keeps its object alive for the process
⚠️ No handle names its owner: any two names reach the same mutable object (M4)



1.1.4 Error

✅ try/except carries a failure to the frame that handles it: a raise is a value that unwinds (Er1)
❌ A failure may arrive undeclared: a raised exception needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it (Er2)
⚠️ A bare except catches everything: the declaration is the handler’s choice, not the raiser’s
❌ A failure is not a value: a raise cannot be folded into an expression, so each level rebuilds the try/except shape around the call (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The interpreter lock serialises bytecode: a CPU-bound program must leave the language, through a process or a native extension, to use a second core (K1)
❌ Shared state is the default: a global or an attribute is reachable from every thread (K2)
❌ Nothing detects a race: the lock discipline is an agreement across modules (K3)
❌ No scope joins a thread: threading.Thread is started and joined by hand, so a task can outlive the code that started it (K4)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: Python is governed by the Python Software Foundation
✅ Several implementations exist: CPython, PyPy, Jython, and IronPython are separate runtimes
✅ The runtime is portable: CPython builds on the era’s operating systems and on many others
✅ The packaging tools are vendor-neutral: the package index and the installer are not tied to one vendor



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Readable syntax vs. hidden rules: the indentation that makes the code readable is also the rule a mixed file breaks silently
A batteries-included library vs. an audit surface: the standard library is large and stable, so a reviewer decides which of its modules are still the right place for a job
Comprehensions vs. the loop: an expression that builds a list hides the accumulation in one line, and a reader who needs the loop’s control flow rewrites it




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Interpreted: the bytecode dispatch, not the algorithm, decides the shape of a hot loop (R1)
⚠️ A C extension helps and binds the program to the C ecosystem: the fast path is a native module
⚠️ Object overhead is high: an integer and a list are heap objects



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The package index holds the ecosystem: a dependency is fetched by the installer
✅ The tooling is settled: pip, virtualenv, and setuptools cover the workflow
❌ A wheel binds to an interpreter: the filename names the Python, ABI, and platform tags, and the installer loads that binary [5], [6] (Ec8)
❌ Stored byte-code binds to the release: the marshal format carries a magic number per release and no cross-release promise [7] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The Python 3 split: print becomes a function, str becomes text, division changes meaning, and the standard library is reorganised, so a 2.7 codebase is revisited across the boundary (V1)
❌ No steward for the line: the series is retired, so a defect in 2.7 is permanent and the only migration path lies outside it (V3)
✅ A bug-fix-only line: 2.7 added no new syntax after 2.7.0, so the definition of the line is stable



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Data analysis is the language’s main work: NumPy, SciPy, and pandas run on 2.7
✅ Scripting and automation: a short program drives an operating system or another program
✅ A web back end is built from it: Django and its peers run on the release



1.2.5 Learning

✅ A gentle start: the syntax reads as executable pseudocode
✅ A large literature: tutorials and courses exist for every level



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Indentation carries the block: the structure is the layout
⚠️ Indentation is also the failure: a mixed tab and space is a syntax error the reader cannot see



1.2.7 Testing

✅ unittest ships with the runtime, and pytest is a standard dependency: a runner and an assertion library are available
✅ pdb ships with the runtime: the toolchain steps through the source
❌ A mistake is found on the path that runs: the compiler decides nothing, so coverage is the only evidence of safety (G3)
❌ The only published clock is the wall: time.time reads the operator’s calendar, and time.clock reports processor time rather than elapsed time (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ No pointer is available: a buffer overflow and a use-after-free are not expressible (Q1)
❌ A value from outside arrives with no declared type: keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer’s check (Q2)
❌ eval and exec turn text into code: a data path can become a control path (Q3)

Ec9 is present when one row carries a break: the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable elsewhere, or a break the probe harness has reproduced.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default: archive metadata and build paths reach the artifact (Y1)
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock: an unpinned requirement is resolved from the index at install time (Y2)
⚠️ The interpreter is not pinned by the project: the release is left to a virtual environment or an image (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ The index publishes signed metadata: the installer verifies a package’s origin (Y3)
❌ The index is a flat name space: a name is a first claim, and a dependency can be redirected without a change in the consumer’s source (Y4)
✅ A vulnerability feed joins advisories to package versions: OSV covers this registry (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ The instrumentation standard publishes an implementation: traces and metrics have a stable expressed form (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit is the run: no build step sits between a change and its effect (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A general foreign-function interface exists: ctypes and the C extension API reach native code in process (Y9)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The specification is public: the language reference states the language, and the enhancement proposals record the changes (Y12)
✅ A published parser exists: the runtime ships ast, and its grammar source is public (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [8]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [9].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [10], [11].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path is published for the language itself; a safety-critical deployment rests on a platform vendor’s qualified runtime, not on the language.

Verdict: Python 2.7 is the last release of the Python 2 line and the clearest example of a language that outgrew its own dialect. It is dynamic, garbage-collected, module-scoped, and readable, and it carries no type system, no effect tracking, and no sum type. Its costs are the costs of its era: print is a statement, str is bytes, a dictionary has no promised order, the only clock is the wall, and no scope runs a release. The interpreter lock forbids parallel bytecode, and the line itself ended in 2020, so a defect in 2.7 is permanent. Main strength: the era’s most productive language for data work and glue code. Main weakness: the 2.x line is a dead end by construction, and the move to 3.0 revisits every file. The family’s Python 3.14 page assesses the successor.

text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PureScript in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 88.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ All Haskell benefits plus algebraic effects: Effect system separates different effect types (unlike Haskell’s monolithic IO)
✅ Row polymorphism for extensible records: Can decouple from exact record shape
✅ Type classes with functional dependencies: More precise abstraction control
❌ JavaScript FFI can bypass type safety: Interop creates coupling holes
❌ The JavaScript backend carries the engine rule: string length counts UTF-16 units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Algebraic data types: A data declaration fixes the set of constructors, so every value is built through a declared shape
✅ Smart constructors: A module can hide its constructors and export a validating function, so an invalid value cannot be built outside it
✅ Records are built from a literal: { field: value } constructs a record directly, with no constructor tied to an allocation step
✅ newtype wrappers are zero-cost: A one-constructor wrapper gives a distinct type without a runtime box
✅ No global mutable state: A module binding is a pure value, so no module couples another to an initialization order



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Compiles to JS, inherits JS GC
✅ Immutability simplifies: No cyclic mutable references
⚠️ JavaScript GC pauses: Non-deterministic, inherited from JS runtime
✅ No space leaks from laziness: Strict evaluation by default (unlike Haskell)
⚠️ JS interop can create leaks: Foreign JS code may hold references



1.1.4 Error

✅ Effect system makes errors explicit by type: Effect (console :: CONSOLE, exception :: EXCEPTION) Unit shows exactly what can fail
✅ Explicit exception handling: No hidden runtime exceptions



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Aff monad for async: Separates async coordination from sync logic
❌ Single-threaded runtime: The compiled JavaScript runs on one thread, so two computations cannot run in parallel (K1)
✅ Effect tracking prevents coupling: Can’t accidentally do async in sync code



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Compiles to JavaScript: The output runs on any JavaScript engine — browsers, Node.js, Deno — rather than inside one vendor’s runtime
✅ No proprietary runtime: PureScript ships no virtual machine of its own; compiled output depends only on the JavaScript platform
✅ Cross-platform host support: Precompiled compiler binaries are published for macOS, Linux, and Windows
✅ Community-maintained compiler: The compiler is developed in the open at purescript/purescript, not owned by a single vendor



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Type Safety vs. JavaScript Interop: FFI boundary loses all guarantees, couples to JS runtime behavior
Effect Granularity vs. Complexity: Fine-grained effect tracking increases cognitive load
Compile Target Constraints: Must fit JavaScript semantics, can’t have true parallelism
Ecosystem Size vs. Quality: Small community means fewer libraries but tighter coupling to available ones




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiles to JavaScript: Inherits JS runtime performance characteristics
⚠️ JS GC couples memory to runtime: No control over GC behavior
✅ Strict evaluation: More predictable than Haskell, no space leaks from thunks
❌ JS interop performance penalty: FFI boundary couples to marshaling cost
✅ Tree-shaking support: Dead code elimination decouples bundle size from library inclusion



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Small ecosystem: Library availability couples to a niche community smaller than Haskell, so a project reinvents wheels or couples to specific libraries
✅ Spago/purs package management: Standardized build system
❌ Depends on JS ecosystem: Must interop with npm packages, couples to JS tooling
✅ Excellent compiler errors: Error messages decouple debugging from trial-and-error
⚠️ Niche community: Support couples to small contributor base



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Stable core: Breaking changes are rare and well-documented
⚠️ Pre-1.0 for long time: Language evolution couples to experimental status
✅ Effect library updates separate: Can upgrade effects without changing core language
❌ Small team: Development pace couples to limited resources



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for frontend development: Type safety in browser decouples from JS runtime errors
✅ Strong for web apps: Effect system handles async/DOM naturally
❌ Limited backend use: Node.js backend couples to JS ecosystem limitations
⚠️ Niche adoption: Team expertise couples to hiring/training challenges



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: All Haskell concepts plus row polymorphism and effect systems
✅ Better than Haskell for JS devs: Familiar runtime, compilation target
✅ Excellent docs: PureScript by Example book decouples learning from experimentation
⚠️ Requires Haskell knowledge: Learning couples to functional programming expertise



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Haskell-like syntax: Familiar to FP developers
✅ Less operator noise than Haskell: More consistent naming
✅ Row polymorphism elegant: Extensible records without boilerplate
⚠️ FFI syntax verbose: foreign import couples JS interop to boilerplate



1.2.7 Testing

✅ QuickCheck/Spec available: Property testing support
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No side effect coupling
❌ Debugging via JS: Must debug compiled output, couples to source maps
⚠️ Browser DevTools help: Can debug in browser, but stack traces couple to compiled code
❌ No monotonic reading published in the language: the Effect time APIs are community packages (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: JS GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safety: Prevents type confusion
✅ Effect system tracks side effects: Can’t accidentally perform unsafe operations
❌ JS interop escape hatch: unsafeCoerce and FFI bypass safety, couple correctness to discipline
❌ The JavaScript backend carries the engine rule: double arithmetic, silent integer change above 2^53 (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Spago resolves package sets at build time. (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ The package set carries no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The registry is a flat name space. (Y4)

1.3.5 Interop

✅ The FFI is the documented escape to JavaScript modules. (Y9)
❌ The compiled artifact runs wherever the host JavaScript runs; the compiler adds no target. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the reference compiler: the documentation defines the language as the compiler behaves, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

title: OCaml (5.4)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses OCaml in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 80.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 86.3/100 · Engineering readiness 59.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Variant types declare a checked case distinction: type shape = Circle of float | Square of float is a closed sum, and the compiler checks that a match covers every constructor
✅ Types are static and inferred: The Hindley–Milner algorithm gives a principal type without annotations, and no value is untyped
✅ A signature hides a type behind an interface: A .mli file can export type t as abstract, so a consumer binds to the operations and not to the representation
✅ A functor makes a type a parameter: Set.Make(String) builds a set module for a given ordered type, so one algorithm is reused across types without run-time dispatch
⚠️ Operators are rebound in scope rather than overloaded (T8): + is int addition and +. is float addition, and a module-qualified form such as Int64.(a + b) or a local let (+) = ... changes which operator is in scope, so the reader must track the binding
⚠️ The object layer is a second type system: Classes and row-polymorphic object types sit beside the core types, so a codebase can mix two paradigms



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Mutable state is the natural default container for shared data (C2): The idiomatic way to hold module state is a ref cell, an Array, or a Hashtbl, each mutable, so any caller of the interface can change what the module holds
✅ A variant constructor is the only way to build a value of the type: Node (l, x, r) names the construction path, so every construction is visible in the type declaration
✅ A record literal states every field: { x = 1.; y = 2. } must be complete unless with is used, so a field cannot be left unset silently
✅ A signature can hide the constructor of an abstract type: With type t abstract and val create : unit -> t, construction goes through the module, so the invariant holds by construction
✅ A let binding evaluates its right-hand side once: let x = expensive () evaluates at that point, and the result is a value rather than a re-evaluable expression
⚠️ A mutable field relaxes the invariant: A record field declared mutable can be assigned at any time, so an invariant over the record is maintained by the code rather than by the type
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the standard library documents Hashtbl iteration order as unspecified (C5)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Collection is automatic with no manual free: The collector reclaims an unreachable block, and a program never calls free
⚠️ Collection is not tied to the last reference (M2): A block stays allocated until the collector decides, so a latency-sensitive path is coupled to a component it never calls
❌ There is no RAII (M3): There is no scope-bound destructor, so a file descriptor, a Unix.file_descr, or another non-memory handle is released by an explicit call or a bracket such as Fun.protect
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties a value to an owner, so a mutable structure that escapes its module is shared without a trace
✅ Fun.protect brackets a resource: Fun.protect ~finally:close body runs the release on the normal path and on the exceptional path, so the release need not be repeated at every exit
⚠️ The major heap is measured and tuned by hand: Gc.set and Gc.stat control and report space_overhead and the major cycle, so a latency-sensitive program reads collector statistics itself
⚠️ C stubs and Marshal sit outside the collector’s view: A value held in a C global must be registered with caml_register_generational_global_root, and Marshal.from_string builds a value the collector then owns, so the boundary is the programmer’s to manage
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a stack overflow in the recursive evaluator is a crash (documented: the native compiler’s stack overflow is fatal), outside the exception surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked (Er2): raise, Failure, and Not_found are not declared in the type of a function, so a caller cannot see the failure set from a signature
✅ result is a composable value: ('a, 'b) result is Ok of 'a | Error of 'b, and Result.map, Result.bind, and Result.fold chain operations without a match at every step
✅ A variant closes the failure set: type error = Not_found | Permission_denied makes the cases finite, so a match over the failure is checked for exhaustiveness
✅ try ... with separates the abnormal path: A handler can match an exception constructor such as Sys_error _ | Unix.Unix_error _ and re-raise cheaply with raise_notrace
✅ Option carries an absence without an exception: Some x and None give a missing result a value, and Option.map and Option.get compose it
⚠️ A wildcard handler hides a fault: try f () with _ -> default catches every exception, including Out_of_memory and an unintended bug, so the cause disappears
❌ A fault ends the process: an uncaught exception in a thread terminates it (documented) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ OCaml 5 runs OCaml code on several cores: Domain.spawn starts a second domain, so the global runtime lock that serialised all code in earlier versions no longer applies
✅ Effects express a scheduler in the language: An effect handler such as Effect.Deep.try_with or Effect.Shallow defines what an effect does, so a concurrency library is ordinary OCaml
✅ Eio supplies structured concurrency: Eio_main.run gives a scheduler with fibers, cancellation, and capability-scoped resources, so a program names a scope rather than a thread
✅ Atomic, Mutex, and Condition are primitives of the runtime: A shared cell of type 'a Atomic.t has defined operations, and Mutex.lock guards a critical section
✅ A channel passes values between domains: Domainslib.Chan with Domain.spawn gives a message-passing design instead of a shared one
⚠️ A library written for one domain must be revisited: Code that relied on the single runtime’s atomicity now shares state across domains, so the migration is a review rather than a recompile



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The native compiler emits machine code for many targets: ocamlopt produces a native executable for x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V, and Power, and ocamlc produces bytecode wherever the virtual machine runs
✅ A C stub reaches any system library: An external declaration plus a small C stub links a C library, so the language’s reach follows the reach of C
✅ MirageOS links an OCaml program into a unikernel: A set of modules builds a freestanding image, so the target needs no operating-system process
✅ The JavaScript backends target the browser: js_of_ocaml compiles bytecode to JavaScript, and Melange compiles OCaml to JavaScript modules
⚠️ The foreign-function interface is manual: An external declaration and its C stub must be kept in step by hand, so the boundary carries the correctness burden of both sides



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The object layer is opt-in: Classes and objects are separate from the module system, so a project can ignore them entirely
Inheritance instead of a functor is a design decision: Using class inheritance where a functor would do is a choice the language permits and does not require
Terse syntax is a stated preference: let f x = x + 1 and the ;; toplevel separator are stylistic, and the adjustment period is not a forced dependency
Persistent structures trade space for sharing: A version-keeping data structure retains the older versions, which is a space cost rather than a coupling mechanism
Interface files are a convention: A project can omit the .mli file, and the abstraction benefit follows from the discipline rather than from the language
Effect handlers are opt-in: A program can ignore effects and write plain code, so the paradigm adds no dependency unless it is used




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ ocamlopt compiles ahead of time to native code: There is no interpreter and no warm-up, so a program starts at full speed
✅ The core type system erases at compile time: An abstract type and a generic function carry no run-time dispatch, so the abstraction costs nothing to execute
✅ A functor is specialised at compile time: Set.Make(String) produces a module whose calls are direct, so the reuse costs no dynamic dispatch
✅ An unboxed representation is available per declaration: An all-float record and an [@@unboxed] declaration avoid a heap indirection, so a numeric structure can be dense
⚠️ A mixed record boxes its float field: type t = { n : int; x : float } stores x in a box, and only an all-float record or an annotation removes it, so the representation is a per-declaration detail
⚠️ Allocation rate drives the collection schedule: A high allocation rate fills the minor heap often, and the program cannot schedule that collection itself



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library ecosystem is small next to Haskell or Rust (Ec3): Fewer general-purpose packages exist, so some work starts from a blank module
✅ opam is a mature package manager: opam resolves versions, pins a package to a revision, and keeps per-project switches, and the opam repository index is curated
✅ dune builds, tests, and documents a project: One file describes a library, an executable, and a test, so no external build system is needed
✅ merlin and ocaml-lsp give editor support: Type-directed completion, jump-to-definition, and error reporting are available in Emacs, VS Code, and others
✅ Substantial systems are written in it: The Rocq (Coq) proof assistant, the Frama-C analyzer, Jane Street’s trading systems, and the Tezos blockchain are OCaml codebases
⚠️ A niche language means fewer answers: The community is smaller, so a team depends on the members it can find



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ OCaml 5 keeps the single-domain case working: A program that ran on 4.x recompiles on 5.x, and the multicore runtime is the same source language
✅ Version changes have been additive in practice: The core syntax and the standard library have stayed stable across decades
✅ A switch pins a compiler version per project: opam switch keeps an old compiler and a new one side by side, so a project upgrades on its own schedule
✅ The multicore change has a migration path: Code that used Threads can move to Domain and a scheduler library such as Eio, with Domainslib bridging the two
⚠️ A single-domain library needs a review for OCaml 5: A global mutable structure that was safe under one runtime becomes shared state when several domains run



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for compilers and static analysis: Algebraic data types, pattern matching, and a module system match a syntax tree and a typed pass directly, and the OCaml compiler itself is written in OCaml
✅ Proven in proof assistants and verification: Rocq (Coq) and Frama-C are OCaml programs, and their term representations are OCaml variants
✅ Proven in finance: Jane Street’s trading systems are OCaml, and the language is used for typed, low-latency systems
✅ A strong fit for parsers and interpreters: menhir generates a parser, and a variant-based abstract syntax tree keeps the grammar’s cases explicit
⚠️ Numeric and tensor work needs a library: Dense array and tensor programming depends on a package such as Owl or on a C binding, not on the core language
⚠️ The object layer is rarely the right tool: Most OCaml code uses modules and variants, and the object system is a separate, optional design



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The abstraction layer is steep even when the syntax is not (L1): A newcomer learns inference, the module and functor system, and pattern matching together, although the language is generally considered easier to approach than Haskell
✅ Inference removes annotation work: let rec fact n = if n = 0 then 1 else n * fact (n - 1) is accepted without a type written by hand
✅ The error messages point at the mismatch: The compiler prints the inferred type and the conflicting type, and Merlin shows the type under the cursor
❌ The module language is a second language: Functors, signatures, and module type of are a topic of their own beyond the expression language
⚠️ Reading an inferred signature is a skill: val f : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a list -> 'b list must be read fluently before an interface is easy to write



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ let, match, and type share one shape: A binding, a case analysis, and a declaration all need no braces, and the toplevel ends a phrase with ;;
✅ Pattern matching is written as data: match xs with [] -> 0 | x :: _ -> x states the cases directly
✅ The keyword set is small and consistent: The same |-case form serves a variant declaration, a match, and an exception handler
✅ Terse for the type information it carries: One line declares a record, and inference fills in the annotations
⚠️ Integer and float operators differ by a character: + is not +., and = is structural while == is physical, so a sign or a repetition changes the meaning
⚠️ Extensions extend the notation: let* binding operators, ppx rewrites, and [@@deriving] attributes are not core syntax, so a reader must know which extensions a file uses



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework lives in the package repository: alcotest and ounit2 provide assertions and runners, and dune runtest runs the suite
✅ Inline and expect tests sit beside the code: let%test and let%expect_test (ppx_inline_test and ppx_expect) keep the expected output in the source and diff it on a run
✅ The type checker catches faults before a test does: An exhaustiveness check reports a missing match case at compile time, which removes a whole class of test
✅ bisect_ppx measures coverage: An instrumented build reports which points were executed
⚠️ A hand-written module is the usual stand-in: There is no dynamic mocking of a module, so a seam must be a functor parameter or a signature
⚠️ An effectful path needs its handler installed: A test of a scheduler runs the effect handler, which is a different setup from a test of plain code
❌ No monotonic reading in the standard library: Sys.time is CPU time, and the wall functions live in the Unix module (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety is the default: The collector and the type system prevent use-after-free, and an out-of-range a.(i) raises Invalid_argument instead of reading adjacent memory
✅ A signature hides the representation: With type t abstract in the .mli, a consumer can neither forge a value nor read its internals
✅ A typed function cannot receive a value of another type: A value that reaches a typed parameter is of that type, so a string cannot become a program structure at that boundary
✅ The runtime bounds an array access: The bounds check is part of the language, so an off-by-one index is a defined exception
⚠️ Marshal.from_string trusts its input: A crafted byte string can build a value that the type system then trusts, so untrusted input must not be unmarshalled
⚠️ Obj.magic and a C stub break the type system: Obj.magic reinterprets a value without a check, and a stub can return an ill-typed value
❌ int is the tagged machine integer; overflow is unchecked (the manual leaves it undefined) (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ opam resolves package versions at install time; lock files are opt-in. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve from the opam repository state. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ opam packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The opam repository is a flat name space. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ print_endline carries no structure. (Y6)
❌ Exceptions carry backtraces only when compiled with -g. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ ocamldebug ships with the compiler distribution. (Y13)
✅ The bytecode loop answers with no build. (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ C stubs are the language’s in-process foreign interface. (Y9)
✅ The compiler targets the common platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the reference implementation: the manual defines the language, the implementation defines the unspecified corners, and no published conformance suite exists (Y17)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

Verdict: OCaml’s design yields low core coupling because its abstraction is checked at compile time. A variant type closes a case set, an abstract type in a .mli hides its representation, a functor makes a type a module parameter, and the inference engine reports a mismatch before the program runs. The coupling that remains is mostly about state and lifetime: there is no ownership rule and no block-scoped release, exceptions are unchecked, and mutable containers are the natural way to hold module state. On the platform side, the small library ecosystem and the concepts of the module language are the real cost, while observation of the collector is a matter of tuning rather than of correctness.
