title: Lua (5.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Lua in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 64.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 86.3/100 · Engineering readiness 49.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no static type check: Every value is a tagged variant and type() answers at run time, so a wrong shape is found when the operation runs rather than when the file loads (T1)
❌ Dispatch is a lookup, not a declared type: obj:m() reads the field m through the metatable chain, so which function runs depends on the table’s metatable rather than on a declared receiver type (T3)
❌ There are no sum types: An alternative is a tag field beside the payload ({kind = "circle", r = 1}), and nothing checks that the branch matches the tag (T4)
❌ There are no generics: Reuse across element types is a naming convention or a documented contract, because the element type of a table is declared nowhere (T5)
❌ There is no namespace (T6): require returns a value and every global name lives in one shared table, so two modules that define the same name collide
⚠️ Metamethods overload the operators: __add, __eq, __lt, __concat, __len, and __call redefine the notation for a table, so an operator at a call site may run a function the reader cannot see (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Globals are the default, so a construction site can write shared state: x = 1 without local creates a field in the global table that every chunk sees (C1)
❌ Nothing is immutable: There is no const and no frozen table, so any code that holds a table can change it (C2)
✅ A table constructor and a closure are values: {1, 2, 3} and function(x) return x * 2 end are built where they are written, with no class or factory in the way
✅ A metatable gives construction its own meaning: setmetatable(t, {__index = proto}) decides how the value answers a missing field, so the object-like behaviour is installed rather than inherited by the syntax
✅ __call makes any table callable: A table with a __call metamethod can be used as a function, so a design need not wrap it in one
✅ An upvalue is private by construction: A variable declared local outside a nested function is reachable only through that function’s closure, so a private field needs no keyword
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the reference states pairs() walks in an order decided by the internal data structures, and the order can change between calls (C5)
❌ require caches the in-progress module; a cyclic require returns the half-built table (documented) (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Collection is non-deterministic in its timing: The collector runs on its own schedule, so the moment a table’s storage is reclaimed is not the moment the last reference to it goes out of scope (M2)
❌ There is no ownership model: The collector sees reachability rather than ownership, so nothing states which part of a program is responsible for dropping a reference (M4)
⚠️ Most values have no destructor: A table’s __gc metamethod runs only if its metatable already carried __gc when it was set, so release is not tied to a scope by default (M3)
✅ A to-be-closed variable releases deterministically: local f <close> = res calls the value’s __close metamethod when the block ends, including on an error (Lua 5.4)
✅ A weak table lets the collector take an entry: With __mode set to "k", "v", or "kv", an entry whose key or value is otherwise unreachable is removed, so a memo table does not pin its values
✅ The collector can be inspected and driven: collectgarbage "count" reports the footprint in kilobytes, and a program can request a step or select the incremental or generational mode (Lua 5.4)



1.1.4 Error

❌ An error carries no declared type: error accepts any value and pcall returns it unchanged, so there is no error type a handler can be checked against (Er2)
❌ A nil result is easy to leave unchecked: io.open and os.remove report a failure by returning nil plus a message, and nothing requires the caller to look (Er3)
✅ pcall and xpcall state the protected call: A call is placed in a protected region and its status is returned, so the recovery path is an explicit second call
✅ A message handler is attached in the language: xpcall(f, handler) passes the error through a function, which is where a traceback from debug.traceback is added
✅ assert states a precondition with its message: assert(cond, "msg") raises when the condition fails, so the check and its text are one call
✅ An error value can be a table: A structured error with a code and a message is an ordinary table, because error raises the value it is given



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Coroutines are the only concurrency in the core: coroutine.create, resume, yield, and status give a cooperative task, so there is no lock, no shared-memory race, and no preemption to reason about
✅ A yield point is explicit: Control returns to the resumer only at a coroutine.yield, so the interleaving is visible at the line it happens
✅ A generator is a coroutine and a call site: An iterator is a function that yields, and for x in gen() do consumes it, so the producer does not know its consumer
✅ coroutine.wrap and coroutine.close complete the protocol: wrap returns a callable that propagates the error, and close closes a suspended coroutine and runs its pending to-be-closed variables (Lua 5.4)
⚠️ There is no scheduler and no parallelism: A coroutine runs only when it is resumed, so one blocking call stops the whole interpreter and parallel work needs a host with several interpreter states
⚠️ A table shared between coroutines is still shared mutable state: The language treats the state as one, so the discipline of not yielding mid-update is the programmer’s



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The reference implementation is portable C: The interpreter builds from one small C library on any platform with a C compiler, and the embedding API (luaL_newstate, lua_pcall, the lua_push* and lua_to* stack functions) is the intended interface
✅ The host controls a script’s environment: A chunk can be loaded with a table as its _ENV, so the set of names a script can see is the host’s decision (Lua 5.2 and later)
✅ Several independent implementations exist: PUC-Rio’s lua, LuaJIT, Luau, and hosted implementations in other languages each provide the language or a near variant
✅ A compiled chunk is data the host decides to load: load and lua_load take text or a binary chunk, so the host chooses what code runs and in which environment
⚠️ The implementations diverge: LuaJIT implements Lua 5.1 with extensions and Luau diverges for its host, so a script that uses goto, integer division, or <close> needs the reference implementation or a recent alternative
⚠️ The default library reaches the operating system: os.execute, os.remove, and io.open are in the standard library, so a host that needs a sandbox must remove them



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One compound structure is a deliberate economy: The language trades a declared type for one constructor that covers arrays, records, objects, and modules
Metatables are an opt-in object model: The core has no classes, and the idiom that adds them is chosen by the program rather than imposed
Embedding is the primary use, so the host owns the runtime: The small library and the C API are the reason to choose the language, not a defect
Cooperative scheduling is a design decision: With no preemption there is no thread of the language’s own, and the host decides about parallelism
The global table is a scripting convenience: It keeps a short script short and lets a host inject functions, and avoiding it is a discipline
A version pin is an adoption cost, not a mechanism: A library written for one version does not load on another, which follows from separate version lines rather than from a coupling in the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The reference implementation is a compact register-based virtual machine: The compiler emits bytecode for a small instruction set (luac -l prints it), so start-up is immediate
✅ LuaJIT traces a hot loop into machine code: The tracing compiler specialises the recorded path, which is why a numeric or table loop runs far faster than in the interpreter (the implementation is Lua 5.1 with extensions)
✅ Strings are interned, so a string key hashes once: Every string is hash-consed and its hash is cached, so a table lookup by string is cheap
✅ Tail calls are proper and do not grow the stack: A tail call reuses the frame, so a state machine written as tail recursion runs in constant space
✅ The collector takes bounded steps: The incremental mode does a small amount of work between bytecodes, and Lua 5.4 adds a generational mode for the allocation-heavy case
⚠️ The array part and the hash part of a table are a performance fact of its shape: The same logical sequence is a fast array or a slow hash depending on how it was built, so a hot path must keep the dense part dense



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small: LuaRocks carries many small modules and few large frameworks, so a project writes its own glue (Ec3)
✅ LuaRocks is a standard package manager and build tool: A rockspec declares a module and its dependencies, and luarocks install and luarocks make build and install it
✅ The language server and the linter are mature: lua-language-server checks the code against annotations such as ---@param and ---@type, and luacheck reports unused variables, globals, and a module’s public surface
✅ The C API is documented and versioned: The manual’s C API chapter and lua.h/lauxlib.h state the stack protocol, and bindings exist for C++, C#, Go, Rust, and Java
✅ The language runs wherever a C library runs: The interpreter is embedded in web servers, editors, games, and network equipment, which is why it is the standard embedded scripting layer
⚠️ The implementations split the ecosystem: A binding written for the LuaJIT foreign function interface or for Luau does not work in the reference interpreter, and the reverse
✅ The C API is documented per release line, and a compiled module links against that line [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A release is a deliberate, documented step: Each version has its own manual and a changes list, and the reference implementation is small enough to read
✅ The C API of a version line is stable within that line: A program builds against one set of headers and the matching library
✅ Feature additions are small and conservative: goto, integer division, the <close> attribute, and the generational collector were added as syntax or library functions rather than as a redesign of the language
⚠️ Source compatibility is not kept across minor versions: 5.2 replaced setfenv, getfenv, and loadstring with _ENV and load, and 5.3 introduced the integer subtype, so a codebase is usually pinned to one version
⚠️ The implementations lag the reference: LuaJIT remains at 5.1, so a program that wants the newer syntax gives up the tracing compiler
⚠️ A dialect can move the language forward on its own: Luau adds gradual typing and performance annotations to its host’s variant, which is not the standard language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Embedding a scripting layer in a host program is the design point: The interpreter is a C library with no external dependency, and the host decides the API it exposes
✅ Game scripting is the widest adoption: The language is the scripting layer of World of Warcraft, Roblox (as Luau), and many engines
✅ Configuration and data description work by construction: A table literal is a data format, and load or dofile evaluates it into a value
✅ Prototype-style objects are expressible with __index: The object model is a library idiom over tables rather than a language feature
⚠️ It is not a systems language: There is no pointer, no placement control, and no unchecked array, so work at that level belongs to the host C code
⚠️ A CPU-bound kernel needs LuaJIT or C: The interpreter is fast for a scripting language and is not a substitute for compiled numerical code



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The core syntax is small and regular: About two dozen keywords, one compound structure, and no declaration ceremony, so the language itself is learned quickly
✅ One document is the complete specification: The reference manual covers the syntax, the standard library, and the C API in a single short text
❌ The advanced layer is a second subject: Metatables, __index chains, closures over coroutines, and the C API are where the difficulty is, and the core syntax does not announce them (L1)
⚠️ The types live in the programmer’s head: With no declaration and no annotation, a reader infers a table’s shape from its uses unless the language server’s annotations or Luau types are added
✅ The interpreter reports the line and the call stack: An uncaught error prints its message with a Lua traceback, so a failure is located from the output



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is small and uses words as delimiters: local, if ... then ... else ... end, for ... do ... end, and function ... end, with no braces and no required semicolons
✅ A table constructor is a compact data notation: {x = 1, y = 2} is a record and {1, 2, 3} is an array, in the same brackets
✅ Short forms carry the common idioms: #t is the length, a .. b concatenates, t:k() calls a method, and ... is the variable argument list
✅ Multiple assignment and multiple return are one form: local x, y = f() and return a, b pass several values without a tuple type
⚠️ A missing local is a global write: x = 1 inside a function writes a field of the global table, and the mistake is invisible at the line
⚠️ The notation does not state the structure: The same {} is an array, a record, an object, or a module, so the intent is a comment rather than a declaration



1.2.7 Testing

✅ busted gives a describe/it suite with matchers: A third-party runner with luassert matchers runs a spec/ directory from the command line
✅ luaunit gives a single-file test framework: One file supplies the assertions and the runner, which suits an embedded project
✅ A test can substitute a chunk’s environment: load(src, name, "t", env) runs the module against a table the test supplies, so a dependency is replaced without editing the source
✅ The debug library can instrument a run: debug.sethook counts calls and samples, and debug.getinfo reports the source line, so a profiler or a coverage tool is written in Lua itself
✅ Static checks catch mistakes before a run: The language server reports an annotation mismatch and luacheck reports an unused variable and a global leak
⚠️ Testing is not part of the standard library: assert is the only built-in check, so the runner and the fixtures are dependencies
❌ No monotonic reading published: os.clock is CPU time and os.time is the wall; the reference ships no elapsed clock (G4)



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ A binary chunk from an untrusted source is unsafe: The manual states that load does not check the consistency of a binary chunk and that a crafted one can crash the interpreter or run arbitrary machine code
✅ _ENV gives a chunk a restricted global table: A sandbox loads a chunk with an environment that holds only the functions the host allows, and the chunk has no other path to the host’s state
⚠️ The debug library defeats a sandbox: debug.setupvalue, debug.getregistry, and debug.sethook reach past the environment, so a sandbox must remove the library and the host must not reopen it
⚠️ The standard library includes file and process access: io.open, io.popen, and os.execute are available unless the host removes them from the environment
✅ A pure Lua value cannot be a forged pointer: A value is a tagged variant, an out-of-bounds access is a table miss rather than an address, and there is no pointer type or pointer arithmetic in the language
✅ The interpreter imposes no host dependency of its own: It makes no call outside the C library unless the program does, so the attack surface of a script is the surface the host exposed
❌ The manual defines integer arithmetic as 64-bit with wraparound modulo 2^64 (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ LuaRocks resolves rock versions at install time; no lockfile exists by default. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve per install unless a rockspec tree pins them. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin file exists in the official distribution. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ LuaRocks packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The rock registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers rocks. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ print is the whole logging surface. (Y6)
❌ No backtrace or post-mortem ships by default; debug.traceback is opt-in. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the interpreter. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ The C API is the language’s own in-process foreign interface. (Y9)
✅ The interpreter is ANSI C and builds on every common platform. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Lua.org reference manual is public and normative. (Y12)
✅ The interpreter source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Lua’s design yields the low core score of a dynamic scripting language, with the coupling concentrated in its data model. One table type serves as array, record, object, and module, so the shape of the data is a convention and every structure error waits for a run time; the global table is the default and errors are unchecked. The counterweight is that the language is small, orthogonal, and easy to embed, and that its separating constructs are real: __index decouples object-like behaviour from syntax, a coroutine makes every interleaving explicit, <close> and weak tables tie release to a block or to reachability, and the C API decouples the language from its host. Main strengths: exceptional performance for a scripting language, a very small footprint, and mature tooling. Main weaknesses: no static type check, globals by default, an unchecked error channel, and a library pool that is small beside the language’s adoption.

title: Kern (1.1.2)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Kern in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 76.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.4/100 · Engineering readiness 67.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ I/O authority is a parameter, and the compiler enforces it: every authority-bearing call demands a Cap<T> argument in the signature, ambient authority is the compile error E0404 with no off switch, only @cap_constructor functions mint, and the entry module mints the roots — a function that cannot show a Cap<Fs> cannot read a file, which puts the effect where the caller reads it (T12)
✅ Nullability, exhaustiveness and boundaries are type facts: str is never null and str? is the opt-in with flow-sensitive narrowing; unions carry payloads and match must cover every variant; pub and the enforced import list (E0327) are a real module boundary; conversions are named calls (int(), float()) with no implicit narrowing, and bool and int are distinct
✅ Functions are coloured by declaration, not by kind: await composes inside a plain fn body — every example on the async page awaits tasks from a fn main — so the async fn marker does not spread through the call graph the way a second function kind does elsewhere (T13)
❌ Generic type parameters are erased: every generic parameter compiles to an opaque i8*, and integer and float values are boxed crossing generic code; there is no reflection API to reach structure at run time, so the charge is the erasure half — the artifact no longer carries the type argument, as on the TypeScript page (T7)
❌ The systems profile crosses to raw memory and syscalls: a @nogc function, or every function in a @systems file, may call the __mem_* and __syscall intrinsics, and std.cap_unsafe hands out Cap<Unsafe> raw addresses — layout, lifetime and the syscall ABI are hand-written agreements the type system does not check, and the memory-safe guarantee stops at that crossing (T14)
❌ length is named characters and ships bytes: the string module’s docstring reads ‘Returns the number of characters in the string’, and the runtime source states kern_str_length returns ‘the byte-length of a string (excluding NUL)’; the codepoint count ships under a different name (str.char_count, pure Kern, continuation bytes skipped), reverse() has been codepoint-aware since 1.0.0, and char_at and slice index positions whose unit the reference does not state (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ State is local and immutable unless written down: bindings are immutable without mut, structs are immutable without type mut, construction names every field with required fields enforced (E0207) and declared defaults, and every declaration carries its initialiser in the grammar — no value exists off a path that filled it
❌ The default map is a hash table with no order promise: Map<K, V> is FNV-1a with chaining and resize at 75% load, keys() states no order, and the library ships no ordered sibling — code that assembles output, a payload or a report from an iteration agrees with a hash function (C5)
❌ Mutable heap values alias by default: structs are heap-allocated and a type mut struct’s fields mutate through every alias, with the alias set undeclared; list_append appends in place and returns the same list — the reference itself records that ‘several stdlib modules that promise immutability silently mutated their caller’s data’ until the behaviour was written down (C6)
❌ Module-level initialisers run once at program start, in declaration order — within a module: the specification states no order across modules for an initialiser that reads another module’s module-level state, and no rule for a cycle; the create-once constant the race check steers toward (const REQUESTS = atomic_new(0)) stays inside one module, but the cross-module read is the loader’s sequence (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ A tracing mark-and-sweep collector owns the heap: stop-the-world and ThreadSanitizer-checked, with per-request epoch GC on the HTTP path — memory returns when the collector decides, not when the last reference goes (M2)
❌ No ownership model: the collector owns every heap object and no type records who may free or mutate; the mut mark says the value can change, not who may change it (M4)
❌ The fatal classes sit outside the declared surface: panic, .unwrap() on an Err, a failed assert, and overflow-checked arithmetic that ‘aborts the program with a diagnostic’ are faults no catch reaches — the declared failure path is the Result value, and these end the program by design (Er6)
✅ Release and reclamation have named forms: defer schedules a call at scope exit, weak_new holds a reference the collector may clear, cycles are collected, and no malloc/free exists in Kern code
⚠️ The trusted base is C: roughly 42,000 budget-capped lines with a written ledger, ThreadSanitizer on the synchronisation primitives, and a stated programme to shrink it — the memory-safe story stops at the runtime’s own boundary



1.1.4 Error

✅ Failures are values end to end: there are no exceptions; Result<T, E> carries any error type, ? propagates only where the enclosing function declares the same E, match is exhaustive, and a -> never function ends a block for the return analysis
❌ A discarded failure is silence: match is exhaustive where it is used and ? propagates, but no diagnostic stops a Result-valued call from standing as a statement, the Go-shaped content, err = fs.read(path) pair leaves the if err: to the programmer, .unwrap() trades the check for a crash, and str_to_int returns 0 for input it cannot read (Er3)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Mutability is the mark the race check reads: a mut module global written from concurrent code — a spawn target, an HTTP handler or middleware, a service impl method, or anything they call, including the body of a spawned lambda — is the compile error E0309, so the default is not unchecked sharing (K2)
✅ A race class is detected at compile time: E0309 rejects the unsynchronised concurrent write; the scope is the checker’s own — module globals and what concurrent code reaches — and container read-modify-write is a W0005 warning in the default edition, becoming E0309 only under edition 2027 (K3)
❌ A spawned task is joined by hand: spawn returns a handle, await all joins an explicit list, and no construct scopes a task’s lifetime to a block — a scope can end while work it started still runs (K4)
✅ The concurrency kit is first-class: cooperative routines on a libuv loop with per-coroutine preemption, dedicated spawn_thread for CPU-bound and blocking work, channels with a required capacity (0 is a rendezvous), mutex, RWLock, semaphore, atomics, and select — a routine that awaits parks, never an OS thread
⚠️ The 1.1.x line shipped with concurrency defects its own changelog names: a cooperative Mutex<T> that could freeze the scheduler thread when a holder was descheduled (fixed in 1.1.2), the same defect in RwLock<T> documented as unfixed at this release, and multi-worker await windows — ‘avoid KERN_WORKERS > 0 in production until v1.1.3’



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One implementation is the language: a self-hosted compiler with no second front end, one vendor’s release calendar, and no independent implementation to compare against — the working reality is one toolchain (P2)
✅ The artifact is a single static native binary: LLVM to the named target triple, no runtime loaded at run time, and therefore no runtime/program version skew to manage — the upgrade is a rebuild



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The type system is the seccomp profile: the compiler derives a seccomp-BPF deny set from the program’s Cap<T> mint set and emits the kernel seal first in @main, inherited across execve — Linux only, no-op on macOS
Forensic record-replay is opt-in and env-gated: KERN_RECORD/KERN_REPLAY capture and re-feed the nondeterministic values the runtime hands the program under a SHA-256 chain that detects an edited trace — bought with per-record capture overhead and an operator’s decision to run traced, which is why it is a deployment tool and not a default
Closures are single-expression by rule: multi-line request handlers are named functions registered on a route — the parser never guesses a body’s extent inside an expression, and the multi-line logic lands in a named, testable function, paid in a line of ceremony per handler
The manifest accepts unknown keys in silence: a section or key the kern.toml parser does not know is read past with no warning — the lenient read keeps a manifest carrying newer keys building on an older toolchain, and costs a typo’d key that sits in the file looking effective and doing nothing, as the documentation itself warns for [runtime] and authors
Reserved names carry the runtime: the kern_ prefix is refused for user functions (E0405) precisely so the C symbol set can move between minor versions
Shadowing a builtin is module-scoped: a function defined with a builtin’s name wins in its own module and its importers, and reaches the builtin through its capability wrapper — one of the two naming rules the reference says ‘trip newcomers’




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Collector pauses are in the timing budget: stop-the-world marking bounds the pause and does not remove it; per-request epoch GC keeps a request’s collection local, and the schedule is still the runtime’s (R2)
✅ Ahead-of-time native, no JIT tier: LLVM emits the binary the machine runs, so cold starts carry no warm-up; the project’s own 55-workload matrix against Go, Node, Python, Rust and C states its losses (file I/O, hashing) beside its wins, with per-cell ceilings — self-reported, not independent



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The supply is one vendor’s: 309 standard-library modules and ten first-party packages against a third-party pool measured in single repositories — zero stars and two watchers on the forge at assessment — so more is written than found, and hiring follows the same curve (Ec3)
⚠️ The standard library is the platform by design: HTTP, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, JSON, crypto, containers and a microVM monitor ship in-tree, so the concentration the supply and implementation criteria price is a deliberate trade — the dependency tree that would diversify the supply is the thing the design avoids, and that choice is charged under Ec3 and P2, not as a community framework monoculture
❌ The runtime bundle crosses as a binary with the promise set to nothing: published so a build can skip roughly 36,000 lines of C, version-paired by convention, with the stability policy stating the C runtime’s symbol names ‘are NOT part of the stable surface’ and can change between minor versions; the v1.1.1 bundle linked on an mbedTLS-2.28 host and SIGSEGVd at the first TLS use, and 1.1.2’s answer — per-ABI bundles and a build-time soname gate (E0504) — is a check at link, not a promise (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The stable line has already broken code, by its own documented exception: 1.0.3 landed in a patch release with nine host-state functions retyped to take Cap<Container> — ‘BREAKING for direct importers’ — removed std.ai, and moved runtime internals behind E0408, under the stability policy’s rule that closing a fail-open path is a fix even when a program depended on it; elsewhere the frozen corpus is compiled on every change, and edition 2027’s three promotions wait for an opt-in (V1)
⚠️ What changed: two isolation defaults moved within the stable line. 1.0.2 made the allowlist the default process-container seccomp profile, where the previous default allowed everything not on a denylist; 1.0.3 defaulted KERN_VM_DATAPATH to vhost and refuses to start a guest when it cannot be opened rather than falling back. Why: fail-closed isolation defaults. How a deployment reverses it: InstanceSpec.seccomp set to denylist per instance, and KERN_VM_DATAPATH=user; both are documented per release, and the stability policy reserves the right to move tuning-knob defaults (V5)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The target is ordinary backend service work: registered handlers are plain functions, a service block generates the RPC plumbing from a typed interface, and the deployment unit is one static binary — no host framework owns the program’s shape



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The capability discipline is the language: every I/O function threads a Cap<T>, only the entry module mints roots, taint tags decide which sinks accept which values, and failures arrive as values to match or propagate — a compile-time discipline with no mainstream analogue in the daily syntax, however Python-like the surface reads (L1)
⚠️ The official reference is strong, and has drifted: a normative specification with the grammar embedded from a canonical file, a 72 KB diagnostics catalogue with one page per code, and per-module references are far above the pre-1.0 norm — and the async page’s own summary table still shows ch.send(...) method forms its body says do not exist, while the spec’s governance paragraph describes an elected technical committee the governing documents do not name



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ The grammar is embedded in the normative specification, so the syntax’s ground truth is one document.
⚠️ The capability discipline shapes every expression form, so a C-shaped reader re-learns the plumbing.



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The verification path ships with the compiler: kern test is stable CLI, assert/assert_eq/assert_ne are builtins, ## kern-time: declares a test’s run-time budget, fuzz targets run in CI, DWARF is emitted for the standard debuggers, and the LSP answers from the real typechecker



1.2.8 Security

✅ The exploit classes are named and closed in the type: memory-safe managed runtime with no eval; injection sinks demand literals (@sql_literal E0300, @shell_literal, @url_literal, @regex_literal) or an Untrusted<T> discharge; a Secret compared with == is the compile error E0317; and overflow arithmetic aborts rather than wrapping
⚠️ The guarantee is young, and its holes are documented by the project: the rc3 external scan found method arguments never type-checked, so every compile-time security rule was bypassable by ordinary idiomatic code; 1.0.3 closed capability bypasses that reached 203 gated builtins, a world-readable container state root carrying env values, and state-record field injection; and the formal proofs cover models — only the lexer’s model is measured against the shipped code, the taint model has no heap, aliasing or concurrency, and the external audit was removed from the plan

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ Byte-reproducible by gate, not by aspiration: the same source, toolchain version and seed give a byte-identical binary, asserted on every push by rebuilding a clean-room compiler from the minimal seed and comparing two full bootstraps (seed to gen1 to gen2), with diverse double-compilation alongside (Y1)
✅ The resolution is a function of the manifests: Minimal Version Selection pins the whole transitive graph in kern.lock, and kern.sum carries two content hashes per version, trust-on-first-use and then immutable; .kern-version beside the source makes the compiler warn when a different toolchain builds it (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ Packages are signed, checksummed and fail-closed: kern-pkg verify refuses a missing hash line, a mismatch, or an unverifiable signature; publishing packs byte-reproducible tarballs; release tags and artefacts are signed with keys whose public halves are pinned in the repository (Y3)
❌ The registry name space is flat: names like kern-postgres resolve on the forge’s generic package registry with the owner a publish credential rather than a namespace in the module path — substitution is answered by the hash-and-signature verification, not by the name space (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed joins vulnerabilities to package versions: kern audit exists in the CLI and the dependency documentation names no database behind it; the 1.0.3 security release’s own advisory was still ‘to be published at coordinated disclosure’ at this tag (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ The stdlib defines the contract: structured logging, latency metrics, W3C tracing and health checks ship in-tree, with kern_otel as the OpenTelemetry package — no per-project instrumentation convention is required (Y5)
❌ A crash documents no post-mortem: the reference and release notes document no default backtrace with source locations — the FATAL diagnostic line is the crash’s printed record, and the forensic record-replay trace and the async wedge trace are env-gated opt-ins (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ Compile speed is a stated design goal with its own programme: the compiler bootstraps from source in seconds and the project carries a go-parity matrix with per-cell ceilings — the project’s own measurements, not an independent one (Y7)
❌ No debugger ships with the toolchain: the CLI is build, check, fix, lint, test, new, explain, audit-caps, bootstrap, version — DWARF is emitted for the standard debuggers, which the distribution does not include (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ The foreign surface exists in-process: the @nogc intrinsics, std.cap_unsafe raw addresses, and the C runtime the compiler links are reachable without leaving the language — the charge is the boundary being unchecked (T14), not its absence (Y9)
❌ No portable target ships at this release: the normative spec’s target table lists WebAssembly as ‘Future’ and the v1.1.2 README names none — the project website’s wasm32-wasip1 row tracks the newer line, not the assessed release (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ PUA Group decides: breaking, governance and licence changes are the company’s decision after a public review period, releases are cut by a maintainer acting on its behalf — and the spec’s own governance paragraph, ‘no single corporate owner, decisions made by elected technical committee’, describes a body the governing documents do not name (Y11)
✅ The specification is public and normative: a 72 KB document that defines the stable surface, embeds the grammar verbatim from a canonical file a CI gate keeps in sync, and states its stability policy as a contract with named tests beside each claim (Y12)
❌ The oracle is one toolchain: the conformance and negative suites are the implementation’s own, no published suite exists for an independent implementation to run, and the project states the limit itself — the capability and flow models are proved about models, with the 54-probe grid as the evidence the shipped checker implements them, and the external audit removed from the plan (Y17)
✅ The compiler is the published parser: the source is EUPL and the canonical grammar lives in the tree, with a CI gate failing on drift between grammar and specification (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Compiles ahead of time to native code via LLVM, so the interpreter-tax class does not apply; the runtime pays stop-the-world collector pauses and drives a libuv event loop. The project’s own benchmark matrix (55 backend workloads against Go, Node.js, Python, Rust and C, losses stated beside wins) reports its methodology and date; independent measurements do not yet exist.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse corpus: the first stable release (2026-10-03) postdates the training data of public coding models, and the project’s own documentation records model-shaped inventions that do not exist — a parse_int builtin, items.map, ch.send — so models write plausible Kern that the compiler refuses. The per-code diagnostics catalogue and kern explain E0xxx are the compensation.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems. The systems profile (@nogc, a deterministic arena allocator, bounds-checked DMA windows, a locked systems surface) targets hypervisor-class software rather than a certification regime, and the formal proofs cover models — the lexer-to-compiler correspondence is measured, the capability and flow links rest on a probe grid.

Verdict: Kern’s Core coupling (76.0) lands above every managed mainstream neighbour assessed so far, because the inventory’s rarest absences are its design facts: effects in the signature (Cap<T> under an unconditional E0404), nullability in the type, errors as exhaustive values, immutability by default, overflow trapped rather than wrapped, cycles collected, defer at scope exit, and a public normative specification. What it keeps is the managed-runtime invoice — the collector’s schedule and pauses, erased generics, aliased mutable heap state, an unordered map, join-by-hand tasks — plus its own additions: a fatal class (panic, unwrap, overflow) outside the declared Result surface, and a length API that names characters and ships bytes. Its youth is priced where youth lives: a one-vendor supply and governance, a single implementation as the only oracle, a flat registry name space, no portable target at this release, no bundled debugger, no documented crash post-mortem, and no advisory feed. The page records what the project documents about itself, which is unusually much: the changelog names its own security holes and known memory-safety defects, the stability policy states which promises are not made, and the formal-scope page draws the line between proved models and shipped code. Main strengths: capability tracking the type carries, and a verification culture — reproducible, double-compiled, signed, specified — that outpaces the language’s age. Main weaknesses: everything below the Core score is time — supply, independent governance, a second implementation, an advisory base — and those are not bought in a first year.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925201
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

title: Java (Java 7)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 65.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
✅ Generics enable type parameterization (Java 5): List<T> decouples a container from its element type
✅ The diamond operator removes a repeated type argument (Java 7): new ArrayList<>() states the element type once
✅ switch accepts a String (Java 7): A string case is checked by the compiler and compared without a chain of equals
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: The run-time type argument is gone, so a consumer recovers it at a cast site the compiler cannot check (T7)
❌ Null is in every reference: NullPointerException is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A closed set of cases is a class hierarchy or an enum with a discriminator, and a switch over it is not checked for exhaustiveness (T4)
❌ A package is not a boundary: Every public class is reachable on the classpath, and nothing declares what a library exports (T11)
⚠️ Inheritance is available: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is final
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Dependency injection decouples construction from use: Spring supplies an object’s collaborators from outside the class
✅ The diamond operator shortens a generic construction (Java 7): The type argument is not repeated
❌ A field is mutable unless declared final: A setter is the ordinary way to change state (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The JVM collects garbage: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ There is no manual deallocation: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The collector’s schedule is not the program’s (M2)
✅ G1 is available (Java 7): A region-based collector can be selected for a large heap
⚠️ JNI reaches outside the heap: A native call is unchecked



1.1.4 Error

✅ A checked exception states a recoverable failure: throws IOException puts the failure in the signature
❌ An unchecked exception bypasses the signature: A RuntimeException can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
❌ Try-catch does not compose: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over (Er4)
✅ Multi-catch and try-with-resources (Java 7): Two failures are caught by one clause, and an AutoCloseable is released at block exit



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A thread pool is the unit of concurrency: A task is submitted to an executor
✅ Fork/join joins the standard library (Java 7): A recursive task divides work without a hand-written thread
⚠️ A thread is an operating-system thread: The number of threads a service may hold is a platform limit
⚠️ A future blocks on get: CompletableFuture does not exist yet
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: synchronized, volatile, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race (K3)
❌ A task holds a platform thread: Each task reserves one until it ends, so the number of tasks is bounded by the platform; Java 21’s virtual threads remove the cost (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The specifications are public: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Several vendor runtimes run the same class files: OpenJDK, the Oracle JDK, and IBM each shipped a JVM
✅ Bytecode is portable: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, and a switch over a hierarchy is not checked for exhaustiveness
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: Old codebases lag behind the language, and the 1990s APIs stay in service
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null, and nothing in the type marks the check
Type erasure vs. runtime types: A generic type argument is gone at run time
Inheritance vs. composition: A hierarchy is the only way to express a closed set of cases, and the compiler does not check it




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The JIT optimises the hot path: A method is compiled after it proves hot
⚠️ A GC pause is part of the timing: The collector decides when memory returns (R2)
⚠️ Startup pays for interpretation: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles (R3)
✅ The JDK ships VisualVM and Flight Recorder: VisualVM monitors a running JVM, and Flight Recorder (commercial) profiles it



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Maven Central is the registry: A dependency is declared in a POM and resolved from the central repository
⚠️ Spring dominates the server stack: The alternatives are not really alternatives (Ec6)
⚠️ The ecosystem carries old APIs: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one (Ec7)
✅ The IDE and build tools are mature: IntelliJ, Eclipse, NetBeans, and Maven
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A class file from an older release still runs
✅ A feature release was deliberate: Java 7 was a multi-year release, and the six-month cadence had not begun
⚠️ There is no preview mechanism: An experimental feature is a flag or an incubator module



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend and enterprise work: The standard choice for a large service
✅ Android runs it: The platform’s language level is Java 7 for years
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
⚠️ JavaFX 2 ships with the JDK (Java 7): A rich client can use the JDK’s own UI toolkit beside Swing, and the applet plugin still runs in the browser
⚠️ Systems programming is out of reach: A collector and a managed runtime



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Widely taught: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
✅ The documentation is exhaustive: Javadoc and the tutorials
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the standard library, and the enterprise APIs (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The diamond and try-with-resources reduce boilerplate (Java 7): A generic construction and a resource are written once
✅ switch on a String reads as a mapping (Java 7): The case is the value
⚠️ A generic type is spelled out in a signature: The declaration repeats the type



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit is the standard test runner: Mature and ubiquitous
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through and breakpoints in the IDE and on the command line



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: The collector prevents a use after free
✅ Type safe: A static check runs before the program
⚠️ Deserialization is an attack path: A crafted stream constructs an object graph the program did not choose
⚠️ A null check is the caller’s: A reference can be null, and nothing states the guard
❌ Integer arithmetic is two’s-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the toolchain reads: the JDK compiler consumes the command line, and the dependency contract lives in third-party build tooling the platform does not ship (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The JDK ships no package channel: jars move through Maven Central, a third-party repository whose terms are its own.



1.3.3 Observability

✅ JDK Flight Recorder ships a stable recording standard for latency, allocation, and method sampling in the JVM itself. (Y5)
✅ The runtime writes hs_err_pid files, thread dumps, and heap dumps by default, so a crash carries its own post-mortem. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The compiler reports an error in the editor: An IDE compiles a file as it is saved, so a type error is reported without a build



1.3.5 Interop

✅ JNI is the in-process foreign interface, and the Foreign Function and Memory API modernizes it. (Y9)
✅ The JVM is the portable target: the artifact runs wherever a compatible JVM runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Java Community Process runs the language evolution through public JSRs and expert groups. (Y11)
✅ The Java Language Specification is published and complete. (Y12)
✅ The JCK conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation. (Y17)
✅ javac and the JDK libraries are public source in OpenJDK. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: Java 7 is the last release before lambdas, and it spends its language budget on syntax that removes a repeated declaration: the diamond operator, multi-catch, try-with-resources, and a String case. The standard library gains a fork/join pool, so a divide-and-conquer computation is expressible without a hand-written thread. Main strength: resource release is now a language construct. Main weakness: no module boundary, no checked alternative to a hierarchy, and a null in every reference.

title: Java (Java 5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 65.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
✅ Generics enable type parameterization (Java 5): List<T> decouples a container from its element type
✅ Annotations state metadata (Java 5): A declaration carries a marker the compiler and a tool can read
✅ An enum is a closed set of constants (Java 5): The type names every case, though a switch is still not checked for exhaustiveness
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: The run-time type argument is gone, so a consumer recovers it at a cast site the compiler cannot check (T7)
❌ Null is in every reference: NullPointerException is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A closed set of cases is a class hierarchy or an enum with a discriminator, and a switch over it is not checked for exhaustiveness (T4)
❌ A package is not a boundary: Every public class is reachable on the classpath, and nothing declares what a library exports (T11)
⚠️ Inheritance is available: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is final
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Dependency injection decouples construction from use: Spring supplies an object’s collaborators from outside the class
✅ Autoboxing and varargs shorten a call (Java 5): A primitive and an array are written without the wrapper
❌ A field is mutable unless declared final: A setter is the ordinary way to change state (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The JVM collects garbage: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ There is no manual deallocation: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The collector’s schedule is not the program’s (M2)
⚠️ The default collector stops the world: A throughput collector pauses every thread
⚠️ JNI reaches outside the heap: A native call is unchecked



1.1.4 Error

✅ A checked exception states a recoverable failure: throws IOException puts the failure in the signature
❌ An unchecked exception bypasses the signature: A RuntimeException can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
❌ Try-catch does not compose: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over (Er4)
⚠️ finally closes the resource: There is no try-with-resources before Java 7



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ java.util.concurrent arrives (Java 5): An executor, a concurrent map, and a latch are in the standard library
✅ A thread pool is the unit of concurrency: A task is submitted to an executor
⚠️ A thread is an operating-system thread: The number of threads a service may hold is a platform limit
⚠️ A future blocks on get: CompletableFuture does not exist yet, so a stage is hand-written
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: synchronized, volatile, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race (K3)
❌ A task holds a platform thread: Each task reserves one until it ends, so the number of tasks is bounded by the platform; Java 21’s virtual threads remove the cost (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The specifications are public: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Several vendor runtimes run the same class files: Sun, IBM, BEA, and Oracle each shipped a JVM
✅ Bytecode is portable: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, and a switch over a hierarchy is not checked for exhaustiveness
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: Old codebases lag behind the language, and the 1990s APIs stay in service
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null, and nothing in the type marks the check
Type erasure vs. runtime types: A generic type argument is gone at run time
Inheritance vs. composition: A hierarchy is the only way to express a closed set of cases, and the compiler does not check it




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The JIT optimises the hot path: A method is compiled after it proves hot
⚠️ A GC pause is part of the timing: The collector decides when memory returns (R2)
⚠️ Startup pays for interpretation: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles (R3)
✅ The JDK ships monitoring tools: jconsole (Java 5), jstat, and hprof



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Maven 1 and Ant manage the classpath: A dependency is declared and resolved from a repository
⚠️ EJB and Spring split the server stack: A session bean or a Spring bean, and neither is a settled default (Ec6)
⚠️ The ecosystem carries old APIs: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one (Ec7)
✅ The IDE is mature: IntelliJ, Eclipse, and NetBeans compile and debug
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A class file from an older release still runs
✅ A feature release was deliberate: Java 5 was a major language change, and it arrived two and a half years after the previous release
⚠️ There is no preview mechanism: An experimental feature is a flag or an incubator module



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend and enterprise work: The standard choice for a large service
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
⚠️ A rich client is Swing, and the web path is an applet: A browser plugin runs it, and the plugin is a support burden
⚠️ Systems programming is out of reach: A collector and a managed runtime



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Widely taught: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
✅ The documentation is exhaustive: Javadoc and the tutorials
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the standard library, and the enterprise APIs (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Generics remove the cast (Java 5): A collection states its element type
✅ Enhanced for and varargs shorten a loop (Java 5): The iteration and the call are written without an index
⚠️ A generic type is spelled out: The declaration repeats the type argument



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit is the standard test runner: Mature and ubiquitous
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through and breakpoints in the IDE and on the command line



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: The collector prevents a use after free
✅ Type safe: A static check runs before the program
⚠️ Deserialization is an attack path: A crafted stream constructs an object graph the program did not choose
⚠️ A null check is the caller’s: A reference can be null, and nothing states the guard
❌ Integer arithmetic is two’s-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build (Q4)

⚠️ The JDK ships no package channel: jars move through Maven Central, a third-party repository whose terms are its own.

1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The compiler reports an error in the editor: An IDE compiles a file as it is saved, so a type error is reported without a build



1.3.5 Interop

✅ JNI is the in-process foreign interface, and the Foreign Function and Memory API modernizes it. (Y9)
✅ The JVM is the portable target: the artifact runs wherever a compatible JVM runs. (Y10)

✅ The Java Community Process runs the language evolution through public JSRs and expert groups. (Y11)
✅ The Java Language Specification is published and complete. (Y12)
✅ The JCK conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation. (Y17)
✅ javac and the JDK libraries are public source in OpenJDK. (Y19)

Verdict: Java 5 is the release that gives the type system a parameter: generics remove the cast from a collection, annotations carry metadata the compiler can read, and an enum names a closed set of constants. The library gains the concurrency toolkit that the later line keeps. Main strength: generics and the concurrent library remove the cast-per-read and hand-written-latch costs. Main weakness: the type argument is erased at run time, a closed set of cases is still not checked for exhaustiveness, and null is in every reference.

Note: The score reflects Java 5’s language: generics, annotations, and enums are present; the module boundary and the sum type are not.

Analysis against Java 26 (March 2026). Java 26 finalises no language feature: the release changes the runtime, the standard library, and the preview set, so every scored mechanism holds the value it held for Java 25 and the score is identical. What the release changes is recorded where it bears on a dimension.
This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].
Snapshot Java 26 — released 17 March 2026 · lifecycle superseded (current at the October 2026 analysis date; superseded by Java 27 on 15 September 2026)
Family Java — shelf: Application
The language’s main business is building general application software, with a managed runtime or a rich standard library. A shelf groups; it does not classify — the tags below carry every use, paradigm, and platform of this snapshot.

title: Java (Java 26)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 72.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: Can program to interfaces
✅ Generics enable type parameterization: List<T> decouples from concrete types
✅ Sealed classes (Java 17): Controlled inheritance hierarchies — the class author decides which subclasses exist, decoupling from unknown extensions
✅ Records (Java 16): Immutable data carriers with auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString — construction decoupled from mutation
✅ Pattern matching (Java 21): switch expressions + sealed types enable exhaustive, compositional dispatch
❌ No higher-kinded types: Can’t abstract over generic types
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: Runtime loses type information (T7)
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Unchecked class extension possible (unless final or sealed)
❌ Null still exists: NullPointerException possible (no non-nullable types in the language) (T10)
⚠️ Module system (Java 9+) limits reflection: Strong encapsulation of non-exported packages became the default in Java 16, so reflective access to them now needs an explicit --add-opens — reflection is no longer a free-for-all
❌ Package-private couples to package structure: Visibility tied to organization
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Records are immutable by default: record Point(int x, int y) — no mutation coupling, auto-generated components
✅ Immutable collections (Java 9+): List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of() produce unmodifiable collections
✅ Copy-with-change without mutation: Records have no withers or copy constructors, so a copy-with-change is a hand-written call that supplies the new value and copies the rest
✅ Dependency injection frameworks: Spring/Guice decouple construction from usage
⚠️ Records eliminate builders for simple cases: Complex multi-step construction may still need builders
⚠️ Constructors couple creation to initialization: Not eliminated, but records and patterns reduce the problem
❌ Static methods couple to global state: Singleton pattern creates hidden dependencies
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Modern GCs (ZGC, Generational ZGC, Shenandoah) provide sub-millisecond pause times
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have dangling pointers
✅ Foreign Function & Memory API (Java 22): Safe memory access without JNI, decoupling native interop from unsafety
✅ AOT object caching with any GC (Java 26): Ahead-of-time object caching reduces startup time and memory pressure regardless of GC choice
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Minimized by modern GCs but not deterministic (M2)
❌ Memory leaks from static references: Static collections couple to application lifetime (still possible)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Checked exceptions separate error paths: throws IOException makes errors explicit
✅ Pattern matching for switch + sealed types (Java 21): Exhaustive error handling — compiler verifies all error cases covered
✅ Primitive types in patterns (preview, Java 26): Extends pattern matching to primitive types, enabling exhaustive switching over numeric domains
❌ Try-catch doesn’t compose: Can’t map/flatMap over exceptions without wrapping (Er4)
⚠️ RuntimeException bypasses checks: Unchecked exceptions defer error-coupling detection to runtime (sealed hierarchies with pattern matching help) (Er2)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Virtual threads (stable, Java 21+): Lightweight threads — each task gets its own thread, eliminating callback coupling
✅ Structured concurrency (preview, Java 21+): StructuredTaskScope — subtask lifetimes scoped to lexical block, preventing thread leaks
✅ A task scope is a block: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, and close() waits until every task submitted to it has completed, so a try-with-resources block joins the work it launched; the richer StructuredTaskScope is still a preview (K4)
✅ Scoped values (final, Java 25+): Thread-local data with guaranteed cleanup, decoupling context from global state
✅ CompletableFuture: Composable async primitives when needed
⚠️ Shared mutable state still possible: synchronized, volatile, and manual lock patterns remain available (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Open specifications: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are public standards that any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Multiple vendor runtimes: OpenJDK, Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, and GraalVM run the same class files
✅ Open-source core: OpenJDK is developed in the open under the GPL with the Classpath Exception
✅ Portable bytecode: Compiled classes run unchanged on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, though a sealed hierarchy is checkable
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: Old codebases lag behind records, sealed types, and virtual threads, and the applet API leaves the platform while the older APIs beside it stay
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null
Type erasure vs. runtime types: A generic type argument is gone at run time
Preview features vs. availability: The StructuredTaskScope API is still a preview, so production code waits, or joins through a block-scoped ExecutorService whose close() is final but blunt — it waits for every task and reports no subtask’s failure
A warning is not a guarantee: Deep reflection that mutates a final field is reported and not blocked, so an ecosystem that depends on it has no deadline to move




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JVM optimization: Excellent JIT, fast steady-state
✅ Virtual threads: Low-overhead concurrency scales to millions of threads
⚠️ GC pauses: Tunable; ZGC offers sub-millisecond pauses (R2)
⚠️ Startup time: JIT warmup (mitigated by AOT object caching (Java 26), GraalVM native image, CDS archives, and CRaC) (R3)
✅ G1 throughput improvements (Java 26): Reduced synchronization overhead in G1 GC improves throughput
✅ HTTP/3 client (Java 26): Native HTTP/3 support decouples networking from legacy protocol constraints
✅ Mature profilers: Excellent performance tooling



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: Maven Central has everything
⚠️ Enterprise monoculture: Spring dominates the server stack, so the alternatives are not really alternatives (Ec6)
⚠️ Legacy burden: The enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2026 one, so a library supports both (Ec7)
✅ Standardized build: Maven/Gradle industry standard
✅ Excellent IDEs: IntelliJ, Eclipse, NetBeans
✅ Mature tooling: Debuggers, profilers, monitoring
✅ Cross-platform: Write once, run anywhere (mostly true)
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Strong backward compatibility: Rarely breaks
✅ Regular releases: 6-month cadence, LTS every 2 years
✅ Preview features: Opt-in features decouple experimentation from production stability
⚠️ Legacy burden: Old APIs accumulate (though deprecated-for-removal process is active; applet API removed in Java 26)
✅ final mutation now warns (Java 26): Deep reflection that mutates a final field reports a warning, ahead of a future release that blocks it



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend/enterprise: Industry standard
✅ Good for Android: Primary language (with Kotlin)
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks
⚠️ Poor for frontend: Applet API removed (Java 26); JavaFX remains niche
⚠️ Not for systems programming: GC, overhead



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle: Widely taught, lots of resources
⚠️ Modern Java is growing in surface: Records, sealed types, pattern matching, virtual threads, modules — more to learn than Java 8 (L2)
✅ Excellent docs: Javadoc, tutorials, books
⚠️ Legacy/Modern split: Learning the “right” modern way requires guidance



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Records eliminate getter/setter boilerplate: record Person(String name, int age) replaces 50-line POJO
✅ Pattern matching reduces verbosity: switch expressions + sealed types
⚠️ Still verbose compared to Kotlin/Scala: Type erasure, generics syntax
⚠️ Checked exception syntax: Verbose, couples signatures



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit industry standard: Mature testing
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through, breakpoints, virtual thread debugging
✅ Mocking frameworks: Mockito, EasyMock
✅ Profiling tools: VisualVM, YourKit, JFR



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safe: Static typing
✅ Module system: Restricts reflective access to non-exported packages by default (Java 16+)
⚠️ Null: NullPointerException still possible
⚠️ Serialization vulnerabilities: Deserialization attacks (mitigated by records + modern serialization frameworks)
❌ Integer arithmetic is two’s-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build (Q4)

Verdict: Java 26 is a runtime release, and no scored mechanism moves: the language the compiler accepts is Java 25’s, so records, sealed types, exhaustive matching, virtual threads, and modules hold their values, and null in every reference, erased generics, failures that do not compose, and an unproven locking discipline hold theirs. What the release changes is what the platform does — ahead-of-time object caching moves startup work into an archive, the HTTP client speaks HTTP/3, G1 sheds synchronization overhead, the applet API is removed, and deep reflection that mutates a final field now reports a warning rather than passing silently. The preview set moves too: primitive types in patterns are re-previewed, so an exhaustive switch over a numeric domain still needs --enable-preview. Main strength: the modern toolkit of a long-lived line on a runtime that starts faster. Main weakness: null, erasure, and a failure that does not compose, beside a warning where the language still cannot refuse the mutation it reports.

Note: No scored mechanism differs from Java 25. Java 26 adds no language construct that the inventory prices; it changes startup, throughput, and the preview set, which the observations record and the score does not.
