title: Java (Java 21)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 72.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
✅ Generics enable type parameterization: List<T> decouples a container from its element type
✅ Records state their components (Java 16): record Point(int x, int y) declares the data and the accessors together
✅ Sealed types close a hierarchy (Java 17): A sealed interface names its implementations
✅ Pattern matching for switch is final (Java 21): A switch over a sealed type is checked for exhaustiveness
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: The run-time type argument is gone, so a consumer recovers it at a cast site the compiler cannot check (T7)
❌ Null is in every reference: NullPointerException is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise (T10)
⚠️ Inheritance is available: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is final
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Dependency injection decouples construction from use: A framework supplies an object’s collaborators from outside the class
✅ A record is immutable by default (Java 16): A component is final
✅ List.of and Map.of build an immutable collection (Java 9): A literal collection is unmodifiable
❌ A field is mutable unless declared final: A setter is the ordinary way to change state (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The JVM collects garbage: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ There is no manual deallocation: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The collector’s schedule is not the program’s (M2)
✅ G1 is the default collector (Java 9): A region-based collector is the default on a server-class machine
⚠️ The Foreign Function and Memory API is a preview (Java 21): A native call is still written through JNI, an incubator, or --enable-preview



1.1.4 Error

✅ A checked exception states a recoverable failure: throws IOException puts the failure in the signature
❌ An unchecked exception bypasses the signature: A RuntimeException can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
❌ Try-catch does not compose: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over (Er4)
✅ An exhaustive switch over a sealed type (Java 21): The compiler verifies that every case is handled



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A thread pool is the unit of concurrency: A task is submitted to an executor
✅ Virtual threads are final (Java 21): A blocking task gets a thread that costs a fraction of an operating-system thread, so the thread-per-request shape scales
⚠️ Structured concurrency is a preview (Java 21): A scope that bounds a subtask’s lifetime is behind --enable-preview
✅ A task scope is a block: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, and close() waits until every task submitted to it has completed, so a try-with-resources block joins the work it launched; the richer StructuredTaskScope is still a preview (K4)
✅ CompletableFuture composes asynchronous work: A stage chains a continuation
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: synchronized, volatile, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The specifications are public: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Several vendor runtimes run the same class files: OpenJDK builds, Oracle JDK, Temurin, Corretto, and Zulu
✅ Bytecode is portable: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, though a sealed hierarchy is checkable
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: Old codebases lag behind records, sealed types, and virtual threads
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null
Type erasure vs. runtime types: A generic type argument is gone at run time
Virtual threads vs. pinning: A task that holds a monitor or a native frame can pin its carrier, so the old concurrency discipline is still needed in places




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The JIT optimises the hot path: A method is compiled after it proves hot
⚠️ A GC pause is part of the timing: The collector decides when memory returns (R2)
⚠️ Startup pays for interpretation: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles (R3)
✅ Mature profilers and monitoring: VisualVM, JFR, and the platform tooling



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Maven Central is the registry: A dependency is declared in a POM or a Gradle build and resolved from the central repository
⚠️ Spring dominates the server stack: The alternatives are not really alternatives (Ec6)
⚠️ The ecosystem carries old APIs: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one (Ec7)
✅ The IDE and build tools are mature: IntelliJ, Eclipse, Maven, and Gradle
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A class file from an older release still runs
✅ A preview feature is opt-in (Java 12+): An experimental construct needs --enable-preview



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend and enterprise work: The standard choice for a large service
✅ Android runs it: A primary language on the platform, with Kotlin
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
⚠️ Front end is out of scope: The applet is gone from the browser, and JavaFX is niche
⚠️ Systems programming is out of reach: A collector and a managed runtime



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Widely taught: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
✅ The documentation is exhaustive: Javadoc and the tutorials
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the standard library, and the enterprise APIs (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ A switch expression returns a value (Java 14): The arrow form states a mapping and removes the fall-through
✅ Records remove the accessor boilerplate (Java 16): A component is declared once
✅ A record pattern destructures a value (Java 21): case Point(int x, int y) reads the components without accessors
⚠️ A generic type and a checked exception are spelled out: The signature stays long



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit is the standard test runner: Mature and ubiquitous
✅ Mocking frameworks are mature: Mockito and EasyMock
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through and breakpoints in the IDE and on the command line



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: The collector prevents a use after free
✅ Type safe: A static check runs before the program
✅ The module system restricts reflection (Java 9): A non-exported package is not open by default
⚠️ Deserialization is an attack path: A crafted stream constructs an object graph the program did not choose
⚠️ A null check is the caller’s: A reference can be null, and nothing states the guard
❌ Integer arithmetic is two’s-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build (Q4)

Verdict: Java 21 adds the concurrency change the platform had promised for a decade: a virtual thread is cheap enough that a blocking style scales, so the callback shape is no longer forced. Pattern matching for switch completes the sealed-type story, and the compiler checks that every case is handled. Main strength: virtual threads and exhaustive matching remove the concurrency-shape and missing-sum-type costs. Main weakness: the locking discipline is still manual, null is still everywhere, and the ecosystem is still Spring-shaped.

Note: The score reflects Java 21’s language: virtual threads and exhaustive switch are final; scoped values are a preview.

title: Java (Java 11)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 68.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
✅ Generics enable type parameterization: List<T> decouples a container from its element type
✅ The module system declares a boundary (Java 9): module-info.java states what a module exports and requires, and the compiler enforces it
✅ var removes a redundant local type (Java 10): The compiler infers the declared type once
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: The run-time type argument is gone, so a consumer recovers it at a cast site the compiler cannot check (T7)
❌ Null is in every reference: NullPointerException is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A closed set of cases is a class hierarchy or an enum with a discriminator, and a switch over it is not checked for exhaustiveness (T4)
⚠️ Inheritance is available: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is final
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Dependency injection decouples construction from use: A framework supplies an object’s collaborators from outside the class
✅ List.of and Map.of build an immutable collection (Java 9): A literal collection is unmodifiable
❌ A field is mutable unless declared final: A setter is the ordinary way to change state (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The JVM collects garbage: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ There is no manual deallocation: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The collector’s schedule is not the program’s (M2)
✅ G1 is the default collector (Java 9): A region-based collector is the default on a server-class machine
⚠️ The native boundary is Unsafe and JNI: A foreign call is unchecked



1.1.4 Error

✅ A checked exception states a recoverable failure: throws IOException puts the failure in the signature
❌ An unchecked exception bypasses the signature: A RuntimeException can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
❌ Try-catch does not compose: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over (Er4)
✅ try-with-resources closes a resource: An AutoCloseable is released at block exit



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A thread pool is the unit of concurrency: A task is submitted to an executor
✅ CompletableFuture composes asynchronous work: A stage chains a continuation
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: synchronized, volatile, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race (K3)
⚠️ A thread is an operating-system thread: The number of threads a service may hold is a platform limit
❌ A task holds a platform thread: Each task reserves one until it ends, so the number of tasks is bounded by the platform; Java 21’s virtual threads remove the cost (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The specifications are public: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Several vendor runtimes run the same class files: OpenJDK builds, Oracle JDK, Temurin, Corretto, and Zulu
✅ Bytecode is portable: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, and no sealed type checks that every case is handled
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: The classpath keeps the old idioms valid, and the module path is adopted unevenly
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null
Type erasure vs. runtime types: A generic type argument is gone at run time
Modules vs. the ecosystem: A library that stays on the classpath erases the boundary the module system declares




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The JIT optimises the hot path: A method is compiled after it proves hot
⚠️ A GC pause is part of the timing: The collector decides when memory returns (R2)
⚠️ Startup pays for interpretation: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles (R3)
✅ Mature profilers and monitoring: VisualVM, JFR, and the platform tooling



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Maven Central is the registry: A dependency is declared in a POM or a Gradle build and resolved from the central repository
⚠️ Spring dominates the server stack: The alternatives are not really alternatives (Ec6)
⚠️ The ecosystem carries old APIs: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one (Ec7)
✅ The IDE and build tools are mature: IntelliJ, Eclipse, Maven, and Gradle
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A class file from an older release still runs
✅ The six-month cadence began with Java 9: A feature release arrives every six months, and an LTS every three years (later two)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend and enterprise work: The standard choice for a large service
✅ Android runs it: A primary language on the platform, with Kotlin
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
⚠️ Front end is out of scope: The applet is gone from the browser, and JavaFX is niche
⚠️ Systems programming is out of reach: A collector and a managed runtime



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Widely taught: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
✅ The documentation is exhaustive: Javadoc and the tutorials
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the standard library, and the enterprise APIs (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ var shortens a local declaration (Java 10): The type is written once
⚠️ A generic type and a checked exception are spelled out: The signature stays long
⚠️ Checked exception syntax is verbose: A signature carries the failure set



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit is the standard test runner: Mature and ubiquitous
✅ Mocking frameworks are mature: Mockito and EasyMock
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through and breakpoints in the IDE and on the command line



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: The collector prevents a use after free
✅ Type safe: A static check runs before the program
✅ The module system restricts reflection (Java 9): A non-exported package is not open by default
⚠️ Deserialization is an attack path: A crafted stream constructs an object graph the program did not choose
⚠️ A null check is the caller’s: A reference can be null, and nothing states the guard
❌ Integer arithmetic is two’s-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the toolchain reads: the JDK compiler consumes the command line, and the dependency contract lives in third-party build tooling the platform does not ship (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The JDK ships no package channel: jars move through Maven Central, a third-party repository whose terms are its own.



1.3.3 Observability

✅ JDK Flight Recorder ships a stable recording standard for latency, allocation, and method sampling in the JVM itself. (Y5)
✅ The runtime writes hs_err_pid files, thread dumps, and heap dumps by default, so a crash carries its own post-mortem. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The compiler reports an error in the editor: An IDE compiles a file as it is saved, so a type error is reported without a build



1.3.5 Interop

✅ JNI is the in-process foreign interface, and the Foreign Function and Memory API modernizes it. (Y9)
✅ The JVM is the portable target: the artifact runs wherever a compatible JVM runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Java Community Process runs the language evolution through public JSRs and expert groups. (Y11)
✅ The Java Language Specification is published and complete. (Y12)
✅ The JCK conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation. (Y17)
✅ javac and the JDK libraries are public source in OpenJDK. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: Java 11 is the first LTS on the six-month train, and it carries the two changes that outlast a feature release: the module system makes a boundary a language artifact, and var removes a redundant type from a local declaration. It has no records, no sealed types, and no pattern matching, so a closed set of cases is still a hierarchy the compiler does not check. Main strength: a real module boundary and a predictable cadence. Main weakness: the type system cannot express a sum, and an ecosystem that stays on the classpath limits what the boundary can enforce.

title: Haskell (GHC 9.12)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Haskell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 92.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73.8/100 · Engineering readiness 59.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Pure functions separate side effects from pure logic: The type system (IO monad) keeps effects isolated, preventing hidden coupling to global state
✅ Type classes enable polymorphism without inheritance coupling: Abstraction through type classes (Functor, Monad, etc.) decouples interface from implementation
✅ Parametric polymorphism prevents coupling to concrete types: map :: (a -> b) -> [a] -> [b] works for any types without knowing their internals
⚠️ Monad transformers can create coupling: Stacking monads (ReaderT, StateT, ExceptT) creates order-dependent coupling
❌ IO monad couples all effects: Can’t separate file IO from network IO from randomness at type level (without effect systems)
❌ Global type class instances couple: Orphan instances create action-at-a-distance coupling



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Data constructors separate shape from creation logic: ADTs (Algebraic Data Types) decouple data structure from construction
✅ Smart constructors enable validation without coupling: Can wrap raw constructors to add invariants
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction doesn’t couple to global state



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory from logic: Don’t think about deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: No cyclic references from mutable structures
⚠️ GC pauses couple to runtime: Non-deterministic pauses affect real-time requirements
⚠️ Space leaks from lazy evaluation: Thunks accumulate, so evaluation strategy and computation order couple to memory usage
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free or double-free bugs
✅ The class is declared: stack overflow raises StackOverflow (the threaded runtime’s documented catchable exception) inside the handler surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Either/Maybe separate success from failure: Either Error Result makes error path explicit and separate from success path
✅ Exceptions are typed: IO exceptions are contained in IO monad, preventing hidden coupling
⚠️ Partial functions (head, tail) can couple: Runtime errors bypass type system unless avoided



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ STM (Software Transactional Memory) decouples concurrency from logic: Composable transactions separate concurrent coordination from business logic
✅ Immutability prevents temporal coupling: No shared mutable state means concurrent operations don’t interfere
✅ Async/threading is explicit in types: Concurrency concerns are separate via type signatures



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owns the language: The Haskell 2010 report is a community standard, and GHC — the de facto reference compiler — is open source under a permissive BSD-style licence
✅ Native-code targets: GHC emits native executables for Linux, macOS, and Windows, so no virtual machine must be installed on the target host
✅ Free, redistributable toolchain: GHC, Cabal, and Stack are open source and freely redistributable, with no vendor licence gate
✅ Open package distribution: Hackage and Stackage index open-source packages under open licences, so dependencies are not gated by a vendor registry



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Performance vs. Abstraction: Lazy evaluation optimizes for composability but couples performance to evaluation strategy
Purity vs. Practicality: IO monad is all-or-nothing—can’t separate different IO types without mtl/effect systems
Type Class Coherence vs. Modularity: Only one instance per type globally couples modules that define instances
Laziness vs. Predictability: Space/time behavior depends on evaluation order, creating hidden coupling
Monad Transformer Order: ReaderT (StateT (ExceptT ...)) ≠ StateT (ReaderT (ExceptT ...)), order matters




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Lazy evaluation couples performance to evaluation strategy: Space/time behavior is non-obvious, creating coupling between logic and performance
⚠️ GC pauses unpredictable: Non-deterministic pauses couple timing-sensitive code to runtime behavior
✅ Immutability enables parallelism: No data races, can parallelize without coupling to synchronization
❌ Thunk accumulation: Space leaks couple memory usage to evaluation order



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Cabal/Stack standardized: Build system is consistent
⚠️ Package ecosystem smaller than mainstream: Library availability couples to niche community
✅ GHC is excellent: Compiler quality decouples from platform-specific quirks
❌ Dependency hell with base library versions: Breaking changes couple code to GHC version



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ GHC extensions allow gradual adoption: Can opt into new features without breaking existing code
⚠️ Extensions create fragmentation: Different codebases use different language subsets
✅ Haskell 2010 standard stable: Core language doesn’t break compatibility
❌ Extension proliferation: Code couples to specific GHC versions and extension combinations
❌ Build variants multiply: -XCPP runs the C preprocessor over Haskell source, so #ifdef trees select which declarations GHC compiles (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for parsers, compilers, DSLs: Type system supports these domains naturally
⚠️ Struggles with I/O-heavy, stateful systems: IO monad creates friction for imperative domains
❌ Poor for systems programming: GC, unpredictable performance couples to domain requirements
✅ Strong for financial, formal verification: Correctness guarantees match domain needs



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Monads, functors, type classes couple productivity to deep expertise
❌ Lazy evaluation surprises: Space leaks require expertise to debug
✅ Excellent documentation: Books, tutorials decouple learning from trial-and-error
⚠️ Multiple ways to do things: Mtl vs. transformers vs. effect systems couple to architectural choices



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Concise, expressive: Minimal boilerplate
⚠️ Type signatures can be verbose: :: Monad m => (a -> m b) -> ... couples readability to type system knowledge
✅ Function composition natural: f . g . h decouples steps
❌ Operator overload: Custom operators (<$>, <*>, >>=) couple readability to library knowledge



1.2.7 Testing

✅ QuickCheck property testing: Built-in support for generative testing
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No setup/teardown coupling
❌ Debugging lazy code hard: Stack traces don’t show evaluation order
⚠️ GHCi debugger limited: Couples debugging to printf-style techniques



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents use-after-free, buffer overflows
✅ Type safety prevents many bugs: Can’t mix incompatible types
✅ Immutability prevents mutation bugs: No race conditions on shared state
⚠️ Timing attacks possible: Lazy evaluation can leak information through timing
❌ Int is machine-bounded and wraps; Integer is the opt-in exact type, a mitigation at every site (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Cabal and stack resolve package versions from Hackage at build time. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve per build unless a freeze file pins them. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Hackage packages carry no signed provenance by default. (Y3)
❌ The Hackage name space is flat. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ putStrLn and Debug.Trace carry no structure. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ GHC compile times are the documented cost of the toolchain. (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ foreign import is the in-process C interface. (Y9)
✅ GHC maintains ports for the common platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The report enumerates, and a published suite runs: the Haskell report defines the language, and the Haskell Test Suite runs against independent implementations (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

title: Groovy (5.x)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Groovy in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 64.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 86.3/100 · Engineering readiness 79.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Dynamic typing is the default: A def declaration defers method resolution to the runtime metaclass protocol, so a mismatch is reported when the line runs rather than when the file compiles (T1, T3)
✅ @CompileStatic and @TypeChecked restore compile-time checking: Groovy 2 and later can compile a class to direct bytecode, and the annotated class is checked in the manner of Java
⚠️ Generics are erased on the JVM: List<String> is a List at runtime, so a cast or a reflection call can reach a type the declaration does not admit (T7)
✅ Traits compose behaviour without inheritance: A trait may carry default methods and state, so behaviour is mixed in rather than inherited from a superclass
✅ Safe navigation separates the test from the call: a?.b short-circuits to null at the point of use, so the absence test stands where the value is read
⚠️ Operator overloading is by method name: a + b may call plus and a[i] may call getAt, so a dense expression can invoke user code the syntax does not show (T8)
❌ Inherits the JVM answer: string length counts UTF-16 units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ Mutability is the default: A field is mutable unless it is final or the class is annotated @Immutable (C2)
✅ GroovyBeans generate the accessors: A property declaration is compiled with its getter and setter, so the boilerplate leaves the source
✅ Map constructors separate the arguments from their order: new Point(x: 1, y: 2) names each value at the call site, so the call does not depend on positional order
✅ @Immutable makes a value type in one annotation: It generates the tuple constructor, equals, hashCode, and a defensive copy of the fields
⚠️ AST transformations decide the shape at compile time: @Canonical, @TupleConstructor, and @Builder generate constructors whose signatures are not written in the source
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Groovy compiles to JVM classes: class initialization is first-touch with the documented cycle, inheriting Java’s rule (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The JVM owns deallocation: There is no free operation, and a collection is scheduled outside the program’s control (M2)
⚠️ No RAII: @Cleanup and withCloseable release a resource at the end of a declared block, but nothing runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A reference may alias or be shared freely, and the collector decides when the object dies (M4)
✅ withCloseable binds release to a closure: stream.withCloseable { ... } closes the resource when the block returns, including on an exception
✅ @Cleanup names the release point: A local annotated @Cleanup is closed at the end of its enclosing block
✅ Collection is invisible in the source: An allocation is a new, and no deallocation call is ever written



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: Groovy requires no throws clause and the compiler does not check that a handler exists, so an exception may propagate from any call (Er2)
✅ try/catch/finally is the structured path: A catch clause names the type it handles, and finally runs on every exit
✅ @TypeChecked turns a type error into a compile error: A call to a method that does not exist fails the build rather than the run
⚠️ Dynamic dispatch failure is a runtime exception: A missing method or property raises MissingMethodException or MissingPropertyException at the call
⚠️ ?. and ?: suppress a failure by design: Safe navigation returns null where an exception would otherwise report the fault



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The JDK concurrency library is available: Thread, synchronized, java.util.concurrent executors, and atomics are reached directly
✅ @Synchronized puts the monitor on the declaration: The annotation transformation wraps a method in the object’s monitor, so the lock is stated beside the method
✅ GPars adds dataflow, actors, and parallel collections: The abstractions are a library over the JDK, so a concurrent design is not limited to threads and locks
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: A field is reachable by every thread, and the compiler checks no access pattern (K2)
❌ No structured concurrency in the language: A task tree, a scope, and a join are the JDK executor’s responsibility, and Groovy adds no scope construct of its own (K4)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Runs on the JVM and interoperates with Java: Any Java class is callable, and most valid Java is valid Groovy
✅ Compiles to standard JVM bytecode: The output is a class file, so any JVM accepts it and the JDK’s tools apply
❌ The JVM is the only target: There is no non-JVM implementation of Groovy, so a program couples to one runtime (P2)
✅ Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline give it a first-class host: The build and CI systems execute Groovy directly, which is why the language is present in most Java builds
⚠️ @Grab resolves a dependency from the script: The annotation fetches an artifact from a repository at compile time, so a script couples to a repository and a version



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic or static compilation is a per-file choice: @CompileStatic buys speed and checks at the cost of the metaprogramming forms it cannot compile
DSL-friendly syntax trades precision for brevity: Optional parentheses and dots make a DSL read well and a fragment ambiguous
def is a productivity trade: Less typing now, a later failure at run time
ExpandoMetaClass is a deliberate escape hatch: It is a scope and architecture decision, and its hidden reach is the price of the flexibility
Java source compatibility is a target: Most valid Java remains valid Groovy, which constrains the syntax as much as it helps
There is no fixed release cadence: The release schedule is the project’s own decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ @CompileStatic approaches Java: The annotation emits direct bytecode calls, so the dynamic dispatch cost is removed for the annotated class
✅ The JVM JIT optimises a hot path: The HotSpot compiler applies its full pipeline to the generated bytecode
⚠️ Collection pauses are inherited from the JVM heap: A stop-the-world or concurrent cycle is scheduled by the collector the program chooses, not by the program (R2)
⚠️ Dynamic dispatch costs in dynamic mode: A call site without @CompileStatic goes through the metaclass protocol, so the per-call overhead is higher than Java’s
⚠️ JIT warm-up precedes peak speed: A short script or a test run finishes before the compiler has optimised the hot path (R3)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Apache top-level project: The language is governed by the ASF, so it is not owned by one vendor
✅ The whole Java library ecosystem is available: Any Maven artifact is usable from Groovy, resolved by the ordinary Java build tools
✅ Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline are built on it: The two most common build and CI systems make Groovy a mainstream presence
✅ Grails and Spock are established projects: The web framework and the testing framework are mature and maintained
⚠️ Groovy-specific libraries are few: Most dependencies are Java libraries, so a Groovy-only package is less likely to exist
✅ The class file carries a published promise: Groovy reaches consumers as JVM bytecode [5] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Apache governance with published release notes: A change is recorded in the release notes and the language documentation
✅ Java source compatibility is maintained: Most valid Java keeps compiling as Groovy
✅ Groovy 5.x improves performance and JDK support: The 5.x line raises the runtime baseline to the modern JDK
✅ @CompileStatic can be adopted file by file: A project migrates incrementally rather than all at once
⚠️ There is no fixed release cadence: The timing of a release is the project’s decision, so a needed fix has no promised date



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Build automation is a primary domain: Gradle’s build scripts are Groovy, and the DSL reads as a configuration
✅ CI pipelines are a primary domain: Jenkins Pipeline scripts are Groovy, in the Jenkinsfile form
✅ Web development is supported by Grails: The framework carries the persistence, routing, and view layers
✅ Testing is supported by Spock: The specification framework defines a given/when/then DSL in Groovy
❌ The host framework can own the architecture: A Gradle build script and a Jenkins pipeline run inside the host’s execution model and its conventions, so the code couples to that model (D3)
⚠️ Application code usually prefers Java or Kotlin: Groovy’s share of general JVM application work is smaller than its share of scripting and build work



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a Java developer: Most valid Java is valid Groovy, so an existing file compiles
✅ Typing is optional: A script can start with def and add @CompileStatic later
✅ The closure and builder idioms read like the domain: each, collect, and the builder pattern remove loop and assembly boilerplate
⚠️ The dynamic model is a large corner: The metaclass protocol, method-missing dispatch, ExpandoMetaClass, and the differences of @CompileStatic from Java must each be learned
⚠️ Two compilation modes are two languages: Code that compiles under @CompileStatic is a subset of dynamic Groovy, so a developer must know which rules apply where



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Concise and Java-compatible: A statement needs no semicolon, no type, and often no parentheses
✅ Properties replace explicit accessors: x reads getX() and x = v calls setX(), so the accessor is not written
✅ GString interpolation is built in: "Hello $name" embeds an expression in a string literal
✅ Optional return and statement-value rules shorten a method: The last expression is the result
⚠️ Operator syntax invokes methods: a + b, a[i], and a << b may call plus, getAt, or leftShift, so the notation hides the call
⚠️ Parenthesis omission can be ambiguous: foo bar baz depends on the method-call rules, which the reader must resolve



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Spock is a first-class framework: given/when/then blocks, data tables, and mocks are a Groovy DSL over JUnit
✅ JUnit works directly: A plain JUnit test class is a Groovy class
✅ assert prints the intermediate values: A power assertion reports each subexpression of a failed assertion, which localises the failure without a debugger
✅ Metaprogramming builds test doubles: ExpandoMetaClass and map coercion can stub a method without a mocking library
⚠️ A dynamic failure appears only when the test runs the line: For a def call path the test is the first check
⚠️ @CompileStatic changes what a test can patch: A statically compiled class does not consult the metaclass, so a stub installed that way has no effect



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety is the JVM’s responsibility: A buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Groovy code
✅ The JDK security stack is available: TLS, the cryptography providers, and the access-control APIs are directly usable
⚠️ Metaprogramming can cause type confusion: ExpandoMetaClass, methodMissing, and invokeMethod change dispatch at runtime, so a call may reach code the source does not name
⚠️ Script execution is a code-execution surface: GroovyShell, Eval, and evaluate run arbitrary text, so untrusted input must never reach them
⚠️ An AST transformation executes at compile time: A build-time transformation runs code in the build, which is a supply-chain surface
⚠️ @Grab pulls code into the build: The resolved artifact is loaded onto the script’s class path from a remote repository
❌ Inherits the JVM rule: integer wraparound (the int/long path) (Q4)

1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The JDK ships no package channel: jars move through Maven Central, a third-party repository whose terms are its own.



1.3.3 Observability

1.3.4 Feedback

✅ javac compiles the edit-run loop in seconds. (Y7)
✅ Editor analysis rides the javac API, so IDE diagnostics match the compiler. (Y8)
✅ jdb ships with the JDK. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The maintained target is the JVM; nothing in the language runs without one. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ The specification documents the language, the implementation defines the rest, and no published conformance suite exists (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [7]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

Verdict: Groovy’s design yields moderate core coupling, and a platform cost driven by the JVM and its dynamic dispatch rather than by the syntax. @CompileStatic and @TypeChecked convert the dynamic default into a checked and fast one, traits compose behaviour without inheritance, and safe navigation puts the absence test at the point of use. Main strengths: the whole Java ecosystem is reachable, Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline give the language a mainstream host, and Spock makes testing first-class. Main weaknesses: def defers failure to run time, the JVM is the only target, exceptions are unchecked, the metaclass protocol can change dispatch invisibly, and no structured concurrency exists in the language.

title: Go (1.26)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Go in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 74.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 95.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Implicit interfaces radical decoupling: No declaration of implementation, duck typing at compile time
✅ Composition over inheritance: No inheritance, only struct embedding
✅ Small interfaces: Convention is single-method interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer)
✅ Generics (stable since 1.18): Type parameters eliminate interface{} casts — slices.Sort, maps.Clone, cmp.Or are type-safe (note: sync.Map remains a non-generic any-keyed type)
✅ Range-over-func (1.23): Custom iteration patterns via iter.Seq[T] decouple iteration protocol from data structure
⚠️ No higher-kinded types: Generics are first-order type parameters only
✅ min/max/clear builtins (1.21): Built-in operations eliminate unnecessary function coupling
❌ Nil everywhere, and no sum types: nil pointers and nil interfaces couple code to nil checks, and the language has no sum type to replace them (T4)
⚠️ Interfaces can be nil with non-nil value: (nil, *T) couples interface semantics



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Zero values make sense: Default initialization doesn’t couple to constructors
✅ Constructors are conventions: NewX() functions, not special syntax
⚠️ Can couple to package-level state: init() functions run at import
❌ Global package state: Package-level variables couple to initialization order
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the specification states map iteration receives no order guarantee, and the runtime randomizes the seed deliberately (C5)
❌ One value, many names: slices and maps share backing structures — append to a slice can write a buffer another name reads, and the parameter type names a value, not the sharing (C6)
✅ Every transfer names a call: deferred calls are written at the site (the defer statement is the call), and the interfaces dispatch by method value, not by string (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Concurrent mark-sweep GC with sub-millisecond pause targets
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ Escape analysis optimizes: Stack allocation when possible, decouples from explicit allocation
✅ Profile-guided optimization (1.22+): Compiler uses runtime profiles to optimize, decoupling performance from manual tuning
⚠️ Defer couples cleanup to function exit: Not immediate, but predictable
✅ Simple memory model: No complex ownership rules
✅ The class is declared and recoverable: panics are values in the frame, recover reaches them (documented), and the fatal classes (the runtime’s) sit outside the language’s surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Explicit error returns: func foo() (Result, error) makes errors visible
❌ No error composition: Can’t map/flatMap errors natively, so call sites repeat if err != nil; generics enable Result types but not idiomatically
⚠️ Panic exists but rare: Explicit, but not in type system
⚠️ errors.Join (1.20): Can combine multiple errors, improving composition slightly
❌ A fault ends the program: an unrecovered panic terminates the program (documented), and the panicking path unwinds the goroutine it ran on (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Goroutines separate concurrency: Lightweight, easy to spawn
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples
✅ Select decouples multiplexing: Wait on multiple channels independently
✅ Structured logging (slog, 1.21): Decouples logging concerns from application logic
⚠️ Can share memory: Mutexes allow traditional coupling, but discouraged



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Open-source toolchain: The Go compiler and standard library are BSD-3 licensed and developed in the open
✅ Alternative implementations: Gccgo (GCC front end) and TinyGo (microcontrollers, WebAssembly) implement Go independently of the main toolchain
✅ Portable binaries: A Go program builds to a static native binary with no installed runtime or virtual machine
✅ Broad cross-compilation: One toolchain emits Linux, macOS, Windows, and WebAssembly binaries by setting GOOS and GOARCH



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The language is deliberately small: Exceptions, operator overloading, and pattern matching are left out, so programs are longer and each construct is plain — a scope decision
One formatter settles style: gofmt writes a single canonical layout, trading some expression for a uniform codebase — a tooling convention
Tooling ships in the go command: Formatting, testing, vetting, and documentation come as one package, so the choice of tools is made by the toolchain rather than by the team
The Go 1 promise freezes the standard library: The compatibility guarantee keeps old code building and makes early API decisions permanent — a stability trade
The standard library is the framework: net/http and encoding/json are used directly rather than through a third-party layer, a design choice whose cost is the conveniences such a layer would add




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Fast compilation: Extremely fast builds
✅ Fast startup: No JIT warmup
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic but low-latency (R2)
✅ Predictable: Simple performance model
✅ Static binary: Single executable



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Standard tooling: Go build, go test, go fmt
⚠️ Project-local conventions: Build tags, code generation, and layout conventions grew outside the toolchain, so each project’s tooling is partly its own (Ec2)
✅ Great stdlib: Batteries included
✅ Excellent docs: Godoc, tour, effective go
✅ Growing ecosystem: Good library availability
✅ Cross-compilation: Easy to build for different platforms
❌ The plugin path is unpromised: plugin.Open requires the application and its plugins to be built with the same toolchain version and flags [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored data crosses on a published design: a gob stream is self-describing, fields match by name and compatible type, and out-of-date receivers keep working as a type gains fields [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Go 1 compatibility promise: Extremely stable
✅ No breaking changes: Code from 2012 still compiles
✅ Conservative evolution: Generics took 10 years
✅ Predictable: No surprises
❌ Build variants multiply: //go:build constraints select which files enter the build, so a package is a platform and tag outcome, not only a directory (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend services: Cloud-native standard
✅ Great for CLI tools: Fast startup, single binary
✅ Strong for networking: Stdlib excellent
❌ Poor for frontend: Not applicable
⚠️ Systems programming: GC limits use cases



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Extremely gentle: Simple, small language
✅ Quick to productivity: Can be productive in days
✅ Excellent docs: Tour, Effective Go
✅ Few concepts: Generics are additive; core language remains small and learnable



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Simple, readable: Minimal syntax
❌ Verbose error handling: if err != nil everywhere
✅ Opinionated: Gofmt eliminates style debates
⚠️ Limited abstraction: Sometimes too simple



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Built-in testing: Go test standard
✅ Benchmarking: Go test -bench
✅ Profiling: Pprof built-in
✅ Delve debugger: Good debugging experience
✅ Table-driven tests: Idiomatic, clear



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ Nil everywhere: Panic on nil dereference
✅ Type safe: Static typing
⚠️ Error handling: Easy to ignore errors
❌ The specification defines integer arithmetic as wraparound (module 2^size) (Q4)

Verdict: Go’s implicit interfaces provide exceptionally low coupling by decoupling implementation from declaration without explicit implements clauses. Goroutines and channels separate concurrency from shared-memory synchronization. Generics, stable for over three years, eliminate interface{} casts. Range-over-func enables custom iteration without coupling to built-in loop constructs. Main strength: simplicity prevents complex coupling from emerging. Main weakness: nil is still everywhere, error handling does not compose, and the language has no sum types or pattern matching.

title: Gleam (1.19)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Gleam in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 90.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 93.8/100 · Engineering readiness 61.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static types with full inference: A function’s types are checked at compile time, and an annotation is optional almost everywhere
✅ A custom type is the only way to add a case: A case over a custom type is checked for exhaustiveness, so a new variant breaks every site that must handle it
✅ There is no null: Absence is Option(a), and the compiler rejects a use of the option as a plain value
✅ There is no inheritance and no class: Data is a custom type and behaviour is a function, so there is no hierarchy to couple to
✅ An opaque type hides its representation: A module can export a type without its constructor, so the invariant is enforced at the module boundary
✅ Generics are parametric and checked: Result(a, e), List(a), and a user type take type parameters with no cast
⚠️ There are no type classes or traits: Reuse across types goes through a record of functions passed to a generic function, not through a shared interface
❌ A call’s effects are not in its type: A signature says what a function returns, not that it reads a process dictionary, sends a message, or panics (T12)
❌ The foreign boundary is a promise: An external function names its Erlang or JavaScript counterpart by hand, and nothing checks that the two agree (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A constructor is the only way to make a value: A custom type’s constructor checks every field, and a case cannot build one that the type does not declare
✅ A record updates by copy: Person(..person, name: "Ada") returns a new value and leaves the original alone
✅ A module holds functions, not mutable state: There is no global variable to read or write during construction
⚠️ Construction is explicit: There are no default values and no implicit conversions, so every field is passed at the call site



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The BEAM collects each process separately: A process has its own heap, and the pause is the runtime’s to schedule (M2)
✅ Data is immutable: A value is never changed in place, so two holders cannot disagree about its contents
✅ A process owns its heap: A value is copied between processes, so no reference is shared across a process boundary
✅ There is no manual deallocation: The runtime frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur
⚠️ No destructor runs at scope exit: A resource follows the process lifetime or an explicit close, not a block boundary
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: Gleam rides the BEAM atom table (documented), and node failure outranks every rescue (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A failure is a value: A fallible function returns Result(a, e), and the type says so
✅ use threads the failure path: use x <- result.try(f()) returns a failure to the caller without a match at each step
✅ A panic is a process crash: panic ends the process and is not a channel for a recoverable failure
⚠️ The error type is the module’s choice: Nothing in the language forces one error type across modules



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A process is the unit of concurrency: A Gleam process is an Erlang process with its own heap and mailbox
✅ A message replaces shared memory: Two processes exchange a value by copy, so a data race between them cannot occur
✅ OTP supervises the tree: A supervisor restarts a failed child, so failure handling is a supervision tree rather than a try block
✅ There is no second function kind: A function does not become async; the runtime schedules processes, so no colour spreads through the call graph
⚠️ The actor library is a package: gleam_otp supplies the actor and supervisor abstractions, so their version is a dependency



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One source compiles to two runtimes: gleam build --target erlang emits for the BEAM and --target javascript emits for Node and the browser
✅ The Erlang back end emits abstract forms: The compiler produces Erlang’s intermediate representation and skips the Erlang front end, so a crash report names a Gleam line
✅ Interop on the BEAM is zero-cost: A Gleam module and an Erlang or Elixir module call each other without a marshalling layer
⚠️ The two targets have different runtimes: A program that runs on both meets the BEAM scheduler on one target and the JavaScript event loop on the other



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A small ecosystem is the price of a young language: Fewer packages mean more code written locally; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
Two targets, two runtimes: A program that runs on the BEAM and in JavaScript meets two schedulers and two sets of libraries
No OOP is a deliberate subtraction: Reuse goes through functions and records, so a team accustomed to inheritance rewrites its habits
The foreign boundary is untyped: An external function is a hand-written promise on both the Erlang and the JavaScript side
Immutability copies at the process boundary: A message is copied between processes, which is safe and not free
The cadence is fast and the language is young: A short release cycle is a fix rate and a moving target




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler is fast: A full build of the published benchmark project completes in a fraction of a second, and a rebuild is incremental
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The BEAM collects a process independently, and the pause is a latency budget’s cost (R2)
✅ The BEAM compiles the hot path: The runtime’s JIT compiles a hot function, so a long-running service does not run interpreted
⚠️ The JavaScript target inherits the engine’s limits: Speed on that target is the JavaScript engine’s, not the language’s



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ gleam add and Hex are the whole dependency story: A manifest, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the toolchain
✅ One binary holds the toolchain: build, format, test, add, and the language server ship together
❌ The ecosystem is small: The package pool is younger and thinner than the mainstream registries, so more code is written than found (Ec3)
✅ The BEAM ecosystem is reachable: A project can depend on Erlang and Elixir packages and call them directly
⚠️ The language is young: A library can change quickly, and a tutorial can lag a release
✅ The NIF ABI is versioned and checked at load on the BEAM runtime it runs on [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Releases follow semantic versioning: A 1.x release keeps the language compatible, and a package states the version it requires
✅ The cadence is short: A release arrives every six to eight weeks, so a fix is not held for a year
✅ Mechanical migrations ship with the compiler: A deprecation arrives with a fix in the compiler or the formatter
⚠️ A pre-1.0 package can break: A dependency that has not reached 1.0 may change in a breaking release



1.2.4 Domain

✅ A web service is the ordinary project: Wisp and the OTP libraries make an HTTP service the default shape
✅ The browser is a supported target: Lustre compiles a Gleam program to the front end through the JavaScript target
✅ A command-line tool is supported: An escript packages a single-file program for the BEAM
⚠️ The centre is server-side: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward backend work on the BEAM



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The language is small: The official tour covers the whole language in an afternoon
✅ An error carries the fix: The compiler names the mismatch and often prints the corrected code
✅ The language server is the compiler: Completion, rename, and go-to-definition come from the same binary
⚠️ Inference hides a type at the boundary: A reader sometimes has to ask the editor for an inferred type



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Every construct is an expression: A case, a let, and a function body produce a value, so a value is defined where it is computed
✅ The pipeline reads left to right: value |> f |> g states the data flow without an intermediate name
✅ A label names the argument at the call site: request.new(method: Get, path: "/") reads without the definition
⚠️ The braces and commas are load-bearing: The syntax is small but strict, and a missing comma is a compile error



1.2.7 Testing

✅ gleam test runs the suite: The toolchain discovers and runs the test modules
✅ gleeunit is the standard harness: A test is a function, and a failed assertion stops the module
✅ The compiler checks the test: A test is type-checked with the project, so a broken test does not compile
⚠️ The harness is a package: gleeunit is a dependency, and its version must match the compiler’s expectations



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety belongs to the runtime: A program cannot read or write outside its data, and the language has no unsafe
✅ Immutability removes a class of bugs: A value cannot change under a holder
✅ There is no eval: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
⚠️ The foreign boundary is unchecked: An external function’s signature is a promise, and the other runtime does not verify it

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The build does not check reproducibility: gleam build writes BEAM or JavaScript output and never compares a rebuild against a published artifact, so a consumer cannot confirm the two match (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A package carries no build attestation: The registry signs its own index, but nothing in a release states who built it or from what source, so a compromised build is not distinguishable from a genuine one (Y3)
❌ Hex names are global: A package name is unique across the registry, so an owner is not separated by a namespace (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: A project chooses an OpenTelemetry package and its own conventions, and the standard library states none (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The compiler is the language server: An error is reported in the editor as the file is saved, and a rebuild is incremental



1.3.5 Interop

✅ Interop is a language feature: A module calls Erlang, Elixir, or JavaScript through a declared external function, so the boundary is written down



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the compiler riding the BEAM: the documentation describes the implementation’s behavior, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)

Verdict: Gleam’s design yields low language-imposed coupling. Static inference removes the dynamic-typing mechanisms, custom types and exhaustive matching remove the missing-sum-type mechanism, and Option and Result put absence and failure in the type. The BEAM gives it process isolation, so no shared-memory race is expressible, and it avoids function colouring because a process, not an async function, is the unit of concurrency. Main strength: a small language whose defaults — immutability, exhaustive matching, errors as values — leave few coupling mechanisms to price. Main weakness: the ecosystem is young and thin, the foreign boundary is unchecked, and the runtime’s collector still schedules the heap.

title: Erlang (OTP 29)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Erlang in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 77.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 90.6/100 · Engineering readiness 66.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing: A value carries its type at run time, so a type fault appears when the expression executes (T1)
❌ No declared parameter or return types: -spec is optional metadata, and the language has no generic type parameters (T5)
❌ No sum types: A tagged tuple such as {ok, Value} or {error, Reason} is a convention, and no type checks the union (T4)
❌ Dispatch is checked at run time: Mod:Fun(Args) resolves when called, so a missing function fails there rather than at compile time (T3)
✅ -spec and Dialyzer give optional static analysis: A success-typing pass over the compiled BEAM files detects inconsistent calls
✅ Atoms serve as named constants: An atom such as ok, error, or undefined is a distinct value, so the language needs no null



1.1.2 Construction

✅ All data is immutable: A term cannot be changed after it is built
✅ A pattern in the clause head selects the construction path: The arguments decide which clause runs
✅ Records and maps declare named structure: -record(user, {name, age}) gives compile-time named fields over a tuple
✅ State is a value threaded through recursion: An OTP behaviour receives its state and returns the new state, so no object owns it
✅ A process is the unit of mutable state: A gen_server owns its state and exposes it by message
⚠️ A record is a tuple: Field access is positional at run time, so the record definition must be shared by every module that uses it



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Collection is per-process and non-deterministic: A process collects its own heap on its own schedule (M2)
✅ A private heap confines a pause: A collection affects one process, and there is no global stop-the-world pause
✅ No manual deallocation: The VM reclaims memory, and a program never frees a term
✅ Off-heap binaries are reference counted: A binary above the heap threshold is shared between processes rather than copied
⚠️ A large live set costs more per collection: A process that accumulates state pays a higher collection cost
⚠️ An ETS table lives outside the collector: The table persists until its owner deletes it or dies
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: atom-table exhaustion fails the node (documented), outside every catch clause and outside the supervision tree (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: throw, error, and exit are not declared, so a caller cannot see the failure set from a signature (Er2)
✅ “Let it crash” makes failure a supervision event: A supervisor restarts a failed process, and the normal path carries no recovery code
✅ Links and monitors define propagation: link/1 couples the fates of two processes, and monitor/2 reports a failure without dying
✅ A pattern-match failure raises a defined error: An unmatched value raises badmatch, and an unmatched clause raises function_clause
✅ try/catch/after is available when recovery is local: A catch clause separates throw, error, and exit
⚠️ A restart resets process state: Supervision restores the process, not the data it held, so state must be recoverable
✅ The runtime publishes the isolation unit: a fault in a supervised process restarts a process under a declared strategy, and the supervision tree is what the program declares (OTP, documented) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The actor model is the core of the language: Processes share no memory and communicate by message
✅ spawn, link, and monitor are primitives: Starting and observing a process needs no library
✅ The BEAM schedules preemptively by reductions: A process cannot hold a scheduler indefinitely
✅ Messages are immutable values: A message is copied or shared by reference count, never aliased mutably
✅ Distribution is built into the VM: net_kernel and epmd let a process send to a node as if it were local
⚠️ Distribution is designed, not automatic: Node failure, network partition, and message loss must be handled by the application



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The BEAM is portable and open source: The Erlang runtime runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, and BSD
✅ Hot code loading is a runtime feature: code:load_file/1 replaces a module while the system runs
✅ A release bundles the runtime and the application: release_handler and reltool produce a deployable node
✅ Distribution across nodes is a platform feature: Nodes discover each other and pass messages without an external broker
⚠️ The runtime must be present: An Erlang program runs on the VM, so the artefact is not a native binary on its own
❌ Poor fit for CPU-bound numerical work: The VM is not built for dense numeric computation, so that work belongs in another language (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The syntax is Prolog-derived: The form is unfamiliar to most developers; this is a learning property, not a coupling
Distribution is a design task: The language supplies the transport, and the application decides the failure semantics
Weak CPU-bound performance is a domain fit note: The VM is built for I/O concurrency, not for numeric loops
Hot upgrade constrains state handling: The running system can change module code, so the application must supply a code_change/3 callback to migrate state
Atoms are named constants in place of null: Absence is carried by an atom convention such as undefined
Records are tuples by design: The representation is a deliberate choice made for compactness and speed




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The BEAM handles very many concurrent I/O processes: A process is cheap and needs no thread
✅ BeamAsm compiles hot code: The JIT added in OTP 24 means bytecode is not always interpreted
✅ Per-process collection avoids a global pause: A collection affects one process
✅ Reduction scheduling bounds latency: A process yields after a fixed number of reductions
⚠️ CPU-bound computation is weak relative to native code: A tight numeric loop trails C or Rust
⚠️ A NIF runs on a scheduler thread: A native function that runs long blocks other processes on that scheduler



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Hex.pm and rebar3 cover packages and builds: A registry, dependency resolution, and release builds are all present
✅ OTP ships with the language: Supervision, gen_server, application, and release handling are part of the distribution
✅ Elixir libraries are reachable through interop: The two languages run on one VM and call each other directly
✅ The flagship projects are long-lived and battle-tested: RabbitMQ, CouchDB, Riak, and WhatsApp’s messaging stack are Erlang systems
✅ OTP is documented as a first-class topic: The OTP design principles document the behaviours
⚠️ The library count is smaller than the mainstream: Fewer general-purpose packages exist outside messaging and telecom
✅ The NIF ABI is versioned and checked at load, and an older major is accepted for two releases [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored terms cross on a published promise: the external term format carries its version, and Erlang/OTP systems as of R16B decode the minor-version-2 encoding that is the default as of OTP 26.0 [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The language has kept backward compatibility for decades: Code written against an old OTP release continues to run
✅ Hot code loading decouples deployment from runtime: A module is replaced while the system runs
✅ code_change/3 migrates state across a version change: An OTP behaviour converts old state to the new shape
✅ OTP release handling gives a controlled upgrade path: release_handler applies a version change to a running node
⚠️ A hot upgrade must be designed: State migration and dependency order are the application’s responsibility
❌ Build variants multiply: -ifdef, -ifndef, and -define select which clauses compile, and -D flags set the space (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for distributed, fault-tolerant systems: Supervision, distribution, and the actor model match the problem directly
✅ Proven in telecom and messaging: WhatsApp, RabbitMQ, and Discord’s infrastructure run on the BEAM
✅ Binary parsing is a strength: The bit syntax <<A:8, B:16/little>> matches a protocol frame directly
⚠️ Distribution across nodes requires explicit design effort: The application must decide how to handle a lost node



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep: A developer learns functional programming, the actor model, and OTP at once (L1)
❌ The Prolog-derived syntax is unfamiliar: The ., ,, and ; delimiters and the term syntax differ from the mainstream (L1)
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the OTP behaviours, and the VM’s semantics are separate bodies of knowledge (L2)
✅ The official documentation is thorough: The Erlang reference manual and the OTP design principles are authoritative
✅ The community is established: Decades of accumulated material and answered questions exist



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The term syntax is uniform: Every construct is a term, and a module is a sequence of forms ending in a period
✅ The delimiter roles are consistent: A comma separates expressions, a semicolon separates clauses, and a period ends a form
✅ Bit syntax is compact for protocols: A binary pattern states field widths and endianness in one expression
✅ Pattern matching is part of the function-head syntax: A clause states its cases directly
⚠️ The comma, semicolon, and period distinction is easy to get wrong: One misplaced delimiter changes the meaning of a form
⚠️ Atoms and variables differ only by case: ok is an atom and Ok is a variable



1.2.7 Testing

✅ EUnit and Common Test ship with OTP: Unit tests and system tests are part of the standard distribution
✅ Property-based testing is available: PropEr and QuickCheck generate inputs from a property
✅ Tracing and observer inspect a running system: dbg, recon, and the observer tool expose processes, messages, and scheduler load
✅ Common Test runs a distributed suite: A test can start several nodes and drive them together
❌ Errors surface at run time: Dynamic typing defers a type fault to the executed path (G3)
⚠️ Dialyzer catches some faults and not all: Success typing proves the absence of some inconsistencies, not the presence of correctness



1.2.8 Security

✅ Process isolation contains a fault: A crashed process does not corrupt another process’s memory
✅ Messages are immutable values: No shared mutable state exists to race on
✅ The supervision tree bounds a failure: A restarted process returns the system to a known state
⚠️ The atom table has a fixed limit: list_to_atom/1 or binary_to_atom/2 on untrusted input can exhaust the table, whose default ceiling is about one million atoms
⚠️ binary_to_term/1 on untrusted input is dangerous: Decoding an external term can allocate a large structure unless the safe option is used
⚠️ A NIF and a Port reach unsafe code: Native code can break the VM’s guarantees

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Rebar3 resolves dependency versions from Hex at build time. (Y1)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Hex packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The Hex name space is flat. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; the runtime ships its own tools. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The shell compiles and runs with no build step. (Y7)
⚠️ No analyzer ships in the distribution; dialyzer ships with it, editor analysis rides third-party plugins.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ NIFs are the in-process foreign interface to C. (Y9)
✅ The BEAM is the portable target: the artifact runs wherever Erlang/OTP runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the BEAM: the documentation describes the implementation, and no published conformance suite exists for an independent implementation (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [7]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].

Verdict: Erlang’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling in the domain it was built for. The actor model removes shared memory from concurrency, immutability removes in-place mutation, and “let it crash” with OTP supervision moves recovery out of the business logic.
