title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Eiffel in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.7/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Design by Contract (DBC): require (preconditions), ensure (postconditions), and invariant (class invariants) make an element’s change conditions explicit. This is the coupling-relevant feature: contracts name the requirements an element realizes, so a change in one element’s requirements that forces another element’s contract to change is visible at the boundary
✅ Void safety (attached types): x: attached T vs x: detachable T separates non-null from nullable at compile time (Eiffel 6+). Eliminates the null-checking coupling class at compile time
✅ Strong static typing: No implicit coercion, no unchecked casts as escape hatches
✅ No argument overloading: Each feature name within a class maps to exactly one feature — “one name, within one class, means one thing.” This eliminates method-resolution ambiguity coupling and is what makes Eiffel’s multiple inheritance safe
✅ Command-Query Separation: Queries (which return information) must not modify the instance — a Meyer design rule that prevents side effects hidden in value retrieval from coupling unrelated elements
✅ Generics with constraints: LINKED_LIST [G -> COMPARABLE] decouples containers from element types
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: Supported with rename, redefine, and select — powerful feature reuse but creates hierarchy coupling and diamond complexity
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Class hierarchies couple behavior to the inheritance tree



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Creation procedures (create): Separate allocation from initialization; create x.make(...)
✅ Invariants validate object state: invariant clauses check well-formedness after every feature call
⚠️ Creation procedures can have side effects: Nothing enforces pure construction
❌ Once routines create global singleton state: once routines run once (per thread by default, configurable per process or per object) and cache their result — a memoized shared-state coupling across the system
❌ One value, many names: by-reference semantics are the design — every object is reached through references, and a feature call mutates one object from any attached name (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Automatic GC: No manual deallocation, no use-after-free, no dangling pointers
✅ No pointers: Memory safety by construction; expanded types give value semantics
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, couple timing-sensitive code to runtime
⚠️ Void references possible (legacy code): Without attached-type discipline, dereferencing a void reference raises a Void_call exception at runtime



1.1.4 Error

✅ Rescue/retry: Structured exception handling where rescue + retry separates error recovery from error detection — failure handling decoupled from the code that triggered it
✅ Contract-driven exceptions: Exceptions arise from precondition/postcondition/invariant violations, making failure points explicit and first-class rather than accidental
⚠️ Exceptions not used for control flow: Eiffel treats exceptions as contract failures, so error recovery is limited to what the contract model supports
⚠️ Contracts can be disabled at compile time: EiffelStudio can compile an executable to include or exclude any set of contracts (workbench vs. deployment modes), coupling correctness to build configuration



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ SCOOP (Simple Concurrent Object-Oriented Programming): Separates concurrency from logic via processor- and handler-oriented design; decouples “what runs concurrently” from “how it synchronizes” (e.g. multiple threads without explicit mutex management). Available in EiffelStudio, though not yet part of the official language definition
✅ Agents: Wrap operations into objects, closely connected with closures and lambda calculus — decoupling callbacks from the calling code
⚠️ SCOOP is complex and niche: Correct concurrent design requires deep expertise; low adoption
⚠️ Shared mutable state possible: No compiler-level race detection



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Native compilation without a runtime: EiffelStudio compiles to a native executable, so a deployed program does not depend on a vendor runtime
✅ Portable across the major desktop platforms: EiffelStudio targets Windows, Linux, and macOS
⚠️ One vendor owns the ISO-conforming implementation: EiffelStudio is the ISO-conforming implementation and is commercial software from Eiffel Software, so the platform’s evolution depends on that single vendor



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Contract vs. Runtime Cost: Contract checking adds overhead; disabling it (deployment mode) removes the enforcement
Inheritance vs. Composition: Eiffel encourages inheritance as its primary reuse mechanism; multiple inheritance couples but enables precise feature reuse via renaming
SCOOP vs. Pragmatism: The concurrency model is elegant and low-coupling but hard to adopt in practice
Once Routines vs. Independent Units: Memoization decouples repeated computation but couples the element to global shared state that other elements may depend on
Contract Depth vs. Discipline: DBC only helps if teams actually write contracts; without them Eiffel degenerates to a plain typed OOP language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled to native code: EiffelStudio generates efficient native executables
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, though modern GCs keep them short (R2)
⚠️ Contract overhead: Runtime checks add cost; disablement improves performance but removes guarantees
✅ Deterministic when contracts disabled: Predictable execution in deployment mode



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Small ecosystem: Far fewer libraries than the JVM or .NET, so a solution couples to the few that exist and to a niche community
✅ EiffelStudio is a complete IDE: Integrated compiler, debugger, and contract-aware tooling
⚠️ Dated tooling: Modern build systems and package managers are weak relative to mainstream
⚠️ Niche community: Limited third-party support and resources
⚠️ Fragmented implementations: EiffelStudio, “The Eiffel Compiler” (tecomp), Gobo Eiffel, SmartEiffel, and LibertyEiffel differ; the GNU implementations track an older language version and do not fully implement the ISO standard



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ ISO/ECMA standard: Eiffel is an ISO/IEC standard (ISO/IEC 25436:2006, ECMA-367), giving a stable language core
⚠️ Slow, conservative evolution: The standard is stable but innovation is glacial
⚠️ Implementations diverge: EiffelStudio and the GNU-based implementations have drifted on language features
❌ Niche survival concern: Long-term support depends on a small commercial base



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for high-integrity and contract-heavy domains: DBC is ideal where correctness is paramount and reliability is the design goal
✅ Good for teaching design-by-contract: The language enforces the discipline
⚠️ Poor for mainstream web/systems: GC, niche ecosystem, dated tooling
⚠️ Little adoption in modern development: Hard to hire for



1.2.5 Learning

✅ DBC is a clear mental model: Contracts make intent explicit
⚠️ Multiple inheritance + renaming complexity: Advanced Eiffel is hard to master
⚠️ SCOOP adds a second learning curve: The concurrency model is non-trivial
⚠️ Fewer modern resources: Documentation is dated relative to mainstream languages



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable, English-like: if x then ... else ... end, require/ensure/invariant read naturally
✅ Explicit contracts: The syntax makes specification a visible part of every feature
⚠️ Verbose: end clauses and full declarations add ceremony
⚠️ Non-standard keywords: Keywords (e.g. feature, deferred, attached) are unfamiliar to most programmers



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Contracts enable automated testing: preconditions/postconditions/invariants act as built-in test assertions
✅ EiffelStudio debugger: Contract-aware, can inspect invariant violations
✅ Exception handling tools: rescue/retry makes error paths debuggable
⚠️ Few third-party test frameworks: The ecosystem is thin



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC, no pointers, no use-after-free, no buffer overflows
✅ Void safety: Prevents null-pointer vulnerabilities by default (with attached types)
✅ Strong typing: No type-confusion bugs
✅ No argument overloading: Unambiguous feature resolution reduces surprising dispatch
⚠️ Once-routine shared state: Can create hidden shared-state vulnerabilities
❌ ECMA-367 defines INTEGER as a machine integer; overflow wraps (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ ECF configurations resolve libraries from the installed cluster. (Y1)
❌ Library versions resolve from the environment at melt time. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)

1.3.6 Governance

✅ The ECMA working group and the community maintain the language. (Y11)
✅ ECMA-367 publishes the specification. (Y12)
✅ The EiffelStudio compiler is public source under GPL. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

title: D (2.112)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses D in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 71.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 87.9/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing with inference: auto, template argument deduction, and typeof infer most declarations, so the type is fixed at compile time without being written at every site
✅ Templates avoid the angle-bracket problem: Instantiation uses the ! syntax (foo!int, foo!(int, string)) with if (isInputRange!R) constraints, so generic code carries none of C++’s nested <> noise
✅ Modules are the compilation boundary: A module is declared with module in one source file and consumed with import, so there are no headers and no include guards tying a declaration to a textual include order
✅ UFCS decouples call syntax from the definition site: x.f(y) is rewritten to f(x, y), so a free function composes into a method-call chain without being a member of the type
✅ immutable and const are transitive: A qualifier reaches through pointers and members, so a read-only view is stated once rather than per access
⚠️ Operator overloading is not visible in cost: opBinary, opCmp, opIndex, and opAssign let a type redefine +, <, [], and =, so a dense expression can hide work the call site does not show (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Structs are constructed in place: struct is a value type, so a local, a field, or an array element is constructed where it is declared without a heap allocation
✅ Contract programming separates the specification from the body: in, out, and invariant blocks state preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants as separate declarations, so a check is not buried in the implementation
✅ scope guards attach cleanup to the construction site: scope(exit), scope(success), and scope(failure) run at block exit beside the code that acquired the resource
✅ @disable this() forbids an illegal construction: A type can delete a constructor, so an object cannot be built by calling new
⚠️ Mutability is the default: A variable is mutable unless it is declared immutable or const, so immutability is opt-in rather than the default reading of a declaration (C2)
❌ One value, many names: class references and pointers alias; ScopedAlias and Unique are opt-in attributes the default code skips (C6)
❌ C++-style module init: cross-module order is not stated in source (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Garbage collection pauses are non-deterministic: The default new path allocates on the collector’s heap, and a collection runs on the collector’s schedule rather than the program’s (M2)
⚠️ RAII is partial: Struct destructors (~this) and scope(exit) release a value type deterministically, but a class instance is collected, so its destructor has no defined run time (M3)
❌ No ownership or lifetime checking: The compiler does not track which reference owns an allocation, so a dangling pointer or a double release in @system code is not diagnosed (M4)
✅ @nogc removes the collector from a call tree: A @nogc function may not allocate through the GC, so its pauses are excluded at compile time
✅ -betterC excludes the runtime entirely: The program links without druntime or the collector, which is what the embedded and no-GC case needs
✅ destroy releases a value at a chosen point: destroy(x) runs the destructor and resets the value, giving an explicit release where the collector would otherwise decide
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: cast between unrelated pointer types compiles unchecked, and the specification hands the representation question to the programmer as undefined behaviour (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer on the GC heap (the @system-safety escape, documented) corrupts memory, below every catch clause (Er6)
❌ Class references are counted by default; cycles leak unless the GC mode is enabled (M7)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Unchecked exceptions are the only error channel: throw needs no declaration in the signature and the compiler does not check that a handler exists; nothrow is an opt-in promise (Er2)
✅ nothrow names the functions that cannot fail: A nothrow function may not throw, so the property is checked at the declaration
✅ scope(failure) separates the recovery path from the normal path: Cleanup written there runs only when the block leaves by an exception
✅ try/catch/finally is the standard shape: A catch clause names the type it handles, and finally runs on every exit
⚠️ Contracts and assertions disappear under -release: in, out, and assert are compiled out in a release build, so their guarantee is a debug-time one
❌ A fault ends the process: an uncaught exception in a thread terminates the process (documented) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The shared qualifier makes cross-thread state visible: Data declared shared cannot be read or written through an ordinary reference, so the cast that crosses a thread boundary is the place the synchronisation is declared
✅ std.concurrency gives message passing: spawn starts a thread with its own message queue, and send/receive pass values between threads without a shared lock
✅ std.parallelism gives structured parallel loops: parallel and taskPool map a loop body over a range, so the common data-parallel case is stated rather than hand-threaded
✅ Atomic primitives are in the standard library: core.atomic provides atomicOp, cas, and atomicLoad, so a lock-free update has a named primitive
❌ Synchronisation is manual and unchecked: synchronized, Mutex, and core.atomic are the only tools, and the compiler does not prove the locking discipline or detect a race (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Three independent compilers target the same language: dmd uses its own Digital Mars backend, ldc uses LLVM, and gdc uses the GCC backend, so a program is not bound to one vendor’s toolchain
✅ Native code is produced for many targets: Linux, Windows, macOS, and the BSDs on x86, x86-64, ARM, and AArch64 are supported targets
✅ C and C++ interoperability is a language feature: extern(C), extern(C++), and the importC compiler feature let a D module call existing C and C++ binaries without a binding generator
✅ -betterC removes the runtime dependency: A BetterC program links like a C program, without druntime or a GC
✅ The C preprocessor is not part of the language: There is no textual include and no macro layer above the module system
⚠️ The three compilers advance at different rates: ldc and gdc follow dmd’s front end with a lag, so a version-specific feature may not be available on every compiler at once



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Better C++ is a target, not a guarantee: Porting C++ to D is a rewrite with its own cost, and the two languages interoperate at the ABI rather than at the source
GC or manual memory is a per-program choice: -betterC and @nogc buy determinism at the cost of the collector’s convenience
Compile-time execution is a deliberate shift of work: CTFE, static if, and string mixins move computation to the build, so it is not a runtime mechanism at all
Multiple paradigms widen the surface: Imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming styles are all supported, and the choice is the programmer’s
Niche adoption is a market fact, not a language defect: The smaller library pool follows from adoption, not from a construction of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Native compilation with no interpreter: dmd, ldc, and gdc emit machine code, so there is no bytecode dispatch or JIT warm-up between the source and the CPU
✅ ldc and gdc reuse mature optimisers: The LLVM and GCC backends apply the optimisation pipeline that compiles C and C++
✅ CTFE moves work to compile time: static if, mixin, and template instantiation are evaluated by the compiler, so the runtime pays nothing for them
✅ @nogc bounds the runtime cost of a call tree: A function that cannot allocate has no collector interaction at all
⚠️ The collector remains a latency risk: Throughput is good, but a collection can still lengthen a pause in code that allocates, so a latency-sensitive path needs @nogc (R2)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small: dub’s package registry is far smaller than crates.io, npm, or Maven, so a project is more likely to write a library than to find one (Ec3)
✅ dub is a standard package manager and build tool: dub.json or dub.sdl declares dependencies and targets, and dub build, dub run, and dub test cover the ordinary workflow
✅ The C and C++ ecosystems are reachable: extern(C), extern(C++), and importC reduce the need for a D-specific binding
✅ vibe.d supports web services: An asynchronous I/O framework covers HTTP and socket work on the D runtime
⚠️ Corporate backing is weak: The language is carried by its contributors rather than by a large vendor, so long-term support is the community’s



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A deprecation cycle precedes a removal: A feature is deprecated for a release series before it is removed, and the changelog records both steps
✅ -preview flags gate changes to the front end: A new language behaviour ships behind a flag first, so a change can be tested before it becomes the default
✅ The DIP process documents proposals publicly: The D Improvement Proposal repository holds the rationale for a language change
⚠️ Removals do happen: The changelog records deprecated features that were later dropped, so older source can need an edit at a major front-end step
⚠️ Front-end versions differ across the three compilers: A change fixed in dmd reaches ldc and gdc later, so a project can be pinned to one compiler for a period



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Systems and performance work is the design target: Native code, value types, and direct C interop are the native idiom
✅ Game development is a stated fit: The GC can be excluded, structs stay in place, and templates specialise per case, which is what a game loop needs
✅ Embedded and no-runtime work is supported by -betterC: The program links without druntime, so it fits a bare-metal or constrained target
✅ Web services are supported by vibe.d: The framework covers asynchronous HTTP on the same runtime
⚠️ The collector is the wrong model for hard real-time: A latency bound requires @nogc or BetterC throughout the allocating path
⚠️ D is rarely the default choice in any of these domains: The fits are real, but the surrounding library and hiring pool is smaller



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Moderate for an experienced C++ developer: Templates, RAII-style cleanup, and value types have direct C++ analogues
✅ Templates are easier to read than C++ templates: The ! instantiation syntax and if constraints remove the ambiguity of nested angle brackets
✅ Contract programming is a small notation: in, out, and invariant are a few keywords over the ordinary function body
⚠️ The metaprogramming surface is large: Templates, static if, CTFE, traits, and string mixins each have their own rules
⚠️ The memory model is two models at once: A developer must know which allocations are collected and which are not, and @nogc makes the distinction a compile-time obligation
⚠️ Four paradigms are available at once: Imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming styles widen the surface a newcomer must choose from



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Cleaner than C++ for similar expressive power: A module is one file, there is no header text, and there is no preprocessor
✅ ! makes template instantiation unambiguous: foo!int cannot be confused with a comparison, which is C++’s parsing problem
✅ auto removes a declaration without hiding the type: The type is inferred and still checked at compile time
✅ scope(exit) is a compact cleanup notation: One line states the release that other languages spell as a try/finally
⚠️ Attributes accumulate on a signature: @safe @nogc @property nothrow pure and their variants stack up, and the combination is part of the contract
⚠️ String mixins hide the generated code: mixin("...") inserts source the reader cannot see in the file’s order



1.2.7 Testing

✅ unittest blocks are part of the language: A unittest { ... } block sits beside the code it tests, and it is compiled in when the -unittest flag is passed
✅ dub test runs the blocks: The package manager builds and runs the test configuration
✅ Contracts are executable invariants: in, out, and invariant checks fail with a trace when a precondition is broken
✅ Coverage is built in: dmd -cov writes a per-line coverage report from a normal run
⚠️ Tests are compiled only with -unittest: A release build carries no test code, so the test set is a build configuration rather than a language guarantee
⚠️ The test library is third-party: Fixture, mocking, and property-test helpers come from packages such as unit-threaded rather than from the standard library



1.2.8 Security

✅ @safe is checked by the compiler: @safe code may not do pointer arithmetic, lose a type through a cast, or call @system code, so the unsafe operations are the ones that were declared
✅ Bounds checking is kept where it is required: An array or a slice carries its length, and @safe code retains the index check
✅ Variables are initialised by default: A variable starts at its .init value, so the uninitialised-read class of bug does not arise as it does in C; the = void opt-out is named at the declaration, and @safe code forbids it for types that may hold pointer values
⚠️ @trusted and cast are the escape hatch: A @trusted function or a pointer cast re-opens the unsafe surface, and its correctness is the author’s claim
⚠️ The collector and the runtime are part of the attack surface: A bug in druntime or the collector is reachable from a @safe program
⚠️ -release removes the contract checks: Assertions and contracts are compiled out, so a release build relies on the checks that @safe keeps
❌ Machine integers follow C semantics: overflow is silent (Q4)

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Dub resolves dependency versions at build time. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve from the registry unless pinned. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Dub packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The package registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Dub packages. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the compilers. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ extern(C) calls any C library in process; the C model is native to D. (Y9)
✅ dmd and ldc target the common platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The D Language Foundation and the community govern in the open. (Y11)
✅ The language specification is public. (Y12)
✅ dmd and ldc are public source. (Y19)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

Verdict: D’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling for a language of its reach. The module system replaces headers, UFCS separates call syntax from definition, and contract blocks separate the specification from the body. Predicates such as @safe, @nogc, and nothrow turn several memory and error properties into declared and checked facts. Main strengths: compile-time execution removes metaprogramming from the runtime, three independent compilers keep the toolchain from locking in, and -betterC reaches the embedded case. Main weaknesses: unchecked exceptions are the only error channel, the collector’s pauses are not deterministic, no ownership model detects aliasing, and the ecosystem stays niche with weak corporate backing.

title: Common Lisp (ANSI X3.226-1994)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Common Lisp in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 85.9/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing defers every check to run time: No declaration states an object’s type, so a call with a wrong argument type fails when the operation executes (T1)
❌ Generic dispatch resolves at run time: defmethod chooses a method from the run-time types of its arguments (T3)
❌ No sum types: Alternatives are tagged lists or structures by convention, so the set of cases is neither declared nor checked (T4)
❌ No generics: A function accepts any object, so no compile-time check constrains its arguments or its result (T5)
⚠️ Operators are ordinary functions: + and slot-value can be redefined or shadowed, so a reader must resolve a symbol from the current package (T8)
✅ CLOS decouples polymorphism from a class hierarchy: A defgeneric method specialises on any number of argument types, so behaviour is not owned by one class



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global functions are the default: defun interns a function in the current package, so two modules that define the same name collide unless they use separate packages
❌ No immutability by default: Lists, vectors, and structures are mutable, and setf changes them in place (C2)
❌ Special variables create implicit dependencies (C1): A defvar or defparameter marked special is dynamically scoped, so a binding is visible to every function in the dynamic extent, not only the lexical one
✅ Packages give a namespace boundary: defpackage with :use and :export controls which symbols a module exposes and which it imports
✅ Macros decouple surface syntax from evaluation: defmacro expands a form before evaluation, so the core evaluator stays small while the notation is extensible
✅ Structure and class accessors decouple callers from layout: defstruct and defclass generate constructors and accessors, so a caller names a field rather than a position
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the standard states hash-table iteration order is unspecified (C5)
❌ One value, many names: cons cells are shared, and setcar/setcdr mutate every name that reaches the cell (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The garbage collector pauses the program: The generational collectors in SBCL and CCL stop execution for collection (M2)
❌ No RAII: Destruction is not tied to scope, so cleanup needs unwind-protect or a finalizer (M3)
❌ No ownership model: Any object can be referenced from anywhere, and a cycle is reclaimed only by the collector (M4)
✅ unwind-protect gives deterministic cleanup: The cleanup form runs on every exit path, including a non-local exit, so a resource is still released
✅ Weak pointers observe liveness without holding an object: sb-ext:make-weak-pointer and the portable trivial-garbage library let a program act when an object becomes unreachable
✅ dynamic-extent keeps short-lived data off the heap: A declaration lets the compiler place a value on the stack, decoupling allocation strategy from the object



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked and untyped: error and signal do not declare what a function may raise, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the signature (Er2)
✅ Signalling is separated from handling: error and signal raise a condition, and handler-case or handler-bind decides recovery, so the raiser need not know the handler
✅ restart-case offers recovery strategies: The failing code publishes named restarts such as retry and use-value, and a handler selects one, decoupling the recovery policy from the code that failed
✅ handler-bind runs before the stack unwinds: A handler inspects the live stack and can continue, unlike a try/catch that unwinds first
✅ Conditions are classes: define-condition makes a condition a CLOS class with slots, so error data is structured and inspectable
⚠️ An unhandled condition reaches the debugger: An error with no handler enters the interactive debugger, which a batch run must suppress
✅ The condition system declares recoverable boundaries: handlers and restarts are first-class, documented recovery points inside a running computation (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The standard defines no threads: ANSI X3.226-1994 leaves threading to the implementation, so a program that uses none is portable
✅ SBCL provides a thread API: sb-thread supplies make-thread, mutexes, and condition variables
✅ bordeaux-threads is a portable wrapper: One API maps to SBCL, CCL, ECL, and other implementations
✅ lparallel gives data-parallel abstractions: A task and channel library builds on the implementation’s threads
⚠️ Thread support is not standardised: Code that spawns a thread couples to one implementation or to a compatibility library
⚠️ Shared mutable state needs an explicit lock discipline: With no ownership model, correct synchronisation is the programmer’s responsibility
❌ A thread is an operating-system thread: SBCL’s sb-thread reserves one per task (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Native code on several implementations: SBCL, CCL, ECL, Allegro, and LispWorks compile to machine code on Linux, macOS, and Windows
✅ Open-source implementations are actively developed: SBCL and CCL are freely available and maintained
✅ CFFI gives a portable foreign-function interface: defcfun and cffi:with-foreign-object work across implementations
✅ ASDF defines systems portably: defsystem states components and dependencies, and every implementation loads it
⚠️ Behaviour outside the standard differs: Thread APIs, finalisation, and compiler internals are implementation-specific
⚠️ Standalone delivery is implementation-specific: Building an executable uses save-lisp-and-die or dump-image, so packaging couples to the implementation



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Parentheses are the price of homoiconicity: The uniform S-expression is what makes macros possible, and the readability trade is deliberate
Dynamic typing is a scope decision: No declarations suit interactive development in a running image, and the run-time checks follow from that choice
The large standard library is a design value: ANSI CL defines format, loop, CLOS, and a condition system in the standard itself
Implementation extensions are a portability trade: sb-ext, ext, and mp packages buy capability at the cost of portability, by choice
The frozen standard is a stability trade: ANSI X3.226-1994 has never been revised, which keeps existing code stable and freezes the language
Lisp is not a systems language: The image-based, collector-reliant model assumes a runtime host, which is a scope boundary rather than a defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Garbage-collector pauses: The generational collector in SBCL and CCL stops the program for collection (R2)
✅ Ahead-of-time native compilation: SBCL compiles to machine code, so ordinary code runs without interpreter overhead
✅ Type declarations enable optimisation: (declare (type fixnum x)) and (the ...) let the compiler emit unboxed, specialised code
✅ dynamic-extent keeps data on the stack: A declared value can avoid heap allocation
✅ time and disassemble expose the compiled result: A program can inspect allocation (bytes consed) and generated code
⚠️ Performance varies by implementation: SBCL and CCL differ, so a program tuned for one may not be fast on another



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and fragmented across implementations: SBCL and CCL are separate worlds, and libraries support one or several implementations (Ec3)
✅ Quicklisp provides a package manager: ql:quickload fetches a library from a curated, versioned distribution
✅ ASDF orders the build: defsystem declares dependencies, so a build is reproducible
✅ A long history of libraries for symbolic work: AI, NLP, and theorem-proving packages reach back decades
⚠️ Library maintenance varies: Some widely used libraries are stable but low-activity, so a project may need to vendor or fork them



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The standard is stable: ANSI X3.226-1994 has not changed, so conforming code keeps working
✅ Implementations evolve without breaking the standard core: SBCL and CCL add capability in their own packages
⚠️ The standard is frozen, so new needs are met by extensions: Modern features arrive as implementation extensions or libraries, so a project couples to one implementation to use them
⚠️ Conservative evolution keeps legacy conventions alive: Slow change leaves older idioms and library styles in current use
❌ Build variants multiply: #+ and #- reader conditionals select which forms read, and the feature set is the build’s, not the file’s (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for AI and symbolic computation: List processing, macros, and CLOS suit symbolic algorithms
✅ Strong for exploratory, image-based work: The REPL and save-lisp-and-die images fit incremental development
✅ CLOS multiple dispatch fits multi-argument domains: Simulation and rule systems that dispatch on several arguments map onto it directly
⚠️ Poorly suited for modern web and systems development: The ecosystem has little of the tooling mainstream web and systems work expects
⚠️ Numeric and low-level work is uncommon: Collection and dynamic typing make it unusual for kernels and HPC



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep: Parentheses-heavy syntax and the macro system must both be learned (L1)
✅ The core forms are few and regular: defun, let, lambda, cond, quote, and cons build most programs
✅ The image gives immediate feedback: A form is evaluated in the running image, so a mistake surfaces at once
⚠️ Macros are the hard second step: Understanding expansion, hygiene, and evaluation order takes practice
⚠️ loop and format are mini-languages: These widely used forms are learned separately from the core



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Parentheses are dense: Deep nesting is hard to read without an editor that matches and highlights delimiters (S3)
✅ S-expressions are uniform: Code and data share one representation, so there is no grammar beyond lists
✅ Prefix notation removes precedence rules: (+ a (* b c)) states the order explicitly
✅ loop provides a prose-like layer where wanted: (loop for x in xs collect (* x 2)) reads almost as English
⚠️ Reader macros add notation: #(...), backquote, comma, and #' are terse and easy to confuse



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The image supports interactive testing: A function is redefined and re-run without a restart
✅ FiveAM and Prove provide test frameworks: Both are available through Quicklisp
✅ assert and check-type are in the standard: A program states and checks an invariant without a library
✅ Conditions let a test assert on a failure class: handler-case and handler-bind distinguish the condition type
⚠️ No test runner is in the standard: The harness is a library, so a suite couples to it



1.2.8 Security

✅ Typed objects and a collector give memory safety: References are checked, and unreachable memory is reclaimed
✅ No raw pointers in the standard: A program cannot forge an address without implementation-specific foreign interfaces
❌ Dynamic typing permits type-confusion bugs: A value of the wrong type is a run-time error, and an unchecked path can act on the wrong shape
⚠️ read and eval execute data: (eval (read ...)) on untrusted input is code execution, and the reader’s #. form evaluates at read time
⚠️ CFFI bypasses the safety model: A foreign call can reach arbitrary native code, so safety at that boundary is the programmer’s concern

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ ASDF systems build from whatever the image and source-registry hold. (Y1)
❌ Quicklisp resolves distribution versions at load time. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin exists; the implementation version is a fact of the machine. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Quicklisp distributions carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The package registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Quicklisp systems. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ format and standard-output carry no structure by contract. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ Each image carries its own debugger; the ANSI condition system is the shared part.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs where its implementation and image run. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No vendor owns ANSI Common Lisp; the community maintains implementations in the open. (Y11)
✅ ANSI INCITS 226 publishes the standard. (Y12)
✅ The ANSI CL test suite is published for independent implementations to run. (Y17)
✅ SBCL, CCL, and CLISP are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Common Lisp decouples syntax, dispatch, and error handling well: S-expressions make code and data one representation, macros expand notation without changing the evaluator, CLOS methods dispatch on any number of argument types, and the condition system separates signalling, handling, and restarting. Core coupling stays high because typing is dynamic, global functions and special variables tie modules together implicitly, and every value lives on a collected heap. The platform dimension is middling: several mature native compilers plus Quicklisp and ASDF for distribution, but a small ecosystem fragmented across implementations, a standard frozen since 1994, and a steep learning curve built on parentheses and macros.

title: Ada (2022 / 2012)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ada in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 84.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.2/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing rejects mismatched use at compile time: Every object, parameter, and function result carries a declared type, so an incompatible assignment or call is a compile error, not a run-time surprise
✅ Subtypes and range constraints narrow the value set: A subtype refines a base type with a range or index constraint, and a value outside it raises Constraint_Error at the boundary
✅ Variant records declare a sum type: A case part in a record declaration selects on a discriminant, so the alternatives are a closed, compiler-checked set
✅ Generic units decouple an algorithm from the types it operates on: A generic declaration names formal types and subprograms, and an instantiation binds them without editing the generic body
✅ Access values are checked: Dereferencing a null access value raises Constraint_Error, no pointer arithmetic is possible, and access designates a typed object
⚠️ Operator overloading makes a symbol mean whatever its package declares: Defining "+" or "=" for a private type is legal, so a reader must resolve an operator from the package that declares it (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Package specification and body are separate units: package X is ... end X; declares the visible interface and package body X holds the implementation, so a client compiles against the declaration
✅ Private types hide the representation: private and limited private make the record fields invisible outside the package, so callers cannot couple to the layout
✅ Child units extend a parent without reopening it: package X.Y adds declarations in its own unit, so a subsystem grows without an edit to the parent body
✅ Constructors are ordinary functions: function Make (...) return T creates a value with no allocation and no special constructor syntax, so creation does not couple to a memory strategy
❌ Variables are mutable unless declared constant: There is no immutability by default, so a package body holds state that clients can reach and every call must re-establish (C2)
⚠️ Library-level variables share one elaboration order: A variable declared in a package body is initialised once, so a client’s behaviour depends on when that elaboration runs
❌ One value, many names: access types designate shared objects, and the parameter mode names copy semantics, not an alias set — the named flow contract is SPARK’s, not Ada’s (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: a controlled type’s Adjust runs at an assignment the source shows as a plain assignment, and dispatching calls resolve at run time to a body the site does not name (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No garbage collector in the standard: The storage of a declared object is reclaimed at scope exit, so reclamation timing is not coupled to a collector’s pauses
✅ Controlled types give deterministic finalisation: A type derived from Ada.Finalization.Controlled runs Initialize, Adjust, and Finalize at defined points, giving RAII-style cleanup
✅ Storage pools decouple allocation from the type: Storage_Pool and Storage_Size are set per access type, so the allocator changes without a change to any client
✅ Representation clauses fix layout where needed: Size, Alignment, and Bit_Order state the representation explicitly, so memory layout is declared rather than inferred
⚠️ Unchecked_Deallocation is manual: An object created with new on the standard heap is released only by an explicit call to Ada.Unchecked_Deallocation, so lifetime is the programmer’s duty
⚠️ There is no ownership model: An access value can outlive its designated object after a deallocation, and the compiler does not prevent it
✅ Reinterpretation is a named artifact: each Unchecked_Conversion is an explicit instantiation over one type pair, reviewable and provable in SPARK (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: storage exhaustion raises Program_Error outside recoverable scope (documented) and can end the partition (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Exceptions are named and scoped: An exception section handles by exception identity with when E : Some_Error =>, so recovery does not depend on an error code
✅ Language-defined checks raise exceptions instead of corrupting memory: Range, index, discriminant, and access checks raise Constraint_Error or Program_Error at the point of violation
✅ Contracts raise Assertion_Error at the boundary: The Ada 2012 aspects Pre and Post and type invariants check a subprogram against its callers
✅ An exception carries diagnostic strings: Ada.Exceptions.Exception_Message and Exception_Information attach a message and a state snapshot to an occurrence
❌ No composable result type: A fallible operation reports through raise, so a caller cannot thread a success-or-failure value through an ordinary expression (Er4)
⚠️ pragma Suppress removes checks: Suppressing a check removes the exception with it, trading safety for speed
✅ The runtime publishes the isolation unit: an unraised exception terminates the task that raised it (RM 11.1, documented), and the partition survives the task (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Tasking is part of the language: task, task type, protected objects, and entries give concurrency without an external library
✅ Rendezvous decouples communication from shared memory: A caller and a task meet at an entry and exchange parameters directly, so the task’s data need not be globally visible
✅ Protected objects serialise access without hand-written locks: A protected body runs one action at a time, so the program does not write mutex code
✅ select states waiting and timeouts declaratively: select ... or accept, or delay, and else express the waiting alternatives in the construct
✅ Annex D states the real-time policy in code: pragma Priority, pragma Task_Dispatching_Policy (FIFO_Within_Priorities), and pragma Locking_Policy (Ceiling_Locking) declare priorities and locking
⚠️ Tasking couples a program to a run-time library: The GNAT run time and the chosen profile decide which tasking constructs exist



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The language is an international standard: ISO/IEC 8652 defines the language and ISO/IEC 18009 defines conformity, so no single vendor owns it
✅ Several independent compilers exist: GNAT (FSF and AdaCore) and other implementations compile the same standard
✅ Restricted profiles target bare hardware: pragma Profile (Ravenscar) and No_Tasking remove constructs a small target cannot support
✅ Hardware access is a language feature: pragma Import, pragma Export, and representation clauses reach registers and foreign code directly
⚠️ Certified toolchains are few: DO-178C qualification kits and ARINC 653 bindings come from a small set of vendors, among them AdaCore, DDC-I (SCORE-Ada on Deos), and Green Hills (AdaMULTI), so a certified build couples to one of them
⚠️ Outside the certified targets, porting is unusual: An untested platform gets few guarantees, because few ports are exercised
❌ The fit outside its niche is poor: Web, data-science, and scripting work have little Ada support (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Verbosity is a deliberate trade: begin/end pairs and spelled-out names make each construct readable at the cost of keystrokes; that is a style choice, not a dependency forced on a caller
Restricted profiles are a scope decision: pragma Profile (Ravenscar) removes dynamic task creation to make a program analysable, trading flexibility for a schedulability bound
No garbage collector is a scope decision: The standard leaves reclamation to the program, which suits real-time work and gives up the convenience of a collector
Ada is not a scripting language: Compilation and the Alire package manager assume a build step, which is a scope boundary rather than a defect
Certification effort is a process cost: DO-178C evidence follows from the domain’s safety obligation, not from a property of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Ahead-of-time native compilation: GNAT emits machine code, so no interpreter and no JIT warm-up sits on the critical path
✅ No garbage collector: Reclamation is deterministic, so no collector pause enters a control loop
✅ Inlining and representation clauses give explicit control: pragma Inline, Size, and Address let a program fix code and layout where latency demands it
✅ The real-time policy is declared in code: Priority and locking pragmas state the scheduling behaviour the program assumes
⚠️ Checks cost run time unless suppressed: Range, index, and access checks are cheap but not free, and pragma Suppress trades them away
⚠️ The GNAT run time is large for small targets: A tasking-enabled build needs the run time, so bare-metal work uses the restricted profiles



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and niche: Alire and the available library set are a fraction of what mainstream languages offer (Ec3)
✅ GNAT is mature and production-quality: The same front end serves FSF GNAT and AdaCore’s GNAT Pro, and certified projects depend on it
✅ Alire provides a package manager: alr resolves dependencies and pins toolchains, so a project build is reproducible
✅ Reference material is complete and stable: The Ada Reference Manual (ISO/IEC 8652:2023), the Rationale, and the SPARK documentation are authoritative and long-lived
⚠️ The community is small: A developer usually meets Ada through an employer’s code base rather than through a public library ecosystem
❌ No object-code promise across compiler releases: GNAT records the dependence graph in the .ali file, and the link step binds that pair to the same compiler release [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: Ada 2022 followed Ada 2012 by about a decade, so a needed feature waits for a revision (V4)
✅ Backward compatibility is strong: Ada 2012 and Ada 2022 add features and keep earlier conforming code compiling
✅ GNAT tracks the current standard: The compiler implements the latest revision and the certification profiles
⚠️ A new feature reaches users through GNAT: Adoption follows the compiler release cycle rather than the standard’s publication
❌ Build variants multiply: GNAT ships the documented -pp C-style preprocessor, and guarded units select which declarations compile (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for safety-critical and real-time systems: Avionics, defense, rail, and space projects use Ada with DO-178C evidence
✅ Annex D and the Ravenscar profile cover hard real-time work: Priorities, ceiling locking, and static scheduling are language-level concerns
✅ Representation clauses reach embedded hardware: Registers and device layouts are declared, not accessed through undefined behaviour
⚠️ Certification artifacts are domain-specific: A DO-178C evidence set is not reusable in another regulated domain without rework



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The language is steep: Tasking, generics, representation clauses, contracts, and the Annexes present several distinct models (L1)
❌ The surface is large: The standard library, the Annexes, and the profiles add to the core language (L2)
✅ Reference material is comprehensive: The Reference Manual states every construct, and the SPARK documentation covers the proof subset
✅ A regular syntax helps after the first step: Statements end in ; and blocks are delimited by keywords, so there is no precedence puzzle
⚠️ Tasking is the hardest single topic: The rendezvous model and protected objects take practice to use well
⚠️ Mentors are scarce: The small community gives fewer examples and reviews than mainstream languages offer



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose: begin/end pairs, full keywords, and repeated identifiers make even small programs long (S1)
✅ English-like and consistent: Ada.Text_IO.Put_Line ("x") reads as prose, and keywords are reserved words
✅ Block structure is explicit: Every construct closes with a keyword, so a reader never counts indentation
⚠️ Identifiers are Mixed_Case with underscores: The convention differs from camelCase and snake_case neighbours, though it is uniform
⚠️ Qualified names add verbosity: A fully qualified call such as Ada.Text_IO.New_Line is long where use clauses are avoided



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Contracts are executable: pragma Assert, the Pre and Post aspects, and pragma Assertion_Policy check invariants in the built program
✅ GNAT ships a test-generation tool: gnattest generates AUnit test skeletons from a package specification
✅ GNATprove proves the stated contracts on the SPARK subset: Sequential and concurrent SPARK code can be proved free of run-time errors
✅ GNATcoverage measures coverage: The tool reports statement and branch coverage for certification evidence
⚠️ No test framework is in the language: AUnit and gnattest are tools, so a suite couples to the GNAT toolchain



1.2.8 Security

✅ Typing and checks prevent memory misuse: Array, range, discriminant, and access checks catch violations before they become memory errors
✅ The standard defines the effect of constructs: Within the defined subsets there is no undefined behaviour, and SPARK removes the remaining cases
✅ No pointer arithmetic: An access value designates a typed object, so an address cannot be incremented into another object
✅ SPARK proves absence of run-time errors: The subset supports proof of freedom from run-time errors and of the stated contracts
⚠️ Unchecked_Conversion and System.Address re-open the unsafe surface: These features can defeat the type system where a program uses them

✅ The ACVS conformance suite runs against validated implementations. (Y17)
✅ GNAT is public source in the GCC tree. (Y19)

Verdict: Ada’s own constructs impose little coupling: strong static typing, package specification and body separation, generic units, tasking with protected objects, and Ada 2012 contracts each separate a caller from the thing it depends on. The cost sits in the platform and ecosystem dimension, where the language is verbose, the standard moves slowly, the library base is small, and tasking plus the Annexes take a long time to learn. For safety-critical and real-time work Ada is close to ideal; outside that niche the small ecosystem is the dominant cost.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
Under a single partitioning rule, a module can deviate in exactly two ways: it can hold elements that do not belong, or it can be missing elements that do. These defects are independent — a module can have either, both, or neither — and they demand opposite repairs. That structure forces the answer to a natural question: how many numbers must a cohesion metric report?
This page proves that the answer is two. One axis cannot distinguish the two failure modes; two axes can; and no third axis adds anything for this purpose. The pair — purity and completeness — is the minimal adequate output for a rule.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
1 One rule, two opposite defects
Fix a partitioning rule PP [1] and assess a module MM against the class CC it should realize.

Impurity. MM contains an element outside CC. The remedy is to remove it — to split.
Incompleteness. Some element of CC lies outside MM. The remedy is to add it — to merge.

Write the two axes as
purity(M)=|M∩C||M|,completeness(M)=|M∩C||C|.
\text{purity}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|M|},
\qquad
\text{completeness}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|C|}.

Both lie in [0,1][0,1]. The two defects are independent in the strict sense: all four combinations occur.

The two failure modes point in opposite directions. Merely knowing that “cohesion is low” is therefore of no help: the correct action could be to split or to merge, and the two actions are opposites.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
2 One axis is not enough

Proposition (dimensional necessity). Let s(M)=g(purity(M),completeness(M))s(M) = g(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) be any scalar that factors through the pair. (a) If gg is symmetric, there are two modules of opposite defect whose scores are exactly equal. (b) If gg is continuous and strictly increasing in each argument, the two defect classes are indistinguishable to any finite precision, and no threshold on the score separates them.

Proof. Fix a rule with a class CC of size 44, and four foreign elements x1,…,x4x_1,\dots,x_4 from another class.

M1=C∪{x1,…,x4}M_1 = C \cup \{x_1,\dots,x_4\} has purity=4/8=1/2\text{purity} = 4/8 = 1/2 and completeness=4/4=1\text{completeness} = 4/4 = 1: impure but complete.
M2={a,b}M_2 = \{a,b\} for a,b∈Ca,b \in C has purity=2/2=1\text{purity} = 2/2 = 1 and completeness=2/4=1/2\text{completeness} = 2/4 = 1/2: pure but incomplete.

Both are realizable in one system.
(a) A symmetric gg gives s(M1)=g(1/2,1)=g(1,1/2)=s(M2)s(M_1) = g(1/2, 1) = g(1, 1/2) = s(M_2) — exactly equal scores for opposite defects. The geometric mean pc\sqrt{pc} scores both at 1/21/\sqrt{2}; so does the arithmetic mean, and every other symmetric aggregate.
(b) The impure-but-complete modules trace the curve B1={(p,1):0<p<1}B_1 = \{(p,1) : 0<p<1\}; the pure-but-incomplete modules trace B2={(1,c):0<c<1}B_2 = \{(1,c) : 0<c<1\}. Strict monotonicity makes g(1,1)g(1,1) the supremum of gg on both curves; continuity makes each image g(B1)g(B_1), g(B2)g(B_2) an interval with that same supremum. Two intervals with a common supremum overlap, so some (p*,1)∈B1(p^*,1) \in B_1 and some (1,c*)∈B2(1,c^*) \in B_2 satisfy g(p*,1)=g(1,c*)g(p^*,1) = g(1,c^*). An impure-complete module and a pure-incomplete module therefore share the same score, and their images approach one another without limit as either defect shrinks. No threshold on the score line can separate “split” from “merge.” ◼\blacksquare
This is why “low cohesion” as a single graded quantity cannot guide a repair. The score is monotonically related to both faults, but it cannot tell the designer which of the two is present — the one thing the designer needs to act.
A caveat keeps the claim honest. The impossibility is for scalars that behave as measurements — symmetric, or continuous and monotone in the two axes. A pathologically discontinuous injection could in principle pack the pair into one real number, but such a function is not a score: it carries no magnitude or ordering that corresponds to defect severity, and it does not arise from the purity/completeness semantics. Every actual cohesion score — a product, a mean, a weighted sum, a distance from the ideal — is continuous and monotone, and every one of them falls to the proposition.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
3 Two axes are enough
The pair not only fails to lose information — it loses none that matters. It determines the failure mode exactly.

Proposition (sufficiency). The pair (purity(M),completeness(M))(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) determines which of the four states a module is in.

Proof. Two equivalences, immediate from the definitions.

purity(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|M|⇔M⊆C\text{purity}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |M| \iff M \subseteq C: no element of MM lies outside its class, i.e. MM is pure.
completeness(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|C|⇔C⊆M\text{completeness}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |C| \iff C \subseteq M: no member of the class lies outside MM, i.e. MM is complete.

So the pair (p,c)(p,c) reports, coordinate by coordinate, whether the module is impure (p<1p<1) and whether it is incomplete (c<1c<1) — the two booleans the remedy depends on. The four cases of the table are read off directly, and with them the correct action. ◼\blacksquare
Together the two propositions give the result: one axis is insufficient; two axes are sufficient. For a single rule, two metrics are necessary and enough.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
4 Why exactly two — not three
Two axes are the minimum, and they are also the maximum needed for the failure-mode question, because a partition admits exactly two failure modes.
The reasoning is a counting one. Relative to the class CC, each element of the module is either inside CC or outside it, and each member of CC is either inside MM or outside it. Two independent questions therefore arise — does MM hold foreign elements? and is MM missing class members? — and they are independent because all four combinations are achievable (the table above exhibits each). To determine the failure mode is to answer both booleans; two coordinates answer two independent booleans minimally. A third coordinate could describe the module more finely (which elements are foreign, how the class is scattered), but it would carry no additional information about which failure mode applies — the axis count the schema requires.
This is why a pairwise, two-axis reading is the correct working form, not a convenience: it is exactly the dimension at which the failure mode becomes visible and no further.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
5 Many rules, many pairs
A system is often assessed under several partitioning rules at once — logical structure, deployment, security, platform. Each rule is its own partition of the same element set, and each admits the same two failure modes, so each contributes its own (purity, completeness) pair. For kk rules the cohesion profile is the 2k2k-tuple of pairs [1].
The necessity argument applies rule by rule: one number cannot serve a single rule, so one number certainly cannot serve the joint requirement. And the pairs are genuinely irreducible across rules. When two rules cross-cut — neither refines the other — placement under one carries no information about placement under the other. The same physical placement can be correct under one rule and wrong under another, and a repair that improves one pair can degrade another. Each rule must be read on its own terms.
When one rule refines another, the pairs are still both needed: the coarse rule frames the fine one, and a clean finer-rule pair does not vouch for the coarser placement that contains it. The coarse pair is load-bearing and must be read first.
The general form, then: two axes per rule; 2k2k axes for kk rules. Collapsing across rules to a single scalar repeats, one level up, the error the proposition already rules out within a rule — it discards the distinction between defects that call for opposite actions.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
6 Where this comes from
The two-axis structure is Condition 4 (adequate dimensionality) of the cohesion metric conditions, and the 2k2k-tuple is the cohesion profile, both developed in On the Nature of Cohesion [1]. The companion page Why cohesion has no scalar metric extends the same obstruction from diagnosis to the placement verdict: a scalar cannot decide whether an element is misplaced, and any scalar that appears to is the rule in disguise.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
The cohesion survey [1] reviews every metric in the literature that carries a “cohesion” label: 24 metrics, from LCOM1 (1994) to MOGA (2010). Its finding is stark: every one of them measures a structural property of the code — shared fields, call connections, dependency edges, execution traces — and none measures cohesion itself. The proliferation is itself a symptom: the field has never agreed on what cohesion is, so each metric chose a different structural graph to stand in for the concept.
This page summarizes what each metric actually measures. For the series’ positive account — cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule — see core conclusions.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
1 Measuring cohesion by its absence
The best-known family is literally named for a lack: LCOM stands for Lack of Cohesion in Methods. Higher LCOM means less cohesion. This is not a polarity quirk that a sign change would fix. An LCOM variant counts something structural — method pairs that do not share fields, connected components that are absent — and negating the score yields only the negation of the proxy, not cohesion.
There is a deeper confusion beneath the naming. Every LCOM variant operates on the method–attribute access graph: the raw input is a coupling relation. LCOM counts pairs for which that coupling does not hold and reports the count as cohesion. By its own data, the LCOM family is a family of coupling metrics that have been called cohesion metrics since their origin.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
3 Why this matters
The metrics differ in which coupling relation they extract, which transformation they apply, and which normalisation they prefer. They do not differ in what they measure: all measure coupling and report it as cohesion.
This has three practical consequences, developed in the survey:

The cohesion–coupling tradeoff is an artifact of measurement convention. Cohesion metrics count internal edges and coupling metrics count cross-boundary edges of the same graph. Designers balancing the two are balancing one dependency relation against itself under two labels.
A high score can mask a mess. When elements that belong apart happen to share many fields or call each other, LCOM, TCC, and LCC all report high cohesion. Structurally cohesive modules receive a quality signal the metric cannot support.
LCOM-triggered refactoring can reward the wrong direction. Standard heuristics treat LCOM thresholds as extract-class triggers. But LCOM detects structural clustering, not principled misgrouping.

None of this makes the metrics useless. Correlation with fault-proneness and maintenance effort has been reported across multiple studies, so structural scores work as screening heuristics and change predictors. The limitation is interpretative: the score measures coupling density, and domain knowledge about grouping conditions is needed to say more.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
section: 4 Where the series goes from here
text:
4 Where the series goes from here
The survey establishes the negative result: no structural metric measures principled cohesion. Later papers in the cohesion series give cohesion a positive definition — correctness relative to a partitioning rule — and derive a metric from the reason elements change rather than from the footprint of their co-location. See core conclusions and knowledge embodiment.

title: Cohesion

1 Where cohesion sits
Cohesion and coupling are the two classical “quality” measures of modular structure. The cohesion series gives cohesion a principled definition: correctness relative to a partitioning rule [1]. The coupling page does the same for coupling — and shows that within any single dimension, coupling is a consequence of cohesion, not an independent objective.
Cohesion is distinct from IVP, though the two are related. IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment. Cohesion is the more general measure of correctness relative to any partitioning rule. The change-driver rule is one instance of that general idea — the instance IVP is built on.
