Both draw on twenty threads by default, and executeBlocking is ordered by default, so tasks from one context run one at a time. Blocking work leaves the loop; its concurrency and ordering move into two settings nobody wrote down.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The offload does not remove the limit; it relocates it to two settings: pool size and ordering. The worker pool is the concurrency limit for everything that blocks, and its queue is where latency accumulates. Ordering is the second half: an ordered flag serialises independent work, and dependent work marked unordered returns out of sequence.
The gap question: which code blocks — measured — and what pool size keeps the worker queue bounded?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Blocking segments offloaded deliberately — a legacy driver, a render, a filesystem sweep — onto a named pool sized from measured concurrency. Each path states its ordering requirement, and queue depth is watched at peak.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



executeBlocking wrapped around everything to make handlers safe. The pool becomes an unsized thread pool, raised to a hundred threads to stop queueing. Ordering flips quietly: a path that needs sequence is marked unordered, or one that could parallelise keeps the default and serialises, and the results arrive in an order nobody can re-sequence. It reads as non-blocking and behaves as an unmeasured pool.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which code blocks — measured — and what pool size keeps the worker queue bounded?

If yes → the offload is a stated fact. Confirm the pool covers concurrent blocking segments at peak, and each path’s ordering flag matches its callers.
If no → both the pool and the order are guesses. Size the pool from measured concurrency, and state per path whether results may arrive out of sequence.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure each blocking segment’s hold time, and how many are in flight at peak.




#VertX #Java #WorkerVerticles #ThreadPools #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
text:
Case study: Event loop count
A pod with a two-CPU request and no CPU limit starts sixteen event loops, because the JVM sees the host’s eight cores and the default doubles them.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Vert.x sizes its event loop pool, by default, at twice the processors the JVM reports, and each loop is one thread carrying many connections. The number is the process’s unit of parallelism. Too few loops and the cores idle; too many and the threads compete for a quota they never had. The processor count the JVM reports follows the cgroup quota — a CPU request without a limit leaves it reading the host.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The setting encodes a claim about CPU: this process owns that many cores, and all of them may serve handlers. In a container that claim must come from the cgroup, not the host, and even then it is half the fact — workers, GC and any sidecar draw on the same quota. The team must know the quota, then decide how much of it the loops may claim.
The gap question: how many loops does this process actually run — and does that match the quota rather than the host?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The loop count is set explicitly from the CPU quota and logged at startup beside the worker pool size. Utilization stays low at peak, and task durations stay short — a blocked loop also runs idle.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A two-CPU request without a limit running sixteen loops because the host has eight cores and the default doubles them. Nothing fails outright: latency spikes at random, the throttling counter climbs, and every trace blames the database. Or the quota shrinks in a later release and the loop count is never revisited, because the two numbers live in different repositories.








TipThe faithfulness test



How many loops does this process actually run — and does that match the quota rather than the host?

If yes → the loop count is a stated fact. Check that workers and heap were sized against the same quota, then watch throttling.
If no → the loops compete for CPU they do not have. Set the count from the quota, leaving headroom for workers and GC.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Read the loop count at startup, the quota from the cgroup, and the throttling counter under load.




#VertX #Java #Containers #Kubernetes #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
text:
Case study: Backpressure
A slow client never raises an error. It just grows the server’s outgoing buffer until the heap does.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A write returns before the bytes leave. Each connection holds a queue of pending writes, and writeQueueFull turns true when that queue passes its maximum; a drain handler fires when it falls back to half. Check the queue and it stays bounded while a consumer catches up; skip the check and that queue is the heap.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
Backpressure claims some producer can outrun some consumer. That is a fact about the workload — a result set streamed to a mobile client, a fan-out to a reporting replica — and it is invisible in a test where the client reads at server speed. The team must know which paths produce faster than they consume, and which sources can be paused.
The gap question: what bounds the in-flight bytes to a slow consumer — stated — and is it tested with a throttled peer?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Streaming writes where every path checks the queue, sets a drain handler that resumes, and pauses the source while the queue is full. Bytes in flight per connection stay at the bound, memory is flat against a deliberately throttled consumer, and the bound is a chosen number.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Rows written without a queue check, because the local client was fast. The slow client’s buffer grows to the whole result set, a hundred such clients finish the heap, and the crash points at an allocation unrelated to the peer. The second variant: an upload read into memory because nothing paused the request. The code reads as streaming, because each chunk is written.








TipThe faithfulness test



What bounds the in-flight bytes to a slow consumer — stated — and is it tested with a throttled peer?

If yes → backpressure is a stated bound. Check it is enforced on every write path, and the throttled-peer test runs in the suite.
If no → the bound is the heap. Add the queue check and drain handler, pause the source while the queue is full, and state the maximum.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure bytes buffered per connection against a throttled consumer, and the largest result it can stream.




#VertX #Java #Backpressure #Streaming #Memory #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: Deployment instances per verticle
text:
Case study: Deployment instances per verticle
An in-memory counter deployed with eight instances is eight counters, and seven of them count for nobody.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: setInstances deploys N copies of a verticle across the event loop threads; each copy has its own fields. The count is a parallelism claim: N instances may serve handlers at once, and no two share an instance field — static state is common to all of them. Instances buy throughput, and every field becomes per-instance state whether meant or not.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The setting asserts two facts: the work per message is independent, and nothing the verticle holds may be visible to another message on another thread. Both are properties of the workload. The team must know what state the verticle holds and who reads it, then choose the count from that answer, not the core count.
The gap question: does this verticle hold state — and is the instance count consistent with that answer, by design?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Stateless verticles at N instances, the count set from the CPU quota because the parallelism is real. Stateful ones held at a single instance, or their state moved to a shared store or map, with each field’s scope written beside the deployment.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An in-memory counter — a rate limiter, a cache, a session map — deployed with eight instances because scaling out looked right. Every increment lands in one instance, the dashboard reads one of the eight, and the tests pass on a laptop at one instance. The number is wrong by a factor of eight and nothing throws. The other variant is as quiet: one instance for safety, so one thread carries the traffic.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does this verticle hold state — and is the instance count consistent with that answer, by design?

If yes → instances and state agree. Check that no field assumes a single writer across messages, and the count still matches the CPU quota.
If no → the count and the state contradict. Either take the state out of the instance, or set the count to one and say why.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every field on the verticle, mark each mutable or constant, and name which component reads it.




#VertX #Java #Verticles #Scaling #StateManagement #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: The event bus and its scope
text:
Case study: The event bus and its scope
A clustered event bus delivers a message once and keeps nothing — and three services treat it as a queue that survives a restart.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Vert.x has one EventBus API and two scopes. Local passes messages between verticles inside one JVM, often by reference. Clustered sends the same call over a network transport. The scope changes the route, not the promise: at-most-once, no bus persistence, no bus redelivery after a node dies. The calling code is identical.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The bus promises ordering between one sender and one receiver, and that a registered handler runs. No arrival is promised. Whether a lost message is acceptable is a fact about the workload, never about the bus. The gap question: does any consumer here need the message to arrive after a crash?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Intra-process decoupling. A verticle announces an order was placed; three local handlers update their own state; a lost event costs nothing because that state rebuilds from the database. The claim is local and best-effort, and the bus is exactly that claim.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The clustered bus as a work queue. Work goes to a worker verticle on another node, the sender moves on, nothing records the job. The node restarts mid-job and the work is gone, because no retry was ever designed. It has a bus, an address, and a handler, so it reads as messaging. It is a fire-and-forget network call to an address, with no ledger.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each bus message: what delivery guarantee does it need — stated — and what does this bus actually provide?

If yes → the bus is the shape the claim requires. Confirm no consumer’s correctness rests on redelivery, and that a lost message is recoverable from another source.
If no → a broker buys durability at the cost of a component to run. Keep the bus for best-effort paths; route durable messages to the broker.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every message this bus carries and mark each one durable or best-effort.




#VertX #Java #EventBus #Messaging #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: Shared data, local versus cluster-wide
text:
Case study: Shared data, local versus cluster-wide
One network hop per read, times your request rate: the cluster-wide “cache” now answers over the network what the heap answered for free.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Vert.x SharedData offers a local map and a cluster-wide map behind one API. The local map reads in heap with no encoding. The cluster-wide map serialises every value and crosses the cluster manager on each operation, so a read is a roundtrip and a write is a roundtrip plus replication.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The choice is a claim about who needs the truth. Local says: this process is the only reader whose freshness matters. Cluster-wide says: every node must see the same value, and the domain pays a hop for it. The gap question: must a node see a write made on another node, or must it read fast?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Hot read paths use the local map: a per-node lookup table, flags refreshed by an event, a counter only this node’s handlers touch. Nobody asked for cross-node consistency, so the local map states the fact. The cluster-wide map earns its hop where staleness is a bug — a leader flag, a token held by exactly one node, a drain switch whose wrong value corrupts work.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The cluster-wide map used as a cache. Someone adds a lookup table to shared data to stop hitting the database, and every read becomes serialisation plus a hop, inside the handler that could have read the heap. Latency budget spent on lookups, plus a codec cost nobody measured. It reads as a cache and bills as a remote call.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who reads this map, how often, from where — measured — and does it need cross-node truth or local speed?

If yes → confirm the reads are off the hot path, and count the hops each request pays. Verify the hit rate beats the hop, not just the database query.
If no → split it. Local map for the hot reads, cluster-wide only for the few values whose staleness is a correctness bug.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Instrument reads per node per second, then the tolerable staleness of each value.




#VertX #Java #SharedData #Caching #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: Future and Promise composition
text:
Case study: Future and Promise composition
One compose step forgets to complete its promise, and the caller does not fail — it waits, holding a connection, until a timeout that may not exist.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A Promise is the writable end, a Future the readable one. Compose, map, and recover chain steps without blocking a thread. The chain is one error channel: the first failure skips every downstream step until a recovery claims it — and a step that never fails its promise stops every step after it.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
Composition moves the failure path into the shape of the chain, away from the code you read. Each link is a claim about who owns the error. Recover turns a failure into a value; otherwise supplies a fallback value; no handler means the error is dropped and nobody hears it. The gap question: for each link, who receives the failure — a named handler, or no one?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Recovery composed exactly where the domain names it. A cache lookup fails and recover serves the database read, because the cache was always optional. A metrics call fails and otherwise completes with an empty result, because metrics are not load-bearing. The fallback is a decision written where it applies, not scattered.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The chain with a lost failure. A middle step calls an async API, subscribes with onSuccess only, and never completes its own promise on error. Upstream fails, downstream never starts, the promise stays pending, the request hangs. Nothing looks wrong: a handler exists, a chain exists, no exception is thrown. The error died inside the chain, and the symptom appears as latency.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each composed chain: who handles the failure path — named — or does the error die inside the future?

If yes → check each link completes or fails its promise on every branch, including the branches that throw.
If no → add a recovery at the boundary that owns the decision, and fail the promise in every terminal branch, not just the happy one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Count the futures that can stay pending, and the timeout that would end each one.




#VertX #Java #Futures #ErrorHandling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: Non-blocking database clients versus the JDBC bridge
text:
Case study: Non-blocking database clients versus the JDBC bridge
Every handler is non-blocking, the event loop never stalls, the dashboard is green — and the JDBC bridge pool is the wall the service hits.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Two database clients wear the same API shape. The reactive client speaks the wire protocol itself and never blocks. The JDBC bridge wraps a blocking driver and runs each query on a worker thread from a pool. One occupies no thread per query; the other occupies one for the whole roundtrip.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
The bridge is not a lie, it is a borrow. It says: this driver blocks, so lend me a thread from a pool you must size, and the loop stays safe. The claim it encodes is that the pool is the real concurrency limit for the database. The gap question: how many queries are in flight at peak, and how large is the worker pool under the bridge?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The bridge where the driver forces it: a database with no reactive client, a vendor driver only JDBC exposes, a nightly batch far from the hot path. The bridge’s pool is sized from measured in-flight queries and kept separate from the general worker pool.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The reactive application whose data layer is the bridge. Twenty worker threads, five hundred concurrent requests, the rest waiting on a queue nobody sized. Latency climbs while CPU idles, and the trace blames a database that is healthy. It reads as reactive because the call returns a Future. It behaves as a thread pool with extra steps.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which database client is actually non-blocking — verified — and what pool sits under the bridge, sized how?

If yes → count in-flight queries at peak against the pool, and confirm the bridge pool is separate from the general worker pool.
If no → the loop is safe but the path is not non-blocking end to end. Measure the wait, then either adopt the reactive client or size the bridge deliberately.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure concurrent queries at peak, then the time each one occupies its thread.




#VertX #Java #Reactive #JDBC #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Vert.x and the Event Loop
section: Case study: HTTP client connection pool sizing
text:
Case study: HTTP client connection pool sizing
Fifty concurrent calls, a default pool of five connections, and forty-five callers queueing on a limit nobody chose.
Writing a Vert.x handler? Ask “which claim does this design make about blocking — what may wait, and what may never wait?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the event loop enforces a guess. If you can, the design is knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The Vert.x HTTP client keeps pooled connections per endpoint, and WebClient sits on it. Reuse is the point: a pooled socket beats a handshake. Max pool size caps the connections; requests beyond the cap wait in a queue. Idle and keep-alive timeouts decide when a socket is dropped. They must end before the server ends its own, or the pool hands out sockets the server is closing.


The Vert.x knowledge gap it signals
Pool size is a claim about measured concurrency, never about caution. Reuse assumes calls are frequent enough to beat a handshake. The queue assumes the wait costs less than the alternative. Neither is free, and both are decisions. The gap question: what is the peak concurrent call count per endpoint, at the peak hour?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The pool is sized above the measured concurrent-call count and states a wait policy: bounded queue with a fast failure, or unbounded with a measured timeout. Timeouts are set together — connect, request, and idle below the server’s keep-alive.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The default small pool under real load. Nobody set the maximum, so it stays at five; the wait queue has no bound and no policy; the p99 belongs to the queue, not to the service. Then the idle timeout outlives the load balancer’s: the first call on a stale socket fails as a read timeout, and the retries read as flakiness. Somebody did set a timeout, so it looks tuned. Nothing was sized. Under HTTP/2 one connection multiplexes streams, which moves the bound from sockets to streams — not away from it.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured concurrent-call count per client — and is the pool above it, with a stated wait policy?

If yes → check the idle timeout against the server’s, and that the queue bound fails fast instead of growing silently.
If no → the pool is the bottleneck by construction. Raise it to the measured count, or bound the queue and let the caller see the rejection.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the design wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure concurrent calls per endpoint at peak, then the wait each one records.




#VertX #Java #WebClient #ConnectionPools #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Every structure below rests on a number. A ceiling, a rate, a timeout, a count, a majority. Each post states the bound, gives its value, and asks whether the structure follows from it.
The first list in this topic asks whether the domain mandates a coupling. This list asks a narrower question, and a harder one: what is the number?
Three things decide. The constraint must be named — a fact about the machine, the runtime, the network, or the bill, not a layer called “infrastructure”. The value must come from this system, at this load, on this release. And an obligation must exist that the value breaches: the fact measures, the obligation rules out.
A real number can still fail to bind. It is borrowed from another system, stale after a release, negotiable by a contract, or idle against the measured peak. Each post names the case where the bound does force the shape, and the case where it does not.
For the same reading of design patterns over domain knowledge, see the first list. For the bounds a data type imposes, see the encoding list.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Vertical scaling (the capacity ceiling)
text:
Case study: Vertical scaling (the capacity ceiling)
“Just give it more RAM.” That is a claim about a ceiling: a bound per unit, a bound in count, a bound in total. The claim has a number. Check it.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A ceiling is a hard upper bound the substrate places on capacity: how large one unit may grow, how many units may exist, and what all of them may spend together.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The ceiling is knowledge only when someone can name it and trace it to its source — measured on this system, or documented by the vendor. “We cannot fit this in one node” is a claim about a value. The gap question is whether anyone knows the value, where it came from, and which release or licence sets it. A headroom figure read off a laptop measures a laptop. An unstated ceiling still binds; it is a constraint nobody can design against.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The limit is named, traced to its source, and binding: every larger unit is exhausted or priced out. A licence that caps seats. A device with fixed flash. An engine whose maximum is documented. Then the system must fit inside the named unit and state its headroom. Which mechanism enforces that — bounded retention, a smaller working set, a reduced requirement — is a further choice the ceiling does not make.








WarningWhen the ceiling does not force it



A real value fails to force a structure in four ways, and they overlap. It is borrowed — measured on another system. It is stale — a release removed it. It is negotiable — a contract term cited as physics, which a different signature lifts. It is idle — the headroom is large against the measured peak. In each case the value is cited and prescribes nothing. The structure pays for a wall it may never reach.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can one person name the ceiling, say where the number came from, and state the price of the next size?

If yes → the value is known, and the structure is answerable to it. Check next whether the working set approaches it; a known ceiling that stays idle indicates nothing.
If no → the ceiling is inherited, stale, or negotiable. Name it, or stop paying for it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the ceiling, or read it from the documentation, before you size the node.




#VerticalScaling #CapacityPlanning #Scaling #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Horizontal scaling (shared-nothing partition)
“Just add more instances.” Horizontal scaling by shared-nothing partitioning assumes one thing: no mutable state passes between instances. That assumption is a precondition, not a fact.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Shared-nothing means no mutable state crosses an instance boundary: no shared memory, no shared transaction manager, no shared storage. A failure does not propagate through state — but the failed instance’s own slice goes dark.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
No mutable state is shared between two instances, so any domain invariant that spans them has no substrate support: it must be paid for explicitly — a partition key, an idempotency key, a compensating step, or a distributed transaction with its own coordination cost. First question: is there state to split at all? A stateless tier needs no key. If there is state, the gap question is whether the partition key is one the domain can name, or one only the deployment can.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



An alignment holds when the coarse-grained failure domain contains the domain’s consistency unit: each ledger, tenant, or account lies wholly inside one failure domain. A failure then removes units whole instead of tearing one. Orders in different tenants may sit on two machines; orders on the same ledger may not. Alignment is contingent, and must be re-checked when the platform changes: failure domains nest.








WarningWhen the key does not force it



The key exists to fit the deployment: session stickiness, a hash of a user id, a round-robin. The domain has one consistency unit — a ledger, a seat map, an inventory count — and distribution moves that invariant into coordination code. Where that cost is not payable, the unit must stay on one node, and the split stops at the unit boundary. The load figure that justified the split may never have been measured on this system.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain own a partition key that matches the platform’s failure domain — and was the load measured here?

If yes → the partition is admissible: splitting along it needs no coordination inside each unit. Whether to split is a separate question, answered by a measured load.
If no → the key was chosen to fit the deployment. Keep the consistency unit on one node, and stop the split at the unit boundary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Name the key and count its cardinality before the split.




#HorizontalScaling #Sharding #Partitioning #DistributedSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Scalability

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Connection ceiling (the pool is the allowance)
text:
Case study: Connection ceiling (the pool is the allowance)
Twenty instances at twenty connections each is four hundred connections. One database accepts a hundred. The pool size is a multiplication, and it is easy to skip.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A connection pool is a local allowance. The engine’s maximum concurrent connections is a hard limit; a licence maximum is a contractual one. Both refuse the connection; only one can be lifted by a purchase.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The limit is documented, and the deployment often never consults it. Where it is consulted, the pool size still arrives by copy from an example, and threads per instance outnumber connections. Timeouts stay unset, so a starved caller waits until a timeout nobody chose. The gap question is what the engine allows and which component may spend it. The engine’s maximum is a substrate bound; whether the domain names the pool count is a separate question. Instances × pool size is the first multiplication, and it costs one line. Reserved, administrative, and replication connections spend from the same allowance.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The limit is documented, binding, and below peak demand. Then access to it must be arbitrated, and the arbitration is a choice: queue the surplus, shed it with a fast failure, or refuse admission upstream. The limit forces that a decision exists. It does not choose which.








WarningWhen the limit does not force it



The pool is an arbitrary knob that nobody traced to the engine. Or the limit is idle: a hundred allowed, five in use. That makes the pool non-binding today, not wrong — size it to the peak the system must survive, and name that peak. Or the pool is oversized and holds connections open that no caller uses; each still counts against the engine, so the component next door is denied capacity. An undersized pool is a different fault: callers queue for a connection the engine would have granted.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has anyone multiplied instances by pool size and compared it with the engine’s limit?

If yes → the product is known and compared. Above the limit, the defect is already live; below it, the pool still has to match measured concurrency.
If no → the pool asserts a bound nobody computed. Do the multiplication; the number is in the engine’s documentation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the limit, then multiply. Both take a minute.




#ConnectionPool #Databases #CapacityPlanning #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Scalability

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Latency budget (the p99 subtraction)
text:
Case study: Latency budget (the p99 subtraction)
Every synchronous hop spends from the same budget: the one you stated, or the one nobody did. It is rarely divided.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A latency budget is an allowance of time, stated end to end and divided among the hops that must fit inside it. The sum of per-hop p99s is the envelope the chain must fit inside — a conservative one, because the tails of different hops do not necessarily align.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The budget is a subtraction, not an average. Averages hide the tail, and the tail is what the unlucky caller experiences. Physics sets a floor that no code removes. The gap question is who divided the budget, and what is left at the last hop. Hop speed alone does not answer it.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



An end-to-end obligation exists and is stated: a payment authorisation window, a control loop, the point where a person stops waiting. Per-hop p99s are measured on this system and their sum exceeds the budget. Then something must give: a hop is removed, batched, or made asynchronous. The arithmetic requires one of these. It does not choose, and the three cost differently — asynchrony shortens the chain and moves a synchronous obligation into the consistency contract.








WarningWhen the budget does not force it



The budget was invented by the team and never tied to an obligation. Averages stand in for tails. Each hop is fast enough on its own; the measured sum exceeds the budget. Or the per-hop figures were borrowed from a development machine with no network and no contention. The structure optimises a number that no obligation outside the team required — not a customer, not a contract, not a downstream service.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has anyone stated the end-to-end budget and summed the measured per-hop p99s?

If yes → the arithmetic holds with the margin stated, provided the tails do not amplify. Confirm it against the measured end-to-end p99, including the work after the last hop.
If no → the hops spend a budget nobody set. Name the obligation, or drop the claim.
If you can’t answer → unclear. State the deadline and subtract each measured p99 from it.




#Latency #Performance #SLO #DistributedSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Reliability

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Availability arithmetic (the serial product)
text:
Case study: Availability arithmetic (the serial product)
Five serial dependencies at 99.9%, each failing independently, give 99.5%. Let them share a rack, a region, or a pipeline, and the real figure drops below the product.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Serial availability multiplies, and only when the failures are independent. A dependency that must succeed takes its own share of the remaining uptime.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The obligation is a contract number. The chain length is a design decision. The gap question is how many independent dependencies must succeed, and what their product is. Per-service reliability does not settle it. Five serial hops at 99.9% give 99.5%. To deliver 99.9% over five independent hops, each must clear 99.98%. The product is one line of arithmetic, and it is rarely done.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



A stated obligation exists — a contractual SLA, a safety function, a payment window — and the product across the synchronous chain falls below it. Then the chain is shortened, or part of it becomes independently available. The product is known, and the structure is answerable to it.








WarningWhen the product does not force it



A component’s figure is often quoted as if it were the system’s. Redundancy is counted without correlated failure: two nodes in one rack share a power feed and a switch; one region shares a control plane; one pipeline shares a defect. A shared cause can take both, so the pair’s availability is bounded by the shared resource, not by the product. They do not always fail together — price the pair against the shared resource, and keep the protection the second node still gives. Or the figure came from a vendor page and was never composed with the rest of the chain.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has anyone stated the obligation, multiplied the availability across the synchronous chain, and separated the correlated failures?

If yes → the chain is counted under independence, and the shared causes are priced. The next check is whether each figure was measured or merely quoted.
If no → the claim is unsupported. The product may fall below it, and a shared cause can put it further below.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Count the hops that must succeed, then multiply.




#Availability #SLA #Reliability #DistributedSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Durability contract (the domain and the substrate join)
text:
Case study: Durability contract (the domain and the substrate join)
“How much data may we lose?” is a domain question. “What does each step of protection cost?” is a substrate price. The two answers set one contract; either alone sets half.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A durability contract is the platform’s claim about what survives which failure — a process, a disk, a region — from the point the caller is told the write succeeded. The claim is a promise; what survives is measured. Retention is a separate promise.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Two knowledge sources meet here. The acceptable loss window is domain knowledge — a ledger, an audit obligation, a commanded action. The price of each step up is a substrate fact: fsync costs a write round trip; synchronous replication costs a network round trip, about a millisecond per hundred kilometres between the replicas; an append-only log costs storage growth. The gap question is whether anyone wrote the loss window down, and whether the contract covers the failures the domain faces. One source justifies half a structure.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The domain states a loss window in seconds or events, and the platform’s claim is weaker for the failures that matter. Then the difference is paid for explicitly, and the design record names the price. A ledger that must lose no acknowledged write needs an acknowledgement after a durable write to replicas that cannot fail together, at a stated quorum. One replica does not cover a zone; no replication covers a bad migration.








WarningWhen the claim does not force it



The loss window was never stated, so the team bought the strongest contract everywhere and pays for it on data that could be rebuilt. Or the window is stated and the claim covers the failures the domain faces; only then is the extra mechanism ceremony. Or a recovery figure was quoted from a vendor page and never mapped to the domain’s own window. A contract must be read for the failures it excludes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the loss window written down, does the contract claim to cover the failures you face, and is the price stated?

If yes → the join is explicit on paper. The remaining step is to confirm the production configuration implements it, for each failure mode.
If no → one side of the join is missing. Write the window, or stop paying for the promise.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Write the loss window in seconds or events, then read the contract against it.




#DataDurability #Replication #DataLoss #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Databases

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Ephemeral ports (the client’s own ceiling)
text:
Case study: Ephemeral ports (the client’s own ceiling)
A client host with one address can hold about 28,000 connections to one destination address and port. At one connection per request, that caps it at about 470 new connections a second.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Every outbound connection takes a local port from an ephemeral range — the Linux default, 32768 to 60999, which is 28,232 ports. The port stays reserved for about a minute after the client closes the connection — the TCP TIME_WAIT hold, fixed by the kernel.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The client host carries its own bound: the ephemeral port range its stack draws from. It belongs to the client, so the server’s pool size does not raise it. The gap question is how many connections the client may hold to one destination address and port, and how fast it opens new ones. The arithmetic is the range divided by the hold time.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The design opens a short-lived connection per request to one destination, and the rate approaches the bound. Then the port range is the binding constraint: 28,232 ports divided by a 60-second hold gives about 470 new connections a second. Connection reuse keeps the workload away from the bound; a larger pool does not.








WarningWhen the range does not force it



The client holds long-lived pooled connections, so the port count is never approached. Or the client opens connections to many distinct destinations, so the range applies separately to each, not once for the host. One load-balancer address on one port is one destination, so the range applies to it in full. Or the rate is far below the bound.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the counted connection rate to one destination address and port inside the range divided by the hold time?

If yes → the rate is inside the bound; reuse is optional.
If no → the rate is at or above the bound. Reuse connections, or accept the ceiling.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range and count the rate.




#Networking #TCP #Scaling #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Retry amplification (the product across layers)
text:
Case study: Retry amplification (the product across layers)
Three attempts at three layers is twenty-seven requests. One user click can become twenty-seven, and each layer believes it made three attempts.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A retry policy multiplies. If each layer makes three attempts — one call plus two retries — the layers below see 3ⁿ attempts for one request, where n is the number of layers that retry.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The retry count is local; the amplification is global. The gap question is which layer owns the retry, and how many layers retry at all. Twenty-seven attempts is a product no single policy computes. The downstream capacity must absorb the product, and while the retries nest inside the caller’s deadline, that deadline divides by it.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



Every layer retries with its own three attempts, so the product reaches twenty-seven. A single downstream stall can produce a retry storm, and the retries spend the capacity the dependency needs to recover. One owner with a stated attempt budget closes it: the layers below fail fast, each layer’s deadline is shorter than its caller’s, and the capacity is sized to the product.








WarningWhen the product does not force it



The product is small — one layer retries, or none does, and the capacity absorbs the attempts. Then a retry budget is ceremony. Or one owner already bounds the attempts, so the multiplication adds no new constraint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the product of the retrying layers fit the downstream capacity?

If yes → one owner suffices, and the capacity is sized to the product.
If no → the attempts multiply past the capacity. Name the owner, and bound the product.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Count the retrying layers, then multiply.




#Resilience #Retries #DistributedSystems #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Connection setup (the round trips before the payload)
text:
Case study: Connection setup (the round trips before the payload)
Before the first byte of a request, TCP and a full TLS 1.3 handshake each cost a round trip. At 50 ms, that is 100 ms of a 200 ms budget gone before the call starts.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A new connection pays for its setup before any request bytes move: one round trip — a message out and its reply back — for TCP, one more for a full TLS 1.3 handshake. At a round-trip time of 50 ms, that is 100 ms.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The setup cost is paid once per connection. It is paid per request exactly when the client opens a connection per request, which is why reuse, or a shorter round trip, is what removes it. The gap question is the round-trip time and the connections one request opens. DNS adds a round trip on the first lookup, and none after that if the answer is cached.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The client opens a connection per request over a long link, and the round trips are a large share of the obligation. Then reuse, session resumption, or termination at the edge reduces the setup to one handshake, or to zero with 0-RTT. Reuse also keeps the client inside its port range, and it does not raise one connection’s throughput. The measurement is the round-trip time and the connection count.








WarningWhen the setup does not force it



Connections are already pooled, so setup happens once and the cost is amortised. Or the client and server sit in the same datacenter, where the round-trip time is under a millisecond and the setup is noise. Then keep-alive saves no latency. It still leaves an idle connection for a timeout to reap.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the measured setup a large share of the end-to-end budget?

If yes → the setup is the dominant term. Reuse connections, resume the session, or terminate at the edge.
If no → the setup is noise, and keep-alive adds an idle connection for nothing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the round-trip time and count the connections per request.




#Networking #TLS #Latency #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Partition count (the ceiling on consumer parallelism)
text:
Case study: Partition count (the ceiling on consumer parallelism)
In one consumer group, twelve partitions support twelve consumers. The thirteenth consumer idles, however many cores the host has.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A partition is the unit of both order and assignment. Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to one consumer, so useful parallelism is bounded by the partition count.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The partition count is chosen when the topic is created, and it can only rise. An increase remaps keys across partitions. The gap question is how much parallelism the throughput target needs, and whether the partition count supplies it. Twelve partitions cap a group at twelve working consumers; the thirteenth is idle, not faster. A skewed key can put the load on one partition while the group waits on it.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The throughput target divides into a required consumer count above the partition count. Then the partitions must increase before the consumers do, and the key distribution must keep the load even. The order is fixed: derive the required consumer count, then compare it with the partition count.








WarningWhen the count does not force it



The partition count already exceeds the required parallelism, so extra consumers would idle. Or ordering requires one partition for the key space, so the ceiling is the price of the order. Then adding partitions buys idle consumers and costs a rebalance.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the partition count cover the required consumer count?

If yes → the parallelism is covered. Check next that the key distribution keeps the load even.
If no → the consumers exceed the partitions. Raise the count, or accept the limit.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Compute the required consumers from the throughput target.




#Kafka #Partitioning #Throughput #Scaling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Restore time (the copy time is a floor)
text:
Case study: Restore time (the copy time is a floor)
A 100 GB restore at 200 MB/s takes 500 seconds — about eight minutes — before verification and replay. The copy is a division, not a promise.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Recovery time is at least the data size divided by the restore rate: the copy is the floor, and every step after the copy adds to it.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The recovery target is an obligation in minutes. The restore rate is a measured property of the backup medium, the network, and the target. The gap question is the size, the rate, and the obligation. Eight minutes of copy is the floor; verification, replay, and the decision to restore add to it. A backup that has never been restored has an unknown rate.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



A recovery target exists and the division misses it. Then the design must change: a warm replica, a smaller restore unit, or continuous replication. The division sets the requirement; which mechanism meets it is a second decision.








WarningWhen the division does not force it



The restore has been timed and fits the target with margin. Then a warm replica pays for a risk the restore already covers. Or the recovery target is unknown, so no division can be compared with it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the measured end-to-end restore time inside the recovery target?

If yes → the division fits with margin. The copy is one step of the path; the backup stays the fallback until the whole path is timed.
If no → the division misses the target. Change the mechanism, or state the longer time.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Restore a copy and time it end to end.




#Backup #DisasterRecovery #RTO #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Databases

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Page write amplification (the engine’s page is the unit)
text:
Case study: Page write amplification (the engine’s page is the unit)
An eight-byte update to a random row dirties a four-kilobyte page. That is at least 512 times the bytes the application changed, before the log and the index.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: The storage engine reads and writes in pages — 4 KiB here, 8 KiB in PostgreSQL, 16 KiB in InnoDB. A random update to a few bytes still costs a whole page on write-back.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The page is the smallest unit the engine writes back. Below the page, the device has its own unit: a sector, and an erase block for flash. So the write path can multiply again. The gap question is the page size and the size of the update. Eight bytes into a four-kilobyte page is 512 times the changed bytes. The workload spends the device’s sustained write budget, not the application’s byte count.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The workload is random small writes at a rate the device cannot absorb, and the amplification is measured. Then batching, an append-only layout, or a larger write unit follows. The arithmetic sets the requirement: changed bytes multiplied by the amplification.








WarningWhen the page does not force it



Writes are sequential or batched, so many updates share one page. Or the working set sits in memory and the page is written once. Or the device is far from its write budget, so the amplification is real and unbilled.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the amplified write rate inside the device’s sustained write budget?

If yes → the amplified rate fits when measured. Record the headroom and treat the fit as a threshold to monitor.
If no → the workload spends more than the device allows. Batch the writes, or change the layout.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Divide the page size by the update size, then compare with the rate.




#Storage #Databases #WriteAmplification #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #CapacityPlanning

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Receive window (the bandwidth-delay product)
text:
Case study: Receive window (the bandwidth-delay product)
One connection with a 64 KiB receive window and a 100 ms round trip caps at 5.2 Mbit/s. The link may be 10 Gbit/s; the window decides.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A sender may have only the smaller of the congestion window and the receive window in flight. The receive window divided by the round-trip time is the ceiling of a single connection: 64 KiB over 100 ms caps it at 5.24 Mbit/s.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
One connection carries only what its window allows, whatever the link is rated at. The gap question is the window and the round trip. Without window scaling — the option that multiplies the 16-bit window field — the window is capped at about 64 KiB, so a long link is filled by many connections or not at all. The division is an upper bound: loss, and the congestion window (the sender’s estimate of what the network will accept), can hold the rate lower.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs more than one connection’s worth of throughput over a long round trip, and the window is not scaled. Then parallel connections, or a larger window, follow. Reuse removes the setup cost, and it cannot raise one connection’s throughput. The measurement is the achieved rate per connection against the window divided by the measured round trip.








WarningWhen the window does not force it



Window scaling is enabled, the receive buffer is large enough, and the window has grown to the product of bandwidth and delay, so one connection already fills the link. Or the round trip is short and the window never binds. Then adding connections adds overhead rather than throughput.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the required rate per connection fit the window divided by the round-trip time?

If yes → one connection can carry it. Scale the window only if the rate must grow.
If no → one connection cannot carry it. Scale the window, or spread the load.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the window, measure the round trip, then divide.




#Networking #TCP #Throughput #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Integer key width (the positive range of the type)
text:
Case study: Integer key width (the positive range of the type)
A signed 32-bit key holds 2,147,483,647 positive ids. The next insert fails, and the failure arrives long after the schema decision that set the limit.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: An identifier has a width. A signed 32-bit integer spans 4,294,967,296 values, and an identity column spends the positive half: 2,147,483,647 inserts, after which the next one fails.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The key width is chosen at schema time. The gap question is how many rows this table will ever hold, and whether the width covers it. The arithmetic is the usable range, 2³¹ − 1, not the current row count. Migrating the live table is one price of getting it wrong.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation implies a row count above the type’s positive range. Then use a wider key, a sequence with a larger type, or a generated identifier. The bound is the range, and the requirement is a count.








WarningWhen the range does not force it



The table is bounded by the domain — a fixed set of regions, currencies, or statuses — so the range is never approached. Or the projected count stays below the limit for the table’s life. Then widening the key buys nothing and can cost a rewrite of the table and its indexes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the projected row count stay below 2,147,483,647?

If yes → the range covers the obligation, and the schema stays.
If no → the projected count passes the limit. Widen the key before the migration becomes urgent.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Project the count, then compare it with 2,147,483,647.




#Databases #SchemaDesign #CapacityPlanning #Scaling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DataModeling

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Quorum (the majority is arithmetic)
text:
Case study: Quorum (the majority is arithmetic)
Five nodes, and three must agree. Two groups of two cannot both write — within one membership view. The rest is policy.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A majority is ⌊n/2⌋ + 1. Five nodes need three; four need three; three need two. A membership view is each node’s current list of voting members; two nodes can disagree on it. Two disjoint groups cannot both hold a majority of the same member set.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The node count decides how many independent failures the system tolerates, and whether a network partition can split the write path. The gap question is the node count and the failure the deployment must survive. Two nodes lost to one hypervisor or one deploy are one failure, and 2f + 1 does not count it. A majority of four is also three, so the fourth node adds cost without adding tolerance.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation names a failure count. Tolerate f independent crash failures over a fixed voting set, and the cluster needs 2f + 1 voting members. Then the node count follows from the failure count, not from the budget.








WarningWhen the count does not force it



The count is even, so the extra node adds cost without adding tolerance. Or the deployment counts copies, not voting members, so two network partitions can each believe they are the writer — the count is cited and never applied. Or the write quorum is set below a majority, which permits two writers by design.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the node count give a majority above the number of failures the system must survive at once?

If yes → the arithmetic holds for one membership view. Confirm that every member shares it, and that an old writer is fenced — cut off before the new one starts.
If no → the count does not cover the failure. Add voting members, or state the lower tolerance.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Start from the failure count, double it, and add one.




#DistributedSystems #Consensus #Quorum #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Databases

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Thread stack (the concurrency model has a memory bill)
text:
Case study: Thread stack (the concurrency model has a memory bill)
On a 64-bit host, ten thousand threads with an 8 MB stack reserve about eighty gigabytes of address space. None of them has done useful work yet.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Each thread reserves a stack. Eight megabytes is the Linux default, read with ulimit -s. Ten thousand threads therefore reserve about eighty gigabytes of address space, whether or not they touch it.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The stack size is a setting, and the thread count is a design decision. Together they are a memory bill. The gap question is the stack size and the concurrency model. Reserved, committed, and resident are three measures of the same memory: the reservation spends address space (the virtual range, not RAM), the commit charge is what a cgroup limit counts, and only resident pages consume RAM.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The address space or the memory budget is finite, and the product exceeds one of them. Then a smaller stack, a fixed thread pool, or an event loop follows. The arithmetic is a multiplication, and it is done before the first thread starts.








WarningWhen the reservation does not force it



The host is 64-bit with address space to spare, and the touched stack pages are the real cost. Then the multiplication overstates the address-space bill, and the thread count binds on scheduling and kernel memory instead. Or the pool is fixed and small, and the stack size never matters.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the reserved stack memory fit the address space and the memory budget?

If yes → the product is known. Compare it with both budgets before you commit to the model.
If no → the reservation exceeds one budget. Shrink the stack, bound the pool, or change the model.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Multiply the stack size by the maximum thread count.




#Concurrency #Memory #Threads #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: DNS TTL (the staleness bound)
text:
Case study: DNS TTL (the staleness bound)
A 300-second TTL lets a conforming resolver serve a stale answer for five minutes. The failover plan is bounded by the record’s lifetime, and by every client that caches past it.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A DNS answer carries a time to live. A caching resolver may serve the old answer until that time expires. A 300-second TTL therefore bounds a conforming resolver’s staleness at five minutes.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The TTL is a promise about how fast a change propagates. The gap question is the TTL and the failover time the system promises. The staleness window is the remaining lifetime on each cached copy, not the TTL on the record just changed. A client that caches past the TTL extends the window.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The failover obligation is shorter than the TTL, and the clients re-resolve inside it. Then the TTL must fall, and a lower TTL costs more queries. The trade is arithmetic: propagation time against query volume.








WarningWhen the TTL does not force it



The TTL is short and the obligation is long, so the record’s life is not the bound. Or clients cache past the TTL, so the TTL is a hope rather than a limit. Then the propagation time is unknown, and the plan must not depend on DNS alone.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the TTL inside the time a change may take?

If yes → the TTL fits. Confirm the clients re-resolve inside it, and keep one path that does not depend on DNS.
If no → staleness outlasts the plan. Lower the TTL, or move the switch off DNS.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the TTL, time a change against it, and check each client stack you ship.




#DNS #Failover #Reliability #Availability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Message size (the payload ceiling)
text:
Case study: Message size (the payload ceiling)
A message ceiling of 1 MiB belongs to the broker. Amazon SQS enforces it; above it, the vendor ships the workaround: claim check.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A broker accepts messages up to a stated size. Amazon SQS accepts 1,048,576 bytes of encoded message, which is 1 MiB. Above that size the broker rejects the message; the application stores the payload and sends a reference.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The ceiling belongs to the broker, not to the domain. The gap question is the largest message the domain produces, and whether it fits. A 1 MiB ceiling rules out sending a 20 MB document as one message: it travels as chunks, or as a reference plus a store. The ceiling counts the encoded message, so a binary payload inflated by base64 may not fit even when the raw bytes do.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The domain’s messages exceed the ceiling, the ceiling is fixed, and the payload has an owner and a lifetime. Then the store-and-reference split follows, and the reference must stay valid for as long as the message can be redelivered.








WarningWhen the ceiling does not force it



The domain’s messages fit the ceiling with margin, so the split adds a store and a failure mode for nothing. Or the limit is configurable, so the split is not forced yet. Or the payload has no stable identity, so a reference cannot be built.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the largest message the domain produces fit the broker’s ceiling?

If yes → today’s largest message fits. Check the growth in payload size before dropping the store path.
If no → the payload exceeds the ceiling. Store it, and make the reference durable.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the largest message, then read the broker’s limit.




#Messaging #ClaimCheck #PayloadSize #EnterpriseIntegration #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: File descriptors (the per-process limit)
text:
Case study: File descriptors (the per-process limit)
A process spends one descriptor per open socket, file, and pipe. At the soft limit the next open fails with an error, not a slow request.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Every open socket, file, and pipe consumes one descriptor, and so does every other handle the kernel returns. The soft limit caps how many a process may hold; the next open fails with EMFILE.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The soft limit is per process; the kernel’s file-max is per host, and it fails with ENFILE. Each is read from its own file. The gap question is the soft limit and the descriptors one unit of work holds. A connection-per-request design spends a descriptor for the life of each connection, and a leak spends it forever. The arithmetic is a multiplication: concurrent work times descriptors per unit.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The product approaches the soft limit under load, and the limit is the binding constraint. Then pool, close the handles, or raise the limit. Raise it in three places, in this order: the hard limit (the ceiling the soft limit cannot exceed), then the soft limit, then any supervisor that resets both.








WarningWhen the limit does not force it



The pool is bounded and small, the files are few, and the product sits far below the limit. Then the descriptor count is not the bound, and raising the limit can hide a leak rather than fix it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the descriptor product fit the soft limit under peak load?

If yes → the product fits. Record the peak count and watch the gap to the limit.
If no → the product exceeds the limit. Bound the pool, close the handles, or raise the hard and soft limits.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read /proc/PID/limits for the service, then count the descriptors per request.




#OperatingSystems #FileDescriptors #CapacityPlanning #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Inodes (the file-count ceiling)
A filesystem with a fixed inode table can run out of files before it runs out of bytes. The error says “no space left on device” while the disk is half empty.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: An inode is the record the filesystem keeps for one file. A filesystem with fixed inodes allocates one per file, directory, and symbolic link; a hard link adds a name and no inode. When the table is full, creating a file fails with ENOSPC (no space left on device) even though bytes remain.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The inode count is set when the filesystem is created, and it is a ratio of inodes to bytes. The gap question is how many files one unit of work keeps alive, and whether the ratio covers it. The arithmetic is files per unit times units in flight — a deleted file returns its inode. A zero in the total column of df -i means no fixed table.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The workload keeps many small files alive, and the product exceeds the inode count. Then use fewer, larger files, a different store, or a filesystem with dynamic inodes.








WarningWhen the inode count does not force it



The workload writes few large files, or stores data in pages inside a database. Then the file count is not the bound. Or the filesystem allocates inodes on demand, so no fixed table exists. Check whether it still caps them by a share of the volume. XFS does.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the peak number of live files fit the inode count?

If yes → the store can hold the workload, and the inode table is not the bound.
If no → the files run out before the bytes. Merge the files, or move the store.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read df -i, then count the files per unit of work.




#OperatingSystems #Filesystems #Inodes #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Storage

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Replication lag (the staleness bound on reads)
text:
Case study: Replication lag (the staleness bound on reads)
A read from an asynchronous replica is stale by up to that replica’s lag. At a two-second lag, a write made in the last two seconds is likely missing from the replica.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Asynchronous replication applies changes after the primary commits. A read served by a replica returns data from the point the replica has reached, which trails the primary by up to that replica’s lag.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The lag is a measured property of the link, the write rate, and the replica’s capacity, and it is a distribution rather than a constant. The gap question is the staleness the domain allows, and the worst lag it gets. Read-your-writes is the sharpest case: the user writes, then reads, and the replica may not have caught up.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The domain requires read-your-writes, and the measured lag exceeds the tolerance. Then the read goes to the primary, waits for the replica to pass a position, or the replica becomes synchronous. The measurement rules out the replica read; which of the three to adopt is a second decision.








WarningWhen the lag does not force it



Some reads tolerate staleness by design: a dashboard, a search index, a report. Then the tolerance is what matters, and the measured lag must be shown to sit inside it before routing to the primary is called unnecessary. Or the replica is synchronous and the lag is zero by construction.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the worst replica’s lag, under peak write load, inside the staleness the domain allows?

If yes → the lag sat inside the tolerance when measured. Confirm it again at peak and during catch-up.
If no → the read can return older data than the domain allows. Route it, or wait for the position.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the lag on the replica that serves the read, under peak write load.




#Databases #Replication #Consistency #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Heartbeat detection (the detection bound)
text:
Case study: Heartbeat detection (the detection bound)
A 30-second heartbeat with a one-beat death timeout detects a dead node in up to 60 seconds. Detection is twice the interval; failover runs past it.
