Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A cluster notices a dead member by missing its heartbeat. Detection takes up to one interval plus the death timeout (the wait after the last beat before the member is declared dead) — two intervals when the timeout is one interval. With k tolerated missed beats, the bound is k + 1 intervals.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The detection time is a design parameter, and it trades against false positives. The gap question is how long a dead node may hold its role, and how many beats fit in that time. A 30-second interval allows up to 60 seconds of a dead node, which may be longer than the lock it holds or the client timeout above it.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The tolerance is shorter than the detection bound, so the interval must fall. Then the setting follows the tolerance: interval ≤ (tolerance − failover time) ÷ (k + 1). A shorter interval costs more traffic, and more false positives on a slow network.








WarningWhen the interval does not force it



Detection comes from the client’s connection failing, not from a heartbeat, so the interval does not bound the window. Or the tolerance is long, and the interval sits well inside it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does one interval plus the death timeout fit inside the time a dead node may hold its role?

If yes → detection fits the tolerance. Failover adds election and promotion on top, so check those too.
If no → the interval is too long for the tolerance. Divide the interval by k + 1, or change how detection works.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Subtract the timeout and the promotion time, then divide what remains by k + 1.




#DistributedSystems #Failover #Heartbeats #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #HighAvailability

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Retransmission timeout (the floor under a lost tail)
text:
Case study: Retransmission timeout (the floor under a lost tail)
A lost packet that only the timer can recover costs at least 200 milliseconds. When later packets arrive, a fast retransmit recovers it in about one round trip instead.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: When a segment is lost and nothing later recovers it, the sender waits for a retransmission timeout. The kernel clamps that timeout at a minimum — 200 ms on Linux. Fast retransmit — resending as soon as later packets reveal the gap — recovers many other losses in a round trip or two.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The timeout is not the round trip. The gap question is the measured loss rate and the tail budget (the latency allowed for the slowest requests). At one percent packet loss, a request of k packets meets a loss about 1 − 0.99^k of the time — 9.6% at ten packets. So the tail is set by the loss and by the packets per request.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The path loses packets, and the tail budget is below the timeout. Then retransmission cost enters the budget, and the design must remove the loss or tolerate the timeout. Fewer round trips and fewer packets reduce the exposure.








WarningWhen the timeout does not force it



The path is clean and the loss rate is near zero, so the timeout is never paid. Or the protocol runs over a transport with its own recovery, and this floor does not apply. Then the floor is real and idle.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the tail cost of one loss inside the tail budget?

If yes → the loss cost fits the budget. The floor is real and unused.
If no → the loss sets the tail. Remove the loss, or widen the budget.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the loss rate and the packets per request, then compute 1 − (1 − p)^k and multiply by the timeout.




#Networking #TCP #TailLatency #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Character length (the byte ceiling behind it)
text:
Case study: Character length (the byte ceiling behind it)
A VARCHAR(255) holds 255 characters. In UTF-8 that is up to 1,020 bytes, and the index limit is measured in bytes.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A character column is declared in characters and stored in bytes. UTF-8 encodes a code point in one to four bytes, and the column counts code points, so 255 code points occupy up to 1,020 bytes.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The column’s declared length is not its storage length. The gap question is the maximum code points per value, and the byte limit of the index or the row. A four-times factor can exceed an index’s byte limit, fail a migration, or truncate the value silently in a non-strict mode. The arithmetic is code points times four.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The value can hold non-ASCII text, and the index or row limit is in bytes. Then size the column, the index prefix, or the validation from the byte count. The requirement is the maximum bytes, not the maximum characters.








WarningWhen the byte count does not force it



The data is ASCII by constraint: a check constraint or a validation rule enforces it, so one byte is one character. Or the type counts bytes and the question does not arise. Then sizing by characters is exact.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the maximum code points per value, times four, fit the byte limit of the index or row?

If yes → the worst case fits the limit. Whether 255 is the right declared length is a separate question.
If no → the value can exceed the limit. Bound the code points, or use a prefix.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Multiply the maximum code points by four.




#Databases #Unicode #SchemaDesign #Indexing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DataModeling

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Send buffer (the buffer divided by the round trip)
text:
Case study: Send buffer (the buffer divided by the round trip)
One connection on a 10 Gbit/s link moves 17 Mbit/s when its send buffer is 212,992 bytes and the round trip is 100 ms. The buffer sets that number.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A sender may leave only its send buffer’s worth of bytes unacknowledged. net.core.wmem_max caps the buffer an unprivileged process may request — 212,992 bytes in the upstream default, larger where a distribution or an operator raised it — and at a 100 ms round trip that is 212,992 × 8 ÷ 0.1 = 17.04 Mbit/s.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
A socket’s rate is one division: the buffer it may leave unacknowledged, over the round trip, per connection and per direction. The buffer is a setting; the round trip is a measurement. Autotuning raises the buffer toward that setting, so the ceiling is the setting’s value, not the link’s rating. A single connection that holds 17 Mbit/s on a 10 Gbit/s link is usually this division.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs more than 17 Mbit/s from one connection over a 100 ms path, and the buffer sits at its default. Then raise wmem_max and set the socket’s send buffer, or spread the flow across connections. The division names how much each remedy must buy.








WarningWhen the buffer does not force it



The buffer is already sized to the bandwidth-delay product — the link rate times the round trip — so the sender can keep the pipe full, and the bound is loss and congestion control. Or the round trip is short: at 1 ms the same 212,992 bytes allow 1.7 Gbit/s, and the buffer is nowhere near the limit. Then enlarging it changes nothing.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the send buffer divided by the round-trip time cover the rate the obligation needs?

If yes → the buffer covers the rate. Measure loss and the congestion window next.
If no → one connection cannot carry the rate. Raise the buffer, or spread the flow.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read net.core.wmem_max, measure the round trip, then divide.




#Networking #TCP #Throughput #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Linux

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Little’s law (the concurrency product)
text:
Case study: Little’s law (the concurrency product)
A service at 1,000 requests a second, each living 100 ms, holds 100 requests in flight on average. The pool size is that product, never a round number.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: In a stable system, the average number of items in it equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there. At 1,000 requests a second and 100 ms end to end, 1,000 × 0.1 = 100 requests are in flight on average — a mean, not a count you will read at any moment.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Two measurements multiply into the pool size: the arrival rate and the time in the system, taken together. The pool size, the queue depth, the connection count, and the thread count are all this one product, applied once per dependency. Below it the requests queue and latency grows; above it the workers idle. A pool chosen by feel is a guess at this product.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The required concurrency exceeds the pool, and the pool is what queues. Then size the pool from the product, and sum it across the dependencies the request waits on in series; the peak hour, not the mean day, is the input.








WarningWhen the product does not force it



The time in the system is short, so the product is small and any sane pool covers it. Or nothing on this side holds the work — a fire-and-forget send, a response streamed without buffering — so there is no pool for the product to size.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the concurrency limit cover the arrival rate times the time in the system, at the peak hour?

If yes → the product does not rule the pool out. Watch the time in the system, which moves with the load.
If no → the requests queue by construction. Raise the limit, or cut the time in the system.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the peak arrival rate, then the end-to-end time at that rate.




#Performance #CapacityPlanning #Queues #Scaling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Reliability

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Queue wait (the headroom is the latency)
text:
Case study: Queue wait (the headroom is the latency)
A queue at 80 percent utilisation waits four service times on average. At 90 percent it waits nine, and at 95 percent nineteen. The last slice of headroom is the whole latency budget.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: For one server with random arrivals and a random service time — the M/M/1 model — the mean wait in the queue is the service time times ρ ÷ (1 − ρ), where ρ is utilisation. At 0.8 that is 4 service times, at 0.9 it is 9, and at 0.95 it is 19. A scheduled arrival, or a second server, changes the curve.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Utilisation and waiting time are not two independent numbers; one divides into the other. The curve is not linear; it is a division by the headroom. A design sized at 90 percent takes ten times as long per item as an idle one, and a capacity report calls that healthy.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The latency obligation is tight and the design runs near saturation. Then either capacity must hold utilisation where the obligation’s wait allows — a 90 percent target costs nine service times — or the per-item service time must fall, which batching buys only where a fixed per-job cost is amortised. The arithmetic sets the headroom; which remedy to take is a second decision.








WarningWhen the queue does not force it



The load sits far below saturation, so the wait is a small multiple of the service time. Or the arrivals are scheduled — a nightly batch — rather than random, so no queue forms by luck. Then the formula overstates the wait, and headroom is not the constraint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the utilisation the design runs at keep the mean wait inside the latency obligation?

If yes → the wait fits at that utilisation. Check the peak, which sits above the mean.
If no → the queue alone breaches the obligation. Add capacity, or shorten the service time.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the service time, then the utilisation at peak.




#Performance #Latency #CapacityPlanning #Queues #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Durable-write rate (the device’s confirmations)
text:
Case study: Durable-write rate (the device’s confirmations)
One durable write per request, at one millisecond each, caps a device that serialises its flushes at a thousand requests a second. Each confirmation is a millisecond the next request waits.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A durable write waits for the device to confirm that the data is on stable media — an fsync. That confirmation costs about 1 ms on an SSD and 5 to 10 ms on a spinning disk, which caps one device at roughly 1,000 and 100 to 200 such waits a second.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The obligation needs durable writes per second; the device offers confirmations per second, and one confirmation serves one flush. A device that accepts several flushes at once — a modern flash device with parallel queues — raises the ceiling, so measure the rate at the concurrency you will actually use. Batching the commits turns many waits into one, and the batch size is the term the design controls.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs a durable write per request, and the required rate exceeds the device’s confirmations. Then batch the commits: 5,000 writes a second against 1,000 confirmations is a batch of five. The arithmetic gives the batch size, and the latency obligation judges whether that batch is payable.








WarningWhen the confirmation rate does not force it



The writes are already batched, so one confirmation serves many. Or the durability obligation is weaker — a buffered write, or a replica that acknowledges before the flush. Then the confirmation rate is not the bound.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does one batch of commits absorb the gap between the required write rate and the device’s confirmations per second?

If yes → the batch covers the gap. Check that the wait for a batch fits the latency obligation.
If no → the device cannot absorb the rate. Add devices, or weaken the durability claim.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Time one fsync on the real device, then count the writes per second.




#Storage #Databases #Durability #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #CapacityPlanning

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Drive endurance (capacity is not the bound)
text:
Case study: Drive endurance (capacity is not the bound)
A 1 TB drive rated at one drive-write per day absorbs a terabyte a day for five years. At ten terabytes a day it spends that whole budget in 182 days, and the capacity report still says 1 TB free.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Drive writes per day is the sustained write volume a drive’s endurance covers, as a multiple of its capacity. One DWPD on a 1 TB drive is 1 TB a day for the warranty period — 1,825 TB over five years. At 10 TB a day that budget is gone in 182 days.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Endurance is priced in bytes written, and those are not the bytes the application sent. The drive rewrites a whole block to change part of it, and keeps a log besides, so one written byte can cost several. A drive that looks empty can be wearing out.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The amplified daily volume exceeds capacity times DWPD. Then the layout must write less, or the drive class must change; the ratio of daily bytes to capacity times DWPD is the wear rate.








WarningWhen the rating does not force it



The workload is read-heavy, so the written volume never approaches the rating. Or the writes already arrive in whole pages and whole erase blocks, so the drive multiplies nothing on the way to the media. Then the rating is real and idle.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the daily written volume, after amplification, stay inside capacity times DWPD?

If yes → the drive outlives the workload at that rate. Recheck when the write path changes.
If no → the drive wears out before the warranty. Cut the writes, or change the drive class.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure bytes written per day at the device, then divide by capacity times DWPD.




#Storage #SSD #CapacityPlanning #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Databases

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Context switch (the core’s switch budget)
text:
Case study: Context switch (the core’s switch budget)
A blocking call costs two context switches. At two microseconds each, one core completes 250,000 blocking calls a second, and the work itself is not counted yet.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A thread that blocks gives up the core and is scheduled back later, and each transition costs one to three microseconds. Two transitions at two microseconds allow about 250,000 blocking calls a second on one core, before the work itself is counted.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Every blocking call costs two switches, and a core completes only so many of them. The count is per core, so the core count multiplies it. A design that blocks once per item pays this for every item, whatever the item costs. The cost does not appear in a profile that measures work; it appears in the wall clock.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs more blocking operations per second than a core’s 250,000 switches allow. Then batch the items, wait on readiness rather than blocking, or shard across cores. The arithmetic gives the batch size that closes the gap.








WarningWhen the switch cost does not force it



The operations are batched already, so one switch serves many items. Or the threads compute rather than wait, so the switch count is small. Then the switches are not the bound, and the core is spent on work.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the blocking-operation rate, times the switches each costs, fit the switches one core completes in a second?

If yes → the switches fit on the core count you have. Watch the count as the batch shrinks.
If no → the switches alone consume the cores. Batch the items, or wait on readiness.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Count the blocking calls per second, then the switches per call.




#Concurrency #Performance #OperatingSystems #Scaling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Latency

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Heap against the cgroup limit (two numbers, one wrong)
text:
Case study: Heap against the cgroup limit (two numbers, one wrong)
A 2 GB container on a 64 GB host: the runtime sizes its heap to 16 GB and the kernel kills it at 2 GB. Both numbers came from the same machine.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: The default maximum heap is one quarter of the memory the runtime detects. In a container on a 64 GB host that detection can return 64 GB, so the heap limit is 16 GB. The cgroup — the kernel’s per-container memory limit — allows 2 GB, and the process dies at the second number, with no heap error to read.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The process has one memory limit, and the runtime reads a larger one. The heap is not the whole process either: thread stacks, class metadata, and off-heap buffers live outside it, so the limit must leave room for them.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The detected memory exceeds the cgroup limit. Then set the maximum heap explicitly, and subtract what lives outside it. The arithmetic is the limit minus the non-heap, and it is a subtraction, not a fraction.








WarningWhen the limit does not force it



The runtime reads the cgroup limit and sizes from it. Or the limit is set explicitly and the default never applies. Then the detected memory is irrelevant, and the fraction is harmless.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the runtime’s maximum heap below the cgroup limit, with room for what lives outside the heap?

If yes → the heap fits the container. Confirm the non-heap has its own headroom.
If no → the kernel kills the process at the limit, without a heap error. Set the heap, and size the non-heap.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the cgroup limit, then the runtime’s reported maximum heap.




#Containers #JVM #Memory #Kubernetes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Operations

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: CPU quota (the period is the pause)
text:
Case study: CPU quota (the period is the pause)
A container that burns its 50 ms quota inside a 100 ms period is stopped for the other 50. The average says half a core; the tail says a 50 ms pause.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: CPU quota is enforced per period, 100 ms by default. A quota of 50 ms lets the threads run for 50 ms and then stops them until the next period begins — if they ask for that much. A workload that wants less is never throttled; one that wants more is throttled in every period it runs. The work still fits the average; the wall clock does not.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The quota is enforced per period, so the pause is the unit that matters, not the average. A request needing 60 ms of a core never completes inside one 100 ms period, whatever the utilisation says. A pause lasts until the period ends.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation is on the tail, and the request’s work exceeds one period’s quota. Then raise the quota to a whole core, or pin the work somewhere the quota does not throttle it; a quota of one core per period removes the pause entirely.








WarningWhen the quota does not force it



The workload is throughput-only and the average meets the obligation, so the pauses cost nothing measurable. Or the quota is a whole core per period, so no period is ever throttled.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the work one latency-critical request needs fit inside one quota period?

If yes → the request can complete inside a period. Check the period boundary, which can still split it.
If no → the request is throttled mid-flight in every period it runs. Raise the quota, or pin it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the quota and period, then time the request’s CPU demand.




#Containers #Kubernetes #Latency #CPU #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Fibre latency (the distance is the floor)
text:
Case study: Fibre latency (the distance is the floor)
Light in glass covers 200 kilometres in a millisecond. A 1,000 km round trip costs 10 ms before any software runs.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Light travels at about 200,000 km/s in fibre. One way, 1,000 km is 5 ms; a round trip is 10 ms. This is a property of the medium, so no release and no setting moves it — only a shorter path does.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The distance and the round trips the obligation allows decide this, and the physics is not negotiable. Nothing in the software layer divides the trip: a faster NIC, a bigger buffer, and a new release all leave it where it is. Caching and replication shorten the distance the data travels; none of them makes the light faster.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation is short and the interactions cross a long distance repeatedly. Then cache the answer, replicate the data, or move the computation — each removes round trips, not kilometres.








WarningWhen the distance does not force it



The callers sit near the data, or the interactions cross the distance once. Then the distance is a small share of the budget, and the software is what to measure.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the round-trip count, times the distance’s trip time, fit the latency obligation?

If yes → the distance fits. Look at the queueing and the software next.
If no → no release closes it. Cache, replicate, or move the computation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the distance, then count the round trips per request.




#Networking #Latency #DistributedSystems #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Architecture

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Loss-limited throughput (the square root)
text:
Case study: Loss-limited throughput (the square root)
One percent packet loss caps a single connection at 1.2 Mbit/s on a 100 ms path. The link may be 10 Gbit/s; the loss is what caps the flow.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A connection that backs off when it sees loss settles near segment size ÷ round trip × 1 ÷ √p, where p is the loss rate. At a 1,460-byte segment, a 100 ms round trip, and 1 percent loss, 1 ÷ √p is 10, so the ceiling is 1,460 × 8 ÷ 0.1 × 10 = 1.17 Mbit/s.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The loss rate that matters is the one on the real path, and it is usually measured on a clean link. The square root is why the number moves so far: a tenth of a percent raises the same ceiling to 3.7 Mbit/s, and a hundredth of a percent to 11.7.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs a rate that one connection cannot reach on this path. Then parallel connections, a loss-tolerant transport, or a fix to the path. The square root sets the price: a tenfold cut in loss lifts the ceiling by only √10, about 3.2 times, and a wider link lifts it not at all.








WarningWhen the loss does not force it



Loss is near zero, so the ceiling sits far above the need. Or the path is short, and the round trip alone allows the rate. Then the formula is not the bound.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the loss-derived ceiling for one connection cover the rate the obligation needs?

If yes → one connection carries it. Measure the loss again under load.
If no → the path, not the link, is the limit. Fix the loss, or add connections.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the loss rate on the real path, then read the round trip.




#Networking #TCP #Performance #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Slow start (the ramp before the rate)
text:
Case study: Slow start (the ramp before the rate)
A new connection starts with 10 segments in flight and doubles each round trip. Nearly filling a 10 Gbit/s, 100 ms path takes 13 round trips — 1.3 seconds of ramp.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A flow begins with an initial window of about 10 segments, 14,600 bytes, and doubles it per round trip. The bandwidth-delay product of 10 Gbit/s and 100 ms is 125 MB, so the ramp needs log₂(125,000,000 ÷ 14,600) ≈ 13 round trips to come within about 4 percent of the link’s capacity.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
A transfer shorter than its ramp never reaches its share of the link, so its rate is set by the ramp and not by the link. The ramp is per connection, so a thousand short connections pay it a thousand times.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



Transfers are short and frequent over long paths, so the ramp dominates the transfer. Then reuse connections, or pre-warm the window so the first request does not pay the ramp.








WarningWhen the ramp does not force it



Transfers are long, so 1.3 seconds of ramp is noise against minutes of payload. Or the path is short, where 13 round trips is 13 ms. Then the ramp is not the bound, and the link’s capacity is.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the transfer last long enough for the ramp to be a small share of its duration?

If yes → the ramp is amortised. Size the transfer from the link.
If no → the rate is the ramp’s, not the link’s. Reuse the connection, or send less.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the round trip, then time one transfer end to end.




#Networking #TCP #Latency #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Packet count (the exposure a response buys)
text:
Case study: Packet count (the exposure a response buys)
A 1 MB response — a million bytes — is 685 packets. At one percent loss, 99.9 percent of such responses lose at least one.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A response is split into segments of at most the MSS. A million bytes over a 1,460-byte MSS is 685 segments, and at 1 percent loss the chance that a response loses none is 0.99^685, about 0.1 percent.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
A response’s exposure is a packet count, and the count is decided by the payload’s size. The tail — the slowest responses, not the average — is set by that count, so a response four times larger is four times more exposed. Shrinking a response is a latency remedy, not only a bandwidth one.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The response is large and the tail budget is tight on a lossy path. Then shrink the response, or split it into pages so one loss costs one page.








WarningWhen the count does not force it



The path is clean, so no packet is lost at any size. Or the loss is recovered well inside the budget, and something else sets the tail. Then the count never shows up.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does a response of this packet count, at the measured loss rate, keep its recovery inside the tail budget?

If yes → the count fits the budget at that loss rate. Recheck after the response grows.
If no → the response’s size sets the tail. Shrink it, or split it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the response size and the loss rate on the real path.




#Networking #TCP #TailLatency #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Clock skew (the ordering bound)
text:
Case study: Clock skew (the ordering bound)
Two healthy hosts disagree about the time by a millisecond, and by ten when the network is busy. Comparing their timestamps is comparing two clocks, not two events.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: NTP holds hosts within a few milliseconds on a good network, and a quartz oscillator drifts up to about 100 parts per million — 8.64 seconds a day if nothing corrects it. The skew between two hosts is the sum of both errors, and it moves with the network.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
An event stamped on one host and compared on another carries the skew between them, and the skew is measured, not assumed. It is not symmetric either: a stamp from the slower clock dates its event earlier than the event happened.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The ordering obligation is finer than the measured skew. Then use a logical clock — a counter, not a time — a single writer, or a sequence from one store; the skew is then out of the argument.








WarningWhen the skew does not force it



The obligation is coarser than the skew, so a millisecond of disagreement does not matter. Or one host stamps every event, and nothing crosses clocks. Then no ordering decision depends on the skew.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the ordering obligation coarser than the measured skew between the hosts that stamp the events?

If yes → the stamps order the events. Record the skew, and watch it under load.
If no → two events can be ordered backwards. Move the order to one clock.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the offset between the hosts that stamp.




#DistributedSystems #Consistency #Reliability #Databases #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Architecture

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Time column width (the last instant it holds)
text:
Case study: Time column width (the last instant it holds)
A signed 32-bit second counter runs out on 19 January 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC. A column of that width cannot store the expiry it was given.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A 32-bit signed integer counts 2,147,483,647 seconds from 1 January 1970, which ends on 19 January 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC. A column of that width cannot hold a later instant: a database rejects the write, and a 32-bit counter in application code wraps, which sends the date backwards.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
A column holds instants up to a computable last one, and the domain’s furthest date is a requirement, not a guess. An expiry, a schedule, or a lease dated past 2038 does not fit. The width is set in the first migration, and changing it later is a migration under load.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The domain stores an instant past 2038. Then widen the column now, while the table is small and the migration is a background job.








WarningWhen the width does not force it



The column holds a duration rather than an instant, so it never approaches the range. Or the domain has no date past 2038 — a fixed historical archive. Then nothing in the table reaches the edge.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the column’s width represent the latest instant the domain must store?

If yes → the column holds the range. Record the latest instant it must represent.
If no → the write fails, or wraps, at a date you can compute. Widen it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Find the largest instant in the domain, then compare it with the type’s range.




#Databases #SchemaDesign #Migration #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Correctness

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Certificate lifetime (the renewal window)
text:
Case study: Certificate lifetime (the renewal window)
A public TLS certificate may live no more than 200 days, and 100 from March 2027. A renewal that needs a person is already out of bounds: the window is shorter than the release cadence that carries it.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Public certificate authorities may issue a TLS certificate valid for at most 200 days, and the ceiling falls to 100 in March 2027 and to 47 in March 2029. Many already issue for 90 days. Renewal must complete before expiry, on a schedule no longer than the certificate’s life.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Two clocks run against each other: the certificate’s life, and the time a renewal takes from decision to deployment. That time includes an approval, a change window, and a rollback. A life of 90 days and a renewal that takes a quarter is an outage with a date on it.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The renewal path includes a manual step and the life is 90 days. Then automate the renewal and exercise the automatic path — an unexercised automation is a manual process with extra steps.








WarningWhen the lifetime does not force it



Renewal is automated and has been exercised, so the life does not bound the schedule. Or the certificate is internal, with a life long enough to cover the process.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the automated renewal complete before expiry, with margin for one failed attempt?

If yes → the schedule fits the life. Exercise the failure path as well as the happy one.
If no → an expiry is scheduled, not possible. Automate the renewal, or shorten the process.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the certificate’s dates, then time one renewal end to end.




#Security #TLS #Operations #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Bit error rate (one error per 125 TB)
text:
Case study: Bit error rate (one error per 125 TB)
A drive with an unrecoverable bit error rate of 10⁻¹⁵ meets one unrecoverable error per 125 TB it reads. A 100 TB restore meets at least one such failure about 55 percent of the time.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: The unrecoverable bit error rate is the chance that a read cannot be recovered: the drive reports a failure rather than returning a wrong bit. At 10⁻¹⁵, one failure falls in 10¹⁵ bits, which is 125 TB. A 100 TB restore reads 8 × 10¹⁴ bits, and if the failures arrive independently it meets at least one 1 − e^−0.8 ≈ 55 percent of the time.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The volume read in one operation is what meets the rate; the rate alone says nothing. A restore reads the whole set at once, so the rate applies to all of it. The rated figure is the failure the drive detects and reports, so the byte is gone, not wrong: a checksum names the block that failed, and only a second copy read on its own returns the byte.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The operation reads more than the rate allows, and the data carries no checksum. Then add end-to-end checksums, verify the stored data on a schedule, and keep a second copy that is read on its own; the operation’s volume is the quantity that decides the risk.








WarningWhen the rate does not force it



The volume read in one operation is small, so the chance of meeting a failure is small. Or a second copy is served on the failed read, so one failure costs a retry and not the restore.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the volume read in one restore stay inside the bytes one error falls in?

If yes → the restore is unlikely to meet an error. Keep the checksums, which catch the rest.
If no → the restore expects an error. Verify with a checksum, and keep a second copy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the drive’s rate, then the bytes one restore reads.




#Storage #Durability #Reliability #Backup #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Databases

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Queue depth (in flight divided by service time)
text:
Case study: Queue depth (in flight divided by service time)
A device holding 32 requests in flight at 200 microseconds each completes at most 160,000 a second. At one in flight it completes 5,000. The depth is a setting you own.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A device can serve many requests at once; a loop that waits for each serves one. A device with a queue depth of 32 and an unloaded service time of 200 microseconds completes at most 32 ÷ 0.0002 = 160,000 requests a second, and it keeps that rate only if the service time holds at that depth. At a depth of one it completes 5,000.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
What the device offers is parallelism; what the code allows is a count of outstanding requests, and the two are set in different places. A loop that waits for each request caps the rate at one divided by the service time, whatever the hardware can do. The depth lives in the application, not on the drive.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs more than 5,000 a second, and the code waits for each to finish. Then issue concurrently, up to the device’s depth, and measure the service time at that depth; an unloaded measurement flatters the device.








WarningWhen the depth does not force it



The device’s service time is long and its parallelism small — a spinning disk, where depth adds queueing and no throughput. Or the code already issues concurrently, so the depth is spent.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the in-flight request count, divided by the service time, cover the rate the obligation needs?

If yes → the depth covers the rate. Measure the service time at that depth, not in isolation.
If no → the loop is the limit, not the device. Issue concurrently, up to the depth.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Count the outstanding requests in the code, then time one at the device.




#Storage #Performance #Queues #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Linux

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Failure domains (nodes are not denominators)
text:
Case study: Failure domains (nodes are not denominators)
Twenty nodes in one rack share one switch. The rack’s availability is the switch’s, and the node count is what the spreadsheet multiplies.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Nodes that share a switch, a power feed, or a hypervisor share a failure: when that component goes, all of them go. A rack of 20 nodes on one top-of-rack switch presents one failure domain, and its availability is that switch’s, not twenty nodes’.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The unit that matters is the independent failure domain, and a node is not one. Counting nodes counts one switch failure twenty times, and a deploy that touches every node is a single failure with no arithmetic at all. That one appears in no availability model.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation names a failure count, and the deployment has fewer independent domains. Then spread the nodes across domains, or state the lower tolerance; the deploy’s blast radius belongs in the same count.








WarningWhen the domains do not force it



The nodes share nothing that can fail together — separate power, separate switches, staged deploys — so a failure takes one domain. Then the node count is the domain count, and the multiplication is honest.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the number of independent failure domains cover the failure count the obligation names?

If yes → the domains cover the failure. Confirm that no deploy touches two domains at once.
If no → one event takes more than the obligation allows. Spread the nodes, or state it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. List what each node shares with its neighbours.




#Reliability #Availability #DistributedSystems #Operations #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: MTU (frame size, and the payload behind it)
text:
Case study: MTU (frame size, and the payload behind it)
A link carries 1,500 bytes per packet, of which 1,460 can be your data. One tunnel header takes 50 of those, and if the network cannot tell you it dropped an oversized packet, a large response never arrives — it just times out.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: The MTU is the largest packet one link carries: 1,500 bytes here. Take away the IP and TCP headers, 40 bytes, and one connection may send 1,460 bytes of payload — the maximum segment size. A tunnel adds its own header first, so VXLAN leaves 1,410 and IPsec about 1,400. A packet above the path’s MTU is dropped rather than split whenever fragmentation is disallowed — always on IPv6, and on TCP over IPv4.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The MTU that matters is the smallest one on the path, and it is measured at the far end, not at the host. When the router’s “fragmentation needed” message is filtered, the drop is silent, so the connection stalls rather than fails.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The path’s MTU is below the sender’s and that message is filtered. Then set the MSS explicitly, clamp it at the tunnel, or keep messages under the smallest MTU; the tunnel’s header is the part you can size, and the path’s MTU is not.








WarningWhen the MTU does not force it



The path is uniform and the message arrives, so the sender learns the limit. Or every message is smaller than the smallest MTU on the path.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the largest message the design sends below the smallest MTU on the path?

If yes → the messages fit every hop. Recheck when an overlay is added.
If no → a hop drops the packet and the message may not arrive. Clamp the MSS, or send less.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Probe the path’s MTU end to end, then read the overlay’s overhead.




#Networking #MTU #Cloud #Operations #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Zone boundary (the cost of crossing it)
text:
Case study: Zone boundary (the cost of crossing it)
One call across zones costs a millisecond or two. Twenty of them in one request cost 30 ms; the same twenty inside a zone cost five.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: Round trips inside one availability zone — a separate datacenter with its own power and network — take about 0.25 ms. Across zones in one region they take one to two. A request making 20 sequential round trips spends 5 ms inside a zone and 30 ms across.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
A deployment diagram shows where the services run, not where the data crosses. Each sequential call pays the boundary once; parallel calls pay it once for the batch. The crossing is a property of the data flow, not of the drawing.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The request makes many sequential round trips and they cross a zone boundary. Then batch the calls, or co-locate the data with the work; the round-trip count is what batching changes.








WarningWhen the boundary does not force it



The calls are few, or they run in parallel, or the boundary is crossed once. Then the zone is a small share of the budget, and the service time is what to measure.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the number of sequential round trips, times the boundary’s cost, fit the latency obligation?

If yes → the boundary fits. Count the round trips again after the next refactor.
If no → the topology, not the code, sets the latency. Co-locate, or batch.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Trace one request, count its sequential calls, note where each lands.




#Cloud #Latency #Architecture #DistributedSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Route convergence (the failover it sets)
text:
Case study: Route convergence (the failover it sets)
A withdrawn route usually disappears in 30 to 180 seconds, and the tail runs to fifteen minutes. A failover plan that waits on routing is a plan measured in minutes.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A routing change spreads as each router learns the new path and passes it to its neighbours; worldwide, the common case is 30 to 180 seconds and the tail runs to fifteen minutes or more. Anycast — one address announced from several sites — moves the flows with the route, so a moved flow loses its connection state.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The failover the obligation allows meets a propagation time that runs on routers, not on your schedule. The route is withdrawn only after a health check fails, so the health check adds to it. The client’s resolver and its connection reuse add again.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation is shorter than convergence. Then put the switch above routing: a load balancer, a health-checked endpoint, an application-level redirect — a layer that answers before the routers agree.








WarningWhen convergence does not force it



The failover is regional and the obligation is measured in minutes. Or the clients reconnect and the lost state is acceptable. Then routing is fast enough, and a second mechanism above it is cost without benefit.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the routing convergence time, plus the health check, fit inside the failover time the obligation allows?

If yes → routing can carry the failover. Check the client’s reconnect time on top.
If no → the route is slower than the promise. Move the switch above routing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Time a route withdrawal, then add the health check.




#Networking #BGP #Failover #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Operations

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Socket distance (the share that crosses)
text:
Case study: Socket distance (the share that crosses)
A memory load that crosses to the other CPU socket costs about 1.7 times a local one. A heap spanning both pays it on every access that crosses.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A core reaches memory attached to its own CPU socket in about 80 nanoseconds, and memory on the other socket in about 130 to 140. A working set spread across both pays the remote price on the accesses that cross.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
The cost is decided by the share of accesses that cross, not by the average latency of memory. The share is a property of the allocator and the thread placement, so it is measured, not assumed. Binding a thread does nothing for memory the thread does not own.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The workload is latency-bound and its working set spans sockets. Then shard by socket, allocate on the socket that reads, and bind the threads; the share of crossing accesses is the number the change moves.








WarningWhen the distance does not force it



The workload is throughput-bound and memory bandwidth is the limit, so using both sockets helps. Or the allocator already keeps each thread’s data local, so few accesses cross.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the share of accesses that cross a socket, times the difference between the remote and the local latency, fit the per-access budget?

If yes → the placement fits. Measure the share again after the data grows.
If no → the topology of the memory sets the latency. Shard by socket, or bind.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the remote share, then the local and remote latencies.




#Performance #Hardware #NUMA #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OperatingSystems

title: Substrate Facts as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Timestamp resolution (the events per tick)
text:
Case study: Timestamp resolution (the events per tick)
At ten thousand events a second, ten of them share a millisecond on average. A millisecond timestamp cannot order them, and the column looks precise enough to try.
Choosing a structure? Ask “what measured fact constrains this structure, and what is its value?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, you hold the number. The number rules out a design only where the design breaches an obligation: the fact measures, the obligation rules out. Which of the remaining designs you take is a second decision.

Bound: A timestamp resolves to one tick. At a peak of 10,000 events a second and a millisecond column, 10 events land on each value on average, and the busier milliseconds hold more — so the column cannot order them and cannot break the tie.


The substrate knowledge gap it signals
Ordering needs a resolution finer than the interval between events, and the column has one tick to give. Resolution is a property of the type, and the event rate is a measurement. A sort on the timestamp leaves the tie in storage order, which is not the order they happened.






ImportantWhen the fact bounds the shape



The obligation needs a total order and the events per tick exceed one. Then add a sequence number, widen the resolution, or take the order from the source; the tie is decided in storage, so the fix belongs there.








WarningWhen the resolution does not force it



The event rate is far below one per tick, so ties are rare and any tie is harmless. Or the order comes from a sequence the store assigns, and the timestamp is metadata.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do fewer than one event per tick arrive at the peak event rate?

If yes → the timestamp orders them. Confirm the peak, not the mean.
If no → ties are certain at peak. Add a sequence, or widen the resolution.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Measure the peak event rate, then read the column’s precision.




#Databases #SchemaDesign #Ordering #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Correctness

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
An annotation or a default claims who owns the transaction, what may run later, what may be stale. Each post names the claim and asks which fact of the domain or the workload backs it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
Case study: @Transactional and the proxy
A method calls its own sibling on the same bean, and the sibling’s @Transactional never executes — no boundary of its own, no rollback of its own, no warning.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: By default, Spring applies @Transactional by wrapping the bean in a proxy whose intercepted methods begin, commit, or roll back. The annotation binds to the call, not to the method body. In proxy mode, a self-invocation passes through no proxy, so the annotation is inert: the method runs in whatever transaction the caller opened, or in none.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
The team must know where its transaction boundaries sit relative to its call paths. The annotation claims “this unit of work is atomic”; the proxy enforces it only on entry from outside. Two facts stay unasked: which paths enter through the proxy, and which failures the domain calls faults. By default, Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions only, so a checked business failure commits and the claim quietly becomes false.
The gap question: which call path enters this method — through the proxy?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Boundaries at entry points that controllers, consumers, or scheduled jobs call from outside the bean. The domain fact is that the step is atomic: the order, the payment, and the reservation succeed or fail together.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



@Transactional on an internal helper “for safety.” The helper joins whatever its caller opened, so it documents an intention and enforces nothing. A test passes because the caller happened to be transactional; the one path without one half-writes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which call path enters this method — through the proxy? And which failures should roll back, by domain rule rather than by default?

If yes → the annotation holds on that path. Check the rollback rules name the domain’s fault classes, checked ones included.
If no → the call is internal. Move the boundary to the entry point, or split the bean so the call crosses the proxy, and price the extra edge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List every caller, then every failure the domain calls a fault.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Transactions #ProxyPattern #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Propagation levels (REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, NESTED)
text:
Case study: Propagation levels (REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, NESTED)
The audit log says the order was placed, the order was rolled back, and REQUIRES_NEW let the audit row outlive the fact it describes.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: REQUIRED joins the caller’s transaction, so one rollback takes both. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller and commits its own, so it survives the caller’s rollback. NESTED takes a savepoint inside the caller’s transaction, on a JDBC-backed manager that supports savepoints, rolls back to it, and lets the outer work continue. The trade is whose failure set is shared with whose.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
Propagation states which facts live and die together: REQUIRES_NEW declares an independent fact; NESTED declares one that may be abandoned while the larger survives. Neither is a safety setting. Propagation is honored only across a proxy call (Spring’s wrapper around the bean), and its consequences appear only at the first partial failure — the case no test scripts.
The gap question: for each boundary, must this fact survive the caller’s rollback — answered in domain terms, or copied from a default?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



REQUIRES_NEW where a stated business rule says the attempt must outlive the failure: a compliance record of a rejected application, a security event for a denied login. The rule is written, and the team can state its converse — what must not be recorded.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



REQUIRES_NEW everywhere “to be safe.” Every attempt writes, including attempts the domain considers non-events, and the log reports orders that were never placed — safe against lost writes, unsafe against false ones. NESTED on a store without savepoint support is the same guess in another form: it compiles, and the driver refuses when the first nested call asks for a savepoint.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each boundary: must this fact survive the caller’s rollback — answered in domain terms, or copied from a default?

If yes → the level is a domain decision. Write down, per boundary, which facts share a fate and which do not.
If no → the level is the default or a habit. Remove it, or restate it in domain terms first.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the level wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which partial failures the domain accepts, and what the log must say about a refused action.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Transactions #AuditLog #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Lazy versus eager bean initialization
text:
Case study: Lazy versus eager bean initialization
Startup drops from nine to four seconds in the Boot log. A missing property surfaces at 02:00 as a 500 on one endpoint, in front of a customer.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: An eager bean is built while the application context refreshes; a lazy one on first lookup. The trade is where a wiring or configuration failure lands: at boot, in front of the deploy pipeline, or at first use, in front of the first caller. Boot 3.x makes the whole context lazy with one property, spring.main.lazy-initialization.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
Laziness relocates failures; it does not remove them. A bean that cannot be configured still fails — the only question is whether the log says “deployment refused” or “request 4471 failed”. That is a claim about consequence: which subsystems must be proven before traffic is admitted, and which may wait. Laziness also stops at the injection point: a lazy bean injected into an eager singleton without an @Lazy injection point is still built at boot.
The gap question: which beans would you rather fail at boot than at first use — did anyone decide, or did a property decide for them?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Lazy for paths only some traffic reaches: an admin report, an optional integration. Eager, deliberately, for the beans whose misconfiguration must stop the release — datasource, security chain, listener containers.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Global lazy initialization “for startup time.” The broken bean is found by the first user, inside a request thread; the deploy that should have failed becomes an incident. The cost does not vanish: it moves to the first call on each cold path, so the p99 of rarely used endpoints becomes the startup you saved, paid by a customer. Every dashboard looks better.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which beans would you rather fail at boot than at first use — and did anyone decide, or did a property decide for them?

If yes → keep those eager by name, make the rest lazy per bean, and check the cold-path latency.
If no → nothing was decided. The property bets on which failures nobody notices; you are not the one who pays it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the property wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which subsystems must be proven before traffic, and what the lazy path costs cold.




#Spring #SpringBoot #StartupTime #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
Case study: Prototype scope
A bean is annotated @Scope(“prototype”) and injected into a singleton. One instance is ever built — and four million requests share it.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: A prototype bean is built for each lookup, configured, handed to the caller, and forgotten — the container keeps no record, so it never calls the destruction callback. The trade is lifecycle ownership: a fresh instance per use against a cleanup obligation the container will not discharge. A prototype injected into a singleton is resolved once, at creation, and captured for the singleton’s lifetime.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
Prototype is a claim about per-item state: this object accumulates something a second user must not see — a buffer, a mutable parse tree. It is also a claim about ownership of cleanup. Neither claim is checked. The container hands a prototype to a singleton without a warning, and never runs @PreDestroy on it, so what it holds is released only if the caller does.
The gap question: who creates and destroys this bean — the container at every lookup, or whoever injected it once?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Work whose state belongs to one unit of use, fetched through ObjectProvider at the moment of need and discarded after: a report builder per export, a stateful parser per payload. The domain says the state is per-item, and the caller owns the end of it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The annotation plus a singleton field. The scope claim is then silently false: mutable state crosses request boundaries, and the bug arrives as another user’s data in a response — intermittent, unreproducible, and naming nothing in the stack trace. A quieter variant: expecting @PreDestroy on a prototype, so connections leak per lookup.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who creates and destroys this bean — the container at every lookup, or whoever injected it once?

If yes → hold it behind an ObjectProvider, fetch per use, and give the caller an explicit end-of-life.
If no → the singleton holds one instance. Make the state immutable, or inject an ObjectProvider instead of the bean.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the scope wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which state belongs to one use, and who closes what the object opens.




#Spring #SpringBoot #BeanScope #Lifecycle #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: @Async and the executor nobody named
text:
Case study: @Async and the executor nobody named
One @Async on the nightly import, and every @Async handler now queues behind the batch.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: @Async lifts a method body off the caller’s thread and returns a future. It runs on an executor you name or do not: Boot 3.x auto-configures a pool of eight with an unbounded queue; the thread-per-task fallback belongs to plain Spring, or to virtual threads. Name nothing, and every @Async method shares that default.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
An executor is a capacity claim about a workload, and the workload is a domain fact. Peak concurrent invocations, thread hold time, the share of that spent waiting on I/O — a pool sized from those three is measured; one sized from a default is inherited. The team must also know which workloads may share a fate: a saturated batch is a different risk from a saturated checkout.
The gap question: which pool runs this method — named, sized — and from what measured task profile?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A dedicated executor per workload, sized from its own profile. The reconciliation job gets two threads because two saturate the source database and more only contend. The request path gets a pool sized from the concurrency its latency budget allows. They share nothing, so a first-of-month spike cannot starve the health check.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



@Async on a method, no executor configured anywhere. It compiles, the single-call test passes, and the annotation reads as “we made it async”. Under load the import, the audit write, and the mail send compete for one pool designed for none of them. The unbounded default is worse: nothing is refused, the queue grows without bound, and the heap fills with work that never runs.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which pool runs this method — named, sized — and from what measured task profile?

If yes → an executor per workload, with a number behind each size. Check its queue: a large queue turns saturation into latency that a refusal would have made visible.
If no → it runs on whatever the framework chose. Name the executor, size it, and decide what happens when it is full.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found @Async wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your workload. Measure the peak concurrent calls and the thread hold time.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Async #ThreadPools #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: @Cacheable, @CacheEvict, and the TTL that is not there
text:
Case study: @Cacheable, @CacheEvict, and the TTL that is not there
A @Cacheable method that reads the current user, under a key that never names the user, serves one customer another’s price.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: @Cacheable stores a return value under a key built from the arguments and serves it to the next caller with that key. @CacheEvict drops entries. Neither carries a TTL — the abstraction offers key, keyGenerator, condition, and unless, so it lives in the CacheManager underneath or nowhere: stale until evicted, forever if nothing does.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
A cache is a staleness contract the domain must state: which reads tolerate lag, and how much. The key is a second claim — an assertion that two calls with equal keys have equal answers. Every input that changes the answer belongs in it, including ones off the parameter list: the principal, the tenant, the locale.
The gap question: what may be stale, for how long — stated by the domain? And does the key capture every input that changes the answer?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A price list that may trail five minutes is a business statement a person can defend: the five-minute TTL sits in the CacheManager entry beside the annotation that cannot express it, the key carries sku, currency, and tier, and eviction hangs off the write that changes it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



@Cacheable on a method whose result depends on the authenticated user, keyed by product id alone. The first caller populates the entry; every other customer reads their price. Nothing fails; the numbers are another customer’s. A self-invoked call bypasses the AOP proxy, so those calls never touch the cache.








TipThe faithfulness test



What may be stale, for how long — stated by the domain? And does the key capture every input that changes the answer?

If yes → the lag is a decided fact and the key is the identity. Check eviction against every invalidating write, and set the TTL in the CacheManager — the annotation will not.
If no → you have a correctness defect no test can see: the wrong answer is a cached one. Add the missing key input, or drop the cache.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found @Cacheable wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which reads tolerate lag, on which inputs.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Caching #Staleness #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Auto-configuration and its embedded guesses
text:
Case study: Auto-configuration and its embedded guesses
The connection pool maxes at ten because ten is the HikariCP default, and nobody in the room ever chose ten.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Auto-configuration adds beans when conditions match: a DataSource from a classpath driver, an ObjectMapper, a pool of ten connections, a thirty-second connect timeout, unknown JSON fields ignored rather than rejected. Each is a decision taken by a condition, not by a person.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
A default answers a question the framework asked on your behalf: how many connections may exist in total, what a consumer does when a payload gains a field, how long a socket may hang. The multiplication is what the default hides — ten per instance, twelve instances, one database accepting one hundred: the last two lose.
The gap question: which defaults is this application running on — listed anywhere — and which did anyone consciously accept?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Each active auto-configuration reviewed once, each exclusion recorded with its reason. The pool is eight because the database’s limit divided by the instance count gives eight, and that arithmetic sits in the configuration comment. Jackson’s conventions are pinned because a contract test asserts them.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“It works” as the only evidence. The pool is ten because ten is the default, and staging never ran twelve instances. The ObjectMapper swallows unknown fields, so an upstream rename becomes a null three layers deeper instead of a parse failure. Dates serialize as ISO because Boot disabled the timestamp form, and the consumer reading epoch numbers never noticed.
