TipThe faithfulness test



Which defaults is this application running on — listed anywhere — and which did anyone consciously accept?

If yes → configuration is a stated set of choices, and an upgrade is a diff against them. Check each value’s arithmetic against the constraint behind it.
If no → the application runs on inherited answers. Enumerate what auto-configured, then accept or override each in writing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found auto-configuration wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Compare what the deployment needs with what the framework supplied.




#Spring #SpringBoot #AutoConfiguration #Defaults #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Actuator endpoints and what they expose
text:
Case study: Actuator endpoints and what they expose
A heap dump endpoint sits one curl away, left open for a demo, and a heap holds every live session token.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Boot exposes only health over the web by default; env, heapdump, threaddump, and configprops need an explicit include. Enabled means switched on for the app; exposed means reachable over HTTP; the network interface is the port that answers, and a management port moves the exposed ones off the application port. The sensitive ones read configuration and memory — env every property, heapdump the heap itself.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
An endpoint is a read of the running system, and the domain decides who may perform it and from where. Env and configprops mask values whose key name looks sensitive — password, secret, token — so masking follows naming, and a credential under an unrecognized name prints in clear. A heap dump is never masked: it is memory, with tokens inside it.
The gap question: which endpoints are enabled, on which interface, reachable by whom — stated anywhere?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Health and metrics on the internal interface, where the load balancer and the scrape job reach them and the internet cannot. Env and heapdump unreachable from outside, behind authentication if enabled at all, the reason written down. In an incident the dump is taken deliberately, then deleted.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A wildcard include added “for the demo”, kept because the demo still runs, with management on the application port so the link works from a laptop. Every step was locally reasonable: the wildcard unblocked a deadline, the public port fixed reachability, and the endpoint “only reads”. Months later an env response appears in a chat channel and a heap dump is a URL.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which endpoints are enabled, on which interface, reachable by whom — stated anywhere?

If yes → exposure is a decided surface with an owner. Check it against the network path from outside, and the masking rules against the property names here.
If no → the surface exists and nobody chose it. Drop the wildcard, move management to its own interface, and gate what remains.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the actuator wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Enumerate what is exposed, then trace each path from the internet.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Actuator #Security #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
Case study: @Scheduled cron expressions
A month-end report fires at 23:00 UTC on the last day of the month. In Berlin that is already 00:00 on the 1st — November’s numbers land in December’s file.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: @Scheduled(cron = “0 0 23 L * *“) hands the trigger to the framework: six fields, seconds first, with L for last day of month. Spring evaluates it in a zone — the JVM default unless you name one — and every instance runs its own scheduler, so nothing in the annotation limits how many machines fire. The annotation buys automation; the bill arrives in the meaning of”when.”


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
“Month end” is a business-calendar fact before it is a trigger: a zone where the month really closes, an accounting boundary, a tolerance. None of that lives in the cron string. Nor does cardinality — whether two runs are a duplicate or a partition of the work. The gap question: whose calendar is “month end,” and how many copies of this job may exist at one instant?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Every expression carries zone = “Europe/Berlin”, reviewed as an accounting fact rather than a default, and a lock holds exactly-once: a ShedLock row, a clustered Quartz trigger, or a database advisory lock — a lock the second instance cannot take.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



No zone field, inheriting whatever the container reports, so a base-image change shifts the run by hours and no test notices. Or a 02:30 local trigger on the DST night, firing in an hour that does not exist, or in one that occurs twice, depending on a resolver nobody read. Or nobody asked, and three replicas each send the invoice email — found by a customer, not a monitor.








TipThe faithfulness test



In which timezone does “month end” actually mean what it says — and how many instances may run this concurrently, by design?

If yes → the expression is an accounting fact. Check the zone at every call site, and that the lock fails loudly rather than skipping.
If no → it is a default wearing a schedule. Set the zone, decide cardinality, and price the lock before adding one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask finance which calendar closes the period, and operations how many replicas run.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Scheduling #DistributedSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Profiles and per-environment configuration
text:
Case study: Profiles and per-environment configuration
One key exists only in production, added years ago by an engineer who has left. Staging has never had it, and never failed that way.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Spring Boot merges application.yml with application-{profile}.yml, selected by spring.profiles.active; @Profile gates beans on the same switch. The merge is additive and silent: a key in one profile and absent in another gives no warning, no diff, no error — only a different object graph. The trade: environment knowledge placed deliberately against profile sprawl, where nobody can name which keys differ.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
A profile claims two environments differ in stated ways and agree elsewhere. Each difference is a fact someone owns: another database, another bucket, a live gateway instead of a sandbox. Sprawl begins when a difference is added for convenience and never stated — a timeout tuned once under load, a key nobody owns. The gap question: which keys differ between production and staging, and does each difference match a reason you can say out loud?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The environments differ in few named ways: a datasource URL, a credential from the environment, a log level, a sandbox endpoint. Secrets stay out of the YAML, injected as variables or fetched from a vault, so the file records shape only.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



application-prod.yml drifting for years, one line at a time, each urgent when added. The result is a key only production has — the one that makes the service start there — and a failure only production has, reproduced nowhere, debugged by diffing files at 2 a.m. Worse: a profile per developer, so the active set is a local ritual.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which keys differ between production and staging — listed — and does each difference correspond to a stated environment difference?

If yes → the profiles are environment knowledge. Check that secrets live outside the files, and re-read the diff each release.
If no → drift. Move the stray key to the shared file, or write down why it differs.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Diff the resolved key sets, then ask who added each.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Configuration #Environments #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
Case study: @ConfigurationProperties versus scattered @Value
A property key is renamed, the build stays green, and forty @Value sites read a default that nobody set — or fail on the first request.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: @ConfigurationProperties binds a prefix to one class — constructor binding, ideally a record — so acme.pool.* arrives as typed fields, and @Validated with JSR-380 constraints — Bean Validation, provider on the classpath — rejects a bad set at startup. @Value(“${acme.limit}”) binds one converted value at one injection point, with no shared home and no link between key and field. The trade: typed, validated, grouped configuration against keys scattered across forty classes.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
Configuration is where the domain states its bounds: a pool size above zero and below the database’s ceiling, a timeout short enough that a stuck dependency does not eat the request budget. A scattered @Value records the key and forgets the bound: every limit is a string that parses or does not. The gap question: which values carry constraints the domain would defend, and does anything enforce them before startup?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The bound is cheap to state: pool sizes, timeouts, retry counts. One properties class per bounded area, constructor-bound, valid on arrival, with @Min, @Max and duration constraints on exactly those fields. A pool of zero becomes a startup failure naming the field, not a stall an hour into load.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



@Value(“${acme.limit}”) in forty places, each with its own default. The key is renamed where it is documented, and nothing connects that string to the code: with a default the fallback wins silently, without one the failure waits for whichever bean initializes first — for a lazy bean, a request.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which configuration values carry domain constraints — and does anything check them before the application starts?

If yes → the configuration is domain knowledge, enforced early. Check that each constraint matches a bound the domain would defend.
If no → the values are strings the domain hopes are sane. Group and type them, constrain the ones that matter.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the keys, then ask which values have a bound you would defend.




#Spring #SpringBoot #Configuration #Validation #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: Circular dependencies (the refused start)
text:
Case study: Circular dependencies (the refused start)
Two beans each demand the other in their constructor, and the container refuses to start — that refusal is the most useful thing the framework says today.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Bean A takes B in its constructor and B takes A, so neither can be built first — a constructor cycle has always failed. From Boot 2.6 the container also refuses a setter or field cycle: spring.main.allow-circular-references defaults to false, and the context fails with the cycle printed in full. @Lazy on one injection point restores the old behaviour with a container proxy resolved at first call. The trade: refusal as design information at build time, against a patch that keeps the cycle and defers resolution to call time.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
A bean cycle is a concept cycle. Each constructor argument claims the object cannot be described without the other, and both cannot hold unless the two are one thing. The team must know which direction is a genuine, conditional use, and which is a need at construction.
The gap question: what is the shared concept both beans need?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A cache and the loader that fills it. The cache cannot fetch on a miss, the loader has nowhere to store the result, and the second direction is deferred — called on a miss, never at construction. Inject a provider (an ObjectProvider, which yields the bean on demand), and “may be called later” is a domain fact, not a workaround.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



@Lazy added to clear the startup error. Initialization order becomes a runtime lottery — whichever entry point touches the proxy first decides when the other bean gets built, so wiring that worked on the web path fails under a scheduled job; no stack trace names the cycle. One annotation, green build, a startup refusal reclassified as a deferral.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the shared concept these two beans both need — extracted, or hidden behind a proxy?

If yes → give it its own bean, and let both depend on that.
If no → the deferral is priced, not proved: the cycle persists, resolved one call later under production load.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List what each bean does with the other, then ask which use must be at construction.




#Spring #SpringBoot #DependencyInjection #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Java

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
section: Case study: RestClient and WebClient timeouts
text:
Case study: RestClient and WebClient timeouts
A client with no read timeout waits forever on a stalled upstream, and takes every calling thread down with it.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Spring’s HTTP clients inherit the bound of the library beneath them, and several stock paths leave the read timeout unset — an unbounded wait: RestClient with its default factory, WebClient on Reactor Netty with no responseTimeout. The trade: a latency budget per dependency, enforced by the client, against a default that reads as “nothing to configure”.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
A timeout is a claim about the dependency, not a setting: this call is worth at most N ms. Only the dependency’s owner can state N; only the caller can enforce it. The team must know, per dependency, the promised response time and what the caller does when it is missed — fail, retry, or serve stale.
The gap question: for each dependency, how long may it take, and who said so?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Two numbers per dependency, both derived. Connect is short and local — the network reaches the host or it does not. Read equals the slowest response its budget permits. Set them per client: each failure stays bounded by its own promise.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The client that keeps the library default. While answers are fast nothing shows; on the first stall every calling thread blocks, the pool can drain, and the endpoints sharing that pool fail together. The seduction: one autoconfigured bean everyone reuses, and an absent setting looks like nothing to review.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each outbound dependency: how long may it take — stated by whom — and does the client enforce that number?

If yes → the budget is knowledge, and the client enforces it. Check that the overall timeout exceeds the callee’s read timeout, so the inner failure fires first.
If no → a library default that knows nothing about this dependency. Set it per client, and decide what the caller does at the limit.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the response-time distribution, then ask its owner what they promise.




#Spring #SpringBoot #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Resilience #Timeouts

title: Spring Decisions as Knowledge Claims
text:
Case study: ApplicationEvent and @EventListener
A listener confirms the order, the transaction rolls back, and the customer keeps the email for something that never happened.
Adopting a Spring annotation or default? Ask “which fact does this choice claim — who owns this transaction, what may run later, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework enforces a guess. If you can, the annotation is knowledge embodied — the framework catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: publishEvent calls each matching non-async listener on the publisher’s thread, inside its transaction, and names none of them. @TransactionalEventListener adds a timing claim: AFTER_COMMIT by default, else BEFORE_COMMIT or AFTER_ROLLBACK — and with fallbackExecution false, a listener is skipped outright when no transaction is active. The trade: decoupling from the call graph, against timing someone must pick.


The Spring knowledge gap it signals
An event asserts that others care about a fact; it is not an instruction to one collaborator. The team must list who consumes the fact, and say whether the reaction belongs inside the transaction, as one atomic outcome, or outside it, surviving a rollback. Both are domain claims, not defaults.
The gap question: who consumes this event, and must their reaction survive the producer’s rollback?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An order is placed, and three things react that the order service need not name: the confirmation mail, the analytics counter, the warehouse pick. The fact is stated once in the past tense, and the reactions run after commit, because a mail cannot be unsent.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An event used as a method call with extra steps: one publisher, one listener, no other consumer. The edge has left the source, so a reader who follows publishEvent finds nothing, and deleting the listener leaves a silent no-op.
The timing variant is quieter and worse. A before-commit listener mails or writes a file, acting on state the transaction may still discard — a phantom no rollback undoes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who consumes this event — listed — and must the reaction survive the producer’s rollback?

If yes → the list is real and the phase is explicit. Check each phase against its job: after-commit for the irreversible.
If no → nobody else consumes it, or the phase is unstated. Call the method, or state the phase; let the compiler keep the edge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask what the listener does on rollback, and whether the domain accepts that.




#Spring #SpringBoot #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DomainEvents #Transactions

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
The compiler checks a fact — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and the check costs something. Each post names the fact checked and the price paid.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: The borrow checker
Two threads borrow the same vector mutably and the build stops — the compiler ruled the pairing out before the binary existed.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Rust allows many immutable borrows or exactly one mutable borrow, checked on every path. Aliasing plus mutation is the pair it forbids, and a data race needs exactly that pair — so safe code cannot race. The guarantee follows from the typing rule, not from a convention the team promises to honor.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The checker asks one question: right now, how many readers, and is anyone writing? A design that answers this has one shape. One that cannot has two owners, or a cache behind a lock, or a callback outliving its caller — and the compiler forces the developer to name which, at the line where the ambiguity sits.
The gap question: which sharing pattern is this program’s real shape — and did the types encode it, or was the checker defeated?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A widget tree with one owning parent and borrowed children. A handler taking &Request and returning owned data. A batch pass reading a large buffer immutably while writing results elsewhere. The rule costs nothing, because the sharing really is many readers or one writer.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Rc<RefCell<T>> on every field. The borrow rules rejected the graph, so shared mutable state came back wrapped and the check moved to runtime: RefCell panics on a conflicting live borrow, deep inside a request, far from the line that caused it. The signature now reads “anyone may mutate at any time” — the claim the compiler declined to verify. It compiles.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which sharing pattern is this program’s real shape — and did the types encode it, or was the checker defeated?

If yes → the types are the design record. Check that the owning side is the one the domain names.
If no → name the aliasing the program actually has, then choose: restructure to one owner, or admit shared mutation and pay for it explicitly.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Draw the ownership graph of the live values and compare it with the signatures.




#Rust #BorrowChecker #Ownership #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: Ownership and moves
A function hands back a 10 MB buffer and no byte of the buffer is copied, no allocator runs, no collector wakes — the signature alone decided where the memory went.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A value has one owner. Passing a non-Copy value moves it, and the old binding is dead; when the owner leaves scope the value drops, in an order the compiler fixes. No tracing collector runs, so no pause interrupts the program. The trade is ergonomics: a signature that moves its argument ends the caller’s use of it.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Ownership is a claim about handoffs. Either the caller still needs the value or it does not. A move says its work in that scope is finished and its future belongs to the callee; a borrow says the caller keeps it and the callee only looks. The compiler accepts the move and rejects the later use — then accepts a clone and rejects nothing.
The gap question: which clones are real copies the domain needs — counted — and which are compiler-appeasement?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A builder consuming self and yielding the finished value, because the caller has no use for the half-built thing. A message sent through a channel, where the sender’s value is dead by definition. Accessors taking &self and returning borrowed fields.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



.clone() scattered until it compiles. The borrow rules refused a second use, so the value was duplicated instead of the design corrected. Each clone duplicates a whole value the rules never required, and it asserts a fact nobody stated: that two copies of this value may diverge. It hides the real lifetime structure, so the next reader cannot tell an intentional snapshot from a truce with the compiler.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which clones are real copies the domain needs — counted — and which are compiler-appeasement?

If yes → count them, and say why each copy exists in the domain, not in the borrow checker.
If no → give the callee a reference, or move once at the real handoff, and let the original die there.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found ownership wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Trace each clone back to the call that demanded it, and ask what the caller did next.




#Rust #Ownership #MemoryManagement #APIDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: Lifetimes
The signature says the returned reference lives as long as the input, and the checker enforces it — so a cache cannot outlive the store it reads.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A lifetime is a named scope, and a reference may not outlive the data it points at. The compiler infers most; where a function without a self parameter returns borrowed data from several inputs, the developer writes the relation down and every call site is checked against it. The trade is annotation overhead exactly where the data flow is complex.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
An annotation states how long a value stays alive relative to another. It forces the developer to say which object owns the memory, which merely looks at it, and for how long that stays legal. That is a domain fact, not syntax. Elision hides it only while the shape is simple.
The gap question: for each reference, what is its real scope — and does the signature say so, or was ’static a shortcut?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A cache holding &’store Entry values into a longer-lived store: the annotation states the store outlives the cache, true by construction and worth stating. A parser returning a slice of its input.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



’static added until the errors stop. It compiles, so the reference now claims to live for the whole program — true by construction, false as a design statement. The real relationship was never modeled and the structure bent around the annotation: the borrow became an owned copy, or a leak, or an Arc with no sharing. The signature says “forever” because nobody could say “as long as the store”.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each reference, what is its real scope — and does the signature say so, or was ’static a shortcut?

If yes → the scope is a domain fact and the signature repeats it. Check that the owner outlives every borrower on every path.
If no → name the real scope, write the lifetime that carries it, or move the data so no reference crosses.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found lifetimes wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List each reference, its owner, and the longest path on which it is used.




#Rust #Lifetimes #BorrowChecker #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: Send and Sync
A type that was never thread-safe fails to compile the moment it enters a channel — the compiler rejects a bug with no runtime symptom before anyone writes it.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Send marks a type that may move to another thread; Sync marks one whose shared references may be used from several threads. Both are auto traits derived by the compiler from the fields; unsafe impl overrides that. A thread spawn or a channel send requires Send, so the crossing is checked at compile time. The trade is the wrapper maze wherever the requirement bites.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Thread safety here is a type property: the developer must know which values genuinely cross a thread and which never leave theirs — a fact about the program’s execution structure. The compiler checks the types it is given; it cannot check whether the crossing was real.
The gap question: which values genuinely cross a thread boundary — and does the type structure say exactly that, no more?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A channel carrying only Send types, its receiver on another thread. A job struct owning its inputs and taking no references, because it must outlive the scope that built it. A shared counter behind Arc<AtomicUsize>, where many threads really read and write.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Mutex<T> around values that never cross a thread. The lock asserts concurrent access and no second thread exists to contend for it. The cost is real: a lock on every read, a poison path nobody designed, guards in the API — a compile-time claim about contention that no measurement supports. Worse, unsafe impl Send on interior-mutable state silences a correct check.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which values genuinely cross a thread boundary — and does the type structure say exactly that, no more?

If yes → the wrappers mark real crossings. Check what happens on the panic path, when a lock poisons.
If no → drop the wrapper, keep the value on its thread, and let the type say so.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Draw the threads, then the values passing between them.




#Rust #Concurrency #SendSync #ThreadSafety #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: Monomorphisation versus dyn Trait
text:
Case study: Monomorphisation versus dyn Trait
One generic function called with twelve types compiles twelve times, and the release binary grows tens of kilobytes for code that runs on two.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A generic function is stamped out once per concrete type: fn area<T: Shape>(s: T) becomes one function per T, each specialised and inlinable. A dyn Trait call goes through a vtable, so one function serves every type at a pointer hop. Static dispatch buys inlining and a known callee; dynamic dispatch buys one code path and a binary that does not grow with call sites.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Monomorphisation is a claim that this call site is hot enough to pay per-type code — in compile time, binary size, and instruction cache. The developer must know which paths are measured hot, and which boundaries want one code path for an open set of types. The gap question: which call sites are hot enough to pay per-type code — measured — and which boundaries want exactly one code path?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A numeric kernel over f32 and f64 on a measured hot path, where inlining removes the call and lets the vectoriser see the loop. Two instantiations, both benchmarked faster than the dyn version by a measured margin. And at the plugin boundary, dyn: the type set is open, the call happens once per item, and one code path is the requirement rather than a compromise.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Generics over everything, because generics are faster. The binary bloats, compile time triples, and the extra instantiation shows no gain in any benchmark. The mirror trap: dyn in an inner loop, because dyn keeps the binary small — the indirection blocks inlining on the one path the profiler flags.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which call sites are hot enough to pay per-type code — measured — and which boundaries want exactly one code path?

If yes → the dispatch matches the profile. Re-check every release; hot paths move.
If no → you chose dispatch by slogan. Profile the path; instantiate where it is hot, box where the type set is open.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Time both builds, compare size, and read the profile.




#Rust #Monomorphisation #Generics #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Compilers

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: Zero-cost abstractions
An iterator chain of map, filter and sum compiles to the loop you would have written — until one closure fails to inline, and it compiles to a chain of direct calls.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: “Zero cost” is a claim about one compilation, not a property of the language: the abstraction costs nothing when the optimiser erases it into the code you would have written. An iterator chain, a trait bound, a closure — each disappears in release when inlining succeeds, and each survives as real work when it does not.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
A zero-cost claim is narrow: this chain, this profile, these settings. The developer must know whether the machine code was compared, or the benchmark timed, on that path — and which constructs defeat inlining: dyn dispatch, a boxed closure, bounds checks the optimiser cannot hoist. The gap question: was zero cost measured on THIS path — assembly or benchmark — or assumed from the slogan?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A filter-map-sum over a Vec<u64> in release, checked against the manual loop: identical instructions, timings within noise, no calls and no bounds checks in the disassembly. The abstraction is verified — the compiler wrote the loop, and the source stays composable. A trait bound on a numeric function, inlined at both call sites, shows the same.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Zero cost” as folklore. The closure boxed as Box<dyn Fn>, so the call is indirect and the chain never flattens. The release profile with LTO off and sixteen codegen units — code split before inlining, so nothing crosses a boundary. The abstraction that failed to inline, found only because someone finally looked at the assembly.








TipThe faithfulness test



Was zero cost measured on THIS path — assembly or benchmark — or assumed from the slogan?

If yes → the abstraction earned its name here. Re-measure after every toolchain upgrade; inlining moves between releases.
If no → you hold a hope, not a fact. Compare the disassembly with the hand-written loop, or time both, before the claim ships.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Compile with debug symbols, read the disassembly, and count the calls.




#Rust #ZeroCostAbstractions #Iterators #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Optimisation

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: Rc, Arc, and interior mutability
text:
Case study: Rc, Arc, and interior mutability
A forum’s comment graph builds, passes its tests, and its memory climbs for 6 days straight — nothing is wrong except that no reference count ever reaches zero.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Rc counts owners on one thread, Arc counts them across threads, and RefCell, Mutex and RwLock let a shared handle mutate. The count is a claim: several owners, no single one responsible for the end. A cycle makes the count never fall to zero — and Weak is the only edge that does not count.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Sharing is a structural fact about the program: which nodes genuinely have more than one owner, and which edges are back-references that must not own. The developer must also know which lock is contended, and for how long, measured. The gap question: which nodes genuinely have multiple owners — stated — and are the cycles broken with Weak, checked?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A tree or graph with parent links: Arc on the nodes several readers hold, Weak on each parent back-edge, so the child never keeps the parent alive. The sharing is visible in the signature, the cycle is broken by construction, and a test drops the root and asserts the nodes are freed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Arc<Mutex<T>> as a default shared state — the lock nobody measured, the contention nobody profiled, and every read serialised behind a write-capable handle. Cloning an Rc purely to silence a borrow error, which invents a second owner to satisfy the checker. And the parent-owns-child, child-owns-parent cycle that leaks until the process dies, invisible to every test.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which nodes genuinely have multiple owners — stated — and are the cycles broken with Weak, checked?

If yes → the count states the structure. Confirm every cycle has one Weak edge, and that the lock’s wait was measured at load.
If no → the count is hiding the shape. Draw the ownership graph, name the owners, and break each cycle with a Weak edge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Watch the memory over hours, not minutes, and graph who owns what.




#Rust #Ownership #ArcMutex #MemoryLeaks #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Concurrency

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: unsafe
An unsafe block added to skip a bounds check in 2025 still runs in 2027, and the invariant it assumed was broken by a refactor in 2026 — the compiler checked neither claim.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: unsafe moves to the human a check the compiler cannot perform: an FFI call, a SIMD intrinsic, a self-referential structure, a hand-rolled arena. Inside the block a specific set of safety checks is lifted — the block is a promise that the invariant holds, and a promise is not evidence.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Each block names an invariant the type system cannot state: this pointer is valid and aligned, this memory is initialised, nothing else aliases it, this thread has exclusive access, this layout matches the C struct. The developer must know which invariant, and where it is written. The gap question: which invariant does each unsafe block uphold that the compiler cannot check — written where?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Blocks kept minimal, each with a SAFETY comment naming the upheld invariant and the surrounding code that establishes it. A test exercises the unsafe block. Miri (the interpreter that checks undefined behaviour) checks its Rust-only paths. The module that reads uninitialised buffers is fuzzed, the FFI wrapper is called against the real library, and a debug assertion states what the optimiser now assumes.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



unsafe for speed — get_unchecked in the loop, the invariant documented nowhere. Variants of the same mistake: one unsafe fn wrapping a whole module, so the boundary is invisible and every caller inherits the burden. A transmute reinterprets bits the type system wanted to check. An unsafe impl Send rests on a comment no test can reach.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which invariant does each unsafe block uphold that the compiler cannot check — written where?

If yes → the promise is auditable. Re-read each comment against the code whenever the block or its callers change.
If no → the burden moved to everyone who reads the file later, and they were not told. Write the invariant, or drop the block and pay for the check.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Run Miri on the module, grep every unsafe, and write the missing comment.




#Rust #Unsafe #MemorySafety #FFI #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Invariants

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: Rayon (the work-stealing pool)
Sixteen cores, a build step at 40 seconds on one core and 41 on sixteen — the loop was parallel, the work was not.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: par_iter splits a range across a thread pool, steals from busy threads, and collects results in order. The split pays only when the chunks are equal, independent, and CPU-bound; a lock or a shared counter inside the closure re-serializes them without a word. The trade is a scheduling cost per split against parallelism that exists only if the work divides.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
Speedup is a fact about the work. The developer must know three things: how much of the runtime is CPU, how evenly it divides, and what each closure touches. Rayon checks the closure is Send and Sync. It does not check that the work is CPU-bound or the chunks balanced.
The gap question: is the work CPU-bound and independent — measured — and does any closure share state that serializes it secretly?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Per-pixel work on an image, a numeric grid reduced to one scalar, a batch of documents tokenized. Each chunk costs the same, touches nothing shared, holds the CPU throughout. Speedup tracks the cores up to memory bandwidth.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



par_iter over a loop that makes a blocking call per item behind a single connection or disk. Sixteen threads park on it, the pool saturates, wall time lands where the sequential version was — the parallelism lived in the API. Or one Arc<Mutex<Vec>> collecting results: it compiles, and every chunk queues on one lock while the cores idle. The benchmark ran once and never repeated.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the work CPU-bound and independent — measured — and does any closure share state that serializes it secretly?

If yes → the pool matches the work. Check that chunks stay coarse enough to amortize the split.
If no → the parallelism is nominal. Keep the loop sequential, or move the waiting out of it first.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Time one core’s CPU, then list every shared value a closure touches.




#Rust #Rayon #Parallelism #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: async/await (the compiled state machine)
text:
Case study: async/await (the compiled state machine)
A request is cancelled mid-flight, the handler returns, and the database transaction is still open — nothing failed, the future was simply dropped.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: An async fn compiles to a state machine: one variant per await point holding the locals live there, driven by poll. Sized and non-recursive, the future sits inline in the caller’s frame, no allocation per call; recursion or dyn forces Box::pin. The trade is allocation-free futures against cancellation that can land only at an await, and a Drop that cannot await.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know where this future may be dropped, which state is live at that line, and which of it needs an await to undo. The compiler checks, where a spawn demands it, that the future is Send across its awaits and that locals live long enough. It does not check that a dropped future leaves the system consistent.
The gap question: where may this future be dropped — and what cleanup must survive that point?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A hot path of nested async fns, no Box::pin: futures inline. A timeout or select! around a future owning nothing that needs rollback — an idempotent read, a reference-counted buffer. Cancellation drops it, the state machine goes, nothing was half-done.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A transaction held across an await, with rollback in Drop. Cancel at the wrong await — a select! arm, a client disconnect — and Drop runs, which cannot await, so the ROLLBACK never reaches the server. The connection returns to the pool still inside a transaction, and the next request inherits it: a write that fails for reasons no one traces to a cancellation three layers up. It compiles, is idiomatic, untested on the cancel path.








TipThe faithfulness test



Where may this future be dropped — and what cleanup must survive that point?

If yes → the awaits are the cancellation map. Check what Drop does at each of them.
If no → the cleanup sits after a suspension, not before it. Move it, or own the work in a task that no caller can drop.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the await points, then name what each one leaves half-done.




#Rust #AsyncRust #Cancellation #Tokio #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: no_std (the target without an OS)
text:
Case study: no_std (the target without an OS)
The firmware tests pass on the laptop, and the first cross-compile for the microcontroller fails four dependencies down.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: #![no_std] removes the std crate, leaving core and, if you opt in, alloc: no threads, no files, no clock, and no allocator unless you supply one. Every crate in the tree must make the same choice, and Cargo features are additive and unified, so one dependency enabling its std feature turns std on for the build. The trade is a small binary with no OS assumptions against an ecosystem split along that exact seam.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which crates in the tree need an allocator, a heap, or an OS, and which of those the target ships. core is portable; alloc needs a global allocator you supply; std needs a system. The compiler checks the tree builds for the target — but only when someone builds for the target.
The gap question: does every dependency support no_std for this target — checked at which feature set?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A core-only tree: fixed buffers, embedded-hal traits (portable hardware interfaces), defmt logging, a parser with no allocation. Built for thumbv7em-none-eabi in CI, then flashed and exercised on the board. Every dependency is pinned to the feature set that keeps it allocation-free.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The crate is no_std and a dependency’s default features pull std in. On the host the tests pass because std exists; on the target the break surfaces at the layer that never touched the hardware. Or a Vec appears, someone bolts on an allocator, and the firmware links — until the first large allocation exhausts a heap nobody measured, at runtime, on a device with no console.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does every dependency support no_std for this target — checked at which feature set?

If yes → the tree is this target’s tree, not the host’s. Check next the allocator budget and the panic strategy.
If no → the no_std claim covers your crate, not your program. Cut the dependency, or gate it, then prove it stays off on the target.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Build for the target triple, then read the resolved feature set per crate.




#Rust #EmbeddedRust #NoStd #Microcontrollers #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
text:
Case study: wasm32-unknown-unknown (the browser build)
The same crate compiles for the browser and the server, and only one target honors a thread by default.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: The target compiles a crate to a WebAssembly module the browser loads; wasm-bindgen marshals values across the JS boundary. Ownership and lifetimes are checked as natively; platform capability is not. std::thread::spawn compiles, then fails at the first call: this target has no threads without atomics and shared memory, and both need the page cross-origin isolated (the COOP/COEP headers). Blocking work compiles and blocks the main thread. The trade is one codebase against bundle size, a thread model the target lacks, and a boundary that copies.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The target states what the platform provides: a heap, no file system, no threads by default, no clock to borrow. The program states what it needs: a pool, a blocking read, a buffer copied per call. Nothing compares the two lists. The gap question: does this program block, spawn, or sleep on the main thread — and does the artifact pay for the feature it carries?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Core logic shared to wasm with the boundary drawn thin: pure functions over owned buffers, a measured bundle against a stated budget. It pays because it is the same logic — same tests, same fixes — and every platform difference sits outside it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The whole crate shipped because it compiled: megabytes where two hundred lines of JavaScript would serve, a framework pulled in to avoid writing a fetch. Then the ported worker pool that panicked in production — the build was green throughout.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the bundle size measured — and does the program stay clear of spawning, blocking, or sleeping on the main thread?

If yes → the target is this feature’s platform, not the project’s default. Check crossings and what runs on the main thread.
If no → the portability is nominal: you shipped a runtime to reuse syntax. Write the thin JS version, or move the feature server-side.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the target wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Measure the gzipped artifact, count crossings, list every blocking call.




#Rust #WebAssembly #Wasm #Frontend #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: Cargo feature flags (the compile-time switch)
text:
Case study: Cargo feature flags (the compile-time switch)
Two features that each pass CI meet in a combination never compiled, and the failure appears in the customer’s build.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A feature is a named set of optional dependencies, code, and features. The resolver unifies them once per build across the whole graph: enabling one anywhere enables it everywhere, except through the build-dependency seam, so “optional” is a claim about the artifact, not the caller. The trade is optional functionality compiled in or out against combinatorics — n features give 2^n builds, and CI runs n+2.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The domain decides which optionality is real: a deployment choice, one binary per customer; a platform choice, one build per target; a debugging aid. Cargo cannot tell those apart. Additive-only is a convention the build does not enforce. The resolver will turn a feature back on through a crate three levels down — which is how a no_std tree grows a hidden std dependency the host never misses. The gap question: are the shipped combinations written down, and does anything reject a build outside them?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Features additive-only, the shipped combinations the tested ones: CI builds --no-default-features, each feature alone, all features; mutually exclusive backends guarded by compile_error! so the bad pair fails at the first crate.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Mutually exclusive features accepted by the build. Both backends compile, a cfg! selector picks one silently, and the broken pair waits for the profile nobody runs locally — release, with a customer’s feature set. Also: an “optional” dependency the team believes is off, switched on by a crate nobody read.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which feature combinations actually ship — tested — and is “additive-only” enforced by the build or assumed by the team?

If yes → features are a supported interface. Keep them additive, and let CI own the matrix: a new feature arrives with its combinations.
If no → every combination you did not build is a configuration you did not design. Shrink the matrix, or reject pairs that must not meet.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flags wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own build. List the artifacts you ship, then the features each sets.




#Rust #Cargo #BuildSystems #Configuration #CICD #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Rust: The Compiler as Knowledge Enforcer
section: Case study: Monomorphisation (speed bought at compile time)
text:
Case study: Monomorphisation (speed bought at compile time)
A 40-minute build is a design decision that never appeared in a review.
Writing a Rust construct or choosing a target? Ask “which fact did the compiler check for me — what owns this, what may alias, what may wait — and what did it cost?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the borrow checker enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Rust compiles a generic function into one machine-code copy per concrete type it is called with. Those copies cost nothing at run time and everything at build time: compile minutes scale with the number of instantiations, and macro-heavy code adds expansion on top. cargo build --timings shows which crate pays. The trade is runtime speed bought with compile minutes against crate boundaries that keep iteration fast.


The Rust knowledge gap it signals
The fact here is the shape of the work: how often one edit is compiled, how long CI may take, how many people wait on it. Code does not carry that; the workspace does. A crate boundary is a build boundary — an edit recompiles its own side, not the other, and costs inlining for code that is neither generic nor marked #[inline]. The gap question: which dependency edge, named, costs the most build time, and what budget must it fit?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Crate boundaries drawn so CI builds stay under a stated budget: a clean build of 6 minutes, an incremental edit of 20 seconds, both measured with cargo build --timings and tracked as numbers, not feelings.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



One giant crate with generics everywhere — 40-minute builds, and the velocity tax nobody put on any budget, because compile time is not a line item anyone owns. “Zero-cost abstraction” is true of the running program and false of the day: the cost moved from the user’s CPU to every developer’s edit. Add a proc-macro derive on every type and watch the tax compound.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured CI build time — and which dependency edge drives it, named?

If yes → the generics are inside their budget. Watch the edge that grew this month, and keep the incremental path short.
If no → the abstraction is not free. Split the workspace at the boundary the work actually crosses, or cut an instantiation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the generics wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own build. Time the edges, not the total.




#Rust #CompileTimes #BuildSystems #Monomorphisation #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DeveloperProductivity

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: Build-time augmentation
The key was changed in production, the service restarted, and the new value took effect nowhere.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Quarkus moves what a framework used to do at boot — bean discovery, bytecode transformation, config resolution — into a build step called augmentation. The shipped artifact is already resolved, so startup is tens of milliseconds and the footprint stays small. The trade is exact: a key fixed at build time cannot change after the build — the binary ignores any value the deployment sends. quarkus.http.root-path, the datasource kind, ORM schema generation — read at build time, fixed in the binary.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
The team must know which config is a fact about the deployed environment and which about the build. One artifact runs everywhere, so any value that differs between environments belongs to the run, not the build: port, credentials, URLs. A key miscategorized the other way loses its dynamism silently — the binary keeps the baked value and logs a warning nobody reads.
The gap question: which keys are build-time, and would we have decided the same knowing they can never change without a rebuild?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A scale-to-zero service behind a queue: the platform bills cold start on every wake-up, and measured startup decides if the design holds.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A build-time key edited in the production config map, deployed, restarted. The service comes up green. The value is ignored, so the change did nothing — and the team learns this days later, debugging what the change was meant to fix. The quieter reverse trap: making everything runtime-overridable for “flexibility,” returning the boot cost to every replica for dynamism nobody used.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which config keys are build-time — listed — and who knows they cannot change without a rebuild?

If yes → augmentation carries the workload’s facts. Check the list is in the readme, not just the config reference.
If no → the artifact holds decisions nobody tracked. Diff the build-time keys against what ops believes is runtime.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure startup, then count deploys that changed a build-time key.




#Quarkus #Java #BuildTime #CloudNative #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: Dev Services
Dev Services started a database for you. It is the image your Quarkus platform version pins, not the one production runs.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: When no datasource URL is configured in dev or test mode, Quarkus starts the container itself — Postgres, Kafka, Redis, Keycloak — and wires the connection. A new developer clones and runs, with no setup. The image is pinned by the Quarkus platform version you build with, not by your production manifest. The trade: parity nobody had to configure, against an environment nobody configured.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
The container is a stand-in for a versioned external service, and it may differ where dev and production were never compared: image version, extensions, collation, timezone, TLS, roles, and data already present. Each difference is a fact about production the developer never met. Tests pass against the substitute and say nothing about the original.
The gap question: which versions does dev actually run, and how were they verified against production?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A team whose production images are pinned and whose CI job compares each Dev Services image tag to the deployed tag. Parity is then a checked fact, and the zero-config start costs nothing but the check.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Dev Services pulls the platform default — a newer Postgres than production runs — and the schema, the JSON functions, and the query planner all behave differently. Everything works locally. The migration passes in CI. Production rejects the syntax, or accepts it and returns a different order. The opposite failure is quieter: tests that pass only because something was listening on the port, never asserting they reached the intended store.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which versions does dev actually run — pinned — and are they verified against production, how?

If yes → the stand-in is constrained by the same facts. Check the comparison runs on every build, not once at setup.
If no → dev parity is a coincidence that holds until a version differs. Pin the images, then align them to production.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every container dev starts and the tag it resolves to.




#Quarkus #Java #DevServices #TestContainers #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: Native image builds
The native build took 14 minutes, and the hot service it produced lost a quarter of its peak.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: GraalVM compiles the application ahead of time under a closed-world assumption: reachable code is fixed at build time, reflection needs explicit registration. The trade: minutes of CI per build, harder debugging, and slower peak throughput on long-running CPU-bound work, against startup in the tens of milliseconds and resident memory a fraction of the JVM’s.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
Native pays back only where startup or footprint is billed. The team must know which of its services is charged for cold start, which is memory-constrained in density, and which runs hot and long enough to prefer the JIT. Those are three different services, and the build profile is a claim about all of them.
The gap question: which services pay their native build cost back in startup and footprint, measured?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The services that scale to zero, where the platform bills the wake-up and the measured cold start and RSS decide whether the trade pays back. The native profile applies there and where footprint is billed. Everything else stays in JVM mode, deliberately.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Native for every service, because “Quarkus is fast.” CI accumulates hours per day, reflection failures surface late in the cycle, and the profile attached to the pipeline stops being readable. A throughput regression on the CPU-bound service ships with the build; an operator finds it months later, not a benchmark. The build cost was real; the payoff was never measured, only assumed.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which services pay their native build cost back — measured?

If yes → the profile is a fact about each service. Check the numbers are recorded per service, not per organization.
If no → the build is a habit. Measure cold start and RSS in both modes on the services that scale to zero.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Time the native build, then measure what it bought.




#Quarkus #Java #NativeImage #GraalVM #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: JVM-mode footprint tuning
Quarkus means small, so someone set a 256 MB limit. The first traffic spike killed the container.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: In JVM mode Quarkus starts fast, but the heap is still the JVM’s: sized from the container limit, a quarter by default, with GC headroom, metaspace, thread stacks, and native buffers living outside it. The trade: defaults calibrated for a modest workload — small heap, quick start, a default collector — against the headroom a real peak load needs, where allocation spikes push the process past its limit.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
Resident memory is heap plus what sits outside it; the peak is the number. The team must know its live set at peak, its allocation rate at peak, and the RSS that follows from both, per replica. Density is computed from RSS; a limit set from a heap estimate or from an idle reading is a guess about a number nobody took.
The gap question: what is the measured RSS at peak load, and is the container limit above it with stated headroom?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A platform that bills density, not idle: RSS measured per replica at peak, the limit set above it with headroom named in the manifest, and density computed from that RSS rather than from the heap. The small footprint is then a fact the platform can plan against.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Quarkus is small” carried into JVM mode with the default heap: a 256 MB limit, a 64 MB heap, and thread stacks and direct buffers outside it. It works in dev, works in the load test at half rate, and dies on the first real spike: RSS crosses the limit while the collector spends the spike collecting. The kill looks like an infrastructure fault, not a sizing decision. Idle RSS measured once, then multiplied into a density plan, sets the same limit.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured RSS at peak load — and is the container limit above it with stated headroom?

If yes → the footprint is a measured fact. Check the reading is at peak, not at idle.
If no → the limit guards nothing. Measure RSS under the peak profile before setting it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure RSS at peak, then compare it to the limit.




#Quarkus #Java #JVM #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
section: Case study: The reactive REST layer
text:
Case study: The reactive REST layer
One JDBC call in a Uni-returning endpoint, and every other request on that event loop waits behind it.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: quarkus-rest dispatches by return type: a plain return goes to a worker thread, a Uni or Multi return stays on the event loop. A reactive method that blocks holds the loop, and every request assigned to that thread waits for it. @Blocking forces a worker, @NonBlocking forces the loop. The trade: event-loop dispatch — no thread per request, high concurrency on few threads — against blocking endpoints whose stall is paid by requests that never blocked.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
The return type is a claim about the endpoint’s behavior: a reactive return promises no blocking, and dispatch trusts it. The team must know which reactive endpoints still block — JDBC, file I/O, a synchronous client, heavy CPU work — because the type promises and the body decides.
The gap question: which endpoints block — listed — and is that marking deliberate or trusted by default?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Reactive dispatch for the I/O-bound endpoints, returning Uni and Multi so the thread is released while waiting. Plain returns, or @Blocking, on the CPU-heavy and JDBC-backed ones, chosen per endpoint and written down. The dispatch model then matches what each endpoint does.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A blocking JDBC call in a Uni-returning endpoint. It passes in dev, passes under a light load test, then degrades nonlinearly: one stall per event-loop thread stalls every request queued behind it, and latency rises without CPU rising. The diagnosis is hard because nothing is saturated. The opposite trap is tidier — @Blocking on everything, which queues every call on a small fixed worker pool and gives up the reason the reactive layer was chosen.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which endpoints block — listed — and is that marking deliberate or trusted by default?

If yes → dispatch matches behavior. Check the list is reviewed when an endpoint gains a database call.
If no → the default is doing the deciding. Walk the resource methods and mark the blocking ones.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every endpoint, then its I/O.




#Quarkus #Java #Reactive #REST #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
section: Case study: Config profiles and build-time keys
text:
Case study: Config profiles and build-time keys
A manifest sets the database kind to Postgres for production, the pipeline applies it, and the application keeps talking to the H2 database the build chose — no error, no restart, no diff anyone reads.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Quarkus sorts every configuration key into a phase: runtime keys are read at startup, build-time keys once on the build machine, then written into the artifact. Profiles (%dev, %test, %prod) select values in either phase. A %prod value for a fixed build-time key is baked, and no environment variable moves it; some build-time keys still keep their value overridable at run time.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
A phase is a claim about the workload. The database kind, its JDBC driver, and the extension set are shipped decisions; the URL, the credential reference, and the pool ceiling belong to the deployment. Getting the split wrong is not a framework bug — it is a missing statement about which facts belong to the artifact. The gap question: for each key, is it build-time or runtime, and does anyone on the team know?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Runtime keys change per deploy and arrive from the environment: a pool size the operator tunes, a region flag set per cluster. Build-time keys stay identical everywhere and are documented in the artifact. The split then matches how the platform actually differs, and the build records what it decided.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An environment-specific value placed in runtime configuration for a build-time key. It looks right in the manifest, it sits beside keys that do work, and it is ignored: the jar starts, serves traffic, and uses whatever the build baked in. The failure reads as “staging works, production is slow” with identical configuration files.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each key: build-time or runtime — known — and how is that verified at deploy time?

If yes → the configuration follows the workload. Check that verification runs where the deploy happens, not in a wiki page.
If no → the key is a wish. Look up its phase, then move it to where it is actually read.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Dump the resolved configuration at startup and compare it against the keys the build fixed.




#Quarkus #Java #Configuration #BuildTime #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
section: Case study: SmallRye health and metrics
text:
Case study: SmallRye health and metrics
The readiness probe calls the payment gateway. The gateway slows past the probe timeout, every replica leaves the load balancer at once, and the outage arrives before the dependency does.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: SmallRye Health exposes /q/health/live and /q/health/ready, each aggregating CDI checks run on every probe call; readiness decides Service membership, liveness decides a container restart. The trade is which remedy a red probe triggers, against checks that are green while useless or red while the application is healthy.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
Readiness answers “should traffic reach this instance now” — a fact about dependencies cheap to check per call. Liveness answers “can this process still make progress” — a fact that must never depend on a peer, because the remedy is a restart. A team needs to know which dependencies are fatal, which degrade, and which a restart cannot repair. The gap question: what does readiness check, and which failure is it meant to catch?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Readiness inspects its own pool and each datastore no request survives without, with a timeout shorter than the probe period. Liveness stays minimal: the event loop answers, nothing else. The platform’s remedy then matches the fault.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Readiness fanning out to every downstream: gateway, search, the broker. Each was added after an incident and looks responsible. Then one slow peer marks the whole fleet NotReady, traffic has nowhere to go, and fleet availability equals the weakest dependency’s. The companion trap: green checks on /q/health while the app returns 500s on the paths that matter.








TipThe faithfulness test



What does readiness actually check — and would a failed dependency flip it, tested how?

If yes → the probes state the fault tolerance. Check that a test breaks the dependency on purpose and watches endpoints drain.
If no → the probe measures nothing. Make it check the one dependency a request cannot survive.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List the dependencies per request, then ask which failures a restart repairs.




#Quarkus #Java #Kubernetes #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture
