title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: Generated Kubernetes manifests
During an incident someone raises a memory limit to 2Gi on one cluster. The generated manifest still says 512Mi, so every pipeline run proposes to revert the fix — and nobody runs the pipeline.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The Quarkus Kubernetes extension writes target/kubernetes/kubernetes.yml at build time from the same properties that configure the application: replicas, resource limits, probes. The manifest is an artifact with a version, not a hand-edited document. The trade is deployment knowledge living in the build against the risk of divergence from hand-edited production YAML.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
A limit is a claim about the workload: a memory ceiling the heap fits under, a CPU request matching measured usage, a replica count derived from load. When those live in the build, one writer owns them: the build. A hotfix then costs a rebuild. A team needs to know which facts are environment-specific — an ingress host, a secret — and which belong to the artifact. The gap question: is the deployed manifest the generated one, or has the cluster become the source?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Manifests generated from the same keys that set the application’s configuration, so heap maximum and container limit come from one number and cannot drift apart. The manifest is versioned with the code, and CI diffs it against the live cluster before applying.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An ops-edited limit that exists on one cluster only. The generated file and the running system disagree, neither is authoritative: the next apply reverts the fix, the next incident re-applies it. The companion trap: hand-maintained YAML drifting until it describes a service that no longer exists.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the deployed manifest the generated one — diffed regularly — or did operational drift become the truth?

If yes → deployment knowledge lives where it is versioned. Check that the diff runs on a schedule, not when someone remembers.
If no → the cluster is the configuration, the build a suggestion. Adopt the live change back into the properties, or write down why it stays local.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Fetch the live manifest, diff it against the generated one, and name who changed each line.




#Quarkus #Java #Kubernetes #Deployment #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
section: Case study: Panache (active record and repository)
text:
Case study: Panache (active record and repository)
A resource class calls Order.findAll() and reads order.customer.email. The query layer, the fetch strategy, and the entity boundary now sit in the web tier — and nothing failed to compile.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Panache offers two shapes. PanacheEntity puts static find, list, and count on the entity and rewrites public field access at build time; PanacheRepository puts the same queries in a repository bean. Both are supported, and the documentation asks a project to pick one. The trade is terse entities and queries against a pattern decision: where a query lives, and who owns it.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
A query states which facts the domain asks for — by identity, by state, by date range — and where it lives marks who may change it. On the entity, the query is part of the model; in a repository, it has an owner and a name. Panache is terse because it assumes that decision is made, and terseness amplifies whatever you assumed. The gap question: can you state which style this service chose, and why?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Panache adopted deliberately per service, the style written down where a reviewer sees it, and every query landing where that style puts it: simple lookups on the entity or in the repository, field access inside the model, so the rewritten access has one owner.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



findAll and field access drifting into controllers. Each hop is one line and reads well, and after a year the web tier builds predicates, the entity is an anemic data bag, and one query exists four times with three fetch strategies. The framework made every step easy, and easy is not decided.








TipThe faithfulness test



Where does a query live in this service — stated — and can a reviewer find it in one hop?

If yes → the pattern is a decision, not a drift. Check that new queries land in the same place and that field access stays inside the model.
If no → the web tier is the persistence layer. Move the queries behind one boundary and name the style where they land.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List the queries the service runs, then map each to the file that owns it.




#Quarkus #Java #Panache #Persistence #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Quarkus Build-Time Decisions
text:
Case study: Hibernate Reactive
Four event-loop threads are offered 8,000 requests a second. One legacy validator makes a blocking JDBC call on every request, and at most four run at once — the loop count, not the request rate.
Accepting a Quarkus default? Ask “which decision did the framework make — at build time or at run time — and which fact did it bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Hibernate Reactive pairs the ORM API with reactive SQL clients. Queries return Uni and Multi, and @Transactional scopes a transaction to the reactive context. The constraints are real: no lazy loading, a reactive driver per database, and no mixing with classic Hibernate ORM in one persistence unit. The trade is a non-blocking path end to end against driver support and transactional semantics that must be verified.


The Quarkus knowledge gap it signals
Non-blocking is a property of the whole path, not of an annotation. The facts to hold: every dependency speaks a reactive protocol natively, every transaction is short, every association is fetched where needed, and nothing in the dependency tree opens a JDBC connection. One blocking call returns the stall to the event loop, and the damage scales with concurrency, not request count. The gap question: which step in this path can block, and has anyone checked?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An IO-bound service, reactive end to end, driver included, with a build that rejects a blocking driver. Quarkus flags a blocked event-loop thread in dev and test mode, so the property is observed, not asserted.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



One blocking call inside the reactive chain. A JWT validator that reads a key from a database, a legacy cache client, a driver that advertises reactive support and hands back a JDBC connection. Each arrives as “just this once”, passes a smoke test, and stalls every request sharing that event loop.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is every step of the request path non-blocking — verified — and does the driver truly support it?

If yes → the choice is the workload’s. Check the warning log for blocked threads, and that no lazy association is traversed in the chain.
If no → the annotation is a costume. Find the blocking step, then wrap it off the event loop or remove it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Trace every endpoint’s path once and list each library it touches.




#Quarkus #Java #HibernateReactive #Reactive #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
A mapping claims what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale. Each post names the claim and asks what the domain says about it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
Case study: FetchType.LAZY versus EAGER
One @ManyToOne marked EAGER pulls the customer and the customer’s billing address into every query that only wanted an order total.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: An association declares when its rows travel: LAZY defers them to first touch, EAGER joins them to every load of the owner. JPA defaults to LAZY for collections and EAGER for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne. The asymmetry is the trade: EAGER is baked into the mapping — a fetch graph can subtract it per query, a load graph can only add — while LAZY has no plan of its own, so an unplanned read becomes one query per row.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Fetching is a claim about use cases, not about tables. “Orders need their lines” asserts that every path reading an order also reads its lines. The team must know which reads of the parent go on to the child. The gap question: does any consumer of this association exist that does not need it loaded?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Associations lazy by default, and each query stating what it fetches — a join fetch or an @EntityGraph on the read that needs the child, a DTO projection where the read model differs. The fetch plan lives with the query, where the use case is visible, and a test asserts the query count.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



EAGER everywhere, “for convenience”: the entity that drags half the schema on every lookup, and the one query that needs three tables now joins nine. Its mirror is lazy with no fetch plan anywhere — the N+1 under every page, invisible until the list passes a hundred rows. Both hide one missing fact: nobody named the use cases.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each association: which use case actually needs it loaded — can anyone name it?

If yes → lazy plus a fetch plan at that query. Check the query count at realistic row counts.
If no → the association is eager by inertia or lazy by default, not by decision. Make it lazy where a fetch plan exists, and count queries at real sizes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the read paths per entity and the child data each one uses.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EfCore #LazyLoading #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Open Session in View
text:
Case study: Open Session in View
A report endpoint calls a payment provider inside a transaction, and the database connection it opened before the first query waits through the whole HTTP round trip.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: spring.jpa.open-in-view defaults to true: one persistence context is bound to the request thread, so lazy loading still works after the service returns, during rendering and serialization. The price is lifespan — the persistence context outlives the transaction and survives every slow call in the view layer, and a connection rides along for the life of any open transaction. Setting it false closes the context at the service boundary.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
A response is assembled from data, and only some of it is persistence data. OSIV asserts that the view’s needs are unknown at service time — that any association may be touched during rendering. The team must know which parts of the response are read after that boundary, and what non-database work runs inside it. The gap question: does rendering still touch entities, or only finished values?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



OSIV off, and fetching completes in the service — a DTO built from a fetch join, so the controller renders plain values with no persistence context open. Queries belong where the transaction is. EF Core reaches the same place differently: its scoped DbContext outlives the service, so a lazy-loading proxy — opt-in, via an option — fires during serialization unless the read is projected.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



OSIV left on because turning it off broke something, and that breakage — the price of the fix — was read as a warning instead of the finding. Then a slow third-party call lands inside the controller’s transaction: each request pins a connection for 1.5 s, the pool sized for query latency starves, and every endpoint times out together. The stack trace names the pool, never the mapping.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does rendering the response still touch the persistence context — and what holds a database connection while it waits?

If yes → keep the fetch inside the service. Check each association the view touches, then the outbound calls in the same window.
If no → switch OSIV off. You will learn immediately which reads depended on it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the setting wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Log connection hold time per request against query time.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #SpringBoot #ConnectionPool #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
Case study: The persistence context
A developer changes a field to test a hypothesis, issues no save, runs a finder — and the row in the database moves.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: The persistence context is an identity map: within it one row is one object, so a == b for two loads of the same key. Dirty checking compares each managed object with its loaded snapshot and writes the differences at flush — the moment pending writes reach the database. The trade is identity against implicit writes — writes the code never asked for, produced by state nobody decided to commit.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
“Same row, same object” is a claim about scope and about commitment. The team must know where the transaction boundary sits, which objects inside it are managed, and whether an object outside it is a stale copy or a live one. In EF Core the identity map is the same and the moment is not: tracking is automatic, but nothing is flushed or committed until SaveChanges. The gap question: at which line does this change become the database’s problem?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



One transaction, one unit of work: load, mutate, commit, with identity and dirty checking relied on deliberately. Read paths say so — @Transactional(readOnly = true) or AsNoTracking() — so a stray mutation cannot reach the database. Equality by key, never by reference, in any object that leaves the boundary.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An entity modified “just locally” while debugging a mapping: AUTO flush writes it before the next query on the same tables, and the change ships. Or two objects for one row, loaded in different sessions, compared by reference and found unequal — so the code adds an update to reconcile what was never two things. Or a detached object merged back in, overwriting a writer it never read.








TipThe faithfulness test



Within this transaction, which objects are managed — and who decided when the flush happens?

If yes → the unit of work is the domain’s. Check that read paths are marked read-only and that no entity escapes the boundary still managed.
If no → the mapping commits state nobody chose. Find the flush: explicit, at commit, or AUTO before an unrelated query.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Map the transaction boundaries, then the entities that cross them.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EfCore #UnitOfWork #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Transactions

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
Case study: The second-level cache
A price update commits on node one, and node two quotes the old price for the whole TTL window — from a @Cacheable that outlived its developer.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: The persistence context dies with the session; a second-level cache lives in the session factory and serves rows to every session on the node. Hibernate 6 needs a region factory — a region is one named partition of the cache — JPA’s @Cacheable per entity, and a per-region strategy: READ_ONLY, NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, READ_WRITE, TRANSACTIONAL. Each is a staleness contract, and the cluster must broadcast invalidation. EF Core ships none of this.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Caching asserts a rate of change and a cost of being wrong. The team must know how often a table’s rows change, how long a reader may see a stale row without harm, and whether invalidation reaches the other nodes. The gap question: what is the measured write rate of this table, and what does the domain lose when a reader sees last hour’s version?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Reference data: country codes, currency tables, category trees — written by a migration, read constantly, changing monthly. Cache it under a JCache region factory with an expiry that matches the publication cycle, and invalidate on the one write path allowed to change it. The staleness window is a published number, not an accident.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The second-level cache enabled globally because reads were slow, applied to orders and inventory. Each node now serves rows another node already changed; NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE returns them until TTL, and with the query cache also enabled it drops whole regions on any write, so hit rate collapses and the wrong rows stay. The invalidation path was never tested with two nodes, because staging runs one.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which tables change rarely enough to cache — measured — and how do the other nodes hear about a change?

If yes → cache those regions only. Check invalidation with two nodes and a write, then the TTL against the write rate.
If no → the cache is a guess about write frequency. Remove it and measure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Instrument writes per table per hour, then price a stale read.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #Caching #EfCore #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Schema generated from mappings (hbm2ddl.auto)
text:
Case study: Schema generated from mappings (hbm2ddl.auto)
One field renamed in an entity class: the new column ships empty, a million rows keep their values in a column nothing reads.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: Hibernate 6 reads the annotations and emits DDL: validate compares mapping to schema and fails at boot, update adds what it thinks is missing, create drops and rebuilds. update has no concept of a rename — a renamed field becomes a new column while the old one keeps its data and its NOT NULL constraint. Nothing it emits is a reviewed artifact.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
A schema carries a history: the column’s author, its type, its nullability, and the migration that moved the rows. update asserts that history does not exist — that the mapping is the whole truth. True only where the mapping generated the schema.
The gap question: can you rebuild production’s schema from reviewed files?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Throwaway environments: create-drop for tests on a containerised database, and validate in production so a mapping that disagrees with the schema fails before traffic. The DDL lives in versioned migration files a person reviewed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



update in production, because it is one property instead of a migration pipeline. It feels safer than create, since it never drops anything — the trap, because never dropping is also never removing. A deleted field leaves its column. Then create on a fresh environment omits every object a person added — the partial index, the check constraint, the trigger — and staging drifts from production, unrecorded.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who owns the DDL — a migration history a person approved, or a diff the ORM guessed at startup?

If yes → the schema is an artifact with an author. Check that validate runs at startup, so a mapping edit that forgets its migration fails the build, not the release.
If no → the mapping is the only schema, and its history is whatever the annotations say this morning. Move the DDL into versioned migrations, then switch to validate.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask who applied the last production DDL change, and which file records it.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #SchemaMigrations #DDL #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Optimistic locking (@Version, concurrency tokens)
text:
Case study: Optimistic locking (@Version, concurrency tokens)
Two support agents open the same ticket, both change the priority, both save. One change vanishes, and neither agent sees an error.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: A version column makes every UPDATE carry its old value: UPDATE ticket SET priority = ?, version = 8 WHERE id = ? AND version = 7. Zero rows updated means somebody wrote first, and Hibernate raises OptimisticLockException while EF Core raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException. The trade: detect the conflict instead of preventing it, against a pessimistic write lock that serialises writers.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
The version column claims two facts: two writers can reach the same row inside the same window, and when they do, somebody is told and something resolves it. The first is a fact; the second a decision the domain must make.
The gap question: which entities have genuinely concurrent writers, and what happens to the loser?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A row humans edit concurrently for minutes: a ticket, a case file, an insurance claim, a shared document header. The conflict surfaces as a domain event — the second agent is told the record moved and re-reads it, or a merge rule keeps both edits.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



No version on a hot row, because “the second write wins and that is fine” — that is a lost update nobody detects. The mirror trap is a version on everything: every entity carries the column and a retry loop, so unrelated rows colliding fire needless retries, a non-idempotent write is duplicated, and nobody has seen the conflict handler fire.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each entity: can two writers conflict — measured from real flows — and when they do, who is told?

If yes → the write path detects the conflict instead of erasing it. Check the resolution exists: a bounded retry, a merge rule, a message to the person who can redo the edit.
If no → either two writers cannot collide on this row, so the column buys nothing, or they can and nobody is told, which is a lost update with a column beside it. Add the version only to the entities that measurement finds in conflict.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Read which flows write the same row inside one second, then read the exception handler.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EfCore #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Batch fetching and fetch size
text:
Case study: Batch fetching and fetch size
An order list renders in 40 ms against 20 seeded rows and takes 9 seconds in production, because each row’s customer was fetched by its own query.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: A lazy association fetched row by row issues one query per owner: 100 orders, 101 queries, and each roundtrip costs real latency. Batch fetching collapses the uninitialised proxies — lazy placeholders for unloaded rows — of one type into IN clauses of a fixed batch size: 32 turns 100 follow-up queries into 4. The JDBC fetch size is a different knob: rows the driver buffers per roundtrip. The trade in both: fewer roundtrips against the memory each page holds.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Both settings claim how much of the graph a page reads, and how many rows fit its working set. That is a fact about the use case: a list screen renders 25 rows and needs each row’s label.
The gap question: what is the measured roundtrip count for one page, and how many rows does each roundtrip cost in memory?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A page of fixed size — 25 rows, each needing one association — with a batch size of sixteen chosen against a measured count: 1 query for the page plus 2 for the associations, not 1 plus 25. Or a streaming report at a few thousand rows.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A fetch size of ten thousand “so we make fewer roundtrips”: every user’s list buffers ten thousand rows in the driver and discards 9,975 — a spike per request. The quieter variant is no batching at all: lazy access inside a loop, one query per row, which passes in every suite that seeds 20 rows and dies on the first real account.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured roundtrip count per page — and what does each fetch cost in memory?

If yes → the width is a fact about this page. Check the count with query logging at realistic page size, and confirm the batch size divides the typical page, not the largest.
If no → one cost is paid blind. Log the queries for one page, then set the batch size and count again.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the page’s row count, its associations, and the heap while it renders.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EfCore #Performance #NPlusOne #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
Case study: Flush timing (FlushModeType.AUTO, SaveChanges)
A test asserts that one UPDATE reaches the database. It passes until a query is added above it — now two run, one against a row the test never touched.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: JPA’s default AUTO flushes pending changes before a query that might read them, so the query sees writes this transaction has not committed — and the UPDATE lands at an instant nobody wrote. EF Core inverts it: SaveChanges is the only write, so the database never sees pending state; identity resolution — one instance per key — still returns the tracked instance with its modified values. The trade: queries agree with memory, against write timing removed from the code that caused it.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know when the transaction writes: that instant decides what a constraint violation means, which trigger fires, which audit timestamp is recorded. In Hibernate it is the flush before a query — even a native one.
The gap question: at which statement does this transaction reach the database — traced, not assumed?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Flush timing understood and explicit at the transaction boundaries where it matters: the write moment chosen at a boundary instead of inherited from statement order, and SaveChanges called once per use case.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Nobody chose anything, and the extra UPDATE appears in the log — dirty managed state written before an unrelated query, a version incremented, a trigger fired for a change nobody meant to save. The tell is a test whose failures move when a query is added: the assertion was never about the write, it was about the flush. The repair that feels right — FlushMode.MANUAL everywhere — makes reads return stale rows.








TipThe faithfulness test



When does this transaction actually write — traced — or is flush timing folklore on the team?

If yes → the boundary is known. Check that a failing constraint maps to one statement, and that a flush is explicit where a native query needs it.
If no → the write instant is an emergent property of statement order. Log SQL for one use case, mark each flush, make the boundary explicit.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which statement must precede the write, and which read must not.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EfCore #Transactions #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Entity equals and hashCode (the sameness claim)
text:
Case study: Entity equals and hashCode (the sameness claim)
Two references to the same customer sit in one HashSet; the set holds both, and after the save neither can be found.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: equals and hashCode are the only statement your class makes about sameness. At the Object default, two instances of one row are unequal; overridden, they are a domain rule every Set depends on. The trade: equality by a business key holds in every state; equality by a generated id holds only after the flush — false exactly when the aggregate (the object graph saved as one unit) is assembled.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
The domain knows what makes two customers the same: the tax number, the receipt number. A generated id is a storage artifact — absent while the object is built, decided by nothing in the domain. Equality leaning on it is a database claim dressed as a domain rule.
The gap question: what makes two entities “the same” — the domain rule — and does equals implement it even before the id exists?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Equals by business key, consistent before and after persistence. An order is the same order by its number, assigned in the domain; a book by ISBN. Two references compare equal the moment both are constructed, so a HashSet deduplicates new objects before any session exists.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Equals on a generated id. Two references to the “same” customer are unequal until saved, so the set stores both; the persist assigns ids, the hash moves, and lookups miss an element still in the bucket. Lombok makes it one annotation and worse: a generated equals compares every field, so a lazy association is initialized to answer the comparison — twenty orders, twenty more selects, or a throw outside the session.








TipThe faithfulness test



What makes two entities “the same” — the domain rule — and does equals implement it even before the id exists?

If yes → equality is a domain statement, true in every state. Check its key fields never change.
If no → it is id equality — storage, undefined before the flush. Keep those entities out of hash-based collections, or give them a business key.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which fields the business uses to tell two records apart.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #EntityMapping #Java #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Inheritance mapping strategies (the shape claim)
text:
Case study: Inheritance mapping strategies (the shape claim)
One table holds every subtype, forty columns wide, and no row fills more than eight of them.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: SINGLE_TABLE keeps the hierarchy in one table, with a discriminator and a nullable column per subtype field; JOINED gives each class its table and rejoins per query; TABLE_PER_CLASS gives each concrete class a full table and turns polymorphic reads into a UNION. The trade: a wide table with nulls is fast, joined tables are normalized and pay a join per level, per-class tables read one type cheaply, the base type only as a UNION.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Two facts are encoded here, and the domain never hands them over. The shape is countable from the model: depth, width, columns per subtype. The query mix is countable from the logs: what fraction of reads asks for every type at once. Both are measurable, and the pair decides.
The gap question: how is this hierarchy actually queried — polymorphically often, or per type — measured?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Shallow and wide: two levels and many subtype columns. SINGLE_TABLE reads a subtype in one row with no join, and a check constraint per discriminator value lets the database enforce which columns belong to which type. Deep and rarely polymorphic: JOINED lets each table hold NOT NULL where its type demands it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



SINGLE_TABLE “for simplicity” over forty columns, a schema cost against the read win: every column is sometimes meaningless, none can be NOT NULL, and the database stops enforcing the domain — the invariant moves to a validator some path skips. TABLE_PER_CLASS under a polymorphic report: the report becomes a UNION over five tables, and no foreign key can point at the base type, because no table holds it.








TipThe faithfulness test



How is this hierarchy actually queried — polymorphically often, or per type — measured?

If yes → the strategy can follow the count. Write it down; revisit when the hierarchy gains a level.
If no → it is a bet on a query mix nobody recorded. Count the statements that name the base type.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask product which screens show mixed types, then read the query log.




#Hibernate #JPA #ORM #InheritanceMapping #DatabaseDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
text:
Case study: AsNoTracking (the tracking claim)
SaveChanges returns zero with no exception, the page reloads, and the old value is still on screen.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: A default EF Core query registers every materialized row in the change tracker — one instance per key, original-value snapshots — so SaveChanges can diff. AsNoTracking skips all of it: less memory, faster materialization, no change tracker — objects the DbContext has never met. The trade: cheaper detached reads against writes that silently do nothing on untracked entities.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Two facts decide this, and both belong to the application. The role: a projection, or a working set someone will modify and save. The cost: rows, memory per row, whether tracking was ever measurable. Untracked results also lose identity resolution: one key, two objects.
The gap question: is this query’s result read-only — stated — and is the tracking cost measured as worth paying?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Read-only queries untracked as a rule, measured. A report grid, a twenty-thousand-row export: nothing downstream mutates the result, so the snapshot is pure overhead and the saving is a number someone wrote down. Where identity matters, AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution keeps one instance per key.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



No-tracking reads fed into SaveChanges: the entities were modified, the context never saw them, zero rows update, no error — the page keeps the old value. The repair looks like the fix and is worse: Update on a detached graph marks every column modified and overwrites a concurrent edit wholesale. The mirror trap is a tracked ten-thousand-row export: detection scans (its per-save comparison) grow with the graph, and memory doubles for rows nobody modifies.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this query’s result read-only — stated — and is the tracking cost measured as worth paying?

If yes → no-tracking is the domain’s own claim. Check that no path downstream hands those instances to SaveChanges.
If no → the result is a working set, and detachment is a bet nobody writes. Track it, or reload before writing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure memory and duration with tracking on and off; list which callers write.




#EfCore #JPA #ORM #ChangeTracking #DotNet #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: ORM Mapping and Loading
section: Case study: Client versus server evaluation (the placement claim)
text:
Case study: Client versus server evaluation (the placement claim)
A page renders twenty rows, the database reports almost no reads, and the request still takes nine seconds.
Mapping an association or tuning the session? Ask “which fact does this mapping claim — what loads when, what counts as the same thing, what may be stale?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the mapping enforces a guess. If you can, the mapping is knowledge embodied — the ORM catching up to what the domain already decided.

Mechanism: EF Core translates a LINQ expression tree to SQL. What it cannot translate either throws — since EF Core 3.0, client evaluation is legal only in the final projection — or, in older code, silently fell back and filtered in memory. The trade: any C# expression compiles, and at run time the query either fails fast or the filter moves into the application as data transfer.


The ORM knowledge gap it signals
Every predicate is one of two things, and the domain decides which: a selection over data, which must run where the data and its index live, or presentation logic, which may run over a reduced page. The ORM reports only what it can translate; conflation reads every row to discard most, and the bill arrives in bytes, not in a slow plan.
The gap question: did the filter run on the server — checked how — or did it move into the application?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Queries verified on the server before they ship: ToQueryString inspected in a test, the statement EXPLAINed, predicates kept translatable. Where a rule resists translation, the filter runs as SQL over a key projection — only keys come back — and presentation logic stays in C#, over twenty rows, not two million.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An AsEnumerable placed before the Where clause: the whole table is transferred so twenty rows can be chosen. The page is called slow, the database called healthy, and both are true — near-zero reads on the server, a memory spike in the application process. And it reads like style: nothing in the query looks wrong.








TipThe faithfulness test



Did the filter run on the server — checked how — or did it move into the application?

If yes → the selection runs where the data is. Confirm the plan uses an index, and that the check lives in a test.
If no → the filter runs in your process over rows already shipped. Move the predicate into the query, or project keys first and fetch by key.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mapping wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Dump ToQueryString for the hot path; compare rows returned with rows the process examined.




#EfCore #JPA #ORM #QueryTranslation #DotNet #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
The framework learns about the application at build time. Each post asks what it learned, and from whose knowledge.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: Compile-time dependency injection
Two services hold the same beans: one boots in 40 ms, the other in 3 seconds. One framework read the graph at build time; the other reads it at every start.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Micronaut’s annotation processor emits a definition per bean, so the container builds graphs from generated classes instead of scanning a classpath reflectively. Startup is a bounded sequence of constructor calls, and a native image has no reflection metadata to guess at. The trade: the candidate set is fixed at compile time, so a bean that only appears at run time — registered, scanned, or loaded later — has no definition at all.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
The framework learned which beans exist, what each constructor needs, and the order they must be built in — from your source code. That is a claim: every bean is knowable statically; any bean the source cannot see breaks it, and none appears in the artifact.
The gap question: is the bean graph a build-time fact or a runtime surprise?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Cold starts on serverless and container platforms, where boot time is billed and a fixed graph is what makes the number small. Measure the start on the target runtime with the production bean count.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Runtime-DI habits carried across unchanged: a factory scanning a directory for handlers, a registry filled from ServiceLoader at first use. It compiles, tests pass, and the container wires exactly what the generated definitions describe — the late registrations riding alongside, invisible to the compiler and absent from the native binary.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which beans are decided at runtime, by condition — can you list them — or is the graph fully known at build?

If yes → the graph is a build-time fact and the startup number is its consequence. Check that nothing registers after startup.
If no → name the conditions, then move each to a compile-time requirement or accept that this part sits outside the framework’s knowledge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Compare the bean count at startup with the count of generated definitions.




#Micronaut #Java #DependencyInjection #GraalVM #StartupTime #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: AOP without proxies
Three interceptors wrap one method — retry, trace, transaction — a patch bump reorders them with no annotation changed, and the first symptom is a duplicate charge.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Micronaut resolves interception at compile time: an advised bean gets a generated subclass whose interceptors run in an order the processor fixed, with no runtime proxy and no reflection. That class is ordinary Java in your build output. The trade: cross-cutting behavior costs nothing at startup and survives native image, but the composed behavior of stacked advice lives in that file, not in the annotations.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
Annotation order is not call order: the processor learned each method’s interceptors and emitted one order, and whether that suits the domain is a fact about your workload. A retry outside a transaction re-runs the whole transaction, commit included; inside, it re-runs one statement. A span outside the retry records one per attempt; inside, one total.
The gap question: what fixes this interceptor order, and has anyone read the answer? For this bean the answer is the generated chain, stated nowhere else.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Retry and tracing advice on an outbound client, with the generated order read once, noted in the design notes, and asserted by a test. An upgrade that reorders the chain fails loudly.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Advice stacked three deep from three libraries, assuming annotations imply sequence. Nobody opens the generated subclass. The behavior is real, ordered, and determined, in a file no reviewer reads — so a patch bump that reorders one library changes the system silently, and the first symptom is a duplicate charge.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the final call order for this bean — read from the generated source, or assumed from the annotations?

If yes → the chain is known and reviewable. Record and assert it, so the next upgrade cannot move it quietly.
If no → you are running an order you never chose. Read the generated class for one advised bean and write the order down.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Open the generated source for the most-advised bean and diff the order after each upgrade.




#Micronaut #Java #AOP #Interceptors #GraalVM #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: Bean introspection
The same serializer returns a complete object on the JVM and an empty one in the native binary — same classes, same annotations, different runtime.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Annotate a class with @Introspected and the processor generates BeanIntrospection metadata at build time, so a serializer using it reads properties without reflection. The trade is coverage: a class with metadata serializes anywhere, native image included; a class without it falls back to reflection, which works until reflection is gone.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
The framework learned which properties each class exposes, for the classes it was told of. That is a claim: the serialized types are enumerable from the source, and the claim covers your annotated types, not your controllers. Error payloads, cache entries, message bodies, types nested in your own DTOs — each crosses a serialization edge, and each is a fact the build learned or did not.
The gap question: is the bean graph a build-time fact or a runtime surprise? For serialization the set is the types with generated metadata; the gap is all the rest.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A boundary that must run native: JSON routed through introspections, every payload type round-tripped in the binary’s test run.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A library deserializes by reflection on classes with no introspection — a third-party type, a DTO from a module built without the processor. On the JVM nothing looks wrong: tests pass, staging is green, the fallback returns the right object. Under native image the same call returns an empty payload, and the trace points at the library, not the annotation missing three modules away. Silent by design.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which classes are serialized — and is their metadata generated, verified for the native build?

If yes → the boundary is a build-time fact. Check that no nested type was forgotten: an outer introspection does not imply the inner.
If no → the fallback is doing the work. Annotate the type, or use a serializer path that refuses what it cannot generate.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Round-trip every payload type in a native build and list those that came back empty.




#Micronaut #Java #Serialization #GraalVM #NativeImage #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: @Executable and introspection boundaries
The endpoint passes every test, every JVM build, every staging deploy — and returns 404 in the native binary that ships.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: @Executable marks a class so the ExecutableMethodProcessor registers its methods where bean conventions would not; @Introspected does the same for serialization metadata. Both are opt-in declarations telling the processor to emit code. Opt-in is a boundary with no middle where conventions are silent: what is declared is generated, what is missed is not, and the miss is silent on the JVM.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
The gap is not in what the processor emitted but in what nobody asked it for. The question is whether the annotated set equals the set your runtime needs. A bean in a library module built without the processor, a class the build never treated as a bean, a nested payload without introspection — each is an omission with no local symptom.
The gap question: is the route set a build-time fact or a runtime surprise? The omission is the surprise, and the JVM hides it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A build output enumerating every generated definition and every registered method, read in review and diffed per release. A route without a generated entry then fails the review, not the deploy.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A controller in a library module compiled without the processor: the JVM falls back to a reflective definition, the native image has no reflection, and the route 404s only in the binary that ships. Every JVM test says the route exists. The seduction is the evidence — green tests, a working local build, a production report that reads like a routing bug in a component nobody touched.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the build report list every route — checked — or is the gap found by a user?

If yes → the route set is a build-time fact. Check the diff, not the list: an omission shows up as an unintended deletion.
If no → the artifact asserts routes the build never generated. Compare the list with the API contract.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Enumerate the generated definitions, then call every documented route in a native build.




#Micronaut #Java #GraalVM #NativeImage #AnnotationProcessing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: Declarative client (@Client interface)
One annotated interface becomes an HTTP client — and one hand-rolled call for an awkward endpoint splits the contract in two.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: An @Client interface declares one method per remote endpoint. Micronaut generates the implementation at compile time and binds the base URL from micronaut.http.services.<id>.url. Timeouts and a @Fallback sit beside the declaration. The trade: one contract that the compiler checks and every caller reuses, against a hand-rolled client whose paths, headers, and error handling drift from the provider’s.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
A declared client asserts that the remote service has a stable contract, that callers share it, and that the address is configuration rather than code. Each is a claim about a service you do not own that can be false. The gap question: for each remote service, is there exactly one declared contract — single-sourced — and where does its URL come from?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



One service, many callers, one provider contract: checkout calling payments, a gateway calling identity. Then declare a single client per service, put timeouts and fallback beside the declaration, and let every caller inject the same interface. A provider change becomes one edit in one file.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Simpler to write it by hand.” One awkward call gets a second client on RestClient or raw HTTP, because the interface felt heavy for one endpoint. The contract now lives in two places, only one is reviewed, and they disagree the day the provider answers 429 — the declared client had a fallback, the hand-rolled one had none, and the busiest caller was the one without it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each remote service: is there exactly one declared contract — single-sourced — and where does its URL come from?

If yes → the client is the contract. Check that timeouts and the fallback sit beside the declaration, not in a caller.
If no → the contract is duplicated, and the duplicate is already wrong. Fold the hand-rolled call in.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every outbound call per service, then the file each contract lives in.




#Micronaut #Java #DeclarativeClients #APIContracts #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: Validated configuration (@ConfigurationProperties)
Every key was marked optional, and the one feature that needs a real value finds out in production.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A @ConfigurationProperties bean binds a key group to typed fields, and the annotation processor generates that binding at build time. With @Validated, @NotNull, and @Context scope, a missing key fails startup — the context-scoped bean is created at startup, and startup fails if a required property is missing. The trade: required keys declared and enforced before the application serves a request, against an optional-everything configuration where every key’s presence is discovered at runtime.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
Marking a key required is a claim that the feature cannot function without it — not that it is usually set. Only the team that owns the feature can supply that claim. The gap question: which config keys are required for this feature to work — enforced at startup — or discovered when it first runs?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A key without which the feature is meaningless: a signing secret, a database URL, a tenant identifier. Then bind it as a required field with a constraint, and let a bad deployment die at startup, not at 3 a.m. in the one path that reads it. Bind the type too: a duration as a duration.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Keep it optional for flexibility” — a @Nullable field or an empty default, applied to every key because one is genuinely optional. The group now boots in any state. The missing key surfaces when the rarely-used feature runs: the nightly export, the regional failover, the admin path nobody exercises — in production, on the day it matters. Optionality spread over a group hides which single key was ever the exception.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which config keys are required for this feature to work — enforced at startup — or discovered when it first runs?

If yes → the group encodes what the feature needs. Check each key has a type, not just a presence rule.
If no → the group encodes nothing, and startup proves only that the process can boot. Make the true requirements fail fast.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Remove each key in a test profile and record which feature breaks.




#Micronaut #Java #Configuration #FailFast #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
section: Case study: Netty server (thread selection and event loops)
text:
Case study: Netty server (thread selection and event loops)
A handler that returns a reactive type is assumed non-blocking — put JDBC inside it and every request on that event loop queues behind the database.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Micronaut serves HTTP on Netty, with a small set of event loops derived from the processors the JVM sees and a blocking pool behind them. Thread selection AUTO reads the handler’s return type: a reactive type stays on the loop, a plain object moves to the blocking pool. The trade: thread economy on the loop against blocking handlers moved to a bounded pool.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
Deciding where a handler runs requires knowing what its body does — wait on a socket, wait on a database, or compute. That is a property of your code, invisible to the framework, which is exactly why AUTO guesses from a type. The gap question: which endpoints run blocking code — listed — and on which pool, sized from what measurement?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Blocking endpoints that are known and counted: JDBC, a filesystem read, a legacy client without async support. Then mark them with @ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING), size that pool from the concurrency the dependency tolerates, and verify the loop count against the container’s CPU quota — the count follows the processors the JVM sees, which in a container may be the host’s, not the quota’s.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A handler declared reactive, returning a Mono, while its body runs a blocking JDBC query — often wrapped to look asynchronous. AUTO trusts the return type, keeps it on the loop, and one slow query stalls every connection that loop owns. Under default configuration the symptom is polite: throughput can halve as load rises, latency climbs, and no thread dump shows a blocked pool.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which endpoints run blocking code — listed — and on which pool, sized from what measurement?

If yes → the placement is a fact. Confirm the pool each blocking handler runs on — not the loop count.
If no → some loop is running a database call. Mark the handler, and size the pool it moves to.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Time each endpoint’s body, then read loop count and pool saturation under load.




#Micronaut #Java #Netty #EventLoop #Blocking #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Micronaut Compile-Time DI
text:
Case study: Bean conditions (@Requires)
A bean exists in production and not in the test suite, and no test ever fails — the wiring is simply absent on one side.
Accepting a Micronaut default? Ask “what did the framework learn about my application at build time, and which fact did that bake in?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the framework decided on your behalf. If you can, the default is knowledge embodied — the build catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: @Requires makes a bean definition conditional — on a class, a property, an environment, another bean’s presence or absence. The processor bakes the definitions into the build, and the context resolves the conditions at startup, against the classpath and configuration it actually has. The trade: wiring declared per environment and fixed at startup, against a container that decides at runtime.


The Micronaut knowledge gap it signals
A condition is a claim about which environments and classpaths this application runs in, and those combinations are the team’s to enumerate, not the framework’s. The build answers only the question it was asked. The gap question: under which conditions does each conditional bean exist — enumerated — and do the tests cover the production combination?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Genuinely different environments: an in-memory queue, a broker client where the client library is on the classpath, a stub for an external provider in the test profile. Then write the conditions down per bean, and let the test profile differ only where production differs, so the coverage gap stays visible.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A bean gated on @Requires(classes = SomeClient.class) where the test profile, lean on dependencies, lacks that library. The bean is absent in CI, the endpoint that injects it is absent too, and the build succeeds because nothing ever asked for it. The path ships unexercised, exists in production, and is first run there — a startup decision made against a test classpath that never matched the deployment.








TipThe faithfulness test



Under which conditions does each conditional bean exist — enumerated — and do the tests cover the production combination?

If yes → the conditions are documented facts. Check the test profile’s differences are the intended ones, not missing dependencies.
If no → some path is greened by absence. Add the dependency to the test classpath, or delete the condition.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List conditions, then diff the production classpath against the test one.




#Micronaut #Java #ConditionalBeans #CompileTime #Testing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Every knob below moves two numbers: the one it aims at, and one it did not. Each post names the knob, states the trade, and asks which measured fact of this workload answers it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: IO scheduler choice (none, mq-deadline, bfq, kyber)
text:
Case study: IO scheduler choice (none, mq-deadline, bfq, kyber)
An NVMe box hands a measurable share of its IOPS to a scheduler reordering what the drive reorders in silicon.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Four schedulers front the device, each selling a different ordering service. none reorders nothing; mq-deadline bounds one request’s wait; bfq divides bandwidth by cgroup weight; kyber caps queue depth per operation type. Three of the four add per-IO CPU work — overhead where hardware already reorders; none buys no ordering and pays no CPU, and it runs no fairness layer.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The choice encodes two claims about your own system: how much contention the device sees, and how much ordering its hardware still lacks. Both belong to your device class and tenant count, not the kernel. The gap question: which blocking behavior does this class still lack, and is the CPU you pay buying what the drive already does?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



bfq where many tenants compete on spinning or slow storage: one backup job stopped starving the foreground path, its p99 read latency falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds. mq-deadline on a database box whose writes must not queue behind a read burst. none on NVMe once request merging above the scheduler is confirmed: more IOPS, less CPU per IO.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The copied tuning guide. bfq is the “low latency” scheduler in every post for spinning disks, so it lands on NVMe, where the drive reorders in hardware and the bookkeeping runs on every submitting core. The quieter trap: none on a SATA SSD with many concurrent fsync writers, because “none is fastest” — one queue, no fairness layer, one fsync-heavy writer takes the disk while the rest wait.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the device class, the contention level, and the p99 target — and did you measure the scheduler’s effect on this box?

If yes → you hold the three facts it rests on. Re-measure when the device or tenant count changes.
If no → the scheduler is an inherited default, not a decision. Name the device and tenant count, then measure an alternative at production queue depth.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Run the workload under two schedulers and read p99, IOPS and CPU per IO together.




#Linux #Kernel #IOScheduler #Storage #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: CPU frequency governor
One config line buys a front-end box back its p99 tail, and bills the choice in watts on every idle core.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Three governors, three claims. performance pins the clock at the top P-state; schedutil derives a target from scheduler utilization; powersave on intel_pstate hands frequency to the hardware’s own control loop. The trade is a latency floor against energy and heat — a constant clock removes the ramp, a scaled clock charges ramp delay on wakeup and saves the watts between.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The governor encodes a claim about load shape: whether the CPU is busy enough that the top clock is nearly always right, and whether a wakeup arriving mid-ramp is visible to your SLA. Neither ships with the kernel. The gap question: which tail number did the ramp actually move, and what does the watt delta cost at your fleet size?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A front-end box whose p99 spiked: a frequency trace put the spike at the ramp, the CPU dropping clock between requests before the next arrived. Pinning performance removed it. An idle-heavy fleet at 5% utilization went the other way: schedutil cut energy with no p99 change that fleet measured.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



performance copied from a gaming guide onto a fleet idling 95% of the day. The gain is real for the benchmark behind it — single-thread latency — and the bill is every idle core holding its top P-state: power, heat, less turbo headroom for the cores at work. The reverse is subtler: schedutil on a trading or audio path where the ramp is the spike. Those boxes idle by design between events, so utilization reads low and each event can pay the delay the governor was meant to avoid.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who owns the SLA — and which currency did the choice spend, watts or wakeup delay, at fleet size?

If yes → you can defend the line in both currencies. Re-check when the idle fraction changes.
If no → the governor is a copied default. Measure the tail under both, then multiply the watt delta by fleet and month.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Trace frequency beside latency for an hour of real traffic.




#Linux #Kernel #CPUFrequency #Latency #Energy #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Kernel preemption model
A kernel built for latency can cost a render fleet several percent of throughput, and no dashboard shows what it bought.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Voluntary preemption runs kernel code to completion at safe points; full preemption allows it nearly anywhere; real-time adds threaded IRQs and priority inheritance. Since 5.12, PREEMPT_DYNAMIC picks among the built variants at boot, so the choice can be per boot, not per build. The trade is throughput against wakeup latency: fewer involuntary switches mean better cache behavior and a longer wait for the task an interrupt woke.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Both sides belong to your workload: how long the longest kernel path gets under your IO pattern, and how much runqueue delay your SLA tolerates. A distro default is a compromise across workloads it never saw. The gap question: which wakeup-latency number does your SLA name, and was it measured on the kernel build you run?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A capture path dropping buffers: full preemption cut worst-case wakeup from 3 ms to 20 µs on the same hardware, and the dropouts stopped — the batch job on the same host lost 4% throughput and had the slack to absorb it. A render farm took the opposite line: voluntary preemption, no latency target, maximum throughput under a full runqueue.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The custom kernel built once “for performance” and never re-measured: full preemption everywhere, so the throughput cost is paid continuously against an unmeasured win. The commoner version is quieter: the distro default assumed adequate for a latency SLA it never heard of. Tests pass because tests are idle, and the first production burst can show a wakeup delay nobody has a number for.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which SLA measured the wakeup path — on which kernel build, and how often is that re-checked?

If yes → you know what preemption buys here and its cost. Re-check after a kernel upgrade, which changes both.
If no → the model is a distro artifact. Measure worst-case wakeup latency under real IO and CPU load, then decide.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Read the worst wakeup, not the mean.




#Linux #Kernel #Preemption #Scheduling #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: CPU isolation and IRQ steering
text:
Case study: CPU isolation and IRQ steering
Four cores reserved for a latency-critical thread that spends its life sleeping on a lock held on a housekeeping core.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: isolcpus stops the scheduler placing ordinary tasks on named CPUs; IRQ affinity policy keeps interrupts off them; a cpuset or taskset must then put the threads there. The trade is direct: quiet cores for the workload against fewer cores for everything else — housekeeping, softirq work, and the rest of what it runs.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Isolation answers a measured jitter question, so it needs a jitter number and a named noise source. You must know whether the spikes came from interrupt delivery, from migration, or from cache contention with a neighbour — each needs a different fix; all three are served by moving work off the core, by a different lever: the IRQ mask, isolcpus, or pinning the thread away. The gap question: which jitter number did isolation improve, measured before and after, and what do the reserved cores cost the rest of the box?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A tail-sensitive service whose p99.9 spikes lined up with NIC interrupt and softirq activity: moving the queue interrupts off four cores, pinning the workers there, and leaving housekeeping on the remainder removed the spikes, with both numbers recorded. The half usually skipped: the remaining cores must still cover the ordinary work.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The cargo cult: cores isolated, threads never scheduled onto them, because the pool’s affinity was never set or the workers sleep on a lock held elsewhere. So the quiet cores idle while the real path stays as noisy as before, on a box with fewer cores for the work. Its fleet cousin reserves those cores on every instance for one benchmark that ran once.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which jitter number improved, measured before and after — and what do the reserved cores cost the rest of the box?

If yes → you have a measured win and a named noise source. Re-check when the interrupt layout or core count changes.
If no → the cores are reserved on faith. Trace the spikes first, then isolate only what the trace implicates.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Compare the tail with and without isolation, not the mean.




#Linux #Kernel #CPUIsolation #Affinity #Jitter #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: cgroup limits as contract
text:
Case study: cgroup limits as contract
A memory limit set at current usage plus ten percent, and the OOM killer arrives on the first busy afternoon.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: memory.max and cpu.max are ceilings the workload may not exceed; io.weight is a share, not one. On breach the kernel throttles per period, or reclaims then kills; under contention a low io.weight deprioritises the cgroup’s IO. The trade is a guarantee for the neighbours against a throttle or a kill for the limited workload itself.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
A limit claims a peak, so it needs that peak measured — not one inferred from a quiet afternoon — with the working set apart from the cache it borrows. It also needs a breach policy: who is paged, what restarts, which counter proves it happened. The gap question: what measured peak does this limit assume, and on breach what happens and who is told?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A batch pod with memory.max above its largest observed resident set plus headroom for the biggest input, and memory.events on a dashboard: the limit held, one breach paged a human, and the pod restarted clean. cpu.max sized so the interactive path kept its share, with cpu.stat throttling displayed rather than discovered.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Current usage plus ten percent, sampled on a quiet afternoon: the first legitimate spike exceeds it, direct reclaim eats the response time, then an OOM kill can take a pod that would have survived. The fairness variant looks principled and is worse: a cpu.max quota set “for fairness” with no definition of fair and no measurement of burst shape. A job needing a 100 ms burst each second is throttled at every period boundary, and the symptom is a mysterious 100 ms p99 stall nobody traces to the quota.








TipThe faithfulness test



What measured peak does this limit assume — and on breach, what happens and who is told?
