If yes → the limit is a contract with a number and a policy. Re-measure the peak when the inputs change.
If no → the limit is a number, not a contract. Measure peak usage and working set, then write the breach policy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Read memory.events and cpu.stat under real load.




#Linux #Kernel #Cgroups #ResourceLimits #SRE #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: vm.swappiness
vm.swappiness=0 read as “never swap” turns a slow box into a dead one, mid-transaction.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The knob biases reclaim between anonymous pages and file-backed page cache: a high value moves anonymous memory toward swap sooner, a low value drops the page cache first and swaps anonymous pages later. It does not switch swapping off — on kernels since 3.5 even zero still evicts anonymous pages rather than OOM while swap exists. The trade is warm file data against the reclaim order of process memory.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The setting presumes two numbers about your workload: the anonymous working set at peak, and how much file traffic is re-read after eviction. A database reaching files directly answers differently from one reading through the page cache, and neither number lives in the kernel. The gap question: what is the measured anonymous working set against RAM, and what does the box do on the first full reclaim walk?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A database box whose anonymous working set was measured to fit in RAM at peak, with scan, page-steal and swap-in rate on a graph. Low swappiness kept the working set resident at the price of file-cache warmth, and any swap-in would have appeared on the latency path immediately.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Zero treated as an off switch. The box has swap, so zero still pages out — but only once the file cache is gone. The workload grows past RAM, direct reclaim storms as swap fills, and the OOM killer lands mid-transaction once swap runs out too. The escalation is turning swap off entirely, which removes the valve and the slow degradation it buys, so the failure changes from slow to sudden.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured anonymous working set against RAM — and what does the box do on the first full reclaim walk?

If yes → the value follows from two measured numbers. Watch swap-in rate on the latency path, not just the swap used column.
If no → the value is a slogan, not a setting. Measure peak anonymous usage, then decide whether swap is the valve or the crutch.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Read scan, page-steal and swap-in through one real peak.




#Linux #Kernel #MemoryManagement #Swap #Databases #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Transparent huge pages (the stall on the allocation path)
text:
Case study: Transparent huge pages (the stall on the allocation path)
A database on 128 GB of RAM stalls 11 ms once a minute, and no query is running when it does.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: THP backs a 4 KB request with a 2 MB page, so one TLB entry covers 512 times more memory. The bill arrives at allocation: when no free 2 MB block exists, the kernel compacts to assemble one, and the thread that asked waits. enabled=madvise limits big pages to regions marked MADV_HUGEPAGE; defrag=madvise keeps compaction off the allocation path.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The knob encodes a priority you must state: throughput on a large footprint, or bounded pause on a shared host. Neither value is the right default — both are properties of your workload and your latency budget. Two boxes want opposite settings, yet the config file is identical. The gap question: which latency number improved on this box — and what did throughput do in the same measurement window?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A jitter-sensitive database shows the stall in its worst-case latency: with THP forced on, the slowest query moved from 0.4 ms to 11 ms; set to madvise, it left the tail and throughput stayed inside the noise. A big-heap batch job that never reports the stall keeps THP on and collects the TLB win.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Disabling THP fleet-wide because a tuning guide said so. Defensible on the database, wrong on the analytics job two racks over, which quietly loses its TLB win and pays 4 KB walks over a heap it touches constantly. The mirror trap is worse: THP left on for the database, where the millisecond pauses stay unexplained for a year because nobody connects them to the knob.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which latency number improved on this box — and what did throughput do in the same measurement window?

If yes → both numbers are yours, so the trade is a decision. Re-read defrag when the allocation pattern changes.
If no → the tweak is a copied default. Toggle THP on one box, same workload, and read p99 and throughput together.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the compaction stall (thp in /proc/vmstat) against your own latency budget.




#Linux #Kernel #TransparentHugePages #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Memory overcommit (the promise the kernel cannot keep)
text:
Case study: Memory overcommit (the promise the kernel cannot keep)
At 02:10 a cache forks to write its snapshot, and the OOM killer takes the parent, not the child.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: vm.overcommit_memory decides what the kernel answers to an address-space request it has no pages for: 0 is heuristic, 1 always says yes, 2 refuses anything past CommitLimit — swap plus overcommit_ratio percent of RAM. The trade: optimistic promises against a hard commitment. The fork path needs the second: with copy-on-write the child’s pages materialise when the parent writes, so a fork the kernel grants must be backed when the writes arrive.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
How much your service forks, how much it writes after forking, and what swap you sized are facts about your system, not the kernel. A snapshot rewrite and a preforking server both duplicate pages; a single-process allocator does not. The gap question: which process forks how much, measured — and who survives the first failed allocation, the requester or a random victim?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A fork-heavy service runs mode 2 with CommitLimit sized to twice the snapshot — the fork charges the COW child in full: the fork fails fast if it cannot be served, and the snapshot is protected instead of dying at 02:10. A single-purpose box whose application counts its own allocations runs mode 1, where the kernel stops second-guessing a plan the process made.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Heuristic mode, no swap, a fork-heavy service. It survives a year because the parent’s dirty pages stay small until the dataset grows; then one night the fork is refused mid-snapshot, or the killer picks its victim by score. The cousin trap is the operator who says “we have swap” while the ratio ignores how the check counts: swap plus a percentage of RAM, not free memory.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which process forks how much, measured — and who survives the first failed allocation, the requester or a random victim?

If yes → the mode matches fork behaviour. Re-check the ratio when RAM or swap changes.
If no → you are betting the snapshot on a heuristic. Count the forks, then size swap to the largest copy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure peak anonymous memory and fork frequency.




#Linux #Kernel #Overcommit #Memory #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Dirty writeback (the flush wall)
text:
Case study: Dirty writeback (the flush wall)
A log writer stalls 1.8 seconds every few minutes, and the CPU sits at 30% the whole time.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: vm.dirty_background_ratio is the share of RAM at which the flusher starts writing dirty pages; vm.dirty_ratio is the share at which a writer must write its own pages and block. Between them the kernel absorbs bursts — a delay, not a capacity. A large buffer smooths short bursts and turns the overflow into one long stall: every writer waits at the wall.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The ratios mean something only against two facts you hold: the write rate this box sustains, and whether a tail-latency budget shares the box with the flusher. In a container the percentage is of host RAM, not of the limit — inherited, never sized. The gap question: what is the measured write pattern of this box — and does any tail-latency budget share the box with the flusher?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A team measured the pause first: writers blocked 1.8 s when dirty pages crossed the hard ratio, and the flusher had started too late. Lowering dirty_background_ratio turned one cliff into a sawtooth with no stall above 20 ms, at the cost of more small writes. Latency-sensitive writers get small ratios; a bulk staging disk keeps large ones.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Raising dirty_ratio “to buffer more”, because the stall looked like a capacity problem. It is seductive: the pause leaves the test window and can return later and taller, since the same megabytes must still reach the disk in one burst. Worse is the inherited default: 20% of RAM on a machine with forty times the memory of the guide that wrote it, buffering 40 GB before stopping for minutes.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured write pattern of this box — and does any tail-latency budget share the box with the flusher?

If yes → the ratios match a write rate you can state. Re-check them when RAM or the writer changes.
If no → you are buffering against a wall you never measured. Size both ratios from a write rate you can state.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the peak write rate and the worst pause together.




#Linux #Kernel #Writeback #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: NUMA policy (bandwidth against locality)
text:
Case study: NUMA policy (bandwidth against locality)
A scan reads 40 GB at 3 GB/s, the profiler blames the code, and numastat says 62% of the allocations are remote.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: On a multi-node box an access is local or remote; remote costs latency and shares an interconnect. numactl --interleave spreads allocations for bandwidth; --membind keeps pages on one node for the lowest access time. The trade: whole-machine bandwidth, or latency for one working set. vm.zone_reclaim_mode still makes a node reclaim its own pages instead of allocating remotely; since 5.9 it defaults to 0.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Which share of accesses must stay local belongs to your access pattern, not the machine. A join walking a 20 GB index wants locality; a 200 GB table scan wants bandwidth and does not care where the bytes live. The gap question: what share of this workload’s allocations is remote, measured — and did the policy move that number?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A team read numastat, saw 62% remote on a bandwidth-bound scan, and interleaved it: throughput reached the aggregate and the remote share stopped mattering, since bandwidth was the goal. For the database the same measurement pointed the other way — bind to the node sharing its interrupts, the remote share falls, the p99 follows.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Interleaving everything “for balance”. It reads like fairness and is wrong for a database whose working set fits one node: every page can now be remote, the free locality is gone, and the slowdown shows up as unexplained query time. The companion trap is a host that inherited zone_reclaim_mode=1 from a template for a two-node machine — stalls that nobody traced to a knob older than the hardware.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of this workload’s allocations is remote, measured — and did the policy move that number?

If yes → the policy answers a number you can state. Re-read numastat after a placement change.
If no → the policy is a preference. Measure the remote share before and after.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Map the working set to nodes, then name the resource you buy.




#Linux #Kernel #NUMA #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Kernel same-page merging (density bought with CPU)
text:
Case study: Kernel same-page merging (density bought with CPU)
Forty containers run the same base image, the host reports 22 GB used, and the sum of their limits is 60 GB.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: KSM scans pages marked MADV_MERGEABLE, hashes them, and merges identical ones into one copy-on-write page; the first write faults and copies. pages_to_scan and sleep_millisecs set the rate. The trade: RAM density per host, paid in CPU for hashing and in fault latency at every write to a shared page.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Whether density is the product or a side effect decides this knob. A fleet of near-identical guests selling memory per tenant buys density; a database host selling latency does not. You must also know the scan cost against your CPU budget, and how much is shared: pages_sharing counts the duplicate mappings, pages_shared the unique merged pages. The gap question: what does the dedup save on this host, and what CPU does the scan cost — measured in the same units, over the same week?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Forty identical images measured 0.8 GB saved per guest, with the scan under a few percent of one core: density was real and priced. They graph the sharing ratio beside the scan cost: a rising ratio with rising CPU is the point, a rising ratio with falling throughput the warning.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Switching KSM on for a latency-sensitive database host because memory is tight. The premise is sound — identical pages are wasted pages. What it misses: a database writes constantly, merged pages copy on every write, and the churn becomes background load on a machine whose tail latency is its purpose. Nothing on the dashboard attributes it: the fault appears as a slower query, the scan as system CPU.








TipThe faithfulness test



What does the dedup save on this host, and what CPU does the scan cost — measured in the same units, over the same week?

If yes → density is a priced decision. Watch the ratio as the workloads diverge.
If no → you bought an unmeasured discount. Budget the scan’s CPU share on one host before the next.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure saved bytes and scan cost on one host for a week.




#Linux #Kernel #KSM #Memory #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: The free-page reserve (headroom against the burst)
text:
Case study: The free-page reserve (headroom against the burst)
A 512 GB host with 200 GB free spends 300 ms in direct reclaim, and the workload has not grown.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: vm.min_free_kbytes reserves free pages for atomic allocations that cannot sleep or reclaim. The reserve must cover the largest burst between wakeups, and every kilobyte of it is page cache the workload cannot use. The default is four times the square root of lowmem, the directly mapped zone, and is capped at 256 MB, so on a large host it grows far slower than the burst does.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
How large a burst arrives between kswapd runs is a fact about your drivers and interrupt load, documented nowhere. The reserve also subtracts from the cache your reads depend on, so it is never free. The gap question: what does reclaim look like at peak, measured — and does the reserve cover the burst without shrinking the cache the workload reads from?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A team saw direct reclaim in network bursts: pgscan_direct climbed and latency followed, while kswapd was never behind. Raising min_free_kbytes moved the work back to kswapd and removed the 300 ms stalls; the cache loss was a few hundred megabytes on a host with 200 GB free. On kernels that expose watermark_scale_factor, scaling beats a fixed number copied between hosts.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Leaving it at default because “we have plenty of RAM” — true and irrelevant, since it answers for the worst instant, not the total. The failure is a direct-reclaim spiral: each thread stops to free pages it needs, and the stall looks like an application bug at 40% free memory. The opposite trap is cranking it to gigabytes until the page cache shrinks and the read-heavy workload misses its cache.








TipThe faithfulness test



What does reclaim look like at peak, measured — and does the reserve cover the burst without shrinking the cache the workload reads from?

If yes → the reserve answers a measured burst. Re-check after a NIC or workload change.
If no → the number is inherited. Read pgscan_direct and the cache hit rate before and after.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure reclaim at peak load, then the reserve it needs.




#Linux #Kernel #MemoryReclaim #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: io_uring (the syscall amortiser)
A flame graph puts 38% of on-CPU time in syscall entry and exit at 90k IOPS. That number, not a 100k-connection benchmark, decides the rewrite.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: epoll waits for readiness, then enters the kernel once per read or write. io_uring moves submission and completion into shared-memory rings, so a batch crosses the boundary once, and on kernels that support it SQPOLL keeps a kernel thread polling, so the submission path never enters. The trade: fewer transitions per operation, paid for with a new completion model, buffer lifetime rules, and failure modes — partial completions, ring exhaustion — that epoll never had.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The measured fact is not the ring. It is your operation rate at your concurrency, and your syscall share. You need your own IOPS, payload size, and whether latency is spent in the kernel or on the peer. The gap question: what is your syscall share at production IOPS, and what does the ring cost?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A storage node doing small random reads at high rates. perf and strace put syscall entry and exit near 40% of on-CPU time; after batching submission through a ring, the same workload holds its IOPS with that share in single digits, and the freed core returns to the application. The evidence is the production flame graph.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Rewriting a working epoll service because a benchmark showed io_uring winning at 100k connections. At 50 concurrent connections the ring is pure CPU overhead: two ring operations and a reaping step cost more than the one system call they replaced. Worse, request lifetime now spans two queues, so a buffer freed between the two is corruption epoll could not express.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of on-CPU time is syscall entry and exit at production concurrency — and does the rewrite pay for itself there?

If yes → the ring answers a measured fact. Check latency at your own concurrency, not throughput alone.
If no → the rewrite is a bet on a stranger’s workload. Keep epoll, and profile where your time goes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found io_uring wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the syscall share under production load.




#Linux #Kernel #io_uring #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SystemsProgramming

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: read-ahead (the sequential bet)
A 4 MB read-ahead on the database host reads four megabytes to serve a 4 KB lookup. The bytes arrive; nobody counts them.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: read_ahead_kb tells the kernel to fetch pages past the one you asked for. When the next read is adjacent, those pages sit in cache and the queue stays deep; when it is not, the kernel fetched pages nothing will touch. The trade: deeper prefetch for sequential streams, against wasted reads and displaced cache for random access.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Read-ahead encodes a claim about your access pattern, and the claim belongs to your workload. You need the sequential share of reads, the fetched-to-used ratio, and the cache hit ratio before and after — from your own device. A backup reader and an OLTP engine seeking an index need opposite values. The gap question: what share of reads is sequential, measured, and what did the cache hit ratio do after the change?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A bulk loader streaming a multi-gigabyte file. At the 128 KB default the queue never fills and the load runs at a fraction of the device’s sequential bandwidth; at 1 MB it saturates, and every fetched page is consumed, so the fetched-to-used ratio stays near one. Bandwidth at the device’s ceiling, and that ratio, are the evidence.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Raising read-ahead to 4 MB on every host, because the analytics box liked it. The index-heavy OLTP workload now pulls megabytes per random page touch, the working set may no longer fit in page cache, and the hit ratio decays slowly enough that the first symptom is a p99 nobody attributes to a sysfs write.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of reads is sequential, measured — and what did the cache hit ratio do after the change?

If yes → the value answers a fact about this device. Then watch the fetched-to-used ratio, which shows over-prefetch early.
If no → the value is borrowed. Revert it, and measure the access pattern before choosing any number.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Instrument the device for sequential share first.




#Linux #Kernel #ReadAhead #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Storage

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: atime, relatime, noatime (the metadata write)
text:
Case study: atime, relatime, noatime (the metadata write)
On a strictatime mount, noatime removes a write per read, and removes the answer to “when was this file last read?” — the tool that asked gets no answer.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: On a strictatime mount, a read updates the access time, which is a write to inode metadata — costly on a file read many times. relatime, the default on most distributions since kernel 2.6.30, updates it only when the old value predates the modification time or is a day stale. noatime stops the update entirely. The trade: the atime writes avoided, against the knowledge of when a file was last read.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
atime is an ambient service any process may consume, per filesystem. You must know which of your own processes reads it — backup rotation with find -atime, dedup and hierarchical-storage (HSM) tools, cache eviction — and whether the write reduction matters at your write rate. The gap question: which process reads atime, and what did the write reduction actually buy?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A build server on a strictatime mount, serving millions of reads from files whose timestamp nobody consults. Measured, metadata writes dominate the small-write load; with noatime they vanish and filesystem write amplification drops, while every atime consumer was enumerated first and none existed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



noatime because a tuning guide listed it. A backup rotation job on that mount reads atime to decide what to retire, and a dedup scan uses it to find cold extents. Nothing fails. The timestamps stop advancing, so the rotation keeps everything and the dedup tier stops tiering — found months later, when someone asks why storage grows. The middle ground, relatime, was never considered, though on hot files it yields the same reduction while keeping atime meaningful.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which process reads atime — can you name it — and what did the write reduction actually buy?

If yes → you found the consumer: noatime would break it, so use relatime, or cache that answer elsewhere.
If no → the flag is safe here. Record that no consumer exists: a later tool that reads atime inherits the break silently.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Enumerate atime readers first.




#Linux #Kernel #FileSystems #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Storage

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: descriptor limits (the runway a leak consumes)
text:
Case study: descriptor limits (the runway a leak consumes)
A connection leak ran for four months because someone raised the descriptor limit until EMFILE stopped. The error was the alarm, not the fault.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Three limits stack: fs.file-max caps the system, ulimit -n caps the process, and a systemd unit’s LimitNOFILE sets what the service inherits. Raising them admits more concurrent descriptors — the aimed number. The unaimed one is how far a leak now runs before it fails: bounded by a low limit, a leak is a crash, and a crash is a signal.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
A limit is a claim about your peak descriptor count, measured over weeks, with an alert that makes growth visible below it. A limit is the point at which demand is declared abnormal, not a cap on demand. The gap question: what is the measured descriptor curve, and does this raise serve a real peak or hide a leak?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A gateway whose descriptor count follows a known diurnal peak. The limit moved from 4096 to 65536, and the weeks after it measured peak 41k, alert at 80% of the limit, load test past the peak. The curve stays flat between peaks, so the higher limit answers a named peak rather than a rumour.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Raising the limit toward infinity to silence EMFILE. The competent version is worse: the engineer sets ulimit -n 1048576 in a shell profile, restarts the service from that shell, and confirms the error is gone — gone because that shell carried the higher limit. Months later systemd restarts the unit, and LimitNOFILE still holds the old value. The service dies at its original count, the drift invisible, since the earlier fix taught everyone this error was solved by raising a number.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured descriptor curve over weeks — and does this raise serve a real peak, or hide a leak?

If yes → the limit encodes a measured peak. Add the alert, so growth stays visible.
If no → you disabled a signal. Fix the leak, and keep the limit low enough to fail early.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the limit wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Graph the descriptor count per unit, for weeks.




#Linux #Kernel #ResourceLimits #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Reliability

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: io.weight and ionice (the priority claim)
text:
Case study: io.weight and ionice (the priority claim)
The transactional p99 triples during the nightly analytics run, so the batch job’s IO weight gets lowered. The tail recovers — until the batch misses its window.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: cgroup v1 called it blkio; cgroup v2 calls it io.weight, a relative share honoured by schedulers that implement proportional service. ionice does a related job per process, though its classes bite only on schedulers that respect them — with none or mq-deadline the effect is small. The trade: a latency share for one IO class, against throughput the yielding class gives up.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
A weight states which workload holds the IO path under contention, an entitlement from an SLA, not a scheduler page. You need the transactional tail split by device queueing time, the batch deadline, and the window where both overlap. The gap question: which SLA owns the IO path, and did the transactional tail improve or just the batch job slow down?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A payments service with a written p99 target, and a nightly report on the same volume. Measured, the nightly spike is device queueing time; on the bfq volume the batch is weighted down, and the following nights show the payments p99 back inside its target while the report still fits its window.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



ionice -c 2 -n 7 applied to whatever process looks greedy. If the latency comes from a row lock, an exhausted pool, or a queue in the application, the IO scheduler has nothing to reorder and the tail does not move — yet the change is recorded as a fix, so the real cause gets another quarter. The quieter variant keeps every weight equal and calls it fairness, when no SLA named an IO class.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which SLA owns the IO path — and did the measured transactional tail improve, or just the batch job slow down?

If yes → the weight encodes a real priority. Confirm the batch still meets its deadline.
If no → you moved latency sideways. Decompose the tail first; check locks and queueing outside the block layer.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the weight wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure queueing time per class against the SLA that owns it.




#Linux #Kernel #Cgroups #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Accept queue sizing (somaxconn and the listen backlog)
text:
Case study: Accept queue sizing (somaxconn and the listen backlog)
A tuning guide says net.core.somaxconn=65535, the listen drop counter goes to zero, and p99 climbs from 40 ms to 400 ms at the same 8,000 requests a second.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: net.core.somaxconn caps the accept queue: connections whose handshake completed and which wait for accept(). tcp_max_syn_backlog caps the half-open queue, and the listen(fd, backlog) argument is clipped to somaxconn, so the smaller of somaxconn and the backlog sets the accept depth. Raise them and the kernel holds connections it would have dropped, while the loop drains — and each held connection spends the wait inside your response time.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The queue is a buffer between the arrival rate and your accept loop’s drain rate. Depth buys time only if the loop drains faster than connections arrive; otherwise a fast refusal becomes a slow success. The team must know its accept-loop concurrency, its burst shape, and whether a caller prefers a refusal to a late reply.
The gap question: what p99 does a queued connection wait for — and who chose that over refusal?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



TcpExtListenOverflows and TcpExtListenDrops rise while CPU sits idle, and the accept loop is single-threaded or blocked after accept(). Then raise the backlog and the accept concurrency together, and read both numbers again: drops can fall to zero while p99 stays flat, because the loop now drains what the queue admits.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The queue lifted without the accept loop behind it: backlog and somaxconn both raised. Drops vanish, the dashboard turns green, and every connection that would have been refused now waits — p99 at 400 ms — for a slot the slow loop never frees; the loss moved from a visible counter to invisible latency. The tell: 65535 copied from a guide before anyone ran nstat.








TipThe faithfulness test



What did the accept-queue counters measure before the change — and what happened to p99 after, at the same load?

If yes → the depth answers a measured overflow and the loop keeps pace. Watch queue occupancy as load grows.
If no → you bought a buffer, not throughput. Fix the drain side first, then re-size.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Read ListenOverflows, ListenDrops, and p99 at one fixed request rate.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Congestion control (BBR versus cubic)
text:
Case study: Congestion control (BBR versus cubic)
BBR lifts one 120 ms path from 40 Mbit/s to 180 Mbit/s, and the cubic flows sharing that 200 Mbit/s bottleneck can be squeezed to what is left.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control picks the sender’s algorithm. Cubic probes until it sees loss, so it treats every drop as congestion. BBR instead estimates bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, paces to that model, and keeps going through shallow-buffer loss. The trade: it stops backing off where cubic would, which is exactly why it wins on a lossy path and exactly why it can take more than its share of a shared one.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
BBR’s model is only meaningful if the path has enough buffering to measure, an RTT that is mostly propagation, and no other sender whose fairness depends on loss signals. The team must know this path’s loss profile, its buffer depth, and who else crosses the same bottleneck. The gap question: what are the measured RTT, bandwidth, and loss profile of THIS path, and which other flows share it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A long fat pipe or a lossy last mile where cubic collapses on loss that is not congestion: 120 ms RTT, 1% random loss, throughput stuck at 40 Mbit/s against a 200 Mbit/s path. On kernels that ship BBRv1, enabling BBR and re-measuring gives 180 Mbit/s on this path, with retransmits unchanged — the gain measured here, not borrowed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



BBR everywhere, because it was measured somewhere else. On a shallow-buffered shared link a BBRv1 sender can starve the cubic flows beside it, and on a 0.2 ms LAN the bandwidth model has nothing to estimate. Nothing in the local numbers said this path needed it.








TipThe faithfulness test



What are the measured RTT, bandwidth, and loss profile of THIS path — and which other flows share it?

If yes → the algorithm answers a measured loss that was not congestion. Watch fairness against the other flows as they change.
If no → you adopted a result from another network. Revert, and fix the loss or the buffer instead.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure RTT, achieved and bottleneck bandwidth, and loss with both algorithms at the same hour.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #CongestionControl #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: TIME_WAIT knobs (tw_reuse, fin_timeout, port range)
text:
Case study: TIME_WAIT knobs (tw_reuse, fin_timeout, port range)
A scraper opens 10,000 connections a second, exhausts its 28,000-port ephemeral range in TIME_WAIT, and someone sets net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: tcp_tw_reuse lets an outbound connection reuse a TIME_WAIT socket after one second, given RFC 1323 timestamps. tcp_fin_timeout shortens FIN_WAIT_2, not TIME_WAIT — that stays 60 seconds. ip_local_port_range widens the ephemeral pool. Together they relieve port and socket-memory pressure by shortening or bypassing what TIME_WAIT guarantees.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Every TIME_WAIT socket is a connection the application opened and did not keep. The knob treats the symptom; the count is churn times the 60 s dwell, and the churn belongs to the client. The gap question: how many connections per second does the application actually open — and what, specifically, stops it from reusing them?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A legitimately churning workload: short-lived scrape targets, one connection per target per interval, keep-alive impossible. Pooling was applied first and measured — churn fell from 10,000 to 470 a second — yet 28,000 TIME_WAIT sockets remain and the port range still exhausts. With RFC 1323 timestamps confirmed at both ends, widening the range and enabling tw_reuse answers a measured shortage.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



tw_reuse as the cure for a missing pool. The client opens 10,000 connections a second because it never learned to hold one, and the knob makes that sustainable instead of visible. tw_reuse also needs timestamps at both ends: behind a carrier NAT that rewrites or strips them, SYNs are dropped silently and retried. tcp_tw_recycle, removed in kernel 4.12, is that trap with a tombstone.








TipThe faithfulness test



How many connections per second does the application actually open — and what, specifically, stops it from reusing them?

If yes → the churn is inherent and the knobs answer a measured shortage. Watch socket memory and NAT behaviour at the peer.
If no → the fix is a pool or keep-alive in the application. Revert the knobs.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Count TIME_WAIT sockets and new connections per second at the client, then test a pooled client.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #TimeWait #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: IRQ affinity, RSS, RPS, and XPS
text:
Case study: IRQ affinity, RSS, RPS, and XPS
Every NIC interrupt lands on core 0, that core sits at 60% softirq, and the eight application threads pinned to cores 0–7 wait on a CPU busy receiving their packets.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: RSS gives the NIC multiple receive queues; /proc/irq/N/smp_affinity decides which CPU runs each queue’s handler; RPS spreads that work in software when the NIC has one queue; XPS picks the transmit queue per CPU. The trade is a core: whatever core runs the interrupt cannot run application threads at full speed, and a core given to networking is a core taken from the application.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The right mask depends on where the application threads run, how many cores the box has, and whether the bottleneck is receive processing or the application. The team must know the IRQ layout and the thread layout before moving anything. The gap question: what is the measured softirq share per core — and where do the application threads actually run?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



/proc/softirqs shows NET_RX concentrated on two cores at 55% while six sit near idle, and the application’s threads are pinned across six only. Steer those IRQs to the two cores carrying no latency-critical thread, apply RPS for the queues the NIC lacks, match XPS to the transmit queues: softirq on the application’s cores falls to 8%, and requests per second rise with p99 flat.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



irqbalance disabled “for determinism” with no mask plan, so every IRQ stays where boot left it — usually core 0. Or the opposite: a mask spread across all cores, the ones the application pinned included, so pinning meant to isolate latency amplifies contention. Both look like tuning; neither read a softirq counter.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured softirq share per core — and where do the application threads actually run?

If yes → the mask answers a measured imbalance. Re-read /proc/softirqs after traffic shifts.
If no → you moved work into the application’s way. Revert the mask until both layouts are measured.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Sample /proc/softirqs per core under production load, and read the thread affinity masks.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #Performance #NUMA #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Jumbo frames (MTU 9000)
MTU 9000 on the backup LAN: 14% more throughput at 40% less CPU per byte, until one switch port in the path stayed at 1500 and the job ran slower than before.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A 9000-byte MTU carries 8960 bytes of payload per frame instead of 1460, so the same byte count costs roughly six times fewer frames: fewer interrupts, fewer headers, less work per packet. The trade is consent — every hop must agree. One port at 1500 forces IPv4 fragmentation or an oversized drop, and filtered ICMP “fragmentation needed” turns that drop into a blackhole.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The benefit scales with bytes per packet, the cost with hop count, so the team must know the exact path its traffic takes, whether it stays inside one broadcast domain, and what encapsulation sits underneath. The gap question: which hops does this traffic traverse — and what did the measured throughput and p99 do at each size?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Storage replication and nightly backup inside one broadcast domain: switch ports confirmed at 9000, NIC and driver jumbo-capable, ping -M do -s 8972 succeeding end to end before anything changes. Throughput then rises 14% and CPU per byte drops 40% — both read on this path.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Jumbo frames “for performance” on a path nobody walked. One hop stays at 1500, so either every large packet fragments — more work than small frames ever cost — or the ICMP that would report it is filtered and the connection stalls. The quiet common case: the path leaves the datacenter, or VXLAN’s 50 bytes push the encapsulated packet past an underlay nobody raised.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which hops does this traffic traverse — and what did the measured throughput and p99 do at each size?

If yes → the size answers a measured per-byte cost on a path you enumerated. Re-check the path when topology changes.
If no → the frame size is a guess with a fragmentation bill. Revert to 1500 until the path is verified hop by hop.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Trace the path, read every MTU, then measure throughput and p99 at both sizes on one transfer.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #MTU #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: tcp_slow_start_after_idle
A pooled connection idles three seconds between bursts, so every burst starts at ten segments and pays a slow-start climb the application blames on the database.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: After about one retransmission timeout of idleness, a kernel honouring RFC 2861 collapses the congestion window to the initial window and re-enters slow start. The rule assumes the path may have changed while you looked away. The trade: re-probing safety after silence, against a re-climb stall on every burst of a connection kept open on purpose.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Service-mesh links, database pools and message consumers idle for seconds over a path that has not moved; a short-lived HTTP client has no gap at all. The gap question: how long are the measured gaps here, and does the path after a gap match the path before it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A sidecar link on a 40 ms path idles three seconds between 400 KB bursts: the window returns to ten segments, and about five RTTs pass before a burst clears, so roughly 200 ms of each burst runs below capacity (qalc: 5 × 40 ms). With the reset off, the burst leaves at bandwidth-delay rate from the first packet.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The trap is tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0 in a base image, justified by one slow dashboard. On a host of short one-shot connections the knob is inert — every connection starts cold — so it buys nothing and hides the real culprit, churn. It bites where idle means something: a device that roams, a NAT that rebinds, a route that failed over during the quiet hour. The switch is per namespace, not per socket.








TipThe faithfulness test



How long are the measured idle gaps on these connections — and is the path after idle the same path as before?

If yes → the reset costs exactly what the gaps cost. Read the gap distribution per connection type, then scope it to the host that owns those links.
If no → the connections are short-lived and the knob does nothing, or the path genuinely moves. Leave it on and chase connection reuse.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Capture the gap distribution and the RTT before and after each gap.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #CongestionControl #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: conntrack table sizing
At peak a NAT gateway refuses new connections with nf_conntrack: table full, and every refused one works when the user retries a minute later.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The conntrack table is what makes NAT and stateful firewalling possible: each tracked flow gets an entry that lives until a timeout reaps it — while the table has room. Sizing is Little’s law on flows — entries are the new-flow rate times the hold time — so the trade is memory against silent drops. A full table drops packets for untracked flows, and a dropped SYN is a connection that never opens.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Your peak new-flow rate is your traffic; your hold time is your timeout policy, and it counts flows the application finished long ago. The gap question: what is the measured concurrent-flow count at peak, and what happens to a NEW flow at the ceiling?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An edge router measures 8,000 new flows a second at peak and cuts the established timeout to 120 s — above the longest idle gap any live flow needs: steady state is 960,000 entries (qalc: 8000 × 120) in a table sized near twice that, with nf_conntrack_count scraped and an alert at seventy percent.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The seductive version is the kernel-computed default on a busy box: connections fail at peak, succeed off-peak, and the failure reads as random because it is a race with the reaper. The reflex is to double nf_conntrack_max and move on — but max without hash size lengthens the chains, so every packet walks a longer list and silent drops become a CPU tax. The other half is the timeout: five-day entries for flows that ended hours ago.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured concurrent-flow count at peak — and what happens to a NEW flow at the ceiling?

If yes → it is sized from your traffic. Check that hash size grows with the maximum, that the timeout matches the flow lifetime, and that table pressure alerts before drops.
If no → the ceiling arrives unannounced at the worst hour. Raise both numbers together, shorten the timeout, and watch insert failures in conntrack -S.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Record nf_conntrack_count and conntrack -S for a week, then recompute at peak.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #Netfilter #Conntrack #NAT #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: TCP_NODELAY against Nagle and delayed ACK
text:
Case study: TCP_NODELAY against Nagle and delayed ACK
A median button press in a trading UI takes 41 ms, the server logs 0.8 ms of work, and one socket option removes the other 40.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Nagle’s algorithm holds a small segment while earlier data is unacknowledged; delayed ACK holds the ACK up to about 40 ms. Together they stall a write-write-read pattern until the peer’s delayed ACK fires. TCP_NODELAY sends each write at once, TCP_CORK batches until released, and the trade is latency against packets.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The flag is a claim in two halves: these writes are latency-bound, so a queued millisecond is lost, and the application does not already coalesce them. The gap question: which writes are latency-bound here, and what does the flag cost in packets?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An RPC path measured 41 ms p50 with 0.8 ms of server time. A capture showed the request leaving in two writes, header then body; the body waited for the header’s ACK. Setting TCP_NODELAY on those sockets cut p50 to 1.2 ms and raised packets about eight percent: latency found by measurement, packets counted, budget satisfied.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The trap is applying the flag wherever latency is praised. On a bulk transfer assembled from 1 KB writes, TCP_NODELAY turns every write into a segment: packet rate climbs, the NIC queue pays per packet, and the throughput delivered was never latency-bound. Its quieter mirror is an interactive service carrying a mystery 40 ms blamed on the network, the database and the GC — never on Nagle waiting for a delayed ACK. Both failures come from one gap: nobody read the write pattern on the wire.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which writes are latency-bound, measured — and does the application’s write pattern batch naturally without the flag?

If yes → the flag encodes a requirement the path proved. Set it on those sockets and leave bulk sockets default or corked.
If no → you are buying latency with packets on a path that never queued. Leave the default and coalesce header and body into one write.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Trace the packets and measure the gap between the second write and its segment.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #Nagle #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: socket busy polling
A market-data receiver shaves 45 µs off its median receive latency, and two cores now read 100 percent CPU while the box serves no packets.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Busy polling spins the CPU inside the receive call for up to net.core.busy_poll microseconds instead of sleeping to the wakeup, so the packet arrives with no scheduler round trip. The trade is two-sided: every microsecond of latency comes out of a core doing nothing else, burning power whether or not a packet arrives.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The knob assumes three things, none a default: that the tail you chase is microseconds of wakeup, not milliseconds of queueing; that the waiting is idle, so spinning beats sleeping; that the cores are reserved, not borrowed. The gap question: what latency does this path measure without the spin, and which cores pay for it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A colocated feed handler runs on a dedicated box, thread and interrupt affinity set on one NUMA node, two cores reserved. Polling per socket takes wakeup-to-receive latency from about 60 µs to about 15 µs at the median: the number the box exists to produce, and the spin is its price.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The seductive move is one line — net.core.busy_poll=50 — applied fleet-wide because the low-latency service liked it. Every front end now spins fifty microseconds after each empty poll: at tens of thousands of polls a second that is real CPU and real watts waiting for absent traffic, and the autoscaler reads it as demand, adding replicas that spin too. The bill arrives as instance count, never as a sysctl, and the tail the knob serves was never measured.








TipThe faithfulness test



What microsecond gain does THIS path measure — and which cores pay, at what monthly fleet cost?

If yes → it is a priced instrument. Reserve the cores, pin the interrupt, set the socket option, not the global default, and re-measure after each upgrade.
If no → you are buying latency nobody measured with cores nobody accounted for. Leave it at zero and find the real tail, usually queueing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure receive latency with the option on and off on one host.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #LowLatency #Scheduling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: CPU vulnerability mitigations off
text:
Case study: CPU vulnerability mitigations off
Three to five percent more throughput on a compile workload with mitigations=off; the same line on a hypervisor removes a boundary for every tenant.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Spectre, Meltdown and their successors are hardware flaws; the mitigations — page-table isolation, retpolines, bounds masking — cost cycles on the paths they guard: switches, indirect calls, indexed loads. Turning them off is a security decision carrying a performance number, not a performance setting with a security footnote — throughput traded for attackers you assume away.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The gain tracks how many of those instructions your workload executes; another workload’s number predicts nothing. The decision needs a threat model: which code runs, who wrote it, who schedules beside it, who accepts the loss. The gap question: what does the measured gain justify, and who owns the boundary the switch removes?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A single-tenant build farm, physically controlled, runs only its owner’s code, with no untrusted execution, no co-tenants. Its compile workload gains four percent, accepted in writing against a threat model naming the assumed-away attacker, the owner, the review date, the reversal condition.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The trap: the benchmark travels, the threat model does not. Three to five percent on a kernel build becomes “free throughput” on a multi-tenant host running customer code, where the assumed-away attacker is the tenant next door. The ticket says performance; the change says page tables are no longer isolated. Then the deferral — “we will re-enable after the migration” — with no owner and no date. On a hypervisor it compounds: the guest is the attacker the host’s mitigations exist to bound.








TipThe faithfulness test



What does the measured gain on THIS workload justify — and who owns the boundary this switch removes?

If yes → the risk is priced. Write the threat model, name an owner, date the review, record the number from the workload that runs.
If no → it is a bet with someone else’s chips. Re-enable the mitigations and optimize the workload.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the gain on your workload, then ask who accepts its cost.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #Security #Spectre #Performance #ThreatModel #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: eBPF at tracepoints, kprobes and XDP
text:
Case study: eBPF at tracepoints, kprobes and XDP
One kprobe on the hottest syscall answers a real question in an afternoon; a year later it is still loaded, costing double-digit CPU.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: An eBPF program runs on every event it attaches to: a tracepoint, a kprobe, an XDP path. XDP is cheapest per packet, running earliest; a kprobe is dearest: a function called a million times a second becomes a million entries into your code. The trade: visibility at the point you need it, against a per-event cost and a pin to kernels you have not run.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Attaching is easy; the decision hides inside it. Which question does this program answer, and is it still open? What does it cost per event? Which kernels must it survive, given that kprobe targets are not a stable interface? The gap question: which question is still open, and what does it cost per event?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A p99 regression points at contention; no metric names the holder. A bounded program on the contention tracepoint records holder, wait time and stack for slow waits: the blind spot closes for under one percent of CPU, and the program goes with the fix. XDP earns its place the same way: an edge host drops a measured flood before the stack spends a cycle.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The trap is instrumentation nobody reads. A program added because the tooling was easy answers a question closed last quarter, on a path running ten million times a second. Its cost is booked as “kernel overhead” nobody owns. The second cost arrives at upgrade: a kprobe on an internal function may fail to load next time. CO-RE — compiled against BTF, so the program relocates onto a newer kernel — reduces the load failures, not the dependence on kernel internals.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which question does this program answer, at what per-event cost — and which kernel versions must it survive?

If yes → it is instrumentation with a budget. Bound the maps, filter at the source, name a removal date, test the load on the next kernel.
If no → it is a debugger left running. Detach it, keep the answer, keep only programs whose cost you can state.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure per-event cost with and without it.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #eBPF #Observability #XDP #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Real-time scheduling classes
A control loop misses its 1 ms deadline under load. One sched_setscheduler call can fix it — and hands the box a failure mode it never had.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR outrank every fair-share task: a runnable RT thread preempts CFS at once, and SCHED_FIFO never yields it back, so wakeup latency is bounded by the scheduler, not by queue depth. That thread gains a guarantee; every other task on the core loses one. The fuse is sched_rt_runtime_us: by default RT tasks may take 950000 of every 1000000 microseconds, then the throttler stops them.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
A guarantee pays only where the domain has a deadline the measured distribution violates. That needs the thread’s worst-case runtime, not its mean, and what else lives on the core. The gap question: which wakeup number needed a guarantee, measured — and does the thread’s worst-case runtime fit the budget the fuse allows?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A control loop sampled a sensor at 1 kHz and measured 4 ms p99 jitter under load against a 1 ms deadline. The sampling thread got SCHED_FIFO at rtprio 10; the logging and metrics threads stayed in CFS. Jitter p99 fell below 200 µs and samples stopped dropping, with the throttle left at its default.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Make it real-time so it runs faster.” On a lightly loaded box SCHED_FIFO does run sooner, because it preempts, and the benchmark improves. Then a CPU-bound loop wearing that policy owns a core until the throttle fires. The throttle stops it, the period restarts, and the machine lurches once a second in a rhythm nobody ties to a scheduler edit. The quieter variant applies the policy by template to every thread, so work with no deadline outranks sshd.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which wakeup number needed a guarantee — does the RT thread’s runtime fit the fuse, and what else lives on that core?

If yes → policy is per thread, fuse armed, alert on the throttling counter.
If no → you bought a priority boost, not a guarantee: nothing else on that core is safe.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the wakeup distribution under load, then worst-case runtime per period.




#Linux #Kernel #RealTime #Scheduling #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Compressed swap in RAM (zram, zswap)
text:
Case study: Compressed swap in RAM (zram, zswap)
A 16 GB host serves a 38 GB anonymous working set and touches no disk. It did not get more RAM. It compressed the difference and paid in cycles.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: zram presents a block device whose contents live in RAM, compressed; zswap compresses pages in front of a real swap device. Both trade swap I/O for CPU spent compressing and decompressing, and both spend RAM on the compressed store: you pay memory to hold shrunk memory. Effective capacity is device size times ratio, and the ratio is a property of your pages.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The team must know its anonymous working set, the ratio on its own pages, and the CPU headroom on cores already at the bottleneck. A heap of zeros compresses beautifully; encrypted pages barely compress. The gap question: what is the measured compression ratio and CPU cost under pressure — and does the leak it postpones have an owner?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A build host with 16 GB measured a 38 GB anonymous peak and a 4.1:1 ratio with zstd on its own pages, read from mm_stat. Swapping in a compiler’s cold pages then cost microseconds instead of a seek. Its CPU cost was measured at that peak.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A leak, hidden by the memory headroom compression buys. zram is sized large enough that the OOM never fires, so the graphs look solved for weeks: no kills, no disk swap IO, flat latency. The truth is a compressed corpse — the OOM can land later, with a working set several times physical RAM and a decompression path between the operator and the evidence. The tweak did not fix the leak; it rescheduled the discovery.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured compression ratio and CPU cost under pressure — and does the leak it postpones have an owner?

If yes → size the device from your own ratio, alert on compressor CPU share, keep the leak on someone’s list.
If no → you inflated capacity by an unknown factor and moved the failure somewhere worse.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure the anonymous peak, your own ratio, and the CPU cost at that peak.




#Linux #Kernel #Memory #Swap #Zram #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Pinning pages (mlock, the memlock limit)
text:
Case study: Pinning pages (mlock, the memlock limit)
A database’s p99 read latency doubles whenever reclaim walks its hot index. The fix pins 12 GB; four months later a second service cannot start.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: mlock marks a range resident: those pages leave the reclaim and swap paths until munlock or exit. The trade is a hard residency guarantee against RAM held forever, including on an idle replica. RLIMIT_MEMLOCK was the ceiling that stopped over-pinning, and on kernels from 5.14 a process holding CAP_IPC_LOCK is largely exempt from it.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Pinning claims these pages are hot enough to justify starving the page cache. That claim needs a measurement: which pages stalled on reclaim, and what fraction of RAM stays un-reclaimable afterwards, summed across every service on the host. The gap question: which pages were measured to stall on reclaim — and what share of RAM is now permanently un-reclaimable?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A read-heavy database showed major faults spiking on a 12 GB index region exactly when reclaim ran, p99 doubling with them. That region was pinned deliberately, the un-reclaimable share written down as 12 of 64 GB, with a per-service pin budget on the host. Reclaim stopped touching the index; the cache still had 52 GB.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



mlockall in the service template, so nothing ever swaps. On one box it looks like a clean win: no swap IO, latency variance down. The working set was never measured, so the pinned region is whatever the process touched, held forever and idle; the host runs out of pinnable memory on a later deploy. Pinning removes the reclaim path too, so the OOM arrives with no pages to evict — the leak survives no better for the pin.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which pages were measured to stall on reclaim — and what share of RAM is now permanently un-reclaimable?

If yes → state the pinned share per host, give each service a pin budget, re-measure after each traffic change.
If no → you converted a reclaim problem into an allocation problem that surfaces on the next deploy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure major faults with and without the pin, then the sum of all pins against RAM.




#Linux #Kernel #Memory #Mlock #PageCache #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Write barriers and the ext4 commit interval
text:
Case study: Write barriers and the ext4 commit interval
commit=60 tuned for throughput, then a power cut erases 59 seconds of transactions — and the auditor finds it before monitoring does.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: commit=N sets how long ext4 may hold dirty data and metadata before forcing a journal commit, so anything acknowledged but not fsynced can vanish up to N seconds back. nobarrier drops the device cache flush and FUA the journal relies on, letting a device’s write cache reorder freely. Both buy throughput against a crash-consistency window measured in seconds of lost writes.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The window is acceptable only if someone can price the loss, which needs two facts: what the file holds, and whether the layer below honors flushes. The gap question: which loss window did someone accept, in seconds — and does the storage below actually honor flushes, verified how?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An index cache rebuilt in twelve minutes had commit=60 set deliberately: up to 60 seconds of writes lost on power failure, the rebuild documented, a name on the decision, barriers left on. Throughput rose enough to end a nightly backlog, and the window went into the runbook in seconds rather than a config line.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



nobarrier on a VM. It is genuinely faster — double digits on metadata-heavy work — and from inside the guest the flush looked honored, because the host cache acknowledged it. It stops being real when the host loses power or the array’s battery has been dead for a year: the fsync returned in microseconds and never reached a platter. The quieter variant is commit=60 on the accounting database, where the code writes and never fsyncs. Sixty seconds of acknowledged transactions, found in an audit.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which loss window did someone accept, in seconds — and does the storage below actually honor flushes, verified how?

If yes → write the window beside the data’s rebuild cost, keep barriers on, verify flush honoring on real storage.
If no → you accepted a window you cannot price. Keep barriers on, and cut the interval until the loss fits the rebuild cost.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure fsync latency with barriers on and off, then pull power.




#Linux #Kernel #FileSystems #Durability #Ext4 #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: NIC and stack offloads (GRO, GSO, TSO, LRO)
text:
Case study: NIC and stack offloads (GRO, GSO, TSO, LRO)
tcpdump on the sending host shows 64 KB TCP segments; the receiver’s shows 1460-byte ones. Both are correct, and neither holds the bug.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: GSO and TSO pass one large buffer down the stack to be segmented below it. GRO reassembles received segments before the stack sees them; LRO does so inside the driver, less faithfully. Throughput rises and CPU per byte falls, against granularity: pacing, forwarding and capture see fewer, larger units than the wire carries.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The team must know whether this endpoint moves bulk bytes or paces packets, and what its capture shows. Offloads are wrong for a forwarder whose two sides run at different shaped rates — a rate-domain boundary, where a coalesced frame must be re-segmented, and harmless for bulk transfers that never inspect a packet. The gap question: is this endpoint bulk or pacing-sensitive — and when you captured packets, what did you actually capture?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A replication link at 3 Gbit/s saturated a core in the softirq path; TSO and GRO cut CPU per byte by more than half at the same throughput, measured both ways.
