The routers between rate domains kept LRO off and per-packet shaping intact. Same kernel, opposite settings, each decided by what the hop does with a packet.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A latency complaint gets a tcpdump on the server; the capture shows 64 KB packets that never existed on the wire while the receiver sees 1460-byte segments, and the two never reconcile until someone remembers offloads. Hours burn on a phantom MTU problem. Batching across a rate boundary costs more: a forwarder emits bursts, the shaper paces what it sees, and the next hop’s buffers overrun in a pattern the sender’s metrics call clean.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this endpoint bulk or pacing-sensitive — and when you captured packets, what did you actually capture?

If yes → turn offloads on for bulk paths with CPU per byte measured, off for hops that pace or forward.
If no → you optimized a hop whose job is granularity and are measuring something other than the wire.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure CPU per byte both ways, and check where the capture point sits.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #TCP #Offloads #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: socket buffers (the in-flight window)
text:
Case study: socket buffers (the in-flight window)
A 200 ms round trip over a 1 Gbit/s path needs 25 MB in flight to fill the pipe — an untuned receive buffer starts at a few hundred kilobytes.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The buffers decide how much data may sit unacknowledged on one connection. tcp_rmem holds min, default, and max, and the autotuner grows toward that max; net.core.rmem_max caps only an explicit SO_RCVBUF, which fixes the size and, on Linux, disables autotuning for that socket. You buy throughput on long paths with memory per connection and queue depth for everyone.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The buffer you need is the product of two facts about your peers: their RTT and your bandwidth to them. That product spans three orders of magnitude between a datacenter neighbour and an intercontinental client, so one global value fits almost none of them. A large buffer also costs latency, because the queue that fills it delays the next packet too. Which connections are long fat, measured — and what does the per-connection buffer cost at the connection count you actually run?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An intercontinental replica pair measured 190 ms RTT at 800 Mbit/s: the buffer maximums were raised above the 19 MB product, and the transfer left the few-hundred-KB plateau while per-connection memory stayed inside the peak-count budget.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A fixed multi-megabyte SO_SNDBUF on every socket, because the long transfer got faster. Then ten thousand connections times four megabytes is 40 GB of unreclaimable kernel memory, and each queue holds four megabytes of segments, so one slow consumer adds tail latency to all. Its mirror is worse: a small SO_RCVBUF set “to be safe”, which disables the autotuner and caps the window, so the long-haul transfer that motivated the change crawls.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which connections are long fat, measured — and what does the per-connection buffer cost at the connection count you actually run?

If yes → the size follows from your peers, not a habit. Check the maximums against the peak product.
If no → the value is a guess about an unmeasured distribution. Leave autotuning on, and cap the maximum only for measured long-fat peer groups.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure RTT, throughput, and peak connection count.




#Linux #Kernel #TCP #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: TCP Fast Open (data in the SYN)
text:
Case study: TCP Fast Open (data in the SYN)
Up to two thirds of a short request’s latency is handshake — and the knob that removes it lets a duplicated SYN replay your request.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: TFO carries request bytes in the SYN, so the first response arrives a round trip earlier; first contact trades a server-issued cookie, cached for later SYNs, instead of data. net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen takes 1 for client, 2 for server, 3 for both. You buy one RTT per connection with a SYN payload that must be safe to execute twice, on a path that must carry the option intact.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
The saving is one RTT, so it matters only where setup is a large share of end-to-end time — short-lived connections, on a path you control end to end. It also asserts a property of your service: the SYN’s request may arrive twice, so the handler must be idempotent. What share of end-to-end latency is connection setup, measured — and is the SYN payload safe to execute twice?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Handshake share measured on short-lived connections in a controlled domain: a CDN edge, a datacenter link, a mesh with no middlebox. The arithmetic is concrete — a 40 ms RTT inside a 60 ms request is two thirds of the budget.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



TFO on across the open internet because the internal benchmark improved. A middlebox that strips the option silently returns you to a plain handshake: the gain evaporates. And a duplicated packet replays the request — bytes reach the application before the handshake completes, so the non-idempotent operation, the charge or the insert, runs twice, and no counter calls it out.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of end-to-end latency is connection setup, measured — and is the SYN payload safe to execute twice?

If yes → the RTT is worth buying. Check that no middlebox strips the option, and that the handler deduplicates.
If no → you pay replay risk for latency you cannot see. Leave it off, or only on paths you own.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure handshake share per request class, then audit which handlers mutate state.




#Linux #Kernel #TCP #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Networking

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: reverse path filtering (the spoofing check)
text:
Case study: reverse path filtering (the spoofing check)
One sysctl turns an asymmetric two-provider box into one that drops half its inbound packets — and only a counter names the culprit.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter tests an inbound packet’s source against the route table: 1 demands the reverse path leave by the interface it arrived on, 2 accepts any interface that could route back, 0 skips the test. You buy source-address validation with a rule your routing table must satisfy.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Strict mode claims this host’s routing is symmetric: every peer’s reply leaves by the door it came in. That claim is about your topology — provider links, policy routing, tunnels — not the kernel, and the kernel cannot verify it. Asymmetry is legitimate and common on multi-homed edges. Is this box’s routing symmetric by design — and which counters showed the drops before anyone looked?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Strict mode where the topology is single-homed and the claim is true: a plain application host, a single-uplink bastion whose drop counters stayed flat across a month, the spoofed-source probe rejected at the door. On asymmetric boxes, loose mode on the interface whose reverse path fails only — the symmetric interfaces kept strict — the reason written down, the drop counters named in the runbook.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Strict mode inherited from a hardening baseline onto a box with two providers. Packets from the second provider are dropped, so roughly half the traffic fails at random, and the hours go into cables and switch ports while nothing bills the sysctl. The hardening is defensible — a checklist asks for it. The recovery is the second trap: loose mode everywhere “to fix it”, which restores traffic and quietly relaxes the spoofing check the knob existed to impose, now with no owner.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this box’s routing symmetric by design — and which counters showed the drops before anyone looked?

If yes → strict filtering costs nothing real and closes a real surface. Keep it, and keep the claim in the platform docs.
If no → your policy collides with your topology. Set the mode per interface, and name the compensating filter for the check loose mode relaxes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Trace the reverse path per peer group, and read the drop counters under load.




#Linux #Kernel #Networking #Security #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: the adaptive tick (nohz_full, rcu_nocbs)
text:
Case study: the adaptive tick (nohz_full, rcu_nocbs)
A trading gate passes at one tick per second — while one core absorbs every displaced timer and RCU callback.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: nohz_full names cores whose running task sees no periodic timer tick; rcu_nocbs moves that core’s RCU callbacks elsewhere; isolcpus keeps the scheduler off them. All three are boot parameters, not sysctls, so the decision never appears in a config review. You buy undisturbed userspace with a housekeeping burden that must land somewhere.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
A tick-free core is worth its cost only where the tick injects jitter the workload can feel — a market-data loop, a control path, an audio buffer. The rest of the machine still needs a core for timers, interrupts, RCU callbacks, and the scheduler — one core now carrying the work of fifteen. So the change moves a known load onto an unknown capacity. What jitter did the tick actually inject, measured — and what runs on the core left holding the housekeeping?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A market-data loop on a 16-core box measured 40 µs worst-case wakeup with the tick and 6 µs without; nohz_full plus isolcpus held it there, and the housekeeping core sat at 30% at peak — the cost stated before the line shipped.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



nohz_full enabled for a vanity number, “one timer tick per second”, on a workload that never measured tick jitter. The mechanism is real, the metric impressive — on a dashboard tied to no latency budget. Meanwhile one core takes the migrated timers and RCU callbacks, plus whichever IRQs you steer there, and can saturate at peak: the spikes return from a new direction, and the team concludes tick suppression “does not work”.








TipThe faithfulness test



What jitter did the tick actually inject, measured — and what runs on the core left holding the housekeeping?

If yes → the trade is priced. Verify that core’s headroom at peak.
If no → you moved the work and kept the risk. No nohz_full until a latency histogram shows the tick.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Measure worst-case wakeup latency with and without ticks, then the housekeeping core’s load.




#Linux #Kernel #RealTime #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #LowLatency

title: Kernel Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: the instrument guard (perf_event_paranoid, kptr_restrict)
text:
Case study: the instrument guard (perf_event_paranoid, kptr_restrict)
The hardening ticket closes, the fleet is “secure”, and six weeks later a tail-latency spike is answered with folklore.
Setting a kernel knob? Ask “which measured fact does this tweak answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the config line is a superstition. If you can, the tweak is knowledge embodied — the system catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: kernel.perf_event_paranoid gates perf events by privilege: negative values allow kernel and CPU-wide sampling, 1 restricts CPU events, 2 blocks unprivileged kernel profiling, and level 3, where defined, closes unprivileged perf entirely. kptr_restrict hides kernel addresses. You buy a smaller exposure surface with your ability to measure production.


The kernel knowledge gap it signals
Every other knob’s justification is a measurement, and this knob decides who can take it. That is an organisational fact, not a kernel one: which team holds the profiling role, how it authenticates, who answers the pager at 03:00. The cost stays invisible until an incident. Who may measure production, by design — and when the tail spikes tonight, can anyone answer with data, or only with folklore?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A production fleet at paranoid=2, the profiling service on a privileged account: during a p99 spike the on-call pulled kernel stacks in four minutes and named the spinlock, not a regression reconstructed from log lines — restrictive defaults elsewhere, one named owner in the docs.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The restrictive default shipped fleet-wide “for security”, with no compensating path. Every clause is defensible alone: addresses leak, counters leak, least privilege is right. The consequence arrives later and elsewhere — nobody can profile production, so every tail-latency question is settled by seniority, and “reproduce it on staging” hides that staging never carried the real load. The measurement gap becomes a knowledge gap, then a policy.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who may measure production, by design — and when the tail spikes tonight, can anyone answer with data, or only with folklore?

If yes → the guard has a door with an owner. Check it works under incident pressure.
If no → you removed your only instrument and called it security. Open a scoped, logged path.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tweak wrong — you’ve found incomplete system knowledge. Ask who profiled production last month.




#Linux #Kernel #Observability #Security #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SRE

title: The Java Language
text:
A language claim meets the compiler: erasure, boxing, pattern matching. Each post compares the claim with the compiled reality.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: The Java Language
text:
Case study: Type erasure
A method declares List<String>, the bytecode declares List, and the String is gone before the first call — the only trace is a checkcast where you read the element.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A type argument is checked by javac, then discarded: List<String> compiles to List, T to its bound or to Object. A checkcast at each read is what remains. The trade: a type check that costs nothing at runtime, since no type is left, against interoperability with pre-generics code — raw types, wildcards, unchecked conversion at every old boundary.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
Whether any decision depends on T at runtime. Arrays of T, instanceof T, static state shared across type arguments, overloads that differ only in a type argument — each wants T to be a runtime fact, and javac declines.
The gap question: which decisions in this code depend on T at runtime, and does any of them survive compilation?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A repository over T whose methods accept and return T. Nothing inside branches on what T is, so nothing needed it at runtime: the type argument documents intent at each call site, and the compiler checks the wiring.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A (T) cast under @SuppressWarnings, no Class token at the entry: the cast checks nothing, so a wrong type argument throws ClassCastException at the first read — far from the mistake, and the trace names the reader, not the writer.
The overload pair differing only in its type argument does not compile, same erasure. The seductive repair collapses both into one List<?> or raw List method: it compiles, accepts both, and enforces the distinction nowhere.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which decisions in this code depend on T at runtime — listed — and does any of them survive compilation?

If yes → T is a runtime fact. Hold the Class token, check where values enter, and keep the unchecked cast to one line.
If no → T is a compile-time label. Keep it out of fields, arrays, and instanceof; the erasure costs you nothing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List every instanceof, array creation, and ClassCastException catch, and trace each to the type argument it leans on.




#Java #Generics #TypeErasure #StaticTyping #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The Java Language
text:
Case study: Boxing and unboxing
Two user ids compared with == return false, both 1000 — the same comparison passed last year, when every fixture used an id below 128.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: javac inserts Integer.valueOf wherever a primitive meets a reference type, intValue wherever a wrapper meets a primitive. valueOf must cache −128..127, so small values share identity; with default JVM settings, larger ones do not. The trade: wrappers let a primitive enter a generic collection or state absence as null, against a possible allocation per conversion past the cache and an == that compares references while reading like a value.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
Where the program stops doing arithmetic and starts handling an object. The conversion is silent both ways: in a loop condition, in a ternary whose branches differ in type. A developer who does not know which values are objects knows neither their allocation rate nor the meaning of their ==.
The gap question: where does boxing happen in this loop, and does any == compare boxed values?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Primitives for the computation, wrappers only where the domain hands you objects. A total as a long, a counter as an int; the box appears once, where the value enters a Map<Long, Order>. The collection needs objects; the arithmetic does not.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Long sum = 0L, then sum += values.get(i) in a hot loop: each iteration unboxes, adds, and boxes a fresh Long past the cache — one allocation per element, invisible in the source.
The comparison trap is quieter. == on two separately boxed Integers is true only while the cache covers the value, so the suite proves it works and the first real order number disproves it. equals was right on every value; == only on what the fixtures used.








TipThe faithfulness test



Where does boxing happen in this loop, measured by allocation — and does any == compare boxed values?

If yes → the box is in the loop, or the comparison is on identity. Hoist the accumulator to a primitive, box once at the exit, change == to equals.
If no → boxing sits where objects genuinely begin. The cost is the boxing’s cost, not the loop’s.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the wrapper wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Measure allocations per iteration, then list every == on wrappers.




#Java #Boxing #Performance #JVM #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The Java Language
section: Case study: Pattern matching for switch over a sealed hierarchy
text:
Case study: Pattern matching for switch over a sealed hierarchy
A fifth payment state ships; eleven switches keep compiling. Each has a default that throws “unreachable”.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A sealed interface states its permitted implementations are a closed set. A pattern switch that names every permitted type is proved exhaustive by javac, no default needed — the switch final since 21, the seal since 17. The trade: completeness checked wherever the switch is recompiled, against a default that ends the check.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
Whether the domain closes the set, and whether every consumer sits inside the proof. Exhaustiveness is a property of switch and seal read together at one compile, not of the switch alone. Know which switches are load-bearing, and whether the default is a case or an exemption.
The gap question: does every switch over this hierarchy prove completeness — or does a default clause end the proof?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A payment state machine as a sealed interface, one record per state, switches that name every case and carry no default. Adding a state is a compile error in every consumer, named in one build: eleven files, or the one that forgot.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A default that throws IllegalStateException(“unreachable”) passes review and converts a compile-time promise into a runtime one: the compiler calls the switch total, stops reporting the missing variant, and the new state reaches a branch nobody wrote. A consumer compiled against the old seal has no arm for the new variant and throws MatchException on it — correct, and late.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does every switch over this hierarchy prove completeness — or does a default clause end the proof?

If yes → the compiler owns the list of cases. Add the variant, let the build name every file, and keep the seal closed.
If no → the default is where new variants go to be forgotten. Delete it from the exhaustive switches, or narrow the switch to the type it handles.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the switch wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List every switch on the hierarchy, mark which carry a default, and check which files built on the seal.




#Java #PatternMatching #SealedTypes #Exhaustiveness #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The Java Language
section: Case study: var and type inference
text:
Case study: var and type inference
One var on a factory result, and nothing on that line says what the variable holds.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: var changes nothing at runtime. javac infers the initializer’s static type, writes it into the class file as an ordinary local-variable entry, and rejects the sites where no standalone type exists: null, a lambda, a method reference, a bare array initializer. What moved is the declaration — the type claim now lives in the expression on the right, and only there.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know the initializer’s static type, not its runtime type, and where the two diverge. javac holds that fact; the reader no longer does. A file full of var resolves its types one hover away — fine for whoever has the IDE open, invisible in a diff, a review, or a stack trace.
The gap question: for each var, can the reader reconstruct the type from that line alone?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



var orders = new ArrayList<Order>(); — the constructor names the class, so var keeps it and drops the interface. The same holds for var names = new HashSet<String>(ids); and any initializer whose right-hand side is a constructor call, a cast, or a literal. The reader reads the type where it is written.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



var report = ReportBuilder.of(tenant).withRange(range).build(); The line states a name and a pipeline. The type is whatever build() returns — a decision inside another file that can change without touching this line. List.of() is the sharper trap: var gives E no target to infer from, so it falls back to Object — List<Object> where the team assumed List<Order>. It compiles; the type claim is quietly weakened.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each var: can the reader reconstruct the type from that line alone — or must they open another file?

If yes → the inference is local knowledge. Check that the inferred type is the interface you meant, not Object.
If no → the type claim left the code the reader has. Write the type on the left, or make the factory’s return visible on the line.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found var wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the declarations a reviewer could not name.




#Java #TypeInference #Readability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #CodeReview

title: The Java Language
text:
Case study: String concatenation
The report takes 9 seconds to build, and the only fault is a + inside a loop.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: a + b reads like arithmetic and compiles to a call, constants aside: since JDK 9 javac emits invokedynamic against StringConcatFactory, binding a makeConcatWithConstants handle that builds the result in one allocation. One expression is efficient and exact. Inside a loop, each s += row concatenates onto the whole prefix, so N iterations copy 1 + 2 + … + N row-lengths — quadratic work the source never announces. The JIT does not remove it: each result is live into the next iteration, and each iteration allocates a new String.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know the iteration count’s growth, not just the syntax. Concatenation cost is invisible at one call site and cumulative at N. The gap is a claim about the data: how many iterations, and how long the accumulated string gets. Nobody wrote that down; the code pays.
The gap question: is any concatenation inside a loop whose iteration count grows with the data?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A log line, an exception message, a cache key of three fields, a URL built once per request. One concatenation, one allocation, and javac’s invokedynamic path is as good as the StringBuilder you would write by hand. The string is built here, once, from parts known here.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



+= in a loop assembling a report over rows from a table. The line reads like an append, and every append copies everything already appended. Ten thousand rows of eighty characters copy four billion characters. The variant that hides best is concatenation inside a toString() called from a loop: the loop looks innocent, the copying lives in another class.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is any concatenation inside a loop whose iteration count grows with data — measured?

If yes → count the characters copied: iterations × average accumulated length. Use a sized StringBuilder or StringJoiner, passed in rather than returned from inside the loop.
If no → one expression, one allocation. Leave it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found + wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Find the loops, then the rows each iterates.




#Java #Performance #StringHandling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #JVM

title: The Java Language
section: Case study: The enhanced for loop
text:
Case study: The enhanced for loop
A loop removes an order from an ArrayList it walks, and the next next() throws.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: for (Order o : orders) over a collection compiles to an Iterator: javac calls hasNext() and next() for you, so the loop has no index and no direct handle on the list. The ArrayList iterator compares a modification counter on next() and throws ConcurrentModificationException when the structure changed under it. The trade: the loop claims “walk every element” only while the structure holds still.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know three facts: whether the collection is structurally modified inside the loop, whether that change is a removal or an addition, and whether this walk is the only reader. Removal is a claim about structure — the list shifts and the iterator cannot see it. Fail-fast is best effort, not a guarantee, and not thread safety.
The gap question: which loops mutate the collection they walk?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



iterator.remove() after next() — the removal goes through the structure that owns the position, so the iterator stays consistent. Or collect the doomed elements and call removeAll after the loop: the walk stays pure, the mutation happens once.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



orders.remove(o) inside the for (Order o : orders) loop. Single-threaded, no other thread — and it throws on the next advance, because the claim is structural, not concurrent. The silent version is worse: on a CopyOnWriteArrayList the iterator holds a snapshot, so the removal never appears and the loop processes an already-deleted element. No exception, and the report is wrong by one row.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which loops mutate the collection they walk — listed — and does each one use the mutation path the structure defines?

If yes → the mutation goes through Iterator.remove() or after the loop. Check that each remove() follows a next() and that no second remove() follows it.
If no → the loop mutates through a path the iterator does not track. Move the mutation out, or use an indexed loop whose index you correct on removal.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the for-each wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the loops, then the collections each writes to.




#Java #Collections #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Debugging

title: The Java Language
section: Case study: Default methods on interfaces
text:
Case study: Default methods on interfaces
A default method ships in a minor release, and a class nobody edited returns the wrong answer.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A default method carries its body inside the interface. Implementors compile unchanged: they do not override it, and invokeinterface falls through when the class declares none. Binary compatibility usually holds: old class files inherit behavior they never compiled. The trade: evolution without breaking implementors, against behavior arriving on types that never opted in.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know whether a behavior is universal across every implementor the interface will ever have, and whether the body needs state the interface cannot hold. A default sound across all implementors relies only on the interface’s contract; otherwise declare it abstract.
The gap question: for each default method, do all implementors honestly satisfy its claim?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Comparator.thenComparing, reversed, Iterator.remove throwing UnsupportedOperationException, List.sort. Each body follows from the interface’s contract alone, so any correct implementation behaves as the default expects and the default adds no assumption. thenComparing says “every comparator chains this way”, true by the meaning of comparator.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A default that assumes implementor state. default String describe() { return name() + " " + version(); } where half the implementors return null from name(), so the default prints “null 2.1” for years. Or default boolean isEmpty() { return size() == 0; } where some implementations compute size() by traversal: an O(1) check becomes a full scan. Every implementor inherits a claim it never read.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each default method: do all implementors — present and future — honestly satisfy its claim?

If yes → the body is derivable from the interface’s contract. Keep it free of assumptions about state.
If no → the behavior belongs to some implementations only. Make it abstract — it breaks implementors — or move it to an interface the willing implementors extend.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the default wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the implementors, then the methods the default calls.




#Java #Interfaces #APIDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Evolution

title: The Java Language
text:
Case study: Annotation retention
A validator that checks every request, a green build, and validation that never ran once.
Writing a Java construct? Ask “what does javac and the runtime actually do with this claim — what survives compilation, what is erased, what is checked and when?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: @Retention decides which artifact holds the annotation. SOURCE is read by the compiler and processors, then discarded. CLASS is the default: written into the class file, invisible to the reflection API. RUNTIME is written into the class file and materialized by reflection. The trade is one enum constant: a framework that reflects sees the annotation only if you said RUNTIME, and javac warns nothing if you did not.


The Java knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know two things: which reader sees this annotation, and when — compile time through a processor, or runtime through reflection. Retention is that claim. Omitted, it defaults to CLASS — invisible to the reflection API your validator uses.
The gap question: for each annotation, which retention was chosen deliberately, and which framework is supposed to see it?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) on annotations a framework reflects over: a validation constraint, a JSON field mapping. The reader exists at runtime; the declaration says so. Compile-time annotations — @Override, @SuppressWarnings — carry SOURCE and vanish, correctly: no runtime reader needs them.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A custom @PositiveAmount without @Retention. It compiles, it reads well in review, and it defaults to CLASS. The validator loops over field.getAnnotations(), finds nothing, and passes every field — silently, on every request, for months. The failure looks like success: no exception, no log line, a check iterating zero times.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each annotation: which retention was chosen — deliberately — and which framework is supposed to see it?

If yes → the retention names its reader. Assert it: reflect over one annotated element; fail if the annotation is absent.
If no → the annotation is a comment the compiler keeps. Add @Retention, or delete it and the dead validator with it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the annotation wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Find the code that reads it, then when that code runs.




#Java #Annotations #Reflection #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Validation

title: Haskell
text:
Laziness is an evaluation-order claim; a type class is a fact about the domain of types. Each post reads the claim and what GHC makes of it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Laziness (the default evaluation claim)
text:
Case study: Laziness (the default evaluation claim)
A million-element fold returns the right number and holds 30 MB of unevaluated additions — one apostrophe (foldl') would have freed them.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: By default a binding is not a value but a recipe: GHC emits a thunk and runs it only when something demands the result, and only to weak head normal form (one constructor deep). That buys infinite structures and short-circuiting, and costs a heap profile set by demand sites the type never names.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
foldl and foldl' share one type: (b -> a -> b) -> b -> [a] -> b. Nothing in that signature separates the version that forces each step from the version that stacks a million thunks: strictness is not carried in a Haskell type. It sits in a bang pattern, a $!, StrictData, or whatever GHC’s strictness analyser inferred. The developer must know, accumulator by accumulator, which chains are forced on purpose and which by luck.
The gap question: which accumulators are forced on purpose, and which by the optimiser?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Demand is incremental: take 10 . filter p over an infinite enumeration, zipWith of two generated sequences, the first hit from find. The producer never runs ahead of the consumer, and GHC’s foldr/build fusion can rewrite the pipeline into one loop with no intermediate lists.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



foldl (+) 0 over a million-element list. Each step allocates ((0+1)+2)+3 …; nothing forces the accumulator until the last demand, so the sum arrives as a million thunks and tens of megabytes for one number. foldl' was one apostrophe away. -Wall stays silent, and -O2 can rescue this exact shape — so the leak shows in the test run, not the benchmark. It type-checks, terminates, and is correct: the cost is absent from every artifact except the heap.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which accumulators in this program are forced — measured in a GC profile — or is every fold a thunk chain waiting to happen?

If yes → the demand sites are the ones you can name. Keep the profile in CI so a refactor cannot move them silently.
If no → the fold is a thunk chain priced by the optimiser. Use foldl', or force with $!.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found laziness wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Read peak live heap (maximum residency) under +RTS -s.




#Haskell #Laziness #SpaceLeaks #GHC #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Purity and the IO boundary
text:
Case study: Purity and the IO boundary
The signature says the function cannot print. Its return value came from a cache populated at a moment nobody chose.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: An IO in the type marks a computation that may touch the world; an arrow without it promises referential transparency, so GHC may reorder the call, share one result, or delete it. The trade is the plumbing: every effect shows at every call site, and every caller carries IO up to main.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
The type tracks effects, not totality. f :: Int -> Int may still loop forever or crash on error — divergence and pure-code exceptions are not in the signature. The arrow therefore promises interchangeable calls, not a delivered result. The developer must know which claim the module makes, and where its effects may sit.
The gap question: which module may decide when an effect happens?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



The domain draws the boundary where the signature does. Parsing, validation, and the state transition are pure functions from data to data; main reads the file, calls them, writes the answer. The core is property-testable without mocks, safe on many threads — and GHC may inline and merge duplicate expressions there precisely because nothing can be observed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



{-# NOINLINE cache #-} around unsafePerformIO (newIORef Map.empty), memoising a lookup the signature calls pure. The effect fires once per thunk, on whichever demand arrives first, and a value read from the environment at first use is that environment forever. The purity claim survives in the type and dies in the runtime. unsafePerformIO asserts the effect is order-independent — the same answer whenever it runs — and nothing checks the assertion — not the type checker, not the tests that keep passing.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which functions in this system can affect the world — exactly those with IO in the type, or are there smugglers?

If yes → the boundary belongs to the type. Check that main reads in one screen, and that error counts as an effect.
If no → the signature is a claim the runtime does not honour. Move the effect into IO, or into ST when it is local mutation (pure once runST closes the scope).
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found purity wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Grep unsafePerformIO and every error.




#Haskell #Purity #IO #UnsafePerformIO #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #FunctionalProgramming

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Type classes (instances as global facts)
text:
Case study: Type classes (instances as global facts)
The same nub (removes repeats by ==) returns a different list in two builds; no source line changed, only a dependency.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A type class is a record of functions GHC passes implicitly: Eq a becomes a dictionary argument, resolved once per type, at compile time. That buys composition across packages — every consumer of Eq User gets one equality — and costs the freedom to declare instances anywhere.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
The compiler checks that an instance exists and its methods type-check. It does not check that == is an equivalence or compare a total order; Data.Map and sort assume those laws and go quietly wrong. The developer must know who owns each instance, and which law it satisfies.
The gap question: for this type, is there one defensible meaning of equality?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Instances sit beside the type or the class. Coherence holds by construction: one candidate exists, every package sees it, and a dependency cannot change a result. A second legitimate meaning gets a newtype — newtype ByName = ByName User — so the choice is written at the call site, not inferred from imports. -Worphans in CI, failing the build, keeps it that way.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Two orphan instances for one pair: Eq User by id in the service package, Eq User by every field in reporting. Each package compiles; its tests pass. A program whose closure reaches only one compiles and uses it; the second arrives as a duplicate-instance error when a dependency adds it. Same expression, different result, chosen by a build file. Orphans seduce because they are local: the instance sits where you needed it, and the bill goes to every program that later combines yours with another.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each instance: who owns it — and could two packages disagree about the same instance in one program?

If yes → ownership is structural and the meaning cannot move. Check the laws as tests; the compiler checked signatures only.
If no → a global fact has a local owner. Move it beside the type or the class, or wrap the type in a newtype.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found type classes wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your program. Run -Worphans on the tree.




#Haskell #TypeClasses #Coherence #OrphanInstances #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #FunctionalProgramming

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Strictness annotations and forcing
text:
Case study: Strictness annotations and forcing
A record with eight lazy fields allocates eight thunks, and the bill lands in whichever function reads them first — rarely the one that built them.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A field without ! holds a thunk: the expression stays unevaluated until something demands it. A ! forces it to weak head normal form (one constructor deep) when the record is constructed, and -XStrictData makes that the module default. The trade is placement and amount: a lazy field can skip work nobody needs and can also pile up deferred computation; a strict field pays at every construction, including those whose record nobody reads.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
Whether a field is always consumed is a fact about your program, not the record type. You must know which parts of the value a consumer touches, and when. A field left lazy because “it might be expensive” is a guess about a consumer you have not listed; a bang added because “laziness is slow” is the same guess in reverse.
The gap question: which fields are forced at construction, and who forces the rest?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Strict fields on records whose components are always consumed: a config read in full at startup, a metrics record whose every counter is summed. No thunk is built that nobody forces, and no field is forced that costs more than it saves.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The record crossing an API boundary with every field lazy. The library builds it cheaply, the boundary benchmarks beautifully, and the caller pays the forcing — one thunk at a time, inside whatever loop touches the fields, with the cost attributed to the caller. Deferred work is not free work. It is work with an unstated owner.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each record: is the forcing site named — or is it somebody else’s problem?

If yes → the strictness is a contract the writer states and the reader can check. Verify the forcing is not repeated per access, and that no thunk retains a large structure.
If no → you have a thunk with no owner. Name each field’s consumer, then force at the last point that still has the information.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Trace each field to its reader, or profile for retention.




#Haskell #Laziness #Strictness #GHC #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Haskell
section: Case study: SPECIALIZE and cross-module inlining
text:
Case study: SPECIALIZE and cross-module inlining
The pragma sits at the top of the module, the dictionary (class-method record) calls sit in the inner loop, and only the dumped core (GHC’s intermediate form) tells you which one shipped.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In an optimised build, {-# SPECIALIZE f :: Int -> Int #-} asks GHC to build a monomorphic copy (one fixed at Int) and rewrite matching calls to it. The copy is a rewrite rule (a compile-time substitution), and a rule fires only where the compiler can see the call’s types. Across a module boundary, the rule needs the function’s unfolding (its body, kept in the interface file), which INLINABLE exposes. Without it, the callee compiles, the caller compiles, and no specialization exists.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
You must know which call sites are hot, at which types, and in which module. That is a fact about execution, not syntax. A pragma says “specialize this”; it never says “this is called a million times at Int from a module that cannot see me.” The cost of polymorphism is the dictionary: a record of methods, called through at every un-specialised site.
The gap question: which call sites did you measure, and at which types?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



The hot polymorphic function marked INLINABLE, with SPECIALIZE for exactly the two types the profile shows, checked in the generated core: the specialized name present, the dictionary arguments gone, the loop monomorphic. The cost is paid where it was measured.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The numeric inner loop behind a module boundary. The function was compiled without INLINABLE, so no unfolding left the module; every iteration takes a Num dictionary and calls + through it. Nothing in the source mentions a dictionary. The benchmark is read as “GHC is slow at abstraction”, when the abstraction was never resolved. The mirror trap: INLINABLE sprayed everywhere, inflating code size and compile time to specialize functions called twice.








TipThe faithfulness test



Was the specialization verified in the generated core — or assumed from the pragma?

If yes → the specialization is a fact here. Re-check after a refactor changes its types.
If no → you have a wish, not a specialization. Dump the core, grep for the specialized name and dictionary parameters.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Profile first, then read the core of the hot path.




#Haskell #GHC #Specialization #Inlining #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Making illegal states unrepresentable
text:
Case study: Making illegal states unrepresentable
The smart constructor validates on the way in, and the module exports Email(..) — so the next module writes the illegal value by hand.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Three mechanisms: a newtype that gives a validation its own type, a sum type (one constructor per case) that gives the impossible state no constructor, a phantom parameter that pins the phase. Each moves an invariant from a comment into the type checker. The trade: an escape hatch — an exported raw constructor, an unsafeCoerce — puts the invariant back into the programmer’s head, silently, with nothing to catch a breach.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
You must know the invariant, who may break it, and which module boundary enforces it. “Non-empty” is a claim about the values the program can produce, not a property of the list type. If the only rule is a mkNonEmpty that calls error on [], the invariant is a crash, not a type.
The gap question: at which boundary can the illegal value still be constructed — and is that boundary named?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Data.List.NonEmpty where the domain guarantees at least one element, so head is total. A sum type whose constructors are exactly the states the protocol has. A phantom parameter so open and closed connections do not type-check interchangeably.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The smart constructor whose raw constructor is exported — Email(..) beside mkEmail — “for tests”. Or unsafeMkEmail in the same module. The invariant is documented, the check runs on some paths, and one module constructs the illegal value with a clean type. The types still read as proof, and reviewers trust a type that no longer means what it says.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each invariant: does the type make it unrepresentable — or is the check sitting next to a raw constructor?

If yes → the compiler is the enforcement, and a bypass is a compile error. Read the export list; the invariant lives there.
If no → the check is a convention. Close the constructor, or admit the invariant is unchecked and test it at every producer.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the invariants, then the constructors that can build each type.




#Haskell #TypeDrivenDesign #Newtypes #PhantomTypes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Correctness

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Partial functions (head, tail, !!, fromJust)
text:
Case study: Partial functions (head, tail, !!, fromJust)
head on the list that is empty “never” — until a refactor lets it be empty, at 3 a.m., in production.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: head :: [a] -> a is total in its type and partial in its value: the signature promises an a for every list, and the empty list has none. !! promises an element for every index, fromJust promises a Just. -Wall reports -Wincomplete-patterns for a case expression you wrote, and says nothing about a head you called: the partiality is in the library. The trade is convenience against a claim that appears in no type.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
“This list is non-empty” and “this key exists” are facts about the program’s states. They live in the programmer’s head, and the signature does not repeat them. Every call to head is an unverified assertion, and the compiler cannot count the assertions it was never told about.
The gap question: which functions here can fail at runtime without their type saying so?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Total functions whose signatures state every outcome: an exhaustive match over a sum type, NonEmpty a where the domain guarantees an element, Maybe where absence is a real outcome. The caller is forced to handle each case, and the empty list is impossible or handled.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A filter, a takeWhile, or a new caller produces [] where the author assumed otherwise. Then fromJust on the Maybe the author did not want to match: the absence was known, felt as noise, and deleted with a function that throws. Each one is a Maybe-shaped fact turned back into an exception, and the type stops reporting it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does every function here state its failure in its type — or is a partiality hiding behind a total-looking signature?

If yes → the signature is the contract. Check that -Wincomplete-patterns is on and clean.
If no → each partial call is an assertion with no witness. Replace head and tail with a match or NonEmpty, fromJust with a case.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List every head, tail, !!, fromJust, and ask who guaranteed the precondition.




#Haskell #Totality #PartialFunctions #GHCWarnings #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Reliability

title: Haskell
section: Case study: Numeric defaulting and fromIntegral
text:
Case study: Numeric defaulting and fromIntegral
fromIntegral narrows an Int64 to an Int32 with no line that says so, and the defaulting rule quietly picks Double for money.
Writing a Haskell definition? Ask “which fact does the type system carry — purity, totality, strictness — and what does GHC actually do with it?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the types enforce a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: An ambiguous Num constraint is resolved by a defaulting rule you never wrote: Integer if it satisfies every constraint, else Double. let n = 1000000 is Integer; 1/2 is Double; a module-level default (Int, Double) changes the first, not the second. fromIntegral :: (Integral a, Num b) => a -> b wraps or truncates when the target is narrower. The trade: one conversion site against a type that no longer says what was converted.


The Haskell knowledge gap it signals
You must know the width of every numeric value at every boundary, and which conversions run there. The compiler knows the types it inferred; it does not know the identifier is 18 digits, or that money needs exactness. A defaulted type is a decision made by a rule, attributed to no one.
The gap question: which numeric type did the compiler choose here, and did you choose it?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Numeric types pinned by signatures where the width matters: Int64 for identifiers, Natural for counts, a decimal type for money, Word32 for a hash. Explicit fromIntegral at the boundary, with a range check beside it, so the narrowing is a site a reader can find and a test can hit.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The Int64 identifier narrowed by fromIntegral into an Int32 at the serialization boundary: no line mentions narrowing, values past the bound go negative or wrap, and the failure surfaces as a wrong lookup rather than an exception. Defaulting that silently chose Double for a money field, because the literal 0.1 needed a Fractional type and nobody wrote one.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each numeric boundary: which conversion runs — written down — and could it truncate or lose precision?

If yes → the conversion is a decision with a visible site. Check the range assumption against real data, not test data.
If no → the compiler chose. Pin the type in a signature and make the narrowing explicit.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Turn on -Wtype-defaults and annotate every boundary it reports.




#Haskell #NumericTypes #Defaulting #GHC #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Correctness

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
The GoF catalogue read as a completeness check: each pattern names a grouping the domain must already have decided — the product family, the algorithm family, the event, the part-whole recursion.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Abstract Factory Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The set of concrete types that must vary together (the “product family”) is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when you’re in context X, you use implementations A₁, B₁, C₁; in context Y, you use A₂, B₂, C₂” — and that these groupings are cohesive units in the domain (e.g., a regulatory regime, a hardware platform, a deployment tier) — then an Abstract Factory is just embodying that knowledge. The factory interface is the domain’s own abstraction; the concrete factories are its real partitions.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates product-family coherence but the language offers no native construct to express “these N types co-vary.” The Abstract Factory is a technical artifact that closes the gap — it prevents each client from individually selecting concrete types, which would scatter the family-binding knowledge across the system and create accidental coupling (every client must know which concrete A goes with which concrete B).








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of product families. The concrete types vary independently. Forcing them into an Abstract Factory imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize — it bundles change-drivers that are actually independent, creating a single point of modification for unrelated changes. That’s the cohesion-reducing move.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the concrete-type groupings as a thing?

If yes → applicable. The Abstract Factory is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing knowledge the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #EIP #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #Domain #Knowledge #DesignPrinciples #Java #C# #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Strategy Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The existence of multiple algorithms for the same operation is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this operation admits variants A, B, C, and there is a domain rule that selects among them,” then Strategy is just embodying that knowledge. The strategy interface is the domain’s own abstraction (the what); the concrete strategies are its real alternatives (the how).






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates algorithmic substitutability — it recognizes that the operation meaningfully differs across contexts, and a domain rule dictates which variant applies. The Strategy pattern closes the gap: it prevents each caller from embedding variant-selection logic inline, which would scatter the selection rule across the system and create accidental coupling (every caller must re-encode which variant to use under which conditions). The pattern collects each variant behind a shared interface; the selection rule lives wherever the strategy reference is assigned.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of multiple algorithms for this operation. The “variants” are a decomposition artifact, not a domain partition — the developer split one algorithm into pieces for readability or reuse and wrapped them in a strategy interface as organizational glue. This imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize: it bundles what the domain treats as one thing into an interface-plus-implementations structure, adding ceremony that signals a richness of variation that isn’t there. If the variants also pull in different data dependencies, Strategy scatters data-acquisition logic across implementations that must each independently discover their inputs.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize multiple algorithms for this operation as a real thing?

If yes → applicable. Strategy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing variation the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.





References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Observer Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that “a change in A constitutes a domain event that B, C, and D must know about” is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that certain state transitions are meaningful events to other entities — that the event is a first-class domain concept — then Observer is just embodying that knowledge. The subject interface is the domain’s own event source; the observer interface is the domain’s own event consumer.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain state changes constitute events with multiple consumers, and the set of consumers is open-ended. Observer closes the gap — it prevents the event source from encoding the full list of consumers and their reaction logic inline, which would bundle every downstream concern into a single class and couple the event source to each consumer’s change-drivers.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “event” is not a domain event — nothing in the domain recognizes the state transition as meaningful in itself. B must recompute when A changes not because the domain treats A’s transition as an event, but because the developer chose to cache or denormalize. Observer used for technical consistency (UI model-view synchronization, the GoF’s canonical example) is valid engineering. The cohesion risk is when notification cascades for technical reasons (cache invalidation, denormalization-update chains) are presented as domain event propagation, inventing event semantics the domain model never had.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this state transition as an event even if the system weren’t software?

If yes → applicable. Observer is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code manufacturing events the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #CodingPatterns #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Adapter Pattern

GoF Intent: “Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn’t otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that two entities must talk to each other but speak incompatible languages is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “system A understands protocol α, system B understands protocol β, and there is a domain rule requiring A and B to interoperate,” then Adapter is just embodying that knowledge. The adapter is the domain’s own translation rule; the adapted interface is the domain’s own target vocabulary.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates interoperability across a boundary the domain itself recognizes — a third-party service, a legacy subsystem, an external standard, a different bounded context. The adapter closes the gap: it isolates the translation logic in one place rather than forcing every caller of B to speak B’s protocol directly. Without it, each caller would embed translation logic inline, coupling unrelated code to B’s vocabulary and scattering the adaptation rule across the system.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “incompatibility” is not a domain boundary — it’s a pair of self-owned interfaces that encode the same concepts differently. Wrapping one in an adapter to match the other adds a permanent translation layer between abstractions that should be unified. Sometimes this is transitional — two teams built different interfaces that need reconciliation. But when the adapter becomes permanent without a unification plan, it institutionalizes an interface mismatch the domain never imposed. The distinguishing test is whether both sides have independent change-driver authorities: an adapter between domain port and infrastructure adapter (Hexagonal/Ports-and-Adapters) embodies a domain-imposed boundary, not duplication disguised as adaptation.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the two sides of the adapter as genuinely separate things that must interoperate?

If yes → applicable. The adapter is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s indirection the domain didn’t impose — which may still be legitimate if the sides have distinct authorities (e.g., domain port vs. infrastructure), but warrants unification if the same team owns both.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #AdapterPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Builder Pattern

GoF Intent: “Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so that the same construction process can create different representations.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that constructing an object is a multi-step process whose steps are domain-significant — not just parameter-passing — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “creating an X requires collecting parts A, B, C from different sources, in an order that matters, with validation between steps,” then Builder is just embodying that knowledge. The builder is the domain’s own construction protocol; each step is a domain operation.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that construction is a process, not a one-shot operation. The object cannot be created atomically because its parts come from different domain sources or require intermediate domain validation — and a partially-built object is a meaningful domain state (a draft, an incomplete form, a staged assembly). Builder closes the gap: it isolates the construction logic so the object doesn’t expose setters allowing mutation after construction, and so callers don’t each re-encode the construction sequence.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of incremental construction. All parts are available at once, and a partially-built object has no domain meaning. Builder is often reached for here to emulate named parameters — e.g., Pizza.builder().size(12).crust("thin").sauce("marinara") reads better than positional new Pizza(12, "thin", "marinara"…). But this ergonomics problem exposes a deeper gap: the constructor arguments are weakly typed. crust isn’t a String, it’s a Crust. Once the domain is properly typed — Pizza(Size, Crust, Sauce, Set<Topping>) — the constructor is self-documenting and Builder adds nothing. Builder here isn’t fixing a language limitation, it’s masking underspecified types.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat “in the process of being built” as a real state?

If yes → applicable. Builder is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. Check first whether weak typing or some other issue is the real gap. When the domain is properly typed and construction is still painful, the language genuinely lacks expressive constructors — but this is rare and worth distinguishing from a type-design gap.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #BuilderPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Command Pattern

GoF Intent: “Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.” [1, p. 233]

The pattern decouples invoker from receiver — the invoker must NOT know which concrete receiver handles the request. This is structural: the invoker dispatches to a Command interface and stays receiver-agnostic. (Queuing, logging, and undo follow from the encapsulation.)

The knowledge gap it signals
Command needs the invoker to be receiver-agnostic. The question is not “would the domain break if the invoker knew?” — the pattern exists because the invoker must NOT know. The gap: does your architecture need receiver-agnostic dispatch?






ImportantWhen it’s needed



The invoker must dispatch to different receivers without knowing which at compile time: a menu dispatches to dialogs, a scheduler to job handlers, a transaction manager to rollback actions, an event bus to subscribers. The invoker cannot name the receiver — requests are queued, parameterized, or submitted by unknown clients. Command closes the gap: the interface abstracts over receivers the invoker was never meant to know.








WarningWhen it’s not needed



The invoker always calls the same concrete receiver. Wrapping every service-method invocation in a Command interface because “we might need undo later” adds indirection where the invoker already knows its target. The interface adds maintenance and dispatch overhead to a call that should be direct. Command here guesses at flexibility no requirement demands.








TipThe faithfulness test — a 3-step decision procedure




Does the invoker need to dispatch without knowing the concrete receiver?
Is there more than one receiver, or will the receiver be determined at runtime?
Decide. If yes → applicable (Command provides the receiver-agnostic dispatch your architecture needs). If no → inapplicable (call directly). If you can’t answer → unclear — you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.



CQS/CQRS “Command” is a different concept — a message that mutates state (contrast: Query) — and is not covered here.

#GoF #CommandPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: GoF Design Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composite Pattern

GoF Intent: “Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.” [1]

The GoF Composite pattern composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. It lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through a shared Component interface.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The domain recognizes a part-whole hierarchy where the whole and its parts answer the same questions. A department and its sub-departments both have budgets. A file and a directory both have sizes. When you find yourself reaching for Composite, the gap is: does the domain actually treat wholes and parts uniformly, or are you imposing a tree structure on something the domain views as flat or differently?






ImportantWhen the pattern follows domain knowledge



The domain has genuine part-whole recursion where the same operations apply at every level. Making “a department contains sub-departments, and both compute a budget” explicit in the domain model is the work. Composite’s uniform interface then prevents callers from branching on “is this a single thing or a group?” before every operation — the hierarchy delegates recursively, and callers operate on the abstract type.








WarningWhen the pattern overreaches



The domain has no part-whole recursion. The hierarchy is a tree-shaped data structure for navigation convenience, not a domain fact. UI component trees are the GoF’s canonical Composite example and are valid — they address the domain of UI toolkit design, where the part-whole relationship IS the problem space. A file-system directory tree is domain recursion; an internal cache organized as a tree for lookup efficiency is not.
