The messages the design will check and the probability the obligation allows are two numbers, and only one of them is measured. The width is fixed by the format. The rate is per message, so it scales with traffic, and a wider checksum costs bytes on every one.






ImportantWhen the width bounds the shape



The message count over the system’s life makes the expected false negative exceed the obligation. Then use a wider checksum, or a cryptographic hash — the width is a format choice, so changing it later changes every message.








WarningWhen the width does not force it



The count is far below the width’s reach, so a false negative is not expected within the system’s life. Or the transport already detects corruption, and the checksum guards something else.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the message count times two to the minus the checksum width stay inside the obligation?

If yes → the width covers the count. Record the count the estimate assumes.
If no → a false negative is expected. Widen the checksum.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Read the checksum width, then count the messages per year.




#Reliability #Encoding #DistributedSystems #Correctness #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Architecture

title: DSA
text:
Algorithms and data structures: each choice encodes facts about the workload — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands.

Algorithms — 22 posts. Each algorithm is a claim about its workload; the gap question asks whether the facts are known or hoped.
Data Structures — 24 posts. Each structure keeps a contract: the order it holds, the cost it promises, the operations it refuses.

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Almost every design pattern/principle can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge. For DDD’s tactical patterns, the justification is explicitly domain-driven — which makes the gap check sharper: is the pattern the knowledge itself, or ceremony wearing its clothes?
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Value Object

Evans: “An object that describes some characteristic or attribute but carries no concept of identity.” [1]

A Value Object is a small immutable type that code compares by field values, not by identity.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing is defined by its attributes and has no identity is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a €10 note is any €10 note,” “an address is whatever its fields say,” or “two measurements of 5 kg are the same measurement,” then equality-by-value is a domain rule, not a convenience. A Value Object is that rule made executable: immutable, interchangeable, replaceable wholesale.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats the concept as a measure, a quantity, a description — something with no “which one is it?” question. A Value Object closes the gap: it prevents the concept from being tracked by identity, which would let two domain-equal instances be distinguished by accident. Immutability is the domain’s own “a value doesn’t change; you get a new one” rule, and validation in the constructor is the domain’s own “a value cannot exist in an invalid state” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The concept has real identity the domain tracks over time — this customer, this order, this account — even when every attribute changes. Forcing it into a Value Object erases the “which one is it?” question the domain asks constantly. Conversely, wrapping every string and number in a Value Object because immutability is fashionable is still a decision, but it signals “the domain distinguishes these” when the domain never named a distinction. That is the gap — the distinction is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert ask “which one is it?” about this thing — or only “what is it?” If equality of attributes settles the matter, it’s a value.

If yes (identity matters) → inapplicable. Model an Entity; identity is the domain’s own question.
If no (attributes settle it) → applicable. The Value Object is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #ValueObject #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Entity

Evans: “An object that is not fundamentally defined by its attributes, but rather by a thread of continuity and identity.” [1]

An Entity is a type whose instances code tracks by an identity separate from their fields.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing remains itself while everything about it changes is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the customer who moves house and changes her name is still the same customer,” then identity over time is a domain rule, not a database convenience. An Entity is that rule made executable: identity that persists through state changes, and a lifecycle the domain tracks.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain distinguishes this instance from that one by identity, not by attributes, and tracks each through birth, change, and closure. An Entity closes the gap: it prevents the thing from being copied or compared by fields, which would let the domain lose track of which customer is which. Equality by identity is the domain’s own “same customer even after moving” rule; the lifecycle methods are the domain’s own “what may happen to it, and when” rules.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “entity” has no identity the domain cares about — it is a measure, a description, a quantity, where attribute equality settles every question. Assigning it an ID invents a “which one is it?” question the domain never asks, and forces the code to maintain identity maps for things that are interchangeable. The ID signals “the domain tracks this through time” when the domain only reads its value.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain track this thing through time as “the same thing” — same customer, same order, same account — even as its attributes change?

If yes → applicable. The Entity is the code catching up to the knowledge; identity is the domain’s own thread.
If no → inapplicable. Model a Value Object; inventing identity fabricates a domain question.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Entity #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Aggregate

Evans: “A cluster of associated objects that we treat as a unit for the purpose of data changes.” [1]

An Aggregate is a group of objects that code loads, changes, and saves as one unit through a single root.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that these things change together, and that this rule must hold at every moment, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “an order’s total can never disagree with its lines,” or “a reservation may not exceed the room’s capacity,” then the invariant is a business rule and the boundary around it is the domain’s own consistency claim. An Aggregate is that claim made executable: one root, one transaction, invariants enforced inside.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain names a rule that must always hold, and every path that could break it is known. An Aggregate closes the gap: it funnels all change through the root, so the invariant cannot be bypassed. The boundary is the domain’s own “these change together, or not at all” rule; references by identity to other aggregates are the domain’s own “these stay independent” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. Grouping a screen’s data into one Aggregate is still a decision: someone chose that boundary. But the boundary asserts one transaction and one invariant. It fits only when the domain names the rule that must always hold inside it. If the domain allows eventual, separate change, it never named that rule, and the Aggregate’s lock asserts a consistency nobody decided. That is the gap — the invariant is unwritten, not a save-a-join trick.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert name the invariant — the rule that must always hold inside this boundary, the way a banker names “the balance always equals the sum of entries”?

If yes → applicable. The Aggregate is the code catching up to the knowledge; the boundary is the domain’s own consistency claim.
If no → inapplicable. Draw the boundary around the actual invariant — or discover there isn’t one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Aggregate #AggregateRoot #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Repository

Evans: “A mechanism for encapsulating storage, retrieval, and search behavior which emulates a collection of objects.” [1]

A Repository is an interface that gives code collection-like access to stored domain objects.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain speaks of a collection of these things is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “all active orders are here; we add orders; we find open ones,” then the collection metaphor is the domain’s own vocabulary. A Repository is that vocabulary made executable: an in-memory-collection facade (add, find, remove) over persistence, named in domain terms.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain genuinely reasons about a set of things — “all overdue invoices,” “the customer by number” — and the queries map to expert phrases. A Repository closes the gap: it gives the domain its collection language while hiding storage, and it confines query logic to interfaces the experts can read. It prevents persistence calls from scattering through domain code, which would couple business rules to SQL.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A method that mirrors one screen, one report, or one ORM call is still a decision, but a Repository asserts that the domain speaks of collections. It fits only when an expert phrase matches the query. If no phrase matches, the Repository supplies vocabulary the domain never adopted — the collection is unwritten, not “merely technical.” Repositories over Value Objects or read-only projections add a facade with no collection semantics behind it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can each repository method be read aloud to a domain expert as something they say — “find open orders,” “get customer by number” — rather than as a data-access operation?

If yes → applicable. The Repository is the code catching up to the knowledge; the collection is the domain’s own concept.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a DAO; name it honestly or reshape the queries around domain phrases.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Repository #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Domain Service

Evans: “An operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model, without encapsulating state, as entities and value objects do.” [1]

A Domain Service is a stateless operation that holds a domain rule belonging to no single entity.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this operation belongs to the domain yet has no natural home on a single entity is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “transferring money involves two accounts and a rule neither owns alone,” then the Domain Service is that fact made executable: a stateless operation named in domain language, placed where the domain says it lives.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain performs an action that spans several entities or needs domain knowledge no single entity should hold. A Domain Service closes the gap: it prevents the operation from being squeezed onto one entity (wrong owner) or diluted into an application helper (no domain home). Its name is the domain’s own verb — “transfer,” “allocate,” “renegotiate” — and its logic is the business rule, not orchestration.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “domain service” is where logic went because no one could decide who owned it — an entity skirted of its own behaviour. Then the service is an anemic-model accelerant: entities hold data, the service holds all rules, and the domain’s own subjects stop carrying their own knowledge. Likewise, a service that only fetches, orchestrates, or calls infrastructure is an application service wearing the wrong name.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the operation in the experts’ words, and is it genuinely homeless — belonging to no single entity — rather than parked there for convenience?

If yes → applicable. The Domain Service is the code catching up to the knowledge; the verb is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Move the behaviour to the entity that owns it, or rename the service to what it really is.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #DomainService #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Domain Event

Fowler: “A Domain Event is a full-fledged part of the domain model, a representation of something that happened in the domain.” [2]

A Domain Event is a message that records something meaningful that happened in the domain.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business talks about this occurrence — that it has a name, a time, and consequences — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “when an order is placed, fulfilment and invoicing both react,” then “OrderPlaced” is a domain fact, not a messaging artefact. A Domain Event is that fact made executable: something that happened, named in the experts’ words, with the past tense the experts use.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognises the occurrence as a milestone: experts refer to it, reports count it, other parts of the business respond to it. A Domain Event closes the gap: it prevents the occurrence from being a side effect buried in a method, and it lets reacting parts subscribe without the placer knowing them. The event name is the domain’s own vocabulary; the timestamp is the domain’s own “when it happened.”








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A table change such as “OrderSaved,” “FieldChanged,” or “RowUpdated” is still a decision, and publishing it asserts a named occurrence. It fits only when the experts name the moment and its consequences. If the experts do not, the Domain Event asserts a milestone nobody decided and forces consumers to reconstruct meaning the producer should have named. That is the gap — the occurrence is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert use this occurrence in a sentence — “the order was placed, so we…” — with the same name and the same consequences?

If yes → applicable. The Domain Event is the code catching up to the knowledge; the milestone is the domain’s own fact.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a change notification; name the integration honestly instead of borrowing domain dress.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #DomainEvent #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Factory

Evans: “Shift the responsibility for creating instances of complex objects and aggregates to a separate object, which may itself have no responsibility in the domain model.” [1]

A Factory is a construct that wraps the code that creates an object.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that creating this thing involves rules — what must be true for it to exist at all — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “an order cannot exist without a customer and at least one line,” or “a policy is created through quotation, not directly,” then the creation rules are domain invariants. A Factory is that fact made executable: the domain’s own birth rules, stated once, at the birthplace.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has creation rules the experts could state — required companions, initial state, eligibility. A Factory closes the gap: it prevents half-born objects from existing, which would push invariant checks into every method that touches the thing afterwards. Creation through the factory is the domain’s own “it may only come into existence this way” rule; a complex constructor argument list is often the factory’s knowledge looking for a name.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. Creating an object is still a decision, and a Factory asserts that creation follows a rule. It fits only when the experts can state the conditions under which the thing may come into existence. If the domain attaches no conditions to creation, the Factory claims governance nobody decided. That is the gap — the creation rule is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert state the conditions under which this thing may come into existence — and would violating them be a domain error, not a null-pointer?

If yes → applicable. The Factory is the code catching up to the knowledge; the birth rules are the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Construct directly; the ceremony invents governance the domain never claimed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Factory #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Specification

Evans: “A predicate that determines if an object does or does not satisfy some criteria.” [1]

A Specification is a rule object that code can check and combine with other rules.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this predicate is a named business rule — one the experts evaluate, discuss, and sometimes change — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “eligibility for the discount” is a thing the business defines, audits, and redefines, then the rule is a domain concept in its own right. A Specification is that fact made executable: a first-class, nameable, combinable rule object.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts name the rule, apply it in several places, or change its terms without changing the surrounding process. A Specification closes the gap: it prevents the rule from being re-implemented in a validation here, a where-clause there, and a report query somewhere else — three copies drifting apart. The specification’s name is the domain’s own phrase (“OverdueForRenewal”), and combining specifications mirrors how the experts combine the rules.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A predicate such as “id != null” or “createdAfter(threshold)” is still a decision, and a Specification asserts that the rule is named policy. It fits only when the experts have a phrase for the rule and own it. If the experts never pronounced it, the Specification claims a policy nobody decided. That is the gap — the rule is unwritten, not “merely plumbing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the experts have a phrase for this rule, and would they recognise their policy when they read the specification’s name?

If yes → applicable. The Specification is the code catching up to the knowledge; the rule is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep it as a plain predicate; the wrapper fabricates policy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Specification #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Bounded Context

Evans: “A description of a boundary (typically a subsystem, or the work of a particular team) within which a particular model is defined and applicable.” [1]

A Bounded Context is a boundary inside which one model and one set of terms apply.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the same word means different things to different parts of the business is domain knowledge. If your organisation crystallises that “a ‘product’ to sales is a SKU with margin; to logistics it is a box with weight; to support it is a warranty scope,” then one shared model is a falsehood, and the boundary between the meanings is the domain’s own division. A Bounded Context is that division made executable: inside this boundary, each term has exactly one meaning.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business genuinely divides — distinct vocabularies, distinct rules, distinct teams — and the split is discoverable in how experts talk past each other. A Bounded Context closes the gap: it prevents a single “unified” model from being stretched across conflicting meanings, which forces every term into nullable, optional, “sometimes it means” contortions. The context border is the domain’s own “here, this word means this” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “contexts” are team territories or microservice quotas, drawn where the vocabulary is actually shared. Splitting one coherent model into several contexts adds translation layers between meanings that never diverged, and every context boundary the domain doesn’t recognise becomes a mapping tax. The boundary signals “the words differ here” when only the org chart does.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the experts themselves divide — does “order” or “customer” actually mean different things across these groups, with different rules attached?

If yes → applicable. The Bounded Context is the code catching up to the knowledge; the border is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep one model; the extra contexts invent translation the vocabulary doesn’t need.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #BoundedContext #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Ubiquitous Language

Evans: “A language structured around the domain model and used by all team members within a bounded context to connect all the activities of the team with the software.” [1]

A Ubiquitous Language is the shared vocabulary that both domain experts and code use.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a term has an agreed meaning between experts and code is itself the completeness-check. Ubiquitous Language is not a structure but a claim: “the words in the code are the words the business uses, with the meanings the business gives them.” Wherever the claim breaks — a “record” that the business calls a “booking,” a “status” no expert recognises — you have found the gap directly.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The terms are settled: experts use them in conversation, the code uses the same words, and a glossary would have one line per term. The language then closes the gap continuously: renaming a class is renegotiating meaning with the business, and a new expert can read the domain model as their own vocabulary. Each named term carries its rules with it.








WarningWhen it exposes the gap (cohesion-reducing)



There is no clean “doesn’t fit” here; the failure mode is pretence. Code that borrows domain words without domain meaning — an “Account” that is really a database row, a “Policy” that is a config entry — manufactures false recognition: experts nod at words that do not behave as they say. That is worse than honest technical naming, because it hides the missing knowledge behind familiar dress.








TipThe faithfulness test



Could a domain expert read the class and method names aloud in a meeting — and would every statement made with them be true in their terms?

If yes → the language is real; it is the completeness-check running all the time.
If no → you’ve found a knowledge gap by name: the term’s real meaning is not settled, or the code’s meaning is not the business’s.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the naming wrong; you’ve found knowledge that isn’t settled yet.




#DDD #UbiquitousLanguage #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Anti-Corruption Layer

Evans: “Create an isolating layer to provide clients with functionality in terms of their own domain model.” [1]

An Anti-Corruption Layer is a translation boundary between your model and a foreign one.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the foreign system’s model is not our model — and must not become it — is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “the legacy system’s ‘customer’ is a billing record, not our customer,” then the translation between the two models is a domain decision. An Anti-Corruption Layer is that decision made executable: one place where foreign concepts are converted into ours, and ours never leak out raw.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The external model genuinely conflicts with yours — different identities, different meanings, a different way of slicing the world — and you cannot change the source. An ACL closes the gap: it prevents legacy concepts from leaking into the new model, where each foreign quirk would become a permanent local rule. The layer is the domain’s own “we translate at the border; inside, our words only” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “ACL” wraps a model you actually share — a well-designed API whose vocabulary matches yours — adding a translation layer that converts identical concepts into slightly renamed copies. Then the layer hides agreement, doubles maintenance, and signals “their model is foreign” when it is simply upstream. When the real problem is that your model was never built, an ACL around the foreign model doesn’t protect your model; it replaces it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the two models genuinely disagree — same word, different meaning, different identity — or do they differ only in naming and technology?

If yes → applicable. The ACL is the code catching up to the knowledge; the border is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Use the shared model directly or a thin adapter; a full ACL manufactures foreignness.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #AntiCorruptionLayer #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Anemic Domain Model (anti-pattern)

Fowler: “The fundamental horror of this anti-pattern is that it is so contrary to the basic idea of object-oriented design — to combine data and process together.” [3]

An Anemic Domain Model is a model of data classes that hold no behavior of their own.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A model of data classes with no behaviour claims, implicitly, that the domain has facts but no rules — that orders merely have totals but nothing enforces validity. That claim is almost never true. The anemic model is therefore a standing question: where did the rules go? The answer is usually “into services no expert named,” and that displacement is the knowledge gap made visible.






ImportantWhen the domain justifies it (rare, but real)



Some boundaries are genuinely data-only because the knowledge genuinely lives elsewhere: DTOs crossing a process boundary, persisted projections in CQRS read sides, integration messages. There the domain itself says “this is an envelope, not a model” — and dressing these up with fake behaviour would be the misplaced structure, not the anemia.








WarningWhen it’s a knowledge gap



The “entities” are the domain model — experts speak of orders, policies, claims — yet every rule about them lives in XxxManager or XxxHelper services. Each such service is an unnamed domain concept: the experts’ verbs exist, but no one found their owner. The anemia signals “the rules had no discoverable home,” which means the model-building stopped before the knowledge was placed. Adding getters does not fix it; finding who owns each verb does.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each behaviour sitting in a service: would an expert name the thing that performs it — “the order validates itself at submission”? Or is the performer genuinely a process, not an object?

If a thing performs it → the behaviour has a home; move it there.
If it’s genuinely a process → keep the service, but name it in the domain’s words.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found a style problem; you’ve found knowledge with no assigned owner.




#DDD #AnemicDomainModel #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Module (tactical packaging)

Evans: “Choose modules that tell the story of the system and contain a cohesive set of concepts.” [1]

A Module is a named package that groups related domain concepts.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that these concepts belong together in the experts’ minds is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “leasing, maintenance, and resale are different parts of the fleet business — each with its own vocabulary,” then the module divisions are the domain’s own chapters. A Module is that division made executable: a named, cohesive packaging of a piece of the domain, whose name an expert would recognise.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The module corresponds to a piece of the business that experts name — “Underwriting,” “Fulfilment,” “Billing” — with a vocabulary used only inside it. A Module closes the gap: it prevents concepts from different vocabulary areas being interleaved until nothing can be discussed in one place, and it makes the domain’s own sections visible in the code layout. High cohesion inside, low coupling across — because the business itself works that way.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. Grouping code into models/, services/, utils/, or helpers/ is still a decision, but a Module asserts that the grouping matches the experts’ own sections. It fits only when the domain names those sections. If the domain’s groupings were never consulted, every business concept is smeared across the drawers and no module can be shown to an expert. That is the gap — the domain’s own structure is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Could you read the module names to a domain expert and hear “yes, those are the parts of our business” — and would each module’s terms be used by exactly that part?

If yes → applicable. The Module is the code catching up to the knowledge; the packaging is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Repackage around the domain’s own sections; the drawers hide the knowledge’s structure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Modules #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Policy / Process (tactical)
A Policy is a rule object that expresses “when this happens, do that.”

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business responds to occurrences with prescribed actions — “when a claim is filed, assign an adjuster within two days” — is domain knowledge. A Policy is that fact made executable: a rule in the experts’ own if-then shape, attached to the occurrence it responds to. It is the domain’s own “when X, then Y” made first-class instead of buried in a sequence of ifs.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts state the rule as a standing instruction, and it may change without the surrounding process changing. A Policy closes the gap: it prevents the response from being smeared through whatever code happens to trigger the occurrence, and it gives the rule one name, one home, one audit trail. The trigger is the domain’s own event; the response is the domain’s own obligation.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A reaction such as “retry three times” or “log a metric” is still a decision, and a Policy asserts that the business prescribed it. It fits only when an expert would state the rule and expect to be consulted before it changed. If the library set it and no expert decided, the Policy claims authority nobody granted. That is the gap — the rule is unwritten, not “merely technical.” The structure also obscures real policies: when everything is a policy, nothing is.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert state this rule in a meeting — “when this happens, we do that” — and would they expect to be consulted before it changed?

If yes → applicable. The Policy is the code catching up to the knowledge; the if-then is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep it as a plain default; dressing it as policy invents authority nobody granted.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Policy #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Domain-Driven Design as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutable Value Objects

Evans: “Value objects should be immutable: rather than modifying one, you create a new one in its place.” [1]

A value object is an immutable type identified by its values; you replace it instead of changing it.

The overlap, and the one thing this post adds
#85 established the construct: a value object makes executable the domain rule “a €10 note is any €10 note.” Immutability is the other half of that same claim, and #85 named it only in passing. The OOP angle is narrower: immutability is a language-level commitment that the domain replaces this fact rather than revises it. An address correction is a new address, not a mutated one. If the business speaks that way, immutability is the code catching up. Where it goes wrong is on both sides. Immutability adopted without a domain warrant — chosen for thread safety, cacheability, or safe sharing on things the domain revises — forces contortions: builders and copy-methods emulating updates the domain actually performs. The choice is still a decision, but the domain never named a replacement rule, and that is the gap — not that immutability is “merely technical.” The inverse is a mutable value-shaped object, whose shared aliasing silently couples changes the domain never coupled.






TipThe narrower test this post adds



For a value-shaped class: when this fact “changes” in the business language, does the old one stop being true, or does the same thing acquire a new state?

If the old one stops being true (the domain replaces it) → immutable. The Value Object is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the same thing acquires a new state (the domain revises it) → not a value object at all. The identity question is #85/#86, not the language mechanism.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ValueObjects #Immutability #DDD #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Every construct below encodes a fact — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be. Each post names the construct, states the encoding, and asks whether the fact is the domain’s or the developer’s.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Natural vs surrogate primary key
text:
Case study: Natural vs surrogate primary key
Two customers, same email, same address, same person — and the database is happy, because both rows carry a different id.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A natural key is an attribute the domain already treats as unique and stable: a serial number, an ISBN, a national identity number. A surrogate key has no domain meaning, so identity survives a change to real attributes. Both enforce a unique column; only the natural key makes the domain’s uniqueness claim.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Identity is a domain decision before it is a column choice. The domain names an attribute that is unique and never reused, or admits it has none. With none, a surrogate is honest — but the sameness rule still needs a home: a UNIQUE constraint over the columns a human compares. The gap question: is the sameness rule written anywhere the database can enforce it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An attribute the domain already guards: a serial number stamped on a device, an IBAN, a legally issued invoice number. Nobody reuses it, so it is the identity. Equally sound: customer_id BIGSERIAL with UNIQUE (email_normalized) WHERE email_normalized IS NOT NULL beneath it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Add id, declare it the key, leave email an ordinary nullable column because emails change. Nothing fails, and the reasoning is sound: surrogate keys are more stable. Then the form double-submits on a flaky connection and the CRM export loads twice. Merging means rewriting foreign keys, and the id has leaked into invoice numbers and URLs — so it becomes the identity nobody can change while the human’s own identity stays unconstrained.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can someone name the rule that makes two rows the same customer — and is that rule enforced anywhere?

If yes → identity is a domain fact with an owner. Verify the constraint exists in the schema, not only in a service method.
If no → the rule exists with no enforcement. A UNIQUE constraint on the natural candidate is the repair — and it rejects the emails that legitimately change.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask whoever merges customer records today which columns they compare.




#Database #PrimaryKeys #DataModeling #SchemaDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Normalization vs denormalization
The product price lives in two tables. The catalog job updates one of them. The customer finds the other.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Normalization stores each fact once, in the table whose key determines it, so every fact has one home, and a change has one place to happen. Denormalization stores a copy so a read avoids a join. The first encodes “this fact changes and must not diverge”; the copy encodes “this read dominates, and someone reconciles it”.


The database knowledge gap it signals
A copy is a prediction about the read-to-write ratio, plus an owner for the day the copies disagree. The choice needs both: a measured read pattern, and a named reconciler — refresh job, trigger, event consumer — with a stated staleness bound. The gap question: what ratio was measured, and who owns the reconciliation?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Boyce-Codd normal form — one home per fact — wherever facts change: price, address, status. Denormalize where one read dominates and the maintenance is real: an order_total kept by a trigger, a search index rebuilt from the event stream, a report table refreshed on schedule.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Denormalize for performance”, applied before anyone measured. The plan shows a join over a million rows, and a stored order_total recomputed on every line-item change looks cheaper. The copy lacks two things: a measured ratio and an owner. Then the trigger misses the refund line, the reconciliation job writes its own version, and finance reads whichever ran last. Two mechanisms now maintain one total, and nothing compares their answers.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does a measured read dominate — and is a reconciler named for the copies?

If yes → a measured pattern and a named reconciliation exist. Verify the staleness bound is written where readers can see it.
If no → say which half failed. No measured read: normalize. Read measured, no reconciler: name the reconciler before keeping the copy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Instrument the read and write counts for a week, then name who owns reconciliation.




#Database #Normalization #Denormalization #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Nullability
The report counted 4,112 non-rejected customers. Another 611 were never counted at all — their status was NULL, and WHERE status <> 'rejected' had dropped them.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A nullable column admits absence: the row exists without a value. The model gives absence one representation, NULL, and one consequence — three-valued logic: any comparison against NULL is unknown, apart from IS NULL and IS DISTINCT FROM. The column encodes “absent”, never which kind of absence.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Absence has at least three meanings a schema must separate: not known yet, not applicable, not yet reached in a process. NULL stores none of them. The domain must say, per column, which one applies — and whether “not yet” is a state the process will leave. The gap question: which absence does this column carry, and did anyone decide?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



shipped_at NULL means “not yet shipped”: a state the fulfilment process leaves, so WHERE shipped_at IS NULL is exactly the open-orders query. terminated_on NULL means “still active”, and the domain says so.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Nullable as the default for every column not supplied at insert. It never rejects a valid row, so it never fails a test. Now status is NULL for three populations: the row the webhook created before the state machine ran, the row imported from a legacy system with no status, and the row where status does not apply. The logic then works silently — <> 'rejected' is unknown for NULL, so those rows vanish from the count; NOT IN against a subquery yielding one NULL returns no rows at all. The report undercounts while every query looks correct.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does every nullable column carry one decided absence — and does every query agree on which one?

If yes → absence is a modeled state. Check the <> and NOT IN filters against it.
If no → say which half failed. Undecided absence: make it NOT NULL or split it. Decided absence, disagreeing queries: fix the queries, not the column.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count NULLs per column and per source; the split counts your hidden meanings.




#Database #Nullability #SQL #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Soft delete vs hard delete
text:
Case study: Soft delete vs hard delete
A customer asked to be forgotten. The row is still there, with deleted_at set, an email and an address — and erasing it would break last year’s revenue report.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Soft delete keeps the row and marks it: a deleted_at timestamp, an is_active flag. Hard delete removes it. The retained row encodes “the domain must still reason about this thing after it stops being current” — history, audit, and the records that cite it.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Forgetting is a rule from outside the schema. Accounting retains invoices for a decade, a regulator names the period, an erasure obligation says personal data must go. These conflict; only the domain resolves it per table. A tombstone — the retained row with its flag — must redact the personal fields to serve an erasure request; whether keeping them is lawful is a judgment the schema cannot make. The gap question: does the domain forget this thing, and who states the retention rule?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



deleted_at where the domain states the rule, deletion is a modeled state, and one filtered view is the only way to read the table: an invoice voided rather than removed, because the ledger must still balance; a user archived because their orders cite them. The rule lives outside the schema, and a named process owns the purge.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



deleted_at added as a habit — “we never really delete, it is safer”. It is safer, and that is the trap: nothing fails, no data is lost, the choice looks conservative. Then every query must remember WHERE deleted_at IS NULL forever, including ones written next year. One forgotten filter leaks tombstones into a production report. Meanwhile the personal data is still physically present, so the erasure request is refused for a reason the schema cannot express.








TipThe faithfulness test



Must the domain still reason about this thing after it stops being current — and who states the retention rule?

If yes → retention is a domain fact with an owner. Verify a purge process exists and that queries filter through one shared view.
If no → delete for real, or split the live table from an archive whose access is deliberate.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask legal and finance how long each table must keep a row.




#Database #SoftDelete #DataRetention #Compliance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: ENUM, lookup table, or free text
text:
Case study: ENUM, lookup table, or free text
“U.S.”, “USA” and “us” were the top three countries by customer count. One country, three rows, and no way back to one.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: An ENUM closes a column to a fixed set; an FK lookup restricts it to the rows present; free text constrains nothing. The closed form encodes “the process owns this set and can enumerate it” — values are states a workflow moves through, not labels the world invents.


The database knowledge gap it signals
The domain decides whether the set is closed by rule or open by nature. Payment states are closed: the gateway returns a fixed list, and a new one is a version change. Lead sources are open: the world adds one whenever a campaign runs. The gap question: is this set closed by a rule, or open by nature?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Payment states — pending, authorized, captured, refunded, failed — as an enum or a lookup table with an FK: the process owns the transitions, and a typo breaks reconciliation.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An enum for a set the world extends: categories, lead sources, product families. It ships well — fast, typo-proof, cleanly aggregated. Then a value arrives that the enum lacks, and adding it is a migration: a deploy coordinated with the reporting team. After six rounds someone adds other and stops. A year later 40% of rows say other, and the constraint enforces only that the real category lives in a free-text note. The inverse trap: free text where aggregation is required, so the country report needs a hand-written mapping table.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can someone state the complete value set today — and who is consulted when a new value is needed?

If yes → the set is closed by rule. Verify the owner exists and that a new value arrives through that owner, by a deploy if the rule says so.
If no → say which half failed. No complete set today: the set is open, so store it as data. Set known, no intake path: build the path and keep the constraint.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the production values and count the variants.




#Database #Enums #LookupTables #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Valid-time columns
The audit asked what a SKU cost on 14 March. The table answered with today’s price, on one row per SKU: valid_from and valid_to were never added, because nothing asked for a past price until the audit did.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: valid_from and valid_to state the interval over which a row’s fact held, keeping superseded rows instead of overwriting them. The interval encodes “the domain asks about the past”, and it carries a rule the columns alone do not: per entity — per SKU, say — no overlapping intervals.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Keeping history is a different claim from current state, and it costs an interval per fact and an integrity rule no writer may violate. The domain must say who closes an interval when a new one opens. The gap question: which decisions were made by reading an old price?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Domains that reason over the past by rule: rate cards, insurance cover evaluated on the incident date, audits of the configuration then. The interval is the domain’s own fact; an enforced exclusion constraint closes the old one as it opens the new one.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Temporal columns added for one report. Nothing enforces the intervals; they are maintained by hand, by whoever remembers. Three failures follow. Overlaps: a rate change inserts the new row and forgets to close the old one, so it has two open intervals and queries pick one at random. Gaps: a backdated correction closes the old interval too early, or the new rate starts late, so “price on that date” returns no row. And the current-row convention differs per query — valid_to IS NULL here, a sentinel there — so two teams get two answers from one table.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does anyone ask about the past in domain terms — and who maintains the integrity of the intervals?

If yes → history is a domain fact. Verify one shared definition of “current” and an enforced no-overlap rule.
If no → say which half failed. Past queried, no interval owner: name the owner and enforce no-overlap. Past not queried: keep current state only.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask which decisions were made by reading an old price, then count open intervals.




#Database #TemporalData #DataModeling #Auditability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE
text:
Case study: Foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE
A migration set amount = -1 on 340 ledger rows. Nothing raised an error. The application would have rejected it — the migration never went through the application.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A constraint is a rule the database evaluates on every write, from any client. Someone can still defer it, disable it, or outrank it. Three shapes: a foreign key forbids a reference to a missing row, CHECK a value outside a predicate, UNIQUE a duplicate. Each encodes “an invariant of the fact”, not a step in one code path.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Every rule has a population of writers: the API, the import, the migration, the hotfix, the second service, the analyst with a console. Application validation covers one of them, and the rest arrive later. The question is not whether the app checks, but who may break the rule. The gap question: if a bug or a second writer bypasses the app, what stops this rule from being violated?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A ledger entry’s account_id references accounts(id): a posting to a nonexistent account must not exist, whatever wrote it. CHECK (amount > 0), UNIQUE (invoice_number).








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Rules kept in application code “for flexibility”. The reasoning is defensible: validation belongs near the domain logic. It holds while one writer exists. Then the reconciliation script runs at 2 a.m. and writes rows the service never sees; a partner CSV import bypasses every check; a second service ships its own copy of the rules. The constraint dropped for a bulk load “temporarily” is never restored, and nobody notices while production data is valid.








TipThe faithfulness test



If a bug or a second writer bypasses the app, does the database still stop this rule from being violated — and is that acceptable?

If yes → the rule is a domain invariant with a database owner. Verify no writer holds a privilege that skips it.
If no → the rule is unenforced, or not acceptably. Name the writers you accept; their number is a chosen risk.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Enumerate every path that writes this table, including scripts, then compare the rule sets.




#Database #Constraints #DataIntegrity #SchemaDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: JSON columns and EAV versus typed columns
text:
Case study: JSON columns and EAV versus typed columns
Every order carries a metadata JSON column. Counted over one month, nine in ten rows repeated the same twelve attributes, and every report reached them by path.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A JSON column, or an EAV table — one row per attribute, no declared columns — stores a shape the schema does not declare. The database reads the stored shape as text: a type, a CHECK, and statistics arrive only with an extracted column. It encodes “the shape is open and decided outside this schema” — a claim about who controls the data.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Openness has a source. A provider webhook payload is open because the provider decides its shape. A domain attribute you have not named yet is not open — it is unknown, and the schema records your uncertainty as a permanent storage format. The gap question: who outside this system decides the shape?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A webhook payload stored opaque inside a typed envelope: event_id, type, received_at, payload as JSON. The envelope is typed and constrained because the domain owns those facts; the payload stays opaque because the provider owns its shape.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Core attributes moved into JSON because a column “felt permanent”. Each step was reasonable: the attributes differ per category, adding columns meant a migration, and JSON was there. Soon metadata->>'colour' sits in a dozen queries, and those numbers are strings, so ‘10’ sorts before ‘9’. No type, no constraint, no statistics — on engines that keep none for expressions, the planner guesses. And the schema cannot be diffed: two environments with “the same” schema hold different shapes in one column.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the shape genuinely open from outside the system — or is this a domain attribute you postponed naming?

If yes → the payload is opaque by contract. Verify a typed envelope around it and a version check at every read.
If no → the shape was never open; it was undecided. Extraction costs the migration the untyped column avoided, and it is the only place the type can live.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the column wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count the distinct paths used in queries; that list is the schema you have not written.




#Database #JSON #SchemaDesign #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Views vs tables
Two revenue reports disagree by 4% and both are labelled revenue: one sums the table, the other a view an analyst filtered last year, and no one can say which number finance signs.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A table stores facts; a view stores a definition — a query text plus the name and owner that govern it. Its rows are computed at read time, so it encodes a claim about meaning: this derived fact has one definition, many readers, and one owner who changes it in one place. It predicts the derivation is cheap enough to recompute per read, and that nobody needs the result pinned.


The database knowledge gap it signals
A named view is a domain term wearing SQL. Someone decided what “active” means, which rows qualify, and who may change the rule — before CREATE VIEW ran. If that decision lives only in the WHERE clause, the schema enforces a guess. Is this a governed term, or a query that happened to get saved?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The domain already names the question. Support, billing, and the churn model all need “active customers”; the finance team owns the definition; a policy change — refund window, trial length — edits the view once, and every consumer that holds no copy moves in the same deploy.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Both traps look like good practice. The first is view stacking: v_active on v_orders_recent on v_orders_clean, twelve layers deep, each hiding one filter. On engines that flatten the nested views into one query it works until the plan degrades, and the debugger then has twelve places to look. The second is drift: active was one filter, then silently became “has an order in 90 days.” Who decided 90, and which of the two views is the term now?








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this a named domain question — or a query that got a name because it was pasted twice?

If yes → the view is the domain’s vocabulary. Check that one owner can change the definition, and that no caller re-implements the filter locally.
If no → it is a saved query. Keep it inside the module that needs it, or make it a table if the derivation is expensive.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the view wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count how many callers duplicate the filter, then ask who signs off when the meaning changes.




#Databases #SQL #Views #SchemaDesign #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Materialized views
The finance dashboard says €1.24M. The ledger says €1.31M. Both numbers are right: the dashboard is a materialized view six hours old, and the freshness was never written down.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A materialized view stores the result; on most engines refresh is an explicit job — scheduled, triggered, or manual. It encodes two predictions: the question is asked far more often than the underlying rows change, and an answer of a stated age is acceptable to whoever acts on it.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Staleness is a domain fact with an owner and a decision boundary. Someone has to accept “up to six hours old” for this consumer, and name the decision that would flip at the edge of that window. Has anyone accepted that age in writing, for this report?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The dashboard refreshes once at 03:00, the team acts on yesterday’s numbers, and no consumer reads the last day. The refresh cost is known — ninety seconds of I/O, measured — and the slot sits outside the load window. The staleness is printed on the page; the last successful refresh is monitored.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The materialized view added “to make the report fast,” with no freshness contract. Trap one: a decision that needs the last hour gets made on stale data, quietly and confidently. Trap two: the refresh window that outgrew its slot — minutes to forty as the data grew — and now overlaps the business day, blocking readers exactly when the report is read. A failed refresh is silent too: the view serves yesterday, then last week, and the number still looks plausible.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has someone accepted a stated staleness — with the decision that changes at the boundary named?

If yes → staleness is a stated domain fact. Check the refresh is scheduled, timed, and alerts on failure.
If no → a cache with no expiry contract. Someone must accept an age in writing; until then the age is whatever the refresh happened to produce.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the materialized view wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the refresh duration against the change rate, then ask each consumer what age they would refuse.




#Databases #MaterializedViews #DataFreshness #Caching #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: CTE vs subquery vs temp table
text:
Case study: CTE vs subquery vs temp table
A 400-line query with eleven CTEs ran in 90 ms on an engine that inlined them; as temp tables, 40 ms, because stage five was read three times. The cost nobody measured: which of the eleven names a domain concept.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: WITH names a subquery — a common table expression. On engines that inline it (non-recursive, referenced once, unless you write MATERIALIZED), the name costs nothing. On older engines, or with MATERIALIZED, it is a fence: computed once, stored, and hidden from the rest of the query. A temp table is a stronger promise — the result is read more than once and the materialization is deliberate.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Readability, reuse, and a materialization boundary are three different claims, and the domain decides which it needs. Steps that mirror domain concepts — billing period, eligible cohort, prorated amount — are knowledge; eleven CTEs that exist because the query grew are not. Does each named step correspond to something the domain names?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



CTEs naming the steps of a domain computation, one step per concept, so a finance reviewer can read the query as the policy it implements: cohort, eligibility, proration. A temp table for a genuine multi-pass pipeline that reads stage one three times.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Cargo-culting “CTE for performance.” The folklore came from planners that fenced every WITH; on modern engines the measured plan shows the CTE is inlined. The engineer adds MATERIALIZED to force the old behavior, and it is slower only where the CTE is referenced once. Second trap: the single 400-line statement of nested CTEs, adopted for modularity, that no reviewer can hold in one reading.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does each named step correspond to a domain concept — and did you confirm on this engine’s plan that the fence is real?

If yes → the naming is domain knowledge. Keep the steps, then confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on this engine version.
If no → say which half failed. Steps without domain names: collapse them. Named steps, unconfirmed fence: read the plan before trusting the boundary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the CTE wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Time each stage, read the plan, then ask which steps a domain expert names.




#Databases #SQL #QueryPlanning #CTE #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Indexing (single and compound)
One insert-heavy table carries twelve indexes and pays about 40 ms per insert at its current size; at one index it paid about 4 ms. Nine of the twelve serve no query anyone can name.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: An index is a second access path over the key columns — sorted in a B-tree, hashed in a hash index — plus whatever the engine needs to reach the row. An index on one column serves predicates on that column at any value; a compound index serves a filter shape, and its column order is part of the claim — equality columns first, then the range. It encodes a claim about a named query and a write tax.


The database knowledge gap it signals
An index is a statement about the queries the domain asks: which lookups are named, what they filter and sort by, how often each runs. It also adds write amplification — extra writes per row.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Every index traced to a real query, quoted. Orders filtered by tenant and date get a compound index on (tenant_id, created_at) — equality first, range second — and the ORDER BY needs no sort node. Each index has a caller, an owner, and a measured cost on the insert path.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Index every column, just in case.” The table is insert-hot; twelve indexes each need maintenance per row; writes queue and latency climbs. Second: the compound index in the wrong column order, (created_at, tenant_id), which serves a date-only filter beautifully and cannot serve the tenant-and-date query by plain descent. Third: the unused index nobody dares drop, because whoever added it has left and its scan count has stayed at zero for a year.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can every index be traced to a named query — and is the write cost of each measured?

If yes → the index is the query’s shadow. Check the column order; before dropping a zero-scan index, check what it enforces.
If no → finish the audit, not the index. Remove the ones with no named query; measure the write cost of the ones that have one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the index wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Log the queries this table serves for a week, then compare their filter shapes to the index list.




#Databases #Indexing #QueryPerformance #SchemaDesign #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Clustering
A table clustered by id is read by customer_id. Ten thousand matching rows scatter across most of its pages, so the plan promises 12 ms and the wall clock reports 4 s.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A clustered index, an index-organized table, and CLUSTER all store rows in key order in the physical structure. A table carries one physical order at a time — one per partition where it is partitioned — so the choice encodes a claim that one read pattern dominates and the others can pay.


The database knowledge gap it signals
The domain must have a dominant read path, measured: what queries this table, in which order, how often, and whether that order survives three more features. What does the domain read together — and is that the order you chose?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Orders read by customer and date range: cluster on (customer_id, placed_at); on an engine that maintains clustering the matching rows sit in one contiguous run, so readahead works and the query reads only the pages holding them. A time-series table read by timestamp window, clustered on it. The competing paths were counted and are rare enough to pay for.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Clustered on the generated id because ids are “the key,” while every query filters customer_id: reads stay scattered and the clustering buys only rewrite cost. The subtler trap is treating re-clustering as one-time. On engines that maintain clustering (SQL Server), an insert into a random key position splits a page and leaves both halves half empty. On engines where CLUSTER is a one-time rewrite (PostgreSQL), new rows land wherever there is free space, rows per page drift toward random at a rate set by inserts against size, and the rewrite takes an exclusive lock.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the dominant read path counted — and does that read order hold as features are added?

If yes → the physical order matches how the domain reads. Check the key’s insert order does not churn, or schedule the rewrite and watch the drift.
If no → say which half failed. No counted path: the cluster key is decorative, so keep the heap and a secondary index. Counted path that drifts: schedule the rewrite, or accept the drift.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found clustering wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure rows-per-page for the dominant filter, then ask which order survives the roadmap.




#Databases #ClusteredIndex #StorageLayout #QueryPerformance #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Sharding and partitioning
A query that took 20 ms takes 320 ms after sharding. It reads one row per tenant, so it now opens sixteen shards in turn and pays each one’s latency.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A shard key routes each row to one shard at write time. Choosing it pre-commits every query path: a query that carries the key reaches one shard, a query without it fans out and pays the slowest. It predicts the domain’s unit of access is that key, that the key has many distinct values, the distribution is even, and cross-unit queries are rare.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Two facts outside the framing list decide this: the load that made one database insufficient, and the measured skew of the key.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



B2B software where one database is measurably out of room and every query filters tenant_id: the key is carried by construction, and moving a tenant is an explicit migration, not an accident. Table partitions for retention — no shard key needed — where dropping a month is a metadata operation, not a million-row delete.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Hashing user_id when the domain’s unit is the account: no query carries the key, so every report fans out and joins across shards in application code, and shared-nothing (each shard independent) behaves like a slow single database. Second: a key chosen for assumed evenness that the queries do not carry. Third: the skewed key found in production. One tenant holds 40% of the rows, its shard is the bottleneck, and re-sharding means moving live data while serving traffic.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the domain’s queries carry this key — and what is the measured skew, not the assumed evenness?

If yes → the key is the domain’s unit. Verify cross-shard queries are enumerated, and that a resharding plan exists.
If no → say which half failed. Queries do not carry the key: change it. Carried but skewed: split the hot tenant, or isolate it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found sharding wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count how many queries carry the candidate key, then measure the top-tenant share of rows.




#Databases #Sharding #Partitioning #Scalability #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Function vs stored procedure vs query
text:
Case study: Function vs stored procedure vs query
A month-end close moves forty thousand postings, and one endpoint in a small service posts without calling the procedure that owns the rule, so one debit lands without its credit and the trial balance is off by €4,200.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A procedure is a named body of SQL the server compiles and keeps; a function returns a value inside a query; an inline query lives only in the client that sent it. The first two give one rule one home, and claim that the invariant holds for whoever writes.


The database knowledge gap it signals
A rule in the schema asserts that this writer is not the only writer, now or later. That is a fact about the domain, not about speed: no caller may be trusted to remember the rule. The gap question: which writers must obey this rule, and who can currently write without it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Double-entry posting: a debit and its credit must land in one transaction, the sum must be zero, and the rule must hold for the API, the importer, and the service nobody has written yet.
