One posting procedure covers every caller that uses it, and revoked write grants cover the rest — plus computation that must not travel: sum a hundred million rows in the server, return one number.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Put it in a procedure, it is faster” seduces because it is sometimes true; the trap is the unowned one — a rule the write paths never mention. The app grows a discount rule, the procedure grows one too, and two truths drift until a customer is charged twice. The inverse dogma fails alike: “no procedures, ever,” so five services re-implement the balance rule, and the hundred-million-row sum never travels.








TipThe faithfulness test



If a second application writes to this table tomorrow, do the same rules survive — and does a reviewer see them?

If yes → the rule is domain-owned, and placement follows. Check one copy exists, the same body runs for every writer, and no grant bypasses the procedure.
If no → one client’s habit, not a schema fact. Keep the logic in the application, in version control, with tests.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List every current and planned writer, then ask which rules the domain requires of each.




#Database #StoredProcedures #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #SchemaDesign

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Row-level triggers
A balance is corrected at 09:25 and wrong again at 09:33, and the cause is a trigger that recomputes it from a rule nobody on the team had read.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A row trigger is a body of SQL the database fires by itself, once per row a statement touches; a statement-level trigger fires once per statement and does not carry the per-row cost below. It encodes knowledge no caller invokes: the table declares the consequence, for anyone who writes.


The database knowledge gap it signals
A trigger says no writer may be trusted to remember the rule and, while enabled, none may opt out — a strong, sometimes true claim. The rule gains no name at any call site, which is where accountability sits. The gap question: would a developer who never opens the table definitions (the DDL) predict that this happens?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An audit row on every inserted, updated, or deleted row of a regulated table, written in the same transaction, so trail and fact cannot diverge. Or a derived column the schema owns and arithmetic determines — a line total, where the alternative is hoping six code paths agree.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A business rule in a trigger: recalculate loyalty on every order update. It looks stronger than a service call, and it is invisible to everyone reading the application: no call site, no signature, nothing in the trace. It fires per row, so a two-million-row load means two million firings; on engines that allow nested firing it cascades into other triggers. Then comes the week spent answering “who updated this row.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Could a developer who never opens the DDL predict that this happens — and does the rule survive that test?

If yes → the table owns the consequence, and it is visible where the table is defined. Check it covers every write path and stays cheap per row.
If no → an application rule hiding in the schema. Move it to the code that owns the decision.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the biggest write, then ask which rules the domain wants for every writer.




#Database #Triggers #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DataIntegrity

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Object-relational mapper (ORM) lazy loading (the N+1 query)
text:
Case study: Object-relational mapper (ORM) lazy loading (the N+1 query)
One page takes 40 ms in staging and 700 ms in production, and the number of queries per row is identical in both.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A navigation property — a reference from one object to its related rows — loads on first touch, so the ORM issues one query per parent row and the query count becomes a function of the data. It encodes an unstated cardinality — this list is short, this relation is optional here — and defers the second query until someone asks.


The database knowledge gap it signals
Cardinality per parent — rows loaded per navigation — is a domain fact the schema almost never records, and it is a size, measured at the largest page the product offers. Nothing in the access decides it; the code assumes “a few,” and the assumption stays invisible until the list grows. The gap question: what is the real cardinality of this relation at production page size, and did anyone count it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Singular navigation. Load the order header, then load its lines when a person opens that order: one extra query for one row, and nothing paid for the orders nobody opens. The reader waits for one query, not two hundred.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Lazy loading inside a list render. Each row follows the relation, so one statement becomes two hundred, and the defect is invisible until a real list appears: staging has twelve rows, production has two hundred, and the page slows about seventeenfold with no error to grep. Then the fix: load everything up front, which multiplies rows at each join level until a three-level fetch returns the product of all three lists and the ORM de-duplicates them in memory. Both placements encode a cardinality guess; in neither was the number counted.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each navigation the ORM will follow, do you know the cardinality it loads — counted, at production page sizes?

If yes → the load matches the domain. Verify it against the largest page the product offers, not the sample data.
If no → it is an assumption about size, not a fact about the domain. Eager fetch is the other guess: it multiplies rows at each join level. Neither is a fact until the cardinality is counted.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Log the query count per request and the row count per relation, at production scale.




#Database #ORM #NPlusOne #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Database Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Isolation levels
Two withdrawals of 200 from an account holding 300 can both commit, and the balance can end at 100 — at the default level, with read-modify-write.
Choosing a schema construct or a database mechanism? Ask “which fact does this choice encode — what exists, what repeats, what must stay true, what gets read together, how fresh an answer may be, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the schema enforces a guess. If you can name those facts, the schema is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: An isolation level names the standard anomalies the engine permits — dirty read (a value never committed), non-repeatable read (a row that changes mid-transaction), phantom (a row that appears on re-query). Each engine adds its own, such as lost update (one write erasing another). Choosing one claims the domain can absorb exactly these — a claim about the business, not a setting.


The database knowledge gap it signals
The domain must already know which anomaly costs money — not which level sounds safest. A level that forbids more than needed is paid in retries; one that forbids less is paid in wrong balances. The gap question: which interleaving would lose money here, and does the chosen level exclude it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Read committed where the domain needs only that independent rows stay independent: two agents editing different orders. Serializable, or an explicit row lock, where two reads feeding one write must not interleave — read both balances, then write both. There the domain can name the loss: an account debited twice, a seat sold twice.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Shipping the default and calling it correct. Read-modify-write in code — read 300, compute, write the absolute value back — can lose an update on engines that give each statement a fresh snapshot, with no error. On engines where a transaction reads one frozen snapshot, the second writer on the same row aborts while write skew — two rows, each written on the other’s stale value — still commits. The over-defence is equally competent: the strictest level everywhere, buying deadlocks and retries for anomalies that never mattered.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the chosen level rule out the anomaly that would actually hurt this domain, on this engine? Name the transaction and the loss.

If yes → the level is chosen, not inherited. Check the engine enforces it, not merely that the standard lists it.
If no → you inherited a default. Name the money-losing interleaving first, then take the lowest level that excludes it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the transactions that read then write, and ask which pair the business would refuse.




#Database #IsolationLevels #Transactions #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Concurrency

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: LINQ deferred execution
A query runs twice, the collection changes in between, and the count stops matching the items it counted.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A LINQ chain over IEnumerable compiles to a tower of iterator objects, one per operator, not to a loop. Nothing reads the source until something calls MoveNext. The trade: you get a composable description that always reflects the source as it is at that moment, and you pay for it by re-running the whole pipeline on each enumeration.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The result is a function of the source at enumeration time, not at the line the query sits on. To know what the code does, you must know every site that enumerates it, how often each runs, and whether anything writes to the source between them. The variable looks like a value and behaves like a method.
The gap question: how many times is this query enumerated, and can the source change between the enumerations?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A pipeline built in stages — filter in one method, project in another, order in a third — materialized once at the end. Deferral is what lets the stages compose without a list per stage, and the result equals the query.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The query held as a value. It is logged, counted, and iterated by a foreach, and the source is a list something else appends to: the count disagrees with the items, and the report states a total from before the last write. Or it is enumerated inside a loop over ten thousand rows, and each row re-reads the store — N+1 produced by deferral, in code that reads as one query assigned to one variable.








TipThe faithfulness test



How many times is this query enumerated — counted — and can the source change between them?

If yes → one enumeration, and no writer between. The deferral is the composition and costs only what you planned. Check the source’s lifetime next.
If no → the query was a description where you needed a result. Materialize where it is consumed, and the second execution disappears.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Count the enumeration sites, then find every writer to the source.

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: IQueryable versus IEnumerable
One AsEnumerable() mid-chain, and every filter after it reads rows the database already sent.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: They share extension-method names, not methods, and compile to different artifacts. IEnumerable<T> binds to Enumerable: each operator becomes an iterator object over the sequence. IQueryable<T> binds to Queryable, so each operator appends a node to an expression tree that a provider reads and translates — the filters become one statement in another language. The trade: the query travels to the data, at the price of every operator being translatable.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The type of the sequence is the claim about where the work runs. Reading a chain, you must know which operators the provider can translate, whether an untranslatable one throws or falls back to memory, and where the type changed. Same syntax, two locations, nothing in the line announcing the switch.
The gap question: does each chain’s type say where it runs, and is the location the one you need?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Each segment declares its type: the repository hands back IQueryable for the part the store can answer — filter, project, order, page — and the method that needs a regex, a compiled delegate, or a domain object materializes explicitly. The declaration reads as a map of execution.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An AsEnumerable(), a ToList(), or a helper taking IEnumerable<T> inserted mid-chain to satisfy a signature. It compiles, returns the right rows, and the rest of the query runs in memory: the filter that should have shrunk the result set scans it, and the cost grows with the table. In review it reads as a style preference: both sides are sequences.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each LINQ chain: does its type say where it executes — and does the execution location match the claim?

If yes → the type transition is deliberate. Check that the operators left on the provider side are translatable, and watch the fallbacks.
If no → the sequence acquired a type nobody chose. Move the materialization to the type transition, and widen the helper to IQueryable; keep the filter with the data.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Print the expression tree and read the provider’s translation.

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: Iterator blocks (yield return)
The null check in your iterator throws three frames from the caller, inside someone else’s foreach.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A method containing yield return is not compiled as an ordinary method. The compiler emits a class implementing the returned interface — IEnumerable<T> or IEnumerator<T> — with fields for the current item and a state number; your body becomes MoveNext, resumable at each yield. The trade: a lazy, resumable sequence, against a body that has not run at all when the call returns.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The call returns the state machine, not a value: the arguments are captured now, and the body, guard included, waits for the first MoveNext. A guard belongs to the consumer’s schedule, not the caller’s. To know when the guard fires, you must know who enumerates, and when — knowledge your signature does not carry.
The gap question: which of these iterator methods validate their arguments, and does that validation run when the caller expects it?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



An iterator paired with a wrapper: the public method validates eagerly — null guard, range check — then returns the private iterator. The guard runs at call time, in the caller’s frame, and the body stays lazy. The split is the knowledge.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The guard inside the yield method, because that is where the parameter is used. It looks defensive, reads as validation, and fires at the first MoveNext — after the caller’s try block has closed, in another layer’s foreach. A unit test asserting a throw on construction fails while the guard is present. Worse, the method is called for a side effect — a logger, a connection opened in the body — and none of it happens: nobody enumerated.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which iterator methods validate their arguments — and does that validation run when the caller expects?

If yes → eager guards, lazy body. Make sure the guard set is complete, then check what the body does on disposal — the last resumption it triggers.
If no → the validation is on the consumer’s schedule. Split the method, keeping the body lazy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the callers, then mark where the first MoveNext happens.

title: The C# Language
section: Case study: Expression trees (code as data)
text:
Case study: Expression trees (code as data)
A pricing rule is written once as C#, handed to a database as SQL, and never runs in the process that wrote it.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Expression<Func<Order, decimal>> compiles to IL that builds a tree, not to IL that runs the rule. The compiler emits a tree of node objects — ParameterExpression, MemberExpression, BinaryExpression — that a library reads, rewrites, and hands to another engine. The trade is inspection for expressiveness: a statement body, an assignment, or an await in the lambda is a compile error, so the code-as-data boundary announces itself at the lambda and nowhere else.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The type claims a second engine can reproduce this code. That claim is about your program, not about C#: only you know whether the rule means anything apart from the machine evaluating it. The compiler checks the tree’s shape; it never checks that two engines agree on what the shape means.
The gap question: does every expression survive translation — verified — or is something lost in transit?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A rule that must run twice: expr.Compile() over one order in memory, the same tree translated to SQL over a million rows. Both engines read the rule as data, so one edit reaches both — the disagreement, when it comes, comes in the translation.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A call the provider cannot translate: a culture-sensitive ToString(), a local helper, a DateTime comparison with an unstated Kind. Sometimes it throws — loud, survivable. Sometimes it translates to different semantics: collation (the database’s text-comparison rules), null ordering, decimal rounding. Zero test failures, because both sides pass their own tests.








TipThe faithfulness test



For this code-as-data boundary: does every expression survive translation — verified — or is something lost in transit?

If yes → the tree is the domain’s rule, portable by construction. Check each provider’s translation of collation, null ordering, and date handling against the local delegate.
If no → the code is a delegate wearing a tree’s type. Write it as a delegate and run it where it was written.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Enumerate the tree’s node types, then the provider’s translation table, and diff the two.




#DotNet #CSharp #ExpressionTrees #LINQ #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
section: Case study: Extension methods (the static call in member clothing)
text:
Case study: Extension methods (the static call in member clothing)
The call reads like a member on your own type, resolves to a static method a using brought in, and accepts null as a legal receiver.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: value.Normalize() compiles to TextExtensions.Normalize(value), the receiver as first argument. No virtual dispatch: binding is fixed at compile time by the namespaces in scope, and an instance member of that name always wins. The trade is methods on a type you do not own, paid for with scope resolution — and a this parameter that may arrive null.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The syntax claims the operation belongs to the type. Whether it does is your program’s fact, not C#’s. The compiler resolves by scope — innermost level first, then outward, and ties inside a level are ambiguous — so a call site rebinds after a using someone added for another reason.
The gap question: is the receiver checked — and would the reader know this is a static method, not a member?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Extensions in one namespace per concern, imported only where it applies — WhereActive on IQueryable<User> — each guarding this with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull, so the call fails at the entry point it really has.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



maybeNull.OrEmpty(). The syntax reads like a safe member call, so nobody asks whether the receiver could be null — and without a guard the NullReferenceException is thrown inside the extension, not at the call site.
The silent one: a later package version adds a real member of that name, every call site recompiled against it binds to the instance method (same syntax, different body), and behavior changes with no diff in your repository.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each extension call: is the receiver checked — and would the reader know this is a static method, not a member?

If yes → a deliberate widening of a type you do not own. Keep the guard, keep the namespace narrow.
If no → a static helper wearing instance syntax: bound by scope, invisible to dispatch, unguarded on null. Make it an explicit static call, or a type you own.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the using directives each file needs, then check whether the type already ships that member.




#DotNet #CSharp #ExtensionMethods #APIDesign #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
section: Case study: Nullable value types (absence as a value)
text:
Case study: Nullable value types (absence as a value)
A total goes null at one unguarded multiplication, and the invoice ships with a zero nobody chose.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: int? is Nullable<int>: a bool and an int in one struct. The compiler lifts every int operator, and the families disagree. Lifted arithmetic returns int? — null + 5 is null, and the null spreads. Lifted comparison returns bool — null < 5 is false, and so is null >= 5. The trade is declared absence, with operators that answer silently instead of throwing.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
Whether “no value” is a fact about this number is your program’s knowledge, not the type’s. The type admits absence and steps aside: it never asks what absence means for a sum or a threshold.
The gap question: where does null enter this computation — listed — and is each entry point a stated decision or a lifted operator nobody chose?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A measurement that may not exist: a sensor reading. HasValue guards the branch that needs a number, ?? throw kills the path that must have one, and GetValueOrDefault(fallback) writes the substitute down, because 0 is a legal price.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The arithmetic chain. subtotal * discountRate * taxRate, every factor nullable: one null and the result is null, flowing until a ?? 0m makes it a zero someone signs.
The comparison is worse. if (x < threshold) Alert(); never fires when x is null; as if (!(x < threshold)) Alert(); it fires on every missing reading. Two branches, opposite failures, one absent value.








TipThe faithfulness test



Where does null enter this computation — listed — and is each entry point a stated decision or a lifted operator nobody chose?

If yes → absence is modeled with declared semantics. Check that every ?? fallback is a domain decision, not a zero-fill.
If no → a lifted operator chose for you: null propagates through arithmetic and becomes a bool through comparison. Test HasValue at the entry; never compare a nullable to a threshold without deciding what absence means.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List every ?? and lifted operator on the path, and name the null each handles.




#DotNet #CSharp #NullableValueTypes #ValueTypes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: Generic constraints
“where T : IComparable<T>” tells the compiler every T can be compared — and the path that crosses as object passes a type that cannot.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A where clause compiles to metadata on the method, not to a check inside the body: the runtime verifies it when a concrete type argument closes the method, and the compiler verifies it at every call site that names one. Both checks are free and total — and scoped to the generic door: the call path that names a type argument. A path that never closes the method never instantiates it.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
A constraint is a claim about every type that closes this method: comparable, constructible, a reference type, non-null. The developer must know which of those the body actually uses — a new() constraint on a method that never calls new states a requirement the algorithm does not have. The gap question: which types reach this code, and do they all arrive through the constrained door?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



The constraint states exactly what the algorithm does with T and nothing more: IComparable<T> on a sort, new() on a factory, class where the null check depends on it. Every call site becomes a proof obligation the compiler discharges, and the signature documents the requirement.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Developers trust the constraint past the generic door. The same algorithm is reached through object and through a non-generic interface. On those paths the promise is checked nowhere, so the failure surfaces as an InvalidCastException deep in a library that “cannot” receive it. The constraint was never wrong. The door beside it was unguarded.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each constraint: does every caller reach this code through the checked path — or is there a door that skips the check?

If yes → it is enforced where the traffic is. Check next that no constraint claims more than the body uses.
If no → it guards a fraction of the callers. Close the non-generic door, or validate at it — a check you now maintain by hand.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the constraint wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own call graph. List every entry into the method, generic and not.




#DotNet #CSharp #Generics #TypeSafety #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
section: Case study: checked and unchecked arithmetic
text:
Case study: checked and unchecked arithmetic
Two positive amounts sum to a negative total, nothing throws, and the report prints that total as a number.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Integral arithmetic is unchecked by default: the compiler emits the wrapping add and multiply, and an overflow disappears in silence. A checked block or expression emits the overflowing forms, and the runtime raises OverflowException as the result leaves the type’s range. The trade: a condition the program can detect, against a number it cannot tell from a correct one. Decimal throws on overflow; int and long wrap.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know the stated upper bound of the operands, and whether the code enforces it before the arithmetic runs. A bound in a comment is not enforced; a bound validated where input enters is. The gap question: what is the largest value this expression can reach, given every input path into it?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Checked context on the arithmetic whose operands are user-sized: amounts in cents, record counts, buffer indexes. There the domain already fixed a bound — the invoice maximum, the page size — and checked arithmetic turns that stated bound into a failure at the exact expression that breached it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The sum that silently wrapped. Every test uses small numbers, the default emits no overflow check, and nothing warns. A year of correct totals ends negative, found only when the figure fits no report. The wrapped value sat inside the type, plausible, and traveled through three aggregates before anyone read it as impossible. The code never stated what it assumed about magnitude, so the language assumed nothing.








TipThe faithfulness test



For this arithmetic: what is the stated upper bound of the operands — and does the code enforce it, or wrap around it?

If yes → the bound is a fact the code holds. Check next that validation sits on every path, not only the parsed one.
If no → the range is an assumption, not knowledge. State the bound and validate it where input enters — checked only throws at the breach.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the arithmetic wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Measure the largest operands in production; compare them to the type.




#DotNet #CSharp #Arithmetic #Correctness #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: string comparison
The same identifier matches on your laptop and fails on a server whose locale is Turkish, with no code change.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: Equality is ordinal: == on string compiles to String.Equals, which compares characters exactly and consults no culture. Ordering is not: string.Compare and CompareTo default to the current culture, so they return 0 for some strings that are not byte-equal, and produce an order that moves with the host’s locale. Casing sits between them: ToUpper() reads the current culture too. Three truths — byte, culture, case rule — and one operator that picks the first.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know what the string is: identifier, key, or a label a human reads. An identifier needs byte truth; a sorted display list needs the reader’s culture; a case-insensitive login needs a case rule. One type serves all three, so the mode is a claim the code never checks. The gap question: which truth does this comparison claim, and is that the truth this key needs?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



The mode is chosen per use: Ordinal for identifiers, keys, file paths; OrdinalIgnoreCase where case carries no meaning but characters do; culture rules only where a human reads the difference, as in a sorted list for a German UI. Then each comparison states its fact.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The Turkish-i problem. An identifier is normalized with ToUpper() and no invariant culture, so the lowercase i becomes İ on a tr-TR host and the key stops matching itself. The developer never chose a culture; ToUpper() chose the host’s. Beside it, Compare(a, b) == 0 used as equality: two distinct keys declared identical because the culture ignores the difference, and a duplicate slips past the uniqueness check meant to catch it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each string comparison: which truth does it claim — byte, culture, or case — and is that the truth this key needs?

If yes → the mode is knowledge. Check next that the culture you get is the one you meant, not the host’s.
If no → the comparison is a default, not a decision. Name the mode at the call site and remove the ToUpper().
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the comparison wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own key. Ask what the string identifies, then who reads it.




#DotNet #CSharp #Strings #Localization #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: The C# Language
text:
Case study: the event keyword
One assignment to a public delegate field erases every subscriber; no compiler error marks the line.
Writing a C# construct? Ask “when does this code actually run — now, on enumeration, at the provider — and what claim does its type make?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the language catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A field-like event compiles to a private delegate field plus two public accessors, add and remove. Any code may subscribe; only the declaring type may invoke or reassign it, and the compiler enforces both. A public delegate field compiles to no accessors at all: read, invoke, assign, all legal from anywhere. The trade is one rule — who may raise this — held by the compiler or by convention.


The C# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know two facts about their own program: which object owns the decision to raise, and which object outlives which. The second is a lifetime fact. Every subscription is a reference from publisher to subscriber, so a long-lived publisher holds every subscriber that never unsubscribed. The gap question: who may invoke this, and does each subscriber unsubscribe when its own lifetime ends?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Events with subscribe and unsubscribe written as a pair: handler added in a constructor, removed in Dispose or on detach. The publisher is the only raiser, so every raise site sits in one file. The lifetime relation is stated, not assumed: the window subscribes to the store and unsubscribes before it closes.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A public delegate field: any caller invokes it, any caller assigns it, wiping every other subscriber. The event semantics exist in a comment; the bytecode has none. Beside it, the subscriber that never unsubscribed: a view model on a singleton, closed, alive because the singleton holds its handler. The leak grows an object per navigation, and the retained object still receives events after its window closes.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each event: who may invoke it — enforced — and does every subscriber unsubscribe when its lifetime ends?

If yes → the rule and the lifetime are both knowledge. Check next that the unsubscribe runs on the failure path too.
If no → you hold the semantics in convention. Replace the field with an event, and detach when the subscriber closes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own object graph. Draw the publisher and its subscribers, then mark which dies first.




#DotNet #CSharp #Events #MemoryLeaks #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
An architecture question usually arrives with a safe generic answer: microservices scale, queues decouple, a cache makes it fast. Each post below takes one such question, states the generic answer, and asks which fact of this system decides it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Monolith, Modular Monolith, or Microservices

Question: “How do you decide between a monolith, a modular monolith, and microservices for a new system?”

The question hides two independent decisions.

Where the boundaries go — what belongs together.
Whether the pieces deploy independently — monolith versus microservices.

A modular monolith and a microservices system can have identical boundaries. They differ only in redeployment: “microservices” answers the deployment question, not the boundary question.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Decision 1: the boundaries — three principles, not three answers
Three principles can govern where boundaries go: - IVP: group elements that change together; separate those that change apart. - Cohesion: group elements that are functionally related. - Coupling: place boundaries to minimise dependencies across them.
They are not independent. When cost is dominated by maintenance — the common case — all three converge on nearly the same partition: keep together what changes together, separate what changes apart. Three vocabularies, one structure; that is why the boundary question feels like a single question.
They diverge only when another cost dominates: performance, distribution, security. Then coupling and cohesion stop meaning change locality, and the principles disagree — marking where a non-maintenance cost governs the design.
Decision 2: redeployment independence — the domain also decides
Deployment separation buys three things: independent release cadence, independent scaling, independent failure isolation. Each is a domain fact, not a default. Two modules need separate deployment only when the domain makes one of them true: - Cadence: they change at different rates and must ship separately. - Scaling: one faces different load and must grow on its own. - Isolation: one must survive, or be contained, when the other fails.
If the domain requires none of these, microservices buys an independence nobody asked for — and pays a network, a consistency window, and a failure mode for it.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



Boundaries follow the change structure; the three principles agree. Deployment is split only where cadence, scaling, or isolation differ.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Boundaries cut across things that change together — or services are split for “scale” while the domain forces lockstep releases. The topology asserts an independence the domain never granted.








TipThe faithfulness test



Two questions, kept apart:

What belongs together? → the domain’s change structure answers it; the three principles agree here.
Must these deploy apart? → cadence, scaling, and isolation answer it.

If you can’t answer either, the diagram is choosing both.
Start with the domain, then choose the packaging. The architecture is underneath; the topology is downstream.



#Microservices #ModularMonolith #Modularization #IVP #Cohesion #Coupling #DomainDrivenDesign #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Principle of Least Surprises

Question: “How do you apply the Principle of Least Surprises when designing components?”

Least surprise is usually taught as consistency: don’t be clever, don’t hide side effects. The domain-knowledge reading is stronger. Surprise is what the caller could not predict because the component answered a domain question the caller did not know was being answered.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A component surprises when its behavior encodes domain knowledge the caller cannot see — a default, an ordering, a rounding, an implicit rule. Every default is a silent claim: “this is the normal case.” Every surprising side effect is a domain decision the interface failed to name.
Least surprise is therefore not a style preference. It is a completeness check on whether the domain knowledge is visible where it is used.






ImportantThe domain mandates clarity



The domain rule exists and the interface names it. The caller can predict the outcome because the rule is in the vocabulary. A payment method that rejects amounts below one cent is not surprising — the minimum is a stated business rule.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The rule hides in an implementation default: the “sensible” timezone, the “usual” tax rate, the “standard” retry. The caller is surprised because an unstated domain decision fired. The fix is not less surprise in the code; it is naming the domain fact the code already assumes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a caller who knows the domain, but not this implementation, predict the behavior?

If yes → the knowledge is visible.
If no → a domain decision is buried; surface it.
If unclear → you have found knowledge nobody wrote down, which is exactly why it surprises.




#LeastSurprise #API #Defaults #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DesignPrinciples

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Accidental Complexity at Scale

Question: “How do you avoid accidental complexity when scaling a system?”

The usual answer is a checklist: cache, shard, queue, replicate, split. That checklist is where accidental complexity is born. The domain-knowledge lens separates the complexity the problem forces from the complexity a technology choice adds.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Scale itself is not a requirement until the domain names it. “Handle more traffic” is not a domain fact; “the month-end close must finish before the regulator’s deadline” is. Distribution, caching, and sharding each add a coupling — consistency windows, failure modes, partition keys. Those couplings are justified only when a domain property requires them.
Complexity added ahead of the domain reason is accidental by definition.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



A real forcing condition exists: data must survive an availability zone, a workload must finish inside a legal window, two regions must stay live for latency the customers contracted for. Then the added machinery encodes a known requirement, and you can name the domain fact each piece serves.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



You cannot name the domain fact any component serves; the architecture exists “to be scalable” for load nobody measured or promised. Now every added piece is a coupling with no mandate — the accidental complexity the question warned about, introduced by the very attempt to avoid it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each scaling mechanism, name the domain fact it satisfies.

If every component has one → the complexity is essential and justified.
If some have none → remove them; you added the accident.
If unclear → the requirement is unwritten; write it before the code, not after.




#Scalability #AccidentalComplexity #DistributedSystems #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #YAGNI

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Synchronous or Asynchronous

Question: “How do you choose between synchronous and asynchronous communication?”

The decision is usually framed as a performance and resilience trade-off. The domain-knowledge lens reframes it: sync versus async is a statement about time — and a measured limit can revise that statement.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Synchronous says: the caller needs the answer now, as part of this activity. Asynchronous says: the caller can continue before the answer exists, and the answer will be handled later. Both are claims about what the business expects — whether a step is part of the current act or a separate future act. The transport (HTTP, message, stream) merely encodes that expectation.






ImportantThe domain mandates it




Synchronous: the customer is waiting to see the seat confirmed before payment; the answer must exist before the activity can continue.
Asynchronous: a shipment is arranged after the order is accepted. The order does not need the courier’s answer to be an order. The domain treats the step as a later act with its own life.

A second source: processing time
Sometimes the caller wants the answer now, but the computation cannot finish inside any tolerable window. Processing time rules out the synchronous form. A test reveals this. Once measured, the limit revises the temporal expectation itself: the step is now known to be a later act. The domain knowledge switches to async in intent — it is no longer a sync step the machine fails to serve. The revision is scoped to the tested platform, hardware, OS, and configuration; change the environment, and the fact must be re-established.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Choosing async for throughput, or sync for “simplicity,” while the domain expects the opposite. A customer told “order placed” over an async pipeline that later fails has been promised something the flow could not deliver. A synchronous chain for a step the business treats as separate couples the two activities and makes a failure in one look like a failure in both.








TipThe faithfulness test



Two questions:

Does the current activity need the answer, or is the answer a separate later act?
If it needs the answer, can the machine deliver it inside the tolerable window?

Match the interaction to both. If unclear → the temporal expectation is unwritten, and the technology default is deciding. If a measured limit rules out the synchronous form, the knowledge switches to async in intent — record the limit with its platform and configuration.



#SyncVsAsync #Messaging #EventDriven #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance #DistributedSystems

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Idempotent Operations

Question: “How do you design idempotent operations for systems with retries?”

The standard answer is a dedup key and a seen-set. The domain-knowledge lens shows that the hard part is not the mechanism. It is deciding what “the same operation” means — and only the domain can.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Retries are a transport concern. Duplicates are a domain possibility with domain meaning. Idempotency is the rule “doing this again with the same identity is a no-op.” The identity is the domain’s: the order number, the trade reference, the invoice id.
If the dedup key is a message UUID, the system catches transport retries but misses the real duplicate: the customer who clicked twice, the two batches carrying the same instruction.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain already defines when two things are the same act, and repeating it changes nothing: paying invoice 7 twice pays it once. The idempotency key is that identity, and the handler enforces the domain’s own rule. This removes the dependence on at-most-once delivery the domain never should have trusted.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The key is technical and the domain identity is absent. Duplicate orders, double bookings, and double charges slip through under different message ids. The system is idempotent for the infrastructure’s duplicates, not the domain’s.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert use this key to decide “this was already done”?

If yes → idempotent at the right level.
If no → you deduplicate the transport and miss the domain.
If unclear → the identity concept is unwritten.




#Idempotency #Retries #DistributedSystems #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #EIP #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Race Conditions

Question: “How would you prevent race conditions in a high-throughput workflow?”

The reflex is locks, transactions, and actors. The domain-knowledge lens asks first: is the contention a fact about the world, or an artifact of how we built it?

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A race condition matters only when two conflicting operations touch something the domain says cannot be shared inconsistently. Sometimes that is real: one seat, one parking spot, ten license seats, one account balance. The constraint — “only N at once,” “only one owner” — is domain knowledge. Other times the “contention” is an implementation accident: two workers updating the same cache row or the same counter that exists only for bookkeeping.






ImportantThe domain mandates protection



The domain names the scarce resource and its rule: “a seat belongs to one booking.” Then the lock or the atomic transition encodes a real invariant, and the throughput question becomes “how do we respect the constraint quickly,” not “how do we avoid locks.”








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The contended object has no domain meaning — it is a technical counter, a shared cache, a statistics row. Locking it serializes the whole workflow to protect a fact nobody in the business needs protected. The throughput loss is real; the invariant it defends is not.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the contended thing a domain-scarce resource with a stated rule?

If yes → protect the invariant.
If no → remove the shared state or confine it; you are racing to protect a fiction.
If unclear → the resource and its rule are unwritten.




#RaceConditions #Concurrency #Locks #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #HighThroughput

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Queues, Streams, or Direct Calls

Question: “How do you decide when to use queues, streams, or direct calls?”

The comparison usually weighs latency, durability, and ordering. The domain-knowledge lens reduces it to one question: does the domain treat this as one activity, or as a fact others will care about?

The architecture knowledge gap it signals

A direct call says: this is part of one activity; I need the answer to continue.
A queue says: do this later, once; the work is addressed to a consumer.
A stream says: this happened; anyone who cares may observe it, possibly many times, possibly replaying.

Choosing the mechanism encodes a claim about who cares, how many, and when — all domain facts.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



A direct call when the step is inseparable from the caller’s activity. A queue when the domain has a piece of deferred work with one owner (“send this statement”). A stream when the domain has events others legitimately need and history matters (“a payment cleared,” seen by billing, fraud, and reporting).








WarningThe domain doesn’t



A queue for something with many real consumers, losing the later ones. A stream for what is really a command one consumer must execute. A direct call for a step the domain treats as a separate later act, coupling both lives. The mechanism asserts semantics the domain never assigned.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who cares that the fact happened, how many, and may they replay?
The answer sorts the three. If unclear → the domain’s event and command structure is unwritten, and the tool is deciding.



#Queues #EventStreaming #EventDriven #DomainEvent #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #EIP

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Sagas for Long-Running Workflows

Question: “What’s the role of sagas in long-running workflows?”

A saga sequences local steps and, on failure, compensates the completed ones. The domain-knowledge lens: a saga is legitimate only when the domain itself knows how to undo each step.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Compensation is not a technical rollback. It is a domain act — cancel a booking, refund a charge, restock a shipment. The domain must already perform these reversals in the real world. If it does, the saga is the domain’s own “how we undo this” rules made executable, and it correctly refuses to pretend a cross-boundary process is atomic.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The process spans boundaries that cannot be one transaction, and each completed step has a real, named reversal. Then a saga is the code catching up to knowledge the business already holds. This is the pattern’s whole justification: the domain knows how to reverse each act.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The “compensation” is a data cleanup only engineers understand, or the steps are atomic within one boundary. The saga then invents undo actions the business never named. It asserts per-step reversibility nobody decided.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain perform these reversals — a cancellation, a refund, a restock — or would the “compensation” be a cleanup only engineers understand?

If yes → applicable; compensations are the domain’s own reverse acts.
If no → inapplicable; name the reversals or keep one transaction.
If unclear → the undo knowledge is unwritten.




#Saga #CompensatingTransaction #DistributedTransactions #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Concurrency

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Exactly-Once Processing

Question: “How do you design for exactly-once or effectively-once processing guarantees?”

Exactly-once delivery across a network is a myth. Effectively-once is achievable — but only if the domain defines “once.” The domain-knowledge lens: the guarantee lives in the domain identity, not the transport.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
“Exactly-once” means: the effect happens once even if the message arrives many times. To know it happened once, you must know what “it” is — a domain identity. Effectively-once is idempotent handling keyed by that identity, plus durable state. Without the domain identity, you can suppress transport duplicates but not semantic ones.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain defines the operative identity and treats repeats as the same act (“invoice 7 may be paid once”). Then exactly-once is a domain rule enforced by an identity and a recorded outcome. The guarantee is real because the identity is real.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The key is a transport id, and two genuine domain duplicates carry different ids. The system claims exactly-once while double-processing the very cases the business fears.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain say when two messages describe one act?

If yes → effectively-once is achievable on that identity.
If no → you have exactly-once for retries and none for reality.
If unclear → the identity is unwritten; that is the gap.




#ExactlyOnce #Idempotency #Messaging #DomainKnowledge #DistributedSystems #SoftwareArchitecture #EIP

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Partial Failures

Question: “How do you handle partial failures in distributed systems?”

Retries, timeouts, compensations, let-it-fail — the menu is technical. But “what should happen when this step fails midway?” is a business question: legal deadlines, SLA promises, manual fallbacks, who gets notified.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A partial failure is not just a technical state. It is often a domain state with a name: “order accepted but not confirmed,” “payment captured but not settled.” The domain decides whether that intermediate state is allowed, how long it may persist, and who resolves it. The failure-handling strategy should encode those decisions.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain names the partial state and its remedy: escalate to a human after N hours, refund automatically, hold the order for a promised window. Then retries, timeouts, and compensations carry real meaning — each is a domain rule for a named intermediate state.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The failure handling is generic: infinite retry, silent drop, a log line. No one asked what the business wants to happen when step three of five fails. The technical default decides the outcome, and the domain consequence surfaces as a customer complaint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain name the intermediate state after a partial failure and what must happen in it?

If yes → the strategy encodes knowledge.
If no → you have left a business outcome to a retry policy.
If unclear → the intermediate-state knowledge is unwritten.




#PartialFailure #Resilience #DistributedSystems #DomainKnowledge #ErrorHandling #SoftwareArchitecture #SLA

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Consistency Across Services

Question: “What patterns help maintain consistency across multiple services?”

Eventual consistency, sagas, outbox, two-phase commit — the patterns are tools. The domain-knowledge lens: consistency is not a global setting. It is a per-fact claim about which things must agree at once, and the domain owns that claim.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
“Consistent” is meaningless without the unit. The domain decides what counts as one indivisible fact: an order and its line items must agree always; an order and its analytics record may lag. Cross-service consistency is a set of domain-drawn transaction boundaries, expressed across process seams. The pattern should follow the boundary, never define it.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



Two facts are one unit in the domain and must change together: money debits and credits, a booking and its seat. Then the pattern — a saga, a single transaction, an outbox — preserves a real invariant.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Two facts are independent in the domain but bolted together by a pattern “for safety,” or two parts of one unit are split and reconciled “for scale.” The first adds coordination the domain never needed; the second risks violating an invariant the domain always had.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which facts must agree at the same instant, in the domain’s own terms?
That defines the boundary. Pick the pattern to honor it. If unclear → the unit of consistency is unwritten, and the framework is deciding.



#Consistency #EventualConsistency #Saga #Outbox #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Microservices

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Resilience to Dependency Failure

Question: “How do you design a resilient system that survives external dependency failures?”

Circuits, bulkheads, retries — but resilience is not a property you bolt on. It is a set of decisions about what to do when a dependency dies, and those decisions are domain ones.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
When an external system fails, the domain must say what is acceptable: keep serving from a cached or alternate source, degrade a feature, queue and reconcile later, or fail loudly. Each is a business stance. A circuit breaker is only the mechanism; the fallback is the knowledge.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain names the fallback: use the secondary supplier, take payments offline and key them in later, show the last-known price. Then the resilience pattern encodes a real business rule, and the failure has a designed, lawful outcome.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The fallback is an engineering guess — serve stale data, return a default, silently drop. No one asked whether the business permits it. The system “survives” the outage by doing something the domain never sanctioned.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain name what must happen when this dependency fails?

If yes → the mechanism encodes knowledge.
If no → resilience is cosmetic; the outage still decides the outcome.
If unclear → the fallback rule is unwritten.




#Resilience #CircuitBreaker #Fallback #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems #SLA

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Detecting and Isolating Slow Services

Question: “What’s your approach to detecting and isolating slow services?”

Dashboards, timeouts, bulkheads. But “slow” is relative to a promise. The domain-knowledge lens: a service is slow only against a deadline the domain cares about, and isolation serves that deadline.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Latency is not a domain fact by itself; a promised response time is. “Checkout must answer in 2 seconds” or “the nightly settlement must finish by 6 a.m.” is domain knowledge. Timeouts and bulkheads should encode those promises, not arbitrary constants.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



A stated deadline exists — an SLA, a legal window, a customer expectation. Then the timeout is that promise, and isolating the slow dependency protects the paths that carry promises. The threshold is defended by a named commitment.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The timeout is a round number pulled from a template; nothing breaks differently at 1s versus 3s in domain terms. Then calls are cut off arbitrarily, and “isolation” protects no promise — it protects a guess.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which domain promise does this timeout defend?

If a real one → the threshold encodes knowledge.
If none → you have invented a deadline.
If unclear → the promise is unwritten; write it before picking the number.




#Latency #Timeouts #Bulkhead #SLA #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Observability

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Caching Layers

Question: “How do you design caching layers (L1/L2) to avoid stale data and thundering herds?”

TTLs, jitter, single-flight — but the first question is not “how long” in technical terms. It is “how stale may this answer be?” — and that is a domain freshness tolerance.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A cache is a bet that a slightly old answer is acceptable. The size of “slightly” is domain knowledge: account balances may be seconds fresh; a product description may be hours stale; a tax rate changes once a year and is not stale for months. L1 versus L2, TTL, and invalidation all encode that tolerance. Thundering herds are technical, but they exist because the tolerance was set and the refresh synchronized.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain states a freshness tolerance per fact. Then each layer’s TTL is that tolerance, and invalidation is triggered by the domain event that makes the value wrong.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



A uniform TTL from a default, unrelated to what any fact tolerates. Some data serves stale and violates a promise; other data is refreshed needlessly, wasting capacity. The cache asserts a freshness policy the domain never set.








TipThe faithfulness test



What staleness does the domain permit for this value, and which event invalidates it?

If stated → the TTL encodes knowledge.
If not → the number is a guess.
If unclear → the freshness tolerance is unwritten.




#Caching #CacheInvalidation #ThunderingHerd #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Vertical or Horizontal Scaling

Question: “What are the signals that a system needs vertical scaling vs horizontal scaling?”

CPU graphs and cost curves are the usual signals. The domain-knowledge lens: the real signal is whether the domain allows the workload to be split, and whether growth is in a shared resource or independent ones.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Horizontal scaling assumes the work can be partitioned and the state replicated without breaking a domain invariant. Vertical scaling assumes it cannot — one big node is the honest shape. Which is true depends on the domain: can two orders be handled by two machines with no shared invariant? Can one ledger be?






ImportantThe domain mandates it



If the domain’s units of work and state partition cleanly, horizontal scaling matches reality. If the domain has a genuinely single, centralized thing — one account sequence, one authoritative counter — vertical scaling respects that.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Horizontal “scaling” applied to something with a global invariant, forcing distributed coordination to preserve what one machine held naturally. Or vertical scaling of something trivially partitionable, paying ever-larger machine prices for no domain reason.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the domain’s work and state be split without breaking an invariant?

If yes → horizontal.
If one invariant must stay whole → vertical, or re-architect the invariant.
If unclear → the domain’s decomposition is unknown.




#Scaling #VerticalScaling #HorizontalScaling #Partitioning #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Read-Heavy Workloads

Question: “How do you design read-heavy workloads for maximum throughput?”

Replicas, caches, denormalization, CQRS. But “maximum throughput” is the trap. Throughput is bounded by what the readers are allowed to see. Freshness tolerance, not horsepower, sets the ceiling.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Reads are cheap to scale only if they may be served from a copy. Whether they may — and how stale the copy may be — is domain knowledge. A price shown to browsing users may lag; a price shown at checkout may not. CQRS and read replicas are domain claims that reads are separable from writes and tolerate a delay.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain distinguishes reads that tolerate staleness from reads that do not. Then replicas and read models serve the tolerant ones, and the strict ones read the source of truth. Throughput rises along the line the domain drew.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Every read is pushed behind a replica or cache “for throughput,” including the ones that must be current. The system is fast and wrong at the moment it matters — the final stock check, the balance at withdrawal.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which reads must reflect the latest write, and which may lag?

If the domain answers → scale the lagging ones.
If not → you are trading correctness for speed blindly.
If unclear → the freshness split is unwritten.




#CQRS #ReadReplicas #Throughput #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Database Load Without Losing Consistency

Question: “What patterns help reduce database load without harming consistency?”

The question already concedes the constraint — consistency — but which consistency? The domain-knowledge lens: “harm” is domain-specific, and the patterns only work once you know which invariant is load-bearing.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
Denormalization, caching, materialized views, and read models all reduce load by keeping a second copy. They are safe exactly when the copy may lag for the domain’s purposes. The load reduction is real; whether it “harms consistency” depends on whether the lagged fact is one the domain requires to be current.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



A fact is read-tolerant in the domain — reporting, browsing, search — even though it is written strictly. Then a read model or cache absorbs the load without touching any invariant.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



A lookup that participates in an invariant is served from a lagging copy: the overdraft check reads a five-second-old balance. Load fell; the invariant silently broke. Nobody asked which reads were allowed to lag.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each offloaded read, does the domain require the value to be current when read?

If no → offload it.
If yes → keep it on the source.
If unclear → the invariant is unidentified.




#Database #ReadModels #Denormalization #Consistency #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Hot Partitions

Question: “How do you approach hot partition problems?”

The obvious move is to salt the key or spread the load. The domain-knowledge lens: a hot partition usually means the domain funnels many operations through one entity — and that entity often exists for a reason.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A partition key is an identity choice: what makes a thing the same thing. A hot key says “most activity touches this one identity” — the current account, the flagship customer, the singleton counter, the day’s date. The heat is a domain fact before it is a scaling problem. Salt it and you may break the very grouping the domain needs.






ImportantThe domain mandates spreading



The heat is accidental — a skewed key format or a monotonically increasing id. Then re-keying to a domain-meaningful distribution removes the hotspot without touching meaning.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The hot key is a real, single domain entity — one ledger, one tenant, one sequence. Salting splits it and forces coordination to restore the invariant. The scale technique fights the domain.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the hot key a real, singular domain entity or an implementation artifact?

If artifact → re-key.
If real → redesign the invariant or accept the scaling limit honestly.
If unclear → the identity is undecided.




#Partitioning #HotPartition #Sharding #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DistributedSystems #Scalability

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
High-Volume Writes

Question: “How do you handle high-volume write workloads?”

Batching, async writes, log-structured storage, sharding. The domain-knowledge lens: write volume is manageable only after you know whether the domain needs the history, the current state, or both.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
High-volume writes stress the current-state store. If the domain is event-shaped — it needs to know what happened and when — an append-only log is the honest fit and absorbs volume naturally. If the domain cares only about the present value, in-place updates suffice. Choosing between them is a domain claim about history.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain needs the sequence of facts: audit, replay, temporal queries, dispute resolution. Then event-sourced or append-only storage serves a real requirement while scaling writes.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The domain only ever asks for the latest value, yet a log is piled on “for safety.” Storage grows without a consumer of the history; the machinery serves no domain question.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain ever need to ask what happened, not just what is?

If yes → append the facts.
If no → keep current state and scale it.
If unclear → the temporal requirement is unwritten.




#EventSourcing #WriteScaling #AppendOnly #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Database

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Relational or Document Store

Question: “How do you pick between relational vs document database?”

The comparison lists schema flexibility versus joins. The domain-knowledge lens: both really ask “is this one fact or several?” — and that is an aggregate boundary question.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A document database suits data the domain treats as one thing, fetched and changed together — an order with its lines. A relational database suits data whose parts are independent facts that must be queried across — customers, orders, products. The storage model should mirror the domain’s own unit of consistency and retrieval.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain has self-contained aggregates read as a whole and rarely joined. Then documents fit: one read, one write, one invariant. The domain has independent entities joined in many ways. Then relations fit.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



Documents chosen for “flexibility” over data the domain requires to be consistent across kinds. Or tables over data the domain always handles as one unit, forcing artificial joins to reassemble a fact the domain never split.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the data one fact the domain reads together, or several the domain joins?
Match the store to that. If unclear → the aggregate boundary is undecided, and the database is choosing it.



#RelationalDatabase #DocumentDatabase #Aggregate #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DataModeling

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Distributed Transactions or Eventual Consistency

Question: “When would you use distributed transactions vs eventual consistency?”

This is the cleanest domain question in the list. Both patterns answer “what must be true at the same time?” — and only the domain knows.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A distributed transaction asserts: these changes are one indivisible fact across systems. Eventual consistency asserts: these changes are separate facts that will converge. The choice is a domain claim about whether the parts are one unit.






ImportantThe domain mandates one unit



The domain treats the changes as inseparable: a debit and its credit, a stock decrement and its reservation. Then a transaction — or a saga with real reversals — preserves the invariant. Eventual consistency would admit a state the domain forbids.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



The changes are genuinely separate: an order and its search index, a profile and its recommendations. Then eventual consistency is honest — and forcing a distributed transaction buys coordination for two facts the domain never tied together. The coordination cost is the fee for a boundary that does not exist.








TipThe faithfulness test



Are these changes one fact or several, in the domain’s own terms?

If one → atomicity is required.
If several → converge.
If unclear → the unit of consistency is unwritten; that is the gap, not the choice.




#DistributedTransactions #EventualConsistency #Consistency #Saga #DomainDrivenDesign #SoftwareArchitecture #Microservices

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Audit-Friendly Systems

Question: “How do you design an audit-friendly system without killing performance?”

Audit is usually framed as overhead. The domain-knowledge lens: who must be able to answer who-changed-what is a domain — often legal — fact, and what it requires dictates both design and cost.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
“We must be able to prove who changed what” is regulatory, contractual, or safety knowledge. It decides whether you keep an immutable log, for how long, whether history is queryable, and whether current state may be derived from it. The performance tension appears only once those requirements are known — and sometimes disappears, because the audit store is what makes the system fast.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



A real obligation exists — a regulator, a contract, a safety case. Then an append-only history is not overhead but a requirement, and event sourcing may serve both audit and performance at once.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



“Audit” is copied in as a generic nicety, with no rule about what must be reconstructable and for how long. The system pays for history nobody is obliged to consult, or logs too little for a rule that does exist.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is there a named obligation to reconstruct who changed what, and for how long?

If yes → the requirement defines the design.
If no → trim it.
If unclear → the obligation is unwritten and being guessed.




#Audit #Compliance #EventSourcing #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Observability

title: Architecture Problems as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Schema Evolution Without Downtime

Question: “What’s your strategy for schema evolution without downtime?”

Expand-contract, dual writes, versioned APIs. The domain-knowledge lens: backward compatibility is about your consumers, and who they are — and how fast they can move — is domain knowledge.

The architecture knowledge gap it signals
A schema is a shared vocabulary. Changing it disrupts whoever reads and writes it. Whether that disruption is acceptable depends on the domain: who the consumers are (other teams, old app versions, external partners), whether old and new must coexist, and for how long. Expand-contract is only the mechanical shape; the policy is the domain’s release reality.






ImportantThe domain mandates it



The domain identifies slow-moving or external consumers and a period during which both old and new must work. Then expand-contract, versioning, and dual reads encode a real compatibility window.








WarningThe domain doesn’t



An “evolving schema” with consumers unknown or ignored. A migration runs in one step, and a consumer that could not move in time breaks. The absence of policy was itself a decision, made by not deciding.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who must keep working during the change, and for how long?

If the domain answers → the migration encodes it.
If not → you have assumed consumer agility you never verified.
If unclear → the consumer knowledge is unwritten.




#SchemaEvolution #BackwardCompatibility #ZeroDowntime #API #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Migration

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Almost every design pattern/principle can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge. Analysis patterns are the purest case: they ARE recurring domain structures — so the gap question is simply “is our situation genuinely one of these?”
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Party
