Fowler: Model people and organizations with a common supertype, Party. [1]

Party is the analysis pattern that lets a person and an organisation stand in for each other wherever a role applies.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a person and an organisation can play the same role — both can be a customer, a supplier, an employee — is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “whoever we invoice may be a person or a company, and downstream we don’t care which,” then Party is that fact made executable: a common abstraction above Person and Organisation, where the roles live.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain assigns the same roles and rules to people and organisations: both order, both pay, both are contacted. Party closes the gap: it prevents duplicating every role (“CustomerContact” vs “CorporateContact”) and every rule for each subtype, and it lets contracts, accounts, and addresses point at one concept. The abstraction is the domain’s own “who matters, not what kind of who” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here people and organisations look like separate kinds, with different lifecycles and different rules. But it is still a domain decision whether they share a role. Party fits only when the domain names a role that is true of both. If the domain has not named one, the abstraction asserts a sameness nobody decided, and every consumer branches on type to escape it. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert state a rule using only “the customer” / “the contact” — a phrase that is true whether it is a person or a company?

If yes → applicable. Party is the code catching up to the knowledge; the shared role is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Model Person and Organisation separately; the abstraction fabricates a role the domain doesn’t share.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Party #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Organization Structure

Fowler: Represent an organization structure as a hierarchy of Parties. [1]

Organization Structure is the analysis pattern that models an organisation as typed units joined by rule-carrying relationships.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the organisation has formal relationships with rules — “regional offices report to headquarters,” “this division owns these cost centres” — is domain knowledge. Organization Structure models those relationships as typed, rule-carrying structures: a parent, a child, a type, and the constraints each type implies.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain reasons about the org chart: who may approve, who consolidates to whom, which unit is liable. Organization Structure closes the gap: it prevents the reporting rules from being hardcoded paths or ad-hoc parent pointers that change shape with every reorganisation. Each relationship type is the domain’s own “this kind of unit relates to that kind this way” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the need looks like a simple directory — an org picker, an email list. But the shape is still a domain decision: someone chose what a unit is and how units relate. Organization Structure fits only when the domain attaches rules to the shape — approvals, liability, consolidation. If it attaches none, the typed relationships assert governance nobody decided. The same gap appears when the real structure is informal: typing an expertise network dresses politics in constraints nobody wrote down. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the business attach rules to the org shape — approvals, liability, consolidation — or do people just need to find each other in a list?

If yes → applicable. Organization Structure is the code catching up to the knowledge; the typed relationships are the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. A simple directory expresses the need without fabricating governance.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #OrganizationStructure #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Organization Hierarchy

Fowler: An organization hierarchy in which each organization has at most one parent. [1]

Organization Hierarchy is the analysis pattern that treats every unit as having exactly one superior.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the organisation is a strict tree — every unit has exactly one superior, authority flows one way — is a domain claim, and often an unexamined one. Organization Hierarchy is that claim made executable: single-parent structure with transitive rules (“the whole branch reports up through here”).






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain genuinely is a tree: command chains, statutory consolidation, single ownership. The hierarchy closes the gap: transitive queries (“all subunits”), single-line accountability, and roll-up rules become simple and correct because the domain guarantees one parent. The strictness is the domain’s own “no shared bosses, no dotted lines” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the organisation looks like a tree, and a hierarchy looks purely structural. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed authority is single-threaded. Organization Hierarchy fits only when the domain names exactly one superior per unit. If the real authority is many-threaded — matrix, shared services, dotted lines — the domain has not named a single parent, and the tree asserts a chain nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can every unit in the business name exactly one superior — and would experts confirm there are no “it depends” reporting lines?

If yes → applicable. The hierarchy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. Model a graph or multiple typed structures; the tree would encode an org that doesn’t exist.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #OrganizationHierarchy #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Accountability

Fowler: Record the accountability of one party to another. [1]

Accountability is the analysis pattern that records who answers to whom, for what, and for how long.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that one party is answerable to another for something — with a scope, a start, and sometimes an end — is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “this doctor is responsible to this clinic for patient care until further notice,” then Accountability is that fact made executable: a responsibility relationship between parties, typed, scoped, and time-bounded.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business distinguishes responsibility from mere org position: who answers for the patient, the account, the project — and since when. Accountability closes the gap: it prevents responsibility from being inferred indirectly (“whoever is head of X”) or hardcoded to one person. Each accountability is the domain’s own “this party answers to that party for this” rule, with a lifetime the domain recognises.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the need looks like a duty roster or a contact route, not answerability. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose who is answerable to whom. Accountability fits only when the business names an answerer for each thing — with a scope and a lifetime. If responsibility is genuinely diffuse and nobody is named, the relationship asserts an owner nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the business name who answers for each thing — and would they accept “responsible until replaced” as a real state of the world?

If yes → applicable. Accountability is the code catching up to the knowledge; the responsibility is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Model routing or staffing instead; the pattern would invent a responsible party.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Accountability #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Knowledge Level

Fowler: Separate the knowledge level (the rules) from the operational level it governs. [1]

Knowledge Level is the analysis pattern that separates the rules about kinds of things from the things themselves.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business distinguishes kinds of things from the things themselves — job positions vs. the people in them, account types vs. accounts, ward categories vs. wards — is domain knowledge. A Knowledge Level is that distinction made executable: one layer defines the types and their rules; the other holds the operational objects that must obey them.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts maintain the rules about kinds separately from the instances: HR defines positions, finance defines account types, and changes to one never touch the other. The knowledge level closes the gap: it prevents type rules from being copy-pasted onto each instance, where a rule change means editing every record. The level is the domain’s own “the rules of the kind live with the kind” structure — a classic and legitimate use of meta-data.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the types never vary and never carry rules — it looks like one kind, with a config table only developers edit. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the business owns rules about kinds. Knowledge Level fits only when the experts maintain those rules and change them without touching the instances. If the table is only a developer lookup, the layer asserts business governance nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the experts maintain rules about kinds of things — and do they change those rules without touching the individual things?

If yes → applicable. The Knowledge Level is the code catching up to the knowledge; the meta-layer is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep types in the schema; the extra layer fabricates business governance.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #KnowledgeLevel #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Quantity

Fowler: A number together with a unit of measure. [1]

Quantity is the analysis pattern for a number that carries its unit of measure.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a number in this domain is never just a number — it is an amount of something, in a unit, comparable only to its own kind — is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “5 kilograms cannot be added to 3 metres,” then Quantity is that fact made executable: a value carrying its unit, with conversion and comparison rules that respect the physics the business lives by.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain measures, doses, ships, or prices things where unit confusion is a real error — medicine, logistics, engineering, energy. Quantity closes the gap: it prevents raw floats from mixing, which would let litres meet tonnes and nobody notice. The unit is the domain’s own “of what?” rule; permitted conversions are the domain’s own “how these kinds relate” knowledge; comparison within kind is the domain’s own ordering.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the numbers look dimensionless — counts, scores, percentages. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed these are plain counts, not measurements. Quantity fits only when the domain names a unit for the value. If no expert would say “five of what unit?”, the wrapper asserts dimensional rules nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the business state amounts with units — “42 tonnes, not 42” — and would adding unlike units be a business error, not just a bug?

If yes → applicable. Quantity is the code catching up to the knowledge; the unit is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Use plain numbers; the wrapper invents dimensional rules that don’t exist.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Quantity #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Money

Fowler: A quantity whose unit is a currency. [1]

Money is the analysis pattern for an amount that carries its currency.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an amount in this domain always belongs to a currency — and that mixing currencies is a domain error, not a rounding detail — is domain knowledge. Money is that fact made executable: amount plus currency, with addition restricted to like currency and comparison routed through explicit conversion. It is Quantity specialised to the one domain every business shares.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business prices, bills, budgets, or reports — and experts never say an amount without a currency, or totals that silently mix pounds and euros. Money closes the gap: it prevents double arithmetic from merging currencies, which produces numbers no accountant can sign. Rounding rules belong here too: where the penny goes is domain knowledge (who keeps the fraction), not a Math.rint call.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the amounts look like single-currency internal metrics — estimates, scores, capacity. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed these numbers carry no currency. Money fits only when the domain names a currency for the amount. If the number is a plain metric, the wrapper asserts currency baggage nobody decided. The opposite misfit is the same gap from the other side: raw doubles for billable amounts surface later as penny-discrepancy postmortems. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert say “that’s euros” about every amount — and would adding a pounds figure to a euros figure be a business mistake even if the code allowed it?

If yes → applicable. Money is the code catching up to the knowledge; currency is the domain’s own constraint.
If no → inapplicable. Keep plain numbers for dimensionless metrics; the wrapper invents currency.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Money #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Observation

Fowler: A value observed or measured about something. [1]

Observation is the analysis pattern that treats a recorded statement as a first-class thing, separate from the truth it records.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a statement about a subject was made by someone, at a time, against a protocol is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “a blood pressure reading is an observation — taken by a clinician, at a moment, interpretable against reference ranges,” then Observation is that fact made executable: the recording as a first-class thing, separate from the truth of what it records.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain keeps observations as evidence: clinical findings, inspections, sensor readings, survey answers. Observation closes the gap: it prevents measurements from being overwritten columns, where history, provenance, and the observer vanish. Each observation carries the domain’s own “who saw what, when, how” rule — and later corrections add new observations rather than rewriting evidence.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the need looks like the current value of a field, and the domain seems to care about the state, not the act. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether the record of the act matters. Observation fits only when the domain names the recording as evidence — who saw what, when, how. If only the latest value is ever needed, the dated record asserts provenance nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would experts ask about a past observation — “what was measured, by whom, when?” — or do they only ever need the current value?

If yes → applicable. Observation is the code catching up to the knowledge; the recording is the domain’s own evidence.
If no → inapplicable. Keep a plain current-value field; the observation log invents an archive no one reads.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Observation #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Measurement

Fowler: An observation of a value, together with its unit of measure. [1]

Measurement is the analysis pattern for a value that carries the procedure that produced it.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a measured quantity comes from a procedure, against a defined scale, with a normal range — that how a value is obtained is part of its meaning — is domain knowledge. Measurement is Observation specialised for quantities: the value carries its protocol, because the domain says a number without its method is not interpretable.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain’s experts judge values only relative to how they were taken: lab assays, calibrations, instrument readings. Measurement closes the gap: it prevents bare numbers from being compared across protocols, where “the same test” done differently yields different answers. The protocol reference is the domain’s own “this number means this, taken this way” rule; reference ranges are the domain’s own norms.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the quantity looks directly meaningful — a stated price, an entered weight — and no expert would ask “measured how?”. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the value stands without a procedure. Measurement fits only when the domain names the method as part of the value’s meaning. If the value stands on its own, the protocol reference asserts methodology nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do experts need to know the method to interpret the number — would the same figure from different procedures be a different fact?

If yes → applicable. Measurement is the code catching up to the knowledge; the protocol is the domain’s own context.
If no → inapplicable. A Quantity suffices; the protocol reference fabricates methodology.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Measurement #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Phenomenon / Category (typed observations)

Fowler: A controlled vocabulary of phenomena and categories for typed observations. [1]

Phenomenon and Category are the analysis patterns that model a controlled vocabulary of things that can be observed or classified.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business has a controlled vocabulary of things that can be observed or classified — diagnosis codes, defect types, product categories — and that free text is not acceptable, is domain knowledge. Phenomenon types and categories are that fact made executable: the vocabulary itself is modelled, with each observation pointing at a term the domain owns.
🧠 Why it matters here Whether the list of valid values is closed is one of the most consequential hidden gaps in data modeling: an open set sneaks in as varchar, and surfaces years later as a migration.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts maintain the term list, report against it, and change it deliberately (“add a new defect class”). Modelling categories closes the gap: it prevents free-text classification, where “scrached” and “scratch on surface” are the same defect and reporting dissolves. Each term is the domain’s own vocabulary item; adding a term is a domain decision with an owner.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the values look genuinely open — notes, descriptions, keywords the experts never control. But the list is still a domain decision: someone chose whether the vocabulary is closed. Phenomenon and Category fit only when the domain owns a fixed term list and admits new terms deliberately. If the business owns prose, the closed table asserts a vocabulary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would experts agree on the complete list of valid terms today — and insist new terms go through them, not around them?

If yes → applicable. Categories are the code catching up to the knowledge; the vocabulary is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep free text; a closed list would censor the domain.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Category #ControlledVocabulary #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Inventory / Asset

Fowler: Separate things tracked individually (assets) from things tracked by quantity (inventory). [1]

Inventory and Asset are the analysis patterns that separate things tracked individually from things counted in bulk.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business distinguishes things it owns and tracks individually from stuff it counts — this van (serial number, service history) vs. 400 litres of diesel — is domain knowledge. The Inventory/Asset distinction is that fact made executable: discrete trackable assets vs. aggregate quantities, with different identity, valuation, and lifecycle rules.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts manage some things individually — “vehicle F-112 needs servicing” — and others in bulk — “we hold 400 litres.” The split closes the gap: it prevents one representation from serving both, where either the van is counted in litres or the diesel gets serial numbers. Each side carries the domain’s own rules: assets take maintenance and depreciation; inventory takes quantities, batches, and expiry.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “asset vs inventory” line looks like a finance-policy detail. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose which things are tracked individually and which are counted. Inventory/Asset fits only when accounting and operations agree on the split. If the two halves disagree, the pattern encodes one side and the split is unwritten. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the business distinguish “track this one” from “count this stuff” — and would both accounting and operations sign the same split?

If yes → applicable. The distinction is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no (they disagree) → unclear — resolve the split with the business first; that’s the gap.
If the domain is all-one-kind → inapplicable. Model only the kind that exists.
If you can’t answer → you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Inventory #AssetManagement #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Account / Entry

Fowler: An account whose balance is derived from an append-only list of entries. [1]

Account with Entries is the analysis pattern that derives a balance from an append-only list of entries.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a balance in this domain is derived, never stored — the result of an append-only list of entries — is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallises that “every change must be traceable to a recorded event,” then Account with Entries is that fact made executable: entries are the facts, the balance is their consequence.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business audits: ledgers, loyalty points, leave balances, phone credit — anywhere “where did that number come from?” is a real question with legal or customer-facing weight. Account/Entry closes the gap: it prevents the balance from being an overwriteable column, which makes every discrepancy unexplainable. The entry is the domain’s own atomic fact; the running total is the domain’s own derivation rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the number looks like a setting, not a history — a discount rate, a stock level corrected by cycle counts. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether the provenance of the number matters. Account/Entry fits only when the domain names the trail as a requirement. If nobody asks for the changes behind the value, the ledger asserts an audit nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert ever ask “show me the changes behind this balance” — and must the answer reconcile exactly?

If yes → applicable. Account/Entry is the code catching up to the knowledge; the trail is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Store the current value; the ledger invents an audit the domain doesn’t require.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Account #Ledger #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Posting Rule

Fowler: A rule that maps a business event to the accounting entries it books. [1]

A Posting Rule is the analysis pattern that maps a business event to the accounting entries it books.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business has named derivation rules — “when we bill, the service account is credited and the tax account is charged” — is domain knowledge. A Posting Rule is that fact made executable: the trigger-to-entries mapping as a first-class thing, owned by accounting logic rather than scattered through process code.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts state the derivations and expect them to hold everywhere, all the time — invoices, fees, taxes, accruals. Posting Rules close the gap: they prevent the debit/credit logic from being hand-written inside each workflow, where three billing paths produce three slightly different ledgers. The rule is the domain’s own “this event books those entries” law, and changing it is a domain decision in one place.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the postings look like developer bookkeeping — cache counters, usage stats, with no accountant. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose how these numbers are derived. A Posting Rule fits only when the domain names the derivation as fiscal and owned. If the counters are merely convenient, the rule engine asserts fiscal discipline nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the rule be read to a finance expert and confirmed as the way the business books this event — identical across every path that triggers it?

If yes → applicable. Posting Rules are the code catching up to the knowledge; the mapping is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep simple internal updates; the rule engine fabricates governance.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #PostingRule #Accounting #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Action & Resource Allocation (planning)

Fowler: Link a planned action to the resources it consumes. [1]

Action & Resource Allocation is the analysis pattern that links planned work to committed resources.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business plans work against committed resources — this technician, this room, this window — and distinguishes a commitment from a request, is domain knowledge. Action & Resource Allocation is that fact made executable: actions that consume resource allocations, with request/commit/withdraw as real domain states.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts book, schedule, and juggle scarce things — operating theatres, consultants, equipment — and speak of “holding,” “confirming,” “releasing.” The pattern closes the gap: it prevents a calendar slot from being a mere string field, where double-bookings are discovered by humans. An allocation is the domain’s own “this resource is promised to this action for this period” fact, with the commitment states the domain itself uses.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the resources look uncommittable — work runs when a worker is free, and no expert “books” anything. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether resources are held or merely used. Action & Resource Allocation fits only when the domain names commitment as a real act. If nothing is scarce or held, the allocations assert a scheduling vocabulary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the business commit resources by name — “we reserved the MRI for Tuesday 10:00” — and treat a failed commitment as a real event?

If yes → applicable. Action & Allocation is the code catching up to the knowledge; the commitment is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. A plain queue expresses the domain; allocations would invent scarcity.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Planning #ResourceAllocation #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Identification Scheme

Fowler: A named, owned rule that says how a thing is identified. [1]

An Identification Scheme is the analysis pattern for a named, owned rule that says how a thing is identified.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business has an agreed way to point at a thing — “by passport number,” “by our customer number,” “by the vehicle registration” — is domain knowledge. An Identification Scheme is that fact made executable: a named, owned rule for mapping identifiers to objects, so “which one is it?” has an official answer.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business issues or recognises identifiers with rules — who assigns them, what they cover, whether they expire. The scheme closes the gap: it prevents each part of the system from guessing its own identity rule, which is how one customer becomes three and invoices point at strangers. Each scheme is the domain’s own “we know things by this” rule, with an owner and a scope.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the identifier looks like a private surrogate — a database sequence with no meaning outside one table. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose how things are identified. An Identification Scheme fits only when the domain names the identifier as the one the business uses. If the business never speaks it, exposing it as the scheme asserts an identity nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do experts identify things this way in conversation — “order 4711 from March” — and would a duplicate or missing identifier be a business problem, not just a key violation?

If yes → applicable. The scheme is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. Keep surrogate keys private; promote only what the business recognises.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #IdentificationScheme #DomainModeling #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Object Merge

Fowler: Unite two records found to be the same thing while keeping their separate identities. [1]

Object Merge is the analysis pattern that unites two records found to be the same thing while keeping both histories.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that two records can turn out to be the same thing — and that the business has a way to reconcile them — is domain knowledge. Object Merge is that fact made executable: a merge act that preserves both histories, redirects references, and remains undoable, because the domain says “we may discover sameness, but we do not erase what we knew.”






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Duplicate customers, patients, and parts are a recognised business phenomenon with a reconciliation procedure. Object Merge closes the gap: it prevents duplicates from being “fixed” by deleting one and hand-editing references, which destroys the history experts still ask about. The merge is the domain’s own “these were two names for one thing, as of this date” rule — with the trailing pointer kept because past records cite the old identity.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the records look like duplicates but are distinct things that resemble each other — twins, neighbouring addresses, two orders for one product. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether the business reconciles identities. Object Merge fits only when the domain names a procedure and an owner for it. If the business has no such act, the merge asserts a sameness nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the business have a word and a procedure for this — “merge the accounts,” “link the duplicate patient records” — with someone authorised to decide?

If yes → applicable. Object Merge is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. Fix data entry upstream; a merge feature invents a reconciliation the business never practises.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Transaction

Fowler: Group several entries as one business act. [1]

Transaction is the analysis pattern that groups entries as one business act.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that these entries belong together — one act, several consequences, atomic or not at all — is domain knowledge. The Transaction pattern is that fact made executable: a grouping of entries that records “these happened as one business event,” so the ledger can answer “what did this act consist of?” as well as “what is the balance?”






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has events with multi-legged consequences — a sale is a debit here and a credit there, plus tax. Transaction closes the gap: it prevents the legs from being written independently, where a crash or a bug produces half an event and no way to say what the whole was. The grouping is the domain’s own “this is one act” claim, and reversal means booking the mirrored transaction, not deleting history.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the entries look independent, grouped only by a batch job, with no business event joining them. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether these entries happened as one act. Transaction fits only when the domain names the grouping as one business event. If the grouping is only a batch job’s output, the wrapper asserts an event nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert call this grouping one thing — “the sale,” “the transfer” — and expect to see all its legs together in a statement?

If yes → applicable. Transaction is the code catching up to the knowledge; the grouping is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Enter the entries individually; the wrapper fabricates an event.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Transaction #Accounting #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Contract

Fowler: Model standing agreed terms between parties, separate from any single act. [1]

Contract is the analysis pattern that models standing agreed terms between parties, separate from any single order.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that two parties are bound by agreed terms — obligations that outlive any single order or payment — is domain knowledge. The Contract pattern is that fact made executable: parties, roles, and terms as a first-class thing that products and services hang off, so “what did we agree?” has an address in the model.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business honours agreements over time: supply contracts, leases, service levels. Contract closes the gap: it prevents the terms from being re-typed into every order, where the agreement drifts per transaction. The contract is the domain’s own “these parties, these roles, these terms” fact, and each order inherits from it rather than restating it.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the deal looks like one exchange with no standing terms — a cash sale, a spot trade. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether terms outlive the transaction. Contract fits only when the domain names an agreement that binds across many orders. If the deal is complete in itself, the contract object asserts standing terms nobody decided. The other gap is the reverse: hardening a verbal, shifting agreement ossifies terms the business never fixed. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would experts say “under the contract, we…” — citing it as a constraint on individual transactions, with terms that hold across many?

If yes → applicable. Contract is the code catching up to the knowledge; the standing agreement is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Model the transaction; the contract wrapper invents obligations nobody agreed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#AnalysisPatterns #Contract #Trading #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Quote

Fowler: A dated offer to sell at a price, with a lifetime. [1]

Quote is the analysis pattern for a dated offer to sell at a price, with a lifetime.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a promise to sell at a price has a lifetime — it exists, it binds for a while, it expires — is domain knowledge. The Quote pattern is that fact made executable: a dated offer with conditions, distinct from both the inquiry that preceded it and the sale that may follow it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business makes offers that bind: “this price holds for thirty days.” The Quote closes the gap: it prevents the offered price from being overwritten when the sale happens — the history of “what did we promise, and when?” vanishes exactly when disputes arise. The quote is the domain’s own “we offered this, under these conditions, until then” fact, and its expiry is the domain’s own rule, not a cache timeout.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the price is computed fresh on every inquiry, and no expert treats it as a commitment — “that’s just today’s price.” But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether an offer binds. Quote fits only when the domain names the offer’s lifetime as a promise. If the price is recomputed on demand, the persisted quote asserts a binding promise nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would honouring last month’s price be a business obligation — or just a mistake the business would correct without ceremony?

If yes → applicable. Quote is the code catching up to the knowledge; the offer’s lifetime is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Compute prices on demand; the quote record invents a promise.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Analysis Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Portfolio

Fowler: Treat a group of positions as one owned thing. [1]

Portfolio is the analysis pattern that treats a group of positions as one owned thing.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business treats a group of positions as one thing — this client’s holdings, this fund’s assets — is domain knowledge. The Portfolio pattern is that fact made executable: an owning collection with its own identity, valuation, and rules, where “the whole” answers questions the parts cannot.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts reason about the aggregate: exposure, diversification, total value, “the fund’s” performance. Portfolio closes the gap: it prevents positions from being grouped ad hoc by query, where every report re-derives membership differently and two reports disagree. The portfolio is the domain’s own “these belong together, under this owner, for these purposes” fact — membership is a domain decision with a timestamp.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the group looks like a filter — all trades this week, all red cars — with no owner and no standing membership. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose whether the group is a managed thing. Portfolio fits only when the domain names the group as one entity with an owner and rules. If the whole is only a query result, promoting it asserts an entity nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do experts speak of the group as a thing — “the portfolio is up,” “the client’s holdings” — with a member who manages it and rules that apply to it as a whole?

If yes → applicable. Portfolio is the code catching up to the knowledge; the group is the domain’s own entity.
If no → inapplicable. Keep it a query; the entity fabricates an owner and membership rules.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: IVP
text:
The Independent Variation Principle applied to software architecture: elements assigned to the same change driver belong in the same module; elements assigned to different drivers belong in different modules [1].
This section covers the formal theory of IVP for software — the system tuple, change drivers, the Γ-equivalence partition, unit purity and completeness, and the axioms.

title: IVP
text:
1 Core theory
The theory is developed in detail in the core theory pages:

The software system tuple — the model the principle is stated over.
Change drivers and assignment — what a change driver is and how elements are assigned to them.
The structural formulation of IVP — the statement of the principle and its four conditions.
The Γ-equivalence partition — the object the principle produces.
The partition theorem — the unique compliant module structure.
Scope and validity conditions — the premises, preconditions, and applicability gates the results depend on.
Consequences and application — what follows, and the six-step procedure.

title: IVP
text:
2 Consequences

How to apply IVP — the six-step process and a fully worked example.
Software clustering — how IVP dissolves the modularisation optimization problem.

The knowledge-embodiment theorem, which connects maximal cohesion to the embodiment of domain knowledge, is a result of the cohesion theory rather than of IVP itself. It is covered under cohesion.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332

All published papers

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text: This is the statement of the Independent Variation Principle itself. Everything else in the core theory — the partition, purity and completeness, the partition theorem — is either an ingredient the principle needs or a consequence it produces. This page states the principle.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
1 The principle in one sentence
For a software system S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma), IVP prescribes the partition of the element set EE induced by the equivalence relation
e1∼Γe2⇔Γ(e1)=Γ(e2). e_1 \sim_\Gamma e_2 \iff \Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2). 
The modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ-equivalence classes of the element set: elements assigned the same set of change drivers belong in the same module, and elements assigned different sets belong in different modules.
That single sentence is the whole principle. The four conditions below are not additional rules — they are that sentence stated as four obligations a module structure must satisfy.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
2 The four conditions

IVP-1 — Element Admissibility. Every element has at least one change driver: |Γ(e)|≥1|\Gamma(e)| \geq 1. No element floats free of the change structure.
IVP-2 — Change-Driver Assignment / Element Form. Every element is pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite. The model admits only elements whose driver set is exactly what the domain requires.
IVP-3 — Unit Purity / Separation. Elements with different driver assignments reside in different modules: Γ(e1)≠Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)≠M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) \neq \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) \neq M(e_2).
IVP-4 — Unit Completeness / Unification. Elements with the same driver assignment reside in the same module: Γ(e1)=Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)=M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) = M(e_2).

Separation (IVP-3) is the “do not mix” half: elements that answer to different change drivers must not co-reside. Unification (IVP-4) is the “do not split” half: elements that answer to the same change drivers must co-reside. Together they force exactly one module structure — the Γ-equivalence partition.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
3 Why the two halves matter
Each half corrects one classic failure.
A module that violates separation mixes elements that change for different reasons. When one change driver activates, the module must change in part, dragging unrelated elements into the blast radius.
A module that violates unification splits elements that change for the same reason. When that change driver activates, the change must be made in several places, and keeping them consistent is coordination cost.
Both are placement errors. Both are named by a condition, which makes them diagnosable.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 4 Admissibility and element form set the model
text:
4 Admissibility and element form set the model
The first two conditions govern what counts as an element at all. IVP-1 says every element belongs to the change structure. IVP-2 says every element’s driver set is exactly what the domain requires — an element is single-driver, or multi-driver in a way that is irreducible, never accidentally bloated.
These two prepare the element set EE for the grouping that IVP-3 and IVP-4 then prescribe.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 5 The principle is a criterion, not a recipe
text:
5 The principle is a criterion, not a recipe
IVP is stated over a system tuple that is read off the domain. Once Γ\Gamma is fixed, the principle determines the structure. This is what makes IVP a criterion: it does not suggest a structure, it names the structure the change drivers require.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 6 How the rest of the core theory follows
text:
6 How the rest of the core theory follows

The Γ-equivalence partition is the object the principle produces.
Purity and completeness are the two properties a module gets from the partition.
The partition theorem says the compliant structure is uniquely this partition.

The statement above is the foundation; the other core-theory pages develop what it implies.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
7 Where the derivation lives
The derivation that this is the unique cost-optimal structure under the change-management hypothesis is proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], and the proof that the four conditions — Admissibility, Element Form, Separation, Unification — are necessary and jointly exhaustive is developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2]. The purity and completeness properties the conditions produce are defined formally in the paper on the nature of cohesion [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
Cohesion and Change Propagation: Four Necessary Conditions for Optimal Modularization — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362420
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

All published papers

title: The Partition Theorem
text: The four conditions of IVP do more than describe what a compliant module looks like. They determine the module structure uniquely.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
1 The claim
A modularization that satisfies all four IVP conditions must be the Γ-equivalence partition — unique up to coarsening ties.
Two elements with the same change-driver assignment must co-reside (Unification), and two elements with different assignments must not co-reside (Separation). These two constraints together fix which elements belong together: exactly the Γ-equivalence classes, and nothing else.
There is no latitude in a compliant structure. Once you have read the change-driver assignment Γ\Gamma off the domain, the partition is determined.

title: The Partition Theorem
section: 2 Why this is not a design choice
text:
2 Why this is not a design choice
This is the force of the result. Classical modularization advice often treats “how to cut modules” as a judgement call, one of many defensible choices. The partition theorem says that under the change-management criterion, it is not a choice. If your goal is to contain change — to make the module that must change together and nothing else — then the Γ-equivalence partition is the answer, and it is the only answer.
This is what makes IVP diagnostic rather than suggestive. Given the domain, it reads off the structure the domain requires.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
3 Up to coarsening ties
The phrase “up to coarsening ties” records one genuine freedom. Within a single Γ-equivalence class, all elements are identical with respect to change: they answer to the same drivers. You may therefore subdivide a class into smaller modules, or keep it as one, without violating any condition. The subdivision is free for readability, team structure, or packaging — it does not change the change-containment behaviour.
What is not free is merging across classes or splitting within a class so that elements respond to different drivers are mixed. The partition’s boundaries between classes are forced; its internal subdivision is not.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
4 Where the proof lives
The derivation that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique cost-optimal structure is proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], which gives a counting argument on the element–change-driver incidence graph showing that grouping elements by their change-driver sets minimizes change propagation cost. The cost-minimisation of the partition is further developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2] and the paper on minimizing change propagation and maintenance cost [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
Cohesion and Change Propagation: Four Necessary Conditions for Optimal Modularization — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362420
Why Minimizing Change Propagation Minimizes Maintenance Cost — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362542

All published papers

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
IVP prescribes one module structure: the Γ-equivalence partition. This page explains that object — what the equivalence relation is, what properties its classes have, and how multi-driver elements fit.
The principle itself — its one-sentence statement and the four conditions — is stated on the structural formulation page. Here we work with the object the principle produces.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
1 The equivalence relation
Define the relation Γ̃\tilde{\Gamma} on the element set EE by:
e1∼Γe2⇔Γ(e1)=Γ(e2) e_1 \sim_\Gamma e_2 \iff \Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) 
Two elements are change-driver-equivalent when they are assigned the same set of change drivers. This relation is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Therefore it partitions the element set into equivalence classes.
The Γ-equivalence partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} is the set of these classes. Each class collects exactly the elements that respond to the same change drivers.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
2 Purity and completeness
A module drawn from this partition has two properties.

Purity. The module contains no element from outside its Γ-equivalence class. Every element in the module is Γ-equivalent to every other. When a change driver activates, every element affected lives in this module — and nothing unrelated lives here.
Completeness. The module contains every element of its Γ-equivalence class. Nothing that should be here has been placed elsewhere. When a change driver activates, no element that must change is scattered across other modules.

Purity is the module-level form of Separation (IVP-3): no foreign elements. Completeness is the module-level form of Unification (IVP-4): no missing elements. A module that is both pure and complete is maximally cohesive with respect to the change-driver rule. It is the unit that contains exactly the elements a change driver forces to change together, and nothing else. The formal account of purity and completeness as correctness relative to a partitioning rule is given in the published paper on the nature of cohesion [1], and the change-driver-assignment instantiation of the schema is developed in the paper on causal cohesion [2].

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
3 Multi-driver elements
Not every element is pure. An adapter that must satisfy both the domain’s rule and a foreign interface has |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1. Its driver set is irreducible: it genuinely needs all of its drivers.
An element is single-driver or multi-driver. The word “impure” applies to a module, not an element: a module is impure when it groups elements that are not Γ-equivalent. A module containing a multi-driver element is necessarily impure, because that element answers to drivers its pure neighbours do not. The adapter is well-designed; the impurity it forces on its module is necessary, not a mistake.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
section: 4 The partition is what IVP produces
text:
4 The partition is what IVP produces
Because IVP prescribes exactly this partition, the partition theorem is the result that the compliant structure is unique — the structure is determined once Γ\Gamma is read off the domain.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193
Causal Cohesion — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703156

All published papers

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text: Change drivers are the engine of the whole theory. Everything the Independent Variation Principle prescribes follows from the set of change drivers and the way elements are assigned to them.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
1 What a change driver is
A change driver is a discrete, identifiable source of variation that can cause elements to require modification. It is an external condition in the operating domain: when it activates, part of the system must change.
The tax legislation is a change driver. When it changes, every element that embodies tax knowledge must change. A payment-routing standard is a change driver. The target platform is a change driver. A security classification is a change driver.
At the leaf level, a change driver is identical to a coupling dimension: both name a dimension along which elements vary together.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
section: 2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
text:
2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
This is the load-bearing fact about change drivers. The set CC is a fact about the domain, not a design choice. The analyst discovers which external conditions force the system to change; the designer does not invent them.
Change drivers are external and fixed by the domain. No design move adds, removes, or transmutes a driver. A change driver exists because the domain’s causal structure produces it, not because a designer decides it should exist.
This is why the theory is a diagnostic instrument rather than a recipe: it tells you to read the change structure off the domain, not to impose it.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
3 The assignment function
The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to the set of change drivers that force it to change.

An element with |Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1 responds to exactly one change driver. Such an element is pure.
An element with |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1 responds to several. It is composite.
A composite element is irreducibly composite when no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose — it genuinely needs all of them. Adapters and translators are typical examples: a module that must both follow the domain’s rule and satisfy a foreign interface is irreducibly multi-driver.

The assignment is read from the domain’s causal structure. Whether an element is pure or composite is not a label the designer attaches; it follows from which external conditions actually force the element to change.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
4 Driver independence
Two change drivers are independent when their knowledge slices do not overlap and activating one does not logically force the other. Driver independence is a well-formedness condition on the driver set, not a hypothesis the theory requires. If two drivers are mutually coupled — each activation forces the other — they do not individuate two distinct sources of change and are correctly treated as one.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
5 Driver omission and refinement
The granularity at which you read the driver set is a modelling choice. You may split one change driver into finer ones, or merge several into one coarser driver. The structural results of the theory are invariant under this refinement: a finer grain yields a richer CC with no loss of structural validity.
Omitting a driver — failing to record a genuine source of change — is a different matter. It coarsens the optimal partition and leaves that change uncontained. Driver omission is the failure mode the theory warns against: if a real change driver is missing from CC, the modules built from the incomplete set will not contain the changes that driver produces.
The taxonomy of change drivers and the discovery tests used here are developed in the published paper on the change-driver taxonomy [1], and the question of what counts as the source of a change driver is examined in the paper on whether a change driver is an actor or a document [2]. The formal account of the assignment function and of driver independence is part of the Independent Variation Principle paper [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Change-Driver Taxonomy — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21669704
Change Driver: Actor or Document? — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21669958
The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332

All published papers

title: Independent Variation Principle
text:
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) is a theory of how structured systems are organized around the sources of change that act upon them.
A system’s structure should separate the elements that vary independently — elements driven by different sources of change belong in different modules — and unify the elements that vary dependently — elements driven by the same source of change belong in a single module.
The principle and the proof that this module structure is the cost-minimising one are published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].
This site is the working home for that theory and its applications.

title: How to Apply IVP
text:
Applying the Independent Variation Principle is an iterative design activity, not a mechanical algorithm. It follows a six-step cycle; you revisit earlier steps as understanding deepens. The depth of analysis should be proportionate to the system’s expected lifetime and how often it changes.
This page first lays out the six steps, then works through them on a complete example, following the principle as stated in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].

title: How to Apply IVP
text:
1 The six-step process

Identify the elements. Choose the grain of artifact the analysis operates on — functions, classes, methods, data structures, modules. Every element is something that can change in response to a change driver.
Identify the change drivers. Read the external conditions whose activation forces the system to change. This is discovery, not invention. Apply the “who asks for this change?” and “independent clock” tests: a change driver is a source of variation that can change without forcing the others to change.
Map drivers to elements. Assign each element the set of change drivers that force it to change — build the assignment Γ\Gamma. Record whether each element is pure (one driver) or composite (several).
Assess the current modularization. Compare the existing module structure to the Γ-equivalence partition. Name the violations: which modules are impure (IVP-3), which are incomplete (IVP-4).
Refactor toward compliance. Move elements so the structure converges to the partition. Merge modules that scatter one driver’s elements; split modules that mix different drivers.
Verify and iterate. Re-check the assignment and the partition as understanding deepens and as the domain changes.

title: How to Apply IVP
section: 2 A worked example: a notification system
text:
2 A worked example: a notification system
To make the process concrete, consider a notification system of the kind found in any SaaS application. It is small enough to fit one page yet rich enough to exhibit both a Unit Purity and a Unit Completeness violation.

2.1 The starting point
The system sends notifications to users when events occur — account creation, order placed, payment failed, subscription expiring. It supports three delivery channels (email, SMS, push) and enforces business rules such as user preferences and rate limits.
A developer has implemented all of this in a single class, NotificationService, containing these nine methods:







Element
Responsibility




e1e_1: resolveTemplate
Selects the message template for a given event type

2.2 Step 1: System description
The element inventory is the table above; at this granularity, each method is an element. The system’s purpose FF: deliver event-triggered notifications to users through their preferred channels, subject to business rules.


2.3 Step 2: Change driver identification
Apply the “who asks for this change?” and “independent clock” tests.

Message content changes when the marketing team redesigns templates, when the UX team changes wording, or when a new event type is added. None of these affect delivery or channel preferences.
Delivery infrastructure changes when operations switches SMTP providers, when the SMS gateway publishes a new API version, or when a new channel (e.g. WhatsApp) is added. These do not affect message content or business rules.
Business policy changes when the product team modifies rate limits, when legal requires changes to audit logging, or when new preference options are introduced. These are independent of formatting and delivery.

The “independent clock” test confirms their independence: a template redesign (γcontent\gamma_\text{content}) can happen without changing the SMS gateway (γchannel\gamma_\text{channel}) or the rate-limiting rules (γpolicy\gamma_\text{policy}), and vice versa.

Unit Purity (IVP-3). Three of the four modules are mixed — they group elements that answer to different drivers. McontentM_\text{content} mixes content and policy (because e2e_2 is composite), MtransportM_\text{transport} mixes channel and content (because e9e_9 is composite), and MlogicM_\text{logic} mixes policy and channel (because e7e_7 is composite). The technical-layer decomposition fails on both directives. A change in business policy touches three modules; a change in a channel’s infrastructure touches three modules. This is shotgun surgery spread wide, plus hidden coupling: the composite elements land in whichever layer their technical category suggests, silently wiring together drivers that should be separated.
Why this mistake is common. Decomposing by technical layer (presentation, logic, data) is a deeply ingrained habit. Technical layers sometimes conform to change drivers, but not always — and the more composite elements a system has, the more the two diverge. The test is not “what kind of thing is this element?” but “what causes this element to change?” A composite element belongs with the elements it shares drivers with, not with the layer its name suggests.

2.8 Step 6: Reflecting on the result
The three modularizations differ in how far a change propagates. The measure that matters is not how many modules are touched, but how many elements must be inspected or modified when a change driver activates — and how many of those were touched unnecessarily.
When a driver activates, the elements that must change are fixed by the domain: γcontent\gamma_\text{content} forces e1,e2,e9e_1, e_2, e_9; γchannel\gamma_\text{channel} forces e3,e4,e5,e7,e8,e9e_3, e_4, e_5, e_7, e_8, e_9; γpolicy\gamma_\text{policy} forces e2,e6,e7,e8e_2, e_6, e_7, e_8. The monolithic design places all nine elements in one module, so every driver activation touches all nine elements, even though only a fraction of them actually vary — up to six unnecessary touches per change. The IVP-compliant design touches exactly the elements that must change and nothing else — zero unnecessary touches, because every module holds only the elements of its driver. This is what IVP’s partition theorem guarantees: the IVP-compliant modularization minimizes change propagation — the scope that must be read and modified when a change driver activates.
The composite elements make the per-driver footprint larger than in a pure system — γchannel\gamma_\text{channel} alone forces six elements across three modules — but this is the domain’s cost, not a defect: each of those elements genuinely must change when the channel changes. IVP cannot reduce the required set; it only ensures that nothing outside it is touched.


2.9 What about dependencies between modules?
The modules in ModuleSet2\text{ModuleSet}_2 will have structural dependencies between them: the orchestration that calls resolveTemplate, then checkPreferences, then deliverEmail introduces inter-module coupling.
IVP does not eliminate dependencies — it organizes them. Dependencies between modules conforming to different change drivers are expected and manageable. Dependencies within a mixed module are the hidden ones that cause maintenance surprises. The composite modules sit between the pure ones by necessity: e9e_9 bridges content and channel, e2e_2 bridges content and policy, e7e_7 and e8e_8 bridge policy and channel. Each is an explicit bridge the domain requires — better a few named bridges than a hidden tangle inside a monolithic module.
