title: Software Clustering
text:
Software clustering is the problem of recovering or prescribing the modular structure of a software system. For three decades it was studied as an optimization problem over a dependency graph. IVP reframes it: the difficulty of the problem is not an intrinsic feature of modularisation, but a consequence of doing it without a semantic criterion.
This page explains what IVP concludes about software clustering — why the traditional problem is hard, how IVP dissolves that hardness, and what the shift costs.

title: Software Clustering
text:
1 The traditional problem is NP-complete
Classical software clustering treats modularisation as an optimization problem: given a dependency graph, find the partition of elements that maximises cohesion and minimises coupling.
Mitchell and Mancoridis established in 2006 that this problem is NP-complete [1]. The field responded with metaheuristic search — hill-climbing, genetic algorithms, weighted graph partitioning — each searching for structurally good partitions that, in the worst case, cannot be found exactly in polynomial time.
The hardness is real, but it characterises the difficulty of partitioning without a semantic criterion, not an inherent difficulty of modularisation itself. Without knowing why elements change together, the optimiser cannot distinguish a well-motivated partition from a coincidental one. It must search exponentially many groupings, with no basis for preferring one structurally plausible partition over another.

title: Software Clustering
text:
2 What “cohesion” means in clustering
Classical clustering does not define cohesion by intent. It defines it operationally, as the internal connectivity of a cluster.
Given the dependency graph and a candidate partition, count for each module the edges inside it (cohesion) and the edges that cross its boundary (coupling). Every objective in the field is built on those two counts:

Modularisation quality (MQ). The cluster factor CF(M) = μ / (μ + ½·ε) combines the counts, and MQ averages it over the modules. TurboMQ weights edges by shared source file for multi-file systems. [2]
Modularity. The Newman–Girvan objective replaces the raw internal count with the excess of internal edge mass over a degree-preserving null model. [3] Optimising it is strongly NP-complete. [4]
Pattern-based clustering. ACDC recognises a subsystem as a body that dominates a cluster, then adopts orphans by connectivity — no scalar, but the same criterion of internal connectivity. [5]
Association-matrix clustering. Similarity is computed from shared data or calls, and cohesion is the sum of intra-cluster similarities. [6] [7]
Within-cluster compactness. Tools that borrow a data-clustering objective use the within-cluster sum of squares directly.

Cohesion and coupling therefore read the same graph. They differ only in which edges they count. A survey of the cohesion-metrics literature reaches the same conclusion from the metric side: cohesion metrics and coupling metrics examine the same graph and differ only in which partition of the edge set they report. [8]

title: Software Clustering
text:
3 IVP supplies the missing criterion
IVP provides the semantic criterion the traditional problem lacks.
Every element is governed by one or more change drivers: external conditions that, when they change, require the element to be modified. The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to its set of governing drivers. The IVP partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} — grouping elements with identical driver assignments — is the modularisation that minimises both module-touch count per driver activation and within-module contamination cost.

title: Software Clustering
text:
4 Given Γ, clustering is polynomial
Once Γ\Gamma is in hand, no search is needed. Each element already carries its own module membership in Γ(e)\Gamma(e): two elements belong to the same module precisely when they share the same driver-assignment set. The bound O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) falls out of the mechanics of that grouping, not from any deep theorem — you can count the operations yourself.
Deriving the cost, step by step, using the six-step application procedure:

Identify the elements (step 1). The analysis has n=|E|n = |E| elements to place. Every element appears once in the pass.
Map drivers to elements (step 3). Each element ee carries its assignment set Γ(e)\Gamma(e), of size |Γ(e)|≤dmax|\Gamma(e)| \le d_{\max}. Set equality does not depend on the order of its members, so each element needs a canonical form before it can serve as a grouping key.
Canonicalise each element’s key (step 5, preparation). Sorting the drivers inside each set makes every element’s key unambiguous: {a,b}\{a, b\} becomes the same key as {b,a}\{b, a\}. Sorting one set of size at most dmaxd_{\max} costs at most dmaxlog⁡dmaxd_{\max} \log d_{\max} operations. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Group by identical key (step 5, main pass). Elements that share a driver-assignment set produce the same canonical key and therefore hash to the same bucket. Inserting one element costs O(dmax)O(d_{\max}) — hashing the set and comparing it against the keys of existing buckets. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}).
Read off the modules. Each bucket is one equivalence class — one module. The number of modules is the number of distinct keys, never more than nn. Emitting them costs O(n)O(n).

Step 3 dominates the total: hashing (step 4) is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}) and read-out (step 5) is O(n)O(n), while sorting is the only step carrying a log⁡dmax\log d_{\max} factor, so it sets the rate. So the whole pass is
O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax) O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) 
When dmaxd_{\max} is bounded by a constant — the practical case, where no element answers to more than a handful of drivers — each element’s work is one small sort and one hash, so step 3 costs O(n)O(n) and the whole pass simplifies to O(n)O(n).
The result is deterministic. Every module in the IVP partition satisfies maximal causal cohesion Hcausal(M)=(1,1)H_\text{causal}(M) = (1, 1), and no other partition achieves (1,1)(1, 1) for all modules.
The same problem is strongly NP-complete over the dependency graph alone and polynomial when the driver assignment is supplied. The complexity class tracks the availability of the semantic criterion.

title: Software Clustering
text:
5 Clustering is not IVP
The output of clustering and the output of IVP share a shape: both partition the elements into modules. The relation that defines the partition differs, and the relation is the content.

Clustering partitions by graph connectivity (or by co-change similarity). Elements go together when they connect.
IVP partitions by Γ-equality. Elements go together when they share the same change drivers.

When dependencies track drivers, the two relations induce the same partition, and clustering acts as a search for the IVP partition. When they diverge, they diverge in both directions. An element that responds to two drivers is adjacent to both driver groups; a connectivity objective keeps it with one of them, while IVP isolates it. Two renderers for the same format that never call each other carry no edge between them; a connectivity objective separates them, while IVP joins them. Neither error is visible from the dependency graph, because both are defined relative to a Γ the graph does not carry.
This is why IVP does not derive from clustering, and does not replace it as a search method. IVP supplies the criterion the clustering objective lacks; clustering supplies a heuristic that approximates it when the criterion is not yet known. The clustering objective scores a partition by the same quantity it optimises — internal edge density — so it cannot say whether the partition is right. IVP is the independent criterion that the cohesion survey found missing from the literature. [8]
One clustering signal samples a different relation and is worth distinguishing, though it is not a better-measured one. Co-change groups elements that historical commits modified together. [9] A call edge records a standing interaction that a change may never exercise; a co-change records an actual modification, so co-change bears on the same question a change driver answers — what varies together — where connectivity does not. That is an alignment of modality, not of accuracy. Co-change fires both when a shared condition forces two elements to change and when a change to one element propagates to a dependent element, and it also fires on commit batching and on refactoring churn. Its error runs in both directions, and its size is not measurable from the co-change data alone. Co-change is a different proxy, not an established better one.
The confound has a direction. Shared-driver pairs co-change symmetrically; change propagation is one-directional, from the element depended upon to the element that depends on it. The directed conditional frequencies therefore carry more than a symmetric co-change count — but only as a filter that rules pairs out. Symmetry is necessary for driver-equivalence, not sufficient (mutual dependencies and commit batching produce it for the wrong reason), and asymmetry alone cannot separate genuine propagation from one element carrying every driver of the other.

title: Software Clustering
text:
6 The cohesion-coupling tension dissolves
The classical imperative — “maximise cohesion, minimise coupling” — treats the two as a trade-off to be balanced with weights. Under IVP, the trade-off was an artifact of optimising without a criterion.
Once every module achieves maximal causal cohesion, the coupling that modularisation can eliminate is eliminated by the same construction that maximises cohesion. The normative decomposition simultaneously maximises cohesion and minimises avoidable coupling — one optimum, not two. The weights encoded a problem that a principled criterion removes rather than solves.

title: Software Clustering
section: 7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
text:
7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
The polynomial result is conditional on Γ\Gamma being known. The complexity of the modularisation problem depends on what information is available:

Γ\Gamma fully known — polynomial: O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Γ\Gamma partially known — a mix: polynomial for the assigned elements, the traditional hard case for the rest.
Γ\Gamma entirely unknown — the NP-complete traditional case.

The polynomial advantage is therefore proportional to the completeness of the driver analysis. The hard part shifts from combinatorial search to driver identification — an epistemic problem that domain analysis must address.
The shift is an improvement, not a cost-shifting trick. Driver identification yields reusable knowledge about the domain. Partition search yields a configuration that is discarded on every requirements change.

title: Software Clustering
section: 8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
text:
8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
When change drivers resist identification, structural clustering does not vanish — it changes role. It is demoted from design criterion to hypothesis generator.
Two reasons drive identification difficulty:

Epistemic. The change drivers exist and are well-defined, but the analyst cannot see them — missing domain expertise, absent artifacts, an inherited system with no design records. The drivers are there to be found.
Structural. The domain itself resists a clean decomposition — dense driver overlap, single-authority greenfield systems, rapidly changing driver sets. No sharp partition exists to recover.

Structural clustering helps with the first and not the second. In the epistemic case, dependency density and co-change history carry indirect evidence about the hidden driver structure and can be mined for it. A cluster the algorithm produces is a question worth asking: these elements are structurally close — is there an external condition whose activation would require all of them to change together? In the structural case, the underdetermination is real: no method recovers a sharp partition, because none exists.

title: Software Clustering
text:
9 Scope and limitations
The polynomial result holds when Γ\Gamma is known. The IVP advantage narrows in three cases:

Single-authority greenfield systems — all elements governed by a single driver; the partition is one module, and the analysis is trivial.
Systems with dense driver overlap — many elements with large, overlapping driver sets; the module count is genuinely large because the domain’s change structure is entangled.
Systems in rapid-change domains — driver assignments change frequently; the partition must be recomputed, and while each update is polynomial, the cumulative cost may be non-trivial.

Driver-equivalence does not put every element in its own module. Two elements share a module precisely when they share a driver assignment, and in any real system many elements do. The number of modules is the number of distinct driver-assignment sets, not the number of elements.

title: Software Clustering
text:
10 Where the proofs live
The claim that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique partition achieving maximal causal cohesion for all modules, and that the cohesion-coupling tension dissolves, follows from the partition result proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [10], with the causal cohesion metric developed in the paper on causal cohesion [11] and the cost-minimum of the partition in the paper on change propagation and maintenance cost [12].

title: Consequences and Application
text: The core theory — system tuple, change drivers, Γ-equivalence partition, and the partition theorem — has direct consequences for how software is structured, and it yields a concrete procedure for applying it.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
1 Consequences
Several practical consequences follow from the core theory.
Change is contained. A module built as a Γ-equivalence class contains exactly the elements a change driver forces to change together, and nothing else. When a driver activates, the developer opens one module, changes what is inside, and nothing unrelated is disturbed.
Coupling is explained, not traded off. The partition removes the coupling that comes from misplacement: no element that changes together is split across modules, so no accidental cross-boundary dependency remains. The coupling that survives is the coupling the domain itself imposes between distinct driver classes — necessary coupling, not accidental.
Cohesion is a consequence of the partition. A module that is one Γ-equivalence class is pure (no foreign elements) and complete (no missing elements). That is maximal cohesion under the change-driver rule. Cohesion is not a separate knob to tune; it follows from grouping by the correct criterion.
Structure is read from the domain. The partition theorem says the compliant structure is determined once Γ\Gamma is known. Architecture becomes a reading of the domain’s change structure rather than a stylistic choice.
Wrong groupings are diagnosable. A module that mixes elements answering to different drivers, or that scatters one driver’s elements across several modules, violates a named condition. The theory names the violation and points at the fix: reunite the Γ-equivalence class.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
2 The six-step application process
Applying IVP is an iterative design activity, not a mechanical algorithm. It follows a six-step cycle; you may revisit earlier steps as understanding deepens. The depth of analysis should be proportionate to the system’s expected lifetime and how often it changes.

Identify the elements. Choose the grain of artifact the analysis operates on — functions, classes, data structures, modules.
Identify the change drivers. Read the external conditions whose activation forces the system to change. This is discovery, not invention.
Map drivers to elements. Assign each element the set of change drivers that force it to change: build Γ\Gamma.
Assess the current modularization. Compare the existing module structure to the Γ-equivalence partition. Name the violations: which modules are impure, which are incomplete.
Refactor toward compliance. Move elements so the structure converges to the partition.
Verify and iterate. Re-check the assignment and the partition as understanding deepens and as the domain changes.

title: Consequences and Application
section: 3 What IVP does and does not tell you
text:
3 What IVP does and does not tell you
IVP is a theory of where to place elements so that change is contained. It is precise about that and silent about several other things.
It does not tell you how to implement an element, only where it sits. It does not decide whether a system is correct — placement is not correctness. It does not optimize performance, security, or other quality attributes directly, though those can enter the analysis as change drivers. It is one criterion applied to one decision: where does each element belong.
Those limits are the subject of the theory’s formal treatment, not hidden in the small print. The premises and preconditions the theory assumes, and the gates that decide whether it applies to a system, are collected on the scope and validity conditions page.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
4 Where the proofs live
The theorems — the partition theorem, the uniqueness result, the consequences derived from the axioms — are proved in the published papers: the partition and its cost-optimality in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], the four conditions in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2], the maintenance-cost minimum of the partition in the paper on change propagation and maintenance cost [3], and the purity and completeness properties in the paper on the nature of cohesion [4].

title: IVP Core Theory
text:
This is the formal heart of the Independent Variation Principle as applied to software. Here we explain the model the theory works on, the principle itself, and what follows from it.
The principle is stated and proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].
The core theory has seven parts.

The software system tuple. The model of a software system the principle is stated over: purpose, domain knowledge, elements, coupling, change drivers, and the change-driver assignment.
Change drivers and assignment. What a change driver is, how elements are assigned to them, and how the assignment is discovered from the domain.
The structural formulation of IVP. The statement of the principle itself — the one-sentence Γ-equivalence rule and the four conditions.
The Γ-equivalence partition. The object the principle produces, and what purity and completeness mean.
The partition theorem. The result that the compliant module structure is uniquely the Γ-equivalence partition.
Scope and validity conditions. The premises, preconditions, and applicability gates the results depend on.
Consequences and application. What the theory implies for structuring software and the six-step procedure for applying it.

The knowledge-embodiment theorem — which links maximal cohesion to the embodiment of domain knowledge — is a result of the cohesion theory, not of IVP itself. It is treated on the cohesion page, because it states a property of cohesion, and cohesion is a design principle distinct from IVP.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
The partition theorem is a conditional result. It holds for systems that meet a set of premises and preconditions, and it returns a stronger conclusion when two further premises hold. This page states all of them in one place: the assumptions the derivation rests on, the preconditions that must hold for the result to apply, and the gates that decide whether IVP is the right tool for a given system.
The principle itself is stated on the structural formulation page, and the object it produces is described on the Γ-equivalence partition and partition theorem pages. This page records the conditions those results assume.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
1 The three unconditional premises
Three premises are required for the derivation to apply at all.

The change-driver hypothesis. Elements change because external conditions change. Each element’s driver assignment Γ(e)\Gamma(e) captures that causal structure: γ∈Γ(e)\gamma \in \Gamma(e) exactly when activating γ\gamma creates a requirement to modify ee, established by the counterfactual test against the domain artifact that anchors γ\gamma.
A causal domain model. The system has a functional purpose FF and relevant causal domain knowledge κF\kappa_F, and every element embodies some part of κF\kappa_F.
Change-propagation minimisation as the objective. Cost is measured as access cost plus interference, so the target is the modularisation that minimises the scope read and modified when a change driver activates. The change-management hypothesis supplies this objective — minimise the lifetime cost of change — and change-propagation minimisation is how the derivation measures it.

Premises 1 and 2 together support Admissibility and Element Form. Premises 1 and 3 support Separation and Unification.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
2 The two conditional premises
Two further premises are required only for the stronger forms of the result.

The contamination premise — strict Separation and uniqueness. A γ\gamma-irrelevant co-resident in a touched module imposes non-zero verification overhead. Under this premise, Separation is strictly forced between classes with disjoint driver sets, and the optimal partition is unique. Without it, Separation is a propagation-neutral tie, and the Γ-equivalence partition is one propagation-minimal modularisation but not the only one.
The coefficient condition (⋆)(\star) — total-maintenance-cost optimality. For every irreducibly composite element e*e^{*} and every pure element ee whose driver set is a proper subset of Γ(e*)\Gamma(e^{*}), write S=Γ(e)S = \Gamma(e) for the shared drivers and U=Γ(e*)\Γ(e)U = \Gamma(e^{*}) \setminus \Gamma(e) for the unshared drivers. The condition is
(⋆)α∑γ∈Uλ(γ)+2ωc≥∑γ∈Sλ(γ), (\star)\quad \alpha \sum_{\gamma \in U} \lambda(\gamma) + 2\omega_c \;\ge\; \sum_{\gamma \in S} \lambda(\gamma), 
where λ(γ)\lambda(\gamma) is a change driver’s activation frequency, α\alpha is the interference coefficient (reading plus disturbance penalty per irrelevant co-resident), and ωc\omega_c is the cognitive cost per co-located pair. When (⋆)(\star) holds, the propagation minimum also minimises total maintenance cost. When it fails at some composite/sharer pair, a coarsening of the Γ-equivalence partition achieves lower total cost, and that pair needs a direct cost comparison.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
3 Precondition: driver independence
The companion results assume that distinct change drivers are independent: their knowledge slices are disjoint, and their activation events are logically independent. The load-bearing requirement is weaker. The partition prescription stays valid whenever no pair of drivers has both overlapping knowledge slices and mutual activation-coupling.
If two drivers always activate together in both directions, they are not two drivers: no element can be governed by one without the other. Merge them into a single driver, and the partition is correct for the merged driver. A pair with overlapping slices but no mutual coupling is harmless: an element that carries both drivers becomes an irreducible composite in its equivalence class, and the overlap is orthogonal to partition correctness.
Driver independence is therefore not an external stipulation. It is a well-formedness condition on the driver set CC.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
4 Precondition: decisional autonomy
The organisational unit that owns a module must be able to modify, test, and deploy within its scope without cross-unit coordination. If every change needs external sign-off, even a pure and complete module carries coordination overhead that the cost model does not capture.
Decisional autonomy is an organisational property, not a property of the code or the causal structure. The theory derives the module boundaries that minimise change propagation; it does not guarantee that those boundaries align with decision-making authority. When autonomy fails, real cost is change-propagation cost plus coordination overhead, and the partition that minimises the first may not minimise the sum. Two remedies are available: align team boundaries to the Γ-equivalence classes (reverse Conway’s Law), or add the organisational objective to the analysis and accept a composite optimum.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
section: 5 Does IVP apply to your system?
text:
5 Does IVP apply to your system?
Two gates decide applicability: is the system maintenance-dominated, and is its causal structure known?








Maintenance-dominated?
Causal structure known?
Result




Yes
Yes
The Γ-equivalence partition unconditionally minimises change-propagation cost; under (⋆)(\star) it also minimises total maintenance cost; under the contamination premise the partition is unique.


Yes
No
IVP applies in principle; driver identification is the blocking step. Proceed with domain analysis.


No
Yes
IVP is not cost-optimal for this system’s dominant objective. Parameterise the analysis with the actual objective and derive the analogous conditions.


No
No
Neither gate is open. IVP is inapplicable as a cost-minimisation result, though it may still supply useful structural vocabulary.



Within the yes/yes cell, the preconditions and conditional premises above further qualify the result. When driver independence holds and decisional autonomy holds, the partition minimises propagation cost directly, and minimises total cost when (⋆)(\star) holds. When the driver set contains mutually activation-coupled overlapping pairs, merge them. When decisional autonomy fails, extend the objective or restructure the teams. When (⋆)(\star) fails at a composite/sharer pair, use a direct cost comparison over candidate coarsenings for that pair.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
section: 6 What the derivation does not supply
text:
6 What the derivation does not supply

Driver identification. The assignment Γ\Gamma is assumed available; the derivation does not perform domain analysis for any specific system. Driver identification is domain analysis, grounded in the counterfactual test against domain artifacts.
Irreducibility determination. Reducibility judgments assume that the element’s purpose specification is available; the derivation does not decide reducibility from code alone.
Driver coverage. A system whose causal structure has not been documented is not a system that defies IVP — it is a system awaiting domain analysis. Whether every such system yields to driver analysis is an empirical question the theory does not settle.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
7 Where the analysis lives
The three unconditional premises, the two conditional premises, and the two preconditions are examined in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1]. The four conditions as necessary and jointly exhaustive, and the contamination premise for strict Separation, are developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2]. The coefficient condition (⋆)(\star) and the total-maintenance-cost result are developed in the paper on minimising change propagation and maintenance cost [3].
What IVP does not address at all — runtime behaviour, performance, security, teams, process, and tooling — is recorded on the consequences and application page.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
The Independent Variation Principle is stated over a model of a software system. This model names every object the theory needs to reason about change. It is called the software system tuple.
The tuple is written S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma). Each entry is one ingredient of the model.
The first five ingredients are inputs. They describe the system and its environment as the analysis finds them. The sixth, Γ\Gamma, is the pivot: it is the map the whole principle operates on.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
1 What the tuple is for
The tuple gives the theory a fixed vocabulary. When the site says “a change driver,” “an element,” or “the coupling relation,” it means exactly the object named in the tuple. The tuple does not describe a new kind of system. It describes any software system in terms that make its structure under change visible.
The tuple is defined and discussed in the formal papers. Here we explain what each entry means and why the tuple is built this way. The software system tuple S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma) is the model the Independent Variation Principle is stated over, as defined in the published paper on the principle [1]. The role of the causal domain knowledge κF\kappa_F in the model is developed in the paper on the nature of cohesion [2].

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
2 Elements respond to change drivers
The central modelling move is Γ\Gamma: every element is assigned the set of change drivers whose activation would force it to be modified. A computeTax() function is assigned the tax-legislation driver, because when the tax rate changes, the function must change. A sanitizeInput() function is assigned the sanitization-policy driver.
The assignment is not arbitrary. It is read from the domain: which external conditions, if they activate, force this element to change. Whether an element responds to one driver or several is a property of the domain’s causal structure, not a choice the designer makes.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
3 Two sets must be distinguished
Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is the set of change drivers that force element ee to change. The module driver set Γ(M)\Gamma(M) of a module M⊆EM \subseteq E is the union of the driver sets of its elements.
These are different objects. Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is a set of drivers for a single element. Γ(M)\Gamma(M) is a set of drivers for a group of elements. Keeping them separate matters when the theory reasons about how elements group into modules.

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Every algorithm below rests on a claim about the workload — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands. Each post names the algorithm, states the claim, and asks whether the facts are known or hoped.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Linear scan
A scan over nine statuses costs about nine comparisons, which is nothing. Point the same scan at ten thousand candidates, call it once per row over ten thousand rows, and it costs a hundred million comparisons — with no profiler line looking slow.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A linear scan examines elements in sequence until it finds the match or the collection ends: O(n) per lookup, O(1) memory, no index assumed. It encodes one claim — the collection stays small enough that the per-lookup constant dominates every alternative.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
For the scan to be knowledge rather than inertia, the domain must supply the bound: seven days in a week, a status set closed by a state machine. Where that rule holds, the constant wins: 200 lookups over 50 rows cost 10,000 comparisons, with no build, memory, or write-path cost. The gap question is whether the bound is a domain fact or a hope about tomorrow’s data.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The bound is small, stated, and enforced elsewhere: ISO country codes, a closed set of order states, a fixed feature-flag list. Any growth past the stated bound breaks a validation before it reaches the scan.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The collection is unbounded and already in the thousands, kept alive by “optimize later.” The subtler form is a scan inside a loop: checking membership per row, or deduplicating against a list, gives O(n²) — a hundred million comparisons where no line looks wrong. The set grew from five statuses to four thousand tenant codes, and nothing re-examined the scan, because the claim was never written down.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the bound on the size that makes the scan acceptable — and is it a domain fact or a hope?

If yes → the bound is a domain fact; with it enforced, the scan is correct. Record the number where a check can break.
If no → the bound is a hope, so the bill grows with the collection and the caller cannot see it. An index moves that cost to the write path.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the scan wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the set’s size and its growth rate, then ask which rule could close the set.




#Algorithms #DataStructures #Complexity #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #CodeReview

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Binary search
Binary search finds any key among a million in about twenty comparisons. Insert one row out of order and it still answers in twenty comparisons — a wrong answer, with no exception.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Binary search halves the search interval per step: O(log n) per lookup, O(1) memory. It is correct only under an invariant — the collection is ordered, and it stays ordered at every read. It encodes the claim that someone produces the order and someone restores it on every write.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Sorted order is not free; it is a maintained property with an owner. Either the domain produces it as a side effect of its own rule, or a write path pays to restore it after each insert. The gap question is not whether the array is sorted today but who keeps it sorted under insertion.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The domain emits order itself: an append-only ledger ordered by posting timestamp, a version index whose numbers increase monotonically. The sort costs nothing extra, because it is what the domain already did.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Two traps, both competent-looking. Sorting on every lookup to search once costs O(n log n) per query to save O(log n) — worse than the scan it replaced. The second is the classic bug: sort once at construction, then let inserts happen. The invariant has no owner and nothing revalidates, so the first write path added after construction — an admin endpoint, a batch import, a repair script — makes every later lookup plausibly wrong.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain both produce the sorted order and maintain it under insertion — or is the order a bet?

If yes → the order is a domain product. Binary search is the code catching up. Verify the insert path is the only write path.
If no → name which half is missing. Order produced, one write path escaping: close it. No producer at all: sort once where writes end, or keep an ordered structure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found binary search wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the lookup-to-insert ratio, then ask whether any domain rule orders the keys.




#Algorithms #BinarySearch #Complexity #DataStructures #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Quicksort
Quicksort on a million records takes about 25 million comparisons on average. Feed it a sorted array with a first-element pivot and it takes about 500 billion — same data volume, same code, and a recursion depth that overflows the stack.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recurses on each side: O(n log n) expected, O(n²) worst, in place, not stable. One call encodes four claims — no user chooses the keys, the average case is what production sees, equal keys carry no order, and the sort is a one-shot over data already in memory.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The expected case is a prediction about the input distribution, and a prediction is not knowledge until someone states where the input comes from. Four decisions hide inside one call. The gap question is whether that distribution is a domain fact: who produces these records, and can a user shape them.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A batch the system itself assembled, sorted once and discarded. Distinct keys, so equal-key order cannot mean anything. No user reaches the key sequence, and a randomized pivot is accepted. Sorting one report’s rows by order id is the shape: one shot, in memory, no adversary, no ties.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Line items sorted by amount when the input order was the customer’s line numbering: ties shuffle between runs and the diff inverts. A deterministic pivot over keys a user can submit is an O(n²) denial of service with extra steps. Re-sorting a million rows inside a 50 ms request path, where 25 million comparisons no longer fit the budget. Each is defensible alone, and each is a bet on benign input, invisible ties, or batch cadence.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is equal-key order truly irrelevant, and is the input distribution a domain fact or a hope?

If yes → quicksort is correct and cheap. Pin the pivot policy so the average case is not left to chance.
If no → choose stability where ties matter, a worst-case bound where input is reachable, incremental insertion where updates are the rhythm.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found quicksort wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Sample the input distribution, then ask whether any consumer compares equal-key order.




#Algorithms #Sorting #Quicksort #Complexity #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Stable sort
Sort a payment batch by amount with an unstable sort and two payments of 50.00 land in a different order after a routine re-import. The totals match. The audit trail no longer does.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal keys. Mergesort is stable at O(n log n) with O(n) extra space; heapsort is O(n log n) in place and unstable; the textbook quicksort partition is unstable. Stability encodes one claim: the order of equal keys is a domain fact, and something downstream reads it.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Ties are rarely ties. When two records compare equal on the sort key, a second criterion decided their order earlier — submission time, arrival sequence, posting order — and the domain already ruled on it. Stability guarantees that the earlier ruling survives the sort. The gap question is whether that criterion is a written rule or an accident of how the data arrived.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Multi-level ordering where a domain rule set the earlier order: sort by name within department, preserving the sequence the intake rule produced. Latest-first within equal priority, where the sequence carries the tie. The buffer costs O(n) and the domain states what it buys.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Both directions look plausible. Paying for stability where equal keys cannot exist — sorting by a unique id, where the extra O(n) buffer buys nothing. And the subtler one: enshrining an accident. The tie order arrived from a hash map’s iteration or from whatever order the file had, stability preserved it, a test asserted it, and now an incidental upstream order is a contractual guarantee nobody designed.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does anyone downstream depend on the order of equal keys, by a rule the domain states?

If yes → stability is domain knowledge. Document which criterion the tie order encodes, and where it comes from.
If no → use the unstable sort, keep the memory, and stop pretending the tie order means something.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found stability wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Find who reads the output, then ask whether that tie order came from a rule or from how the rows happened to arrive.




#Algorithms #Sorting #Stability #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DataStructures

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Counting and radix sort
text:
Case study: Counting and radix sort
Sorting a million records by comparison costs about 20 million comparisons. Counting instead spends one pass over the data and a table of 121 counters — because ages stop at 120, and that bound is the whole algorithm.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Counting sort tallies each key into a table indexed by the key, then writes the output in key order: O(n + k), where k is the size of the key universe. Radix sort repeats that per digit at O(d(n + b)) for d digits over a b-symbol alphabet. Both encode one claim: the keys come from a small, known, closed universe.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Comparison sorting assumes only a total order on the keys; these assume the key universe itself. The table’s size is a written claim about which values the domain can produce, and an alphabet bound is a claim about key width. The gap question is whether that universe is closed by a rule you can state, and who is notified when it opens.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Ages from 0 to 120, bounded by biology. IP octets from 0 to 255. Country codes closed by a published list. A fixed-width integer ID, where alphabet and width are facts of the type. A validation rule that already rejects anything outside the range — the constraint restated as an array.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The table sized for a universe that grew: twenty status codes, then one tenant-specific code numbered 4000, and the array is now two hundred times the data. Direct indexing over an open identifier space allocates a billion entries for a thousand user IDs. Keys of unfixed width, such as arbitrary strings, make the digit count depend on the data. Each works on test data.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the key universe closed by a domain rule you can state — and who is notified when it opens?

If yes → counting sort fits; radix also needs a fixed key width. Assert both in code, so growth fails loudly instead of allocating.
If no → the table is a bet on a universe you do not control. A comparison sort costs O(n log n) and needs no such claim.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found counting sort wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the key cardinality and range over a real sample, then find the rule that could close the universe.




#Algorithms #Sorting #RadixSort #Complexity #DataModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Topological sort
An approval chain ran for nine months with finance signing before legal, while the policy document named legal before finance. The sort printed both edges and reported a cycle on its first run — the contradiction sat in two documents, and the sort compared them.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so every edge’s source precedes its target, in O(V + E). It encodes a strong claim: the domain’s before/after relation is a partial order — asymmetric, transitive, acyclic — and pairs with no order between them are genuinely unordered, not missing information.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
A partial order cannot be inferred from observations; it must be declared — in policy, in a document the domain owns. Every edge is a domain rule; every absent edge is a claim too — that either order is acceptable — unless transitivity already decided the pair. The gap question is whether an expert can name the pairs, and which unordered pairs the domain leaves free.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Build steps whose dependencies come from declared imports. Migration ordering a database administrator can draw on a whiteboard. An approval chain written in policy. The graph is a domain artifact, the expert draws it, and the cycle check runs as a domain-consistency check — a contradiction detector, not an inconvenience.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Precedence invented to make the sort succeed: a tie between two unordered tasks, broken by list position or by ID, so the run completes and the order looks settled. Then the second trap — suppressing the cycle. Catch the exception, log a warning, fall back to declaration order, ship. The system now hides a contradiction, and the wrong order looks like a right one: no failure, no alert.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the domain expert name the before/after pairs — and for unordered pairs, is “either order is fine” the domain’s answer?

If yes → the sort embodies a real partial order. Keep the cycle check as a domain check, never as noise to route around.
If no → any acyclic output is luck. A cycle means two domain rules conflict; resolve the rules, not the graph.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the sort wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Enumerate the pairs with the expert, and treat every cycle as a question about requirements.




#Algorithms #Graphs #TopologicalSort #Dependencies #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #BuildSystems

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Breadth-first search
Six degrees of separation on a graph of a billion people: breadth-first search finds the shortest chain by expanding ring by ring — six rings, not a billion nodes, and every hop counts as one — because in that domain a hop is the unit of cost.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: BFS explores a graph in order of hop count: it visits every node at distance k before any node at distance k+1, in O(V + E) time. The queue is the whole mechanism, and a queue can only count edges. So the algorithm encodes one claim — every step costs the same, and the smallest number of intermediate stops is the domain’s notion of best.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Unit weights are a domain statement, not a default value. The claim says two routes of equal length are equally good, and that nothing distinguishes the third step from the first. The gap question is whether the domain ever decided that.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The steps are genuinely interchangeable. Degrees of separation, fewest clicks to a checkout, minimum moves in a puzzle, fewest screens in a flow — the unit is an action, and the domain counts actions. BFS is then exact, at O(V + E).








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The weights exist — in a price table, a contract, an SLA — and the traversal ignores them because a queue was easier to write and BFS is the traversal everyone knows. It returns a real path with a plausible length, so the team reports “the cheapest route” — the domain asked which route costs least, and the code answered which route is shortest. The gap stays invisible until finance compares the two routes and finds the shipped one more expensive.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain count steps — or price them? Who said all steps are equal?

If yes → hops are the domain’s unit. Check that no edge in the data carries a weight the traversal silently drops.
If no → it is a shortest-hop answer to a shortest-cost question. Read the weights, or record in writing that hops are what the domain measures.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Find two routes of equal hop count that differ in domain value, and ask the domain owner which one they would ship.




#Algorithms #GraphTraversal #BreadthFirstSearch #DomainModelling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Depth-first search
A cycle detector over a build graph of 40,000 nodes touches each node and each edge once and answers a yes/no question. Ask it for the cheapest way to break the cycle and it hands you whichever loop it stumbled into first.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: DFS follows one branch to its end before it backtracks, with a visited set to stop revisiting and a stack of depth equal to the longest path. It costs O(V + E) and returns reachability; ranking is not its product. The algorithm encodes one claim: existence or completeness is what matters, not which path is best. The first path it finds is a valid path and nothing more.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Accepting any valid answer is a strong domain decision. Either the question was “does one exist”, “is there a cycle”, or “enumerate them all” — or the domain compares answers and needs the best one. The gap question is which of those the domain asked, because DFS is honest about existence and enumeration and silent about which is best.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The domain wants the full set or the bare yes. Cycle detection on a dependency graph, all reachable accounts for a permission audit, every descendant of a category node, a topological order from postorder where the graph is acyclic. The domain never asks which answer, because every member of the set is equally wanted.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



DFS returns a path, the path is valid, and the product presents it as the route. Nobody asks whether a better one exists until a customer compares today’s route with yesterday’s and finds it longer. The trap is seductive because the output is correct in the only sense the code checks. The second trap is the visited rule keyed on the wrong field: a node reached by two paths is silently omitted, and the set is wrong in a way no test names.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the question “does one exist / enumerate all” — or “which is best”? Does the domain accept any valid answer?

If yes → existence or enumeration is the question. Check that the visited rule covers cycles and the depth covers the data.
If no → an arbitrary valid path is being read as an optimal one. Say which answer the domain compares, then compute the comparison.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask whether two valid answers are ever compared, and by what rule.




#Algorithms #GraphTraversal #DepthFirstSearch #DomainModelling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dijkstra’s shortest path
Dijkstra returns the cheapest route only while someone can name the unit of cheap. An edge weighted 3.7 minutes is a domain quantity. An edge weighted 3.7 is a number someone tuned until the demo looked right.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Dijkstra settles nodes in order of tentative distance, using a priority queue: O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap, and correctness requires non-negative weights. It encodes three claims at once — the weights are numbers the domain recognizes, costs add along a path, and the sum is what “best” means. Take away the first or the third and it still returns an optimal answer to a question nobody asked; take away additivity and the answer is optimal for nothing.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
A weight is a unit before it is a number. Minutes, euros, kilometres: each carries a decision that units are comparable, and that two routes cost the sum of their parts. The gap question is whether the domain made that decision in public, or a developer made it privately.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The weights are quantities the domain already trades in. Route planning over measured minutes, cost-optimal planning over invoice lines. Someone can check the unit with a stopwatch or a bill, and re-derive it when the contract changes. Non-negativity holds because a refund is not a journey.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The weights are invented: 0.5 because that partner is “preferred”, 1.0 because that route is “strategic”. The algorithm is textbook-correct and returns a provably optimal answer to an objective no one owns. The harder version is multi-attribute — cheapest and fastest at once — collapsed into one number that fixes an exchange rate between money and time nobody can defend.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can someone name the unit of the weights, and defend addition as the way they combine?

If yes → the weights are domain quantities. Check non-negativity, and record where each weight comes from.
If no → it is an optimizer over an invented objective. Name the attributes separately and let the domain rule compare them.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found Dijkstra wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Find who owns the trade-off, then ask what one unit of weight buys.




#Algorithms #ShortestPath #Dijkstra #DomainModelling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Optimisation

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: A* search
A* keeps the optimal route only while its estimate never overestimates. Raise one constant in the heuristic by 10% and the route comes back at most 10% longer than the best one — a bound nobody wrote down, and nothing compares the result with the optimum.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A* orders its frontier by f(n) = g(n) + h(n): cost so far plus an estimate of cost remaining. It encodes two claims. The domain supplies that estimate, and the estimate is trusted: admissible, it never overestimates the remaining cost, so optimality holds; consistent — never overestimating by more than one edge — so no node is reopened, when efficiency is required too. The heuristic is domain knowledge expressed as a number, or it is a tuning knob.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
h is a prediction, and every prediction needs a warrant. A warrant is a domain fact that bounds the remainder from below in the cost’s own unit: the straight line between two points, because no road is shorter than the line joining its ends. The gap question is where the estimate came from, and which fact keeps it from overshooting. Without that fact, faster search is bought by giving up the answer.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A principled estimate exists and someone can derive it: straight-line distance for road networks, the triangle inequality doing the proof.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The heuristic is guessed to make the search fast. It is fast, and the answers are plausible, so the returned route ships. The optimality claim stays in the comment above the function while the estimate quietly overestimates in the one region of the graph that matters. The optimality claim leaves without a test failing, because no test compares the result with the true optimum.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the domain fact that bounds the remaining cost from below — and does it hold everywhere the search runs?

If yes → A* is optimal, and the estimate is domain knowledge in numeric form. The fact you named is its warrant.
If no → say where the fact stops holding. No fact at all: drop the optimality claim. A fact that holds in part: scope the claim to that part.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found A* wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Compare h against true remaining cost on instances you can solve exactly.




#Algorithms #Search #AStar #Heuristics #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Optimisation

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Greedy algorithms
Greedy coin change is optimal for 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and wrong for 1, 3, 4: on an amount of 6 it returns three coins where two will do. Same code, opposite verdicts — the difference is a fact about the currency.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A greedy algorithm takes the locally best option at each step and never reconsiders. Interval scheduling by earliest finishing time is optimal; coin change is optimal only when the coin system is canonical; first-fit packing carries no optimality guarantee and is often good enough. The algorithm encodes a claim about the input’s structure: that the local best choice leads to a globally acceptable outcome.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
That claim is a theorem about the domain, not a property of the code. It survives when two choices can always be swapped without loss — as the 1, 2, 5, 10 coins allow and 1, 3, 4 do not. The gap question is whether the domain has that structure, or has issued a policy accepting a suboptimal answer. Both are legitimate. Neither is “it worked on our examples”.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The structure holds, or the policy is explicit. Interval scheduling by earliest finish, where the swap argument is one paragraph. A minimum spanning tree, where an edge can be added only if it joins two unconnected parts. First-fit packing where an operations rule accepts wasted capacity above a threshold.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The counterexample is one step away. A non-canonical coin system invented by a loyalty programme. Scheduling with prerequisites, where the earliest-finishing task is not the one that unblocks the rest. Greedy on this shape is seductive because it is O(n log n), short, and correct on every example it was shown — and the examples were chosen by the person who wanted it to work.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state why local optimality survives to the global level — or has the domain explicitly accepted a possibly-suboptimal answer?

If yes → the structure holds, so optimality survives. If the policy was merely accepted, say so, and never call it proved.
If no → it is a heuristic wearing a proof’s clothes. Search for the counterexample, or compute the optimum.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found greedy wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Brute-force the small inputs; one counterexample settles it.




#Algorithms #Greedy #Optimisation #Complexity #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Correctness

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dynamic programming
Edit distance between two 1,000-character strings is a million cells. The table is not the algorithm’s overhead — each axis is a domain statement: these two prefixes, this cost.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: DP solves a problem by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems over a state space: edit distance over prefix pairs in O(mn), knapsack over items times capacity in O(nW). It encodes two claims — the subproblems genuinely overlap, and optimal substructure holds, meaning the best answer assembles from the best answers to its parts — over a state space the domain recognizes. The state definition is the domain model. Two axes of a table are two distinctions the domain is willing to pay to keep apart.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Writing the state is a modelling act, and it is the whole decision. Items times capacity says the domain cares which items and how much room is left, not arrival order. Positions in one string times positions in the other says the strings are compared as sequences. The gap question has two halves: can the axes be named in the domain’s vocabulary, and do the subproblems genuinely overlap — the same state reached by several routes.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Optimal substructure is real, and the state is a domain object. Edit distance, knapsack where capacity is a measured space. The table is large because the domain is that large, and the size is the honest cost of an exact answer.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The state carries distinctions the domain never asked about: the identity of the request, the tenant. The table then grows with traffic instead of with the problem, and the explosion gets blamed on “combinatorics”. Size is read as rigour: the table is big, so the state is assumed to have been thought through.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you define the state in the domain’s words, and say why the subproblems overlap — or is the table just where the complexity went?

If yes → the state is the domain model. Check each axis against a question the domain actually asks.
If no → drop the axis, or drop the table. Either the distinction is not the domain’s, or the subproblems do not repeat.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found DP wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the state’s axes, then ask the domain owner which of them it distinguishes.




#Algorithms #DynamicProgramming #Complexity #DomainModelling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Optimisation

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Divide and conquer
Splitting an 8-second job into eight independent parts finishes in 1 second — and the job still takes 8, because recombining them costs the other 7.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Solve the problem by splitting it into subproblems, solving each, and combining the answers. The choice encodes two claims the framing list does not name: the subproblems share no state, and the combine is cheaper than the work the split removed. Merge sort earns Θ(n log n) this way — merging two sorted halves is a linear pass, and there are log n such passes.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must state that the split follows a real separation: the halves share no state, and no rule couples one half’s answer to the other’s. Sorting halves works because the position of one value does not depend on the other half — a domain fact about total orders, not a property of the code.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The domain genuinely decomposes. Records partition by account, and one account’s aggregate is independent of every other’s, so combining is an addition over disjoint keys. A map covers disjoint regions, so each region’s answer stands alone. The combine is a sum, a max, or a union — cheap next to the piece work.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The halves are only apparently separate. Both write the same counter or session record, so the “independent” subproblems serialize at the combine and the split buys latency it cannot deliver. Or the merge dominates: a combine that passes over the whole output at every level turns the algorithm into its own combine step with recursion attached. The combine is where the claim is priced: eight partial sums is eight additions, eight merged runs is a pass over the whole output.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the independence of the pieces a domain fact — and is combining cheaper than the work the split removed?

If yes → the split follows the domain’s own separation. Watch the combine as the data grows; it scales with the whole, not with a piece.
If no → say which claim failed. Coupled state: the pieces serialize. Dominant combine: the split gave back the work it removed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Time the combine against the total. If the combine is the majority, the split is not the decomposition.




#Algorithms #DivideAndConquer #Decomposition #Parallelism #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Backtracking
A timetabling problem with 12 rooms and 30 lectures has 30! orderings. The solver answers in about 40 milliseconds, because one conflict rule rejects a bad prefix long before it is a schedule.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Build a candidate one decision at a time and abandon a partial candidate the moment a constraint fails, then try the next option at that depth. The choice encodes one claim: the domain’s constraints are checkable on incomplete candidates, and they prune enough that the remaining search is affordable. The worst case stays exponential — O(b^d) for branching b and depth d — pruning lowers constants and effective depth, never that bound.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must supply the rule that kills a prefix. A partial timetable is already wrong when two lectures claim one room at one hour, and that check is local and cheap. The recursion only carries the domain’s constraint structure; without such a rule the search has no reason to stop anywhere.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Real constraint propagation exists. Scheduling with hard room and lecturer conflicts, where a conflict is decidable from the assigned prefix. Dependency resolution, where a version conflict is visible before the full set is chosen.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Brute force wearing the name. The recursion walks every subset and the “constraint check” runs only at the leaf, so nothing prunes and the run time grows with the whole space. Pruning that is unsound returns a wrong answer faster, which is worse than being slow.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does a domain rule kill a partial candidate early, near the root rather than near the leaf?

If yes → the search mirrors the domain’s constraint structure. Check next that the rule is sound and that it fires near the root, not near the leaf.
If no → it is enumeration with a stack. Bound the space before you run it, or accept that the run time grows with the whole space.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Time a run at n items and at n+1. If the time doubles per added item, nothing is pruning.




#Algorithms #Backtracking #ConstraintSolving #Search #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Sliding window and two pointers
text:
Case study: Sliding window and two pointers
A fraud rule looks back 100 transactions because 100 is a round number. The two events that correlate sit 101 apart, so any window of 100 cuts a real relation and joins an unrelated one.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Keep a contiguous span between two indices, plus a rule that decides whether the span is valid. Both indices move forward only, so each element enters and leaves at most once and the pass is O(n) instead of O(n·k) for rescanning every window of size k. The choice encodes two claims: the answer is a property of a contiguous span, and validity is monotone in span length, so shrinking is the correct repair.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must state the span rule and its bound: at most K distinct items, no more than X consecutive failures, sessions no longer than T. The algorithm assumes such a rule exists and that adjacency in the data means something. Where the domain never stated a span, the window has nothing to be faithful to.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The domain states the span. Rate limits over the last T seconds. A rolling count or sum over five minutes, where shrinking the span is a subtraction. A circuit breaker opening after N consecutive failures, where “consecutive” is a domain word. Run-length constraints in validation.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The window sits over data whose relevant pairs are not contiguous. Two transactions that correlate may lie a month apart with unrelated rows between them. The size is often chosen because the algorithm needs one — 100 rows because 100 is round — so any pair separated by 101 rows is invisible. And non-monotone validity breaks it silently: if adding an element can restore validity, shrinking is the wrong repair and valid answers are skipped.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain state the window rule and its size — or do the algorithm’s needs supply them?

If yes → the window is the domain’s own span rule and the bound is a number the domain stated. Check the ordering: a window means something only if adjacency means something.
If no → the window is a reading habit. The span is a pair the data never promised to keep adjacent, and the size is arbitrary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask what makes two records adjacent in this ordering. If nothing does, no window is faithful.




#Algorithms #SlidingWindow #RateLimiting #Streaming #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Quickselect and order statistics
text:
Case study: Quickselect and order statistics
A dashboard needs the 99th percentile of 50 million latencies. Sorting all 50 million to read one value costs about 1.3 billion comparisons; quickselect gets it in about two linear passes.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Partition around a pivot and recurse only into the side containing rank k, discarding the rest. Average O(n), worst case O(n²) with bad pivots, O(n) guaranteed with median-of-medians. The choice encodes one claim: the domain consumes the k-th order statistic — the median, the top-k set, the percentile — and the ordering of the other n−1 values is work nobody reads.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must state k and state that only the k-th value is consumed. A p99 SLA threshold is such a statement. So is a median with no requirement on the rest of the distribution. Where the domain never said which statistic it acts on, selection is a guess about what the reader will want.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Percentile SLAs at p99, with a randomized or median-of-medians pivot, where nothing else is read. Median response time reported as one figure. Top-N by score where the set matters and order within it does not. Each case pays O(n) for one answer and never asks for the rest.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The median is computed, then the same report paginates and ranks the rows, so the sort happens anyway and the selection was a wasted extra pass. Or k is unstable: page size sets k, so the domain re-asks with a different k on every request, and each request pays O(n) over the same 50 million rows a hundred times a minute — where one sort and one index would have answered every k. Right per call, wrong per workload.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the partial answer genuinely what’s consumed — or does the next step need the full order?

If yes → selection is the answer. Check next whether k is stable across requests, since that decides pass-per-request against sort-once.
If no → the full order is the real product. Sort or index once and answer every k from it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Trace the value one step downstream; that step decides.




#Algorithms #Quickselect #Percentiles #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Reservoir sampling
A log stream at 20,000 events a second produces 1.7 billion events a day. A 1,000-item reservoir estimates the error rate to about ±3% and keeps a thousand of them.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Keep k items from a stream of unknown length so that every item seen so far is in the sample with probability k/n. The classic form holds the first k, then keeps the i-th item with probability k/i in place of a uniformly chosen one. The choice encodes one claim: a uniform sample answers the question, and a census is neither needed nor possible.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must pose a question about the population and accept a sampling error. For a proportion, the 95% margin is 1.96 × 0.5/√k, so a thousand items give about ±3% — a number someone states and accepts, not one discovered later. Where the domain asks about a particular item, no sample size helps.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Population-level questions with a stated error. The fraction of requests that fail, to a margin someone wrote down. The share of requests slower than 300 ms. In each case the answer is a rate over the population, the error is written beside it, and no individual item is the subject. A distribution’s shape is a different question, and a reservoir answers it only at the quantiles it can support.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Fraud review, compliance audit, incident triage: the question is per item, and the rare event is exactly what a uniform sample misses. At one event in 10,000 and a sample of 1,000, the chance of missing it is about 90%. Then sample statistics get reported as facts — “the sample shows no failures” becomes “there were no failures”.
