Uniform inclusion is itself a claim: where rare events matter, stratified sampling — sampling within each group — is the right instrument, not the cheap one.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the question about the population — and is the sampling error a stated, accepted bound?

If yes → a sample of stated size answers it, and the error is a number someone wrote down beside the metric.
If no → say which half failed. Per-item question: no sample size answers it. Population question with no stated bound: state one and accept it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask what decision the number feeds. If one missed item changes that decision, the question is per item.




#Algorithms #Sampling #Statistics #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Streaming approximate algorithms
Counting distinct users over a day needs memory proportional to the users. HyperLogLog answers the same question from a fixed 12 KB, and states its standard error.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality from the longest run of leading zeros in each of m registers; with 16,384 registers of six bits, 12 KB, the standard error is 1.04/√m, or 0.81%. Count-Min Sketch estimates item frequencies from d arrays of counters and only ever over-counts. Both encode one claim: an estimate carrying a stated error bound is acceptable, and exactness is not a requirement.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The domain must accept a bound and name the decisions the number feeds, so the acceptance is explicit rather than accidental. Where nobody can say which decision reads the number, nobody can say whether 0.81% is acceptable, and the Count-Min is a guess about tolerance.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Dashboards, alert thresholds, and capacity planning, where 9,980 and 10,000 distinct users lead to the same decision. Cardinality of a label set when the question is “ten series or ten thousand”. Trend detection, where the movement matters and the last digit does not.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Billing and reconciliation counts: the approximate answer becomes a money number someone acts on. A 0.81% standard error on four million events is 32,500 events at one sigma, 65,000 at two, and at a per-event price that is an invoice line. Count-Min only over-counts, so a “block above 1,000 requests” rule fires early and never late — maybe fine, never chosen. Often the bound is unstated: a Count-Min sized for 1% error then answers a decision that needs 0.01%.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does an error of the stated size leave every decision that reads this number unchanged?

If yes → the estimate is the knowledge and the error is its contract. Put the bound next to the number.
If no → the number became a fact by accident. Exact counting is the repair, and it costs the memory that made the sketch attractive.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the consumers of the number. If any of them acts per item, the estimate is the wrong tool.




#Algorithms #HyperLogLog #ApproximateComputing #Metrics #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Consistent hashing
Ten cache nodes become eleven, and modulo hashing remaps ten of every eleven keys. The key count did not change. Only the number of nodes did.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring, and a key belongs to the first node at or after its position. Adding a node splits one arc, so roughly 1/n of the keys move instead of (n−1)/n. The choice encodes one claim: membership changes, and remapping the whole key space on each change costs more than the ring costs to keep.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
For the ring to be knowledge, the domain must have decided that the node set is dynamic. It must also decide that the remap cost matters: at ten nodes a full remap loses ten of every eleven warm entries, and that loss must outweigh the ring’s complexity. The gap question: does membership actually change here, and what does one change cost?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A cache tier or shard cluster that scales with load, where nodes join on a capacity schedule and leave on failure. The misses that follow a join are bounded by the fraction that moved. The domain owns the fact: capacity is elastic, and churn is its normal state.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Three nodes, provisioned by hand, in a deployment that has not scaled in two years — and has no plan to. The ring remains. So do the virtual nodes (several ring positions per node), the rebalancing tool, and the key-placement debugging. None answers a question this deployment asks. The seductive form runs the other way: a fleet that scales weekly, where the team skips the ring because “we only have a few nodes,” and pays a full remap every Monday.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does membership actually change on this system — how often, measured? Is the remap cost real here or inherited from another system’s scale?

If yes → the ring is the knowledge. Record the churn rate and the fraction of keys each change moves.
If no → it is a fixed placement carrying a ring’s maintenance bill. Take modulo, or a static table.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count the membership changes in the deploy log over six months.




#DistributedSystems #Caching #Scaling #Partitioning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Join algorithms (nested loop, hash join, sort-merge)
text:
Case study: Join algorithms (nested loop, hash join, sort-merge)
A join assumed to return 200 rows returns 2 million. The plan chose nested loop, the query runs for 9 minutes, and the optimizer did exactly what the numbers it was given said to do.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A nested loop reads the outer input once and the inner input once per outer row: n × m reads without an index on the inner side, about n × log m with one. A hash join builds a table on one input and probes with the other in linear time, and needs the build side to fit in memory. A sort-merge join sorts both inputs and merges them, which is also the one that serves range predicates. All three encode the same claims: which input is small, how much of it survives the filters, and which of an index, a memory budget, or sorted input the domain supplies.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
For the plan to be knowledge, someone must know that the domain produces tables at these sizes, and that these predicates keep this fraction of rows. The gap question is the size ratio and the selectivity — the fraction of rows each filter keeps — on this data, with these filters, not a ratio a benchmark reported for another schema.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The sizes are measured on the real tables: a 50-million-row fact table joined to a 2,000-row currency dimension, where building the hash on the dimension and probing with the fact reads each table once. The domain supplies the ratio, and the plan follows from it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The plan carries yesterday’s statistics. “The filter makes it small” states a selectivity nobody measured, and the estimate holds until one customer’s data arrives. It all works in development, on ten-thousand-row fixtures, where every plan is fast and every plan is wrong for the same reason: nothing was measured at production size.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has the small side been measured on this data, with these filters — and recently enough to trust?

If yes → the plan follows, if the build side fits memory and the index exists. Recheck counts after each backfill.
If no → the plan pays for an unmeasured prediction. Read the actual row counts, then choose.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the join wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Run the join with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare estimated to actual rows per node.




#Databases #QueryPlanning #Joins #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Recursion instead of iteration
text:
Case study: Recursion instead of iteration
A recursive descent over a partner’s JSON overflows the stack at four thousand nesting levels. Every fixture had seven. The bound was never written down, so nothing could enforce it.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Each recursive call takes a stack frame: parameters, locals, return address. The stack is finite — typically 8 MB on Linux for the main thread, around 1 MB default on a JVM thread, and Python stops itself at 1,000 frames. Recursion therefore encodes one claim about the input: the depth is bounded, and the bound is comfortably under what the stack holds.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
The depth bound is a claim about the shape of the input, not about the code. For recursion to be knowledge, the domain must have decided that shape: a grammar with a declared maximum nesting, a hierarchy with a known height, a tree the system itself builds. The gap question: is that shape a domain fact, or a property of the fixtures the tests happened to use?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An org chart eight levels deep. A category tree whose schema declares four levels. Balanced tree traversal, where depth is log n and n is bounded by memory anyway. An expression tree the parser builds from its own grammar, so its depth is bounded by the nesting the language defines. Here the bound is a domain fact, and the recursion states it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Recursion over user-supplied nesting: JSON from an API, reply threads, folder hierarchies, XML from a third party. The producer decides the depth and has published no limit. Recursion is clearer to read, the tests use shallow fixtures, and the single input that breaks it arrives from one customer’s import at 3 a.m. The guard is worse than the recursion: a depth limit of 1,000 chosen because the test passed at 900 is an enforcement of a number nobody owns.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain bound the depth, with a limit you can cite?

If yes → the recursion states the bound. Record it next to the function that relies on it.
If no → the recursion bets on a bound nobody owns. Iteration pays in clarity; a guard pays in a number you must justify.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the recursion wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the deepest input the producers actually send.




#Recursion #Robustness #Parsing #StackOverflow #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Algorithms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Batch versus incremental recomputation
text:
Case study: Batch versus incremental recomputation
A dashboard recomputes its whole aggregate on every keystroke in the filter box. Eight analysts typing all day at 40 ms per recompute is an afternoon of database time spent on numbers nobody read.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Batch recomputes the whole answer from the whole input. Incremental applies only the delta to the answer already held. The choice encodes two claims the framing list does not name: how often the input changes, and how stale the answer may be.


The algorithmic knowledge gap it signals
Both claims are domain facts. The ledger posts at 23:00 and prices change hourly — that is a change rate. The report is read at 07:00 by a controller who accepts yesterday’s close — that is a staleness tolerance. Neither is a property of the code. The gap question: has anyone stated the freshness number, and has the person who reads the number accepted it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Nightly totals for a morning report, where the freshness is stated and accepted in writing. Incremental maintenance where reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude and each change touches a small fraction of the answer, so the delta path pays for itself. In both cases the change rate and the tolerance were named before the mechanism was chosen.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The mirror image of the hook is the seductive one: a change log, incremental tables, and a reconciliation job for a report a nightly forty-minute batch already answered, because nobody measured that the input changes twice a day. Behind both sits the same artifact — a “real-time” requirement that traces to no business rule, defended by the fact that it sounds like a requirement.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has someone accepted how stale the answer may be — and is the input’s change rate measured?

If yes → choose the cheaper mechanism that meets both numbers.
If no → the choice is a preference, not engineering. Write the two numbers down first.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the choice wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count the writes per day, then ask the reader what staleness they would notice.




#DataPipelines #BatchProcessing #Caching #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Architecture Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Each architecture pattern names a boundary the domain must already have drawn. The five styles get their full assessments under Verdicts: Hexagonal, Onion, Clean, Layered, Vertical slice.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Architecture Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Command Pattern

GoF: Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an action is a first-class thing — not just a method call — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an operation must be recorded, queued, undone, or scheduled — the action itself is a domain entity with identity and lifecycle,” then Command is just embodying that knowledge.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats actions as entities: they can be stored, replayed, reversed, and audited. An order-fulfillment system where “ShipOrder,” “CancelOrder,” and “RefundOrder” are domain commands — with undo semantics, execution timestamps, and audit trails — is the domain speaking. Command closes the gap: it prevents the action logic from being a method buried on some service class, which would make the action invisible to the domain model. Instead, each command is a domain object with its own data, validation, and undo path.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “commands” are not domain commands — they’re method-call wrappers. Wrapping every service-method invocation in a Command object because the framework expects it doesn’t reify a domain concept; it wraps function calls in infrastructure ceremony. Command here adds object-allocation and indirection costs to what should be a direct call, signaling entity-richness where the domain has none. Event-sourcing architectures are a valid exception — commands as persisted entities with identity serve a persistence/routing infrastructure that IS the architecture.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain expert talk about this operation as a thing that exists — “the shipment,” “the refund,” “the approval request”?

If yes → applicable: Command is the code catching up to the knowledge. If no → inapplicable: it’s function-call packaging. If you can’t answer → unclear: you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #CommandPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Architecture Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dependency Injection

Fowler: A form of Inversion of Control in which a component is given its dependencies rather than creating them itself. [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
With dependency injection, a service declares: I need these dependencies — but I do not need to know where to get them, or how to build them; give them to me. A faithful declaration carries domain knowledge: an order service needs persistence and messaging. Even which database, which queue, and how they are built is a domain decision: someone chose them. The interface states the need; the composition root supplies the answer. The gap it signals is whether the need is real and whether the supply can vary.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The need is real and the supply can vary. The order service always needs persistence; which database serves it can change. The interface declares the need once; the composition root supplies the answer.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The need is invented, or the need is real but the supply cannot vary. Either way the injection point asserts a boundary the domain never decided: the external seam is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the need real, and can the supply vary?

If the need is real and the supply can vary → applicable. Dependency injection is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the need is invented → inapplicable; nothing to abstract. If the supply cannot vary → inapplicable; no variation justifies it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Architecture Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: DI is not the composition root
text:
DI is not the composition root
DI is a technique: how a service declares its dependencies and receives them from outside.
The composition root is a place: where the application assembles its object graph, at the entry point. Only applications should have one — composition belongs to the application. A DI container belongs only there.
DI does not specify where the object graph is assembled; the composition root answers that.
Two failures hide when the names are conflated: - Scattered wiring: composition at each use site, with no root. A deployment change touches many files. - A frozen choice: a root that bakes a per-operation choice in at startup.

#DependencyInjection #CompositionRoot #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Architecture Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composition Root

Seemann: A single, logical location in an application where modules are composed together. [3]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The assembly looks purely technical, but it is still a domain decision: the same modularization rule decides where the composition root goes, what each service receives, what belongs inside each service, and whether each dependency is fixed for the object’s lifetime. The root decides those choices once, for the whole graph. The rule is derived from domain knowledge: it follows from which choices the domain owns and which it leaves open. The service’s content is fixed by the rule, not by the wiring that supplies it. The gap is the rule: if you cannot say which choices the domain owns, you cannot say where the composition root goes or what the services contain.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The modularization rule is clear, so the composition root sits where it belongs, and each service receives what the rule assigns. A change to one choice touches one place.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The rule is unstated. A choice the domain owns is supplied at the composition root, so the domain can no longer vary it — every such change now edits the composition root. Or the composition root sits in a library or framework, so it carries choices that belong to its caller.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the rule that places the composition root and assigns what each service receives?

If yes → applicable. Composition Root is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The composition root is placed by guesswork.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CompositionRoot #DependencyInjection #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Modularization #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
The concurrency constructs below encode facts about the workload: what may interleave, what must be ordered, how long a wait is acceptable, and how much may fail together.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Actor Model

Hewitt et al.: The actor model represents concurrency as independent actors that communicate only by asynchronous messages. [1]

An actor is an isolated unit that owns its state and processes arriving messages one at a time.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a domain entity owns its state and reacts to the work that arrives to it is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “this entity processes its work one unit at a time, in isolation, and the only way to influence it is to hand it a new unit of work,” then the Actor Model embodies that knowledge. The heart of an actor is the behaviour: the entity’s own rule for each unit of work. However the code is dressed, this entity owns its state and changes it only in response to what it received.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that each entity is a self-contained unit that owns its state and changes it only in response to the work it is given. Actors close the gap: they stop outside code from reaching in and rewriting that state, which would scatter ownership across every caller. The queue of arriving work is the domain’s own “work is consumed as it arrives” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain treats the work as one immediate, ordered step with nothing to protect. The actor still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone chose to model this work as an isolated entity with a queue. It fits only when the domain names the state ownership and the queue as requirements. If not, the actor asserts a boundary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert describe this entity as owning its state and responding to the work it is given — a thing that “handles what arrives, in isolation,” not a thing you reach into and change?

If yes → applicable. The Actor Model is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The construct asserts an ownership boundary the domain never drew. Decide it, or use a plain call that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ActorModel #Concurrency #MessagePassing #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Semaphore / bounded resource

Dijkstra: A semaphore is an integer with atomic wait and signal operations used to coordinate access to a shared resource. [2]

A semaphore is a counter that limits how many tasks may use a shared resource at once.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that only a fixed number of these things may be in use at once is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallises that “there are exactly eight loading docks,” “we hold at most fifty concurrent licences,” or “the lot has two hundred spaces,” then the bound is a fact about the world. A semaphore is that fact made executable. The count is the domain’s own “how many can exist at once” rule; the acquire/release discipline is the domain’s own “hold one only while the world lends it” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a hard ceiling on concurrent use, and exceeding it is a domain error, not just a slowdown. A semaphore closes the gap: it stops the code from treating a limited resource as unlimited, which would let callers exceed a limit the world does not permit. The permit count is the domain’s own capacity; the wait is the domain’s own “queue until one frees” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the bound looks like a performance knob — a connection-pool size, a thread count, a rate limit. But even a capacity limit is a domain decision: someone chose the bound. A semaphore fits only when the domain names the resource as a bounded shared pool. If the number is an arbitrary, freely changeable knob, the domain has not named a bound, and the semaphore asserts a constraint nobody decided. That is the gap — the bound is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert name the limit — “eight docks, fifty licences, two hundred spaces” — as a fact of the business rather than a setting someone picked?

If yes → applicable. The Semaphore is the code catching up to the knowledge; the count is the domain’s own capacity.
If no → inapplicable. The count asserts a bound the domain never set. Name the bound, or use a plain limiter that does not claim one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Semaphore #Concurrency #BoundedResource #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Read-Write Lock

Courtois et al.: A readers-writer lock permits concurrent readers or a single writer. [3]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that many parties may look at the same thing at once, but only one may change it, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a timetable may be read by every dispatcher while a single edit is in flight,” or “a catalogue may be browsed while one price is corrected,” then the read-write asymmetry is a fact about the world, not a performance guess. A read-write lock is that fact made executable: readers share, writers exclude.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain distinguishes observation from modification, and the two are asymmetrically compatible — many observers may coexist, but a change must be alone. A read-write lock closes the gap: it gives readers concurrent access while keeping the writer exclusive, which is the domain’s own “look freely, change carefully” rule. Using a plain mutual-exclusion lock instead would needlessly serialise observers the domain says may proceed together.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “readers” and “writers” split may look purely technical. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed these operations differ in kind. A read-write lock fits only when the domain names observation and modification as distinct activities. When everything is an update, the domain has not named that distinction, and the second lock state and writer-starvation risk assert a role nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat reading and changing this thing as genuinely different activities — many may look, one may alter — or is that distinction only about performance?

If yes → applicable. The Read-Write Lock is the code catching up to the knowledge; observers and changers are domain roles.
If no → inapplicable. The split asserts an observer role the domain never named. Name the distinction, or use a plain mutex that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ReadWriteLock #Concurrency #SharedState #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Producer–Consumer

Dijkstra: A producer–consumer system decouples production from consumption through a bounded buffer. [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Producer–Consumer is a pattern where one side adds work to a queue and the other takes it off. The fact that work arrives on one rhythm and is handled on another is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “orders arrive whenever customers click, but the kitchen cooks one ticket at a time,” then the queue is not an optimisation — it is the domain’s own buffer between two activities that run at different rates, with the bounded queue as the domain’s own “we can hold only so much waiting work” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain contains two distinct activities — arrival and handling — that proceed at different rates, and the gap between them is real waiting work. Producer–Consumer closes the gap: it prevents the arrival side from being coupled directly to the handling side, which would force clicks to block on cooking and cooking to be paced by clicks. The queue decouples the rhythms the domain already treats as separate.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain sees one immediate, ordered step: the work arrives and is done in the same breath, with no waiting state. A queue still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone claimed arrival and handling are separate. Producer–Consumer fits only when the domain names a real waiting state. If not, the queue asserts a waiting room nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a real waiting state — work that has arrived but is not yet handled — or is arrival and handling one immediate act?

If yes → applicable. Producer–Consumer is the code catching up to the knowledge; the queue is the domain’s own waiting room.
If no → inapplicable. The queue asserts a waiting state the domain never named. Name it, or use a direct call that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ProducerConsumer #Concurrency #BoundedQueue #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Barrier (phase synchronization)

Goetz et al.: A barrier makes a set of threads wait until all have reached a common point. [4]

A barrier makes every participant wait until all have arrived, then releases them together.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a stage cannot begin until all participants have finished the prior stage is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the meeting cannot start until every attendee has arrived,” or “the tally is only valid once every ward has reported,” then the barrier is the domain’s own rendezvous rule made executable.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a rendezvous: the next step is well-defined only when every participant has completed the current one, and a partial set is meaningless. A barrier closes the gap: it stops fast participants from racing ahead into a stage the domain says is not yet valid, which would let a premature actor act on an incomplete world. The barrier is the domain’s own “wait for all” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “wait for everyone” looks like a technical staging device — a synchronisation point that exists because one task happens to depend on several results. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the participants form one collective. A barrier fits only when the domain names the group as a real unit and the moment as shared. If the domain has not named a collective, the all-must-arrive rule asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat the stage as meaningful only when all participants have completed the prior one — is the group itself a domain entity?

If yes → applicable. The Barrier is the code catching up to the knowledge; the rendezvous is the domain’s own rule.
If no → inapplicable. The rendezvous asserts a collective the domain never named. Name it, or use a future or gather that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Barrier #Concurrency #PhaseSynchronization #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Double-Checked Locking / lazy initialization
text:
Case study: Double-Checked Locking / lazy initialization

Goetz et al.: Double-checked locking tests a flag, then locks and tests again before creating an object, to avoid locking on the common path. [4]

Double-checked locking tests a flag first, then locks and tests again before it creates the object.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing should not come into existence until it is first needed is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a ledger is opened only when the first entry is posted,” or “the archive is materialised only when someone asks for it,” then laziness is the domain’s own “existence begins on demand” rule. Double-checked locking makes that rule executable safely. When the domain has not named when existence begins, that is unwritten knowledge.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the object’s lifecycle begins on first use: its creation has a real cost or meaning, and eager creation would assert existence before the domain says it exists. Double-checked locking closes the gap: it keeps creation lazy while avoiding the cost of serialising every access. The laziness is the domain’s own “not until needed” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the laziness looks purely technical — a startup-cost optimisation. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose when the object exists. Double-checked locking fits only when the domain names that moment as meaningful. If creation timing is a free choice the domain never named, the volatile flag and null-check assert a lifecycle rule nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain care when this thing begins to exist — does it recognise a real “not yet” state — or is creation timing purely a performance question?

If yes → applicable. Double-Checked Locking is the code catching up to the knowledge; laziness is the domain’s own lifecycle rule.
If no → inapplicable. The laziness asserts a lifecycle rule the domain never named. Name it, or create eagerly without the memory-model ceremony.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DoubleCheckedLocking #LazyInitialization #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutable Snapshot / copy-on-write

Goetz et al.: An immutable snapshot exposes a consistent instance while writers replace it copy-on-write. [4]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an observation must reflect a single consistent instant is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a quote is the price at the moment it was issued,” “a bank statement is the balance as of the closing date,” or “a submitted tax return is frozen,” then a snapshot is the domain’s own “this reading is a point in time” rule made executable. Copy-on-write is one encoding: the reader sees a stable version while a writer prepares a new one.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain requires point-in-time consistency: what an observer sees must be one coherent state, not a mixture of before and after. An immutable snapshot closes the gap: it prevents a concurrent reader from observing a half-applied change, which would show the domain a state that never legally existed. The snapshot is the domain’s own “freeze this reading” rule; the writer’s new version is the domain’s own “changes take effect as a new whole” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the snapshot is taken to avoid locks or allocations, so it looks purely technical. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed a reader must see one consistent moment. Copy-on-write fits only when the domain names the instant of observation as meaningful. If the domain has not named it, copying the whole structure adds allocation and garbage pressure for a rule nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat this reading as a fact fixed at a moment — a quote, a statement, a frozen submission — rather than a casual glance at whatever is current?

If yes → applicable. Immutable Snapshot is the code catching up to the knowledge; the frozen reading is the domain’s own fact.
If no → inapplicable. The snapshot asserts a frozen instant the domain never named. Name it, or read directly without inventing one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CopyOnWrite #Snapshot #Immutability #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Saga / compensating action

Garcia-Molina and Salem: A saga splits a long-lived transaction into steps, each with a compensating action to undo it. [5]

A saga runs local steps in sequence and, on failure, compensates each completed one.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain knows how to reverse or offset each step is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a booking can be cancelled,” “a shipment can be returned and restocked,” and “a charge can be refunded,” then a saga is the domain’s own set of reverse actions made executable. Each compensating step is a domain rule — the reverse of a domain act — not a technical rollback invented by the transaction machinery.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain comprises several long-running steps across boundaries that cannot be made atomic, and each step has a reversal the business already performs. A saga closes the gap: it prevents a distributed transaction from pretending that the whole process is atomic, which the domain does not permit. The compensations are the domain’s own “how we undo this” rules; the sequence is the domain’s own business process.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “compensation” looks purely technical — a data cleanup to fix a failed write. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the steps are separately reversible. A saga fits only when the domain names a real reversal for each step. When the steps are atomic within one boundary, the domain has not named a reversal, and the undo path asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain perform these reversals in the real world — a cancellation, a refund, a restock — or would the “compensation” be a cleanup only engineers understand?

If yes → applicable. The Saga is the code catching up to the knowledge; compensations are the domain’s own reverse acts.
If no → inapplicable. The saga asserts reverse steps the domain never named. Name them, or keep one transaction that does not invent undo.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Saga #CompensatingTransaction #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Circuit Breaker

Nygard: A circuit breaker trips after repeated failures and short-circuits calls until the dependency recovers. [6]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain names a dependency as unavailable is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “when the card processor is down, we take the order on account,” or “when the address service is unavailable, we route to manual review,” then the domain has named the failure state: this dependency is down. A circuit breaker is that state made executable — after repeated failure it trips open and stops the calls. The trip threshold is a chosen bound; the down state it acts on is the domain’s rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain names the condition under which a dependency is unavailable, and it accepts that calls must stop while the dependency is down. A circuit breaker closes the gap: it prevents the code from hammering a failing dependency, and it records the domain’s own down state. The open state is the domain’s own “stop calling” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain treats every call as independently worth attempting, with no named state in which the dependency is down. The breaker still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone claimed this dependency has a failure state. A circuit breaker fits only when the domain names that state. If the domain has not named it, the trip threshold and open state assert a failure boundary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain name a state in which this dependency is unavailable — a real down state — or is every call independently worth attempting?

If yes → applicable. The Circuit Breaker is the code catching up to the knowledge; the open state is the domain’s own down state.
If no → inapplicable. The open state asserts a failure boundary the domain never named. Name it, or retry plainly without inventing one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CircuitBreaker #Resilience #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Scheduler / time-triggered job
A scheduler runs a job at a set time or on a recurring timetable.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that something happens at a particular time is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the books close at end of business on the last working day,” “interest posts on the first of the month,” or “the report runs every Friday before the stand-up,” then the trigger is a domain rule and the cron expression is merely its encoding. The schedule is the domain’s own calendar made executable; the job is the domain’s own “this must happen then” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain attaches meaning to the moment: a deadline, a settlement date, a statutory filing window. A scheduler closes the gap: it prevents the timing from being buried in an operator’s habit or a manual reminder, and it records the domain’s own calendar. The trigger time is the domain’s own fact; the recurring run is the domain’s own recurring obligation.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “schedule” looks like an operational convenience — a nightly cache warm, a log rotation, a cleanup at 03:00. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose the time. A scheduler fits only when the domain names the moment as meaningful. If the time is a free choice the domain never named, the trigger asserts an obligation nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert say the business requires that this happens at that time — a deadline, a settlement, a statutory date — or is the time just when it is convenient to run?

If yes → applicable. The Scheduler is the code catching up to the knowledge; the trigger is the domain’s own calendar.
If no → inapplicable. The trigger asserts a business date the domain never named. Name it, or run an interval that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Scheduler #Concurrency #TimeTriggered #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Concurrency Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Thread Confinement / thread-local state
text:
Case study: Thread Confinement / thread-local state

Goetz et al.: Thread confinement restricts an object to a single thread, removing the need for synchronization. [4]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that one worker handles one case from start to finish is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the assigned caseworker owns the case until it closes,” or “one clerk processes one application throughout,” then confinement of the working state to that worker is the domain’s own “this caretaker owns this case” rule made executable. Thread-local state is one encoding: the state belongs to the worker, not to the shared code.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain assigns a case to a single owner for the duration of its handling, and no other party may touch the in-progress work. Thread confinement closes the gap: it prevents the in-progress state from being shared and mutated by unrelated workers, which would let a case be advanced by two clerks at once. The confined state is the domain’s own “one owner while in progress” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the confinement looks like an accident of the runtime — state stashed in a thread-local to avoid passing it explicitly. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed a single worker owns this work. Thread confinement fits only when the domain names that owner. If ownership is whatever thread happened to pick the work up, the domain has not named an owner, and the thread-local asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain assign this work to a single owner for its whole duration — one clerk, one case — or is the “ownership” only whatever thread happened to pick the work up?

If yes → applicable. Thread confinement is the code catching up to the knowledge; the confined state is the domain’s own case ownership.
If no → inapplicable. The confinement asserts an owner the domain never named. Name it, or pass the state explicitly.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ThreadConfinement #ThreadLocal #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Where the algorithm list reads the order of operations, this list reads what holds the data: the order it keeps, the cost it promises, the operations it refuses. Each post names the structure, states the contract, and asks whether the domain supplied it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Dynamic array (the doubling vector)
text:
Case study: Dynamic array (the doubling vector)
A vector that doubles at three million 8-byte elements copies 24 MB in one call — inside whichever request happened to trigger the growth.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: One contiguous block, a count, a capacity. Append is O(1) amortized: a resize copies n elements, and doubling spreads that copy over the next n appends. Positional access is O(1). Insert in the middle is O(n). The predictions: appends dominate writes, positional access dominates reads, an occasional pause is acceptable, insertion order is the order the domain means.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The array bets on the operation mix, the scale, and the pause. All three are domain facts: a log is appended to, a price list is read by index, a nightly job absorbs a 24 MB copy; a 5 ms request does not, and that copy is about 2.4 ms at ten gigabytes a second.
The gap question: which operation dominates, and is the resize pause acceptable at the size the domain reaches?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Collect-then-process workloads: buffer a query result, iterate all of it, discard it. Appends dominate, iteration dominates, and the order kept is the order received — the order the domain produced. Positional access is a need here, not a convenience.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Edits in the middle of a long-lived list. The call reads like O(1); each call shifts half the array — 100,000 moves per edit at 100,000 elements, behind one method name. Or the count reaches millions and nothing records that anyone compared the doubling pause to a latency budget.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do appends or index reads dominate — and is the resize pause within the budget at peak size?

If yes → the pause fits the budget. Check the peak size the doubling reaches, then the copy cost there.
If no → say which half failed. Mix unmeasured: count the operations. Pause over budget: reserve capacity, or move the copy off the request path.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the array wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count appends, middle inserts, and index reads for a week.




#DataStructures #Arrays #Performance #CacheLocality #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Linked list (the splice contract)
text:
Case study: Linked list (the splice contract)
A linked list makes insertion O(1) and then charges a cache miss per element: walking 100,000 nodes touches 100,000 scattered cache lines.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: Node plus pointer, allocated one at a time. Given a reference to a node, insert and remove are O(1): rewire pointers, shift nothing. Search is O(n), positional access is O(n), and each traversal step is a dependent load from an address neither the compiler nor the prefetcher can predict. The predictions: splice at a held position dominates, random access never happens, the cost per element is acceptable.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The O(1) claim is conditional. The structure is fast only when the caller already holds the position. If the caller holds an index or a key, the structure finds the node first, and the find is O(n).
The gap question: is the position already in hand when the write arrives?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Cursor-and-splice workloads. An LRU (least recently used) cache keeps an eviction chain: the hash map holds the node, so moving it to the front is O(1) pointer surgery that copies nothing. An allocator free list pops a block from the head. A kernel intrusive list embeds the node in the object, so one object sits on many lists.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Insertion is O(1), so the list beats the array.” The workload builds the list, then checks whether a key already exists — search, then insert. The search is O(n) with a cache miss per step, and a contiguous array scans the same data faster. Or the list is long and read hot: pointer chasing over 100,000 nodes turns a sub-millisecond scan into milliseconds.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do you hold a position and splice — or search, then insert?

If yes → the O(1) claim holds. Check what the splice touches, and that no one else holds a stale pointer.
If no → the O(1) claim is false for you: the search dominates. Measure the search against a contiguous scan.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the list wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the insert sites, and mark which ones arrive holding a node.




#DataStructures #LinkedLists #CacheLocality #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Stack (the last-in rule)
An undo stack pops the newest edit first. Do that with support tickets and the calmest one closes first while the outage waits.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: One end is both readable and writable; the other is sealed. Push, pop, and peek are O(1), and nothing below the top is reachable without popping what sits above. The structure can serve only the most recent item, so it encodes the claim that of everything it received, the most recent matters now, and first.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The structure does not prefer recency; it makes recency the only rule. Reversal is a real domain relation where the last edit is the first to undo, or the innermost block the first to close.
The gap question: is “most recent first” the domain’s own rule for what happens next, or a container default standing in for a rule nobody stated?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Undo history reverses in exact reverse order, because the edits were causally ordered and only the newest is safe to reverse. A parser tracks open brackets: the innermost is the only legal closer, and the grammar bounds the depth. Depth-first traversal keeps its frontier here, so backtracking resumes where it stopped.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A severity queue that happens to use a stack. Arrival order becomes priority without anyone deciding it: a low-severity ticket filed a minute ago outranks a payment outage filed an hour ago. The structure authored a policy the domain never agreed to, and the policy is invisible in the push and pop calls. Or a stack holds a history the domain wants to browse, and nobody can jump to a known revision or compare two.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is “most recent first” the domain’s own rule for what happens next?

If yes → LIFO is the domain’s rule. Check the depth the domain permits, and what bounds it.
If no → the order is a container artifact. Name the rule the domain does have — priority, deadline, revision — and let it into the structure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the stack wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask who decides which item is handled next.




#DataStructures #Stacks #Undo #Parsing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Queue and deque (the arrival-order contract)
text:
Case study: Queue and deque (the arrival-order contract)
FIFO is a fairness rule that a domain either adopts or inherits by default. One urgent item behind 40,000 batch items waits for all 40,000, and nobody chose that policy — the container did.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A queue adds at the tail and removes at the head, both O(1) in a ring buffer. A deque frees both ends for O(1) reads and writes. The queue encodes one rule — service order is arrival order — and the deque encodes two: both ends carry meaning, neither is a leftover. That is a fairness claim before it is a data-structure claim.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The structure fixes the ordering rule and hides the backlog inside itself. An unbounded queue is also a latency store: when arrival outruns service, waiting time grows without limit and the container never objects.
The gap question: is arrival order the rule the domain chose, or the one it inherited?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Fair service in arrival order, where the domain names the fairness: job queues, request lines, print spools, a connection pool’s wait queue. Each promises that no later arrival overtakes an earlier one. A deque earns its second end the same way: undo consumes one end, redo returns items to the other, and the two ends are two domain facts.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



FIFO as accidental policy. One queue carries nightly batch work and customer-facing work, and the batch fills it, so urgency is irrelevant by construction and no line of code decided that. The deque has its own version: one end is used, the other is a field no code path reads — the structure claims two domain facts and the domain supplied one.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is first-come-first-served a rule the domain recognizes?

If yes → FIFO is the domain’s fairness rule. Check what bounds the queue when service is slower than arrival.
If no → the order is accidental. Name the rule the domain has — priority, deadline, tenant quota — and put it in the structure or the scheduler above it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the queue wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure arrival rate against service rate at peak.




#DataStructures #Queues #Fairness #Backpressure #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Hash map (the exact-key index)
text:
Case study: Hash map (the exact-key index)
One release changes a map’s initial capacity, and every record is written in a different order — same input, same data, different bytes.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A hash function maps a key to a bucket: lookup, insert, and delete are O(1) expected, O(n) worst case when every key collides. The buckets encode no order a reader may rely on; iteration follows the hash, the capacity, and the insertion history. It predicts that lookup by exact key dominates, key order carries no meaning, keys are unique, and the hash is a pure function of the key’s value.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
Uniqueness and orderlessness are domain claims, not storage options. A map enforces the first — a second insert on the same key overwrites — and hides the second, so a display path built on iteration order turns nondeterministic the day the capacity changes.
The gap question: does any downstream consumer read the order the entries came back in?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Identity lookup where the key is the identity: a user by id, a session by token, an order by number, a cache entry by URL. Counting occurrences, deduplicating a stream by key, joining two collections on a shared identifier. The domain asks what belongs to this exact key, and nothing about sequence or proximity.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Order taken from the map. A file records it and a test asserts it, so the next capacity change turns the diff into noise and the failure into an intermittent one.
Range queries cost a full O(n) scan: a hash has no proximity to exploit, so “all users from A to M” reads every entry. Mutable keys rot in place: change a hashed field after insert, and the entry becomes unreachable and undeletable.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is lookup by exact key the only access pattern — and is “no meaningful order” a domain fact or an oversight?

If yes → the map is the domain’s index. Check that keys stay immutable while stored, and that the uniqueness it enforces is the domain’s rule.
If no → you need order or range, which a hash cannot answer. Use an ordered index, and keep the map only where exact lookup pays.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the map wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. List the queries the domain asks, then the order it presents results in.




#DataStructures #HashMaps #Determinism #Indexing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Hash set (the membership contract)
text:
Case study: Hash set (the membership contract)
A cart that holds its line items in a set merges two identical items into one, and the customer receives one of what they ordered twice.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A hash set answers one question: is this value in the collection? Membership, insert, and delete are O(1) expected. There is no index, no position, no count per value, no second copy — inserting a value already present changes nothing and reports nothing. It predicts that membership is the only question, duplicates are not distinct facts, and order is not a fact.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The set stores one fact per value — presence — and drops multiplicity and sequence. Correct where the domain asks only whether something is present, and a silent rewrite where two identical arrivals are two events.
The gap question: what does the domain do when the same thing arrives twice?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Membership as the whole question. Deduplicating event ids so a retried delivery is processed once. A permission check against granted roles. Tags on an entity, where a repeated tag is the same tag. Here the domain has no multiplicity and no order, and the type states that.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Duplicates the domain keeps apart. Two identical line items are two items: quantity, a unit price, a customer decision to buy twice. The set merges them, the total is half, and the bug looks like arithmetic rather than representation.
A set standing in for a relation the domain enumerates in order. Grants are fine unordered; the audit log of when each was granted is not. Or two records share a key, the set calls them one member because equality is defined on that key, and a dedup rule nobody stated is now in force.








TipThe faithfulness test



Did the domain decide that two identical submissions are one fact?

If yes → they are one fact. Check that the equality the set uses is the domain’s identity rule.
If no → membership is the wrong question. You need multiplicity, or distinct entities with their own identity, and a set carries neither.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the set wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Ask what the domain does when the same thing arrives twice.




#DataStructures #HashSets #Dedup #DomainModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Sorted array
A price list of 10,000 rows rebuilt nightly, read 40 million times a day, answers each lookup in 14 comparisons. Insert one row between rebuilds and 5,000 rows move.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A sorted array keeps keys in order in one contiguous block: binary search O(log n), range scan O(log n + k), random access O(1), and insertion or deletion O(n), because every later element shifts. The prediction is that order is a property of the data, and that writes are rare enough to pay for in bulk.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The choice assumes that reads dominate writes, that order is a domain fact rather than a display preference, and that the working set fits one block. The gap question is the measured write rate against the read rate, and who owns the order when a write does arrive. A sorted array with an unasked question behind it is a sort nobody consumes.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Reference data rebuilt in batch: price lists, tax brackets, ranking tables, leaderboards recomputed by a job. Writes happen inside the batch that owns them, reads hit a finished artifact, and the same array serves an ordered report without a second structure. The batch interval is the staleness the domain accepted when it scheduled the rebuild.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Interleaved inserts on a live stream: at 100,000 rows and a thousand writes a second, the shifts are 10⁸ element moves a second, spent preserving an order nothing asked for. The seductive version keeps the invariant by hand — two code paths inserting “in the right place”, a background re-sort, a flag asserting the array is sorted. Sortedness then becomes a distributed invariant with no owner, holding until one writer appends and forgets.








TipThe faithfulness test



Measured, do reads dominate writes — and is one owner named for the sort?

If yes → the order is a domain property and one owner holds the writes. Check the rebuild interval against the staleness reads tolerate.
If no → say which half failed. No owner: name one. Writes outrun reads: the sort is decoration — a hash map or a tree pays less.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the array wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Count peak inserts per second, then count the code paths that write.




#DataStructures #Algorithms #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance #Caching

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Binary search tree (unbalanced)
Load one million keys into a plain binary search tree in ascending order and each lookup costs one million comparisons — a linked list, with pointers paid for.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A binary search tree orders keys by construction, so search, insert, and delete cost O(h) in the height h, and a full traversal costs Θ(n). The O(log n) claim holds only while the height stays a small multiple of log₂ n, and the height is not a property of the algorithm. It is a property of the order the keys arrived in.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The domain must say what insertion order looks like: a sequence, a migration, a sorted export, a replay of an ordered log, or users typing. Uncorrelated input keeps the height a small multiple of log₂ n, in expectation; the bound is probabilistic, so the structure is knowledge. If the domain ever emits keys in order, the bound fails, and it fails silently. The gap question is the worst realistic insertion order, not the average.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Keys genuinely arrive uncorrelated with their order: random identifiers, hashes, names typed by people. Writes and reads interleave, ordered traversal is used, no single writer controls the sequence, and the tree delivers its bound with two pointers per node — cheaper to build and to restructure than a balancing variant.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Sorted or sequential input: auto-increment identifiers, timestamps, a sorted CSV import, a replay of an ordered log. Bulk-loading sorted data builds a spine instead of a tree: every operation degrades to O(n), and a recursive insert can exhaust the stack. It passes every test, because the fixtures are shuffled; production feeds it what the database returns, ordered by primary key. The complexity claim was never earned, only assumed from the name.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the insertion order under your control — no import, no migration, no sequential id that could arrive sorted?

If yes → the bound is earned. Trace each input path once for correlation, then leave the tree unbalanced.
If no → the bound is not delivered: the order arrives. Balancing is the repair, and it costs the pointers and rotations the unbalanced case was avoiding.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tree wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Instrument the depth in production, and sample the insertion sequence.




#DataStructures #Algorithms #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Complexity #Correctness

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Self-balancing binary search tree (AVL, red-black)
text:
Case study: Self-balancing binary search tree (AVL, red-black)
An AVL tree holds a million keys within 29 levels whatever order they arrive in. If the domain cannot produce the input that breaks a plain tree, you bought a policy against a risk nobody can name.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A self-balancing tree restores its own height after every write: AVL keeps child heights within one and rotates on violation, red-black keeps a colour and rotates less often for a looser bound. Both give O(log n) worst case for search, insert, and delete under any insertion order, paid for in per-node bookkeeping and rotation work on the write path.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
The domain must say whether input order is outside its control — user-supplied keys, imports from unknown sources, an adversary choosing keys to degenerate the tree — or whether a latency bound is a requirement someone signed. The gap question is whether that input can occur, and whether the guarantee was ever stated rather than assumed.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Ordered maps and sets whose contract requires any input to work: C++ std::map, Java TreeMap. Any input, guaranteed logarithmic bounds, ordered iteration available. Key spaces an untrusted party contributes to also qualify.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A red-black tree hand-rolled for a 5,000-key table whose insertion order the team could have declared, so the balance covers a risk nobody tested for. The policy covers a risk the domain excludes, and it is paid for in rotation logic that must be right.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can adversarial or sorted input actually occur here — or is the worst-case guarantee a requirement someone stated?

If yes → the balance is knowledge. Record the threat or the bound that demanded it, next to the structure.
If no → unrequested insurance. Compare a sorted array for read-mostly use, a hash map for unordered lookup, and a heap when only the extreme is read.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the tree wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Find who required the bound, then measure the input order.




#DataStructures #Algorithms #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Complexity #Latency

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: B-tree
A B-tree with branching factor 500 stores a billion keys in four levels. Four page reads, not thirty. The win is not the tree — the node is the size of the transfer unit.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A B-tree is a balanced multi-way search tree whose nodes hold many sorted keys, sized to the storage block. Height is log base b of n, so a billion keys at b = 500 sit three or four levels deep, and linked leaves make a range scan a sibling walk rather than a re-descent.


The data-structure knowledge gap it signals
Two facts must exist for the width to be knowledge: the actual transfer unit of this medium, and a measured volume that made memory insufficient. Without them the node size is a copied constant. The gap question is what this medium transfers per read, and what measurement showed the working set no longer fits in RAM — a B-tree over data that does fit pays for an I/O it never performs.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



On-disk indexes and databases: SQLite, PostgreSQL, InnoDB, LMDB. Wide shallow trees matched to the block amortize one read across hundreds of keys.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



B-trees over in-memory data, justified by borrowed authority: databases use B-trees, so the service uses one for a 5,000-entry lookup table that fits in 400 KB of RAM. In memory the unit is a 64-byte cache line. A 4 KiB node spans 64 of them, so each comparison jumps to an address the CPU did not fetch. A sorted array reads one contiguous pass. The second trap is sizing carried across media: disk reasoning applied to flash, or a 16 KiB node inherited from a database default on a device that reads 4 KiB, so each node read is four transfers.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the node width matched to this medium’s measured transfer unit — and has a measurement shown the working set no longer fits in memory?

If yes → the width is knowledge. Size the node to the unit; the height then follows arithmetically.
If no → say which fact is missing. Width unmatched: size the node to the transfer unit. Working set fits: an in-memory array is cheaper than an I/O you never make.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the B-tree wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge. Measure the read transfer size, then the working set, then compare against RAM.




#DataStructures #Databases #Storage #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: Data Structures as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Heap / priority queue
A scheduler with 100,000 pending jobs does not need them sorted — reading the next job is free, and about thirty comparisons restore the heap after each change.
Choosing an algorithm or a data structure? Ask “which facts does this choice encode — the operation mix, the scale, the ordering, the exactness the domain demands, among others?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the structure pays for a prediction nobody wrote down. If you can name those facts, the structure is the knowledge embodied — the code catching up to what the domain decided.

Construct: A binary heap is a complete tree flattened into an array, each parent no greater than its children. Reading the extreme is O(1); inserting and extracting it are O(log n).
