title: .NET Knobs and Practices
section: Case study: Server GC versus Workstation GC
text:
Case study: Server GC versus Workstation GC
Same build, same load: server GC returns 44,000 requests a second holding 690 MB, workstation 31,000 holding 380 MB — each team calls its number correct.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Server GC gives the process one heap per core, each with its own allocation budget and collection thread; workstation GC gives it one heap, collected by the triggering thread. The trade is parallel collection against footprint and pause shape: per-core heaps and helper threads are memory the process must be granted. In a container, server GC sizes its heap count from the CPU limit, not the host’s core count — unless GCHeapCount pins it.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know how many cores it gets, and whether a human waits: throughput on a batch job is invisible to users, pause on an editor is visible on every keystroke. The gap question: which of throughput and pause does this workload sell, and how many cores does the scheduler really give the process?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A request service on 16 cores, same allocation profile: workstation 31,000 requests a second at 380 MB peak RSS (resident set size), server 44,000 at 690 MB with p99 pause flat. Nobody watched the process and memory was free, so the mode was chosen by the number the customer pays for. An editor takes the opposite side: one heap, a smaller resident set.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Server GC copied into a small container because “web APIs use server GC”. The pod gets 1.5 CPU and 512 MB; the host has 64 cores. The limit should size two heaps; a teammate pinned GCHeapCount to 64, copied from the host’s spec. Sixty-four heaps and their helper threads divide a core and a half, each keeps its own gen0 budget, and the pod is OOM-killed while reporting low CPU.








TipThe faithfulness test



What do the measured throughput and pause profile need — and how many cores does this process really get?

If yes → it answers a stated requirement. Re-measure when the CPU limit or traffic shape changes.
If no → a default inherited from another machine. Let the CPU limit, not a config value, decide the heap count.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mode wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure requests a second and p99 pause per mode at the real CPU limit, with peak RSS.




#DotNet #CSharp #GarbageCollection #Performance #Containers #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
section: Case study: DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes)
text:
Case study: DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes)
The pod’s memory bill halved and its collection count rose 2.4× — memory was the scarce resource, and the four percent of throughput was the number nobody wrote down.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: DATAS — server GC only, opt-in on .NET 8, default on .NET 9 and later — derives heap count from the live data instead of the core count, shrinking the gen0 budget when that live set is small. The trade is footprint against collection frequency: a smaller budget fills sooner, so collections arrive more often and each does less work.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know which resource is scarce here: a memory limit is a number in a manifest, throughput a number in an SLA, and the runtime reads neither. A mode that shrinks the heap where memory is free and cores are busy turns a non-constraint into a cost. The gap question: is the binding constraint memory or throughput — measured, and for which SLA?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A queue worker in a 900 MB container, live set 210 MB, over a week. DATAS off: peak RSS 940 MB, three OOM kills. On: peak RSS 480 MB, collection count up 2.4×, throughput 18,400 to 17,600 messages a minute. A four percent loss against a ceiling the pod was breaching is a trade one sentence defends.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



DATAS left on for a throughput-bound server GC batch job on a 32-core host with memory to spare. The live set is small — millions of objects a second, most dead within a pass — so the budget shrinks and the collector runs several times as often. Throughput drops nine percent, the memory saving is invisible because nothing there counts memory, and a default charged the number the SLA names.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the binding constraint memory or throughput — measured, and for which SLA?

If yes → it is aimed at the constraint. Watch collection count beside RSS.
If no → a default doing an unrequested favour. Disable it, or write down the memory it protects.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure peak RSS and collection rate on and off, at the limit that would kill the pod.




#DotNet #CSharp #GarbageCollection #Memory #Containers #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: Span<T> and Memory<T>
A parser’s allocations fell from 1.2 GB per 10,000 requests to 40 MB — then the same span types made an async method uncompilable.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Span<T> is a ref struct — a pointer and a length over existing memory — so a slice costs two integers, where string.Substring copies. The trade is allocation-free slicing against a lifetime the compiler enforces: no boxing, no class field, no lambda capture, no crossing an await. Memory<T> is the heap-safe sibling for slices that outlive their method.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know whether this path’s cost is allocation, and where each slice must live. A slice is free only while its buffer lives; once it outlives the method, Memory<T> or a copy comes back — the old allocation in new syntax. The gap question: is this path measured as allocation-bound, and can every slice die inside its own method?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A log and CSV parsing path over 10,000 fixed requests: 1.2 GB allocated, 210 gen0 collections, 11 percent of wall time in GC. Parsed over ReadOnlySpan<char> from the request buffer instead: 40 MB allocated, 12 gen0 collections, 1 percent in GC, throughput up 11 percent. No slice escaped the parse method.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Span spread through a codebase because spans are faster. A 200-byte model is built with stackalloc, the stack frame grows, and a method that must await a database call cannot hold the buffer — so the code grows a synchronous twin and a defensive copy. The path allocated once per request, a number nobody had taken. On .NET 9 and later a ref struct local may live in an async method that crosses no await — removing the compile error, not the reason for it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this path measured as allocation-bound — or is Span fashion?

If yes → the slices encode a real lifetime fact. Keep the measurement, so a later return to Substring shows its price.
If no → a constraint bought for an unmeasured number. Keep Substring; revisit when the profiler names this path.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found Span wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure allocated bytes per request and GC time share.




#DotNet #CSharp #Performance #Allocations #Span #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: Sync-over-async (.Result, .Wait())
One .Result in a shared library passed every unit test, then deadlocked the first request from a UI handler.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: .Result and .Wait() block the calling thread until the task completes. Where a synchronization context exists — WinForms, WPF, MAUI, legacy ASP.NET — the awaited continuation is posted back to it, and the thread it needs is the one blocked on .Result. Without a context, as in ASP.NET Core, the deadlock becomes starvation: every blocked pool thread must be replaced by injection, the pool adding a thread on demand.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know two facts about every call site: whether a synchronization context is ever present on the calling thread, and how many callers reach it at peak. Both belong to the host, not the method: the same line is safe in a console job, fatal in a UI handler. The gap question: is this path ever called with a synchronization context, or at production concurrency?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Genuinely synchronous code kept synchronous. A CLI import tool reads, transforms and writes a file on its own thread, with no context and one caller, calling a library it cannot change. It blocks with GetAwaiter().GetResult(), which keeps the original exception: 4,000 files a minute.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



One .Result inside a library method, “just here”, since the caller was synchronous. The tests pass: the console harness has no context, and the runner’s is not the UI’s. Then a WPF screen calls it and the window stops responding on the first click, the stack trace showing an incomplete task whose continuation never ran. In ASP.NET Core the same line starves: 200 blocked pool threads, p99 from 40 ms to 12 seconds at 15 percent CPU.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this path ever called with a synchronization context or under load — measured?

If yes → it is a defect with a schedule. Await to the top of the stack, or make the entry point synchronous end to end, priced against every signature it changes.
If no → blocking describes the work, and claims something about the host. Keep the call behind a context-free boundary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the block wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Grep for .Result and .Wait(), then measure queue length at peak.




#DotNet #CSharp #AsyncAwait #Deadlock #ThreadPool #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: ConfigureAwait(false)
ConfigureAwait(false) skipped the post-back on every continuation after it — and a control that needed its UI thread was touched from the pool, four frames below.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: An await captures the current SynchronizationContext and TaskScheduler, then posts the continuation back to them. ConfigureAwait(false) skips the capture, so the continuation resumes on any thread pool thread. It buys the post-back and spends the assumption that the continuation lands on the synchronization context’s thread — the UI thread that must touch a control.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The knob answers a question about your callers, not your code: which re-enter on a specific thread, and which read ambient state after the await. A library that touches no UI and reads no ambient state can suppress the capture. The gap question: who is downstream of this await, and what does each one need from the context?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A library exercised under a UI dispatcher, where each captured post-back costs a hop nothing below it uses. Ten thousand awaits hold ten thousand post-backs; false removes all ten thousand. Default the library to false, and let the app layer keep the context deliberately, because the app is the layer that owns it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



False copied across application code because a style guide said so. A WPF handler awaits a call, and its continuation touches a control from a pool thread — no exception at the await, only a cross-thread failure four frames down, in a path no test covered. The win is a hop nobody measured; the loss is a crash the console harness never produced.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does anything downstream need the context — can you name it — or was false copied from a style guide?

If yes → keep the capture here, and suppress it inside the library.
If no → the suppression is free, and the hop was never doing work for anyone.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure which continuations resume on a specific thread, then list every ambient read after each await.




#DotNet #CSharp #AsyncAwait #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: ValueTask
ValueTask removed the allocation from a cache lookup that usually hits — and then two consumers awaited the same instance, which the type forbids.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A Task is a heap object, so a synchronous completion still allocates one unless the runtime hands back a cached instance. ValueTask is a struct wrapping a result, a Task, or an IValueTaskSource, so the synchronous case allocates nothing. It buys the allocation and spends a discipline: one consumption, one await, never stored, never awaited twice. Break it and the behavior is undefined, not merely slow.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The knob presumes two facts about your path: that it completes synchronously most of the time, and that exactly one consumer touches the result. The first is measurable; the second is structural. A hot cache lookup satisfies both. A method whose result gets logged, branched on, and returned satisfies neither. The gap question: is single consumption guaranteed by the shape of this code, or by hope?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A measured hot path that usually returns without awaiting — a memory cache hit, a buffer already filled. Ten million calls, and each cache hit still allocates a Task where the ValueTask path allocates nothing; the count on that path goes to zero. The discipline holds because one caller awaits it once.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Less allocation” adopted everywhere. A method returns ValueTask, and an interceptor awaits it, then the caller awaits it again: a second await is undefined behavior when the source is an IValueTaskSource — it throws, or it corrupts. Or the value gets handed to two consumers that both start it. The allocation win was nanoseconds; the failure is a corrupted result in production.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the measured path usually complete synchronously — and is single-consumption guaranteed by structure, or by hope?

If yes → ValueTask is the honest type here. Verify no call site awaits twice or stores it.
If no → use Task. The allocation is the price of a contract your code actually uses.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the synchronous completion rate, then count the consumers per result.




#DotNet #CSharp #AsyncAwait #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: IAsyncEnumerable
IAsyncEnumerable streamed a four-million-row report at constant memory — and the caller called ToListAsync, and the memory came back all at once.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The consumer awaits MoveNextAsync and processes each item before the next arrives. It buys constant memory and a first result before the query ends. It spends the total count, unknown until the stream finishes, and the simpler code that took a materialized list.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
Streaming presumes two facts: the result set is large enough that materializing hurts, and the consumer acts on each item as it arrives. Both are measurable. A consumer that buffers, sorts, or shows a page count has already given up the win, whatever the type promises. The gap question: what is the measured result size — and does the consumer process incrementally, or buffer anyway?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A measured large result set: four million rows at 200 bytes is 800 MB materialized, against a stream that holds one row plus its buffer. The consumer writes each row to a file or a response before the next arrives, so first byte leaves earlier and memory flatlines. The async enumeration per row now buys something: the producer is I/O-bound, and the consumer keeps pace.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



IAsyncEnumerable over a twelve-row lookup table. Twelve rows fit in one page, yet the streaming machinery adds an async state machine, an await per row, and a caller that must step it — and the caller buffers it straight into a list to get the count. Paid for, never collected.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured result size — and does the consumer actually process it incrementally, or buffer it anyway?

If yes → streaming is the honest shape. Check that nothing downstream sorts, counts, or materializes before use.
If no → materialize. A list is simpler, and the total count is knowledge you get for free.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the rows and the bytes per row, then trace whether the consumer holds them all.




#DotNet #CSharp #AsyncStreams #Memory #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
section: Case study: NativeAOT, ReadyToRun, plain JIT
text:
Case study: NativeAOT, ReadyToRun, plain JIT
NativeAOT took a CLI’s startup from about 80 ms to about 10 ms — and then the JSON serializer threw at runtime on a type the compiler never saw.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: JIT compiles IL on first call and re-optimizes hot paths from real profiles, so steady state wins and startup pays. ReadyToRun precompiles IL to native while keeping the JIT available: startup improves, the binary grows. NativeAOT compiles the whole closed world ahead of time, so startup and footprint drop and reflection stops being free.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The knob presumes startup dominates and every dependency survives a closed world. Startup-dominated is measurable; AOT-safe is knowable only by trying. Tiered compilation with dynamic PGO, on by default since .NET 8, means the JIT’s peak is the number you give up. The gap question: does startup or steady state dominate, measured — and is the dependency tree known to be AOT-safe?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A measured startup-dominated workload: a CLI at about 80 ms to first output, mostly compiling methods it never runs, against about 10 ms under AOT.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



NativeAOT on a long-running, reflection-heavy API. Startup was never the bottleneck — the process lives for days — so the win is invisible and the cost permanent. Plugins loaded by assembly name, a serializer mapping by reflection, proxies built at runtime: each becomes a runtime failure the compiler never saw, at the first request that touches it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does startup or steady state dominate, measured — and is the dependency tree known to be AOT-safe?

If yes → AOT or ReadyToRun is knowledge, not fashion. Check the trim and AOT analyzer warnings, and test every reflection path.
If no → stay on the JIT. Keep the throughput: startup is paid once, throughput every day.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure time to first useful output against throughput at sustained load, then list every reflection call in the tree.




#DotNet #CSharp #NativeAOT #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: IL trimming
The publish folder dropped fifty-four percent, and the first request with an unregistered subtype died on missing metadata.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The linker walks the call graph from entry points and deletes the IL nothing calls. Reflection is not a call edge: a type named in a serializer attribute or emitted by an ORM proxy is reachable only at run time, so the linker trims it unless an annotation roots it, and the app fails at first use. The trade is size and cold start against every path only reflection knows; .NET 8’s annotations narrow that surface, not the trade.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know its own reflection surface: which types the runtime resolves by name, and which the tests exercise. The library’s annotations describe the library, not your use of it. The gap question: which types are reached only via reflection — enumerated how — and is that list tested after trimming?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A self-contained or AOT deploy where size and cold start are constraints: enumerate the reflection surface in a descriptor (files that list reflection-reached types) or a source-generated context, and run the integration suite on a trimmed publish. Measured: publish 210 MB to 96 MB, cold start 2.4 s to 0.9 s, eleven metadata exceptions caught in that first trimmed run.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Trimming a service dense with runtime polymorphism — dynamic JSON, assembly scanning, lazy proxies — because the folder looked big. It publishes, it starts, the unit tests pass because they never touch the artifact. Weeks later an unforeseen subtype throws a metadata exception naming a type the source contains. Suppressing the warnings to get green makes the guess permanent.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which types are reached only via reflection — enumerated how — and is that list tested after trimming?

If yes → the trim states a checkable reachability claim. Re-check it per library upgrade, not the build.
If no → the trim was a size decision that deleted reachable code. Enumerate the surface first, or leave the reflection-heavy assemblies untrimmed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Run a trimmed publish under the integration suite and log every metadata failure.




#DotNet #CSharp #Trimming #NativeAOT #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: Nullable reference types
Nullable went on across the solution, the build went green in a day, and nobody can say which parameters may now be null.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The compiler tracks flow for reference types and warns when null can reach a dereference. It checks nothing at run time — the annotation is a claim, not a guard. The gain is a compile-checked nullability claim; the price is the annotation discipline legacy code owes, since every signature becomes a statement somebody must defend. Since .NET 6 templates enable it project-wide, an enable is a commitment, not a sprinkle.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
Nullability is a domain fact at each boundary: which inputs may be absent, which invariants hold after construction. The compiler proves a local flow; it cannot know whether absent means “not yet set” or “caller broken”. The gap question: is every nullable annotation backed by a stated invariant — or silenced to make the build pass?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Enabled per project, warnings as errors, each resolved into a real decision: handle the null, or non-null the parameter and make callers prove it. Measured on a forty-project solution done this way: 1,900 warnings, 61 that a reviewer traced to a real null path — 61 latent bugs in code declared fine.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Enabled wholesale with <NoWarn>CS8600;CS8602;CS8618</NoWarn>, or a nullable-disable atop the files that complained. The build is green: every warning silenced, and a string? with no invariant behind it reads as a contract. The seduction is real: the property is on, the dashboard says “adopted”, and every consumer trusts a contract nobody checked.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is every nullable annotation backed by a stated invariant — or silenced to make the build pass?

If yes → the annotation is knowledge the compiler enforces. Check the ! suppressions next; each is a hand-written exception to it.
If no → at least one annotation is decorative. Fix those, or revert the enable.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Count the suppressed warnings, then trace what each flagged.




#DotNet #CSharp #NullableReferenceTypes #StaticAnalysis #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: C# records
An order in a HashSet has its status flipped to Shipped, and the lookup misses — its hash moved to another bucket, and the set never rehashed it.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A record gets compiler-written equality over its fields, a matching hash code, and with expressions that copy and modify in one line. The trade is value semantics — equal by data, replaced by convention rather than enforced — against identity semantics, equal by reference or id, which an entity needs to stay itself while its data changes. record struct adds struct rules — copies on assign, no inheritance; with copies shallowly, so nested mutable state stays shared.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know, per type, whether the domain identifies it by its data or by a persisted id. Money, a date range, a DTO — data is the identity. An order, a user, a document — the id is the identity, and two versions with different data are one thing. The gap question: is this thing a value (equal by data) or an entity (equal by identity) — decided, not defaulted?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



DTOs, messages, and domain values as records, so copy-and-modify collapses into order with { Status = Shipped } — no builder, no forgotten field. Measured on a mapping layer converted this way: 1,400 lines of copy code became 260, and three bugs where a copy kept a stale field left with them.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Records for entities. The instance goes into a set, someone sets a property, and the entity can no longer be found under the key it was added with — no exception, no trace. Then mutable properties undercut the claim: init becomes set, and equality changes while the object is in use.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this thing a value (equal by data) or an entity (equal by identity) — decided, not defaulted?

If yes → equality by fields is the domain’s rule. Check the record is immutable, so the hash cannot move under its container.
If no → it is an entity. Give it reference or id-based equality, and never key a set on mutable fields.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the record wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Ask what the domain calls the same thing twice.




#DotNet #CSharp #Records #DomainModeling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: Structs versus classes
A 200-byte struct crosses four methods per call, and the profiler puts 11 percent of sampled time in the copy.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A struct is a value: it lives inline in its container, allocates nothing, and sits close to the data beside it. Every by-value assignment copies the whole thing: a by-value parameter, a return, a field store, each a memcpy. The trade is allocation and locality against copy cost, and the cost scales with a size nobody wrote down. readonly struct with in parameters — pass by reference, no copy — is the lever; a non-readonly member on a readonly field still copies.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know two numbers about its own workload: the struct’s byte size, and how often it travels. A sixteen-byte value passed once per request is free; the same value in a four-million-element array walked twice is the hot path, where locality wins. The gap question: what is the measured size of this struct — and is it immutable, so copies are safe?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Small immutable value types on a measured hot path: an identifier wrapper, a coordinate, a key. Measured on a parsing loop over four million price points: the class version spent 38 percent of its time in garbage collection, the readonly struct with in parameters spent 6 percent, and the pass went from 210 ms to 95 ms — allocation removed and locality gained, not a cleverer algorithm.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A 200-byte struct passed everywhere because structs are “faster”, and the copies add up. Then the mutable struct: a method sets a field, the caller sees nothing, because the mutation landed on a copy that died at the closing brace. The code compiles, the value changes nowhere, and no compiler diagnostic names the copy.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured size of this struct — and is it immutable, so copies are safe?

If yes → the struct is a value whose copies cost what you measured. Check no per-call path copies it needlessly, and nothing boxes it.
If no → the copy is unmeasured or unsafe. Shrink it and make it readonly, or make it a class if size dominates.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Print Unsafe.SizeOf<T>(), count the copies, compare the allocation profile.




#DotNet #CSharp #Performance #ValueTypes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: ArrayPool (the rented buffer)
A 128 KiB buffer allocated per request at 2,000 requests a second: 250 MiB/s onto the Large Object Heap, and a Gen2 pause no call stack explains.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: ArrayPool<T>.Shared lends an array and takes it back on Return, so each rent reuses a pooled array instead of a fresh allocation. Above 85,000 bytes that is the difference between an LOH segment and none, and LOH objects are reached only in Gen2 — the pause you are reading. The trade is a lifetime obligation: every rent needs a return on every path, and the buffer comes back dirty.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know its allocation profile: which buffers cross 85,000 bytes, how often, and whether Gen0 already absorbs them. Reuse pays where the churn measures as LOH pressure; where it is Gen0 churn, the pool buys nothing and adds a return path. The gap question: is this churn LOH-heavy by measurement, and does every path return what it rents, exceptions included?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A gateway copying bodies into 128 KiB buffers at 2,000 requests a second puts about 250 MiB/s on the LOH. Pooling a bounded set takes LOH allocation to near zero and Gen2 from about 30 a minute to 2 — the unexplained Gen2 pause gone — with the pool size now setting the ceiling.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Pooling 64-byte arrays in a hot loop because “allocation is expensive.” Gen0 allocation is a pointer bump and Gen0 collection is cheap; the pool adds a return obligation on every branch, a dirty-data bug on the first path that forgets to clear, and a stale byte from another request in a response.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the churn measured as LOH-heavy — and does every code path return what it rents, even on exception?

If yes → the pool answers a measured fact. Check it is bounded, that buffers carrying request data are cleared, and that used length is tracked apart from array length.
If no → no on the churn means nothing pays for the pool — measure first; no on a path means a missing return — fix it. Gen0 churn takes a plain allocation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the knob wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure bytes allocated per second by size bucket, then Gen2 pause time and cause.




#DotNet #CSharp #ArrayPool #Performance #GC #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
section: Case study: Service lifetimes (the claimed scope)
text:
Case study: Service lifetimes (the claimed scope)
A singleton holding a scoped DbContext serves last week’s prices, and the cause is one line in a constructor signature no build check reads.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A registration declares how long an instance lives: transient one per resolution, scoped one per scope — per request in a web host — singleton one for the life of the container. The trade is a claim about who shares an instance. A mismatch fails quietly: a singleton that takes a scoped dependency captures it, and that instance then lives as long as the process.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know, per service, whose lifetime it shares — per request, per operation, per process — and whether it is thread-safe. Injection makes the claim implicit: a scoped service injected into three singletons shares whatever the first capture gave it. The gap question: for each dependency, is the lifetime stated on the registration, or discovered the first time data goes stale?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An order API scopes its DbContext to the request — the request is the transaction boundary — and keeps the configuration reader singleton, since the process owns it. With ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild, the capture becomes a container exception at boot: a failed deploy instead of a pricing incident later.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A singleton holding a scoped DbContext, because “the context is expensive to construct and we wanted one.” The first request’s context is captured and served to every later request — last week’s prices — and under overlap it corrupts across threads: a DbContext is not thread-safe, so callers interleave on one change tracker (its per-request entity set) — “A second operation was started on this context instance” at load, or request A’s entities saved by request B.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each dependency, whose lifetime does it share — stated, or discovered at runtime?

If yes → the container serves the claims. Enable scope validation everywhere, and check any captured dependency is thread-safe for that sharing.
If no → you have a captive dependency, not a caching problem. Move the scoped service behind a factory or an explicit scope.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the lifetime wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Read every constructor argument’s registration, then the concurrency it implies.




#DotNet #CSharp #DependencyInjection #Lifetimes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
text:
Case study: IHostedService and BackgroundService
The nightly import job loses its last fourteen rows on every deploy, and the log shows no error because there was no error — the process ended.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A hosted service is started by the host, receives a stopping token, and must stop before the process exits: services start in registration order, stop in reverse, and the host waits up to its shutdown timeout — 30 seconds by default — to drain them all. The trade: the host now owns your work’s lifetime, so the work must be cancellable and a partial batch safe to reread.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know what the work does when interrupted: which writes are idempotent, and how long a batch takes. Start order and the shutdown timeout are usable only if the work has a checkpoint the next start can find. The gap question: what happens to in-flight work when the process stops — stated, and does the shutdown path honor it?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A worker consuming 400 messages a second: on deploy it stops accepting, finishes the batch in flight, and exits in 1.8 seconds, queue depth zero. Across 50 deploys: zero truncated batches against a handful before, and no longer deploy time, since the drain finished inside the timeout.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A Task.Run fired from startup “for the background job.” The host does not await it, so shutdown has nothing to drain. The next deploy ends the process mid-write: no commit of the pending write, no retry, no error. It worked locally, because no debug session raced a deploy. The work looks asynchronous and is unowned.








TipThe faithfulness test



What happens to this work when the process stops — stated — and does the shutdown path honor it?

If yes → the lifetime is owned. Check the stopping token reaches the deepest loop, a batch commits or abandons atomically, and the drain fits the timeout.
If no → the work is fire-and-forget, and its failures are silent by construction. Move it into a hosted service, or a queue with an acknowledged checkpoint.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the practice wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the longest batch, then watch one deploy stop mid-batch.




#DotNet #CSharp #HostedServices #BackgroundJobs #Reliability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: .NET Knobs and Practices
section: Case study: Task.Run wrapping (the false offload)
text:
Case study: Task.Run wrapping (the false offload)
A controller awaits Task.Run around an HTTP call, the throughput halves at 800 requests a second, and the work was never CPU-bound.
Changing a .NET knob or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every knob moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the knob is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Task.Run queues a delegate to the pool and returns a task. The trade is a thread hop to shed the caller’s context: the delegate’s synchronous part runs on a pool thread, and the caller’s continuation needs one again, so a wrapped call pays two pool work items where one would do. On ASP.NET Core there is no synchronization context to escape, so the hop buys nothing.


The .NET knowledge gap it signals
The team must know the shape of the work: CPU-bound or waiting on IO, and which thread pool the caller already occupies. Wrapping wait-bound work relabels it; wrapping CPU-bound work moves it to a pool thread the pool must still supply, and the demand is unchanged. The gap question: is the wrapped work CPU-bound by measurement, and does the caller sit on the pool it starves?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A desktop application recomputing a 400 ms report on the dispatcher thread at every filter change leaves the window at about 2.5 frames a second. Moving the compute behind Task.Run with a cancellation token holds the UI at 60 frames, and the calculation still takes 400 ms — one pool thread against a responsive window.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Task.Run around an awaitable inside a server request, “so it does not block the request thread.” Nothing was blocking: async IO frees the thread at the first await. Under load the pool queue grows, the pool injects a thread about once a second, and p99 triples while the CPU sits idle. Wrapping a synchronous call is worse: one pool thread parks while another works.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the wrapped work actually CPU-bound — and does the caller sit on the same pool it starves?

If yes → the offload is real. Pass a cancellation token, keep the delegate short, and check the thread pool has threads at peak.
If no → no on CPU-bound means IO in disguise: await it directly, remove the wrap. No on the pool means the offload stands.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found Task.Run wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure CPU time against wall time for the call, then pool queue length at peak.




#DotNet #CSharp #AsyncAwait #ThreadPool #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Most design patterns and principles can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Content-Based Router Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we handle a situation where the implementation of a single logical function (e.g., inventory check) is spread across multiple physical systems?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that messages carry content that determines their destination is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “an order from region R goes to warehouse W, a payment above threshold T goes to fraud-check,” then Content-Based Router embodies that knowledge. The routing table is the domain’s own dispatch logic; each destination is a domain actor that receives specific kinds of work.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that which component receives a message depends on the message’s content — and the classification rule is a domain rule, not a technical convenience. When a claims-processing domain says “auto claims under $5,000 go to fast-track; auto claims over $5,000 go to full review; all property claims go to property adjustment,” the router encodes domain knowledge that would otherwise be buried in each receiving component’s guard clause. Without the router, every receiver must independently re-implement content-based filtering, scattering the routing rule across the system and creating accidental coupling — each receiver must know about every message type it could receive.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “routing” is not a domain rule — it’s a technical partition masquerading as a content decision. “Based on the message XML namespace, route to parser version 1 or version 2.” Or “route to the service instance with the lowest current load.” The domain doesn’t recognize XML namespaces, parser versions, or load distribution as input variables — it sees “process this order.” Content-Based Router here becomes a technology-level dispatcher that hides the real domain concern (what happens to the order?) behind a mechanical classification the domain expert would never produce. When the routing criteria are implementation details, every domain change that affects content may invisibly re-route without the domain expert knowing.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert produce the routing table from their own knowledge, without asking an engineer what’s “technically easier”?

If yes → applicable. Content-Based Router is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a technical switchyard disguised as domain routing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #ContentBasedRouter #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Publish-Subscribe Channel Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can the sender broadcast an event to all interested receivers?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that multiple parties independently care about the same occurrence is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when an order is fulfilled, the warehouse needs to restock, the customer needs a notification, the loyalty program needs to update points, and the finance system needs to recognize revenue,” then Publish-Subscribe is just embodying that knowledge. The topic is the domain event; the subscribers are domain actors who, by the rules of the domain, must react when that event occurs.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that one occurrence triggers multiple independent responses — and the publisher has no domain reason to know about the subscribers. A publisher should not know who consumes its events; the event itself is the coupling point, and the downstream reactions are separate domain responsibilities. Publish-Subscribe closes the gap: it prevents the publisher from growing a list of explicit callbacks for each new consumer, which would couple the publisher to downstream concerns it has no domain interest in. Each subscriber declares its interest in the event independently; the publisher emits once and the domain network reacts.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “subscribers” are not domain-independent — they are implementation partitions of a single domain concern. Splitting a single logical operation into multiple subscribers bound by a publish-subscribe channel creates an invisible coupling: the subscribers depend on each other’s execution to complete the operation, but neither the channel nor the subscribers encode this dependency. The domain says “one procedure does X, then Y, then Z” — but Publish-Subscribe scatters X, Y, Z into independent endpoints whose ordering is implicit. A domain expert would say “no, X and Y and Z are the same thing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the event and every subscriber using only domain vocabulary, with no implementation words?

If yes → applicable. Publish-Subscribe is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. You’re broadcasting for technical convenience, not because the domain broadcasts.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #PublishSubscribe #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Dead Letter Channel Pattern
text:
Case study: Dead Letter Channel Pattern

EIP Intent: “What will the messaging system do with a message it cannot deliver?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that some messages cannot be delivered and that the domain has rules for what happens then is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an insurance claim missing a policy number is undeliverable and goes to manual triage; a payment with a mismatched currency code goes to the reconciliation desk; and anything else unrouteable gets queued for the operations team,” then Dead Letter Channel is just embodying that knowledge. The dead-letter queue is the domain’s own undeliverable-work queue; the dead-letter consumer is the domain’s own exception-handling actor.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes that messages can legitimately fail to reach a destination, and the domain itself distinguishes categories of failure with different remediation paths. Dead Letter Channel closes the gap: it prevents each sender from embedding fallback logic for the failure it caused, which would scatter undeliverable-work handling across every component and create accidental coupling — each sender would need to know about manual triage, reconciliation desks, and operations queues. The dead-letter queue consolidates exception routing into one place, reflecting the domain’s own classification of failure modes.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The dead-letter channel is a catch-all for anything the developer didn’t handle — “put failed messages here and we’ll figure it out later.” The domain has no classification of failure modes, no notion of undeliverable work as a distinct domain state, and no remediation process. The dead-letter queue becomes silent data loss: messages accumulate in a queue no one monitors, and the domain event they represented is simply dropped. A domain expert would say “what do you mean the order disappeared — did it ship or not?”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a named process, role, or procedure for handling work that cannot reach its destination?

If yes → applicable. Dead Letter Channel is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a black hole with a tidy name.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #DeadLetterChannel #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Message Filter Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can a component avoid receiving uninteresting messages?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a component should only receive a subset of the messages flowing through the system is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the premium-customer system cares only about orders from customers at loyalty tier 3 or above; the standard-order pipeline should never see test-mode orders,” then Message Filter embodies that knowledge. The filter predicate is the domain’s own membership condition.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain assigns different message subsets to different domain actors — and the subset condition is a domain rule, not a performance optimization. Message Filter closes the gap: prevents each receiver from re-implementing the filter in a guard clause at the entry point, which would couple the receiver to message types it should have no knowledge of. A receiver that filters out orders below $1,000 at its own entry point must still know that such orders exist — spreading knowledge of the full message universe into every receiver. The filter externalizes the membership rule so each receiver sees only its domain-relevant messages.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The filter is adopted without a constraint that selects which messages to drop — “drop messages when queue depth exceeds 500” or “route every other message when CPU is > 80%.” Queue depth and CPU load tell you that you need to shed load — not which messages to shed. The filter predicate (drop oldest? drop lowest-priority? drop at random?) is undetermined by the constraint. When selection is arbitrary, the filter couples message survival to infrastructure state without a defensible rule.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the filter predicate as a domain rule — a sentence that starts with “The system is only interested in messages where…” and mentions no implementation concepts?

If yes → applicable. Message Filter is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (membership condition, regulatory boundary, domain scope rule) selects which messages pass.
If no → inapplicable. You’re dropping messages without a constraint that identifies which ones.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #MessageFilter #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Recipient List Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message to a list of dynamically specified recipients?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message has a domain-determined list of recipients — where the list itself is a domain artifact, not a configuration file — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a customs declaration must go to the importing country’s customs authority, the exporting country’s customs authority, the carrier, and the importer of record; a trade confirmation goes to both counterparties’ settlement desks,” then Recipient List is just embodying that knowledge. The list of recipients is the domain’s own distribution rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a single message be delivered to a specific, domain-determined set of recipients — and those recipients are each domain actors, not technical mirroring targets. Recipient List closes the gap: it isolates the distribution logic so the sender doesn’t embed a hardcoded list of downstream systems, which would couple the sender to the topology of the integration landscape. Without it, adding a new regulatory recipient means modifying the sender’s code — making the sender change with the regulatory environment even though its domain logic (produce the trade confirmation) hasn’t changed.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The recipient list is an availability tactic — send to primary and backup instances, or fan-out to multiple replicas. The domain doesn’t recognize “instance 1” and “instance 2” as distinct recipients; it recognizes one recipient (the order-processing system) — the fact that it runs on two machines is an implementation detail. Recipient List here masks infrastructure redundancy as domain distribution, creating coupling between the sender and deployment topology. A domain expert would say “just send it to order-processing — how many machines that runs on is not my concern.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, given only knowledge of the business process, produce the same list of recipients without knowing how the system is deployed?

If yes → applicable. Recipient List is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s deployment topology leaking into domain logic.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #RecipientList #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Splitter Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can we process a message if it contains multiple elements, each of which may have to be processed in a different way?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a composite message is domain-recognized as containing independently processable parts, and that the decomposition rule is a domain rule, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an insurance claim package contains a claim form, a police report, medical records, and repair estimates — each processed by a different team,” then Splitter is just embodying that knowledge. The decomposition rule is the domain’s own partitioning; each sub-message is a domain-recognized unit of work.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a composite message be decomposed into independent parts that travel different paths — and the decomposition corresponds to a domain-recognized partition. Splitter closes the gap: it prevents each downstream processor from re-extracting its own piece, which would couple each processor to the composite message format and scatter extraction logic across the system. Without it, the medical-records processor must know how to locate its section within the full claim package — structure knowledge that belongs in one place (the splitter), not in every downstream handler.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The composite message is a technical envelope — a batch of messages bundled for transport efficiency — and the domain sees the individual messages as the real units of work that were always separate. Splitter here just unwraps a transport artifact. Worse: if the original messages were produced independently at different times, splitting them doesn’t re-establish their original arrival order or context, and a later aggregator may produce results that arrived in a different sequence than they were produced.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the composite as a single thing that contains multiple independently meaningful things — like an “order” containing “line items” — rather than as a bunch of messages in a box?

If yes → applicable. Splitter is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s unwrapping a transport artifact and calling it domain decomposition.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Aggregator Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we combine the results of individual, but related messages so that they can be processed as a whole?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that multiple independent messages together form a domain-recognized whole — and that the domain specifies when the whole is complete — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a trade is complete only when we have both the execution report from the exchange and the allocation from the trader; a purchase order is fully processed when all its line items have been fulfilled from their respective warehouses,” then Aggregator is just embodying that knowledge. The completion condition is the domain’s own completeness rule; the aggregated result is the domain’s own composite state.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a result is the composition of multiple independent sub-results — and the domain itself defines when “enough sub-results have arrived” (by count, by timeout, by content, by domain predicate). Aggregator closes the gap: it prevents each downstream consumer from tracking partial state and re-implementing the completion check, which would scatter the aggregation logic across every consumer. Without it, the trade-settlement system must know when both the execution report and the allocation have arrived — knowledge that belongs at the aggregation point, not at every settlement subsystem.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “aggregation” is a technical re-assembly of parts that were split for transport — the splitter split by count, the aggregator reassembles by count, with no domain knowledge involved. The completion condition is “got all three pieces” rather than a domain predicate like “we have both the execution report and the allocation.” Aggregator here becomes a stateless reassembly mechanism that adds latency and a stateful waiting point for no domain reason.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain define the completeness condition — and would a domain expert state it in domain terms (“we need both the execution report and the allocation”) rather than as a count (“all three parts arrived”)?

If yes → applicable. Aggregator is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s re-gluing what was unnecessarily split.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Scatter-Gather Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do you maintain the overall message flow when a message needs to be sent to multiple recipients, each of which may send a reply?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a single request requires answers from multiple domain sources, and that the best answer is a domain-defined composition of those answers, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “to price a shipment, you need quotes from carrier A, carrier B, and carrier C, then you select the lowest; to approve a loan, you need a credit-score check, an income-verification check, and a fraud check — all must pass,” then Scatter-Gather is just embodying that knowledge. The recipients are the domain’s own information sources; the aggregation rule (lowest, all-pass, majority) is the domain’s own decision procedure.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a fan-out to multiple domain actors whose results must be combined by a domain rule — and the rule itself (not just the data) is domain knowledge. Scatter-Gather closes the gap: it prevents the requester from invoking each source sequentially, collecting results, and combining them inline — which would couple the requester to the list of sources, their invocation patterns, and the combination rule. Without it, adding a fourth carrier means modifying the pricing module’s internal loop.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “scatter” is a technical fan-out for performance — send the same query to all three replicas and take the fastest response. The domain doesn’t recognize replica voting; it recognizes one source (the product catalog), and the fact that it has copies is irrelevant. Scatter-Gather here masks a latency-hedge as a domain composition, introducing a gather step whose “aggregation rule” is “first one back” — a rule with no domain meaning. A domain expert would say “you’re asking the same question to three copies of the same book and taking whichever page turns first.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, asked “how do you decide the answer?” produce the same aggregation rule that the Scatter-Gather uses — without mentioning system architecture?

If yes → applicable. Scatter-Gather is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a race condition dressed as a decision procedure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Routing Slip Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message consecutively through a series of processing steps when the sequence of steps is not known at design-time and may vary for each message?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message must visit a sequence of processors, and that the sequence itself is a domain process that changes based on domain rules, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a purchase order above $10,000 goes: budget check → compliance review → director approval → procurement; a purchase order below $10,000 goes: compliance review → procurement — and for international orders, add export-control review after compliance,” then Routing Slip is just embodying that knowledge. The slip is the domain’s own process definition; each step is a domain actor in a domain sequence.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a variable multi-step process whose steps are domain operations — and the step sequence depends on domain conditions (order value, jurisdiction, product category). Routing Slip closes the gap: it prevents the process logic from being embedded in a central process manager that must know every step for every variation, which would couple all process variants together. Without it, the process manager becomes a god object that grows with every regulatory change.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The routing slip encodes a technical pipeline, not a domain process: “validate the message, transform the format, enrich with reference data, persist, notify.” The domain doesn’t recognize these as distinct business steps — it sees “process the order.” Routing Slip here wraps a technical ETL pipeline in the vocabulary of a business process, adding domain-coded step names (compliance, approval) to steps that are really validation, transformation, and persistence.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert, given a specific scenario (e.g., “an international order above $10,000”), list the steps in the correct sequence without consulting anyone technical?

If yes → applicable. Routing Slip is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The “process” is a technical pipeline with domain window-dressing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Process Manager Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message through multiple processing steps when the required steps may not be known at design-time and may not be sequential?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a long-running multi-step process has a domain-defined state machine — where states, transitions, and compensating actions are all domain concepts — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a trade lifecycle is: initiated → allocated → affirmed → confirmed → settled; an insurance claim lifecycle is: filed → assessed → approved/rejected → paid; and each state transition has domain preconditions and domain rollback procedures,” then Process Manager embodies that knowledge. The state machine is the domain’s own lifecycle; each transition is a domain event; compensating actions are the domain’s own reversal procedures.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a long-running process whose intermediate states are domain-recognized states — and the domain itself specifies what can happen from each state and what undoes a failed transition. Process Manager closes the gap: prevents the process logic from being scattered across the message handlers that implement each step, where each handler must independently decide whether the step is valid given the current state and what to do if it fails.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “process” is a saga — a technical transaction-coordination mechanism that chains service calls with compensating actions to simulate distributed atomicity. The domain doesn’t recognize compensating actions like “refund the payment” as a business process; it recognizes “the payment was refunded” as an independent event. Process Manager here becomes a distributed-transaction coordinator that hides failure-handling code behind state-machine syntax. A domain expert would say “the payment shouldn’t have been taken in the first place if the rest of the process couldn’t complete — fix the order of operations.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a name for each intermediate state, and can a domain expert draw the state machine from memory — states, transitions, and what goes wrong at each transition — using only business vocabulary?

If yes → applicable. Process Manager is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a distributed-transaction coordinator wearing a state-machine costume.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Message Broker Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can you decouple the destination of a message from the sender and maintain central control over the flow of messages?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the systems in a domain are decoupled — that system A should not know about system B, that the topology is a domain property not a deployment detail — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the order-entry system produces orders; the warehouse system consumes orders; the revenue-recognition system consumes fulfilled orders — and none of them should know about each other because they’re separate bounded contexts with different ownership and release cadences,” then Message Broker embodies that knowledge. The broker is the domain’s decentralized hub; the channels are the domain’s communication paths.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that components communicate without direct knowledge of each other — because they evolve independently, are owned by different teams, or sit in different bounded contexts. Message Broker closes the gap: prevents each producer from maintaining a registry of consumers and each consumer from knowing the producer’s endpoint, which would couple the entire ecosystem together. Without it, changing the warehouse system’s endpoint means modifying the order-entry system — coupling two systems that the domain says should be independent.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The systems are in the same bounded context and the “decoupling” is architectural dogma — “we always put a broker between things” — when no external constraint mandates it. A broker between services sharing the same team, repository, domain model, and release cadence turns a function call into a message round-trip with serialization and new failure modes. The knowledge gap is adopting a decoupling structure without a constraint that demands decoupling.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the two sides of the broker as genuinely separate things — different bounded contexts, different owners, different evolution cadences — or are they one logical system that you split across two services?

If yes → applicable. Message Broker is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s adding a network boundary where the domain already had a module boundary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Content Enricher Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we communicate with another system if the message originator does not have all the required data items available?” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message arrives with incomplete information and that the missing information has a domain-designated source is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an order message carries a customer ID, but the warehouse needs the shipping address — which is owned by the customer profile service,” then Content Enricher is just embodying that knowledge. The missing field is domain information that belongs to a different domain authority; the enricher is the domain’s own information-completion step.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain information belongs to a specific domain authority — and the downstream consumer legitimately needs that information but shouldn’t own the authority to produce it. Content Enricher closes the gap: it prevents the consumer from calling the authority directly, which would couple the consumer to the authority’s interface and create a runtime dependency that the domain didn’t intend. Without it, the warehouse system must know how to call the customer profile service — coupling the warehouse to customer-profile concerns, when its domain job is “ship to this address,” not “look up addresses.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “missing” information is not missing from a domain perspective — the downstream consumer doesn’t need it, but the developer thinks it’s “nice to have” or is preemptively enriching for a future use case. Or the information belongs to the producer and should have been in the original message — the producer was lazy and Content Enricher is doing the producer’s job post hoc. A domain expert would say “if orders always ship to the customer’s default address, why doesn’t the order-entry system put the address on the order to begin with?”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the missing piece of information belong to a different domain authority than the producer — and does the consumer legitimately need it to do its job?

If yes → applicable. Content Enricher is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s either gold-plating or compensating for a producer that skimped on its domain responsibility.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.
