#FP #PatternMatching #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Lazy Evaluation

Hughes: Lazy evaluation defers a computation until its result is needed. [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a value may never be demanded — and that deferring it is a domain decision, not only a performance optimization — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “most requests never open the full report detail; only a few accounts need the risk breakdown; the customer may never submit the form and so never need a premium quote,” then Lazy Evaluation embodies that knowledge. The thunk is the domain’s own “derive only if demanded” contract: the value is computed only when something asks for it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats the derived value as demand-driven — computing it eagerly would do work the domain may never ask for. Lazy Evaluation closes the gap: the value is not computed unless it is demanded. The laziness is a domain rule here, not merely a caching trick.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Even a “purely performance” deferral is a domain decision: someone chose when the value is needed. Lazy evaluation fits only when the domain names that timing — compute on first request, or compute at period close. If the timing is an arbitrary knob the domain never fixed, laziness asserts a demand schedule no one decided. If the domain always demands the value, laziness asserts a suspension no one asked for. That is the gap: the timing is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain expert describe a scenario where this computation genuinely should not happen — not “should happen later,” but “may never happen at all”?

If yes → applicable. Lazy Evaluation is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The timing is an arbitrary knob — the domain has not named when the value is needed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #LazyEvaluation #Thunk #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Trampoline

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A trampoline is a loop that runs recursive steps as plain returns, so deep recursion does not overflow the stack. Stack safety is one axis. The domain question is the other: when the computation has meaningful discrete phases the domain recognizes, the trampoline’s steps are those phases. If your domain model crystallizes that “processing a batch of claims requires progression through validation, assessment, approval, and payout — each step is a domain phase,” then the trampoline’s structure is the domain’s own.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates stepwise execution where each step is a meaningful domain unit — AND the computation is deeply recursive, requiring stack safety. Trampoline closes the gap: its steps are the domain’s phases, and it runs them without overflowing the stack.








WarningWhen the steps are not domain phases (cohesion-neutral)



Stack safety is not knowledge-free: the runtime’s stack bound is a fact about the environment the code runs in, and the trampoline fits it. The inapplicable case is naming each step a domain phase when no rule or state the expert recognizes stands behind it. Then the phase names are invented, not discovered — calling each step a “phase” asserts a domain granularity no one decided. That is the gap: the phase boundaries are unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Beyond the need for stack safety, would the domain expert describe the computation as a sequence of distinct, named domain phases?

If yes → applicable. Trampoline is doubly justified — runtime safety AND domain fidelity.
If no → no phase knowledge. It remains correct for stack safety — a real environment fact, never a mistake.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Trampoline #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Memoization

Michie: Memoization stores a function’s result under its arguments so a repeated call reuses it. [4]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Memoization stores a computation’s result under its inputs, so a repeated call reuses it. That a result is determined solely by its inputs — and that caching it is a domain guarantee, not just a performance optimization — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a tax table lookup for a given bracket always returns the same rate; a risk score for a given exposure profile is immutable for the scoring period,” then Memoization is just embodying that knowledge. The cache is the domain’s own “this value, once computed, is stable” guarantee.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates determinism: for a given key, the same inputs always produce the same output. When validity is period-bounded, the period is part of the key. Memoization closes the gap: it avoids redundant recomputation and fixes one value per input set. The cached value becomes the single source of truth — matching the domain’s own “the rate doesn’t change mid-period” constraint.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Even a caching optimization is a domain decision: someone chose to reuse the result, and how long. Memoization fits only when the domain names a stability window. When the output changes for reasons external to its inputs, the window is unfixed; memoizing a database query, a time-dependent computation, or a stateful function then adds staleness risk. The cache asserts a stability the domain never guaranteed. That is the gap: the validity window is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain guarantee that the same inputs always yield the same output — and would a differing result for the same inputs be a domain error?

If yes → applicable. Memoization is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The function’s output is time-dependent or externally mutable, and caching risks domain-incorrect results.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Memoization #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Pure Function

Hughes: A pure function has no side effects: its result depends only on its arguments. [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a domain demands deterministic, side-effect-free computation is domain knowledge. Purity is also the FP default, but the domain’s demand for it is still a choice. The question is whether the domain demands referential transparency. If your domain model crystallizes that “computing a tax liability from income and bracket must yield the same result every time for the same inputs — and must not depend on or modify anything outside those inputs,” then the Pure Function matches the domain’s own determinism constraint. Purity is double-counted: computational correctness AND domain fidelity. Domain-essential effects are handled with effect types, not by violating purity.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain computations are deterministic and side-effect-free. Pure Functions close the gap: they prevent the system from introducing hidden dependencies (global state, clock time, random seeds) into computations the domain says should be deterministic. Testing, reasoning, and caching become trivial — consequences of that determinism, not just technical benefits.








WarningWhen the determinism constraint is unstated (cohesion-neutral)



The pattern does no harm here. It also gives no signal. In functional code, purity is the default, so the code reads the same whether or not the domain requires determinism. Two cases collapse into one: “the domain requires this result to stay stable” and “this function is pure by habit.” The code cannot tell them apart. The requirement is real, but it is unwritten. The gap is the missing statement, not a missing constraint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain impose determinism constraints on certain computations — and would a non-deterministic result (same inputs, different output) be a domain error?

If yes → applicable. The pure function is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → no named constraint. It remains FP’s default — never wrong, but the requirement is unstated.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #PureFunction #ReferentialTransparency #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Recursion Scheme

Meijer et al.: A recursion scheme is a reusable function that captures a standard traversal of a recursive data type. [5]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
A recursion scheme is a reusable function that captures a standard traversal of a recursive data type, such as a fold. When a domain operation is defined over such a type and the recursion pattern is domain-meaningful — not just algorithmic convenience — that is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “an org chart folds to its root to compute headcount,” then a Recursion Scheme encodes that knowledge. The fold captures bottom-up reduction; the unfold captures top-down generation. Unlike structural patterns, where the code is the domain structure, the recursion scheme is an encoding choice. A recursive function or Visitor gives the same behavior, but loses the clean separation of traversal from per-node logic.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Recursion Schemes close the gap: they separate “how to walk the structure” from “what to do at each node.” When the data type changes, only the per-node function changes; the traversal updates.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The data structure is not domain-recursive — it is a tree-shaped intermediate representation. A JSON AST, parse tree, or object graph recurses structurally. But the shape is still a decision: the domain chose it. A recursion scheme fits only when the domain names the tree as a hierarchy it owns. If the shape is a format detail the domain never named, the scheme formalizes an artifact and couples operations to a shape that changes when the format evolves. That is the gap: the tree’s domain standing is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the recursive structure a domain concept — would an expert describe the tree as “an organization of sub-organizations” or “an expression of sub-expressions”?

If yes → applicable. Recursion Schemes are one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The tree is a format detail the domain never named — a recursive function expresses the same traversal without formalizing it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #RecursionScheme #Catamorphism #Anamorphism #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Functional Programming as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Continuation

Reynolds: A continuation is a function that represents the rest of a computation. [6]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
A continuation is a function that represents “the rest of the computation,” passed in so the caller decides what happens next. That a computation’s next step is a domain decision passed at runtime — that “what happens after” is not fixed — is knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “after payment processing, send a confirmation email on success or queue a fraud review on failure,” then Continuations encode that knowledge. CPS captures the domain’s “here’s what to do next” parameterization. Unlike structural patterns where the code is the domain structure, CPS is an encoding choice: a Strategy, a callback, or an event emitter gives the same behavior, but loses CPS’s composable control flow.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the “and then” is itself a domain decision, not a fixed algorithm. Continuations close the gap: they prevent the computation from hardcoding its successor, which would couple the processor to the notification and fraud systems. The continuation is supplied at the call site — the business process determines the next step.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “and then” is always the same — but even a fixed callback is a domain decision: someone chose that the step must happen. The construct fits only when the domain names the next step as a decision point. Passing a logger, a metrics collector, or a response writer as a continuation transforms plumbing into CPS when no rule varies the step. The interface then signals a choice no one makes. That is the gap: the fixed step is unstated, not “merely plumbing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have multiple, different “what happens next” paths — and would an expert describe the continuation as a business-process decision point?

If yes → applicable. Continuation is one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The step never varies — a direct call expresses the same fixed step without passing a continuation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Continuation #CPS #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: F# Constructs
text:
Computation expressions, units of measure, type providers — compile-time knowledge drawn from data. Each post names what the construct knew, and when it knew it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: F# Constructs
text:
Case study: Computation expressions
Two builders both called “result”: one stops at the first failed step, one collects all of them. The call sites look identical.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A computation expression is a builder object plus syntax. let! x = e desugars to builder.Bind(e, fun x -> ...) (or a fused Source form when the builder defines one), return to Return, and! to MergeSources or a BindN, whatever the builder defines. The builder decides what a bind means — stop on first error, accumulate all, await, retry — and the syntax hides that decision behind let!.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
Know your workflow’s failure semantics first: does one failed step end the run, or must every failure report in one pass? A payment authorization stops: the second step is invalid once the first refused. A form validation reports all fields; no user should submit five times to learn five things. Both look like let!, and only the author knows which this is.
The gap question: for this workflow, what does one failed step mean — stop, accumulate, retry — and does the builder actually do that?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Steps as sequential obligations: read the order, charge the card, write the receipt. Any failure aborts, and a short-circuiting Bind is exactly that rule. Or a validation builder where and! accumulates every violation into one pass.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The computation expression was adopted “for readability”. The builder comes from a library because let! beats nested matching, and nobody reads its Bind. A record then fails two rules, the short-circuiting builder returns the first, and the second error waits for the next submission. The syntax matches an accumulating builder’s, so review sees nothing. The elegance was real; the failure semantics were never decided.








TipThe faithfulness test



For this workflow: what does one failed step mean — stop, accumulate, retry — and does the builder actually do that?

If yes → the syntax carries the domain’s rule. Check the builder’s Bind, not the call sites.
If no → the construct asserts a failure rule your domain lacks. Swap the builder, or handle what it drops.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Write down what happens to the other steps when one fails, then read Bind against it.




#FSharp #DotNet #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #ComputationExpressions #ErrorHandling #TypeSafety

title: F# Constructs
text:
Case study: Units of measure
A length in metres plus a length in feet refuses to compile — and the same two numbers, cast to float for a library call, add up silently.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: [<Measure>] type m makes float<m> a dimensioned number, and arithmetic keeps the dimension: metres times metres is float<m^2>, metres plus feet is a type error. The check runs entirely in the compiler — the units are erased, so nothing exists at runtime and nothing re-checks it later. Conversions become explicit factors like 0.3048<m/ft>.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
Dimension is a claim about the quantity itself, and the author must know which quantities have one: is this number a length, a duration, a rate, a count, money? float<m/s> and float<kg/s> are both “a rate” and are not interchangeable. A type says which.
The gap question: which numbers in this system carry units — typed — and at which boundary do the units disappear?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A measured calculation: structural spans in metres against a specification table in feet, with the conversion written once as 0.3048<m/ft>. The mixup that ships elsewhere is a compile error here, at the line. Dosages, flow rates, fuel per distance behave alike.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The dimensional claim stops at the interop edge. The core is typed, then a DTO needs double Length for JSON, a column is float, a plotting call takes plain floats — and the unit is stripped by a cast to float, at the boundary, where no reviewer looks twice. The metre/foot mixup now lives exactly where the compiler was told to stop caring, and the runtime has no units left to disagree with.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which numbers in this system carry units — typed — and at which boundary do the units disappear?

If yes → the compiler guards the interior. List the boundaries and check each conversion factor by hand.
If no → the numbers are plain float and the dimensional claim lives in a comment or a variable name. Add the measures, starting at the boundary that hurts.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Walk the data path and name the unit of every stored number.




#FSharp #DotNet #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #UnitsOfMeasure #TypeSafety #DomainModeling

title: F# Constructs
text:
Case study: Type providers
A column gets renamed upstream. The build stays green, because it read a sample file committed in March.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: CsvProvider<"sample.csv"> reads that file at compile time and generates a row type with the columns it found; an OpenAPI or SQL provider does the same from a document or a live schema. Your code is then checked against those types, so a misspelled column fails the build. But the schema was read once, at that build — and erased providers leave nothing at runtime to re-check it.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
The author must know whether the schema is a contract they control or a snapshot they observed. A provider turns an observation into a type: as true as the document read, as durable as the next change to it. The knowledge is not “these columns exist” but “these columns exist in version N, which is what production serves”.
The gap question: when was this type last generated — and from which version of the schema?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A contract that is stable and fetchable at build time: the provider regenerates in CI against the current schema document, so a renamed column or an added field breaks the build instead of a nightly job. The generated type is that agreement, dated.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The committed sample. Someone checked in a CSV, or pointed the provider at last quarter’s schema document, and every build since has asserted that old shape. Then the API renames a field: the build reads the stale document, compiles clean, tests pass on recorded fixtures, and the runtime serves the new one. The failure arrives as a null under the old field’s name — right type, missing value, no exception — and “it compiles” had felt like validation.








TipThe faithfulness test



When was this type last generated — and from which version of the schema?

If yes → the type is a claim about a named version. Pin it in the build and fail when the source document moves.
If no → the type is a claim about a snapshot nobody tracks. Regenerate, or drop the provider and validate where the data enters.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Find the file or URL the provider reads, and date it.




#FSharp #DotNet #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #TypeProviders #SchemaEvolution #APIContracts

title: F# Constructs
section: Case study: Discriminated unions and the incomplete-match warning
text:
Case study: Discriminated unions and the incomplete-match warning
A union gains a case, the build prints four warnings among three thousand lines, and the missing arm throws at 2 a.m. in production.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A multi-case reference-type discriminated union compiles to a tagged class hierarchy; a match compiles to a tag test with the arms inlined. Incompleteness is FS0025 — a warning, not an error — so a match that omits a case compiles clean and throws MatchFailureException when that case arrives. The trade: the type carries the whole case set, and the compiler reports the mismatch only at the volume you configured.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know the case set is closed, that every consumer was rebuilt against it, and that no wildcard arm stands in for cases not yet written. The wildcard is where the next case is swallowed: the warning disappears and the new case takes the fallback branch. An old binary does not warn at all — it throws.
The gap question: does an unmatched case break this build — configured — or only a production run?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



FS0025 promoted to an error in the project file, and no wildcard arms on the union. A new case then breaks the build in every consumer that has not handled it: the compiler enumerates the sites you would otherwise grep for, and both stay in lockstep.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A developer adds the case, the warning lands in the log, and nobody reads it. Four matches have no arm for the new case — the warning was their only check. The build stays green, and the one path that reaches the case throws in production.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does an unmatched case break this build — configured — or only a production run?

If yes → the union is the authority on its case set. Check which arms are wildcards; those are the ones the next case will not reach.
If no → the exhaustiveness claim is prose, not a checked fact. Promote FS0025 to an error and rebuild every consumer.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List every match over the union, then the arms that name no case.




#FSharp #DotNet #DiscriminatedUnions #PatternMatching #TypeSafety #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: F# Constructs
text:
Case study: Immutability by default
One unguarded mutable field turns a record you could hand to ten threads into a record you must hand to one.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: A record compiles to a class with get-only fields, and a list to a linked chain no operation modifies; a change produces a new value. The trade: the compiler checks nothing about sharing. It makes mutation hard to write, then trusts you to know what is actually shared. Declare one field mutable and the type is immutable in shape, mutable in fact, and nothing warns.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which values more than one owner reads at once, and which of those hold state that changes once another thread can see it. Immutability by default keeps that question cheap only while it holds — and one unguarded mutable field ends it.
The gap question: which types in this module contain mutable state — listed — and is each one’s sharing story stated?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Records updated by explicit with expressions, so a change yields a new value and the old one stays valid for every reader holding it. Lists shared by prepending, where the tail is reused without a copy and both owners hold it safely.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The record is immutable except for one field, declared mutable to avoid threading an update through six call sites — a real saving, and why the trap works. Two threads now share the instance and the field crosses a thread boundary with no synchronization and no symptom until the read lands stale. The mutable list says it louder: a ResizeArray handed to two owners, both appending, one growing under the other’s loop.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which types in this module contain mutable state — listed — and is each one’s sharing story stated?

If yes → the default is doing its job and the exceptions are deliberate. Check that each mutable field is confined to one owner or guarded.
If no → the type says immutable and the program says otherwise. Confine the mutation to one owner, or make the sharing explicit and synchronized.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the mutable fields, then the threads that reach them.




#FSharp #DotNet #Immutability #ThreadSafety #RecordTypes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: F# Constructs
section: Case study: Async of T versus Task of T
text:
Case study: Async of T versus Task of T
An async workflow that never runs throws nothing — it is a value built, passed on, and dropped.
Writing an F# construct? Ask “which fact does the type carry — units, effects, exhaustiveness — and when is it checked?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the construct enforces a guess. If you can, the code is knowledge embodied — the types catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: An async workflow compiles to a function taking a cancellation token and a callback that resumes it — cold: nothing runs until something starts it. A Task is hot when its factory starts it: work begins there, and the bare constructor leaves it cold until Start(). Both are generic over the result: the type says “this produces a T” and nothing about who starts it or whether cancelling reaches the work. The trade: coldness with an implicit token against immediacy with an explicit one.


The F# knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which token the work observes — a fact no signature records. Async threads cancellation through the workflow context, so a started workflow inherits the token given to Start; a Task observes only the token its factory was given. Convert and the answers diverge.
The gap question: for each async value, who starts it, and does cancellation cross the Async and Task boundary — verified?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



One world per Async/Task seam, chosen once and named. Async inside the domain where composition and inherited cancellation matter, converted where a .NET library returns a Task — named, so a reader sees the task is already hot. Startup is one explicit Start at the top, and its token is the one the workflow observes.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Start called inside a function to make sure the work happens: it fires, returns, runs under Async’s default token, so the caller’s cancellation never reaches it. Or the reverse — an async wrapper awaited around a Task created without a token, so cancelling the workflow is a request the Task never received.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each async value: who starts it, and does cancellation cross the Async and Task boundary — verified?

If yes → the boundary is explicit and the token path is real. Check the one place startup happens, and that it is not repeated deeper.
If no → the workflow may never run, or may never stop. Make startup explicit, and pass the token into every factory that creates a Task.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Trace each value from its creation to its Start or await.




#FSharp #DotNet #AsyncProgramming #Cancellation #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
text:
The closed-world assumption encodes what exists, what is reachable, what may load later. Each post names what the image assumed, and which fact it stands on.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: GraalVM Native Image
text:
Case study: The closed-world assumption
A native binary decides, before it runs, every class it will load — and nothing met later can revise any of it.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: Native Image compiles against GraalVM’s closed world: reachability is walked from the entry points, and everything unproven is folded away. Startup falls to tens of milliseconds — no class loader to bootstrap, no JIT to warm — and no unreachable class ships. The trade is exact: every path that reaches a class by a computed name (reflection, resources, JNI, proxies, serialization) must be declared, or the image omits it.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The closed world is a claim about your application, not about Java: these are all the types this program will ever touch. Making it true requires knowing your own dynamism — every name your code computes instead of writing, and every access that depends on it. A team that never enumerated those paths inherited the claim.
The gap question: which classes reach the program only through a string?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A dependency set that is fixed and known, audited for reachability, every dynamic access declared and reviewed. Then the image is a fact: the build reproduces, the start-up budget is real, a deleted class leaves the binary.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“It runs on the JVM, so it will build native.” The trap is the successful build. On the JVM, Class.forName resolves against a class path holding everything; here it resolves against a set frozen before the program ran. A missing entry is a run-time failure, not a compile error, so the image builds green, and the gap waits — on a plugin loader, an optional driver, an error path reached once a quarter. Toolchains warn at build time, but only for accesses they can see.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which classes load only by reflection — enumerated — or is that an article of faith?

If yes → the closed world matches the application. Check the entries are regenerated when code moves.
If no → the image enforces a guess. Run the tracing agent over the suite, diff, declare what it reaches.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Find the string-based entry points, then run the tests under the tracing agent.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #AOT #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Reflection and resource configuration
text:
Case study: Reflection and resource configuration
One absent entry in a metadata file turns a passing service into a MissingReflectionRegistrationError at two in the morning — and no compiler saw it.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: Reachability metadata names what static analysis cannot see: classes reached by reflection, resources fetched by name, proxy and serialization targets. Declared, they enter the image; undeclared, they are compiled out. The trade is one configuration line per dynamic element against a run-time failure on precisely the element you forgot.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The metadata is a written record of the application’s dynamism. Producing it means knowing which types your frameworks resolve by name: the DTO a serializer reflects over, the entity an ORM maps, the handler built from a config string. A hand-written file records what someone remembered that day; a generated one records what a run reached — a smaller claim, and an honest one.
The gap question: who generated this metadata, and does the generator run where the code changes?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Metadata generated by a test run through the tracing agent, then reviewed and committed: the diff is readable, the entries name real types, and CI regenerates it so a new DTO arrives with its entry. Coverage is the suite’s coverage — a limit you measure rather than discover.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A framework builds proxies by reflection, and the metadata covers the DTOs the tests touched. One rarely used DTO, added last spring, has no entry — so it fails when that endpoint is first called, weeks after deploy. The build was green every day in between. A hand-maintained file rots quieter: nobody deletes the entry when a class is renamed, so the failure surfaces on the new name.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who generated this metadata — and is it regenerated when the code changes, inside CI?

If yes → the declarations track the code. Check a review step exists, so generator noise never becomes an unreviewed grant.
If no → the file records a past run’s memory. Regenerate from a production-like suite, diff, commit the delta.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. List the frameworks that reflect, then the types they reflect over.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #Reflection #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Build time, class initialization, run time
text:
Case study: Build time, class initialization, run time
A static initializer reading config at build time freezes the build machine’s answer into the binary — every later environment inherits it.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: A native image has three phases: build, the class initialization the build performs, and run time. By default initialization runs at start-up; classes marked --initialize-at-build-time run their static initializers on the builder, and their state lands in the image heap. That is the trade: start-up work moves to the build, and every build-time side effect happens once, on a machine that is not production.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The choice is a claim about each class: nothing it computes depends on where or when it runs. So what is its domain — the environment, the locale, the time zone, the clock, a random seed? A class touching these describes a deployment, not a program — and the deployment is unknown at build time.
The gap question: which classes run their initialization during the build, and would any of them read something that differs per environment?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The order reviewed class by class, every class touching environment, locale, or time kept at the run-time default. Pure lookup tables — parsers, registries, compiled regexes — stay at build time, costing the build and never the start-up.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The build succeeds, the binary starts in 20 ms, so nobody asks what ran at build time. A configuration holder, marked for build-time initialization, caches System.getenv; the staging value ships to production. A default time zone is captured from the builder; a random seed is drawn once, so every replica shares it. None of these crash. Each yields a wrong answer, quietly and uniformly — the harder failure to find.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which classes run code at image build — listed — and would any of them read something that differs per environment?

If yes → the split is a decision. Check the list is regenerated when classes move, and measure start-up, where deferred init returns.
If no → the build froze a deployment fact. Move those classes to run-time initialization, re-measure start-up.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Enumerate the initializers that touch the environment, then trace what the build ran.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #ClassInitialization #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
text:
Case study: Profile-guided optimization
A native image has no JIT to learn hot paths at run time. A training profile decides them months before production does.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: PGO builds the image twice: an instrumented build records a profile from a training run, and the optimized build uses the captured branch and call frequencies to lay out code and choose inlining. The trade is a training run to maintain against much of the peak throughput the JIT would have found by itself. Without it, the image keeps the compiler’s guessed layout; with a stale one, the layout for traffic you no longer serve.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The profile is a claim about workload: these calls dominate, these branches stay cold, these types appear here. A team must know its real traffic shape — endpoint mix, argument distributions, the true rarity of the rare path — as a measurement, not an architecture diagram. The profile is workload knowledge, encoded where the compiler can act.
The gap question: what traffic trained this profile, and when was it last validated against real load?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



PGO trained from production-like traffic — a replay of recorded requests, or a load test built from measured distributions — with peak throughput compared before and after, recovering toward the JVM’s numbers. The training run is a maintained artifact, regenerated as traffic moves.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A profile recorded in the first month, from synthetic traffic, never regenerated. The code has moved since: a path that was cold is now the main one, so the compiler inlines the old favourite and leaves the new hot path out of line. Nothing fails, no test changes colour. Throughput is simply below the JVM’s, invisible unless someone compares.








TipThe faithfulness test



What traffic trained this profile — recorded — and when was it last re-validated against real load?

If yes → the profile is evidence. Check it still matches the measured traffic, and the measurement uses peak, not the average day.
If no → the optimizer aims at a workload that left months ago. Record the traffic shape, retrain, compare peak.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Measure the call and branch mix of real traffic first.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #PGO #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Truffle and polyglot embedding
text:
Case study: Truffle and polyglot embedding
An embedded second language runtime is a two-runtime decision: one serves the feature, both cost warmup and footprint.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: Truffle implements languages on GraalVM’s shared runtime, and the polyglot API lets them call each other through one interop protocol. The trade is one process and one infrastructure set — collector, threads, debugger — against per-language warmup, footprint, and marshalling on every value that crosses the boundary. Each embedded language adds a language runtime on the shared VM, not a library call.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The choice is a claim about a feature: this capability cannot be expressed in the host language without reimplementing one. Defending it requires knowing which feature that is, how much users exercise it, and what a crossing costs — the interop boundary is where latency and allocation concentrate. A team that cannot name the feature has chosen a platform, not a solution.
The gap question: which feature genuinely needs a second runtime — measured against what it costs?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



User-supplied scripts evaluated in an isolated polyglot context under resource limits. The users write the language, so the language is the requirement, and warmup is measured against a script’s expected lifetime.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Polyglot chosen because it is impressive. A rules expression evaluates in an embedded Python interpreter: one language’s worth of feature, and the interpreter that runs it in every replica — an interop hop per evaluation. The demonstration was convincing; the steady state was never measured. The second runtime is a permanent tax on a feature a hundred lines of the host language would serve.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which feature genuinely needs a second language runtime — measured against what it costs?

If yes → the embedding is a requirement. Check context isolation and per-language warmup are measured, and crossings are bounded.
If no → one runtime is doing the work of two. Re-express the feature in the host language, or move it out of process.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Name the feature, then count the calls that cross the boundary.




#GraalVM #Java #Truffle #Polyglot #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Native image versus JIT peak throughput
text:
Case study: Native image versus JIT peak throughput
A payments service boots in 90 ms, then runs for six weeks — the native image saves the 90 ms it pays once.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: A native image compiles ahead of time under a closed-world assumption: the build decides what code exists, and the result runs without a profiling JIT. The JVM instead profiles the running program and recompiles hot paths. The trade is startup and footprint against peak throughput, which the JIT reaches over minutes and keeps only at steady state — profile-guided native builds narrow the gap.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know the process’s life: how long it runs, and whether the hot code that dominates CPU arrives in the first minute or the fortieth. A short-lived process is mostly warmup; an always-on service lives at steady state, where a per-request throughput difference outweighs a startup difference paid once. The gap question: is this lifetime, measured as a distribution, short enough that the gap never amortizes?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The decision comes from a measured workload shape. Short batch jobs, CLI tools, functions, and scale-to-zero workers live for seconds, and native wins on start-up. A fleet autoscaling on a tight latency objective belongs here too. The mirror case is a result, decided by the same lifetime measurement.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Native chosen for the always-on service, because a demo booted fast on a laptop. Startup improves by a figure nobody disputes; the steady-state gap appears as more CPU per request, so the team adds replicas and calls it capacity planning. The seductive part: the startup number is cheap to reproduce, while the peak gap needs an hours-long test — so the cheap measurement settles the expensive question.








TipThe faithfulness test



How long does this process live — measured — and does the startup win amortize against the peak gap?

If yes → native is admissible. Confirm both builds reached steady state.
If no → throughput was traded for a boot time. Measure sustained throughput at production load.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Measure the lifetime distribution, then sustained throughput on both builds.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #JIT #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
text:
Case study: Native memory footprint
The native image dropped the metaspace and the code cache — and the container limit, halved by folklore, was filled by the first burst.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: A native image is one executable: class metadata is baked in, code is compiled at build time, and no metaspace or code cache grows with traffic. What remains is real — the image’s size, a runtime heap for allocations still collected (Serial GC by default), thread stacks, native buffers. The trade is a predictable resident size against an image of tens to hundreds of megabytes, plus an allocation rate the collector still serves.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know its memory curve: resident size at peak load, not at boot, and how much the application allocates per request. The removals are easy to predict; some remaining terms are workload-dependent and decide whether the claim holds. A native image that allocates heavily lands close to the JVM build’s resident size, minus the code cache. The gap question: what is the measured resident size at peak load?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Density per node is measured, and the choice follows the number. A team benchmarked a native build under production load, found peak resident size well below the JVM build’s, and raised replica count on the same hardware. The mandate is a schedule paid per gigabyte-hour, or a fixed node count.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Native means small” assumed without measuring resident size under load. The container limit is then set by folklore — the JVM number halved, or a round 256 MB — and a burst drives allocations past it, so the container dies for a limit nobody sized. The seductive part: boot-time resident size looks tiny, and that is the figure on the slide.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured resident size at peak load — and what density did it actually buy per node?

If yes → the claim is knowledge. Check the limit covers image baseline, stacks, and collector headroom.
If no → the footprint is a story. Measure resident size under sustained peak load on both builds.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Measure peak resident size and allocation rate, then recompute density.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #MemoryFootprint #Kubernetes #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Native builds in the pipeline
text:
Case study: Native builds in the pipeline
11 minutes of CI per commit, sixty commits a day, and one of those binaries ever reaches a running node.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: Producing a native image is a compile job: closed-world analysis and whole-program optimization — one pass over every class, minutes of several cores and a few gigabytes. Its inputs are a pinned JDK, a GraalVM version, the dependencies, and the reachability metadata — the declarations naming what reflection reaches by string. The trade is build time and cache storage against reproducibility; a cache keyed on those inputs decides it.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know which artifacts ship as images and which exist only to be tested. That fact is often unrecorded: services claim to be deployable, so pipelines build the deployable form. The other fact is the input set — toolchain, dependency lock, metadata, build arguments — because a cache that ignores one returns a stale binary. The gap question: which pipelines build native, and does each deploy what it builds?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Native builds are layered and cached, produced only for artifacts that ship as images: release tags, or published artifacts. The cache key covers toolchain and dependency lock, so a hit is a real match, and a per-commit JVM build carries the code’s test signal. The image job costs minutes on the builds that matter, and its binary is the one that ships.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A native build on every commit, for every branch: hours of CI per day for binaries nobody deploys that night, and a cold cache blocks merges that touch nothing native. The seductive part: it looks like thoroughness. Building the same way everywhere is consistent, consistency feels like safety, and it produces a green badge.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which pipelines build native — and does every one of them actually deploy the result?

If yes → the build is knowledge: the image job’s inputs match what ships. Check the cache key covers toolchain, lock, and metadata.
If no → you pay for a compile nobody consumes. Move native builds to the artifacts that ship, keeping a JVM build for the test signal.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pipeline wrong — you’ve found incomplete delivery knowledge. Map each shipped artifact to its producing pipeline.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #CI #BuildEngineering #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
section: Case study: Virtual threads on a native image
text:
Case study: Virtual threads on a native image
The service passed every concurrency test on the JVM — the carrier pool ignored its parallelism setting under the native binary, and the first Friday in production found it.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: Virtual threads made blocking code cheap: many of them ride a small pool of carrier threads. A native image can inherit the feature through the same libraries, and no declaration is needed for it: the scheduler is reachable through the API. Support and behavior vary by GraalVM and JDK version, so the artifact to validate is the native binary, not the JVM run.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know which concurrency behaviors its code depends on: carrier parallelism, thread-local use, pinning inside synchronized blocks or JNI calls, timing assumptions in tests. Those are facts only the team holds. A feature list is a general claim; a build is specific. The gap question: is the concurrency behavior validated on the native build, or only on the JVM?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The virtual-thread service is validated under the native build: the full suite plus a sustained load test, pinning scenarios exercised, blocking I/O at high virtual-thread counts, throughput compared against the JVM build. The parity claim is then a measurement on the artifact that ships.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Parity assumed: the feature is documented as supported and the JVM mode passed, so the native build is declared equivalent. Under load the difference surfaces only in the native binary: a carrier count that ignores the setting, a pinning path that stalls. The team debugs application code before suspecting the image. The seductive part: passing tests are the evidence people trust most.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this feature validated on the native build — tested — or assumed from the JVM mode?

If yes → the parity claim is knowledge. Check the validation exercised load, on the shipping toolchain.
If no → you hold an untested claim about the artifact you deploy. Add native concurrency tests and one sustained load test.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the image wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. Enumerate the concurrency behaviors you rely on, then test each on the native binary.




#GraalVM #Java #VirtualThreads #Concurrency #NativeImage #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: GraalVM Native Image
text:
Case study: Library reachability metadata
A library takes a minor upgrade, the metadata still matches the range, and one class stops being registered for reflection.
Building a native image? Ask “which fact does the closed-world assumption encode — what exists, what is reachable, what may load later?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the image enforces a guess. If you can, the build is knowledge embodied — the binary catching up to what the application actually does.

Mechanism: A native build must know which classes reflection, serialization, JNI, and resource loading reach — closed-world analysis cannot see a runtime-computed name. The GraalVM Reachability Metadata Repository collects community metadata. Entries are tested against particular versions and consumed across declared ranges. The trade is coverage against entries authored for another version.


The GraalVM knowledge gap it signals
The team must know the exact library versions in the build and whether the matching metadata was tested against them. That is a fact about the resolved dependency graph, not the repository. A version bump can rename a class or move the reflective path out of coverage. The gap question: which library versions does this metadata target?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Metadata is pinned to the exact library versions in the build, refreshed with every upgrade — range coverage forgone — and matched strictly with GraalVM’s exact-metadata mode, so a version mismatch can fail the build. The version then matches; whether every reflected path has an entry is still the suite’s question.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Metadata carried over from a different version of the library. The range overlaps, so the entry applies and most classes register; the one class that changed between versions is missing, and the failure appears on the single code path that reflects on it. The seductive part: the build is green and quiet. The analysis found a metadata entry — any entry — so it had no warning to give.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which library versions does this metadata target — pinned — and how does the build verify yours match?

If yes → the metadata is knowledge. Check the pin comes from the dependency lock.
If no → coverage is assumed. Pin metadata to resolved versions and test the reflecting paths natively.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the metadata wrong — you’ve found incomplete application knowledge. List the libraries that reflect, then the versions the build resolves.




#GraalVM #Java #NativeImage #ReachabilityMetadata #Reflection #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Almost every design pattern/principle can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge.
When you’re reaching for a pattern, ask “does the domain knowledge mandate the coupling this pattern would add or remove?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the knowledge prescribes the structure directly — the pattern adds nothing the domain hadn’t already decided.

Nothing here was decided
A design review, the ordinary kind. Eight engineers, one whiteboard, a service to build. The lead walks the room through the choices: a Strategy for the payment variants, a Facade over the gateway, a fifth of the heap for the young generation, a week’s retention for the audit log, a soft delete for the orders. Each choice gets its trade-offs spoken aloud, gets challenged once, gets nodded through. The minutes record them as decisions. Leaving the room, everyone agrees the session was good: hard choices, made well.
Then someone asks one question, and the meeting starts over. For each item on the board: which fact made it so? Not why did you choose it — what made it true? The Facade: someone finds the gateway’s rate-limit page, and the shape stops looking optional — the mediation had to exist, and it had to sit in one place. The Strategy: the product owner names the three payment methods and the rule that routes among them, and the pattern turns from a choice into a description — the code catching up to something the domain already said. The retention week: the auditor names the regulation, and the choice dissolves into compliance arithmetic. The heap fraction: nobody finds anything. No allocation profile, no burst curve, no measurement at all — the fifth was a number somebody remembered from another system.
By the end of the second pass, the board looks different. Nothing on it was decided. Every shape that survived was caused — by a vendor number, a domain rule, a regulation, a measured load. The shapes that fell were guesses wearing decision clothes: placeholders for facts nobody had. The team had not spent those months choosing. They had spent them guessing, and the guessing had felt like choice because the facts were still missing.
Design, on this evidence, is not a decision discipline. It is a knowledge discipline. The structure of a system is derived from what is true — of the business, and equally of the machine. Domain here means all of it: the bounded contexts, and also the infrastructure, the hardware, the runtime, the bill. There is no line where business knowledge ends and technical detail begins. There are only facts, nearer to or farther from the invoice. Where the fact is known, nothing is left to pick: any competent designer lands on the same shape, because the shape follows. Where the fact is missing, several shapes look defensible at once, and the picking feels free. That feeling of freedom is what a knowledge gap feels like from the inside. A decision is the shape a structure wears while its facts are missing.
One boundary needs naming. Facts can bind against each other — the regulation that orders the record erased, the statute that orders it kept — and where the domain writes no priority, the shape follows whichever obligation somebody ranked higher. The priority is the part that must be written down; until it is, the shape wears a decision. The boundary is narrower than it looks, and the rule holds for the majority of situations. The facts usually do not collide. And when several structures fit the same facts, they are rivals only if one of them adds meaning the knowledge does not carry — an ordering nobody mandated, a coupling nobody owes. Encodings that embody the knowledge without adding incompatible meaning are one design in different syntax; choosing between them changes nothing the system owes. Where a fact is missing, where two collide, or where an encoding adds what the domain never said, the posts say so: that is what their inapplicable halves are for.
This reading is hard to prove in theory, and no page here tries. The proof on offer is the pile. Across this section, the same question runs over patterns, algorithms, data structures, database constructs, kernel knobs, JVM flags, hardware ceilings, and encoding widths — several hundred cases, from the shape of a collaboration down to the width of a counter — and every case returns the same outcome. Where the causing fact can be named, the structure was already determined. Where it cannot, the structure stands on a guess. The most technical entries are the strongest cases: nobody defends a kernel knob as taste. Read a dozen posts and you will start predicting how each one ends. That predictability is the argument. The stories all end the same way: nobody chose. Something was true, and the system grew around it.

Each family of patterns sharpens that question in its own way. Where a family frames it differently, its framing opens above that family’s posts. The section holds eight areas, and each area holds one or more lists of posts:

Software Patterns — 170 posts in eleven family lists, from the GoF catalogue down to platform idioms and the architecture questions.
Substrate Facts — 47 posts on the bounds the machine imposes: capacity, time, failure, and topology.
Encoding Limits — 16 posts on the widths a type holds and the bytes an encoding adds.
DSA — 46 posts across algorithms and data structures.
Databases — 42 posts on the schema, the storage mechanism, the mapping, and the query.
Kernel & Runtimes — 94 posts on the kernel, the JVM, .NET, and GraalVM.
Frameworks — 42 posts. What Spring, Quarkus, Micronaut, and Vert.x decide for the code.
Languages — 51 posts. What the compiler checks, and what it erases.

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Every flag or practice below moves two numbers: the one it aims at, and one it did not. Each post names the flag, states the trade, and asks which measured fact of this workload answers it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Collector choice (G1, ZGC, Parallel)
text:
Case study: Collector choice (G1, ZGC, Parallel)
A checkout path passes its load test at 40 ms p99.9, ships on the collector nobody chose, and the first busy Tuesday spends the budget on stops.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: G1 is the default: it hides most collection work behind concurrent threads while keeping a young generation. Generational ZGC, the default ZGC mode since Java 23, pushes pauses towards sub-millisecond with a per-reference barrier cost and larger headroom. Parallel GC stops everything and spends the cores on throughput.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
A collector answers a pause budget the SLA states and a throughput number the peak hour carries. G1’s mixed collections, the ones that also collect old regions, land in the low hundreds of milliseconds by default, so a path with no written budget inherits that number by accident. The gap question: what is the measured pause budget you must meet, and what did throughput cost under the chosen collector at peak?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A payment path with a stated 50 ms p99.9 budget on a 6 GB live set: generational ZGC held stops under a millisecond, for a tenth less throughput against G1 in the same harness and a heap target raised from 8 GB to 12 GB. A nightly reconciliation nobody waits on stayed on Parallel, finished fastest, and counted its multi-second stops as nothing.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



ZGC everywhere, because low pauses read as strictly better. On the batch box it buys pauses nobody observes and pays the barrier tax plus headroom the limit must now cover. The mirror image is quieter: G1 at default on a user-facing path, mixed collections to 200 ms against a budget nobody wrote down, the incident blamed on the network.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured pause budget from the SLA — and what did throughput cost under the chosen collector, at peak?

If yes → it answers a number you hold. Watch the pause distribution, not the mean, and re-measure after any heap change.
If no → you have a default, not a decision. Write the budget down, then run one harness under two collectors.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure pause distribution and work completed per collector at peak.




#Java #JVM #GarbageCollection #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Heap sizing (-Xmx, MaxRAMPercentage)
A container gets 8 GB of memory, the heap gets 8 GB, and the process is killed with gigabytes of heap still free.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The heap flag caps the heap; the container limit caps everything the process touches. Between them sit metaspace (class metadata), the code cache, GC native structures, thread stacks, and direct buffers (off-heap IO memory) — none of them inside -Xmx. Sizing sets that gap deliberately, or loses it to a kill.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The live set at peak gives the heap floor; the distance from it to the limit gives headroom for bursts and the native reservation, which follows thread count, class loading, and direct buffer use. The gap question: what is the measured live set at peak, and how much of this container’s memory lives outside the heap?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A service with 900 MB live after a full collection at peak, the heap bursting to 1.6 GB between collections, 40 threads in a 4 GB container: heap at 2 GB via -Xmx, leaving 2 GB for metaspace, code cache, stacks, and direct buffers; MaxRAMPercentage, where -Xmx is unset, tuned against the limit rather than a bare-metal value. A 24-hour soak held at 82% of the limit, non-heap charted, no kill.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



-Xmx equal to the container limit, because the container is “the memory” and the heap is “the memory” — the arithmetic feels complete, and it passes in staging, where nothing else grows. In production the kill can arrive before any collection can act. MaxRAMPercentage at 100 is the same choice in percent form. The opposite failure is quieter: native exhaustion with gigabytes of heap free, as metaspace, direct buffers, or threads grew into an unreserved gap.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured live set at peak — and how much of this container’s memory lives outside the heap?

If yes → the heap is derived from a number. Check native growth at peak and watch the headroom.
If no → you have a budget, not a heap size. Take the live set, add a growth factor, then check that total against the limit less the native reservation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the live set after a forced full collection at peak, and read RSS against the limit.




#Java #JVM #Containers #MemoryManagement #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #CapacityPlanning

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Compact object headers
Every object on the heap carries a header, and on a 64-bit JVM those headers have been twice the size they need to be.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders, product-ready in Java 25, shrinks an object header from 16 bytes to 8. The saving lands on footprint, then on cache locality, then on collection frequency — young collections fall with bytes allocated. The direct cost on a modern 64-bit JVM is negligible; the real work is measuring the migration, since some instrumentation agents assume the old header layout, and vendor support still differs.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The win is proportional to the object count in the live set, not to the heap total. A heap dominated by large primitive arrays — sample buffers, matrix rows, byte payloads — carries few headers, so the saving rounds away. The gap question: what share of the live set is object-dominated, measured, and did the heap and the collection frequency actually move?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A service holding 44 million live order objects with references: 2.4 GB before the flag, 2.05 GB after, in the same staging harness. Roughly 15% off the live set, young collections from 22 to 18 per minute, throughput unchanged, no tooling objection in a soak run.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Enabling it because the release notes call it free. On the array-heavy service the flag works, the migration runs, the heap barely moves, and the team records a win it cannot reproduce under load. The cost is the soak run, the instrumentation audit, and a benchmark built on small objects quoted where the live set holds arrays.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of the live set is object-dominated, measured — and did the heap and the collection frequency actually move?

If yes → it answers an object-count fact you hold. Compare heap and collection rate before and after, at peak.
If no → the saving scales with header count, so at your object count it rounds away — expect no measurable move.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Take a heap histogram by class and instance count, then compare the live set with the flag on and off.




#Java #JVM #MemoryFootprint #Java25 #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: MaxGCPauseMillis as an SLO knob
text:
Case study: MaxGCPauseMillis as an SLO knob
A team sets the pause target to 5 ms to fix tail latency, and gets a busier CPU with the same tail.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: On G1 the value is a goal, not a guarantee: the collector shrinks the young generation, the nursery area where new objects are allocated, and collects fewer regions per mixed cycle to approach it. A smaller target means more collections and more CPU for shorter stops, so the same live young generation is copied more often.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The number belongs to the SLA, and it must be defended against the measured distribution — the tail, not the mean. A target of 5 ms against a 100 ms budget buys nothing and costs CPU; the 200 ms default against a 50 ms budget fails silently while looking configured. The gap question: which SLA derived this target, and does the measured pause distribution meet it at what CPU cost?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A request path with a stated 100 ms p99.9 budget carried a measured pause tail of 190 ms at default. Given a target of 50 ms for headroom: the pause p99.9 settled at 55 ms, young collections rose from 12 to 30 per minute, and process CPU moved from 55% to 68%. Request p99.9, re-measured, settled at 92 ms inside the budget; the CPU rise was recorded beside the win.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Setting 5 ms on G1 to obtain ZGC behavior. The reasoning holds as far as it goes: pauses are latency, latency is the complaint, so lower the target. It fails on the mechanism. G1 buys shorter stops with more of them and more marking between, so CPU rises while the tail stays where the young generation puts it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which SLA derived this target — and does the measured pause distribution meet it, at what CPU cost?

If yes → the target encodes a number you hold. Re-read the distribution after every heap change.
If no → you have a wish, not a target. Derive the number from the budget, or drop the flag.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Log pause durations at peak and plot the tail before and after.




#Java #JVM #GarbageCollection #SLO #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Latency

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: String deduplication on G1
text:
Case study: String deduplication on G1
A 200,000-record cache, and 38% of its character data is the same field names copied again and again.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: -XX:+UseStringDeduplication spends collection time hashing the backing arrays of surviving strings and pointing duplicates at one copy. It touches the character data behind each string, not the objects, and reaches only strings old enough to survive a collection. The trade is collector CPU against footprint, which moves only where duplicates exist.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The saving equals the duplicated character bytes, a property of what the workload stores: key-heavy caches, parsed documents repeating field names, payloads carrying the same codes. A heap of numeric arrays holds little character data, so the pass finds nothing. The gap question: what share of the live set is character data in duplicated strings, measured, and could a design fix hold the dedup instead?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A parsed-document pipeline holding 200,000 records with repeated field names: character data at 1.1 GB of a 2.8 GB live set, roughly 38% duplicated. Dedup brought the live set to 2.4 GB, and collector CPU for the pass stayed under 3%.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Enabling it as a general memory optimization: it costs nothing to add and reads as strictly good. On a numeric-array workload the pass runs over every collection and finds nothing, yet full collections grow longer — a small tax with no invoice. The subtler version uses it in place of a design fix: keys that should be interned (one shared instance), shared by construction, or replaced by enum constants stay duplicated, and the flag compresses the waste.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of the live set is character data in duplicated strings, measured — and could a design fix hold the dedup instead?

If yes → the pass answers a duplication fact you hold. Keep its CPU share under watch: it is paid on every collection.
