If no → the flag cannot pay for itself. Duplication is a code lever — fix it where it is created — then re-measure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Break the live set down by content type.




#Java #JVM #StringDeduplication #MemoryFootprint #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Performance

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Virtual threads (waiting made cheap, and only waiting)
text:
Case study: Virtual threads (waiting made cheap, and only waiting)
Two hundred platform threads, 1,800 requests a second, p99 stuck at 240 ms — every thread parked on a downstream wait.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A virtual thread is a task the JVM mounts on carrier threads, one per detected CPU by default. Blocked on integrated IO it unmounts and frees the carrier, so a parked request costs a heap object, not an OS thread. Final (no longer preview) since Java 21; since Java 24 synchronized no longer pins the carrier it is mounted on. The trade: waiting becomes cheap, computing does not, and the pool stops capping waiting tasks.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
You must know the waiting-to-computing ratio here, and where this workload’s threads stop being virtual — a native call holds its carrier until it returns. You must also know what replaces the pool as the gate. The gap question: is the measured waiting of this workload IO-blocking rather than CPU — and does anything still pin a carrier thread?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An API gateway measured 92 percent of request time in downstream waits, saturated at 210 concurrent. On virtual threads the same heap held 80 in-flight requests on 8 carriers — p99 90 ms, kilobytes of stack per parked request. A semaphore held 500 concurrent database calls, the number the connection pool would serve.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The seductive version: read “threads are cheap” and parallelize a CPU-bound job over 10,000 tasks. Nothing waits, nothing unmounts, every task holds a carrier to the end — throughput equals the carrier count. The pool then reappears as a virtual-thread “pool” capped at 500: it bounds little: creating a thread costs nothing, so the semaphore stays the control.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the measured waiting of this workload IO-blocking rather than CPU — and does anything still pin a carrier thread?

If yes → the win is the waiting, and the gate is a semaphore sized from the connection pool.
If no → you bought heap-resident stacks for a workload that computes, and you still need the pool.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the practice wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Sample thread states at peak, pinning event on.




#Java #JVM #VirtualThreads #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Thread-pool sizing (a number that states a claim)
text:
Case study: Thread-pool sizing (a number that states a claim)
Sixteen threads, a queue toward its 40,000 bound, a p99 of 9 s — and a pool that was the ceiling, not the workload.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A platform thread pool carries one number, and that number asserts a task profile: on N cores, CPU-bound tasks want N threads, IO-bound tasks want N × (1 + waiting ÷ computing), per Goetz’s pool-sizing rule. The trade: the pool turns the claim into a ceiling and a queue — correct, the queue drains; wrong either way, the queue is where the damage shows.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The formula needs two measurements of your workload, CPU time per task and waiting time per task, taken at peak hour, not the average day. It also needs the consequence of a full queue. The gap question: what is the measured CPU-to-waiting ratio of these tasks — and who sized the pool from that number?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An image service measured 12 ms of CPU and 60 ms waiting on object storage per task — a multiplier of six — on 8 cores: 48 threads, a queue bounded at 200, a rejection handler returning 429. At 400 tasks/s it held p99 at 180 ms. The 16-thread pool before it ran the queue bounded at 40,000 at p99 9 s: the ceiling was the pool, and the damage sat in a queue no dump shows.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Two shapes, both respectable. A cached pool under IO load: threads are created until the load stops, so 3,000 threads at a megabyte of stack each, and a process that hits its thread limit before the queue fills. Or 4 × cores “for IO”, applied to tasks that block on a lock: the wait ratio is real, the conclusion is not, and the queue never drains.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured CPU-to-waiting ratio of these tasks — and who sized the pool from that number?

If yes → the pool is a priced claim. Re-measure when the dependency changes, and read queue depth first.
If no → the number is a guess with a queue attached, which absorbs the error as latency.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the sizing wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure CPU time and waiting time per task at peak, then divide.




#Java #JVM #Concurrency #ThreadPools #CapacityPlanning #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Parallel streams (a shared pool you never sized)
text:
Case study: Parallel streams (a shared pool you never sized)
One parallel() on a stream that calls a REST endpoint, and an unrelated report in the same JVM takes 4 s instead of 200 ms.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: parallel() splits a stream across the JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool — seven workers by default on an eight-core box; a CPU quota shrinks it to max(quota − 1, 1) — and joins the results. The trade: one line buys data parallelism, spent from an account every parallel stream shares, a pool whose size and failure behaviour nobody in your code chose.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The pool’s size is a default, its tenants are someone else’s code, and its work-stealing assumes tasks that finish on their own. You must know whether the operations are side-effect-free CPU-bound work, whether the data amortizes the forking, and who else draws on the pool. The gap question: are the operations strictly CPU-bound and the data large enough to amortize forking — measured how, and who else shares this pool?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A nightly report aggregates 10 million rows through a 12 µs arithmetic transform: 120 s serial, 18 s measured across seven workers, against a 17 s ideal. Nothing else in that JVM uses parallel streams then, and the transform allocates too little to make the collector a bottleneck.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The line reads fine. Then a downstream call goes inside the stream — 80 ms against a service that is usually fast — and it parks one of seven workers. Six concurrent requests can exhaust the common pool, and the unrelated report sharing it measured 4 s instead of 200 ms, its stack trace saying it waited. Equally common and cheaper still: parallel() on a hundred elements, where splitting and joining outweigh the work.








TipThe faithfulness test



Are the operations strictly CPU-bound and the data large enough to amortize forking — measured how, and who else shares this pool?

If yes → the common pool is adequate, while nothing blocking enters the stream.
If no → you are spending a shared resource on work that does not repay it. Use a sequential stream, or a pool you own, sized and bounded deliberately.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found parallel streams wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Time the serial loop, then the parallel one, at your real element count.




#Java #JVM #ParallelStreams #ForkJoinPool #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: ScopedValue (context with a visible lifetime)
text:
Case study: ScopedValue (context with a visible lifetime)
A request ends, its platform thread returns to the pool, and the next task’s log names the previous customer.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A ScopedValue binds a value for the dynamic extent of a block — ScopedValue.where(TENANT, t).run(...) — readable inside, gone on return. Final in Java 25. The trade: you give up a mutable per-thread slot that survives until someone removes it, for cleanup that cannot be forgotten and inheritance from a task scope, which is still a preview in 25.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The question is not which API is newer; it is whether the context is immutable for the request’s life — mutate it downstream and the scoped version cannot express that. You must also know who owns the boundary: a value bound in the wrong scope is invisible where needed. The gap question: which context values are effectively immutable — and who guarantees the cleanup that ScopedValue makes structural?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A service carries tenant, actor, and trace id four levels down into a data layer that reads them without an argument in any signature. On virtual threads at 4,000 concurrent requests it binds once at the edge and reads everywhere inside, with no remove() on nine exit paths. It measured no faster: the win is correctness — handlers nobody wrote cleanup for are still correct.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



ThreadLocal keeps working, which is the trap. A forgotten remove() can land on a reused platform thread, and the next task inherits the tenant — a defect that shows in logs, not in tests, which start fresh threads. Then the invisible-parameter variant: a method needing the user id takes no argument for it, so the dependency hides from every signature.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which context values are effectively immutable — and who guarantees the cleanup that ScopedValue makes structural?

If yes → bind them at the boundary of the work; delete the remove() calls only once every exit path is migrated.
If no → the context is mutable by design, and no scoping API fixes that; find the mutation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found ThreadLocal wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. List every thread-local the path sets, and where each is cleared.




#Java #JVM #ScopedValue #ThreadLocal #Concurrency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Container CPU detection (one number, many consumers)
text:
Case study: Container CPU detection (one number, many consumers)
Two CPUs in the quota, forty-three GC threads in the JVM, and a p99 that worsens each time the heap is raised.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The JVM reads the container’s CPU allowance at startup and publishes it through Runtime.availableProcessors(). GC threads, concurrent marking threads, the common ForkJoinPool, and the JIT compiler threads all size from that number. The trade: right-sizing when detection is right, correlated over-allocation when it is wrong.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
You must know which number the runtime sees, which number the quota grants, and which of your settings came from it. Detection reads quotas and shares by rules that vary across cgroup versions: confirm it, do not trust it. The gap question: how many CPUs does the runtime actually see — and do the GC and ForkJoin thread counts agree with the quota rather than the host?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A worker under a two-CPU quota reported availableProcessors 2: two parallel GC threads, common-pool parallelism 1, heap 1 GB, p99 collection pause 40 ms. Where detection returned 64 — shares set, no quota — the same worker ran 43 parallel GC threads inside two CPUs and spent 30 percent of its quota collecting. Setting ActiveProcessorCount=2 took that to 4 percent — until the next rescale.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Latency rises, so heap is raised — the lever everyone trusts. Forty-three GC threads then share two CPUs, the collection has more heap to walk, and the pause grows, so the fix turns a latency problem into a memory problem for a quarter. The quieter variant: a ForkJoin pool of sixteen on the same two CPUs, matched to the host it was born on — sixteen pool threads for a quota that schedules two.








TipThe faithfulness test



How many CPUs does the runtime actually see — and do the GC and ForkJoin thread counts agree with the quota rather than the host?

If yes → the sizing chain is consistent, while quota and detection agree.
If no → every derived count is wrong at once. Set the count deliberately, then re-measure the collection share.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Print the flag values at startup, then compare them with the quota.




#Java #JVM #Containers #Kubernetes #GarbageCollection #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: AOT cache and ahead-of-time compilation
text:
Case study: AOT cache and ahead-of-time compilation
A function answers one webhook and exits: 1.4 s of JVM startup to do 40 ms of work.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: An AOT cache (Java 24, JEP 483) and ahead-of-time method profiling (Java 25, JEP 515), the Leyden work, move class loading, linking, and some code generation into the build: run the application once, record what it touched, ship what was learned. The trade is a training run and a cache artifact as build inputs, against code that never gets as hot as C2, the optimizing JIT compiler, would make it.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Two facts decide this, and teams rarely hold either: how long the process lives, as a distribution not a mean, and where the steady-state cost surfaces — p50 means every request pays it, p99 means only the saturated tail does. The gap question: what share of this process’s life is measured as startup-to-useful-work — and where does AOT’s steady-state cost land, p50 or only p99?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Serverless handlers, command-line tools, short batch jobs: anywhere startup was measured at most of the process’s life. One team shipped a trained cache for a webhook handler and cut startup to first request from 1.4 s to 240 ms, because the linking that request needed had happened at build time.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The same cache shipped to a service that runs for weeks. Startup improves by a figure nobody disputes, and the regression surfaces as a fatter right tail on the busiest nodes, months later, blamed on the release after. The training run is the seductive part: a real measurement, taken once, against an artifact changed twice since — profiling a program that no longer exists.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of this process’s life is measured as startup-to-useful-work — and where does AOT’s steady-state cost land: p50, or only p99?

If yes → the trade is cheap only if that share dominates. Rebuild the training run in CI on every release.
If no → throughput was traded for a startup gain nobody observes. Measure sustained throughput with and without the cache.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the lifetime distribution, then p50 and p99 at steady load.




#Java #JVM #AOT #Startup #Leyden #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: JMH and the discipline of measurement
text:
Case study: JMH and the discipline of measurement
A change measured four times faster in a timed main() method was four times faster at being optimized away.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: JMH, the JDK’s microbenchmark harness, runs warmup iterations, then measurement iterations, in forked JVMs — a fresh JVM per run — consumes every result through a black hole so the compiler cannot delete the work, and reports a confidence interval instead of a number. The trade is time and care — minutes per benchmark, code written for the harness rather than the product — against an answer that holds outside the harness.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Three facts about the measurement, not the code: whether steady state was reached before counting began, whether the timed work still existed after optimization, and whether variance between runs is smaller than the effect claimed. Without warmup you measure the interpreter’s first steps; with one fork you measure that fork’s luck. The gap question: was this “faster” claim measured with warmup, several forks, and dead-code control — or did it feel faster?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Any decision that changes a hot path, or that will be argued in a design review. One team kept a serialization library only after measuring both: warmup discarded, five forks, a GC profiler attached, a 12% throughput gain whose confidence interval did not cross zero.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The plain main() with nanoTime around it, seductive because it looks honest: a real JVM, real input, real elapsed time. Three things vanish. Dead code — the result is never read, so the computation goes. Warmup — early iterations are interpreted, so two programs’ opening steps are compared. Fork isolation — one run in one JVM becomes the number in the ticket, carried into a migration nobody benchmarked.








TipThe faithfulness test



Was this “faster” claim measured with warmup, several forks, and dead-code control — or did it feel faster?

If yes → the number is an estimate with a range. Compare it to the effect size.
If no → it is not a measurement, it is an anecdote with units. Re-run it under a harness before it hardens into code.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete workload knowledge. Rewrite the benchmark in JMH with warmup, three forks, and a profiler.




#Java #JVM #JMH #Benchmarking #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Java Flight Recorder, left on
text:
Case study: Java Flight Recorder, left on
At 02:14 last night p99 tripled for forty seconds. The answer comes from a recording already running, not a reproduction that will never happen.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: JFR records runtime events — allocation, GC pauses, lock contention, code cache occupancy — into a bounded ring buffer, and it can stay enabled in production. The trade is a measured cost near one percent, plus storage discipline, against no evidence at the moment the anomaly arrives.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Whether the question you will ask at 3 a.m. is answerable from events the runtime already emits, and what always-on costs on this workload. One percent is a measurement, not a law: allocation-heavy services pay more. The gap question: can tonight’s anomaly be answered from recordings — and what does always-on cost, measured on this workload?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A payments service kept a continuous recording at the default profile and measured 1.1% of CPU with no shift in p99. Three weeks in, a nightly batch degraded at 02:14; the recording answered it from one file: allocation pressure in a single code path, a wrapper object built per row, inside the exact forty seconds everyone had argued about.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Two failures that look like opposites. “Enabled for emergencies only” sounds prudent, but the emergency is when no data exists, so the incident is argued from theory and the postmortem concludes “likely GC” without a single allocation event. The other wears a lab coat: every event at maximum detail on the busiest nodes, until the observer effect is real and the team blames the release for the slowdown the configuration caused. Both are one gap: nobody measured observability’s cost on the workload carrying it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can tonight’s anomaly be answered from recordings — and what does always-on cost, measured on this workload?

If yes → the evidence exists before the question does. Check retention and that files survive the node.
If no → the incident will be reconstructed from memory. Enable a bounded recording now.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete workload knowledge. Measure p99 and CPU with the recording on and off at peak.




#Java #JVM #JFR #Observability #Production #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: The code cache and its eviction
text:
Case study: The code cache and its eviction
Nine days after a deployment one hot method stopped being compiled. Latency rose by an order of magnitude: no exception, no log line.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The JVM reserves a bounded region for code the JIT — the just-in-time compiler — produces, sized by ReservedCodeCacheSize. When it fills, the runtime sweeps and frees compiled methods; if nothing can be freed, compilation stops and the affected methods run interpreted — an order of magnitude slower, no exception. The trade is memory reserved for compiled code against a silent ceiling.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Two facts: how fast this workload’s compiled-code footprint grows, and whether growth is bounded or continuous. A steady application plateaus; one that generates classes at runtime — proxies, hidden classes for lambdas, script engines — climbs until it hits the ceiling. The gap question: what is the measured fill trend of the code cache — and when it fills, does an alert fire or does silence fall?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A long-running application where the footprint was charted before the flag was touched: occupancy over a week, a slow rise at peak hours toward the default, no plateau. The size was raised deliberately, fill curve in hand, kept as a dashboard so the next rise is a signal, not a surprise.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The value copied from a tuning guide, doubled to be safe. It removes the symptom and keeps the cause: if occupancy climbed because a library generates a class per request, a bigger ceiling buys weeks and arrives at the same cliff, further from the change that caused it. The quieter failure: on a live redeploy, methods still needing compilation stay interpreted, latency rises by an order of magnitude, and the only symptom is a slow afternoon until someone reads occupancy. Nothing alerts — nobody decided a full cache was worth watching.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured fill trend of the code cache — and when it fills, does an alert fire or does silence fall?

If yes → you know the slope and the ceiling. Watch the slope; a change in it is the finding.
If no → a latency cliff with no instrument. Chart occupancy, find what generates classes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong flag — incomplete workload knowledge. Sample occupancy across a week, including a redeploy.




#Java #JVM #JIT #CodeCache #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Records and sealed hierarchies
text:
Case study: Records and sealed hierarchies
A new order state shipped on Friday. Nothing failed the build, and on Monday three consumers handled it — the other eleven silently ignored it.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A record states the type is a transparent holder of its components: final fields, accessors, equals and hashCode from them. A sealed hierarchy states its implementations are a closed set, and a pattern switch over it — no default branch, Java 21 — turns a missing case into a compile error. The trade is two claims — value and closure — checked at compile time, against the flexibility classes grant.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Whether the domain makes those claims. A record is wrong when identity or mutation is part of the meaning; a sealed type when someone outside the Java module legitimately adds a case. Each is a statement about the domain, enforced in every exhaustive switch over it. The gap question: is this set genuinely closed by the domain — and does the next variant break compilation everywhere, or break production somewhere?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A payment state machine as a sealed interface with one record per state. Adding a state was a compile error in every consumer: fourteen files, named in one build. The switch turned a production incident into a failing case before anything shipped.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Sealing a set the domain left open: a plugin interface, an extension point, a hierarchy the test suite stubs. It compiles beautifully, then a case arrives the author never imagined, and the closed-set claim is exposed as a convenience — with an escape hatch worse than the interface it replaced. Records fail from the inside: a record holding a List is only as immutable as the list, so a caller mutates the component and the hashCode the map keyed on shifts.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this set genuinely closed by the domain — and does the next variant break compilation everywhere, or break production somewhere?

If yes → seal it and let the exhaustive switch carry it. The compiler finds the missing case.
If no → the set is open. Keep the interface open and test the default path.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete domain knowledge. List who may add a case, then whether the value is ever mutated.




#Java #JVM #Records #SealedTypes #PatternMatching #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Foreign Function & Memory, final since Java 22
text:
Case study: Foreign Function & Memory, final since Java 22
A native decoder was replaced and p99 halved — not because the new API is faster, but because the rewrite batched crossings that each pinned a carrier before.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The Foreign Function & Memory API calls native code — a downcall — through a bound method handle, a callable to a native entry point, and manages native memory as segments in an Arena, a region whose memory is freed all at once, not per object. The trade is managed safety — a segment cannot outlive its arena, no hand-written glue to get wrong — against a per-crossing cost intrinsic to the boundary, whatever the API.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The deciding fact is a frequency: how often control leaves the JVM per unit of work. A thousand crossings of a 200 ns function are dominated by the boundary; one crossing per 10 MB buffer is not. Safety is priced per crossing too. The gap question: how often does control cross this boundary, measured — and does each crossing pay for the safety it buys?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An image pipeline crossing once per tile: a segment over an arena-confined buffer, one downcall per 4,000-element block, results read back through the same segment. Crossing frequency was counted before the rewrite, about 250 per second, so the boundary budget was under a millisecond per second of work.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



JNI, the older calling convention, kept because it was always there, around a library that blocks inside a native call. That call pins the carrier it runs on for the duration, invisible until the service moves to virtual threads and the scheduler runs out of carriers. The seductive opposite: FFM adopted, then called once per element in a tight loop, where crossing cost dominates what the native code saves. The fix is batching, which nobody had measured.








TipThe faithfulness test



How often does control cross this boundary, measured — and does each crossing pay for the safety it buys?

If yes → the boundary is the cost centre: batch it, amortize over a buffer, or move the loop into native, then count crossings again.
If no → crossings are rare; leave the loop where it is, and keep the managed boundary for the safety it buys.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete workload knowledge. Count crossings per request and per second at peak.




#Java #JVM #FFM #JNI #VirtualThreads #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Compressed oops and the 32 GB boundary
text:
Case study: Compressed oops and the 32 GB boundary
A host goes from 31 GB of heap to 40, gains nine gigabytes, and holds fewer objects per gigabyte. Nothing crashed. The 32 GB boundary did it.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Below a maximum heap of roughly 32 GB, HotSpot stores a reference in 4 bytes instead of 8, scaling by object alignment so the short form still spans the heap — compressed oops, on by default since Java 6u23. At or above the boundary the scaling fails, references widen, and every object holding one grows. The trade is pointer width against reach: more addressable memory, less of it usable.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
What matters is objects reachable per gigabyte, a ratio set by how many references each live object carries. Small nodes with many fields pay nearly double to cross; large byte arrays barely notice, since their bytes are not references. The gap question: which side of the boundary is this heap on — and did capacity per GB move the day it crossed?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A cache team counted entries against heap used: 38 million fit at 28 GB, so the team held the heap there and ran three smaller JVMs instead of one large one.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Memory pressure — add heap.” The 31 GB box becomes 40 GB, the flag stays default, and the work is declared done because the alert stopped. Underneath, references widened, pointer-heavy objects inflated, promotion rose, and the collector does more work per gigabyte while holding a smaller live set. Pressure can return; someone proposes more heap. The seductive part is that the change did help — a heap near its ceiling always does — so the story writes itself backwards.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which side of the boundary is this heap on — and did capacity per GB move the day it crossed?

If yes → you can size deliberately: stay under it and scale out, or accept the widening for the reach.
If no → the resize was arithmetic on a number you never measured. Compare entries per gigabyte before and after.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure objects reachable per GB, then read the effective reference width on a live process.




#Java #JVM #HeapSizing #GarbageCollection #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: G1 humongous objects
The service throws “OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space” while its own GC log shows four gigabytes free. No contiguous run of free regions was left to allocate into.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: G1 splits the heap into fixed power-of-two regions, derived from the heap, between 1 MB and 32 MB. An allocation at or above half the region size is humongous: it lands in contiguous regions and skips the young generation’s copying path. The trade is speed through the young path against contiguity.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The allocation-size distribution is the fact; the flag is not. You must know your largest allocations, how they die, and what region size your heap implies — the same 2 MB buffer is ordinary on a 32 MB region and humongous on a 2 MB one. The gap question: what is the measured allocation-size distribution against the region size — and who owns the giant arrays?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A document service profiled its allocations: 99.9 percent under 4 KB, plus a 3 MB paging buffer. Raising the region size to 8 MB would stop it being humongous; splitting the buffer into 64 KB pages removed it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A request handler allocates a 2 MB byte array per call on a 4 GB heap — 2 MB regions, so every array is humongous. Hundreds are in flight at once, and the dead ones wait for the next collection before eager reclaim frees their regions. The old generation fills with live giants, the next large allocation finds no contiguous run, and the failure reads as heap exhaustion. The team adds heap, the symptom eases, and they credit the memory — but region size derives from the heap, so 8 GB only buys 4 MB regions, the 2 MB arrays stay humongous, and the easing is headroom, not a fix.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured allocation-size distribution against the region size — and who owns the giant arrays?

If yes → you can choose knowingly: larger regions, fewer giants, or a paged design that removes them.
If no → every large allocation is a lottery ticket on fragmentation. Profile the sizes, then decide who changes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found G1 wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Histogram allocation sizes, then compute the region size your heap implies.




#Java #JVM #G1 #GarbageCollection #Allocation #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Direct buffers and -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
A service with 8 GB of heap dies with OutOfMemoryError, and the dump left behind is almost empty. The memory it ran out of was never on the heap.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect returns a buffer whose bytes live outside the heap, in memory the collector does not trace. It exists for one reason: to hand an address to the operating system — socket, file, TLS — without a copy. -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize caps the total, defaulting to roughly the maximum heap. The trade is a copy saved against memory the collector learns about only through a Cleaner — a free that runs when a collection finds it dead.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The deciding facts are how many direct-memory bytes per second must reach the operating system, and how long each buffer lives. A buffer allocated per message pays malloc and a Cleaner registration per message; a pooled buffer pays neither while traffic lasts. And because the default cap derives from -Xmx, raising the heap raises the direct-buffer cap too, though other off-heap memory is untouched. The gap question: how many direct-memory bytes per second does this workload allocate, measured — and what frees them?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A gateway writes every response to a socket. Buffers are pooled and sized once at startup, direct memory is capped explicitly, and allocation profiling shows the count flat after warm-up. Bytes per second never fell; allocations per second went to zero.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



“Off-heap is faster, so move the cache off-heap.” A 12 GB cache in direct buffers, allocated on demand, no cap set — and the direct-memory bytes are only freed when a heap collection happens to run, so the memory moved out of the heap is still reclaimed by the heap collector. When the process dies, the dump is nearly empty and the alert names a heap that is not the problem.








TipThe faithfulness test



How many off-heap bytes per second does this workload allocate, measured — and what frees them?

If yes → pool the buffers, cap direct memory explicitly, and keep the copy you saved.
If no → direct memory buys the copy the heap path cannot skip, and this workload saves none. Measure the direct-memory allocation rate, not heap occupancy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete workload knowledge. Read the direct-buffer pool’s used bytes against the container limit at peak.




#Java #JVM #DirectMemory #OffHeap #ByteBuffer #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: System.gc() and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC
Someone adds System.gc() to a request path to silence an alert. The pause lands on whichever user is unlucky — and the alert returns.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: System.gc() is a suggestion, not an instruction. G1, the default collector, answers it with a stop-the-world full collection by default; -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent makes G1 and ZGC answer concurrently, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC makes the call a no-op. The trade is timing. The collector schedules from occupancy and a pause target; an explicit call overrides that with a caller’s guess about when memory should be returned.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The fact to establish is what the call releases. Some resources free themselves only when a collection runs: direct buffers, freed by a Cleaner once a collection sees them dead; remote references in RMI (the JDK’s remote-call service), released only by its distributed garbage collector; and unmapped-file regions, freed by the next collection. So disabling explicit collection removes a release path together with the pause. The gap question: name what this call releases, measured — and what breaks if it never happens?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A nightly import calls it once, between phases, where no request is in flight. Measured before adoption: the pause is 1.2 seconds, each phase runs 40 seconds, and the intent is to keep the previous phase’s garbage out of the next phase’s budget. One call, at a boundary someone chose.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A library calls System.gc() after closing a mapped file, and the call runs inside a service that maps files too. The team then disables explicit collection to remove a 400 ms pause — and silences the call the library depended on, so a resource that was released by force now waits for whatever collection happens next, or for none if the heap never fills. The fix belongs at the one bad call site; the flag cuts a mechanism the library needs.








TipThe faithfulness test



What does this call release, measured — and what breaks if it never happens?

If yes → keep it, at a chosen boundary, and log when it fires.
If no → remove the call site, not the mechanism, and let the collector schedule.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong practice — incomplete resource knowledge. Track allocation and free rates for direct buffers and file mappings before touching the flag.




#Java #JVM #GarbageCollection #SystemGC #ResourceManagement #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and HeapDumpPath
A production OOM at 03:00 earns a container restart. By 09:00 the evidence is one log line and a theory.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: When a memory pool is exhausted the JVM can write the live set to an HPROF file before it dies: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError enables the write, -XX:HeapDumpPath names the file or directory; the JVM writes the dump, then the uncaught OutOfMemoryError ends the process. The trade is a file the size of the live set, written at the worst possible moment, against the only snapshot of the state that failed.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The flag is a few characters; the obligation is a reader, a volume, and a retention rule. A 30 GB heap writes up to 30 GB in tens of seconds to minutes, into whatever filesystem the path names — often the ephemeral layer of a container, which then fills. The file also holds every string that was in memory, credentials included. The gap question: who opens this dump, and is there room to write it where it lands?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A 4 GB heap, the path on a mounted volume with a retention rule, and a triage step that opens the newest dump in an analyser. Three OOMs produced three dumps, and one of them named the leak. The flag cost nothing because the reader and the disk existed first.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Flag on, path left at the default inside a pod with a 10 GB ephemeral disk. The dump fills it, the kubelet evicts the pod, and the dump is deleted with the pod — while the team concludes the flag does not work. The seductive part: it did work. It wrote the file, and the file was thrown away by the platform.








TipThe faithfulness test



Who opens this dump, and is there room to write it where it lands?

If yes → keep it on, keep the path on durable storage, and set a retention rule.
If no → the dump is a file nobody reads. Fix the path and the reader first, then enable.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong flag — incomplete operational knowledge. Check free space at the mount — your platform team’s volume room — and whether the kill is even a heap OOM.




#Java #JVM #HeapDump #OutOfMemoryError #Observability #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
A service starts in 40 seconds, then spends its first ten minutes stepping down in latency as the heap fills page by page.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: The JVM reserves the heap as virtual address space and commits pages only as objects touch them, so a 40 GB heap is cheap until it is used. -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, with -Xms at -Xmx, walks the whole heap at startup and writes to every page, forcing the kernel to map frames now. The trade is paid before the first request: a longer startup and a resident set, the physical pages held, equal to the heap, against page faults — the kernel’s per-page charge on first touch — and kernel zeroing spread across live traffic.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The fact that decides it is how long the ramp lasts. A service whose heap reaches its full committed size in seconds amortizes a one-time cost; one whose heap grows for an hour pays faults while serving. Pre-touch also makes commitment visible: a heap larger than the container limit fails at startup instead of being killed at peak. The gap question: how long until this heap reaches steady state, measured — and does the container limit allow the whole heap to be committed up front?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A batch aggregator with a 40 GB heap and a load phase that fills it at once. Pre-touch adds 40 seconds before the job, resident memory equals -Xmx from the first second, and the load phase runs without a page fault. The cost is outside the measured phase and the benefit is inside it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



-Xms64g -Xmx64g inside a 32 GB container. Pre-touch commits all of it at startup, the kernel sees the limit, and the process is killed before it logs anything. The lazy version would have run to the peak, where the death is diagnosable. Pre-touch moved the death to startup — the diagnosis was the loss, a crash nobody can explain.








TipThe faithfulness test



How long until this heap reaches its full committed size, measured — and does the container limit allow the whole heap to be committed up front?

If yes → enable it, and keep the ramp inside a phase you already budget for.
If no → the walk is a tax on a heap that never grows. Leave the pages lazy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong flag — incomplete workload knowledge. Plot committed heap pages against time after startup — RSS is the proxy — and compare it with the container limit.




#Java #JVM #Startup #MemoryManagement #AlwaysPreTouch #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Escape analysis and scalar replacement
text:
Case study: Escape analysis and scalar replacement
A pricing path allocates 40 MB a second and young collections run twice a minute — almost none of those objects leave the method.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: HotSpot asks whether an object can be reached outside the method or thread that allocated it. Where it proves the object local, the compiler dissolves it into registers and stack slots — scalar replacement — and the allocation disappears. The trade: objects proven local become free; everything else keeps a real allocation plus the analysis spent on it.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The analysis gives up on what real code makes: objects stored in a field, returned, or captured by a lambda that outlives the call. So the team must know which of its references escape by construction. The gap question: which allocations actually escape — checked how — and is there a pool maintaining objects the JIT would have erased?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A pricing step builds a small value object per line item, 30 million per batch, with a collection every 30 seconds. Every reference stays inside the method. Once the object is small and no reference to it leaves the method, allocation on that path falls by most of its volume and collections grow to 90 seconds apart.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The object pool. It sounds responsible: bounded, reused, sparing the collector. But a pooled object lives in a field, so the analysis proves it escapes and every instance is traced for the life of the process. The team buys reset bugs and concurrency defects to avoid allocations that were free. Under C2, a hot-path call site with many receiver types turns megamorphic, inlining stops, and the scalar-replaced objects return as garbage.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which allocations actually escape — checked how — and is there a pool maintaining objects the JIT would have erased?

If yes → the shape is right. Keep objects small, final, and out of fields, and re-profile when a call site changes.
If no → measure before moving code: allocation profiling per call site, and what the pool retains.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Record the allocation rate, the collection interval, and the survival share.




#Java #JVM #EscapeAnalysis #Allocation #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Tiered compilation, C1 and C2
text:
Case study: Tiered compilation, C1 and C2
A build step lives four point two seconds. One point six of them go to compiling methods the process will never call twice.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Tiered compilation, the default since Java 8, runs two compilers: C1 compiles fast with light optimization, C2 compiles slowly and optimizes hard, and a method climbs as it proves hot. -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 stops the climb at C1. The trade: compile time during startup against peak throughput for the rest of the process’s life, with that lifetime as the exchange rate.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
Whether the exchange is good is a fact about the process, not the JVM: how long it runs, how much is warmup, and whether steady state arrives before exit. A service alive for a week amortizes every C2 compile to nothing; a command-line tool finishing in seconds never collects the payoff. The gap question: what is the measured lifetime of this process — and does steady state ever arrive before it exits?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A code-generation step in CI, measured at 4.2 seconds wall clock, 38% of it in compilation. C1 only: 2.9 seconds, identical output, no throughput requirement beyond finishing. It runs 400 times an hour, so the saving compounds.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The flag copied from a build-tool tuning guide onto a long-running service. It arrives with plausible provenance. It improves a startup dashboard nobody reads twice, and its cost shows nowhere: peak throughput drops a few percent, latency at saturation rises. Because nothing was measured beforehand, nothing looks wrong. A competent engineer makes this move, because the flag was correct where they found it. The transport was the error, not the reasoning.








TipThe faithfulness test



What is the measured lifetime of this process — and does steady state ever arrive before it exits?

If yes → keep the default tiers; C2 pays back before exit.
If no → stopping at C1 is the priced choice: the process never collects C2. Startup work is a different lever, with its own measurement.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure the lifetime distribution and the share spent before hot methods reach C2.




#Java #JVM #TieredCompilation #JIT #StartupTime #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Class Data Sharing, application classes from Java 10
text:
Case study: Class Data Sharing, application classes from Java 10
On a Java 17 service, 1.9 seconds of a 3.4-second startup are class loading: 4,800 classes parsed and verified before the first request.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Class Data Sharing writes pre-parsed class metadata into an archive the JVM maps read-only — the OS keeps one copy in the page cache, so co-located processes share it. Application Class Data Sharing (Java 10) covers application classes; the dynamic archive (Java 13) records what a training run loaded, so no class list needs maintaining. The trade: startup work leaves every process, against a snapshot.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The payoff is a share, not a boolean: how much of this startup is class loading, measured, and how many JVMs on one host load the same classes. A short-lived process gains little; a host running eight gains both. The archive also needs an owner in the build. The gap question: what share of startup is class loading, measured — and who regenerates the archive when the application changes?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A 17-only fleet starting 300 times a day, class loading at 56% of startup by profile. The dynamic archive ships with the artifact: startup falls from 3.4 to 2.2 seconds. Regeneration is a build step per JDK and per artifact, so the archive matches what ships — a bump or dependency change rebuilds it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



Two ways to get this wrong, both reasonable. The archive dumped once and never again: a framework upgrade changes the class set, the archive serves what it still matches, the rest loads the old way, and the team concludes sharing does not work here. Or the practice dismissed as obsolete because the newest JDK ships ahead-of-time cache work — on a fleet that cannot leave 11.








TipThe faithfulness test



What share of startup is class loading, measured — and who regenerates the archive when the application changes?

If yes → ship the archive from the build, and treat regeneration as a build step.
If no → your startup is spent elsewhere. Profile it before adding a file to the deployment.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the mechanism wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Measure startup phases, and count the JVMs per host.




#Java #JVM #ClassDataSharing #AppCDS #StartupTime #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Biased locking, off by default since 15, removed in 18
text:
Case study: Biased locking, off by default since 15, removed in 18
A cache guarded by a synchronized block, hit by one thread 40,000 times a second, costs almost nothing — on a JDK where the mechanism that made it true is gone.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: Biased locking assumed most monitors are taken by one thread for their whole life, so the first acquisition recorded that owner in the object header and later ones by the same thread skipped the atomic compare-and-swap. A second thread revoked the bias — a stop-the-world operation to walk and repair stacks. The trade: uncontended acquisition approaches free, against revocation stalls. Java 15 disabled it by default; later releases removed the implementation.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
It paid off under conditions to verify, not assume: one owner, no second thread arriving, thousands of acquisitions a second, and a JDK where the code exists. Three are workload facts, one a fleet fact. The gap question: which JDK does this fleet actually run — and would anyone notice the flag being ignored?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The honest case is from the era it served: a shared map, uncontended — one owner and no revocation events in a peak hour of JFR lock records, not a thread dump. On Java 8 that is the shape it was built for.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The tuning guide, still in the repository, still shipping -XX:+UseBiasedLocking to fleets on 17 and 21. On 17 the flag still works; on 21 the launcher warns that support was removed in 18 — a line nobody reads — and the script still reads as tuned. The worse outcome is the diagnosis. Latency gets blamed on revocation, on a JDK with no bias left to revoke. That cause is plausible enough to close the investigation before anyone reads the safepoint log. The guide never had a version column.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which JDK does this fleet actually run — and would anyone notice the flag being ignored?

If yes → check the flag does what the guide claims on that exact version, and delete it elsewhere.
If no → the mechanism may be gone on this fleet’s JDK; the latency has another cause. Read the safepoint log — time-to-safepoint, the wait before a pause — for what stalls threads.
If you can’t answer → unclear. Not a wrong flag — incomplete fleet knowledge. Inventory JDKs per environment, then test one change.




#Java #JVM #BiasedLocking #Locking #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Concurrent Mark Sweep, removed in Java 14
text:
Case study: Concurrent Mark Sweep, removed in Java 14
A service pinned to Java 8 for its pauses, where every full collection arrives a little later and lasts a little longer.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: CMS marked and swept while the application ran, so pauses were short — and it never compacted. Free space fragmented, a large allocation failed, and the fallback was a single-threaded full collection with compaction: the debt paid at once, or a concurrent mode failure — the concurrent pass falling behind and giving up — that stopped everything. The trade: short pauses now, against fragmentation that picks when the long pause comes. Deprecated in Java 9, removed in Java 14.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
What the team must know is a trend, not an average: pause length between compactions, the promotion rate — the young-to-old flow — driving fragmentation, and the JDK the fleet runs in three years. A collector chosen for its pauses is chosen for a shape of heap use; a workload churning large objects breaks it. The gap question: is this fleet on a JDK where CMS still exists — and what is the measured trend of pause length between its compactions?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



The Java 8 latency service CMS genuinely served: a 400 ms pause target met at p99, tenuring — the age at which an object is promoted — tuned by measurement, fragmentation bounded by a derived heap size, an upgrade scheduled, not assumed.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The fleet stays on the old JDK because the collector works fine. Each full collection tends to be a few percent longer than the last, and none crosses the alarm — the tail grows while the average holds. The runbook still recommends flags of a collector removed in Java 14; on a new JDK, startup fails. The reasoning was sound when written; only the calendar moved.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this fleet on a JDK where CMS still exists — and what is the measured trend of pause length between its compactions?

If yes → track pause trend and fragmentation, with a dated plan to leave the collector.
If no → the flags are inert or fatal. Measure the pause distribution under the collector you run; re-derive heap size.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the collector wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Record the JDK per environment and the last ten full-collection pauses.




#Java #JVM #GarbageCollection #CMS #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Safepoints and time-to-safepoint
A service stalls 600 ms every few seconds; the GC log shows 8 ms pauses, so nobody looks at the collector again.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: To collect, the JVM stops every thread at a safepoint, a point where its state is known. That stop has two parts: the wait for the last thread to arrive, time-to-safepoint, and the operation itself, the pause the log prints. The log bills the second part.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The stop you can read is half the stop; the other half is decided by a loop or a native call, not by the heap. Whether your fleet holds the world at a poll it reaches slowly is a fact about your code paths. The gap question: when the world pauses, does the pause appear in the GC log — and if not, who measured time-to-safepoint?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A p99.9 of 700 ms against a 200 ms budget, collector pauses at 8-12 ms. Safepoint logging put 600 ms in time-to-safepoint: one counted loop, a loop whose end the compiler knows, over a large array in a hot path. Before Java 10 such a loop could run past its poll and finish before the world stopped; loop strip mining, since Java 10, places a poll inside it, so older JVMs carry more of the stall in the loop. After the loop was restructured to yield inside it, the stall went; the pauses never moved.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The heap is resized, the collector swapped, the flags shuffled. A fair move: you have a latency complaint and a pause log, so you tune what it measures. It misses because the log is honest and incomplete. On a pre-10 JVM the loop keeps every thread hostage every few seconds, no collector flag touches it, and each round tells a convincing story about the young generation, which was never the problem.








TipThe faithfulness test



When the world pauses, does the pause appear in the GC log — and if not, who measured time-to-safepoint?

If yes → you see the stops you have. Alarm on time-to-safepoint beside every pause.
If no → the missing stop is in an uninstrumented thread. Read time-to-safepoint at peak, not pause duration.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the practice wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Record time-to-safepoint for a peak hour, then find the repeating frame.




#Java #JVM #Safepoints #GarbageCollection #Latency #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Finalization and its successors
text:
Case study: Finalization and its successors
A nightly job dies at 1,024 open files, and every test passes: the close sits in finalize(), which runs when the JVM pleases.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: finalize() runs at most once, after the object becomes unreachable, and only if a collection happens. The object is enqueued for finalization first, so freeing it takes a second collection: every finalizable object that dies costs two passes, and it can resurrect itself by publishing this. Deprecated for removal in Java 18; the successors are try-with-resources on AutoCloseable and java.lang.ref.Cleaner, a deferred free the collector runs (Java 9+).


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
An eventual close is a claim about the collector’s schedule, which answers to allocation. You must know which resources are finite, their exhaustion symptom, and which path acquires each; finalization hides all three. The gap question: which resources still rely on finalization today — and would explicit closing be measurable work or a refactor hiding behind “it works”?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Descriptors closed by try-with-resources: a batch job walking 200,000 files held a steady 40 descriptors, and a leak test failed loudly instead of drifting.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The handle released in finalize(), and it does run — you see the close in the log, which is why review passed it. It runs whenever the collector schedules it: let the service idle and allocations stop, collections stop, finalizers stop, and the handle stays open, and the table fills. Then the cache whose values override finalize: every evicted entry still costs two collections, and nothing tells you which are queued.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which resources still rely on finalization today — and would explicit closing be measurable work or a refactor hiding behind “it works”?

If yes → you hold the inventory. Move each to try-with-resources; keep a Cleaner as the net.
If no → the close is a hope about the collector. Rewrite the acquisition sites; from Java 18, plan for removal.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the practice wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Count open descriptors at idle, not under load.




#Java #JVM #ResourceManagement #GarbageCollection #Cleaner #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: JVM Tuning as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: The perf-data file and -XX:-UsePerfData
text:
Case study: The perf-data file and -XX:-UsePerfData
A flag is added to stop a JVM writing into /tmp. Two months later the dashboard is a flat line, and no alarm fired.
Changing a JVM flag or adopting a practice? Ask “which measured fact of this workload does it answer, and what does it trade away?” Every flag moves two numbers — the one you aim at, and one you did not. If you can’t name both, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the flag is a superstition. If you can, it’s knowledge embodied — the runtime catching up to what the workload demands.

Mechanism: A running JVM memory-maps a small perf-data file under /tmp, named for the user and pid, holding counters the runtime keeps: heap, threads, classes, GC totals. jstat, the JDK command for runtime stats, reads it, and a generation of monitoring agents reads it through the same door. -XX:-UsePerfData stops the JVM creating it; some vendors and images ship that flag by default.


The JVM knowledge gap it signals
The file is a published contract, not a by-product. Disabling it is safe only when you can name every consumer and each has another source. That means knowing whether /tmp is per-container, wiped by a reaper, or mounted noexec, and whether your agent reads the file or attaches to the process. The gap question: which tools read this JVM’s perf counters — the platform team’s list, by name — and do they have a fallback when the file is gone?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A hardened image whose /tmp is noexec and cleared hourly: the perf-data file is deleted under the process, so it should not exist. It was disabled deliberately, once the monitoring stack was confirmed to read JFR recordings and MXBeans, the runtime’s management beans, over the attach API, and the exported series showed no gap across the rollout.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The flag added “to clean up /tmp” across a fleet. /tmp warnings are genuine and the flag name reads like tidiness. What ships is silence. jstat reports no data, the agent exports nothing rather than failing — an empty series is not an error — and the dashboard can render a flat line no alarm watches. Months later nobody can date the change, because nothing broke.








TipThe faithfulness test



Which tools read this JVM’s perf counters — confirmed by name — and do they have a fallback when the file is gone?

If yes → disable it and keep the visibility. Alarm on the replacement series.
If no → you are trading an instrument for disk hygiene. Find the consumers first.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the flag wrong — you’ve found incomplete workload knowledge. Check the effective flag on a live process, then trace who reads that file.




#Java #JVM #Observability #Monitoring #jstat #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

text:
