title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
The OOP principles read as completeness checks: each names a rule about what a module should hold and what a caller should know — and each holds only where a domain fact stands behind it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Encapsulation

Parnas: Modules should hide a design decision behind an interface so that the decision can change without affecting clients. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
An encapsulation boundary splits a type into what callers may depend on and what they never see. The real claim is not “something is hidden here” but “this interface is exactly what callers need.” That claim has content only if the team knows the callers’ needs — which parts the domain assigns to this thing, and which are one way of fulfilling them. The gap shows when the split is drawn by habit: the interface carries choices no caller asked about, or withholds something needed. Where the domain fixes a concrete detail, that detail belongs in the interface; an abstraction above it asserts a concept nobody decided.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The team can point at each exposed operation and name the need it serves: “converting a payment uses the current rate” is a domain-assigned responsibility, and how the rate is stored is one way of fulfilling it. Callers depend on the responsibility, not the fulfillment, so reworking the internals touches no one.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Encapsulation as a default virtue. Private fields with public getters and setters: the representation becomes part of the commitment, so an internal choice and the callers’ needs are fused — reworking the internals means renegotiating with every caller. Interfaces wrapped around things no caller needs: commitments with nobody to commit to. Where the domain mandates the concrete detail, the abstraction asserts a concept nobody decided; the concept is unwritten, and callers couple to the invention. The mirror failure: withholding what callers need produces workarounds — reflection, duplicated internals, paths that bypass the boundary. The mechanism runs without the knowledge.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each thing this type exposes: which need does it serve? For each thing it withholds: why may no caller reach it?

If you can answer both → applicable. The boundary is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the answer is “private by default” → inapplicable. The mechanism runs without the principle.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You found incomplete domain knowledge, not a wrong pattern.




#Encapsulation #InformationHiding #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Inheritance / Subtyping

Liskov and Wing: A subtype must be usable in place of its supertype without altering the correctness of the program. [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every extends freezes a classification into the code: the child is declared a kind of the parent, for all time. That claim has content only if the domain draws the distinction — if a domain expert would state the classification as a fact of the business, and if substitution holds under every change the domain can force. The gap shows when the hierarchy answers a question nobody asked the business: the taxonomy reflects how the code happens to be organised, not how the domain classifies. The square–rectangle trap is the textbook case; the everyday version is a parent class that exists only because two classes shared three methods.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The classification is a domain fact with a forcing condition. Banking regulation distinguishes account types, and a savings account IS a bank account in the regulator’s own language — substitution is a legal truth, not a programming nicety. When the business itself reasons through the subtype (“any account may be frozen; savings accounts additionally accrue interest”), the hierarchy is the code catching up to the knowledge.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Inheritance used to reuse implementation. Two classes share code, someone extracts a base class, and the child is coupled to every future change of the parent — while the code asserts a classification the domain has not stated; that knowledge is unwritten. The parent’s change reasons and the child’s diverge, but the hierarchy forces them to travel together: a change the domain aims at one concept lands on both. The taxonomy hat hides the actual structure, which was coincidence of code, not identity of concept.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given extends: would a domain expert state this classification as a fact of the business — and does the subtype remain substitutable under every change the domain can force on the parent?

If yes to both → applicable. The hierarchy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the honest answer is “we wanted to share the code” → inapplicable. Reuse wearing a taxonomy hat.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Inheritance #Subtyping #LSP #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composition over Inheritance

Gamma et al.: Favour object composition over class inheritance. [3]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Choosing inheritance freezes a relationship as permanent taxonomy; choosing composition says the relationship is a role — attached, detachable, reassignment-capable. An employee is a person who plays the employee role; a discount policy is attached to an order, not what an order is. The gap shows when the structural choice was made for reuse or convenience without asking which reading the domain supports — the choice still encodes a claim about the business, and that claim is unwritten until the domain states it. Only one reading is true.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Composition wins when the domain itself reassigns roles: a contractor becomes an employee; a customer is also a supplier; a policy attaches to this order today and that one tomorrow. Roles vary independently of the carrier’s identity, and composition encodes exactly that independence — a change in the role’s rules arrives without touching the thing that plays it. Inheritance stays honest in the opposite case (#136): the domain holds the classification fixed, and a changed relationship would mean a different thing entirely.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Composition adopted as a blanket slogan. The relationship is a stable domain classification, but the code models it as an attachable role “for flexibility” — flexibility against a change no domain mechanism can force. The price is real: indirection, identity workarounds (the composed parts re-deriving what “the same thing” means), and a structure that invites the domain-illegal move — swapping a component the business considers constitutive.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given relationship: can the domain change it without changing the thing’s identity?

If yes — the business reassigns, swaps, stacks roles → composition. The domain treats it as played, not inherited.
If the domain would say “it would then be a different thing” → the classification is stable; inheritance may be the honest encoding.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The structure is a guess about permanence the business never confirmed.




#CompositionOverInheritance #Inheritance #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself)

Hunt and Thomas: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous representation within a system. [4]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
DRY is about knowledge, not text — but the only instrument the programmer has operates on text. Two fragments look alike, someone extracts the common code, and the extraction itself is a claim: “these are one rule, and a change to it must reach both.” That claim has content only if the domain agrees. The gap shows when the team merged by similarity without asking whether one domain decision stands behind both fragments — the merge couples two change drivers, and when one rule moves and the other must not, the shared abstraction breaks in production.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Both fragments encode the same domain decision: the same VAT rule, the same rounding policy, the same eligibility criterion. The domain itself guarantees they change together — when the rule is revised, every place that applies it must move in lockstep, and a single representation is what makes that guarantee structural rather than hopeful. The deduplication is the code catching up to the knowledge.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Merging by text similarity. Two price calculations that coincide today because the numbers happen to align; two validation blocks that share a shape but answer to different authorities. The duplication was the faithful structure — two rules, two drivers, two futures — and the merge planted a coupling no rule behind the fragments mandates; if each fragment answers to a different authority, each rule is unwritten and the merge hides both. Every later change now starts with an archaeology dig: which of the callers may follow this edit, and which must be peeled off first?








TipThe faithfulness test



For a candidate merge: if the domain rule behind fragment A changes, must fragment B change with it — always, by the domain’s own logic?

If yes → one knowledge, one representation. Merge.
If no → the duplication is faithful. Extracting couples two drivers.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The similarity is visible; whether it is one rule is exactly the knowledge you’re missing.




#DRY #DontRepeatYourself #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Law of Demeter

Lieberherr and Holland: A method should talk only to its immediate collaborators, not to their collaborators. [5]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every reach-through chain asserts that the caller’s business genuinely depends on the far object along this route — that the path is a stable domain relationship, not an accident of object layout. Sometimes it is: an order’s customer’s billing address is a path the business itself reasons about. Sometimes it is digging: the caller exploits an implementation trail, following a route that exists only in the object graph. The gap shows when nobody can say which of the two a given chain is — the coupling exists, its legitimacy unexamined.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The law earns its keep where the chain is NOT a domain path. Rewriting a.b().c() into a direct ask keeps the caller coupled only to the object whose job the operation is — so when the intermediate structure changes for its own reasons, the caller doesn’t move. The caller now depends on what the domain mandates (the outcome) and not on what it doesn’t (the route). Note the asymmetry: the law is a heuristic about structure; its violations are the signal worth auditing, one chain at a time.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Mechanically eliminating every chain. Where the chain is a domain relationship the business itself reasons about, the rewrite replaces a recognised route with a direct ask nobody decided; where it was an implementation route, wrapper methods tunnel the same dependency and only move the coupling out of sight. The caller’s real dependence on the far object is hidden, not removed.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given chain: is this path a relationship the domain itself recognises, or a traversal of an object graph that exists only as implementation?

If the domain recognises it → the coupling is mandated; keep it visible and direct.
If not → the path exists only as an implementation route; the chain couples the caller to structure the domain never mandated.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The navigation compiled, but nobody checked it against the map.




#LawOfDemeter #TellDontAsk #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: YAGNI

Fowler: Build only what the requirements demand now; do not add speculative generality. [6]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every “we’ll need this to be flexible” asserts that the domain can force a variation here — a forcing condition exists, and the structure stands ready for it. The gap is anticipating variation no domain mechanism can force: a plugin point for providers the market does not contain, a config switch for a rule the business holds fixed, an abstraction layer against a change nobody can cause. The reverse gap is costlier: “you aren’t gonna need it” said about a variation the business has already announced — the seam was domain knowledge, and YAGNI was invoked to unsee it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



No forcing condition exists for the anticipated change, and the team can say so honestly — not “we didn’t ask,” but “we asked, and the domain holds this fixed.” Deleting the speculative structure removes a coupling to a phantom driver: the code now covers exactly the variations the domain can produce, and nothing pays rent for the rest. YAGNI here is knowledge applied, not effort avoided.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two failure modes, same root. YAGNI invoked against a variation the domain demonstrably forces — a regulator who can change the rule, a market that adds channels, a pricing policy with a history of revision — because “we’ll add it when we need it,” as if adding structure under deadline pressure were free. The refusal asserts that no forcing condition exists; the domain has one, so the seam’s absence is a structure nobody decided. And the mirror: building for a forcing condition nobody can name. Both share one gap: the future change was decided without consulting the domain that owns it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given piece of flexibility (or a refused one): name the forcing condition that would make you use it.

If you can name the domain mechanism → the structure is knowledge, whether you build it now or deliberately defer it.
If the answer is “someday, maybe” → the structure is a guess; YAGNI applies.
If you can’t answer either way → unclear. The decision to build or not build is currently a coin flip dressed as engineering judgment.




#YAGNI #DesignPrinciples #ExtremeProgramming #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Information Hiding (Parnas)

Parnas: Decompose a system by hiding the design decisions most likely to change behind stable interfaces. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Parnas’s rule works at the system level: derive module structure from the inventory of decisions, grouped by what could force them to change. One module may hide several decisions — when the same conditions force them to change together — and one decision may not be split. The likelihood reading asks for a forecast that can never be checked when it is made. The recoverable reading lists decisions whose forcing conditions are demonstrable today — a regulator who has revised the rule. The gap shows as a break in the correspondence: co-changing decisions split across modules, or change-apart decisions hidden behind one wall.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The correspondence holds both ways. Every module hides a cluster of decisions that share their forcing conditions, so one change event has one address; every decision with a demonstrable forcing condition lives in one such module. The structure is a complete map of the domain’s known forcing conditions.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two failures, same root. Decomposition by likelihood guess: boundaries drawn around decisions someone felt were change-prone, with no forcing condition anyone can name — speculation wearing Parnas’s hat. And decomposition by data shape or technical layer: all DTOs here, all controllers there, all “utilities” in a third drawer. Such a module hides no domain decision; its secret is a formatting convention. Meanwhile the genuinely volatile decisions — pricing policy, eligibility rules, regulatory thresholds — leak across five modules each, and the inventory of real forcing conditions is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Compare the modules with the decisions whose forcing conditions are demonstrable today. Are decisions grouped by shared forcing conditions?

If the correspondence holds both ways → applicable. The decomposition is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If co-changing decisions are split, or change-apart decisions share a wall → the correspondence breaks; that break is the gap.
If a module hides no decision → it is a drawer, not a module.




#InformationHiding #Parnas #Encapsulation #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Tell, Don’t Ask

Hunt and Thomas: Tell an object what to do rather than asking it for its state and acting on it yourself. [4]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
if (account.balance > amount) account.withdraw(...) looks harmless — but the overdraft rule just lived in the caller. Every “ask then decide” asserts that the decision belongs outside the object whose state feeds it; every “tell” asserts it belongs inside. Both are placement claims about domain knowledge, and both can be wrong. The gap shows when the placement was never reasoned about: rules drift into whichever file was open, and the object that owns the state no longer owns the rule that governs it — so a change to the rule hunts through every caller.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The decision is a function of one object’s own state and constitutes one domain rule: overdraft policy on the account, eligibility on the application, validity on the certificate. Telling places the behavior where its change driver points — when the policy is revised, exactly one module moves, and no caller needs to know that anything changed. The placement is the code catching up to where the knowledge already lives in the business.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Dogmatic “never return data.” Objects swallow decisions that belong to collaborators, growing into gods of their own state; or tell-methods sprout callback and lambda parameters so the caller can smuggle its decision back in through the tell — the knowledge moved syntactically while the dependency stayed exactly where it was. The deeper miss: a decision that consults several objects’ state is a collaboration, and no amount of telling removes that coupling — it only hides which object is actually deciding.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given decision: which object’s state does the domain rule consult?

If one object’s → tell it. The rule lives where its data lives.
If several objects’ → the decision is a collaboration; place it explicitly (a policy, a service) instead of tunnelling it through a tell.
If you can’t say whose state the rule reads → unclear. The behavior is placed, but nobody knows by what knowledge.




#TellDontAsk #LawOfDemeter #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Extension Points

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every extension point — a plugin interface, a strategy slot, a template method — claims “the domain varies here, and not there.” No slogan tells you which point to build or when; a module can be extensible somewhere, never everywhere, so every seam is a bet about the location of change. The gap is the bet placed without the knowledge that settles it. Two failure signatures follow: seams on axes the domain holds fixed, and hardcoding on the axis it varies — the pricing formula’s shape changes while the seam sat at the rates.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Current domain knowledge selects the seam — not clairvoyance, but a forcing condition the business can point to now: tax rules the jurisdiction already revises on a schedule, payment methods the market keeps adding, report formats a regulator has already changed twice. Build the seam where change has already shown itself. The next variation arrives as a new implementation plugged into the same seam, and the code already written stays untouched.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Speculative extension points: abstractions for a second backend never funded, hooks for customizations never requested, strategies for jurisdictions never entered. Each wrong seam is worse than dead code — it looks deliberate and nothing flags it for removal, so the coupling accumulates as the codebase ages. And the inverse failure: the axis of demonstrated volatility was hardcoded, so every real change edits the code that was supposed to stay fixed.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given extension point: which change has the domain already shown it can force along this axis — and is everything outside the seam safe from the changes shown elsewhere?

If you can point to demonstrated volatility → applicable. The knowledge selected the seam.
If the justification is “we might need it” → inapplicable. Speculation wearing a principle’s hat (#140 applies).
If you can’t answer → unclear. The structure bets on a change map nobody has drawn — that map is the missing knowledge.




#ExtensionPoints #YAGNI #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutable Value Objects

Evans: Value objects should be immutable: rather than modifying one, you create a new one in its place. [7]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Post #85 covered the identity question: a value object claims that identity doesn’t matter, that equality by content is the domain’s own notion of sameness. What remains for this folder is the mutation question. Making a class immutable asserts: “when this fact changes, the domain replaces it — the old one stops being true.” An address correction is a new address, not a mutated one; a price revision supersedes the old price. Where it goes wrong: immutability chosen for technical convenience — thread safety, cacheability — applied to facts the domain revises. Thread safety is a real requirement, but it does not decide whether a fact is replaced or mutated; the domain does. If the domain revises the fact, immutability asserts a replacement nobody decided — the rule is unwritten — and builders and copy-methods must emulate updates the business performs. And the inverse gap: mutable value-shaped objects whose shared aliasing silently couples changes that should be independent.






TipThe faithfulness test



For a value-shaped class: when this fact “changes” in the business language, does the old one stop being true — or does the same thing acquire a new state?

If the old one stops being true → replace, and immutability is the code catching up.
If the same thing acquires new state → this was never a value question; the identity question from #85 (and #86) decides the structure.
If the domain language has no answer yet → unclear. The keyword is written; the knowledge it encodes is not.




#ValueObjects #Immutability #DDD #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: OOP Principles as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Static Fields and Methods
text:
Case study: Static Fields and Methods

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every static is a placement claim: this fact or behavior exists independent of any particular thing — it holds for the type itself. That claim has content only if the domain speaks that way: a conversion constant the physics fixes, a rule that governs the concept rather than its instances, construction logic that is merely named creation (#91). The gap shows when static was chosen so the code could reach something without knowing which thing owns it — the knowledge lives nowhere, so it lives everywhere.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The fact is genuinely instance-independent in the domain: a mathematical constant, a classification rule that holds for the type as such, a factory method that names a construction the business names (“Money.euros(amount)”). No instance could carry the knowledge, because no instance is what the knowledge is about.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two classic traps, same root. Static mutable state — the cache, the counter, the registry — asserts “the whole universe of discourse shares one of these.” Sharing scope is a domain decision. If the domain has not named it, the assertion is a claim nobody decided — the mandate is unwritten, not absent — and the result is a hidden global that couples every caller to one change driver. And the static utility class: behavior that acts on instances, parked at the type level — the class asserts a type-level fact the domain never stated. Even static final deserves suspicion: TAX_RATE = 0.21 hardcodes a domain decision with a forcing condition — the value is fixed so far, the speculative seam’s mirror image (#140, #143).








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given static member: does the domain state this fact without referring to any particular instance — or did the code lose track of which thing owns it?

If the domain speaks instance-free → applicable. The keyword encodes the knowledge’s true level.
If the knowledge consults one thing’s state → inapplicable. Place the behavior with the thing.
If it’s shared mutable state nobody justified → unclear at best. The coupling is real; the mandate for it was never checked.




#Static #GlobalState #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Language and Platform Idioms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
A platform idiom encodes a fact about the environment: what owns a resource, when it is released, what the runtime charges for it.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Language and Platform Idioms as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dispose Pattern

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a resource has a bounded lifetime — that acquiring it and releasing it are two ends of a single domain transaction — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this resource must be acquired before use and released after, and the interval between acquisition and release is a meaningful domain scope (a session, a connection, a lock window),” then Dispose is just embodying that knowledge. The disposal interface is the domain’s own “bounded lifetime” contract; the using block is the domain’s own scoping rule made mechanical.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a resource has a deterministic end-of-life tied to a domain scope. Dispose closes the gap — it prevents each caller from manually pairing acquire and release calls, which would scatter the lifetime knowledge across the system. Every call site would need to know both the acquisition protocol and the release protocol, coupling unrelated code to resource lifecycle details it shouldn’t own.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “resource” is not a domain resource — it’s a memory-management artifact. The developer wraps a plain object in IDisposable because the GC won’t finalize it soon enough, not because the domain mandates a bounded lifetime. Dispose here addresses a runtime behavior, not domain knowledge. Infrastructure resources — file handles, database connections, network sockets — have bounded lifetimes by OS nature, and Dispose is correct for them even when the domain is silent. The inapplicable case: domain objects with no resource semantics beyond memory, where disposal introduces lifecycle coupling the domain never defined.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this resource as having a defined end-of-life — or is the resource inherently finite by the nature of the computing environment?

If yes → applicable. Dispose catches up to domain knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. But the resource is infrastructure (files, sockets, connections) or the domain is resource-constrained (embedded/real-time), it remains valid — the bounded lifetime comes from the environment. If purely a GC workaround, the pattern adds lifecycle coupling the domain didn’t require.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DotNet #CSharp #IDisposable #DisposePattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #OOP

title: Kernel & Runtimes
text:

title: Software Patterns
text:
A pattern is a structure the domain may or may not have decided. Each list below reads one family of patterns the same way: name the structure, then ask which fact of the domain makes it so. The last list turns that question on the answers an architect gives under questioning.

title: SQL Statement Semantics
text:
A query’s shape claims something about the domain — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means. Each post states the claim and the fact it needs.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: Three-valued logic (NULL in a comparison)
text:
Case study: Three-valued logic (NULL in a comparison)
A revenue report comes up short by 2,190 orders. The table also holds 2,190 rows whose status is NULL, and no clause of the query ever mentions them.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: NULL is not a value; it marks the absence of one, so it equals nothing, not even itself. Every value comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. status <> 'cancelled' is TRUE for shipped, FALSE for cancelled, UNKNOWN for NULL — and NOT (status = 'cancelled') is UNKNOWN as well. Neither predicate covers the NULL rows.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The query splits the table’s rows into three parts while the writer holds a two-part mental model. Writing the filter requires knowing whether the column is nullable, and what the NULL means here: not yet decided, not applicable, or unknown to the source system. Under “unknown”, excluding those rows is a lie about coverage.
The gap question: for each comparison in this query, where do the NULL rows go?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



WHERE status <> 'cancelled' OR status IS NULL — the writer knew the NULL rows were in scope and said so in the statement. The standard goes further: IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a value, so each such comparison answers TRUE or FALSE.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The exclusion query that drops every NULL-status row. It is seductive because the query is well-formed, the filter reads like the English requirement, and a NULL status is invisible in the output. The count then falls short by exactly the unknowns, and the complementary report falls short by the same rows, so the two totals never reconcile to the table and nobody can say why.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each comparison in this query: where do the NULL rows go — stated, or unknown?

If yes → the row set is closed and the aggregate is meaningful. Check the aggregates next: COUNT(col) skips NULL, COUNT(*) does not, AVG divides by the non-NULL count.
If no → the comparison is a filter with an unstated third outcome, answering a question nobody asked. Add IS NULL, or make the column NOT NULL so the guess cannot recur.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Find the column’s nullability, then count the NULLs before trusting any total.




#SQL #ThreeValuedLogic #NullHandling #DataQuality #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: LEFT JOIN demoted by a WHERE clause
text:
Case study: LEFT JOIN demoted by a WHERE clause
A LEFT JOIN kept all 9,400 customers. One WHERE condition on the right table removed 1,340 of them, and the join became an inner join without anyone editing the join.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: A LEFT JOIN promises at least one output row per left row even when the right side has no match, padding the missing right columns with NULL. A WHERE condition on a right-table column then tests those padded rows too: b.type = 'purchase' is UNKNOWN when b is NULL, so the row is discarded. The keyword still says LEFT; the result is INNER.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether the domain needs every left row: every customer including those who never ordered, every account including those with no transactions. Missing purchases appear as gaps in the output; missing customers do not.
The gap question: does any WHERE condition on the right table exist — checked — and did anyone intend an INNER JOIN?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Right-table conditions live in the ON clause, where the promise survives: the left row stays and the right columns come back NULL. The deliberate anti-join WHERE b.id IS NULL asks the outer join’s question directly.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



LEFT JOIN orders b ON b.customer_id = c.id WHERE b.type = 'purchase'. Every customer without a purchase vanishes and the count drops to the match count. It is seductive because the LEFT JOIN looks like the careful choice, the author believes the guarantee is preserved, and no error is raised: the query returns a smaller, well-formed, plausible table. The shortfall is exactly the left rows with no right row of type purchase.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each LEFT JOIN: does any WHERE condition on the right table exist — checked — and did anyone intend an INNER JOIN?

If yes → the outer join is an inner join wearing an outer join’s name. Move the condition into ON, or delete the LEFT keyword and stop claiming a guarantee the query does not give.
If no → every left row survives — the rows are the join’s full result, not a filtered one. Check that consumers expect NULLs there.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(b.id): the difference is the left rows with no right.




#SQL #Joins #LeftJoin #DataModelling #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: NOT IN against a set that contains NULL
text:
Case study: NOT IN against a set that contains NULL
The exclusion query returned zero rows for three weeks. The blocklist held 40 values, one of them NULL.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: NOT IN is shorthand for a conjunction of inequalities. id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means id <> 1 AND id <> 2 AND id <> NULL. The last conjunct is UNKNOWN for every id, UNKNOWN absorbs the conjunction, and no row can satisfy the predicate. The answer is empty for every id — unsatisfiable, not merely over-selective.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether the subquery’s column can return NULL: a nullable foreign key, an optional attribute, or a LEFT JOIN inside the subquery each produce one. The negation is only safe when that column is provably total, and “nobody inserts NULL there” is a belief, not a proof.
The gap question: can the subquery return NULL — proven — or should this be NOT EXISTS?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



NOT IN over a subquery column declared NOT NULL, where the constraint is the proof rather than the hope. Or NOT EXISTS for the negation: it tests row existence, not value equality, so a NULL in the subquery cannot match and the intended answer survives.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The exclusion list that gains one NULL row — an import left a cell blank, or a LEFT JOIN in the subquery padded one in. It is seductive because the query is idiomatic, the list is short and looks curated, and the empty result reads as “nothing was excluded” or “the filter cleaned everything” — when it is the correct answer to an accidental question: is this id different from every listed value, including an unknown one?








TipThe faithfulness test



For each NOT IN: can the subquery return NULL — proven — or should this be NOT EXISTS?

If yes → any NULL in the list disables the whole predicate. Rewrite as NOT EXISTS, then compare the row counts before and after.
If no → the NOT NULL constraint is doing the work, so check it survives every load path: staging tables, imports, and backfills each need it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Read the subquery column’s definition and every writer of it, then count its NULLs directly.




#SQL #NullHandling #Subqueries #DataQuality #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: GROUP BY as a grain claim
text:
Case study: GROUP BY as a grain claim
A revenue report groups by region and prints a sales rep’s name beside the total. The named rep did not earn the total — the query picked an arbitrary row.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: GROUP BY states the grain of the answer: one output row per distinct combination of the grouped columns. Every selected column must therefore be grouped, aggregated, or functionally dependent on the grouped columns; standard SQL rejects the rest. MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off, and SQLite by default, accept it and return a value from an arbitrary row of the group.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know the grain of the business question: one row per region, per region per month, per rep per month. The grain is a domain fact, not a formatting choice — a total is defined at a grain, and the label beside it must live at the same one.
The gap question: what is one output row of, exactly — stated — and is every column grouped, aggregated, or dependent?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Every selected column is grouped or aggregated, and the groups match the report’s claim: one row per region per month, said in the header and true in the query. Then every label in a row belongs with the number.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The lenient GROUP BY returning an arbitrary row’s value for the ungrouped column. It is seductive because the query runs, the total is right, and the name belongs to a real rep who does sell in that region — so nothing looks broken. The report is a total joined to a person who did not earn it, and the name can move when the plan does.








TipThe faithfulness test



For this query: what is one output row of, exactly — stated — and is every column grouped, aggregated, or dependent?

If yes → the aggregate is defined at a named grain. Check it is the report’s grain, not a coarser one summed into a finer label.
If no → the query aggregates at a grain nobody wrote down, and the ungrouped column is a pick, not a fact. Add it to GROUP BY, or replace it with an aggregate the domain permits.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Find the table’s key, then name the business entity one output row denotes.




#SQL #GroupBy #Aggregation #DataModelling #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
text:
Case study: HAVING versus WHERE
A row filter moved into HAVING drops whole groups or counts the excluded rows, so the total is wrong either way.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: WHERE evaluates rows before grouping; HAVING evaluates groups after aggregation. Two grains: the row and the group. The shape claims which grain the rule belongs to.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether “more than three orders” filters rows before counting them, or counts a customer’s orders and tests the total. Both readings yield a number; only one is the question. A condition that each row meets or fails belongs before the count, because afterwards it changes what is counted.
The gap question: which grain does this rule belong to — the row or the group?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



WHERE on the raw rows: shipped orders only, one region, a closed range. HAVING on the aggregate’s meaning: accounts whose summed balance exceeds the limit, customers with more than three orders. The test is the subject, not the grammar: does the condition speak about one row or about the group? One row is WHERE; a group is HAVING.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The aggregate condition pushed into WHERE, which standard SQL rejects — it moves to HAVING to make it run, and the row condition follows. MySQL without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, and SQLite, accept HAVING status = 'shipped' on an ungrouped column, evaluate it on one arbitrary row of the group, and drop the whole group on that row’s value. The mirror image: HAVING used as “WHERE for grouped queries,” filtering groups by a fact about their members while the writer thinks they filtered rows. It runs, the totals look plausible, and they span rows the rule meant to exclude.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each filter: does it constrain the rows or the groups — stated — and is that the question being asked?

If yes → the clause records the grain. Check that the filters before the count are the ones the count’s definition assumes.
If no → the count is taken over the wrong grain. Move each condition to the clause matching its subject.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Write each metric as one sentence, then place each condition against the noun it constrains.




#SQL #Grouping #Aggregation #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: No ORDER BY, no ordering guarantee
text:
Case study: No ORDER BY, no ordering guarantee
A report has come out sorted for six years. A parallel plan appears, no code changes, and rows arrive in a different order.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: A table is an unordered multiset: rows have no position, and no operator reading them promises a sequence. Without ORDER BY the engine returns rows in whatever order the plan produces — index scan, hash build, worker arrival. The statement claims nothing about sequence, so a consumer reading sequence relies on an unstated fact.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether sequence is part of the answer or only part of the reading habit. Order belongs to the question, not the storage. A client rendering rows top to bottom turns an accident into an expectation the database never agreed to.
The gap question: does any consumer of these rows depend on their sequence?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Every consumer depending on sequence states it: the API page, the feed, the ledger statement, the migration applying changes in order. Order belongs on the outermost query — ORDER BY in a subquery or view is not carried outward as a contract, and engines that keep it do so by accident.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The report that always came out sorted, until the parallel plan or the new index. Nothing was tested, because the test asserted rows exactly as its environment produced them — a green suite proving the plan, not the query. The failure reads as an intermittent bug, and the fix gets filed against the export layer.
The sharper variant: LIMIT 10 with no ORDER BY, labelled “top ten.” It returns ten rows, not the ten highest, and they can change with the plan.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each query whose consumer cares about order: is ORDER BY written — or is the order an accident being trusted?

If yes → the sequence is a stated claim. Check that the sort key is unique, or that a tie-breaker follows.
If no → nothing was promised. Add ORDER BY at the outermost query, or drop the consumer’s dependence on sequence.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. List the consumers, then mark which would change output on shuffled rows.




#SQL #Ordering #Determinism #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: Ties without a tie-breaker
text:
Case study: Ties without a tie-breaker
One row appears on page two and again on page four. Its neighbour appears on no page, and the SQL is correct.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: ORDER BY created_date imposes a partial order: rows sharing a date are equal, and the engine may return them in any sequence. LIMIT and OFFSET re-execute the whole query per page, so a tie straddling a page boundary can be cut at a different place each time — the same row can surface twice, or slip between two pages and land nowhere. Pagination needs totality: no two rows compare equal.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether the sort key is unique, or which second column makes it so. Timestamps, prices, scores, and truncated dates can be non-unique in practice; a tie can be rare in staging and routine the day one batch writes two records. Pagination claims something about every pair of rows, so one duplicate breaks it.
The gap question: is the sort key unique, or is there a stated tie-breaker?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A unique tie-breaker appended — ORDER BY created_date, id — makes every page disjoint and complete while the table holds still, and the proof is one line: distinct sort tuples. Keyset pagination goes further, seeking WHERE (created_date, id) > (?, ?) instead of counting rows to skip, so the boundary is a value, not an offset, and ties cannot shift it, giving up the jump to a page number.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



ORDER BY created_date LIMIT 20 OFFSET n. It looks right on every page a developer opens: stable while the plan is stable, and ties near boundaries are absent in a small table. OFFSET reads like a cursor resuming where the last page stopped; it is a skip count computed by re-running the query and re-deciding ties. Add a second non-unique key, and the illusion holds while the guarantee does not.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the sort key unique — or is there a tie-breaker — stated, so pagination is provable?

If yes → the order is total. Check that the tie-breaker is unique on the data, not only on today’s sample.
If no → pages overlap and leak by construction. Append a unique column, or switch to keyset pagination.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT sort_key) on the real table.




#SQL #Pagination #Ordering #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
text:
Case study: ROW_NUMBER versus RANK
Two players tie for first. The report numbers them 1 and 2, the medal table shows two golds, and the ceremony disagrees with both.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: All three number rows in a partition, each claiming something different about equality. ROW_NUMBER promises distinct consecutive integers, so equal keys get an order the engine picks and a plan change re-picks. RANK promises equal ranks for equal keys and skips what a tie consumes: 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK promises equal ranks with no gap: 1, 1, 2. Three claims about ties: none, equal with a gap, equal without.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know what a tie means before choosing. Two rows with the same score: same standing, or a deterministic order that must be provable, or labels for a list? Top-N needs exactness: a unique tie-breaker belongs in the ORDER BY. Standings need the opposite — equality preserved, gaps included: after two joint firsts no row is second.
The gap question: what does a tie mean here, and does the function chosen say the same thing?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Arbitrary-but-total for top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) = 1 picks the latest order reproducibly: a unique column breaks ties. RANK where shared standing is the truth: competition results, exam grades, severity bands.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



ROW_NUMBER used as “the ranking” for a leaderboard. Tied players are numbered 1 and 2 by storage order; the report stays stable until the table is rewritten or the plan changes, then the medals can swap between two people with identical scores.
The mirror trap: RANK for top-N returns eleven rows for WHERE rank <= 10 once a tie straddles the cut.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each ranking query: what do ties mean to the domain — and does the function chosen say the same thing?

If yes → the numbering encodes the domain’s tie rule. Check that the window’s ORDER BY is unique where exactness is demanded.
If no → the numbering imposes a tie rule nobody stated. Switch function, or add the tie-breaker the domain recognizes.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Count duplicate sort keys, then ask what equality means.




#SQL #WindowFunctions #Ranking #Database #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: DISTINCT as a bug mask
text:
Case study: DISTINCT as a bug mask
A join returns 4,000 rows where the domain expects 1,000. Someone adds DISTINCT, the count drops back to 1,000, and the fan-out (row multiplication) that produced the extra rows stays in the query.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: DISTINCT compares each complete result row against every other complete result row and discards the duplicates. It claims that the data can produce identical rows and that the result must not contain them. That claim concerns the output alone: the duplicates are removed after the join multiplied them, so the count a reader sees no longer measures what the join did.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know which of two facts holds: the duplicates came from the data, or they came from the join. If the join generated them — a missing condition, a fan-out on a one-to-many key — the query now returns a correct count over an incorrect row set. The gap question: what in the data makes these rows identical?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



Counting uniques. “How many distinct customers ordered this month?” The column holds duplicates because one customer orders many times, and the question asks for customers, not orders. DISTINCT is that question, written down. The same holds for a list of distinct shipping countries, or distinct product ids across a set of invoices.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



DISTINCT appended after a row count “came out too high.” The dedup restores the number, the review passes, and the missing join condition stays. The duplicates are now invisible: a region total sums correctly because each duplicated row collapsed, and nobody sees that one order was joined to four addresses. The keyword reclassifies a wrong join as a property of the data.








TipThe faithfulness test



Was DISTINCT written because the domain counts uniques — or because the join produced too many rows?

If yes → the keyword is the domain’s question. Check that distinctness is stated over the columns that matter, and that the dedup is not collapsing rows the domain counts twice.
If no → the join is the defect. Remove DISTINCT, then fix the condition or the grain (what one row denotes).
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Count rows before and after each join, and name the key that should be unique.




#SQL #Database #QuerySemantics #Joins #DataModelling #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: UNION versus UNION ALL
text:
Case study: UNION versus UNION ALL
Two branches that cannot return the same row. One keyword still sorts or hashes the whole result on every run to prove that they don’t.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: UNION combines the branches, then removes duplicate rows across the combined result — typically through a sort or a hash — and returns each surviving row once. It claims that the branches can produce identical rows and that the result must not contain them. UNION ALL concatenates the branches and claims nothing about overlap; every row from every branch appears.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know whether the branches can overlap. They can when one source is queried twice under predicates that do not exclude each other, or when a current table and an archive table share key values. They cannot when the branches read disjoint sources, or one source under mutually exclusive predicates — and the projection keeps the rows apart. The gap question: can branch A and branch B return the same row?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A partial migration leaves the current orders table and the archive table with overlapping id ranges, and a mailing list needs each customer once. Or one branch selects buyers, another selects complainants, and a recipient must appear once. The branches genuinely can return the same row.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



UNION between branches that are disjoint by construction: one predicate on status ‘open’, one on status ‘closed’, both over the same table, and status in the select. Every run pays a sort or hash over the full result to remove duplicates that cannot exist. The inverse trap is quieter: UNION ALL over a current table and a history table that started to overlap after a re-import. Then one customer is counted twice, and the total is wrong with no error to show for it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can these branches return the same row — proven — and was the dedup cost accepted knowingly?

If yes → UNION states the domain’s rule. Check the cost against the result size, since the dedup — sort or hash — is paid on every run.
If no → UNION ALL, and say in the query why the branches are disjoint.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Read the predicates: the disjointness you rely on is either written down or it is not.




#SQL #Database #QuerySemantics #SetOperations #Performance #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
text:
Case study: The scalar subquery
A lookup starts returning two rows, and the query does not return the first one. It fails at runtime, on the one row that broke the assumption.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: A scalar subquery stands where one value is required: in the SELECT list, or in a comparison. It claims the inner query returns at most one row for that position, and most engines enforce it: two rows raise a cardinality violation (SQLite takes the first). Zero rows yield NULL, so “none” arrives as a value and the claim stays at most one, never exactly one.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know what holds the inner result to one row. Three things can: a constraint, such as a unique index on the lookup key; an aggregate, such as MAX, which collapses any number of rows to one; or hope. The gap question: for each scalar subquery, which of the three?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



An aggregate over a set: the highest price in a price history, the maximum approval date for an order. A lookup by primary key, where the constraint guarantees the cardinality. A correlated subquery reading a unique index per outer row. In each case the guarantee is written where the engine and a reader can both inspect it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The lookup runs on a business key only believed unique — an email address, a SKU, a national identifier — and stopped being unique when an import merged two systems. It works for a year. Then production fails on the single duplicated row in a query nobody changed. The seduction is the first thousand runs: a working query looks like a proven claim. Where the inner query carries a LIMIT 1, the failure disappears and the query picks a row arbitrarily — worse than the error.








TipThe faithfulness test



What guarantees at most one row — a constraint, an aggregate, or hope?

If yes → the claim is grounded. Check that the constraint still holds in the data, not only in the schema.
If no → the subquery is a bet. Add the constraint, add the aggregate, or make the multi-row case explicit in the query’s shape.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Group the inner key and count the rows where the count exceeds one.




#SQL #Database #QuerySemantics #Subqueries #Constraints #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: SQL Statement Semantics
section: Case study: Implicit type coercion in comparisons
text:
Case study: Implicit type coercion in comparisons
A varchar column compared to a number turns an index lookup into a full scan — and the stored value into something nobody wrote.
Writing a SQL statement? Ask “which claim does this query make about the data — what exists, what counts, what order means, what NULL means?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap: the query enforces a guess. If you can, the query is knowledge embodied — the statement catching up to what the data actually contains.

Construct: When a comparison puts two different types side by side, the dialect’s coercion rules decide whether they compare at all. The statement claims these values are comparable, and that one side converts to the other’s type without loss. Two costs follow. The conversion happens per row, so an index on the converted column cannot be read. The conversion may also change the value.


The SQL knowledge gap it signals
The writer must know the declared type of both sides and whether the conversion keeps the meaning. The gap question: are both sides the same type, stated in the query — or is the engine translating a claim nobody wrote?






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it



A cast at a boundary where the types genuinely differ, with the conversion named. A legacy text column of identifiers is cast once, on the parameter side, so the indexed column keeps its type and the cost is one conversion. A date literal written as DATE ‘2027-01-01’, not left as a string. The conversion is visible, so a reader can check it.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



An order reference stored as varchar, compared to a numeric parameter. Every row is converted, the index goes unread, and the query scans the table while looking identical to an indexed one. Dates stored as strings are the quieter variant: lexical order matches calendar order only while every row is zero-padded and formatted alike. One ‘2027-2-1’, or a locale format, silently reorders the result. Dialects disagree, and that changes the claim. PostgreSQL raises an error. MySQL converts the string to a number — zero when it has no numeric prefix — so = 0 matches every row without one.








TipThe faithfulness test



Are both sides the same type — stated in the query — or is the engine translating a claim nobody wrote?

If yes → the comparison is grounded. Check that the cast sits opposite the indexed side.
If no → state the type, or cast deliberately at the boundary, knowing the cost.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the query wrong — you’ve found incomplete data knowledge. Read the column definitions, then the parameter types, and compare them.




#SQL #Database #QuerySemantics #TypeSystems #Indexing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Unison
text:
Effects are declared in types, and a definition’s hash is its identity. Each post asks which knowledge the type carries and which the hash replaces.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Unison
section: Case study: Abilities (effects in the signature)
text:
Case study: Abilities (effects in the signature)
A function that logs, reads the clock, and can fail carries all three in {IO, Exception} — visible before the first line runs.
Writing a Unison definition? Ask “which fact does the hash and the signature carry — what this does, which version this is — and what can no longer be a guess?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the definition is knowledge embodied — the codebase catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In Unison’s documented model an ability declares operations, and a function’s type records the abilities it requires: {} pure, {IO} writing. A call site must handle each one or propagate it, so effects travel inside the type. The trade: no effect hides behind the signature, at the cost of threading abilities through every caller in between.


The Unison knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which effects the program performs — which reads, which writes, which failures — and who is responsible for each. An ability in a type is a claim about how the function touches the world; a handler is a claim about where that responsibility stops. A signature assembled by habit describes a program nobody verified.
The gap question: does the effect set name every way this function touches the world?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A report job that reads a file and writes a summary needs {IO}; a validator with no effects gets {}, and the compiler will not let it print. Every caller shows what it inherits, so the boundary where effects are discharged — one main, one test harness — is visible in the types.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The team arrives from a language where the type read Promise<User> and the database call inside was invisible. A review step grew to catch what the compiler did not: does this touch the database, can this throw. In Unison that step hunts effects the signature already lists, and what remains is a checklist that always passes. The trap is keeping the ceremony and calling it rigor.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each function: do its effects match its signature — and is that checked by the compiler or by hope?

If yes → the signature is the contract. Check that each ability is handled where the program wants the responsibility, not merely somewhere.
If no → the type does not describe the function. Narrow the ability set, or move the effect to its handler.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List what it reads, writes, and can fail with, then compare it to the type.




#UnisonLang #Abilities #EffectSystems #TypeSystems #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Unison
text:
Case study: Content-addressed definitions
Rename a function across a thousand files and its hash does not move; change one character inside it and every dependent’s hash does.
Writing a Unison definition? Ask “which fact does the hash and the signature carry — what this does, which version this is — and what can no longer be a guess?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the definition is knowledge embodied — the codebase catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In Unison’s documented model a definition’s identity is a hash of its normalized form, including the hashes of everything it references; the name is a separate, editable annotation. Renaming changes nothing, and an edit changes its hash plus every definition above it. The trade: an identity that cannot drift, against a name that no longer tells you what you are calling until you follow it.


The Unison knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which definitions the program depends on at the level of the individual definition, not the repository. “We use library X” becomes a set of hashes, and two identical-looking call sites may sit on different ones.
The gap question: for each shared definition, is the consumer’s copy the same definition, or a copy that drifted?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



Two codebases referencing the same hash hold provably identical code — not “the same version”, the same term. A security review or an audit transfers with the hash: whoever verified that hash verified the code your build runs; a measurement does not — it describes one run.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



A helper “shared” by two services, edited on separate days, now sits at two hashes with quietly different behavior — and in Unison the divergence is visible, because the hashes differ. The seductive trap runs the other way: believing a shared name means shared code. A name is a claim; the hash is the fact, and a diff between hashes is not a formality.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each shared function: which hash do the consumers reference — and is any divergence visible, or buried in git blame?

If yes → the hash is the identity. Compare the hashes across consumers that claim to share a definition; a mismatch is a fork, not a version.
If no → the name is carrying an identity it cannot. Record the hash where the dependency lives, and compare before assuming behavior.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Check whether “same function” is a claim about a name or about a hash.




#UnisonLang #ContentAddressing #CodeIdentity #Refactoring #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Unison
section: Case study: The escape hatches that do not exist
text:
Case study: The escape hatches that do not exist
A function that can fail returns Either Failure Success — no caller reaches the success path without matching the failure first.
Writing a Unison definition? Ask “which fact does the hash and the signature carry — what this does, which version this is — and what can no longer be a guess?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the definition is knowledge embodied — the codebase catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In Unison’s documented model there is no null and no unchecked exception: absence is Optional a, failure is Either e a, and a partial operation such as list head returns an Optional rather than throwing. Matching is exhaustive, so a new case breaks every match with no wildcard branch. The trade: every case is handled where it arises or carried explicitly to a caller, against the verbosity of matching at each step.


The Unison knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which failures the domain admits and what should happen at each, because the type is now the list of them. The construct forces the belief open: a crash and an unhandled None are both statements about what the program assumes.
The gap question: is every failure a caller can meet named in the return type?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A parser returns Either ParseError Ast, so the syntax error is a value the caller destructures and reports; adding a second error case fails compilation at every match that assumed one. Nothing reaches Right by accident, and no failure survives only as a log line.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The habit from other languages: a defensive check for the value that cannot be null, a catch-all handler around a call that cannot throw. Both compile. Then the optimism returns as a wildcard match branch that turns exhaustiveness back into a guess, or a helper that crashes on None, reinstating the exception the language removed. The compiler audits the match; it does not audit the wildcard you added to silence it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each failure path: is it in the return type — where every caller sees it — or in an exception nobody declared?

If yes → failure is data. Check that each match names every case, and that no wildcard branch hides a case someone must handle.
If no → failure is an implementation detail, invisible at the boundary. Return it as a value, or declare it in the signature.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List how each call can fail, then read the type back.




#UnisonLang #Exhaustiveness #ErrorHandling #TypesAsKnowledge #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Unison
section: Case study: The codebase as a database
text:
Case study: The codebase as a database
Nothing in the build says “4.2.x”. It says the hash of one definition, and that definition is the one that runs.
Writing a Unison definition? Ask “which fact does the hash and the signature carry — what this does, which version this is — and what can no longer be a guess?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the definition is knowledge embodied — the codebase catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In Unison’s documented model the codebase is a database of definitions keyed by hash, and a dependency is a set of exact hashes rather than a package version. There is no range to resolve and no “compatible with 4.2.x” — either the definition your code calls is present, or it is not. The trade: the build’s contents are decidable in one lookup, against ranges that let a patch version flow in without a decision.


The Unison knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know which definition each dependency resolves to, and for each upgrade what actually changed. A range encodes a hope about compatibility; an exact hash encodes a fact somebody recorded. “Which version am I running” stops being archaeology and becomes a lookup — so the honest answer is available, and therefore expected.
The gap question: for each dependency, can you name the definition the build contains?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



An upgrade is deliberate: a dependent moves to a new hash, its own hash changes, and every consumer of it sees a hash it must re-verify. Nothing arrives by accident through a resolved range, and two builds of one commit contain the same definitions by construction.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The range “4.2.x” that behaves two ways in two builds, and a lockfile cited as proof that the code is known. A lockfile records what a resolver chose; it does not name definitions, so two lockfiles can agree on a version string while the code underneath differs. Carry that habit over and “we pin it” becomes a sentence nobody can check.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each dependency: which exact definition does this build contain — answerable in one lookup — or is it a range and a hope?

If yes → the dependency is pinned to a definition. Check that the hash in the build is the hash anyone reviewed.
If no → compatibility is a belief, not a record. Replace the range with the hash you verified, and note what changed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. Read the dependency’s hash out of the codebase, then read its diff.




#UnisonLang #DependencyManagement #ContentAddressing #Builds #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Unison
section: Case study: Publishing and consuming definitions
text:
Case study: Publishing and consuming definitions
A consumer does not depend on “the library” — it depends on eleven definitions inside it, each one pinned by hash.
Writing a Unison definition? Ask “which fact does the hash and the signature carry — what this does, which version this is — and what can no longer be a guess?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the definition is knowledge embodied — the codebase catching up to what the program means.

Mechanism: In Unison’s documented model publishing makes a codebase’s definitions available, and consuming brings a definition into your own codebase by its hash, where it can be browsed and diffed like local code. The trade: upgrades become explicit — take one function’s new version and leave the rest — against a project that tracks many hashes and keeps docs as a separate artifact.


The Unison knowledge gap it signals
The developer must know what the consumer actually uses, and what changed between two hashes of it. “We use the whole library” stops being true once the dependency is a set of definitions, and the set says which ones you took. A changelog is someone’s summary of a diff; the diff is available, so the summary is convenience, not evidence.
The gap question: can a consumer state, definition by definition, what it depends on?






ImportantWhen the types encode reality



A library’s consumers pin exact hashes, and an upgrade is a reviewed hash change per definition. A consumer using four of a hundred definitions says so, and a change to any definition the four do not reach never enters that consumer’s build — the pinned set is the dependency and the inventory of trust.








WarningWhen it’s a guess dressed as engineering



The hand-maintained changelog, drifted from the code: “Renamed X” when the break was a changed error type, no entry because nobody wrote one. In Unison “what changed” is answered by comparing hashes and reading the term diff, so the trap is trusting the prose, not the hash — and releasing under a label that promises more than the definitions deliver.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a consumer state exactly which definitions it depends on — by hash — or does “what changed” live in a document someone forgot?

If yes → the dependency set is the contract. Check that each pinned hash was reviewed, and diff the old and new before releasing.
If no → a label carries the claim. Publish the hashes, and let consumers pin what they verified.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the construct wrong — you’ve found incomplete knowledge of your own program. List the definitions the build contains, then diff them against the ones you meant.




#UnisonLang #UnisonShare #PackageManagement #ContentAddressing #CausalKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture

title: Workflow Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Process models are different from design patterns: the artifact claims to describe the domain, so the gap question is not “should we use this?” but “does this model tell the truth?” Between the process (a knowledge claim) and the notation (modelling vocabulary) sits every silent misrepresentation.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Workflow Patterns as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Deferred Choice

van der Aalst et al.: A point where the choice among alternatives is deferred until an event enables one of them. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the world picks the branch, at the moment it happens, is domain knowledge. If the business says “either the customer pays or the order expires — whichever comes first,” the choice is not made by the process but by an external event that commits one path and withdraws the others.
