title: Delphi (12.3 Athens)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Delphi in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 58.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 27.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Unit interface sections separate the declaration from the implementation: A consumer compiles against the interface part of a unit and never sees its implementation part, so either part can change without the consumer being rewritten
✅ Class, record, and interface types are declared and checked at compile time: A method call, a field access, and an argument are resolved against the declared type, so no name lookup happens at run time
✅ Dotted unit names give a namespace: System.SysUtils, Vcl.Forms, and the project’s unit scope names qualify every entity, so two units may declare the same identifier without a collision
⚠️ A variant record is a sum type without a checked tag: A case part in a record lays alternatives over the same storage, but reading the field of the wrong alternative is not diagnosed, so the tag lives in the programmer’s discipline (T4)
⚠️ Generics exist but the constraint vocabulary is small: Generic classes and records (TList<T>, TDictionary<TKey, TValue>) have been in the language since Delphi 2009, but a type parameter can be constrained only by a class, a record, a constructor, or an interface, so older library code still passes TObject and TValue
⚠️ nil is a value of every class, interface, and pointer type: There is no non-nullable reference type, so a call through nil is a run-time fault rather than a compile-time error
❌ Char is a WideChar unit; UnicodeString length counts units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A property separates the name from the accessor: property Count: Integer read GetCount write SetCount lets a consumer use one name while the class moves between a field and a method without touching the consumer
✅ An event separates the publisher from the subscriber: property OnClick: TNotifyEvent and anonymous methods let the framework raise a notification without knowing which handler is attached, which is the observer pattern in the language
✅ A class helper extends an existing type from outside it: A helper adds a method to a class declared in another unit, so an extension does not require editing the type or inheriting it
✅ A constructor is an ordinary method named Create: Construction is a call rather than a special form, and Create may be virtual, so a factory returns the right subclass
✅ initialization and finalization give a unit a declared start and end: The start-up and shutdown code of a unit has a named place, so a unit-level resource is not acquired in a random procedure
❌ Mutability is the default: A field, a global variable, and an ordinary parameter are writable unless the declaration says const or constref, so the default reading of a variable promises nothing about it being unchanged (C2)
❌ One value, many names: objects are references — a field, a parameter, and a closure share one instance; records copy, objects alias (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: a record’s Implicit class operator runs at an assignment the source shows as a plain assignment (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Nothing ties a release to the end of a block: An object from Create is released by an explicit .Free, usually inside try/finally, and no destructor runs at scope exit, so cleanup is a written obligation (M1, M3)
❌ There is no ownership model: The compiler does not track which reference owns an instance, so a double .Free, a use after .Free, and a leak are neither diagnosed nor reported (M4)
⚠️ Managed types are reference-counted and the rule differs by compiler: string, dynamic arrays, and interface references release their storage when the last reference goes away, but an object is reference-counted only on the mobile compilers, so the lifetime rule depends on the target
⚠️ An interface reference cycle is never released: The reference count of a cycle never reaches zero and there is no tracing collector, so the cycle leaks unless a weak reference breaks it
✅ TComponent.Owner gives a declared lifetime to a component graph: A component frees the components it owns when it is freed, so the object graph of a form is released deterministically
✅ A managed record extends scope-tied release to a value type: Initialize, Finalize, AddRef, and RemoveRef operators let a record run code at the end of the block that holds it (Delphi 10.4 and later)
❌ Raw storage arrives uninitialized: managed types (strings, interfaces, Variants, dynamic arrays) initialize to nil and zero, but plain records, static arrays, and out-parameters carry indeterminate content, and the compiler only warns (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: variant records and absolute declarations overlay one storage with unrelated layouts, unchecked (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer on a raw PChar writes past the string’s bounds, and an access violation in non-managed memory has no reliable catch site (Er6)
❌ Interface reference-counting (ARC) leaks cycles; the documentation names the discipline (M7)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: raise needs no declaration in the signature and no caller is obliged to handle the exception type, so the failure set of a routine is not part of its interface (Er2)
✅ except with on E: T do binds the handler to a type: The handler names the exception class it catches and an unmatched exception propagates, so the recovery region is stated
✅ try/finally separates cleanup from recovery: A finally block runs on both the normal exit and the exceptional one, which is where a release belongs
✅ An exception object carries its own data: A class derived from Exception can carry context and raise propagates it unchanged, so a caller does not parse a message string
⚠️ A bare except swallows the cause: An except block without on catches everything, including an access violation, and the recovery code may not know which failure it is covering
⚠️ A memory fault arrives as an exception: A read through a dangling pointer raises EAccessViolation at the faulting instruction, so an unsafe pointer becomes a run-time error that the program may or may not handle
❌ A fault ends the program: an unhandled exception ends the application (documented); a thread is not an isolation unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Synchronisation is manual and unchecked: System.SyncObjs supplies TCriticalSection, TMutex, TSemaphore, TEvent, and TInterlocked, but the compiler does not check the locking discipline or diagnose a race (K3)
✅ System.Threading gives a task abstraction: TTask.Run, TParallel.For, and futures carry work across a thread pool, so a parallel loop is stated rather than hand-threaded
✅ TThread wraps a thread as an object with a lifetime: The execution and the termination of a thread belong to one object, and Synchronize and Queue marshal a call back to another thread
✅ A queued call separates a worker from the UI thread: TThread.Queue, TThread.ForceQueue, and PostMessage deliver work without a shared lock
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: An ordinary field or global variable is reachable from every thread, and the language does not mark which state is confined to one thread (K2)
⚠️ The VCL is single-threaded by contract: The GUI may be touched only from the main thread, and that rule is documented rather than enforced
❌ TThread reserves an operating-system thread: A task holds it until it ends (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One source targets Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and Linux: The Object Pascal front end and the RTL are shared, and only the GUI framework differs between the targets
✅ A second compiler implements the same language: Free Pascal and Lazarus compile Object Pascal in a Delphi-compatible mode ({$MODE DELPHI}), so a program is not bound to one vendor’s binary alone
✅ The RTL is usable without the GUI framework: A console or service program links the runtime alone, so a non-GUI program does not depend on a windowing framework
⚠️ FireMonkey is the cross-platform GUI path and it is second to the VCL: The component sets and the visual behaviour of the two frameworks differ, so a GUI program depends on the one it was written for
⚠️ A program that calls the Windows API is bound to Windows: The Windows unit, COM, and the registry are used beside the RTL, and that part of the program is not portable
⚠️ The compiler and the IDE are one vendor’s licensed product: The direction of the language follows that vendor, even though a compatible open compiler exists



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The VCL/FireMonkey choice is a GUI decision: A RAD component couples the program to the framework it was dropped onto, and the alternative is to build the user interface against the raw platform
Single inheritance is a deliberate simplification: The language gives interface types for the shared-behaviour case and keeps the class tree one level deep
The RAD model trades control for speed of construction: A designer-saved form and a live object graph are why the framework owns the lifetime of the components
nil is a convenience as much as a hazard: An unset reference has a natural empty value, and the discipline of an assigned check is the programmer’s
Pointer arithmetic is opt-in in practice: Pointer, GetMem, and System.Move exist for the low-level case, and ordinary code need not use them
The language is an Object Pascal dialect, not Pascal: The dialect follows from the RAD requirement, and the compatibility with Turbo Pascal is historical




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits native machine code: dcc32 and dcc64 produce an executable directly, so no interpreter or JIT sits between the source and the CPU
✅ A desktop release does not scan the heap: With reference-counted strings, dynamic arrays, and interfaces, the runtime has no tracing collector, so there is no collection pause to plan around
✅ inline, const parameters, and record passing control cost at the declaration: The call convention is stated beside the routine rather than inferred from its use
⚠️ The classic optimiser is modest beside a modern back end: The vendor compiler does not apply the cross-module inlining and vectorisation that Clang or LLVM at -O2 applies, so a numerical kernel is usually delegated to a library
⚠️ An interface call is an indirect call: Dispatch through an interface adds an indirection the compiler cannot resolve across units



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small and centered on the vendor’s own packages: A project draws on GetIt, the bundled RTL/VCL/FireMonkey, and a small third-party set, so a missing library is often written in-house (Ec3)
✅ The IDE is a complete tool: Editor, visual designer, debugger, profiler, and refactoring sit in one product, with no plugin assembly required
✅ GetIt and open source cover the common needs: The IDE’s package channel, and community projects such as DUnitX, Spring4D, and ORM and JSON libraries, supply the usual layer
✅ The vendor documentation is a reference work: The DocWiki holds an entry per type and per routine of the language, the RTL, and the VCL
⚠️ The platform is one vendor’s commercial product: The compiler, the IDE, and the frameworks are maintained by Embarcadero, so support and direction are commercial decisions
⚠️ Adoption is declining and the community is concentrated: The hiring pool and the library pool shrink with the Windows desktop market, and the active community is organized around a few sites
❌ A runtime package binds to a release: Embarcadero states that an application deploys with the .bpl packages it uses and that the developer must make sure users have the correct versions of them [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Annual releases add features with a published changelog: Each 12.x release records its language and RTL additions in the release notes
✅ Backward compatibility is long-lived: Turbo Pascal-era source mostly still compiles with warnings, so a codebase is rarely rewritten for the toolchain alone
✅ A deprecation is reported with a replacement: The compiler warns on a deprecated routine and names its successor, so a migration is guided
⚠️ The roadmap is one vendor’s: A needed language feature waits for the vendor’s release decision, and the community cannot change the language
⚠️ A program that uses the VCL cannot leave Windows: The framework choice fixes the platform, and the cross-platform path is a separate framework
⚠️ A project is often pinned to an older IDE: The compiler version becomes part of the codebase, and an upgrade is a project of its own
❌ Build variants multiply: {$IFDEF} and {$IF} directives select which units and statements compile, and the flag set lives in the IDE’s project options (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Windows desktop line-of-business software is the native target: A database front end, a form, and a grid are the idiom the framework is built for
✅ Rapid UI construction is a documented strength: The visual designer, the data-aware components (TDataSet, TDataSource), and live bindings make a screen quick to build
✅ A cross-platform client is supported through FireMonkey: One source produces a Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android client, although that path is secondary to the VCL
✅ Native Windows integration is direct: The Windows unit, COM, and the registry are reachable from the same code as the language
⚠️ The market the language fits best is now a legacy market: New Windows desktop development is a smaller share than web and service development
⚠️ The fit outside a GUI application is thin: A service, a web back end, or an embedded program is written against the RTL alone, with little framework support



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The curve is gentle for a Pascal or C-family developer: begin/end, a single-pass declaration order, and readable identifiers make the language quick to read
✅ The IDE teaches the framework interactively: Dropping a component and reading the generated code is the standard on-ramp
✅ A reader sees each name’s type at hand: var, const, and type sections and typed parameters put the declaration beside its use
⚠️ The framework is a second subject beyond the language: The VCL/FireMonkey object model, the streaming of a form (.dfm), and the RTTI layer are knowledge the language does not imply
⚠️ The Windows mental model is required for real work: The message loop, handles, threads, and COM are needed as soon as the program touches the system



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keywords delimit blocks and the statements read as English: if ... then ... else, for ... do, while ... do, and begin/end
✅ Identifiers are case-insensitive and the layout is free: The compiler ignores case, and the IDE’s formatter keeps the source uniform across a team
⚠️ The language is verbose: Each declaration opens a var, const, or type section, and a unit needs an interface, an implementation, and a closing end. even for a few statements (S1)
⚠️ try and begin pairs nest into an end ladder: An ordinary routine with two try/finally blocks ends in a run of end; lines
⚠️ Attributes and compiler directives share the bracket notation: [Weak], {$IFDEF}, and {$WARN} mix the language and the compiler controls in the same text



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework ships with the toolchain: DUnitX, and the older DUnit, provide fixtures, attributes, and assertions, and the IDE runs the suite
✅ The debugger steps through a test and shows the fault: The IDE debugger shows the call stack, the locals, and the thread state at the failure
✅ Assert is in the RTL: Assert(cond) raises EAssertionFailed when assertions are enabled, so a precondition is stated in the code
⚠️ The checks that would catch a fault are off by default: Range and overflow checking ({$R+}, {$Q+}) must be enabled per project, so an out-of-bounds index in a release build is undefined
⚠️ Assertions are compiled out of a release build: {$ASSERTIONS OFF} removes them, so their guarantee is a debug-time one
⚠️ Debugging is the vendor’s IDE’s: A command-line debug session is not the standard workflow, so a headless build server runs tests without the interactive state



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Memory safety is not guaranteed: Pointer, GetMem/FreeMem, System.Move, and PChar arithmetic are available, nothing marks the part of a program that uses them, and in that part the type system is not in the path, so its safety is the author’s claim
✅ Managed types carry their length and are checked when range checking is on: {$R+} makes an out-of-range index raise ERangeError, and a string or a dynamic array knows its own length
✅ There is no dynamic evaluation of source text: The language has no eval that compiles a string, and reflection reaches only published members through the RTTI, so an injection path needs the program to build the call itself
⚠️ The language offers no sandbox and no capability model: A program runs with the authority of the process, and the mitigations (DEP, ASLR, control-flow guard) are linker and loader options
❌ Range checking is off in the default release configuration; Int64 wraps the bound in silence (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds embed component-library and IDE state; no reproducible default exists. (Y1)
❌ Third-party component versions resolve from the installed library. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Third-party components carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The component market is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers component vendors. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ The VCL logging surface is application code. (Y6)
❌ An RTE dialog without a dump is the default failure face. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer beyond the compiler ships with the toolchain. (Y8)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs on the platforms the compiler releases target. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the toolchain: the vendor’s reference documents one compiler’s behavior, and no conformance suite exists for an independent implementation (Y17)
❌ No parser published: the grammar is diagrams in the reference, the compiler is closed, and no parser API ships (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Delphi’s design yields a middling core score, because its separating constructs sit beside its coupling ones. The interface section of a unit, a property, an event, and an interface type each decouple a consumer from an implementation, while the single-inheritance tree is the one hierarchy the language imposes. Main strengths: native compilation, a gentle Pascal-derived syntax, and a mature IDE and framework for Windows desktop work. Main weaknesses: exceptions are unchecked, a release is written rather than tied to scope, references are nilable with no ownership check, and the platform is one vendor’s commercial product in a declining market.

title: Elixir (1.20)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Elixir in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 79.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 90.6/100 · Engineering readiness 70.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing: A term carries its type at run time, so Map.get/2 on a list fails only when the call executes (T1)
❌ No declared types on functions: A def head names patterns, not types, and the language has no type parameter or generic (T5)
❌ No sum types in the type system: Alternatives are tagged tuples such as {:ok, value} and {:error, reason}, checked by pattern matching rather than by a type (T4)
❌ Dispatch is by run-time shape: A protocol or a pattern chooses a clause from the value it receives, so no static check selects the branch (T3)
✅ @spec and Dialyzer give optional static analysis: A success-typing pass detects a call whose arguments contradict the specification
⚠️ Gradual set-theoretic types are being added: The work is in progress, so the language is dynamic today



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Every value is immutable: A term cannot be changed in place, so construction never aliases mutable state
✅ defstruct declares the record shape: %User{name: "Ada"} builds a struct, and an unknown key is a compile-time error
✅ @enforce_keys validates at construction: A struct with required keys cannot be built without them
✅ The pipe operator decouples data flow from nesting: data |> parse() |> validate() reads left to right as a chain of transformations
✅ Processes hold state, not objects: A GenServer keeps its state inside its own process, and a caller reaches it by message
✅ Mutable state lives in a named process or table: Agent, ETS, and :persistent_term give shared state an explicit owner, so a reader can find it and an owner can delete it
✅ Nothing mutable is shared: terms move by value semantics, so a write has no second name to reach (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ BEAM collection is non-deterministic: A process collects its heap when it grows, so the program does not choose the moment (M2)
✅ Each process has a private heap: A collection pause is per-process and short, and there is no global stop-the-world collection
✅ No manual deallocation: The VM reclaims memory, and a program never frees a term
✅ Large binaries live off-heap and are reference counted: A binary above the heap-binary threshold is shared between processes rather than copied
⚠️ A large live set costs more to collect: A long-lived GenServer that accumulates state pays a higher collection cost
⚠️ An ETS table lives outside the collector: The table persists until its owner deletes it or dies
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: BEAM’s atom-table exhaustion fails the node (documented), beyond the supervision tree’s restarts (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: raise and throw appear in no signature, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
✅ “Let it crash” plus supervision decouples recovery from business logic: A Supervisor restarts a failed child, so the recovery path is not interleaved with the normal path
✅ Tagged tuples are the idiom for an expected failure: {:ok, value} and {:error, reason} keep the failure inside the returned value
✅ with composes a chain of expected results: Each <- clause fails through to the else branch without nesting
✅ Links and monitors make propagation explicit: spawn_link and Process.monitor define which process observes a failure
⚠️ The tagged-tuple convention is not a type: Nothing forces a caller to match the :error case, so the discipline is social



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Processes are the unit of concurrency: A BEAM process shares no memory and communicates by message, so a race between processes cannot occur
✅ The BEAM schedules preemptively: A long computation is reduced and rescheduled, so one process cannot block a scheduler
✅ OTP gives structured, supervised concurrency: Task, Task.Supervisor, GenServer, and Supervisor are library primitives over the process model
✅ Immutability removes locks from the model: A message carries a value, and the receiver holds its own copy of the terms
✅ Task.async and Task.await pair a spawn with a result: The caller collects results without a hand-written join
⚠️ A slow consumer accumulates messages: An unbounded mailbox grows until the process is restarted



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The BEAM is the only requirement: Elixir code runs on any platform that runs an Erlang VM
✅ Erlang interop is direct: Elixir calls Erlang modules and libraries without a binding layer
✅ Releases bundle the runtime: mix release packages the BEAM, the application, and its dependencies into one deployable
✅ Nerves keeps the same model on embedded devices: The build produces a firmware image, and the runtime model is unchanged
⚠️ The runtime is not a native binary: A release carries the VM, so the artefact is larger than a compiled C program



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic typing is a deliberate trade: It buys the flexibility of pattern matching and hot code loading at the cost of static checking
Ruby-like syntax is a familiarity choice: It lowers the barrier for developers from a scripting background
LiveView keeps the UI state on the server: This is a deliberate architectural choice that removes client JavaScript, not a language mechanism
Nerves adds an embedded build layer: The added layer is scope, not coupling
Macros are a metaprogramming power: A macro rewrites code at compile time, and that power carries the usual hygiene discipline
The BEAM is a virtual machine, not an operating system: The runtime boundary is scope, not a coupling defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The BEAM is a mature bytecode VM with a JIT: BeamAsm, added in OTP 24, compiles hot code, so bytecode is not always interpreted
✅ Excellent for I/O-bound workloads: Hundreds of thousands of processes can wait on I/O without one thread each
✅ Per-process collection avoids global pauses: A collection affects one process, not the whole system
✅ Reduction-based scheduling keeps latency even: No process starves another for long
⚠️ Weaker for CPU-bound computation: The BEAM trails native-compiled languages on a tight numeric loop
⚠️ A NIF runs on a scheduler thread: A long-running native function can block other processes on the same scheduler



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Hex.pm is a mature registry and mix is the build tool: Dependency resolution, build tasks, and release packaging come from one toolchain
✅ Phoenix, Ecto, and LiveView cover web applications end to end: Routing, database access, and server-rendered UI are provided by one family
✅ Erlang libraries are usable through interop: The OTP libraries arrive with the runtime
✅ Livebook gives executable notebooks: Interactive exploration and live documentation are part of the ecosystem
❌ The ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP: One framework family dominates, so alternatives are few (Ec6)
⚠️ The library count is smaller than the JVM or npm: Fewer general-purpose packages exist
✅ The NIF ABI is versioned and checked at load on the BEAM runtime it runs on [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored terms cross on the BEAM promise: Elixir encodes terms in the external term format, and the format’s version rule is published — systems as of R16B decode the current default encoding [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ mix.exs pins an Elixir requirement: A project states the version range it needs, and mix enforces it
✅ The BEAM is stable across decades: Code written years ago continues to run
✅ Deprecations warn before removal: The compiler emits a deprecation warning ahead of a change
✅ mix format settles style across the ecosystem: One formatter removes style drift
⚠️ A hot upgrade needs a state migration callback: code_change/3 must convert old state to the new shape, so an upgrade is a design task
❌ Build variants multiply: an if in a module body evaluates at compile time, so only the taken branch becomes code, and its condition comes from the build configuration (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for real-time web: Phoenix Channels push over WebSockets, and LiveView renders on the server
✅ Excellent fit for distributed, fault-tolerant systems: OTP supervision and the distribution protocol cover process and node failure
✅ Nerves deploys to embedded devices: The same runtime runs on a device image
✅ Back-pressure pipelines are a supported domain: GenStage and Broadway build pipeline stages over processes
⚠️ Not aimed at CPU-bound numerics: The BEAM is not designed for tight numerical loops



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Ruby-like syntax lowers the barrier: Developers from Ruby or another scripting language recognise the form
✅ The documentation culture is excellent: HexDocs, guides, and doctests sit with the code
✅ The community is welcoming and growing: Questions are answered and the ecosystem keeps expanding
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the OTP behaviours, macros, and the process model must all be learned (L2)
⚠️ Macros and quote/unquote are hard: Metaprogramming is powerful and easy to misuse



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Ruby-inspired syntax is readable: The do/end block form and the keyword style read naturally
✅ The pipe operator reads as data flow: |> threads a value through a chain of calls
✅ Pattern matching replaces nested conditionals: A multi-clause function is a case analysis
✅ Structs and maps have literal syntax: %User{name: "Ada"} and %{key: value} build data directly
⚠️ Macros can hide the code they generate: A DSL built with macros is opaque without the expansion
⚠️ The pipe passes the first argument: An awkward argument order forces a wrapper function



1.2.7 Testing

✅ ExUnit ships with the language: mix test runs the suite with structured assertions and tagged tests
✅ Doctests run the examples in documentation: An iex> example in @doc is executed as a test
✅ Property-based testing is available: StreamData generates inputs from a property
✅ mix test --trace and coverage reporting are built in: Test order and line coverage are visible without extra tooling
❌ Errors surface at run time: Dynamic typing defers a type mistake to the executed path (G3)
⚠️ Testing concurrent code needs process-aware assertions: A test must wait for a message or a process state, so timing is a factor



1.2.8 Security

✅ Immutable data removes a class of shared-state faults: No two processes share a mutable value
✅ Process isolation contains a fault: A crashed process does not corrupt another process’s heap
✅ Pattern matching makes an unexpected shape fail loudly: A bad message raises a FunctionClauseError rather than corrupting state
⚠️ String.to_atom/1 on untrusted input can exhaust the atom table: Atoms are not collected, so untrusted conversion is a denial-of-service risk
⚠️ Code.eval_string/1 executes arbitrary code: Dynamic evaluation must be kept away from untrusted input
⚠️ A NIF and a Port reach unsafe code: Native code can break the BEAM’s safety guarantees

Verdict: Elixir’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling. Immutable terms, the process model, and OTP supervision remove shared-memory races, turn failure into a supervision event, and keep state inside a process instead of in shared objects. Main strengths: the pipe operator and pattern matching decouple data flow and case analysis, the BEAM supports code loading without stopping the system, and the runtime is proven by decades of fault-tolerant operation. Main weaknesses: the language is dynamically typed, so a type fault surfaces at run time; exceptions are unchecked; collection is non-deterministic; and the ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925201
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

title: F# (9)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses F# in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 77.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 88.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Discriminated unions separate cases: Like Haskell ADTs
✅ Type providers decouple data access from code: SQL, JSON, etc. accessed via types generated from schemas
⚠️ OOP interop allows inheritance coupling: Can use C# classes with inheritance and other C# patterns, coupling subclasses to base classes
❌ Nulls from .NET: Nullable references from C# libraries reintroduce null-checking coupling
❌ Inherits the CLR rule: char is a UTF-16 code unit (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Immutable records by default: Construction doesn’t couple to mutation
✅ With-copy syntax decouples updates: { person with Age = 30 } doesn’t modify original
⚠️ Can use .NET constructors with side effects: Interop allows coupled construction
❌ Mutable cells exist: Can create ref cells, coupling to mutable state



1.1.3 Memory

✅ .NET GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: Fewer mutable references, cleaner collection
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Non-deterministic pauses, though .NET GC is mature
⚠️ Can use IDisposable from .NET: Manual resource management via use keyword couples cleanup
✅ Garbage collection handles closures: Captured references are traced by the .NET GC, not by reference counting



1.1.4 Error

✅ Result type separates success/failure: Result<'T, 'Error> makes errors explicit
⚠️ Can throw .NET exceptions: Interop allows unchecked exceptions
✅ Railway-oriented programming pattern: The community embraces this functional error-handling style where success and failure paths are composed like parallel railroad tracks using Result types
❌ A fault ends the process: an unhandled exception in any thread terminates the process (documented by the runtime) (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Async workflows decouple async from sync: async { } blocks separate concerns
✅ MailboxProcessor for actors: Message passing decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ .NET threads allow shared mutable state: Interop permits coupling



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Cross-platform .NET runtime: The same F# assembly runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows
✅ Open-source compiler: The F# compiler (dotnet/fsharp) is MIT-licensed and developed in the open as a .NET Foundation project
✅ Freely available, cross-platform toolchain: The dotnet SDK and NuGet run on Linux, macOS, and Windows at no cost, and Visual Studio is optional rather than required
✅ Multiple compile targets: Fable compiles F# to JavaScript, so the language reaches the browser as well as the .NET runtime



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Functional Purity vs. .NET Interop: Can’t enforce purity when calling C# code
Type Safety vs. Practical Libraries: .NET libraries use null, exceptions, mutation—F# must accommodate
Railway-Oriented Programming vs. Exceptions: Community promotes Result types but .NET uses exceptions
Immutability by Default vs. Performance: Persistent data structures slower than .NET mutable collections
FP Culture vs. OOP Platform: F# encourages FP but runs on OOP-first platform




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JIT compilation: Fast steady-state performance
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, but tunable
✅ Tail call optimization: Decouples recursion from stack size
✅ Immutability optimized: Persistent data structures perform well
⚠️ Startup time: JIT warmup couples cold start to performance



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Full .NET ecosystem access: Massive library availability
✅ dotnet CLI standardized: Consistent build experience
✅ Excellent IDE support: Visual Studio, Rider, VSCode with Ionide
⚠️ Some .NET libraries couple to OOP patterns: Not all libraries are functional-friendly
✅ NuGet package management: Well-established, reliable
✅ CLR metadata carries a published promise: F# compiles to IL under the runtime’s standardised format [5], [6] (Ec8)
❌ Stored payloads bind to the runtime: F# runs on the .NET runtime, and from .NET 8 BinaryFormatter throws across nearly all project types, with .NET 9 removing the in-box implementation [7], [8] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Strong backward compatibility: Code rarely breaks between versions
✅ Follows .NET release cadence: Predictable updates
✅ Active development: Regular improvements and new features
⚠️ Coupled to .NET platform evolution: Must follow .NET’s direction
❌ Build variants multiply: #if directives select which declarations compile, with the flags set at the command line (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend services: Async, type safety, .NET performance
✅ Strong for data analysis: Type providers for data access
✅ Great for financial/scientific: Immutability, correctness, units of measure
⚠️ Web frontend less common: Fable exists but smaller ecosystem than mainstream
✅ Cross-platform: .NET Core runs everywhere



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentler than Haskell: More pragmatic, less abstract
✅ Good docs: F# for Fun and Profit, official docs
⚠️ Requires functional mindset shift: For OOP developers
✅ Can adopt gradually: Mix FP and OOP as needed



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean, concise: Significant whitespace, minimal boilerplate
✅ Pipe operator: |> decouples data flow
⚠️ Type inference limitations: Sometimes need explicit annotations
✅ Pattern matching expressive: Clear, readable



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Standard .NET testing tools: xUnit, NUnit, MSTest
✅ FsCheck property testing: Built-in support
✅ Excellent debugger: Visual Studio debugger is world-class
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No hidden state



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: .NET GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safe: Strong static typing
✅ Immutability by default: Prevents many mutation bugs
⚠️ C# interop escape hatches: mutable, null, unsafe code possible
❌ Inherits the CLR rule: integer arithmetic wraps unchecked by default (Q4)

title: GML (2026.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses GML in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 54.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 63.3/100 · Engineering readiness 41.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Variables are dynamically typed: A name takes any value, and typeof reads the type at run time (T1)
❌ A script is a value: script_execute and a method variable dispatch at run time (T3)
❌ There are no sum types: A state is an integer and a switch (T4)
❌ There are no namespaces: Every script, object, and global lives in one project scope (T6)
❌ There are no generics: A data structure holds any value (T5)
❌ An unset variable is undefined: The type does not carry the check (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ An instance’s Create event is its constructor: The engine calls it once
❌ Instance and global variables are shared by default: A global. variable is reachable from every object (C1)
❌ A variable is mutable by default: A struct is the only value with a copy semantic (C2)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: script execution by name (with(script), asset_get_index) resolves the string to code at run time (C7)
❌ Scripts and objects initialize in room-load order; the source names no sequence (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The runtime frees an instance: instance_destroy and the collector release memory
❌ There is no scope-exit release: A data structure or a surface is freed by a call (M3)
❌ Aliasing is unrestricted: Two references can hold one struct, and nothing marks the owner (M4)



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no exception path: A failed call writes a message and continues, and show_error aborts (Er1)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The game loop is the only thread: Everything runs on one thread and one frame (K1)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A program runs inside the GameMaker runtime: The engine provides the loop, the renderer, and the objects (P1)
✅ The same project exports to many targets: Windows, macOS, Linux, HTML5, mobile, and consoles



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The engine buys the loop and the renderer: A game starts from objects and events, not from a window
The project scope is flat: A global is reachable from every object, and the name is the contract
The runtime is the platform: An extension is a DLL or a marketplace asset, and it is not portable
The language follows the engine’s cadence: A project pins an LTS line, and an update is a decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ The default target is a bytecode VM: The YoYo Compiler can emit C++ for a native build (R1)
✅ A native build is available: The YYC path trades a long build for native speed



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The engine is proprietary: GameMaker is licensed, and the source is closed (Ec4)
❌ The IDE is the toolchain: The editor, the debugger, and the build are one application (Ec5)
❌ The engine is the ecosystem: A library outside the asset marketplace is rare (Ec6)
✅ The asset marketplace is the package source: An extension is installed from the IDE
❌ An extension binds to the toolchain: GameMaker documents extension packages built against the IDE and runner release [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored projects cross on a documented conversion: the IDE detects a pre-2.3.0 project on import, converts it, and generates a compatibility report to check [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The engine ships on a monthly and an LTS channel: A project can pin a stable line
⚠️ The language follows the engine: A runtime rewrite can change an idiom
❌ The preprocessor selects the compiled source: #if, #ifdef, #elif, #else, #endif, defined(), and the configuration macros decide which code the compiler keeps, and the definitions live in the project configuration, not in the source the reader sees (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is 2D games: The engine’s objects, sprites, and rooms are the model (D1)
❌ The event model sets the architecture: A game is a set of objects and event handlers (D3)



1.2.5 Learning

✅ A beginner can ship a game quickly: Drag-and-drop actions and a small language



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Two dialects share the editor: GML Visual and GML code state the same action (S2)
✅ The syntax is C-like: Braces, semicolons, and functions



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The debugger steps through an instance: Watches and breakpoints are in the IDE



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ A dynamically typed value fails late
✅ There is no eval: The engine does not run a string as code
❌ Numbers are doubles: integers above 2^53 change value in silence (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The build embeds the project and the runtime: The artifact is not byte-identical across machines (Y1)
❌ The engine version is the dependency: A project records the runtime version (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ An extension is installed without a signature check (Y3)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ There is no tracing standard: show_debug_message writes to the console (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The IDE reports a compile error in place



1.3.5 Interop

✅ Extensions bind native code in process on the desktop targets. (Y9)
✅ The export targets are the maintained portable targets. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ One vendor governs the engine and the language (Y11)
❌ The language specification is the manual (Y12)
❌ Semantics rest on the shipped runtime: the manual documents the IDE’s and runner’s behavior, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)
❌ No parser published: the manual documents the syntax in prose, the compiler is closed, and no parser API ships (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ No independent energy or time benchmark for the language is recorded.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse public training data: models write it less reliably than a mainstream language [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Go (1.27)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Go in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 74.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 95.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Implicit interfaces radical decoupling: No declaration of implementation, duck typing at compile time
✅ Composition over inheritance: No inheritance, only struct embedding
✅ Small interfaces: Convention is single-method interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer)
✅ Generics (stable since 1.18): Type parameters eliminate interface{} casts — slices.Sort, maps.Clone, cmp.Or are type-safe (note: sync.Map remains a non-generic any-keyed type)
✅ Generic methods (1.27): A method can declare its own type parameters, so a helper that belongs to one type no longer needs a package-level function
✅ Range-over-func (1.23): Custom iteration patterns via iter.Seq[T] decouple iteration protocol from data structure
⚠️ No higher-kinded types: Generics are first-order type parameters only
✅ min/max/clear builtins (1.21): Built-in operations eliminate unnecessary function coupling
❌ Nil everywhere, and no sum types: nil pointers and nil interfaces couple code to nil checks, and the language has no sum type to replace them (T4)
⚠️ Interfaces can be nil with non-nil value: (nil, *T) couples interface semantics



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Zero values make sense: Default initialization doesn’t couple to constructors
✅ Constructors are conventions: NewX() functions, not special syntax
⚠️ Can couple to package-level state: init() functions run at import
❌ Global package state: Package-level variables couple to initialization order
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the specification states map iteration receives no order guarantee, and the runtime randomizes the seed deliberately (C5)
❌ One value, many names: slices and maps share backing structures — append to a slice can write a buffer another name reads, and the parameter type names a value, not the sharing (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Concurrent mark-sweep GC with sub-millisecond pause targets
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ Escape analysis optimizes: Stack allocation when possible, decouples from explicit allocation
✅ Profile-guided optimization (1.22+): Compiler uses runtime profiles to optimize, decoupling performance from manual tuning
⚠️ Defer couples cleanup to function exit: Not immediate, but predictable
✅ Simple memory model: No complex ownership rules



1.1.4 Error

✅ Explicit error returns: func foo() (Result, error) makes errors visible
❌ No error composition: Can’t map/flatMap errors natively, so call sites repeat if err != nil; generics enable Result types but not idiomatically
⚠️ Panic exists but rare: Explicit, but not in type system
⚠️ errors.Join (1.20): Can combine multiple errors, improving composition slightly
❌ A fault ends the program: an unrecovered panic terminates the program (documented), and the panicking path unwinds the goroutine it ran on (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Goroutines separate concurrency: Lightweight, easy to spawn
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples
✅ Select decouples multiplexing: Wait on multiple channels independently
✅ Structured logging (slog, 1.21): Decouples logging concerns from application logic
⚠️ Can share memory: Mutexes allow traditional coupling, but discouraged



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Open-source toolchain: The Go compiler and standard library are BSD-3 licensed and developed in the open
✅ Alternative implementations: Gccgo (GCC front end) and TinyGo (microcontrollers, WebAssembly) implement Go independently of the main toolchain
✅ Portable binaries: A Go program builds to a static native binary with no installed runtime or virtual machine
✅ Broad cross-compilation: One toolchain emits Linux, macOS, Windows, and WebAssembly binaries by setting GOOS and GOARCH



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The language is deliberately small: Exceptions, operator overloading, and pattern matching are left out, so programs are longer and each construct is plain — a scope decision
One formatter settles style: gofmt writes a single canonical layout, trading some expression for a uniform codebase — a tooling convention
Tooling ships in the go command: Formatting, testing, vetting, and documentation come as one package, so the choice of tools is made by the toolchain rather than by the team
The Go 1 promise freezes the standard library: The compatibility guarantee keeps old code building and makes early API decisions permanent — a stability trade
The standard library is the framework: net/http and encoding/json are used directly rather than through a third-party layer, a design choice whose cost is the conveniences such a layer would add




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Fast compilation: Extremely fast builds
✅ Fast startup: No JIT warmup
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic but low-latency (R2)
✅ Predictable: Simple performance model
✅ Static binary: Single executable
✅ Small allocations are size-specialised (1.27): The compiler calls an allocation routine sized for the object, which removes up to 30 percent of the cost of a small allocation



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Standard tooling: Go build, go test, go fmt
⚠️ Project-local conventions: Build tags, code generation, and layout conventions grew outside the toolchain, so each project’s tooling is partly its own (Ec2)
✅ Great stdlib: Batteries included
✅ Excellent docs: Godoc, tour, effective go
✅ Growing ecosystem: Good library availability
✅ Cross-compilation: Easy to build for different platforms
✅ The standard library keeps absorbing the common dependency (1.27): encoding/json/v2, a uuid package, and the post-quantum crypto/mldsa package remove three third-party dependencies
❌ The plugin path is unpromised: plugin.Open requires the application and its plugins to be built with the same toolchain version and flags [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Go 1 compatibility promise: Extremely stable
✅ No breaking changes: Code from 2012 still compiles
✅ Conservative evolution: Generics took 10 years
✅ Predictable: No surprises
⚠️ A removed setting stops being accepted (1.27): The compiler now reads a removed GODEBUG setting only at its final default value and fails on an older one, and go no longer fetches from bzr
❌ Build variants multiply: //go:build constraints select which files enter the build, so a package is a platform and tag outcome, not only a directory (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend services: Cloud-native standard
✅ Great for CLI tools: Fast startup, single binary
✅ Strong for networking: Stdlib excellent
❌ Poor for frontend: Not applicable
⚠️ Systems programming: GC limits use cases



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Extremely gentle: Simple, small language
✅ Quick to productivity: Can be productive in days
✅ Excellent docs: Tour, Effective Go
✅ Few concepts: Generics are additive; core language remains small and learnable



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Simple, readable: Minimal syntax
❌ Verbose error handling: if err != nil everywhere
✅ Opinionated: Gofmt eliminates style debates
⚠️ Limited abstraction: Sometimes too simple



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Built-in testing: Go test standard
✅ Benchmarking: Go test -bench
✅ Profiling: Pprof built-in
✅ Delve debugger: Good debugging experience
✅ Table-driven tests: Idiomatic, clear
✅ Leaked goroutines are a profile (1.27): The goroutineleak profile reports a goroutine blocked on a primitive that can never unblock, so a leak is visible in the runtime’s own output



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ Nil everywhere: Panic on nil dereference
✅ Type safe: Static typing
⚠️ Error handling: Easy to ignore errors
❌ The specification defines integer arithmetic as wraparound (module 2^size) (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ go.mod is the contract the go command reads and validates, with the lockfile it writes. (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ The checksum database signs the module graph, and go.sum records it. (Y3)
✅ Module paths are namespaced by repository. (Y4)
✅ The project publishes security advisories with CVE mappings. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ runtime/trace and net/http/pprof ship in the standard library. (Y5)
✅ log/slog ships structured logging in the standard library. (Y6)
✅ Panics print full goroutine stack traces by default. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the toolchain; delve is a separate project. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ cgo is the in-process foreign interface to C. (Y9)
✅ Cross-compilation to the common GOOS/GOARCH pairs needs no toolchain changes. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Evolution runs through a public proposal process under Google stewardship. (Y11)
✅ The Go specification is public. (Y12)
✅ The suite gccgo runs is the published check on the specification. (Y17)
✅ The compiler and standard library are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [9], [10].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Go’s implicit interfaces provide exceptionally low coupling by decoupling implementation from declaration without explicit implements clauses. Goroutines and channels separate concurrency from shared-memory synchronization. Generics, stable since 1.18, now extend to methods (1.27), so a type can carry its own generic helper. Range-over-func enables custom iteration without coupling to built-in loop constructs. Main strength: simplicity prevents complex coupling from emerging. Main weakness: nil is still everywhere, error handling does not compose, and the language has no sum types or pattern matching.

title: G# (0.5.212)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses G# in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 79.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.3/100 · Engineering readiness 81.9/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ T? is a distinct type with nil, ?., ??, ??=, and flow narrowing: if let, guard let, and while let strip the nullable layer, and a violated non-null assumption fails at a written !!
✅ Null-safety gate at the call site: a nullable value at a non-nullable parameter is an error (GS0154), so an imported T! (platform) reference cannot flow unchecked into a non-null position
✅ Generics are reified end to end: GenericParam rows, TypeSpec encodings, and closed instantiations land in the emitted metadata, so a type argument survives into the artifact
✅ A package scopes names, imports are selective, and visibility is declared: package, import (+ aliases and per-file static imports), and public/internal/private are real boundaries
✅ Polymorphism without an inheritance chain: interfaces with default methods and static-virtual slots, explicit qualifiers func (IFoo) M, and adapt[I](source) structural adaptation; classes are sealed unless declared open
✅ Payload-bearing enums are discriminated unions: enum Shape { Circle(r float64); Square(s float64) }, sealed hierarchies, and pattern switches the compiler checks for exhaustiveness
✅ The numeric lattice is width-named: canonical int8–int64/uint8–uint64 names with binder-resolved friendly aliases; lossless widening, explicit T(x) narrowing, constant-expression narrowing only as in C#
❌ Reflection reaches private members through the ordinary .NET runtime APIs, and object boxes any value, so a declared boundary is not a ceiling; the charge rests on this reflective reach, the half the C# page also charges — the erasure half does not apply here (see the reified-generics bullet above) (T7)
❌ Signatures carry no effect set: a throw needs no declaration, and a call’s I/O, mutation, suspension, and lock footprint is read from its body (T12)
❌ await colours the function that spells it: the function compiles to a ValueTask state machine, suspend func pins the shape at fixed-shape signatures, and a suspending call made from a plain function blocks with warning GS0558 (T13)
❌ @DllImport/@LibraryImport, @MarshalAs, and unmanaged function pointers are hand-written ABI promises: layout, marshalling, lifetime, and calling convention land outside the type system (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Every binding states its kind: const (compile-time constant), let (immutable binding), var (mutable); the form is spelled per site, not defaulted
⚠️ let freezes the rebinding, not the graph behind it: the referenced value stays writable, so write permission is read from the declaration form the team chooses
✅ Value aggregates build in place: struct literals, adapt[I](ref handle), slice[T] views, stackalloc, and structural projection Target{ ...source, Member: override } construct over storage the caller chose
✅ data class/data struct synthesize equality, deconstruction, and with-copy (C# record ABI since 0.5, ADR-0199); classes carry primary constructors and init blocks



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The CLR garbage collector decides when memory returns: the release schedule belongs to the runtime, not to the program (M2)
❌ A managed[T] handle provides GC reachability, not exclusivity, synchronization, native ownership or race freedom; a slice[T] view retains the entire owner array (M4)
✅ using let binds a disposable to scope exit, and defer call(...) schedules a call at scope exit with a cancellation grace budget
⚠️ The by-ref discipline is a scope rule, not an ownership analysis: ref/out/in/scoped parameters, ref locals and ref returns are checked by a simple non-escaping rule; the full ref-safe-to-escape analysis is not implemented



1.1.4 Error

❌ Failures are CLR exceptions with no signature list: no throws clause exists, so the set of failures a call can raise is discovered on the path that raises it (Er2)
✅ try/catch/finally with four catch forms, when filters emitted as real CLR filter regions, and rethrow: a detected failure travels to a handler through a language construct
✅ The shipped Gsharp.Extensions.Optional composes T? through expressions: Map, FlatMap, OrElse, OrCompute, IfPresent, Filter, and OrThrow carry the absent value as a value (Gsharp.Extensions is referenced automatically; imports stay explicit per file)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ A go task shares the parent’s heap by default: closures capture the enclosing bindings, and a plain map[K,V] is explicitly not goroutine-safe (K2)
❌ The ordering discipline lives outside the type: the concurrency guide prescribes lock, SyncMap[K,V], and BCL concurrent types, and nothing proves the discipline or detects a missing lock; the project’s own contract checks are named as the substitute for a race detector (K3)
✅ scope { } joins its go children before control moves on, cancels siblings on first failure, and aggregates failures as a ScopeException; an async let binding cannot be stored, returned, or collected
✅ Channels, select, and directional in/out handles are language constructs with no import: chan[T] is System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T>



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The language has one implementation: a bespoke self-hosted compiler (written in G# since 0.5.3) with Roslyn deliberately kept out of the compiler process (ADR-0027); cs2gs migrates C# source, it is not a second compiler, so every consumer works on one compiler’s release cycle (P2)
✅ The emitted artifact is standard ECMA-335 PE with Portable PDB: it runs on CoreCLR and Mono, on Windows, Linux, and macOS, and the compiler cross-targets net8.0/net9.0/net10.0 through an isolated metadata-load context



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Nullability checking is a compiler option: /nullability:enabled|platform-types|oblivious sets the enforcement level per compilation, so a project states its own contract — the incremental adoption path C# used
Pre-1.0 churn is managed by a written policy: diagnostic IDs are never reused, retired spellings ship replacement diagnostics, breaking changes require an ADR plus migration guidance, and production is told to pin exact versions
The language-defined library stays deliberately small, so BCL interop carries the everyday APIs; the guide’s rule is “use CLR interop instead of wrappers”
Concurrency inherits the Go shape — go, channels, select — onto CLR channel primitives: a language-level spawn with chan[T] identical to System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T> (adapters stay spare), paid in rendezvous and capacity decisions a plain spawn never asks
data class/data struct compile to the C# record ABI (ADR-0199): a G# data type and a C# record are shape-compatible for the BCL and for C# consumers that deconstruct or pattern-match them, at the cost of committing G# data types to C#’s record semantics rather than its own
The compiler owns its emit path end to end: the metadata writer, the PDB writer, and the binder are the project’s own code — independence from the platform’s compiler stack, paid in maintaining all three




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ GC pauses are part of the timing budget: server and background GC modes bound the pause and do not remove it, and the collector decides when it arrives (R2)
❌ The CLR tiers its compilation, so the first requests measure slower than steady state and a benchmark has to agree on a warm-up (R3)
✅ Every driver emits CIL: the single-file gsc run, the gsi REPL, and the SDK build share the emitter; the tree-walking evaluator was removed, and the emitted executable is the differential oracle for the other drivers



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is young and small: 55 releases since the first alpha (2026-05-29), six first-party NuGet packages, and a handful of third-party G# libraries, so a G# project more often writes what it needs than finds it, and the hiring market is correspondingly small (Ec3)
✅ The library supply behind it is .NET’s: any NuGet package is reachable through interop, and the guide’s rule is to use CLR interop instead of wrappers
❌ Stored payloads bind to the runtime: G# emits .NET assemblies, and the .NET runtime that reads serialized payloads states the break: NotSupportedException from .NET 8, in-box implementation removed in .NET 9 [10], [11] (Ec9)
❌ The assembly boundary carries no release promise: the CLI standard fixes the format, and the language’s own policy declines API stability before 1.0 — a consumer recompiles after a compiler upgrade, and production pins an exact version (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Pre-1.0 evolution reaches the source: the 0.5 line retired the chan T spelling (GS0567), the Go-style built-ins (GS0566), record (GS0535), and := (GS0305), and array length became part of the type, so a program written on 0.4 is edited, not recompiled, on 0.5 (V1)
⚠️ What changed: 0.5 adopted the C# record ABI for data class and data struct (ADR-0199), so the synthesized ToString, equality, and PrintMembers output of unchanged source changed with the toolchain; a record-shaped consumer that prints a data type sees the 0.4 text until it edits. Why: interop parity with C# consumers — the record shape is what BCL and C# code already understands. How a deployment reverses it: pin the toolchain to a pre-0.5 release (the compatibility policy instructs pinning exact versions for production), which restores the 0.4 synthesized surface; a pinned deployment never sees the change (V5)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The target is ordinary .NET application work: console, library, web, and TUI samples ship in the templates, and the Trail tutorial builds a worker-pool inventory app from the language’s own constructs



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Several paradigms arrive at once: Go-shaped concurrency, Kotlin/Swift-shaped data and nullability, CLR-shaped members, and the unsafe/span/ref machinery; one shape can be modelled as struct, data struct, data class, inline struct, anonymous object, or adapt[I] wrapper, so “the way we do it here” is a written team convention the language will not narrow (L2)
✅ The reference material is unusually complete for a pre-1.0 language: a normative specification with an EBNF appendix, a 512-ID GS#### diagnostics catalogue with cause and remedy per ID, a feature matrix with explicit Partial and Removed rows, four bridge guides (C#, Go, Kotlin, Swift), and 215 recorded ADRs



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ The grammar is embedded in the normative specification, so the syntax’s ground truth is one document.
⚠️ The surface borrows from several languages at once, and no inconsistency is charged.



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The official distribution ships a test path: Gsharp.Templates includes a gsharp-xunit template, the SDK integrates with dotnet test, and the Visual Studio extension carries native Test Explorer for xUnit, NUnit, and MSTest
✅ Debugging runs on Portable PDBs through the official VS Code and Visual Studio extensions (coreclr debug resolution, F5 managed debugging), with dotnet watch hot reload and a logical view for suspending functions



1.2.8 Security

❌ A lambda converts to Expression[TDelegate] when the target demands it, so a G# program can build and compile code at run time (unsupported shapes diagnose GS0473) (Q3)
⚠️ Memory safety is the CLR’s: unsafe, stackalloc, and cast[ptr](addr) bypass it by design — an opt-in escape hatch
✅ There is no eval facility and the evaluator backend was removed from the compiler: the only run-time code path is the typed expression tree the source writes, recorded by the Q3 mark — G# builds no code from untyped text
❌ .NET arithmetic wraps in silence by default: an operation whose result leaves the type’s range discards the overflow in unchecked context, the compiler’s default, and the checked context that raises System.OverflowException is the opt-in the program must ask for (Q4)

1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [12]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [13]. The project’s own compile-time measurements (self-host parity 1.04x time, ReadyToRun payload +31% on hello-world compiles) are reported with their provenance and expiry stated on the page.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse corpus: the first public release (2026-05-29) postdates the training data of public coding models, so models write it unreliably; the bridge guides and the cs2gs pipeline exist precisely because human C# and Go experience transfers better than model output.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: G# outscores the C# page on Core coupling (73.7 against 72.3; F# stays ahead of both): the constructs the inventory prices in its managed neighbours are the ones G# supplies — tasks joined by a scope, null checked by the type, payload enums with checked exhaustiveness, reified generics, declared module boundaries, defer and using release, deterministic emit, and a public specification. What it keeps is the platform’s invoice: the GC’s schedule and pauses, tiered compilation, function colouring (aggravated by inference), unchecked exceptions, and the hand-written ABI of P/Invoke. Its own youth is priced too: one compiler, a pre-1.0 contract, a small supply of libraries, solo governance, and no portable target. Main strengths: structured concurrency and nullability are language facts, and the documentation (spec, diagnostics catalogue, feature matrix, ADRs) is stronger than most post-1.0 languages. Main weaknesses: most of what sits below the Core score is ecosystem and governance, and those take years to buy.

title: Java (Java 1.4)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 64.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
❌ There are no generics (before Java 5): A collection holds Object, so every read is a cast the compiler cannot check (T5)
⚠️ Reflection reads the structure at run time: java.lang.reflect reaches a field or a method by name, outside the type check (T7)
❌ Null is in every reference: NullPointerException is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A closed set of cases is a class hierarchy, and a switch over an int constant is not checked for exhaustiveness (T4)
❌ A package is not a boundary: Every public class is reachable on the classpath, and nothing declares what a library exports (T11)
⚠️ Inheritance is available: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is final
❌ char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A field is mutable unless declared final: A setter is the ordinary way to change state (C2)
✅ A factory method states the contract: A static method returns a cached instance or a subtype
⚠️ A complex object needs a builder: A telescoping constructor couples the call site to the field order
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The JVM collects garbage: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ There is no manual deallocation: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
❌ A collection pause is part of the timing: The collector’s schedule is not the program’s (M2)
⚠️ The default collector stops the world: A serial collector pauses every thread
⚠️ JNI reaches outside the heap: A native call is unchecked
✅ The class entered the declared surface: Java 1.4 made OutOfMemoryError a thrown value (documented) — the memory-exhaustion patch moved the fault into the catchable class, and the JLS/JavaDoc contract names it (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A checked exception states a recoverable failure: throws IOException puts the failure in the signature
❌ An unchecked exception bypasses the signature: A RuntimeException can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
❌ Try-catch does not compose: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over (Er4)
⚠️ finally closes the resource: There is no try-with-resources before Java 7



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A Thread is the unit of concurrency: A task is a Runnable handed to a new thread, and a pool is hand-written
✅ wait and notify are the primitives: A monitor and a condition variable are in the language
⚠️ java.util.concurrent does not exist yet: A latch, a queue, and an executor are hand-written or bought
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: synchronized, volatile, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race (K3)
❌ A task holds a platform thread: Each task reserves one until it ends, so the number of tasks is bounded by the platform; Java 21’s virtual threads remove the cost (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The specifications are public: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Several vendor runtimes run the same class files: Sun, IBM, BEA, and Hewlett-Packard each shipped a JVM
✅ Bytecode is portable: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked exceptions vs. composition: Explicit errors do not compose natively, and a switch over a hierarchy is not checked for exhaustiveness
Backward compatibility vs. modern features: Old codebases lag behind the language, and the 1990s APIs stay in service
Null as default vs. safety: Every reference can be null, and nothing in the type marks the check
A collection holds Object: A read is a cast, so the element type is a convention the compiler cannot check
Inheritance vs. composition: A hierarchy is the only way to express a closed set of cases, and the compiler does not check it




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The JIT optimises the hot path: A method is compiled after it proves hot
⚠️ A GC pause is part of the timing: The collector decides when memory returns (R2)
⚠️ Startup pays for interpretation: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles (R3)
✅ The JDK ships a profiler: hprof and a thread dump are in the distribution



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Ant builds the classpath: A build is an XML script, and a dependency is a jar in a directory
⚠️ An application server is the deployment target: J2EE and EJB set the architecture
⚠️ The ecosystem carries old APIs: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one (Ec7)
✅ The IDE is mature: IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse compile and debug in 2002
✅ The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [4] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A class file from an older release still runs
✅ A feature release was deliberate: Java 1.4 was one of the multi-year releases, and it added assertions and NIO
⚠️ There is no preview mechanism: An experimental feature is a flag or an incubator module



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend and enterprise work: The standard choice for a large service
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
⚠️ A rich client is Swing, and the web path is an applet: A browser plugin runs it, and the plugin is a support burden
⚠️ Systems programming is out of reach: A collector and a managed runtime

✅ Widely taught: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
✅ The documentation is exhaustive: Javadoc and the tutorials
