title: Tcl (9.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Tcl in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 70.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 87.5/100 · Engineering readiness 49.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static type checking: A variable holds any value and a command converts its arguments when it runs, so a type error appears at the point of use rather than at compile time (T1)
❌ No sum types and no generics: A choice between alternatives is a string, a list, or a dict with a discriminating key, and a proc declares no type parameter, so neither the alternative read nor the types a body expects are checked (T4, T5)
❌ No null-safety: There is no null type; an empty string, an empty list, and an unset variable are distinct states, and $x on an unset variable aborts the script (T10)
❌ One global namespace and no module boundary: A proc declared at the top level is a global command, namespace eval is opt-in, and source evaluates a file into the current interpreter without restricting what that file makes visible (T6, T11)
❌ A protocol is not a declared type: TclOO, in the core since 8.6, provides classes, mixins, and multiple inheritance, so a shared protocol is captured by a class hierarchy or a mixin rather than by an interface the interpreter checks (T9)
✅ A value’s subtype is inspectable: string is and the expr conversions such as int(), double(), and boolean() let a script test a value before it is used



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global state appears at the first assignment: At the top level a name becomes a global variable when it is assigned, so two scripts in one interpreter share those variables (C1)
❌ Nothing is immutable: set is the only declaration a variable receives, and it can reassign or unset the value at any time (C2)
❌ No constructor or validation hook: A value is whatever a command stored, and a proc cannot reject a malformed argument unless it checks by hand (C4)
✅ proc gives a body its own local scope: A procedure is a named command with a parameter list, and its parameters and locals do not touch a caller’s variables unless global, variable, or upvar says so
✅ namespace eval gives a scope of its own: A namespace holds its own variables and commands, so a package need not write into the global scope
⚠️ upvar and uplevel reach into the caller’s frame: A procedure that binds a caller’s variable, or evaluates in the caller’s scope, depends on where it was called from, and global and variable make a shared variable explicit but still shared



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The interpreter owns the heap: There is no allocate or free command, and a script never names an address
✅ A value is reclaimed when its last reference goes away: Reference counting releases a Tcl_Obj without a lifetime written in the script
✅ The dual representation keeps a compiled form beside the string: A Tcl_Obj holds its string and, once used as a list or an integer, an internal representation that is reused
✅ A C extension allocates through the interpreter: An extension uses Tcl_Alloc and Tcl_Free, so the interpreter’s accounting still applies
⚠️ A reference cycle is not reclaimed by counting alone: Two objects that reference each other are released only by the interpreter’s cycle collection, and a cycle held by an extension is not collected at all
⚠️ Taking the string form discards the internal representation: An operation that needs the string regenerates it, so a hot loop can pay the same conversion more than once



1.1.4 Error

❌ A failure can be ignored by design: catch returns a status and nothing requires the caller to test it, so an unchecked return value discards the failure (Er3)
✅ Every failure is a value: catch returns a status such as ok, error, return, break, or continue, together with the result and the error options
✅ errorInfo and errorCode carry the detail: After an error the interpreter records the stack trace and a machine-readable code such as POSIX ENOENT
✅ error raises and return -code states a status: A command states the status it wants to propagate to its caller
⚠️ A handler that matches the message text is bound to the wording: The message is a string, and errorCode is the documented field to test instead
⚠️ catch also catches return and break: A nested return arrives as a status, so it must be passed on deliberately rather than by accident



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ I/O is a channel: chan reads and writes a stream, so a program composes I/O without naming a file descriptor
✅ after and vwait give an event loop: A callback runs on the interpreter’s event loop, and the script does not block the process while it waits
✅ Coroutines are in the core since Tcl 8.6: coroutine, yield, and tailcall express a suspendable computation as an ordinary command
✅ Threads are available when the core is built with them: Each thread runs its own interpreter and threads exchange values through a thread-safe channel queue rather than shared variables
⚠️ A script runs on the thread that calls it: One Tcl_Interp is not usable from two threads at once, so state is partitioned per thread
⚠️ A callback can outlive its intended state: An after script or a channel handler holds the interpreter’s state, so a cancelled operation must be cancelled explicitly



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One implementation is portable across platforms: The core builds and runs on Windows, macOS, and Unix-like systems from one source base
✅ Embedding is a first-class use: The C API (Tcl_CreateInterp, Tcl_Eval, Tcl_CreateObjCommand) lets a host application embed an interpreter and expose its own commands
✅ A script needs no build step: A .tcl file runs as written through tclsh
❌ The implementation is one project: Tcl and Tk are maintained by a single core team that sets the language direction, so the platform has one centre (P2)
⚠️ Tk and every extension are separate packages: GUI work requires Tk beside the core, and a package must be found on auto_path or TCLLIBPATH
⚠️ A native extension is built per platform: A package that wraps a C library ships a compiled binary for each target, and the binary must match the interpreter version



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Everything is a string is a design choice: One representation for scripts, lists, and data buys uniform introspection at a conversion cost
A command is the only abstraction: The language has no operator table and no macro layer, so a domain language is built by writing commands
A small core plus packages is a scope decision: Tcllib, Tk, and Expect are separate distributions, and a program chooses which to depend on
There is no compile step by design: A syntax error appears when the script reaches the command
Tcl 9.0 treats compatibility with 8.6 extensions as a non-goal: The project states that ABI compatibility was not an aim, so the rebuild cost is a stated trade rather than an accident
A Tcl program is meant to be a layer over a host: The design point is a C or C++ program with a Tcl configuration and control layer




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The core compiles a script to bytecode: The bytecode compiler added in the 8.x series means a loop body is not re-parsed at each iteration
✅ expr compiles arithmetic: An expression is compiled to instructions rather than dispatched as a sequence of commands
✅ A C extension removes the interpreter from the hot path: A command implemented in C runs compiled code, which is how performance-critical work is normally done
⚠️ Each command still costs a dispatch: A loop written in Tcl pays parse and dispatch overhead per iteration, so the speed comes from moving the loop into C or into expr and string operations
⚠️ A re-generated string form costs again: An operation that needs the string representation discards the internal one, so a hot loop can convert repeatedly
⚠️ Tk redraw bounds GUI throughput: A large widget tree redraws at the rate the toolkit can service it



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and largely legacy: The active package field is far smaller than that of a mainstream language, and much Tcl code still in use was written decades ago (Ec3)
✅ Tcllib and Tklib are maintained standard libraries: Pure-Tcl packages for containers, lists, and protocols, distributed separately from the core
✅ The distribution is a complete tool: tclsh and wish need nothing else installed to run a script
✅ A package system names and resolves packages: package provide, package require, and the teacup distribution machinery locate and version a package
⚠️ A binary package is distributed per platform: A compiled extension must match the platform and the interpreter version, so a pure-Tcl package travels more easily
⚠️ The documentation corpus is stable but old: The manual pages are complete, and most tutorials and examples date from the 1990s and 2000s
❌ A compiled extension binds to a release line: Tcl states that extensions built against 8.6 and before will not work with 9.0, and ABI compatibility was a non-goal for 9.0 [5], [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Tcl 9.0 is an actively released line: Tcl/Tk 9.0 appeared in September 2024 after the long 8.x series, and 9.0.x maintenance releases continue
✅ Scripts are largely backward compatible: The migration notes list a small set of removed pre-8.0 legacies such as the old case, puts, and read forms
⚠️ Tcl 9.0 broke the C extension interface: Tcl_Size replaced int for lengths and indices and Tcl_UniChar became 32-bit, so an extension built for 8.6 must be rebuilt
⚠️ A major release arrives rarely: 9.0 came 27 years after 8.0, so a core change can wait a long time
✅ The project publishes a migration guide for scripts and for extensions: “Migrating scripts to Tcl 9” and “Migrating C extensions to Tcl 9” state each required change



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Embedded scripting is the native domain: A C or C++ host embeds an interpreter and exposes its own commands, which is how Tcl is most often used
✅ Tk is a mature cross-platform GUI toolkit: Tcl/Tk remains a workable choice for a simple desktop GUI
✅ Expect automates an interactive program: The Expect extension drives a terminal program through its prompts and is the standard tool for that job
✅ Tcl is used as a test and build harness: The core’s own test suite and many command-line tools use a Tcl driver
⚠️ General application work is rare: Outside embedded scripting, GUI, and automation a new project rarely chooses Tcl
⚠️ The heavy computation is normally in C: A Tcl program is usually a thin layer over an extension that does the work



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is tiny: A script is a sequence of commands, and set, proc, if, and foreach cover most of the surface
✅ The manual is uniform: Every command has a manual page with the same sections, so the reference is easy to navigate
✅ An interactive shell is part of the tool: tclsh evaluates a line as it is typed, so an experiment is immediate
⚠️ Substitution and quoting need care: $var, [command], braces, and backslash interact, so a command that builds another command is a skill of its own
⚠️ The single-value model surprises a newcomer: A list, a number, and a script are values of one kind, and the difference appears only when a command interprets the value
⚠️ The object systems are additional: TclOO is built in and [incr Tcl] is an extension, so object-oriented Tcl is a layer above the command core



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ A command is words separated by whitespace: puts hello is a command with one argument, and the language uses almost no operator punctuation
✅ Braces group a block without substitution: { ... } passes the enclosed text unevaluated, which is how if, proc, and foreach receive a body
✅ A script is data: Because a script is a list of words, a command can build and evaluate one
⚠️ expr has its own grammar: An expression uses operators and functions rather than command words, so the syntax changes inside its braces
⚠️ Substitution is dense: $, [, and \ each start a substitution, and a missing escape changes the meaning of a line
⚠️ An unbalanced brace or bracket changes the parse: A newline ends a command, so an unclosed group swallows the following lines



1.2.7 Testing

✅ tcltest is part of the core: The standard test package supplies test, testConstraint, and a summary, so a suite needs no external framework
✅ A test is a script the same interpreter runs: The check and the code under test share one language
✅ catch makes a failure assertable: A test states the expected status and message, and the return value of catch is the assertion
✅ trace observes a variable or a command: A test can watch a variable write or a command call without changing the code
✅ tclsh is the debugger: An interactive shell with info and trace exposes the state without a separate tool
⚠️ Nothing checks a command before it runs: A misspelled command name or a wrong argument count appears only when that line executes



1.2.8 Security

❌ Untrusted input can become code: eval, subst, uplevel, and expr evaluate text, so a value built from input can be executed as a command (Q3)
❌ The single-value model cannot reject a malformed input at the boundary: Because every value is a string, an injection that forms a valid command is not distinguishable from a legitimate one by the type system (Q2)
✅ A safe interpreter removes the dangerous commands: interp create -safe makes an interpreter without exec, open, source, and load
✅ A host can define the whole command surface: An embedded interpreter exposes only the commands the host creates, which is the usual Tcl sandbox
✅ catch and error bound a failure: A failing command can be reported instead of ending the interpreter
⚠️ Correct quoting is the mitigation and it must be uniform: list and lindex build a command safely, but only at every site where input becomes code

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Package installs resolve per environment; no lockfile exists by default. (Y1)
❌ Package versions resolve from the path at run time. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Tcl packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The package registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Tcl packages. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ puts is the whole logging surface. (Y6)
✅ errorInfo and errorCode record the stack and code of every failure. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer ships with the standard toolchain. (Y8)
❌ No debugger ships with tclsh. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs where a tclsh is built and installed. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Tcl Core Team governs in the open. (Y11)
✅ The manual pages are the public reference. (Y12)
✅ The interpreter source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [7]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Tcl’s design yields a moderate core score, and its losses cluster where declaration is absent: the type is dynamic, a variable defaults to the global scope, and nothing is immutable or validated. What the language does provide is a small, uniform command core that separates a procedure from its call sites, a real namespace construct with namespace eval, and an interpreter that manages memory for the script. Main strengths: embedding through the C API, the mature Tk toolkit, the built-in tcltest package, and a bytecode compiler that keeps the loop cost off the parser. Main weaknesses: everything is a string, so injection is an inherent risk and no type error is caught before run time; the implementation is a single project; the ecosystem is small and largely legacy; and the upgrade to Tcl 9.0 obliges every compiled extension to be rebuilt.

title: Visual Basic (6.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Visual Basic in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 62.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 64.8/100 · Engineering readiness 27.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Implements decouples the caller from the class: A class can implement an interface without inheriting an implementation
❌ Undeclared variables are Variant: Option Explicit is opt-in, so a name can accept anything (T2)
❌ There are no namespaces: Every public name in a project shares one global scope (T6)
❌ There are no generics: A collection holds Variant, and a read is a cast (T5)
❌ COM dispatch resolves at run time: IDispatch and TypeOf reach a member by name (T7)
❌ An object variable can be Nothing: Nothing in the type says whether it is set (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A closed set of cases is an enum or a set of constants, and a Select Case is not checked for exhaustiveness (T4)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Class_Initialize is the constructor: The object states its own setup
❌ A module-level variable is global: A public variable in a .bas module is reachable from the whole project (C1)
❌ A property is read/write by default: A field is mutable unless the author writes a getter only (C2)
❌ One value, many names: ByRef is the default parameter mode (documented), so the callee’s writes land in the caller’s variables (C6)
❌ Module-level initialization runs at load in loader order; the startup form is not a source-visible order (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Objects are reference-counted: The last released reference frees the object, so release is deterministic
⚠️ A reference cycle leaks: Two objects that point at each other are never freed
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: On Error covers statement-level errors, and a stack overflow in the recursive call ends the program (the documented crash class) outside every handler (Er6)
❌ COM reference counting leaks circular references; the process never releases them (M7)



1.1.4 Error

❌ On Error GoTo is the failure path: The failure travels by a jump and a global Err object, and no signature states it (Er1)
✅ On Error Resume Next is explicit: The skip is written at the site



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ An ActiveX EXE can run a unit out of process: The mechanism is a separate component
❌ There is no first-class thread or channel: Concurrency is a COM apartment and a separate process (K5)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A program runs on Windows through COM: The registry, the apartment, and the binary format are the platform (P1)
⚠️ The VB6 runtime must be installed: msvbvm60.dll ships with the operating system, not with the program



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A Variant default buys speed of writing: An undeclared variable accepts anything, and the type error arrives at run time
COM is a real boundary: A server is called through an interface, and the implementation is replaceable
Reference counting is deterministic but fragile: A cycle leaks, and the release order is the program’s to know
The language is frozen: A program written for 6.0 will not move to a modern runtime unchanged




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits native code: A project can be built to a native executable
⚠️ Late binding is slow: An IDispatch call resolves a name at run time



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The platform is proprietary: Visual Studio 6 and the VB6 runtime are Microsoft products (Ec4)
❌ The IDE is locked to Windows: The designer and the debugger are Windows applications (Ec5)
❌ A large body of VB6 code remains: A component written in 1998 still runs on a supported Windows (Ec7)
✅ The component model is standard: An ActiveX control or a COM server is callable from any COM client
✅ A component publishes a COM type library, the platform’s binary interface for its consumers [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The language is frozen at 6.0: No release after it changes the language
❌ The line is discontinued: Support ended in 2008, and no successor accepts the source (V3)
❌ Build variants multiply: #If blocks with project-defined constants select which code compiles into the binary (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The centre is the Windows desktop and COM: A line-of-business form over a database (D1)
❌ The form and the event set the architecture: A program is a set of controls and handlers (D3)



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The language is small and widely taught: BASIC syntax and a drag-and-drop designer



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Dim, Set, and End If are spelled out: The declaration and the block are verbose (S1)
⚠️ The default-property syntax is dated: Text1.Text and the line-continuation underscore



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The IDE debugs in place: Breakpoints, watches, and the immediate window
❌ No monotonic reading published: Timer() answers with the wall date, and the runtime ships no elapsed reading (G4)



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ A Variant hides the type until run time
❌ ADO and dynamic SQL take a string: A WHERE clause built by concatenation is an injection path (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The project build is not reproducible: A .vbp build embeds paths and a timestamp (Y1)
❌ A dependency is a registered DLL: Nothing in the project pins the component version (Y2)
❌ No contract the toolchain reads: references are IDE checkboxes in a registry entry, and no machine-read manifest travels with the project (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A component carries no signature: Registration is a registry entry (Y3)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ There is no tracing standard: A program writes a file or the event log (Y5)
❌ There is no structured logging facility: Output is a string (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The IDE reports a syntax error as it is typed



1.3.5 Interop

❌ There is no portable target: A binary runs on Windows only (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ One vendor governs the language: Microsoft defines the runtime and the tooling (Y11)
❌ The specification is a vendor document: The language is documented, not standardised (Y12)
❌ Semantics rest on the product documentation: the manuals define the language as the shipped IDE behaves, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)
❌ No parser published: the grammar is prose in the IDE documentation, the compiler is closed, and no parser API ships (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ No independent energy or time benchmark for the language is recorded.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse public training data: models write it less reliably than a mainstream language [6].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Visual Basic 6 is a form-and-COM language: the interface and the component model decouple a caller, and reference counting frees an object deterministically, but the default Variant, the flat namespace, On Error GoTo, and the Windows-only runtime keep the coupling high. Main strength: a small language with a real component boundary. Main weakness: the failure path is a jump, and the program runs only inside COM on Windows.

title: X++ (10.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses X++ in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 67.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61.3/100 · Engineering readiness 59.6/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ A class and an interface state the contract: X++ follows the .NET type system
❌ There are no sum types: An enum or a base class plus a discriminator (T4)
❌ Reflection reaches the metadata: .NET reflection reads a type at run time (T7)
❌ A reference can be null: The type does not say whether it is set (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ new runs a constructor: A class states its invariants
❌ A field is mutable by default: A property is read/write unless the author restricts it (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation does not define X++ Map’s iteration order (C5)
❌ One value, many names: Dynamics class objects move by reference; a map, a local, and a field reach one record object (documented) (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: newQuery/dynamic resolution and the run-time class lookup (Class::new for a string name) build calls from text (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The CLR collects: The pause is the runtime’s (M2)
❌ There is no scope-exit release: try/finally closes a resource (M3)
❌ There is no ownership model: Aliasing is unrestricted (M4)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: the CLR’s stack overflow in the recursive X++ interpreter is fatal (documented: the runtime crash is not catchable in the CLR contract) (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ An exception bypasses the signature (Er2)
❌ There is no result type: A failure is an exception (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The batch framework runs a job: A runnable class is scheduled by the platform
❌ Locks are manual: ttsbegin and the transaction scope are the discipline (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A program runs only in Dynamics 365: The AOS, the database, and the metadata are the platform (P1)
✅ The runtime is the CLR: X++ compiles to CIL and uses the .NET libraries



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ERP model is the language’s domain: A table and a form are the unit of design
The CLR is a real runtime: The language inherits a mature collector and library
The base application is both platform and constraint: An extension is written against a moving base
The release wave is the upgrade path: A program moves when the service moves




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ A collection pause is part of the timing (R2)
⚠️ The database round trip dominates: A loop over a table must be set-based
✅ The AOS caches metadata and data: A hot path can avoid a round trip



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The platform is proprietary: Microsoft licences the ERP and the toolchain (Ec4)
❌ The tooling is Visual Studio plus the Dynamics extension: Deployment is the platform’s (Ec5)
❌ One platform is the ecosystem: An X++ program serves one ERP (Ec6)
❌ The base application is a compatibility surface: An extension must respect it (Ec7)
❌ A deployable package binds to a platform release: Microsoft documents it as a binary update for one platform release, and the environment that receives it cannot rebuild it [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The platform is updated in release waves: A program moves with a service update
⚠️ The base application changes under an extension: A chain of command can break
❌ Build variants multiply: #if, #ifdef, and #define select which X++ code compiles, and the flags follow the model and build configuration (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is ERP: Finance, supply chain, and manufacturing (D1)
❌ The framework sets the architecture: Forms, tables, and the SysOperation framework (D3)



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The language and the ERP model are learned together: Two bodies of knowledge at once (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is C-like: Braces, classes, and a SQL-like select
⚠️ The embedded SQL is a dialect: A select statement is part of the language



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The SysTest framework runs a unit test: A test class is a model element
❌ No monotonic reading published: systemDateGet and systemDateTimeGet read the wall (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ A dynamic query takes a string: A query built from input is an injection path (Q3)
✅ The role and duty model is enforced: An entry point checks a privilege



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The deployable package is not reproducible: The package embeds build metadata and paths, and two builds are not compared (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ A deployable package can be signed: A certificate signs the package for deployment



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ Diagnostics ride the platform’s telemetry and trace parser, not the language.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The Visual Studio integration debugs X++ in the standard IDE. (Y13)
✅ Builds integrate with the incremental Visual Studio build. (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ X++ binds .NET assemblies in process through the runtime. (Y9)
✅ The cloud runtime is the maintained target for the artifact. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ One vendor governs the language (Y11)
❌ The specification is the vendor’s documentation (Y12)
❌ Semantics rest on the vendor runtime: the toolchain documentation defines the language as the vendor’s runtime behaves, and no published conformance suite exists (Y17)
❌ No parser published: the syntax pages define the surface, the compiler is closed, and no parser API ships (Y19)

title: Solidity (0.8.x)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Solidity in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 60.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Statically typed and compiler-checked: Every state variable, parameter, and return value has a declared type
✅ Value and reference types are distinguished: uint256, address, and bool are value types, while arrays, structs, and mappings are reference types
❌ No sum types: A choice between alternatives is an enum plus a struct, or a separate contract, and the compiler cannot check the union (T4)
✅ Contracts and interfaces declare the ABI: A function signature in an interface fixes the external call shape
✅ No null: A uint256 starts at 0 and an address starts at the zero address, so absence is a value convention
⚠️ The data location is stated at every use: memory, storage, and calldata must be written for a reference type, and a wrong location changes the meaning of an assignment



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A constructor is optional: A contract without an explicit constructor is deployed with default state, so deployment validation is optional (C4)
✅ Contracts are the unit of encapsulation: State and functions live in one contract, and external, public, internal, and private state the visibility
✅ Inheritance with C3 linearization gives a defined order: contract B is A orders the bases linearly, so super resolves predictably
✅ Mappings and structs are declared members: A mapping(address => uint256) and a struct state the storage shape
✅ Constructors and initializer functions validate deployment: constructor(...) and an initializer modifier set and check the initial state
⚠️ delegatecall couples two contracts to one storage layout: The callee runs against the caller’s storage, so the layouts must agree exactly



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No garbage collector and no collection pause: The EVM memory is a per-call byte array that is discarded when the frame returns
✅ The data location makes copying visible: memory copies a value into the call, and calldata reads it in place
✅ Values are freed when a call frame returns: The caller never frees memory
✅ constant and immutable remove a storage read: A value fixed at compile time or at construction is embedded in the bytecode
⚠️ Persistent storage is expensive and manual: A write to a fresh storage slot costs 20 000 gas, so layout and write count are economic decisions
⚠️ A storage pointer aliases contract state: A local storage reference points into state, so a write through it is persistent



1.1.4 Error

❌ Failure is checkable but not exhaustive: require and revert abort a call, and nothing forces a caller to handle the failure (Er3)
❌ An unchecked low-level call is silently ignored: (bool ok, ) = addr.call(...) compiles even when ok is discarded, so a failed external call can pass unnoticed
✅ require(cond, "reason") states a precondition: A failed precondition reverts with a message
✅ Custom errors carry structured data cheaply: error InsufficientBalance(uint256 available); and revert InsufficientBalance(a) return named fields
✅ try/catch handles an external call failure: Since 0.6 a failed external call can be caught
✅ Arithmetic is checked by default since 0.8: An overflow or underflow reverts, and unchecked { ... } is the explicit opt-out



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The language has no concurrency: A transaction runs sequentially on a single EVM thread, so there is no concurrent primitive (K1)
❌ Execution is coupled to the gas limit: A call that runs out of gas reverts, so control flow depends on the gas the sender supplies
✅ A transaction is atomic: The state changes commit together or revert together, so no partial state remains
✅ External calls within one transaction are ordered deterministically: The sequence is fixed by the bytecode
⚠️ Reentrancy is an ordering hazard: An external call can re-enter the contract before it returns, so checks-effects-interactions or a reentrancy guard must be applied by hand
⚠️ Atomicity stops at the transaction boundary: Two contracts touched in one transaction succeed or fail together, and no further coordination exists



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The EVM is the only target: The compiler emits EVM bytecode, and there is no other runtime (P1)
❌ The chain context is injected into every contract: msg.sender, msg.value, block.timestamp, block.number, and tx.origin are globals, so logic is coupled to the caller, the block, and the chain
✅ EVM-compatible chains share the runtime: A contract deploys to Ethereum, an L2, or any other EVM chain
⚠️ The context globals differ in meaning per chain: On an L2 block.number may be the L1 height and the sequencer sets block.timestamp, so a timing assumption does not transfer
⚠️ An upgradeable contract separates logic from storage: A proxy delegates to an implementation, and the storage layout must stay compatible



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Gas metering is the execution model: A deliberate economic constraint, not a language defect
Turing completeness is an expressive-power choice: Decidable automated verification of arbitrary properties cannot follow from it
The domain is on-chain contracts: Outside that domain the language has no use, which is a scope decision
Inheritance is provided: The language includes single and multiple inheritance, and C3 linearization orders multiple bases
Static typing helps but does not remove domain risk: The type system checks types, not economic or adversarial behaviour
The 0.8 release line changes semantics: Checked arithmetic and removed implicit conversions are a deliberate tightening, not a defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The cost model is explicit in gas: Every operation has a known price, so cost is stated rather than measured
✅ The solc optimiser reduces the emitted bytecode: The compiler optimises the code it produces
✅ Execution is deterministic across nodes: Every node computes the same result, which consensus requires
⚠️ Performance is not measured in wall-clock time: Gas, not throughput, is the design constraint
⚠️ Storage reads and writes dominate cost: A warm storage read costs 100 gas and a write costs far more, so a layout decision sets the cost
⚠️ The EVM is slow in general-computing terms: A loop over state is expensive by construction



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Foundry, Hardhat, and Truffle provide build and test tooling: Compilation, testing, and deployment are covered
✅ OpenZeppelin Contracts gives audited base contracts: Standard tokens and access control arrive as reviewed libraries
✅ solc is a released, versioned compiler with a range pragma: A file states the compiler versions it accepts
❌ The ecosystem is niche, young, and chain-specific: Package reuse is limited to an EVM audience, and the tooling field is small (Ec3)
⚠️ Tooling churn is high: The build-tool field has shifted toward Foundry, and older tooling is losing support
⚠️ There is no language-level package manager: Dependency management comes from the build tool, such as npm or a git submodule
✅ The contract ABI is published by the language as an encoded, typed signature the EVM enforces [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The compiler is released on an active cadence: 0.8.x releases add features and fixes
✅ pragma solidity ^0.8.0 pins the compiler range per file: A source file states the versions it accepts
✅ Breaking changes are grouped into release lines: 0.8 turned on checked arithmetic and removed implicit conversions
✅ The release notes state every breaking change: A migration path is documented for each release
⚠️ The 0.x versioning carries no compatibility promise: Every minor release may break, so a compiler range is mandatory in practice
⚠️ A deployed contract cannot be changed: The bytecode on chain is fixed, so an upgrade needs a proxy pattern from the start



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The language is the right tool for EVM smart contracts: The ABI, the storage model, and the chain context match the problem
✅ The type-safe ABI supports standard interfaces: An ERC-20 or ERC-721 contract is expressed as an interface with typed functions
❌ Domain lock-in to on-chain contracts: Outside the EVM the language has no application (D1)
⚠️ Blockchain-specific concerns are only partly covered by constructs: Reentrancy, front-running, and key management have no dedicated language construct
⚠️ The gas model is part of the domain semantics: Every construct has an economic effect the programmer must consider



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep: The blockchain model — accounts, gas, storage, reentrancy, and the ABI — must be learned on top of the language (L1)
✅ The syntax is familiar to JavaScript developers: The grammar is ECMAScript-like, with braces, semicolons, and dot access
✅ Modifiers give a readable access-control idiom: modifier onlyOwner states a precondition at the function
✅ The documentation and community resources are good: The Solidity documentation and the OpenZeppelin guides are maintained
⚠️ A mistake has a direct economic cost: A vulnerability in a deployed contract can be exploited immediately, so experience is expensive to acquire



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ ECMAScript-style syntax: Braces, semicolons, and the . member operator match JavaScript
✅ Modifiers are a declarative precondition: A modifier wraps the function body and names the condition at the signature
✅ Data locations are stated in the signature: function f(uint[] calldata xs) shows where the argument lives
✅ Contract and interface declarations read as a module: The contract is the top-level unit and names its own scope
⚠️ Inline assembly { ... } uses the lower-level Yul syntax: A low-level block changes the language inside the braces
⚠️ A modifier hides the code it wraps: The reader sees the modifier name, not the rewritten body



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Foundry runs tests written in Solidity: forge test executes contracts as tests
✅ Hardhat runs a TypeScript test suite against a local chain: Accounts, deployment, and assertions are scripted
✅ Fork testing reproduces mainnet state: forge test --fork-url runs against a pinned block
✅ Fuzzing and invariant testing are built into Foundry: A property is checked over generated inputs
✅ Coverage and gas reporting are available: forge coverage and forge snapshot report coverage and cost
⚠️ The compiler does not catch reentrancy or access-control faults: Those faults pass every type check



1.2.8 Security

❌ The domain has canonical vulnerability classes: Reentrancy, front-running, and access-control faults are the field’s recurring failures, and Solidity was partly blamed for The DAO hack in 2016 (Q3)
⚠️ Reentrancy needs an explicit ordering discipline: Checks-effects-interactions or a reentrancy guard must be applied by hand
✅ Arithmetic is checked by default since 0.8: An overflow or underflow reverts rather than wrapping silently
✅ require and custom errors make a failure explicit: A failed precondition reverts with a reason
⚠️ delegatecall and low-level calls bypass type checking: The callee and the target are chosen at run time
✅ Static typing and the ABI prevent type confusion at the boundary: An external call is encoded against a declared signature

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Compiler and library versions resolve from the toolchain unless pinned with a lock file. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ npm-published contracts and libraries carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The npm name space is flat for contract packages. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; events are the convention. (Y5)
❌ Events and revert strings are the whole logging surface. (Y6)
❌ A reverted transaction returns its reason and no post-mortem. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the compiler; IDE debuggers ride the tool vendors. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Solidity calls only inside the EVM; no in-process interface leaves it. (Y9)
❌ The artifact runs only on EVM chains. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Ethereum improvement proposals run the EVM in the open; no single vendor owns the language. (Y11)
✅ The grammar and the documentation are public. (Y12)
✅ The solidity test suite and the EVM conformance work are public. (Y17)
✅ solc is public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

The type system is static and the data locations are explicit, but the EVM injects the chain context into every contract, execution is single-threaded and gas-metered, and the language runs nowhere else. title: AQL (ArangoDB 3.11)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses AQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 87.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.4/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL and absent values are not type-safe: A missing document, an absent edge, and a NULL property all reach an expression, and comparisons over them form a three-valued logic (T10)
❌ A function’s signature does not state its effects: A user-defined function runs inside the server, and the query text shows the call, not what the body reads, mutates, or reaches out to (T12)
❌ User-defined functions cross into JavaScript unchecked: A JS function is declared by name, and the engine does not check its body against the query’s expectations (T14)
✅ The query is analysed before execution: ArangoDB’s query analysis rejects malformed expressions and constant-folded type mismatches at prepare time



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Data-driven blocks compose without shared state: FOR, LET, sub-queries, and COLLECT build intermediate results inside the query
✅ Graph traversal is a first-class clause: OUTBOUND, INBOUND, and depth ranges state a traversal in the query, not in host code
⚠️ Views store queries server-side: A stored view is a dependency a reviewer must fetch from the deployment to read a query in full



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The engine owns allocation: Query buffers, index pages, and traversal state are managed by the server, not by the query
⚠️ Deep traversals can exhaust engine memory: An unbounded depth range over a dense graph can still fail the operation



1.1.4 Error

✅ Syntax and analysis errors are caught at prepare time: Unknown collections, malformed expressions, and unparsable queries are reported before the query runs
⚠️ Runtime failures depend on the data: A type mismatch on an untyped JSON field, a division by zero, and a unique-constraint violation surface only on the documents reached



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group writes atomically: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a set of AQL writes commit or abort as one
⚠️ Isolation is engine-specific: A write conflict raises an engine error the caller handles outside the query language



1.1.6 Platform

❌ AQL runs only inside ArangoDB: The language is defined for one product, and no other engine implements it (P1)
❌ AQL is a poor fit outside database work: General application logic, external I/O, and multi-pass algorithms are pushed to a host language (P4)
⚠️ Editions split features: ArangoDB’s Enterprise line adds security, caching, and graph features the community edition lacks



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One language over three models: Documents, graphs, and key-value reads share AQL; the breadth is real, and each model’s idioms coexist in one syntax
NULL and missing keep optional data natural: The document model needs no placeholder, and three-valued comparisons become a cost every reader pays
User-defined functions extend the query: JavaScript functions buy expressiveness at the cost of an unchecked foreign boundary
Community edition versus Enterprise: The language’s core is open, and the features an enterprise query needs sit in the licensed edition




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The optimizer chooses index and traversal strategies: explain() reports the plan, and optimizer hints steer it
⚠️ Plan quality depends on the indexes and statistics: The same query is fast on an indexed collection and a scan on a bare one



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments by edition and driver: Drivers, the web console, and migration tools target ArangoDB’s editions at different support levels (Ec2)
❌ The AQL ecosystem is niche: The library pool, hiring market, and third-party tooling are thinner than for SQL, Cypher, or Gremlin (Ec3)
✅ The server is open source: ArangoDB ships under a community licence, and its source and documentation are public



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Releases are published with changelogs: ArangoDB’s release notes name each AQL change before it ships
⚠️ AQL has no standards committee: The language moves on the vendor’s release schedule, and features arrive engine-first



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting AQL means adopting ArangoDB’s multi-model store: One language spans documents, graphs, and key-value collections, and its clauses assume that model (D1)
✅ AQL is used to query stored document and graph data: FOR d IN users retrieves documents, and graph traversal clauses walk edges and paths
⚠️ Graph semantics are new material for SQL readers: Traversal direction, depth ranges, and path objects extend the SQL-shaped surface



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The SQL-shaped core transfers: FOR, FILTER, SORT, and COLLECT read as SELECT-FROM-WHERE to anyone with SQL experience
⚠️ Sub-query scoping and LET semantics take practice: A newcomer must learn where a variable is bound and how nested data flows through a query



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ JSON expressions sit inside SQL-style clauses: FOR-RETURN reads like SQL until an expression nests JSON objects, arrays, and ternary operators
⚠️ Collection and field access lean on punctuation: Backtick-quoted collections, doc.field paths, and arrow traversal operators carry the structure
✅ Queries read linearly: A clause list in order states the data flow, and a short query is legible without a schema at hand



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test harness ships with the language: Testing an AQL query requires a running ArangoDB deployment and a harness each project builds for itself (G1)
❌ Schemaless collections move type faults to execution: An expression on untyped JSON fields fails only when a matching document is reached, so an untested path gives no evidence (G3)
❌ No monotonic clock is published in the language: DATE_NOW() and NOW() read the wall clock, so elapsed-time tests depend on the server’s clock (G4)
✅ explain() and profile report plans and timings: Inspecting a query’s plan and execution statistics is standard practice



1.2.8 Security

❌ String-built queries are an injection surface: Concatenating untrusted input into a query text lets that input change the parse (Q3)
❌ Untrusted documents enter queries untyped: Field types in schemaless collections are data, so an expression must re-check each type at every use (Q2)
✅ Parameterised statements remove the injection surface: Bound parameters carry data out of band, so a value cannot become syntax



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is a request text: The same query submitted to the same server version and dataset produces the same result, and there is no build artifact to reproduce (Y1)
⚠️ Queries live beside the application that submits them: A deployment stores no manifest naming the server version the query was written against



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published drivers carry no signed provenance by default: A consumer must trust the package they install (Y3)
✅ Drivers publish in registries with an ownership model: The arangojs npm package names its publisher, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
❌ No vulnerability advisory feed joins published drivers to known vulnerabilities at the package-version level: A consumer reads release notes to learn a driver is affected (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: Observability is provided by the server and its drivers (Y5)
❌ No structured logging is defined in the language: Diagnostics are server log entries with their own format (Y6)
✅ Slow and failed queries are recorded by the server: The slow-query log and query trace name the query and its timing (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit-test loop is a text submission: There is no compile step between editing a query and running it (Y7)
❌ No fast in-editor analysis ships for AQL: Query syntax is checked when the query is submitted; editors have no incremental analyser for the language (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger ships with the language: Debugging is done through query plans, logs, and the web console (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ User-defined functions call host-language code: JavaScript functions extend the engine without leaving the process (Y9)
❌ The query runs only inside ArangoDB: There is no portable target outside that product (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is ArangoDB Inc.-led: The language ships with the server, and the roadmap follows the vendor (Y11)
✅ The AQL manual is public: The language surface is documented and can be implemented by others (Y12)
❌ No conformance suite exists: Independent implementations cannot run a shared test suite against the manual (Y17)
✅ The parser is open source: ArangoDB publishes its query parser in the server source, so third-party tools can parse AQL (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside the ArangoDB server: energy and time are the engine’s, not the query’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ The manual and tutorial are public with many examples: current models write common AQL queries reliably, though traversal semantics need review.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: CQL (Apache Cassandra 5.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses CQL (Apache Cassandra 5.0) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 77.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 46.1/100 · Engineering readiness 70.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Columns are typed at the DDL: the types reference opens by stating CQL is a typed language, and native, collection, UDT, tuple, vector, and custom types bind to the declared table
❌ No sum types: a column is one type, and an alternative — a value that is text today and a number tomorrow — is modeled by two columns, not by a type (T4)
❌ No parameterized type: CREATE TYPE hard-codes every field type, and a reusable shape is copied table by table (T5)
❌ Null is a plain value, not a type: reads return null for absent columns, IS NULL is the only distinction the language names, and a query over an absent value behaves like a query over a stored null (T10)
❌ No import mechanism: USE switches the session’s keyspace, a UDT is bound to the keyspace that created it, and nothing in CQL imports definitions across keyspaces (T11)
❌ Statements state no effect: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, and USING TTL mutate rows, INSERT JSON replaces rows, and no signature records the write (T12)
❌ A custom type is a Java class name: the types reference defines custom_type as a string naming a server-side class on every node’s CLASSPATH, and no CQL-side check bounds its values (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The schema declares the storage order: CREATE TABLE names the partition key and clustering columns, and the row layout on disk follows the declaration
❌ Rows mutate in place: UPDATE SET rewrites columns, counters increment through UPDATE, and there is no immutability option in the language (C2)
❌ No validating constructor: collection literals build maps, sets, and lists from bare terms, and a bad element — a missing list position, an unbindable marker — surfaces as a server-side error at execution (C4)
❌ Default order is the storage order: a SELECT returns rows in clustering order, ORDER BY exists only over clustering columns, and no clause pins an order the partition layout does not already give (C5)
⚠️ List appends read like values: scores = scores + [14, 21] mutates a stored list, the docs mark append and prepend non-idempotent, and a timed-out retry may add the value twice



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Storage is the node’s: commitlog, memtables, and SSTable files live in the server’s storage, and the statement text allocates nothing
⚠️ Some list operations read before they write: setting or deleting a list element by position incurs an internal read-before-write the docs state runs slow, a storage-engine cost inherited from the schema choice



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured path in the language: a read timeout, an unavailable coordinator, and a list position that does not exist are server-side faults reported through the driver, and the statement carries no path around them (Er1)
❌ Conditional writes report applied, not failed: UPDATE … IF EXISTS answers an [applied] row carrying the current values when the condition fails, and no error the language can branch on is raised (Er3)
❌ Counters fail without a result type: the docs state a counter update that times out leaves the client unable to tell applied from lost, and re-incrementing after a delete is guaranteed to misbehave — success, failure, and unknown share one silent surface (Er4)
✅ Clauses are checked before data is touched: the grammar and the WHERE restrictions fail at prepare time, so a misspelled clause or an unbound partition key never reaches a scan



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency is the server’s: statements execute on the coordinator under its thread pools, and the language defines no threads, tasks, or channels
⚠️ Conditions serialize per partition: LWT IF clauses order writes inside one partition, and multi-part transactions arrive only with the 6.0 Accord line, now in alpha



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Two open implementations speak CQL: Apache Cassandra (Apache-2.0) and ScyllaDB implement the language and the native protocol, and official drivers ship on Maven Central, PyPI, npm, and Go
❌ A poor fit outside partition-keyed data: WHERE is bound to the PRIMARY KEY, joins do not exist, ad-hoc filters across the table need ALLOW FILTERING’s full scan, and application logic stays in a host language (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Partition-keyed design is the language’s bargain: WHERE bound to the PRIMARY KEY buys predictable reads at known cost, and the price is that ad-hoc analytics needs a second table — a materialized view — built and repaired through the same language
LWT pays a consensus round per partition: IF EXISTS conditions serialize updates and answer [applied], and the same mechanism keeps range-wide conditions out of CQL until Accord lands in 6.0
Counters traded atomicity for convergence: counter updates are non-idempotent last-writer merges, documented as un-retryable after a timeout, where a plain column write is idempotent by design
5.0 extended the language while its function surface contracted: the vector type, Storage-Attached Indexes, and Dynamic Data Masking arrived, the JavaScript UDF line reached removal, and Java UDFs ship sandboxed and switched off by default — what a 4.x-era query can express and what a 5.0-era query can express are not the same set




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Prepared statements are cached plans: the native protocol prepares a statement once and reuses the server-side plan per node, so repeated queries skip the parse
⚠️ Collections read whole: the docs state an individual collection is not indexed internally, so reading one element reads the collection — a performance fact the data model must design around



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments across the stack: cqlsh and nodetool ship with Cassandra, ScyllaDB carries its own CLIs, DataStax ships its own workbench and drivers, and monitors are per-distribution (Ec2)
❌ A niche market: wide-column expertise concentrates in high-write operational stores, and the hiring pool is a fraction of SQL’s (Ec3)
❌ Compatibility surface kept on life support: the types reference labels custom types as existing mostly for backward compatibility and discourages their use, and list and counter non-idempotence is documented as inherent (Ec7)
✅ The core stack is open: Cassandra’s source, Java/Python/Node.js/Go/C#/Rust drivers, and the native protocol specification are published, and downloads ship PGP signatures and checksums



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Major releases cut script UDFs: 4.0 removed Thrift and Python UDFs, 4.1 deprecated JavaScript UDFs with removal in progress for 5.0, and 5.0 documents Java as the function language of record — sandboxed, opt-in, off by default in shipped config (V1)
❌ The language moves with the engine’s roadmap: CQL changes ship as Cassandra design docs and CEPs tied to a release, with no independent language process — the CQL 3.0 surface of 2013 underlies the 5.0 grammar today (V4)
✅ 5.0 added real surface: the vector type, Storage-Attached Indexes, and Dynamic Data Masking entered CQL with 5.0, and the 6.0 line designs in the open (quarterly alphas through late 2026, 5.0.x current GA)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting CQL means adopting a wide-column store: the unit is the partition-keyed table, replication is declared in the DDL, and the schema is built per query workload (D1)
❌ The language forces a partition-first architecture: WHERE must bind the PRIMARY KEY, ORDER BY is clustering-only, and the docs open the data-modeling chapter with Hint: it’s not relational and define application queries before the schema — the store’s shape follows from what the language can express (D3)
✅ CQL queries and mutates stored wide-column table data: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE read and write the tables the schema declares



1.2.5 Learning

❌ SQL-shaped syntax with non-relational rules: a SQL reader must unlearn joins, re-derive the PRIMARY KEY as the query surface, learn that UPDATE SET writes rows, and read ALLOW FILTERING as a scan alarm rather than a flag (L1)
❌ The surface is long: native, collection, UDT, tuple, vector, counter, date, time, duration, and custom types plus DDL, DML, indexing, materialized views, JSON, masking, triggers, and operators — the reference gathers them across a dozen pages and a single-file edition (L2)
✅ The reference is readable: the CQL chapter carries BNF grammar and worked examples per type, from quickstart inserts to compaction options



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Property bags on every DDL: CREATE KEYSPACE … WITH replication = {‘class’: ‘SimpleStrategy’, ‘replication_factor’ : 3} and CREATE TABLE … WITH compaction = {‘class’: ‘SizeTieredCompactionStrategy’} — every declaration drags a map of engine knobs (S1)
❌ The surface is uneven: UPDATE SET writes, counters increment through UPDATE, list appends ride on +, LWT adds IF [NOT] EXISTS and answers an [applied] row, DELETE demands the full PRIMARY KEY, and USING TTL prefixes a write (S2)
❌ Punctuation carries meaning: { } for maps and sets, [ ] for lists, vector<int, 3>, frozen<list>, quoted “MixedCase” identifiers, and the [applied] bracket in conditional results — a misread token usually parses and changes meaning (S3)
✅ Statements are short: INSERT INTO t (id, k, v) VALUES (0, 0, ‘val0’) is one line, and cqlsh echoes the result as a table



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard query-test harness in the language: Testcontainers and cassandra-unit wrap a test cluster for driver code, and CQL itself names no harness for query regression (G1)
❌ No plan tool in the language: the 5.0 command list carries no EXPLAIN statement, and diagnosis goes through nodetool stats, system.log, and the JMX meters — the query author never sees the plan the coordinator builds (G2)
❌ Restriction and position faults land on the data: scores[1] = 7 errors only when the list is shorter, ALLOW FILTERING pays only when the scan is wide, and a counter re-increment after a delete is documented as undefined behavior (G3)
❌ Only the wall clock: currentTimestamp(now()) and toTimestamp() read server time, and the language names no monotonic clock for elapsed-time tests (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ String-built statements are the injection surface: concatenating user input into a statement lets that input add clauses, and the drivers’ prepared statements and named parameters exist precisely to keep values out of syntax (Q3)
✅ Named and positional parameters are first-class: every driver binds values out of band against a prepared statement, and bind_marker appears in the language grammar itself
❌ Overflow is documented as the aggregate’s risk: collection_sum and SUM return the same type as the input elements with the docs’ own ‘risk of overflowing the data type’ warning, AVG truncates ([1, 2] answers 1, not 1.5), and CAST ‘relies strictly on Java semantics’ — a narrowing cast truncates silently (Q4)
✅ Width-typed native columns: tinyint, smallint, int, and bigint carry declared bit widths, varint is arbitrary precision, and a constant outside the declared width is rejected when the write executes

What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

Ec9 is present when one row carries a break: the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable elsewhere, or a break the probe harness has reproduced.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A statement is a request text: the same statement on the same cluster, schema, and version reproduces the same rows, and there is no build artifact (Y1)
✅ Drivers are pinned by registry versions: the Java driver ships on Maven Central with release versions (4.19.4 in late 2026), and a project pins it as an ordinary dependency (Y14)
⚠️ The deployment is the result’s home: a read reproduces on the cluster’s token ring, replication, and version, not on the statement text alone



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published libraries carry no signed provenance by default: drivers on Maven Central, PyPI, and npm name their publishers, and a consumer trusts the package installed (Y3)
✅ Maven Central, PyPI, npm, and the Go module proxy namespace every package, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
✅ Advisories are published: the Apache Security Base and the project’s security page carry Cassandra CVEs against releases, and the GitHub advisory database covers the driver packages (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: latency and cache meters are the node’s JMX beans and virtual tables, and the statement text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: system.log, audit logging, and full query logging are server configuration, and the statement defines no logging construct (Y6)
✅ The node records running queries: full query logging and audit logging are published operating features, and nodetool stats, netstats, and compactionstats report the work behind a result (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ cqlsh is submit-and-run: paste a statement, get a result table, with no build step (Y7)
❌ No maintained in-editor analyzer: CQL syntax and restriction checks land when the statement reaches the server, and the vendor IDE plugins are per-tool toys, not a language server the ecosystem maintains (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger: diagnosis goes through EXPLAIN output, nodetool stats, system.log, and the repair and compaction meters (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ Function definitions are published in the grammar: CREATE FUNCTION carries LANGUAGE and AS clauses, CREATE AGGREGATE composes state and final functions, and the 5.0 functions reference documents Java as the language of record — sandboxed and disabled by default in shipped config (user_defined_functions_enabled)
❌ No portable target: a statement runs on a Cassandra-protocol engine, and nothing in the language runs without one (Y10)
✅ The native protocol is a published spec: Java, Python, Node.js, Go, C#, and Rust drivers interoperate with any conformant node because the wire protocol is documented, not implied



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Governance is an Apache project: Cassandra is a top-level Apache project with a public PMC, design docs and CEPs on GitHub and the mailing lists, and the 6.0 feature line lands publicly (Y11)
✅ The specification is published: the CQL chapter carries the grammar, types, statements, and indexing rules, with a single-file edition of the whole language (Y12)
❌ No conformance suite decides cross-engine CQL: Cassandra exercises its parser through dtests, ScyllaDB carries its own CQL test line, and no shared suite with published conformance reports tests the language across engines (Y17)
✅ Published parsers: Cassandra’s CQL parser ships in the Apache-2.0 source, cqlsh’s Python parser ships with it, and drivers carry their own grammars (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a JVM node: energy is the server’s, and the language’s own levers are the partition design, the compaction strategy in the DDL, and collection size.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A well-documented SQL-shaped language: models write INSERT and SELECT reliably, and the partition-key restriction — WHERE bound to the PRIMARY KEY, ALLOW FILTERING — is where generated queries go wrong.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the reliability record is the store’s replication and repair design, declared in the DDL and audited outside the language.

Verdict: CQL is SQL-shaped syntax on a storage model that refuses the relational bargain: WHERE is bound to the PRIMARY KEY, joins do not exist, and ad-hoc filters are a documented full scan behind ALLOW FILTERING. The language’s costs are that bargain’s own surface — statements with no effects, null as a plain value, no module boundary, list and counter semantics documented as non-idempotent, aggregates documented as overflowing their input type, and a custom type that is a Java class name on the node’s classpath. Its evolution is the engine’s roadmap: 5.0 added the vector type, Storage-Attached Indexes, and Dynamic Data Masking, and ships its function surface sandboxed and switched off by default with the script languages of the 2.x era removed from the grammar’s reach. Main strengths: a fully public grammar and types reference, Apache governance with two open implementations, named parameters in the grammar itself, and published drivers in six languages. Main weaknesses: no query-test harness in the language, no plan tool in the 5.0 command list, no conformance suite between engines, tooling split across Cassandra, ScyllaDB, and DataStax surfaces, and restrictions that make the data model a prerequisite for writing a correct query.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925201
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193
