title: PL/SQL (Oracle)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PL/SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 41.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, constant, parameter, and function return declares a type, and a mismatch is a compilation error
✅ %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor a declaration to the schema: emp%ROWTYPE follows the table’s column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
✅ Subtypes declare a constrained domain once: SUBTYPE and a constrained type such as NUMBER(7,2) state a range or a shape and reuse it
❌ NULL is not type-safe absence (T10): An unassigned variable and an unused column are NULL, and NULL propagates through expressions, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL
✅ A REF CURSOR carries a row set without fixing its row type: SYS_REFCURSOR passes a result between program units, so the producer and the consumer need not share a record type



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The package separates specification from body: The spec declares the public interface — types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, and subprograms — and the body holds the implementation, so a consumer binds to the spec
✅ Subprogram overloading is available in a package: Two subprograms with one name differ by parameter list, so a family of operations shares one name
✅ A cursor FOR ... LOOP iterates the query result directly: Iteration ends at the result’s last row, so the code does not track a row count
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): A package variable is declared once and lives for the whole session, so every caller that touches the package sees and changes the same value
⚠️ Package initialisation runs on first use: An initialisation block in the body runs when the package is first touched in the session, so setup timing follows call order
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to an insert, update, or delete, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The Oracle server owns SGA and PGA memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
✅ The server sizes the work areas: Automatic PGA management gives a sort or a hash operation its memory from PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET, so the block does not reserve it
⚠️ A session-scoped collection holds its memory: An associative array or nested table kept in a package variable stays for the session, so retained state is a standing cost
⚠️ A bulk fetch needs a deliberate size limit: BULK COLLECT ... LIMIT bounds a fetch, and its absence can materialise a whole result set in PGA
✅ A cursor is released by CLOSE: The server reclaims the cursor’s memory, so the program does not track bytes



1.1.4 Error

✅ The block separates the normal path from the recovery path: DECLARE ... BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END; gives a named handler section
✅ Exceptions are matched by name: A predefined exception (NO_DATA_FOUND, TOO_MANY_ROWS, ZERO_DIVIDE) and a user-declared EXCEPTION are caught by name, and WHEN OTHERS catches the remainder
✅ RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR sets a code and a message: A custom failure carries a number in the application range −20000 to −20999, so a caller can branch on it
⚠️ WHEN OTHERS hides the class of the failure (Er3): A handler that catches everything without logging SQLCODE and SQLERRM, or that does not re-raise, lets the enclosing block see a normal return where the inner block failed
⚠️ No composable result type (Er4): A failure cannot be returned as a value the caller must inspect, so error information does not compose through a call chain



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions are the unit of concurrency: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT make a unit of work atomic, so a block does not coordinate with other sessions statement by statement
✅ An autonomous transaction decouples a log write: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION commits on its own, so the entry survives the caller’s rollback
✅ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE names the rows to lock: The lock is declared by the cursor text rather than by a separate call
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): A package variable is shared with every program unit that runs in the session, and nothing in the declaration marks it private
⚠️ Serialisation across sessions is the application’s to arrange: Where row locks and DBMS_LOCK calls do not apply, the ordering between two sessions’ work is nowhere declared
✅ DBMS_LOCK provides an explicit lock service: A named user lock serialises a critical section across sessions



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The block and package model follows the SQL/PSM shape: Persistent stored modules are specified in ISO/IEC 9075 Part 4, and the package and block model follows that concept, though the language itself has no public specification
⚠️ It is implemented outside Oracle Database: TimesTen and IBM Db2 support PL/SQL, so there is more than one implementation, though the dialects are not fully interchangeable
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database, so the unit of deployment is an Oracle schema
❌ The useful surface is Oracle-specific: DBMS_* server packages, ROWNUM, sequences, and SQL%ROWCOUNT are Oracle features, so the code cannot move to another engine unedited
⚠️ A port to Transact-SQL is a rewrite, not a translation: Feature differences and different concurrency and locking models separate the two dialects



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A session-scoped package variable is a deliberate cache: Keeping a value for the session avoids a repeated read; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the cached value when the underlying data changes
A trigger is a data-integrity mechanism: A rule kept in the database is enforced for every writer; the cost is that a reader of the application source cannot see the rule
Logic beside the data is the purpose of the language: A procedure that runs in the database avoids shipping rows to a client; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application’s test suite and profilers
Dynamic SQL buys flexibility: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs DDL and changes object names in a statement, which static SQL cannot do; the cost is that the statement’s shape is known only when it runs




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compilation happens at deployment: A package or procedure is compiled once and the stored form is reused, so a call does not re-parse the source
✅ Native compilation is selectable: PLSQL_CODE_TYPE = NATIVE compiles to machine code, so a hot subprogram does not pay the interpreter
✅ Bulk processing amortises the SQL boundary: FORALL and BULK COLLECT move many rows per round trip, so per-row context switches do not dominate
✅ The optimiser and the SGA serve the data path: Plan selection and buffer caching are the server’s job, not the block’s
⚠️ Cost follows the plan and the retained state: A poorly chosen plan, or a package variable holding a large collection, is a cost the unit cannot see



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Oracle under licence
✅ Tooling is mature and long-established: SQL*Plus, SQL Developer, and third-party IDEs have existed for decades
✅ Published practice is extensive: The PL/SQL language reference, the database manuals, and decades of books and courses document the language in detail
⚠️ Capability follows the licence: Tooling, support, and advanced features are licensed per seat or per processor, so a team reaches only what it has bought
⚠️ Enterprise code bases are long-lived and heavy: A schema commonly spans many versions, so a change has to keep the oldest callers working



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A program written for an early Oracle release generally still compiles and runs in the current one
✅ Edition-based redefinition supports an online change: EDITIONABLE objects let a new version of a package be deployed and switched over without downtime
✅ Deprecation is announced before removal: Oracle documents deprecated features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
⚠️ A language feature arrives with a database release: Adoption timing therefore follows the customer’s upgrade cycle, not a separate language release
⚠️ A new feature is unavailable on a pinned older database: Code that must run on an old release cannot use a recent construct
❌ Build variants multiply: $IF and $THEN directives select which PL/SQL statements compile, evaluated against package state at compile time (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for data-centric business logic: A procedure operates on tables with SQL directly, so a rule runs where the data is
✅ The language is a full procedural language inside SQL: Loops, records, collections, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
✅ Server packages reach outside the schema: UTL_FILE, UTL_HTTP, and DBMS_SCHEDULER give file, network, and job facilities from inside the database
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain
⚠️ A trigger can hide a domain rule: An invariant implemented in a trigger is enforced for every writer, but a reader of the application source cannot see it
⚠️ The language is not a general-purpose runtime: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a high-rate service belongs in another language beside PL/SQL



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Moderate for a SQL-plus-Pascal background: The block structure follows Ada and Pascal, so a developer from those languages reads it quickly
⚠️ The SQL-to-PL/SQL boundary needs practice: A SELECT inside a block must return exactly one row, so NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS are everyday cases
⚠️ Package semantics take time: Spec versus body, per-session package state, and initialisation timing are not visible in the syntax
⚠️ Exception semantics reward careful reading: An exception in a nested block propagates to the enclosing handler unless it is handled there
✅ The reference documentation is complete: The Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference documents every construct with examples



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable and keyword-led: Statements read as verbs — INSERT INTO, FETCH, RAISE — so intent is visible
✅ Blocks nest visibly: An inner BEGIN ... END holds its own declarations and handler, so scope follows the indentation
❌ Verbose (S1): Even a small unit needs a declaration section, a BEGIN ... END, and an exception section, so the block structure adds lines to every subprogram
⚠️ END closes several constructs: END IF;, END LOOP;, and a package END must each be matched, so a long body is read against its terminators
⚠️ A large package body is one long file: The spec and the body are a unit boundary, not a file-per-subprogram rule



1.2.7 Testing

✅ utPLSQL is the established framework: An open-source test framework runs suites with assertions and reporting, so tests need not be hand-rolled
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run and ROLLBACK, leaving the database unchanged
✅ The toolchain traces execution: DBMS_PROFILER, DBMS_TRACE, and the hierarchical profiler report call counts and coverage
⚠️ A suite depends on grants and deployment: The framework is installed in the database it tests, so permissions and schema state are preconditions
❌ No monotonic reading published: SYSTIME and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are wall readings anchored per session (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Bind variables remove the injection surface: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ... WHERE x = :1' USING v passes the value out of band, so it cannot change the parse
✅ DBMS_ASSERT validates an identifier before interpolation: SIMPLE_SQL_NAME, QUALIFIED_SQL_NAME, and ENQUOTE_NAME check the string
✅ The rights model is explicit: AUTHID DEFINER and AUTHID CURRENT_USER select whether a unit runs with its owner’s privileges or the caller’s
✅ Privileges are granted per object: GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg TO role scopes access, and the package specification is the grantable interface
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and DBMS_SQL build a statement as text, so concatenated input can become code
⚠️ Definer’s-rights code can escalate: A unit that runs with its definer’s rights reaches more than the caller, so it needs an audit

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Compilation state lives in the dictionary; no reproducible build exists outside the database. (Y1)
❌ Units resolve dependencies against the schema at compile time. (Y2)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Schema sources and third-party packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to PL/SQL libraries. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO is a convention. (Y5)
❌ DBMS_OUTPUT is the whole logging surface. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the database; the IDE debuggers are separate products. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The unit runs only in Oracle-family databases. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Oracle decides the language’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists; the manuals document one implementation. (Y12)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

❌ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: PL/SQL’s coupling is set by its host, not its syntax. The package separates a specification from its body, blocks and named exceptions give a structured failure path, and bind variables close the injection surface. Main strengths: interface and implementation are separable, error handling is structured, and server-side code runs beside its data. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside an Oracle database, a package variable is shared session state, every variable starts as NULL and NULL propagates, dynamic SQL turns concatenated text into code, and WHEN OTHERS is a standing invitation to swallow a failure.

title: PL/pgSQL (PostgreSQL 18)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PL/pgSQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 82.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 63.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and return value declares a type, and a body that violates its declarations fails when the function is compiled
✅ %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor a declaration to the schema: emp%ROWTYPE follows the table’s column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
✅ Polymorphic parameters keep one algorithm generic: anyelement and anyarray let a single function run over many types, with the type fixed per call
⚠️ Operators resolve by operand type (T8): +, ||, and && name different operations for different types, and CREATE OPERATOR lets an extension add meanings, so an expression’s sense follows from the operand types
⚠️ A record variable defers its row type to run time: The row shape is known only when a value is assigned, so a mistyped field surfaces on the path that reaches it
❌ NULL is the default value and it propagates (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, three-valued logic applies, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL
❌ A signature says what a function returns, not what it does (T12): A function that mutates tables, reads a foreign table, or sends notifications looks like any other function



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A function is a closed unit: Local variables are private to the call, and the signature is the whole interface, so a caller cannot reach inside
✅ CREATE FUNCTION and CREATE PROCEDURE compile at creation: The body is checked once when it is deployed, and a caller binds to the name and the signature
✅ Anonymous DO blocks run ad-hoc logic without a deployment step: A one-off migration or maintenance script is a block, not a schema object
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger function runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ SECURITY DEFINER is decided in the definition, not at the call: A caller sees only a function name; whether it runs with the owner’s rights follows from the definition



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The PostgreSQL server owns process memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
✅ The server sizes the work areas: A sort or a hash inside a function’s statements gets its memory from work_mem, which is a setting, not a statement property
⚠️ RETURN QUERY materialises its result before returning: A set-returning function builds its whole output in a tuplestore, so the call’s memory follows the result size
⚠️ A CREATE TEMP TABLE inside a function outlives the call: The table persists for the session, so a local act leaves a session-scoped resource behind



1.1.4 Error

✅ The block separates the normal path from the recovery path: BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN ... gives a named handler section, and conditions match by code or by name
✅ RAISE EXCEPTION carries a code and a detail: RAISE EXCEPTION 'msg' USING ERRCODE = '23505' raises a failure a caller’s handler can match on
✅ GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS reports the caught error: A handler can read the error’s code, message, constraint, context, and line
⚠️ A handler can swallow (Er3): An EXCEPTION block that catches and returns normally lets the caller see success, and WHEN OTHERS is the widest net
❌ A failure cannot travel as a value (Er4): The failure path is the exception path, so a fallible operation cannot be folded into an expression or returned as a result the caller inspects



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A procedure can manage its own transaction: A CALLed procedure may COMMIT and ROLLBACK (since PostgreSQL 11), while a function always runs inside its caller’s transaction
✅ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE names the rows to lock in the query text: The lock is declared by the statement rather than by a separate call
✅ Advisory locks give an explicit lock service: pg_advisory_lock serialises an application-level critical section across sessions under a declared key
❌ Session state is shared by default (K2): Custom session parameters set with set_config, session temp tables, and current_setting are visible to every function that runs in the session
⚠️ Transaction isolation and declared locks do not order independent work: Two sessions’ multi-step work is ordered only by the locks its statements name, so any ordering the source relies on is an agreement no declaration carries



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Cannot function outside one engine (P1): A PL/pgSQL program needs PostgreSQL or a compatible fork, so the unit of deployment is a database schema
❌ Portability is the engine’s, not the artifact’s (Y10): The program runs wherever its PostgreSQL release runs, and the language has no build target of its own
⚠️ Managed services track the engine’s calendar: A managed PostgreSQL carries the PL/pgSQL of its engine version, so the available surface follows the provider’s upgrade
⚠️ Foreign languages load in-process (T14): LANGUAGE C and the untrusted PLs such as plpython3u run outside PL/pgSQL’s checks, so a boundary no signature can see separates the two sides
✅ Client interfaces are standard: libpq, ODBC, and JDBC reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: A rule that runs beside its tables is enforced for every writer; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application’s test suite and profilers
A session cache in custom parameters is deliberate: set_config keeps a value for the session without a table; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the value when the underlying data changes
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible filter: EXECUTE with format() reaches names a static statement cannot; the cost is the plan, since a built string is parsed and planned on every execution
SECURITY DEFINER is deliberate for gated access: It exposes one narrow operation instead of table grants; the cost is an audit duty, since the function runs with its owner’s rights




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Statements inside a function use cached plans: A function’s static SQL is planned once per session and reused, so a call does not re-parse
✅ Set-based statements in the body do the heavy lifting: One INSERT ... SELECT inside the function carries the optimiser’s plan, so the procedural wrapper is not the hot path
⚠️ Row-by-row loops pay per-row context switches: A loop that fetches one row at a time runs far slower than its set-based equivalent
⚠️ A plan regression arrives hidden inside the call: A caller cannot see the queries inside a function, so a changed plan surfaces as the function being slow



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The extension ecosystem supplies the libraries: CREATE EXTENSION loads packaged capabilities such as PostGIS, pg_trgm, and pgcrypto into the database
✅ PGXN catalogs shareable extensions: A public registry indexes community extensions with releases and metadata
✅ PostgreSQL’s popularity carries the market: Documentation, books, courses, and hiring are abundant
✅ The stack is open and permissively licensed: The engine, the client tools, and the documentation carry no per-seat licence
⚠️ Tooling centres on the engine’s own tools: psql, pg_dump, and pgAdmin cover administration and query work, and the procedural language has no dedicated environment of its own



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Major releases keep the language: A PL/pgSQL function written years ago compiles in the current release
✅ Deprecation is announced before removal: The release notes and the documentation mark obsolescent features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
⚠️ A feature arrives with the engine’s major release: Adoption follows the server a deployment can upgrade to, not a separate language release
⚠️ The community’s own decisions govern the change: No independent standard bounds the syntax, so the release notes are the definition’s change log



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for data-centric logic: A function runs beside its tables with SQL directly in the body, so a rule executes where the data is
✅ A full procedural language inside SQL: Loops, records, cursors, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
✅ The engine reaches beyond its own schema: Foreign data wrappers and dblink read remote sources, and other PLs run beside PL/pgSQL in the same database
❌ Domain lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside PostgreSQL, so the PostgreSQL data tier is the only domain
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a long-running service belongs in another language beside PL/pgSQL



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a SQL developer: A block with DECLARE, BEGIN, and END reads like SQL with control flow added
✅ The documentation is complete and canonical: The PL/pgSQL chapter of the PostgreSQL manual documents every construct with runnable examples
⚠️ SELECT INTO is silent on an empty result: A plain SELECT INTO assigns NULL when the query returns no rows, and STRICT is the opt-in that makes it error
⚠️ Engine behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Locks, MVCC, and transaction semantics matter more than syntax for correct code



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose (S1): Every unit needs CREATE FUNCTION, a dollar-quoted body, and DECLARE, BEGIN, and END sections before it does anything
✅ Keyword-led and readable: Statements read as verbs, and the block boundaries are visible in the source
⚠️ The body is one dollar-quoted string: $$ ... $$ hides the body from the outer statement’s parser, so a function deploys as a single statement
⚠️ Function overloading hides the signature: Two functions may share a name and differ by argument types, so a call’s target follows from the argument list



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ No test framework ships with the engine (G1): psql and the server tools provide no assertion or runner, so a suite depends on pgTAP or a hand-rolled harness
✅ pgTAP is the established framework: An open-source test framework runs database tests with xUnit-style assertion functions
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run inside a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database unchanged
✅ The engine traces execution: RAISE writes to the server log with line numbers, and auto_explain logs the plans of statements inside functions
⚠️ A suite needs a server: Tests run inside the database they exercise, so the harness depends on a PostgreSQL instance and on deployment rights
❌ No monotonic reading published: now() and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP anchor the transaction’s wall time (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Static SQL in the body is parameterised automatically: The function’s variables become $n parameters of the planned statement, so values cannot change the parse
✅ GRANT and roles express least privilege: EXECUTE on a function is granted per role, and the function signature is the grantable interface
✅ SECURITY DEFINER states the effective identity in the definition: ALTER FUNCTION ... SECURITY DEFINER plus a pinned SET search_path makes the rights and the environment explicit
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): EXECUTE with a built string turns concatenated input into code, and format() with %I and %L is the mitigation, not a guarantee
⚠️ Definer’s-rights functions can escalate: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner’s rights, so it needs a pinned search path and an audit

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The distribution records no toolchain version per project; the server and extension versions are facts of the installation. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ PGXN and community extensions carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The extension registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to extensions. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; the server’s log stats are the instruments. (Y5)
❌ RAISE is the whole logging surface. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer ships with the server; editor analysis rides third-party tools. (Y8)
❌ No PL/pgSQL debugger ships with the server; pgAdmin’s is separate. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The routine runs only in PostgreSQL-family servers. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The PostgreSQL community governs in the open; no vendor owns the language. (Y11)
✅ The documentation set is complete and public. (Y12)
✅ The server and the procedural handler are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Procedural SQL is thin in model training data relative to mainstream languages, so generated PL/pgSQL mixes in other dialects’ syntax [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

❌ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: PL/pgSQL’s coupling is set by its host engine and governed by its community. Functions are closed units with typed declarations, the EXCEPTION ... WHEN section gives a structured failure path, static SQL in the body is parameterised automatically, and the extension registry, the open licence, and community governance give this shelf’s most open ecosystem. Main strengths: open source end to end, an independent steward, complete documentation, automatic parameterisation, and real modularity at function granularity. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside PostgreSQL, NULL starts in every declared variable and propagates, signatures carry no effects, dynamic SQL turns built strings into code, a handler can swallow a failure and return success, RETURN QUERY materialises its result, and the block structure adds boilerplate to every unit.

title: R (4.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses R in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 76.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68.0/100 · Engineering readiness 54.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A value carries its type at run time, so a type error surfaces when the expression evaluates
⚠️ An atomic vector holds one type and coerces silently: c(1, "a") becomes a character vector with no error, so a mixed vector changes type
⚠️ A factor stores integer level codes behind printed labels: A comparison and an ordering can therefore differ from the text a reader sees
⚠️ library() copies a package’s exported names onto the search path: A package has its own namespace and pkg::name reaches any of its objects, but the habitual library(pkg) attaches the exports to the search path, so two packages that export one name collide and the later attachment masks the earlier
✅ A function is a first-class value with its own type: is.function, formals, and body expose a function as data
⚠️ Attributes travel with a value invisibly: A names, class, or dim attribute changes dispatch and printing, so two values that print alike can behave differently



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A data frame is the central structured-data abstraction: Named columns of one length form a table, and a model function accepts it without knowing how it was built
✅ Functions are first-class and an environment is a lexical home: A function can be stored, passed, and returned, and it closes over its defining environment, so deliberate state is possible as a closure instead of a global
✅ The formula interface separates a model from a caller’s data: y ~ x1 + x2 names the columns, so the same call works on any data frame that has them
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): <- at top level writes into the global environment, and <<- writes into an enclosing environment, so a name is shared across the session
❌ No immutability by default (C2): A binding is assigned freely, and attr(x, "a") <- v, names(x) <- v, and a reference-class field change a value in place
⚠️ Many functions capture their arguments non-standardly: subset, with, and most modelling functions evaluate an argument inside a data frame, so the call does not follow the usual rule



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Copy-on-modify protects the reader: A value is copied only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives a vector does not change the caller’s value
⚠️ Copy-on-modify raises peak memory: Modifying a large object can duplicate it, so the footprint exceeds the logical size of the data
⚠️ The collector runs on R’s schedule (M2): Collection happens when R decides, and gc() reports heap use, but there is no block-scoped release
❌ No RAII (M3): There is no destructor at block exit, so a connection, a file, or a graphics device is closed by on.exit or explicitly
❌ No ownership model (M4): No static rule ties a value’s storage to one binding
✅ on.exit registers exit-time cleanup: An action runs when the function returns or raises, which is the R idiom for releasing a resource
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: memory exhaustion at the allocator aborts the session (documented as the R-session crash), below the tryCatch surface (the nested-depth error is a catchable condition; the allocator abort is not) (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Conditions are classed objects: stop, warning, and message signal a condition with a class, so a handler matches a class rather than a message string
✅ tryCatch separates recovery from cleanup: An exiting handler returns a value, and finally runs on every path
✅ withCallingHandlers allows a non-unwinding response: A handler can log a warning and let evaluation continue
❌ Unchecked exceptions only (Er2): A signalled condition propagates until something catches it, and no caller is required to handle it
⚠️ A warning is not an error: It prints and evaluation continues, so an ignored warning can leave a wrong result
⚠️ No composable result value: A failure is a thrown condition or a sentinel such as NULL or NA, so it does not compose through a call chain



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ parallel ships with the base distribution: mclapply forks workers on Unix, and makeCluster with parLapply runs across sockets, so independent work splits without a shared-memory protocol
✅ A socket cluster passes results, not shared state: A worker returns a value that is serialised back, so workers do not share an address space
✅ future and %dopar% give a declarative parallel surface: Code written for a sequential lapply is unchanged when it runs in parallel
⚠️ Base R evaluates one expression at a time: Vectorised operations are the usual substitute for a second thread
⚠️ A forked worker copies on write: mclapply shares the parent’s memory until a worker modifies it, and then it duplicates
⚠️ Reproducibility needs explicit seed handling: A parallel random stream requires clusterSetRNGStream or the future seed mechanism



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One open-source implementation with several distributors: The R Core Team maintains the interpreter under the GNU GPL, and CRAN ships source and binaries
✅ Official builds cover the three desktop platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows binaries are published for each release
✅ The interpreter is not tied to one editor: RStudio, VS Code, Emacs ESS, and the plain console drive the same R
✅ Package installation is declarative: install.packages fetches from a named mirror, and renv records exact versions in a lockfile
⚠️ A source package with C or C++ needs a toolchain: The published binary avoids the compiler, but a source install needs headers and a linker



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Copy-on-modify is a deliberate trade: Immutability by copy protects callers and costs peak memory
Non-standard evaluation is a deliberate design: It makes subset(d, x > 1) and a formula interface readable and lets a modelling call record the variable names it was given, at the cost of evaluation that is not visible at the call site
The global environment is for interactive analysis: A session-wide namespace suits exploratory work at the console
A factor encodes categorical data: The hidden integer code is the price of ordered levels and of a compact representation
One-based indexing and <- are convention choices: They follow the S language and the statistics literature, so the cost is familiarity, not a forced dependency
R is for statistics, not general programming: The assumption of a data-analysis workload is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Vectorised and matrix operations call compiled C, C++, and BLAS/LAPACK code: colSums, %*%, and lm do their work in compiled libraries, so the interpreter is not in the inner loop
✅ A large set of compiled packages exists: data.table, Rcpp, and Matrix move hot paths into compiled code, and CRAN distributes them
⚠️ Interpreted with no ahead-of-time compilation (R1): Base R executes an interpreted form, so a scalar loop is slower than its compiled equivalent
⚠️ The just-in-time compiler helps only where it applies: The byte-code compiler (level 3, cmpfun) speeds up a loop, but the gain is bounded
⚠️ Memory pressure shows up as time: Copying and collection cost time that the source does not show



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ CRAN is a large, curated, central repository: Tens of thousands of packages pass an automated check before publication
✅ The RStudio IDE is a first-class environment: Console, source editor, plots, and a debugger sit in one window
✅ Reproducibility tooling is mature: renv records a project library, and a package manager can pin a date-based snapshot
⚠️ Package quality varies: The CRAN check verifies correctness and portability, not statistical validity, so a method needs its own reading
⚠️ A deployment needs the full environment: R, a build toolchain, and system libraries for compiled dependencies make a project heavier to ship than a single binary
❌ Binaries bind to an R major release: R 4.0.0 required every package to be reinstalled, and the C API manual promises notice, not binary stability [5], [6] (Ec8)
❌ Stored workspaces bind to the release: serialization format 3 is the default since R 3.6.0, R states that format-3 data cannot be read by versions prior to 3.5.0, and version = 2 is the documented way to write a file an older R opens [7] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong and documented: The Core Team publishes a NEWS file per release and keeps the language API stable, so an old script generally still runs
✅ A regular release cadence exists: An x.y.0 release appears each spring and a patch release follows in the same year
✅ The tidyverse and r-lib provide deprecation discipline: The lifecycle package marks a function as experimental, deprecated, or superseded before removal
⚠️ A third-party package can break across a major release: A package that used an internal API can fail after an upgrade, and the fix belongs to its maintainer
⚠️ A package can be archived from CRAN: An unmaintained package is removed from the index, so code that depends on it needs a replacement or a frozen snapshot



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for statistical computing: lm, glm, aov, and t.test are in the base distribution with a formula interface
✅ CRAN and Bioconductor cover the applied fields: Biostatistics, econometrics, time series, and genomics each have dedicated packages
✅ A report is generated from the analysis itself: knitr, rmarkdown, and Quarto run the code and place its output in the document
❌ Domain lock-in to statistics and data analysis (D1): The core value types, the formula interface, and the modelling packages assume a data-analysis workflow
⚠️ A production service in R is unusual: A service with a high request rate is usually written elsewhere and calls R for the model



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ Steep (L1): The idioms — vectorisation, the apply family, environments, and S3 dispatch — take time for a programmer from an imperative language
⚠️ Non-standard evaluation surprises newcomers: An argument can be evaluated inside a data frame, so subset and dplyr code does not follow the usual call rule
⚠️ Factor semantics are unfamiliar: A factor compares by its integer level code, so an ordering or a comparison can differ from the printed text
⚠️ The apply family is confusing: sapply varies its return type with the input, so a result is not predictable from the call alone
✅ Documentation is generated, complete, and mandated: Every CRAN package must document every exported function, and ? reaches the reference page



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The formula interface and the pipe are compact: y ~ x and x |> f() read as a data pipeline
✅ Indexing follows one rule across atomic, list, and data-frame values: [, [[, and $ behave consistently, so a new structure needs no new syntax
⚠️ Two assignment operators exist: <- binds a name in the current environment, and = also assigns at top level but separates a named argument inside a call, so the meaning depends on position
⚠️ . is overloaded: It means every other variable in a formula and the piped value in a magrittr pipe
⚠️ A print method hides structure: Printing a data frame or a model object shows a summary, so str() is needed to see the actual shape



1.2.7 Testing

✅ testthat is the de facto standard framework: It provides expectations, a runner, and a per-file test structure
✅ A package must pass R CMD check: CRAN runs the check, which executes the tests and the examples, so a package is not published with a failing test
✅ Property-based and snapshot testing exist: hedgehog generates inputs, and a testthat snapshot records output for comparison
✅ Interactive debugging is available: browser(), traceback(), debug(), and the RStudio debugger stop at a line and inspect its environment
⚠️ Errors are runtime-only (G3): A type error appears when the line runs, so the test suite is what reaches the untested path
⚠️ A suite depends on the installed environment: The tests run through the package machinery, so the environment must be installed first



1.2.8 Security

❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): eval(parse(text = ...)), do.call on a string, and system() turn text into code or a command, so concatenated input is an injection surface
❌ Dynamic typing carries its risk into security code: A check written for one class can pass an object of another class, and dispatch then runs a different method
⚠️ system2 reduces but does not remove shell risk: It passes arguments as a vector, yet a shell is still involved
⚠️ load and readRDS restore an object, not only data: A serialised object can carry an environment, so restoring untrusted state is a code-execution path
⚠️ The interpreter runs with the user’s full privileges: R has no sandbox of its own, so code in a session has the user’s access to files and the network

Verdict: R’s design yields moderate coupling for statistical computing and higher coupling outside it. Vectorised operations and compiled linear algebra remove per-element iteration from the source, and the formula interface separates a model from a caller’s data. Main strengths: a curated package ecosystem, first-class functions and environments, and a strong fit for data analysis. Main weaknesses: dynamic typing with no static check, the global environment as the default destination of <-, copy-on-modify memory cost, non-standard evaluation that hides where an argument is evaluated, a steep learning curve, and dynamic code paths (eval, system) that carry injection risk.

title: RQL (RavenDB 7.2)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses RQL (RavenDB 7.2) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 65.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 47.3/100 · Engineering readiness 59.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ The query states the result: from ... where ... select declares the projection to produce, and the reference lays the clause order over the server’s pipeline
❌ The server checks values at execution: RQL carries no static check against the document shape — a document missing the filtered field ‘may return unexpected results’ in the docs’ own words, and a nulls first clause against a Lucene index answers InvalidQueryException at runtime (T1)
❌ Dynamic fields drive the dispatch: a query on an unindexed field creates an auto-index from the documents found, in and all in behave per array flattening, and a field’s type follows the JSON document, not a schema (T3)
❌ No sum types: a field holds a string, number, array, or nested object from the document, and an alternative is modeled by collection naming and exists() guards, not by a type (T4)
❌ No parameterized query: the declare block defines one JavaScript function per query, values arrive as $param markers, and reusable logic is copied query to query (T5)
❌ One flat name space: collections, indexes, and declared functions are named strings inside a database, and nothing in RQL imports definitions across databases (T6)
❌ Null and absent share the filter: where on a missing field matches by index semantics, the 7.2 nulls first/last clauses exist to pin where missing-field documents land (Corax only), and exists() is the documented anchor for the distinction (T10)
❌ No module boundary: declare is query-local, static-index definitions live in the server’s own map-reduce languages, and RQL text imports nothing (T11)
❌ Statements state no effect: update runs a JavaScript patch over every matched document, load pulls related documents into the projection, and no signature records the write (T12)
❌ JavaScript is the language’s second surface: declare functions and update patches execute server-side, and values cross between JSON documents and script objects with no typed boundary check (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The pipeline mirrors the syntax: from, where, include, order by, limit, and select are the server’s pipeline stages in the order the reference states them
❌ Documents mutate in place: update patches stored documents with a script, counters increment, time series append, and patching is the language’s own write surface (C2)
❌ No constructor validates a patched document: a patch script can produce any JSON shape, the server ships JSON Schema validation as a feature beside the language (7.2), and the patched document’s shape is checked by the deployment, not by the query (C4)
⚠️ Conditional patches race writers: an update script runs server-side over a query’s results, and RavenDB’s per-document change vectors resolve what the language does not scope



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the server’s: Voron pages, index files, and query results live in the RavenDB process, and the query text allocates nothing
⚠️ A query is served by an index the server builds: a dynamic query on an unindexed field creates and maintains an auto-index, and the 7.2.5 notes fix non-ASCII index terms truncated after a 2048-character value lands in the same field — storage-engine facts the language hides



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured path in the language: a type-mismatched comparison is logged by the engine and the document drops from the result, a clause the index engine rejects raises InvalidQueryException as a server error, and the query text carries no path around either (Er1)
❌ Non-matching filters are the error: a document without the filtered field falls out of where results, NOT cannot start a clause so the docs prescribe an exists() anchor, and the anchors behave differently on scoring (exists() adds a constant score, where true adds none, 7.2.6) (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: documents, projections, included relateds, counters, time series, and explanations share one flat response envelope, and success and absence are read from the collection’s emptiness (Er4)
✅ The response can carry its own diagnostics: include exposes query timings and explanations, published in the keyword list, so a caller reads a defined report about the query beside the data



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency is the server’s: indexing, ETL, subscriptions, cluster transactions, and replication run as server tasks, and the language names no threads, tasks, or channels
⚠️ A patch-all races writers: an update over a dynamic query’s results runs per document, and per-document change vectors and cluster transactions resolve conflicts outside the language



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One product speaks RQL: the language is RavenDB’s query surface — its index engines, its Studio, its client APIs — and nothing in the language runs against another database (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside document data: the unit is the JSON document, every query runs through an index the reference states as universal, and relational and analytic workloads move to the server’s ETL side (P4)
✅ A typed front end shares the surface: LINQ and the high-level session methods translate to RQL before sending, per the reference, so application code plans queries through the same pipeline statically



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Every query pays for an index: the index-first pipeline publishes fast, sorted reads and auto-index convenience, and the price is write-time index maintenance every document write pays, queried or not
Two engines, one language, not one language: the reference states 7.2’s nulls clauses as Corax-only and answers InvalidQueryException on Lucene indexes, so the same text carries two legalities inside one product line
Embedded JavaScript buys projection power and server trust: declare functions format results and update scripts rewrite documents inside the query, and the language’s security surface becomes script execution bounded by admin access
The upgrade is a ratchet: the 7.2.5 revisions schema update publishes no downgrade path, so a deployment that adopts the newest RQL surface cannot roll its data back to the version it came from




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The index serves the query: every RQL query runs on an auto or static index, the 7.2.6 notes ship bitmap evaluation for large Corax result sets, and the projection stage reads stored fields, not documents
⚠️ Auto-indexes pay at write time: a dynamic query on an unindexed field creates an auto-index the server then maintains, a cost the docs attribute to the server’s decision, not the query’s



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments across the stack: Studio and RavenCLI ship with the server, the monitoring integrations (SNMP, Telegraf, Grafana) are per-vendor plugins, and the client tooling is per-language SDK (Ec2)
❌ A niche market: RavenDB expertise concentrates in .NET-lineage application shops, and the hiring pool is a fraction of SQL’s (Ec3)
❌ Source-available under the vendor’s license: the server source is published on GitHub under RavenDB’s source-available terms with usage caps, so a deployment reads the vendor’s license before its code (Ec4)
❌ A .NET monoculture: the client APIs, Studio, the LINQ provider, and the deployment tooling center on .NET, and the 7.2 notes ride .NET 10 updates with a multiarch server image (Ec6)
❌ Two engines kept alive under one language: the 7.2 nulls clauses are published as Corax-only, InvalidQueryException on a Lucene index, and the docs maintain a client-migration guide for the API surface the language rides on (Ec7)
✅ The reference layer is open: docs.ravendb.net publishes every version 1.0 through 7.2, the Query view ships in every license, and the community channel is a click from every page



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The vendor renames, reparses, and ratchets: RQL gains keywords per release (when() conditional filtering, nulls first/last, vector.search()), the client migration guide publishes breaking changes per major, and the 7.2.5 What’s New page states the revisions storage schema update as a one-way door — after upgrading, downgrading to an earlier version is not possible (V1)
✅ A yearly line with LTS points: 5.4, 6.2, and 7.2 are LTS releases with published support end dates, patches ship quarterly (7.2.7 in late 2026), and the What’s New pages state each release’s surface
✅ The language moves on the product’s clock: RQL gains surface in quarterly patches, not committee drafts, so a feature arrives in release notes before it settles in the reference



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting RQL means adopting RavenDB’s index model: every query is served by an index, collections and fields are named strings inside a database, and counters, time series, spatial fields, and vectors are extensions the language reaches through its own keywords (D1)
❌ The index-first pipeline forces the architecture: the reference states that all queries in RavenDB use an index as universal, an auto-index appears when a query needs one, and static indexes are map-reduce code in the server’s language — the application’s shape follows from what the query language can bind to (D3)
✅ RQL queries stored document data: from names the source, where filters the index, and select projects the matching documents



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Index semantics under SQL-shaped syntax: a SQL reader meets auto-indexes, all in answering empty where in answers full, NOT needing an anchor, and where true scoring documents differently from exists() — the reference devotes sections to these traps (L1)
❌ Three syntaxes, one server: RQL text, the LINQ provider, and the DocumentQuery methods all land on RQL, JavaScript rides inside declare and update, and Lucene full-text syntax embeds inside where via lucene() (L2)
✅ One reference page covers the language: the 7.2 RQL page lists every clause with worked examples, the pipeline order, and the keyword-method table



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The surface is uneven: = and == are interchangeable, NOT cannot start a clause, limit 5, 10 and limit 10 offset 5 and offset 5 coexist for the same paging, the nulls clauses are Corax-only, and declare function embeds JavaScript in a SQL-shaped text (S2)
❌ Punctuation carries meaning: Lines[].ProductName for flattened arrays, all_docs? for the all-collection source, $param1 for parameters, quoted “Collection/Name” strings, // and /* */ comments — a misread token usually parses and changes the result (S3)
✅ The common query is one line: from “Employees” where FirstName = “Laura” select FirstName states the projection in three clauses, and keywords are case-insensitive



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard query-test harness in the language: the documented test story is a client-side base class over an embedded server for application code, the Query view is manual, and RQL text names no regression harness (G1)
✅ The language can report its own execution: include carries query timings and explanations in the published keyword list, and Studio’s Query view runs RQL against the live database with code assistance
❌ Type and field faults land on the data: a comparison against a field typed as the other type is logged and the document skipped, and the docs’ where true / exists() caveat — unexpected results when documents lack the field — is a data-shape fact found at execution (G3)
❌ Only the wall clock: today() and now() compare against the current server date per the reference, when() evaluates its condition against query parameters at evaluation time, and elapsed-time tests read the server (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Values coerce at evaluation: order by … as long casts at the sort stage, between requires matching border types, string-and-number comparisons ride on index collation, and the 7.2.5 notes fix control-character equality and hashing as a storage consistency bug, rejecting control characters in document ids for new databases (Q2)
❌ String-built queries are the injection surface: RQL is request text the RawQuery path sends as written, so concatenated user input can add clauses to a where expression, and the documented mitigation is binding values through $param markers out of band (Q3)
⚠️ Stored script is the server’s trust decision: declare functions and patch scripts execute on the server, so write access to the language grants script execution, bounded per database by admin-level access



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.2.10 Stored data formats
What the toolchain stores that outlives the program, and what the vendor publishes about reading it across a release boundary. Ec9 is present when one row carries a break: the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable elsewhere, or a break the probe harness has reproduced.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is a request text: the same RQL on the same server version and dataset reproduces the same documents, and there is no build artifact (Y1)
✅ Drivers pin by NuGet version: the client packages ship per release with the server’s version (the 7.2 notes track .NET 10.0.9), and an application pins them as ordinary dependencies (Y14)
⚠️ The deployment lives server-side: results reproduce on a cluster’s topology, index state, and version — the 7.2.5 storage-schema note makes even the version a one-way fact



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published libraries carry no signed provenance by default: the client SDKs ship on NuGet named to their publishers, and a consumer trusts the package installed (Y3)
✅ NuGet namespaces every package, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
❌ No maintained advisory feed names the product: security fixes land in release notes and vendor communication, and no CVE-mapped public advisory database tracks RQL-era releases the way Apache and CNCF projects publish theirs (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No stable tracing standard is part of the language: OpenTelemetry export is a server monitoring feature (the 7.2.5 notes add service-name configuration), SNMP and Grafana integrations are server-side, and the query text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: the server routes logs through NLog, keeps an audit log, and added a Studio admin logs view in 7.2.6, and the language defines no logging construct (Y6)
✅ The server ships its own post-mortem: the debug package for a (sharded) database named in the 7.2.5 notes, the audit log, and the cluster dashboard give an operator the artifacts around a failure (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ Studio is submit-and-run: the Query view runs RQL against the open database with code assistance, and RavenCLI answers with no build step (Y7)
✅ A maintained analyzer ships with the product: RQL code assistance in Studio’s Query view is published as part of the server, so syntax and completion land in the vendor editor before the server sees the text
❌ No source-level debugger: diagnosis goes through include-explanations, query timings, the server’s logs, and Studio’s views (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ JavaScript is the published extension point: declare function defines server-side functions callable from a projection, update runs patch scripts over matched documents, and values cross as JSON — the function mechanism is in the language, if untyped
❌ No portable target: a query runs on a RavenDB server, and nothing in the language runs without one (Y10)
✅ HTTP, ETL, and wire protocols move data across systems: queries answer over HTTP, ETL sinks publish Parquet, SQL, Kafka, and queue paths, and the PostgreSQL-protocol integration answers BI tools



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is the vendor: RQL gains keywords when Hibernating Rhinos ships them — the What’s New pages are release notes, not a standards process — the LTS schedule and license terms are the vendor’s, and no external body owns the language (Y11)
✅ The reference is published: the clause list, keyword-method table, and per-feature guides are on the public docs site, and the server’s source is readable on GitHub (Y12)
❌ No conformance mechanism exists: RQL has one implementation, so conformance is the vendor’s own test suite, and no published suite with implementation reports decides a third-party claim (Y17)
✅ The parser is readable in the source: the server repository is public and source-available, and RQL parses in published code the ecosystem can inspect (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a RavenDB server: energy is the engine’s, and the reader’s levers are the index choice — auto versus static, Corax versus Lucene — that the language’s from clause makes visible.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ A SQL-shaped language models write fluently, and 7.2 ships an AI Assistant in Studio that generates RQL — the index-first semantics and the all in, NOT, and exists() traps are exactly where generated queries need review.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; RavenDB ships ACID writes, optimistic concurrency, and cluster transactions, and its safety record is the vendor’s, stated in release notes.

Verdict: RQL is a SQL-shaped surface over a document store that refuses to answer a query without an index: from, where, order by, and select read the index the server builds, an auto-index appears when a dynamic query needs one, and JavaScript rides inside the language for projection and patching. Its costs are RavenDB’s own: values coerce at evaluation, a where over a missing field drops documents silently, two index engines publish two legality rules for the same 7.2 clauses, and governance, licensing, and the roadmap are one vendor’s. Main strengths: a one-page reference with worked examples and a published trap list, query diagnostics inside the language itself (timings, explanations), Studio code assistance the vendor maintains, and LINQ as a static front end that shares the pipeline. Main weaknesses: single-vendor governance with no conformance mechanism, no portable target at all, a source-available license with usage caps, a .NET-centered ecosystem, and a published one-way storage schema on the newest line.

title: SAS (9.4 / Viya)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SAS in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 79.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 71.1/100 · Engineering readiness 25.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A variable takes its type when the DATA step first builds the row, so a mismatch appears at run time
⚠️ Two types exist and a character length is fixed at first use: A variable is numeric or character, and a later longer value is truncated to the length already set
⚠️ The dataset carries the schema, not a declaration: A variable list comes from the dataset descriptor, so a variable’s type is read from data rather than from source
✅ LENGTH and ATTRIB declare a variable explicitly: A length, a type, and a format can be fixed before the data arrives, which decouples the variable from the value that first creates it
✅ FORMAT and INFORMAT separate presentation from storage: A date is a number with a DATE9. format, so a reader sees a date and the value stays numeric
❌ There is no type beyond a column in a dataset: SAS has no user-defined type, generic, or interface, so a richer value is encoded in columns



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The DATA step separates data handling from analysis: A DATA step reads, merges, filters, and derives; a PROC step analyses and reports, so the two are distinct statement kinds
✅ A PROC step names its analysis and takes a dataset: PROC MEANS data=work.sales; performs one analysis on one input, so the analysis is not tangled with retrieval
✅ SET, MERGE, and BY compose datasets declaratively: A join is declared with a BY key, so the key is the join condition rather than a hand-coded loop
❌ No immutability by default (C2): A DATA step can overwrite the dataset it reads (data work.x; set work.x;), and every variable is reassignable
❌ A macro is the only module mechanism: %MACRO is text substitution, so an expansion depends on the macro symbol table and on the place of the invocation
⚠️ The DATA step’s implicit loop carries state across rows: RETAIN and the automatic _N_ follow the row stream, so row order becomes part of the result
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: call symput-generated code names, the CALL EXECUTE site runs the string as a statement (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The SAS supervisor allocates and frees the buffers of a step, and the program never names an address
✅ The program-data vector bounds per-row state: A step holds one row’s variables in a fixed vector, so the program does not size buffers
✅ The resource envelope is a configuration choice: SORTSIZE, MEMSIZE (on the hosts that provide it), and the Viya CAS memory settings are set outside the program
⚠️ A large sort spills to the work library: A sort or a hash join that exceeds its memory writes to the utility library, so the temporary footprint follows the data volume
⚠️ A macro variable persists for the whole session: A %LET value stays until it is reassigned, so it is shared state that outlives the step that set it
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: an ABEND-class runtime failure ends the session (documented), below the ON ERROR surface (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ OPTIONS ERRORABEND stops the session on an error: An error ends the run instead of continuing, which turns a silent failure into a visible one
✅ A macro-level guard can abort the run: %IF &SYSERR %THEN %ABORT reads the error status and stops the batch
❌ No structured error path (Er1): SAS has no exception construct, so a DATA step records an error, writes a note to the log, and by default continues to the next observation
⚠️ An error is reported in the log, not to the caller: A step sets &SYSERR and the automatic _ERROR_ flag, so detection is by log inspection or a macro check
⚠️ Error checking is opt-in per step: The default continues on many data errors, so a batch run can finish with a wrong dataset



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Procedures can use several threads: OPTIONS THREADS lets PROC SORT, PROC MEANS, and PROC SQL use more than one processor
✅ SAS/CONNECT and MP Connect distribute work across sessions: A job can be split over several SAS sessions on one host or across hosts
✅ A dataset is locked per member: Two writers do not share a row buffer, so member-level locking prevents a concurrent overwrite in one library
⚠️ The language offers no lock or atomic primitive: Coordination is the platform’s library locking and the scheduler’s, not a construct in the DATA step
⚠️ The macro symbol table is shared session state: One step’s %LET or CALL SYMPUT is visible to every later step in the session



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): The language needs a SAS installation, and a program’s unit of deployment is a SAS library on a SAS host
❌ SAS datasets are the interchange unit: The persistence format is a proprietary member of a SAS library
⚠️ Viya is a second runtime under the same vendor: Viya runs the language on the CAS engine with cloud deployment, but it is the same vendor’s platform, not an independent implementation
✅ A dataset can be written to the documented XPORT transport form: The XPORT engine with PROC COPY produces the openly documented transport format that the FDA requires for electronic submissions, and other tools can read it
⚠️ Open-source interop exists from inside the platform: PROC PYTHON and PROC R call R and Python, so part of a workflow can use an open tool



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The DATA-step/PROC-step split is a deliberate separation of concerns: Retrieval and analysis are distinct statement kinds by design
The dataset is the only data abstraction: One table shape for all data keeps the language uniform, at the cost of encoding a richer value in columns
A macro is a text-substitution preprocessor: It keeps a repeated block in one place, at the cost of visibility at expansion time
Point-and-click Enterprise Guide serves a non-programmer task: Hiding the language suits a code-free workflow, so the GUI’s coupling to the engine is the product’s purpose
A proprietary platform is traded for a regulated-industry toolchain: One vendor with documented releases and validation packages suits a regulated deliverable
Viya chose coexistence over replacement: Modernising the architecture while keeping SAS 9.4 running is a compatibility decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The DATA step and the procedures run compiled code: A step is compiled to a program-data-vector loop executed by the supervisor
✅ Multithreading and the CAS engine parallelise heavy work: Threaded procedures and distributed in-memory execution in Viya carry the large jobs
✅ An index or the SPD engine avoids a full scan: A lookup by an indexed key or by the multi-threaded SPD engine reads fewer pages than a sequential pass
⚠️ A sort can dominate a job’s time and space: A sort that exceeds memory spills to the work library, so a job of a given size needs a matching utility allocation
⚠️ A BY-group analysis requires sorted input: Many procedures need the data sorted by the BY key, which makes a sort a precondition of the analysis



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The library is large and mature inside its industry: SAS ships statistical, econometric, clinical, and operations-research modules with long support windows
✅ Regulated statistical practice has decades of SAS convention: Clinical and regulated reporting follows CDISC standards and platform validation practice
✅ Viya adds open-source tooling: Jupyter, Python, R, and REST interfaces connect to a Viya deployment
❌ Proprietary (Ec4): The product is licensed by subscription, and its modules are licensed separately
❌ Small, niche, and increasingly legacy (Ec3): The language’s own market has shrunk against R and Python, so new analysts and new packages arrive more slowly
⚠️ The ecosystem is closed: A shared contribution is an in-house macro or user-defined format, not a package drawn from an open index
✅ Stored data sets cross on a published engine rule: SAS states that its engines enable SAS to access different formats or versions of SAS files [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Long-term stability is a stated commitment: A program written for an earlier release of the same generation still runs on a later one
✅ The vendor carries validated code forward: Existing 9.4 language support continues in Viya, so a submission program is not stranded
⚠️ The language has evolved slowly: SAS 9.4 has been the reference release since 2013, and the DATA-step and PROC syntax is largely unchanged
⚠️ The modern architecture is a second platform: Viya changes deployment, engines, and administration, so a move to it is a platform migration rather than a language upgrade
⚠️ Evolution follows the vendor’s roadmap: A new feature appears at the vendor’s next release, not at a date the community fixes
❌ Build variants multiply: the macro language’s %IF %THEN generates code at compile time, so the step that runs is a macro outcome, not the source text (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for regulated statistical reporting: A DATA step plus a PROC produce a documented, reproducible table
✅ Clinical and financial workflows have a fixed vocabulary: PROC LIFETEST, PROC PHREG, PROC FREQ, and PROC LOGISTIC name the standard analyses directly
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language is built for statistical analysis on a SAS platform, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
⚠️ The regulatory transport requirement has narrowed: The FDA still requires the open SAS V5 XPORT transport format for datasets, but CDISC standards define their content and other tools can write the format, so the language’s old regulatory moat has shrunk
⚠️ General-purpose programming sits outside the design centre: Text processing, user interfaces, and systems work are not the intended use
⚠️ Analysts increasingly use R and Python beside it: An open-source language is cheaper per seat and easier to hire for



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The DATA-step/PROC-step division is teachable: A beginner learns retrieval in a DATA step and analysis in a PROC, and the two do not mix
✅ Documentation and training are complete and vendor-provided: SAS documentation, courses, and certification cover every module
⚠️ Steep (L1): The DATA step’s implicit loop, the program-data vector, and the two-match step of MERGE are unlike any other language’s execution model
⚠️ DATA-step syntax is idiosyncratic: Statements are KEYWORD variable=value; lines whose effect depends on their order in the step
⚠️ Macro programming is a second language on top: %MACRO, &var, %eval, and the quoting functions (%str, %bquote) have their own rules



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Statements are keyword-led and read as English: PROC SORT data=a; by x; run; states the operation and the key
✅ A PROC block is small per analysis: An analysis reads as PROC name data=...; plus a few statements
❌ Verbose (S1): A typical step is a list of KEYWORD option; lines, and necessary statements such as LENGTH, FORMAT, and LABEL add lines before any data is touched
⚠️ Every step must be closed by RUN or QUIT: A missing RUN; means the step does not execute, and a missing QUIT leaves a procedure open
⚠️ The semicolon and the % sigil each carry meaning: A missing semicolon changes the statement, and a macro reference without % or & is treated as text
⚠️ Formats and informats add a name to every value: date9., $char20., and best12. decorate a declaration, so a reader learns a second vocabulary



1.2.7 Testing

✅ PROC COMPARE reports differences by variable and observation: A regression test is a dataset comparison with a named result
✅ A check step can assert its own expectation: A step can read the result and %ABORT on a wrong value, and OPTIONS ERRORABEND turns a data error into a stop
✅ The log is the primary diagnostic instrument: With MPRINT and MLOGIC it names the step and the macro line that failed
⚠️ No test framework ships with the language: A test is a SAS program, so the harness is a script or a scheduler around it
⚠️ Errors are runtime-only: A wrong type or a missing file appears when the step runs, not before
⚠️ A passing run can still contain errors: The default continues after many errors, so a clean exit code does not imply a clean run
❌ No monotonic reading published: the SAS datetime functions read the wall clock, and the reference ships no elapsed reading (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ No pointers and no manual memory access: The language offers no address arithmetic, so the memory-corruption class does not apply
✅ Access control is a platform feature: Library and table permissions, metadata-server roles, and Viya identities control who reads a dataset
✅ Viya records an audit trail: A deployment logs who ran which action against which resource
⚠️ A macro variable can build a statement: &SYSFUNC and a resolved macro variable are expanded into syntax, so a value that carries user input can become code
⚠️ Encryption and transport security are configuration choices: A library can be encrypted and a connection secured, but the default is the site’s decision
⚠️ A dataset member is a binary file with no per-row rule: A leaked member is a full data dump, so row-level restriction must be built above the format
❌ All numbers are IEEE-754 doubles: integers above 2^53 change value in silence (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.2.10 Stored data formats

Verdict: SAS’s design yields moderate core coupling and a weaker platform position. The DATA step and the PROC step are genuinely separate concerns, and the language is strong for regulated statistical reporting. Main strengths: the retrieval/analysis split, a mature module library, and long-term stability that carries validated code forward. Main weaknesses: dynamic typing with no static check, no structured error path, a proprietary platform with a closed ecosystem, a shrinking market against R and Python, and an idiosyncratic DATA-step syntax that makes the learning curve steep.
