title: SPARQL (W3C Recommendation 1.1)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SPARQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 77.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 58.2/100 · Engineering readiness 70.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Expressions reuse a published type system: SPARQL 1.1 conforms to the XPath/XQuery 1.1 function library and its typed value model, and the operator semantics are stated in the specification
❌ No sum types: a bound term is an IRI, a literal, a blank node, or a value in the expression type lattice, and an alternative is modelled by UNION and a post-check (T4)
❌ No generic type parameter: a query cannot be parameterised over a type, and reusable logic is copied, templated by the caller, or moved to engine-specific procedures (T5)
❌ An absent match leaves UNDEF, not a typed value: OPTIONAL leaves variables unbound, and an expression over an unbound position is a fault the specification defines — absence is not a type the query names (T10)
❌ No module boundary in 1.1: a query is one unit, PREFIX names a vocabulary, and nothing in SPARQL 1.1 imports definitions from a published document (the SPARQL 1.2 drafts carry an IMPORT clause) (T11)
❌ The text shows the graph, not the effect: SERVICE reaches a remote endpoint and INSERT/DELETE write the store, and no signature states the effect (T12)
❌ A SERVICE block sends the inner pattern to an endpoint the query cannot validate: the remote graph’s shape arrives as bindings (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The query states the result: CONSTRUCT { ?s ?p ?o } WHERE { ... } declares the graph to produce, and the engine computes the mapping
❌ The dataset is mutable in place: SPARQL 1.1 Update writes named graphs and the default graph as a language surface, with no immutability option (C2)
❌ No constructor validates a produced term: a CONSTRUCT template composes IRIs and literals from bound parts, and a malformed term surfaces as a type fault at runtime (C4)
❌ The default order is a set: a SELECT result is a sequence of solution mappings, and GROUP_CONCAT leaves element order to the engine unless an ORDER BY fixes it (C5)
⚠️ Store rules run outside the query: an INSERT WHERE races writers, and the engine’s transaction layer handles what the language does not scope



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the engine’s: query results, join state, and index pages live in the store’s runtime, and the query text allocates nothing
⚠️ A dense match materializes in the engine: an unbounded variable-length property path over a large graph is an operation whose memory the operator plans for



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path in the language: a type fault in BIND, a ?x/0 division, and an unbound term in a template are runtime faults the specification defines, and the query carries no path around them (Er1)
❌ FILTER swallows a type fault: an expression that evaluates to UNDEF filters its row out, and the row’s disappearance is the definition, not an error (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: bindings, booleans, and UNDEF share the expression slots, and success and absence compose by spec rules, not by a type (Er4)
✅ The protocol defines a transport outcome: the SPARQL Protocol names the HTTP status a service returns for a malformed request, so a caller sees a defined result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Federation is a clause, not a thread: SERVICE <remote> { ... } composes remote evaluation into the query, and the engine schedules it
⚠️ Isolation is store-specific: a write racing a writer is handled by the engine’s transaction layer, outside the language



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The language is a W3C Recommendation, not a product: Apache Jena, Oxigraph, Blazegraph, GraphDB, Virtuoso, and Amazon Neptune all implement SPARQL 1.1 query and update
❌ A poor fit outside RDF data: triple-pattern matching, named graphs, and dataset semantics assume an RDF store, and application logic stays in a host language (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Default-graph semantics are deliberately left open: the same query over the same files answers differently across stores until the deployment states its default-graph rule
SERVICE federation evaluates on the remote endpoint under the join order the language fixes: a federated subpattern can re-run per binding solution, and the remote bill lands outside the local plan
The graph answers only what the vocabulary asked: a query reads the triples the modeling chose, and modeling debt lands in the data before the first query runs
ShEx and SHACL carry the schema layer the standards group has not standardized for queries: the ecosystem validates graphs with published schema languages, and a query author pairs them with 1.1 by hand




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The store’s planner runs the join: engines cost joins, order OPTIONAL left-to-right, and expose plan inspection (Jena’s Explain, Blazegraph’s EXPLAIN, Oxigraph’s plans)
⚠️ Property-path depth is the tuning surface: + and * path expressions plan as variable-depth traversals, and the engine’s limits are the practical constraint



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling fragments by engine: Fuseki, Oxigraph’s server CLI, GraphDB Workbench, and Blazegraph’s GUI each carry their own query console, loader, and monitor (Ec2)
❌ A niche market: RDF query expertise concentrates in semantic-web, library, research, and knowledge-graph systems, and the hiring pool is a fraction of SQL’s (Ec3)
✅ The reference stack is open: Jena (Apache-2.0) and Oxigraph (MIT) ship the language end to end, and RDF’s exchange formats (Turtle, N-Triples, RDF/XML) are published standards



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The committee moves on a decade’s clock: SPARQL 1.1 became a Recommendation in March 2013; the SPARQL 1.2 First Public Working Draft arrived in May 2023, and the 1.2 documents are Working Drafts in late 2026 (V4)
✅ 1.1 is stable and conformance-tested: the W3C 1.1 test suite is maintained with implementation reports, and engines report passing it as a compatibility fact



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Adopting SPARQL means adopting an RDF store: the language’s unit is the RDF dataset, and its patterns are triple matches (D1)
✅ SPARQL is used to query stored RDF graph data: SELECT and CONSTRUCT read triples, and Update writes them back
⚠️ Linked-data plumbing travels with the language: SERVICE federation, the Graph Store Protocol, and entailment regimes are companion standards, and using the ecosystem means reading them too



1.2.5 Learning

❌ SQL-shaped syntax carries RDF semantics: OPTIONAL is a left join under set semantics, MINUS is a difference, and blank-node scoping in CONSTRUCT templates is new material for a SQL reader (L1)
❌ SPARQL 1.1 is five specifications plus a data model: Query, Update, Graph Store, Protocol, and Federated Query, over the RDF 1.1 model — the ‘language’ is a family of documents (L2)
✅ The reference is one readable page: the W3C Query Recommendation carries definitions, examples, an ABNF grammar, and the worked test suite behind it



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ A query wears its vocabulary: a PREFIX block, the full clause list (SELECT ... WHERE ... OPTIONAL ... FILTER ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT), and BIND/AS scaffolding for computations that fit one expression line in a host language (S1)
❌ The surface is uneven: OPTIONAL is not a SQL LEFT JOIN, MINUS is not EXCEPT (its scoping is not compositional under bag semantics), and SERVICE and GRAPH clauses read as extensions bolted onto SQL-shaped clauses (S2)
❌ Punctuation carries meaning: ?x, a, ->, !, ^^, @en, and SERVICE { } blocks — a term’s type is its punctuation, and a misread pattern still parses (S3)
✅ The core pattern is compact: ?s pred ?o . states one triple match in four tokens



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard query-test harness in the language: ShEx and SHACL validate the data, the W3C suite tests the specification’s conformance, and an application’s query regression is its own harness (G1)
❌ Debugging is set-semantics tracing: an OPTIONAL that drops rows, a MINUS that empties under bag semantics, and a property path that binds nothing are diagnosed by engine logs, not by a language tool (G2)
❌ UNDEF faults surface at execution: a BIND on an unbound variable, a type-mismatched comparison, and a division by zero report only on the data reached (G3)
❌ Only the wall clock: the expression library is XPath’s, fn:current-dateTime() reads wall time, and SPARQL 1.2 drafts add NOW() — elapsed-time tests read the engine’s clock (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Literals carry datatypes, and expressions coerce at runtime: xsd:integer("x") is a runtime fault, a plain literal against a typed number is UNDEF, and data crossing the datatype boundary is re-checked per row (Q2)
❌ SPARQL injection is a documented attack: string-built queries over untrusted input let that input add clauses (UNION, SERVICE, Update blocks), and the research literature names the pattern (Q3)
✅ Parameterized execution is an engine API: Jena’s parameterized queries and the engines’ binding APIs carry values out of band, so a value cannot become syntax

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A query is a request text: the same query on the same engine version and dataset reproduces the same solution sequence, and there is no build artifact (Y1)
⚠️ The deployment lives server-side: an endpoint stores its graphs and serves the queries, so reproducing a result is an act on a deployment, not on the query text alone



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Published libraries carry no signed provenance by default: Jena artifacts on Maven Central and pyoxigraph on PyPI name their publishers, and a consumer trusts the package they install (Y3)
✅ Maven Central and PyPI namespace every package, so there is no flat namespace to hijack (Y4)
✅ Advisories are published: Apache Jena’s security page lists CVEs against releases, and the GitHub advisory database covers Maven and PyPI (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing and metrics standard is part of the language: metrics are the engine’s (Fuseki’s statistics endpoint, Blazegraph’s meters), and the query text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: the engine logs queries in its own format (Jena’s ARQ logging, Fuseki request logs), and the language defines none (Y6)
✅ Engines record running queries: Fuseki’s query log, Jena’s ARQ logging, and Neptune’s query profile report the query text and timings (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ Submit-and-run is the loop: Fuseki’s web form, Oxigraph’s CLI, and GraphDB’s playground run a query with no build step (Y7)
❌ No maintained in-editor analyzer: SPARQL syntax and type checks land when the query reaches the engine, and the editor plugins are per-IDE toys, not a language server the ecosystem maintains (Y8)
❌ No source-level debugger: diagnosis goes through engine traces, EXPLAIN output, and the store’s own monitors (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No published function interface: SPARQL 1.1 defines no user-defined function (Jena and Virtuoso extension functions do not transfer), and function declarations are 1.2 draft material (Y9)
❌ No portable target: a query runs in an RDF store’s engine, and nothing in the language runs without one (Y10)
✅ HTTP carries the language: the SPARQL Protocol defines query requests, and the Graph Store Protocol moves RDF files, so any HTTP client interoperates with an endpoint



1.3.6 Governance

✅ Governance is a W3C working group: the RDF & SPARQL Working Group publishes the 1.2 drafts under the Recommendation track, with public contribution and implementation-report process (Y11)
✅ The specification is published: Query, Update, Protocol, and the grammar are W3C Recommendations, readable and implementable by anyone (Y12)
✅ A conformance mechanism exists: the W3C SPARQL test suite with implementation reports decides conformance, and it is maintained in the open (Y17)
✅ Published grammars and parsers: the specification carries the grammar, and Jena (Apache-2.0) and Oxigraph (MIT) publish parsers (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside an RDF store’s engine: energy and time are the engine’s, and property-path depth is the plan a reader tunes.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ One of the best-documented query languages: the W3C Recommendation and its test suite are public, and models write common SELECT queries reliably, with OPTIONAL scoping and MINUS semantics needing review.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: SPARQL is the most standards-grounded language in this analysis: a W3C Recommendation with a published grammar, a maintained conformance suite with implementation reports, and an open working group, so its coupling is not vendor-imposed. The costs are the RDF model’s own: an unbound term in an expression is a runtime fault, OPTIONAL and MINUS carry set semantics a SQL reader must re-learn, FILTER’s UNDEF rule drops rows silently, federation crosses an endpoint the query cannot validate, and the standards’ pace — 1.1 in 2013, 1.2 in Working Drafts in 2026 — freezes the surface a developer can use. Main strengths: engine portability, published governance and conformance, open-source reference engines, and a compact triple-pattern core. Main weaknesses: a niche ecosystem, no standard test harness for application queries, no user-function mechanism in 1.1, and runtime-only type and absence faults.

title: SQL PL (Db2 12.1)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL PL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 48.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and return value declares a type, and a body that violates its declarations fails when the routine is created
✅ LIKE anchors a declaration to the schema: DECLARE v LIKE emp.salary follows the column’s type, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
✅ Array types carry their element type: A VARCHAR(20) ARRAY or an associative array keeps a typed collection in one declared variable
⚠️ Overloading resolves a call by argument type: Two routines may share a name and differ by their signature, so the argument list decides the target
❌ NULL is the default value and it propagates (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, three-valued logic applies, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL
❌ A signature says what a routine returns, not what it does (T12): A procedure that mutates tables, commits a transaction, or reads a nickname looks like any other procedure



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A routine is a closed unit: Local variables, cursors, and conditions are private to the call, and the signature is the whole interface
✅ Modules give a namespace and a boundary: CREATE MODULE groups routines, types, and variables, and an unpublished member is invisible to callers outside the module
✅ Compound statements scope declarations: An inner BEGIN ... END holds its own variables, conditions, handlers, and cursors
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger body runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ A module’s variables live for the session: A variable declared in a module keeps its value across calls, so one call can read state another call wrote



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The Db2 engine owns the memory of its agents, and a routine never names an address or frees a byte
✅ The server sizes the work areas: Sorts and hashes inside a routine’s statements take their memory from the engine’s heap configuration
⚠️ A built collection holds its memory for the call: An ARRAY assembled with ARRAY_AGG or element by element materialises in the routine’s memory, so the call’s footprint follows the collection’s size
⚠️ A declared global temporary table outlives the routine: A DECLARE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE persists for the session, so a local act leaves a session-scoped resource behind



1.1.4 Error

✅ Conditions and handlers separate the failure path: DECLARE ... CONDITION names a failure, and EXIT, CONTINUE, and UNDO HANDLER declare what happens when it is raised
✅ Handlers match by class or by name: sqlexception, sqlwarning, and not found catch classes, and a declared condition catches its own
✅ GET DIAGNOSTICS reads the failure’s detail: The handler can read the SQLSTATE, the message text, and the routine’s own diagnostics
⚠️ A handler can swallow (Er3): A CONTINUE HANDLER that records nothing lets the routine proceed past the failure, and silence is indistinguishable from approval
❌ A failure cannot travel as a value (Er4): The failure path is the handler path, so a fallible operation cannot be folded into an expression or returned as a result the caller inspects



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A procedure can manage its own transaction: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT are statements of the language, so a unit of work commits or aborts as one
✅ Isolation and lock intent are declared in the query text: An isolation clause with USE AND KEEP UPDATE LOCKS on a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE names the locking the statement needs
❌ Special registers are session state (K2): CURRENT SCHEMA, CURRENT PATH, and the other special registers are set per session and visible to every routine that runs there
⚠️ Transaction isolation and declared locks do not order independent work: Two sessions’ multi-step work is ordered only by the locks its statements name, so any ordering the source relies on is an agreement no declaration carries



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Cannot function outside one engine (P1): SQL PL runs on IBM Db2, so the unit of deployment is a Db2 database
⚠️ The Db2 family carries dialect differences: A procedure written for Db2 on Linux, UNIX, and Windows is not guaranteed to compile unchanged on Db2 for i or Db2 for z/OS
⚠️ The engine also accepts PL/SQL through a compatibility mode: A registry setting enables Oracle-syntax blocks, packages, and types, so one database can run two procedural dialects side by side
⚠️ External routines run outside the SQL type system (T14): A LANGUAGE C, LANGUAGE JAVA, or CLR routine crosses a boundary no signature check reaches
✅ Client interfaces are standard: ODBC, JDBC, and the CLP reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: A rule that runs beside its tables is enforced for every writer; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application’s test suite and profilers
An unpublished module member is deliberate encapsulation: Hiding internals from callers trades discoverability for a boundary the catalog enforces; the cost is that every consumer must learn which members are public
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible filter: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE reaches names a static statement cannot; the cost is that the statement’s access path is chosen when it runs
A session-scoped module variable is a deliberate cache: Keeping a value across calls avoids a repeated read; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the value when the underlying data changes




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Routines compile into the catalog: A procedure’s body is compiled once at creation and the section is reused, so a call does not re-parse
✅ Set-based statements in the body do the heavy lifting: One INSERT ... SELECT inside the procedure carries the optimiser’s plan, so the procedural wrapper is not the hot path
⚠️ A plan regression arrives hidden inside the routine: A caller cannot see the queries inside a procedure, so a changed plan surfaces as the routine being slow



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from IBM under licence
⚠️ A free community edition exists: Development can run without a licence, while the supported tooling and the enterprise features remain licensed
✅ Decades of published practice: The Db2 documentation set and the wider IBM knowledge base cover the language with syntax and examples
⚠️ Tooling centres on the engine’s own tools: The CLP and the IBM documentation carry the workflow, and the procedural language has no dedicated environment of its own



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Upgrades keep routines: A procedure written for an earlier Db2 release compiles in the current one
✅ Deprecation is announced in the documentation: The knowledge centre marks deprecated and discontinued features before they go
⚠️ A feature arrives with a release or a modpack: Adoption follows the server a deployment can upgrade to
⚠️ IBM’s own decisions govern the change: The knowledge centre is the definition’s change log, and the block model follows the SQL/PSM concept without conforming to a published specification of the dialect



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for data-centric logic: A routine runs beside its tables with SQL directly in the body, so a rule executes where the data is
✅ A full procedural language inside SQL: Compound statements, array types, cursors, and condition handlers live in the same unit as the queries
❌ Domain lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside Db2, so the Db2 data tier is the only domain
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a long-running service belongs in another language beside SQL PL



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a SQL developer: A compound statement reads like SQL with control flow added
✅ The knowledge centre documents every construct: The Db2 documentation covers the syntax with runnable examples
⚠️ The handler model takes practice: EXIT, CONTINUE, and UNDO handlers, condition matching, and handler scope are semantics the syntax does not show
⚠️ Engine behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Isolation levels, locking, and routine registration matter more than syntax for correct code



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose (S1): Every routine needs a CREATE statement and a compound-statement body with its DECLARE section before it does anything
✅ Keyword-led and readable: Statements read as verbs, and the block boundaries are visible in the source
⚠️ END closes several constructs: END IF;, END LOOP;, and a routine’s labelled END must each be matched, so a long body is read against its terminators
⚠️ The deployment script carries a statement terminator: A script must tell the CLP which character ends a routine body, usually @, so the source carries a convention of its own



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ No test framework ships with the toolchain (G1): The CLP and the Db2 tools provide no assertion or runner, so a suite is assembled from third-party harnesses or hand-rolled procedures
✅ Third-party harnesses exist: db2unit and similar frameworks run Db2 unit tests with assertions and reporting
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run inside a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database unchanged
⚠️ A suite needs a server: Tests run inside the database they exercise, so the harness depends on a Db2 instance and on deployment rights
❌ No monotonic reading published: the client’s time functions read the wall, and no elapsed reading ships (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Static SQL in a routine is parameterised: The routine’s variables bind as host variables of the compiled section, so values cannot change the parse
✅ GRANT EXECUTE and roles express least privilege: Access is declared per routine, per module, and per schema
✅ Row and column access control declares visibility in the schema: A row permission or a column mask filters what a statement can see regardless of which routine issues it
⚠️ Static and dynamic privileges differ inside a routine: A routine’s static statements run with the definer’s rights while its dynamic statements check the invoker’s, so the two paths carry different grants
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): EXECUTE IMMEDIATE with a built string turns concatenated input into code



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ The distribution records no toolchain version per project; the server version is a fact of the installation. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Routine sources carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to SQL PL libraries. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ The SIGNAL and message surfaces carry no structure. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer ships with the server; editor analysis rides third-party tools. (Y8)
❌ No SQL PL debugger ships with the server. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The routine runs only in Db2-family servers. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ IBM decides the language’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists; the manuals document one implementation. (Y12)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Procedural SQL is thin in model training data relative to mainstream languages, so generated SQL PL mixes in other dialects’ syntax [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

❌ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: SQL PL’s coupling is set by its host engine and by IBM’s licence. Modules give a namespace with published and unpublished members, compound statements carry named conditions and handlers, static SQL in a routine is parameterised, and the knowledge centre documents the language in full. Main strengths: an explicit module boundary, a structured condition-and-handler error model, typed collections, and complete documentation. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside Db2, the proprietary licence owns the stack and the tooling, signatures carry no effects, a CONTINUE HANDLER can swallow a failure and let the routine proceed, dynamic SQL turns built strings into code, every variable starts as NULL and propagates, no test framework ships with the toolchain, and the block structure adds boilerplate to every routine.

title: SQL (ANSI SQL:2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 89.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 90.6/100 · Engineering readiness 72.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static column typing: Every column, parameter, and result column has a declared type, checked when the statement is prepared or planned
✅ Schema is declared independently of queries: A table declares its structure once; queries consume it without redeclaring it
❌ No sum types: A column carries one scalar type, so alternatives are modelled with nullable columns or separate tables and the caller must know the encoding (T4)
❌ No generics: There is no type parameter, so reuse across types is done by generating DDL, not by the type system (T5)
❌ NULL is not type-safe absence: NULL is compatible with every domain, three-valued logic propagates through expressions, and NULL = NULL is unknown rather than true (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Declarative query construction: A statement states the result set, and the engine chooses the access path, so construction does not couple to a storage layout or an algorithm
✅ Views separate consumers from the query behind them: A view exposes a stable relation whose defining query can change without changing its consumers
✅ Set-based composition: Joins, unions, and subqueries compose relations, so logic composes without imperative sequencing or shared cursors
✅ Schema and use are separated: Tables declare the data, and normalisation stores each fact once so a fact duplicated across columns cannot drift out of agreement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Stored procedures couple construction to the engine: SQL/PSM standardises persistent stored modules (Part 4 of ISO/IEC 9075), but the dialects used in practice — PL/pgSQL, PL/SQL, and T-SQL — share little beyond the basics, so the code depends on one engine



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The storage engine owns buffers, caches, and page allocation, and a statement never names an address or frees anything
✅ No explicit allocation in queries: The engine materialises or streams a result set, so query text does not couple to a memory layout
✅ Resource limits are declarative configuration: Work memory and temp-file behaviour are engine settings, not properties the query must manage
⚠️ Large intermediate results still cost memory: An unbounded sort, hash join, or SELECT * spool can exhaust the engine’s memory even though the language hides allocation
⚠️ Materialised views and temporary tables persist engine-side state: They pin storage and need a refresh policy, coupling the data to a refresh lifecycle



1.1.4 Error

✅ Standard SQLSTATE: An error carries a five-character SQLSTATE class and subclass, so a handler matches a portable code instead of a message string
✅ Structured handlers in SQL/PSM: DECLARE ... HANDLER and EXCEPTION blocks separate the normal path from the recovery path
✅ Constraint violations are errors, not silent writes: A primary-key, foreign-key, UNIQUE, or CHECK violation aborts the statement
⚠️ Vendor error codes extend SQLSTATE: PostgreSQL SQLSTATE codes, Oracle ORA- numbers, and SQL Server error numbers differ outside the standard classes, so handlers are not portable
⚠️ Some failures depend on the data: Name and type errors are caught at prepare time, but division by zero, overflow, and constraint violations are detected only at execution



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one, so a statement does not coordinate with others by hand
✅ Isolation is selectable: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE let the application declare the visibility contract it needs
✅ MVCC in PostgreSQL and Oracle: Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, so read and write traffic decouple
✅ Set-based statements reduce explicit locking: One UPDATE moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
⚠️ Default isolation permits anomalies: READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, so non-repeatable reads and write skew are possible unless the application raises the level
⚠️ Explicit locking couples code to the engine: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, LOCK TABLE, and advisory locks are vendor-shaped and must agree with the lock ordering of the whole application



1.1.6 Platform

✅ A standard core is portable: DDL, DML, and joins written to core SQL run on PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and SQLite with little change
✅ Standard call interfaces: ODBC and JDBC let one client reach many engines, so an application does not bind to one engine’s binary protocol
✅ Multiple independent implementations: No single vendor owns the language, so the standard cannot be changed unilaterally
⚠️ Dialects diverge outside the core: String functions, date arithmetic, LIMIT versus FETCH FIRST, and window-function details differ by vendor
⚠️ Vendor extensions bind queries to one engine: JSON operators, array types, regex syntax, and identity or sequence clauses are engine-specific



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Denormalisation is a modelling choice: Storing a value in two places trades redundancy for fewer joins; the language permits it but does not force it
NULL versus NOT NULL is a modelling decision: Making a column nullable widens its value set, and the three-valued-logic cost follows from that decision, not from a forced dependency
The optimiser owns the execution plan: A declarative statement gives up control of access paths, so plan hints are a choice about how far to override the engine
Schema migration is a process, not a mechanism: Changing a column couples deploy order to schema version, but the coupling follows from sharing one schema, which is the purpose of a relational store
Vendor-specific SQL may be worth the portability cost: Writing to one dialect buys features and performance; the loss of portability is a deliberate trade, not a property of the language
SQL is not a general-purpose language: The assumption of a database engine and a set-based workload is a scope decision, not a coupling defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Decades of query-optimisation research: Cost-based planners, index selection, join reordering, and predicate pushdown produce good plans without hand-tuning in the common case
✅ Set-based execution: One statement moves many rows, so per-row interpreter overhead is amortised by the engine
✅ Indexes and partitions are declarative: An index is declared once and then used by any matching query
✅ Engines are written in C or C++ with mature storage layers: Throughput and buffer management are the engine’s responsibility, not the query’s
⚠️ Plan quality is an engine property: The same query can be fast on PostgreSQL and slow on another engine, and the language guarantees no plan
⚠️ Plans can regress without a query change: New statistics, a version upgrade, or changed data volume can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling is fragmented by dialect: ORMs, migration tools, linters, and formatters commonly target one engine’s dialect, and there is no single SQL toolchain (Ec2)
✅ The standard interfaces are universal: ODBC, JDBC, and ADO.NET drivers exist for nearly every engine and host language
✅ Mature, independently maintained engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and SQLite are all long-lived and actively developed
✅ A very large body of published knowledge: Standards documents, engine manuals, and books are abundant and stable over decades



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard evolves slowly: SQL:2023 appeared six years after SQL:2016, so a needed feature can wait years for standardisation (V4)
✅ The language is broadly backward compatible: New editions add features and rarely remove them, so decades-old queries keep running
✅ Vendor implementations lead the standard: PostgreSQL, Oracle, and others ship features before standardisation, which gives users early access
⚠️ Adoption lags publication: An engine may take years to implement a newly standardised feature, so code written to the standard may not run everywhere yet



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for relational data: The model of relations, tuples, and set operations matches tabular data directly
✅ One language spans several data domains: Analytics with window functions, transactional writes with DML, and semi-structured data with SQL/JSON all live in the same language
✅ SQL/PGQ in SQL:2023 adds property-graph queries: Graph patterns are expressible without leaving SQL
⚠️ Procedural logic is awkward: Row-by-row algorithms and complex control flow read poorly in SQL/PSM and are usually pushed to a host language
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: SQL assumes a database engine and a set-based workload, which limits use outside data management



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Basic queries are gentle: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE is readable and learnable within days
✅ The declarative surface hides the hard part: A beginner writes a correct query without knowing the plan the engine will choose
⚠️ Advanced work is steep: Query optimisation, join ordering, and window semantics take years to master
⚠️ NULL semantics surprise newcomers: Three-valued logic makes an intuitive predicate such as a <> 5 fail to match rows where a is NULL
⚠️ Dialect knowledge is required in practice: Beyond the standard core, a developer must learn one engine’s functions, types, and plan output



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: Statements read close to English and do not lean on punctuation or symbols
✅ Compact for the result produced: A join and filter over several tables fits in a few lines
⚠️ DDL is verbose: CREATE TABLE, constraints, indexes, and ALTER TABLE statements are long and repetitive
⚠️ Identifier quoting differs by engine: Double quotes, backticks, and square brackets each mark an identifier in a different dialect



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Plan inspection is standard practice: PostgreSQL and MySQL report the chosen plan and actual timings through EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and Oracle and SQL Server expose equivalent plan and runtime statistics
✅ Constraints are executable invariants: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, and NOT NULL reject bad data at write time, so tests need not re-check them
✅ Transactions isolate a test: A test can run inside a transaction and roll back, leaving the database unchanged
✅ Standard schema introspection: INFORMATION_SCHEMA and catalog views let tooling verify structure
⚠️ No in-language test framework: Test harnesses live in the host language, so a suite couples to the driver and to a fixture loader
❌ No monotonic reading published: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is the session’s wall clock, anchored per transaction and no elapsed reading ships (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Injection is the canonical failure: Because a statement is text, building it by concatenating untrusted input lets that input become code (Q3)
✅ Parameterised statements remove the injection surface: Bind variables and prepared statements carry data out of band, so a value cannot change the parse
✅ GRANT and REVOKE express least privilege: Access is declared per object and per role
✅ Views and row-level security restrict visibility: A view, or PostgreSQL row-level security, limits what a statement can see
⚠️ Dynamic SQL re-opens the risk: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, dynamic PL/pgSQL, and string-built queries defeat parameterisation where they are unavoidable
⚠️ Definer’s-rights procedures can escalate: A procedure that runs with its definer’s rights (SECURITY DEFINER) can grant more access than intended unless it is audited

❌ Schema scripts move as text with no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed exists for the standard’s ecosystem; fixes land in engine release notes. (Y16)

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ No logging facility exists in the language. (Y6)

❌ No debugger exists for the language; the engines’ EXPLAIN tools are the instruments. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The dialect-specific parts run where an engine that implements them runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ ISO/IEC JTC1 SC32 maintains the standard through national bodies. (Y11)
✅ ISO/IEC 9075 is published. (Y12)
✅ The NIST SQL conformance suites historically checked implementations. (Y17)
✅ The engine parsers are public source in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [5], [6].

Verdict: SQL’s design yields low language-imposed coupling for the work it is built for. The declarative model separates what a result is from how it is computed, and the schema separates data structure from the queries that consume it. Views decouple consumers from the query behind them, and transactions decouple statements from each other’s timing. Main strengths: the standard core is portable across many independent engines, types come from the schema, and a mature optimiser takes on execution plans. Main weaknesses: NULL is not type-safe, no sum types or generics exist, the standard moves slowly, tooling fragments by dialect, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard unless parameters are used.

title: SQLScript (SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 08)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQLScript (SAP HANA Platform 2.0 SPS 08) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 83.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 40.9/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ NULL is a member of every domain: procedure parameters, locals, and table columns carry NULL unannounced, and no signature states whether a value may be absent (T10)
⚠️ No sum types: an alternative is a nullable column or a table variable’s shape, and the consumer re-derives the encoding from the body
❌ Statements state no effect: the reference defines the functional extension as side-effect free by intent, but the signature of a procedure states nothing about the writes, reads, or calls inside it (T12)
❌ R rides an external boundary: procedures can be written in RLANG, executed by an external R environment the server calls, and the crossing between SQLScript tables and R data frames is checked by neither side’s compiler (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Table variables are the unit: the data extension defines table types without tables, and procedures pass and assign table variables the optimizer can treat as sets rather than rows
⚠️ The reference argues against its own imperative layer: the motivation chapter sets one-tuple-at-a-time semantics against set-oriented SQL because loops are “hard to optimize and parallelize”, so the procedural constructs carry a documented performance warning the declarative ones do not



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocation is the engine’s: column store, delta merge, and statement memory live in the HANA process, and the SQLScript text allocates nothing



1.1.4 Error

❌ The EXIT HANDLER decides, or the procedure dies: handlers catch declared conditions and SQL error codes, and without one the error leaves the procedure — no value carries the failure (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: failures travel by exception and results by output table variables and result sets, and neither threads through an expression (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Session state is shared: session variables and temporary tables are visible across every procedure the connection calls, so two callers share what the session holds (K2)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The procedure runs only in HANA: the parser, the table-type system, and the deployment model (HDI containers) are the engine’s, and nothing in the language runs elsewhere (P1)
❌ A poor fit outside the data tier: the language has no general libraries or error values, so application logic beyond data flows builds every abstraction itself (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Pushdown is the design goal: table types, set-oriented bodies, and in-engine parallelism exist to keep data from moving, and the price is that the imperative layer carries a documented optimization warning
Deployment is the database: HDI containers version procedures and table types as artifacts, and the price is that the application’s logic lives inside a commercial engine’s deployment model
Handlers are optional: EXIT HANDLER gives structured recovery against conditions and SQL error codes, and the price is that unhandled errors surface at the caller
Embedded R and Python buy in-database analytics: foreign-language procedures run beside SQLScript bodies, and the price is an unchecked boundary between two type systems




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The optimizer is the point: the reference’s stated goal is pushdown with “massive parallelization”, and declarative bodies (UNION ALL with implicit parallelism, MAP_MERGE-style operations) are the constructs the engine optimizes
⚠️ Imperative bodies carry a documented penalty: the reference motivates SQLScript itself by the cost of row-wise logic, and the same warning applies to loops written inside the language



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A proprietary stack end to end: the server, the deployment infrastructure, the IDE (Business Application Studio), and the support model are SAP products under commercial terms (Ec4)



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ The SPS calendar governs the surface: HANA 2.0 moves in support-package stacks, and the reference’s own version selector decides which constructs a deployment’s procedures may use



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists to serve SAP’s data tier: procedures deploy through HDI into containers, the calculation and SQL engines define what they can say, and the S/4HANA application world is the domain (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Two styles, one language: set-oriented SQL and imperative blocks share the surface, and the reference’s own guidance on when each applies is required reading before a body will perform (L2)



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Standard-shaped, SAP-flavored: the statements read like ISO SQL, and the table-type system, handler syntax, and deployment annotations are HANA’s own layer on top



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No standard test harness for user procedures: SAP’s own QA is internal, and the documented testing story is application-side tests and the SQL analyzer against a live system (G1)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic SQL is string-built: EXEC runs SQL text assembled at run time, so concatenated user input reaches the parser, and the mitigation is the privilege model plus bound inputs (Q3)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ A procedure is deployed source: the same HDI artifact on the same server version and data reproduces the same result, and nothing is compiled ahead of the call outside the deployment
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the artifact: the repository names no server revision — the executing release is a deployment fact the HDI container records elsewhere (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No signed provenance for published procedures or add-ons: deployment artifacts move through SAP’s channels under commercial terms, with no signature-checked public channel (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed names the language surface: security fixes land in SAP notes and support packages, with no public CVE-mapped advisory database for the engine’s dependencies (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard is part of the language: PlanViz, the SQL analyzer, and the trace configuration are server features, and the procedure text carries no trace hook (Y5)
❌ No structured logging in the language: messages leave through SIGNAL and the server log, and no logging construct exists in SQLScript (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The vendor’s IDE completes the code: SAP Business Application Studio publishes SQLScript tooling with code completion and the SQL analyzer beside it (Y8)
❌ No procedure debugger ships in the standard toolchain: diagnosis goes through the SQL analyzer, PlanViz, and handler instrumentation (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No portable target: the body compiles in one vendor’s engine, and nothing in the language runs without a HANA server (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Governance is SAP: the release calendar, the roadmap, and the language’s direction are one company’s, and no independent body can change them (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists: the SQLScript Reference documents the implemented behavior of one product line, and no independent implementation follows from it (Y12)
❌ Correctness is what HANA does: no conformance suite exists for SQLScript, and the one implementation is the oracle (Y17)
❌ The parser is closed: the grammar lives as prose in the SQLScript Reference and the parser inside the closed engine, so analysis tooling reads the manual and guesses (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Energy is the HANA process’s: column store, delta merges, and the application’s license bill pay, and the reader’s levers are set-oriented body design the reference argues for.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Generated procedures appear in SAP migration and extension work, and the traps are the layer the reference warns about: imperative bodies, handler scope, and dynamic SQL that no generated snippet prices.



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified path; the engine’s transaction and recovery guarantees are SAP’s, stated in its own documentation and support terms.

Verdict: SQLScript is SAP HANA’s collection of SQL extensions — table types without tables, side-effect-free functions, and imperative procedure bodies — deployed through HDI into the engine’s containers. Its costs are the platform’s own: NULL in every domain, failures that travel only by exception, session-wide state, a proprietary stack end to end, and a reference that documents row-wise constructs as the thing the optimizer exists to avoid. Main strengths: a stated design goal of pushdown and parallelism, table variables the engine treats as sets, in-database R and Python for analytics, vendor IDE tooling with the SQL analyzer, and one-volume reference documentation. Main weaknesses: no debugger or user-procedure test harness, no structured logging or tracing in the language, string-built dynamic SQL, single-vendor governance with no specification or conformance suite, and logic whose reproducibility rides a commercial engine revision the artifact does not name.

title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Transact-SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 84.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 55.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and column has a declared type, and a block that violates it fails at parse or bind time
✅ Table variables and table-valued parameters carry a declared row type: DECLARE @t TABLE (...) and a user-defined table type pass a typed row set between units
✅ A procedure parameter declares its type and direction: @p int OUTPUT fixes the type and the direction, so a caller binds to a signature
⚠️ DECLARE @name defaults to NULL (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, so an unassigned variable is valid and propagates NULL into the expression
⚠️ NULL comparison needs three-valued logic: With ANSI_NULLS ON (the default, and the only supported setting since SQL Server 2017), @x = NULL is unknown, so a check needs IS NULL
⚠️ sql_variant is the one escape hatch: A column or variable of sql_variant holds values of different base types, and every consumer must discover the stored base type at run time



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A stored procedure provides modularity with a declared interface: CREATE PROCEDURE names the unit, its parameters, and its result, and can return a status value and OUTPUT parameters
✅ A view or an inline table-valued function separates consumers from the query: The exposed relation is stable while its defining query can change
✅ A table-valued parameter passes a row set without a shared temporary table: A user-defined table type plus a TVP parameter removes the need for a global temporary table
✅ Set-based statements compose without a cursor: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM, and MERGE express the whole transformation in one statement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: An AFTER or INSTEAD OF trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Session SET options change the meaning of a statement: ANSI_NULLS and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER are captured when a stored procedure is created, while DATEFORMAT applies when the statement runs, so the same text can parse or convert differently elsewhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The SQL Server buffer pool and the query workspace own the memory, and a batch never names an address
✅ The server grants memory to a query: The query’s memory grant comes from the server’s calculator or the Resource Governor, so the batch does not request bytes
✅ Buffer pool and tempdb behaviour are server configuration: max server memory, the tempdb files, and a Resource Governor pool are settings, not batch properties
⚠️ A sort or hash can spill to tempdb: An operation whose grant is too small writes to tempdb, which costs I/O even though the language hides allocation
⚠️ A cursor allocates per fetch: A row-by-row cursor uses workspace per fetch, so the memory pattern follows the loop



1.1.4 Error

✅ TRY ... CATCH gives a structured path: The CATCH block runs on error and exposes ERROR_NUMBER, ERROR_MESSAGE, ERROR_SEVERITY, and ERROR_LINE
✅ THROW and RAISERROR raise with a number and a message: THROW 50001, 'msg', 1 carries a number, so a handler can branch on it
✅ XACT_STATE() and @@TRANCOUNT tell the handler whether the transaction is committable: A doomed transaction is detectable inside CATCH
⚠️ Errors ignored or non-exhaustive (Er3): A CATCH block that swallows the error, or a skipped @@ERROR check, lets the batch continue past the failure
⚠️ Errors do not abort the batch by default: Without SET XACT_ABORT ON, a statement error rolls back that statement and the batch continues
⚠️ Severity decides whether the caller sees the error: A low-severity error is informational, so the same statement text can pass a caller by



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one
✅ Isolation levels are selectable and versioned: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, and SERIALIZABLE, while the database options READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT and ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION switch READ COMMITTED to row versioning and enable SNAPSHOT
✅ Snapshot isolation removes reader–writer blocking: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON, a reader uses row versions and does not block a writer
✅ Set-based statements reduce explicit locking: One UPDATE moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): SET options, CONTEXT_INFO, and a global temporary table ##t are visible to code the caller did not write
⚠️ A locking hint couples the query to the engine’s concurrency model: WITH (NOLOCK), UPDLOCK, and READPAST are engine-shaped and must agree with the application’s lock ordering



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Client interfaces are standard: ODBC, JDBC, OLE DB, and ADO.NET reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol
✅ Bulk interfaces are documented: bcp and BULK INSERT use a documented format, so data exchange is not tied to an application API
⚠️ Two implementations exist under separate vendors: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP ASE share a lineage and a core syntax, but the two diverge, and Microsoft and SAP document them separately
⚠️ Azure SQL is the same vendor with a different deployment: The managed service changes availability, administration, and some features, so code targets a specific surface
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): The language needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE
❌ The T-SQL surface is engine-specific: TOP, IDENTITY, GO, the sys catalog views, and the sp_ procedures are SQL Server features, so a port to another engine is a rewrite



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: Keeping a rule in the database guarantees it for every writer; the cost is that the rule now deploys and versions with the schema rather than with the application
A cursor is a deliberate trade for row-by-row work: It makes a per-row algorithm expressible, at the cost of the set-based model
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible query: sp_executesql and EXEC reach constructs a static statement cannot name; the cost is that the statement’s shape is known only when it runs
NOLOCK trades consistency for concurrency: A reader that accepts dirty reads avoids blocking




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A cost-based optimiser with a plan cache executes a statement: A procedure’s plan can be reused, so the caller does not choose an access path
✅ A columnstore index and batch mode scan analytically: CREATE COLUMNSTORE INDEX plus batch mode processes a large scan in vectorised batches
✅ Query Store records plans and regressions: An operator can see a plan change and force a previous plan
✅ In-memory OLTP tables are lock-free and memory-optimised: MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON tables and natively compiled procedures remove latch contention
⚠️ Parameter sniffing can choose a plan for the wrong input: A cached plan built for one parameter value can be poor for another
⚠️ A plan can regress without a query change: New statistics, a version upgrade, or a changed data volume can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Tooling is mature and first-party: SQL Server Management Studio, Azure Data Studio, and sqlcmd cover administration and query work
✅ The market and the hiring pool are large: SQL Server is widely deployed in Microsoft environments, so documentation, training, and consultants are abundant
✅ Cloud deployment is a first-party service: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance run the same engine with a managed administration model
❌ Proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Microsoft (and, for ASE, from SAP) under licence
⚠️ The ASE toolchain is separate from the SQL Server toolchain: SAP maintains its own documentation, tools, and support, so knowledge does not transfer freely



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The release cadence is regular and active: SQL Server ships a major release periodically, and Azure SQL receives continuous updates
✅ A compatibility level keeps old behaviour: A database at an older compatibility level keeps the older optimiser and syntax behaviour while the engine is upgraded
✅ The engine leads the standard: TRY ... CATCH, MERGE, window functions, and JSON support arrived as engine features, so users get them without waiting for the standard
⚠️ A deprecated feature is warned and then removed: The documentation lists deprecated features, so a removal can require edits even though a compatibility level otherwise preserves older behaviour
⚠️ Feature availability differs by edition and deployment: An Enterprise feature or an Azure-only feature may not exist on a local Standard edition



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for transactional and analytical logic in the database: A stored procedure runs beside the data with a plan and a transaction
✅ One language spans OLTP and analytics: Set-based DML, window functions, and a columnstore scan all live in the same language
✅ The surrounding pipeline is first-party: Integration Services, the Agent scheduler, and Reporting Services cover the rest of a data workflow
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists inside SQL Server or SAP ASE, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
⚠️ Procedural row logic reads poorly: A row-by-row algorithm in a cursor is verbose and slow beside its set-based equivalent
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: The language assumes a SQL Server database and a set-based workload



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a SQL developer: A procedure with BEGIN ... END, TRY ... CATCH, and SELECT ... INTO is readable to anyone who knows SQL
✅ Documentation and examples are complete: The Microsoft T-SQL reference documents every statement with examples
⚠️ The procedural and the set-based model coexist: A developer must choose between a cursor and a set-based statement, and the wrong choice shows up as a performance problem
⚠️ NULL handling must be learned: With ANSI_NULLS ON, = NULL never matches, and a comparison with NULL yields unknown
⚠️ Plan and locking behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Performance work means reading plans and lock waits rather than syntax
⚠️ The SAP ASE dialect diverges in details: Differences in GO, IDENTITY, and built-in functions mean knowledge transfers only in part



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE and BEGIN ... END read close to English
✅ A procedure is a readable unit: The parameter list, the body, and the RETURN value are declared in one CREATE PROCEDURE statement
✅ GO marks a batch boundary in a script: The client tool sends the batch, so the boundary is visible in the source
⚠️ SET options prefix every script: SET NOCOUNT ON, ANSI_NULLS ON, and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON are usually written at the top, so the boilerplate grows
⚠️ @ and @@ distinguish kinds of variable by convention: A local variable, a parameter, and a global function share the sigil, so a reader distinguishes them by spelling
⚠️ Identifier quoting depends on a setting: [name] and "name" both quote an identifier, and the second form needs QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON



1.2.7 Testing

✅ tSQLt is the established framework: An open-source unit-test framework runs test classes with mocked tables and assertions
✅ TRY ... CATCH makes a unit test expressible in the language: A test procedure asserts and THROWs on a mismatch
✅ A transaction wraps a test and rolls it back: The database is unchanged after the test
✅ Error metadata supports an assertion on a failure path: ERROR_NUMBER and ERROR_MESSAGE inside CATCH let a test check the rejection
⚠️ No test framework ships with the toolchain (G1): SSMS and sqlcmd provide no assertion or runner, so a suite depends on tSQLt or a hand-rolled harness
⚠️ A server-side suite needs a server: The harness needs a SQL Server instance, so the tests couple to infrastructure
❌ No monotonic reading published: GETDATE and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are wall readings (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ sp_executesql with parameters removes the injection surface: EXEC sp_executesql N'SELECT ... WHERE x = @p', N'@p int', @p = 1 passes the value out of band
✅ GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE with roles express least privilege: Access is declared per object, per schema, and per role
✅ Row-level security limits what a statement can see: A SECURITY POLICY with a predicate function filters rows by the caller’s identity
✅ EXECUTE AS makes the effective identity explicit: A procedure can run as its owner or as a named user
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): A statement built with EXEC (@sql) from concatenated input lets the input become code
⚠️ Dynamic SQL and owner-rights execution re-open the risk: EXEC on a built string, sp_OA* procedures, and xp_cmdshell where enabled defeat parameterisation

⚠️ There is no build: the module definition is stored in the catalog and scripted out.



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Module sources and SQLCLR assemblies carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to third-party modules. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; Extended Events is the server’s. (Y5)

1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No T-SQL debugger ships with the server; the SSMS debugger is a separate install. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The module runs only in SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Microsoft decides the language’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ No public specification exists; the documentation documents one implementation. (Y12)

Verdict: Transact-SQL’s coupling follows its host engine. Stored procedures, views, and table-valued parameters give real modularity, TRY ... CATCH gives a structured failure path, and the optimiser, Query Store, columnstore, and in-memory OLTP carry performance work. Main strengths: a mature first-party toolchain, a regular release cadence, and standard client interfaces. Main weaknesses: the language only runs on SQL Server or SAP ASE, the useful surface is engine-specific, NULL starts in every declared variable, an unhandled CATCH continues the batch, cursor code paths are slow, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard.

title: XSLT (3.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses XSLT in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.4/100 · Engineering readiness 77.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ The data model is untyped by default: A template matches a node or an item, and a schema is opt-in (T1)
❌ There is no sum type: A sequence holds any items, and the match decides (T4)
❌ There are no generics (T5)
❌ An empty sequence is a value: Nothing in the type distinguishes absent from present (T10)
✅ A mode separates two transformations of one tree: The same rule can run under a named mode



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A template rule is the only construct: A match and a mode select the rule
✅ The output is built by a literal result element: The stylesheet states the result shape



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The data model is immutable: A node is never changed; a transformation builds a new tree



1.1.4 Error

✅ xsl:try and xsl:catch give a structured path: A recoverable error is caught by type
⚠️ A recoverable error can be recovered silently: The processor may continue with a fallback



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ There is no shared mutable state: A transformation is a function of its input



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The standard is public: XSLT 3.0 is a W3C Recommendation, and several processors implement it
✅ A stylesheet is portable: Saxon, libxslt, and a browser engine read the same source



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A stylesheet is a function: The input tree in, the result tree out, no shared state
The mode is the dispatch mechanism: Two rules for one node under different names
The result is built, not mutated: The immutability is the safety and the copy cost
The standard is the compatibility: A stylesheet runs where a processor is installed, and a 1.0 engine is the floor




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ The stylesheet is compiled to the processor’s own form: That form is executed by the engine, and there is no path to machine code (R1)
⚠️ A naive template chain is slow: A recursive copy of a large tree is the classic cost



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The processors fragment the language: XSLT 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 support differ (Ec2)
❌ XSLT 1.0 remains in service: A 1999 stylesheet still runs in a browser (Ec7)
✅ A processor is a library: Saxon, libxslt, and the browser engine need no vendor



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: XSLT 3.0 is from 2017, and a 4.0 has not arrived (V4)
✅ A version is declared in the stylesheet: version="3.0" selects the rules



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The domain is document transformation: XML to HTML, to text, or to another XML
⚠️ JSON and a general program are out of scope: A transformation is not an application



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The declarative model is small: A match, a mode, and a template
⚠️ The recursion and the sequence model take time



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The syntax is XML: Every instruction is an element (S1)
❌ The angle brackets dominate: A short stylesheet is long (S3)



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A processor reports a static error: A stylesheet is compiled before it runs



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ An extension function calls out of the sandbox: A processor can expose Java or C

1.3.1 Reproducibility

1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ There is no package registry: A stylesheet imports a module by URI, and nothing verifies it (Y3)

✅ The W3C maintains the recommendation in an open process. (Y11)
✅ XSLT 3.0 is a published W3C Recommendation. (Y12)
✅ libxslt and Saxon publish their source. (Y19)

Verdict: XSLT is a declarative transformation language: immutable trees, template rules, modes, and a structured try make a transformation a function of its input, and the standard is public. What it charges is the untyped data model, the absent sum type, the empty sequence, the XML syntax, and a standard that has not moved since 2017. Main strength: a pure transformation with no shared state. Main weakness: the type model is weak, and the processors disagree at the edges.
