title: Racket (8.17)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Racket in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 74.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 90.6/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Typing is dynamic with no static check (T1): A value carries its type at run time, so a wrong-typed use fails when the expression executes
❌ Dispatch is resolved at run time (T3): (send obj 'msg) and a generic method resolve when called, so a missing method fails there rather than at compile time
❌ There are no sum types and no core generics (T4, T5): An alternative is a struct, a symbol, or a tagged list plus a contract, and no type parameter exists in the core language
❌ The numeric operators dispatch on a hidden type (T8): +, *, and = accept any number, and the exact or the inexact result follows the values at run time, so the arithmetic is overloaded without a declared type
✅ A contract checks the module boundary at run time: (provide/contract [f (-> integer? integer?)]) and define/contract reject a wrong call at the boundary and name the module at fault
⚠️ #lang typed/racket types part of a program: A typed module imports an untyped one through require/typed and a contract, so static and dynamic code meet at a checked boundary



1.1.2 Construction

✅ struct declares the constructor with its invariant: (struct posn (x y) #:transparent #:guard check) creates the constructor, the predicate, and the accessors together, and the guard rejects a bad argument
✅ A macro extends the language at compile time: A define-syntax form sees its syntax objects and expands to core forms, so a construct is added without a run-time library
✅ Hygiene prevents accidental name capture: A binding the macro introduces cannot collide with a name at the use site, so the expansion does not depend on the caller’s names
✅ A module scopes what it defines: A binding is private until it is provided, so a helper constructor stays invisible outside the module
✅ #lang fixes the whole surface of a file: A module states its language on the first line, so a DSL and the base language do not mix by accident
⚠️ set! reaches any binding in the core language: A variable can be reassigned unless the language of the file forbids it, so immutability is not enforced by the core
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the default hash’s iteration order is documented as not specified (C5)
❌ One value, many names: pairs are shared, and the mutation operators change every name that reaches the cell (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ A call-with-* form brackets a resource: (call-with-input-file path proc) opens and closes around the call, and with-handlers covers the exceptional path
✅ A place collects its own heap: A place runs on a separate thread with a separate store, so parallel work does not extend one collection pause
❌ Collection is non-deterministic (M2): The collector runs on its own schedule, and (collect-garbage) or the PLTSTDERR collection log is the only control a program has
❌ There is no RAII (M3): There is no scope-bound destructor, so a port, a TCP listener, or a subprocess is released by an explicit close-input-port or by a bracket the author writes
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties a value to an owner, so a shared mutable structure escapes its module without a trace
⚠️ A custodian groups resources only when it is created: make-custodian and custodian-shutdown-all shut down a group of threads and ports together, and the code must ask for that grouping



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked (Er2): raise, error, and raise-user-error are not declared in a signature, so a caller cannot see the failure set from the definition
✅ with-handlers selects the recovery by predicate: (with-handlers ([(lambda (e) (exn:fail? e)) handler]) body) chooses the handler from the exception’s type rather than from a code number
✅ An exception is a struct with fields: (exn-message e), (exn:fail:contract? e), and the continuation marks of exn:fail make a failure an inspectable value
✅ A failure can be a value instead of a throw: A struct with an ok and an error variant, or a pair of values, carries the outcome without an exception
✅ A contract violation blames a party: An exn:fail:contract carries the offending value, the contract, and the module blamed, so a boundary fault is localised
⚠️ A catch-all handler hides the cause: (with-handlers ([void void]) ...) discards the reason, and any cleanup must be arranged with dynamic-wind rather than by the handler



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A place gives shared-nothing parallelism: place runs a computation on its own thread and store, and place-channel-put and place-channel-get pass values, so several cores are used without shared memory
✅ A future parallelises an expression: (future expr) runs on a thread from the pool and (touch f) forces the result, and the runtime keeps a future’s computation safe on its own
✅ A thread is a lightweight green thread: (thread proc) starts one, (sync evt) waits on an event, and channel-put and channel-get pass values between threads
✅ Non-blocking I/O composes through events: sync on a port or on an async-channel waits for whichever is ready, so no callback pyramid is needed
✅ A custodian bounds a thread group: A supervisor custodian shuts down its threads and ports together, so a group of tasks is torn down as a unit
⚠️ A shared box still needs a lock: A box or a vector written from two threads needs a semaphore or box-cas!, and the runtime reports no race



1.1.6 Platform

✅ A program compiles to a native executable: raco exe produces a standalone binary and bundles the runtime and the libraries it needs
✅ The runtime runs on the major platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, and the BSDs are supported from one source
✅ Racket CS builds on Chez Scheme: The default runtime compiles with Chez’s compiler, and the earlier bytecode runtime with its JIT remained available as the alternative
✅ raco covers install, build, and delivery: raco pkg, raco exe, and raco distribute are one tool family for a project’s whole lifecycle
⚠️ The runtime must be present unless it is bundled: A source program needs an installed Racket, and raco distribute is the step that removes that dependency
⚠️ Cross-compilation is limited: An executable targets the platform that built it unless a cross build is arranged



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Language-oriented programming is the premise: Building a DSL is the design centre of the language, and the work of designing the notation is the price of a task-specific language
Contracts are opt-in: A module can leave a boundary unchecked, and the per-call cost of a contract follows from asking for the check
#lang fixes the language for a whole file: A module cannot change its language halfway, which is a deliberate uniformity rather than a coupling defect
A macro can obscure its expansion: A macro is powerful, and the readability cost of an unusual expansion is a style decision
A linked list is the core sequence type: cons, car, and cdr model a sequence as a pair chain, so the cost in memory locality is a representation choice
The λ-calculus core is deliberately small: The core language is tiny because a macro expands to it, which is a design decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Racket CS compiles through Chez Scheme: A module is compiled to native code ahead of time, so an interpreted step is not in the hot path
✅ Hot code is compiled rather than interpreted: The compiler and the JIT of the runtime remove repeated interpretation of a loop
✅ A future and a place use several cores: A computation split across futures runs on the available threads and places
⚠️ Numeric code is moderate: A boxed number and a generic arithmetic operation over the numeric tower cost more than unboxed arithmetic in a compiled language
⚠️ A contract adds a check per boundary crossing: A contract on a hot function is a run-time check on every call
⚠️ A continuation capture does real work: call/cc and dynamic-wind save and restore the control state, so a control abstraction is not free



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The package ecosystem is small (Ec3): The count of published packages is well below a mainstream language’s, so a project may write what it cannot find
✅ raco pkg is a first-class package manager: raco pkg install takes a package name, a file, or a Git URL, so a dependency needs no manual vendoring step
✅ The distribution ships a large library: racket/base, racket/list, racket/contract, racket/class, racket/draw, and racket/gui come in one installation
✅ DrRacket is an IDE for both beginner and expert: The editor, the REPL, and the stepper are part of the distribution, and the stepper shows one reduction at a time
✅ Scribble documents a package in the language itself: Scribble writes prose with Racket syntax and produces HTML, PDF, and the reference pages from one source
⚠️ The community is small: Questions are answered, but by fewer people than in a mainstream ecosystem



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The language is stable and backward compatible: Racket 8.x runs code written for earlier releases, and the compatibility promise covers the core
✅ #lang isolates a change: A DSL fixes the language of its own files, so a change to the base language does not reach a #lang that pins it
✅ The change of runtime kept the language: Racket CS replaced the bytecode runtime beneath the language, and existing source recompiled
✅ A package can be held at a version: An installation can be pinned to a version or to a repository revision, so a build can be made reproducible
⚠️ A library API can change between releases: The core is stable, and a library outside it may change, so an upgrade needs a test run
❌ Build variants multiply: read-conditional barbs select which forms read, and the space is set by the reader’s features (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for language research and DSLs: Macros, #lang, and the reader produce a new language from a module, as the paper “Languages as Libraries” documents
✅ Strong fit for teaching: DrRacket, How to Design Programs, and the teaching languages such as #lang htdp/bsl are built for a first course
✅ Good for compilers and interpreters: #lang plus raco makes a language implementation a package, and the Beautiful Racket book builds several
✅ racket/gui covers a desktop application: The GUI toolkit and racket/draw ship in the distribution, so a windowed program needs no external dependency
⚠️ Commercial adoption is small with notable exceptions: Naughty Dog’s game scripting language and the Arc dialect behind Hacker News run on Racket, but the general production footprint is small
⚠️ Heavy numeric work belongs in a library: Array and tensor computation depends on a package rather than on the core language



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The concepts are many even when the syntax is small (L1): Macros, continuations, modules, and contracts are separate topics, and each takes practice
❌ A macro is a topic of its own: Writing a macro requires the syntax-object model and the phase distinctions, which are separate from ordinary programming
✅ DrRacket and the stepper make evaluation visible: A beginner steps an expression and sees each reduction of the program
✅ A complete curriculum exists: How to Design Programs and its teaching languages are free and aligned with the IDE
✅ The documentation is comprehensive: The Racket Reference and the Racket Guide cover the language and each library with examples
⚠️ A Scheme background helps and misleads: The parentheses and the λ-calculus core transfer, while the module system, structs, and #lang differ from a bare Scheme



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is uniform: Every form is a parenthesised list, so a reader learns one shape and applies it everywhere
✅ A user form looks like a built-in form: A macro-defined form has the same shape as let or define, so no new grammar is needed
✅ A reader extension can change the surface: #lang plus a readtable defines a different notation for one file without changing the language
✅ Prefix notation removes precedence rules: (+ (* a b) c) states the order of operations in its nesting, so no precedence table must be learned
⚠️ The parentheses are dense: A deeply nested expression needs careful counting, and most editors use a paredit or rainbow-paren mode to help
⚠️ A quoted form blurs data and code: '(a b) is a list and (a b) is a call, so one character changes the meaning of a form



1.2.7 Testing

✅ rackunit ships with the language: check-equal?, check-true, and test-case are in the distribution, and raco test runs a directory of tests
✅ A test can live in the module it tests: A (module+ test ...) submodule holds the tests, so no separate test file is needed
✅ A contract is an executable invariant: A contract on an exported function rejects a wrong call, so a test need not re-check the boundary
✅ A failure reports both values: A failed check-equal? prints the expected value, the actual value, and the source location
✅ The debugger and the stepper inspect a real run: DrRacket’s debugger steps the evaluation, and the stepper shows the reduction sequence
⚠️ Dynamic typing defers a fault to the executed path: A wrong-typed call passes the build and fails a run, so the covered paths matter



1.2.8 Security

✅ The runtime is memory-safe: No pointer arithmetic and no manual free exist, so a use-after-free or a buffer overflow cannot be written in Racket source
✅ A contract guards a trust boundary: A contract on a value that arrives from outside rejects a wrong shape at the boundary and names the party at fault
✅ racket/sandbox runs untrusted code with limits: A sandboxed evaluator carries its own language, a memory limit, and a custodian that bounds its run time
✅ eval is explicit and scoped: eval and dynamic-require are visible calls, and the namespace decides what the evaluated code can reach
⚠️ eval on a term built from input is the injection pattern: (eval (read input)) executes the text, and read itself can allocate on a crafted input
⚠️ Two places share the file system: A place shares no memory with another, but two places can still corrupt one file, which the language does not prevent

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Raco resolves package versions from the catalog at install time. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve from the catalog state. (Y2)
❌ No toolchain pin exists in the official distribution. (Y14)

❌ No advisory feed covers catalog packages. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ displayln carries no structure. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ DrRacket ships debugging with the distribution. (Y13)
⚠️ The build-less loop is immediate; compilation pays only where the program opts in.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs where a Racket distribution of the version runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Racket team and community govern in the open. (Y11)
✅ The Racket reference is public and complete. (Y12)
✅ The runtime and DrRacket are public source. (Y19)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

Verdict: Racket’s design yields moderate core coupling and better ecosystem coupling. The language-oriented model is a real decoupling device: a macro expands to core forms without a name from the use site leaking in, a struct carries its own guard, a module hides what it does not provide, and a contract checks a boundary and names the party at fault. The cost sits in the type system and the heap, where typing is dynamic, dispatch resolves at run time, there are no sum types or core generics, and memory has neither an ownership rule nor a block-scoped release, with collection decided by the runtime. Around the language, the package ecosystem is small and the concept load is heavy, while the toolchain, the documentation, and the debugging support are complete.

title: Scratch (3.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Scratch in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 70.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.5/100 · Engineering readiness 47.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no static type check: A block accepts a value of any kind, and a mismatch appears only when the script runs (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative is not a declared type; the script tests a value with an if or a sensing condition (T4)
❌ No generics: A list block is not parameterised by an element type (T5)
❌ One flat namespace for message names: Every message name is project-wide, so a name collision is a naming decision rather than a scope decision (T6)
❌ No null safety: A variable that was never set reads as an empty value, and a block that needs a value can run with none (T10)
❌ No module boundary: The project is one program, and a sprite exposes its blocks without a declared interface (T11)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global mutable state is the default: A variable created “for all sprites” is writable by every script in the project (C1)
❌ No immutability: A value in a variable can be changed by any script that names it (C2)
✅ A sprite is a self-contained unit: Costume, sound, and scripts live together, so one actor’s behaviour is defined in one place
✅ The event model separates the trigger from the action: The green flag, a key press, a sprite click, or a received message starts a script, and the script does not know who started it
✅ Cloning separates an instance from its definition: create clone of myself copies a sprite’s scripts at run time, so a repeated actor is written once
⚠️ A custom block is the only abstraction: define gives a named sequence with inputs, and “run without screen refresh” is the one control over its granularity



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The runtime owns every object: No allocation and no deallocation block exists, and a sprite, a costume, or a clone is reclaimed automatically, so a script never names memory
✅ A clone can be deleted explicitly: delete this clone bounds the number of live actors
⚠️ The clone count is the practical limit: Scratch caps the number of clones, so a forever loop that clones without a delete reaches the cap rather than exhausting memory
⚠️ The media assets are the project’s footprint: Costumes, backdrops, and sounds dominate the size and the load time of a project



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no structured error path: No exception and no error value exists, and a failed block simply does not produce the expected effect (Er1)
❌ Nothing marks a failed operation: A block that cannot do what it says leaves the value unchanged or produces a placeholder, and the script continues (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: A block returns one value, and no value can carry the fact that an operation failed (Er4)
✅ The stage gives immediate feedback: An out-of-stage sprite is visibly off-stage, and a sensing block can test for a touch
⚠️ Debugging is by observation: There is no breakpoint, so the ordinary method is a variable monitor or a say block



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Scripts are concurrent by default: Every hat block in the project runs in parallel, and no script starts or joins another by hand
⚠️ A broadcast is global: Any sprite can listen for any message, so a broadcast couples the sender to every listener in the project
✅ The scheduler is cooperative and single-threaded: The scripts advance one after another within a frame, so an interleaved update does not arise in the middle of a block
✅ A clone runs its own copy of the script: when I start as a clone gives each instance an independent thread of control
⚠️ A shared variable is updated by many scripts without a lock: Correctness depends on where each script yields, which the programmer must reason about
⚠️ One frame is the unit of timing: The green-flag scripts share the frame budget, so the loop rate is the scheduling contract



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The runtime is the same on every target: A project runs in the browser player and in the offline editor with the same blocks
✅ The sandbox bounds what a project can do: A project reaches no file system and no network, so its effect is confined to the runtime
✅ MIT Media Lab maintains the runtime and the community site: The editor, the player, and the sharing site come from one organisation
✅ The project file is an open document: A .sb3 project is a zip archive of JSON and assets, so a project can be read and converted
⚠️ Cloud variables are a hosted service: They work only on the Scratch site, so a project that uses them depends on that host
⚠️ An extension changes the runtime’s surface: The Music, Pen, and video-sensing extensions, and the hardware extensions, add blocks the player must supply
❌ It is not usable for a production application: There is no file access, no network, no performance target, and no general library (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Visual blocks trade expressiveness for legibility: The block shape carries the nesting rule, so a syntax error is not expressible — which is the design goal
The block vocabulary is deliberately small: A small instruction set is the pedagogy, not an oversight
The actor-based organisation mirrors the stage: A project is organised by sprite because the program is a scene
The educational scope is a scope decision: The absence of files, network, and performance is the boundary of the design
Sharing and remixing are community choices: The remix model is a policy of the site, not a property of the language
Turbo Mode is an optional accelerator: It removes the frame wait, and the choice is the user’s




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The runtime executes the blocks directly: The player holds the block scripts and runs them, so there is no build step between the editor and the running project
✅ “Run without screen refresh” removes the frame yield: A custom block with that option runs to completion inside one frame, so a heavy computation can finish without waiting
✅ Turbo Mode removes the frame wait entirely: The option runs the project as fast as the runtime allows
⚠️ Animation is capped near the redraw rate: A loop yields each frame, so smooth motion is limited to the display rate
⚠️ A large script count degrades the frame: Every script shares one frame budget, so the project slows as the script count and the clone count grow



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is the runtime and one community site: The blocks, the media library, and the sharing site are the whole environment, and there is no general package manager (Ec3)
✅ The adoption in education is very large: The project is used in K-12 classrooms worldwide
✅ A large public project corpus exists: Shared and remixed projects are a huge body of worked examples
✅ The media and sprite libraries are built in: Backdrops, costumes, and sounds ship with the editor
⚠️ Third-party players and add-ons are the extension point: TurboWarp, Scratch Addons, and the extension gallery live outside the official editor
✅ Stored projects cross on a documented path: Scratch 3 opens .sb and .sb2 projects and saves them in the current format [5] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The project format carries a version and a converter: An older project is converted when it is opened in the current editor
✅ MIT maintains the editor as a product: The runtime, the editor, and the site receive continuing updates
✅ The offline editor mirrors the online one: A project runs without a connection to the site
⚠️ A block set can change between editor releases: A removed or renamed block can leave an older project needing an edit



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is one thing: teaching programming to beginners: The design goal is computational thinking, and everything outside it is out of scope (D1)
✅ The classroom fit is exemplary: Drag-and-drop, immediate feedback, and shareable projects match the teaching case
✅ It is the first language in many curricula: The adoption in schools is the evidence for the fit
⚠️ The move to a text language is the known gap: A learner must leave Scratch to continue, and the transfer is not automatic



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The curve is effectively zero: The interface is drag-and-drop, and there is no syntax to learn
✅ The block shape prevents the syntax error: A block that does not fit cannot be placed
✅ The stage returns immediate feedback: One click runs the project and shows the result
⚠️ The ceiling is low for a capable learner: After the core blocks there is little further depth
⚠️ “Run without screen refresh” is the one advanced idea: A heavy custom block must use it to finish inside a frame



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is the block shape: An invalid nesting is impossible, because the editor accepts only a shape that fits
✅ The expression blocks nest visually: An operator block occupies an input slot, so the precedence is explicit without parentheses
✅ The blocks are named in the reader’s language: The editor localises the labels and the variable names
⚠️ A small computation becomes a tall column of blocks: The notation is compact per block and long per expression
⚠️ There is no text form in the editor: A script cannot be typed, searched, or diffed as text



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework: No assertion and no runner exists, so a test is a manual run (G1)
❌ An error appears only when a script runs: A wrong block is found by executing the project (G3)
✅ The stage is a built-in observation harness: Motion, sound, and say show the program state directly
✅ A variable monitor exposes a value on the stage: Any variable can be shown and watched as it changes
⚠️ Verification is by inspection: The programmer checks the result by watching the project, not by a repeatable check



1.2.8 Security

✅ A project runs in a sandbox: No block opens a file or a socket, so a project reaches no file system and no network and its effect is confined to the runtime
✅ The runtime is the same for every project: A shared project cannot ship a native binary
⚠️ A cloud variable is shared global state: Every player of the project can write it, so a project that trusts it can be misled
⚠️ The community features are moderated, not secured: The safety of the sharing site is a policy of the site, not a property of the language
⚠️ A third-party player can add an unsafe surface: An alternative player or an add-on can extend the runtime beyond the sandbox
❌ Numbers are JavaScript doubles: integers above 2^53 change value in silence (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

⚠️ Nothing is built; the project file and the editor state are the whole artifact.



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Shared projects and extensions carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers community extensions. (Y16)
⚠️ Extensions are added by URL or palette pick, with no registry contract.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ say and the variable pane carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A script failure stops the sprite silently unless the project handles it. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No in-editor analysis exists beyond the block palette. (Y8)
❌ No debugger ships with the editor. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Extensions run outside the language; no in-process interface exists. (Y9)
❌ The project runs in the Scratch editor or a compatible player. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the shipped VM: the documentation describes the virtual machine’s behavior, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Scratch’s design yields moderate core coupling, and the marks fall where the pedagogy put them. Global variables are the project namespace, a broadcast reaches every sprite, and there is no type check, no structured error path, and no module boundary; the constrained environment keeps the consequence small. The visual block model removes the syntax error entirely, the event model separates a trigger from the action it starts, and a sprite is a self-contained unit. Main strengths: a zero learning curve, an exemplary classroom fit, very large K-12 adoption, and a sandbox that bounds what a project can do. Main weaknesses: it is not usable for a production application, the domain is a single one, the block vocabulary is shallow, and testing is by inspection.

title: Assembly (x86-64, System V AMD64 ABI)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Assembly in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 39.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 81.6/100 · Engineering readiness 49.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no type system: An operand is a register or a memory address of a fixed width, and the assembler does not check that an integer, a pointer, and an address are used consistently (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative must be encoded by hand in a register or in a memory layout the programmer invents (T4)
❌ No generics: A macro can repeat a sequence, but there is no type parameter through which a repeated sequence can be checked (T5)
❌ No namespaces: Every global symbol shares one flat namespace in the object file, so a collision is resolved by naming convention (T6)
❌ No null safety: A null pointer is a zero register value, and a load from it is an ordinary instruction (T10)
❌ No module boundary: Separate translation units share the same global symbol space and ABI, and the only encapsulation is the assembler’s local label (T11)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Registers are global mutable state: Every instruction reads and writes the same fixed register file, so the meaning of a register depends on the whole instruction stream (C1)
❌ Mutability is the only mode: Nothing is immutable unless a section is marked read-only, and that is enforced by the loader rather than by a type (C2)
❌ Construction is allocation: Creating a value means writing a register or a memory cell that must already have been reserved (C3)
❌ No constructor or validation: A value is legal only because the programmer kept it legal, and nothing checks it (C4)
✅ Macros decouple a repeated sequence: .macro in GAS and %macro in NASM let a reusable instruction sequence be named and expanded, so a repeated pattern is written once
✅ Sections separate data from code: .text, .data, .rodata, and .bss place each kind of content in its own segment of the object file



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Every allocation and deallocation is manual: The stack frame, the malloc call, and the free call are the programmer’s responsibility (M1)
❌ No release tied to scope: There is no RAII; nothing runs at the end of a block (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A pointer may alias, dangle, or be freed twice, and the assembler does not see pointers as a type (M4)
✅ The stack is a structured allocation: push/pop and the rsp/rbp frame give a scoped allocation with a defined lifetime for the duration of a call
⚠️ The layout is the ABI’s, not the program’s: The System V AMD64 ABI fixes which registers are caller-saved and how the stack frame is formed, so the layout choices are constrained
❌ Nothing initializes anything: a register or stack slot holds whatever the previous user of those bytes left, and the language has no notion of an unwritten value (M5)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: the fault is the OS’s — no language surface exists to catch a trap in (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no structured error path: No exception, no error type, and no return-result convention; a failed call is signalled by a flag or a register the caller must test (Er1)
❌ An error can be ignored by design: A non-zero value in rax or a set carry flag does nothing unless the code branches on it (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: An error cannot be returned as a value the caller’s code carries in a checked way (Er4)
✅ Flags give a structured condition test: cmp and test set ZF, CF, SF, and OF, and a conditional jump branches on a named condition
⚠️ The recovery path is a jump target: Recovery is a branch to a label, so its structure exists only in the programmer’s discipline
❌ A fault is the process: an OS fault ends the program, and no recoverable unit is declared (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Shared mutable state is the default: Registers and memory are equally visible to every core, and there is no notion of private state (K2)
❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection: A lock is a lock prefix on one instruction or a call into a library, and nothing analyses the program for a race (K3)
❌ No structured concurrency: A thread is a clone or pthread_create call, and nothing scopes or joins its lifetime (K4)
✅ Atomic operations are instruction-level: lock cmpxchg, lock xadd, and mfence express a defined atomic primitive directly
✅ The lock prefix gives a defined ordering: It serialises the decorated instruction across the cores of the machine
⚠️ The memory ordering is reasoned about by hand: The x86-64 model is comparatively strong, but nothing in the language states or checks the ordering the algorithm needs
❌ A thread is an operating-system thread: clone or pthread_create reserves one, and the kernel limits how many a process may hold (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The program is bound to one instruction set: x86-64 opcodes do not run on AArch64 or RISC-V, so the source is not portable across architectures (P1)
❌ The calling convention is one ABI: A call must agree with the System V AMD64 register and stack rules, so the function interface is fit for one platform’s convention
✅ The object format is documented and stable: An ELF object file is linked with the platform linker through a published format
✅ The assembler is a choice within the target: GAS and NASM produce code for the same instruction set
⚠️ Windows uses a different x86-64 convention: The Microsoft x64 ABI differs from System V in its argument registers and its shadow space, so the source is bound to one operating-system convention as well
⚠️ Extension instructions need runtime dispatch: AVX-512 and the other vector extensions require a CPU feature check before they are used
❌ It is a poor fit above the machine: With no types, no data abstraction, and no error handling, ordinary application logic is expensive to write and to change (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Full machine control is the point: The absence of an abstraction layer is a deliberate removal, not a defect
Assembly is a last resort by design: It is used where a higher-level language cannot express the operation
A hand-written kernel can repay the discipline cost: The performance-critical kernel and the cryptographic primitive are the cases where it does
Reverse engineering is a use, not an application: Disassembly is read, not maintained as a product
The dialect choice is a surface choice: The Intel and AT&T notations name the same instruction set
Inline assembly inside a host language is a scoping decision: What remains is a coupling to the compiler’s asm syntax




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The program is the machine code: There is no interpreter, JIT, or runtime between the source and the CPU, so the cost of an instruction is the instruction
✅ Instruction selection is under program control: lea, fused operations, and vector instructions can be chosen for each site
✅ There is no runtime start-up cost: A static executable needs no runtime initialisation beyond the loader
⚠️ The CPU optimises beyond the instruction stream: Out-of-order execution, branch prediction, and the micro-operation cache mean the source-order cost is not the measured cost
⚠️ A hand-written routine can lose to a compiler: Without the optimiser’s cross-block analysis, hand-scheduled and hand-allocated code can be slower than -O2 output



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ There is no package manager: A dependency is an object file or a linked library, resolved by the linker and the build script (Ec1)
✅ The assemblers are standard and maintained: GAS, NASM, and the LLVM assembler are widely available
✅ The code interoperates with C at the ABI: An assembly routine can be called from C and can call C
⚠️ The reusable corpus is small: Most assembly source is written for one program and its ABI, so few libraries exist as assembly source
✅ The source writes against the platform’s published ABI, which is the interface its artifacts need [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The instruction set is specified and backward compatible: x86-64 adds encodings and keeps the earlier ones
✅ New extensions are opt-in: SSE, AVX, and AVX-512 code is gated by CPU feature detection rather than by the instruction set as a whole
✅ The manuals are public and maintained: The Intel SDM and the AMD APM document each instruction
⚠️ Assembler syntax is not standardised across tools: GAS and NASM disagree on directives, operand order, and macro syntax
⚠️ A microarchitecture change invalidates tuning: Code hand-scheduled for one CPU generation can be mistuned on the next
❌ Build variants multiply: assembler conditionals (.if, %if) select which instructions assemble, so a listing is a flag outcome, not only a source file (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The kernel-level operations are the native domain: Hardware access, interrupt entry, context switch, and boot code
✅ Some instructions are reachable only here: The special registers, cpuid, rdtsc, and the privileged instructions have no higher-level equivalent
✅ Vector kernels benefit: A hand-tuned SIMD routine writes exactly the instruction the target supports
⚠️ Even kernel work is mostly C with small assembly islands: The fit is real but narrow



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The curve is extremely steep: The programmer must hold the register file, the instruction set, and the target ABI in mind at once
❌ There is no abstraction to learn instead of the machine: Nothing is hidden and nothing is named above the instruction level
✅ The reference material is complete and public: Intel and AMD document every instruction and every flag
✅ The machine gives immediate feedback: A debugger shows the registers and the memory directly
⚠️ Three bodies of knowledge are separate subjects: The instruction set, the ABI, and the toolchain must each be learned on its own



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ The Intel and AT&T dialects differ in the same instruction set: Operand order reverses and the register and constant prefixes differ, so the notation is a toolchain choice
⚠️ The directive syntax differs by assembler: GAS uses .globl and .section, NASM uses global and section
⚠️ Every operand form is spelled out: %rax, $42, and 8(%rbp) write the addressing mode at each site
✅ The mnemonics are short and uniform: mov, add, and jmp each name one operation
⚠️ A label is a fixed position in the code: A label names a location for a jump, a call, or a data symbol, so a transfer target is coupled to that position in the listing



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework in the language: A test is a program that runs and compares, and the harness lives outside the assembler (G1)
❌ Debugging is low-level: The debugger exposes registers and raw memory, so a fault is found in machine state rather than in a named abstraction (G2)
✅ A single-step debugger is exact: gdb and lldb can run one instruction and show every register and flag
✅ Repetition is deterministic: With no scheduler and no collector, the same input produces the same instruction sequence
⚠️ The usual check is a test in a higher-level language: The assembly routine is called from C and compared there
❌ No clock the language publishes: a program reaches the OS clock through services, not a published reading (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Every memory-safety class is open: A buffer overflow, a use-after-free, a double free, and an out-of-bounds write are all possible and nothing prevents them (Q1)
❌ Return-oriented programming is possible: The stack holds return addresses that are writable, so a memory write can redirect control flow
❌ There is no bounds checking and no guard page by default: An array index is an address calculation
⚠️ Stack canaries, ASLR, and CET are external mitigations: They come from the toolchain flags, the loader, and the operating system, and the source must cooperate with them
✅ Non-executable and write-or-execute pages are available: The operating system can mark the stack non-executable and enforce W^X, which removes some code injection
✅ The sandbox is the operating system’s: A program runs with the privileges the loader grants it, not with a language-level capability model

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the tool reads: the assembler assembles what the command names, and dependencies (if any) are the linker’s command line (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Object files and libraries move with no provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers the library ecosystem. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists; the hardware debugger and simulators are the instruments. (Y5)
❌ Output is whatever the program writes to ports and buffers. (Y6)
❌ A fault lands in the CPU’s vector handler; the state is the register file. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with an assembler; gdb and the simulators are separate. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs on the instruction set it encodes. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No vendor owns the instruction set; the makers publish the manuals in the open. (Y11)
❌ The ISA manuals are documentation, not a grammar a second assembler implements. (Y12)
✅ The assemblers (gas, nasm) are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Assembly’s design produces the lowest core score in this comparison, because it removes every separating construct rather than misplacing one. There is no type system, no release tied to scope, no structured error path, and no concurrency construct; the register file is global mutable state, and the machine is the only abstraction. What the language does give is exact control: the programmer chooses the instruction, the register, and the schedule, and the flags give a defined condition test. Main strengths: no runtime overhead, direct access to the privileged instructions, and a fully public specification. Main weaknesses: the source is bound to one instruction set and one ABI, every memory-safety class is open, and the work is expensive to learn, to test, and to maintain.

title: SPARK (Pro 25)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SPARK in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.8/100 · Engineering readiness 39.2/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ The static type system is Ada’s: Every object, parameter, and function result has a declared type, and the compiler checks every assignment and call
✅ Subtypes carry range constraints: subtype narrows a base type with a range or a predicate, and in the proved subset a violation is a proof obligation rather than a run-time check
✅ Enumeration and discriminated record types express alternatives: An enumeration gives a finite value set, and a variant record’s discriminant states which branch is active
✅ Generics are checked at each instantiation: An Ada generic is analysed where it is instantiated, so a reusable abstraction is verified at its use site
✅ Type_Invariant states a property of a private type: The invariant is an obligation on every value of the type
⚠️ Access types are admitted only under an ownership policy: SPARK allows a pointer when its owner is declared, so indirection is available but constrained
❌ Inherits the JVM answer: string length counts UTF-16 units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Contracts are part of the subprogram declaration: Pre, Post, and Contract_Cases state the obligation beside the parameters, so a caller reads it with the signature
✅ Flow contracts state what a subprogram reads and writes: Global, Depends, and Refined_Global make the data flow a declared artefact
✅ Abstract states confine a package’s state: Abstract_State declares the state as an abstraction, Refined_State binds it to concrete variables, and Initializes states what a package sets up
✅ Separation is proved rather than advised: The ownership policy, the flow aspects, and the contracts are analysed by GNATprove, so a declared separation is verified and not merely recommended
⚠️ The declarations carry more than the code needs: A proof requires a contract for every subprogram on the path, so construction carries an annotation burden
⚠️ A unit can opt out with SPARK_Mode => Off: An analysed region and an unchecked region can sit in the same program
❌ Inherits the Java class-init rule: first-touch, with the documented cycle (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ An ownership policy governs any access type: SPARK’s data-ownership regime gives a pointer a stated owner, so a dangling or duplicated reference is a proof failure rather than a run-time defect
✅ No manual deallocation in the subset: Unchecked_Deallocation is outside SPARK, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ No garbage collector: SPARK compiles to native code and runs without a collector
✅ Bounded containers remove the heap: Ada.Containers.Bounded_Vectors and its siblings hold their storage in the object
✅ A local object’s lifetime is its scope: A stack variable’s extent is fixed by the block that declares it
⚠️ An owned access type still allocates at run time: The allocation is allowed and proved, but the allocator’s behaviour remains a run-time fact
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: the proof covers declared failures; storage exhaustion on the runtime reaches Program_Error, outside the contract (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A failure is a proof obligation: GNATprove reports an unproved check, so a fault is found in the toolchain rather than in a test run
✅ A raise is stated in the contract: Exceptional_Cases names the exceptions a subprogram may propagate, so the failure set is declared
✅ Run-time checks are proved impossible rather than disabled: Once GNATprove proves that an index, a range, or a division cannot fail, the check costs nothing
✅ Assert becomes a proof obligation: pragma Assert states a property that the analysis must establish or report
✅ Assume records an unproved fact explicitly: An assumption is written in the source and appears in the analysis report
⚠️ The proof is no stronger than its assumptions: An Assume, an unproved check, or a SPARK_Mode => Off unit leaves a gap in the guarantee



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Ada tasking is available and analysable: A task and a protected object are language constructs, and SPARK analyses the data flow of the supported subset
✅ A protected object is the synchronisation boundary: A protected operation enforces mutual exclusion and a barrier, so the lock is not written by hand
✅ The Ravenscar profile gives a static task set: No task is created dynamically, and the ceiling-locking protocol prevents priority inversion
✅ Shared state must be declared: A variable shared between tasks appears in a Global or Depends aspect, so the sharing is visible
⚠️ The analysed subset of tasking is smaller than Ada’s: An entry family, a dynamic rendezvous, or an unrestricted task is outside the analysed subset



1.1.6 Platform

❌ SPARK is a subset of Ada and a program is an Ada program: GNAT compiles the code, and the language has no existence apart from the Ada platform (P1)
❌ A foreign call leaves the proved region: An interface to C or another language is declared outside SPARK, so it cannot be analysed with the rest
✅ GNAT is a mature and portable Ada compiler: The same source compiles for x86-64, ARM, and the embedded targets used in avionics
✅ The qualified toolchain targets the certificated platforms: GNAT Pro supports VxWorks, LynxOS-178, and bare metal with a qualification for DO-178C
⚠️ Full support is a commercial subscription: GNATprove is available in the community toolchain, and SPARK Pro adds support, libraries, and qualification
⚠️ The build is a GNAT project: gprbuild and a project file describe the build, so the project couples to the Ada toolchain



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The proved subset is smaller than Ada: A feature outside SPARK is left out or isolated behind a SPARK_Mode => Off boundary
The restriction on pointers is a deliberate exchange: Aliasing is removed in return for an ownership regime and an array or a bounded container in place of a linked structure
The annotation burden is the price of the proof: A contract, an invariant, and a flow aspect are written for each unit on the path
The target domain is high-assurance by design: Aviation, space, and medical devices are the intended context, and the domain mark records that scope
Verification effort is a project decision: Zero-defect software is achievable given sufficient effort, which is a budget choice
The proof checks the contract, not the requirement: A verified program can implement the wrong specification, which no toolchain detects




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiled output is an Ada program’s native binary: SPARK compiles to the same native code, so the verification adds no run-time cost
✅ A proved check need not execute: A check that GNATprove established can be suppressed at that point, so the verified code does not pay for the guard
✅ No collector and no interpreter: The run-time has neither a garbage collector nor a JIT, so the timing is the Ada run-time’s
✅ The Ravenscar profile bounds the run-time behaviour: The task set, the priorities, and the locking are static, which makes the timing analysable
⚠️ The run-time is the Ada run-time: Tasking, the secondary stack, and exception propagation cost what GNAT’s run-time costs
⚠️ The proof is a build-time cost: GNATprove can take far longer than the compilation, which delays the build but not the program



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The SPARK ecosystem is a subset of Ada’s: A library must itself be in the SPARK subset to be analysed with the program (Ec3)
✅ Ada’s tooling serves the project: Alire supplies packages and gprbuild builds the project
✅ GNATprove and SPARK Pro are purpose-built and mature: The analyser and the commercial support layer are actively developed
✅ The industrial community sustains the toolchain: The requirements of the certificated industries drive the analyser and the library work
✅ A verified library base exists: SPARK’s own libraries and verified components ship with the toolchain
⚠️ A library that uses pointers must be isolated: An Ada library outside the subset is reached through an unproved boundary
❌ No object-code promise across compiler releases: the proved library travels as the .ali-bound objects of one GNAT release [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ SPARK tracks a published Ada standard: The subset is defined against Ada 2012 and Ada 2022, so a language change follows the standard revision
✅ Successive SPARK releases widened the subset: The ownership policy, the functional contracts, and the proof of type invariants were added over several releases
✅ Ada’s compatibility record is strong: An older Ada program generally compiles under a later revision
⚠️ A new feature arrives with a toolchain release: The analyser states the subset it supports, so adoption follows the release
⚠️ A proof depends on the toolchain version: A check proved under one GNATprove release can need a new annotation under another
❌ Build variants multiply: the GNAT toolchain’s preprocessor runs over the Ada sources the SPARK checks consume, so a proved unit can compile from a guarded selection (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists for high-assurance systems: Aviation, space, and medical devices, where DO-178C, EN 50128, or IEC 62304 applies, are the intended domains (D1)
❌ Outside those domains it is rarely chosen: A general application gains little from the proof and pays the toolchain cost (D1)
✅ The fit in the intended domain is excellent: The tools, the libraries, and the certification evidence all target it
✅ DO-333 credits the proof against the certification objectives: The formal-methods supplement to DO-178C lets the analysis substitute for some test objectives
✅ The shipping uses are real: Airbus, Thales, and Lockheed Martin build critical software on it
⚠️ The labour pool is small: An engineer with both Ada and formal-methods experience is hard to find



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Two skills must be learned, not one: SPARK requires Ada fluency and formal-methods practice, so contracts, invariants, and the proof tool must all be mastered (L1)
❌ A proof failure must be read as a counterexample: GNATprove reports an unproved check with a path, and turning the report into a fix takes experience
✅ The analysis report is actionable: The tool names the check, the path, and the assumption that blocks the proof
✅ The learning material is complete: AdaCore’s tutorial and the SPARK course material cover the language and the proof method
⚠️ The learning curve is very steep: A first proved subprogram is quick to write, and a first proved package with an abstract state is not



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is Ada’s: A package, a subprogram, and a loop read as they do in Ada, and a contract appears as an aspect or a pragma
✅ The block structure is explicit: A begin/end pair closes a block, and the end repeats the name it closes
✅ Contracts sit beside the parameters: Pre =>, Post =>, and Global => are part of the subprogram declaration
✅ Quantified expressions are first-class: (for all I in A'Range => A (I) > 0) states a property in the source
⚠️ An aspect clause can be long: A Depends aspect over much state is a long expression that needs careful reading



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The proof covers the property the contract states: An obligation is discharged for every value it quantifies, not for a sample
✅ The test suite no longer has to trigger every check: A bounds or range check proved impossible needs no test to reach it
✅ gnattest generates a unit-test harness: It reads a package specification and emits AUnit test stubs
✅ AUnit covers the behaviour a contract does not state: The proof and the test suite answer different questions
⚠️ A property that no contract states is not proved: The analysis reaches exactly the contracts and invariants that are written



1.2.8 Security

✅ The classic memory-safety faults are proved absent: A buffer overflow, a use-after-free, and a null dereference are removed by the subset and the proof, so the vulnerability class does not exist in the analysed code
✅ Input validity is stated and checked: A range constraint or a Pre aspect states what the caller must guarantee, and the proof covers the rest
✅ Unchecked_Conversion and pointer arithmetic are outside the subset: The unsafe operations are not available to analysed code
⚠️ The guarantee stops at the SPARK_Mode => Off boundary: An imported C function, a device driver, or an unchecked allocation is not proved
⚠️ The trusted base includes the prover and the compiler: A defect in GNATprove or in the code generator is outside the proof
❌ Inherits the JVM rule: integer wraparound in UDFs and expressions (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds embed compiler switches and library state. (Y1)
❌ Library versions resolve from the environment unless locked. (Y2)
❌ The distribution records no toolchain version per project. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Alire crates and vendored sources carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The crate registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers SPARK libraries. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ Text_IO carries no structure. (Y6)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The SPARK toolchain includes the GNAT debugger. (Y13)
⚠️ The proof tools are the verification instrument; editor analysis rides GNAT Studio.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The artifact runs on the targets the Pro toolchain ports cover. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ AdaCore decides the Pro toolchain’s direction and release cadence. (Y11)
❌ The SPARK Reference Manual is the vendor’s; the checking contract is not an independent standard. (Y12)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: SPARK’s design yields low core coupling for the work it is built for, and its platform cost is the price of a narrow domain. The static type system is Ada’s, the contracts and flow aspects make every global dependency explicit, an ownership policy removes coupling through shared references, and the toolchain proves the run-time checks that other languages leave to a test suite. The only scored core loss is P1: the language is a subset of Ada and does not exist apart from that platform. Main strengths: GNATprove, a toolchain qualified for DO-178C, DO-333 credit for the proof, and industrial use at Airbus, Thales, and Lockheed Martin; main weaknesses: an ecosystem that is a subset of Ada’s, a domain lock-in to high-assurance systems, and one of the steepest learning curves here.

title: Visual FoxPro (9.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Visual FoxPro in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 63.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.7/100 · Engineering readiness 27.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A variable is loosely typed: A name holds a string, a number, or an object (T1)
❌ A macro substitutes text at run time: &name resolves a name when the line runs (T3)
❌ There are no sum types (T4)
❌ There are no generics (T5)
❌ There are no namespaces: A procedure and a table share one project scope (T6)
❌ A field can be .NULL.: The type does not carry the check (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A class has a constructor: Init runs when the object is created
❌ A public variable is global: A PUBLIC value is reachable from the session (C1)
❌ A property is mutable by default (C2)
❌ One value, many names: user-defined functions receive parameters by reference by default (documented), and arrays alias across scopes (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The database is the runtime: A table, an index, and a cursor are part of the language
⚠️ A form’s object graph is the session’s memory: A large cursor is a sizing decision
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: ON ERROR catches statement errors; the runtime-level crash ends the session below the handler (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ ON ERROR is the failure path: The handler is a procedure, and no signature states the failure (Er1)
❌ An error can be ignored: The handler returns to the next line (Er3)



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ A program is single-threaded: A long scan blocks the session



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A program runs on Windows through the VFP runtime: The runtime is a 32-bit Windows binary (P1)
✅ The database is abstracted by the cursor: A query fills a cursor and a scan reads it



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The cursor is the unit of work: A query and a scan replace a general data layer
The macro operator is the escape hatch: It makes a dynamic name cheap and unsafe
The product is frozen: A program written in 2007 is the last version’s program
The database and the form are one runtime: Deployment is a directory of DBF files




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A cursor is a local in-memory table: A query fills it and a scan reads it
⚠️ A row-at-a-time scan is the classic cost: A set operation is written by hand



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and closed: The vendor stopped the product (Ec3)
❌ The product is proprietary: Microsoft owns the runtime and the IDE (Ec4)
✅ The data format is documented: A DBF table is readable by other tools
❌ A compiled program binds to a release: Microsoft lists .fxp as a compiled program and .fll as a Visual FoxPro library, ships updates as service packs per release, and states that a compiled provider’s requirements match the Visual FoxPro release it is built for [5], [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The product is discontinued: Support ended in 2015, and no successor accepts the source (V3)



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is data-centric desktop software: A form over DBF tables (D1)



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The command language is small: A SCAN and a REPLACE state the intent



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The commands are English words: SCAN, ENDSCAN, REPLACE (S1)
✅ SQL is interchangeable with native commands



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The debugger steps through a program: Breakpoints and the call stack are in the IDE



1.2.8 Security

title: VBScript (6.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses VBScript in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 72.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69.9/100 · Engineering readiness 48.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A variable has no declared type: Dim x declares a name, and the value it holds is a Variant whose subtype is decided at the assignment, so the operator resolves the operands when the statement runs and + adds or concatenates according to the values it receives (T1)
❌ There is no namespace: Every global variable and procedure lives in one flat global scope, so two included scripts share it (T6)
❌ There is no module boundary: A script file exports nothing and imports nothing explicitly, and ExecuteGlobal or a .wsf include writes into the same global scope (T11)
✅ The subtype is inspectable: VarType, IsNumeric, IsDate, IsArray, and IsObject let a script ask what a variant holds
✅ Null and Empty are distinct values with their own tests: IsNull and IsEmpty separate a true null from an uninitialised variant
✅ Class, added in version 5.0, groups state with behaviour: A class declares Private fields and Public property procedures, with Class_Initialize and Class_Terminate
❌ Inherits the engine rule: string length counts UTF-16 units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A global variable appears at its first assignment: Without Option Explicit, x = 1 at file scope creates a global, so state appears wherever a name is first used (C1)
✅ Option Explicit requires a declaration: With it, an undeclared name is an error instead of a new variable
✅ Sub and Function scope their own locals: A Dim inside a procedure belongs to that procedure
✅ A class validates and cleans up in its two lifecycle methods: Class_Initialize runs at creation and Class_Terminate at release
✅ A .wsf file combines several scripts: A Windows Script File includes more than one script file, and the procedures of one are callable from another
⚠️ ExecuteGlobal defines a global at run time: A generated statement can create a name that no declaration lists



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The script engine owns the memory: There is no allocate, free, or pointer operation in the language
✅ A COM object is released by reference count: The object is freed when its last reference goes out of scope, and Class_Terminate runs at that point
✅ No pointer type and no address exist: A value can never name a memory location
✅ A class instance is collected by the engine: The script states no lifetime for a class object
⚠️ A reference cycle between script and COM objects is not reclaimed: The engine’s counter cannot release a cycle, and the process must end to reclaim it
⚠️ Repeated string concatenation in a loop reallocates: A long string built with & is copied at each step, and the language has no string builder



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no structured error path: The language has no try and no catch, only On Error Resume Next and the Err object (Er1)
❌ On Error Resume Next discards a failure by default: The next statement runs regardless, and the failure is invisible unless Err.Number is tested
✅ The Err object makes a failure a value: Err.Number, Err.Description, Err.Source, and Err.Raise let a handler read and create a failure
✅ On Error GoTo 0 ends the suppressed mode: Error handling returns to the default at that statement
⚠️ A host error names its provider: An ADO, WMI, or file-system failure carries a provider-specific number and source, so a handler is bound to that provider
⚠️ An unhandled failure ends the script: There is no caller frame to unwind to, and the default action is to stop



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The language has no shared-memory concurrency: A script runs single-threaded in its host, so there is no race to guard
✅ A script can start another process: WScript.Shell.Run launches a program, and Exec returns a stream of its output
✅ The host delivers an event to the script on its own thread: A callback is serialised onto the host’s thread, so the script never observes a concurrent invocation of itself
⚠️ The host decides the threading model: Windows Script Host, Internet Explorer, and classic ASP each run a script differently, and the host’s apartment model governs a COM call
⚠️ A session-scoped object is shared across requests: In classic ASP, Session state is visible to more than one request, and nothing in the language partitions it
⚠️ A long-running script blocks its host thread: The language has no yield and no cancellation



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The engine is Windows-only: vbscript.dll is the only implementation, and it ships with Windows, so a script runs on no other platform (P1)
❌ Every capability arrives through COM: File access, WMI, ADO, and the shell are COM objects such as Scripting.FileSystemObject and ADODB.Connection, so a script depends on the registered object model
✅ A .vbs file needs no build step: The host runs the text as written
✅ The host is part of the operating system: cscript.exe and wscript.exe are installed with Windows
⚠️ The host decides which objects exist: Windows Script Host, Internet Explorer, and classic ASP present different object models to the same language
⚠️ A .wsf file states its own includes: A multi-file script needs the Job attributes and the <script src=...> elements that name its parts



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Hosted scripting is the purpose of the language: VBScript is designed to be embedded in a host, so the dependence on the host is a scope decision
The classic Visual Basic surface is a familiarity trade: The BASIC syntax is easy to read, and one value type keeps the engine simple, at the cost of the type system
A suppressed error is sometimes deliberate: On Error Resume Next around one statement is a chosen tactic
The language is meant for short programs: A page of automation is the design point, not a system
A fixed parameter list is a deliberate omission: The language cannot pass a variable number of arguments, so a variadic call is written as an array parameter
The deprecation is a lifecycle decision: Microsoft’s removal plan is a product decision rather than a language mechanism




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ The compiled form does not survive the process: The engine compiles the script at load rather than ahead of time, so a fresh host pays the parse again
⚠️ A variant costs at every operation: An operation reads the subtype tag and converts the operands before it acts
✅ The engine is an in-process library: The host loads it once, so a script starts with no separate runtime to launch
✅ The engine compiles the file before it runs: The host parses and compiles the script once at start, and a page host can keep the compiled script for later requests
⚠️ A COM call dominates a data-heavy script: The crossing into ADO, WMI, or a file-system object is where the time goes
⚠️ String handling is the common trap: Concatenation in a loop and a repeated RegExp replace on a large string cost far more than the control flow



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The language is proprietary and discontinued: It exists in one vendor’s product, and Microsoft announced the deprecation in October 2023 (Ec4)
❌ The ecosystem is legacy and frozen: The language has gained no feature since version 5.5 (2000), when the engine moved to sustaining engineering, so the tool field is historical (Ec3)
✅ The runtime tooling is part of Windows: cscript and wscript are installed with the operating system
✅ A large body of published scripts exists: Administrative scripts, examples, and books from the 2000s are widely available
✅ The migration targets are named and documented: Microsoft points to PowerShell and JavaScript and describes the path
⚠️ Many environments block the script host: A security policy or a mail filter commonly disables or rejects a .vbs file



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language is discontinued: Microsoft announced the deprecation in October 2023 with removal planned after 2027, so no further version is expected (V3)
✅ The remaining life is long and published: The phased plan keeps the language available as an on-demand feature for years, so an existing script keeps running
✅ The language does not change under a script: An existing script’s meaning is fixed, which makes a migration predictable
✅ A successor covers each use: PowerShell replaces the administration role and JavaScript replaces the browser and page role
⚠️ New code has no reason to choose it: The direction of the platform is removal, not extension



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is Windows administration and COM: The useful work is expressed through WMI, ADO, the file-system object, and the shell, and none of that exists off Windows (D1)
✅ Administrative automation fits it well: A short script drives WMI and the registry directly
✅ Classic ASP and HTML Applications were real hosting domains: A server page and an .hta file both used VBScript with the full object model
✅ Test automation still uses it: UFT One and similar tools keep a VBScript dialect for their test scripts
⚠️ PowerShell has replaced it for administration: The same task is now written in PowerShell
⚠️ An embedded operator interface is a narrow remaining use: A few industrial and point-of-sale systems still run a VBScript engine for local automation



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is small: If ... Then ... End If, Sub, Function, and For Each are the surface
✅ The curve is gentle for a Visual Basic programmer: The classic Visual Basic surface carries over almost unchanged
✅ The reference is complete: Microsoft’s VBScript Language Reference documents every statement and function
✅ The error model is easy to start with: On Error Resume Next and the Err object are a few lines
⚠️ The real subject is COM: The object model beneath the language is the large part of the work
⚠️ The error model is easy to misuse: It requires a discipline that the language does not enforce



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The keywords are words: If, Then, Else, End If, For Each, and Next
✅ A line is a statement: Statement boundaries are lines, and : separates two statements on one line
✅ Line continuation is explicit: _ continues a statement on the next line
✅ A block closes with its keyword pair: End If, End Sub, End Function, Loop, and Next each close their own construct
⚠️ The language is case-insensitive: myValue and MyValue name the same variable, so a rename is not caught by the case
⚠️ Dim may be omitted: Without Option Explicit, a name is declared by its first use, so a typo reads as a new variable



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework in the language or the host: A check is a script that compares values and reports the result (G1)
✅ A test is a .vbs file run by cscript: The same engine runs the test and the code under test
✅ A harness is only a few lines: WScript.Echo with a comparison gives a report, and a failing check can call Err.Raise
✅ cscript //X starts the script debugger: A step-through debugger is available where the Windows debugging tools are installed
⚠️ A test suite is the programmer’s own: There is no runner, no fixture loader, and no report format
⚠️ A type error appears only in the test run: Nothing checks a value’s use before the line executes



1.2.8 Security

❌ Untrusted input can become code: Execute, ExecuteGlobal, and Eval evaluate text, so a value built from input can run as a statement (Q3)
❌ Script malware is a known, historical class: The ILOVEYOU worm spread as a .vbs attachment, and the file extension is still commonly blocked
❌ The file-system object grants the user’s own rights: Scripting.FileSystemObject can read or overwrite any file the invoking user can
✅ A script runs without elevation by default: It holds the privileges of the invoking user and no more
⚠️ The usual mitigation is policy: A mail filter, an attachment block, or a group-policy restriction, rather than a language feature
⚠️ Correct quoting must be uniform: An injection that forms a valid statement is not distinguishable from a legitimate one by the engine
❌ Numbers are doubles: integers above 2^53 change value in silence (Q4)

What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

⚠️ Nothing is built: the script is the artifact the host loads.



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Scripts include and instantiate components with no provenance. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers the component ecosystem. (Y16)
⚠️ The COM registry is the shared library the script trusts.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)
❌ MsgBox and WScript.Echo carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A runtime error raises a dialog and stops; no post-mortem exists. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No analyzer ships; the editor is a text editor. (Y8)
❌ No debugger ships with the engine; the platform debugger is separate. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ The script runs where the Windows scripting host runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Microsoft decides the language’s direction and its maintenance status. (Y11)
❌ The documentation is the vendor’s; no public specification exists. (Y12)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.
