Verdict: VBScript holds the lowest pair of scores in this group, and the losses concentrate in its defaults and its dependence. A variable is a Variant with no declared type, an undeclared name becomes a global, an error is a mode the caller must enable, and every useful capability arrives through a COM object that exists only on Windows. What the language does provide is a tiny readable syntax, a host that is already installed, lifecycle methods on a class, and Option Explicit to require a declaration. Main strengths: a gentle learning curve, direct WMI and ADO automation, a .wsf file that packages a multi-file script, and a simple way to restrict a script through the Windows Script Host. Main weaknesses: no structured error path, no namespace and no module boundary, a proprietary and discontinued implementation, a domain locked to Windows and COM, weak tooling, and an injection surface that made it a malware vehicle.

title: The Scoreboard: All 125 Languages Ranked
text:
Scores from the model (a fixed inventory, scored by severity share), analysis date October 2026. Each version is the latest stable release at the analysis date, or another release of the same language whose page states why it is assessed — a later general-availability release, or an earlier long-lived line. Rank is the Ranking score: core × (0.85 + 0.15 × readiness / 100). Rows that tie on the ranking score share a rank; the table lists them by Core coupling, then by the newer release when both rows are releases of one language, then by name. Coupling is primary; readiness is a modifier worth at most 15% of the coupling score, so a full 0-to-100 readiness swing is worth 15 points at a core of 100 — about 2.7 High mechanisms on the Core scale — and proportionally less below that. Readiness can therefore settle a close call, and it can never overturn a large coupling gap. Higher is better: each score is 100 minus priced cost, not a general quality measure. Each column has its own scale and its own band; do not compare across columns. The star rating reflects the Core coupling score: 90+ = ★★★★★, 75–89 = ★★★★, 60–74 = ★★★, 45–59 = ★★, below 45 = ★. Ecosystem coupling is a lens and does not enter the ranking, because it is a dependency context rather than a quality. The table sorts by any column, so a reader who wants pure coupling sorts by that column.

title: Bash (5.3)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Bash in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 75.4/100 · Engineering readiness 53.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Everything is strings: No type system whatsoever
❌ No abstractions: Shell functions are commands with positional parameters, and there are no interfaces
⚠️ Associative arrays: Bash 4+ has hashes, but limited
❌ No encapsulation: All variables global unless explicitly local
❌ No modules: Sourcing scripts pollutes namespace
❌ Word splitting: Unquoted variables couple to IFS



1.1.2 Construction

❌ No objects: Not an object-oriented language
❌ No constructors: Everything is imperative scripting
⚠️ Functions: Can simulate construction with functions
❌ No validation: Can’t enforce invariants
❌ Global variables: All variables global unless local
❌ Environment variables: Implicit dependencies everywhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Automatic: Shell manages memory for variables
✅ Process-based: Each script is a process, cleaned up on exit
⚠️ File descriptors: Must manually close, can leak
✅ No manual management: Can’t segfault (unless calling C programs)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exit codes only: Return 0–255, no typed errors
❌ Ignores errors by default: Must use set -e to fail on errors, and a failure is otherwise silent
❌ No exceptions: Can’t catch/throw
⚠️ trap: Can handle signals, but limited



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Background jobs: & runs in background
❌ No coordination: No semaphores, mutexes in pure bash
⚠️ Pipes: Pipeline concurrency, but limited
❌ Race conditions: Easy to create, hard to avoid
⚠️ Process-based: Fork/exec model, heavyweight



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Path dependencies: Couples to external commands availability
❌ Platform coupling: Bash version, coreutils differences
✅ A POSIX subset is portable across systems: A script limited to POSIX sh runs under dash, ash, ksh, and zsh, and the standard is a published specification
✅ The script is the artifact: A Bash program is a text file that needs only an interpreter on the target, so nothing of the language is deployed with it
✅ The shell is a GNU project with no vendor owner: Bash is developed in the open by the GNU Project under the GPL
❌ The dialect is defined by one implementation: The extensions beyond POSIX ([[ ]], arrays, local, mapfile) are Bash’s own, so a script that uses them depends on Bash and its version (P2)
⚠️ The installed Bash version varies by platform: MacOS ships Bash 3.2 while Linux distributions ship Bash 5.x, so a script that uses newer features fails on the older interpreter



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Interactive use shapes the syntax: History expansion, aliases, and prompt escapes are features for a terminal session, and they are why the language reads oddly inside scripts
The pipeline is the composition model: Programs combine as processes joined by pipes, so composition happens between executables rather than inside one program — a design boundary
Arithmetic is integer-only: $(( )) computes on integers, so decimal work calls an external program — a scope decision rather than a dependency
Universal availability is the goal: The language keeps to what an interpreter can supply on any Unix system, which is why new features arrive slowly




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Very slow: Interprets every line, with no JIT and no compilation
❌ Process spawning: Fork/exec for every command
❌ String manipulation: Terribly inefficient
✅ Good for orchestration: Fast when calling other programs



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Ubiquitous: On every Unix system
⚠️ No package manager: Manual dependency management
✅ shellcheck: Excellent linter
❌ No IDE support: Basic syntax highlighting only
✅ Coreutils: Standard Unix tools available



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Stable: Bash 3/4/5 mostly compatible
⚠️ Slow evolution: Conservative changes
❌ Fragmentation: Sh, bash, zsh, fish differ
✅ POSIX: Standard helps portability



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for shell automation: Perfect use case
✅ Good for CI/CD: Build scripts, deployment
✅ System administration: Natural domain
❌ Terrible for applications: Not designed for this
❌ No cross-platform: Windows support poor



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Easy to start: Simple commands work
❌ Hard to master: Quoting, word splitting, and unquoted variables are footguns
✅ Good resources: Advanced Bash Scripting Guide



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Quirky: [ vs [[, quoting rules
❌ Verbose: if [ "$x" = "y" ]; then
✅ Pipe-oriented: Natural for Unix philosophy
❌ Special variables: $?, $!, $@, $$



1.2.7 Testing

✅ bats: Bash Automated Testing System exists
⚠️ set -x: Trace execution, but noisy
❌ No debugger: Just echo/printf
✅ shellcheck: Catches many errors



1.2.8 Security

❌ Code injection: Easy with eval, command substitution
❌ Path injection: $PATH manipulation dangerous
❌ No input validation: Everything is strings
❌ Shell injection: Major attack vector
❌ Arithmetic is 64-bit and wraps in two’s complement (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the shell reads: requirements live in the script text and the invocation, and the shell validates nothing (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A script runs on whatever the PATH resolves; nothing signs the commands it calls. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins vulnerabilities to the programs a script invokes. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists; set -x and redirection are the instruments. (Y5)
❌ echo and printf are the whole logging surface; no structured records exist. (Y6)
❌ A failure leaves an exit code and a terminal, with no post-mortem artifact. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the shell; set -x tracing is the built-in aid. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ A shell reaches other languages only by starting a process. (Y9)
❌ The script runs where bash runs; portability across shells is a discipline, not a target. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The GNU project maintains bash in the open; POSIX scopes the language family. (Y11)
✅ The Bash reference manual and the POSIX standard are public. (Y12)
✅ The bash source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [5], [6].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Bash is a scripting language that trades nearly all separation-of-concerns enforcement for universal availability. Everything is a string, all variables are global by default, and errors are ignored unless explicitly checked. Its main strength is that it runs everywhere and excels at gluing Unix tools together. title: Fish (4.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Fish in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73.8/100 · Engineering readiness 49.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with no declaration: set x 10 and set x abc are the same operation, and nothing states what a name holds (T1)
❌ No sum types: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is a list of words, and the reader decodes the convention from the calling code (T4)
❌ No generics: A function is specialised only by its positional arguments, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data (T5)
❌ One namespace for every name: Functions and variables share one flat space, so collisions are avoided by convention — the __fish_-prefixed helper names in the bundled completions are the visible result (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to an empty list: set -q tests whether a name is set, but nothing forces it to be, so a mistyped variable silently expands to nothing (T10)
✅ Lists are values, not strings to be re-split: set a 1 2 3 and $a expand to exactly three arguments, so element structure survives expansion without quoting



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global is still the default: An assignment without a scope flag reaches the innermost existing scope or the global one, so an accidental write into the caller is easy (C1)
❌ No immutability by default: There is no read-only binding, so any visible name can be reassigned (C2)
✅ set -l gives block scope: A variable declared local inside a function, a begin/end block, a for, a while, or an if disappears at the end of that block
✅ alias is sugar over function: An alias becomes a real function, so the invocation name and the body are separated instead of textually substituted
✅ argparse validates options at the boundary: A function declares its own option spec, so callers do not hand-roll a getopts loop and a bad option fails before the body runs
✅ Configuration lives outside scripts: ~/.config/fish/config.fish, the conf.d/*.fish snippets, and the universal-variable file separate shell setup from script logic



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation syntax: There is no pointer, no address, and no free; lists and strings are allocated by the interpreter
✅ Block scope bounds a value’s lifetime: A set -l list is released at the end of its block, so storage does not leak past the code that created it
✅ Export joins a list on the way out: A list assigned to an exported variable is joined with :, so PATH is edited as a list without building a string by hand
⚠️ Assignment copies the list: set b $a duplicates every element, and there is no way to reference a list without copying it
⚠️ Command substitution is materialised whole: (cmd) builds the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large output is held in memory
⚠️ Universal variables outlive the process: set -U writes to fish_variables, so a value persists after the shell exits until it is erased deliberately



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: A command reports success through $status and text on stderr; there is no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ Errors are not composable: and and or chain status codes, but a status carries no payload and cannot be returned from a function as data (Er4)
❌ A non-zero status is easy to ignore: A function reports the status of its last command, so a failure in the middle of a block is discarded unless or return follows it (Er3)
✅ $pipestatus reports every stage: Each stage of a pipeline keeps its own status, so a failure is not hidden by a successful last stage
⚠️ Syntax errors are reported with a source position: Fish names the file, line, and column, but only for text it has parsed, so a fault inside a function body is reported when the function is defined
⚠️ An unknown command is a hookable event: fish_command_not_found runs when a command is missing, so the message can be replaced, but the failure remains a status code



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no thread, lock, channel, or await; the only parallel construct is backgrounding with & (K5)
✅ Event handlers decouple producer from consumer: function --on-variable NAME, --on-event, --on-process-exit, and emit let a consumer subscribe without the producer knowing it exists
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
⚠️ Process events are the only synchronisation: A script coordinates jobs by watching exit events or by wait, and no value can be returned from a job
⚠️ Background jobs share the environment: A & job inherits every global and universal variable, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No coprocess: Fish cannot keep a two-way conversation with a child, so an interactive child must be driven through files or a while read loop



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Not a POSIX shell: Fish does not implement the POSIX shell language, so a #!/bin/sh script is a different language and sh -c calls a separate program (P2)
✅ One implementation defines the language: With no standard to satisfy, behaviour is fixed by the fish manual and its release notes
✅ Runs on every Unix-like target: Fish ships on Linux, the BSDs, and macOS, and is packaged by every major distribution
⚠️ Windows support is through an emulation layer: Fish relies on Unix APIs and their semantics, so Windows use goes through WSL, Cygwin, or MSYS2 rather than a native port
⚠️ One implementation is one point of failure: There is no second implementation to test the language’s contract against
⚠️ fish is the default login shell nowhere: A user installs it and sets it as their shell, so availability depends on the host’s configuration
❌ It is not a POSIX shell: A fish script runs only under fish, so portable system scripts, configure scripts, and #!/bin/sh entry points cannot be written in fish (P4)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Fish is deliberately not POSIX: Giving up sh compatibility buys the design freedom that removes word splitting and most quoting noise
Universal variables are a convenience with a lifecycle cost: Persisting a value outside the shell trades reproducibility for ergonomics
Aliases became functions because functions are better: The change breaks the textual-substitution habit from other shells, which is the point of the change
The web-based configuration UI is a front end: fish_config writes plain files under ~/.config/fish, so the browser is not a runtime dependency
Autosuggestions and highlighting are interactive features: They cost start-up work and terminal capability, and they are not part of the scripting language
The Rust port is an implementation change: The language contract is unchanged; the gain is in the codebase, not in what a script may rely on




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Every command is parsed and executed as text, and fish offers no ahead-of-time path (R1)
✅ The core is native code: Fish was written in C++ through the 3.x series and was ported to Rust for 4.0, so parsing, expansion, and completion run in compiled code rather than in script
✅ Command substitution does not re-split: (cmd) performs no word splitting or globbing, so a large result is not re-parsed argument by argument
✅ Start-up can be profiled and trimmed: fish --profile-startup measures configuration work and --no-config skips it
⚠️ Start-up runs the configuration snippets: An interactive shell sources config.fish and every file in conf.d, so a heavy prompt or completion setup costs time on each new shell
⚠️ for over a substitution materialises the output: A large (cmd) result is held in memory before the loop starts



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager in the language: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins are copied into ~/.config/fish by third-party managers such as Fisher or Oh My Fish (Ec1)
⚠️ The ecosystem is small but growing: Completions and prompt themes exist for popular tools, and there are far fewer fish libraries than sh libraries (Ec3)
✅ The bundled completion system is large: complete -c declarations ship with fish and cover hundreds of commands, so everyday completion needs no add-on
✅ fish_config gives a built-in UI: Prompts and themes are edited in a browser against files under ~/.config/fish
✅ Documentation is first-class: The manual, the tutorial, and help <builtin> are maintained with each release
⚠️ Third-party plugin managers own the plugin ecosystem: Fisher and Oh My Fish are unofficial, so the plugin supply chain is not part of the language



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: Fish adds features and documents the few incompatible changes in the release notes
✅ Release notes record every incompatibility: The manual lists removals and behaviour changes for each version, so an upgrade is inspectable
✅ The project ships on a regular cadence: Fish 4.0 was released in February 2025, and further 4.x releases followed it
⚠️ No standards body: The direction of the language follows its maintainers rather than a committee
⚠️ Non-POSIX means the language may keep diverging: With no standard to align to, fish is free to change and is not compelled to hold sh semantics



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Strong for interactive work: Syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, and completion make the terminal the primary domain
✅ Good for personal automation on a fixed host: Where the interpreter is guaranteed, a fish script is shorter and clearer than its sh equivalent
✅ Lists map to the filesystem naturally: $PATH and command output are lists of paths, and path and string split operate on them directly
⚠️ Weak for distribution: A fish script cannot be shipped to a host without fish, which rules fish out for bootstrap, packaging, and installer code
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so real data processing moves to other tools



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The tutorial and manual are written for newcomers: Fish ships a tutorial and an FAQ, and each builtin has its own help page
✅ Error messages name the file, line, and column: A beginner sees where the problem is rather than a bare failure
✅ The language is smaller and more regular than sh or zsh: One end closes every block, set is the only binding command, and there is no word splitting to learn
⚠️ Quoting habits from other shells misfire: "$var" and [ -f x ] do not apply, and $var is not split where an sh user expects it to be
⚠️ The builtin vocabulary is large: string, math, path, set, argparse, complete, and status each carry their own option set



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ No word splitting means fewer quotes: $var expands as written, so a path containing a space needs no quoting to survive
✅ One block terminator: end closes if, for, while, switch, and function
✅ One binding form: There is no =, no setenv, and no typeset to choose between
⚠️ and and or begin a line: A boolean continuation puts the operator at the start of the next command, which reads unusually
⚠️ Piping a block needs a wrapper: A multi-command producer must be written as begin ... end before it can be piped
⚠️ switch has no fallthrough: A case ends at the next case, so an intentional fallthrough must be written as a second case



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a function that calls the code and checks $status, with no assertion or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Debugging is breakpoint and fish_trace: Fish can pause with breakpoint and print a stack with status stack-trace, but it has no debugger with breakpoints, stepping, and inspection (G2)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad list index is found during the run (G3)
✅ fish --no-execute checks syntax without running: A script can be parsed before it is executed
✅ fish_indent --check fails on unformatted code: A shipped formatter gives a cheap consistency gate in a test path
✅ fish --private isolates a test from user state: Configuration, history, and universal variables are left untouched, so a test run is reproducible
❌ No monotonic reading published: fish reads date; the sh family’s documented elapsed counter is not in this shell (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Text can re-enter the interpreter: Input assembled from untrusted data and passed to eval, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code (Q3)
✅ No word splitting removes a whole class of injection: An unquoted $var does not split or glob, so a value with spaces or * cannot become several arguments or an unexpected path list
✅ string escape and string collect make quoting explicit: Output can be quoted for re-input instead of being concatenated by hand
✅ argv and argparse keep options out of the parser: A function receives its arguments as a list, so a value beginning with - is not silently taken as an option
✅ No memory-safety surface: Lists and strings are interpreter-managed, so a fish script has no buffer to overflow
⚠️ History and universal variables are unencrypted state: Command history and set -U values are written to disk in the user’s configuration, so a secret typed at the prompt is recorded by default
❌ Arithmetic is 64-bit and wraps in two’s complement (Q4)

❌ No contract the shell reads: requirements live in the script text and the invocation, and the shell validates nothing (Y18)

❌ No debugger ships with the shell; fish_trace and the docs are the aids. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Other languages are reachable only by starting a process. (Y9)
❌ The script runs where fish runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the implementation: POSIX defines the standard sh-family shells, not this one, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification

Verdict: Fish lowers the coupling that a scripting shell normally imposes on construction and on text handling: set -l gives block scope, $var never splits, lists are first-class, and functions replace textual aliases. Its core score still stops at 43, because the value model has no types, every name is global by default, and an error remains a status code rather than a value. The price is paid elsewhere: fish is not a POSIX shell, so a fish script runs only where fish is installed, and start-up configuration, an unofficial plugin supply chain, and the absence of a test framework hold the platform and ecosystem score to 49.

title: Perl (5.42)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Perl in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 36.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.3/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No type system: Dynamic, weakly typed
❌ TIMTOWTDI: “There’s More Than One Way To Do It” creates inconsistency
⚠️ Sigils: $scalar, @array, %hash provide some structure
❌ Context-sensitive: Same code behaves differently in scalar/list context
⚠️ Moose: Object system add-on provides types, not core
⚠️ A method call resolves on the run-time object: $obj->method looks the name up in the object’s class when the call runs, so a rename breaks a caller only at run time (T3)
❌ Regular expressions: Write-only code, couples understanding to expertise



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Bless: Primitive object system, bless {} is manual
❌ Core class syntax is experimental: use feature 'class' provides a core object system, but the implementation is still experimental, so a project cannot rely on it
⚠️ Moose/Moo: Modern OOP libraries improve this significantly
❌ Hash-based objects: No encapsulation enforcement
❌ Global variables: $_, @_, %ENV everywhere
❌ **Implicit $_**: Default variable creates hidden dependencies
❌ Package variables: Global state pervasive
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation states hash order is not the source’s, and Perl randomizes it per process to catch the agreement (C5)
❌ One value, many names: references are first-class, and the language’s containers reach one structure through names the declaration does not count (C6)
❌ require/use executes at load; a cyclic require yields a partially defined package (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting: Deterministic deallocation
⚠️ Cyclic references: Leak unless broken manually
✅ Automatic: No manual malloc/free
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: an interpreter crash (the documented memory-exhaustion and regex blow-up classes) ends the program outside eval’s recovery (Er6)
❌ Reference counts leak loops; the cycle collectors are opt-in, a priced mitigation (M7)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Die/eval: Exceptions not typed, eval catches everything
❌ Return undef: Many functions return undef on error, silent failures
⚠️ $!: Global error variable couples error state
❌ Signatures declare parameters only: A sub’s signature does not state the errors it may raise, so the failure channel is invisible at the call
❌ A fault ends the program: a thread die ends the process (documented in the threading manual); eval recovers frames, not units (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Threads: Available but discouraged, heavyweight
⚠️ Fork: Process-based concurrency common
❌ No modern concurrency: No async/await, no actors
❌ Shared state: Manual locking, error-prone
❌ A thread is an interpreter thread: Each one reserves an operating-system thread, so the program pays per task (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: Perl 5 is released by the Perl 5 Porters under the Artistic License and the GNU General Public License, and no vendor controls it
✅ The interpreter is portable: The same C source builds on Linux, macOS, the BSDs, Windows through Strawberry Perl, and OpenVMS
✅ CPAN is vendor-neutral: The archive is mirrored worldwide and serves any Perl distribution, not one vendor’s package service
✅ A base interpreter ships with most Unix systems: Many Linux distributions and the BSDs install perl as part of the base system, so a script needs no extra platform



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Regexes are woven into the grammar: Pattern matching is syntax rather than a library, which makes text handling concise and the language hard to read — a syntax decision, not a coupling mechanism
Sigils prefix every name: The leading $, @, or % encodes the noun in the identifier, a readability trade expressed in the name rather than in a type system
Scalars carry both a number and a string: The dual-valued scalar is why == and eq are separate operators, a convenience whose cost falls on every comparison
Backward compatibility is the default: Decades of behaviour remain in the language, and use strict and use warnings recover discipline one file at a time — a compatibility cost, not a forced dependency
The successor was released as another language: Raku was developed separately from Perl 5, so Perl 5 continues on its own line — a project decision, not a coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled, and the reference interpreter has no JIT
✅ Regex engine: Very fast for text processing
❌ Memory usage: Higher than C, lower than Ruby/Python



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ CPAN: Comprehensive Perl Archive Network, massive
⚠️ Aging: Fewer new modules than modern ecosystems
⚠️ IDE support: Limited compared to modern languages
✅ CPAN minus: Great dependency testing
⚠️ Tooling dated: Perldoc, prove, but aging
❌ An XS module binds to a Perl build: the C code compiles against one Perl’s headers and build flags [5] (Ec8)
✅ Stored data crosses on a published promise: a Storable header carries the file format version, and a reading Storable defers croaking until it meets a data type it does not recognize [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Perl 6 → Raku: Split into separate language
⚠️ Perl 5 stable: Very conservative, few changes
❌ Declining use: Community shrinking



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for text processing: Regex, sed/awk replacement
✅ Good for system admin: DevOps, automation
⚠️ Web declining: CGI era passed, PSGI exists
❌ Not for applications: Modern alternatives better
✅ Bioinformatics: BioPerl still used



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Steep: Sigils, context, special variables
❌ Write-only code: Hard to read others’ code
⚠️ Good docs: Perldoc comprehensive
❌ Many gotchas: $_, context, references



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Sigils everywhere: $@% visual noise
❌ Context sensitivity: Same code different results
⚠️ Powerful: Can express complex logic concisely
❌ Punctuation soup: Special variables like $!, $?, $@



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Test::More: Good testing framework
✅ Prove: Test runner works well
⚠️ Debugger: Perl -d works but basic
✅ Testing culture: CPAN requires tests



1.2.8 Security

✅ Taint mode: Tracks untrusted data
⚠️ Type confusion: Dynamic typing allows anything
⚠️ Eval risks: Code injection if used carelessly
✅ No memory bugs: GC prevents use-after-free
❌ An overflowing integer is promoted to the floating NV type in place, silent (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Installs resolve from the CPAN index at install time; no lockfile exists by default. (Y1)
❌ Dependency versions resolve per install unless a carton-style snapshot is adopted. (Y2)
❌ The official distribution ships no toolchain pin; perlbrew is third-party. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ CPAN distributions carry no signed provenance by default. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to CPAN distributions. (Y16)
✅ PAUSE registers author namespaces, so CPAN names carry them. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The interpreter runs with no build step. (Y7)
✅ The Perl debugger ships with the interpreter behind -d. (Y13)
⚠️ Editor analysis rides third-party language servers.



1.3.5 Interop

title: Sh (POSIX.1-2024)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses sh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 66.6/100 · Ecosystem coupling 77.0/100 · Engineering readiness 51.5/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ All values are strings, and numbers live in a second grammar: x=1 and x=abc are the same assignment, and $(( ... )) evaluates a signed-integer expression that is re-parsed at each use (T1)
❌ No arrays and no associative arrays: A list is a string split on IFS, and the specification provides no indexed or keyed aggregate (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional parameters, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
❌ One flat namespace: The specification gives a function no local scope, so a function’s working variables are the caller’s variables (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name and an empty name are indistinguishable: set -u turns a reference to an unset name into an error, but it is off by default and an empty value still passes (T10)
✅ Default and alternate expansions are part of the language: ${var:-default} and ${var:+alternate} carry the missing-value case in the expansion itself, so many ad-hoc checks disappear



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: An assignment writes the single namespace, and only readonly fixes a value (C1, C2)
❌ No constructor or validation at the point of assignment: Nothing checks a value when it is bound, so validation is written as a separate case statement or test (C4)
❌ Functions share the caller’s variables: The standard provides no local declaration — local is a ksh and Bash extension, and shells that offer it differ in detail — so a helper must save and restore every name it touches, or run in a subshell
✅ A subshell is a scope: ( ... ) runs in a child process, so a subroutine is isolated from the parent’s values by wrapping it
✅ Positional parameters are the argument list: A function or a sh -c string reads its inputs as $1, $2, and so on, so a routine consumes its arguments instead of reading a global
✅ ENV separates interactive setup from scripts: An interactive shell reads its personalisation file from $ENV, so a non-interactive script starts with none of it



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; the shell owns every string
✅ A subshell releases its memory at exit: ( ... ) ends and its environment is discarded, so temporary state does not survive it
✅ unset drops a name: The shell reclaims the storage, so no free order and no double free can arise
⚠️ Assignment copies the value: b=$a duplicates the string, and there is no way to reference a value without copying it
⚠️ A pipeline is a set of processes: The shell forks each stage, so the memory cost of a pipeline is the sum of its parts
⚠️ Command substitution is buffered whole: $(cmd) collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so the whole result is held in memory and then split



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: The entire apparatus is $? and trap, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ $? is lost by the next command: Any command resets it, so an interposed test discards the failure (Er3)
❌ Errors do not compose: A failure is an exit status, so it cannot carry a payload, be returned as data, or be combined with another (Er4)
⚠️ set -e is not a reliable policy: errexit does not fire in && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes the behaviour of the whole script
⚠️ There is no ERR trap in the standard: Reporting and cleanup must be attached to EXIT, to a named signal, or to an explicit check after each command
✅ trap ... EXIT runs on every exit path: Cleanup can be attached once and will run on a normal exit or on a handled signal



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: No lock, channel, semaphore, or await exists; the only parallel construct is & (K5)
✅ Pipelines are a first-class composition: The pipeline is a core operator of the language, so stages are connected without the script manipulating file descriptors
✅ wait and $! make a job addressable: cmd & records the process id in $!, so a script can wait for one job rather than for all of them
✅ A subshell isolates concurrent state: ( ... ) & gives a job its own copy of the environment, so the job cannot change the parent’s values
⚠️ Background jobs share files and the working directory: A & job inherits the environment, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No value comes back from a job: A status arrives through wait, and a result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a named pipe



1.1.6 Platform

❌ sh is an implementable name, not an implementation: POSIX defines the language but not which program provides it, so /bin/sh is dash, ash, bash in POSIX mode, or a vendor shell depending on the system, and only the standard subset is portable (P2)
✅ POSIX guarantees that a shell exists: Every conforming system provides sh, so a script invokes an interpreter without installing anything
✅ The standard is written for maximum reach: The language contains no optional syntax that a conforming shell may omit
⚠️ Implementations are not equally complete: An older sh may lack behaviour added in Issue 8, so a script that uses pipefail or $'...' is portable only to newer systems
⚠️ sh -c is the universal entry point: system(), make, containers, and cron all use it, which makes the shell the assumed execution layer even when no script is written
⚠️ Extensions are common and not portable: local, [[ ... ]], arrays, and function are available in many sh implementations but are outside the standard



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Minimalism is the point: The language is small because every construct must be implementable on every conforming system, so the absence of arrays is a scope decision
Portability costs expressiveness: Writing to the standard means doing without associative arrays, pattern-replacement expansions, and floating point
No interactive features is a deliberate omission: Line editing, history, and completion are terminal concerns and are kept out of the standard
/bin/sh is a policy choice on each system: A distribution links it to dash, bash, or another shell, and that choice is not the language’s
Integer arithmetic is the standard’s floor: A script that needs floating point calls an external tool, which is a design boundary rather than a defect
The specification is written for implementers: Its precision makes it slow to read, and that is the price of one text that many shells obey




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT (R1)
✅ A minimal implementation starts fast: dash and ash reach the first command in a fraction of the time a feature-rich shell needs, which matters for the many sh -c calls in a build or a boot
✅ Builtins replace processes for common work: printf, read, test, getopts, and parameter expansion avoid an external command
⚠️ Every external command forks: The builtin set is small, so a loop that calls sed, grep, or basename per item pays a process per iteration
⚠️ Command substitution is buffered and re-split: $(cmd) reads the whole output and then splits it on IFS, so a large result is walked twice
✅ Scripts pay no start-up configuration: The ENV file is read only by an interactive shell, so a non-interactive script pays nothing for user setup



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no dependency mechanism for shell code, so shared routines are sourced from a directory or vendored (Ec1)
✅ Every UNIX-like system has an implementation: Dash, ash and BusyBox ash, FreeBSD sh, ksh, and bash in POSIX mode all provide an sh mode, so a script always has a host
✅ The standard is published and maintained: The Open Group Base Specifications define the language in one stable document with a change history
✅ Analysers target sh by default: ShellCheck and similar tools treat sh as the base case, so a minimal script is the best-supported one
✅ checkbashisms detects non-portable constructs: A script can be checked against the POSIX surface before it is released
⚠️ Most published shell libraries assume Bash: They use arrays and [[ ... ]], so they cannot be used in a strictly conforming script



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: Issue 7 appeared in 2018 and Issue 8 in 2024, so a needed feature waits years for the committee (V4)
✅ The standard is backward compatible: Issue 8 adds features and removes only what was already marked obsolescent, so old scripts keep running
✅ Removals are signposted for years: test’s -a and -o primaries were marked obsolescent in Issue 7 before Issue 8 removed them
✅ The change history ships with the text: Every change from the previous issue is recorded in the specification rationale
⚠️ Adoption lags publication: A shipped sh may implement an older issue for years, so a script written to Issue 8 may not run on the host it is deployed to
⚠️ The committee decides on defect reports: A change enters the standard only through an accepted interpretation, so the process is deliberate rather than responsive



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for its intended domain: Boot scripts, installers, container entrypoints, and configure scripts need the one interpreter that is always present
✅ Stop-gap automation is a native use: A two-line sh -c avoids a build step and a binary, which is why build tools, cron, and orchestrators embed it
✅ Portable text filtering composes well: Pipelines over grep, sed, and awk are the idiom the language was designed around
✅ Configuration and environment setup read cleanly: Exporting variables, setting umask, and changing directories is a few lines
⚠️ Data structures push the script elsewhere: Without arrays, a keyed or indexed collection becomes a temporary file and a series of awk invocations
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so a program with real logic belongs in another language



1.2.5 Learning

✅ A small surface to learn: Assignments, if, case, and pipelines cover most scripts, and the standard is short compared with bash or zsh
✅ Skills transfer upward: Everything learned in sh applies to Bash, ksh, and zsh, which is why it is the usual starting point
✅ The specification is the reference: A precise description of every construct exists in one place
⚠️ Quoting and word splitting trap newcomers: $var unquoted splits and globs, so a space or an asterisk in a value changes the command
⚠️ [ is a command, not syntax: test parses its arguments, so an unquoted empty variable changes the argument count and can turn a test into an error or a truth
⚠️ The specification is written for implementers: It is precise about behaviour and thin on explanation, so learners need other material



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The language is small and predictable: Assignments, if, while, for, case, and pipelines cover the whole grammar
✅ Here-documents handle multi-line input: << and <<- embed a block of text in a script without escaping
⚠️ Expansion has five forms to remember: %, %%, #, ##, and ${#var} are compact but each has its own rule
⚠️ Quoting rules are context-dependent: Single quotes, double quotes, and backslash escapes each treat $, backtick, and newline differently
⚠️ [ and test need the operands spaced out: The bracket form requires a space after [ and before ], which is easy to forget
⚠️ No [[ ... ]] in the standard: The construct was removed from the shell language description in an early POSIX proposal, so richer tests are written with case or with expr



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a missing file is found during the run (G3)
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: sh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ set -x shows the expansion: The traced command reveals how a value was split and quoted before it ran
✅ Exit status is a reliable oracle: $? after a command gives one unambiguous value to assert on
✅ A test can be isolated with a subshell: ( ... ) gives each case a fresh copy of the environment, so one case cannot leak into the next



1.2.8 Security

❌ Command construction from text is the classic injection path: A value expanded into a command line or passed to eval becomes code, so unquoted expansion of untrusted input is unsafe (Q3)
❌ Weak typing removes a check the shell cannot make: A value that should be a number, a path, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object (Q2)
✅ test can be made argument-safe: [ "X$response" = "Xexpected" ] or ${var:+...} expansion removes the ambiguity that an unquoted variable introduces
✅ set -f disables globbing: noglob stops an expanded * from becoming a path list
✅ umask is part of the language: File-creation permissions are set inside the script rather than left to the ambient environment
✅ No memory-safety surface: Strings are interpreter-managed, so a script has no buffer to overflow
❌ Arithmetic is 64-bit and wraps in two’s complement (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets
What ships from a producer to a consumer, and whether the interface across a release boundary is promised. Ec8 is present when one compiled target crosses with no promise.

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the shell reads: requirements live in the script text and the invocation, and POSIX names no manifest (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ A POSIX script runs on whatever the environment resolves; nothing signs it. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed covers the commands a script calls. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists; set -x is the instrument. (Y5)
❌ printf and echo carry no structure. (Y6)
❌ A failure leaves an exit status. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with a POSIX shell. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

❌ Other languages are reachable only by starting a process. (Y9)
❌ The script runs where a conforming shell runs. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ ISO/IEC 9945 (POSIX) is maintained by the open Austin Group. (Y11)
✅ The POSIX standard and the shell command language are public. (Y12)
✅ Conforming implementations ship public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [5], [6].

Verdict: sh is the smallest language in the shell family, and its coupling profile is the family floor: every value is a string, one namespace holds every name, a function has no private scope, and an error is an exit status rather than a value. What it returns for that price is reach — one text that every conforming system implements, so a script runs wherever POSIX is present, and its standard is slow to change but never breaks what it already promised. The ecosystem score reflects that trade: the tooling and the specification are complete and stable, while the glacial standardisation cycle and the missing test and error apparatus remain real costs.

title: C++ (C++23)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C++ in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 57.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72.7/100 · Engineering readiness 43.3/100

Note: The score reflects C++23 with modern idioms (smart pointers ≥ raw pointers, std::expected ≥ exceptions, modules ≥ headers, concepts ≥ unconstrained templates). Teams stuck on older standards or pre-modern coding styles will experience significantly worse coupling properties.


1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Templates enable generic programming: Decouple algorithms from types
✅ RAII separates resource management: Constructor acquires, destructor releases
✅ Concepts (C++20) constrain templates: Clean error messages, explicit constraints decouple interface from implementation
✅ Modules (C++20/23) decouple compilation: import replaces #include and removes header coupling, though headers remain for code not yet migrated
✅ Deducing this (C++23): Eliminates const/non-const overload duplication
⚠️ Multiple inheritance still available: Diamond problem possible (though final specifier helps)
⚠️ Template metaprogramming still complex: Despite concepts, advanced templates couple to expertise
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope (though modules reduce header macro issues)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors separate: Copy, move, default constructors are distinct
✅ Move semantics decouple: Transfer ownership without copying
✅ Designated initializers (C++20): Named initialization decouples from parameter order
❌ Constructors can throw: Exception during construction couples cleanup
⚠️ Two-phase initialization still possible: Though discouraged by modern idioms
⚠️ Global state is available: static variables and singletons are permitted, though a local automatic is the default home for a value
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the specification fixes std::map in key order and leaves std::unordered_map bucket-local, so a program that reaches for the hash container keeps the ordering discipline itself (C5)
❌ One value, many names: pointers and references alias freely, and a parameter, a member, and a captured pointer reach one object (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: user-defined conversions run from an implicit constructor, a conversion operator, and overload resolution (C7)
❌ The static initialization order fiasco: a namespace-scope object reading a namespace-scope object from another unit has implementation-defined results [5] (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ RAII decouples resource management: Destructors run deterministically, no GC needed
✅ Smart pointers eliminate manual delete: unique_ptr, shared_ptr are idiomatic (manual new/delete is a code smell in modern C++)
✅ std::span/std::mdspan (C++20/23): Non-owning one- and multi-dimensional views decouple algorithms from container types and memory layout
✅ Explicit lifetime management (C++23): std::start_lifetime_as for safe low-level patterns
⚠️ shared_ptr has atomic ref counting cost: And circular references need weak_ptr
⚠️ Raw pointer escape hatches exist: A raw pointer and a reference can alias the same object with no owner stated, though idiomatic C++23 uses spans and smart pointers (M4)
✅ No GC, deterministic: Full control over allocation timing
❌ Undefined behavior still exists: Buffer overruns, null derefs possible when using raw pointers/functions
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: default-initialization leaves scalars and many class members indeterminate, and reading one before an initializer runs is undefined behaviour (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: reinterpret_cast and unchecked downcasts reinterpret storage with no check, and the object model declares the mismatch undefined (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer’s trap and a stack overflow in the template machinery end the program, outside every catch clause (Er6)
❌ shared_ptr cycles leak; the standard requires the cycle to be broken by hand (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ std::expected and std::optional monadic operations (C++23): and_then, transform, or_else make error and absence handling composable and type-safe
❌ Exceptions still exist and remain unchecked: std::expected is idiomatic and preferred, but exceptions are still in the language and used in the standard library
✅ std::stacktrace (C++23): Provides unwinding visibility, addressing historical debugging pain
✅ std::variant: Type-safe discriminated union for error discrimination
❌ A fault ends the program: an uncaught exception in a thread calls std::terminate (documented); the thread is a scheduling unit, not an isolation unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Shared mutable state default: Mutexes required, though lock-free patterns are achievable
✅ std::jthread (C++20): Auto-joining threads with cancellation via std::stop_token
✅ std::latch, std::barrier, std::semaphore (C++20): Higher-level synchronization primitives
✅ std::generator (C++23): Coroutine-based generator decouples producer from consumer
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No compile-time prevention (unlike Rust)
⚠️ Memory model still complex: Atomic operations require deep understanding
❌ std::thread reserves an operating-system thread: A task holds it until it ends, and a blocked task holds one too (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owner: The language is standardised by ISO/IEC and implemented independently by GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so no single vendor controls the standard
✅ No required platform runtime: A program compiles to native code and needs no C++-specific virtual machine or vendor service
✅ Every mainstream target is supported: Compilers and standard libraries exist for Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded and bare-metal targets
✅ One source base for several implementations: Code that stays in the portable subset compiles under GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so the project is not bound to one compiler



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

RAII vs. Exceptions: Exception during construction couples cleanup to unwinding, may leak
Zero-Cost Abstraction vs. Reading Time: templates and inline code remove runtime cost and add ceremony at every declaration
C Compatibility vs. Modern Features: Legacy C patterns can couple to modern C++ code when used
Standard Versions: C++11/14/17/20/23 couple codebases to version choices; modern C++ is largely additive since C++11
Safety vs. Performance: a bounds check is a written call, so a team decides per loop whether to pay for it




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Zero-overhead abstraction: Pay only for what you use
✅ No GC: Deterministic, predictable
✅ Manual control: Full optimization control
✅ Compile-time computation: Constexpr (expanded in C++23 — now covers std::bitset, std::unique_ptr, std::optional, std::variant, std::string, cmath functions)
⚠️ Binary bloat: Templates can explode size (mitigated by explicit instantiations, LTO)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

⚠️ No standard package manager: CMake + Conan/vcpkg are de facto standards, but fragmentation persists
⚠️ Compilation speed: Templates + concepts + modules improve but still slower than Go/Rust
✅ Excellent IDE support: CLion, Visual Studio, VSCode with clangd — all support C++23
✅ Vast library ecosystem: Decades of libraries, Boost, Qt, etc.
⚠️ Build system convergence improving: CMake dominates; vcpkg/Conan converging
❌ No cross-release binary promise: libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another, and mixing C++ ABIs is not recommended [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Additive since C++11: Code from C++11+ largely compiles under C++23 (removed features are rare and deprecated first)
⚠️ Legacy C++98 burden: Old codebases still exist, but not a language-level problem for new code
✅ 3-year standard cadence: Predictable evolution (C++23 → C++26 → C++29)
⚠️ Feature complexity grows: Each standard adds more to learn
❌ Build variants multiply: #ifdef, feature-test macros, and __has_* probes select which declarations reach the compiler, so a translation unit is a flag outcome, not only a file (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Performance critical code
✅ Great for games: Industry standard
✅ Strong for embedded: (with care, constexpr + templates help)
✅ Good for high-performance: Finance, scientific computing
⚠️ Not for web: Rare use case



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Massive language surface area accumulated over 40+ years
❌ C++23 idioms are learnable but the full language is not: Smart pointers, expected, ranges, modules add to surface
❌ Undefined behavior: Still exists and requires understanding to avoid
✅ Excellent resources: Effective Modern C++, C++ Core Guidelines, cppreference



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Modules reduce header boilerplate: import std; replaces many #includes
⚠️ Template syntax: <> remains noisy, though concepts improve readability
✅ Designated initializers: Named member initialization improves readability
✅ auto, structured bindings (C++17): Reduce verbosity



1.2.7 Testing

✅ GTest, Catch2, doctest: Mature frameworks
✅ Static analyzers: Clang-Tidy, CppCheck, and MSVC Code Analysis find some undefined behaviour before runtime, though no analyzer is sound or complete
✅ Profilers: Excellent tooling (perf, VTune, Instruments)
✅ std::stacktrace (C++23): Runtime stacktrace capture improves debugging
⚠️ Template errors: Concepts (C++20) dramatically improve error messages, but edge cases remain



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Memory safety depends on idiom: std::span, std::mdspan, smart pointers are memory-safe; raw pointers and pointer arithmetic are not
✅ Smart pointers remove most memory bugs when the idiom is kept: unique_ptr prevents a use-after-free and a double-free, and a raw pointer reopens both
✅ AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer: Compiler instrumentation catches memory bugs at test time
❌ Unsafe escape hatches remain: reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic, manual new/delete still compile (Q1)
❌ The inherited C rule: signed overflow undefined, unsigned modulo; the optimizer exploits both (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds embed include paths, ABI choices, and template instantiation state. (Y1)
❌ Libraries resolve from the system and package-manager state at build time. (Y2)
❌ The distribution records no compiler version per project. (Y14)
✅ The build description (Make or CMake) is the contract the builder reads. (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ System packages and vendored sources carry no signed provenance by default. (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins CVEs to the libraries a program links. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ The standard library has no structured logging. (Y6)
⚠️ Tracing rides the platform (ETW, perf, OpenTelemetry SDKs), not the language.
❌ A fault ends in a signal or terminate; core dumps are a platform setting. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ Template instantiation and header recompilation make builds slow. (Y7)
❌ No debugger ships with a compiler; gdb and lldb are separate projects. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ The C FFI is native to the language; any C library is callable. (Y9)
✅ C++ compilers target every common architecture and platform. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the compiler’s conformance tables: the standard lists implementation-defined behavior, and the committee publishes no conformance suite an independent implementation runs (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [7], [8]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [9].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [10], [11].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: C++23 provides substantially better coupling than its reputation suggests. Modules decouple compilation units. std::expected provides composable error handling. title: C++ (C++98)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C++98 in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 48.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69.5/100 · Engineering readiness 43.3/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A conversion narrows in silence: the conversion table is a shared resource no reader is forced to hold, so a checked expression cannot be told from a narrowed one (T2)
❌ No sum type: a union plus a tag is the encoding, and every consumer re-derives which member is live (T4)
❌ An operator takes its meaning from the operand types: << shifts and inserts, and a reader resolves the type to know which (T8)
❌ A pointer may be null and the type does not say so: each consumer writes the guard, and an omission stays invisible (T10)
❌ A header is the only surface, and it is entirely public: there is no construct that declares what a module exposes and keeps (T11)
❌ A signature states no effects: a call may write a file, mutate a global, and throw, and the signature names only the return type (T12)
❌ extern "C" is a hand-written promise: argument order, layout, and lifetime cross a boundary that neither compiler validates (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A binding is mutable until the code says otherwise: const is opt-in, and every holder reconstructs who may write (C2)
✅ Placement construction separates storage from construction: an object is built in storage the caller already holds (C3)
✅ Only the ordered containers ship: std::map and std::set iterate in key order, so the hash container’s unpinned order does not exist in this release (C5)
❌ One value, many names: a pointer, a reference, a member, and a parameter reach one object, and the declaration names none of the sharers (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: a converting constructor and a conversion operator run from the contexts the standard names, not from a call the source shows (C7)
❌ The static initialization order fiasco: namespace-scope init order across translation units is implementation-defined [5] (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Destructors run at scope exit: the release is deterministic and no collector is involved
❌ No handle records its owner: two pointers can share one buffer with no way to say which frees it (M4)
❌ Storage arrives uninitialized: default-initialization leaves scalars indeterminate, and reading one before a write is undefined behaviour (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: a union and a reinterpret_cast reinterpret storage with no check (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a wild pointer’s trap ends the program outside every catch clause (Er6)
❌ Reference-count cycles leak in the C++98 library idioms; breaking by hand is the documented rule (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A structured path exists: throw and catch carry a failure from where it is raised to where it is handled (Er1)
❌ A failure may arrive undeclared: throw needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it (Er2)
❌ A failure is not an ordinary value: nothing folds a fallible operation into an expression, so each level rebuilds the pair (Er4)
❌ A fault ends the program: an uncaught exception in a thread calls std::terminate, and the thread is not an isolation unit (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No thread of control in the language: a second core needs a platform thread library, which is outside the language’s own structure (K1)
⚠️ Shared state is the default once a thread library is in use: nothing marks a value thread-local or immutable (K2)
⚠️ Nothing detects a race: the locking discipline is an agreement across files that no tool checks (K3)
⚠️ No scope joins a task: a task started without a scope can outlive the code that started it (K4)
❌ No first-class lock, channel, or await: coordination lives in the platform’s facilities, and no declaration states the protocol (K5)
❌ A concurrent task is an operating-system thread: each task holds a thread for its whole life, so ten tasks read well and ten thousand do not (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owner: the language is standardised by ISO/IEC, and independent compilers implement it
✅ No required runtime: a program compiles to native code and needs no vendor service
✅ Every mainstream target is supported: compilers exist for the operating systems and embedded targets of the era



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Zero-cost abstraction vs. reading time: templates and inline code remove runtime cost and add ceremony at every declaration
Placement construction vs. readability: building an object in storage the caller chose is a precise control, and the reader reconstructs where that storage came from




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled to native code: no interpreter dispatch sits in the hot loop
✅ No collector: release timing is the program’s, not a runtime component’s



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: a dependency is resolved by a build script or by the platform’s toolchain, so two checkouts can disagree about the graph (Ec1)
❌ Fragmented tooling: the language is split across platform toolchains with different extensions and warning sets (Ec2)
❌ No cross-release binary promise: libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ A needed feature waits for the committee: the 1998 standard was revised only by a defect report in 2003, and the next feature revision arrived in 2011 (V4)
❌ Build variants multiply: the preprocessor’s #ifdef tree selects which declarations reach the compiler, so a translation unit is a flag outcome (V7)
✅ Additive revisions: the committee removed almost nothing, so code written to this standard still compiles under later ones



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Close to the machine: the language serves systems, games, and embedded work
⚠️ Not a web or scripting language: the work it fits least is the work it is least used for



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Steep: templates, multiple inheritance, manual memory, and undefined behaviour build on nothing a mainstream background supplies (L1)
❌ Several paradigms at once: procedural, object-oriented, and generic code all remain available for the same task (L2)
✅ An authoritative standard text and a large literature: the reference is public and complete



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Nested instantiations tax the reader: a template argument can itself be an instantiation, and the reader unfolds the chain to know the type it produces
✅ Declarations state types once: the reader resolves a type at its declaration rather than at each use



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ Testing arrives from outside the toolchain: assert is in the library and no runner is, so a framework and a runner are adopted per project
✅ A mature debugger exists for every platform: the toolchain is the platform’s, and it steps through the source
❌ The only published clock is the wall: time() reads the operator’s calendar, and clock() reports processor time, so no reading the library publishes is monotonic (G4)



1.2.8 Security

❌ Memory-unsafe: a buffer overflow, a use-after-free, and a double free all compile, and any pointer suffices (Q1)
❌ The inherited C rule: signed overflow undefined, unsigned modulo (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default: timestamps and absolute paths reach the artifact, so a third party cannot confirm it matches the source (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ No registry, so no signed provenance: a dependency is a source tree or a library, and its origin is taken on trust (Y3)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ A failure leaves no post-mortem by default: without a debugger and an enabled core dump, an unhandled failure prints nothing (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ A change pays a slow build: templates and a long link step sit on the critical path of every edit (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A general foreign-function interface exists: the platform’s C ABI is the boundary, and the language calls it directly (Y9)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ An open standard with no conformance suite: the standard lists implementation-defined behaviour, and the committee publishes no suite an independent implementation runs (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [7], [8]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [9].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [10], [11].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: C++98 is the standard that made the language portable, and it carries every cost of its era. There is no thread in the language, no smart pointer, no sum type, and no module: concurrency, ownership, and encapsulation are conventions the platform supplies. Templates give generics at compile time, destructors give deterministic release, and the preprocessor gives portability at the cost of a flag-dependent program. Main strength: zero-cost abstraction and direct control of memory and layout. Main weakness: the language supplies no construct for concurrency, for ownership, or for a module boundary, so each is a local invention.
