title: Goose (2026.3)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Goose in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 87.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 83.2/100 · Engineering readiness 45.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static and narrow-checked: Arithmetic happens at the operands’ own width, a literal adapts only to a type whose range holds it (let x: u8 = 256; is a compile error), and same-width signed and unsigned operands do not unify without a cast
✅ Sums and absence in the type: enum is a tagged union in two sizes and match must cover it, case functions dispatch on the tag through a jump table the compiler checks for coverage, and T? is a nullable reference that must be narrowed by if, while, guard, assert, or a null test before it writes through
✅ Generics with nothing erased: An untyped parameter is a generic one and every call is monomorphized, so the type argument travels with the code; function values are compile-time entities that cannot escape, so there is no closure object, no function pointer, and no reflection
✅ No inheritance anywhere: The only dynamic-shape mechanism is the ADT tag, so a type is never placed under a base to be used through it, and x.f(a) is exactly f(x, a)
⚠️ Generics are checked at instantiation: A generic body is typechecked only where every type is concrete, with no trait bounds, so an unconstrained parameter reports its failure at a call site, with the compile-time call chain attached
❌ Namespaces scope names, and stop there: A namespace scopes a name and import … from … fetches a package, and that is the whole boundary mechanism: the reference states “there is no privacy, no re-export and no nesting”, so every declaration of an imported package is reachable from every consumer, and namespace privacy is on the specification’s open-items list (T11)
❌ A signature says what returns, not what happens: A call can print, grow a global, abort, or return … from an outer function, and every function in between keeps its plain signature — “no error parameter, no ? on each call, nothing to propagate” (T12)
❌ The C agreement is hand-written: extern fn rejects a signature with no C shape at the declaration, and the C side’s own prototype, padding, ownership, and lifetime stay outside any check — pad 3 must be written where C pads, library-owned memory arrives as an opaque u64, and callbacks and variadic functions cannot be bound at all (T14)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Built in place, guaranteed: The copy-free construction guarantee builds a value at its final destination through any depth of calls, so items.push(parse(line)) writes the parsed record straight into the array and a function returning a growable array by value writes into the caller’s variable: construction is never tied to a reservation site
✅ No uninitialized value: Every local must be initialized before it is read, on every path; fixed arrays must be fully initialized; and a var global given only a type starts as its type’s declared default, so var log: u8[>..]; at file scope is an empty array, not raw storage
✅ No global by default: let binds a name that cannot be reassigned and const makes contents read-only, so a mutable global must be written as var; a thread_fn is compiled as its own program with its own copy of the globals it touches, so a worker’s write to a global is not a write to main’s
❌ Contents are writable by default: A let stops the name being reassigned and says nothing about the value behind it — let xs = [1, 2, 3]; xs[0] = 9; is fine — and read-only contents require the type to say const, which is inferred per instantiation for parameters and views (C2)
⚠️ Constness is checked at the call: A parameter written u8[:] takes a writable or a read-only argument and its body is checked with what it was given, so the write that fails is reported at the call site with the call chain, not at the definition



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No heap at all: Dynamic values live inline on a compile-time count of data stacks, each a reserved region with a bump pointer; growth is a pointer bump with no capacity check, and freeing a million-element structure at scope exit is one store to the stack top
✅ Release tied to scope, as the model’s only rule: Scope exit is the free — the construct M3 prices by its absence is not an addition here but the whole reclamation mechanism — and a worker’s return releases everything it owned
✅ Ownership, inferred: Every reference and slice has a static root, the variable that owns its target, and the checker rejects a reference that would outlive its root, a store into a shorter-lived location, a view of a temporary, and a shrink that would strand a reference — with no lifetime syntax, no aliasing rules, and no unsafe
✅ References survive growth: Nothing moves, so a reference into a grow-only array stays valid for as long as the array does, which Vec<T> and std::vector<T> cannot promise, and an array of strings is one contiguous block with no pointer in it
⚠️ Lifetimes have to nest: Where a value lives and how long its scope lasts become decisions the source records, because scratch ends at the scope that owns it and a recursive call cannot keep a growable local across the call
⚠️ A reusable pool frees nothing: free records a slot for reuse, every element stays a live value of its type, and a stale slot reads a different value of the correct type, which the reference names “the whole extent of the unsafety”



1.1.4 Error

✅ A failure has a typed, checked path: return E from f returns E as the result of the innermost active call of f, unwinding the frames in between, and the whole-program checker verifies that every call of a function containing it lies inside a call of f, so nothing is uncaught at run time; the exception module packages the same machinery as try and throw
✅ Absence and found-or-not are in the type: T? costs nothing and must be narrowed before use, and a two-outcome call returns a trailing bool as an ordinary value
❌ Nothing forces the decision to be recorded: qput(v); as a statement ignores the answer the reference says a full queue returns, a trailing ok from from_bytes can be dropped with the empty array it came with, and a thread_wait that does not ask for a contained worker’s abort message loses it (Er3)
❌ No result type to compose: The reference states there is no exception mechanism and no Result type, so a success-and-failure pair is destructured by statement and cannot be mapped, chained, or threaded through an expression as one value (Er4)
⚠️ The abort path is a bug trap, not a channel: assert, abort, a bounds check that survives analysis, division by zero, capacity overflow, and data-stack exhaustion end the program, appear in no signature, and are not catchable; a contained worker sends its message to whoever waits for it



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Threads share nothing: A thread_fn and everything it calls are compiled as a separate program with its own data stacks and its own copies of the globals, so the language has no locks, no atomics, and no memory orderings, and there is no race for a detector to find
✅ Coordination is in the language: Typed queues, one per value type, carry flat values by memcpy — qput, qget, qpoll, qlimit — with qlimit bounding how much a queue may hold and a full queue refusing work at once
✅ No function colouring: There is no second function kind; qget blocks, so a plain function calls a plain function and a chain never has to change kind
❌ No task scope: thread_spawn returns an id and thread_wait joins it by hand, so nothing guarantees that a block ends with the work it started finished, and workers still running when main returns are killed (K4)
❌ A worker is an operating-system thread: Each worker carries its own data stacks, and --stacks reports the cap the count puts on hardware_threads(), so the number of tasks a program may run at once is set by its data-stack budget rather than by a construct (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Plain C out: The compiler emits one C file for the whole program, which the machine’s own C compiler builds, so the artifact runs wherever a C compiler and the Goose runtime object reach: Windows x64, Linux x64, and macOS on Apple silicon and Intel, with the in-process TinyCC backend running a program with no build step at all. There is no target beyond native C, and the WebAssembly design is a proposal, not implemented
✅ Plain C in: extern fn binds a Goose signature to a C symbol, extern "lib" { … } binds functions from a shared library by name at program start with no C to compile, and export fn makes a Goose function callable from C, so Goose sits inside a C host as easily as a C library sits inside Goose
✅ No vendor: Language, compiler, specification, standard library, samples, and benchmarks are one Apache-2.0 repository with public issues, discussions, and CI, and the graphics, audio, physics, and UI packages are four packages in two repositories — graphics, audio, and UI share one — fetched at pinned tags
✅ Systems-shaped, general-purpose: The constructs are built around data layout and lifetime discipline. The parts a poor domain fit (P4) charges for are present: nominal structs and enums, generics, namespaced modules, slices, a typed failure path, file access and the process environment in os (read_file, write_file_atomic, list_dir, args, env), and JSON, CSV, and regex parsers, so the samples run from a JSON parser to a spinning cube to a to-do list in windows of widgets. Subprocesses and networking are not in the v1 library and arrive through extern fn, the same boundary that reaches any C library. The subtractions the Learning section lists are deliberate. Three have stand-ins: a block for a closure, an untyped parameter for a function pointer, and the ADT tag with case functions for dynamic dispatch. An array of growable values and separate compilation have none, and the trade-offs below carry them. The artifact is C source that MSVC, clang, and gcc all build, so no single vendor’s platform owns the deployment (P1), the emitted C and the emitted runtime are what a program falls back on if the compiler stops (P2), and the artifact has no platform of its own that could stop developing (P3)



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The speed is bought with one storage model: the data stacks are the only dynamic storage the language offers, and their count is a compile-time constant, so the layout gains arrive with the obligation to decide where a value lives and how long its scope lasts, and with a limit on how many growable values may be live at once
Growable data never moves, at the price of recursion: no growable local can be kept across a recursive call, so scratch ends before the call and what must outlive it is passed in as a pool, and that is what buys references that stay valid and a free that is one store
An array of variable-size elements iterates and does not index: Inline nesting is bought at the price of random access, and the workaround is a second array of references kept beside it as an index
No escaping closures, no function pointers, no dynamic dispatch beyond ADT tags, whole-program compilation only: the zero-overhead guarantee is paid for by removing the runtime’s flexibility
An enum’s layout is chosen per container, and neither mode can change in place: fixed mode is indexable and overwritable at the largest variant’s size, variable mode costs each value only its own variant’s size and cannot be rewritten




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Ahead of time, with no collector and no warm-up: The program is compiled to C and linked by the platform’s compiler, and the in-process backend compiles and runs a program inside the compiler, so no tiering and no pause sits between the source and the measured time
✅ The cost is in the source: Function values are compile-time entities, so xs.filter() { it > 0 } compiles to the loop it looks like and builds its result straight into its destination, and a variable-mode enum gives each value its own variant’s size rather than the largest one’s
✅ Bounds checks are reported, and can be contracted away: Every index and index-type conversion is checked and the compiler removes what it can prove, --bce-lines lists what survives per line, and checkfree fn rejects a kernel if any check remains
⚠️ The margins are the project’s own measurements: The suite reports 1.24x and 1.26x the speed of hand-optimized C++ and 1.13x and 1.19x the best safe Rust row under MSVC and clang, on 1.32x and 1.25x less peak memory, as geometric means over sixteen benchmarks on one machine, whole-process, with the losing rows published beside them, and with speed and memory each selected from a different Goose implementation, so the pair is not the profile of one program [5]



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ A two-month ecosystem: The repository’s first commit is dated 28 August 2026, the standard library is sixteen modules written in Goose, the sample set is thirty-one programs, and the blessed package set is four packages in the two repositories the project chooses, so a team is likelier to write a library than to find one, and the hiring market does not exist yet (Ec3)
✅ Dependencies are declared and fetched: import name from "owner/repo@v1" names a git repository at a tag or a commit, and the compiler fetches it and builds it once into the user’s cache; the root-file rule and what a ref pins are in Reproducibility
✅ One toolchain, not several: The compiler, the language server, the package fetch, the benchmark suite, and the test runners ship together, and goose toolchain says which C compiler a build will use
⚠️ No registry, no third-party supply, no ecosystem around the tooling: Packages arrive from git repositories, the community is a Discord channel and a GitHub discussion board, and editor support is a VS Code extension plus configuration notes for Neovim, Helix, and Emacs



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Nothing is settled: The project states “Goose is new”, keeps its open items in the specification’s Appendix B, and lists five deliberate omissions — moves for resizable values, more than one resizable per struct, labeled break, namespace privacy, and more OS and library access — so a program follows the release rather than the other way round (V1)
⚠️ The runtime object is version-locked: the runtime is compiled once per C compiler and a program built by another version of the compiler fails to link against it, so a toolchain upgrade is a coordinated rebuild — a cost of the whole-program model rather than a change in what the language means
⚠️ Four releases in one week: v2026.0 to v2026.3, dated 14 to 21 October 2026, the releases are calendar-numbered, and there is no long-support line and no 1.0 designation to aim at
✅ No default drift is recorded for this release: The analysis found no change from v2026.0 to v2026.3 that moves the behaviour of code which never named the value it relies on (V5)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Systems work first, games and tools with it: The design targets layout, speed, and bounded memory, and the graphics, audio, physics, and UI modules, the samples’ spinning cube and raining boxes, and the author’s own game-engine lineage make it a game and tools language as well
⚠️ Adoption is unproven: No production deployment is named, so a team adopting Goose adopts a language whose use in anger is undocumented, and the benchmarks are microbenchmarks the project wrote



1.2.5 Learning

❌ A new model, not a dialect: A C or Rust practitioner must learn that every dynamic value lives on a compiler-assigned data stack, that the array kind (T[>..], T[>..<], T[..k], T[varint]) decides what growth does to references, that a reference’s root is its owner, and that return … from unwinds frames by name; the language’s own cost section opens with “You think about where data lives” (L1)
✅ Documentation unusually complete for a new language: a tutorial, a topic-by-topic reference with a compiling example for each feature, a specification with the exact rules, the sixteen standard-library modules, thirty-one samples, implementation and testing notes, and a benchmark report that publishes its losses
✅ The model is traceable to known designs: The project’s own survey ranks the nearest memory models — ML Kit region inference, GNU obstacks, ParaSail, Cyclone’s LIFO arenas, OxCaml’s stack allocation — and states that no prior language or paper combines the ingredients [6]
⚠️ The limits are the language’s, not a style guide’s: No escaping closure, no function pointer, no dynamic dispatch beyond ADT tags, no array of growable values, no separate compilation. A program that needs one of those does not get it in Goose



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ C and Rust familiar: Braces, a conventional keyword set, and Rust’s operator precedence, with postfix type syntax (u8[>..], Node&<u32>?, Shape..) that reads outward from the base type
✅ Terse: An un-annotated declaration takes its initializer’s type, x.f(a) is exactly f(x, a), a block stands in for a closure in a higher-order call, and .= binds a reference where = copies
⚠️ The notation carries the memory model: T[>..] against T[>..<] against T[..k], .= against =, and T&<u32 in pool> each state where a value lives and what happens to its references, so a reader who does not know the model cannot read the type



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Assertion, typecheck-only, and a checking build: assert aborts naming its source line and narrows an optional, goose check typechecks without generating code, --debug turns on the overflow, range, and tag checks, and --bce-lines reports the bounds checks that survived
✅ The project’s own suite is broad: CI runs a fixture suite on Windows, macOS, and Linux with a sanitizer job, and the fixtures include a typecheck-error section that checks 1,668 expected typecheck diagnostics
✅ Answers while typing: goose lsp gives diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition, completion, rename, and symbols, shipped in the compiler and wired into a VS Code extension
⚠️ No test harness beyond the assertion: the language ships assert and the toolchain a typecheck, which is the whole of the provision, so G1 is not charged, and there is nothing more: no test annotation, no runner for a program, no coverage tool for a program, and the project’s own suite is a Python script outside the language
❌ No monotonic reading published: the language reaches time through its Go host (G4)



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety with zero annotations: References carry no pointer arithmetic, no casts, and no way to dangle; every index and index-type conversion is bounds-checked; the lifetime rules reject a reference that outlives its owner; and there is no unsafe to enter
✅ A hostile file is a false: from_bytes verifies the framing, every tag, every length, canonical varints, and every link landing on an element start before the bytes become a value, so a corrupt image yields false and an empty array rather than a wild reference
✅ No text-to-code facility: There is no eval in the language, embed_file reads bytes at compile time, and the C boundary takes typed values, not source
⚠️ A reused pool slot is a type-safe information path: A slot handed back to a reusable pool and still named reads whatever its next owner wrote there, which is a logic bug rather than memory corruption, and exactly the shape an information leak takes in a language that cannot corrupt memory
⚠️ The safety is a young implementation’s: The compiler is about thirty thousand lines of C++, public only since 28 August 2026 and tagged only since 14 October, and its safety properties are the specification’s, enforced by a test suite the project wrote, not by an external proof or audit
❌ Inherits the Go rule: wraparound by specification (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ Dependencies are declared in one place and held to a ref: only the root file declares a package, a library’s own import line is a requirement the root must satisfy, and a git source needs a ref, so a program’s dependency graph is flat and one version of each package exists in a program; a tag can move, so the pin is only as good as the ref it names (Y2)
⚠️ The toolchain is chosen per machine, not per project: ~/.goose/config names a C compiler for the user, and the repository carries no per-project toolchain file, so the dependency graph is fixed by the ref the root file names, and nothing in the project names the Goose compiler’s own version, which the four-releases-in-one-week cadence in Evolution is still moving (Y14)
❌ Two builds do not produce the same bytes: the program’s C is compiled by whatever the machine provides, the runtime object is built once per C compiler into a per-user cache, and packages are fetched at build time, so the artifact is tied to the machine that made it (Y1)
❌ No contract the tool reads: the reference implementation builds what it is pointed at, and no manifest ships (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ There is no flat package name space to squat: a package is named by its repository (owner/repo@ref), so no registry holds a first-come name a dependency can be redirected through (Y4)
❌ A fetched package carries no statement of who built it: git gives source and a ref, and the build happens locally, so nothing attests the artifact’s origin, and a bare hash of a repository’s tag is not provenance (Y3)
❌ No advisory feed joins a vulnerability to a version: OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database cover npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems, Packagist, Cargo, Go, Hex, Pub, and Swift, and none of them covers Goose packages, because the language has no registry — the package documentation says plainly, “There is no registry to register with.” — so each team tracks the graph it declares in its root file (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ A failure leaves no trace: the standard library states it plainly — “There is no stack-trace facility” — so an abort names its own source line and nothing above it, and a contained worker sends its message only to the first waiter that asks (Y15)
❌ Diagnostics are free text: print and str write bytes, and the standard library defines no structured log record, so a question about a running system is answered by parsing text (Y6)
⚠️ No instrumentation contract: with no OpenTelemetry implementation and no standard format, a Goose service built on a C networking library through extern fn agrees with its neighbours on a format the project invents (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The loop is short: goose file.goose compiles and runs a program inside the compiler with no build step, goose check typechecks alone, the whole program is compiled in one invocation, so no per-file build can fall out of step, and goose lsp answers as the author types (Y7)
⚠️ No debugger in the distribution: the toolchain ships checks, a language server, and --debug builds with debug information for gdb and lldb, and no source-level debugger of its own, so the interactive stepping step is external (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A C interface exists in process: the language binds C functions by symbol, binds whole shared libraries by name at start-up, and exports Goose functions to a C host, so a C library is reached without a process boundary and without a binding generator (the mechanism is absent; Platform has the detail) (Y9)
⚠️ No target beyond native C: a browser, sandbox, or WebAssembly deployment is not available, because the data-stack model needs reserved address space and the WebAssembly design is a proposal, not implemented (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No vendor, and an open definition: The language, compiler, specification, and standard library are one Apache-2.0 repository, the specification is the file the implementation is written against, and issues, discussions, and pull requests are public, so nothing about the program’s future is negotiated with a commercial owner (Y11)
✅ The specification is public and complete enough to implement from: It states the size classes, the construction and lifetime rules, the shrink rules, and the representation, and the design notes state the reasoning, so a third party is not reduced to reverse-engineering one implementation’s behaviour (Y12)
⚠️ The exposure is a bus factor of one: The authors section names one language designer and one implementer, and no foundation, steering body, committee, or second maintainer is recorded, so the openness of the artifacts is what continuity rests on today
❌ Semantics rest on the reference implementation: the published documentation defines the language as the reference implementation behaves, and no conformance suite exists (Y17)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ No independent measurement: the language energy and time benchmarks the model cites do not include Goose. The project’s own suite (sixteen benchmarks, one machine, whole-process wall clock, losses published, speed and memory chosen from different implementations) reports 1.24–1.26x the speed of hand-optimized C++ and 1.13–1.19x the best safe Rust row, on 1.32x and 1.25x less peak memory [5].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Minimal training data: the family is two months old at the analysis date, so a coding model’s exposure is close to nothing and it writes the language from the reference and the samples. The README documents the project’s own build route — the compiler was produced almost entirely by a coding model from the author’s design, written in C++ — which is evidence about how the toolchain got made, not about a model writing Goose [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems: a team would have to qualify the toolchain itself, and the compiler behind it has been public only since 28 August 2026, with tagged releases only since 14 October.

Verdict: Goose takes the entire memory dimension of the systems comparison away at once: there is no heap, no allocator, no collector, and no manual free, so the Memory dimension carries no charge at all, and memory-unsafety (Q1) is absent with it, while M3’s release tied to scope is not something the language added but its only reclamation rule. Ownership is inferred — the root of every reference is the variable that owns its target — and a reference that would outlive its owner is a compile error with no lifetime syntax and no unsafe. Construction is never tied to a reservation site, because the in-place guarantee builds a value at its final destination. Main strengths: memory safety carries no annotations, the artifact is as portable as C on the platforms the runtime object is built for, and threads share no memory, so there is no locking discipline to keep and no race to detect. Main weaknesses: the module boundary has no privacy, so an imported package exposes every declaration it holds; failures travel as pairs that nothing forces a caller to inspect, and there is no result type to compose; a worker is an operating-system thread, and how many may run at once is set by the program’s data-stack budget; and the ecosystem is two months old, with no registry, no provenance, no structured logging, and no long-support line.
This page assesses Goose (v2026.3, released 21 October 2026), the family’s only assessed snapshot: the repository’s first public commit is dated 28 August 2026, and the release is the fourth calendar tag of October 2026. title: Rust (1.96 / 2024 edition)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Rust in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 89.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 68.4/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Traits decouple without inheritance: Interface + implementation separate
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Monomorphization prevents abstraction coupling to runtime cost
✅ No null: Option<T> makes absence explicit
✅ Ownership prevents aliasing: Can’t have multiple mutable references, eliminates coupling
✅ Associated types in traits: Decouple trait from concrete types
⚠️ Orphan rules couple trait implementations: Can’t impl external trait on external type



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors are just functions: new() is convention, not special
✅ Builder pattern zero-cost: Type-state pattern at compile time
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction can’t couple to globals
✅ Drop trait separates cleanup: Destruction logic separate from construction
❌ Collection order is unpinned: the documentation states HashMap’s order varies with a per-process random seed; the ordered BTreeMap is the opt-in (C5)
✅ The borrows are named: &mut marks the exclusive path, & the shared one, and the compiler proves the alias set at every call — the agreement lives in the type (C6)
✅ Every conversion is a named trait call: From/Into appear at the site, Drop is an explicit impl, and dispatch is a named method path (C7)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Ownership system prevents memory coupling: Compiler prevents use-after-free and double-free at compile time
✅ No GC, no pauses: Deterministic deallocation via RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, via the Drop trait)
✅ Lifetime tracking decouples: References can’t outlive referents
✅ Zero-cost abstractions for memory: Box, Rc, Arc explicit about allocation strategy
✅ Allocator parameter support: Can decouple allocation strategy from data structures
✅ No implicit copies: Move semantics by default prevent accidental copying
⚠️ Reference cycles with Rc: Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles require Weak to break (M7)
⚠️ Lifetimes can couple: Complex lifetime constraints create dependencies between regions
⚠️ Unsafe blocks bypass memory-safety guarantees: Can violate all guarantees, but explicit
✅ Uninitialized reads are a compile error: the borrow checker proves initialization before use, so a read of storage nobody wrote does not compile (M5)
✅ The class is declared: capacity overflow panics (documented) and catch_unwind recovers the panic class inside the thread (Er6)
❌ Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles leak (the standard-library documentation names it); Weak is the discipline (M7)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Result<T, E> makes errors explicit: Can’t ignore errors without .unwrap()
✅ ? operator composes: Error handling doesn’t obscure logic
✅ No exceptions: All errors in type system
✅ Panics are rare: Explicit unwrap/expect, or Result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Ownership prevents data races: Compiler enforces Send/Sync
✅ Async/await with explicit futures: Concurrency in types
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples concurrent tasks
✅ No shared mutable state without explicit synchronization: Arc/Mutex make coupling visible



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor lock-in: Compiles to native code for every major platform
✅ Broad target support: Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, and bare-metal no_std
✅ Static linking by default: A binary does not couple to a platform’s runtime or shared libraries



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Safety vs. Flexibility: Borrow checker rejects valid programs that don’t fit ownership model
Lifetime Complexity: Complex lifetime bounds couple function signatures to caller context
Async Colored Functions: async fn creates two function worlds (sync/async), couples call sites
Trait Coherence vs. Modularity: Orphan rules prevent implementing external traits on external types
Compile Times vs. Zero-Cost: Monomorphization couples build time to generic instantiation count
Learning Curve vs. Productivity: Steep learning curve couples team productivity to expertise




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Zero-cost abstractions: No runtime overhead
✅ No GC: Deterministic performance, no pauses
✅ Predictable: WYSIWYG performance model
✅ Compile-time optimization: LLVM backend
⚠️ Binary size: Can be large without optimization



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Cargo is excellent: Best-in-class package manager
✅ Great IDE support: Rust-analyzer, IntelliJ, VSCode
✅ Strong ecosystem: crates.io growing rapidly
⚠️ Smaller than JVM/npm: Fewer libraries than established ecosystems
✅ Excellent docs: Rustdoc, The Book
✅ Crates ship source, and Rust-to-Rust binaries do not cross a producer boundary; exported symbols cross to C consumers on the platform ABI [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Editions system: Breaking changes isolated to editions
✅ cargo fix: Automated migration
✅ Strong stability: Post-1.0 stability guarantee
⚠️ Async runtime: Tokio is the de facto standard; async support has stabilized at the language level (2024 edition)
❌ An edition can change what existing code means (V1): Edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of impl Trait, required unsafe extern, and reserved gen, so a crate that adopts it must be revisited
❌ Build variants multiply: cfg attributes and cfg!(…) blocks select which items compile, and –cfg flags set the space (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Memory safety without GC
✅ Great for embedded: No runtime, predictable
✅ Strong for CLI tools: Single binary, fast startup
✅ Good for WebAssembly: First-class WASM support
⚠️ Backend less common: Growing but smaller than Java/Go



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Ownership, lifetimes, borrowing
❌ Compiler fights you: Borrow checker takes time to internalize
✅ Excellent docs: The Book, Rustlings, error messages
❌ Lifetime complexity: Advanced patterns very difficult



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Expression-oriented: Everything returns a value
⚠️ Lifetime annotations: <'a, 'b> syntax noisy
✅ Pattern matching: Powerful, expressive
⚠️ Macro syntax: ! and #[] can be confusing



1.2.7 Testing

✅ cargo test: Built-in testing
✅ Integrated benchmarking: Cargo bench
⚠️ Debugging async code: Can be challenging
✅ gdb/lldb support: Standard debuggers work



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: Ownership prevents use-after-free, double-free
✅ Thread safe: Send/Sync prevent data races
✅ No null: Option prevents null pointer derefs
⚠️ Unsafe blocks: Can bypass safety (but explicit)
❌ The release build wraps in two’s complement (documented); the debug panic is a mitigation, priced, not an exemption (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ Cargo.toml is the contract cargo reads and validates, with the lockfile it writes. (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ crates.io packages carry no signed provenance beyond TLS. (Y3)
❌ The crates.io name space is flat. (Y4)
⚠️ The RustSec Advisory Database is a community project, not a registry feed.



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard ships with the language; the tracing crate is the ecosystem answer. (Y5)
❌ println! and the log facade carry no in-language structure. (Y6)
❌ A panic prints a backtrace only when RUST_BACKTRACE is set. (Y15)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ Monomorphization and crate graphs make release builds slow. (Y7)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ extern blocks are the in-process C interface. (Y9)
✅ rustc targets every common triple, cross-compiling from one host. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Rust Foundation and the teams govern through a public RFC process. (Y11)
✅ The Rust Reference is public. (Y12)
✅ rustc and the standard library are public source. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

1 Assessment
This page assesses Zig in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 74.0/100 · Ecosystem coupling 74.2/100 · Engineering readiness 56.7/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ No hidden control flow: Everything explicit, no operator overloading coupling
✅ Comptime metaprogramming: Type-level computation decouples patterns from instances
✅ Tagged unions: Discriminated unions like Rust enums
⚠️ No interfaces yet: Manual duck typing
⚠️ Comptime can be complex: Metaprogramming couples to compile-time semantics



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Explicit allocation: Separate allocator parameter, decouples memory strategy
✅ No constructors: Just functions, like Go
✅ Zero is sensible: Default values are predictable
❌ Collection order is unpinned: AutoHashMap iterates in hash-dependent order, documented; ArrayHashMap is opt-in (C5)
❌ One value, many names: pointers alias, and slices share a backing array across assignments — the type names an address, not an owner (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Allocator-as-parameter decouples perfectly: Every allocation takes explicit allocator
✅ Manual control: malloc/free style, predictable
✅ No hidden allocations: Compiler never allocates without explicit allocator
❌ No safety: Use-after-free, double-free possible (but less common than C)
✅ Defer for cleanup: defer free(ptr) couples cleanup to scope, predictable
✅ No GC pauses: Deterministic performance
⚠️ Error unions complicate lifetimes: Returning errors can extend memory lifetimes
✅ Comptime allocation separate: Compile-time vs runtime allocation explicit
✅ Uninitialized is an explicit value: storage is zero-initialized, and undefined is the opt-in that removes the guarantee, named at every use site (M5)
❌ Bytes can be read as a type they never were: @ptrCast and @bitCast reinterpret storage in ordinary code, with no unsafe context to mark the crossing (M6)
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: a safety panic aborts the process (documented); the error-value mechanism recovers fallible operations, not bounds, integer overflow, or unwrap traps (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Error unions: !Type makes errors explicit
✅ try/catch syntax: Error handling composes
✅ No hidden exceptions: All errors visible
✅ Panic is explicit: unreachable must be marked
❌ A fault ends the process: a safety panic takes the process down (documented); the error-value mechanism recovers fallible operations, not safety faults (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Still evolving: Async/await planned but not stable
⚠️ Manual synchronization: Like C, explicit
✅ No hidden coupling: Everything visible
❌ std.Thread reserves an operating-system thread: A task holds it until it ends, and the language offers no lighter task (K6)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owner: Zig is developed by the Zig Software Foundation, a non-profit, so no company controls the language or the set of supported targets
✅ Compiles to native code: The LLVM backend emits native executables and libraries, so a program needs no Zig-specific runtime on the target
✅ Cross-compilation is built in: One compiler targets many architectures and operating systems, and bundled libc implementations remove the need for a separate target toolchain
✅ Bare-metal and WebAssembly are first-class: -target selects freestanding and wasm32 targets alongside Linux, macOS, and Windows



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Zig is pre-1.0 by design: The project holds back a stability guarantee until the language settles, so code follows the release rather than the other way round
C headers are the interface to the world: Zig imports C headers and exposes the C ABI, so libraries reach Zig through the platform’s own interface instead of a Zig-specific one
Zig ships a C compiler and a build tool: zig cc and zig build replace parts of the system toolchain, a scope decision that makes Zig a toolchain as well as a language
One formatter fixes the layout: zig fmt is part of the distribution, so style is settled by tooling rather than by a style guide
Error sets can be widened to anyerror: A function may return any error to keep a signature short, a design option whose cost is the loss of the exhaustive set




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ C-like performance: Zero-cost abstractions
✅ No GC: Manual memory management
✅ Comptime: Compile-time execution, no runtime cost
✅ LLVM backend: Excellent optimization
✅ Predictable: Explicit everything



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Small ecosystem: Growing but limited, so a project may couple to the few libraries that exist
✅ zig build: Integrated build system
✅ Cross-compilation: Best-in-class
❌ Pre-1.0: Unstable, breaking changes
⚠️ IDE support: Improving but limited (zls)
✅ export gives the platform C ABI to the functions you name, so a Zig library ships source and comptime instantiations are compiled per build [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Pre-1.0 instability: Frequent breaking changes couple code to a language version
❌ API churn: Standard library changes often
⚠️ Active development: Rapid iteration
❌ No stability guarantee: Code breaks between versions
❌ Build variants multiply: build options feed inline-if on comptime values, so Debug and ReleaseFast compile different programs from one source — the release the consumer runs compiles a program the debug suite never saw (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Memory control, performance
✅ Great for embedded: Small footprint
✅ Strong for C interop: Replace C build systems
✅ Good for CLI tools: Fast, single binary
⚠️ Limited adoption: Few production use cases yet



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Simpler than Rust: No borrow checker
✅ Explicit: Easy to understand what’s happening
⚠️ Comptime complexity: Advanced metaprogramming
⚠️ Documentation: Improving but incomplete



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean syntax: Readable, minimal noise
✅ Error unions: ! syntax clear
✅ Comptime: Powerful metaprogramming
⚠️ Allocator passing: Verbose but explicit



1.2.7 Testing

✅ zig test: Built-in testing
✅ Excellent error messages: Clear, helpful
⚠️ Debugging tools: gdb/lldb work but improving
⚠️ Stack traces: Good but not as polished as mature languages



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Undefined behavior still exists: Signed overflow, unaligned access, incorrect @ptrCast, and unreachable reached are UB (Zig reduces but does not eliminate it; debug mode checks overflow and bounds)
⚠️ Manual memory management: Can have use-after-free (Q1)
✅ Bounds checking: Debug mode has checks
✅ No null: Optional types explicit
❌ The optimized build wraps in two’s complement; the debug panic is a mitigation, priced, not an exemption (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Build caches and system linking state feed the artifact. (Y1)
❌ The distribution records no version pin beyond build.zig.zon itself. (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ The package summit carries no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The package registry is a flat name space. (Y4)
❌ No advisory feed covers Zig packages. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the compiler. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ cImport? and the built-in C compiler make C interop the language’s own surface. (Y9)
✅ Cross-compilation is a first-class target matrix in the compiler. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The Zig Software Foundation governs in the open. (Y11)
✅ The language reference is public. (Y12)
✅ The compiler source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [6], [7]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Zig improves C’s coupling profile by making everything explicit and adding error unions. Allocator-as-parameter decouples memory strategy brilliantly. Comptime separates compile-time from runtime. Main strength: no hidden control flow prevents subtle coupling. Main weakness: concurrency story incomplete, pre-1.0 instability.

title: Rocq (9.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Rocq in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 95.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 87.9/100 · Engineering readiness 52.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Dependent types decouple a specification from its implementation: A type may mention a value, so a sorted list or a length-indexed vector is a type and a term of that type is the proof that the specification holds
✅ The Curry–Howard correspondence equates propositions with types: A proposition is a type and a proof is a program, so logic and computation are written in one language
✅ Inductive types define the data and the proofs over it together: An Inductive declaration fixes the constructors, and recursion over them is checked for coverage
✅ The universe hierarchy stratifies types: Prop holds propositions, Set holds program data, and Type holds types, so a type cannot contain itself
✅ Type classes and records express an interface: A Class or a Record states a structure and instance resolution selects the implementation, so reuse does not require inheritance
⚠️ Definitional equality is the checker’s equality: Two terms that are equal only up to a lemma are not interchangeable without a rewrite, so an implementation must be shaped to compute the way the checker reduces



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The logic core is pure: A Gallina term has no side effect, so building a value cannot change shared state
✅ The tactic language is separate from the term it builds: A proof script constructs a Gallina term, and the kernel checks that term, so the proof strategy and the proof object are distinct artifacts
✅ Definitions are checked terms: Definition and Fixpoint each name a term that the kernel type-checks before it is used
✅ Modules and functors confine names: A Module Type states a signature and a Module implements it, so a name is reachable only through its path
✅ Extraction separates verified construction from the runtime: Extraction emits OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme, so verification is decoupled from the implementation language
⚠️ Totality is required: Every Fixpoint must be shown to terminate, so a construction that is correct but not obviously decreasing needs a measure or a well-founded relation



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The logic core names no memory: A Gallina term has no address, no allocation, and no free operation, so a proof cannot couple to a memory layout
✅ Collection belongs to the runtime: The checker is an OCaml program with its own collector, and the extracted program uses its target language’s collector
✅ Reduction strategy is a tactic choice: cbn, cbv, lazy, vm_compute, and native_compute select how a term is reduced, so checking cost is stated where it is needed
⚠️ A large reduction consumes memory without a visible allocation: A vm_compute or native_compute over a large term can exhaust memory while the source names no allocation
⚠️ native_compute compiles a module through OCaml: It evaluates the term through code the OCaml compiler produced at proof time, trading the kernel’s own reduction for speed



1.1.4 Error

✅ A wrong proof is a type error: A term that does not inhabit the goal is rejected when it is checked, before any extracted code runs
✅ Tactic failure is a structured signal: Ltac combinators such as try, repeat, first, and progress branch on success and failure, so a tactic script has a recovery path
✅ Fail asserts that a command is rejected: A development can test that a wrong proof fails, which keeps a tactic honest
✅ Qed runs the kernel check and Defined records the term: The sealing decision is explicit at the end of a proof
⚠️ Admitted and admit leave a gap the checker accepts: A development can be declared complete with an unproved lemma, so the guarantee holds only if the development contains none
⚠️ Axiom, Parameter, and Hypothesis add an assumption without a proof: The soundness of a result is relative to the axiom set it used



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The logic core is sequential: A Gallina term is a pure value, so there is no shared mutable state in the language to race
✅ A development is checked file by file in parallel: coq_makefile -j and rocq makefile -j compile independent .v files in separate processes
✅ Asynchronous proofs run in a worker process: -async-proofs on delegates a proof to another process, so a document and the proof that fills it are decoupled
⚠️ The tactic monad threads one proof state: A tactic acts on the current goal, so the tactics in a script are ordered even though the resulting term is pure
⚠️ Parallel checking is a tool option, not a language guarantee: An interactive session with -async-proofs off is sequential, and the option is the user’s choice



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Rocq is not a general-purpose programming language: A term is written to be checked, and Gallina has no I/O, no foreign-function call, and no runtime of its own (P1)
❌ A deployed program exists only in the extraction target: Extraction emits OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme, so one development reaches three ecosystems but the verified artifact runs only as a program in another language (P1)
✅ The checker is an ordinary OCaml program: It builds and runs on the platforms OCaml supports, including Linux, macOS, and Windows
⚠️ The OCaml toolchain is required to build the checker: A plugin or a native_compute build depends on the OCaml environment, not only on Rocq itself



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dependent types trade automation for certainty: The specification lives in the type, and every refinement obligation is discharged by a tactic or by hand
The ecosystem is small by scope: Rocq targets verification and mathematics, so a general-purpose library set is out of scope rather than missing
The academic audience is the intended one: The domain mark records a scope decision, not a defect of the language
Tactic scripts are a workflow choice: Ltac, Ltac2, and ssreflect are ways to construct a term, and a proof can also be written directly as a term
Prop erasure is a deliberate design: A proof in Prop is erased from the extracted program, so its cost is a checking cost rather than a runtime cost
Totality is required for a consistent logic: The termination obligation is the price of using one language for proofs and for programs




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The measured workload is proof checking: The kernel checks a term once, so the checking algorithm, not a program’s runtime, sets the cost
✅ Independent files are checked in parallel: -j and -async-proofs spread a build across the available cores
✅ A heavy reduction can run as compiled code: native_compute evaluates a term at the speed of compiled OCaml
✅ Extracted code runs at the target language’s speed: The deployed program’s performance is the target compiler’s concern
⚠️ Checking time grows with the proof: A large vm_compute, a deep induction, or a long auto search can take minutes, and the cost is paid on every rebuild



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and centred on academia: Outside the standard library, mathcomp, and the Rocq Platform, the set of maintained packages is thin (Ec3)
✅ opam installs Rocq, its libraries, and its plugins: The OCaml package manager is the distribution channel
✅ The Rocq Platform pins a compatible set: A Platform release fixes versions of libraries and plugins that are known to work together
✅ The landmark libraries are mature: mathcomp (Mathematical Components), stdpp, and CompCert are long-lived and actively maintained
⚠️ A plugin extends the checker from inside: An OCaml plugin reaches the engine directly, which is powerful and also couples the plugin to a Rocq version



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The rename from Coq to Rocq preserved compatibility: Rocq 9.0 continued to accept the Coq.* module paths and the coq* command names, so an existing development kept checking
✅ A release is versioned and pinned: opam records the Rocq version and the library versions a development was checked against
✅ Deprecation precedes removal: A renamed tactic or lemma warns before it stops working
✅ The changelog names each change: A release records the renamed lemmas and tactics with their replacements
⚠️ Library and tactic names do move between releases: A development that pins no version may need edits when it is checked under a later Rocq



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is formal verification and mathematics: The language states and checks proofs, and it is not chosen for general software work (D1)
✅ It is a strong fit for the domain it targets: Machine-checked mathematics and verified software are what the system is built to do
✅ The CompCert verified C compiler is a landmark result: A realistic C compiler was proved correct in Coq, which is evidence that the domain fit works at scale
✅ Critical cryptography and kernel components have been verified in it: Rocq has been used to verify cryptographic primitives and operating-system kernel components
✅ Extraction bridges to an industrial artifact: A verified algorithm is extracted to OCaml or Haskell and then deployed
⚠️ A proof of a program is not the program: The extracted code is correct relative to the extracted semantics, and a declared axiom weakens the guarantee



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is very steep: Dependent type theory, universes, and the calculus of inductive constructions must be understood before a nontrivial development can be written (L1)
❌ Tactic scripting is a second language: Ltac/Ltac2 and the ssreflect idioms are a distinct skill from writing a term
✅ A first proof is short to write: intros, reflexivity, and Qed complete a small example in the first session
✅ The reference material is thorough and maintained: The Rocq reference manual, the Software Foundations course, and the mathcomp book are stable resources
⚠️ An error message must be read against the goal state: The checker reports a goal and a term, and interpreting the report takes practice



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The core grammar is small: A term is an application, a fun, a match, or a let, and the proof language is a sequence of commands
✅ Notation and scopes localise a symbol: A notation applies only where its scope is open, so + can mean different things in different developments
✅ Inductive and record declarations read as their structure: Record point := { x : nat; y : nat } names the fields in one line
✅ Proof bullets give a proof a tree shape: -, +, *, and { ... } nest the goals, so the structure is visible
⚠️ Notation interaction is local knowledge: Two declarations for the same infix symbol, with associativity and precedence levels, can parse a term in a way the reader does not expect



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Checking is the test of the proved property: A development that compiles has been checked by the kernel, so the property needs no separate suite
✅ Qed seals a proof and runs the kernel check: The term is re-checked at sealing, independently of the tactics that built it
✅ Fail and Succeed test a command’s outcome: A regression test can require that a specific wrong proof is rejected
✅ Example gives an inline test: An anonymous lemma checks a claim at the point where it is stated
✅ coqdoc renders a checked example into the documentation: A documented example is the same checked term
⚠️ Only the stated property is checked: An Admitted lemma or an Axiom is accepted on trust, so the guarantee holds only over the proved fragment



1.2.8 Security

✅ The kernel check gives the strongest assurance available for the stated property: A Qed term is checked against the calculus, so the result holds as long as the kernel is trusted
✅ Gallina has no memory operation to misuse: There is no pointer arithmetic and no manual free in the logic core
✅ native_compute is opt-in: The compiled reduction is selected explicitly and is disabled by default, so the kernel’s own reduction remains the default path
⚠️ The trusted base includes the kernel, the extraction, and any axiom: A kernel defect, an extraction defect, or a declared axiom is outside the proof
⚠️ Extracted code inherits the target language’s safety: An OCaml or Scheme program is subject to that runtime’s own model

Verdict: Rocq yields low core coupling for the narrow work it is built for: dependent types put the specification in the type, tactic scripts are separate from the terms they build, extraction decouples verification from the implementation language, and the logic core is pure and total. The core score loses only through P1, because the language does not function outside the domain of formal proof. The platform cost is the price of that focus — a small academic ecosystem, a domain lock-in to verification, and one of the steepest learning curves here. Main strengths: kernel-checked certainty, the CompCert landmark result, and extraction as the bridge to OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme; main weaknesses: the narrow domain, the thin ecosystem, and the depth of type theory and tactic knowledge required.

title: CFML (2025)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses CFML in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 57.1/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69.1/100 · Engineering readiness 59.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ A variable is dynamically typed: A name takes any value (T1)
❌ A component method resolves at run time: A dynamic call reaches a method by name (T3)
❌ There are no generics (T5)
❌ A variable can be undefined: The type does not carry the check (T10)
❌ There is no sum type: A component or a struct carries a discriminator, and a switch is not checked (T4)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A component is a class: init is the constructor
❌ The application and session scopes are global: A value in application is reachable from every request (C1)
❌ A variable is mutable by default (C2)
❌ Collection order is unpinned: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose (C5)
❌ One value, many names: every object is reached through references, an array’s buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: invoke() and createObject with string names resolve to code at run time, and the source names a string (C7)
❌ Java class initialization under the engine: first-touch, with the documented cycle (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The JVM collects (M2)
❌ There is no scope-exit release: A file or a query is closed by hand (M3)
❌ There is no ownership model (M4)



1.1.4 Error

❌ An exception bypasses the signature (Er2)
❌ An error can be ignored: A failed tag returns false (Er3)
❌ There is no result type: A failure is an exception, and a success is a return value (Er4)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ cfthread starts an asynchronous task: The engine scopes the thread to the request
❌ Shared scopes are the default: application and session are reachable from every thread (K2)
❌ A lock is manual: cflock is the discipline, and nothing detects a missing one (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The runtime is a JVM servlet: A CFML application deploys to Tomcat or a Java EE server
✅ The language has more than one implementation: Adobe ColdFusion and Lucee run the same source



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A page is the program: The request lifecycle is the framework, and the scopes are the state
Two syntaxes, one language: A tag and a script statement do the same thing
The JVM is the platform: A Java library is one call away, and the GC is the JVM’s
The engine is the deployment: A CFML application is a directory of templates on a servlet container




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ A collection pause is part of the timing (R2)
✅ A compiled template is cached: The engine compiles a page once and reuses it



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Two engines dominate: Adobe ColdFusion and Lucee are the choices (Ec6)
❌ A large body of tag-era code remains: A 2005 application still runs (Ec7)
✅ A Java library is reachable: A component calls a JAR directly
✅ The class file carries a published promise: CFML runs on the JVM and consumes JVM bytecode [5] (Ec8)
✅ Serialized objects cross on a published promise: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A release is annual: A named release ships with updates
⚠️ The tag and the script syntax both remain: New code can use either



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The engine sets the architecture: Application.cfc and the scopes decide the structure (D3)
✅ A data-driven web application is the ordinary project: A form, a query, and a page



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The tag syntax is approachable: An HTML-like page reads as markup



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The tag syntax is verbose: <cfquery>, <cfoutput>, and a closing tag (S1)
❌ Two syntaxes share one language: Tags and CFScript state the same construct (S2)



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework exists: TestBox runs a unit and an integration test



1.2.8 Security

❌ evaluate() and cfexecute are ordinary calls: Text becomes code or a command (Q3)
⚠️ Output is not escaped by default: A value is written as it is, and encodeForHTML is the caller’s call
❌ A dynamically typed value is checked at run time: A wrong type fails when the line runs (Q2)
❌ Java numeric semantics under the engine: integer wraparound (Q4)

1.3.4 Feedback

1.3.5 Interop

✅ The engines expose the whole JVM from CFScript, so any Java library is reachable in process. (Y9)
✅ The artifact runs on any CFML engine on any JVM. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ Semantics rest on the dominant runtime: the specification documents the implementation’s behavior, and no conformance suite exists for an independent runtime (Y17)
✅ A published-source compiler ships the parser: Lucee’s compiler is open source, so the CFML parser is published source an analysis tool can run; Adobe ColdFusion’s remains closed (Y19)

Verdict: CFML is a dynamic web language on the JVM: components, tags, and the request scopes make a data-driven page cheap, and the Java runtime is behind it. What it charges is the dynamic type, the shared application scope, the manual lock, the tag verbosity, and a two-syntax language whose engines disagree at the edges. Main strength: a fast path from a form to a working page. Main weakness: the scopes and the lock are the program’s discipline.
