title: Dart (3.13 / Flutter 3.47)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Dart in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 78.3/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84.8/100 · Engineering readiness 70.8/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Sound null safety: String and String? are distinct types, and Dart 2.12 and later check the difference at compile time
✅ Static typing with inference: var, final, and const infer a type, and that type is checked everywhere the value is used
✅ Sealed classes give exhaustive matching: A sealed class hierarchy lets the analyser check a switch expression for exhaustiveness
✅ Records give structural data: (int, String) is a value type with no class declaration, and its fields are named or positional
✅ Pattern matching decouples destructuring from accessors: An object, list, or record pattern pulls values apart without getter calls
✅ Extension methods add behaviour outside the type: An extension on String adds methods without subclassing or changing the class
✅ Primary constructors state the class contract once: class Point(final int x, final int y); declares the fields and the constructor in the header, so the parameter list is not written twice
⚠️ At language version 3.13, final and var are reserved for declaring parameters: A non-declaring parameter can no longer carry either keyword, so code that used one must drop it and, to keep preventing reassignment, enable the parameter_assignments lint
❌ String is documented as UTF-16 code units; length counts units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A primary constructor removes the assignment boilerplate: The header binds each field, so a class no longer repeats its parameters in a constructor body
✅ late decouples initialisation from construction: A late final field is initialised on first access, so the constructor need not compute it
✅ Factory constructors decouple construction from allocation: A factory constructor can return a cached instance, a subtype, or a constant instead of a fresh object
✅ const constructors build compile-time constants: A const value is canonicalised, so equal constants share one instance
✅ State lives in the object: The language forces no global mutable state, and an instance is the natural unit of state
✅ Named and optional parameters state the construction contract: Point({required int x, int y = 0}) names each argument at the call site
⚠️ A library-level var is global mutable state: Mutable top-level variables are permitted, so global coupling needs discipline rather than the compiler
❌ One value, many names: every Dart object is reached by reference; a field, a parameter, and a closure share one instance, and const pins the binding, not the object (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The VM collects garbage: Allocation and reclamation are automatic, and the program cannot choose when a pause happens (M2)
❌ No RAII: The language has no scope-exit destructor, so an opened File or socket must be closed by hand or in a try/finally (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow model: Aliasing is unrestricted, so two references can hold the same mutable object and the VM alone tracks its lifetime (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: Ordinary Dart never frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur in managed code
✅ Each isolate owns a separate heap: An isolate collects its own garbage, so a pause is confined to one isolate
⚠️ Finalizer and weak references are best effort: Finalisation runs when the collector decides, not at a moment the program chooses



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: throw accepts any object and no signature declares what a function can throw, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
⚠️ try/on/catch/finally gives a structured path: The recovery path is separate from the normal path, but the caught type is matched at run time
⚠️ Error and Exception are a convention: Error marks a programming fault and Exception a recoverable condition, and nothing enforces the split
✅ finally separates cleanup from recovery: The block runs whether the body succeeds, throws, or returns
✅ Future failures stay inside the chain: async/await routes a thrown object to the awaiting caller, and catchError handles it beside the value
✅ assert states a precondition in development mode: An assertion runs in development and JIT mode, so a violated invariant fails early



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Isolates share no memory: Each isolate has its own heap and communicates only by message, so a data race between isolates cannot occur
✅ Future and async/await suspend without blocking: An await yields the event loop instead of holding a thread
✅ Stream composes asynchronous sequences: await for and stream transformers chain events without callback nesting
❌ No race detection inside an isolate: The event loop runs each callback to completion, and the language provides no lock or race checker for shared mutable state (K3)
✅ Isolate.run and ports marshal by copy: A message is copied or transferred, so a value cannot be shared accidentally
✅ One event loop per isolate removes most synchronisation: Application code on a single isolate needs no lock
✅ Isolates gained synchronous control: Isolate.runSync, Isolate.create, Isolate.shutdownSync, Isolate.onEvent, and Isolate.handleEvent give a caller an explicit handle and a synchronous path where the async API was the only one



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Ahead-of-time compilation to native code: dart compile exe and the Flutter release build produce native ARM and x64 binaries with no interpreter
✅ Web targets are first class: dart compile js and dart2wasm emit JavaScript and WebAssembly for browsers
✅ The development VM supports hot reload: The kernel VM and the JIT path give an edit-and-reload cycle without a rebuild
✅ No vendor runtime lock-in: One source runs on the Dart VM, as native code, and in a browser
⚠️ Flutter is the dominant consumer: Server use through Shelf and Dart Frog is real but far smaller
✅ dart build cli cross-compiles: The --target-os and --target-arch flags produce a binary for another platform from one host



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ecosystem outside Flutter is small: Most packages target Flutter, so a non-UI project has fewer libraries; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
Null-safety migration of old packages is unfinished: An unmigrated package carries an unsound boundary, and opting out with a // @dart=2.x comment is a legacy choice
JIT in development and AOT in production is a tooling split: Hot reload needs the JIT, and a release build needs the AOT compiler
Familiar syntax is a familiarity choice: The C-style grammar is close to Java and TypeScript, which lowers the barrier but is not a coupling property
dart:ffi reaches native code: FFI is an explicit escape hatch, so the memory-safety guarantees of managed code do not extend across it
Dart is a general-purpose language with a UI-heavy reputation: The reputation follows Flutter, not a scope limit in the language
Language versioning isolates some changes but not all: A library can stay at // @dart=3.12 for the constructor syntax, while the corrected type-promotion rules apply at every version, so pinning does not make the upgrade reversible




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Production code is compiled ahead of time: The Flutter release toolchain and dart compile emit native machine code, so the hot path holds no interpreter
✅ Startup is fast: An AOT binary starts without a warm-up phase, which matters for a mobile cold start
✅ The JIT optimises development runs: The development VM profiles and recompiles hot functions, so hot reload keeps speed
❌ The collector pauses the mutator: The generational garbage collector stops execution during a collection, which appears as a frame-time spike (R2)
⚠️ Throughput is good but not hand-tuned C: AOT output is close to a native compiler’s, but a numeric kernel has no SIMD or arena control in the language
✅ Bit counting is a getter: int.trailingZeroBitCount and int.oneBitCount count set and trailing-zero bits without a loop the caller writes



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ dart pub and pub.dev are mature: Version constraints, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the SDK
✅ The SDK ships the toolchain: dart analyze, dart format, dart test, and dart fix need no extra install
✅ Google backs the language: Funding and staff come from one large vendor, which keeps the toolchain coherent
❌ The package ecosystem is small outside Flutter: The great majority of packages are Flutter plugins, so a server or CLI project finds fewer libraries (Ec3)
⚠️ Null-safety migration is still in progress for old packages: An unmigrated dependency weakens the soundness guarantee at the boundary
⚠️ A single vendor holds the roadmap: The language specification and the Flutter release train come from one company
✅ The analyzer replaced two analysis options with lint rules: no_raw_types and no_dynamic_casts carry what strict-raw-types and strict-casts did, so the strictness setting lives in one place
✅ Native code reaches Dart through the FFI’s C interface, whose ABI the platform publishes [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Dart 3 unified the language at 100% null safety: One soundness model now applies to all migrated code
✅ Language versions are declared per library: A // @dart=3.0 comment pins a library to a language version, so a migration can be staged
✅ dart fix --apply automates migrations: Mechanical rewrites for deprecations ship with the SDK
✅ The language changes on a predictable cadence: Releases follow the Flutter stable train, so a team can plan an upgrade
⚠️ Older packages may lag the current release: A dependency that targets an older language version keeps its old semantics
⚠️ 3.13 corrects unsound type promotion and changes a library type: The corrected promotion rules apply at every language version, and NetworkInterface.addresses now returns List<InterfaceAddress>; both break code that relied on the old behaviour
❌ Build variants multiply: const fromEnvironment with –define, plus URI-conditional imports, select which code the compiler keeps (V7)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for cross-platform UI: Flutter renders one widget tree on iOS, Android, web, and desktop from one source
✅ Server-side use is supported: Shelf and Dart Frog provide HTTP servers and routing on the same runtime
✅ Browser output works through JavaScript and WebAssembly: dart compile js and dart2wasm cover the web target
✅ Command-line tools are a supported target: dart compile exe produces a standalone binary
⚠️ Non-Flutter use is uncommon: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward UI development



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is familiar: The C-style grammar and the type annotations resemble Java, C#, and TypeScript
✅ Inference keeps annotations light: var, final, and collection literals let a beginner write working code early
✅ The official documentation is thorough: dart.dev carries a language tour, codelabs, and the effective-Dart guides
✅ Null safety gives a clear first rule: The compiler’s null-safety errors teach the distinction between T and T? quickly
⚠️ Dart 3 features are recent: Records, patterns, and sealed classes postdate many tutorials, so older material omits them



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Familiar C-style syntax: Braces, semicolons, and the . member operator match the mainstream
✅ Expression-oriented switch: A Dart 3 switch expression returns a value and reads as a mapping from case to result
✅ String interpolation is built in: "value: $x" embeds an expression without a concatenation call
✅ Named arguments make call sites self-documenting: theme: dark, dense: true states the intent at the call
⚠️ Asynchronous code colours functions: An async function returns Future<T>, so a caller must be asynchronous to await it
⚠️ Null-aware operators add punctuation: ?., !, and ?? are concise but stack up in dense expressions



1.2.7 Testing

✅ package:test is the standard runner: dart test discovers files under test/ and reports structured failures
✅ flutter_test covers widget tests: WidgetTester pumps frames and finds widgets by key or text
✅ The analyser catches errors before the test run: dart analyze reports type and null-safety faults without executing code
✅ Asynchronous and golden tests are supported: expectLater and matchers handle Future and Stream results
⚠️ There is no single mocking standard: mockito with code generation and mocktail without it are both common
✅ The analyzer serves inline values to the editor: The LSP textDocument/inlineValue method renders a variable’s evaluated value beside its declaration during a debugging session



1.2.8 Security

✅ Sound null safety removes null dereference: A String? cannot be used as a String without a check or an explicit !
✅ Static typing rejects type confusion at compile time: The analyser rejects an assignment the type system forbids
✅ Bounds checking is always on: An index outside a list’s range throws RangeError rather than reading adjacent memory
✅ No eval and no dynamic code execution: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
⚠️ Web output inherits browser risks: A compiled script still runs inside the browser’s security model
❌ VM integers are 64-bit two’s-complement wraparound; the web backend carries the JavaScript double rule (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Pub resolves dependency versions from the registry at get time; the lockfile is discipline. (Y1)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Pub packages carry no signed provenance. (Y3)
❌ The pub name space is flat. (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

❌ No tracing standard exists in the language; DevTools observes the running app. (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ Dart DevTools ships with the SDK. (Y13)
✅ dart run starts with no build. (Y7)
⚠️ Editor analysis rides the analysis server.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ dart:ffi is the in-process foreign interface to C. (Y9)
✅ The compilers target the common desktop, mobile, and web platforms. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

❌ The language specification is published, and the semantics of the unspecified corners rest on the shipped SDK; the SDK’s tests are a development suite, not a conformance suite (Y17)

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].

Verdict: Dart’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling. Sound null safety, inference, records, patterns, sealed classes, and the primary constructors added in 3.13 decouple the type from absence and from shape, and isolates remove shared-memory races entirely. title: JavaScript (ES5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses JavaScript (ES5) in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 49.4/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 93.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static types: the type of a value is whatever the run time finds, so every agreement is deferred to execution (T1)
❌ The call target is chosen from the value: a property of that name must exist on every object that arrives at the site (T3)
❌ No sum type: absence is undefined or null, and an object shape is the alternative encoding, so completeness stays a convention (T4)
❌ No type parameter: an algorithm over several types duplicates or narrows through one universal value (T5)
❌ One flat name space at the top level: a top-level declaration is a property of the global object, so two scripts that never call each other are joined by the name they both want (T6)
❌ Two absence values: null and undefined both mean missing, and no signature says a value may be absent (T10)
❌ No construct declares a module’s surface: a script’s declarations are all reachable, and the only private scope is a function body (T11)
❌ A signature states no effects: a call may read a global, write storage, and throw, and the signature names only the return value (T12)
❌ A native addon is an unchecked boundary: the engine’s C ABI is a hand-written declaration that nothing validates (T14)
❌ String length and indexing are UTF-16 code-unit operations; charAt can split a surrogate pair (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ The global object is the default home: a top-level var is a property of the global object, and a forgotten declaration writes there (C1)
❌ Bindings are mutable by default: nothing states that a property or a variable will not change (C2)
❌ Enumeration order is the implementation’s: the ES5 specification leaves the order of for...in and Object.keys unpinned, so output built from a dictionary is a hash-function fact (C5)
❌ One value, many names: objects and arrays move by reference, so a parameter, a closure, and a property reach one buffer (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ A collector reclaims memory: no release call exists, so a use-after-free is not expressible
✅ A cycle is not a leak: a mark-and-sweep collector reclaims objects that point at each other
⚠️ A closure holds what it captures: a listener or a timer keeps its captured objects reachable until it is released
⚠️ The collector decides when memory returns: a pause is the engine’s decision, and the program cannot schedule it (M2)
⚠️ No scope runs a release: no destructor exists, so a resource is freed in a finally or by a convention (M3)
⚠️ No handle names its owner: any two references reach the same mutable object (M4)



1.1.4 Error

✅ A throw is a value: a failure is caught as an object at the frame that handles it (Er1)
❌ A failure may arrive undeclared: a thrown value needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it (Er2)
❌ A failure can be dropped: an error-first callback may ignore its error argument, and nothing forces the decision (Er3)
✅ Each script and each Worker is its own boundary: an uncaught error ends that script or Worker, not the page’s other scripts (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ One event loop: a long task blocks every other callback, so a CPU-bound computation has no second core (K1)
❌ Shared state is the default: a global or a captured object is reachable from every callback (K2)
❌ Nothing detects a race: interleaving is the program’s discipline, and no tool checks it (K3)
❌ No scope joins a task: a callback or a timer can outlive the code that started it (K4)
❌ No coordination in the language: a callback and a timer are host facilities, so the protocol lives outside the standard (K5)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owns the language: ECMAScript is standardised by Ecma International as ECMA-262
✅ Independent engines implement it: V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore are separate implementations
✅ Every browser ships an engine, and Node.js runs the language outside the browser: the source is portable between hosts



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Flexibility vs. tooling reach: a program can be changed at run time, and a tool that reads the source cannot see the change
Callback style vs. composition: a callback starts non-blocking I/O without a thread per operation, and the era’s style nests them, so a failure path is duplicated at each level
First-class functions vs. call-site binding: a function is a value, and this is decided by how it is called




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A JIT compiles the hot path: the engine optimizes the code that runs, so a loop is not interpreted statement by statement for long
⚠️ The collector’s pauses reach the event loop: a pause delays every pending callback (R2)
✅ The event loop serves I/O: many pending operations are handled without a thread per operation



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ A package registry exists: npm records, fetches, and resolves a project’s dependencies
❌ A native addon binds to the engine’s release: the addon is built against one major and must be rebuilt for another [5] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The TC39 process is public: a proposal passes fixed stages before it ships
✅ The language is backward compatible: an edition adds syntax and keeps the meaning of what it had
⚠️ The syntax of the era shapes the code: module and class syntax arrive after this release, so the era’s code is written in functions and object literals



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The only native browser language: a user interface that runs in a browser is written in it
✅ A server runtime runs the same source: Node.js loads the language outside the browser, so a project shares one language across client and server
✅ Scripting and glue code: a short program automates a task or connects two programs
⚠️ Poor for systems work: no control of layout or release timing



1.2.5 Learning

✅ A gentle start: a program runs as soon as it is written, and the browser is the development environment
⚠️ this follows the call site, and coercion follows the operand: the two rules a beginner must learn are the two the language explains least



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Object literals and first-class functions express a shape directly: data and behaviour are written side by side
⚠️ Coercion surprises survive reading: [] + {} and {} + [] differ, and the rule is memorised rather than learned



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Test frameworks are mature: a runner and an assertion library are standard project dependencies
✅ The engine’s developer tools step through the source: a breakpoint and a call stack are part of every browser
❌ A mistake is found on the path that runs: the compiler decides nothing, so coverage is the only evidence of safety (G3)



1.2.8 Security

✅ A collector removes memory bugs: a use-after-free and a buffer overflow are not expressible (Q1)
❌ A value from outside arrives with no declared type: keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer’s check (Q2)
❌ Text becomes code as an ordinary operation: eval parses a string at run time, so a data path can become a control path (Q3)
❌ Every number is an IEEE-754 double: integers above 2^53 change value in silence (Q4)

1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ The lock file pins the graph: the package manager records resolved versions and verifies them on install (Y2)
⚠️ The interpreter is not pinned by the project: the language runtime version is left to a version manager or an image (Y14)



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ The registry records signatures: a published package carries a verifiable statement of the publisher (Y3)
❌ The registry is a flat name space: a name is a first claim, and a dependency can be redirected without a change in the consumer’s source (Y4)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ The instrumentation standard publishes an implementation: traces and metrics have a stable expressed form (Y5)



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ The edit is the run: no build step sits between a change and its effect (Y7)
✅ An incremental analyser answers as the code is typed: the editor resolves types and references without a full build (Y8)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ A general foreign-function interface exists: a native addon calls the platform’s C ABI in process (Y9)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ A published conformance suite exists: Test262 runs against every engine, so the language’s meaning is testable outside one implementation (Y17)
✅ A published parser exists: the engine’s parser and the compiler API expose the syntax (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [6]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: PHP (8.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PHP in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 51.7/100 · Ecosystem coupling 78.5/100 · Engineering readiness 73.1/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Type declarations (PHP 7+): Gradual typing, improving
✅ Interfaces decouple: Can program to interfaces
❌ Weak typing historically: Type juggling couples
⚠️ Traits: Multiple inheritance-like, can couple
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: strpos vs str_replace couples to memorization
✅ Namespaces scope every name: A namespace declaration qualifies a class, function, or constant, so two libraries can define the same short name
⚠️ Magic methods can hide coupling: __get, __call obscure behavior



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ Constructors can have side effects: No enforcement
❌ No immutability by default: Everything mutable
⚠️ Dependency injection available: Frameworks support it
❌ Global state tempting: $_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION couple
❌ One value, many names: objects move by handle (documented), so two variables reach one instance; arrays copy, objects share, and the declaration names nothing (C6)
❌ Execution moves with no call in sight: unserialize runs the object hooks the class defines at a site the source shows as data, and the call is the format’s choice (C7)
❌ include/require executes top-level code at load; a cyclic include sees the half-defined file (C8)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting: Immediate deallocation when references drop to zero
✅ Cycle collector: Detects and breaks circular references (M7)
✅ Request-scoped by default: Each request has isolated memory, cleared after request
❌ Long-running processes leak: Traditional PHP has no long-lived processes, but Swoole/ReactPHP do
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free in pure PHP
⚠️ Extensions can leak: C extensions may have memory issues
❌ The undeclared class has no catch: the memory-limit fatal ends the request (the Allowed-memory-size-exhausted fatal error is not a Throwable — the engine cannot allocate to throw it), and the stack-overflow class entered the declared surface in 8.3, where the default configuration throws a catchable Error (zend.max_allowed_stack_size, documented to prevent stack-overflow-induced segmentation faults) (Er6)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
⚠️ Error vs Exception confusion: Two error mechanisms couple
❌ @ operator suppresses errors: Hides coupling
⚠️ Modern frameworks handle better: Laravel/Symfony impose discipline
❌ A fault ends the script: a fatal error terminates execution (documented); the per-request boundary belongs to the SAPI, not the language (Er5)



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Shared-nothing by default: Each request is separate process
✅ Fibers (PHP 8.1): Built-in cooperative concurrency — enables async I/O without external extensions
⚠️ No built-in async event loop: Fibers need a framework (ReactPHP, Swoole) for full async; however Revolt/Amp provide fiber-based event loops
❌ Global state couples across requests: Sessions, databases



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: PHP is maintained by The PHP Group and released under the PHP Licence, a permissive BSD-style licence
✅ The reference implementation is free software: The Zend Engine is developed in the open and shipped by every Linux distribution
✅ The interpreter is portable: PHP runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, under Apache, nginx through PHP-FPM, and IIS
✅ Commodity hosting provides it: Most shared hosts include a PHP runtime, so deployment needs no platform purchase
✅ No single distribution is required: Distribution packages, official builds, and vendor bundles run the same language



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The language began as a page preprocessor: PHP grew from a templating tool, so markup and logic still share one file — a design origin whose cost is mixed presentation and behaviour
Every variable carries a $: The sigil marks a variable at a glance and cannot be omitted, a notation decision rather than a type-system one
The core library assumes one short request: Functions such as header() and session_start() act on the current request, an assumption that costs when the same code must run in a long-lived worker
Frameworks define the architecture: PSR interfaces and the Laravel or Symfony conventions shape practice more than the language does — an ecosystem convention, not a dependency the language forces
Feature growth is version-gated: Enums, readonly classes, and property hooks arrive release by release, so the style a codebase may use follows its minimum supported version — an evolution cost, not a coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled languages
✅ PHP 8+ JIT: Significant improvements for CPU-bound workloads
⚠️ Shared-nothing: Each request starts fresh (couples to memory)
✅ Fibers: Cooperative concurrency without process overhead
⚠️ OPcache helps: But couples deployment to caching



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Composer: Good package manager
✅ Large ecosystem: Packagist has many packages
✅ Laravel, Symfony: Mature frameworks
✅ IDE support: PHPStorm excellent, VSCode good
⚠️ Quality varies: Many low-quality packages
❌ An extension binds to a release: PHP policy updates PHP_API_VERSION and the module API numbers for each new release branch [5] (Ec8)
⚠️ Stored serialized strings bind to the release by silence: the manual states the format is a byte-stream representation that can be stored anywhere, and documents no version field and no cross-release compatibility, so the row is recorded and prices nothing. The probe harness round-tripped every writer and reader pair from 8.0.30 to 8.4.14 with no break reproduced — tested is not promised [6] (Ec9)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Improving rapidly: PHP 8.1-8.5 added enums, fibers, readonly, property hooks, asymmetric visibility, clone with, pipe operator
✅ Regular releases: Yearly cadence
⚠️ Legacy burden: Must support old code (PHP 5.x still in the wild)
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: function_name vs functionName — PHP 8.x is standardizing but still inconsistent



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for traditional web: WordPress, Drupal, Laravel
⚠️ Backend only: Can’t do frontend (obviously)
✅ Fibers enable async: Modern PHP can do async I/O natively
⚠️ CLI possible: But uncommon relative to Python/Ruby
❌ No systems programming: Not suitable



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Very gentle: Easy to start
✅ Lots of resources: Tutorials, documentation
⚠️ Bad habits easy: Superglobals, $ prefix confusion
✅ Quick productivity: Deploy immediately



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ C-like syntax: Familiar but verbose
✅ Property hooks (8.4): Eliminates getter/setter boilerplate
✅ Asymmetric visibility (8.4): Clean access control
❌ Superglobals: $_GET, $_POST everywhere
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: Hard to remember function names



1.2.7 Testing

✅ PHPUnit: Industry standard
⚠️ Xdebug: Works but setup needed
✅ Property hooks + readonly: Easier to test (less setup)
⚠️ Error reporting: Improving with strict types



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ SQL injection: Easy to do wrong (prepared statements help but not enforced)
❌ XSS: Template systems help but not enforced
❌ Superglobals: Injection attack surface
⚠️ Modern frameworks help: But not language-level
❌ An overflowing integer is converted to float in place, documented and silent (Q4)

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ No contract the toolchain reads: the runtime ships no manifest reader, and the ecosystem’s package manager is installed beside it, not with it (Y18)



1.3.2 Supply chain

❌ Composer packages carry no signed provenance by default. (Y3)
✅ Packagist namespaces every package by vendor. (Y4)
✅ The PHP project announces security fixes with each release. (Y16)



1.3.3 Observability

✅ An uncaught error or exception prints a fatal report naming the stack. (Y15)
⚠️ error_log and the SAPI logs are the built-ins; structure is the application’s job.



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ No debugger ships with the interpreter; Xdebug is third-party. (Y13)



1.3.5 Interop

✅ The FFI extension reaches C libraries in process. (Y9)
✅ The interpreter is maintained for every common platform and web stack. (Y10)



1.3.6 Governance

✅ The PHP Group and the public RFC process run the language. (Y11)
✅ The language reference and the RFC archive are public. (Y12)
✅ The interpreter source is public. (Y19)




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [7]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [8].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [9], [10].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: TypeScript (7.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses TypeScript in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 62.9/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80.1/100 · Engineering readiness 93.0/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Structural typing decouples from concrete types: Can pass any object with right shape
✅ Union types separate cases: string | number makes alternatives explicit, and a discriminated union is a checked sum type
✅ Generics enable parametric polymorphism: Decouple from concrete types
✅ strictNullChecks makes absence a checked case: string and string | null are different types, so a possibly-absent value must be narrowed before use, and T10 is absent
⚠️ any is an explicit opt-out: strict bans an implicit any, but a written any still drops the check at that spot
❌ Type assertions couple to implementation: as Type forces coupling
❌ The artifact carries no types: Types are erased at run time, so a consumer recovers a type by convention (T7)
⚠️ A method call dispatches on the run-time value: An interface declares the method, but the call reaches the prototype’s implementation at run time (T3)
❌ Inherits the engine rule: string length and indexing count UTF-16 units (T15)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Object literals decouple construction: { name: "Alice", age: 30 } without classes
⚠️ Class constructors can have side effects: Nothing prevents coupled initialization
⚠️ Dependency injection requires manual wiring: No built-in mechanism
❌ Module side effects: Imports can execute code, coupling load order
❌ Global namespace pollution: window, global create hidden coupling
❌ Objects are mutable unless marked readonly (C2): readonly is opt-in, so any holder of a reference can change the object
❌ One value, many names: objects and arrays move by reference under the type annotations, which name the type, not the sharing (C6)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Generational GC (V8, SpiderMonkey, etc.)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Closure captures extend lifetimes: Closures hold references, prevent collection
⚠️ Event listeners create memory leaks: Forgotten listeners couple to DOM/event system
⚠️ Circular references with DOM: Can create leaks if not careful with event handlers
⚠️ Collection follows the JavaScript runtime’s schedule (M2): A value stays allocated until V8’s collector decides, and the pause is non-deterministic, so the heap’s release schedule is not the program’s to name
✅ using ties a release to the scope (M3 absent): TypeScript 5.2 adds using and await using, so a value with a Symbol.dispose method releases at block exit



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: No throws clause, errors hidden from type system
⚠️ Result types exist but not idiomatic: Libraries like neverthrow exist but uncommon
❌ Promise rejection is unchecked: Async errors not tracked by types



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Async/await separates sync from async: async function makes concurrency explicit
❌ Promises don’t track errors: Promise<T> doesn’t show failure type
⚠️ The event loop is the only unit of work (K1): Single-threaded, so a long callback blocks every other task and no second core is available for CPU-bound work, and callbacks create order coupling
⚠️ Shared module state has no concurrency discipline (K2, K3): A module-level binding is reachable from every callback, and nothing detects a race across interleaved tasks



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The compiler is open source and emits a standard target: tsc is developed in the open under Apache 2.0, and its output is ECMAScript, so no proprietary runtime is required
✅ The emitted code runs on every major engine: The output runs on V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore and on Node.js, Deno, and Bun alike
✅ Several tools compile TypeScript: tsc, esbuild, swc, and Node.js type stripping all accept .ts source, so the build step is not locked to one implementation
✅ No language runtime is deployed: Type checking happens at build time and the artifact is JavaScript, so nothing of TypeScript ships to the platform
✅ The compiler runs on all three desktop platforms: One npm package covers Windows, macOS, and Linux



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Type Safety vs. Runtime Reality: Types are documentation only, no runtime enforcement couples safety to discipline
Gradual Typing vs. Type Holes: any escape hatch couples strict code to untyped code
JavaScript Compatibility vs. Type Safety: Must support all JS patterns, even unsafe ones
Type System Complexity vs. JavaScript Simplicity: Advanced types (conditional, mapped) couple to TS-specific knowledge
Build Step vs. Simplicity: Compilation adds complexity, couples deployment to build tools




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ JavaScript runtime: Inherits JS performance characteristics, JIT optimization
⚠️ Type erasure: No runtime cost but also no runtime enforcement
✅ Event loop: Single-threaded simplifies reasoning
❌ Unpredictable GC: No control over pause times (R2)
⚠️ Bundle size couples to libraries: Frontend deployment couples to dependency graph



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: Npm has everything
✅ Excellent IDE support: VSCode, IntelliJ, WebStorm
✅ Build tools mature: Webpack, Vite, esbuild, tsc
⚠️ Too many build tools: Choice couples to toolchain complexity
✅ TypeScript compiler fast: Incremental compilation
✅ The compiler is a native binary (7.0): tsc is a Go program shipped for each platform, so a build pipeline fetches a binary instead of starting a JavaScript compiler
❌ A node-gyp addon in the dependency tree binds to a Node major; the native compiler changes the toolchain, not the binding [5], [6] (Ec8)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Strong backward compatibility: Breaking changes rare
✅ Regular releases: Predictable cadence
✅ Gradual adoption: Can upgrade incrementally
⚠️ Lib versioning: @types packages couple to library versions
⚠️ The compiler is a new implementation (7.0): A tool that reaches into the compiler’s JavaScript internals must be ported, because the 7.0 toolchain is a Go program



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for frontend: Industry standard for React, Angular, Vue
✅ Great for backend: Node.js/Deno with types
✅ Full-stack: Shared types between frontend/backend
⚠️ Systems programming: Not suitable, GC/interpreted



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for JS developers: Incremental adoption
✅ Good documentation: Official handbook is excellent
⚠️ Type system complexity: Conditional types, mapped types can be confusing
✅ Familiar to C#/Java devs: Similar type system concepts



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ JavaScript syntax: Familiar, minimal new syntax
⚠️ Type annotations can be verbose: Generics get noisy
✅ Type inference: Often don’t need explicit types
⚠️ Any escape hatch: Too easy to bypass types



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Jest, Vitest, Mocha: Mature testing frameworks
✅ Debugging tools: Browser DevTools, VSCode debugger
✅ Source maps: Debug TypeScript directly
⚠️ Runtime vs compile-time gap: Types don’t catch runtime issues



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
⚠️ Type erasure: No runtime validation
❌ Prototype pollution: Object mutation can create vulnerabilities
⚠️ Dependency vulnerabilities: Npm ecosystem size couples to attack surface
❌ Inherits the JavaScript engine rule: double arithmetic, silent integer change above 2^53 (Q4)



1.2.9 Delivery targets

Verdict: TypeScript keeps less of JavaScript’s type coupling than JavaScript does: strict makes absence a checked case, structural typing and discriminated unions remove the dynamic-typing and sum-type mechanisms, and using ties a release to the scope. What its type layer cannot remove is the JavaScript runtime’s: a single-threaded event loop, a collector the program cannot schedule, unowned mutable objects, and failures that no type tracks. title: CUPID
text:
CUPID is a set of five software properties — Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic, Domain-based — proposed by Dan Terhorst-North in 2022 as an alternative to SOLID [1], in the line of earlier critiques of that set [2], [3], [4], [5]. He frames them not as principles but as properties: qualities of code that a team moves towards [1]. Principles, he argues, are rule-like — you are either compliant or you are not — and produce bounded sets of rule-followers; properties instead define a centre, so that code is only closer to or further from it, with a clear direction of travel [1].
He states three criteria a property should meet: it should be practical (easy to articulate, assess, and adopt), human (read from the perspective of people, not code), and layered (obvious by name, deep in use) [1]. The assessment requirement is the sharpest: a reviewer should be able to easily decide how much of the property the code exhibits [1].
This page tests the five properties against that requirement, and then against two standards the criteria do not include — grounding in a theory or a model, and falsifiability.

title: CUPID
text:
1 At a glance
The glosses and the assessments below are read off the essay [1].








Property
Gloss
Meets the assessment requirement?




Composable
“plays well with others”
No: no measure of the centre


Unix philosophy
“does one thing well”
No: no test for “one purpose”


Predictable
“does what you expect”
Partial: sub-properties only


Idiomatic
“feels natural”
Conditional: needs an external standard


Domain-based
“the solution domain models the problem domain”
No: no criterion

title: CUPID
text:
2 Composable
Composable is developed through three characteristics — a small surface area, intention-revealing naming, and minimal dependencies — under a governing statement: the characteristics “are neither necessary nor sufficient to make any guarantees”, and “more is not necessarily better; it is all trade-offs”, with a “sweet spot” between fragmented and bloated [1].
That caution is not, on its own, what makes the property hard to assess. A characteristic can be neither necessary nor sufficient and still support a graded comparison, provided the characteristics share an axis on which to order them. What blocks the comparison is that no such axis is supplied. “More is not necessarily better” denies that more of a characteristic means more of the property; the sweet spot is named but not measured; and the characteristics pull against one another, so improving one can worsen another. With no measure of the centre, a reviewer cannot decide how much of the property a component exhibits.

title: CUPID
text:
3 Unix philosophy
The Unix philosophy is glossed as “does one thing well”, grounded in the Unix tool tradition [1]. Its criterion is “a specific, well-defined, and comprehensive purpose”, and each adjective demands the judgment it is meant to guide. “Specific” and “well-defined” restate the goal — a clear boundary — without a test for when the boundary is clear. “Comprehensive” requires the purpose to be broad enough to be complete yet narrow enough to remain one, with no way to tell when it is broad enough. The example illustrates a design judgment and supplies no test: a designer who kept two tools together would still satisfy the criterion. The property therefore gives no rule for when a purpose counts as one and comprehensive enough.

title: CUPID
text:
4 Predictable
Predictable is glossed as “does what you expect”, with three sub-properties: it should behave as expected, be deterministic, and be observable [1].
Determinism and observability can be assessed against a specification the reviewer states from the component itself — determinism against its functional bounds, observability against a stated output-and-state specification. The headline sub-property is different. “Behaves as expected” is relative to an observer the essay does not fix: obviousness is held by a reader, and readers differ. Its own example — confidence in a low-coverage trading codebase — reports a judgment, not a measure, and credits two properties at once [1]. Predictable is therefore assessable in its deterministic and observable sub-properties, but not in its headline gloss.

title: CUPID
text:
5 Idiomatic
Idiomatic is glossed as “feels natural”, defined against a target audience: an experienced programmer fluent in the language, its libraries, its toolchain, and its ecosystem [1].
How much a reviewer can assess depends on the language. Some languages have strong opinions about how code should look, and a canonical formatter settles syntactic quirks — though idioms reach further than the language definition. Others are deliberately multi-paradigm, where it is left to the team to decide what good looks like [1]. The standard comes from a language community, a tool, or the team, never from CUPID, which supplies the name and the observation that consistency matters but no standard against which idiomaticness is judged.

title: CUPID
text:
6 Domain-based
Domain-based is glossed as “the solution domain models the problem domain in language and structure”, with three parts: language, structure, and boundaries [1].
The advice is actionable: grouping a design by use case rather than by technical type, because type-grouping scatters a change across the codebase [1]. Whether the property lets a reviewer decide how much of it the code exhibits is a narrower question, and it is not answered. All three parts take “the domain” as given: identifying it, and deciding where its parts divide, is the hard problem, and no criterion is given for it. The worked example names several areas but no rule for finding them; a different designer could name others. The level of boundary is likewise left to the judgment the property is meant to guide, and the success criterion — that a casual observer cannot tell whether people are discussing the code or the domain — describes an outcome, not a test [1].

title: CUPID
section: 7 The set against its own criteria
text:
7 The set against its own criteria
The articulation leg of the practical criterion is met: each property is stated in a sentence, with examples and counterexamples [1]. The human criterion is met: the five names are chosen for the perspective of people, not code. The assessment leg is not met for the property as a whole, and the adoption leg does not compensate — a direction whose centre the property does not locate is easy to adopt for the same reason it is hard to assess.
The layered criterion holds in form only. The depth is real, but it is the same content whose assessment fails, so it adds no independent support.
Terhorst-North makes two remarks about how the properties combine: that everything is a trade-off, so context should always be considered; and that the properties are mutually reinforcing [1]. Both can hold, but the essay does not join them, and states no procedure for the case the first describes — two properties pulling in opposite directions on the same code.
What the analysis leaves is a vocabulary and a stance: memorable names for outcomes practitioners value, and guidance as a centre to move towards, with no gate to pass. None of the five properties meets the assessment requirement as a whole.

title: CUPID
text:
8 Beyond the author’s criteria
The assessment above used Terhorst-North’s criteria, and is confined to them. That method cannot place CUPID against the standards of a technical discipline, because the properties answer to no standard outside the essay. Two standards define engineering practice: grounding in a theory or a model [6], [7], [8], and falsifiability [9].
On grounding, the five properties are selected, not derived. They were chosen because they “feel foundational” and stated as beliefs and preferences, with no model, theory, or empirical result behind them [1]. The choice is arbitrary on its own account — CUPID is a backronym, and several candidates existed for each letter — so there is no principled reason to prefer these five [1].
On falsifiability, a claim is falsifiable when some observation could refute it [9]. The properties are stated as centres, and the trade-off remark answers any apparent violation: a codebase that appears to violate a property is either a trade-off or too far from the centre, never a counterexample [1]. No observation can fail a property, and none can be checked against a model because none is offered.
As a replacement for SOLID, CUPID also fails on coverage. SOLID poses five design questions — responsibility boundary, extension, substitutability, interface granularity, dependency direction — and a replacement should engage the same questions [10]. It does not: only the Unix philosophy approaches one, single purpose, and even that is presented as a different, outside-in property [1]. Nothing in the five says how to extend a design, when a substitution is sound, how to split an interface, or which way a dependency should point. The packaging principles that accompany SOLID are untouched as well [10].
The expected reply is that CUPID never claimed to be rigorous, so this section attacks a claim its author does not make. That is correct, and the objection is not to CUPID’s informality. It is to the opposite move: presenting the properties as a replacement for SOLID, and claiming an effect — that the more code has these qualities, the more joyful it is to work with [1] — while disclaiming the standards on which design guidance is judged. The disclaimer cannot have it both ways: if CUPID claims no results and no grounds, it can claim neither to replace SOLID nor to improve anything.

title: CUPID
text:
9 What remains
On its author’s own terms, CUPID fails the assessment requirement he set: the articulation and human criteria are met, the assessment requirement fails for Composable and the Unix philosophy, holds only in part for Predictable, holds for Idiomatic only against an external standard, and has no criterion for Domain-based, while layering adds no independent support [1].
On the standards that define engineering [6], [7], [8], the five properties rest on no model or result and are not falsifiable [9], so they give no basis for expecting improvement. The result is narrow: it does not say the five names are useless, that the recommendations behind them are unsound, or that CUPID is worse than SOLID. Several recommendations have merit on their own — narrow interfaces, observability, domain language, consistent formatting.
What CUPID is, on its own presentation, is a statement of what its author values in code, with no result demonstrated [1]. It belongs to a third category — practitioner advice — legitimate, but neither engineering nor science, and with no reason to believe it is right.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
Onion architecture places a domain model at the centre and wraps it in rings. Around the model sit the application’s other layers; around those sit the infrastructure, the user interface, and the tests. One rule governs every dependency: it points inward. Code may depend on layers closer to the centre, and never on layers further out. The database is external; persistence is reached through interfaces the core defines and an implementation at the rim supplies [1].
Palermo presents onion openly as a named pattern — a set of object-oriented techniques and conventions gathered and named so that they can be communicated [1]. So the question is not whether onion admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut? The argument below is self-contained for onion. The shared machinery — representation, the partition, the shape-versus-rule boundary — is developed on the hexagonal page.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Onion nests a domain model inside a centripetal stability ordering of rings.
The domain model is genuinely stable and the infrastructure volatile; the gradient is monotonic.
The gradient inverts (a volatile model) or is non-monotonic (a stability valley); the model’s state and its mapping are split.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The domain model is the innermost ring, and Palermo says it “is only coupled to itself.” The next ring holds the interfaces the core needs — repository interfaces, for example — while their implementations live at the rim. The rim is “reserved for things that change often”: infrastructure, the user interface, tests. It is isolated from the core.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 3 Onion justifies the ring order by change frequency
text:
3 Onion justifies the ring order by change frequency
The rule that fixes the ring order is the inward dependency rule. Its justification, though, is stated in terms of change: isolating the volatile rim protects the core from churn. That is a claim about how often things change.
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) does not rank change drivers by frequency. Frequency orders work; it does not fix a boundary. A boundary is fixed by which change activates which elements, not by how often [2]. So onion’s stated axis — changes often versus changes rarely — is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition. It does not determine it.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as a domain model at the centre, a repository-interface ring around it, and infrastructure at the rim. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, decisions, responsibilities, and policies. The ring scheme is not among those forms. The rings appear when a designer lays out code; they are an object-oriented encoding. Palermo says so directly: the architecture is “unashamedly biased toward object-oriented programming, and it puts objects before all others.” That is an encoding choice, and the designer makes it. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 5 The domain model is not coupled only to itself
text:
5 The domain model is not coupled only to itself
The strongest of onion’s claims is that the domain model is coupled only to itself. That is a claim about the direction of reference: the model imports nothing from an outer layer. Onion exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling. Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then the model’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment.
Onion puts the model at the centre and its mapping at the rim. The ring boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the model-at-the-centre claim is meant to prevent. The model is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanics the rings were meant to isolate.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 6 What onion embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What onion embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The inward dependency rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Onion’s blanket rule points every dependency inward, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The rings are a claim about the cut. The domain-model kernel, the repository-interface ring, the domain-service and application-service division: none of these is in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable: some structure must carry the knowledge. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A ring is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the ring groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a ring that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Onion’s rings are that deviation. The repository interface is the clearest case: Palermo places it in the core because the model needs to be saved, but the need to persist is an infrastructure fact, and the interface that expresses it is a code artifact. The core does not gain knowledge from holding it; it gains a dependency on a shape the domain never named.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of onion, arrives at the partition and not at the rings. The rings are not a structure a developer arrives at on their own: the impulse to keep business rules out of the database is common, but the ring scheme is a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Onion fails wherever a ring straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s. When the encoding is read as knowledge, the chosen structure goes in as if the domain had asked for it, and the domain never did.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, onion’s rings are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 9 When onion is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When onion is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So onion answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Onion does no harm only where its rings coincide with that decomposition. Where they do not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across rings scatters one change, and a ring that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim.

The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost. The partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states; the pure, disjoint change-driver case is unconditional [4]. Whether the metric matches real economic cost is an empirical question. Palermo’s advice — onion is “not appropriate for small websites” and suits “long-lived business applications” [1] — is a statement about where that cost matters. The placement result does not depend on it: Γ-equivalence is correct placement for every modelled concern, whatever the cost coefficients.
The theory does not discover the rule. It defines what cohesion is; identifying the domain conditions that matter and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.

Beneficial, here, means only that onion does no harm: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own; the partition does the work, and onion packages it. Outside the band, onion is harmful wherever its rings do not coincide with the partition.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties, each attached to a different object: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter the condition. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Onion can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in onion checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the ring diagram looks the same.
Onion is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
11 Summary

Onion directs all coupling toward a domain-model centre and rings the rest around it. Its stated axis is change frequency.
IVP does not rank change drivers by frequency; frequency orders work, not boundaries. The frequency axis is a proxy.
The rings — model kernel, repository-interface ring, service layers, infrastructure rim — appear in no analysis artifact. They are concepts the designer adds; Palermo presents them as a named pattern of conventions.
The domain model is not coupled only to itself: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the ring boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the rings coincide with the partition, onion adds nothing; where they do not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: onion’s rings are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Onion does no harm only where its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where they do not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them, correct under all at once. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare hexagonal architecture, which reaches the same conclusion by a different route.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature or use case. Each slice runs end to end for one operation — request, validation, business rules, persistence — and slices do not share layers. There is no horizontal business layer; each slice holds what its operation needs. Bogard presents it as a response to the cross-layer editing that layering forces for a single feature [1].
So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for layered architecture, onion architecture, and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Slices group elements end to end by feature or use case.
Each feature carries its own change driver and no rule crosses features.
A cross-cutting change driver (tax, audit, authorisation) reaches every slice.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
2 The claim
A slice is a feature. “Place order,” “issue refund,” “cancel subscription”: each is a slice, cut end to end through request handling, rules, and storage. The claim is that a feature change stays inside its slice. Slices do not depend on one another.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 3 Slices divide by feature or use case
text:
3 Slices divide by feature or use case
Slicing’s axis is the feature or use case. Elements are grouped by which operation they serve.
This axis is closer to the domain than the rings of onion or clean, because an analyst names operations. Where a use case is a change-driver class, the slice coincides with the partition. The axis fails when a change driver spans features. IVP groups by which change activates an element; a rule that applies to every order — currency handling, tax, authorisation, audit — is one change driver, and it reaches every slice that processes an order [2]. So the feature axis is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition, when each feature carries its own change driver; it does not determine it.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 4 The slice is not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The slice is not in the domain’s analysis
A business analysis names use cases, processes, and capabilities. It does not organise knowledge as slices of code that each own a request handler and a persistence path. The use case is in the analysis; the slice is the code that encodes it. The end-to-end code unit — the thing that bundles one operation’s request, rules, and storage — appears when a designer lays out code; it is an encoding. This is the distinction the style blurs: the axis is domain-near, the code form is not. Absence of the code form from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 5 A feature is not independent of the others
text:
5 A feature is not independent of the others
Vertical slicing’s strongest claim is that each feature changes independently. That is a claim about change. A slice exists to contain a feature’s change, so the coupling at issue is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, a cross-cutting rule drives every slice together: change the tax rule, and every slice that computes tax changes. Then the shared change driver reaches across slices, and each slice holds its feature change driver plus the shared rule’s change driver — two assignment sets where the slice wanted one. Each slice that must carry the shared rule becomes impure, and the shared rule’s class is scattered across slices — a Unit Completeness failure. The feature is independent only when no change driver crosses slices. That is the style’s hidden hypothesis: that the feature is the whole of its elements’ change story.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 6 What vertical slicing embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What vertical slicing embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The slice boundary is a claim about the cut. When its axis — the use case — is a change-driver class, the cut is domain-near: the business names the operation, and the slice follows it. That is the closest any style on this site comes to the partition, because the analyst already thinks in operations.
The assumption that the feature is the only change driver is the invention. A slice asserts that its feature is the whole of its elements’ change story. Where a cross-cutting change driver exists, the assertion is false, and the slice invents a unity — a feature boundary the domain does not have.

The general criterion applies. A representation is unavoidable; what is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A slice is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the slice groups elements with different change-driver assignments — its feature’s change driver plus a shared rule’s — it invents a unity; if its boundary separates elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a slice that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of vertical slices, arrives at the partition. She groups by what changes together. A slice per operation follows only where the operation is itself a change-driver class — which the analyst’s use cases sometimes are and sometimes are not.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof. The slice’s axis is domain-near, so vertical slicing is the style most likely to coincide with the partition — and the one whose failure is most instructive where a cross-cutting change driver breaks the coincidence. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account

Judged by that standard, a slice is correct where no class straddles it and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped — that is, where its feature is the sole change driver of its elements.
Where a cross-cutting rule is present, it is not correct: the shared change driver makes each affected slice impure and scatters the shared rule’s class across slices — a Unit Completeness failure. Off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
11 Summary

Vertical slice architecture organises code end to end by feature or use case; slices do not share layers. Its stated axis is the feature.
The axis is domain-near: analysts name operations, so a slice frequently coincides with the partition.
It fails under a cross-cutting change driver: one shared rule reaches every slice, making each impure and scattering the rule’s class (a Unit Completeness failure).
The use case is in the analysis; the end-to-end slice is the code form of it, an encoding.
Where the slices coincide with the partition, vertical slicing adds nothing; where they do not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: vertical slicing’s slices are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Vertical slicing does no harm only where its slices coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where they do not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare layered architecture, which cuts the other way, and hexagonal architecture.
